title: Watch: Pomp and toasts - day two of state visit
description: Xi’s first visit to Washington in a decade was a display of pomp and pageantry, with Trump offering his guest a two-month truce on the brewing tariff war.
body: This video can not be played US President Donald Trump put on a warm reception for China's leader Xi Jinping in DC, on the second day of his visit. The world’s two most powerful men held talks, with little progress on big political commitments. The night ended with a state dinner which was attended by major Tech CEO's including Tesla's Elon Musk and OpenAI's Sam Altman. Read more on this story here. title: Zidane waited for France - now can he harness their star power?
description: Zinedine Zidane says he waited for the France job, but what will he bring to the role after five years out of management?
body: Zinedine Zidane won the Champions League three times as Real Madrid manager France will have a new face on the touchline for the first time in 14 years when they face Turkey on Friday. Zinedine Zidane replaced Didier Deschamps after France's fourth-place finish at the World Cup, but his appointment had been an open secret long before Les Bleus' third-place play-off loss to England. Talks between the former Real Madrid manager and the French football authorities kicked off as early as February 2025 - after Zidane's former team-mate Deschamps announced a few weeks earlier he would step down following the 2026 World Cup. When he was unveiled in Paris, Zidane was keen to highlight the time he had spent waiting on the sidelines and preparing for the job. "I had several offers in the last four or five years, but I turned them all down," an emotional Zidane said. "The national team is the only thing I wanted." While his enthusiasm at taking the job was the overarching theme of his first news conference in the French capital, the midfield legend offered few clues to France fans as to how he would approach the role. Even a question on Kylian Mbappe's captaincy was bypassed: "The most important thing for him now is to rest, we'll have the chance to speak in September." Mbappe, speaking to Spanish newspaper AS, has since said having the former Real Madrid star as his national team coach was "like a film". When asked about his preferred style of play, Zidane opted against going into tactical detail. "I can't explain to you in just a couple of words how we're going win. I have to arrive, meet with the players, and explain my plans to them. After that, it'll be up to me to keep this team winning." However, Zidane confirmed his intention "to do things differently" and he has called up five uncapped players for this international break. He went on to signal that there would be a degree of "continuation" from the work of his predecessor, which he made sure to praise. "I'm going to try do what I know how to, but it won't be a complete break either." So what will Zidane bring to the France dugout? Zidane, who retired in 2006, was one of the most exciting attacking midfielders of his generation. He won league titles and European trophies with Juventus and Real Madrid, while he helped France to victory at the 1998 World Cup and Euro 2000. Zidane started his career at Cannes and then moved to Bordeuax. He almost joined Premier League side Blackburn Rovers in 1995, but the move broke down with Rovers owner Jack Walker reportedly asking manager Kenny Dalglish: "Why do you want to sign Zidane when we have Tim Sherwood?" Instead Zidane moved to Juventus, winning six trophies, before he was signed by Real Madrid for a then record £45.8m. For France he was the hero of the home 1998 World Cup, scoring twice in the final, a 3-0 win over Brazil and was named the best player at Euro 2000. He retired after the 2006 World Cup, a campaign full of highs, leading France to the final, and one big low, when his playing career ended after he was sent off in the showpiece match for headbutting Italy defender Marco Materazzi. Zidane and Deschamps - two 1998 World Cup winners - do share a few similar traits in their management, not least in their pragmatism, as well as the laissez-faire approach to attacking phases which Deschamps embraced in the recent World Cup. Given the attacking talent at his disposal, it stands to reason that Zidane would carry on in that vein. "I was a number 10 as a player," he said, hinting he would retain the role Michael Olise thrived in for much of the summer. "What motivates me is the game, it's scoring goals," he added. With the team netting 20 times in North America, Deschamps has arguably laid the foundations for his successor's attacking set-up. Zidane is finding Les Bleus in immeasurably better shape than his predecessor did at the start of his own tenure, at which point the wounds of the 2010 World Cup fiasco were still fresh. The appointment does come with a degree of uncertainty, though. Given that Zidane has spent five years out of management, and the Real Madrid job is the only other senior coaching role of his career, it might seem like a gamble. The 54-year-old himself has acknowledged leading a national team would be an entirely new proposition: "It's new to me, but I'm not scared. This is what I wanted." Predictably, the reaction among players and fans to Zidane's arrival has been almost unanimously positive. He was met with a crowd of supporters carrying flares and banners as he left the French Football Federation's headquarters after his unveiling. "Welcome home," Mbappe wrote on Instagram later in the day. Zidane was met by fans and media after his unveiling as France boss "It's a great day for French football," his former France and Bordeaux team-mate Bixente Lizarazu told France Info later that day. "He is more than fit to manage Les Bleus, given what he did at Real Madrid with great players and big egos." The respect that the former Ballon d'Or winner commands in a dressing room is one of his key strengths. Even more so than Deschamps, a France legend in his own right, Zidane is a figure who can rival - perhaps even overshadow - his own players in terms of star power. In this sense, he may be the ideal manager to get the most out of an attack made up of Mbappe, Ousmane Dembele, Desire Doue and Olise. This international break - lasting four Nations League fixtures over three weeks - will offer the France players a crash-course to the new management style. After facing Turkey, they have two games against Belgium and one against Italy in Paris. Given his iconic status within French football and on the wider national stage, Zidane will invariably enjoy an unprecedented degree of goodwill regardless of his initial results. title: Trump and Xi toast new chapter in friendship at White House state dinner
description: The lavish state dinner included tech billionaires, red tablecloths, bok choy and festive toasts.
body: Xi thanked his hosts for receiving him and his wife with "meticulous care and consideration" US President Donald Trump welcomed China President Xi Jinping to the White House for a lavish state dinner where both leaders touted a new chapter in their friendship. The dinner was attended by billionaire business leaders, Trump administration officials, US tech CEOs and others. Their arrival was marked, however, by protesters loudly shouting from just outside the White House gates, some of whom were arrested. Both Trump and Xi praised one another, pledging to continue talks to ensure stability between their two nations. But experts say that not much concrete has been yielded in talks so far. The dinner came on the second day of Xi's three-day trip to Washington. The noise of protests could be heard inside the White House as guests arrived for dinner Trump thanked Xi for making the long trip to the US, and said the relationship between the two men was strong. "We've never gotten along better," Trump said. He praised the long history of US-China relations, although he did take an unscripted detour to praise his ongoing ballroom project. In the off-the-cuff moment, he said as a "special treat" the Chinese leader and his wife could be the first to enter the ballroom, which is still a year away from completion. "Anybody who wants to walk into a construction site that's nice and clean and sparkling, it's our honour to have you do so," he said. He also presented Xi with a sculpture of a bald eagle, America's national symbol, saying it embodied "the free and soaring spirit of America". "We hope it will find a nice, wonderful place in Beijing. It's your honour," he said. Trump added that he and First Lady Melania had participated in the design of the sculpture. This video can not be played Watch: The world’s two most powerful men just met. How did it go? Xi thanked his hosts for receiving him and his wife with "meticulous care and consideration", making them "feel truly at home". He said the two leaders are "making history in our bilateral engagements". "We agreed to build a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability," Xi said, adding that the two shared "sincere and in-depth exchanges" that will strengthen relations between the two countries. Like Trump's, Xi's remarks were heavy on flattery, focusing on cultural ties and shared history between the US and China. The relationship between the two countries was "forged in blood and fire" during the fight against Japan in the Second World War, before being furthered during the "ping pong" diplomacy of the Nixon administration, he said. Towards the end of his speech, Xi said the US and China's goals can be "mutually reinforcing". He urged both sides to explore a "new approach for major countries to get along". Musk was seen mingling with guests, alongside US Secretary of State Marco Rubio When the BBC entered the dining hall for the dinner, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk was standing over a table and appeared to be telling an entertaining story that had two others nearby barreled over with laughter. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth was at another table, with a serious look on his face. His wife is sat beside him, with Jared Kushner and White House chief of staff Monica Crowley nearby. The White House invited scores of US officials, as well as conservative broadcasters, tech industry bosses, social media CEOs and other corporate executives. Attendees included members of Trump's cabinet, as well as family members like his children Ivanka, Eric and Tiffany. Bosses from the tech industry in attendance included Apple's Tim Cook, OpenAI's Sam Altman, Google's Sundar Pichai, Amazon's Jeff Bezos and Nvidia's Jensen Huang. Both Cook and Huang were seated at the same table as Trump and Xi. As was Musk, who previously worked in Trump's administration leading the effort to shrink government. Other companies whose leaders were in attendance include General Motors, Visa, Paramount Skydance, ExxonMobil and more. Social media mogul Mark Zuckerberg also attended, as well as Jeff Yaas, the American billionaire who owns a share of TikTok. "Everybody wanted to be there," Trump said ahead of the event. "I would say you have the entire tech world, the entire banking world, and a lot more." But one notable absence was Anthropic - one of the biggest and most valuable AI firms in the world. The BBC has asked Anthropic if it was invited, or if they chose not to be there. Business leaders and tech bosses were among those in attendance The office of the First Lady Melania Trump, which planned the event, said the dinner menu would showcase "American ingredients with subtle Chinese influence". For their first course guests enjoyed yellow squash, wild mushrooms and crispy pancetta. The ate off red tablecloths - red being a symbol of luck and good fortune in China. For their main course they dined on a sesame-crusted sea bass, braised bok choy and roasted eggplant. Dessert featured the two leaders and their fellow diners tucking into vanilla crémeux with sour cherry confit, with an accompanying ice cream "made with harvested White House honey". The wine chosen by the first lady included Schramsberg Blanc De Noir - a nod to President Nixon's 1972 "Toast to Peace" with former Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai, when they used a bottle from the same vineyard. Trump and Xi will begin their day with tea at the White House's Red Room with their wives. The group then head to the US National Archives for a tour of the building and its exhibits. Formally called the National Archives and Records Administration, the building holds some of the most important documents regarding the founding of the United States - including the US Constitution, the Declaration of Independence and the Bill of Rights. title: Betty the 'cold-stunned' turtle set for Azores release
description: Betty was washed ashore at Dunwich during storms and has been nursed back to health in Hunstanton.
body: Loggerhead turtle Betty was found cold-stunned on Dunwich beach and has spent seven months recovering at Hunstanton Sea Life Centre A rare loggerhead turtle found "cold-stunned" after coastal storms is preparing to return to the sea after seven months of recovery and rehabilitation. Named Betty by her carers, the turtle was mistaken for "debris" on Dunwich beach in Suffolk by a member of the public in February who called the British Divers Marine Life Rescue (BDMLR). She was transferred to Hunstanton Sea Life Centre in Norfolk, where a second loggerhead turtle, called Olive, has been under care since December. Both will travel to the Azores later this month for release. Katie Robertson, display supervisor at the centre, said: "The moment they finally get released is going to be an emotional time for us." Both turtles were found cold-stunned - when temperatures rapidly decline and the struggle to find warmer waters can make them lethargic and experience decreased circulation. The condition can be fatal. Katie Robertson said sea life centres were preparing for a busy winter as loggerhead turtles cold wash ashore more often Robertson added: "With temperatures changing in the waters during the summertime, our temperatures in the sea are increasing and it's getting into the low 20 [degrees] - which is causing them to travel further north than where they would normally travel. "When our temperatures drop drastically compared to the Mediterranean they get cold-stunned, which basically means the surrounding water for them gets too cold." X-rays and CT scans were carried out on Olive (pictured) who was found in Scotland in December, to make sure she no longer had pneumonia Loggerhead turtles, external are the most common turtle in the Mediterranean and typically nest on beaches from Greece and Turkey to Israel and Libya. They weigh up to 400lb (181kg) and can be up to 48 inches (1.2m) in length. The species is named for their large heads that support their powerful jaw muscles, needed for catching prey. Since the turtles have been in the centre's care they have undergone a range of tests, including x-rays and CT scans checking for pneumonia. Betty, who came straight to the team from the beach, underwent more specialist care. Robertson said it was "a step-by-step process" to get Betty ready to return to the water, as they had to work to increase her body temperature very gradually every day. Betty and Olive are due to travel to The Azores in Portugal and will leave Norfolk on 28 September Robertson said visitors had loved seeing the rescued turtles improve and that the two animals had come a long way. She said: "When we got the all clear for both turtles, the whole team, we just had a moment where we were just so proud of all the work we've put into it but also proud of the turtles themselves." The creatures will leave Hunstanton on Monday before travelling to The Azores in Portugal where they will be monitored for up to two weeks before they are released back into the sea. title: Our son's death could have been prevented by FA - Billy Vigar's parents
description: Billy Vigar's parents says the Football Association could have prevented their son's death.
body: This video can not be played Billy Vigar's parents speak about their son "You swing from sadness to anger because you just feel it could have been prevented." That is the view of Camilla Vigar, whose son Billy, a former Arsenal academy player, died a year ago today from a "significant brain injury", five days after colliding with a concrete wall surrounding a pitch. The 21-year-old striker was playing for Chichester City at Wingate and Finchley FC in north London. In their first broadcast interview since their son's passing, the Vigar family accuse the Football Association of doing "nothing" after previous similar incidents. "[Billy] had his whole life ahead of him. He was 21 years old and he lost it playing football when he didn't need to," she told BBC Sport. "I personally feel that the FA could have stopped Billy losing his life because they had so many warnings." They give the example of amateur footballer Ben Hiscox, who died in 2015 after colliding with a clubhouse near Bristol. After the coroner warned the FA about the risk of future deaths, padding was added to Stoke Gifford United's clubhouse and the run-off between it and the pitch was increased. The Vigars also point to the life-changing injuries sustained by Alex Fletcher in 2022. Fletcher fractured his skull when colliding with concrete barriers next to the pitch at Bath City's ground, and was forced to retire in 2024. The FA conducted a review of clubs after that incident. "As far as I'm aware, nothing was done with that information and it just sat there. One of the clubs as far as I'm aware that was highlighted as being one of the high-risk clubs was Wingate [and Finchley], where Billy then lost his life," said Camilla Vigar. When asked by the BBC what was done with the information it had gathered, the FA provided no comment. Vigar, aged 21, died after sustaining a "significant brain injury" on 25 September 2025 At the time of Vigar's accident, the FA's stadium accreditation criteria, which applies to the National League System in men's football and the Women's National League, said clubs needed to have a "permanent" barrier around the pitch "of sound construction (eg concrete and steel)". In light of what happened to Vigar, the FA launched a safety review of more than 900 clubs, which was conducted by independent experts. As a result, the stadium criteria was updated last month and "no longer permits solid brick, breeze block or concrete barriers around pitches". The BBC has been told 169 clubs in the men's National League System and women's National League were notified they would need to make changes "as soon as is reasonably practicable". Where walls are structural, they must be "covered with suitable protection", such as padding. The FA said: "This important work is under way, and we will continue to fully support the clubs involved." Funding is being provided by the FA and the Premier League. BBC Sport approached hundreds of affected clubs in an effort to gauge their views on the changes and understand the status of their remedial work. Bromsgrove Sporting near Birmingham, which has a concrete wall surrounding its pitch, told BBC Sport the changes were "completely understandable and long overdue". It added: "We are fully supportive of this and are grateful for the 100% funding from the FA." The club said it had been given a deadline of the end of this season but "being high risk it would be good to complete this side of Christmas". Sheppey United are one of the 169 clubs who have been advised to modify their stadium Meanwhile, Sheppey United, in Kent, has a concrete supporting wall around two sides of its 3G pitch, which will be covered in padding. Asked for their thoughts on the changes, the club said: "There is always an element of risk in all sports and they can't all be mitigated, unfortunately in this instance the remedial works are more a reactive response rather than a proactive one. If the funding wasn't in place I think it would make it difficult for some clubs to fund this." Bath City, where Fletcher's incident happened, has solid perimeter walls on all sides of its pitch. The club told BBC Sport: "We welcome the ruling as it seeks to improve player safety and recognises that funding needs to be available to support clubs to implement this fundamental change to the ground grading regulations." Keith Vigar, Billy's father, said: "I work in the health and safety industry, and the main thing is you don't go to work and expect to get injured, let alone even die at work in the workplace." The Vigars want the regulations extended above and below the National League. "It needs to change basically at all levels, not just at the levels that have changed," said Keith Vigar. That is a view shared by Fletcher, who said the FA had "ignored" his years of campaigning on the issue of pitch perimeter safety. "It wasn't until Billy's passing that [the FA] came to the table on this issue," he said. "So for me, that is a complete dereliction of duty on their part, and there should be accountability for that failing." Fletcher also said he is worried the ban on concrete, breeze block and brick walls does not cover all levels of the game and wants that explored urgently by the authorities. "There could be still situations where football is being played at some level, to some degree, organised football in this country, with these unsafe pitch perimeters. I would like to see that guidance, or the regulation, extended to consider all of football." Vigar joined Arsenal's academy aged 14 and spent almost seven years at the club Compared to many youngsters, Billy Vigar joined the football system late - and yet his talent was still recognised. title: Endangered dormice on farm signal healthy landscape
description: Dormice are detected on a farm near Bridport during surveys by the Countryside Regeneration Trust.
body: Dormice have been detected at Babers Farm following the installation of footprint tunnels Endangered dormice have been found on a farm that has been working to improve biodiversity and nature habitats. Babers Farm in Marshwood, near Bridport, Dorset, is under the stewardship of the Countryside Regeneration Trust (CRT), which seeks to create nature-friendly farms. Hazel dormice are a European Protected Species and are considered vulnerable to extinction, but their presence is a marker of a healthy, well-connected landscape. Since it began surveys in May, the CRT has installed 39 footprint tunnels along hedgerows and woodland edges, with nine of the tunnels recording dormouse footprints. Ruth Moss said survey data helped inform CRT's management of its farms Babers is one of the first CRT farms to return positive dormouse results after a fundraising appeal to fund surveys and habitat improvements across its 16 properties. The survival of dormice is dependent on diverse woodland, species-rich hedgerows and connected habitats that provide year-round food and shelter. CRT conservation officer Ruth Moss said: "It's really encouraging to see evidence of hazel dormouse presence on the farm. "As the survey progresses, the results will build up a more complete picture of where, within the areas surveyed, dormice are present on the farm. "Having a current set of data helps us to manage these areas with dormice in mind." The CRT works with tenant farmers to restore soil health, improve biodiversity and strengthen the natural ecosystem while producing food. Footprint tunnels have also been installed at Bere Marsh Farm in Dorset and at Pierrepont Farm and Green Farm in Surrey. Dormouse footprints were detected on nine footprint tunnels The surveys will continue in Dorset throughout September and into November in Surrey. Dormice have also been detected at Turnastone Court Farm and Awnells Farm in Herefordshire. CRT supporters raised £6,000 to fund dormouse surveys and habitat improvements across the charity's farms. As surveying continues through 2026, the CRT hopes to build a clearer picture of dormouse populations across its farms and use the findings to guide future habitat management. The tiny nocturnal species has disappeared from 20 counties in England since the 19th Century. The loss of traditional skills such as coppicing has led to their habitats being lost, which also makes it more difficult for populations to travel between locations. Climate change has also disrupted their hibernation patterns. title: Cotswolds home to UK's first air taxi centre
description: The futuristic air taxis will be built at a new centre at Cotswolds Airport in Gloucestershire.
body: The Valo aircraft take off and land vertically like helicopters Futuristic air taxis that take off like helicopters will be built at a new facility that is the first of its kind in the UK. Bristol-based company Vertical Aerospace has announced a new aircraft assembly centre at Cotswold Airport, near Kemble in Gloucestershire, describing it as a "once-in-a-generation opportunity". The Valo aircraft currently being developed and tested there are electric, carry four passengers and can fly up to 160km (100 miles) with no operating emissions, the firm said. Minister for Reindustrialisation Blair McDougall said the new facility would "help turn British innovation into British manufacturing". The new centre adds 60,000sq ft (5,574sq m) of space to Vertical's existing flight test centre at Cotswold Airport. Council leader voted out after no confidence motion Rare Bronze Age finds unearthed in city dig Man who used police ruse to assault girls jailed Vertical said construction of the new aircraft would begin in late 2027 with an initial 25 being built every year before the company increases that number to 900 a year by 2035. The company said it had 1,500 orders, many of which were from airlines. It said there were plans to get the planes certified for commercial use by 2029. Vertical's CEO Stuart Simpson said the new centre was an "important step" for the company Vertical's CEO Stuart Simpson said: "We're getting really close to this idea of flying cars, flying taxis. "Opening our aircraft assembly centre is an important step in Vertical's transition from prototype developer to aircraft manufacturer. "Bringing a new category of aircraft to market is a once-in-a-generation opportunity and it is especially rewarding to do that here in Great Britain, drawing on the country's proud aviation heritage." Testing of the new aircraft technology was already under way at Cotswold Airport, a spokesperson for Vertical said McDougall said the assembly centre was "exactly the kind of investment we want to see more of as we work to reindustrialise Britain, creating high-skilled local jobs and strengthening our manufacturing base". Suzannah Harvey, CEO of Cotswold Airport, said she was "delighted" to support the new centre which she said strengthened the airport's "growing role as a hub for aerospace innovation". Plans for a separate full-scale production site, intended to support higher-volume manufacturing, are expected to be announced later this year. title: British rapper Yung Filly to face rape retrial in Australia next June
description: Andres Felipe Valencia Barrientos was cleared of several sexual offences in July but a jury was undecided on three rape charges.
body: Yung Filly will face a retrial next June after a jury in Australia failed to reach a verdict on three rape charges British rapper Yung Filly will face a rape retrial in Australia next June after a jury failed to reach a verdict during an earlier trial. In July, a jury acquitted the 31-year-old - whose real name is Andres Felipe Valencia Barrientos - of three counts of rape, one of assault and one of strangulation but found him guilty of two assault charges. No decision was reached for three rape charges, which he has denied. A fan, aged 20 at the time, alleges Barrientos repeatedly raped and assaulted her in his hotel room in Perth, Western Australia, after a 2024 concert. The court previously heard that Barrientos and the woman had consensual sex before she alleged it turned violent and he refused to stop. On Friday, Perth's District Court set 15 June as the start date for the retrial which is expected to last eight days. Barrientos was not required to appear in court and is understood to have returned to the UK after the court granted him permission to leave Australia as part of his bail conditions. Sentencing for the two assault charges that the jury found Barrientos guilty of in July will take place after the retrial. Barrientos, who was born in Colombia and brought up in the UK, is known for his work with the YouTube collective Beta Squad. He has appeared in the celebrity version of Bake Off on Channel 4 and presented BBC Three shows. title: Xi got Trump's red carpet welcome - but not everything he wanted
description: China wanted progress on trade, technology and Taiwan - but hasn't got as much as it would have hoped for.
body: This video can not be played Watch: The world’s two most powerful men just met. How did it go? President Xi Jinping's summits with Donald Trump have one clear aim. China believes the United States is trying to contain its rise as a superpower, and it wants Washington to stay out of its way - particularly when it comes to trade, technology and Taiwan. On this visit, however, despite Trump rolling out the red carpet for him, the Chinese leader didn't get everything he wanted. The trade truce that saw both countries pause a tit-for-tat tariff war and prevent a further escalation, was extended by only a few months - from November to January. Beijing had hoped for at least a year as Xi looks to ride out the remainder of Trump's presidency. This means key disputes on tariffs, China's dominance on rare earth supplies and access to advanced US chips are being kicked forward into yet another round of negotiations. This suggests the US wants China to do more to fulfil its side of the bargain before offering longer-term concessions. Trump and Xi attend a dinner at the White House The uncomfortable truth for Xi is that his domestic economy is in trouble. While the country sells a record number of goods around the world, consumers at home are holding back. Youth unemployment remains stubbornly high and property prices have slumped in a country where 80% of people own their own homes. Trade is helping to prop up growth, making access to overseas markets more important than ever. Xi needs to protect those exports from the kind of debilitating tariffs the US imposed last year. On Taiwan, Xi once again made clear that US arms sales to Taiwan are a red line for China. The US is bound by law to provide the self-governing island with the means to defend itself. In May, Xi warned Trump that mishandling the issue could cause the two countries to "collide or even enter into conflict". Trump then delayed the approval of a $14 billion arms package for Taiwan, describing it as a "very good negotiating chip" with Beijing. Xi may have seized on that opening during the talks and likely argued that restraining support for Taiwan reduces the risk of conflict. On Thursday he reiterated his hope that the US would adhere to the "correct position" of opposing Taiwan independence. However, Trump - who is coming under some bipartisan pressure to continue US support to Taiwan - is yet to make any public response to the Chinese leader's comments. Trade is helping to prop up growth The two leaders did at least discuss artificial intelligence (AI) although it's unclear whether they agreed to any safeguards. All eyes were on whether they would make any concrete decisions on AI - such as an agreement to hold a summit - in the wake of an essay by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei calling for the slowing down of AI development to make it safer. That followed a warning by a top safety researcher from the company that there was a "greater than 10% chance" that AI could cause the extinction of humans. But besides Xi talking about the importance of ensuring AI "is always under human control" we didn't get much else. Trump has most recently dismissed fears of human extinction from the technology as a "hoax". And, of course, let's not forget the pandas. The gift of Ping Ping and Fu Shuang to Atlanta was first heralded in April, but Xi has now announced they will arrive in just a few days as China's panda diplomacy resumes. There may be more announcements to come as the two prepare to have tea and visit the national archives on Friday. Pandas have played an important role in Chinese diplomatic measures But for now, one of the summit's biggest victories for Beijing may have been the optics. The lavish welcome, a personal greeting at the airport and a state banquet featuring sesame crusted sea bass and braised baby bok choy have been welcomed by those watching from China. It will have helped cement Xi's image at home as Trump's equal. Memes contrasting the two leaders have spread widely on Chinese social media. One popular image shows Trump grimacing as bomber jets fly overhead, while Xi remained impassive. Xi has found a way to manage one of the world's most unpredictable leaders. But while Trump talks of a "truly great friendship", China's leader is focussed on something bigger: securing China's place alongside the United States as a superpower. The pandas, the pageantry and the warm words may help smooth this relationship. But beneath the spectacle, the competition between the world's two most powerful countries remains as fierce as ever. title: Why Trump gave Xi an ornate bald eagle statue at the state dinner
description: From redwood benches to DVDs, gifts are an important part of the art of diplomacy.
body: President Trump said he and First Lady Melania helped design the statue US President Donald Trump has presented Chinese President Xi Jinping with a sculpture of a bald eagle, a bird native to North America and his country's national symbol, during a lavish state dinner in Washington. The gift, which was unveiled before VIP guests at the Thursday dinner, embodies "the free and soaring spirit of America", said Trump. He said that he and First Lady Melania Trump participated in its design. The statue is part of a valuable - but sometimes tricky - aspect of international diplomacy: gift-giving. Such gifts are a small but meaningful element of the larger aim of Xi and Trump's three-day summit – forging personal relationships between heads of two global superpowers. "They're going to discuss all of these complicated issues," Daniel Kritenbrink, partner at The Asia Group says. "But at the end of the day, these are still two human beings. "So that personal relationship means something," he says. "I think the gift exchange is one key part of that." Kritenbrink, who spent over 30 years as a US diplomat, mostly in Asia, says personal relationships are of particular importance to Xi. He believes the direct Trump-Xi bond is the glue that is holding together "the most complex and the most consequential relationship in the world". He says Trump, too, values what Kritenbrink calls "leader-level diplomacy". Gifts have had a unique presence in the Trump presidency. The US president has received a luxury jumbo jet, an engraved gold bar, a diamond-and-jewel encrusted gold ring, and more. Ole Jacob Sending from the Norwegian Institute of International Affairs says: "You think about the Trump presidency in that way, I think gift giving, certainly broadly defined, is very much part of how he operates." On Thursday morning, Xi announced a gift of two Chinese pandas to a zoo in Atlanta - and a new student exchange programme, which will welcome 100,000 US students to study in China over five years. "The giant panda have been an envoy of friendship between the Chinese and the Americans," Xi said. "In a few days, two pandas - Ping Ping and Fu Shuang - will come to their new home in Zoo Atlanta and meet with the American people." It's unclear if he gave any further presents. The BBC has contacted the White House. This video can not be played Watch: The world’s two most powerful men just met. How did it go? Today, the practice of giving lavish gifts mostly exists in Gulf states and autocratic governments. "Autocracies like China give much more expensive gifts," says Morten Skumsrud Anderson, who co-authored a study on diplomacy and gifts with Sending. In the West, Anderson says, the tradition has been watered down by democratic guardrails and restrictions. For example, the US Constitution has an emoluments clause that puts a dollar-value limit on gifts a president can receive from a foreign government. Currently, the limit is $525 (£397). Anything higher and it becomes federal property, unless the president chooses to buy it back with his own money. Also, when giving a gift beyond a certain amount, a US president would have to go through Congress, unless he was paying for it personally. "There are a lot of rules and protocols involved," Sending says, "A lot of thought and process relating to what type of gift to to give, where should the gift exchange happen? How should it happen? When? "All of this is highly scripted, and involves negotiation at lower levels that goes on for weeks and weeks in advance," Sending says. Anderson adds: "This is not a last-minute purchase at the airport." During Xi's state visit to the US in 2013, then-President Barack Obama gifted him an inscribed bench made of redwood, native to California where the two had met. They sat on it together afterwards, smiling for cameras. It was a more shining example than in 2009, when then-British Prime Minister Gordon Brown gifted Obama an ornamental desk pen holder made from the timbers of a historic anti-slave ship; while Obama gave Brown a set of DVDs, which reportedly were not formatted for UK DVD players. "That's one example of a kind of an embarrassing exchange," Sending says. Fortunately, Brown and Obama were allied leaders and not deep rivals looking to resolve seemingly intractable differences. "You don't want to mess up," Sending says, adding that the wrong gift could potentially derail any larger objectives. In this case, there is potentially a lot at stake between Trump and Xi. Their third face-to-face encounter since the start of Trump's second term, this summit is happening amid growing fears of an AI-led apocalypse as both countries race for dominance in the quickly growing industry. It's also taking place in the wake of a bitter US-China trade war that has only been resolved by a temporary truce, extended on this trip. So, do the military plane flyovers, cue the performances, fill the wine the glasses, Kritenbrink says. Exchange the gifts. "It's protocol and it's optics and it's gift giving all as a means to an end, which is stable US-China relations," Kritenbrink says. "I'll take a fragile truce over a white-hot trade war any day of the week." title: Miliband tells Iran minister UK will not tolerate 'hostile activity' on British soil
description: The foreign secretary stresses "the UK's unwavering resolve to combat threats from Iranian-linked groups in UK soil, including attacks on the British Jewish community".
body: Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has told Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi that the UK will "not tolerate intimidation, threats or hostile activity on UK soil". The ministers met face-to-face at the UN General Assembly in New York City. The Foreign Office said Miliband spoke to his counterpart about "the UK's unwavering resolve to combat threats from Iranian-linked groups in UK soil, including attacks on the British Jewish community", and discussed war in the Middle East and a British couple detained in Iran. There was no immediate comment from Araghchi. The Islamic Republic News Agency reported the men met and "discussed bilateral ties and international developments during their talks". Miliband's comments follow an arson attack on four Jewish community ambulances in Golders Green in March and other incidents. The BBC understands that British intelligence chiefs were initially keeping an open mind as to whether the Iranian state or organisations working for it had a role in the Hatzola ambulance attack and other attacks against Jewish communities during 2026. They later concluded that secret intelligence pointed to Iran or its proxies being involved in the attack. In July, a small power plant in the UK was also shut down due to a cyber attack, which the Telegraph reported , externalwas carried out by hackers affiliated to the Iranian regime. The Foreign Office said Miliband also spoke to his counterpart about the country's war with the US, telling Araghchi that Iran should choose "de-escalation and diplomacy instead of prolonging the war" and stressing the importance of reopening the Strait of Hormuz. In February, the US and Israel attacked Iran, killing the country's supreme leader. Iran responded by launching strikes on Israel and neighbouring Gulf Arab states which host US military bases. It also effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, impacting the global economy. On Wednesday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told the UN General Assembly that any deal would have to include an end to the US blockade stopping Iranian ships from using the waterway. Responding to US President Donald Trump's threat to "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if a deal is not reached soon, Pezeshkian said his country will never "bend the knee". "The resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying," he said. There was no immediate comment from the US, whose delegation walked out of the chamber at the start of Pezeshkian's address. The Foreign Office said Miliband also used Thursday's meeting to raise the detention of British couple Lindsay and Craig Foreman in Iran. The couple, who are from East Sussex, have been detained for more than 20 months after being arrested while passing through the country on a motorcycle journey. In February, the Foremans were each sentenced to 10 years in jail on espionage charges, which they deny. In Miliband's discussion with the Iranian foreign minister, he reiterated the call for them to be immediately released and stressed that their welfare remains a priority for the government, the Foreign Office said. title: Watch: The world’s two most powerful men just met. How did it go?
description: The BBC’s China correspondent Laura Bicker unpacks how the trip panned out for Beijing and Washington.
body: This video can not be played The world’s two most powerful men – Xi Jinping and Donald Trump – have just met in Washington after days of pomp and pageantry. While there were many symbolic gestures, including Chinese pandas from President Xi, there were few big movements – although they committed to a six month extension of the tariff truce. title: The Papers: 'Xi urges rivals to coexist in peace' and 'It's on at last'
description: Many of the papers include photographs of Chinese President Xi Jinping's historic visit to the White House.
body: Many of the papers on Friday include photographs of Chinese President Xi Jinping's historic visit to the White House. The Financial Times leads on quotes from his address, where Xi said the US and China should "coexist in peace" and avoid being drawn into conflict. US President Donald Trump and his wife Melania are pictured alongside Xi on the front page of the Times, standing on the White House balcony after a military show. The main story for the paper focuses on a sex offender who was repeatedly allowed to return to his home overlooking the playground he targeted. It leads on a statement from the Metropolitan Police commissioner, who said police officers felt "hamstrung" by a system that he said results in "seemingly unfathomable decisions". Sir Mark Rowley told reporters that "the children should be put first, not the paedophile". The Sun says Sarah Ferguson has received offers of up to seven figures for an autobiography, and is just "days away" from a book deal. The paper adds that the Royal Family are still reeling from the revelations in Earl Spencer's memoir about his sister, Princess Diana. The paper's front page also includes a nod to the upcoming fight between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua. The headline reads "It's on at last". People who believe they have ADHD or autism must wait two years before they can be assessed, according to the Guardian. The paper reports that the decision to delay assessments is because the NHS is struggling to meet the "surging demand", and cannot afford the cost of the number of assessments people are seeking. It adds that the NHS disclosure of this approach precedes a major government-commissioned review of the "colossal increases" in diagnoses of ADHD, autism and mental illness. The NHS is also the focus for the i Paper, which reports that overcrowding in A&E has been linked to more than 500 deaths a week across the UK. It says that, on average, emergency rooms are operating at 175% capacity. The Daily Telegraph carries a series of allegations regarding the care of celebrated explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes, who has been open about his battle with Parkinson's disease. "Labour's army of migrants", reads the Daily Mail, which says that the number of small boat migrants who have reached the UK under the Labour government is "larger than the entire British Army". The paper says that 83,279 migrants have reached British shores since the last general election, according to figures quoted by Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp. A photograph of migrants in the English Channel leads the Daily Express under the headline: "Desperate to reach Britain". Former England striker Andy Carroll is pictured on the front page of the Mirror, after he revealed he was sexually assaulted by a man in 2021. The paper reports the incident took place at Carroll's home, with the unnamed attacker set to stay over after arriving to watch a boxing match. Carroll is also the leading story for the Star, which says the perpetrator assaulted the former footballer while he slept. His attacker was jailed for three years following the incident, the paper adds. The UK has launched its first retail facial recognition system in a London coffee shop, which the Metro claims "endangers civil liberties" and "risks unleashing fraud on a dangerous new level". The paper explains that when a customer goes to pay, the system, which is powered by online bank Revolut, checks their biometrics against those provided when they first signed up. title: Treadmills to deadlifts: Why Gen Z are swapping cardio for strength training
description: Gyms are booming, solitary cardio is out - how workouts are changing.
body: When Antonia Duffin, 34, started going to the gym, she wanted to lose weight and tone up. It became such a big part of her life that she decided to become a personal trainer alongside her day job in operations for a supermarket chain - and now runs her own women's gym in Manchester. "Some of my clients want to feel stronger, some want to get in shape for a baby and some are struggling with other conditions like endometriosis and want to feel better," she says. Hybrid training, like Hyrox, which is sociable and competitive, seems to have taken over from running on a treadmill or general cardio on a bike, she explains. Antonia also notes an appetite for more strength training workouts among younger clients, adding: "I think people are now realising the importance of it - we're preventing osteoporosis and things like that." Do numbers bear that out? And how are workouts across the UK changing? This video can not be played Why more young people are switching from cardio to weights According to Sport England, more young adults are going to the gym, using exercise machines and weights to keep fit compared to nine years ago. "Gyms offer broader types of exercise, like resistance training, which can improve body composition and shape more quickly than aerobic exercise training," explains exercise expert Dr Andrew Scott, from the University of Portsmouth. He says social media is having an impact too. "Lots of people are largely learning from influencers, suggesting 'I can do it, this is what I did and so can you'." Student Will Seward, 19, started going to the gym when he was at secondary school because he wanted to "get stronger and build up his physique". His workouts - usually three a week - have changed over time, from using running machines and exercise bikes initially to more explosive training using weights, to help build athleticism. "It's had a real impact on my day to day life," he says, "improving my mood and making me feel generally healthier." Barbells, kettlebells, dumbbells and cable machines are all part of the strength training Antonia offers in her gym space, located in a shipping container. Recent research suggests doing the recommended two hours of strength training each week may offer many of the same benefits as regular aerobic exercise, such as lowering the risk of dying from heart disease or stroke while also protecting the brain and boosting self-esteem. These benefits are not the only appeal of exercise though. Many say they feel a sense of connection when exercising with other people. Dr Hussain Al-Zubaidi, a GP, personal trainer and triathlete, says there is now "an enormous ecosystem" for those who are already active, featuring gyms, running clubs, fitness apps, social media and wearable tech. How different age groups meet overall exercise targets varies. Among nearly 2 million participants in Our Future Health - a health and lifestyle questionnaire - younger age groups were more likely to do shorter bursts of vigorous activity every week like fitness classes, aerobics or football. While running has fallen in popularity overall, it is still the most common form of exercise for young men and women - and in the top two activities for adults overall. And organised, social running is thriving, with children, 20-somethings and over 50s accounting for a growing share of participants in parkruns, which are free to everyone and have over 1,400 events taking place across the UK every weekend. Prof Esther van Sluijs, professor of behavioural epidemiology from Loughborough University, says community exercise offers social connection. When working from home is so common, particularly for young people, "easy access to community clubs close to home is very important", she adds. So how much is keeping active costing exercise goers, at a time when budgeting is tight? More than a quarter of 16-34 year olds say paying for gym membership and keeping fit is a top spending priority, over holidays and eating out, data from UK Active shows - up from a fifth in 2024. A 2026 survey by the Gym Group found a third of Gen Z spent £26-50 per month on health and fitness, with a quarter spending more than £50. Events manager Cordelia Sheridan, 27, who exercises four to five times a week at her gym in Battersea, says she treats her £45 gym membership "like an essential utility bill". "If you go to the pub and you're with a group of mates, you can buy a few pints and easily spend that on a night out," she says. Living just five minutes walk from her gym makes it easy to get there for 6.30am and exercise before work. At the gym, she spends 10 minutes on a stair-climbing machine then 35 minutes using weights and machines to strengthen the thighs, hips and lower back. Before, her routine was all about cardio - but she didn't feel she was getting better or stronger. Now, she says, it's really nice being able to hit targets and lift heavier weights. "I want to go into my 30s being strong." "And it's also weirdly more sociable," she says. Persuading people to exercise is about making it the easy, social and enjoyable thing to do, even if it costs, says Dr Al-Zubaidi. "I think that's why activities like the gym, running clubs and padel have been successful - not because they prevent disease but because they are fun and sociable." Wellness habits you can start now - at no (or little) cost £170 a bag? title: Just how hot and dry was your summer? Use our postcode lookup to find out
description: Most of us experienced drought and heatwaves - but temperatures and rainfall were not the same everywhere.
body: The UK faced its hottest summer on record this year, with much of the country experiencing drought and repeated heatwaves. But temperatures and rainfall were not the same everywhere. Type in your postcode to see what summer 2026 was like in your area. A modern browser with JavaScript and a stable internet connection is required to view this interactive. As a result, we can't show information for your location, but data for the entire UK is available below. Data up to August 2026 In the UK summer temperatures have been above average. The maximum daily temperature was 21.3C on average, which is 2.4C above what it was for summer between 1991 and 2020. Virtually all of the UK experienced above average temperatures, driven by repeated heatwaves. Southern England and Wales saw heat far above usual. Temperatures were closer to normal across Scotland and Northern Ireland. Rainfall in the UK has been below average this summer. Across the country a total of 195mm of rain fell on average, which is 23% below what it was for summer between 1991 and 2020. Summer months tend to be drier, but this year was exceptional. Only north-western Scotland saw more summer rain than usual, as droughts were declared across much of the rest of the UK. This lookup uses data from the HadUK Grid dataset (opens in new tab), which is produced by the Met Office Hadley Centre. HadUK Grid is one of the main products used by scientists to monitor and research the UK’s changing climate. The HadUK dataset displays temperature and rainfall data across a uniform grid covering the entire landmass of the UK. The data does not cover the Channel Islands. Every value on the grid is an estimate for the centre point of a 1km by 1km grid box, the most detailed climate data publicly available for the UK. The values are created using observations from land-based weather stations across the country, and by taking into account additional factors such as altitude, terrain and distance from the coast to scientifically “fill in the gaps” between weather stations. The results displayed for each grid area represents a mean average of that grid cell and its nearest grid cells. For most areas, this represents a 5km square centred on the primary grid cell. Along irregular coastlines and on small islands, the nearest grid cells are chosen to match the shape of the coastline or island, but no cells are further than 7km away. This approach aims to avoid sharp jumps between neighbouring locations which may occasionally arise due to uncertainties in the data, while still making use of the most detailed dataset available to capture local weather conditions across the UK's varied geography. The data for 2026 is provisional, with fewer observations feeding into calculations due to lags in data availability. As such, the precise values could change slightly in future as more data comes available. The historical averages are calculated over a 30-year period from 1991-2020, which matches the standard period used by the UN’s World Meteorological Organization. The average temperature represents the mean average of the selection of grid cells across the month or season. The maximum temperature is the mean average of the daily maximums recorded across all nearest grid cells for the month or season; the minimum temperature is the mean average of the daily minimums. The rainfall is the total amount of rain for the month or season, averaged across the selection of grid cells. Methodology support from Dan Hollis, Amy Doherty and Oli Claydon, UK Met Office. title: New policies, election speculation: What to expect from Burnham's first Labour conference as PM
description: Andy Burnham is under pressure to deliver a compelling vision for the country as he steps from the sidelines on to the main stage.
body: Andy Burnham is gearing up to deliver his first conference speech as Labour leader Andy Burnham had plenty to say about where the government - and the country - was going wrong at last year's Labour conference in Liverpool. But that was at a fringe meeting on the sidelines of the main event. Now, as Labour leader and prime minister, he is the main event - and it is down to him to show party members and the wider public that he has some answers. Earlier this week, he said his debut leader's speech would leave nobody in any doubt about "what I'm trying to do in this role". "People are going to know the direction I want to take this country and I will set it down quite clearly," he told reporters en route to the UN General Assembly in New York. An internal No 10 note has set out the broad themes he will explore when he takes to the stage in Liverpool on Tuesday - including setting out long-term solutions to build a belief that the future can be brighter. The slogan for this year's conference is "Hope Again". So in his speech he is likely to point to his forthcoming 10 Year Plan for the UK – which, he says, will have "making life more affordable" at its core. As for the specifics of what he will say, some of it will be very familiar to anyone who was listening to his conference fringe speech 12 months ago. Back then, he declared then that the country had "lost control" of "the essentials" following the Thatcher-era sell off of utilities and that we were all "overpaying for water, housing energy, transport". He called for a renewed emphasis on technical education and wanted to see a decade of council house building on the scale of the post-war Labour government. For a politician frequently denounced for "flip flopping" he has been remarkably consistent in recent times. He is likely to re-alight on themes from his Labour leadership campaign – saying more about his commitment to greater "public control" – though not necessarily public ownership - of life's necessities; building national resilience in an unstable world; and investing political capital in the reform of social care. A potential crowd pleaser would be to tell Labour activists from the main stage what he told them as Greater Manchester mayor from the fringe last year – that he will set up a commission to examine electoral reform. Such a move would be supported by about a quarter of his own MPs and would tie in with his leadership campaign promise of "a new politics", focused on "problem solving" rather than "point scoring". We are also likely to hear more about getting young people into work or training, with the conclusions of the review by the former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn likely to be published soon. And there is certain to be plenty about his efforts to devolve power away from Whitehall to England's mayors and the new No 10 North. The task for Burnham is to meld these snapshots into a compelling and coherent narrative, culminating in a vision of the Britain he wants to see a decade from now. But there are already worries that this might become a fictional narrative unless he also focuses even more on the here and now. After all, Sir Keir Starmer's "decade of national renewal" was binned after just two bumpy years in office. Unite's Sharon Graham is calling for more help with the cost of living We are told there will be policy announcements on each day of the conference – starting on Saturday. Each announcement will have to fit in with the PM's priorities – "putting power in people's hands" - in other words more devolved powers; "growth in every postcode" – such as investment decisions around the country; and help with cost of living. Party insiders say measures such as removing VAT from electricity bills are just the start of that assistance. But Labour's biggest union funder, Unite, wants to see much more robust action on living costs sooner rather than later. The union does not want the promise of jam tomorrow, but some instant sweeteners. Its leader, Sharon Graham, has called for a "winter fuel in reverse" – a policy from Burnham next week which would be as popular as Starmer's early removal of payments from many pensioners was unpopular. The union has put forward a motion which gives the PM plenty of options such as a cap on energy prices and unfreezing tax thresholds – an issue Burnham himself said had come up on the doorsteps when he was campaigning to be the MP for Makerfield. The union has said revenue can be raised through a windfall tax on banks. The umbrella body for unions, the TUC, has called for an increase in the bank surcharge to subsidise energy bills. All eyes will be on John Healey's first conference speech as chancellor on Monday. With borrowing costs for last month soaring to their second highest level, his room for manoeuvre is limited and he will not scoop his own Budget next month by announcing what is in it. But Labour activists will be keen to know from his language whether Healey's Treasury will opt for continuity or will represent a break from the past two years under Rachel Reeves, not just in rhetoric but reality. Some in Labour's ranks believe Burnham is planning for an early election, with party HQ recently launching "operation second term", to beef up its campaigning and organising strength. Burnham does not have to call an election until August 2029 - but going to the country early - perhaps as early as next spring - could deliver him a mandate of his own and free him from the constraints of Sir Keir Starmer's 2024 manifesto. Recent polling has suggested that a "Burnham bounce" is real, though not dramatic. The party has moved from just under 20% in the polls at the end of the Starmer era to around the mid-twenties now. title: From weeks to hours - the rapid new test transforming brain tumour diagnosis
description: The test means patients can start treatment sooner and are spared weeks of uncertainty.
body: The test means patients can be diagnosed within hours rather than weeks, like Steve Palmer whose case the BBC followed A rapid new test for brain tumours that the NHS has started using can slash the time it takes for an accurate diagnosis from up to eight weeks to two hours. The test, which is used by doctors to diagnose which type of tumour a patient has, should mean patients can start treatment including radiotherapy and chemotherapy sooner, and are spared weeks of uncertainty. Steve Palmer, 55, from Nottingham, is among those to benefit from the new technology - and it meant surgeons were able to get his result while they were still operating to remove his tumour. "Getting that quick diagnosis removed weeks of anxiety," he told the BBC. NHS England said that the genomic test, which works by quickly analysing the genetic code of a sample of the tumour, will be piloted in specialist centres around England. There are around 150 different types of brain tumour ranging from slow-growing to aggressive cancers, each of which can respond differently to treatment. Steve was diagnosed with a brain tumour after he collapsed at the gym, and the test revealed it to be a grade 4 glioblastoma. "It wasn't the result I wanted to hear but it means I can get on with the next phase of treatment and recovery, and get on with fighting whatever it is I've got to fight," he told the BBC. Consultant neurosurgeon Stuart Smith, who led Steve's operation at Queens Medical Centre, part of Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust, told the BBC the test "seems almost magical." "The diagnosis of brain tumours relies on molecular and genetic analysis but it can take up to six to eight weeks to get the full information back. Here it is done while we are still operating." Diagnosing the type of tumour while the patient is still on the operating table could impact how surgeons operate. Smith explained: "For some tumour types, which are curable, surgery needs to be as radical as possible to remove every last bit of tumour that we can find. "Other types, sadly, are too aggressive, and beyond what surgery can remove, so we would be more cautious in order to lower the risk of causing damage to the brain." Neurosurgeon Stuart Smith, who points to a screen during Steve's surgery, says it means patients will also have quicker access to clinical trials The test works by sending small tissue samples taken from the tumour to the pathology lab. The samples are prepared for loading into a shoebox-sized sequencing machine made by Oxford Nanopore, which uses specialist software developed at the University of Nottingham, in partnership with hospital clinicians. The molecules of DNA pass through a nanopore - a tiny hole - which reveals the tumour's unique genomic fingerprint. In Steve's case, after the nanopore machine was running for 20 minutes, the neuropathology team called the theatre to tell them that the tumour was likely to be a glioblastoma. Dr Simon Paine, consultant neuropathologist at Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust, explained that the genomic test was transformative in comparison to what he could determine by looking at tumour cells down a microscope. "I'm crystal ball gazing and can do it reasonably well on a good day, but nowhere near with the clarity of the nanopore, which gives a comprehensive molecular classification," he said. More than 12,000 people in the UK are diagnosed with a primary brain tumour each year. It is the biggest cancer killer of children and adults under 40. Prof Frankie Swords, NHS medical director, said: "For people with suspected brain tumours, getting the right diagnosis quickly can feel like a race against time, while waiting weeks for answers can be agonising for them and their families. "This remarkable rapid test has the potential to completely transform how we diagnose brain tumours, with results reaching patients in a matter of days rather than weeks. "This is a huge leap forward for patients - a faster diagnosis means they can start the right treatment or access clinical trials sooner, while for some patients it could mean surgeons can make potentially life-changing decisions about their surgery while on the operating table." The NHS England pilot will involve five specialist centres in Nottingham, Birmingham, London and Newcastle - they are Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust, University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust, Great Ormond Street Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, King's College Hospital and Newcastle Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust. It will later be extended to sites in Bristol, Oxford, Leeds and Manchester. The pilot builds on an earlier project already under way in Nottingham and Birmingham. The BBC watched the surgery to remove Steve's tumour, shown here on the scan, at Queens Medical Centre, Nottingham Prof Dame Sue Hill, chief scientific officer for England and senior responsible officer for genomics in the NHS, said: "This is another world-leading development for NHS genomics, taking pioneering science and testing how we can use it safely and consistently in patient care. "Rapid genomic testing could dramatically shorten the wait for answers for brain tumour patients and, in some cases, give surgeons vital information before an operation is even over. "Our ambition is to build the evidence for this testing to become part of routine NHS care, so patients across the country can benefit equally from faster, more precise diagnosis." Smith added: "For patients it will mean not only mean quicker access to results and treatment, but because we have a full genetic profile of the tumour, more rapid access to clinical trials." title: From Nagaland to a path to the Oscars: Indian film brings a rarely seen world to global cinema
description: After a major win at Toronto, Angh, a film from northeastern India, is now on a path towards the Oscars.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Indian film brings a rarely seen world to global cinema There is something pleasingly improbable about Angh. The film comes from Nagaland, a mountainous state of fewer than two million people on India's northeastern frontier, and is in Konyak, a tribal language unfamiliar to most Indians, never mind audiences abroad. It was director Theja Rio's first feature and most of its cast faced a camera for the first time. And yet, at the Toronto International Film Festival this month, this quiet film won the Platform Prize, a major juried award. The award is intended to recognise films with a particularly distinctive directorial voice. The jury praised Rio's "refreshing perspective" and the film's portrait of a world rarely encountered on the international screen. The win also gives Angh an unusual route towards the 2027 Academy Awards. Under new rules, winners of designated prizes at six international festivals can qualify for consideration in the International Feature Film category without relying solely on their country's official submission. This does not make Angh an Oscar nominee. But it does place a Konyak-language film from one of India's smallest states inside a global conversation from which such stories have been almost entirely absent. Rio still sounds slightly startled by it. When we speak in Delhi, roughly 72 hours after the win, he has barely had a moment to breathe - Toronto, flights, interviews, more interviews. "There were a lot of good films in the competition", he says, including films by far more seasoned directors. His producers were confident. "They thought we were going to win. I wasn't." He is also less solemn than Angh might suggest. Before cinema, he wanted to be a rapper - "a kid from Compton instead of a kid from Nagaland", as he puts it. His tastes still range happily from Black Thought, the lead rapper of American hip-hop group The Roots, to his favourite filmmaker, the Iranian director Abbas Kiarostami. But for his first feature, he turned close to home. Set in the early 1960s, Angh follows Anghba, the ageing hereditary chief of a Konyak village, and his young son, as the world around them changes. The Konyaks are one of Nagaland's 17 major tribes, concentrated in the eastern district of Mon, where such chiefs are known as Anghs. Even today, some older men bear facial tattoos associated with the Konyaks' historical practice of headhunting. Anghba is the ageing hereditary chief of a Konyak village in Nagaland in the film Anghba and his son are among the last in their region to hold to an ancestral faith as Christianity spreads. Then an American missionary, played by Scottish actor Douglas Henshall, arrives. The father resists but the son is now curious. Rio says the idea for the film came a few years ago, when he was visiting Mon for another project. What struck him was how closely different generations seemed to live alongside one another there. Within a single family, he says, a grandfather might be a former headhunter, his face still tattooed; two generations later, his grandson might play guitar in a rock band. "It feels like you've jumped on a time machine," Rio says. "The past and the present sort of coexist together." The year also matters. Nagaland, which was earlier part of Assam state, formally became an Indian state in December 1963, during a period of profound political and social change. By then, Christianity had been spreading among Naga communities for decades, bringing changes extending beyond religious belief into customs, rituals and everyday life. From right: Theja Rio poses with Nancy Nisa Beso, the film's producer, and actors Anglong Konyak (who plays the village chief, Anghba) and Sobino Rengma (who plays the son, Amao) Dr B Amo Konyak, a scholar of Konyak society, says the changes during this period were almost like a disappearance. Some practices were lost; others "survived in fragments" - in the memories of elders, in family heirlooms. What had once been part of everyday life became heritage. But Dr Konyak says culture did not simply stop. People carried parts of it into new religious and social worlds. Traditions survived, but changed meaning as they changed form. It's this moment of transition that Rio wanted to capture. "The past 50 or 60 years have brought extraordinary churn," he says, widening the distance between generations. In Angh, he explores this through the relationship between the father and son who "intimately love and care about each other very deeply", even as their worlds begin to pull apart. Critic Siddhant Adlakha was struck by the ambiguity the film captures. "Progress and tradition can be nonlinear, even entwined," he says, "rather than strictly opposing forces." Angh traces the relationship between a father and son as they reconcile with larger changes The film is yet to reach a wider audience, but its brief trailer offers a glimpse of how Rio constructed this world. Mist hangs over steep green hills; figures move through forests and village paths; fire and lamplight pick faces out of the darkness. The landscape is beautiful but not merely picturesque - a small world held together by ritual, family and geography, while something larger presses in from beyond its edges. Adlakha singles out the quiet close-ups of Anghlong Konyak, the first-time actor who plays the chief, and the "gentleness" with which Rio captures his "subdued rage". What the camera saw mattered almost as much as where it was looking from. Konyak people have long been viewed from the outside. Dr Konyak points to explorers, colonial officials, missionaries and photographers drawn to tattooed faces, ornaments, weapons and headhunting, while the lives behind them often receded from view. The forest plays a central part in the storytelling of the film Rio was conscious of inheriting that history. "There have been several films and documentaries made about Nagalan

title: Catterick Garrison fire could burn through night, authorities say
description: North Yorkshire Fire and Rescue Service said in a statement that multiple crews were at the scene.
body: Soldiers at the garrison in an undated file photograph Firefighters expect to work all night as a fire blazes at the military barracks accommodation block in Catterick Garrison, North Yorkshire. North Yorkshire Fire and Rescue Service said in a statement that multiple crews were at the scene, along with an appliance from County Durham and Darlington. "The incident is expected to be ongoing throughout the night," the statement said. Unverified videos and images shared online show flames and smoke rising up from a building as bystanders watch. The BBC has asked the Ministry of Defence for comment. Hipswell and Colburn councillor Kevin Foster told local media that details were limited at this stage. "My immediate concern is for the safety and wellbeing of everyone at the camp, including our military personnel, their families and the emergency services responding to the incident," he said. This is a developing story.
