title: Netanyahu defends Israeli military action as delegates walk out before UN speech
description: The Israeli leader labels those who left his speech at the UN General Assembly as "moral cowards".
body: This video can not be played Watch: UN delegates walk out of Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu's speech Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has fiercely defended his country's military campaigns in Iran, Gaza and elsewhere in the Middle East in a speech to the UN General Assembly. After dozens of delegates walked out in protest as he took to the stage, Netanyahu vowed to continue fighting: "We're going to win. We have no other choice." In response to the walkout, he said: "If there are any other moral cowards who haven't left the hall, please do so now." The Israeli leader also rejected accusations that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza. Hours earlier, in a recorded message Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas told the UN that Israeli policies - in particular the illegal expansion of Jewish settlements in the occupied West Bank - threatened "the very life and existence of the Palestinian people on their homeland". He also said it jeopardised the two-state solution, which is an internationally backed formula for peace between Israel and the Palestinians. Abbas said that Palestinians were being subjected to "killing, destruction, starvation and attempts at displacement, as well as a genocidal war" in Gaza by the Israeli military. The Palestinian leader was addressing the annual gathering via a video link because he had been denied a US entry visa. Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza almost a year after a ceasefire came into force Netanyahu, who is subject to an International Criminal Court arrest warrant for alleged war crimes, launched scathing attacks on nations and leaders who have criticised him. "They accuse Israel, tiny Israel, of colonialism - some colonialism. And who's accusing us? Among them are people in Britain and in France. For God's sake, they invented the term," he said. He went on to label Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan a "tyrant", accusing him of supporting the Palestinian armed group Hamas. Erdogan told the UN on Tuesday that the injustices faced by those in Gaza and the West Bank "deeply offends the conscience of humanity". New York City's left-wing mayor Zohran Mamdani - who had previously vowed to arrest Netanyahu but later said he did not have the authority to do so - was also criticised by the Israeli leader. "Since you were elected mayor of this city, many Jews no longer feel safe in New York," the Israeli prime minister said. In a statement, Mamdani's office said Netanyahu "used his speech to repeat baseless lies meant to sanitize his genocide of Palestinians". Netanyahu also thanked US President Donald Trump for his "bold leadership", referring to the air strikes the US and Israel jointly launched against Tehran in February. "Israel and America acted together not only to protect ourselves, but to save civilisation," he said. Much of Netanyahu's speech was pitched at the two audiences he needs to convince the most: Israelis as he faces a critical election at home next month, and Americans as Israel faces growing isolation and fractures in support abroad. In Israel, Netanyahu's once unrivalled image as "Mr Security" has come under increasing scrutiny in what is the first election since the 7 October 2023 attacks. Some political opponents have argued he is unfit for office following Israeli media reports, firmly denied by Netanyahu, that he did not heed warnings of a potential attack by Hamas. His characteristic defiance at the UN podium will be replayed in a campaign seeing his religious-right wing coalition trailing in the polls. Netanyahu appeared to have pre-scripted his comments about "moral cowards" as he faced a mass walkout. It will likely be used as he tries once again to burnish an image as being the only Israeli politician that can truly take on Israel's growing number of global critics. There were also clearly marked references meant for American audiences, including the joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran and his praise for Trump. Netanyahu, who was born in Israel but spent his formative years in Pennsylvania, has always tried to present himself as having a unique ability to pitch Israel's case in the US. Despite continued weapons supply from Washington, he faces an increasingly sceptical public. Polls suggest plummeting support for Israel among Democrats, and a fracture in historically high levels of backing among Republicans which has spread to Trump's Maga base. A number of people protesting against Netanyahu's visit were detained in New York City. Among them were the Oscar-winning actress Susan Sarandon and Emmy-winning Hacks actress Hannah Einbinder. Also detained were Democratic congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier and New York City council member Chi Osse. A spokesperson for the NYPD said officers had responded to reports of an "unscheduled demonstration" where protesters were blocking a junction. Actress Susan Sarandon was among demonstrators detained near the UN The Israeli military launched a ground offensive in the Gaza Strip after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attack against Israel, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others taken hostages. During the Israeli military campaign more than 73,920 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry. Last year, the world's leading association of genocide scholars declared that Israel was committing genocide in Gaza. A resolution passed by the International Association of Genocide Scholars (IAGS) stated that Israel's conduct meets the legal definition as laid out in the UN convention on genocide. Israel has regularly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide and says they are justified as a means of self-defence. On 28 February, Israel and the US started launching massive air strikes on Iran, suspecting it of secretly building a nuclear weapon - a claim denied by Tehran. title: Hundreds of thousands expected in Paris for Pope's visit
description: The highpoint of his time in Paris will be a giant Mass attended by more than half a million people.
body: Pope Leo begins his visit in the French capital, before moving on to Lourdes and Metz Pope Leo XIV embarks on a four-day visit to France on Friday, with the highpoint being a giant Mass attended by more than half a million people in central Paris. For Saturday's afternoon celebration, an altar has been built on the Place de la Concorde and a large area around the Champs-Élysées sealed off by police. Some 600,000 Catholic faithful are expected to cram the avenue up to the Arc de Triomphe and beyond. Large crowds are also due at other stages in the Pope's itinerary, reflecting an enthusiasm that the Church attributes to growing spiritual thirst among the French and other Europeans. President Emmanuel Macron will greet the Pope at Orly airport on Friday morning, and then hold talks with him at the Élysée Palace on geopolitical issues and artificial intelligence (AI). He will also deliver a speech with the Pope in Metz. However, the president will not be at any of the Pope's Masses, largely to avoid breaching France's strict separation of state and religion. Instead, the Champs-Élysées Mass will be attended by his wife Brigitte and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu. Several candidates for next year's presidential election are also due, including Marine Le Pen of the nationalist right, centrists Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal, and conservative Bruno Retailleau. There were reports of tensions between Macron and the Vatican team sent to make arrangements, with the president allegedly frustrated in his wish for a more ceremonial aspect to the visit. This was dismissed this week by Élysée officials, who said it was customary to offer a visiting head of state – which the Pope is – a range of high-profile events, such as a cavalry escort down the Champs-Élysées. But they said it was never expected that the Pope would actually take the offer up. They did confirm that Pope Leo turned down Macron's idea of a meeting with artisans who helped rebuild the fire-devastated Notre-Dame cathedral. This was because his agenda was too tight, they said. After a Popemobile ride through crowds to Notre-Dame cathedral on Friday afternoon, Pope Leo XIV will be joined in the evening by 80,000 young people at the Stade de France in northern Paris. On Sunday 150,000 have signed up to attend mass in the Pyrenean sanctuary of Lourdes. Preparations are taking place in Lourdes ahead of the visit On Monday the Pope will be in Metz, in northeast France, where he will pay tribute to Robert Schuman (1886-1963), a founding father of the European Union and a fervent Catholic who is today a candidate for beatification. The Pope will also meet a group of migrants in Paris, and in Lourdes some victims of sexual abuse by members of the Catholic clergy. Born in Chicago in 1955, Pope Leo XIV was originally called Robert Prevost – a French name. In fact his paternal grandmother was born in Le Havre in Normandy in 1894. When she married in the US many years later she and her Italian husband took the name Prevost, which had been her mother's maiden-name. France has a historically complex relationship with the Catholic Church of Rome. The country was long known as the "Eldest Daughter of the Church" because supposedly, but inaccurately, it was the first kingdom to convert to Christianity. Actually Armenia, Georgia and Ethiopia preceded it. In the 14th Century the papacy came in exile to Avignon in southern France, and over following centuries French armies periodically intervened in Italian politics, where popes were secular rulers as well as heads of the Church. Napoleon held two popes in captivity. Recent popes have all come to France, most notably John-Paul II, who came several times between 1980 and 2004, and Pope Francis who came three times, but avoided Paris, going instead to Strasbourg, Marseilles and Corsica. Pope John Paul II, pictured here in Paris in 1980, visited many times Today France has secularised with the rest of Europe, and less than half of the population identifies as Catholic. The number of regular worshippers has fallen from 35% of the population in 1960 to less than 5% today, while the number of priests has shrunk by two-thirds from 25,000 in 1990 to fewer than 9,000. But in recent years there have been signs of a growing interest in religious tradition, with the number of adult baptisms more than doubling in five years to hit 10,000 in 2025. "France has indeed secularised, but there is a void where God and values used to be," said Cardinal François Bustillo, Bishop of Ajaccio. "People are searching for something. Maybe they go to India or Tibet or the Amazon. And now the Pope comes here from Rome, bringing a reminder to people of their own roots. "It was John-Paul II who awoke the East. Now Leo XIV will awake the West," he said. title: Drumcree parade decision expected to be announced
description: The Parades Commission has been deliberating on whether the parade will be allowed along the Garvaghy Road in Portadown.
body: Since 1998, the Parades Commission has imposed restrictions on the Orange Order's route back from a service at Drumcree Church outside Portadown A decision on whether or not a controversial Drumcree parade by the Orange Order in Portadown is to be re-routed may be announced later on Friday. The Parades Commission has been deliberating since Wednesday on whether the parade will be allowed along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road. Unionist politicians have urged the five-person commission to permit Sunday's march in spite of opposition from a group of local residents. The commission has indicated it hopes to announce its decision on Friday, but it could come on Saturday. The parade by Portadown District Orange Order is due to start at 13:00 BST at Drumcree church on Sunday and finish at Carleton Street in the town centre by 14:30. A total of 60 people would march along the road in silence, without any bands. The last time the commission considered the parade route, it re-routed the march, but that decision in June was later quashed in court as proper procedures had not been followed. The commission's decision, known as a determination, was explained in a nine-page document. A lengthy explanation is expected to accompany the latest determination. The decision could face a legal challenge. The reasons behind the determination are likely to be outlined in detail. Final submissions were made this week by the Orange Order and the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition as well as all of the major political parties in Northern Ireland. The police were also consulted about the planned parade. The Police Service of Northern Ireland says it has activated "mutual aid arrangements to support contingency planning for a policing operation" in Portadown on Sunday. The Parades Commission, led by Professor Evelyn Collins, has been in the political spotlight since its previous Drumcree determination was quashed in the High Court. A review of the commission has since been ordered by the Northern Ireland Office. This video can not be played Drumcree dispute: Explained in a minute The Drumcree parade dispute began in the mid-1990s and it almost derailed the peace process at the time. Violence related to the dispute resulted in riots, roadblocks and murders. When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995 there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years. The Parades Commission began operating in 1998 to regulate parades and try to defuse tension around marches. Its decision not to allow a march down the Garvaghy Road that summer has been challenged by the order for the past three decades. What is the Garvaghy Road dispute all about? title: X-planes: Are they needed in the new era of drones?
description: Where do America's X-plane projects fit in an era of cheap drones?
body: The long nose of the X-59 is designed to damped the plane's sonic boom There's a weird and wonderful jet flying over the US. It has the nose of anteater, parts cannibalised from other planes and a cockpit so far back the pilot depends on a camera to see where he's going. This contraption, the X-59, might just be the future of air travel. The X-59's owes its eccentric design to the problem of sonic booms. The shockwave created by a jet breaking the sound barrier restricted Concorde to flights over the sea and barred it from lucrative routes across the US. Now Nasa is working around that problem using the X-59's elongated snout to flatten supersonic booms into tolerable bumps in the background. On top of its bizarre appearance the X-59 boasts a remarkable lineage. It's the latest in a series of experimental Nasa aircraft dating back to 1947 and the first plane to break the sound barrier, the Bell X-1. Peter Coen, a 43-year Nasa veteran who manages the programme, explains the thinking behind 80 years of X-planes. "Our approach is to pick small goals we aim to prove with flight data and we construct an airframe for that one task." The X-plane philosophy is to "minimise goals, the more goals you have the more expensive it gets." For the X-59 it's about suppressing sonic booms on a budget and nothing else. In the case of the X-1, flown through the sound barrier in 1947 by the legendary test pilot Chuck Yeager, Nasa knew a .50 calibre bullet travelled faster than the speed of sound. So the stumpy little aircraft was shaped like a bullet with wings added. A mere 20 years later the X-15 rocket plane, a cylinder with tiny wings dropped from a B-52 bomber, flew to 6.7 times the speed of sound (4,520 mph) and the edge of space, paving the way for heat-resistant materials vital to the Space Shuttle. In 1947 the Bell X-1 was the first plane to break the sound barrier Nasa is flying the X-59 in conjunction with community surveys to assess what people think when a supersonic boom is bent by the planes stretched nose and hushed up. "We want to figure out what level of boom is acceptable to people on a regular basis," says Coen, who reckons his machine will sound "like a car door being closed across the street" when it flies past Mach 1, around 660mph at airline cruising altitude. With its cockpit and ejector seat taken from a T-38 training jet, its landing gear from an F-16 fighter and engine courtesy of the F-18 this jigsaw of an aircraft was assembled by Lockheed Martin for Nasa. A camera feeding a screen in front of the pilot relies on instantaneous computer processing to get round the lack of forward vision. It first flew in 2025 and is now breaking the sound barrier over chosen US towns. But is there still a place for X-plane projects in a world where relatively cheap drones are being rapidly developed - not least in Ukraine's war against Russia. Even Nasa considered an uncrewed X-59. But drones are not always a cheaper option. Removing the pilot would have added the cost and complication of certifying a robot jet to fly fast over urban areas. Plus the X-59 had to be big enough to resemble an airliner punching through the sound barrier, which in turn allowed space for a cockpit. Nasa is no stranger to drone X-planes. The X-48, a scaled down model of an airliner that blends wing and fuselage to create a single lifting body, flew in 2007. Small was beautiful for the tiny X-48 with its 20ft wingspan as this kept the programme within budget. "It's likely that future X-planes will be uncrewed," says Coen, before adding the vital caveats "unless the technology we're researching relates to piloting or if crewing it is more cost-effective". The X-48 was a scaled-down plane to test a blended wing and fuselage Guy Gratton, professor of Aircraft Test and Evaluation at Cranfield University, gets frustrated at the suggestion crewed test planes have had their day. "There's a belief in certain quarters that drones can do everything. In Ukraine they've done amazing things with drones, but if you want to carry people you can't take short-cuts." Gratton has tested light aircraft and stresses the importance of a human in the loop. "You lose a huge amount without pilots, you miss lessons a pilot would identify, plus it can take four times as many people on the ground to test a drone." Staff monitoring signals from a drone are an indirect cost that keeps some piloted X-planes relatively affordable. The Experimental Aircraft Programme tested systems for the Typhoon fighter. The UK has flown its own technology testbeds and Chris Yeo was in the pilot's seat of one. The Experimental Aircraft Programme (EAP) flew from Lancashire in 1986 and tried out core systems for the Typhoon fighter. Yeo acknowledges the EAP's shared heritage with X-planes. "They all research some facet of flight, and demonstrate the design is working correctly. A lot of people say they can do something, but you only know it works when the design has been tested and certified." Forty years on from Yeo's EAP flights a new UK technology demonstrator is taking shape. It is, says Tony Godbold who runs the project for BAE Systems, "the X-plane of our generation". This BAE Systems initiative pulls together 100 UK suppliers including Rolls-Royce to test out ideas that might make it into the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP), a fighter due to fly in the 2030s. The technology demonstrator will borrow engines from the existing Typhoon and fly sometime in 2028. This has triggered great excitement in the UK's small community of qualified fast jet test pilots. Almost every one, around 14 of them says Godbold, has already tried out this plane on a flight simulator. For many in the aerospace industry, the human element still matters as much as it did in Yeager's day. title: 'We're all broke': Would you chase a friend for £5?
description: What's the smallest amount of money you would ask a friend to pay you back?
body: This video can not be played Watch: We ask New Yorkers to share the smallest amount they'd ask a friend to pay back You pick up the bill for dinner, pay for the taxi home or grab a friend's coffee with the promise they'll pay you back later, but days go by and the money never arrives. At what point do you ask them for it again and how small is too small to chase? For some, $5 (£3.70) is worth a reminder, while for others, asking a friend to repay anything under $20 (£15) feels more awkward than simply taking the hit. Henry Payne says he's "sent a request for $8.50, but I wouldn't go lower than $8". The 21-year-old New Yorker adds that he will chase someone once but "two requests is insane". "I would rather swallow the $8.50 than send another request." He does admit that he's sometimes the person on the other side of the transaction and can be forgetful himself. "For everyone that I haven't sent back money to, I just forgot, feel free to double request me." Nouria (left) and Kaz are two students in New York who say money conversations with friends can be very awkward Kaz Jahanbini, 19, says needing to ask to be paid back in the first place can be frustrating. "If someone bought me something, I'm immediately paying them back. So then I'm thinking for them, what's the delay?" His rule for navigating friendship and finances is to "keep your wallet close but your friends closer". His friend Nouria agrees and says as a student "every extra dollar counts" but she would usually only ask for money back from a friend if it was more than $10. A recent study, external found that 76% of Gen Z who have fronted money for a group expense, like a trip or event, say they were not fully repaid, and 55% say it created tension or negatively affected a relationship. Betsie believes there's a cultural difference between Brits and Americans For British student Betsie Brooke-Taylor, 19, the threshold to ask for money back is a fiver as she says "every little helps". She sees a cultural difference between the UK and US and even though "we are all broke, I think Americans are a bit more generous". Betsie also thinks technology makes settling small debts easier in the US, where payment apps such as Venmo are widely used. Venmo lets users send and request money through an app which includes the function of sending a reminder if someone hasn't paid you. In the US, more than 95 million people have a Venmo account, external. "In the UK you have to ask for the account number and sort code, and not everyone has that on hand," she says. Annika (left) and Hanako feel very differently about confronting a friend who hasn't paid them back For 19-year-old Annika Violet, the amount she would ask back from a friend depends on whether she's consistently paying for them. "I prefer to do something where I get them this time and they get me next time but if I'm consistently paying and you're not, then I will request the $5." Unlike many, Annika doesn't find money conversations uncomfortable. "I am so confrontational, I do not find it awkward. If you're my friend, you would pay me back." Annika's friend Hanako Stepper says she finds it awkward asking for money but wishes she didn't. "I've never chased anyone - I'm just sad if I don't get paid back." Annika's advice to those who do struggle to ask is to "be brave and bold". "If they are going to give you flak about it, maybe it's a sign they are not a good friend." Money expert Laura Pomfret says many people feel embarrassed about asking to be paid back, and Britons in particular can find it awkward. "We're often very British about asking for money back," she says, suggesting people may be worried about being judged as a "cheapskate". Her top tips for asking friends to pay up are: She adds that you shouldn't convince yourself that a debt is too small to justify asking for it as "if you want the money paid back then the amount shouldn't matter". And if the same friend repeatedly fails to pay, Pomfret suggests remembering it the next time you're about to pay for them and think twice. Ella (left) and Katrina have a few friends who rarely pay them back Several people the BBC spoke to said the amount itself mattered less when somebody repeatedly failed to pay. New York student Ella Feuille, 21, says $15 is roughly the point at which she would consider requesting money. If a significant amount was owed, Ella says she would ask around three times before giving up but wouldn't necessarily forget about it. "I have friends who I know now it has to go on their card because they're not going to pay me back." Her friend Katrina Dimingot agrees and says she much prefers a method where "we don't pay each other back, we just take it in turns to get things for each other". My friends always want to split the bill equally, how do I say no? 'I'd be put off if he asked to split it': Who should pay on a first date? title: Bellamy wants more from Wales after loss to Portugal
description: Craig Bellamy believes there is "more to come" from his Wales side in the Nations League following their opening-match loss in Lisbon.
body: This video can not be played Highlights: Watch as Portugal beat Wales in Nations League opener Wales earned plaudits but Craig Bellamy wants more from his side, after admitting they were forced to suffer in their narrow 1-0 defeat in Portugal. Joao Felix's deflected strike proved enough to earn victory in Lisbon for the hosts, who also saw Cristiano Ronaldo's effort ruled out by VAR. It was a winning start to the Nations League title defence for Portugal and for new manager Jorge Jesus. Despite being under pressure for long spells in Lisbon, Bellamy's injury-hit side ended strongly as Brennan Johnson and Lewis Koumas both went close to snatching a draw. "It was a difficult game for us. We had to suffer a lot," said Bellamy. "I think that's the longest we've been in a game without the ball. "We could have done more with the ball but I'm beyond proud as well. "We have a lot of players who weren't here. That's OK, we can handle it. "A lot of players who don't play, week-in, week-out. So for them to use the energy they were able to, we've got to have a big heart to be able to do that. They've always shown that and they showed that again." Felix strike earns Portugal narrow win over Wales When Bellamy watched on as Ronaldo caused lockdown Wales have a short turnaround to their second League A fixture against Denmark in Copenhagen on Sunday (17:00 BST). But Bellamy feels his squad - missing Harry Wilson, Karl Darlow, Dylan Lawlor, Joe Rodon and Nathan Broadhead through injury - are capable of improving. "There's more for us, so that's something we always look at as a positive," he said. "How can we improve? How can we get better?" Cristiano Ronaldo earned his 234th cap in the match against Wales Ronaldo unsurprisingly took the spotlight in the build-up to the contest at Jose Alvalade Stadium - where the 41-year-old began his professional career with Sporting in 2002. The forward missed a big opportunity and had a goal disallowed for offside, which would have been his 980th top-flight goal, before being substituted midway through the second half. He could well line-up against Wales again when Portugal play the return match in Cardiff in November. Amid the noise around the Al-Nassr frontman, Bellamy refused to be overawed and hopes to face Ronaldo again. "If you looked at everything that was going on, it's a £1.4bn squad you're up against, [but] I felt quite calm. The players give me that," added the Wales boss. "Ronaldo is one of the greatest players of all generations, not just this generation. "You have to plan for him because he's beyond dangerous, even at his age. "He's a superstar and I'd love to think I'd have the opportunity to be up against him again, but I don't know, maybe time is ticking." title: Man Utd borrow another £90m as debt tops £1.1bn
description: Manchester United confirm they have borrowed another £90m since 30 June, to take their overall debt to more than £1.1bn.
body: Manchester United's Old Trafford stadium is facing maintenance issues Manchester United have borrowed another £90m since 30 June - and confirmed they spent £191.7m on new players this summer. United bought Andrey Santos from Chelsea on 13 July, Youri Tielemans from Aston Villa on 14 July and Carlos Baleba from Brighton on 25 August. The fees the club stated they spent on the trio at the time the transfers were announced added up to £153m, and it is not clear where the additional sum has been spent. The club have been approached for comment. Confirmation of the additional borrowing of £90m was included in a more detailed filing to the New York Stock Exchange on Thursday, following Wednesday's release of their 2025-26 accounts to 30 June, and showed their overall debt was still more than £1bn despite major cost-cutting measures implemented by Sir Jim Ratcliffe since he became minority owner in 2024. United confirmed it made three further drawdowns from its revolving credit limit, on 29 and 31 July and 28 August, totalling £120m. It then paid back £30m on 21 September. It takes United's overall debt to £1.15bn, made up of the historic debt, which now stands at £578m, the £200m outstanding on its revolving credit facility, and £375m in outstanding transfer fees. That is a £72m reduction on the £447m they stated was owed in transfer fees in the 2024-25 accounts. However, it remains a large sum, with £104.8m due in between one and two years and £51.9m in between two and five years - with the remainder due in the next 12 months. The club say payments for their most recent transfers "are due within the next five years". title: Uefa fears impact of Premier League spending on transfer market
description: Uefa believes "a clear two-speed system" is emerging in the transfer market due to huge spending by Premier League clubs this summer.
body: Morgan Rogers joined Chelsea from Aston Villa in a deal worth £118m Uefa believes "a clear two-speed system" is emerging in the transfer market as a result of the huge spending by Premier League clubs this summer. In its latest European club talent and competition landscape report, European football's governing body laid bare just how dominant the transfer activity of English clubs has become. Uefa's report said that the estimated €4.6bn (£4bn) spend by Premier League clubs is "larger than that of the next eight largest European countries combined". Andrea Traverso, Uefa's executive director of finance, said that this trend "raises concerns". "Transfer values continue to rise sharply, particularly in the English market, increasing future pressure on club financial results," Traverso wrote. "These developments also point to an increasing concentration of talent and a growing polarisation of the market, with the emergence of a clear two-speed system. "English clubs were involved in more than 60% of the deals and paid an average of around €24m (£20.7m) per inbound player, compared with only around €4m (£3.4m) to €5m (£4.3m) in the other major European leagues, underlining a widening gap in purchasing power." Traverso said that any "correction in transfer values" or "slowdown in buyer demand" could have serious implications for any club carrying debt. The report added that the transfer spend of the 20 Premier League clubs this year is "equivalent to 56% of their annual revenue" - much higher than the 33% average of the pre-Covid decade. Uefa also highlighted the increasing trend for English clubs to do big-value transfers between each other, which showed a 44% increase to €1.55bn (£1.33bn). The English domestic market was "as large in fee value as the next five market flows combined". A market flow describes league-to-league deals. After the English domestic market, the next most lucrative was the German Bundesliga to the Premier League, at €690m (£594m). The number of European transfer fees paid above €50m has significantly increased, from 14 in the summer of 2024 to 23 in 2025. In 2026 there was another jump to 35 such deals, of which Premier League clubs were responsible for 29. With pressure to pass financial regulations, clubs have increasingly looked to sell academy players as they provide pure profit on the books. European clubs generated an estimated profit of €6.8bn (£5.85bn) on these sales over the summer, an increase of €655m (£564bn) on 2025. Uefa also found little evidence of clubs using multi-club ownership structures to move players for inflated or reduced fees. Total transfer fees of such deals were €152m (£130.8m) with an estimated market value of €159m (£136.8m). More than half of this spend came from transfers between Chelsea and Strasbourg. title: Yom Kippur shooting outside Canadian synagogue was 'hate-motivated', officials say
description: Const Jeff Smith, who was critically injured in the incident, continued to fend off the attacker after being shot multiple times, police said.
body: Canadian authorities have confirmed a shooting near a synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, was a "hate-motivated" attack targeting the Jewish community. The shooting took place outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue on Sunday night during Yom Kippur, the holiest night in the Jewish calendar. Belleville police chief Murray Rodd said during a Thursday news conference that it was "a deliberate attack directed at members of the Jewish community". A police officer who was critically injured in the incident continued to fend off the attacker despite being shot multiple times, the police chief said. The officer, identified as Constable Jeff Smith, suffered multiple gunshot wounds to his head and body, Rodd said. Smith remains in hospital and is expected to undergo multiple surgeries related to "serious head trauma". "He's making progress every day," the chief said. Smith was shot in his car but sought to fend off the attack on the synagogue until a second officer arrived almost three minutes later. "Despite suffering life-threatening injuries, within moments of encountering the armed suspect, Constable Smith exited his vehicle and engaged the attacker," Rodd said. The second officer, Constable Mike McCurdy, "joined the active gunfight, helping to bring the violent attack to an end", the police chief said. McCrudy was not injured. Both officers discharged their firearms, authorities said earlier this week. Around 20 to 30 shots were fired, leaving the suspect in life-threatening condition and Smith in critical but stable condition. The gunman was identified by police as 29-year-old Sean Ward from Quinte West, a community near Belleville and about 170km (105 miles) east of Toronto. He was sent to hospital with serious injuries and later died. Rodd called the attempted attack a "hate-motivated crime". Toronto police have increased patrols outside synagogues and places of worship out of an abundance of caution. Leaders of the Jewish community, as well as Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and other politicians, condemned antisemitic violence in the aftermath of the incident. Noah Shack, CEO of the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs, said in a statement on Thursday that "if not for the extraordinary bravery of Constable Jeff Smith, Canadians would have experienced the type of mass-casualty terror attack our security services have warned is a realistic possibility". He called on Canadian leaders to "take urgent and concrete actions" against threats toward the Jewish community. Carney wrote on X earlier this week that "Jewish people must be able to worship safely. To live free, open, proud Jewish lives." title: Xi visit to Washington all pomp but little progress so far
description: The summit so far has focused on "positive vibes", says one analyst, with several pressing issues awaiting discussion.
body: This video can not be played A red carpet and military flyover - How Trump welcomed Xi At least so far, Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington has been all pomp and little obvious progress on pressing issues. From the ceremonial welcoming at a military air base on Wednesday to the honour-guard arrival at the White House this morning, President Donald Trump rolled out the red carpet – literally and figuratively – for his Chinese counterpart. The public remarks from the two leaders have teemed with warm words and diplomatic niceties. In a statement before today's formal meetings, Xi announced a gift of Chinese pandas and unveiled a new student exchange programme. "Let us keep advancing the cause of friendship between our two peoples and work together to build a better world," he said. Trump, for his part, outlined some of the topics the leaders planned to discuss in their meetings, including "pressing issues concerning security, technology, and superintelligence" - using his preferred term for artificial intelligence. Trump says he and Xi held 'great meeting' as Chinese leader visits White House "The decisions we make in these areas today can promote peace and prosperity for decades and decades to come," he said. The marching bands and military flyovers on Thursday may serve a larger purpose, however – at least for Trump. "This is a little bit of intentional pageantry to talk up the positive vibes of the summit," Jennifer Welch, chief economic analyst for Bloomberg Economics, told the BBC. "This is very much how President Trump sees the summit and the role he plays in the US-China relationship, as ballast to provide stability." Even so, there is still an edge to some of Xi's rhetoric, she notes. In remarks at the White House, the Chinese leader again mentioned the "Thucydides trap" – a theory that shifts in global power tend to lead to conflict between rising and declining nations. "China and the United States are different in national conditions, but through candid, in-depth and continued dialogue, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust," Xi said. The obstacles in the way of reaching any substantive agreement between the two nations are significant, however. When Trump and Xi met in Beijing in May, the men agreed to form boards of trade and investment to oversee economic interactions, and little more. On Wednesday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said a year-long trade "truce" between the two nations that had kept tariffs lower would be extended another two months. Financial analysts expect a further extension could come before this week's summit ends, given that neither side wants a renewal of last year's trade war. The outlook for progress is much dimmer on other topics, like the US war with Iran, the Ukraine war and regulating AI. China's reneging on promises to buy more American agricultural products and to also sell more rare earth minerals to the US is helping cloud the outlook. China, meanwhile, is watching to see if Trump follows through on a proposed sale of American weapons to Taiwan, which has been on hold for months. This video can not be played Watch: Here's why Trump's been so keen on Xi's visit When it comes to AI, China and the US have two very different goals for any agreement on the race to develop the technology, Robyn Klingler-Vida, a professor of political economy at Kings College London, told the BBC. "On the US side, it's about existential risk and slowing down AI potentially," she said. "Whereas in China, it's about acceleration, maybe winning the AI tech race and the application of AI to the real economy." A number of leading American AI executives plan to attend tonight's formal state dinner at the White House, which many view as a means for the US side to tout its current technological advantage. Muscle-flexing aside, more pageantry – and the promise of stability – may be the end result of Xi's China visit, even with additional face time between the two leaders to come before Xi departs on Friday afternoon. "What China talks about is metaphysical and abstract. The United States wants to solve specific problems," Miles Yu, who served as principal China policy planner and strategist to Secretary of State Mike Pompeo during Trump's first term, told the BBC. "These different approaches are not going to lead to any result." title: What are my children exposed to? Why I want testing for cancer-causing chemicals
description: People living near a lagoon branded "a shame on Britain" want to be tested for cancer-causing PCBs.
body: Natalie Dugdale is calling for public health bodies to test people that are worried they may have been poisoned by years of exposure to toxic waste When she moved to the countryside two years ago, Natalie Dugdale thought it would be the perfect spot to raise her family. Close to a lagoon in north Wales, she thought she could walk her baby, toddler and dogs on public footpaths. But when she watched Michael Sheen's BBC documentary revealing the lagoon's history as a dumping ground of cancer-causing chemicals known as PCBs, Natalie was shocked. Now she is part of a group of people who are worried they may have been poisoned by years of exposure to toxic waste, and are campaigning for voluntary blood testing across Wales. But Wales' public health body has said it does not recommend blood testing for PCBs, saying it would cause more concern. Michael Sheen followed up campaigner Douglas Gowan's concerns about dumping carcinogenic waste Public Health Wales (PHW) said the tests did not provide "a reliable means of assessing an individual's exposure to contamination or the potential health impact". Members of a newly formed campaign group for those living alongside some of the sites concerned have told BBC Wales they had been left "frightened and upset" and said testing would help provide "peace of mind". Natalie could not believe her local lake in Llwyneinion, just outside Wrexham, had actually once been a dumping ground for potentially dangerous chemicals and wants to see blood testing introduced. "I was really upset because having young children, what are they being exposed to?," said Natalie, 33. Llwyneinion lagoon was recently branded "a shame on Britain", following the documentary into historical dumping of PCBs by US chemical giant Monsanto, which had factories in Wrexham and Newport. Michael Phillips played at the lagoon as a child and decades later developed a rare cancer in his shoulder. He said many of his other friends had died because of similarly rare cancers, which he now suspects were linked, although no proven link has been established. "I would say every person that played in the pool that was close to me, apart from one friend who had an operation to get rid of it, is dead," said Michael, 63. Sheen's Buried programme team found elevated levels in soil samples taken in an area open to the public beyond the fenced-off lagoon, as well as at 13 other suspected dumpsites for the firm's toxic waste across the country. Llwyneinion lagoon is one of the most notorious dumpsites of the toxic chemicals Michael Phillips was also found to have "very high" levels of PCBs in his blood, after private testing commissioned for the documentary. The banned chemicals were once widely used and revered for being non-flammable and hard to break down – but are seen today as the first "forever chemicals" - which are building up in the environment, threatening wildlife and human health. What is the truth lying beneath our feet? Michael Sheen uncovers claims of conspiracy, complicity and denial over alleged toxic 'forever chemical' contamination in south Wales. Michael and Natalie have both now joined a newly formed campaign group - made up of hundreds of residents living alongside the former Monsanto works in the villages of Cefn Mawr, Acrefair and Trevor in north-east Wales. One of their calls - alongside a national soil testing programme - is for voluntary blood testing, led by Public Health Wales. One of the group's founders pointed to the fact the documentary had to rely on a large-scale study from the US to assess and compare PCB levels in the local residents it had tested. This video can not be played Michael Phillips played at Llwyneinion lagoon as a child and wants people like him to be tested "There's a huge potential here for Wales... to really lead the way and show the rest of the UK how to handle this risk," said community councillor Katie Witherden. "It would give people answers about what they have or haven't been exposed to - and I think all of us deserve the right to have the choice to know that." Nel Byers said that blood testing was needed "for people's own peace of mind" as well as showing "on a national scale" whether these communities had heightened results. "If they get the blood testing done they might actually start doing something about [the dumpsites]," said the 33-year-old from Trevor. There are 12 locations in Wales that were sites of concern for Douglas Gowan Public Health Wales issued a statement, external in response to calls from residents and politicians - including the Welsh Affairs Select Committee of MPs - saying a programme of blood testing was "not recommended". It argued that testing would "not tell us how or where people may have been exposed" as there were many potential PCB sources in the wider environment - including food, and materials in homes and buildings. There was no treatment for higher levels of the chemicals so there was a risk too of "causing worry among people who are found to have PCBs in their blood", it added. Natalie said she found the response "disappointing", adding: "I think a lot of people are already frightened and it's more frightening not knowing." Katie agreed that "people are already worried" and said: "We know they can't treat PCBs and that's not what we're asking for." Her husband Steve Witherden is the Labour MP for Montgomeryshire and Glyndŵr and described PHW's response as "chilling". Nel Byers, her fiancé Otis Proctor and their three-month-old daughter Wren live near the former Monsanto works in Wrexham and want to know how they may have been affected by toxic chemicals in the ground "My hope is that they revise their position," he said. "There's a real strength of feeling from people who've lived near to these sites or worked in them, a real clamouring." title: Catherine Zeta-Jones bases new role on funny Welsh people she knows
description: Zeta-Jones plays Jackie Price, a former cocaine dealer who is targeted by assassins, in Kill Jackie.
body: Catherine Zeta-Jones plays Jackie Price, a former cocaine dealer who is being targeted by hitmen in a new series Actor Catherine Zeta-Jones says she based her performance in the new series Kill Jackie on people she knows in Wales. The Mumbles star plays Jackie Price, a former cocaine dealer who is being targeted by hitmen, in a new series for Prime. It is the first time she has played a role using her Swansea accent and the first time she has filmed a drama in Wales. "I played on people I know in Wales, people who are comedic and the accent makes it funny and real and true, but the character comes from a tough side of Swansea, which we do have as well," she said. The series is based on a book called The Price You Pay, set in the US, and the central character is a man called Jack. Zeta-Jones said they "flipped it" for her to be a woman with all the quirkiness and craziness that Jack had in the book. She said: "I told my creative team, I want to play her Welsh. And they went OK." "For many reasons. One, I've never played real Welsh Swansea ever, never shot in Wales and I think it would ground me in her character and add nuances that I would know," she told Lucy Owen on BBC Radio Wales. "I'm so glad I did it because she's such a great character and I just wanted her to be Welsh." Óscar Jaenada as Zigor and Zeta-Jones as Jackie Price in Kill Jackie Zeta-Jones, also an executive producer on the series, said she had an idea for one scene to use a song by Welsh singing legend Tom Jones, and have him help save the day. She said: "Jackie has installed this high-tech security system behind these Andy Warhol style prints of Tom Jones. They lift up and out come very dangerous machine-guns that do the bad guys in." "That was my contribution to the scene." Catherine said she did not know if Jones realised he had such a crucial role and said she needed to text him to tell him about it. "I think because I'm playing such a badass, I think he's going to love that we used his song in that particular moment in the show," she said. Zeta-Jones says she "could not believe" how many of her fans noticed the use of her accent in the thriller Zeta-Jones has been praised by fans for using her Welsh accent in the thriller, which begins on 2 October. One fan said they loved hearing the "queen of Wales sounding Welsh". She has previously spoken about her strong connection to Wales, adding in her heart she "never really left". One fan commented on an Instagram post of the trailer, saying: "Her Welsh is out and I love it, can't wait". Speaking on BBC Woman's Hour, Zeta-Jones said she "could not believe" how many of her fans noticed the use of her accent and that it had made her "very happy". The Hollywood actress also revisited comments she made recently about the term "nepo baby", which she said was a "horrific" phrase. During the interview, she said her husband Michael Douglas - son of Hollywood legend Kirk Douglas - was "the ultimate nepo baby". She also said her children Dylan and Carys had dealt with the "intense attention thrown on them profoundly well". Catherine Zeta-Jones on using her real accent in Kill Jackie Despite her Welsh pride, Zeta-Jones has also revealed that she turned down an appearance on Welcome To Wrexham, alongside fellow Hollywood stars Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac. In an interview with Heart Radio she said she was asked several times to feature in the documentary series. "It's really hard to explain to Americans that I'm from Swansea and I was brought up with Swansea City. My uncle Bobby was director of the Swans when John Toshack took us to the premiership." "I was in the front seat of the parade. I have been a lifelong Swansea city fan. I can't go to Wrexham. I can't even go to Wrexham to tell them how much I love Swansea. I think they would throw bricks at me in the street", she joked. title: Anti-migrant activist charged after dinghy slashed in Channel
description: Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas is charged in connection with an incident in the English Channel.
body: Daniel Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, will appear in court on Friday morning Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been charged with criminal damage after he was seen in a video slashing at a dinghy in the English Channel. The 37-year-old, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, has also been charged with failing to disclose the PIN to his phone, Hampshire Police said. He has been remanded in custody to appear at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court on Friday morning. Several hundred people, many wearing black, had gathered outside a police investigation centre in Basingstoke on Thursday evening believing Thomas was inside. They arrived shortly before 18:30 BST and stood on the road outside the building and could be heard chanting "free DT". The crowd began to disperse at about 21:45 after protesters learned of the charges against Thomas. Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary earlier said an arrest had been made after a "boat that had an emergency responder on board" was damaged in the Channel. title: Results awaited in Isle of Man general election
description: Counting begins in the island's 12 constituencies to elect 24 members of the House of Keys.
body: Polling stations across the island opened at 08:00 BST Counting has begun across the Isle of Man in the 2026 general election, with results expected to be declared throughout the evening and into the night. There are 82 candidates contesting the election for the 24 seats available in the House of Keys. Exit polls conducted by Manx Radio predict seven outgoing MHKs will lose their seats, three of whom are current members of the Council of Ministers. They suggest outgoing Environment, Food and Agriculture Minister Clare Barber, Education, Sport and Culture Minister Daphne Caine, and Enterprise Minister Tim Johnston have lost their seats. Former ministers Onchan MHK Julie Edge, Ramsey MHK Lawrie Hooper and Rushen MHK Michelle Haywood, and deputy speaker of the Keys are also predicted to lose their seats. In Ayre and Michael, the exit polls predict that Chief Minister Alfred Cannan is in a fight to retain his place in the House of Keys, with only 1% between him and the candidate in third. Overall the exit polls suggest there will be 15 new MHKs, including eight women, down from 10 elected in 2021. A third of the seats in the Keys are not being contested by outgoing MHKs, which means there is guaranteed to be eight new faces in Tynwald. Arbory, Castletown and Malew: Kirrie Jenkins and too close to call between Jason Moorhouse and Steve Crowther. Ayre and Michael: Stephen Broad and too close to call between Alfred Cannon and Phil Corkhill Douglas Central: Peter Shimmin and Chris Thomas Douglas East: Andy Saunders and too close to call between Joney Faragher and Dave Mackey Douglas North: David Ashford and Damien Ciappelli Douglas South: Sarah Maltby and Claire Christian Garff: Richard Henthorne and Aishlinn Creer Glenfaba and Peel: Katryna Baptist and Geoffrey Pugh Middle: Jane Poole-Wilson and James Cochrane Onchan: Rob Callister and Rachel Glover Ramsey: Juan McGuinness and Robert Cowell Rushen: Michael Crowe and too close to call between Mark Kemp and Simon Williams Among the issues dominating the election in 2026 were keeping young people on the island, the availability and cost of housing, wind farms, healthcare waiting times, and the impacts of spiralling expenses for small businesses. Voting took place across the island from 08:00 BST on Thursday until the polls closed at 20:00. Those who have been elected as a Member of the House of Keys (MHK) will be sworn in on Tuesday by the first and second deemsters. The House of Keys will then sit on 13 October to nominate a chief minister and speaker of the House of Keys. title: Buttler injury halts England as Sri Lanka level series
description: Jos Buttler's bravery comes in vain as Sri Lanka fight back to beat England in the second one-day international at Headingley and set up a series decider at The Oval.
body: This video can not be played Highlights: Mendis hits century as Sri Lanka beat England at Headingley Second Metro Bank one-day international, Headingley Sri Lanka 321-6 (50 overs): Kusal 121, Kamindu 54; Ahmed 2-48 England 305-9 (50 overs): Banton 73, Buttler 69; Wellalage 3-49 Sri Lanka won by 16 runs Jos Buttler's bravery came in vain as Sri Lanka fought back to beat England in the second one-day international at Headingley and set up a series decider at The Oval. Needing 68 from 75 balls, England were cruising towards a target of 322 until Buttler retired hurt on 67 after tweaking a hamstring. When Rehan Ahmed, Gus Atkinson and Jamie Overton fell, Buttler re-emerged with 27 needed from 14 balls and witnessed Will Jacks fall for 52 at the non-striker's end. England were left needing 19 from the last with Buttler on strike but, barely able to hobble a single, he holed out at deep mid-wicket. England finished on 306-9 as Sri Lanka won by 16 runs. Buttler had earlier shown flashes of his vintage best in hitting Sri Lanka's spinners for five sixes, putting England on course after collapse of 3-14 spoiled an opening stand of 143 between Tom Banton and Ben Duckett. Sri Lanka were fortunate for the way he was abruptly halted but deserve credit for the way their seamers used reverse swing afterwards to deny England's lower order. Their captain Kusal Mendis also hit a fine 122 in their 321-6. The series, and the international summer, concludes on Sunday from 10:30 BST. 'The lads wanted me to stick one up him' - Wood relives fastest spells Sri Lanka level ODI series as England fall short in thriller - as it happened Pick your County Championship team of the season This video can not be played Best shots - Brilliant Banton gets England off to excellent start What to make of this dramatic encounter? It is a defeat for England, one which halts their momentum a touch as they build towards next year's 50-over World Cup. It was unlike any other, however. They will do well to find situations like these again when the bigger moments come. "It is always disappointing when you lose," captain Harry Brook said. "Sri Lanka played exceptionally well there, especially the last 10-15 overs. There were plenty of moments in the game we could have been slightly better." One positive was the batting of Buttler before injury struck. He has not scored a century in this format for three-and-a-half years and had his T20 form doubted earlier this year at the World Cup. The way he took down the spinners was brutal. When he was flying, England were on course for their highest chase at this ground. The opening stand between Banton and Duckett was also impressive - reminiscent of England's brightest ODIs days as they thrashed around the bowling at more than seven runs an over. That neither pressed on - Duckett was bowled for 67 and Banton stumped for 73, both to left-arm spinner Dinuth Wellalage - was disappointing. There were also rare failures for Joe Root who made 15 and Brook, the latter also pinned in front lbw for one by Wellalage. Perhaps more concerning was that the lower order were unable to support Jacks in his quest to push England over the line again. That aspect must improve over England's three white-ball series that come before mid-January. This video can not be played 'Fabulous knock' - Watch the best shots as Mendis reaches 100 This has been a difficult tour for Sri Lanka, who were outclassed in the 3-0 T20 series defeat and well beaten by 89 runs in the first ODI at Chester-le-Street. This, especially given the bad start with the ball, will be a significant boost to morale. Kusal was troubled early on by Overton's bouncers, top-edging one into a gap soon after Atkinson dropped a simple chance at fine leg when the right-hander had 17 - another England error. The Sri Lanka captain also had to overturn a caught-behind decision on 99 when Overton was the bowler again. Kusal was eventually caught on the boundary trying to clear deep mid-wicket off Ahmed, who also had Charith Asalanka caught in the same position for 2-48 but did not offer the control usually brought by Adil Rashid. A flat Headingley pitch was a far bigger test of England's seamers than Tuesday's difficult surface in Durham. Josh Tongue struggled with his lines for 0-50 in seven overs. Atkinson, who took 2-55, and Overton, who had another catch dropped in the final over, in taking 0-63 from 10 were England's best bowling performers. "Tight games are always good games to watch and good games to be a part of," Brook added. "Having the opportunity to play in a decider will only benefit us." title: Woman, 40, dies in three-vehicle crash
description: Karen Stewart was one of five people taken to hospital after a crash on the Moira Road on Saturday but later died from her injuries.
body: Karen Stewart, 40, was from Portadown A woman has died following a three-vehicle collision in Lisburn. She was one of five people, including a child, who were taken to hospital for treatment after a crash on the Moira Road at the weekend. Karen Stewart, 40, from Portadown in County Armagh, later died in hospital from her injuries. The crash happened at about 11:06 BST on Saturday. PSNI Det Insp Stewart said the 40-year-old had been driving a Ford Kuga which was in involved in a crash with a Citroen C5 and a BMW at the junction of Crewe Park Road. Police, the Northern Ireland Ambulance Service and the Northern Ireland Fire and Rescue Service attended the scene. title: Italy ministers agree to ban burqa and niqab in school and cap foreigners in class
description: Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni described the measures as "common-sense tools that do not divide but really help to integrate".
body: The Italian government has approved a ban on the burqa and niqab in schools, along with a limit on the share of pupils who speak little Italian in any one class. A 30% cap will be imposed on children without Italian citizenship or poor knowledge of the Italian language in the first year of primary, middle and high school. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni described the measures as "common-sense tools that do not divide but really help to integrate". Opposition parties accuse the government of pandering to the policies of the hard-right Futuro Nazionale party, ahead of a general election next year. Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara has said the limit is "purely linguistic" rather than one of citizenship, while he has sought to frame the ban on the niqab and burqa as a matter of gender equality. "You must go to school with your face uncovered," Meloni said while announcing the plans on Sunday, adding that no-one could decide that a young woman should hide herself in the name of tradition. There were several drafts of the decree ahead of Thursday's council of ministers meeting, however the core details were clear. The veil ban would apply to the burqa and niqab, but not the hijab, which leaves the face visible. The niqab is a veil for the face that leaves the area around the eyes clear. However, it may be worn with a separate eye veil. It is worn with an accompanying headscarf. The burka is a one-piece veil that covers the face and body. Often there is a mesh screen around the eyes to see through. Non-Italian citizens make up 11.6% of pupils in Italy's schools, according to the research institution Fondazione ISMU. The 30% limit on pupils who speak limited Italian will cover separate stages of education differently. In primary schools, it would cover non-Italian citizens who have either not been born in Italy or who have not attended at least two years of nursery school. In lower- and upper- secondary schools, it would cover pupils without Italian citizenship who have not successfully completed at least three years in the Italian school system. Local school offices would be asked to spread pupils with little Italian language skills more evenly among nearby schools. Where that is not possible, exemptions would apply, with extra Italian teaching. The aim was to avoid "ghetto classes", the education minister explained. The draft also goes further on parents, according to the Ansa news agency. Schools would have to report to social services cases in which persistent language barriers among those with parental responsibility hinder a child's integration. Free Italian courses would be offered. The measure is a decree law, meaning it can take effect immediately, but must be ratified by parliament within 60 days. Italy already has guidance on Italian language at schools. A 2010 ministerial notice under then-Education Minister Mariastella Gelmini set a 30% limit "as a rule" on pupils without Italian citizenship. The new decree puts the limit into law. The political opposition says the plan is as much about politics as schools. Opponents accuse Meloni of pandering to Roberto Vannacci, a retired military general who leads the hard-right Futuro Nazionale party and is seen as a threat to the governing coalition's right flank. The leader of the centre-left Democratic Party (PD), Elly Schlein, called the plan propaganda and impossible to implement. PD deputy and chamber vice-president Anna Ascani also accused the government of propaganda at the expense of schoolchildren. Valditara, speaking by video link from New York at a press conference rejected the charge. "We are not chasing Vannacci; if anything, he is chasing us," he said. Vannacci said he agreed with the measures, but they should have come years ago. The League's Matteo Salvini, who launched a separate package of measures on what he called "political Islam" on Wednesday, accused Vannacci of "continually voting against the government". Salvini said he hoped Futuro Nazionale would back the League's new proposals. title: Priest killed and four injured in knife attack at Polish abbey
description: A male suspect from Ukraine was arrested after the stabbings in the town of Jarosław, police say.
body: Polish police have sealed off the area around the abbey A priest has been killed and four other people injured in a knife attack in south-east Poland, officials have said. A 31-year-old Ukrainian man was arrested after the stabbings on the grounds of a Catholic abbey in the town of Jarosław. Polish President Karol Nawrocki said Thursday's attack "has shaken us all and demands a firm response from the state", while his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky said "we are shocked by this evil". Reports in Polish media said the attacker first injured a priest in a nearby cafe, and then another four people inside the abbey itself. A police investigation into the attacker's motives is now under way. Polish police said four men and one woman were stabbed in the attack on Thursday morning on the abbey grounds. The name of the murdered priest has not been publicly released. Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said psychological support was now being provided to all those affected by the incident. Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the perpetrator "will be punished with the full severity of Polish law". Echoing his words, President Zelensky said "the perpetrator of this evil must bear full responsibility according to the law", adding that Ukraine was counting on "a quick and thorough investigation of all circumstances". The Ukrainian embassy in Poland also condemned the attack. In a statement, it said: "In such difficult moments, it is especially important to support each other, remain steadfast in respect for human life, and not allow pain to escalate into hatred or new violence. Responsibility for a crime must be based solely on the law." Poland has recently seen a number of often violent incidents involving its citizens and Ukrainians, many of whom have fled their home country after Russia's full-scale invasion. title: Four civilians killed in Pakistani strikes in Afghanistan, Taliban says
description: Pakistan says it struck 10 targets, adding the strikes were "strictly limited to identified military objectives".
body: Flames and smoke rise from an area struck by an air strike in Kandahar on Thursday Afghanistan's Taliban government said a wave of Pakistani air strikes had killed four civilians in the latest escalation between the two sides. The strikes hit provinces including Kandahar, the Taliban's base of power, sources told the BBC. A resident told AFP news agency they heard a jet, followed by a large explosion and then a fire in the city. Pakistan said its forces had struck 10 targets in Afghanistan, without specifying their locations, adding the strikes were "strictly limited to identified military objectives". It's the second wave of Pakistani air strikes on Afghan territory in the past week, and comes after a deadly attack on a police facility in Pakistan on 18 September. In a statement, the Taliban said there would be an "appropriate response" following the attack, while Pakistan said any further "provocative act" would be responded to. Taliban government spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said the attacks were in Afghanistan's Kandahar, Paktia and Khost provinces. In Paktia, an official said jets had bombed the Afghan Armed Forces' 203 Mansouri Corps, which is controlled by the Taliban, without providing any information on casualties. In Khost, a spokesman said houses were damaged in the strikes, with no casualties reported. Abdullah, a local eyewitness, told Reuters news agency the strikes happened around midnight. "People were shouting, and there was panic all around," he said. "Afterwards, the village elder arrived and called out to the houses, asking if anyone was killed. Thankfully, no one was killed." Another local, Salamat Khan, told Reuters that "there is no military base here, nor are there any military personnel", adding "there are only the homes of ordinary civilians". A Taliban security official inspects the scene of Pakistani air strikes in Khost Zabihullah Mujahid labelled the attack as "reckless, careless, and hostile", and said it "will have adverse consequences for the Pakistani military". Pakistan's Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said the strikes were "deliberate, precise, calibrated, and proportionate, and strictly limited to identified military objectives directly linked to the attempted attacks against Pakistan". The Taliban and Pakistan had enjoyed three months of relative calm, until fighting reignited following an attack on a mosque at a police compound in north-western Pakistan last week, which killed at least 31 people, according to AFP. A group linked to Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which has waged a violent campaign against Pakistan for years, claimed the attack. Islamabad has accused Kabul of harbouring the TTP. Afghanistan's Taliban government denies this, saying militancy is Pakistan's internal problem. Following the attack on the police facility, Pakistan said earlier this week it launched air strikes in the Afghanistan-Pakistan border region, killing 28 militants. Farid Dehqan, a spokesman for the Taliban government in Kunar province, told the BBC that three people were killed and four others were injured in the strike. The UN mission Unama also confirmed that at least three civilians were killed. An attack in Afghanistan's Kunar province has killed at least three civilians, according to the UN Then on Wednesday, Pakistan said it detected drones launched from Afghanistan into its territory and that all of them were "neutralised". Taliban officials denied that their government had launched drones against Pakistan that day. Unama said in July that cross-border armed violence between Taliban government forces and Pakistani security forces killed at least 499 civilians and wounded 1,216 others between October 2025 and June 2026. The worst single incident occurred in March, when more than 269 people were killed, external in a Pakistani air strike on Kabul, which the Afghan Taliban said hit a drug rehabilitation centre. Islamabad denied the charge, saying it "precisely targeted military installations and terrorist support infrastructure". The neighbouring countries had agreed a ceasefire in March, but international mediation has failed to produce a lasting resolution. During a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly earlier this week, Pakistan's Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar called for "concrete and verifiable" measures to ensure that Afghan territory is not used for "terrorism". title: Crisis-hit gender service cancelled 60 surgeries this year, Welsh health minister says
description: It is the first time figures have been given for numbers of surgeries cancelled by the service.
body: Surgeries referred from the Welsh Gender Service were cancelled in August About 60 surgeries via the Welsh Gender Service (WGS) were cancelled for this year after NHS officials paused referrals in August, Wales' health minister has revealed. It is the first time figures have been given for the number of people affected by the decision to pause referrals over concerns that patients who identify as transgender had been "appropriately assessed". In a Senedd debate, Welsh Green leader Anthony Slaughter said patients were facing "unbearable limbo". Reform's Cristiana Emsley said it would be unacceptable to continue when "serious concerns exist". Health Minister Mabon ap Gwynfor said he wanted "to bring certainty" as quickly as possible. The body that took the decision, the NHS Wales Joint Commissioning Committee, external (NWJCC), has commissioned a review that is examining the referrals to see if any of the cancelled surgeries can proceed before the end of the year. BBC Wales revealed in August that some patients found out about the cancellations while they were in hospital. Earlier this month, the NWJCC said in some cases patients did not meet "the basic requirements for surgery". Having an unsuitable body mass index (BMI) - a value derived from an adult's height and weight - was a factor. It also said the proportion of Welsh patients progressing from referral for some types of surgery was "significantly lower" than across the border, while the rate of surgery referrals was "significantly higher". The WGS, external provides referrals for adult patients living in Wales, but all NHS surgeries are carried out in England. The surgery includes both masculinising and feminising procedures. They are not reversible. The Welsh Gender Service is based at St David's Hospital in Cardiff Ap Gwynfor said the NWJCC had appointed a clinical review panel, and it was expected its work would commence "imminently". "This review will prioritise those individuals who are further along the pathway to allow appropriate referrals to proceed as soon as possible," he said. "The JCC has identified that approximately 60 patients were due surgery between the pausing of surgery in August and the end of December. "Our priority is to bring certainty to these people as quickly as possible and the JCC are confident that all 60 of these cases can be reviewed before the end of December." A wider independent review into the service is also taking place, with findings expected later this year. Ap Gwynfor added: "I have met with the JCC and been clear that the urgent clinical review needs to be swift to minimise the disruption and distress for individuals on the waiting list. "I have also been clear that I expect all patients impacted by this pause to have access to the necessary support whilst the review is undertaken." Wales Greens leader Slaughter led the debate and told Members of the Senedd (MSs) that an "unbearable limbo" was being faced by patients. He said some of whom had been left feeling "abandoned, alone and confused, having had the rug pulled from under them". "They had jumped through every hoop asked of them, had arranged and rearranged their lives around this day," he said. Slaughter urged ministers to review what he called "the failure of governance that led to both patients and the government being blindsided" and said "robust measures" should be put into place so that the JCC could be held to account. Slaughter was supported by Plaid Cymru MS for Sir Fynwy Torfaen, Matthew Jones, who accused the committee of "not publicly or adequately" explaining its concerns. But Conservative health spokesperson Natasha Asghar said: "The title of this short debate suggests that pausing sex change operations is unacceptable but that couldn't be further from the truth. "There is nothing unacceptable about pausing irreversible surgery at the Welsh Gender Service while serious concerns are investigated." Cristiana Emsley, Reform MS for Fflint Wrecsam, said she believed the halt was merited, saying: "Whatever our political differences, truth and patient safety must unite us. "I accept that the pause might cause distress and patients must be supported, but what would be unacceptable is continuing irreversible referrals when serious concerns exist about referral appropriateness, clinical governance and patient safeguards". The NWJCC said in an update on Wednesday that it would begin its review looking at patients whose surgery would be due to take place between August and December 2026. "Reviews will start with those whose planned surgery dates were earliest and will continue in date order," it said. "NWJCC has sought confirmation from the NHS England surgical providers that patients who are able to proceed with surgery will be prioritised." It promised that this stage of the review would be completed by the end of December, and says "experienced gender clinicians" will undertake the work. "Patients who are waiting for surgery in 2027, and those who are waiting for a surgical assessment, will also have their referral reviewed to confirm that the requirements for surgery have been met." The NWJCC said it had not identified any patients who had come to harm, but said concerns were raised through "complaints, correspondence and other information".
