title: The compromises and power struggles that shaped Fury-Joshua
description: BBC Sport takes a look at the compromises, power struggles and competing interests behind Tyson Fury v Anthony Joshua.
body: Tyson Fury (left) and Anthony Joshua have been world heavyweight champions twice each After a decade of stalled negotiations, public squabbling and false starts, Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua will finally meet in the ring on 11 December at Cardiff's Principality Stadium. BBC Sport understands the WBA 'Super' heavyweight title is expected to be on the line, although confirmation from the governing body is still awaited. It would give both former world champions the chance to regain a version of the heavyweight crown, although Fury-Joshua has always been about more than belts. The fight arrives later than anybody wanted, with both in the twilight of their careers, but for years British boxing's biggest heavyweight rivalry seemed destined to remain a story of what might have been. Yet Thursday's announcement of an 80,000-capacity showdown, broadcast globally by Netflix, did more than finally provide a date and venue. It also offered a glimpse of the competing interests, egos and power struggles involved in getting one of boxing's most elusive fights over the line. This video can not be played 'None of this is unusual' - Warren on AJ v Fury fight timings Speaking to BBC Sport after the fight was announced, Fury's promoter Frank Warren repeatedly returned to one word: compromise. "Everybody's got to make a compromise," the Queensberry boss said. "Tyson really compromised. He didn't dig his heels in. "He said, 'Fine, wherever they want it, I'll do it. If they want me to go to New York, I'll go. They want it in the UK, I just want to get the fight on." The fighters had already agreed to the contest but the venue was a sticking point. Warren says Netflix wanted New York, while Joshua, 36, was determined to fight in Britain. Predictably, their camps disagree over who finally got it done. Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn described the push to keep the fight in Britain as a "two-man crusade". "AJ has turned down money to keep it in the UK," Hearn told the Matchroom YouTube channel. "I wouldn't be able to look people in the eye if I was part of the movement to take this to the US." Hearn says Joshua had specifically requested protection for a UK fight in his contract and refused to relent. "We were under so much pressure to fold," he added. "It was only really the support of the British public that made Joshua stand 10 toes down and say no." He says Fury, 38, could have insisted on his own contractual position but instead accepted Britain to ensure the fight did not collapse. Fury has won 36 pro fights with two defeats and one draw, while Joshua has won 30 and lost four Perhaps the biggest sideshow has been the struggle for influence around the promotion itself. Saudi boxing powerbroker Turki Alalshikh announced the fight, having previously insisted any confirmation would come from him. "For 15 years no-one has been able to make this fight," he wrote. "Back in April, I said that any announcement would come from me. I can now confirm that Fury v Joshua will be coming to the UK, as I promised British boxing fans. The time for talking is over." Dana White's involvement is particularly intriguing. The UFC chief is partnered with Alalshikh through Zuffa Boxing and featured prominently in the announcement, with Netflix describing the event as a collaboration involving White and Alalshikh's The Ring. Hearn and Warren were absent. Hearn had previously said White would not be involved in promoting the fight, while Warren says both fighters' contracts stipulated the same. Yet Warren says White ultimately helped secure the Netflix deal but believes fans care little about the promotional politics. "I don't know whether he will be front and centre or not," Warren said. Wednesday's news conference in London may tell us more - not least how prominent White is and how he and Hearn share the stage after months of back-and-forth. This video can not be played 'I think Tyson will knock Joshua out' Even Cardiff comes with competing claims of credit. Hearn had publicly pushed for the Principality Stadium in recent weeks, while Warren told BBC Sport Queensberry and Saudi events company Sela spent several months working "quietly" with the venue and local authorities. The stadium's retractable roof makes it well suited to a December event and there is precedent for late night boxing. Joe Calzaghe's victory over Mikkel Kessler there in 2007 took place under a closed roof, with the fight starting after 01:00 GMT to accommodate American television. Fury-Joshua is expected to follow a similar pattern. The exact ringwalk time remains in the hands of Netflix, with Hearn saying his current understanding is around 01:00 or 01:30 GMT. Warren has ruled out anything as late as 04:00. "If it went on in America you'd be watching it five o'clock in the morning," Warren said. "It's a compromise and it's an event." There is no contractual rematch clause, according to Hearn. "We're coming in for the kind of victory that no-one will need to see the fight again," he said. Warren believes the winner can continue towards further world-title opportunities. For the loser, he thinks the road may end in Cardiff. Whatever the outcome, Fury-Joshua has long been defined by the reasons it did not happen. But in just over eleven weeks there will be no more negotiations, competing claims or hypothetical outcomes - just Fury and Joshua, in the same ring at last. title: Watch: UN delegates walk out of Netanyahu speech
description: The Israeli delegation could be be seen cheering in support during Netanyahu's speech.
body: This video can not be played Dozens of United Nations delegates walked out of the hall Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was due to deliver a speech in. Addressing the UN's General Assembly in New York, Netanyahu described those walking out as "moral cowards". Those who remained and felt similarly should leave, he said. The Israeli delegation could be seen cheering Netanyahu in support. Israel has faced condemnation for its actions in Gaza and Lebanon. A UN commission of inquiry has previously accused Israel of committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza - Israel has strongly rejected the accusations. The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage. Israel responded by launching a military campaign in Gaza, during which more than 73,920 people have been killed, according to the territory's health ministry. title: BBC upholds complaints over Victoria Beckham slur on Have I Got News For You
description: Two viewers complained to the BBC over the "gratuitously offensive" comment made during the show.
body: Complaints about the broadcast of a swear word in connection with Victoria Beckham during an episode of BBC One's Have I Got News For You have been upheld, the corporation's executive complaints unit (ECU) has ruled. The show, from 7 November last year, hosted by comic and presenter Katherine Ryan, featured an email allegedly sent by Sir David Beckham in which the word was used. Ryan told the show's panellists: "I don't know that we are allowed to broadcast the c-word, but you did reference Victoria Beckham earlier and we'll allow that." Two viewers complained that this was gratuitously offensive, and the BBC said there was no justification for a comment which "presented Victoria Beckham as equivalent to a particularly offensive word". The ECU finding has been reported to the management of BBC Content. As a result, a version of the programme edited in light of the finding will replace the version currently on iPlayer. The ECU statement in full said: "The relevant BBC Editorial Guidelines do not require programmes to avoid giving offence, but do require that any offence should be editorially justified. "In the ECU's judgement, while the inclusion of the c-word in the programme derived editorial justification from David Beckham's alleged use of it and the satirical reflections this prompted, there was no such justification for a comment which presented Victoria Beckham as equivalent to a particularly offensive word." In November, the ECU responded to complaints from viewers it said were "unhappy with the inclusion of strong language in the programme". It said "the use of the strong language was editorially justified as the panel were discussing a current news story about Sir David Beckham and directly quoting from leaked emails in which he had used the word in question, leading to further discussion". It added that it was "common practice" to carry a clear verbal warning at the start of post-watershed programmes with very strong language, which was what happened for this particular episode of the show. "It is never our intention to offend our audience," the statement added. title: Why Australia chose the world's biggest political stage to reveal OpenAI hack
description: Australia, which has strict social media restrictions and has proposed controls on algorithms and smart glasses, announced the breach at the UN.
body: This video can not be played Australia made a dramatic revelation on Wednesday during the United Nations General Assembly. Rogue AI agents had hacked one of its government bodies - the first known incident of its kind in the world. Private data, but not sensitive information, was taken from Medicare, Australia's universal healthcare scheme. The breach happened in June, but OpenAI says it only became aware of it in August - and then took until 10 September to alert Australia's government, by sending an email to an address used by researchers and academics to alert authorities to concerns of vulnerabilities. While worrying, the timing of the incident is somewhat of a gift for Australia. A middle power that doesn't usually get as much of a platform as its influential allies, the country wants to be seen as punching above its weight on one of the most defining issues of our time - big tech regulation. In the past year alone, it has implemented the world's strictest social media ban, announced what it says are the world's strongest algorithm controls, floated the possibility of "world-leading" limits on smart glasses, and is now the first government to confront AI firms over a rogue attack on its data. The Australian prime minister says he'd had a "frank" discussion with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman about the breach It's entirely possible other governments have been the victim of rogue AI agents. Former Australian government cybersecurity adviser Alastair MacGibbon told the BBC he'd heard whispers that several others have been notified of similar recent breaches by OpenAI agents. "Some have chosen to not be public – that's every government's choice on how it wants to handle these things," the CyberCX chief strategy officer said. "The [Australian] government chose a time to release this to gain maximum publicity which is their wont to do." Revealing a data breach can of course be a risky strategy for governments - it leaves them vulnerable to criticism that their security systems aren't up to scratch. But the fact that no sensitive information was leaked put Australia in a stronger position to use the incident. "Nobody has died," says the University of Queensland's associate professor Michael Noetel, who studies AI risks. "This is another canary in the coal mine. This sort of loss-of-control incident, even though it's minor now, is what CEOs are worried about getting worse over time." Though Australia has made a name for itself by taking a stand against social media companies, taking up the AI mantle now is another way for Australia to rein in big tech, says Tama Leaver, professor of internet studies at Curtin University in Perth. "It's impossible to say for sure, but it seems incredibly likely that this was very carefully planned." All smiles in their selfie but Trump doesn't agree with the Australian prime minister's approach to AI The fact that leaders were all together in New York this week has probably helped. Albanese says he had a "frank" discussion with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman to express Australia's "extreme concern" about what happened. Altman acknowledged "issues with protocols" at OpenAI, he said. The Australian leader also posed with Donald Trump for a selfie - and the two may have had face-to-face talks. But Australia risks the ire of the US president, who wants to encourage AI, "not rein it in", and even rename it "super intelligence". Earlier this week, the Albanese had to deflect criticism from the Trump administration over his government's proposal to give users the ability to opt out of social media algorithms. The US said it amounted to "censorship of protected speech". US criticises Australia's proposed algorithm opt-out laws as 'censorship' Australia to double maximum penalty for platforms in breach of social media ban Back home, Australia's very own eSafety commission is currently arming itself with lawyers, preparing to take on social media platforms objecting to its social media law for under 16s. Australia isn't popular with big tech. But its bold policies on social media and internet safety have been largely supported among Australians themselves, especially parents. The government is taking advantage of the hack to position itself as a leader on one of the biggest talking points of our time. And it's wasting no time in using the incident to advance the country's broader crusade. Within hours of the announcement, Communications Minister Anika Wells told reporters: "This is an example of an unregulated industry where big tech clearly feels like they can do whatever they like, and that's not going to wash here in Australia." title: 'This is the final offer,' says NI secretary over £1.5bn Stormont funding package
description: Some six months have passed since the executive should have set a budget for this financial year.
body: Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant, pictured in early September The Northern Ireland Secretary of State has said the government's £1.5bn financial package for Stormont is his "final offer" and has given executive parties until next Thursday to respond. Sir Chris Bryant said there was "no more money" available and that the Northern Ireland Executive needed to agree a budget. he said he would have to consider "every eventuality" if the executive failed to reach an agreement, including the possibility of a budget being passed at Westminster. "I don't want to legislate for a budget. I want to sit down and I'll be as cooperative as I possibly can," he said. Earlier this month, Bryant made an offer of a financial package worth about £1.5bn over the next three years - that was a rise from an initial proposal of £1.1bn. But executive parties said it did not go far enough and have argued that significant gaps remain before they can agree to a deal that would allow them to set a budget. Some six months have passed since the executive should have set a budget for this financial year. Speaking to BBC Newsline, Sir Chris said he had given executive parties until noon next Thursday to come back to him with a plan for agreeing a budget for this year and the following two years. "It's my final offer. It's a good offer," he said. He added: "There is no more money. The financial situation in the UK government at the moment is very, very tight." Asked whether he was prepared to introduce a budget at Westminster if the executive did not accept the offer, Sir Chris said: "I've got to look at every eventuality. Of course I have. I've got to be responsible about this." He said he did not want to legislate for a budget and would prefer to work with executive parties to reach an agreement. "If it's impossible to set a budget through the executive, then somebody else will have to do it for them," he said. "But I'm not at that stage yet." Sir Chris also said the executive would have to consider raising additional revenue, but that it was not his job to tell ministers how to do so. He said he had not specifically raised the introduction of water charges with executive parties. Northern Ireland Executive parties had rejected an initial £1.1bn package over three years Executive parties have been in negotiations with the government in a bid to get increased funding. Finance Minister John O'Dowd previously said the current published financial pressures facing Stormont departments were around £1.6bn, adding: "So we have a bit to go." A Sinn Féin spokesperson said the "current offer from the British government falls well short of what is required to fund, transform and improve our public services". "The north receives less in funding than Wales and Scotland which if addressed would give us a transformative increase of between £1 billion and £3 billion. "People here pay their taxes and have the right to properly funded public services and our public service workers deserve proper pay settlements." The Ulster Unionist Party (UUP)'s Steve Aiken said that "calling this the final offer does not make it a fair or sufficient offer". "The UK government has moved significantly from its opening position, and that should be acknowledged. However, even with extensive savings, the annual funding on offer would barely meet the pressures in health alone. That puts the scale of the Executive's wider problem into stark perspective." He said it had been made to clear during meetings that our public services need to "deliver to our citizens the same standard of health, education, policing and other services as is available in any other postcode in our nation". The offer on the table from the government includes £450m extra for day-to-day pressures this year, as well as an additional £400m in 2027/28 and 2028/29. title: Sex offender bailed to flat near playground
description: Victims of Zapher Dogen were living close to the 32-year-old, who admitted multiple offences.
body: Zafer Dogan took photographs from his bedroom window A sex offender jailed for taking thousands of pictures of children and using AI software to "nudify" them was repeatedly allowed to return to his home overlooking the playground he targeted. It meant victims of Zafer Dogan, from Enfield in north London, were living close to the 32-year-old, who admitted multiple offences. Met Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley spoke outside Wood Green Crown Court after Dogan was jailed for two years and four months, where Sir Mark criticised the "unfathomable decisions" of the justice system. "The children should be put first, not the paedophile," he said. Speaking outside court after the sentencing hearing, Sir Mark Rowley said one family was left feeling so fearful they moved away Dogan, who works as a mechanic, previously pleaded guilty to multiple offences, including making indecent images of children. According to the police, he had taken more than 5,000 pictures, many from his bedroom window. The mother of a victim under the age of eight described feeling "helpless", adding: "Our lives will never be the same again and I can't do anything about it all because one man exploited my child." The mother of a teenage victim said it was as if she had been "punched in the gut" when police officers told her what had happened. She added: "I'm really worried that my daughter's photos are online and other paedophiles have them." Sir Mark said: "Prosecutors rightly opposed bail on multiple occasions, building on officers' clear assessments of the great risk he posed, and yet bail decisions were ultimately made that prioritised the offender's interests over the safety and the peace of mind of the victims. "A victim and their family found themselves living in close proximity to a man who had admitted targeting them. "They were so fearful, they ultimately felt forced to move to distant temporary accommodation, disrupting their lives and disrupting their children's lives, simply to escape being in the neighbourhood of the offender." He also criticised "some grossly irresponsible technology and AI companies". He said: "Dogan voyeuristically photographed children known to him before using an AI photo-editing technology to manipulate those images for his own sexual gratification. Companies must do more to prevent their platforms and tools from being used to facilitate sexual offending and harm. "Innovation cannot come at the expense of public safety, and industry has a clear responsibility to help prevent these technologies being exploited by predators. "Victims, in this case extremely young children and their families, deserve better from both the tech companies and the criminal justice system." title: Rapper Macklemore announces 'Free Palestine' tour after Ed Sheeran fallout
description: Proceeds from the tour, which begins in Dublin next month, will go to organisations supporting Palestinians, he says.
body: Macklemore performs at the Goldencoast Rap Festival in Corcelles-les-Monts, near Dijon, central-eastern France, on 30 August, 2026 Rapper Macklemore is launching a "Free Palestine" tour, days after being dropped from Ed Sheeran's Loop Tour following pro-Palestinian comments he made onstage earlier this month. "So, as you all know, my schedule freed up a bit," he said upon announcing the tour on Thursday. The American artist - whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty - said proceeds from the tour, which launches in Dublin next month, will go to organisations supporting Palestinians. Macklemore's onstage comments and subsequent removal from the tour led Sheeran's support acts to drop out, while the British singer stressed that the decision to drop the rapper was made by his promoter, not by himself. Everything we know about the Ed Sheeran and Macklemore controversy In a statement on Thursday, the rapper said that the last couple of weeks had shown him there had been "a collective awakening around Palestinian liberation, the power of billionaires that try to censor that call, and what we expect from artists right now". "What happened to me is bigger than one artist or one stage," he said. "When the billionaire class can decide which voices are allowed on stage and which ones are too dangerous to hear, everyone should be paying attention." Macklemore said he had spent the last week contacting artists who had used their platforms to stand in solidarity with the Palestinian people, regardless of the consequences. Due to how quickly the tour came together, several details were still being worked out, he added: "But this is a moment of momentum, and there is work to be done." Macklemore's new tour will begin in Dublin on 26 October followed by Paris on 29 October and London on 30 October. US dates will also be added, he said, with additional tickets going on sale next week. This video can not be played "I cannot hide how I feel anymore": Ed Sheeran addresses Macklemore row at show While performing as the opening act for Sheeran at a concert in early September in New Jersey, Macklemore said: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine." The Thrift Shop rapper then performed a song dedicated to pro-Palestinian protesters at Columbia University. After he was taken off the tour on 14 September, Macklemore accused stadium owners of rallying together to push him out. He was also accused by billionaire stadium owner Robert Kraft of hate speech and antisemitic rhetoric surrounding Israel and Gaza. Sheeran early on said that the decision to drop Macklemore from his tour was made by concert promoter Messina Touring Group. His early remarks led to all of his support acts to drop out of the tour in solidarity, and fans to express frustration. Ticket prices for the tour plummeted as well. Sheeran addressed the controversy head-on during the start of his set in Philadelphia last week. He said he had made "mistakes" handling the fallout, apologising to fans and taking a stand on the Israel-Gaza conflict, which he said was "a humanitarian issue". He described the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks as "horrific", and also called the situation in Gaza "unjustifiable and disproportionate". title: 'It has broken us as a family,' mother of poison seller victim tells hearing
description: Tanya Whitaker broke down before she spoke of how her son Samuel's death had devastated her family.
body: Danielle Cornish died after taking poison sold by Canadian Kenneth Law The mother of a British victim of poison seller Kenneth Law has said his death and the way that he died had "destroyed" their family. Tanya Whitaker broke down at the start of her video statement about the death of her son, Samuel, shown on the second day of a four-day sentencing hearing of Law in Ontario, saying: "He barely had a chance." The University of Warwick student was found collapsed outside his halls after taking poison sold by Law, who has admitted 14 counts of aiding suicide in Canada but has also been linked to nearly 80 deaths in the UK. Debbie Cornish echoed Whitaker's sentiments, telling the hearing that her family was "still fighting" to stay together years on from her daughter Danielle's death. A plea deal with Canadian authorities means Law will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths, but impact statements from their families are being read this week. "The enormity of losing a child is catastrophic," Whitaker told a Canadian court on Thursday. "Samuel was just 19 when he was handed the tools that ended his precious life." She continued: "It has broken me completely and utterly. It has broken us as a family and me as a mother. "Our son died alone at university 100 miles away from his family. We will never be able to forgive ourselves for this happening." Samuel Whitaker's mother said his death had broken her "completely and utterly" Whitaker said Samuel had been the only biological son of her husband, Paul. "He is a shell of himself today. Broken and devastated beyond repair," she added. Cornish, the mother of British victim Danielle, spoke of her anguish in a written statement, in which she referred to Law only by the initials KL. "Words on paper can't even begin to describe the painful loss of our amazing daughter," she said. "Nothing will be the same ever again as we are part of a surreal nightmare. "Nearly four years on, we are still fighting to keep our family together... not to mention the constant thoughts of how she may have died. "KL has changed the life of many many families all across the world as well as ours. We are living a constant nightmare." Authorities say Law, a former chef, sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients from 40 different countries he met in online suicide forums. Roughly a quarter of the packages were sent to the UK. He was arrested in May 2023, following a complex investigation by at least 11 law-enforcement agencies that involved investigators from around a dozen countries, including the UK, Italy and the US. Law, a former chef, sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients whom he met in online suicide forums The court also heard a statement from Faith George, the mother of Faith Ike-Elechi, who referred to her daughter by the nickname Chimma. She found her daughter helpless on the floor after she had taken the poison, and said her last works "echo in my mind every day". She said if she were able to speak to her daughter again she would tell her she had never stopped being proud of her. Maurice Dunham, father of British victim Michael Dunham, said the last time he saw his son alive was on a family holiday to Croatia that Michael had left early to return home. "The last conversation I had with him was an argument," he said in a written statement. Maurice returned home days later and discovered Michael was dead. "The feeling I had was like an electric shock going through me," he wrote. "I blamed myself for not stopping Michael from leaving the hotel room. "I planned to take my own life. I didn't care if I lived or died." Later, the court heard the words of the mother of Yeanu Mistry, who said hearing he had died was "the news every parent fears". And Maureen Cooper, the mother of poison victim Gary Cooper, called the pain of losing her son "unbearable". "A death such as this is the thing of nightmares," her written statement said. On Wednesday, the court heard from a British survivor who was given an antidote that saved her after taking poison from Law. Elisabeth Belien told the court: "I feel guilty for surviving. Although I survived, it has also impacted my loved ones. I feel like my vulnerability was exploited. I still feel a lot of shame about what happened." title: Ministers reject dog ownership licence scheme
description: A taskforce had suggested new legal requirements could help promote dog control and reduce attacks.
body: Pet owners will not have to pay a fee to own a dog, after the government ruled out introducing a licensing scheme. In a report, published on Thursday,, external a panel of animal experts suggested the government should consider new legal requirements for dog owners. The panel did not reach an agreement on which rules should be adopted but the taskforce said any new laws should aim to promote better dog control, reduce the risk of dog attacks and avoid placing an "undue burden" on owners. A spokesperson for the environment department said: "This is a welcome report and ministers are considering the taskforce's recommendations, however we will not be introducing a new dog licensing scheme." The Dog Control Coalition - which includes the RSPCA, Battersea Dogs & Cats Home and the Royal Kennel Club - said it supported the recommendations in the report and that it was "vital" for the government to take action "as a matter of urgency". A spokesperson for the coalition said: "Dog bite incidents continue to have serious consequences for people and dogs, and the time that has passed since the publication of The Middlesex Report, in 2021, makes it imperative that we now see progress." The report made 20 recommendations including calling for councils to provide a service to tackle low-level dog control issues, improved recording of dog bite wounds and legal requirements for dog walkers. Dog attacks are still rising - even after the XL bully ban What are the rules for having an XL bully dog? Dog licences explored to tackle ownership issues The Responsible Dog Ownership Taskforce was established by the government in 2022, following a series of high-profile dog attacks. The taskforce's report noted that since 2011 the dog population in the UK had grown by 35%, while hospital admissions relating to dog bites in England had risen by 77%. It said pet ownership had spiked during the Covid pandemic at a time when it was harder to access support services. "This led to less experienced owners struggling to access services and finding it harder to get help," the report said. Until 1987, dog owners in England, Wales and Scotland had to pay an annual fee to get an ownership licence. The scheme was scrapped on the grounds that the amount of money it raised was outweighed by the operating costs. Dog owners in Northern Ireland still have to buy a licence of £12.50, or £5 if the owner receives an income-related benefit. In France, owners of the most dangerous dogs have to get special permits which can involve passing a training course and putting the dog through a behavioural assessment. Switzerland previously required potential dog owners to complete a knowledge test, followed by a practical, but this condition has been scrapped. The report said that most members of the taskforce backed introducing legal requirements for dog owners but "further consideration would be needed regarding the form that this should take". "Any legal requirement would need careful consideration of its objective and not appear as a tax on already responsible dog owners. "Reintroducing a universal dog licence may amount to another database of responsible owners or an administrative exercise with little public safety benefit or opportunity to promote responsible dog ownership." It said options could include focusing a scheme on high-risk dogs, introducing background checks on owners and requiring potential owners to pass a knowledge test. The Dogs Trust and the RSPCA have commissioned research into the costs and benefits of different systems and their conclusions are due to be published later this year. In a ministerial foreword to the report, environment minister Baroness Hayman of Ullock said: "In recent years, we have seen a concerning rise in dog attacks, alongside changes in patterns of dog ownership." She said the taskforce's report was an "important and timely contribution", adding: "As ministers, we are carefully considering the recommendations alongside the wider programme of work already under way." title: Glasgow City Council to fire and rehire over 23,000 employees
description: It says redundancy notices will be withdrawn if the three unions agree to ballot their members on the pay offer.
body: Glasgow City Council faced a long-running women's campaign for equal pay Glasgow City Council is to sack more than 23,000 members of staff and then rehire them to new contracts after pay talks broke down with unions. The local authority says letters will be sent to its non-teaching staff next week, with new contracts then taking effect from 1 January. Talks earlier this week between the council and the GMB, Unison and Unite unions fell apart on Wednesday when Unison said it would not ballot its members on a proposed new pay offer. The negotiations concerned plans by the council to implement a new pay and grading system, to replace one that was found to discriminate against mostly women workers. However the move meant 11% of employees would see wages cut. The council said redundancy notices would be withdrawn if the three unions agreed to ballot their members on the pay offer. The letters of dismissal will cover every member of non-teaching staff on the council's books, including chief executive Susanne Millar, nursery staff and refuse collectors. Unions called the move a "scandalous threat" and demanded it be withdrawn. Glasgow City Council at 'critical' point over £110m budget gap Glasgow City Council approves plan to cut pay for some workers Hundreds of council workers face wages cut in end to equal pay row In a statement, the council's director of communications and corporate governance Colin Edgar claimed Unison had betrayed its own members by not balloting them. He said talks breaking down meant there was now "no agreed way forward between the council and the joint trade unions". "The council has gone as far as it can," said Edgar. "The new pay and grading scheme removes unequal pay and sees pay rise or stay the same for 90% of staff – the council's total pay bill will be substantially higher. "For those staff who are in detriment our joint trade unions negotiated an increase in pay protection from six months to 12 months. "Additionally, some trade unions are devoting energy to local consultations to mitigate the impact on those colleagues in detriment – focusing on providing specific solutions." Edgar said council officials hoped to meet with Unison earlier but the union had not attended the meeting. He added: "The offer which has been unilaterally rejected by Unison would have taken dismissals off the table and seen additional cash for those members of staff, and members of all unions, who are due back pay. "It beggars belief that they would betray their own members in this way." Unison Scotland regional organiser Mandy McDowall said: "Glasgow City Council staff are not going to be bounced into a shoddy deal by bosses trying to bully them with arbitrary deadlines. "The council's decision to dismiss workers helps nobody and Glasgow City Council risks being labelled a pariah employer if it refuses to negotiate in good faith with its staff." She added Unison would continue to work to secure a fair deal and would ballot its members on an offer once discussions had finished. Graham McNabb, an industrial officer with Unite the Union, said: "Glasgow City Council must remove direct threats to our membership in its proposed new pay and grading structure, whether it is through cuts to terms and conditions, or the scandalous threat of fire and rehire tactics. "If they go down this reckless path then it will be met with the full force of Unite." Glasgow City Council says it will fire around 23,000 workers and then rehire them At a meeting last month, the council agreed to an overhaul of its pay and grading structure after eight years of negotiations. The new system would see 63% of those affected gain financially while 11% will have their wages reduced. The highest drop in wages is expected to be around £11,500. The GMB and Unite had earlier said they secured an additional £110m into the funding package to resolve key issues affecting "the vast majority of our members". The two unions sent out a message to staff earlier warning the fire and rehire policy might be introduced, and saying the extra money was now "hanging by a thread." However Unison said this extra funding would go towards towards "assimilation and arrears", and not help the staff facing wage cuts. GMB and Unite both wanted the council to table the offer so members could make a decision. Both unions stated that if the council pursues the fire and rehire policy then they will "immediately enter into dispute to secure the improved package and halt fire and rehire". A letter to members of GMB and Unite, sent before the council announced it was implementing the policy, stated fire and re-hire would be a "self-defeating step" by the local authority. It added that such a move would "hasten a prolonged industrial dispute" between unions and the council. The letters sent to staff say their new contracts would begin the day after the old ones would end, and that continuity of service would not be affected. Glasgow City Council has been embroiled in problems over pay for years. The local authority previously paid out about £770m after it emerged female workers in roles such as catering or cleaning had for years been receiving up to £3 an hour less than those in male-dominated areas such as refuse collection. The new job evaluation scheme was designed to draw a line under the row by bringing pay scales into line with equality law, but it also meant some staff would face wage cuts, depending on what pay banding the new scheme placed them in. This is a major escalation of the row over the proposed new pay structure at Glasgow City Council. So-called "fire and rehire" tactics are always controversial. Unions often associate them with private sector companies seeking cuts - not major public sector employers. Glasgow City Council had previously said it would explore mitigations for the 11% of staff facing a pay cut. title: Spain's housing crisis in focus after eviction of 87-year-old woman
description: The tenant of the flat in the Retiro area of central Madrid, Maricarmen, was unable to pay her rent set after it was increased by an investment firm.
body: This video can not be played An 87-year-old woman has been evicted from her home in Madrid where she has lived for seven decades, in a case which has put the spotlight on Spain's soaring rents and lack of available housing. The tenant, known by her first name, Maricarmen, was removed from her flat in the Retiro area of central Madrid on Wednesday, with people taking part in a protest at her property clashing with police. Maricarman was left unable to pay her rent after investment firm Urbagestión, which bought the property in 2018, increased it from €500 (£428; $572) to €2,650 (£2,280; $3,020) - although later offering to reduce this to €1,650 (a figure she was still unable to pay on her pension of €1,350). The BBC's Guy Hedgecoe looks at why this eviction has drawn so much attention to Spain's housing crisis. Spain's housing crisis in focus after eviction of 87-year-old woman. title: Greek PM urges Burnham to return Elgin Marbles permanently
description: Andy Burnham said in 2023 the sculptures should be returned to Greece with "no strings attached".
body: The Greek prime minister has called on Andy Burnham to find the "political will" to send the Parthenon sculptures back to Greece. Kyriakos Mitsotakis wrote in the Guardian that returning the classical treasures, also known as the Elgin Marbles in the UK, would "send a powerful signal" but would require "courage". The sculptures have been on display in the British Museum since the 19th Century, though Greece has long disputed the legality of their removal. Mitsotakis and his government have previously held talks with the British Museum about the sculptures, but the two have so far failed to reach an agreement, with Greek authorities seeking their permanent return. The Greek PM used the recent fanfare generated by the loan of the Bayeux Tapestry to the British Museum to restate his country's claim to the Elgin Marbles. "Nobody would seriously contemplate cutting what survives of the tapestry in two and displaying half in London and half in Bayeux, and claiming this was an adequate way to understand it," he wrote on Thursday, external. "Yet that is exactly what happened to the Parthenon sculptures." His comments come after British Museum director Nicholas Cullinan suggested that the recent arrangement struck between the UK and France, after decades of rejected requests to borrow the medieval embroidery, offered hope of a deal with Greece over the Elgin Marbles. Mitsotakis said he was "surprised at the recent suggestion from the museum that the Bayeux Tapestry loan might provide a template for an agreement over the Parthenon sculptures", adding: "I do not believe it does." "Greece cannot accept any arrangement that would require it to recognise the British Museum's ownership of the sculptures, or a scheme that would mean we 'borrow' parts of our own monument," he wrote. Instead, he urged Burnham to stand by his previous comments on the sculptures and find a way of returning them for good. This would be a "decisive step", Mitsotakis said, that would "reunite the sculptures and transform a historic dispute into a unique act of cultural friendship". Back in 2023, several years before he returned to government and became prime minister, Burnham said the sculptures should be returned to Greece with "no strings attached". For years, he supported a change in the law to allow for this. But last month, he told the Financial Times that "ultimately it's an issue for the British Museum", adding that "legally that's where that issue rests". Many of the Elgin Marbles originate from the Parthenon in Athens British ambassador Lord Elgin was granted permission by the Ottoman Empire, the governing authority in Athens at the time, to remove some of the marble statues in the early 19th Century. They were created between 447BC and 432BC to decorate the Temple of Athena - what is now known as the Parthenon, in the Acropolis in Athens. After an 1816 parliamentary select committee deemed Elgin's actions legal, the sculptures entered the British Museum collection by an act of Parliament. The Greeks dispute their removal was lawful and the demands to return the statues have been vocal. The Parthenon gallery in the Acropolis Museum in the Greek capital was deliberately designed with spaces left for the sculptures in the British Museum. Back in 2023, George Osborne, then the museum chair, told the BBC he was looking for a "more co-operative arrangement" after "quite a bitter disagreement" with the Greeks for more than 200 years. Mitsotakis's latest comments appear to suggest a ramping up of rhetoric around the thorny issue once again. Last month, Greece's health minister told Breitbart News he would like to see US President Donald Trump pressure the British to return the Parthenon pieces. The British Museum's position - and that of the UK government - is that the law prevents the permanent return of items held in its collection, though loan agreements are common. Campaigners point out that the British Museum Act could be amended. However, the UK government has not signalled that this is a priority. Elgin Marbles: What are the Parthenon Sculptures? title: Hundreds attend Jacob Elordi lookalike competition
description: The contest, organised by a group from the University of Bristol, included an Australian accent round.
body: This video can not be played Hundreds of people turned out to watch a Jacob Elordi lookalike contest which saw youngsters don their finest tote bags and slouchy sweatshirts. The event, which took place on College Green, was organised by Overheard at UoB - a social media community dedicated to life at the University of Bristol. Acclaimed Australian actor Elordi is best known for his roles in The Kissing Booth, Saltburn, Frankenstein, Wuthering Heights, Priscilla and the HBO series Euphoria. Despite some worthy competitors performing their best catwalk struts and Australian accents, the title was awarded to a 17-year-old girl who did not want to be named. Joey Lush said he trawled through Pinterest for "stylish" outfit inspiration An estimated 500 people showed up to watch the contest unfold. Jamie Crook, who recently moved to the city from Oxford, said he was shocked at the large turnout and "had jelly legs the whole time". He said: "I loved it, it was so fun. I'm still kind of shaking now. "I think it's a really good way to make friends and get to know people. "I feel like one of the most famous blokes in Bristol for a day, which is an experience." NHS staff investigated over access to dead teenager's medical records Mayor believes mass transit system is coming Hovis workers pause strike after fresh pay deal The veterinary medicine student even took the time to thank his doppelganger directly, acknowledging the boost to his street cred. "For the better half of seven years, since the Kissing Booth came out, Jacob Elordi has carried my dating career," he laughed. "Also, shout out to my barber. "Every time he cuts my hair I show him a picture of Jacob Elordi and he just sorts it out. "You've got to go with what works." Lookalike Jamie Crook thanked the Australian actor for boosting his dating life Crook explained the accent round was his downfall. He blamed his croaky impersonation on a lingering "fresher's flu". Joey Lush secured second place in the competition after trawling through Pinterest for outfit inspiration and "grabbing a tote bag from the fresher's fair". He said: "He's a very stylish guy, so I tried my best. "I did not realise what I was signing up for - I was a bit nervous going up." Jacob Elordi is a 29-year-old actor who has starred in leading Hollywood roles But Lush accepted the loss graciously. "The winner did an amazing job," he said. "I'm so okay with it, I lost fair and square. "I saw her in the line and she was the only one I wouldn't have been... hurt about losing to. "She was very much a clear winner. "I think it was her moustache that sold it." Follow BBC Bristol on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to us on email or via WhatsApp on 0800 313 4630. title: BBC Inside Science
description: How do we measure time accurately and why is the rotation of the Earth causing problems?
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations Radio 4,·24 Sep 2026,·28 mins In October members of the General Conference on Weights and Measurements are voting to change how we keep time on Earth accurate. Currently an additional second, known as a Leap Second, can be added to make sure modern atomic clocks stay in sync with solar time. However, all of this might be about to change as the rotation of the Earth speeds up and interferes with our measurements. Tom takes a trip to meet Principal Scientist Setnam Shemar at the National Physics Laboratory to learn how our time lords keep us all on schedule. Plus, Associate Professor Claire Nichols from Oxford University helps us understand why the Earth's rotation puts our timekeeping in jeopardy. Also on the show, Professor of Mathematical Biology Kit Yates has scoured the news to bring us two of the hottest science stories this week. We find out how scientists can tell the body temperature of the Tyrannosaurus rex from fossils, and whether the record has been broken for the warmest temperature complex life – eukariotic cells – can tolerate on Earth. Our coverage of the Royal Society Trivedi book prize is also heating up as the winner is announced next week. Ahead of the ceremony author, former winner and judge Bill Bryson shares with Tom why he holds the prize in such affection. We also hear from shortlisted author Lise Barnéoud whose book, Hidden Guests, uncovers the surprising science of microchimerism and how some of your cells are not your own. To discover more fascinating science content, head to bbc.co.uk, search for BBC Inside Science and follow the links to The Open University. title: Man jailed for two years over throwing bottle at Portsmouth migrant protest
description: Del Somerville, 42, pleaded guilty to violent disorder following an overnight protest at Eastney.
body: Del Somerville was described as a "thug" by the judge A father-of-two has become the first man jailed following an anti-migrant protest in Portsmouth after admitting throwing a plastic bottle and swearing at police. Del Somerville, 42, was given a two-year sentence after previously pleading guilty to violent disorder at the city's crown court following the overnight protest near Eastney Marina on 6 September. Hundreds of protesters gathered after a boat carrying about 120 migrants was brought ashore near Eastney Beach. He pleaded not guilty to a separate charge of assaulting a police officer, relating to an incident on 11 September, and will face trial at Portsmouth Magistrates Court at a later date. Protesters gathered near police lines at Eastney Beach in Portsmouth on 6 September Judge Daniel Sawyer told Somerville that his sentence would act as a deterrent to others following subsequent protests in the area. Describing him as a "thug", he told the defendant: "Police officers dedicate their lives to the protection of the public regardless of their own views, the very least they can expect is that those who engage in protests treat them with respect and the courts punish those who assault them." The court heard Sommerville, from Portsmouth, was among a large group of demonstrators protesting at the arrival of the migrants. They were brought ashore by the RNLI after being picked up in the Channel. A number of volunteer lifeboat crew members were subject to online abuse following the incident. Prosecutor Edward Warren said Somerville was part of an "initially peaceful and lawful" gathering of a number of people on Ferry Road. At shortly before 23:30 BST, he was with a large group of men as they were held up by the police line. The court was told he was identified in police body-worn video as throwing a small bottle and swearing at police. When later interviewed by police, he said he had found the bottle on the ground and was going to throw it into a nearby bush, but was angry and so threw it up into the air. Defence barrister Helen Easterbrook said Somerville had been "caught up" in the disturbances. She said he had been attempting to be a "calming influence" on the crowd but had thrown the bottle "in frustration". Four other men are awaiting sentence having also been charged with violent disorder following the protest in Eastney. title: Activists found guilty of theft of King's lambs
description: They believed the King "would have consented to their rescue" due to being an "environmentalist".
body: (Left to right) Rosa Sharkey, Sarah Foy and Rose Patterson, pictured outside Norwich Crown Court, had denied stealing the lambs Three animal rights activists have been found guilty of stealing three lambs from the King's Sandringham Estate. Throughout a three-day trial, Rosa Sharkey, 26, Sarah Foy, 26, and Rose Patterson, 37, insisted they rescued the animals in 2023. The members of campaign group Animal Rising also said they believed the King "would have consented to their rescue" due to being an "environmentalist". But the jury of five men and seven women at Norwich Crown Court unanimously found all three guilty of theft. They were each sentenced to a 12-month community order of 150 hours of unpaid work, and they must each pay £250 towards prosecution costs. Sentencing them, judge Anthony Bate said their actions highlighted "sensitive and important matters of public interest". He added that the defendants were all "intelligent and capable women who can make a valuable contribution to society". After the hearing, Patterson, director of Animal Rising, said: "We are of course disappointed by the verdict today, but it doesn't change how I feel about rescuing Sammy, Sunny and Sooty." The three activists posed for a photo with the animals The theft took place on 23 May 2023, when the trio spent hours in a field at Appleton Farm in Sandringham, to allow the sheep to become acquainted to them. The court heard they then took three lambs and put them into a van after they came close, and they were driven off to an unknown animal sanctuary. The following day, the women travelled to Windsor Castle, where they attempted to alert authorities to what they called a "rescue" of the lambs. They later handed themselves in to Windsor Police Station and were charged with theft. Videos of the trio taking the lambs were shared on social media Earlier in the hearing on Thursday, defence barrister Sarah-Jane Ewart, representing Sharkey, insisted the trio had acted "honestly" throughout. She highlighted their attempt to alert the authorities at Windsor as an example. In the trial, all three defendants detailed how their personal experiences had led them to become involved in animal rights activism, due to concerns about welfare and the environmental impact of agriculture. The lambs have never been recovered by the authorities but remained alive and well at an unknown sanctuary, the court heard. After the verdict, Patterson said the trio "rescued them because we believed they deserved the chance of a long life", adding: "I don't regret for a moment giving them that chance." Sharkey added: "This isn't the verdict we hoped for, but the most important thing to me is that those three lambs were saved and are now living safely and happily." The three defendants were Foy, of North Street, Alfreton, Derbyshire; Patterson, of Homerton High Street, London; and Sharkey, previously of Mayville Estate, London, but she told the court she now lived in Brighton. title: Gavin and Stacey stars join Ruth Jones for 60th birthday party at social club
description: The party took place at the Porthcawl and Kenfig Hill RAFA Club where her parents were members.
body: Gavin and Stacey co-stars joined Jones at the event Gavin and Stacey's Ruth Jones has celebrated her 60th birthday at a social club with co-stars including James Corden and Rob Brydon. The party took place at the Porthcawl and Kenfig Hill RAFA (Royal Air Force Association) Club on Saturday where her parents were members for several years. Corden, who co-wrote the series and played Smithy - the love interest of Jones' Nessa - helped behind the bar pouring beers, while Jones reconnected with Brydon to sing country classic Islands in the Stream on stage. Sarah Prescott, the club's steward, described the evening as "overwhelming and unbelievable", thanking Jones for choosing the club to host the event. James Corden spent some of the evening serving pints behind the bar The private celebration was also attended by cast members Melanie Walters and Alison Steadman, as well as Steve Speirs, a close collaborator of Jones'. "We didn't realise how big of an event it was until the actual night when they were all coming through the door," Prescott said. "It was quite overwhelming and unbelievable," she said, adding it had been kept private and required careful planning. Prescott said Jones chose the venue because of its strong connection to her family, with both her parents long-standing members. "She used to come here as a child and had her first guitar lesson at the RAFA club, so she does hold the club dearly," she said. Rob Brydon celebrated with Jones and staff The evening also saw Jones and Corden reunited for a rendition of Islands In the Stream, a duet they did on the show, while Corden performed Me and Mrs Jones by Billy Paul. "They were all so lovely and just like normal people really," Prescott said. "She had everything she wanted. She even wanted curry and chips." Prescott also said staff had reported an increase in new booking enquiries since the event. "I think it's definitely put the RAFA back on the map," she said. She also received a message from Jones' team saying the actress was "utterly delighted" and the party was "better than she could have ever imagined". title: Apple Day called off after poor harvest
description: It is the first time the event has been cancelled in 24 years.
body: Head gardener, Simon Tetlow, said the difficulties faced this year demonstrated the pressures on sustainable fruit growing Tatton Park's annual Apple Day has been cancelled for the first time in 24 years after extreme weather and increased pest activity left organisers short of fruit to share with visitors. The event in Cheshire will not take place this October following a significantly reduced harvest from the estate's collection of about 300 apple and pear trees. Head gardener Simon Tetlow said prolonged summer drought had created one of the most challenging growing seasons the team had experienced. He said the cancellation highlighted the challenges climate change posed for sustainable fruit growing. Apple Day celebrates the gardens' orchard collection and is a popular fixture in the park's calendar Head gardener Simon Tetlow said: "For 24 years, our orchards have provided the centrepiece for a fantastic tasting day to celebrate the start of autumn, but this year a combination of prolonged drought and unprecedented pest pressures has left us without enough fruit to share with visitors." He said the gardening team was already adapting what crops were grown, where they were planted and cultivation methods to improve resilience in future seasons. Organisers said they hoped Apple Day would return in 2027. title: Watch: Why has Trump been so eager to welcome Xi?
description: President Donald Trump has been talking about Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit for months, the BBC's Sarah Smith looks at why.
body: This video can not be played US President Donald Trump has been talking for months about Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington DC. He's spruced up the White House, lamented that his new ballroom won't be finished in time and ensured a new marble helipad is ready to show off to the Chinese leader. Trump gave Xi a warm welcome on his arrival at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, complete with a military flyover and a 100ft (30m) red carpet. The BBC's North America Editor Sarah Smith explains how Trump has long made no secret of his admiration for strongman leaders around the world. Here's why Trump's been so keen on Xi's visit. title: Small boat migrant arrivals reach 781 in one day, breaking 2026 record
description: A total of 781 migrants arrive on Wednesday, but the yearly total is below the same point in 2025.
body: The Home Office said 10 migrant boats arrived on Wednesday A total of 781 migrants arrived in 10 small boats on Wednesday, the highest number for a single day so far this year, Home Office figures show. So far this year 18,565 people have made the Channel crossing, which is 42% lower than the same period in 2025 when 32,188 had crossed in small boats. The government said its "progress this year in tackling small boats is indisputable" but it needed to "push further and harder in order to eradicate this vile trade". French authorities reported on Thursday that a man had died after having a cardiac arrest while people attempted to board a vessel at a beach south of Boulogne-sur-Mer. Wednesday's figures include a dinghy carrying 51 people which departed from Normandy, much further west than small boats typically set off, on Monday morning and spent more than 33 hours at sea. About 150 people crossed from France in three small boats on both Monday and Tuesday. This followed five days with no crossings at all. Wednesday's figure was the highest daily total since 803 people arrived on 20 December 2025. The highest total in one day in recent years was on 3 September 2022, when 1,305 migrants made the crossing. Between 1 January and 23 September 2026, a total of 18,565 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 42% on the same period the previous year. These crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020. Nearly all those who arrive by small boat claim asylum. Under international law, this means they are allowed to stay in the country while their asylum application is considered. Small boat arrivals made up 40% of asylum applications between July 2025 to June 2026. Boats that arrived in the UK from 24 September 2025 to 23 September 2026 carried an average of 67 people. This has more than doubled since 2021. Experts say overcrowding in boats makes crossings riskier. At least 84 people died while attempting to cross the Channel in 2024, according to the United Nations (UN). When looking at the scale of small boats crossings, the number of these arrivals is about 5% of the size of total immigration into the UK from January 2025 to December 2025. The government has pledged to “smash the gangs” behind these crossings in order to reduce the numbers. People from Eritrea accounted for 18% of all arrivals from July 2025 to June 2026. In the latest figures covering January 2025 to December 2025, at least 2,335 people who arrived by small boat were found to be potential victims of human trafficking or other forms of modern slavery, according to the Home Office. Another 4,712 people were detected entering the UK without permission via other methods including hiding in vehicles, travelling on ferries or through airports from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 17% on the same period the previous year. There are also individuals who arrive legally, for example via a work or study visa, and then overstay their limit. The total number of people who live in the UK illegally after arriving legally is not known. Crossings are more common during warmer weather and when there are calmer sea conditions, with the highest monthly totals typically between June and September. The English Channel is one of the most dangerous and busiest shipping lanes in the world. Labour Party deputy leader Lucy Powell said earlier that the government had "significantly reduced" the number of people arriving on small boat crossings after "a huge amount of work". "If we had a switch that we could switch tomorrow to stop all small boats we would switch it," she told BBC Radio Kent. She said the government was taking steps to reduce the number of people arriving on small boats, including providing extra resources and new legislation. Cabinet minister Lucy Powell said there was no "switch" to stop small boat crossings "I know that people want this to happen faster," Powell told the BBC. "We are taking those steps, it is working." Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said: "Keir Starmer's pledge to 'smash the gangs' was always a farce and open-borders Burnham has learnt absolutely nothing from his predecessor. "The only way to stop the crossings is to deport all illegal immigrants on arrival, and only the Conservatives have a plan to do that." Liberal Democrats home affairs spokesman Max Wilkinson said the government should "tackle the root cause by entering the EU's landmark migration and asylum pact". Until they did so, he said, people smugglers would "continue to find a way through, lives will be put at risk and taxpayers' money will be wasted". Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said his party would "deploy the Royal Navy and stop the boats". On Tuesday Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood ordered officials to conduct a review after two migrant vessels in as many days made it ashore near Folkestone undetected. Small boat passengers are usually brought to shore by Border Force officials or on rescue boats and uncontrolled arrivals are rare. Mahmood said the beach landings were "not acceptable". The landing on Monday was the first in more than a year and only four have been recorded since the Home Office began keeping data in 2023. title: Firm fined £1m after man killed by window that fell from luxury penthouse
description: Mick Ferris was crushed when the 130kg window fell from The Corniche building in Vauxhall.
body: Mick Ferris was a coach driver for Clarkes of London, and had been returning to his coach when the window pane fell A property developer has been fined £1m after a window fell from a luxury riverside penthouse in south London and killed a coach driver. Mick Ferris, 53, was crushed when the pane of glass weighing 130kg (20 stone) fell 26 storeys from The Corniche in Vauxhall on 2 October 2018. His wife Rachel Ferris told the sentencing hearing at Inner London Crown Court that her husband's death "could have been prevented", after it emerged that a window fell from the same development in August 2017, but the design was not substantially changed as a result. Mitigating for the developer St James Group Ltd, Prashant Popat KC said his client was "deeply remorseful and regretful". Luxury flats at The Corniche, on Albert Embankment, have previously been listed for sale at £3m The father-of-two was hit by the falling glass as he returned to his coach on central London's Albert Embankment that morning. Specialist façade contractor Lindner Prater was also fined £300,000, after it and St James were found guilty of ignoring "foreseeable risks". Luxury architecture firm Foster + Partners and engineering consultants Wintech Ltd were cleared of the same charge. Judge Boyle said St James should have been more robust in "ensuring the critical safety component" of the window was "present and engaged". He added that Lindner Prater "should have done more to complete and document the risk assessment process". In addition to the fine, Judge Boyle ordered St James and Lindner Prater to pay costs of £125,000 each. The window panel was roughly 85 x 190cm (2.7ft x 6ft) and weighed 130 kg (20 stone) Ferris said her husband's death was "so sudden" and "out of the blue". In a statement read out in court, she said: "If somebody had done something differently – anything – it would have changed our lives. We wouldn't be in this position. "I know it wasn't just one person, but one person could have changed this. "What those companies did killed my husband. "The thought this could have happened to anybody is always with me. It could have been a child." She also told the court that 400 people attended her husband's funeral, and said "he is missed by so many it was unbelievable". At the time of the incident, television host and fellow West Ham fan James Corden paid tribute to Mick Ferris on Twitter, saying: "He was a huge West Ham fan and has passed away in the most sudden of circumstances." He added: "Tell your loved ones you love them today." HSE principal inspector James Goldfinch said: "The fact lessons had not been learnt from a near miss the year before makes what happened on that day all the more galling. "For a window to fall once was quite extraordinary, for it to fall again was simply criminal." title: White House 'repeatedly violated' court order to restore press access, say media outlets
description: Lawyers for CNN, Politico and MS Now are seeking an emergency court hearing, saying the White House "repeatedly violated" the order.
body: CNN White House reporter Betsy Klein was reportedly denied access on Thursday Three US media outlets have requested an emergency court hearing, accusing the White House of having "repeatedly violated" a judge's order to restore their access in a stand-off with President Donald Trump. Employees from CNN, Politico and MS Now reported being denied entry on Thursday morning, with some having their credentials confiscated, while others were granted access. Judge Timothy Kelly ruled in the early hours of Thursday that Trump's ban on the outlets should be temporarily lifted because it "likely violated their constitutional due process rights". Trump initially said he banned the outlets because of "fake news". The White House later cited national security. It was unclear whether the refusal to admit some reporters on Thursday morning was because of an administrative lag as the White House potentially worked to comply with the judge's order. The standoff was expected to impact TV coverage as Trump welcomes Chinese President Xi Jinping to the White House on Thursday morning ahead of a state dinner. CNN said some of their journalists had been denied entry, including senior White House reporter Betsy Klein. But a producer was allowed to enter, the outlet reported. Politico said one of its reporters was denied access to the White House and had his press credentials confiscated. MS NOW reported that its White House reporter Laura Barrón-López and a producer were barred and had their passes taken, but another MS NOW producer was allowed in. The White House is yet to comment on the ruling, and lawyers acting for the president may take further legal action. title: German prosecutors investigate 105-year-old for crimes at Nazi PoW camp
description: The suspect is alleged to have been an accessory to murder at the Stalag 326 camp, where tens of thousands of Soviet PoWs died.
body: Thirty thousand Russian prisoners of war are buried at Stalag 326 in Senne German prosecutors are investigating a man aged 105 over allegations that he was an accessory to multiple counts of murder at a Nazi prisoner of war camp in World War Two. The suspect is alleged to have been a camp guard at Stalag 326 VI K in Senne in northwestern Germany. A similar case had also been under way involving a second former camp guard at Senne, Dortmund public prosecutor Sonja Frodermann said in a statement. That suspect died a few months ago at the age of 99, she said. No further details about the two former guards have been made public, however the two cases highlight the difficulties faced by prosecutors who continue to investigate Nazi-era crimes, with most of the remaining suspects already dead. More than 5.3 million soldiers from the Soviet Red Army were held in German captivity during World War Two and half are thought to have died. Many of those who did survive were treated as traitors on their return home. But the PoW camp, or Stalag, at Senne was one of the biggest. One in three Soviet PoWs entering Nazi Germany between 1941 and 1945 went through the complex at Senne, according to the memorial site, and they often ended up doing forced labour in the wider region. Living conditions at Stalag were horrific, and prisoners faced appalling mistreatment and malnutrition. Of the 180,000-200,000 Soviet prisoners of war registered there, many died and tens of thousands are buried there. PoWs from France, Poland, Serbia and Belgium were also held at Senne. More than 9,000 Russian prisoners of war were alive in the camp at the time of liberation in 1945 The prosecutor made clear the investigation surrounding the 105-year-old was still under way and that the allegations of being an accessory to multiple murders related to his activities at Stalag 36. There has been no statute of limitations in Germany for either murder or accessory to murder since 1979, to enable the prosecution of Nazi-era crimes. Another centenarian camp guard from the Hemer Stalag VI A camp is also said to be under investigation. However, bringing perpetrators to justice more than 80 years after the war is now fraught with difficulty. Four years ago a 101-year-old concentration camp guard was given a five-year jail term for complicity in murder at Sachsenhausen. Josef Schütz was the oldest Nazi criminal ever brought to justice. He never served time in jail and died in 2023 while appealing his sentence. A former Nazi concentration camp secretary was convicted in 2022 of abetting murder and given a suspended jail term. She died last year aged 99. Although prosecution of Nazi crimes is handled by the public prosecutors in the western city of Dortmund, cases are initially taken on by the central office for Nazi crime investigations in Ludwigsburg in the south-west. title: Drinking at football matches - would fans welcome it?
description: Andy Burnham has long championed a repeal of the ban which prevents football supporters from drinking alcohol in the view of the pitch. But do fans even want it?
body: The law permits supporters at stadiums from the Premier League to National League to drink alcohol outside the ground and in concourses, but not in their seats When UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham embarked on his trip to the United Nations in New York, he might not have been expecting a question about football fans drinking alcohol in grounds. Burnham firmly believes the law that prevents supporters from having a beer at their seat during a match is outdated. It's a position the Everton supporter has long held, and when asked was happy to reaffirm. "I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination," said Burnham, who feels football fans are singled out compared to those of other sports and events. There is no suggestion this is about to become official government policy, and last year MPs rejected a Conservative amendment to the Football Governance Bill that would have forced ministers to launch a formal consultation on scrapping the rule. That was, of course, before Burnham returned to Downing Street. It is a complicated and divisive issue, about not just safety. But is it something that match-going supporters actually want? Drinking alcohol at football grounds in England and Wales has been strictly controlled since the Sporting Events Control of Alcohol Act was introduced in 1985. It was brought in to counter escalating hooliganism through the 1970s and into the 1980s. The ban impacts clubs in the Premier League down to the National League. While beer can be sold, it must be consumed in areas that do not have a view of the pitch. Yet fans who support teams in the National League North and South and below can drink alcohol around the pitch. The ban is more strict in Scotland, with a law in place since 1981 that alcohol is only available in hospitality areas and not for other fans. It was initially imposed following a riot during the 1980 Scottish Cup final between Rangers and Celtic at Hampden. However, attitudes have been changing in recent seasons. It was lifted as part of a pilot scheme last year, with several Scottish clubs selling alcohol in clearly defined, monitored areas of the stadiums. It started with lower-level clubs, eventually being extended to the Premiership. The Scotland national team joined the trial for the friendlies against Japan and Curacao earlier this year. It has been extended to games against Switzerland on 29 September and Slovenia next month. The Women's Super League in England has just completed two seasons of successful trials and the rule preventing drinking in the stands has now been removed by the league's governing company, WSL Football. The women's game is not governed by the Sporting Events Control of Alcohol Act, enabling the competition organiser to make the change. Is there support for the move within English football's corridors of power? Premier League chief executive Richard Masters said in August the competition had not "got a specific view" and "we'd need to give it some really careful thought". The English Football League, however, issued a statement on Thursday that said it would be "receptive to discussions around reviewing the current legislation". It added member clubs had already provided "a mandate to lobby for appropriate reform" which had "not kept pace with significant developments in stadium management, safety and stewarding". This video can not be played Should alcohol be allowed in football stands? The Football Supporters' Association has for some time backed changing the law. Like the prime minister, it considers it to be unfair on football fans. "I think it is outdated," FSA chairman Tom Greatrex told the BBC Radio 4 Today programme. "If you go to watch football in Germany or in other places around the world, then it's perfectly acceptable. "It is civilised and appropriate. There's no reason why that shouldn't be the case for football fans, as it is for fans of rugby league, watching Oasis, or anything else that happens often in the same stadiums in the same seats." The FSA's position is that clubs should have the choice, in consultation with supporters, to sell alcohol. Clubs might want to offer it in all stands, others in designated areas, while a few might choose not to do so at all. Other sports offer designated alcohol-free sections, something that football clubs may wish to copy for some families and supporters who do not consume alcohol because of their religion. The FSA acknowledges this, but believes having the option to make such decisions is important. It believes relaxing the law would be more popular the further down the leagues you go, where alcohol sales could potentially provide a crucial additional income stream. The UK Football Policing Unit rejected the suggestion, arguing alcohol plays "a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour" and that "other sports simply don't see the violence and criminal behaviour" that football does. Yet for Greatrex, there is already proof police are not open to ideas through their previous opposition to safe standing. Before it was introduced four years ago, Mark Roberts, who has been the national lead for football policing since 2014, told the BBC it would make it "easier to throw missiles, engage in hate chanting, racism, sneak alcohol in, take cocaine". "[The police] were telling everybody that we couldn't have standing at football again, that it would jeopardise safety, " Greatrex said. "Actually, what we saw then was a controlled, managed pilot projects to get that re-established. "There hasn't been the level of disorder that some of the police sources were saying there would be. I think the police should have more of an open mind and engage in this in a sensible and mature way." Scottish football has slowly started to relax the ban of alcohol sales at matches but fans continue to protest for this to move at a faster pace.
