title: Why did an OpenAI system hack Australia's health system - and can it be stopped in the future?
description: News that an automated AI agent hacked a government IT system raises big questions about regulating the tech.
body: This video can not be played Watch: What you need to know about the OpenAI Australian government hack An OpenAI agent has gone "rogue" and "infiltrated" an Australian government website in what cyber-security experts are calling the first hack of its kind. But why did it take the government months to discover what happened - and could it happen again? The hack was carried out by an AI agent - an autonomous computer program that uses AI to complete a task with minimal human oversight. On 18 June one of OpenAI's agents went rogue during a test exercise - the company has said it was supposed to "look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation". In the process it "infiltrated" a private statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said. OpenAI said it only realised the breach had happened at all in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity", and the company sent an email to a generic Australian government inbox some weeks later. That email seems to have gone unnoticed for five days before it was escalated to Australia's cyber-security experts on 10 September. The prime minister described the breach as "obviously unacceptable" and said OpenAI took "way too long" to inform Australian officials. Analysts have also raised concerns over OpenAI's almost three-month delay in noticing and reporting the breach via email. "The way the notice arrived bothers me as much as the delay," chief data and AI officer Simon Liu from cyber-security firm TrustDecision told the BBC. OpenAI is the company behind the popular ChatGPT servie Australia has said this incident is the first of its kind, and experts agree it might be. As far as we know, hacks carried out by AI agents are still quite rare occurrences - but then again, it is largely up to companies themselves to disclose them. Hacks like this have happened before. In July, OpenAI agents went rogue during a test and infiltrated tech start-up Hugging Face's internal systems. The AI agents decided that ignoring the limits on what should be done to achieve their goal was the best course of action. This is what the industry calls "misalignment" - broadly defined as when AI machines do not act in humanity's best interests, such as by bending the rules. It is a problem that is fundamental to making AI safe, and it is proving challenging. To put it simply, the type of AI models at play here - known as large language models - are designed to predict the likeliest output to a given input, rather than consider the consequences of that output as a human would. Companies attempt to prevent negative consequences by placing "guardrails" on the AI but, as the Australian government found out, that is not always enough. Dr Hammond Pearce, senior lecturer at the University of New South Wales Institute for Cyber Security, told the BBC this sort of hack would likely "grow in severity and in frequency", adding: "I do hope that this incident does start ringing alarm bells in governments around the world." Niusha Shafiabady, professor of computational intelligence at the Australian Catholic University, said this incident had shown the need to "judge autonomous AI by its behaviour under pressure, not by the promises in a product launch". "The deeper technical risk is that autonomous AI does not always know when it is wrong, and humans may not be able to see why it made a decision," she said. "Without strong verification and hard boundaries, probabilistic errors can quietly become operational failures." The explosive rise of AI has left governments scrambling to put protective measures in place, with some calling for companies to be forced to build ways to disable their own tech into its systems. One idea backed by some AI firms and lawmakers is a "kill switch" - a way to simply to turn the tech off in a crisis. OpenAI is reportedly, external already working to build automated tools which can shut down its systems if needed. Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, former deputy prime minister and Facebook executive Sir Nick Clegg said the kill switch remains an unproven idea. "There isn't a room with a little fuse box [where] you just pull out the fuse and everything winds down," he said, with AI tools underpinned by global infrastructure. Cyber-security experts said the systems protecting Australia's Medicare were just not strong enough, and a skilled human hacker could have got around them. But other experts say that is not the point - and that this was the latest case of AI agents ignoring laws around how to safely access online information, and perhaps the most serious yet given the information was under government control. Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they? How to stop AI agents going rogue As warnings mount about the potentially devastating impact of AI, many in the industry and in governments around the world are openly wondering about what national and international regulations might be needed to keep it in check. Meanwhile some scientists, experts and workers have dismissed the bleak projections as vague, hypothetical, or an effort by large AI developers to ensure their dominance. As it stands, AI companies largely regulate themselves - but this week, 20 nations, including Australia and Canada, signed a joint statement calling for better safeguards, globally consistent standards, and an international regulator off the back of these concerns. However, the US and China, two nations at the forefront of AI development, have so far resisted calls for greater regulation, raising questions over whether this hack will be the first of many, or the wake up call many experts want it to be. "The immediate harm here appears limited, but the governance lesson is not," says Dr Raffaele Fabio Ciriello, senior lecturer in business information systems at t

title: Is this really the Premier League's 'Bermuda Triangle'?
description: Do the stats back the social media meme that Bournemouth, Brighton and Brentford form a Premier League 'Bermuda Triangle' where teams lose points?
body: How do Brentford, Brighton and Bournemouth fare against the 'big six'? It's the place where points are lost and never to be seen again, according to a popular social media meme. Draw a line from Brighton to Bournemouth to Brentford and back down to Brighton again and you will have formed the Premier League's very own "Bermuda Triangle". Those three clubs have developed a reputation for taking points off the traditional Big Six - Arsenal, Chelsea, Liverpool, Manchester City, Manchester United and Tottenham. Recent results have only fuelled the narrative and helped to push the tongue-in-cheek theory. On Friday night, Brentford beat Chelsea 3-0. Less than 24 hours later, Brighton outclassed champions Arsenal, albeit by the same scoreline - though it was a victory that could arguably have been even more emphatic had David Raya not produced a couple of smart saves. Bournemouth, meanwhile, pushed Liverpool all the way before falling to a gritty 1-0 defeat, with Alisson forced into a brilliant recovery stop to deny the Cherries an early opener. Those are the sort of performances that stick in supporters' minds and help explain why the theory has taken hold. Since the start of the 2024-25 season, Brighton have been the best-performing non-traditional Big Six side against Arsenal, Chelsea, Liverpool, Man City, Manchester United and Spurs, taking 42 points from 26 games - an average of 1.62 points per match. The Cherries are not far behind, collecting 35 points from 26 matches, or 1.35 points per game. Brentford, however, have taken 22 points from 26 matches, averaging 0.85 points per game. Newcastle (1.46), Nottingham Forest (1.46) and Aston Villa (1.38) have all matched or outperformed the Bees against the traditional Big Six over the same period. In other words, the clubs most commonly grouped together by the meme have produced very different levels of success against elite opposition. Brighton and Bournemouth have consistently taken points off the Premier League's heavyweights. Brentford's record is less convincing. In fact, the Opta data suggests Brighton are the main reason the theory has gained such traction. Since Fabian Hurzeler took charge, only Kenny Dalglish's Blackburn have recorded a better points-per-game return against the traditional Big Six among managers of non-Big-Six clubs with at least 10 matches. The popularity of the Bermuda Triangle idea may say as much about perception as results. When it comes to recruitment and spending, Bournemouth, Brighton and Brentford operate in a different world to the Premier League's biggest clubs. They cannot simply outspend Arsenal, Liverpool or Manchester City. That makes their victories more memorable. Upsets also tend to linger longer in the memory because they fit a familiar story: well-run clubs outperforming opponents with significantly greater resources. The meme is not entirely without foundation, although the evidence is considerably stronger for Brighton and Bournemouth than it is for Brentford. Brentford's overall record is weaker, although a series of eye-catching victories under Thomas Frank and now Keith Andrews have helped cement their reputation as a difficult opponent for elite clubs. And the start to this season has helped: their Chelsea success added to by an opening day 3-0 rout of Spurs. But the numbers do not support a three-club phenomenon quite as clearly as social media might suggest. If there is a Premier League Bermuda Triangle, Brighton sit firmly at its centre. The Seagulls' record against the traditional Big Six is not merely impressive by modern standards. According to Opta, it is one of the best any non-Big-Six club has produced in the Premier League era. The only catch is that the evidence points less to a triangle and more to one standout club, with Bournemouth providing strong support and Brentford helping to supply some of the moments that keep the theory alive. title: Russell fastest from Antonelli in Baku practice
description: Mercedes driver George Russell heads both practice sessions at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.
body: George Russell's most recent grand prix victory was in Austria in June Mercedes driver George Russell headed both practice sessions at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix. The Briton led team-mate Kimi Antonelli by 0.552 seconds in the second session. Red Bull's Max Verstappen was Russell's closest rival in the first session, when Antonelli suffered a hydraulic failure. Antonelli's reliability problems also meant he missed the first half of the second session, and overall the Italian had half the amount of running of Russell. Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad had his second crash in consecutive race weekends in practice, clipping the wall on the exit of the tight chicane leading into the section around the castle. In the context of the day, the margin between the two Mercedes drivers is to be expected but Antonelli is likely to close in on Friday in the run up to qualifying. Mercedes spent the first half-hour of the second session finishing off the repair to Antonelli's car, which involved an engine change. That meant he had to go straight into his performance runs on the soft tyre, having missed set-up and development time at the end of the first hour and the beginning of the second. Debris and sparks fly as Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad hits the wall during second practice Antonelli leads Russell by 81 points in the championship heading into this weekend. Verstappen was 0.4secs slower than Russell in the first session, and 0.827secs adrift in the second, when he was third fastest behind the two Mercedes drivers. Ferrari's Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton were next, but more than a second off the pace. And Lando Norris was sixth fastest, 1.484secs back, in a McLaren with a heavy aerodynamic upgrade. Alpine's Pierre Gasly was seventh, ahead of the the second McLaren of Oscar Piastri and Red Bull's Isack Hadjar, who is fit again after missing three races because of a broken wrist. title: On-the-run killer Gary Anderson appears in court
description: Gary Anderson had been serving life in prison for the murder of Karol Kelly in Londonderry in 2018.
body: Gary Anderson, pictured outside a special sitting of Letterkenny District Court on Thursday, following his arrest in County Donegal An on-the-run killer who absconded after being permitted to attend his father's funeral in Northern Ireland 10 days ago has appeared in court in the Republic of Ireland, where he was arrested on Wednesday. Gary Anderson, 29, appeared at a special sitting of Letterkenny District Court on Thursday following his arrest at a campsite near Buncrana, by An Garda Síochána (Irish police). He had been serving life in prison for the murder of Karol Kelly in Londonderry in 2018. The court was told Anderson is charged with being present at Fahan Marina caravan and campsite on 23 September, having escaped from Maghaberry Prison, contrary to Section 3(1) of the Criminal Law (Jurisdiction) Act 1976. Karol Kelly was stabbed to death in Londonderry in 2018 Garda Det Jason Conroy gave details of the arrest, charge and caution during the hearing on Thursday. The detective said Anderson was arrested at about 13:44 local time on Wednesday at Fahan Marina campsite and was told why he was being arrested but made no reply. At 20:47, he was charged, handed a copy of the charge sheet and again made no reply, the court was told. Garda Sgt Jim Collins told the court that there had been no application for bail from Anderson's legal representatives at that time. The court was told Gary Anderson was arrested at Fahan Marina caravan and campsite on 23 September Collins said he was seeking directions from the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) in the case and was seeking to have the accused remanded in custody. He applied to Judge Emile Daly for an adjournment in the case to allow for these directions. Judge Daly adjourned the case for Anderson to appear by videolink at Letterkenny District Court later this month. His solicitor said that while he understood Judge Daly could not direct that Anderson be held in a prison other than Castlerea Prison in County Roscommon, he asked the judge to recommend another prison because of what he termed "other parties involved". title: Reported assaults on Britain's rail services rise by more than a third
description: Recorded incidents of violence and harassment against passengers and rail workers showed a sharp increase in the year to March.
body: Reports of violent incidents and harassment on rail services "rose substantially" last year, figures from the rail regulator show. Reported assaults, including physical and verbal, were up 36% in the year to March 2026 compared with the previous year, according to the Office of Rail and Road (ORR). In total 13,464 assaults against passengers and members of the public were recorded on Britain's mainline railway, the highest number recorded since the series began in 2004. The ORR said the figures were "concerning" and that it was working with the industry to address the problem. According to the figures, harassment increased by 52% compared with the previous year and common assaults rose by 30%. The increase comes against a backdrop of five years of rising reports of incidents and industry campaigns to raise awareness. Assaults on the mainline railway are recorded according to their type. As a result each incident can lead to reports in more than one category, for example if someone is harassed and then physically assaulted. There were also 11,289 reported assaults against members of the workforce on the mainline railway, up 12% compared with the previous year. Of those 2,487 were physical assaults, while more than half (6,390 incidents) involved verbal abuse. The rest were threats. "We're working with industry and our trade union colleagues to address work-related violence and harassment," said Richard Hines, the ORR's chief inspector of railways. "This includes understanding where the risks are, putting effective controls in place, encouraging staff to report incidents and providing appropriate support afterwards," he said. The statistics include mainline rail services in England, Scotland and Wales, but not Northern Ireland. The data release also covers the London Underground, trams, metros and other light rail services. On the London Underground, recorded assaults increased 20% to 5,534 in the latest year, but reported workforce assaults fell 3% to 3,525. Transport for London does not record multiple aspects of each incident. Instead it records the most severe aspect reported. A spokesperson responding on behalf of Network Rail and the train companies said all operators were working to reduce risk and prevent harm by sharing information, improving reporting processes and deploying body-worn cameras. "Keeping passengers and colleagues safe is at the heart of everything we do," the spokesperson said. "Violence, abuse and intimidation directed at passengers or staff are completely unacceptable. The rail industry works closely with British Transport Police to investigate incidents, support victims and bring offenders to justice." The RMT union, representing rail industry workers, said the figures corresponded with the union's own figures indicating two-thirds of its members had experienced violence at work. RMT general secretary Eddie Dempsey called for an increase in staffing on public transport, including an end to lone working, to combat the problem. "We also clearly need stronger legal protections for public transport workers against assaults at work," he said. He said cuts to British Transport Police funding had been "disastrous" and called for outsourced security and enforcement staff to be brought in-house "as a matter of urgency". Other notable figures from the statistical release include that 11 members of the public died at mainline level crossings in the latest year, six more than the previous year. Eight were pedestrians and the others were road vehicle users. Will battery-powered trains change the future of UK rail travel? title: Girl, 16, killed in crash near north London school
description: A 68-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of causing death by careless driving, the Met says.
body: A 16-year-old girl has been killed in a crash near Highgate School in north London. The Met Police said officers were called to North Road, Highgate, at about 08:15 BST following reports of a collision involving a pedestrian and car. The girl was pronounced dead at the scene, near the private school's main site. The driver of the car, a 68-year-old man, remained at the scene and was arrested on suspicion of causing death by careless driving. The girl's next of kin have been informed and are being supported by officers, the Met said. The London Ambulance Service, London Fire Brigade and London Air Ambulance also attended. The Met said road closures were in place, and people are being asked to avoid the area. title: Ethiopia's army says it has repelled attacks in first comment on fresh fighting
description: The military says its soldiers inflicted casualties as fears grow of a resumption of a full-blown civil war.
body: Tigrayan fighters have been seen on the streets of the region's main city but it is relatively quiet there as clashes flare up elsewhere Ethiopia's army says it has repelled attacks from Tigrayan forces and their allies in parts of the north of the country, in its first statement since fighting broke out on Wednesday. The army said hostilities began in an area of Amhara region close to the border with Tigray, adding that its soldiers had inflicted heavy casualties and seized weapons. The developments come as tensions between the federal government and Tigrayan leaders have sharply escalated over the last few days, raising fears that a devastating civil war could resume. On Wednesday, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which dominates the region, seized control of three airports from federal police. The TPLF has not commented on the army's claims and the BBC has not been able to independently verify the army's claims. The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas. There are unconfirmed reports that TPLF forces have launched attacks in the neighbouring regions of Afar and Amhara. A humanitarian source in Afar told AFP news agency on Thursday that Tigrayan forces had launched heavy artillery attacks as they attempted to take control of the town of Yallo, near the border with Tigray. "We are in the situation of full-blown war now," TPLF vice-president Amanuel Assefa is quoted by the news agency as saying. The latest escalation follows months of rising tensions between Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government and Tigray authorities, who fought a devastating war from 2020 to 2022. That ended in an African Union-brokered peace deal but over recent months both sides have been accusing each other of violating the agreement. It was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the AU's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine. On Sunday, the TPLF announced an alliance with six other armed groups to oust the governemnt. Following the seizure of the airports, Ethiopian Airlines has cancelled all flights to Tigray. Residents of Tigray's main city of Mekelle told the BBC that local forces had taken over control of the city's airport from the national police early on Wednesday. This followed reports of drone strikes in Tigray in recent days. A Mekelle resident told the BBC's Newsday programme on Thursday there had been no clashes in the city, unlike in the previous war, with most fighting happening elsewhere. "Mekelle is calm, except the stress from the people," said the resident, only identified as Fitsum for his safety. He added that the biggest problem was economic, with people not having enough cash. "People are in a mood where they are distressed because it's been so difficult, so tough. The last seven or eight months the government has been denying budgets to the civil servants and all the banks were running out of cash." Fitsum said people had been relying on mobile banking but with the risk of communications being cut off, "people are going to be in grave danger because there is almost no cash". With the outbreak of war, people were limiting their movements and the city was all quiet - "it's like a curfew has been placed," he told the BBC. title: 'Cheeky' fees prompts choirs to pull out of Andrea Bocelli gig
description: Choirs say they're withdrawing from the Principality Stadium event because of the £42 per member charge.
body: Andrea Bocelli is one of the most well-known classical musicians in the world Wales is the land of song, but there may be distinct lack of voices at a festival in the Principality Stadium next year, because choirs are being charged thousands of pounds to take part. The event, billed as the The Land of Song Festival, will feature world-renowned Italian Tenor Andrea Bocelli, but choirs are pulling out because of steep costs that include fees for individual singers. Huw Watkins, who has performed in the Royal Albert Hall and at Wales rugby matches with Glynneath Male Voice Choir, said: "We couldn't get over it - we've never paid anything before to participate." The event organisers, The Land of Song Festival and the Principality Stadium, have been asked to comment. The festival next May is being marketed as "one of the world's largest shared singing events", with tenor Bocelli appearing on the Saturday, and up to 20,000 choristers appearing on the Sunday. But choristers believe the event would be fortunate to get a fraction of those numbers, given the costs involved. The festival's own website outlines the costs, with each choir paying a "choir subscription" of £150. Then each individual choir member has to pay an additional £42, which means some choirs having to pay thousands of pounds to attend. The Land of Song festival is due to take place on 8 and 9 May 2027 Glynneath Male Voice Choir, which would have been taking about 20 members to the event, said it would have cost them about £1,000 to sing, and then hundreds of pounds for coach hire, with some choirs from outside Wales also having to pay for accommodation. "Apparently, if you want hard copies of the music, you've got to pay for that also," said Watkins. "Somebody's making a lot of money from this." He said some of the choir's new members were "disappointed" they would not be able to participate in an event on this scale. "It would have been an experience for the new choristers - these opportunities don't come around that often as well, especially in the Principality," he said. "There is a good possibility that it might not go ahead." About 40 choirs or singing groups have taken to social media to say they will not be taking part in the event. Huw Watkins says his choir won't be taking part because of the cost Colin Williams is in Llantrisant Male Choir, which has about 78 members. They had signed up for the event and paid the £150 registration fee but, when they found out the cost was £42 per member, they pulled out. "After paying the registration fee, the communication from the organisers was non-existent as to what we would be singing and the practice needed, then the next thing we saw on social media was that they'd be charging £42 per chorister to sing there, which is unheard of. "I've been singing 44 years in the choir and I've never had to pay to sing, normally we get paid to sing. "We shared that info in our Whatsapp groups and the reaction was unanimous, people didn't want to take part. "We're not stopping our members from taking part but as an organisation we can't commit to it." He continued: "Some of our members haven't done these mass events, so I feel sorry for them, but being asked to pay £42 is a lot, and it's a lot of work and rehearsals, so it's massive cheek to ask for that much." title: No 'switch' to stop small boats, Lucy Powell tells BBC
description: Labour's deputy leader was speaking to BBC local radio ahead of the party's annual conference
body: Lucy Powell spoke to presenters from BBC local radio There is no "switch" to stop small boat crossings, and not every migrant boat can be intercepted, Labour's deputy leader has told the BBC. Lucy Powell's comments came after two uncontrolled landings from the Channel in two days, at Folkestone and Samphire Hoe in Kent. The Home Secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has ordered an urgent review by Border Security Command, calling the failure to intercept the two boats "not acceptable". But the Conservatives say Labour has lost control of Britain's borders, and a "radically different" approach is needed. A total of 781 people were recorded as arriving in 10 boats on Wednesday, the highest in a single day for far this year. In a round of interviews with BBC local radio ahead of Labour's annual conference, Powell told BBC Solent: "We are taking all steps we can to really bear down on and eradicate the small boat crossings altogether. "This has been a mammoth task across a whole range of different policy areas over the last couple of years, which is now starting to bear fruit, in that small boat crossings are significantly down this year - in fact significantly lower than at any time in the last six years. "Obviously as we close down some avenues and we close down routes criminal gangs look to find new ways to deliver their terrible business model." The thousands of migrants crossing the Channel are usually brought to shore by Border Security Command or RNLI boats. Before Monday, no small boat arrivals to the UK coast without an escort had been officially recorded since September 6, 2025. Uncontrolled landings are so rare that last year's incident was the only other one recorded since the Home Office began keeping data in 2023. On Wednesday British rescue boats were sent to collect a group of migrants who had spent more than 33 hours at sea Powell told BBC Kent: "It's not easy, if we had a switch that we could switch tomorrow to stop all small boats, we would switch it". Labour's deputy leader and Education Secretary told Radio 4's Today programme that "(You) can't stop everything all of the time. "Of course, it's a concern. That's why the Home Secretary has demanded and ordered this urgent review, because this is not what we want to see. This is not acceptable." The Conservative Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said on X: "Labour has lost control of our borders. "A radically different approach is needed. "We need to leave the ECHR so anyone entering Britain illegally can be rapidly deported. No hotels. No benefits. No lengthy court process. No asylum claim. Just rapid removal. Then the crossings will soon stop." The Liberal Democrat home affairs spokesperson, Max Wilkinson MP, said closer cooperation with the EU was key to tacking small boat crossings. "Until the government adopts Liberal Democrat proposals to tackle the root cause by entering the EU's landmark Migration and Asylum Pact, these the smugglers will continue to find a way through, lives will be put at risk and taxpayers' money will be wasted," he said. title: Ex-England striker Andy Carroll reveals he was sexually assaulted in 2021
description: Former England striker Andy Carroll reveals he was sexually assaulted in 2021, by a man who has subsequently been jailed for three years.
body: Andy Carroll has also played for Reading, West Brom and French sides Amiens and Bordeaux Former England striker Andy Carroll has revealed he was sexually assaulted by a man in 2021. The 37-year-old, who was automatically granted anonymity as a victim of sexual assault, has made the details public in an autobiography titled 'Owning it'. The incident took place at Carroll's home, during his second spell with his hometown club Newcastle and led to the perpetrator being jailed for three years. Carroll, now a player/co-owner of non-league club Dagenham & Redbridge, says he decided to include the incident in his book "at the very last minute" after discussing it with his girlfriend Lou Teasdale. A friend of his former partner, who was away at the time, was set to stay over after coming to his home to watch a boxing match. Carroll says the incident occurred while he was sleeping and he then threw the man out of the house, before knocking him unconscious as he tried to return. Carroll, who also played in the Premier League for Liverpool and West Ham, called the police and was "sobbing" in the arms of his children's nanny. The unnamed attacker was found guilty of sexual offences and placed on the sex offender register. Carroll testified in court, a process he says was "humiliating and embarrassing and absolutely horrendous". Carroll wrote: "I was sexually assaulted, there I said it. Scary to even think about and only a few people knew about it before now. "Me and Lou spent a lot of time discussing whether to mention it in this book or not. I avoided my publisher for so long that they probably suspected I got cold feet. "Scary to talk about but it's made [me] the person I am today as much as any of the good stuff. And if me talking about it helps just one person then good, it will have been worth it." Carroll, who won nine England caps, added: "What happened to me affected every facet of my life. I'd think about it every day, making it difficult to focus on anything else, including football… The trauma of what happened to me hasn't gone away." Carroll joined Dagenham in July 2025 and has made six appearances in the National League South this season. title: RAF pilots who ejected moments before crash expected to make full recovery
description: The Hawk T2 aircraft had been flying out of the RAF Valley station when it plummeted to the ground.
body: This video can not be played Moment pilots eject as RAF jet crashes in Anglesey Two pilots, a trainee and an experienced professional, who ejected and parachuted out of their plane moments before it crashed are expected to make a full recovery, the RAF has said. The Hawk T2 aircraft had been flying out of the RAF Valley station on Anglesey on Wednesday when it plummeted to the ground in the nearby Pencarnisiog area. Hawk operations have been paused by the RAF as a "precautionary measure" while investigations into the crash are ongoing - the Red Arrows are included in the pause as the aerobatics display team use the T1. On Thursday, the RAF said the two pilots, who were treated for minor injuries, are "doing well" and are "expected to make a full recovery". Captain Gez Currie, Station Commander of RAF Valley said the pilots were in hospital being cared for and were with their families. He would not give personal details about the pilots and said the investigation was in the early stages, adding "it's far too early to even suggest what has happened in this occasion". "The aircraft would have been, aimed in a direction that the pilot believed was open field, in order to avoid built up areas and anybody on the ground." Captain Gez Currie, Station Commander of RAF Valley said the pilots are with their families A video of the crash shared on social media on Wednesday appeared to show the two pilots ejecting from the aircraft before it nosedives and crashes in flames. The footage shows a plume of smoke and fire erupting as the aircraft hits the ground, appearing to narrowly miss homes. In a statement on social media, the RAF said: "Both pilots are doing well, they are in extremely good spirits and expected to make a full recovery. "A formal investigation into the circumstances surrounding the incident is now under way and, as a precautionary measure, the RAF has temporarily paused Hawk T1 and Hawk T2 flying operations." The RAF plane crash happened near Pencarnisiog The Hawk T1, and newer T2 versions are transonic, two-seat training aircrafts used to train fast jet pilots. The Red Arrows, based at RAF Waddington in Lincolnshire, are included in the pause, however they were not due to fly again until Le Touquet Airshow in France this weekend in any event. It is not known when the restriction will be lifted. Fighter pilots are trained at RAF Valley Fighter pilots are trained at RAF Valley. Aircrew are also trained there for mountain and maritime operations, and it is also home to the Mountain Rescue Service. The MOD describes its No 4 Flying Training School as responsible for training the "next generation of world-class fighter pilots, external". It opened in February 1941 and became a staging post for US aircraft to help the war effort from 1943. The Prince of Wales was an RAF search and rescue pilot at the Holyhead base from 2010 to 2013 and lived on Anglesey with the Princess of Wales as newlyweds. He returned in April to mark it 85th anniversary, where he spoke of his "fond memories" of the base. Separately, a publicly-funded airport operated between Anglesey and Cardiff between 2007 and 2020. title: Poland says fire at Starlink station is sabotage as Denmark warns of rising Russian threat
description: The satellite station is used in part to provide internet coverage to neighbouring Ukraine, the government says.
body: A fire at a Starlink satellite station in central Poland was a deliberate "act of sabotage", a government minister has said. Polish Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said the fire in the Masovian Voivodeship province was "deliberately designed to disable the station... disrupting internet access for various institutions, including the Ukrainian army". He told Polish public broadcaster TVP Info an investigation was ongoing but "many indications suggest" the attack fits into a "new Russian doctrine of attack". The Kremlin has not commented. Meanwhile, Denmark's intelligence service issued a new threat assessment saying it expects Russia to escalate hybrid warfare in the coming months. It said an attack remained "highly unlikely" but warned of "a low but growing risk" that Russia could launch a limited military attack against Nato countries. In recent weeks a number of European Nato members have said Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine, which Moscow denies. Earlier this month, Germany blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport, while France has ordered a plan to protect critical infrastructure and defence industry sites. Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary - for example cyberattacks, sabotage or misinformation. Proxies are often used to carry out the attacks and Russia always denies involvement, despite growing evidence to the contrary. Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage - and Russia is the chief suspect The fire at the state-owned Polish satellite station broke out on Wednesday night in Wola Krobowska. It remains operational. The deputy prime minister said it transmits internet traffic through Poland to countries including Ukraine, and uses SpaceX systems that provide connectivity via Starlink terminals. Asked about the incident at a news conference with Bulgaria's leader on Thursday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he disliked "labelling something as sabotage versus an accident without 100% certainty, but it looks bad". On Wednesday Poland also said a Russian military helicopter briefly violated its airspace, forcing it to scramble fighter jets. Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly said Moscow does not plan to attack Nato states. Earlier this month, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said it was Europe speaking about preparing for war, adding: "If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war [from that in Ukraine], and it will be very short." Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory, including the Crimea peninsula annexed in 2014. In Ukraine, Kharkiv and Kyiv experienced the worst of Russia's attacks overnight into Thursday. In Kharkiv, six people were killed and twelve others injured in a Russian strike on a farm in the village of Stara Hnylytsia, Ukraine's state emergency services said. It said they were agricultural workers sorting vegetables, with the head of the Kharkiv region adding that four were women. Onions covered the floor where the six farm workers were killed in Kharkiv In Kyiv, two people were killed and eight others injured overnight, emergency services said. More than 50 civilian facilities were also damaged in the city, including a maternity building. The hospital's director said a woman gave birth to a baby boy in a shelter during that attack, adding: "Even on such a terrible night, life goes on." Russia's defence ministry said it had hit Ukrainian defence facilities, logistics and telecom centres, as well as vessels used by the military. Moldova's president said four Russian drones crossed into its airspace, with at least one exploding, while Romania's defence ministry said one drone crashed in its territory. This video can not be played Watch: Ukraine's race to counter a new type of Russian drone Russian aerial attacks on Ukraine have become more devastating in recent months because of their new jet-powered drones, which are harder to shoot down. Kyiv is racing to develop low-cost weapons that can counter them as the missiles and fighter jets it has to fight them are too expensive. Speaking at the UN General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said, "we need ballistic interceptors to protect lives" and called on the US to help. He said Putin needed to be stopped from continuing the war and "spreading this evil further", adding: "Putin is always looking for someone who can help him kill more, kill more people for every kilometre of land." He said Ukraine would seek to target the Russian energy sector over the winter. The Ukrainian president's comments came as Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev headed to the US to meet Trump administration officials, including Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Reuters reported, citing two sources. Russia's Lavrov told the UN Security Council on Wednesday there would be no pause in the war. title: Date set for long-awaited Fury v Joshua fight
description: Cardiff's Principality Stadium will host Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury's all-British heavyweight fight on 11 December.
body: Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury will contest their long-awaited all-British heavyweight fight at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December. The bout, more than a decade in the making, will be broadcast globally on Netflix. BBC Sport understands the main event could take place in the early hours of Saturday morning in the UK, with organisers considering a late start to cater for audiences in the United States. Joshua and Fury will come face-to-face at a news conference in London on Wednesday, 30 September, as the build-up begins to one of the most anticipated fights in British boxing history. The event is being promoted as a collaboration between Saudi boxing powerbroker Turki Alalshikh's The Ring and UFC chief Dana White, who is also fronting the recently launched Zuffa Boxing. title: Meet Grumpygran1948 - Fornite's record breaking streamer
description: Cath Bowie, from Moray, began playing the online shooter in 2017 and now has an audience of around 24,000 followers.
body: Cath Bowie has an audience of around 24,000 followers on Fortnite A 78-year-old Scottish grandmother has been named the world's oldest female Fortnite streamer by Guinness World Records. Cath Bowie, who is originally from Moray but now lives in Inverurie, began playing the online shooter in 2017 and now has an audience of more than 24,000 followers. She was introduced to the game by her grandson, who was 17 at the time, and says no-one is "ever too old to start gaming". Known on Fortnite her username grumpygran1948, Cath features in the Guinness World Records Gamer's Edition 2027. Fortnite is one of the most popular video games in the world, putting up to 100 players against each other in a fight to be the last one standing. This video can not be played Gamer gran named world's oldest female Fortnite streamer Cath had tried video games before, but none fully sparked her interest until she discovered Fortnite. "I was immediately hooked," she said. She then bought her own console, but her grandson doubted she would grow a following as a streamer. She said: "As a young guy, he just couldn't believe that his grandma would do such a thing and suggested that nobody would join me or watch me. "Saying that was like a red rag to a bull to me. I would show him that I could do it. "Twenty four thousand followers later and he doesn't mention it. I wonder why?" Fortnite is one of the world's most popular online video games Cath says she loves the challenge of the game but also likes chatting to other players Cath said she loves the challenge the game gives her and plays it every day. She told the BBC's Radio Scotland Breakfast programme: "It's a lovely, lovely game. The one I play is Battle Royale Last Man Standing and you go into it either as a solo, duo or squad. "You're trying to get the better of your opponents and eliminate them. "But there's no blood on the scene - you just shoot somebody and they either crawl about until they die or they're just obliterated with the one shot. So there isn't any mess - nothing like that." Cath is welcomed into the 2027 Guinness World Records Gamer's Edition Cath said the community of people playing the game was more important than the game itself. "I play with some wonderful folk - from the UK, quite a few from the USA, from Canada, New Zealand and Australia," she said. "It's super meeting all these folk. The chat we have, it's lovely - I've had folk with me for quite a few years now." Alice Bell, editor of Guinness World Records Gamer's Edition 2027, said: "At Guinness World Records we believe gaming is for everyone. "This edition showcases gamers of different generations and cultures from around the world. title: Elephants use medicinal plants to treat themselves, researchers find
description: African elephants use dozens of different medicinal plants to treat themselves and their families when they are sick, research reveals.
body: Accounts from local experts revealed that wild elephants used more than 35 plants, many of which have known medicinal uses African elephants use dozens of different medicinal plants to treat themselves and their families when they are sick. This is the conclusion of a study which interviewed people who live and work alongside the elephants in the Mount Elgon region of Kenya. These particular animals have long intrigued scientists with their extraordinary behaviour - they are known as salt-mining elephants, because they go into caves and scrape the rock with their tusks to extract minerals for their diet. This newly published research suggests that the same elephants use several different plant species in the forest for medicinal purposes. Camera traps set up by the Mount Elgon Foundation captured the elephants 'mining' for salt in caves, to supplement their diet One of the lead researchers, Dr Elodie Freymann from Brown University in the US, said the study raised the question of whether destruction of forest habitat deprives animals - and humans - of the medicines they need to thrive. "This shows just how entangled our medicines are with the non-human world," Dr Freymann told BBC News. The researchers say the forests are 'natural pharmacies' for the elephants The scientists collaborated with the conservation charity the Mount Elgon Foundation, external. They interviewed local people, including wildlife scouts and community elders. Accounts described elephants selecting particular plants when they seemed unwell, and mothers reportedly giving medicinal plant material to their calves. From this, the researchers concluded that the elephants use 35 different plant species, and that 25 of those are known locally to have medicinal uses. Wild chimpanzees filmed using forest 'first aid' Wounded orangutan seen using plant as medicine The study, published in the journal Scientific Reports, external, did not name the interviewees - keeping participants anonymous so they felt free to share their stories. Their accounts reveal some intriguing details. In one testimony, a wildlife scout described seeing elephants using a plant known as Angurweet "as medicine to give to babies". Angurweet is used as a remedy for ailments including stomach ache. The scout, who described elephant mothers mixing it in their mouths - "removing the leaves and chewing it until smooth, along with the roots of some other trees". He also recounted that he had seen mothers mix this plant material with their own milk. "They give it to the babies, who chew on it themselves and spit out the solids". Professor Michael Huffman, a primatologist based in Japan, currently at Nagasaki University, said this particular account was "tantalising", but more evidence would be needed to prove that elephants provided bespoke medical treatment for their calves. The scientists have already embarked on gathering that evidence - giving the local wildlife experts they worked with cameras to record the behaviour they witness. They are also analysing plants that the elephants use - looking for new medicines that the elephants themselves may have discovered. Another lead reearcher on the project, Dr Fabien Schultz from the Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine in Hamburg, told BBC News: "Local knowledge has given us a map". "We [now] want to follow the elephants and investigate whether they select particular plants in particular health contexts, and whether those plants have relevant biological activity." The study identified 35 different plant species that the animals use Many animals treat themselves with plants and other natural remedies. The earliest scientific accounts of elephants practicing "self-medication" date back to the early third century. Roman author Claudius Aelian in his text De Natura Animalium (On the Nature of Animals) described an elephant that, after being wounded by spears and arrows, consumed flowers and oil from an olive tree. The elephant made a full recovery. Centuries later, these scientists are delving into what we can learn from wildlife about the properties of plants in the forest habitats they evolved in. "There are medicine-producing organisms on this planet that have this incredible capability," Dr Freymann told BBC News." Medicine factories that exist all around us." Researchers worked with local experts to identify plants the elephants use Prof Huffman, who was not involved in this study, added: "We now know that mosquitoes and drosophila (flies) self-medicate, bees self-medicate, as do many other species all the way up the evolutionary ladder to the great apes of Africa and Asia. "WIth each new species studied, we have gained a greater understanding of our medicinal past." For Dr Freymann, the findings also contain a lesson for our future. "So many of the medicines we buy in a pharmacy were derived from compounds from trees, algae, from fungi, from coral reefs. "It's a win-win for us to protect these forests and keep those natural pharmacies around... long enough that we can discover new natural products that could save us down the line." title: Edinburgh Zoo's red panda goes to the vet for toothache
description: Red panda Bruce laid on his back under a general anaesthetic, as vets removed the problem tooth and checked him for other illnesses.
body: Say Pand-aaah: Vets found Bruce was suffering from tooth ache Edinburgh Zoo's red panda makes a visit to the dentist look easy after having his tooth removed during a health check-up. Keepers noticed that Bruce was not eating his food. They sent him to Royal Zoological Society of Scotland vets who discovered he was suffering from toothache. Eleven-year-old Bruce laid on his back under a general anaesthetic, as they removed the problem tooth and checked him for other illnesses. The endangered red panda, who arrived in Edinburgh in 2016, was given a clean bill of health and returned to his habitat. Bruce went back to his habitat after a full check-up by vets Red pandas are native to the eastern Himalayas and south western China. Bruce is now the only red panda at the zoo and is the grandfather of Priya, a female red panda who moved to the Highland Wildlife Park earlier this year. Edinburgh Zoo's baby red panda Roxie was three-months-old when she died from stress caused by fireworks on Bonfire Night in 2024. Her mother Ginger also died unexpectedly five days earlier at the age of nine. Bruce was placed under general anaesthetic by the vets Red pandas have become an endangered species, mainly due to habitat loss, human interference and poaching. They are not related to giant pandas but rather closer to raccoons, skunks and weasels. The World Wildlife Fund (WWF) estimates there are fewer than 10,000 red pandas left in the wild. They are classified as endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). title: Are we back in big tech's 'move fast and break things' era?
description: Despite promises to make safe AI, examples of bots behaving badly are now coming at us thick and fast.
body: This video can not be played Watch: What you need to know about the OpenAI Australian government hack "Move fast and break things." It was a mantra coined by the tech giant Meta and used until 2012, which came to define the bad old days of social media running riot in a feeding frenzy of user data. Yet now we have large companies scrambling to develop ever more powerful AI, in an intense global race to be first to build the world's most advanced models, egged on by US President Donald Trump. Despite numerous pledges, commitments and open letters over the years from the industry, promising to prioritise safe, responsible AI aligned with human values, examples of bots behaving badly – to put it mildly - are now coming at us thick and fast. OpenAI's agents seem to feature quite prominently in the current roll call of AI products taking their remits to extremes. The Australian government is fuming at the firm's most recent disclosure, that its products accessed both public and non-public data from part of the country's online Medicare healthcare system. It happened in June, but OpenAI didn't notice until August. It notified the authorities in September. As Camilla Chan, founder of the cyber-security firm X-Phy, puts it: "The future of autonomous AI cannot rest on companies discovering their own failures and reporting it afterwards." Protests calling for an end to the "AI race" in Silicon Valley and beyond have intensified in recent months Worse still, the agents were reportedly able to plot the attack using a German web forum they secretly took over in June, according to ABC's Cam Wilson, external. When the website's editors noticed and started deleting pages, the agents shared code designed to retrieve them. And that happened before the Hugging Face incident, described at the time as the world's first AI-enabled cyber-attack. It raises a question - if the Medicare incident had been carried out by a person rather than an AI agent, would they be in big trouble? "If this was an individual hacking Australia's Medicare system, they'd be looking at jail time," said Dr Andrew Rogoyski from the Institute for People-Centred AI at the University of Surrey. "The fact that it's an AI seems to allow the company to shrug their shoulders and get away with 'accidents happen'." Australia says it is carrying out an urgent review into whether any laws have been broken, but part of that rests on being able to prove intent – which OpenAI denies. And its government may have to ask itself some awkward questions about the strength of its cyber-security defences, including whether the healthcare data could have been better protected. What is AI and how does it work? Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they? The industry has warned countries and institutions to prepare for a new world of supersized cyber-attacks powered by AI. A popular solution to keeping the tech on the straight and narrow lies in two parts: slowing down the pace of its development, and implementing international regulation to police it. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham highlighted the need for new global AI standards in his first international speech at the UN General Assembly. And last night both Sam Altman from OpenAI and Dario Amodei from Anthropic addressed the UN Security Council and pleaded for both – despite US President Donald Trump not being at all enthusiastic about this approach. "The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the USA has that, in spades!" he posted on Truth Social earlier this month. Although he has since said he intends to appoint an AI tsar, so perhaps somebody has had a quiet word. Yesterday I spoke with a senior executive at the top of one of the US's biggest AI firms, and I asked him what he expected international regulators to be able to do, that he was seemingly unable to do inside his own lab? I didn't get a straight answer, but my interpretation is nobody wants to apply the brakes only to see their rivals race ahead, and they don't trust each other enough to go first. Global regulation would force them all to tow the line - and also remove some of the weight of responsibility from the industry itself. AI is increasingly becoming a toxic brand, but in order to remind people of the benefits of the technology - and why it isn't facing an outright ban - the industry urgently needs some quick wins. The problem is the tech sector has always been very good at promising the future, without delivering so much in the present. And that also applies to future problems. Alarm bells rang loudly when former Anthropic safety researcher Joseph Coxon said he believed the tech had a 10% chance of destroying humanity within the next 10 years. Some experts warn we should be wary of these claims. "There are known risks which are serious enough to be getting on with," Sir Nick Clegg, former head of global affairs at Meta, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme. "Whether it's bioweapons, whether it's cyber-security hacks, whether it is the implications of how people are going to be affected by an increasingly intimate and perhaps in many cases emotionally dependent relationship with AI entities going forward. "There's enough to be really, really worried about already, without thinking that homosapiens [are] going to be eliminated by next Tuesday." title: Rolls-Royce signs 'multi-million' engine deal
description: The order will see 18 engines built and maintained by the company from its Derby aerospace centre.
body: The order includes both the engines and a maintenance package Rolls-Royce has moved forward with a deal to power a new fleet of Airbus long-haul jets for Philippine Airlines. The FTSE-100 firm will provide 18 engines for nine new Airbus A350-1000 aircraft in a deal worth "hundreds of millions of pounds". The agreement, once finalised, also includes a maintenance package, meaning Rolls-Royce will continue servicing and monitoring the engines throughout their operational life, officials said. The government welcomed the deal, saying it would bring "good quality jobs" to the company's Derby base. The order was first announced as a memorandum of understanding at the Farnborough International Airshow in July. At the time, Rob Watson, president of civil airspace at Rolls-Royce, said the company was "proud to continue strengthening our long-standing relationship with Philippine Airlines". While the deal is described as being worth "hundreds of millions", the precise value has not been confirmed. Airbus designs and manufactures wings for all its commercial aircraft at its Broughton site in North Wales. Minister for trade Anas Sarwar said: "This news shows British engineering is flying high with world-class innovation that puts our companies at the front of the pack. "Building these engines and wings brings good quality jobs to Derby and Broughton, and means UK expertise is at the heart of thousands of flights by one of the fastest-growing airlines around the world." The engine involved, the Trent XWB-97, can operate using a 50% sustainable aviation fuel blend, with plans for it to run on 100% sustainable aviation fuel in the future. This order follows Philippine Airlines's previous order for nine Trent XWB-97-powered Airbus A350-1000 in 2023. title: How Man City overhauled their squad from a 650,000-strong database
description: BBC Sport goes inside Manchester City's data team, who have been a key part of their rebuild over the past 18 months.
body: How Man City overhauled their squad from a 650,000-strong database Inside the confines of Manchester City's sophisticated data operation is a fundamental phrase its experts work towards: "What does it take to win?" In practice, the motto is broken down into three sections: identifying players, evaluating them and assessing how the club could improve them, all with a view to enhancing the statistical probability of City winning the Premier League. Last season, the club's data department projected they would be there or thereabouts when it came to the title race, but their metrics indicated Arsenal were favourites to be champions. They were accurate. This time around, City prefer to keep their projections under wraps - but five wins from five Premier League games have prompted predictions from supporters and pundits they will again be the Gunners' closest challengers. City's devotion to data is at the heart of their efforts to close the gap on Arsenal and BBC Sport has been given unprecedent access to the inner workings of the club's metrics machine as we uncover some of the secrets guiding their work - particularly regarding player recruitment and sales. Their work is a sign of the times in the Premier League, with clubs across the top flight and beyond increasingly using data for transfers and monitoring their teams' performance. At City, one of the fundamental aims is to reduce risk of any market transaction, be it a purchase or a sale. City grade players based on: The system they play in at their current club and how the manager is asking him and the team to play. Once those four aspects are observed, City's aim is to understand not just how good the player is but how good he could become at the Etihad. Since winning the Treble in 2023, City's squad has undergone a vast overhaul using this approach. Only four players from that historic campaign remain. It is crucial to stress, however, that while data has made an indefinite impact on how City operate in the transfer market, the work of traditional scouts continues to be the primary gauge of whether they decide to move for a player. "Data plays a role in our decision-making, but it is just one part of the overall picture," City sporting director Hugo Viana told BBC Sport. "We know data cannot tell us everything about a player. It cannot fully show a person's character, mentality or behaviour. "That is why we study data insights but focus on the expertise of our scouts and other specialists." The prominence of data, however, has grown significantly behind the scenes at the Etihad. Here BBC Sport can take you to the core of some of City's key transfer calls from their extensive three-year squad revamp - including the £116m signing of Elliot Anderson. The starting point for any new signing is City's database of 650,000 footballers from around the world. The next step is the brief: what sort of player is the club wanting to recruit. This usually starts with a position, though that process isn't as simple as it sounds. City, for example, categorise their full-backs into three types: those who are defensive, those who come inside, and those who play high and wide. Once the club's data departments have the brief, filters that grade a player's overall ability are applied to whittle down the 650,000-man database to 20-50 names. Juventus full-back Andrea Cambiaso is one player who has been on City's radar after the data highlighted him, particularly his ability to coming inside to build play in midfield. That he is comfortable with both feet rated highly on the data, too. In accordance with the data and the scouting reports it was decided the club would not proceed with their interest in Cambiaso in the previous window, but City's approach is likely to mean he will continue to be monitored. The longlist of 20-50 names is cross-referenced with the scouting longlist. Generally there is a significant overlap between the players identified by data and the ones already on scouts' radar. From there, further, more refined metrics are applied to rank and prioritise the longlist. Scouts will then complete further diligence on the players to reduce the list to a maximum of about six players. At this point, the club will complete deeper dives into the remaining players, including diligence on their injury record, athletic performance and behavioural habits. The information is then collated into individual reports called acquisition packs which contain all the key metrics used to inform the decision on a player. This includes a 'radar chart', which rates a range of specific on-field metrics. For example, when Jeremy Doku was signed in 2023, then manager Pep Guardiola decided he wanted a winger who was direct, akin to Leroy Sane, because at the time they had Jack Grealish and Riyad Mahrez, who preferred to keep the ball and cut inside. Among the criteria applied in City's brief were the following: making (running into) the box, pressure regains, take-on percentage and opposition-half pressure. Doku's overall numbers ticked the boxes Guardiola was looking for, although the Belgian's 'making the box' score was among his lowest readings. Since his arrival, Doku has improved this rating - an example City say shows how their data systems are helping to improve existing players. There is also a 'utilisation chart' that records how often the player has been used over a three-year period, as well as a scouting grade that indicates how highly the traditional scouts rate the individual. Each player is also awarded an overall "current impact score" - which predicts what impression he would be expected to make immediately on signing - and a "potential impact score" that projects the contribution the player could make in the future. Perhaps the most intriguing reading on the acquisition packs is a player's "action value score". This positi

title: The eel-powered 11-year-old making history
description: Primary school student Yuki Kurihara makes a flying start as he becomes the youngest athlete at this year's Asian Games.
body: Puyo Puyo was created in Hiroshima in 1991, with Sega acquiring the franchise in 1998 Primary school student Yuki Kurihara made a flying start as he became the youngest athlete at this year's Asian Games. The 11-year-old eSports star beat opponents almost three times his age in his native Japan on Thursday. The youngster competes in Puyo Puyo Champions, a puzzle game similar to Tetris which was developed in Japan. Players try to clear their screen of coloured blobs by lining them up and popping them, creating chain reactions called 'dairensa'. Kurihara beat all four opponents to top Group A and he will attempt to win gold on Saturday. "The best feeling in the world is winning," Kurihara told the Japan Times., external "When I lose, I cry and try not to think about it too much. When the play doesn't go well it's not fun, so I want to quit. But I always come back. "I hope to win a gold medal for Japan." Japan's youngest athlete in Asian Games history could also become the competition's youngest ever medallist. Indonesia's Bunga Nyimas holds the record, having won bronze in women's skateboarding aged 12 in 2018. eSports has appeared in the previous two editions of the Asian Games, with Puyo Puyo being one of 11 medal events this year. Kurihara says he eats eel to prepare for contests and secured his place on the Japan team at just 10 years old. In February he beat an adult professional to win Sega's Puyo Puyo Grand Prix Final and he turned pro himself in April - two months before his 11th birthday. The Asian Games are being held in Nagoya and the wider Aichi area from 19 September to 4 October. title: NHS trust to reexamine 4,500 breast cancer cases after unnecessary surgeries found
description: Hospital chiefs in County Durham agree to a review after failings including unnecessary surgeries.
body: Hospital chiefs in County Durham have agreed to review up to a further 4,500 breast cancer cases after failings including delayed diagnoses and unnecessary surgeries were found. Hundreds of patients suffered harm under County Durham and Darlington NHS Foundation Trust, according to a review of cases dating back to 2023. The BBC has spoken to multiple women affected by the failings, including one who said she felt "mutilated" and the trust's mistakes were "absolutely unforgivable". Ahead of agreeing to expand the review to cases dating back to 2015, members of the trust's board offered "sincere" apologies for the failings and harm caused. At an extraordinary meeting of the board held in Durham, board chair Alison Marshall said: "I would like to offer a sincere apology to all the women and their families who have been affected by the failings in our breast services. "I can't imagine the impact that has had." She said they could "not turn back the clock" but would be "open, honest and transparent" about the failings. Chief nurse Gill Hunt told the board concerns were first raised in 2015 after a "service reconfiguration" and loss of breast surgical trainee posts. title: The Global Story
description: What can America learn from the rest of the world about protecting journalists?
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations World Service,·24 Sep 2026,·27 mins Available for over a year Last week, President Donald Trump barred CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House, accusing them of spreading "fake news". After their reporters had their press passes revoked and were denied access to the building, the three outlets launched a joint legal challenge, arguing that the move was unconstitutional. How unprecedented is this decision? And how does it compare with the treatment of journalists in other countries around the world? Jason Rezaian, host of the Washington Post podcast Freedom Desk and the paper's former Tehran bureau chief, has a unique perspective on these questions. While reporting from Iran, he experienced restrictions on press freedom and was ultimately imprisoned by the regime. Since his release, he has become a prominent advocate for press freedom around the world. He joins The Global Story’s Tristan Redman to discuss where President Trump's decision fits into a broader pattern in the relationship between political leaders and the media over recent decades. Producers: Xandra Ellin and Cat Farnsworth. Executive producer: Martine Powers Mix: Travis Evans Digital producer: Sam Gruet Senior news editor: China Collins. title: Anti-migrant activist arrested over video of dinghy slashing
description: Police had been looking into footage appearing to show the man, also known as Danny Tommo, slashing at a boat in the English Channel with a knife.
body: The police had been examining live-stream footage appearing to show Daniel Thomas slashing at a migrant boat Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been arrested over a video appearing to show him slashing at a boat in the English Channel with a knife. Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary said a 37-year-old man of no fixed abode had been arrested after a "boat that had an emergency responder on board" was damaged in the Channel. He was arrested on suspicion of criminal damage with intent to endanger life and endangering the safety of a ship on Wednesday. He remains in custody. The force previously said it was looking at the video which Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, had live-streamed on social media on Tuesday. A French coastguard official was on board when Thomas appeared to slash at it. Some 50 migrants who had travelled in the boat from Normandy had already been taken to Dover for processing. Far-right activist Tommy Robinson shared a video of Thomas's arrest on social media late on Wednesday, claiming it was in relation to an attempt to "stop the invasion of our country". Thomas organised anti-migrant protests in Dover and Portsmouth in early September which saw roads blocked by hundreds of demonstrators, including groups of men in black balaclavas. He has been rallying support for "mass resistance" to "take our country back" through his venture Patriot Platform, which he founded earlier this year. title: Why India's Election Commission is in the eye of a storm - again
description: India's polling monitor is facing yet another crisis of credibility with fresh allegations against its chief.
body: India's opposition parties have demanded that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resign from office India's Election Commission (ECI) is facing yet another crisis of credibility after a series of fresh allegations of irregularities against its chief. One of the most trusted public institutions in the world's largest democracy, the three-member commission is headed by the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and includes Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi as commissioners. The latest row broke out after a report in the Indian Express newspaper, external said that in the past few months, CEC Kumar had been repeatedly questioned by his two colleagues over the integrity of the voter database, changes to the way new voters are enrolled and the security of the electoral rolls itself. The report said that Commissioners Sandhu and Joshi objected to several decisions which were taken without their knowledge. There were at least 14 times in the past 10 months when Commissioners Sandhu and Joshi were kept in the dark, it added. In one instance, the report says, the two commissioners even wrote a letter complaining to the chief secretary, the top bureaucrat in the Indian government. The revelations have created a furore, with opposition leaders demanding Kumar's resignation. Sandhu and Joshi have not publicly commented on the report but the ECI said in a statement that "differing views" were part of the "decision-making process". The report comes at a time when the commission is carrying out a controversial country-wide revision of the electoral database. The Election Commission says the aim of this Special Intensive Revision - better known by its acronym SIR - is to ensure that no ineligible name remains on the rolls. It says the last revision was done nearly a quarter of a century ago and the voters' list needs to be updated to account for those who have died, left the country or are registered in more than one place as they've moved to a new address. But the exercise has been mired in controversy from the start with the opposition parties accusing CEC Kumar of manipulating voters' list to favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) during elections. Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the accusations. But the latest revelations are being seen as much more serious as they are about questions being raised from within the Election Commission about the way its chief is functioning. The Indian Express report says that CEC Kumar has been repeatedly questioned by his two colleagues over the integrity of the voter database in recent months From the start, questions have lingered over the robustness of the revision, which has seen 130 million names from across India struck off the voters' list. Millions of voters have also complained to the authorities that their names are missing, saying the new process set by SIR to register as voters is too cumbersome and involves furnishing documents that many don't have. Former CEC SY Quraishi, who says he has "been a critic of the SIR from the beginning", told news agency PTI that he always wondered why Commissioners Sandhu and Joshi had been "keeping quiet". "[Now] I realised that very silently and quietly they were protesting, they were writing notes. That is a good thing, they have gone up in my esteem," he said. How a Brazilian woman became the face of India vote fraud row New voters list in Indian state includes wrong photos and dead people The row over 'vote theft' that has shaken Indian politics The revelations have also provided fresh ammunition to the opposition parties and critics who have repeatedly claimed that SIR is being used to exclude their voters for the BJP's benefit and that elections in India are no longer free and fair. On Wednesday, angry opposition politicians once again questioned the sanctity of India's election process and demanded that CEC Kumar resign, saying he had no right to continue in office, with some even calling for his arrest. The charge was led by MP and senior Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi who has repeatedly accused the Commission of "stealing votes from the opposition". On Wednesday, he also accused the Commission and its officers of "treason". "Vote chori [theft] is a crime against the Indian people and a direct attack on our constitution. The BJP, RSS [Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh] and EC who organised it have committed an act of treason. Justice will be served," he posted on X, external. He also shared a 15-second video telling the commission and its officers that "your time will come. You cannot get away". Mamata Banerjee, leader of the regional Mamata All India Trinamool Congress, called for Kumar's arrest and demanded fresh polls with the pre-SIR voters' list in the state of West Bengal which she lost to the BJP in the recent elections. At least 2.7million voters were removed in the state during SIR - Banerjee and her supporters say that cost them dozens of seats and the election win. Congress leader Rahul Gandhi has repeatedly accused the commission of "stealing votes from the opposition" Within hours of the Indian Express report and statements from opposition leaders, the Election Commission put out a statement, external defending its way of working. "Differing views and observations are a normal part of deliberation in any institution. They are a part of the decision-making process before a final decision is taken. "Not only the three Commissioners, but every officer of the Commission is fully authorised to give his suggestions to the Commission for improving the electoral system," the statement said. The note said that highlighting "certain specific internal notes and observations spread over the period of 10 months while overlooking the much larger body of approvals, decisions, instructions and initiatives" give only part of the picture.
