title: 'Tragic but avoidable' - how serious is heat-death risk in sport?
description: BBC Sport explores the health impact of extreme heat on athletes, following the death of a Fijian rugby player in Japan in August.
body: The Met Office has confirmed that 2026 was the UK's hottest summer, and many other countries around the world have also dealt with extreme heat On Monday, 3 August, Fijian rugby player Saimoni Vunilagi set off from home to train with his team-mates. After the session, he was taken to hospital. A few days later, the 26-year-old was dead. In a statement announcing his death, Japanese second division club Kyuden Voltex said Vunilagi "displayed symptoms consistent with severe heatstroke" during the training session, adding "despite the best efforts of the medical team, he sadly passed away". Japan, like the UK, Europe and many other parts of the world, suffered severe heatwaves this summer. By noon on the day Vunilagi became ill, the temperature in Fukuoka - where Kyuden Voltex are based - had risen to 35C. The humidity was more than 75%. In the weeks before, the daily high was between 32 and 37C. It had been a month since the daily high was below 30C. No formal cause of death has been publicly released, but the link suggested by the club between training in heat and Vunilagi's death has caused alarm, given the increase in global temperatures and the rising frequency of extremely hot days. So, how serious a threat is extreme heat to athletes, what measures could help and do perceptions within sport need to change? There have been a variety of heat-related medical incidents during sports events in 2026. Tennis players Jakub Mensik and Ekaterina Alexandrova collapsed during matches played at more than 30C, and eight runners had to be taken to hospital during a marathon in South Korea in April at which temperatures reached 29C. Tour de France winner Tadej Pogacar called this year's heat "dangerous" during the event, while Matthew Brennan asked "what are we doing?" after the temperature topped 40C at the Vuelta a Espana, in which he won five stages. This summer's World Cup also featured controversial hydration breaks at every match, which Fifa insisted were introduced to aid player welfare. Many sports - including tennis, athletics and cycling - monitor potentially dangerous levels of extreme heat using the Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT), which produces a measure for heat stress levels by assessing air temperature, humidity, wind speed, sun angle and solar radiation. But some experts believe athletes need greater protection, or the risk of further fatalities will increase. "We have seen an increase in the number of heat illness events in rugby and many other sports around the world in recent years," says Dr Madeleine Orr - assistant professor of sport ecology at the University of Toronto. "People assume we've seen such extreme heat before and think, 'it was fine, we pushed through, we can do it again'. "That's not necessarily true - the heatwaves we're experiencing today are hotter than the ones in your childhood, because heatwaves are relative to the local normal, and 'normal' levels have risen." Jakub Mensik was helped by rival Mariano Navone after collapsing at the end of a five-set match which lasted four hours and 41 minutes, and was played in more than 32C heat Though the requirements of each sport mean the impact of high temperatures can differ, there are growing calls for blanket rules to be implemented across sports which offer more cast-iron protection when things become really extreme. "Different leagues have different policies - there needs to be more of a standardised approach so that everyone just knows what to do," says Orr. "It's similar to lightning - most people are familiar with the idea that when there's lightning near a sports event, we take a break for 30 minutes and start once it has gone away. "We need a similar policy on heat and we need it to apply everywhere - it's easier for people to get behind if it's universal that once we get to a certain threshold, we know what happens." One of the big challenges with heat-related illnesses in sport is convincing athletes and their coaches to do what is best for their health. "I've got no doubt that a lot of coaches think that heat regulation is a hindrance," says Christian Day - general secretary of the Rugby Players' Association. "And it's a tough one for the player, isn't it? Because you don't want to be the player who puts their hand up and says they're not feeling well, or that it's too hot to train on a certain day. Players need protecting from themselves sometimes. "It's important for team staff to have a regulatory number that they know if it hits it, there's no discussion, you just stop playing. "It's also about educating players as to what signs to look for to identify one of their team-mates who is struggling in training." World Rugby updated its heat and air-quality guidelines in 2025, including use of a heat stress index - a measure from 0 to 250 used to determine how dangerous hot conditions are for players, with provisions for water breaks and extended half-time periods at low levels of danger, and potentially suspending or postponing matches at the higher end of the scale. But players spend far more time training than they do playing matches. "If this level of heat is going to become the norm, then we need central regulation and governance as to how we help clubs manage their players and how they should react to these kind of temperatures," says Day. "Maybe there are cases where perhaps training needs to be limited in time, or doesn't take place at all that day outdoors. "It's not a matter of trying to call people out or produce problems. It's trying to ensure the safest possible training environment." By early August, the Japan Meteorological Agency had recorded 4,727 instances of 'extremely hot' temperatures across the country since the start of 2026 Pre-season can be an especially dangerous time for athletes across sports. title: Man Utd selling Old Trafford turf cubes for £125
description: Manchester United is selling pieces of its Old Trafford pitch for £125 each, an initiative announced the same day the club reported its overall debt remains more than £1bn.
body: Manchester United have played at Old Trafford since 1910 Manchester United are selling pieces of their Old Trafford pitch for £125 each. The initiative was announced the same day that the club reported that overall debt remains more than £1bn. The first batch put on sale has already sold out. While United recorded a record revenue of £677.6m and a £22.6m operating profit for 2025-26, they had a pre-tax loss of £43m. The 13-time Premier League champions also confirmed £63.5m had been spent on buying land for the team's new stadium, which is expected to cost more than £2bn overall. For the first time in 14 years, the Old Trafford pitch was dug up this summer and stripped back to its foundation. Sections of the turf were preserved, with pieces measuring 7x7cm then being placed in glass cubes. The cubes are presented inside a black case. The club website says that the cubes make a "priceless memento of iconic games played at home and keeps the memories of matchdays alive". title: Alcaraz on late finishes, missing Sinner and Laver Cup return
description: Carlos Alcaraz discusses his US Open return, why he "misses" rival Jannik Sinner and his excitement for this year's Laver Cup.
body: Carlos Alcaraz has won seven Grand Slam singles titles, including this year's Australian Open Most players, after seeing their US Open title defence end at 3.34am after five intense sets, would not walk away smiling. Carlos Alcaraz is not most players. After his loss to Ben Shelton - a match that played out over a gruelling four hours and 28 minutes - the Spaniard was filmed walking down the Arthur Ashe tunnel with a huge grin on his face. Alcaraz had been competing in his first tournament for over five months after suffering a wrist injury that left him in pain every day. He did not defend his French Open title or compete at Wimbledon, and did not know if he would play in New York until a week before. "The quarter-final was great - it was a gift for me," Alcaraz told BBC Sport before this week's Laver Cup in London. "I suffered, but I enjoyed and that's why I smiled when I walked out of the court because I missed that feeling." This video can not be played Sinner says Alcaraz has 'pushed' him to be better The match against Shelton was the latest finish in the tournament's history, and was one of several matches at Flushing Meadows to finish in the early hours. Eventual champion Alexander Zverev finished past 1am in three of his first five matches, while Venus Williams finished her first-round match at 2am. "I think it's too much," Alcaraz said of playing so late. "The last match people stayed but if that match was played earlier, the court could have been packed. "I would like to change the schedule a little with a maximum finish at 11pm or whatever would be better." Alcaraz, 23, is one of a number of players to have missed large chunks of the season with injury. Britain's Jack Draper has had a lengthy struggle with an arm injury, ultimately ending his season early to recover, while Alcaraz's rival Jannik Sinner missed the US Open with a knee injury. The Spaniard said at the US Open that he will miss some tournaments in the future to allow himself to be "mentally and physically healthy". He will compete for Team Europe in the Laver Cup at The O2 in London this week, between 25-27 September. The team tournament pits Europe - captained by Yannick Noah - against a United States team overseen by Andre Agassi. "When you have your team-mates, the best in the world, by your side, it's a weird feeling but it's beautiful," Alcaraz said. "We played like our lives depend on it. That's why the Laver Cup is so good to watch as well." Alcaraz and Italy's Sinner split eight Grand Slam titles between them from 2024 and 2025, establishing a generational rivalry in the process. They have only met once this year because of injuries, with Sinner winning their sole meeting in the Monte Carlo Masters final to become world number one. "I have text him not too much, but a few times when he has been winning everything, mostly at the beginning of the year," Alcaraz added. "I miss him, I miss seeing him around, playing against him. He pushes me to be a better player. "People will be waiting for those matches, so I think it's going to be better." title: Teen rocker Nene Royal becomes first Thai to win America's Got Talent
description: Her heavy metal performance trumped nine other finalists, including magicians and even a robot crew.
body: Nene emerged as a clear fan favourite early in the competition Nene Royal, a 16-year-old rocker, has been crowned the latest winner of America's Got Talent - making her the first ever Thai winner of the long-running talent show. For the show's finals on Tuesday in California, Nene, whose real name is Rattikarn Amloy, performed a rendition of Seven Nation Army by American rock duo The White Stripes. Her heavy metal performances trumped nine other finalists, including magician acts, canine performers and even a robot dance crew. Many in Thailand are celebrating her win, with some saying they were proud that she had made it to "one of the biggest stages in the world". The Thai government has called her an "inspiration to anyone who dares to dream big". Nene emerged as a clear fan favourite early in the competition, after a viral clip of her audition, in which she belted out Zombie by The Cranberries to a stunned panel of judges. The video has racked up 20 million views. On Wednesday night, ahead of the results being announced, Nene took the stage with Linkin Park to perform The Emptiness Machine, a 2024 rock song by the American band. Later that night she broke down in tears, kneeling on the ground as she was crowned the winner of the show's 21st season - which comes with a prize of $1m (£755,000). "I'm very happy and emotional right now," she said, thanking everyone for supporting her. The results show was also eagerly followed by her legion of fans in Thailand, who were unable to watch the live broadcast on the television network NBC. Many in Thailand had to resort to a YouTube livestream instead - and were thrown into distress when the livestream was abruptly cut in the middle of the results announcements. But moments later came sighs of relief and exclamations of joy, as word got around that Nene had secured her historic victory. "History made!" one Thai social media user wrote on Facebook. "Let the world write it down that this Thai kid is incredibly talented," wrote another. Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul congratulated Nene Royal, saying in a statement that she had "brought honour to Thailand" and "instilled pride in the Thai people" with her win. "What makes this win special is that Nene carried her Thai identity with confidence onto one of the world's biggest stages," the Thai government's public relations department said in another statement on Thursday. "She showed that talent, hard work, and determination can come from anywhere, including a young girl from Phuket with a guitar and a big dream." Nene Royal, 16, went viral for her heavy metal performances According to Nene, she started playing the guitar when she was seven years old and harboured dreams of becoming a touring musician. In her hometown of Phuket, a tourist hub known for its beaches and seaside resorts, Nene was known to busk at Naka Weekend Market. Piyarat Na Songkhla, 43, tour guide in Phuket, tells the BBC that he has seen Nene Royal perform since she was young. "She's so adorable," he says. "I feel so elated and happy for her. It's unbelievable that she has gone this far. So proud of her." The Facebook account of Naka Weekend Market posted a tribute to Nene after her victory. "Everyone at Naka Market is so proud to see you shine on one of the biggest stages in the world," its post reads. "Your talent, heart, and courage have inspired so many people, and this victory is a beautiful reminder of what can happen when someone truly gives everything to their dream." Kajonkiet International School in Phuket, where Nene studies, also congratulated her on the win. "We are so proud of you," reads a Facebook post from the school, which posted a video of its students and staff gathering to watch Nene's final performance, screaming and chanting her name. title: Harry Potter play producer says cost of living made two-part show 'impossible'
description: The London production, which has been running for 10 years, will reopen next month as a one-part show.
body: A Harry Potter And The Cursed Child producer has said the rising cost of living made it "literally impossible" to retain the play's original format in two parts. The production has been cut down to a single three-hour show and is set to re-open in the West End next month. "The cost of living has gone up 30-40% since the pandemic, including running shows," producer Sonia Friedman said in comments reported by media at a launch event. "The only way we could continue to run it as a two-parter would be by charging an amount for the tickets that would be unaffordable and inaccessible." The two-part play, a sequel to JK Rowling's books, premiered in the West End in 2016 and closed on 20 September. The changes to the West End production follow the 2021 relaunch of the play as a single show on Broadway in New York City. "The pandemic, the cost of living and the wars going on around the world accelerated that decision in New York, and that's where we are now with London," Friedman said. "Of course we'll miss it but it was absolutely the right call and we've got a beautiful alternate version that we're very proud of." Director John Tiffany said at the launch event that he and writer Jack Thorne - who also wrote acclaimed Netflix series Adolescence - had to be "dragged, kicking and screaming to make the one-parter" due to the success of their original script, the Times reported. However, Tiffany said the new version meant "more people are going to get to see this show and not have to pay a fortune for it", according to The Stage. The play takes place 19 years after the final book and follows Harry's son Albus Severus as he arrives at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry. The production has been seen by more than 14 million people around the world, including over 2.5 million in London. The reimagined one-part production will retain some of its original cast, including David Ricardo-Pearce as Harry Potter, Thomas Aldridge as Ron Weasley and Naana Agyei Ampadu as Hermione Granger. New actors have been cast in the roles of Albus Potter, Ginny Potter, Rose Granger-Weasley, Draco Malfoy and Scorpius Malfoy. title: 'I can't see it stopping' - Middlesbrough's young men discuss gangs after A66 crash
description: Last month's deadly A66 crash shone a light on organised crime and opportunities for young people in Middlesbrough.
body: Dylan says "no one's got the answer" to organised crime in Middlesbrough Inside Hemlington Boxing Club in Middlesbrough, music is drowned out by the sound of gloves hitting pads. For young men here, nights in the ring are far better than the alternative. Because outside, away from the bright lights of the gym, riders wearing balaclavas roar past on quad bikes in the darkness. "You see it all the time," says Dylan, a 20-year-old who trains at the club. "But I just can't see it stopping. The police can't really do much against it." Attention has turned to organised crime in Middlesbrough since seven people, including two police officers, were killed last month in a crash. A Volkswagen Passat that had been pursued by officers travelled the wrong way along the A66 and collided head-on with a police car. For young men like Dylan, who knew one of the lads killed, there are worries about how easy it is to get sucked into a criminal way of life. "You could walk around the corner and there's just a gang of lads stood there and they shout you over," he says. Dylan and other boxers tell BBC Newsbeat they blame a lack of safe activities and opportunities for young people in the area. He says getting into the sport has kept them away from gangs on the streets. "It stops you going down these bad tracks of crime, drugs, and what most of the lads my age are doing," he says. "It's just not something I want to be involved in, really," says Dylan. "I don't think anyone would, but some people just get forced down these routes." Some of the lads at the boxing club had gone to school with men who died in the A66 crash In a report published last month, external, the Centre for Social Justice found that north-east England has the highest rate of NEETs in the UK. About one in five 16 to 24-year olds from the region is not in education, employment or training. Dylan works as a joiner and says he's lucky to have found a job that "keeps you busy and keeps your brain active". "I think that's where it's going wrong, because people haven't got anything to do," he says. "So they go into [crime], and it just spirals from there. "I wish it would all stop, but it's not going to because no-one's got the answer for it." BBC Newsbeat - Bikes and Balaclavas A month after the A66 crash that killed five young men and two police officers, BBC Newsbeat heads to a boxing club in Middlesbrough to hear what life is like in the area. Listen on BBC Sounds or on Radio 1 at 12:45 and 17:45 BST. Michael Cahill, 23, Jakub Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae and Cole Worthy, both 17, were killed in the crash, as were PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, who were in the police car. Of the men in the Passat, only Michael Cahill had no convictions. The other four had 30 between them for crimes including car theft, drug possession, assaulting police officers and driving offences. After the crash, the prime minister called on social media companies to take down posts celebrating dangerous driving. TikTok posts from an account thought to belong to Makai Saddington had appeared to share this type of content. Louis has dreams of pursuing sport as a career once he finishes college Louis, 16, who also trains at Hemlington, says similar clips pop up "everywhere" on his own feeds. "I've seen quite a few videos on driving cars at high speeds," he says. "I just don't think it's cool." He says he'd known Theo Rae since the two were at primary school, and was shocked by news of the fatal crash. Louis says the boxing gym gives him somewhere safe to spend his time, instead of chasing an adrenaline rush from breaking the law. He wants more people to have access to "sports, or something they enjoy which isn't doing dangerous stuff". Alex says he trusts police "to an extent" but crime has given Middlesbrough a bad reputation Alex, 21, has been training at Hemlington for just over two years. "If I wasn't here I'd just be out with my mates, or I'd just be sat at home doing nothing," he says. For Alex, it's not hard to see how others end up spending their time out in the streets. "Realistically, what are you going to do on a night?" he says. "There's nothing to do. Everyone's just out and about, especially the kids." Alex says crime has become "normal" in the area. "You can't hide from it," he says. "People find it a game almost, recording things for TikTok. It's a 'catch me if you can'." Since the A66 crash, Alex says, his family has been telling him to "get out" of the area. "You hear nothing good from Middlesbrough any more," he says. "It's just got a bad reputation. "I wouldn't want to bring my kids up round here with all the stuff that's going on". James says the gym is very important for the community and "keeps people out of trouble" James, 24, who recently moved away to Peterlee, about an hour's bus ride north, says he used to see "quite a lot" of gang activity. "It might be drugs or knife crime or little petty things," he says. Cleveland Police has been criticised since the crash, and some residents previously told the BBC they'd "rather die" than dial 999 because their trust in the force was so low. James and the other boxers who speak to Newsbeat take a more balanced view when it comes to the police, but agree more work is needed to improve relations. The authorities need to "get to know the people more, understand the people more" to build trust, says James. "I think the moment you relate to people, that's the moment you've opened the door to getting people's trust." Cleveland Police Chief Constable Victoria Fuller tells Newsbeat the aftermath of the A66 crash has been hard for the force, with "an incredible amount of grief" for the two officers who died. title: Judge temporarily overturns Trump's White House media ban
description: A court has ordered the US government to reinstate access to the building for CNN, Politico and MS NOW.
body: A judge has ordered the White House to immediately reinstate press access for three news organisations barred from the building last week by US President Donald Trump. A District of Columbia court issued a temporary restraining order against the ban, meaning CNN, MS NOW and Politico must have their access restored for 14 days. The three outlets had launched a legal challenge which called the ban unconstitutional after their reporters had their hard passes for the White House confiscated and were denied access. The Trump administration sought to defend the move in court, accusing the outlets of publishing false information and threatening national security - an argument the court rejected. The White House is yet to comment on the ruling, and lawyers acting for the president may choose to take further legal action. Judge Timothy Kelly ruled CNN, Politico and MS NOW were "likely to succeed" in showing the White House had not exercised "adequate due process" in implementing the ban. He also cast doubt on the Trump administration's arguments that the bans were motivated by national security concerns, pointing out the president made no mention of that in his initial announcement. The ruling continued: "The record lacks factual support for Defendants' contention that the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes will in fact protect national security or that national security will be endangered if the Court orders their passes reinstated while this litigation proceeds." What is the White House pool and why is it in a row with Trump? title: Corrie Mckeague's mum: 'We did all we could to find him'
description: Nicola Urquhart speaks to the BBC on the 10th anniversary of her 23-year-old son's disappearance.
body: Nicola Urquhart spoke to the BBC for the 10th anniversary of the disappearance of her son, Corrie Mckeague "We definitely did all we could and I can honestly sleep at night knowing there was nothing I physically could have done any different." It is 10 years since Nicola Urquhart's son, Corrie Mckeague, disappeared on 24 September 2016 after a night out in Bury St Edmunds, Suffolk. For the months and years that followed, she embodied a mother's love and determination to find the truth: to never give up. The RAF gunner's body has never been found but he was officially declared dead in 2022, when an inquest ruled he had died after climbing into a commercial waste bin before it was tipped into a waste lorry. Nicola is composed and reflective as she recalls when her son went missing. He had just turned 23 and within months would become a dad. She says her son would be forever in her thoughts, but adds: "I've given myself closure; my son is dead." She spoke to the BBC after what would have been Corrie's 33rd birthday and ahead of the 10th anniversary of his disappearance. She says she last saw her son when she went for a birthday meal with him at Cheers in Bury St Edmunds, adding he was a "social hand grenade" who "really did live every moment at a hundred miles an hour". A decade on, she says there is "never an end" to losing somebody but it is about "managing each day". Nicola says she "definitely wouldn't have got through" the loss of her son Corrie without the support of her family "Every time I drive up a road, as I'm driving I still look at the verges, I can't stop myself," says Nicola. "The anniversary is difficult, but we will still try to be positive about it and the universe makes us remember it and generally in a really nice way. "We are fine, but that is a conscious, deliberate effort to be fine because it would be a disservice to his memory if we just shut down and didn't make the best of our lives. "In every single way that you can think, there is not one day, one decision, that doesn't go by without Corrie being at the forefront of it," she adds. The Horseshoe area where Corrie vanished was surrounded by food outlets such as Greggs and McDonald's Airman Corrie, who was based at RAF Honington in Suffolk, had enjoyed a night out drinking when he was thrown out of a nightclub and became separated from his friends. He then went to buy burgers, a kebab and chips, with CCTV captured at 01:20 BST showing him clutching a takeaway as he staggered through the town. After sleeping in a shop doorway for an hour, Corrie disappeared from the view of cameras on Brentgovel Street at 03:25 into an area known as the Horseshoe. He was never seen again. What followed was a huge search and rescue mission, which cost Suffolk Police more than £2m, captivated the country and fuelled conspiracy theorists. It culminated in the excavation of a landfill site at Milton, Cambridgeshire, which lasted several months but found nothing. The moment Corrie walked into an area in central Bury St Edmunds known as the Horseshoe. He was never seen again On 22 March 2022, after nearly six years of speculation, inquest jurors provided an explanation for Corrie's disappearance. Delivering a narrative conclusion they said he died at about 04:20 BST as a result of "compression asphyxia in association with multiple injuries". These injuries, they ruled, were suffered after Corrie, from Dunfermline, Fife, had climbed into a commercial waste bin - something he had used before as somewhere to sleep - before it was tipped into a refuse truck. During the inquest, Suffolk Coroner's Court heard that 30 tonnes of force was exerted during each compaction cycle in the back of a bin lorry and so the chances of someone surviving were "slim". Corrie with his girlfriend, April Oliver, with whom he had a daughter, Ellie While Nicola, a former Police Scotland sergeant, accepts the final judgement, she says only she could truly decide when she could achieve a sense of closure. "No one thing externally can give me closure. The only thing that can give me closure is myself saying, have I done everything I can?" she says. "We definitely did all we could and I can honestly sleep at night knowing there was nothing I physically could have done any different." RAF airman Corrie was said to be a "heavy sleeper when drunk" Corrie's nine-year-old daughter Ellie, who was born nine months after he went missing, has also been a blessing, Nicola says. She adds her son lives on through her "lovely, happy and well-behaved" granddaughter. "She's just like her dad, it's frightening; she looks so much like him, she's got his mannerisms, she's adorable, athletic, sporty," she says. "It's so lovely having a little mini Corrie to remind us of him, she is the very best of him, and she's a very lucky little girl, in some respects, with the family that she's got. "It is fantastic having Ellie in our lives - it genuinely is just a little bit of Corrie." Corrie's mum never gave up in the search for her son Nicola says Corrie's family are doing "so many little things" to ensure Ellie is constantly reminded of her dad in the best and most "positive way". They include going to the Cenotaph in London on Remembrance Day every year and enjoying her dad's favourite activities, such as going to watch Wicked the Musical. One day, Nicola adds, Ellie will be presented with a special gift that once belonged to her car-loving dad Corrie. "[Corrie's brother] Darroch got his MG car that was on the base and spent a lot of time trying to get the car back on the road again," adds Nicola, who lives in Scotland. "The car is going to Ellie - whether it will still be running when she can drive, I do not know, but she's going to be the one that has his car. "She's got a father figure, who is her dad, and he's fantastic, but she also knows exactly who

title: Food banks 'in crisis' amid fears some may have to close
description: According to the Trussell Trust, an anti-poverty charity, some food banks are having pay for 30-50% of the food they are supplying.
body: Paul Dickson is project manager of the Enniskillen Food bank The manager of a food bank in County Fermanagh has said they have enough money for "two months of running costs" before they run out, while another one in West Belfast, has had to "significantly reduce" the sizes of their parcels. According to the Trussell Trust, an anti-poverty charity, some food banks are having pay for 30-50% of the food they are supplying. Enniskillen Foodbank said their "ongoing expenses are continuing and donations are not keeping pace" with project manager Paul Dickson describing it as it a "bleak situation". Edel Diamond from South-West Belfast Foodbank on the Stewartstown Road said they are struggling with stock which is "really upsetting because you've got families coming to you that aren't really coping". Enniskillen Foodbank is part of the Trussell Trust network which can provide support for another three months. "That isn't enough to last a year," Dickson told Radio Ulster's Evening Extra programme. "It's brilliant to get that [support from the trust] but...we need to create network of relationships locally that help make foodbanks sustainable." Food banks in critical need He added that he noticed a drop in donations given to supermarkets but understood that things are becoming more expensive. "Part of the Trussell ethos is that we don't believe that we should be needed, but unfortunately, we are needed at the minute and we need to be here for the people that rely on us." Edel Diamond runs a foodbank on Stewartstown road in west Belfast Edel Diamond said that while she is thankful they are not having to turn people away, it was distressing. "It seems to me like one cost-of-living crisis is just rolling into another and it doesn't seem to have gone away," she said. She added that the rising energy costs have a knock-on effect on charities. "We're not just a food bank, we are places of comfort for people, places where people can come and find that hope," Diamond said. "We want to see the end for the need for food banks, but at this immediate time we are in crisis and we're urgently appealing for donations of food and finance." Fiona Cole, from Trussell Trust in Northern Ireland said it was "heartbreaking" to see food banks in this situation, adding the stress on food bank managers and volunteers is increasing on a daily basis. According to the Trussell Trust, 67,851 parcels were distributed in Northern Ireland, 26,459 of those given to children in 2025. The policy and public affairs manager said in the last four to six weeks food banks have faced a crisis in terms of stock levels. "Our biggest fear is that our food banks are prematurely forced to drastically reduce their support, or worse, close their doors because the income they receive falls short and they can no longer afford their household essentials," Cole said. She said that fewer donations could be a result of people struggling with cost of living and having to cut their own budgets. "Our lifelong contributors, they would give us five pounds of food or £10 of food every time they go to shop in a supermarket," Cole said. "That £10 of food is just simply not the same amount as what you would have got even six months ago." She said three food banks had contacted them directly about concerns with stock and finance, and six in total had to put out emergency appeals for donations on social media. She added food banks have also had to close distribution centres or reduce their hours. Cole said there needs to be sustainable funding for food banks to operate as well as support from government and the Northern Assembly. While food banks are under pressure a Trussell Trust report found that they had been distributing fewer parcels in 2025 than the peak seen in 2023. "Wider data suggests there has been a corresponding fall in need for food banks, not just use, external". title: Why this break has come at the worst time for De Zerbi & Spurs
description: BBC Sport columnist Tony Pulis explains the different factors that mean Tottenham boss Roberto de Zerbi needs time with his players to build a proper team.
body: Big spending always means big ambitions, but shelling out so much money on so many players the way Tottenham did this summer produces problems for any manager, and there is no quick fix. If I was given a bundle of cash and asked to buy an outfit for a wedding, and I spent every penny of it on pink shoes, brown trousers, yellow shirt and orange tie, then I am sure you would all say that just doesn't work. That is similar to what has happened at Spurs, where the board backed Roberto de Zerbi to the hilt with an outlay on new players of around £400m. It was an almost unprecedented occurrence from a club that has always been renowned for being careful with investment in their team, and it sent expectations from many Spurs supporters through the roof. The club had just avoided relegation two seasons running, finishing 17th twice in a row, but suddenly some fans were looking forward to a season competing for trophies and a top-four finish. Their early results and performances have been disappointing, of course, but fans have to understand all the different factors that affect you when you are building a team - and it is ridiculous to suggest De Zerbi should be under pressure already, especially after he kept them up last season. De Zerbi (left) took over as Spurs boss with seven games to go last season and the club 17th in the Premier League. Three wins and two draws were enough to keep them up Finding a way for your club to win takes a manager in lots of different directions but they all involve time - on the grass or with social interaction with the players. Not only has De Zerbi not been given that early time and opportunity, the majority of his players have now been taken away from him for another three weeks on international duty. De Zerbi has many other issues to deal with, from Tottenham's poor home form to their inability to recover from conceding the first goal in games. But his biggest challenge right now will be to fit those players who have just arrived in with the ones already at the club, into a unit that plays as a team and produces results so that the money the club has spent is justified. All of this will take time, and patience, and all the kinds of little detail that supporters never see. In my day, we were given time to create a team, and a family. For today's managers, time seems more limited than ever. We are only five games into the season but there are already some Spurs fans who seem to think De Zerbi is the worst manager in the world, even though he has proved elsewhere how good he is. I like De Zerbi's passion, and his approach. That will count for nothing if Spurs don't eventually produce, but let's give him a proper chance. Spurs, Fulham and Bournemouth are the only top-flight teams yet to win a league game this season De Zerbi is a very passionate, straight-talking and ambitious manager who demands total commitment and backing from his board. He has definitely had that at Spurs, which has left people wondering why he has made such a slow start. But, before the season started, I thought his biggest challenge with so many different types of players arriving would be to put players together that fit as a team, not as a group of individuals. I've been in that situation myself, for example in my early days at Stoke, when I signed Gerry Taggart and Michael Duberry to play together, two centre-halves who were complete opposites in relation to how they dealt with space on the pitch. Gerry always wanted to drop off deeper because he wasn't overly quick, whereas Michael was fast and didn't ever worry about leaving space behind him. I couldn't make Gerry any quicker, so common sense locked in and I had to convince Michael that he would have to take a step away from his main strengths of pace and power and work along Gerry's lines instead. We spent a great deal of time on the grass in training until we finally got both working in unison. Both were different, but they understood the importance of working together as a pair for the benefit of the team. Even so, it still took time for it to click. For any manager trying to build a successful team by developing combinations like that, the main thing you need is time with your players. It can happen where a lot of new players settle in quickly at the same time and the team starts well - like Sunderland last season, or Brighton pretty much every year when they have lost several key players - but the difference is that while those clubs might also have changed their manager, they have not changed their identity. Whether it is Sunderland and Brighton, or Brentford and Bournemouth, they all have a set identity so that when they look for a player to fit in a certain position, he has to have certain strengths. When you don't have that solid base behind you, knowing exactly what is needed for certain positions, then bringing 10 new signings and all in one window like Spurs have just done, is going to create many issues for the coach. Each player has a different personality and needs different amount of time to settle in, not only to a new environment but also to adjust to the demands of a very single-minded and demanding coach like De Zerbi is. This settling-in period would have been covered if all the players had had a pre-season together, to get up to speed with their team-mates and what De Zerbi is asking of them, with his front-foot style of play. That did not happen, and then even after the season started, Spurs were still adding to their squad. This video can not be played Roberto de Zerbi interviewed after Spurs' 3-2 home loss to Aston Villa Coaching a team to be a team takes time, patience and a sound idea of the strengths of all your players. Even when you have got that, trying to knit every player together takes time, and that is still De Zerbi's issue now. For starters, he was always playing catch-up. description: The BBC’s North America technology correspondent Lily Jamali explains how the Medicare breach happened, and why it matters.
body: This video can not be played A rogue OpenAI agent has hacked an Australian government website, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said. The agent hacked a statistics portal containing private data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme, Medicare. title: 'I knew something was wrong when my baby's head was too big'
description: Nancy had to have major surgery after her parents noticed her head was too big for her body.
body: Nancy needed surgery for sagittal craniosynostosis, a rare condition in which the head becomes egg-shaped Not long after Bethany Hardy's daughter was born, she felt something was wrong with her new baby. Nancy's head was a strange shape and much larger than her body, and she struggled to lift it. By the time she was nine months, her parents, from Leeds, were seriously worried about their child. Nancy was a year old when she was eventually diagnosed with sagittal craniosynostosis, a rare condition where the skull does not grow properly - but the delay meant she had to undergo more invasive surgery. She had six operations, including blood transfusions and a skin graft, and spent a month in hospital - but Bethany believes if she had been diagnosed sooner, the treatment would have been less traumatic. Recalling the first few months after Nancy's birth, Bethany says: "She really struggled lifting her head, tummy time, that kind of stuff, because her head was a lot larger than her body. "By nine months her head was on the 98th percentile but her body was on the 24th, which straight away kind of rings alarm bells because they should all be in line." Nancy was referred for an X-ray, but her parents instead decided to book a private consultation at Great Ormond Street Hospital in London. Specialists were able to identify Nancy's condition, which is caused by parts of the skull fusing together before birth, merely by visual observation and she was then offered reconstructive surgery on the NHS. Before the surgery, Nancy's parents noticed her unusually-shaped head "Her head could only grow forwards and backwards, it wasn't circular like a brain, so they put part of the skull at the side to make her a more normal-shaped head," explains Bethany. Her daughter needed further surgery after she developed an infection. After surgery, Nancy developed an infection and needed six operations, blood transfusions and a skin graft An earlier diagnosis would have made her treatment more straightforward, Bethany, from Yeadon, believes. "If she was diagnosed before six months, she could've had small surgery, 45 minutes to an hour, which is still heartbreaking as a parent and you don't want to go through, but it's nothing compared to what she has been through." Nancy is now home and recovering well with mother Bethany Nancy, now two, is now recovering well at home but still bears physical and mental scars from her long stay in hospital. The family are now raising awareness of craniosynostosis and its signs, and promoting the importance of early diagnosis and intervention. "She goes to ballet classes and when they give stickers at the end, she can't take them because it reminds her of that. She sees people in blue and she's terrified, she's damaged from all of it. "But she's an amazing little girl and she's happy." Listen to highlights from West Yorkshire on BBC Sounds, catch up with the latest episode of Look North. title: Debbie Beard and Amanda Thorpe lost their husbands - this is their story
description: Debbie Beard and Amanda Thorpe speak to the BBC's Simon Jack at the launch of a new suicide prevention toolkit.
body: This video can not be played Debbie Beard and Amanda Thorpe on the loss of their husbands Warning: This story contains discussion of suicide and information some readers may find distressing Where do they even begin? Two women, united in grief, are meeting for the first time. Debbie Beard lost her husband just over a year ago. Matt Beard, the former Liverpool Women manager, died in hospital on 20 September 2025. He is believed to have taken his own life, though an inquest is yet to conclude. Amanda Thorpe's husband Graham, the former England and Surrey cricketer, took his own life in 2024. He had "spiralled into depression" after losing his job as a batting coach in 2022. The two women, who had never met before, came together at an event launched by the Prince of Wales and the Royal Foundation to urge sport at every level to make suicide prevention part of its culture through a new nationwide toolkit. There they spoke to the BBC's business editor Simon Jack, who was 17 when his father took his own life. On Your Side, external is a set of resources available online that aims "to make suicide prevention as much a part of sport as warm-up, training and performance". Former England international Graham Thorpe took his own life in 2024 after suffering from depression and anxiety Amanda Thorpe has said previously she believes her husband would still be alive had he received more support from the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) after leaving his coaching role. Following the inquest into his death, the ECB said it was "a profound tragedy" and added Thorpe's passing was a "stark reminder" of the challenges many face with mental health. Matt Beard died a month after leaving his role as manager of Burnley Women. He had been in the post for only two months. When the inquest into his death was postponed indefinitely, Burnley said they were "aware of an ongoing legal process" and would "not be making any comment at this time". Amanda: "Graham had been struggling for the previous year to 18 months during Covid. Graham didn't really like following rules and there were quite a few in Covid - like playing under bubble conditions. So he had been having some medication and therapy in his job. But then Graham lost his job and he didn't see it coming. "He did pride himself with having been in the game his whole life. He just couldn't believe that he was blindsided by it. "I think at least two other people were sacked at the same time, which does happen at the end of disastrous Ashes series. "Also he was probably drinking too much and found the whole of the last trip in Covid very stressful. He then took a playful video at the end of the tour, when they had a few drinks with the opposition. One of the players sent it to two friends and someone unfortunately leaked it, so it was in the Sydney Morning Herald." Simon: "Going for a few drinks with the opposition - you would think that that happens in sport all the time, but they lost?" Amanda: "Yes. It's OK if you win but you're not allowed to have a drink if you lose. He was probably in shock. He couldn't believe it. And he was embarrassed and ashamed about this stupid video, which to me he blew way out of proportion. But he was in this tunnel where he thought he'd messed it all up. So he went into a quick and steep decline." Simon: "During that period, what could have been done? You said that he was seeking some help. What might have made a difference, do you think?" Amanda: "He was having therapy sessions. He had 10 sessions. There's obviously the confidentiality but I found out after he made a very serious attempt on his life, when he really hurt himself very badly, that he'd mentioned suicide. I didn't know about that at the time. Of course, I feel that if I'd known, things could have been different. And I did feel that he wasn't really getting better. It was difficult. I felt like maybe he did need more help - maybe residential but we didn't really know where to find that." Simon: "Debbie, Matt also lost his job..." Simon: "Were there any signs that he was struggling with mental health, and then was there a steep decline afterwards?" Debbie: "I think there were changes in behaviour, looking back. Performance-wise the team weren't doing well so there was a lot of abuse on social media. He could never really speak his truth during media interviews of what was going on behind the scenes and he used to sound off to me at home. "I've found out since that he had spoken to his brother quite a lot about his mental health. But whenever I would say to Matt 'how are things?', he'd be, 'I'm all right, I'm all right', because he always wanted the best for other people. "He didn't want to concern me and the family that he was having these thoughts and that he was going through these different struggles. "The sacking came out of the blue and there was a lot of speculation around that. He was starting to drink more than he would have done normally. In terms of his behaviour, I would say he was taking a lot of risks as well. So maybe that was the start of this with him." Amanda: "Graham was known as a tough competitor. He was a very happy person and loved life, but it can happen to anyone. He wasn't thinking straight really because everything kind of became a vortex. And he just sort of lost the ability to be able to be grounded and think straight. Also you think you're thinking straight when you're not." Simon: "One of the things about sport that's been discussed is that its reach is enormous. Coaches have a very intimate and closely proximate relationship with people. They can see what's going on with them - even at grassroots level. What would you encourage people to do if they see other people struggling, either in their family or in their community?" title: Police arrest 36 in raids on Vietnamese crime gangs linked to human trafficking
description: About 300 officers took part in simultaneous early-morning raids at 47 sites across Scotland.
body: One of the targeted sites was a nail salon in Glasgow One of Scotland's biggest ever police operations has targeted a Vietnamese organised crime group linked to human trafficking and cannabis farms. About 300 officers took part in simultaneous early-morning raids, leading to the arrest of 36 people and the discovery of 14 cannabis-growing operations. In total, police searched or checked 47 addresses in Aberdeen, Dundee, Falkirk, Edinburgh, Glasgow, Ayrshire, Lanarkshire, Midlothian and the Scottish Borders. Police Scotland allege the gang is involved in "poly-criminality," including human trafficking, drug production, fraud, money laundering and organised immigration crime. The force says the activities first came to light after Vietnamese criminals were connected to 150 cannabis farms discovered in Scotland last year. Around 120 people had been arrested - so-called "gardeners"- and drugs worth £26m were seized. Six men to stand trial over £7m cannabis farm in former school Two jailed after police raid on £525,000 cannabis farm Subsequent inquiries linked a single Vietnamese crime group to about a third of the farms, with months of planning leading up to Wednesday's raids. Det Supt Stevie Bertram said: "This was by far the biggest human trafficking investigation that Police Scotland has ever run. "We wanted to disrupt and absolutely cripple that organisation. "We wanted to do it all in one day and I think it's been a huge success. Essentially, they won't be able to function. "All of the targets of this operation have been arrested and they are the ones we believe are running that operation." Cannabis plants were found inside a flat in Edinburgh's South Clerk Street Police Scotland officers arrested individuals in Birmingham as part of Wednesday's enforcement action, which was carried out with support from Home Office Immigration Enforcement and His Majesty's Revenue and Customs. "We think the group runs across the UK and internationally," said Bertram. "We've met with regional crime teams from up and down England and Wales and Ireland, to look at what's happening across the country." Officers from the National Crime Agency based in Hanoi have been liaising with the authorities in Vietnam. A large number of plants were found in a raid in Dundee The addresses raided by the police included a tenement flat in Edinburgh's South Clerk Street, a five-minute walk from one of the capital's busiest police stations. Three rooms were crammed with plants growing behind tarpaulin screens under bright lights. A box of seedlings was discovered in the kitchen. There were signs of occupation, though no-one was in the flat when the police forced entry. In Dundee, a cannabis operation discovered in two neighbouring flats had been extended into a shared loft. The police will now try to establish whether the people arrested include victims of human trafficking. "Vietnamese nationals are still the highest nationality that we see being exploited in Scotland" said Bertram. "A lot of hard work and investigation will go on from today. "We'll examine mobiles, data, paperwork to make sure that if there is a victim of human trafficking, they're quickly identified as a victim." title: The chef turned award-winning author unfazed by 'second book syndrome'
description: Louise Kennedy, the author of Trespasses, says everyone "should give anything they fancy a lash".
body: Louise Kennedy, author of Trespasses, attends The Women's Prize For Fiction Awards in 2023 When your award-winning debut novel is adapted into a Bafta-nominated TV series expectations run high for what might come next. But Louise Kennedy, the author of Trespasses, seems unfazed with the daunting notion of what is often called second book syndrome. Maybe it's her late entrance to the literary world, working in busy kitchens as a chef for decades or dealing with a cancer diagnosis that helps Kennedy cope with pressure. She says she "could very easily never have written a word" and continued her career as a chef. "I'm sure my life wouldn't have been thoroughly miserable," she adds with a half smile. But in 2014, aged 47, a friend asked her to join a writing group. "I had never written in my life. I had no ambition to write. It never entered my head." At first it was short stories, then came Trespasses in 2022. Set during the Troubles in Northern Ireland it was a story of cross-community forbidden love between a young Catholic teacher and a married Protestant barrister. Kennedy's second novel is Stations, currently being serialised on BBC Radio 4, the reader meets Róisín and Red, following their friendship from rural Ireland to London, full of teenage angst, fragile friendships and the romance of escape. "I knew that there were going to be readers for Stations, but I could only write the book that I wanted to write," she tells BBC News. Their story starts in County Kildare in 1982 and follows them for the next 25 years as Róisín follows Red to London. Kennedy describes her relationship with Róisín, as "unfinished business" as the lead character is the same unsympathetic teenager from her 2021 collections of short stories The End of the World is a Cul-de-sac. Kennedy goes to great pains to declare that Róisín isn't her and she's not Róisín, "but there are similarities". Kennedy and her family left Northern Ireland when she was 12 in the 1970s and relocated to the Republic of Ireland where she found herself an outsider in a small, rural village. "I was a very unpopular, awkward teenager but I'm a good mimic. I thought that all my problems in my new school would be solved if I spoke like everybody else. And I was able to change my accent over a weekend." This accent change is also something Kennedy gifts to Róisín and the book pokes at the very pronunciation of her name, "Rawsheen" in the north, but "Rowsheen" in the south. The decision to sacrifice her Belfast accent is something she regrets. However, she explains that when she is writing her early life experiences resurface. "When I speak, I sound like a free stater, but the voice in my head is really northern." Kennedy, pictured at the Women's Prize for Fiction in 2023, says anyone should "give anything they fancy a lash" The parallels don't end there, as Kennedy, similar to the characters in Stations, also emigrated to England in the 1980s. However, Kennedy moved for economic reasons. "Most of us went to London because you didn't have to get a visa. It was cheap and there was a huge network of people there. "You always knew people, and there were always leads for getting a place in a squat or some horrible flat somewhere." There are about 500,000 Irish-born people living in England today. Since the 1930s, England has been the major focus for Irish migration, with big waves during the 1940s to the 1950s and the Irish recession of the 1980s. However, Kennedy was keenly aware of the generation ahead of her who emigrated in the 1940s and 50s. The women ending up in domestic roles or nursing and the men mostly labouring across building sites unable to settle. She says "we weren't so different". "We were better educated, but we had great expectations and great hopes for ourselves." Gillian Anderson, Tom Cullen and Lola Petticrew starred in the Channel 4 adaptation of Trespasses Last year, Trespasses was turned into a Channel 4 drama, starring Gillian Anderson and Lola Petticrew giving the story a "much longer and bigger life" than Kennedy ever anticipated. So has Kennedy thought about where her new novel could go and who she would cast? The short answer is no. Whilst the book has been auctioned for TV and film adaptation rights, Kennedy is putting no names in the mix. "I kind of sat back a lot with that because I just thought it wouldn't be helpful for me to be asking loads of questions." However, with a sly smile Kennedy confesses that her granny "would have been absolutely tickled pink to think of Gillian Anderson playing her". In Trespasses, Anderson plays the character Gina, who has alcoholism and is the broken mother of Cushla, based on a version of Kennedy's grandmother. "Even as a scruffy Gillian Anderson, she'd have been thrilled." In 2019, Kennedy was diagnosed with melanoma skin cancer, which, over the following years progressed to further discoveries and a stage 4 diagnosis. She googled everything - apart from her prognosis. "I never asked. I never said 'how long have I got if these drugs don't work'," she says. The drugs were successful and after eight months the cancer was gone but there are ongoing health challenges as a result. She has previously praised Trespasses for enabling her to "largely ignore all the health stuff, external" as the writing of it Kennedy told The Times “got her through the first melanoma diagnosis", and its publication, sustained her through its return. It's then not surprising that the acknowledgement in her new novel pays homage to the medical team who continue to look after her and "the legend who figured out how to use Chinese hamster ovary cells against melanoma". "I owe you my life." Kennedy never thought she would "earn any money from writing" but is glad it all worked out. "I'm too old to be a chef. I'll be 60 next year, and my hips - was it Shakira who said that the hips don't lie?" As Kenned

title: I had no heating or electricity for more than two years - now I have a new island home
description: Ruari Morgan is one of the first tenants in a new development of 10 social homes on Rathlin Island.
body: Ruari Morgan is enjoying luxuries such as a hot shower in his new home For the past-two-and-a-half years, some basic home comforts have been hard to come by for Ruari Morgan. A fire in the backup generator of his old stone cottage on Rathlin Island left him without electricity, heating or hot water. Now he's enjoying the simple pleasures of being able to come home and put the kettle on or have a shower after he moved in to a new social home two weeks ago. The development of 10 social houses is the first on the island for more than a decade and it is hoped it will allow the unique community to sustain its population and provide a boost to its economy. Rathlin is a small island off the north east coast of Northern Ireland, between Northern Ireland and Scotland, with a population of about 150 people. Morgan, who was born and bred on the island and returned 15 years ago after living and working abroad, said social housing created more opportunities for islanders to come home. "Obviously the more accommodation and the more affordable accommodation on the island is a good thing," he said. "It's not always about encouraging new people to come to the island - which we do of course - but it's about making life here sustainable for the people who live here and have a connection to the island." Morgan had been on the waiting list for four years before being allocated the property. "I travel quite a lot and I volunteer abroad, but Rathlin's my base, this is my home," he said. "We have a really good community here and it's not only people who have a lifelong connection...it's a nice mix." Marina McMullan said the homes were great news for the island The homes in Church Bay came following a housing needs assessment carried out by the Northern Ireland Housing Executive (NIHE), Rural Housing Association and Rathlin Development Community Association (RDCA). The assessment found there was a need for more social housing to help sustain the island's population. When it came to allocating the homes, NIHE's points-based system was used in conjunction with a local Rathlin lettings policy which included having a connection to the island. Marina McMullan, the chairwoman of RDCA, grew up on the island and also lived and worked elsewhere before coming back. She said the new scheme was vital to help keep the island's community thriving. "It means people can stay here, families can stay here for employment, for school," she said. "Social housing means the cost is not exorbitant, it means families don't have to move away and leave the senior citizens at home. "It's great for the school, it keeps a small community. "Some people have had to leave because of the lack of housing, now hopefully with these houses they'll be able to move back, especially young people with families because that's the future." The new homes have just been completed The assessment was carried out in 2016 and it has been a long road to finally getting the homes completed. The scheme was delivered by Rural Housing Association and the NIHE along with the Department for Communities. The task was not made easier by the logistics of getting workers and building material on to the island, with much of it having to be shipped over on a barge. Both Morgan and McMullan were full of praise for the workers, who they said integrated with community life when they were on site. McMullan said it was important an island like Rathlin was able to keep its way of life. "We're the only island in Northern Ireland with a vibrant population that has been there for generations and there's no reason why we can't be here for future generations," she said. Holly Hartley is originally from Kent but now lives and works on the island One of the newer residents in Rathlin was Holly Hartley. She came to the island just over a year ago to volunteer on the RSPB's Life Raft project to eradicate ferrets. She never left and now works at the Manor House Hotel and the primary school. She said she was pleased more islanders would have an opportunity to access social housing. "It's a really good first step because it allows young families to move in and bring that next generation and I think that's really encouraging," she said. "I know a lot of people who have family members who were born and raised on the island but have had to move away because there's nowhere for them to go. "People might say 'why do you need more houses there's not that many people here'? But the point is it encourages people. "I think if you give people that space to grow naturally they will expand and it just provides a longevity to the island." Does she see herself staying? "It's definitely the kind of place I can see myself staying for a considerable amount of time," she said. "I can open my bedroom curtains and see dolphins out my window, it's so surreal, especially being from Kent where you don't really get much of that." title: Rising fuel costs hitting businesses and customers
description: Business owners say higher fuel costs are creating challenges on several fronts.
body: Flower shop owner Mark Nicholas said fuel costs had affected deliveries Businesses and consumers in a town say soaring fuel prices are having a growing impact on both their day-to-day operations and spending power. Hayle in Cornwall is home to a range of independent businesses that rely on regular deliveries, tourism and customers travelling from across the region. Petrol prices rose to an average of 161.3p per litre between July and August, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), the highest level recorded since November 2022, and diesel is expected to top £2 per litre in the coming days Mark Nicholas, who runs flower shop The Big Pink Tree, said: "The fuel increase has really affected really how far we can deliver to serve our customer base." Surf shop manager Justin Lapskas said fuel costs had an impact on imports More news stories for Cornwall Listen to the latest news for Cornwall Nicholas added: "Because of the increase we've had to pull back slightly from the area that we deliver which upsets me because I can't serve every customer that we used to serve." Local residents said filling up their vehicles was also putting pressure on household finances. One worker drives an eight mile round-trip between Carbis Bay and Hayle every day and said fuel costs had become "extortionate". She said she no longer considered making extra journeys at weekends because of the cost. Emma Crossley said customers have been waiting longer between haircuts Businesses are also seeing wider knock-on effects. Hairdresser Emma Crossley said customers were waiting longer between appointments than they had previously. She said: "Since the fuel prices went up I have noticed a difference in how often people have their hair done. About five years ago it would have been about six or seven weeks - it's more like 10 to 12 weeks now." Tourism operators have also noticed a change. Pauline Ellis of the Mad Hatter bed and breakfast, said some visitors had cancelled trips because travel costs had become too expensive. She said: "We are a long way down here and I think it has made an impact on whether people can afford to come this far down, with the prices as they are." At Down the Line Surf Shop, owner Justin Lapskas said the higher fuel costs affected the import and transportation of products. "We bring in products from around the world, so for us, the increase in fuel prices has an effect and something that we've kind of got to deal with moving forward," he said. "So yeah, I'd say fuel has an impact across the board for us." Follow BBC Cornwall on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to spotlight@bbc.co.uk, external. title: Greens aim for first London MP in Holborn race
description: There are 15 candidates standing in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election on Thursday 8 October.
body: Camden Town is at the heart of Holborn and St Pancras constituency On 8 October, voters in the Holborn and St Pancras constituency will choose their next MP. A win in this seat, which has returned Labour MPs for decades, would be a feather in the cap of the Green Party after Sir Keir Starmer stood down from the House of Commons at the start of September, shortly after leaving office as prime minister. Labour are confident of holding on, but the Greens also have high hopes of winning their first London seat - and there are 13 other candidates in the mix all hoping to take this central London constituency. BBC London spoke to five of the leading candidates. Zack Polanski says people in the constituency want change Zack Polanski, the Green Party candidate, told BBC London he was "feeling confident or I wouldn't have put my hat in the ring in the first place, but I'm not complacent". He said he would "work with the Labour government constructively on the things we agree with". He added: "But where they're letting us down on things like housing, on nationalising Thames Water, on tackling the climate crisis - they're talking about drilling for new oil and gas - voting Green and sending me to Parliament is a way to keep this Labour government in check." Polanski, who is a member of the London Assembly and leader of the Green Party in England and Wales, said people in the constituency "desperately need change". "People are telling me over and over again they can't afford the cost of housing, they need more council housing. "Renters who need rent control, leaseholders who need justice for leaseholders. The government said they'd end this feudal system of leasehold and then haven't taken the action." When asked about the last time he ran in Camden, as a Liberal Democrat candidate for the council, he said: "I think in politics we need less politicians who treat political parties like football teams. "Someone picks a team and they have to stick with it for life no matter what they do. "Actually, there's lots of people including Liberal Democrats in this constituency that will recognise I'm the only person in this constituency who can beat Labour." Sagal Abdi-Wali has been the leader of Camden Council since May Sagal Abdi-Wali, Labour's candidate, said the campaign had been "really good" so far. She told BBC London: "It's quite a big deal politically, absolutely, "Andy Burnham's first by-election, standing against the Green Party leader; yeah, quite a big test for the party... you have the responsibility to deliver." Abdi-Wali, whose family came to London from Somalia as refugees in the 1990s when she was a child, has been the leader of Camden Council since May. She told BBC London: "For me, I'm just so excited. "We've got an opportunity to make sure that we send a Labour member of Parliament that would be really local and really visible and committed to this area, someone who comes from this area. "I grew up in this area my whole life. It's made me, Camden made me who I am, and to be able to now represent us in Parliament will be such a major thing." Abdi-Wali acknowledged there were problems with housing and crime in the constituency. "I want to make sure that particularly with housing, for instance, it's an issue. It's a crisis here in Camden. It's a crisis in London. It's a crisis all over the country and it needs a national response." Abdi-Wali praised the former MP, Sir Keir. "The work that Keir did as the member of Parliament for here for 11 years and before that the 30 years that he gave to social justice. "Now with Andy Burnham, we have an opportunity to really work on a lot of those issues." Reform UK's Peter Newman says voters are worried about crime Peter Newman, the Reform UK candidate, said he served in the Metropolitan Police for 31 years from 1978 to 2009. He told BBC London: "I had a good and varied career, but you know the time has come when, you know, woke leadership was getting too far into the Met." Newman said he was standing because "I couldn't walk by any more". "The chaos of the Conservatives and Labour that have left this country in, I had to do something. "Reform is the only option for the people of Holborn and St Pancras, the only option in fact for the country." He said the party was "picking up votes all the time in local elections". "We're improving our percentages in London all the time, and we've got a tough election. And the people of Holborn and St Pancras, they want change. "They've been let down by Keir Starmer, who clearly used it as a stepping stone just to become prime minister." He says on the doorstep, voters are telling him "they're fed up with the crime, disorder. This borough is crime-ridden. It's soaked in crime." If elected, Newman said he would be "relentless in pursuing the police chiefs and the mayor of London and his policing advisers in finding out what's gone wrong with policing in London". Liberal Democrat candidate Patrick Stillman says the party are community champions Lib Dem candidate Patrick Stillman said his party's ground game in the by-election was helping it reintroduce itself. He told BBC London: "We've got a really good liberal message: we care about the things you care about, and we're going to work really hard for you." Stillman is a Camden councillor, representing West Hampstead in the north of the borough. The party led a joint Conservative-Lib Dem administration when the council was under no overall control from 2006 to 2010. He said the by-election "is our opportunity really to sort of re-represent ourselves and say, 'Actually, you know, look at the great work our team are doing, look at the great things we're saying in Parliament - wouldn't you like a bit of that here?'" title: Rise in 'commuter students' due to living costs
description: Some young people are staying at home while attending university as they cannot afford to move.
body: Bethany Fearne, a law student, said she was still involved in university activities such as the Colour Run despite living at home Attending university has traditionally been a rite of passage that involves moving away from home and transitioning into an independent life. However, the reality is different for a growing number of students who say they will instead be staying at home and travelling to their seminars due to the cost of living. In 2017, 535,090 people said they intended to live at home during their university course compared with 748,060 in 2026 - an increase of 39.8%, according to figures from the Universities and Colleges Admissions Service (Ucas). Bethany Fearne, a second year law student, said it was "significantly cheaper" to stay at home in Sittingbourne and drive to Canterbury Christ Church University (CCCU) than live on campus. She said she believed living outside of university "made no difference" in terms of immersing herself in university life. "I don't feel like I miss out at all," she said. " I get involved in activities like the Colour Run." Ez Spring, who studies sports therapy, spoke about the benefits of being a commuter student Ez Spring, a second year sports therapy student, drives 40 minutes each way to university and sees the benefits of living at home. "When I am driving, it's a nice time to relax before attending classes," she said. "I can stay at home with my family and keep my job." This year, more than 81,000 UK 18-year-olds said in their accepted university application they intended to live at home, according to Ucas figures. Dr Susan Kenyon, principal lecturer in politics at CCCU, said: "We have seen this trend across many years now in higher education. " Nick Hillman, director of the Higher Education Policy Institute, said the gradual growth of commuter students was linked to the cost of living. "Aside from tuition fees, the single biggest cost is rent where you can pay up to £1,000 a month depending where you live," he said. "Even if you receive the maximum maintenance loan rate, it may not be enough to cover both rent and other daily expenditures." Hillman said there were advantages and disadvantages to being a commuter student. "If you live at home, you are more likely to keep your network of family and friends, and other support network," he said. "However, you may be not immersing in campus life experience. "Some universities are adapting to this commuter student trend by reducing on-campus attendance to three days a week and offering hotel-style accommodation."
