title: England should stop trying to replicate Spain - Gordon
description: Anthony Gordon says that controlling games is not in the "English DNA" but the Three Lions could still win major tournaments if they stop "trying to replicate Spain".
body: Anthony Gordon has made 25 appearances for England and scored four goals. Anthony Gordon says that controlling games is not in the English "DNA" but the Three Lions could win major tournaments if they stop "trying to replicate Spain". The Barcelona winger was speaking at St George's Park as the England squad prepare to take on world champions Spain on Saturday - their first match together since the World Cup. England lost their semi-final 2-1 to Argentina, before beating France 6-4 in the bronze medal match. Ending on a high meant England achieved their best finish in a World Cup since 1966. But many have criticised the manner in which England were beaten by Argentina, after head coach Thomas Tuchel substituted goalscorer Gordon and went to a back five. The tactical tweak invited pressure, with Enzo Fernandez equalising before Lautaro Martinez scored a stoppage-time winner. Gordon said that he had "never felt worse", after the game and believes that the "scar" left by defeat may mean the England squad take a different approach in the next tournament. "[The] scar doesn't have to be a negative one because it might lead us to victory in the next tournaments," Gordon said. "We can't keep looking at other countries and trying to be like them, because we're not them - we're English and we have our own strengths which they don't have, so maybe we start playing the way we're good at." Signed instead of Rashford, Gordon is proving worth at Barca Gordon moved to Barcelona from Newcastle for £69.3m in the summer. He says that the experience of playing in La Liga - with and against some of Spain's top stars - has made him realise just how different the nation's approach is to football. He is not convinced English players can be taught to play more like the Spanish, with their intricate possession-based game. "I'm speaking from a point of view where I feel like we are trying to replicate Spain," Gordon said. "Because I'm in Spain, I know we have just as good players, but they have different qualities, so why are you trying to make those players the same as the Spanish players? Because the Spanish players lack the things that we have and vice versa." England have lost two consecutive European Championship finals, and been beaten by France and Argentina in the past two World Cups. Those outcomes have led to repeated questions about whether the team are good enough at controlling possession against elite nations. Spain won the World Cup by beating Argentina and dominated with 65% of the ball in the final, restricting opponents led by Lionel Messi to just two shots in 120 minutes of play, neither of which hit the target. Spain's particular style will test England again this weekend, and the Wembley hosts will look to find a response - but perhaps not by copying their opponents. "It's not in the English DNA," Gordon said. "I'm not sure it's something that can be taught because now I think, playing in Spain, I can speak with an educated view on the way they keep the ball is different. "I even look at some of the decisions they take on the ball sometimes and think I'm not sure how you've seen that. "It's the way they're built. I don't know whether it is something that maybe we can't ever put a name to, but they're definitely built different." Gordon's goal in the semi-final capped what was an impressive tournament for the 25-year-old and briefly had England supporters dreaming of World Cup glory. The winger started five of England's games and also provided four assists. He was taken off 17 minutes after putting the Three Lions ahead against Argentina and says that he was surprised to be substituted. He says that after scoring he plays "off adrenaline" and "goes into an untouchable mode of confidence". "It makes me feel on top of the world, especially in that moment on that stage. I felt really good," he said. "But as a winger, to be honest, I come off most games. It's normal [for wingers]. "Obviously that substitution was different but in that moment probably yeah, but in general as a winger I expect it a lot of the time." England had battled to a 3-2 win over Mexico in the Azteca Stadium, where they played with 10 men for over 35 minutes after Jarell Quansah's red card. According to Gordon, the manner of that last-16 victory was a factor in the players' thinking when trying to get over the line against Argentina. The winger also suggested that the team did not match the performances that they were creating in training. If they had, Gordon says, they "would have dominated everyone". He defended Tuchel's "more safe and more defensive" tactics, which sparked external criticism and in-camp disappointment. "We shouldn't try and blame one man who's obviously trying his best and trying to win the cup for us all," Gordon said. "As players, we could have done more to take the initiative to control the [Argentina] game. I think if we do that the manager doesn't make the decision [to use a back five]. "For me, we had the best team, we had the best players on the pitch in that semi-final, and in the last 20 minutes we didn't play the best football. "That's something the manager can't really affect from the sideline, so I think as a group everyone together should take responsibility." title: Mother of teen who died ‘deeply hurt’ that NHS staff may have accessed son’s records inappropriately
description: Oliver McGowan, who died in 2016, may have had his medical records accessed inappropriately after his death by NHS staff in Bristol.
body: Oliver McGowan, pictured here with his mother Paula, died in 2016 after being prescribed anti-psychotic medication at Southmead Hospital in Bristol The mother of a teenage boy who died in hospital has said she is "deeply concerned and hurt" after learning his medical records may have been accessed inappropriately for years after his death. Paula McGowan, whose 18-year-old autistic son Oliver died in 2016, was told that at least five members of staff at Bristol Foundation NHS Trust may have accessed his records without permission as recently as this year. Three nursing staff are under formal investigation, while a doctor who no longer works for the trust has self-referred to the General Medical Council. Another member of staff is having their case reviewed separately. The trust said it was "deeply sorry" for any stress and anxiety caused. It said it had voluntarily referred itself to the Information Commissioner's Office. It is the latest case involving concerns that NHS staff may have accessed patient records without a legitimate professional reason. In July the head of NHS England, Sir Jim Mackey, issued a "stark warning" that staff could face the sack or even prison for doing so. Recent high-profile examples include the victims of the Nottingham and Southport attacks and a child who was injured in a crocodile enclosure in Cambridgeshire. This month an investigation for the Health Services Journal found that at least 214 NHS staff have lost their jobs and around 2,000 been sanctioned for snooping on sensitive patient data over the past five years. Oliver, who had a mild learning disability and epilepsy, died in 2016 at Southmead Hospital in Bristol after being given anti-psychotic medication that his family had repeatedly warned he should not receive. After requesting information about his medical records, his mother was told that 38 people had accessed the data since his death, with 637 items viewed and 67 printed off. A report in 2020 found Oliver's death was "potentially avoidable", with his parents blaming the "ignorance" of medics Most access was appropriate and linked to complaints, legal proceedings, and the coroner's inquest into his death. But three nursing staff not involved in his care are currently under formal investigation after initial inquiries could find no evidence they had a legitimate reason to view her son's records. A fourth member of staff is having their case reviewed separately. McGowan said she was told that one nurse wanted to view the files as they had a general interest in anti-psychotic drugs and the care of patients with a learning disability. The trust is also looking into 13 another cases involving former staff, including doctors, nurses and clerical workers, to establish if that access was appropriate or not. One doctor, who no longer works at the trust, has already referred themselves to the medical regulator, the GMC, after being approached by the hospital. Autistic teen's hospital death was 'avoidable' Oliver, who had epilepsy, was being treated for a seizure when he was given the anti-psychotic drug to sedate him, which caused a rare side effect McGowan told the BBC she was "deeply hurt, deeply disappointed" after being told about the investigation, which is ongoing. "I've always been open and honest but there are deeply personal things in Oliver's [medical] notes that I don't tell anybody," she said. "He died in pain and it's not pleasant if that side of Oliver's death has been accessed." Her husband, Tom McGowan, said that the risk of unauthorised access to medical records had increased as more information is stored on digital, cloud-based platforms. "It's a weakness in the system and action needs to be taken now to tighten up controls," he said. Paula McGowan, with husband Tom, became a prominent patient safety campaigner following Oliver's death and received an OBE in 2021 for her work to improve care for autistic people and people with learning disabilities Bristol NHS Foundation Trust said it was undertaking a "thorough investigation" and it would be "inappropriate to reach conclusions before those enquiries are complete". "Every patient and family has the right to expect that their personal information will be treated with care, respect and confidentiality," said Prof Steve Hams, the trust's chief nursing and improvement officer. "Any concern that records may have been accessed without a legitimate reason is something we take extremely seriously." The trust said that, should any staff misconduct be identified, "appropriate action will be taken through the relevant processes". NHS medical records can contain highly sensitive personal information, ranging from test results and hospital discharge summaries to details of prescriptions and medications. That extends well beyond the information available to patients through the NHS app and may include safeguarding concerns, risk assessments, correspondence between healthcare professionals and detailed consultation notes. There is no single NHS-wide electronic record system that every member of staff can access. Instead, organisations including GP practices, hospitals and specialist clinics maintain their own records and determine who can view particular information. Doctors, nurses and other healthcare staff often need fast access, particularly in emergencies. However, they should only view confidential information when they have a legitimate work-related reason and the right authorisation. IT systems keep an audit trail that should be able to show exactly who accessed a patient's records and when. NHS England said any instance of staff looking at records without a valid reason would be "wholly unacceptable, a disgraceful breach of patients' trust and against the law". title: Prison staff told not to use inadequate cells as overcrowding worsens
description: Workers tell BBC they are increasingly having to put two inmates in single occupancy cells because of overcrowding.
body: Some prisoners will be released early in October to try to tackle overcrowding (file photo) Prison governors in England and Wales have been warned against using unsafe cells to cope with overcrowding, according to documents leaked to the BBC. The six-page letter from the Prison Governors' Association (PGA) has been sent to members urging them to abide by the law when using cells, ensuring they meet health and safety requirements and are suitable for the number of inmates they are holding. Prison staff told the BBC they were increasingly having to put two inmates in single occupancy cells, as overcrowding across the adult male estate worsens. "Keeping two prisoners in cells built for one isn't ideal, but the pressure is on to maintain operational capacity. "We don't have the space. Some cells have problems with heating or plumbing and they [prisoners] shouldn't really be in there to be honest," one governor said. "The infrastructure is failing, especially in the older establishments, and cramming people into cells isn't going to help - especially when the toilet or sink isn't working." A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: "Cells are only doubled up where it is safe to do so." Governors have been warned that cells need to meet health and safety standards, including plumbing The leaked document, called Operational Capacity Guidance, states: "It is a legal requirement under the Prisons Act 1952, the Prison Rules and the Young Offender Institution Rules that no cell shall be used for the confinement of a prisoner or young offender unless it is certified by an inspector that its size, lighting, heating, ventilation and fittings are adequate for health and that it allows the prisoner to communicate at any time with a prison officer." It also says the number of people in a prison must not exceed the number of spaces. There are concerns among some staff that the government is putting pressure on prison management to take more inmates than they can reasonably house. A growing number of prison staff have told the BBC that rules are being stretched or broken to accommodate additional inmates, potentially posing health and safety risks. Some regard the guidance as a "warning shot" to those in charge of setting the maximum operational capacity of prisons. The decision on where the operational capacity of a prison is set lies not with the governor but with their boss - the Prison Group Director (PGD). The PGD sets operational capacity by judging the total number of inmates a prison can hold and takes into account control and security. One prison staffer said: "We don't have enough staff to monitor the extra prisoners. We don't have the infrastructure to house the additional prisoners. So those who make the decisions need to abide by the law or they're the ones who have to justify why they're making governors take all these people". The male adult prison estate is at 98.5% capacity, with some staff claiming they have just a handful of spaces remaining. Prison sources say there are just over 1,200 spaces remaining across the adult male estate - which currently has a total population of around 83,400. Some prisons hold more than 1,000 inmates - like large Victorian jails. Others can be smaller with a more concentrated population in the low hundreds. Former prison governor John Podmore said it was "fundamentally unfair" governors were having to deal with a penal crisis they didn't create. "The public may have little sympathy for prisoners, but that doesn't alter the reality. You can put a second bed in a cell and call it capacity but that doesn't make it sensible or safe. "Meanwhile, the system is quietly putting thousands back into prison through recall. If ministers want more space, they should look at why the revolving door is getting faster, rather than simply squeezing two people into a cell built for one." Violence, overcrowding, self-harm: BBC goes inside one of Britain’s most dangerous prisons Spaces in male prisons fall to lowest level of year, sources say Laundry rooms to be turned into cells to tackle prison overcrowding The government is starting an early release scheme from next month to create more room. In total, around 4,500 offenders will be let out sooner over a ten-month period. Some senior staff believe this will improve the situation in the short-term but worry pressure will continue on prison management to push their capacity numbers to the maximum or even beyond. On October 1, around 700 offenders serving sentences of up to 19 months will be released earlier than initially scheduled after serving a third of their sentence in custody. Then on October 13, governors will release a second tranche of 650 prisoners who have been serving sentences of between 19 months and two years and five months. A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: "The government inherited a prison capacity crisis after places increased by just 500 in 14 years, but we're pulling every lever available to make sure the country never runs out of spaces and we can keep dangerous offenders locked up. "We're delivering 14,000 additional places with nearly 3,300 already delivered, converting suitable existing spaces into new cells, securing land for future prisons, and removing foreign national offenders faster." title: Trump offers warm welcome as China's Xi arrives for US visit
description: The US treasury secretary said that the US and China had reached an agreement to extend a trade truce as Xi began his visit.
body: This video can not be played A red carpet and military flyover - How Trump welcomed Xi US President Donald Trump has greeted his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping with a military flyover and 100ft (30m) red carpet to kick off their three-day summit in Washington. In a rare move, Trump met China's premier at the airport as the US Air Force band marched on the tarmac and US and Chinese flags flew. Trump and First Lady Melania Trump welcomed Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday evening in Maryland. The high-stakes visit - Xi's first trip to Washington since 2015 - is expected to include closed-door meetings, a state dinner, and plenty to discuss, from AI, to the Iran war and Taiwan, and an extended trade truce. This is Xi's first visit to Washington since 2015 The leader of China's Communist Party touched down in an Air China plane at 17:39 local time (22:39 BST). The colour and honour guard marched up to the aircraft and stood on both sides of the red carpet as two limos pulled up. Xi and Peng exited their plane and the two couples shook hands. They spoke briefly before walking side by side down the red carpet and posing for photos. Two B-1s flew over as the Army Air Force Band played the US national anthem. The supersonic aircraft are a key part of the US's combat arsenal. After exchanging pleasantries, the two couples departed in separate vehicles to Washington. This is the first time since 1962 that a US president has personally welcomed a foreign leader at the base, signalling the importance that Trump is giving this visit. In 1962, then-President John F Kennedy greeted British PM Harold Macmillan. Also on Wednesday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that the US and China will extend their trade truce to January. The agreement, which saw Trump lower tariff rates on some goods in exchange for Xi loosening restrictions on rare earth minerals, was set to expire 10 November. Bessent, who spoke after meeting Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, said the two discussed if there can eventually be a more substantive trade deal between the two countries. In a written statement published by China's state news agency Xinhua, Xi said both China and the US are "great nations, and their people are great people". "The two countries should be partners rather than rivals," he said. Melania Trump has said she has been involved intimately with the planning of the itinerary. She told Fox News that Trump made the decision to personally greet Xi himself at the airport "because they have a great relationship". Xi is accompanied on the visit by Cai Qi, a member of the party's Politburo Standing Committee who's widely seen as his right-hand man, vice premier He Lifeng, foreign minister Wang Yi, as well as other delegates and ambassadors from Beijing. "Realising the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can fully coexist, reinforce each other and benefit the world," Xi said in the statement carried by Xinhua, where he also expressed confident that the visit would "yield fruitful results". It is unclear if Xi has brought any business executives with him. Bringing Chinese firms to the US may also raise questions about Chinese business practices, subsidies and overcapacity, all of which may draw more fire and questions than Xi or his party would like. During Trump's visit to Beijing in May, he was accompanied by a group of tech executives from some of the largest US firms, including Apple's Tim Cook, Tesla's Elon Musk and Nvidia's Jensen Huang. Leaders of US AI companies are slated to attend the lavish state dinner set for Thursday. Xi's visit will end on Friday. Trump has dismissed recent warnings about the potential dangers of AI from within the industry as a "hoax" and both countries are racing to try to achieve dominance in the sector. Trump will aim to achieve other deals around trade and tariffs – like lowering Chinese tariffs on American products, increasing imports of Chinese rare earth minerals, and increasing exports of US agricultural products, according to David Firestein of the Bush China Foundation. But China appears have reneged on promises to buy more American agricultural products and to sell more rare earth minerals to the US. Firestein expects Xi to encourage Trump to further stall - or kill - a congressionally approved $14bn (£10.5bn)-arms sale to Taiwan and deepen US-China trade integration. These are the same US-China issues for the ages, he said, but, this time, "there seems to be a greater degree of, let's say, stability within the relationship, or less volatility relative to where we were last year in 2025". White House rolling out red carpet for historic Xi Jinping visit This video can not be played Watch: What’s at stake when Trump and Xi meet in the US? Xi's visit comes at a time when American attitudes towards China appear to be warming. A recent poll by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs indicated that 41% of Americans see China's territorial ambitions as a threat to the US. That number is down from 52% in 2022. More than half of Americans - 57% - believe the US should cooperate and engage with Beijing. Notably, that statistic cuts across the US political spectrum. Of Republicans who do not identify as Maga, 57% favour cooperation, as do most Democrats, both moderate and liberal. However most of Trump's loyal base - 63% - favour limiting US relations with China, putting them at odds with his warm welcome of Xi. Aside from the arrival ceremonies at the White House, Melania Trump has also planned a visit to the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art to show her Chinese counterpart the cultural connections between the two countries. title: They were labelled 'pervert glasses'. Will a camera-free version transform their image?
description: Meta has unveiled audio-only smart glasses, with some questioning whether it is a response to the backlash over privacy.
body: They were labelled 'pervert glasses'. Will a camera-free version transform their image? When Meta first launched its AI-powered smart glasses in 2023, in collaboration with the trendy sunglasses brand Ray-Ban, it unleashed a storm of controversy. There have been multiple reports of the devices being used to harass women and girls in particular, filming them without their consent, then sharing the footage. The image problem doesn't seem to have been cured by Meta's enlistment this summer of Kylie Jenner, Kim Kardashian's sister, as their prime model. The devices have been dubbed "pervert" or "creepy" glasses. In the UK, JD Wetherspoon pubs, a handful of major theatres, Comic-Con, some schools, and Faslane, home of the UK's nuclear submarines, have all chosen to ban them. On Thursday, Meta is unveiling a new version which does not contain a camera at all, called Ray-Ban Meta Audio. They will have the audio functions of the original glasses - including the ability to make phone calls or play music, with the sound funnelled directly into your ear - but with fewer implications for privacy. To some in the industry, it looks like an interesting pivot - a response, perhaps, to the backlash over privacy. Mark Zuckerberg - who wore a set at an event in California last year - predicts that smart glasses will replace mobile phones The tech giant denies that the new glasses have been rushed out in response to public anger. They say the product has been in development for two years. The audio-only version is cheaper than its camera-enabled cousins, and Meta says it has a lighter frame and better battery life. When I put it to Meta Glasses' head of product Ankit Brahmbhatt that I thought they might overtake the original camera-enabled glasses in sales, there was a pregnant pause. "We have, I think, something for everyone," he said, choosing his words very carefully. Does the release of a camera-free option represent a shift in how tech companies see the future of smart glasses? And is Meta's original vision getting further away? Or should we see camera-free glasses as a niche side-product that serves a small market - a bit like how some mobile manufacturers are now releasing internet-disabled "brick" phones for people who are tired of social media? There's no doubt that smart glasses have become controversial. I was lent a pair of Meta Ray-Bans – with cameras - to try out. I was initially nervous about wearing them in public, in case someone got physical: I have heard of people knocking them off wearers' heads and smashing them in the street. The reality was that I wore them on public transport and on foot in several cities including London, Glasgow and Portsmouth, and nobody batted an eyelid. It made me wonder whether awareness of them is really as high as both Meta and anti-glasses campaigners believe. That said, some people quietly told me they would not be confident enough to approach someone wearing them even if they did spot them, for fear of the interaction being filmed and uploaded. The glasses are designed to work as an extension of your phone. They use Bluetooth to sync with a handset via Meta's AI app. They are voice-activated, with open speakers in the arms funnelling sound into your ears. The result is a bit like wearing headphones without the addition of noise-cancelling features, so you can still hear the world around you. My potentially cancellable opinion is that I found many of the glasses' features useful. Interestingly, none of them included the camera. Listening to music and podcasts on the move without having earbuds stuffed into my ears felt safer. I felt more confident about avoiding the gamut of e-bike-riding phone thieves in central London without my phone physically in my hand. Left: Meta's demonstration of a user making a phone call, with an image of the person they're talking to displayed inside their glasses. Right: Zoe Kleinman wearing a set on her commute And as someone with a pitiful sense of direction, I rely a lot on map apps. It was handy to have the directions spoken in my ears. The pay-off for this, however, was having to accept allowing the Meta AI app to know exactly where I was at all times. Meta is notorious for its hunger for personal data. When I posted about using the Meta Ray-Bans on social media, I got a bit of a hard time. Less so when I showed them to people in my everyday life. My hairdresser loved the idea of using them to record her clients' hair transformations. A builder I chatted to at the gym reckoned they would be useful on sites for recording what he was doing, either in the event of an accident or even to teach others new skills. My friend who runs said he would like to wear them on a jog. Plenty of content creators are big fans. My son borrowed them to wash my car, and was proud of his film showing me how he delicately chipped away at a stubborn bit of bird poo without damaging the paintwork (I was pleased, and happy to take his word for it). More broadly, smart glasses have been welcomed by the blind community. One user described them to the BBC as a "game-changer" because they can give audio descriptions of current locations and read out visible text like restaurant menu options. Earlier this year Meta donated 15,000 pairs to a charity for the blind in Ireland. But still, anger over privacy has grown. The glasses have a blinking white LED that switches on when the camera is active, but a whole industry has sprung up around finding technical workarounds to disable that light, some of which involve taking the glasses apart. Meta says less than 0.1% of the frames it has sold worldwide have been physically tampered with. Exact sales figures are unknown, but Ray-Ban's parent company EssilorLuxottica has reported that it sold seven million last year. title: Eight US sailors assigned to USS Abraham Lincoln attempted suicide, Navy says
description: In a letter to Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the crew had adequate mental health support during the long deployment.
body: Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao has said that eight crew members who were assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide during their lengthy deployment. The disclosure was made in a letter to Senator Kirsten Gillibrand of New York on Tuesday in response to questions from the Democrat on the well-being of sailors onboard following mounting concerns. Family members of sailors had raised alarm about deteriorating mental health and grim conditions during a prolonged mission in the Middle East as part of the US war in Iran. The carrier, which had been deployed since last November, is now returning to the US. The BBC has contacted the US Navy for comment. In his letter, Cao said that there were five chaplains and multiple mental health professionals available on board to meet the "spiritual and emotional needs of the crew". He said the eight sailors included "the Lincoln crew and sailors from the carrier airwing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers and all embarked aviation squadrons". While the US Navy has previously acknowledged supply challenges on the carrier, it denied that a mental health crisis was taking place on the Lincoln, which had some 5,000 crew aboard. Cao's letter also denied widespread concerns about broken plumbing and shortages of fresh food, but acknowledged temporary "localized piping failures" and problems with the reverse osmosis desalination units, and some meal options were reduced for a "short time". Senator Gillibrand, a member of the Senate's armed services committee, criticised the Trump administration's previous responses to reports of grim conditions, calling the treatment of service members "completely unacceptable". "What Trump and Secretary Hegseth dismissed as 'fake news' turned out to be serious and deteriorating conditions for our service members," she said in a statement to the BBC on Wednesday. "Our troops and their families make immense sacrifices every single day, yet the president dismissed them with open disrespect," she added. The carrier left California in November for the South China Sea and was sent to the Middle East ahead of attacks on Iran in February. The deployment, which was originally set to end in May, was repeatedly extended. In August, the USS George Washington, an aircraft carrier, was sent to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln following a nine-month deployment. US sailors stopped in Thailand on their way home, hitting bars, malls and beach areas in their first time on land before continuing on to the US. US sailors go shopping before hitting the bars in Thailand after 250-day voyage US sailors arrive in Thailand's Pattaya after record 250 days at sea Suicide remains a leading cause of death in the US Navy and Marines, according to an analysis of military data by USNI News, while veterans have higher rates of suicide than Americans who have not served in the military, according to the Veterans Administration. A study, external of 956 sailors released in January 2025 found that troops aboard US Navy ships suffer the highest rates of "serious psychological distress" compared to other branches of the US military. The study cited "unique stressors, such as poor habitability, noise and demanding schedules that leave inadequate time for sleep and rest". If you or anyone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line or you can call the US Suicide and Crisis Lifeline on 988. title: In Amish country, nurses go door to door to stop deadly spread of measles
description: With four measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania, health officials are hoping to get people on board with vaccines in private.
body: Pennsylvania is home to thousands of Amish, who avoid many aspects of modern life For the past few months, nurse Dale Weiser has been making unexpected home visits. As the state battles the deadliest measles outbreak in recent history, the clinical supervisor drives 30 miles (48.3km), sometimes daily, to a rural corner of Pennsylvania where many Amish people live. Walking into strangers' homes, Weiser says she tries her best to be respectful and non-intrusive as she vaccinates dozens of family members against the measles, sometimes around the kitchen table. "A lot of people that I encounter, they don't have health insurance. They don't have a lot of interaction with the health system, and they just haven't seen the need to get these vaccines," said Weiser, who works for the Chester County Health Department. "When you start talking and you answer their questions, and build that trust, a lot of times they will make a different decision." The at-home vaccinations are part of the county and state health departments' strategy to encourage immunisations in the county, which includes an Amish community who abstain from many aspects of modern life, including regular contact with the western medical system. Weiser has vaccinated around 100 people since the outbreak began, going into people's homes to improve access to vaccines The state health department told the BBC it has administered nearly 4,300 measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccines at pop-up clinics near the epicentre of the outbreak since it began in late April. US measles cases reach 35-year high But even as health officials see success in their vaccine programmes, the state has reported four deaths from measles complications, marking the most deadly outbreak the US has seen since 1992. The infections have led to tensions between state and federal health officials, including vaccine-skeptic Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr. Those politics are back of mind in the Amish community, where people are growing fearful of more deaths as they watch their friends and family fall sick with the disease, which for decades has been eliminated in the US. "They're not a community that's as easy to reach - we can't just put up a social media post," Weiser said. "They are suffering at the moment, and we're trying to reach out and make connections." Pennsylvania is home to thousands of Amish, who avoid many aspects of modern life Amish people began coming to the US in the early 1700s, with the first community settling in Lancaster, Pennsylvania. Known as the "Plain People" for the simple clothes they wear, the Amish are a devout Christian community that does not use many forms of technology, relying on horse and buggies instead of cars. About 90,000 Amish people live in Pennsylvania, with estimates suggesting around only a quarter of Amish people in the Lancaster area have had the MMR vaccine. There is no particular religious text advising against vaccines, but Amish people do not have regular contact with the western medical system, or have a way to easily travel to appointments, experts said. "A lot of people who haven't gotten vaccinated, it's not because they have a strong stance against getting vaccinated for measles. It's just that they haven't gotten around to it. It's not convenient," said Braxton Mitchell, a genetic epidemiologist with University of Maryland School of Medicine who runs a research clinic studying the Amish in Lancaster. Amish people are extremely social, he said, so when the virus hits one church group, it affects everyone who is unvaccinated. "Measles is rampant in the Amish community," he said. "People are concerned about it." He added the community has been especially concerned about the dangers to babies; so far two newborns have died of measles complications, as well as an 18-year-old and a 40-year-old woman, according to state officials. Chester County has vaccinated 538 people against measles Chester County public health officials did not wait long to launch a response to the growing measles outbreak in their community, which shares a border with Lancaster County, the epicentre of the outbreak. Jeanne Franklin, the director of the health department, said officials have been using some of the strategies they employed during the Covid pandemic - knocking on doors in the community to let them know about the outbreak and offering private settings, like people's homes, for immunisations. Since the outbreak started, the county has given 538 MMR vaccines, 340 of which they administered in private settings. "People have called up and said, 'I can't get to your clinic, or, I don't want people to know I've changed my mind," Franklin said. "'If you can come to us, that's a lot easier.'" The boots-on-the-ground approach has helped the health department dispel misinformation and build trust with the community, local health officials said. In recent years, childhood vaccination rates have fallen across the country as false theories about the safety of the measles vaccine have proliferated on social media. Those theories have found roots even in an insulated community with limited access to computers, Weiser said. She has heard people ask if there are heavy metals in the vaccine that could make them magnetic, or if the shot has a computer chip in it. "You're clearly getting information from that hard-core group that is promoting that misinformation and disinformation," she said. People in this "hard-core group", who are staunchly against vaccines, are unlikely to be swayed, experts and officials themselves said. But now, local health officials said, many affected by the Pennsylvania outbreak are seeing their neighbours fall seriously ill and asking thoughtful questions. title: The Papers: 'RAF jet crash escape' and 'Tories to cut benefits'
description: The moment two RAF pilots ejected from a training jet is splashed across the front page of the Daily Mirror.
body: The moment two RAF pilots ejected from a jet is splashed across the front page of the Daily Mirror, which says it is a "miracle" nobody was killed in the incident. The two pilots were taking part in a training exercise in Anglesey when they were forced to parachute from the plane, which the paper reports then "plummeted nose-first into a field" and caused a "huge fireball". Several of the papers lead on the Conservative party's promise to prevent long-term jobless benefit claimants from spending their welfare payments on alcohol, cigarettes and gambling. The Times declares "Tories to cut benefits for long-term unemployed", and includes quotes from party leader Kemi Badenoch, who says she plans to stop joblessness being a "lifestyle choice for those who can't be bothered". The Daily Mail says Badenoch's "ruthless crackdown" would see people who have been unemployed for more than six months have their Universal Credit cut by 30%. Instead of receiving the reduced welfare support in cash, the paper reports, the proposals would see benefits paid onto a "Back to Work" card, which would block spending on alcohol, cigarettes or betting. Similarly, the Telegraph reads: "Tories to ban spending benefits on alcohol". The paper says that the proposal would mirror measures in the US, where claimants receive benefits on cards rather than cash. According to the Telegraph, the Labour Party has called the Conservatives' plan "unworkable". Teenagers will be offered a range of new vocational GCSEs under what the Guardian is calling a "radical shake-up of the school system". It reports that from 2029, students will be able to supplement compulsory GCSE subjects with courses like construction, creative media production and child development. The paper says it is an effort by Prime Minister Andy Burnham to meet his promise of an "education system that offers a path for everyone", and is designed to tackle a "crisis" that has left nearly a million young people out of work or training. The Sun suggests that Burnham could be on the verge of axeing the "ban on boozing" at football matches in the UK. It follows comments from the prime minister where he told reporters there was a "case to remove that discrimination perhaps on a trial basis". Government sources stressed Burnham was restating an opinion he has long held, rather than making any sort of policy announcement. Laws have been in place since 1985 which prevent drinking in view of the pitch at stadiums for clubs in the top five tiers of men's football in England. The Football Supporters' Association (FSA) has said the "outdated" legislation should be reviewed, but police chiefs are warning against relaxing the law. Co-chair of the EU-UK Parliamentary Partnership Assembly Sandro Gozi has told the i Paper that Burnham should drop Labour's "obsolete" red lines to allow for a "deeper" agreement with the European Union. He said he was hopeful that the prime minister will "move beyond" Labour's manifesto restrictions, and achieve a "Canada-style membership deal" for the UK. "Healey weighs smaller fiscal headroom to reduce tax rises", says the Financial Times, reporting that the chancellor's fiscal buffer could fall to £14bn in next month's budget. The paper says investors have signalled that the gilt market "would not be spooked" by a more modest target, adding that the Treasury and Number 10 are "actively debating" the possibility. The Metro leads on the jailing of James Gillingham, who was found guilty of running a £13m ponzi scheme. "Wolf of Essex caged" reads the paper's headline. "Ewe can't count Jez", writes the Daily Star, reporting Jeremy Clarkson has been "left red-faced" after police informed the television personality that he had miscounted the number of sheep in his fields. title: Residents eating garden weeds in Russian-occupied city cut off from food and water
description: The BBC has spoken to residents in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky who say they are being "constantly shelled".
body: Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since 2022 and its people are now trapped "Two more civilians died last night," says Halia, before her phone connection cuts off. She is trapped in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which she says is "constantly shelled" and cut off from food and water. Three days later she tells me the two who were killed were a husband and wife. She knew them well. They were bringing home a bag of food from the closest neighbouring town of Radensk, 23km (14 miles) away, but were unable to get home before a curfew imposed by Russian occupation authorities. They were then killed by a drone. Four separate sources have confirmed the deaths of two civilians carrying food on 20 September. Halia does not want to share their names for fear she might be identified. Her name has been changed to protect her safety. Hers is just one of the many harrowing accounts the BBC has heard from residents in the front-line city in southern Kherson in recent days. Occupied by Russia since 2022, Oleshky is trapped between the Dnipro River, which separates it from Ukrainian positions, and Russian forces. It is also one of the cities where thousands of people lost their homes after the collapse of Nova Khakova Dam in 2023, flooding buildings up to their rooftops. Ukraine and Nato accused Russia of blowing up the dam, while Russia blamed Ukraine. Oleshky was home to 24,000 people before Russia's full-scale invasion. Now the Ukrainian government estimates that some 6,000 people remain in the city and its surrounding areas, including 200 children. Residents say children remaining in wider Oleshky are suffering from malnutrition, a lack of medical services, and are "degrading" without access to education. Many have also told the BBC independently there is only one hospital partially operational, opening a few days a week to perform critical amputations. Ukraine has attempted to deliver supplies to the area but has not had success in recent months. To stay or risk the 'Road of Death' - Ukrainian civilians trapped in frontline city Earlier this week the Kremlin acknowledged that Oleshky faced "a critical situation" and "problems with supplies of food and medicine", but added that "Russia's military was working to resolve them" and blamed Kyiv. The local population is living under a "full blockade" by Russian forces, according to Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha. Speaking at the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, Sybiha called on the international community to pressure Russia into allowing humanitarian aid into the city. Oleshky was flooded after the collapse of the Nova Kakhovka Dam in June 2023. Inside Oleshky, Halia faces a daily struggle to survive. "There is no food here in the city," she says, adding that the last food delivery was back in May. "I eat once a day, a dinner only," she says. "I make some plain bread, sometimes I can have it with a tomato, or with some honey, and a tea. That's it." Many residents have turned to cooking garden weeds as they have run out of the vegetables they managed to grow over the summer, she explains. Oleshky has been without gas or electricity since 2023, so residents have had to find other solutions Which weeds are safe to eat and how to boil them has become a topic of discussion on local Telegram messaging chats, along with calls between residents to sell, swap or share pieces of food. No shops are open any more in Oleshky, with residents unable to source either clothes or hygiene products. The city has had no electricity, gas or water since the Kakhovka dam was attacked three years ago. While some residents have risked travelling on foot along mined roads out of the city in search of supplies, it is now deemed too much of a danger. These residents were able to get out of Oleshky in spring this year Warning: Distressing and graphic descriptions of dead bodies below. Working out how many people have been killed in Oleshky is difficult. The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine has recorded reports this year of at least 29 civilians killed and 54 injured in Oleshky and Hola Prystan, external - about 24km to the east. Local volunteers estimate that number could be significantly higher. Ksenia Arkhipova has been counting the dead since she managed to escape Oleshky in summer 2022 - a few months after it was taken by the Russian army. She is a volunteer who is involved in attempts to deliver food and medicine and facilitating evacuations to Oleshky. Locals trust her with their sensitive personal information. "I've been putting together a spreadsheet of all those who died as soon as I find out about it, with their names and dates of birth – I've got around 1,200 people now," she says. "Sometimes I don't have time to update it, as the list grows one or two people longer every day: someone was killed by a drone, someone else stepped on the landmine." While the BBC cannot independently verify these figures, one local resident has given her personal account of losing her loved ones. Both her parents were killed in Oleshky this summer, said Tetiana - also not her real name. She confirmed their identities to the BBC with their dates of birth and photos, but asked not to have them published for her own safety. "They were shot inside their home. Russian soldiers came there and wanted to take it," she said. Largest attack on Moscow sees Ukraine fire hundreds of drones, mayor says A four-minute warning isn't enough: Russia's new relentless missile tactics exhaust Kyiv residents Russia hits Ukrainian train shortly after Boris Johnson and top European officials leave station Burying the bodies of people killed in Oleshky has been restricted by Russian occupation authorities, residents say. This has made counting the dead even harder. They "do not allow us to bury the dead if they were killed by a drone, stepped on a landmine or were killed in any other way", said Tetiana. Russi

title: OpenAI agent 'infiltrated' Australian government website, PM says
description: Albanese said he expressed "concern" to OpenAI founder Sam Altman, after authorities were informed three months after the breach in June.
body: Albanese said it took "too long" for OpenAI to inform Australian officials of the breach in June An artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI "infiltrated" an Australian government website in June, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has said. The agent hacked a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare, Albanese said in New York on Wednesday, local time. He had a "very frank discussion" with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman for taking "too long" to tell them about the breach, believed to be one of the world's first publicly reported AI-led hacks of a government website. OpenAI said it only became aware of the incident in August "during an ongoing review" of "misaligned model activity", and told Australian officials on 10 September. While the review is ongoing, a spokesperson for the AI firm said that it is not believed that any patient records were accessed. Albanese said the breach occurred in June this year, but OpenAI only informed government officials via email on 10 September. The prime minister said he had also expressed "Australia's extreme concern about this incident" when he spoke to Altman and there will "obviously be legal consequences on it". Albanese said the agent accessed both public and non-public files and a "forensic investigation" is under way to find out if other government systems were affected. The investigation will be led by the Australian Signals Directorate, the country's cybersecurity agency. The public-facing Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal is administered by Services Australia, the main hub to redirect users to government services. He told reporters: "No personal information is believed to have been accessed at this stage, but investigations are ongoing. "Evidence currently available is there is no broader compromise to the Services Australia network. Nonetheless this situation is obviously unacceptable." Earlier this year, OpenAI revealed a group of AI agents it had been testing had escaped from their controls and secretly worked together to hack another tech firm named Hugging Face. title: 'Make women feel seen': Why the Dutch have a new word for labia
description: Campaigners hope the new words will lead to less body shaming and more sex positivity.
body: Shari Klein spoke at a recent march celebrating the new word Can you imagine seeing the words "shame lips" on your medical notes? The term, which can also be translated as "pubic lips", is the Dutch word for a women's body part. But, for some, it's just one of countless examples that are outdated and loaded with stigma. Last month, leading Dutch dictionary Dikke van Dale said it would include a new term for the labia, "vulvalippen" - in its upcoming online addition - alongside the traditional term "schaamlippen". European campaigners have long been calling for a rewrite of terms used to discuss women's bodies, sexuality and health. What unites them is the desire to move away from terms that are often seen as misogynistic or judgmental. "Language shapes how we see ourselves," says Shari Klein, one of the founders of the Schaamteloos campaign, which targets words that use "schaam" or "shame". "It's crucial people have a more neutral, anatomically correct word - not a word that links to shame, whether consciously or sub-consciously," she says. Calls to use vulvalippen aren't new but campaigners say inclusion in the dictionary may be a sign society is "finally ready for change". Esther Van der Valk, part of prominent Dutch feminist group Dolle Mina, says it's also about sex positivity and reducing body shaming. The campaign's next steps are to convince doctors and officials to use vulvalippen in leaflets and consultations. Signs used during a recent march in the Netherlands, the one on the left translates as "afterall there are no shame balls" Ton den Boon, editor of the dictionary, says adding vulvalippen is justified because it is becoming more established in the language and is being used more in the media, biology text books, medical leaflets and is even seen in veterinary medicine. But whether it will be adopted widely is yet to be seen. Other Dutch words, relevant to both men and women, could carry similar connotations - from "schaam haar" (pubic or shame hair) or "schaam been" (pubic or shame bone) to even "schaam lice" for pubic lice. However, critics say changing a word will not necessarily change people's lives. Language around birth should be less judgemental The campaign mirrors attempts in Germany, where in 2018 journalists Gunda Windmüller and Mithu Sanyal started a petition to change "Shamlippen" to "Vulvalippen". Windmüller says she was compelled to after a gynaecologist told her of the shame some women carry when discussing their bodies and having medical examinations. When writing her article, she realised she couldn't even mention anatomy without including the word shame. "Vulvalippen" has not yet been adopted by a German dictionary, but Windmüller has spotted it in conversations, school textbooks and women's magazines. Her hope is the Dutch move will ignite support closer to home. Similarly, in Sweden a new word for "hymen" was added in the academic dictionary after a 2009 campaign. The association for sexuality education (RFSU) felt traditional term "mödomshinna", which translates as maidenhood skin or virginity membrane, was anatomically inaccurate and did nothing to dispel myths around hymens and virginity. The new term "slidkrans" translates as vaginal corona - reflecting the fact the hymen is often folds of tissue in a ring, rather than a seal that breaks once. "With a new word we can challenge the myths that seek to control women's sexuality and freedom," Sonja Ghaderi of the RFSU says. Ghaderi says slidkrans is used particularly by healthcare professionals and in youth clinics but adds misinformation still exists emphasising the "need to change social constructs". Supporters took to the streets in the Netherlands to celebrate and publicise the new word In the UK, feminist podcast host Nicola Denson-Elliott started a petition to replace the word "hysterectomy" (surgical removal of the womb) with "uterectomy". She argues, as others have, that hysterectomy has linguistic links with hysteria, external - once seen as a disease of emotional excess in women - and wants a more "anatomically correct term" not one "associated with emotion." The petition describes it as "medical misogyny", adding: "Women deserve terminology that respects them." Linguistics researcher Dr Beth Malory says any changes need to be researched first. "Will people understand uterectomy? Is simply saying removal of the womb better?" New words cannot be ambiguous, she says, it's important to look at the whole system so there is no confusion. Malory also studies language around pregnancy and loss. One phrase highlighted in her research is "incompetent cervix" used to describe the shortening of the cervix that can increase risks of pregnancy loss and early birth. Women told her it made them feel blamed for the medical issue. "Why do we need judgmental words like failure or incompetence?" says obstetrician Dr Brooke Vandermolen, external. Even though they appear in medical textbooks, she tells me she's moved away from certain terms, including "failure to progress" - which describes labour not moving forward as expected. "Language is incredibly important and the words we choose can show recognition and make people feel validated and seen." In 2022, the Royal College of Midwives produced guidance offering alternative phrases. But Vandermolen says some traditional terms are still being used and still cause distress. "I hope this change in the Netherlands sparks more conversations here about how we speak about women's bodies. What we say can have a lasting impact." title: I didn't know my partner was raping me while I slept
description: Adelle Overton had been with Steven Uden for 13 years when she found out he had been raping her.
body: Adelle Overton, 46, and Steven Uden, 44, were together for more than 13 years "In my eyes, up until maybe the day before he admitted to what he'd done, it was the best relationship I've ever had." Adelle Overton's boyfriend of 13 years, Steven Uden, appeared to be the perfect partner. They met on the set of a zombie film and had lots of shared interests. She says Uden was kind and loving and even gave up work to be Overton's carer when she became disabled. "He was wonderful. I loved him deeply, and I think I still kind of do a bit," says Overton, sitting on a sofa at her home in Derby. Overton trusted Uden, but that trust was shattered when he admitted he had been raping her while she slept. "I instantly felt betrayed. I'd never felt so safe in a relationship before that point," says Overton. Uden had cared for Overton while she was being treated for breast cancer, but he later told police he had raped her while she was under the effects of the medication. "That sense of betrayal, that I thought I knew him, but I don't know who he was," says Overton. "And the thought that he'd been living with me for 13 years, he helped raise my children. "I thought he was safe when he wasn't." Uden is now in prison, and Overton has decided to talk about what happened in the hope it will help others. Uden and Overton were friends before they began dating Overton and Uden met in 2009, during the filming of a zombie film being shot in Nottingham, when she was 29 and he was 27. Uden was doing make-up and acting, and Overton was one of the actors too. They were both in relationships with other people but stayed in touch as friends. They eventually became a couple on 13 January 2012 - Overton remembers the date because they had a Friday the 13th film marathon. Overton said being with Uden felt different from the relationships she had been in in the past. "He was fun and caring and I felt loved by him," she says. The pair worked as zombies for an events company They had met in an unconventional way, and their life together was unconventional too. They worked as professional zombies for a company that ran zombie survival horror experience days. Playing a zombie required Overton to be physically active, but she eventually had to give it up in 2017 after being diagnosed with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, external. Uden then became her carer towards the start of 2018. "He did almost everything for me," she says. Looking back, with hindsight, Overton - nicknamed Dell - thinks Uden did start to become controlling. "He would enjoy telling everybody else what I was capable of doing," she says. "Somebody would come up with a suggestion for doing something, he'd enjoy saying, 'I don't think Dell would be able to manage that, let's think of something else'." Uden seemed like the perfect partner to Overton's friends and family, she says But Overton now knows that Uden's behaviour was far more sinister than she could ever have imagined. She had suspicions in 2020 while having chemotherapy for breast cancer. "I don't know if the discomfort in my body was more apparent, but I woke up while he was doing it," she says. "He made loads of excuses like, 'I thought you were awake, and you were making all the right noises'. "I was thinking about all of the stress we were under, and he's saying he did it by accident." So, Overton brushed aside her concerns. "I guess it was easier to believe the lie than process what the truth might have been," she says. Uden eventually confessed to Overton But Overton started having difficulty sleeping. "I think somewhere in there, in my head, my brain just didn't feel safe while I was asleep," she says. Overton says she also struggled to be intimate with Uden, and started having more nightmares relating to her past experience of sexual abuse. "At the time I thought I was linking it to my trauma, and I was judging him and what he'd done more harshly because of my trauma," she says. "I started to feel guilty and started berating myself internally for it all." Uden didn't confess until five years later, in 2025, when he was having cancer treatment himself - for bowel cancer. "I think something must have been playing on his mind, because now he was seeing what I was going through from the other side," Overton says. "He definitely lingered on the fact that he didn't look after me very well when I was going through treatment." This brought back Overton's memory from five years before, of waking up and finding Uden having sex with her. She says: "I pushed him. 'What do you mean by that? What do you mean you didn't look after me? In what way?'" Uden was arrested by police after his confession to Overton At some point during the conversation, which Overton says was spread over two days, Uden phoned a friend and admitted what he had done, before returning home and confessing to Overton. She felt betrayed, and sickened, but did not immediately end the relationship. She felt like she relied upon Uden, and she loved him too. Overton was already having group therapy for past sexual abuse and mentioned it during her next session. She says: "It was one of the counsellors, one of the therapists that shook me out of it, because I was in bits, I was in floods of tears saying, 'what do I do? How do I stop him from doing it?' "And she said, 'you kick him out and you call the police'. And later on that day she said they'd had a safeguarding meeting, and they would be calling the police about the whole thing, and at that point I kind of knew that it was out of my hands." Det Sgt Eleanor Kirton says Overton's bravery has helped protect other women The case was allocated to Det Sgt Eleanor Kirton, of Derbyshire Police. "The first thing I did was contact Adelle," she says. "Understandably she was incredibly distressed about what had happened." After interviewing Overt

title: I had to learn to walk again after hit-and-run
description: Fiona McGill suffered a shattered pelvis, two broken vertebrae and a broken leg, and wakes up in pain every day.
body: Fiona McGill said she wakes up in pain every day When Fiona Gill was struck by a van she was left with a shattered pelvis, two broken vertebrae and a broken leg. The mother of two said she still wakes up in pain every day. "It was two major surgeries, four months in a wheelchair, and I had to learn to walk again," she said. Antrim GAA footballer Kavan Keenan, who was driving the van in October 2024, was recently handed a nine month suspended prison sentence and a 12 month driving ban. Speaking for the first time since the crash, McGill recounted her injuries and the painful recovery. Fiona McGill was struck by the van in 2024 "My hip needed pinned, my pelvis was shattered, they pulled a piece of car bumper out of my thigh which had cut my muscle away," she said. "The pain was horrendous because I had injuries on every side. The nurses had to turn me [in my bed] and the pain was excruciating." McGill's relatives had to take care of her young boys while she was recovering. "I spent five weeks in hospital, so my sisters had to take a child each. I had to essentially parent from my hospital bed. "My eldest was doing his GCSEs so the impact on him has been significant." Keenan left the scene and initially denied driving the vehicle after the crash in Martinstown, County Antrim, but changed his plea one month before he was due to go on trial. The 27-year-old from Millfield in Ballymena admitted injuring the woman by careless driving and failing to remain at the scene of an accident. He also admitted to driving without insurance and failing to report an accident. Kavan Keenan pictured outside Ballymena Magistrates' Court during a court appearance in August 2025 The footballer's father was given a community service order for trying to take the blame. Asked about the sentence Keenan received, McGill said elements of it were incredibly disappointing. "In terms of his driving, he should have got a bigger ban and he should be retested again," she said. "I wouldn't want his children, or his child, to go through what my children went through, having their parent taken away. "But I feel like his lack of remorse throughout this whole process needed more of a punishment." The van Keenan was driving after the hit-and-run The judge said there were a number of aggravating factors in the case against Keenan, including his failure to identify himself as the driver at the time. During sentencing, the judge said "a common theme" in the character references was Keenan's remorse, and he also highlighted the defendant's contribution to his community. McGill disagrees and said she feels his "remorse is only for himself". "He has shown me no remorse," she said. "Our barrister said in court there had been none shown." McGill said she was speaking now because she wanted people to know the true impact of the crash. "Different people in my community would ask me how my leg was. The truth was it was so much more. "I wake up every day in pain. It has completely changed my life." You can hear Fiona McGill's interview in full on BBC Radio Ulster's Evening Extra at 17:00 BST. title: Indians are discovering the thrill of shopping without paying
description: Dopamine sites mimic shopping’s thrill without the spending, turning the ritual of consumption into a digital game.
body: FoodNeverComes calls itself a 'dopamine kitchen' You are hungry. Or you are not. It doesn't matter. You open FoodNeverComes, pick from 22 cuisines and start scrolling. Butter chicken looks good. So does bibimbap. You add a few dishes, watch the total climb and hit checkout. A tracker says a rider is on the way. Then you get a dummy AI-generated call from inside the site. He is outside your building, he says, but cannot find your street or door. Except there was never any food in the first place. The order exists only on the screen. "Order the food. Skip the bill," says the site., external Its slogan is blunter: "The food never comes - but the dopamine does." Built by two 26-year-old software developers - Purvansh Parmar and Anshul Sharma - from Udaipur in India's northern state of Rajasthan, FoodNeverComes says it has attracted more than 2.7m visitors since its launch in June. It now offers 22 kitchens, 327 dishes and 319 real recipes, complete with fake prices, a simulated checkout and a fictional delivery experience. The site offers 22 fake kitchens, 327 dishes and 319 real recipes FoodNeverComes belongs to a new internet genre: "dopamine sites", which recreate the rituals of consumption without the consumption. There are fake shopping sites, fake delivery services and even fake holidays. The genre took off in South Korea, external and has since travelled well beyond, spawning a growing crop of sites - Dopamine Shop, external or Fakehaul, external, for example - that mimic everything from food delivery and shopping to travel. What, exactly, are we enjoying when we enjoy buying something? The idea began with the founders' own shopping habits. Parmar and Sharma met on a computer science diploma course and later started NeuroX AI, which builds software and AI products and makes Instagram content. They noticed it in their own lives: online baskets filling up with things they wanted, but never actually bought. Sharma would browse electronics, fill an online basket and abandon it. Parmar's mother did much the same. "She would add things to the cart and say, 'I will order this later'," he recalls. Parmar's own version ended at food delivery checkouts. During a two-month project in Mumbai, he says, he was spending 5,000-10,000 rupees a week on food, sometimes ordering treats he did not necessarily need: Belgian waffles, ice cream and, once, a large jar of sour cream he barely wanted and gave away to friends. He believes "perhaps the real craving was not always for the food, but for the ritual of ordering it". Purvansh Parmar says he spent a lot of money on a work trip on food and treats he did not necessarily need What begins as genuine hunger, the two argue, can become associated with the pleasure of ordering. Over time, boredom, anxiety or habit can trigger the urge even when the hunger has disappeared. "Sometimes you're not hungry at all. You're bored or busy, and then you realise that ordering food makes you feel good. You start associating the act of ordering with that dopamine hit. Eventually, it's not just the food you want," says Parmar. Ravi Dhar, director of the Yale Center for Customer Insights, calls this "anticipatory utility" - the pleasure of looking forward to consumption. It is especially strong with things that capture the imagination - a new pair of shoes, a holiday, a restaurant meal - because anticipation becomes part of the experience. Sometimes, Dhar says, anticipation can be more pleasurable than ownership: "The thrill is in the chase." Once the object is acquired and the tension resolved, psychological arousal falls. Neuroscience has a name for this gap between the chase and the catch, and it complicates a popular idea. Dopamine is not simply the brain's pleasure chemical, whatever the internet's talk of "dopamine hits" might suggest. Swiggy, a popular food delivery site in India, alone handled roughly 2.5m consumer orders a day in FY2025 Kent Berridge, a University of Michigan neuroscientist who developed the theory of "wanting" and "liking", says they are separate processes. Wanting is the motivational pull towards something; liking is the pleasure of having it. They often travel together, but not always. Dopamine, in his account, drives the first, not the second. Tempting food or products online are likely to activate this wanting system, which Berridge calls "incentive salience". "Some situations can trigger 'wanting' by itself," he says. We can pursue something intensely even when the eventual pleasure is weak - or, in more everyday terms, want something more than we ultimately like it. Dr Anna Lembke, a Stanford University addiction psychiatrist and author of Dopamine Nation, makes a similar distinction. "To call dopamine a chemical of pleasure is an oversimplification," she told me. "Dopamine is the molecule that says 'get more of' or 'do more of', but it doesn't necessarily equate to pleasure." TripNeverLeaves lets users plan a holiday before sending them on a virtual flight that never leaves the runway. What she adds is the role of ritual. Cues and habits attached to a reward can become reinforcing in their own right, she says: in addiction, the routines leading up to drug use can eventually matter as much as the drug itself. "Anticipation of reward can be as reinforcing as the reward itself," she says. Can repeatedly ordering imaginary food satisfy a real craving? Berridge says the ritual could produce a "dopamine hit and strong 'wanting', and also evoke faint conditioned 'liking'". But he would expect the "novelty to soon wear off", and would be "surprised" if many people returned to place more than about 10 imaginary orders. Dhar is more open to the possibility that simulated consumption could serve as a kind of release valve. title: How the oil capital of the US welcomed a solar power boom
description: Texas is now the country's biggest producer of solar-farmed electricity.
body: Farmer Steve Cargil is now paid $200,000 a year for hosting a solar farm on his land Steve Cargil's family has farmed the flat, dry land around Uvalde, a small city in southwest Texas, since 1953. Cargil, 67, had always assumed that one of his three children would eventually take it over, the way he had from his father. But that assumption took a hit one night in 2018 after a violent hailstorm. Cargil and his son, Ryan, had spent months nursing crops of cabbage and onions to harvest. Then a storm rolled through and destroyed them overnight. "I remember my son saying, 'Dad, I just don't know if I can do this. You do everything right, and we work so hard, and you come out one morning and it's all gone'," Cargil says. Cargil's farm was at risk of ending with him, he says, with none of his three children wanting to farm full time. For years, that left him wondering what would happen to the land, and to his own retirement, since farmers rarely have a pension to fall back on. Then in 2001 Cargil signed a deal to lease 600 acres of his land, about a quarter of the total, to a company called OCI Energy which built a vast solar farm. "Never in my wildest dreams did I think that a solar project would be on my farm," Cargil says. Looking back now, he calls it a blessing. The lease, which pays Cargil $200,000 (£150,000) a year, has let him keep his farm running through a punishing drought. He has been able to concentrate his water irrigation allowance on the land he still farms, and he has stopped losing sleep over rises in the price of things such as diesel and fertiliser. "It's changed my life." Texas, which remains the largest oil producer in the US, earlier this year overtook California to become the country's biggest generator of electricity from solar farms., external And in March of last year, more electricity was produced by solar in Texas than from coal for the first time, according to the US Energy Information Administration. Solar farms can stretch out across the flat lands of Texas On hot afternoons, when demand for power peaks, solar is now regularly supplying around a third of the electricity used across Texas, says Mark Stover, executive director of the Texas Solar and Storage Association. He says that the solar boom is being driven by two main things. Firstly, it is cheap and quick to connect solar farms to Texas' power grid, which is separate to the rest of the US. Secondly, Texas has a huge and growing appetite for electricity, driven by a burgeoning population. Between 2015 and 2025, Texas's population increased by 15.8%,, external making it one of the fastest-growing states in the nation. "We need a whole lot of power in Texas, and we need it quickly," Stover says. Solar has also become inexpensive. James Scott, vice president of project development at OCI, says the technology has had years of small manufacturing gains that brought the price down to the point where it is now the cheapest way to generate power in the state. "No one would have believed that 20 years ago," Scott says. Once a project is built, he says, the price of the electricity it produces can be fixed for decades, since the fuel, sunlight, is free. "We'll charge you $40 a megawatt hour for the next 25 years," Scott says, adding that large buyers such as Amazon and Apple value being able to lock in a price for that long. By contrast, new coal plants in the US produce power at nearly $90 megawatts per hour, says the Energy Information Administration. Farmers have become central to that growth because solar developers need large stretches of flat land. Stover says the industry is now paying out multigenerational income to families through leases that typically run 25 to 30 years and rise in value each year, letting some retire, set up family trusts, or simply keep a farm solvent. Stover argues solar's footprint is smaller than critics assume. "The industry is utilizing less than 0.15% of Texas land," he says. Texas is now the largest producer of solar farm power in the US Yet solar has its opponents. In Franklin County, in northeast Texas, a small group of residents has spent the past few years fighting its growth. BF Hicks, a local lawyer whose family has owned land in the county since the 1800s, says he watched neighbours sign 30-year leases with solar companies and bulldozers clear centuries-old oak trees near his property. He describes a summer when smoke from burning cleared land hung over his town for weeks. "It got real personal," he says, when a solar farm was built next to his family's cemetery. His relatives have been buried here dating back two centuries. David Truesdale, a retired federal law enforcement agent who moved to the county to get away from city life, says he became involved after learning that a neighbouring solar project would sit near his home. And that under Texan law no environmental review was required. "We're destroying the world as we're trying to save it," Truesdale says of the land clearing he has seen. He also points to the large lithium-ion battery units installed alongside many solar farms, drawing a comparison to fires that have occasionally engulfed similar batteries in electric bikes. "If one of those things catches fire, they go off in series, so each one will progressively cause another one to go off," he says. Lawyer BF Hicks fights the building of new solar farms Both men say their objections are not about politics. Franklin County is solidly conservative, but its residents helped push through one of the state's first county-level moratoriums on new solar construction, before it was later rescinded under legal pressure from developers. Their complaints echo a broader unease that has followed solar's expansion into rural Texas - worries about visual impact, water runoff after land is cleared, and battery storage units that scorch their land.
