title: 'Proteinflation': Meet the people paying up to £100 for a bag of protein
description: Consumers are feeling the squeeze from the rising price of protein.
body: The cost of the whey protein Amarpreet Singh buys has almost tripled since 2020 Amarpreet Singh has been drinking protein shakes since he was 16. The 30-year-old, who lives in London and works in banking, started going to the gym at a time when he says protein supplements were mostly associated with bodybuilders. Fourteen years later, shakes are still part of his routine, but they have become considerably more expensive. He says a 4.5kg bag of the whey protein he buys cost around £60 in 2020. By last year, the price had gone up to £120, though he managed to get one from eBay for £90. Now the same bag is £170. "I was a bit gobsmacked," he says. Among his gym friends, the rising prices have even been given a nickname – "proteinflation". Student Evie says the tub she buys is quite expensive for the size of it Over the years, protein powders and shakes have attracted a much broader customer base, while food manufacturers now offer high-protein versions of everything from bagels to water. Evie Lewis is a more recent buyer of protein powder. The 19-year-old University of Manchester student began using it a few months ago because she felt she wasn't getting enough protein in her diet. "You hear a lot more about protein now on social media," she says. But at £32.99 for a 420g tub, she's feeling the high price and tries to make the product stretch. "I've been rationing it and using less than what's suggested," she admits. Max Longman, 32, from Manchester, works in real estate and has been taking protein supplements for 10 years, originally to help him gain weight. He now drinks a protein shake every day and says his monthly spending on whey protein has risen from around £45 a year ago to £60 now. "Loads of foods have protein added to them now. Up until a few years ago, I'd never heard of high-protein yoghurt, and now I eat it three or four times a week," he says. Max Longman has been taking protein supplements for 10 years More recently, weight-loss drugs such as Wegovy and Mounjaro have added another source of demand. People taking these drugs typically eat less, and are often encouraged to make sure they get enough protein while losing weight to help preserve muscle. But that growing appetite for protein is running up against a problem - supply has not kept pace. And the result has been a sharp rise in the wholesale price of some key ingredients, and consumers are feeling the squeeze. High whey protein prices take chunk out of THG profits Food firms scramble to meet the high-protein craze According to global market intelligence platform Expana, the European price of one widely used type of high-protein whey was 130% higher in late August than a year earlier, and more than four times its level three years ago. There is no equivalent UK measure, but Expana says the UK market is closely linked to mainland Europe, where some British businesses source their whey protein. Other dairy proteins have also become more expensive, with another type of whey protein up 60% over the year, while one type of milk protein concentrate was up 80%. Manufacturers say that increasing production takes time and is costly, as producing high-protein whey requires specialist processing and drying equipment. So some are starting to adapt what they make, by changing recipes or looking for cheaper sources of protein. Kieran Fisher's company Warrior is launching a product using cheaper sources of protein Warrior, a UK sports nutrition company, is one of those looking for alternatives. "Our whey protein powder was £12.50 on the shelf last year. We've put that up to £17.99 and we're still subsidising that from other aspects of the business," says its founder Kieran Fisher. The company is now launching a product using other sources of protein, which Fisher says costs around half as much as whey. The effects are also being felt outside the fitness market. Dairy proteins are used in infant formula, and Expana says higher dairy protein costs have contributed to price rises there too. There are, however, early signs that the market is starting to adjust. Wholesale prices for high-protein whey have begun to level off over the past couple of months, although they remain much higher than they were a few years ago. For now though, the higher prices aren't putting off Max. "It feels like protein is so important now, a lot more than it used to be. It's pushed out everywhere," he says. "If you're doing exercise and not taking any, you feel like you wouldn't be recovering properly." But for students like Evie, managing on a much tighter budget, it's a different story. "It was affordable on my gap year [when she was working], but now I'm at university, I don't think I'll continue buying it. It's not a necessity right now," she says. Amarpreet says he will continue buying protein, but admits "it's becoming a luxury". He says £170 for a bag is too much for him, so he's switching to a cheaper brand, which he can get for about £100 a bag. title: What video footage tells us about RAF training jet crash
description: The RAF said training on their Hawk jets had been "temporarily" paused while an investigation is under way.
body: This video can not be played Moment pilots eject as RAF jet crashes in Anglesey The RAF is investigating a crash involving one of its high-speed Hawk fighter jets after two of its pilots ejected and parachuted out of their plane moments before it crashed and burst into flames. The RAF said that training on these jets had been "temporarily" paused as a "precautionary measure". North Wales Police said the pilots, who had been flying a training aircraft, were being treated for minor injuries. While an investigation is under way, here is what we know so far and what the crash footage shows us, according to one expert. The Hawk T2 aircraft had been flying out of the RAF Valley base on Anglesey when it plummeted to the ground at nearby Pencarnisiog. RAF Valley is used to provide both basic and advanced fast-jet training. According to BBC Security analyst Mikey Kay, who also served in the RAF for 20 years, the area was "perfectly situated for training pilots" and was part of the "low-flying system". According to the Ministry of Defence, there are 20 low-flying areas - also known as tactical training areas. They are located in central Wales, northern Scotland, the borders area of southern Scotland and northern England. RAF Valley is also close to the Machynlleth Loop - a series of valleys between Dolgellau in Gwynedd and Machynlleth in Powys. The loop, also known as the Mach Loop, is an attraction for aviation enthusiasts and photographers. "These pilots they train in low level, they train in instrument flying, formation flying, general handling, so that area, the Anglesey area and its accessibility to all of those landscapes for the requirement of training is perfect," said Kay. The RAF plane crash happened near Pencarnisiog The jet involved was Hawk T2 - a two-seat training jet by BAe Systems used for advanced jet training, and designed with similar controls to the Typhoon fighter jet. According to the RAF, it comes with an advanced "glass cockpit", and the aircraft is also used for the "most advanced fast jet training for RAF pilots". The older version of the T2, Hawk T1, is also used by the Red Arrows, which the BBC understands are also included in the pause. However, they were not due to fly again until Le Touquet Airshow in France this weekend. It is not known when the restriction will be lifted. Kay, a former RAF pilot who grew up three miles away from RAF Valley, shared video on social media appearing to show flames rising from the rear of the T2 jet, external as it rolls down the runway. As the jet climbs, the flames seem to disappear. It is not clear how long after take-off the pilot's ejection from the plane took place. Kay told the BBC that the Hawks are non-reheated jets, which means they do not have reheat - also known as afterburn in the US. This is a secondary combustion system that injects raw fuel directly into a jet engine's exhaust stream behind the turbine, which gives the jet a big short-term boost in thrust. It is different to an F18 or a Tornado where orange flames will come out of the jet, Kay explains. "You never ever see flames coming out of the back of a Hawk," he said, adding that in the video, the flames can be seen coming off the side of the engine - where the main hydraulics system is, which controls how the plane flies - and not out of the engine. Kay says that while it is too early to say, it is possible that the cause of the crash was not an engine failure. Kay told the BBC that the video he shared on X also showed a red and white van parked on the side. He said that van is not part of air traffic control, and it was actually spotters, and therefore did not have direct communication with the jet and did not have the authority to tell the jet to abort. Kay said the van, however, does have a direct line to air traffic control, but "by the time that conversation has happened, the jet is already airborne". A video of the crash shared on social media appears to show the two pilots ejecting from the aircraft before it nosedives, crashes and bursts into flames. The footage shows a plume of smoke and fire erupting as the aircraft hits the ground, appearing to narrowly miss residential properties. Kay - who hosts the BBC's Security Brief - described footage of the pilots ejecting being caught on camera as "quite remarkable" and said the pilots' ejection seat was "one of the big lifesavers in this whole story". He said there are two options for ejection that can be taken in a T2 jet - which usually involves an experienced pilot trainer and a student. One option involves both pilots ejecting individually by pulling a black and yellow ring placed between their legs on the jet, the second option is called "command ejection" where one pilot ejects both seats, with whoever sitting at the back going first. According to Kay, once the pilot decides to eject the seats, it sets off a miniature detonation cord (MDC), a thin explosive line that is used to shatter the canopy of a jet in the event of an emergency. "The aircraft seat is designed for the pilot to be able to eject at zero speed and zero height, and that will allow enough time for the parachute to inflate, and then the pilots hit the ground," he added. "As far as I'm aware this is the first known case of this variant, the T2, ejecting pilots out of it," he said, adding that the safety record for these jets is "obviously very good". title: OpenAI and Anthropic bosses push UN for global terms on AI
description: OpenAI's Sam Altman has called for risk evaluation standards, as have Anthropic's Dario Amodei and Hugging Face's Clement Delangue.
body: Sam Altman of OpenAI has become a key figure in the AI technology development. The heads of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Hugging Face have told the UN that the current pace of artificial intelligence (AI) development, and the risks it poses to society, demands international coordination. Altman called for common risk evaluation standards, as did Dario Amodei of Anthropic, a main rival of OpenAI, and Clement Delangue of Hugging Face. Earlier this month, Amodei wrote an essay welcomed by Altman and others calling an AI development slowdown in response to fears about the technology's threat to humanity. However, at the same UN conference, a key technology advisor to US President Donald Trump, rejected the idea any new form of AI regulation. Michael Kratsios, a former Scale AI executive, admitted that the speed of AI development is increasing and that there are risks presented by the technology, but told the UN this was not reason enough "to pause development or constrain it with new global governance structures". "International dialogue in this forum and others cannot be allowed to drift toward global governance," Kratsios added. Kratsios's comments echoed similar statements made by Trump in recent weeks. Trump told the UN on Tuesday he wanted to rebrand it "super intelligence" and has strongly opposed any idea of an AI slowdown because of the US's competitive advantage in the sector. "We're leading China on AI... and, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins," he said earlier this month. Sam Altman of OpenAI and other AI chief executives expressed a different view in their talks to the UN on Wednesday. "If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone," said Altman. He told the UN that he wanted countries to start working together toward "the collective good in the face of powerful new technology". He called for "national and international" AI standards on measuring the capabilities of an AI tool, assessing related risks, AI safeguards, and the degree to which human oversight over such tools is maintained. He also called for "speedy incident reporting, classification, and reporting protocols so the world can learn from failures before they become catastrophes". "We need common standards so countries can compare evidence, verify compliance, and have a shared language and understanding what is happening," Altman added. Not all AI workers think the tech could kill everyone AI 'kill switch' may need to be mandatory, Anthropic co-founder tells BBC AI staff 'genuinely frightened' for humanity's future, ex-Anthropic researcher tells BBC Anthropic's Amodei and Hugging Face's Delangue made similar comments in their speeches. Amodei said that AI "if managed poorly... could be a risk to humanity as a whole". He added that further development of AI tools calls for "even more stringent standards of safety". "We will slow down as much as necessary in order to make sure that every successive AI technology that we release is actually safe," Amodei added. "But regardless of what we do, managing these risks is ultimately bigger than any one company, and it has an industry-wide and global scale." Hugging Face's Delangue said: "The global community needs stronger standards for monitoring and incident disclosure." All three of the executives are based in the US and directly involved in the development of AI technology. Hugging Face, a platform for AI developers, more recently rose to prominence after it admitted to being hacked by AI agents, or AI bots that operate somewhat autonomously, that came out of OpenAI. Hugging Face has since been acquired by AI chipmaker Nvidia. The Hugging Face hack has been treated as a 'wake-up call' within the industry for the ways in which AI technology has advanced and could hypothetically act in ways that could harm humanity. title: Will.i.am backs campaign for Sir Tom Jones to return to The Voice
description: Sir Tom Jones, 86, has appeared as an on-off coach on the ITV show since 2012.
body: Will.i.am collaborated on an Instagram post sharing the petition to reinstate Sir Tom Jones Will.i.am has endorsed a petition to have Sir Tom Jones reinstated on ITV's The Voice. Sir Tom told his social media followers earlier this month that the broadcaster had "fired" him as a judge on the show. The 86-year-old singer from Treforest, Rhondda Cynon Taf, has appeared as an on-off coach on the singing competition since it premiered in 2012. Superfan Aaron Howlett, 50, from Kingston-upon-Hull, started the petition which has received more than 63,000 signatures from around the world. ITV thanked Sir Tom for all of his years on The Voice and the "countless incredible and unforgettable moments" he gave the show. Speaking on BBC Radio Wales Breakfast on Wednesday, Howlett said he had been a fan of Sir Tom for four decades. "Sir Tom is one of the last living legends," he said. "His voice resonates with so many people, young and old." Aaron Howlett says he had the pleasure of meeting Sir Tom 10 years ago, and found him "incredibly humble" "If he stopped singing and performing, then he wouldn't be Sir Tom anymore," continued Howlett. "I think singing is Tom. He resonates from the inside and he becomes alive on stage." Howlett referenced a recent show Jones performed in Milwaukee, USA, where he "was given a standing ovation at 86". "He rocked the crowd. He had the crowd in the palm of his hand. He still does it on the television, and he's the reason that most people watch The Voice," he said. US rapper and songwriter Will.i.am, who has also appeared as a coach on The Voice alongside Sir Tom, collaborated on a Change.org Instagram post on 15 September which shared Howlett's petition. Howlett said he was "overwhelmed" by the response as, when he started it, he was unsure if "anybody [was] going to follow". Howlett believes the other judges on The Voice look up to Sir Tom A spokesperson for The Voice previously said: "We have loved working with Sir Tom Jones over the past nine years on The Voice UK. "While he will no longer be a full-time coach on series 15, we continue to talk to Sir Tom and his team about his involvement in the next series." In a social media post published earlier this month, Sir Tom said: "They are offering a much-reduced role where I would make an appearance but without being actually involved from the start, and I'm not thrilled about that. "So the only thing I know right now is that there's never a good time to fire an 86-year-old who's still pretty good at his job." The programme's 2027 series was due to begin production soon. In the most recent series of The Voice UK, Sir Tom featured as a coach alongside McFly stars Tom Fletcher and Danny Jones, Will.i.am and Destiny's Child singer Kelly Rowland. He has also appeared alongside singers Jessie J, Olly Murs, Kylie Minogue and Rita Ora in previous series, and mentored three competitors on the programme who went on to win. Sir Tom has appeared as an on-off coach on the singing competition since it premiered in 2012 Fans from across the world have commented on the online petition, including Alison, from Peterborough, who wrote: "I, like so many people, watch The Voice because of Sir Tom and will stop watching if he's not on it." Carmela, from Montreal in Canada, said: "My mom passed away 3 years ago. On her death bed she had to watch Tom Jones on TV and on YouTube. Us Canadians love him. My mom and I went to see him in concert 3 times when he came to visit my city." An ITV spokesperson said: "ITV would like to thank Sir Tom Jones for all his years on The Voice UK, and the countless incredible and unforgettable moments he gave the show. "He has brought joy to audiences, and to every singer who performed for him and with him." title: AI superpower ambitions take centre stage as Trump and Xi meet
description: The US and China are vying for AI supremacy while seeking to keep it under human control.
body: The US and China are locked in a race to develop AI US President Donald Trump has been blunt about his AI ambitions, as well as about who he considers the US's main rival to be: China. His Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, has not said anything so forthright - but it seems he holds a similar view. "China very much sees it as a race, they very much think China should be the leading force in AI - they see AI as a power maximiser," says Rebecca Arcesati, from the Mercator Institute for China Studies. You can look beyond the rhetoric for evidence of this: AI has been a cornerstone of China's technological ambitions for more than a decade, whether Xi emphasises it publicly or not. For Trump, beating China to AI supremacy outweighs any risks of the technology to humans - something he has described as "a hoax". China's foreign ministry warned that "narratives of threat" and confrontation hinder global AI governance, calling for cooperation to ensure it benefits all. It means when the two presidents sit down on Thursday there will be few more important topics than their AI ambitions - and what they say and decide will matter to the whole world. There's no doubt the US and China are global leaders in AI but who is ahead depends on how success is measured. American companies lead on so-called frontier models, with the highest-performing systems on most benchmarks coming from firms such as Anthropic, Google and OpenAI. In February 2025, an AI model by China's DeepSeek "briefly matched the top US model" and as of March 2026, Anthropic's top model led the pack "by just 2.7%", according to researchers at Stanford University, external. Part of the US advantage stems from the vast sums being invested in leading AI companies as the frontier labs burn through mountains of cash to build the infrastructure to train new models. OpenAI boss Sam Altman called for a coordinated slowdown of advanced AI development The stock market is booming and a large part of the US economy's expansion relies on the enormous growth - and projected profitability - of AI companies. So that might partly explain why President Trump sees AI as key to US success. Another factor limiting China's ability is the sweeping government restrictions placed on US companies that prevent them from selling advanced microchips to Chinese firms - these are crucial for developing cutting-edge models. Despite the chip restrictions, new AI models are coming out almost monthly in both countries and it's unclear what "winning" the AI race would actually mean, or whether there is a finish line at all. Many companies are racing to develop artificial general intelligence (AGI), a theoretical form of AI capable of learning, reasoning and performing a wide range of tasks at or above the level of humans. The Chinese AI industry has so far focused not on creating frontier models but releasing what is known as open weight models - downloadable and tweakable in a similar way to open source software. This contrasts with the approach taken by many US firms, which largely focus on proprietary models accessed through paid subscriptions or company platforms. Chinese open weight models are being released at a rapid pace, with benchmarks showing the country's top models trailing US rivals by only a few months. Models such as Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 have become popular in China and overseas because they perform close to the frontier models while remaining freely downloadable and adaptable. Beijing's focus is more about deploying the technology across its economy, China analyst Lizzi Lee from the Asia Society Policy Institute said. "AI isn't the moon landing," she said. "The US may lead at the frontier, while China could still gain enormous economic and geopolitical leverage by making capable AI cheap, open and ubiquitous." Yang Zhilin co-founded Moonshot, one of China's most successful AI models, in 2023 AI is also very energy hungry, and China is very well placed there, Rebecca Arcesati told Tech Life on the BBC World Service. "Chinese AI companies are able to access the electricity they need for a much lower cost and that really is an advantage," she said. In robotics - a field of AI that some believe will be world-changing - China has become the world's biggest manufacturer of robots, with more than two million working in the country's factories, the International Federation of Robotics estimated. The nation is also the world's biggest maker of humanoid robots, accounting for more than nine-tenths of global shipments in the first half of the year, according to independent policy institute Chatham House. Chinese AI developers have showed "remarkable resilience and innovation" in spite of the shortage of advanced American chips, analyst Lian Jye Su from tech research firm Omdia said. But US officials and AI firms have also alleged that Chinese developers closed the gap by using distillation - a technique that enables models to learn from more advanced platforms. China's foreign ministry said in response that AI development was "fuelled" by the country's "vision of extensive consultation and joint contribution for shared benefit". China and the US may be in fierce competition, but their governments' approaches to safety concerns are markedly different. While some in the industry have recently warned that AI could pose an existential risk to humanity, Chinese researchers seem less concerned about that and are more worried about potential misuse of the technology and cyber war. Responding to concerns over AI, Trump has said the US already has sufficient rules in place and that the only guardrails AI needs are a "high IQ" president. "We're leading now over China by a lot, and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way," Trump said this week, adding that the US was not going to "stifle the growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution

title: I couldn't live with the agony of migraines any more but my GP called me dramatic
description: Lauren had to abandon her career in the NHS after being left "in agony" due to her migraines.
body: Lauren Evans was just seven-years-old when she started getting chronic migraines Warning: This article contains details and references to suicide When Lauren Evans told her doctor she was suicidal because of the "pure agony" of her chronic migraine, she was told she was being dramatic. Lauren, 29, was seven when she got her first migraine and went on to have them regularly - by the time she was 24, they were happening every day. "People need to understand that a migraine is a full body experience," she said. Migraines are often misunderstood as "just a headache" despite being a neurological condition that can leave people unable to work, socialise or function in everyday life, according to a migraine expert. The Welsh government said it was working to improve access to neurological services. Lauren said when she is having a migraine attack, one eye droops, goes quite puffy and watery Lauren, from Swansea, said: "Although the 'headache' is in the head it can affect body temperature, digestive system, speech, light sensitivity, limb numbness, ability to walk and carry out a journey, brain fog, sleep, neck pain, mood swings, visual aura, sound sensitivity, cravings, vertigo. "I would wake up daily either in pain or worried about when it would start." She also spent a huge amount of time researching triggers and spent "hundreds on various things just to see if that would help" - from vitamins to chiropractors. Lauren was training to become a biomedical scientist in the NHS but the lights and overstimulation of Singleton Hospital were so intense she had daily migraines. Lauren says she had her first migraine when she was a child She added that she often felt dismissed by colleagues who implied she was faking her condition but was lucky that her manager was supportive. Some colleagues would accommodate her by turning off the lights, she said, but others said: "If you don't get your annual leave approved, you can just say you've got a migraine and you won't come in. "That was so untrue. So you're battling, not just your physical health. You're battling all the mental side that comes with it as well. "If I went home every day at the sight of a migraine, I would never be in work. There wasn't a day without pain and if there was, I'd be waiting for it." To manage her symptoms, Lauren changed her working hours, starting at 08:00 BST and finishing at 16:00 so she could get home to take medication, but was still "in agony". "I couldn't make plans because I knew I'd be suffering in the evening. My weekends would basically be spent recovering," she said. The NHS says there is treatment to help manage symptoms Lauren said frequent attacks affected her relationship and left her feeling isolated: "It was a dark time. It got to the point where I was like, 'I can't do this for another year'." Lauren said she went back to the doctor to try to find another option. "I was like I've tried quite a lot of things. Is there any referrals I can have? "I actually disclosed that I'm starting to feel suicidal and I'll never forget the words out of her mouth because I burst into tears immediately - she said: 'That sounds very dramatic, doesn't it?' "I told her I had written a note to my family to say I couldn't live with the pain anymore." She was referred to a neurologist, but four years on and she still has not been able to speak to them. Lauren studied to become a biomedical scientist Lauren saw a crisis team in December, was signed off work for a month and her migraine attacks began to ease. She decided it was time to leave her biomedical scientist career and now has a job at an insurance firm, and feels like a different person. "I have never done so many hobbies in my life," she said. "Jewellery making, painting... and running 50k in September for a charity." Her new medication is working well, but she added: "If it got bad again, I honestly wouldn't know where to turn to." Swansea Bay health board said it was "very sorry to hear of the patient's concerns" but could not comment on individual cases without consent and "would welcome the patient getting in touch with us so we can discuss this further". It said it had a "specialist headache clinic that covers conditions such as migraine, which GPs can refer people to when appropriate". Lauren, pictured on a trip to north Wales with her dog and boyfriend, says her new medication is working well now Experiences like Lauren's are all too common, said Katy Munro, senior GP headache specialist at the National Migraine Centre and host of the Heads Up podcast. "There are various barriers to people getting good help for migraine," she said. "What we're trying to get away from is that preconception that migraine is just a very bad headache." Munro said headaches were a symptom of migraine attacks, but so too are "visual disturbances, nausea and vomiting, sometimes numbness and tingling, sometimes abdominal pain, sometimes dizziness". They are also a spectrum condition, she said, from episodic - meaning people have mild or rare attacks - to chronic where they have more than 15 days a month affected by migraine symptoms. "If you have a migraine attack and you put up with it and then you have another one and put up with it, your brain actually gets more irritable," she said. That means the migraines become more regular and can become chronic if effective treatment is not applied. The first barrier to treatment, Munro said, is that a lot of people believe they are "normal headaches". She said people should always get repetitive headaches checked out by a GP. The next barrier is that GPs often just note down the headaches as a symptom rather than diagnose migraine. The third barrier is the medication that was offered in the past, though this has improved in the last five years, she said. "We need better education throughout the whole of society about how sign

title: 'Perfect storm' could lead to rubbish piling up on Scotland's streets, experts warn
description: There are warnings over a combination of significantly reduced landfill space and a breakdown of Glasgow's main incinerator.
body: The large landfill site at Mount Vernon, Glasgow, has just a few weeks of 'void' space left Scotland's waste sector is on the verge of a crisis which could see rubbish piling up on the streets, experts have warned. They say the combination of significantly reduced landfill space and a breakdown of Glasgow's main incinerator have created a "perfect storm" which could see waste left uncollected. Industry representatives are due to meet ministers to discuss their concerns but say there's no obvious short-term solution to avoid the crisis. The Scottish government said was working with stakeholders to maintain resilience and identify contingency arrangements should they be required. Landfill capacity in Scotland has been shrinking as operators wind down their operations ahead of a forthcoming ban on sending black bag waste to landfill sites. That had been due to come into effect at the start of this year, but was delayed until January 2028 after a Disclosure investigation reported that 100 lorry loads of waste would have to be sent to England by road each day. David Balmer says rubbish will soon have nowhere to go and be left on Scotland's streets Last year there were 10 sites which took in most of Scotland's residual waste – the material left over after recyclable and compostable materials have been separated out. However, that has now been reduced to just three, one of which is in administration. The problems have been exacerbated by the breakdown of Glasgow's main incinerator at Polmadie, which has been out of action since April. Welding cracks were identified during routine inspections and the facility is not expected to resume operations until next March. Much of the city's household waste is currently being diverted to a large landfill site at Mount Vernon - but its operator, Patersons, says it only has a few months of space available for burying the rubbish. The amount of rubbish being processed there has increased from about 2,000 tonnes to 5,000 tonnes a week. An application to extend the site has been refused on appeal by the Scottish government. The operator estimates that it will be full by the end of the year. The ban on sending black bag waste to landfill was designed to encourage more recycling, with the residual waste being sent instead to incinerators where it is burned to create electricity. The proposals sparked a rapid rise in plans to build waste to energy facilities, which led in 2022 to a ban on new applications This was introduced because of concerns that Scotland would end up with more incinerators than needed to deal with the available waste, particularly if recycling rates increased. But the amount of household waste being recycled has barely changed in a decade. A fresh report published last month by Zero Waste Scotland concluded that most incinerators are operating well below their maximum capacity, which suggests the capacity gap might have been miscalculated. Several more sites are under construction, including the South Clyde Energy Centre at North Cardonald, but are not expected to be ready quickly enough to address the current issues. Several sites in the north of England, some of which are understood to have received waste from Scotland, have been shut down by the Environment Agency following investigations into suspected illegal waste activity. Landfill manager David Balmer, who works with Mount Vernon's operator Patersons, said it was possible that Scotland would quickly run out of landfill space. He said the Polmadie breakdown had created a perfect storm. "Could you see waste on the street? Absolutely," he said. Balmer said councils and waste management contractors were under an obligation to collect the rubbish. "But if they can't process it further down the line, what's the easier solution? "The easier solution is to leave in the streets at the moment, pending a solution. The problem is we can't see a solution." Waste consultant Alasdair Meldrum, of Albion Environmental, says he has not seen such a looming crisis in almost 40 years of working in the industry. He says there are already commercial operators who are struggling to find outlets to send their waste, with some being sent hundreds of miles to locations in England. Meldrum added: "There's no easy solution. There are a number of landfill sites that could develop more void space but you can't do the engineering work in the winter. "There's no real short-term solution. We've got ourselves into a real problem." Experts say 80% of the waste in black bags could be recycled One possible solution is for householders to reduce the amount of black bag waste they generate by sending more for recycling. However, rates of recycling have barely changed in Scotland over the last decade. Zero Waste Scotland has estimated that more than half of domestic residual waste could be recycled. One of the biggest elements is food waste which, if collected separately, could be processed through anaerobic digestion. However, environmental group Friends of the Earth Scotland believes its policy which is to blame rather than the actions of individual households. Kim Pratt, circular economy campaigner, says there has been far too much focus on incineration and not enough on reducing how much waste is in the system. She added: "That makes all these problems much easier to solve. It reduces the expense for households, it makes it easier to meet the landfill ban and it reduces the need for incineration." The Grrec energy-from-waste incinerator in Glasgow has been out of action since April Glasgow City Council said general waste was being disposed of at a range of alternative sites, including other energy from waste facilities. A spokesman added: "We are satisfied there is sufficient capacity in the overall system to ensure general waste is disposed of appropriately while the Grrec is offline for repair. title: Teenagers to be offered new vocational GCSE subjects in school
description: New GCSE subjects could include child development and building and construction as vocational courses are being introduced.
body: New vocational GCSEs will be introduced from 2029 for 14-year-olds alongside existing core academic subjects in England. The new subjects could include building and construction, business management and finance, and child development. A new national target for employers to help create 200,000 work experience opportunities for under 16s is also being set by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, as part of reforms to shake-up the education system to better prepare young people for the world of work. Education unions said the ideas were welcome but a clear strategy was needed to make them happen. The Conservatives said the plans risked "throwing away" progress made in recent years. Standards for the new qualifications will be set nationally by the regulator Ofqual to ensure grades are in line with other GCSEs, and will gradually replace other qualifications at this level such as BTec tech awards. The vocational GCSEs will be designed to allow teenagers to progress at 16 to studying similar courses at college, including the new V-levels which colleges are teaching from autumn 2026, and T-levels. The idea is to create a clear pathway for teenagers into different types of work through a ladder of qualifications. Education Secretary Lucy Powell argued the new vocational GCSEs would give young people a "stronger connection" to careers, while the prime minister said it was a change from a "one size fits all" education system. VCSEs, external, a new style of vocational qualification unique to Wales, will be taught in schools and colleges from September 2027. Learners in Wales can choose from 15 VCSE subjects including Animal Care​, Nature Restoration​ and Motor Vehicle Maintenance​. Daisy is taking business studies at BTec Level 2 - this is the kind of subject that could be replaced by a new Vocational GCSE Vocational subjects at 16 currently make up 7% of the entries for qualifications in England and it is up to each school how many subjects with hands-on learning they offer. Wright Robinson College in Gorton, East Manchester, already offers 10 practical or vocational subjects for study in Year 10. Daisy, in Year 11, is taking business studies as a BTec Level 2 which she said is giving her "practical experience" and building her confidence to progress to an A-level in the subject. This is the kind of subject that may be replaced by one of the new vocational GCSEs. Many of these existing tech awards have their standards set by the examining organisations, not the regulator. The standards for the new VGCSEs will be national. Sarjo, also Year 11, already knows she wants to be a flight attendant so she is taking hospitality and catering as a BTec Level 2 alongside GCSEs. She said she "learns faster" in the practical subject and most teenagers want to do something they enjoy alongside core academic subjects. Martin Haworth, executive headteacher at Wright Robinson College, said any new qualifications had to "add value" to what was already on offer and labelling them as GCSEs might help with credibility. He said schools would need to recruit specialist staff if the courses and exams were going to be "robust", and it would cost schools money to convert existing classrooms for practical learning. Sarjo enjoys the practical elements of her hospitality and catering BTec New analysis of school funding by the independent Institute for Fiscal Studies shows the budget per pupil is growing faster than expected, by 9% in real terms between 2025-26 and 2028-29. This is partly because of various government top-ups to the budget and falling pupil numbers in some areas. Economist Luke Sibieta said asking schools to offer more vocational routes would be a "big change" on top of the significant reforms to support for pupils with special educational needs and disabilities. He said there was a "big question mark" over whether there were enough people to teach technical and vocational subjects, with further education colleges already struggling to recruit. The Association of Colleges (AoC) suggested schools worked with them because they could offer "industry standard facilities" and qualified staff. David Hughes, from the AoC, said this would help ensure learning was "authentically different to school and properly employment focused". Daniel Kebede, from the National Education Union, said "sustained investment and resources" was needed to make a success of the new qualifications. While Pepe Di'Iasio, of the Association of School and College Leaders, described the government's plans as "well intentioned" but without making sure schools had the staffing and resources would not remove barriers to young people. He welcomed the national push for work experience and said with placements "extremely difficult" to secure more support was needed from employers. The existing statutory career guidelines for secondary schools in England already require "meaningful" work experience for 14 to 16-year-olds. Employers are now being asked to contact their local careers hub to offer placements. Laura Trott MP, who is the Conservative Party's shadow Education Secretary said she was concerned the changes risked losing the progress England had made in improving standards, and "ripping up the system" could mean "sabotaging young people's futures". "Better schools will continue to protect rigorous subjects but disadvantaged children will be steered towards easier routes, lowering expectations for the very pupils who need high standards most", she said. title: FBI investigates apparent theft of its personnel data by hackers
description: The hackers claim they have every agent's name, role, badge number and personal details including home address, phone numbers and spouse information.
body: The FBI says it is investigating a reported breach of its system after a cybercrime group claimed to have stolen sensitive information on thousands of bureau personnel. The hackers, Shiny Hunters, say they now hold private data on all the bureau staff - around 38,000 people - including anyone who applied to join the investigative agency. The group says it has every agent's name, role, badge number and personal details including home address, phone numbers and spouse information. In a statement posted on X, the FBI said it was aware of the claim and the agency was "actively and aggressively investigating the matter". The criminals claim to have breached the FBI's servers on Monday night and began contacting reporters on Tuesday sharing samples and screenshots of the stolen data. The BBC has seen a small portion of the data which appears to be genuine. According to Reuters, some of the data contains details about officials' ​job assignments, including sensitive work against Chinese spies, Russian intelligence and drug cartels. ShinyHunters is an international collective of hackers, believed to have originally started in France. It has been behind a number of high-profile breaches including on Rockstar Games in April and a highly disruptive hack on education platform Canvas in May. The group claims to have found a vulnerability in the Oracle cloud storage system used by the FBI to breach multiple systems including FBIJOBS, FBI BEAST, which does background checks on employees and applicants, FBI MedLink, which holds agent's medical records and FBI BICS, which holds investigation information. In its message on darkness web, the group said it did not hack the FBI system for money. Instead, the cybercriminals are asking the agency to retract an advisory that it issued about the gang, saying it was "offended" by its characterisation. That FBI's public service announcement, external described ShinyHunters as "threat actors" who often "use their real or exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims". "They target major companies across tech, finance, and retail, often stealing millions of customer records at once," the advisory said. ShinyHunters said it would give the bureau one week to correct or remove what it says are false allegations or they would publish the full databases. The FBI did not respond to multiple requests for comment from the BBC. In its statement on X, the agency said it was trying to determine whether or not the hackers had breached its systems or a third party. "We are actively and aggressively investigating this matter and working closely with those third-party providers that support FBIJobs.gov to mitigate any and all risk," the post said. In a statement to the BBC, a cybersecurity expert said it was a "retaliation attack", which demonstrated that "no organisation is safe from the group". "The group clearly wants to control the narrative around their activities, ensuring nothing is said that could dent their reputation," said William Wright of Closed Door Security. title: Watch: The arms race in space and how the UK is defending itself
description: The UK has jammed satellites to defend itself from hostile threats, the BBC has been told.
body: This video can not be played The head of Britain's Royal Air Force has warned that we we now face an unprecedented threat in space, which could have a devastating effect on the satellites we rely on for communication, internet, bank transfers and satnav. A defence source has told BBC defence correspondent Jonathon Beale, that Britain has already used a ground based system to jam or block the satellite communications of a hostile state. Beale explains there is now a new arms race going on in space. Watch: The arms race in space and how the UK is defending itself. title: Lidl banned from selling copycat Birkenstock sandals, Dutch court rules
description: Lidl must also compensate Birkenstock and pay its legal fees, according to the court ruling
body: Lidl must stop selling copycat versions of Birkenstock's famous sandals in the Netherlands, a Dutch court has ruled. The discount supermarket chain faces a fine of €5,000 (£4,200) per day if it fails to comply and must also hand over sales data to Birkenstock, according to the ruling. Lidl must also compensate Birkenstock and pay its legal fees, with the amount to be decided in separate court decisions. Birkenstock said the judgement sent a clear message that "copycats must not be allowed to free-ride on [our] creativity and innovation". The BBC has reached out to Lidl for comment. The ruling, which can still be appealed, means Lidl cannot sell its copycat versions of Birkenstock's Arizona, Madrid, Gizeh, Boston, and Florida models across the Netherlands, after the court found the discount grocer infringed on the brand's trademark "footbed design". It is the latest in a string of court decisions on Birkenstock designs. In November 2025, a Dutch court order stopped retailer Scapino from selling similar lookalikes in a judgment which is being appealed. And in December 2025, Europe's highest court ruled everyday commercial products can hold copyright if they represent creative design choices, a decision which Birkenstock said was relevant to its "iconic" sandals. However, Birkenstock also faced a setback in Germany's highest court in early 2025. The sandals may have been cool enough for Margot Robbie to wear in the Barbie film, but the German judges ruled they were practical products rather than works of art – an outcome Birkenstock called a "missed opportunity" at the time. Following Wednesday's ruling, Birkenstock said it will "continue to defend its rights vigorously and will use all available legal means to combat imitations of its iconic products". "To protect its retail partners and consumers, Birkenstock will continue to take decisive action against copycats seeking to profit from the company's creative ideas and innovations," it added. Birkenstock is far from the only fashion brand locked in battles with mass retailers over design mimicry. Footwear giants like Dr. Martens have repeatedly taken online big-box sellers to court over boot designs, while luxury house Christian Louboutin spent years in global litigation defending its signature red soles against high-street copycats. title: UK survivor of Canadian poison seller says he exploited her despair
description: Elisabeth Belien tells Kenneth Law's sentencing hearing she took the poison when she was just 23 years old.
body: Law, a former chef, sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients whom he met in online suicide forums A British woman, one of the survivors of Canadian poison seller Kenneth Law, faced him in court on Wednesday to describe how he had exploited her vulnerability. Elisabeth Belien told the four-day sentencing hearing of Law in Ontario, Canada she had been at her lowest ebb when he sold her toxic chemicals when she was just 23. Belien, who until Wednesday had not been known as one of his customers, said she had physically recovered after being successfully given an antidote by medics. But as she faced him as he sat in the glass-panelled dock, she revealed she had suffered "survivor's guilt" after learning from police others had died. Law has admitted 14 counts of aiding suicides in Canada after meeting people in suicide forums online. But there are almost 80 deaths in the UK that have also been linked to him. As part of a plea deal with Canadian authorities, Law will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths. But impact statements from their families are being read during the sentencing hearing this week. Man who sold toxic chemicals should rot in hell, says mother of woman who killed herself Belien told the court: "I had struggled with my mental health for a long time before this. Kenneth Law made it a lot easier to act on that despair. "I continue to struggle with intrusive thoughts and flashbacks of that day. "I made a full recovery. However, emotionally and psychologically, the effects are far more long lasting. "I feel guilty for surviving. Although I survived It has also impacted my loved ones. I feel like my vulnerability was exploited. I still feel a lot of shame about what happened. "I felt like the purchasing from Kenneth Law, I enabled him to continue his business, supplying his products, to other people who might have been vulnerable, like I was. I felt guilty for surviving." Belien, who said she took the poison in January 2023, said being in court reminded her "how easily" it could have been her own parents there talking about her. "I'm learning that things can get better," she said. "I'm learning to be excited to see what the future holds for me. But the gratitude I'm feeling for being alive today doesn't take away from the trauma of the experience." The Ontario Superior Court of Justice on the day of the sentencing hearing of Kenneth Law Authorities say Law, a former chef, sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients he met in online suicide forums in 40 countries. Roughly a quarter of the packages were sent to the UK. He was arrested in May 2023, following a complex investigation by at least 11 law-enforcement agencies that involved investigators from around a dozen countries, including the UK, Italy and the US. David Parfett, whose son Tom died in October 2021, said in a victim impact statement: "Since Tom died, I've struggled with my mental health. "Initially, in the months after he died, I didn't properly mourn him, because my focus was on understanding, and then exposing the harm caused by the internet platforms that allowed Law to trade suicide to kids. "I'm still, after five years, unable to fully process Tom's death. I'm a very different person to who I was before Tom took his own life, having previously been gregarious, outgoing. I find it difficult to enjoy life." A statement was also read from the parents of Henry Tucker, a 14-year-old British boy who died in October 2021. Kate and Henry Tucker said Henry had been diagnosed with autism but actually had a neurological condition that could have been treated with antibiotics. "The realisation that his suffering and his death could have been prevented is a weight that is impossible to bear," they said. "The death of a children under these circumstance is a heavy burden to carry for the rest of our lives. "We will carry it however with Henry's blessings until we meet again. We love you Henry." David Parfett, father of Thomas, who bought poison from Kenneth Law Norson Harris, the father of British victim Ashleigh Harris, read a statement in person on the agony of losing his daughter. He said: "The circumstances of Ashleigh's death have been incredibly tough to bear. "We all feel we should have been able to prevent Ashleigh's death. "Rather than offer the help needed that individual Kenneth Law sold her a chemical that Ashleigh took to end her life. "I still hope over time Mr Law will recognise the answer to Ashleigh and the myriad of others who reached out to him should have been that they were loved and there was help available to them." Earlier Stephen Mitchell Sr, the father of Canadian Stephen Mitchell Jr, told of the aftermath of his death on March 25 2023. "He was ill, he needed help, and I tried my best to bring him that help," he said. "Mr Law robbed my son of that chance to be well." Mr Mitchel Sr, addressing Law in court, said: "I'm willing to accept that during Mr Law's time in incarceration, he might have had brief moments of regret, or even despair and helplessness. "Perhaps he may have even thought during those moments: my life is meaningless, what is the point of living. "That was the same thoughts that my son Stephen had before he took the chemicals that Mr Law sold him. "When my son was well, he would have gladly helped Mr Law work out his depressive thoughts, if asked, because he believed in the value of people." Sandra Scott, whose daughter, Amara Scott, died on February 9 2022 aged 25, said she and her family were trying to help her through a mental health crisis. "Our efforts were cut short when, in her most vulnerable state, she made contact with the accused, she said. "The day I and her friends found Amara, and the way that she died – it broke my heart. title: Tories would prevent long-term jobless spending benefits on alcohol and cigarettes
description: The proposals would also see benefits cut for people who are able to work but have failed to hold down a job.
body: The Conservatives have promised to prevent long-term jobless benefit claimants from spending their welfare payments on alcohol, cigarettes and gambling. Under the party's proposals, claimants who have been unemployed for more than six months would see their Universal Credit cut by 30% if they have not previously paid enough into the system, despite being able to work. This reduced rate would be paid onto a "Back to Work" card, which would not allow cash withdrawals or spending on these items. The Tories said the proposals were designed to encourage people back into work and cut the soaring welfare bill but Labour branded the scheme "unworkable". A Labour Party spokesperson said: "The Conservatives had 14 years to fix our welfare system but they completely failed to make meaningful reforms. "Now they are proposing an unworkable new card scheme, which does nothing to tackle the numbers of people their system left signed off and written off." It's too easy to claim benefits in UK, Badenoch says Reform proposes £50bn welfare bill cut with changes to disability payments for millions The Tories estimate the proposed changes would move about 350,000 claimants onto the lower rate of Universal Credit, saving around £538m a year. Under the proposals, anyone fit to work would get six months on full benefits to find a job. Every two years a claimant has previously worked would buy an extra year on the full rate of Universal Credit - but those who have not contributed enough would drop to a new "Subsistence Allowance", worth 70% of the full rate. The party said this would protect "those with a strong employment record". For example, a 58-year-old who has worked since leaving school but has been made redundant would keep the full allowance up to state pension age. Claimants who are sick, disabled or already in work would also be exempt, with only those judged capable of work affected. The Tories said loading the "Subsistence Allowance" onto a pre-paid card, with restrictions on what the money can be spent on, would ensure taxpayers' money supports claimants with essentials like food. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the current system "where someone who can work chooses not to, and earns more benefits than someone in a job" was "unfair". "The best welfare is a well-paid job. So, we will be tough on those who exploit the system because the current system is unfair to workers, taxpayers and those who truly need support," she said. "Welfare must be a safety net for those who genuinely need it, not a lifestyle choice for those who can't be bothered." However, Helen Barnard, director of policy and research at the anti-poverty charity Trussell, said the proposals were "deeply misguided". "Universal Credit already falls well short of what people need to afford the essentials like food and heating, forcing people across the UK to the doors of food banks," she said. "We see people's health being damaged and their ability to find and maintain work undermined by the severe hardship so many are facing." Reform UK's economy spokesman, Robert Jenrick, said the Tories had left record numbers on long-term benefits and the proposals "won't even put a dent" in the welfare bill. The Conservatives have already pledged to scrap Personal Independence Payment, the main disability benefit in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, for "low-level" mental health conditions to help cut the welfare bill. The party also wants to make it harder to claim sickness benefits, which it said would mean more people are required to look for work. Spending on benefits has ballooned in recent years and is forecast to rise to £408.6bn in 2030/31, according to figures from the Department for Work and Pensions. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has insisted he will get the welfare bill down, for example by tackling but number of young people not in education, employment or training, but not through "crude cuts". title: Burnham brands ban on football fans drinking alcohol in stands as 'discrimination'
description: The prime minister opposes the law - in place since 1985 - and believes there is a case to remove it.
body: A Wrexham fan holds his pint of beer while watching his team play Charlton Athletic Andy Burnham has branded a ban on fans being allowed to drink alcohol in the stands during men's football matches as "discrimination". The prime minister told reporters that "I don't think it's fair for football fans to be singled out", as he suggested a change could be trialled. Laws have been in place since 1985 which have prevented drinking in view of the pitch at stadiums for clubs in the top five tiers of men's football in England. Other sports do not face such a restriction. The Football Supporters' Association (FSA) said the "outdated" legislation should be reviewed, but police chiefs have warned against relaxing the law and would like to meet the PM to "explain the challenges". The legislation was introduced in 1985 by Margaret Thatcher's government for English and Welsh football grounds. At the time, then-Home Secretary Leon Brittan said that alcohol was a "major contributory factor in violent and disorderly behaviour" in football grounds. Burnham is a keen football fan and a season-ticket holder at Premier League team Everton. Shortly before he became prime minister, he criticised the restriction on football fans as he attended a rugby league game at Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium where it was possible for supporters to have a drink in the stands. Speaking to reporters on his trip to the United Nations in New York, Burnham was asked if it was still his view now he is in Downing Street. Burnham replied: "I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different. "And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination. There are different ways it could be done. It could happen on a trial basis. "But I'm not going to back away from what's been a long held view of mine. I don't see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently." A trial or pilot scheme to look at whether a change would be possible is not being ruled out by government sources. But any wider move would require extensive consultation involving football clubs, fans and the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport - none of which is currently planned. A UK Football Policing Unit (UKFPU) spokesman warned that changes to the law would pose "challenges" to policing and the "safety of staff and fans at football games". He said: "Other sports simply don't see the violence and criminal behaviour from their supporters that football does, albeit a minority, with alcohol often playing a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour. "It would be irresponsible to fuel this by allowing greater alcohol consumption during games." He added it would be "incredibly rash to make fundamental changes without a full examination of the evidence and meaningful consultation with police practitioners who have the expertise in this area". FSA chairman Tom Greatrex said it was "unfair to criminalise football fans for having a pint while watching the match - especially since you can sit in the same seat drinking alcohol whilst watching an Oasis gig or rugby league". He said "many clubs" were in favour of a change, adding: "We welcome the prime minister's comments and totally agree that the legislation is outdated and deserves to be reviewed." A fan-led review of football governance in 2021 called for the law to be re-examined. The rules have been relaxed this season with all Women's Super League (WSL) clubs allowed to offer alcohol to supporters in the stands following two seasons of successful trials. The law is more restrictive in Scotland, where the general sale of alcohol has been prohibited in Scottish football stadiums since 1981, but trial sales have been taking place recently and fans can now buy alcohol at Hampden Park games. title: Blood tests find high level of cancer-causing forever chemical in residents near factory
description: People living near a major chemical factory in Lancashire are told they could be at risk of serious health conditions.
body: Residents like Sam told the BBC they were shocked by their blood test results Blood tests have found "really high levels" of a cancer-causing forever chemical in dozens of people living near a major chemical factory in the UK. The residents, from Thornton-Cleveleys, Lancashire, have been told they could be at elevated risk of serious health conditions from the substance, known as PFOA. The village has been under investigation for years by the Environment Agency over contamination of soils and locally grown food from the substance, which is a type of forever chemical - so-called because they do not easily break down. That investigation said high levels likely came from the nearby AGC Chemicals factory, which used it to manufacture coating for frying pans until 2012. Sam and her husband, both from the village, have been told they were at increased risk of health impacts from PFOA. However, she told the BBC was more shocked by her son's result. "When we opened the results...it was like, my God, that is ridiculously off the scale. "I feel guilty because I've introduced [my children] to that way of life. I know it isn't my fault, but the guilt is horrific. Knowing that I've offloaded what levels I probably had over the years into those children when I breastfed them - that's heartbreaking," she said. Forever chemicals are a group of substances, also known as PFAS, that are resistant to water and oil and are in thousands of everyday products, such as clothing and cookwear. But because they do not break down easily they have raised health concerns. PFOA has been banned in the UK since 2020 because it was classed by the World Health Organisation (WHO) as a Group 1 carcinogen, which means there is clear scientific evidence it can increase the risk of cancer. The Environment Agency and Wyre Council have been testing the area close to the AGC Chemicals factory since 2024 to determine if it has been contaminated. They found PFOA at elevated levels in the soil, eggs and locally grown vegetables. Two allotment sites have now been closed and are due to be classified as contaminated land, while residents within 1km of the factory have been advised to peel any fruit or vegetables grown in their gardens. Those investigations concluded the PFOA was likely to have come from the factory having been carried in the air. Two allotments in Thornton-Cleveleys have been closed and are due to be classified as contaminated land Residents previously asked the council to test their blood for the chemical. But according to the UK Health Security Agency, PFAS monitoring is not currently recommended because "tests are unlikely to provide clear information for individuals". Instead independent tests were offered by Manchester Metropolitan University, paid for by investigative journalists Watershed and Law for Change - which funds cases covering environmental issues. Forty-nine residents volunteered, and they were told their blood test readings on Wednesday. Andrew Molloy found out he was in the highest-risk category. "I was half expecting it to be just normal," he said. "Because the investigation here has all been focused on - you're only really being at risk if you eat fruit and veg from the garden or grow your own eggs - which I don't." Andrew's home was built on land that used to be part of the factory. He underwent the tests because he was worried about persistent health problems in his family. "One of the first things I'm going to do is take [the results] to my GP and at least get it on my record. They seem to refuse to do anything related to this, but now I have hard information and data," he said. Mario Panteli, who was visibly shaken by his results, which were among the highest, said it was "quite emotional, a shock". He added: "I bought a property, assuming that this is our forever home. I'm going to have to stop my children from going in the garden, front and back. I feel constricted, like I'm in a cage now." Dr David Megson, who carried out the testing at Manchester Metropolitan University, said the results made him feel sick. "To me, it shows something seriously wrong has happened to that community in that area, that the levels were far higher than anything we would have ever expected to see in the general population." Andrew Molloy expected his results would be normal The UK does not have any recommendations about acceptable PFAS levels in people, although the US and Germany do. Of the 49 residents tested, 70% had readings that could leave them at increased risk of adverse health effects, according to these countries' guidelines. Possible effects include a higher risk of reduced thyroid function, kidney cancer, testicular cancer, elevated cholesterol, pre-eclampsia and ulcerative colitis. Having elevated forever chemicals in their blood is not a guarantee residents will develop these conditions, but US and German authorities have suggested anyone with elevated levels should be offered further health screening. More than 100 residents, including those who had their blood tested, are now considering taking a group legal action against AGC Chemicals to claim damages for the contamination Sarah Moore, partner at law firm Leigh Day - which is representing some residents - said compensation could be sought for financial losses on residents' homes and the impact it has had on their use and enjoyment of the land. She said damages could also be sought "in relation to the health risks, which we now consider to be a significant issue as a result of the testing we've been doing locally". The case would be "groundbreaking in the UK," she added and would be the first time a community has brought a legal claim over contamination from forever chemicals in the country. Overseas, one of the biggest legal cases over PFOA contamination was in West Virginia, in the US, which was depicted in the 2019 film Dark Waters. In that case, DuPont and Chemours Co settled

title: Essex cricketer Das charged with two counts of rape
description: Essex cricketer Robin Das is charged with two counts of rape and will appear in court in October.
body: Robin Das last appeared for Essex in a One-Day Cup match against Middlesex on 21 July Essex cricketer Robin Das has been charged with two counts of rape. The 24-year-old will appear at Inner London Crown Court on Friday, 9 October after he was charged on 23 July. Das was arrested on 27 August last year following reports of a woman being raped in Brixton in March 2024. The Metropolitan Police said in a statement: "Robin Das of Queens Road, Waltham Forest, was charged on 23 July 2026 with two counts of rape. "The charges follow his arrest on 27 August 2025 following reports of a woman being raped in Brixton on 30 March 2024. The woman continues to be supported by specialist officers." Das, a top-order batter, has made 60 appearances for Essex and last appeared for the club in a One-Day Cup match against Middlesex on 21 July, his only senior appearance in the 2026 season. Essex have confirmed that he has been suspended since his arrest, two days after his last appearance for the club. Essex said in a statement: "Essex County Cricket Club can confirm that a male member of the playing staff, currently under contract with the club, recently appeared in court in relation to an incident that took place outside club activities. "Throughout, the club has remained in contact with the ECB, PCA, the Cricket Regulator and the player with regard to the matter, which included an immediate and ongoing suspension. The club will continue to follow all appropriate legal processes and guidance. "As a club we have strict safeguarding and HR procedures in place, and all employees of Essex County Cricket Club are required to meet the highest standards of professional conduct at all times. "As legal proceedings are in progress, the club are unable to make any further comment at this time." Das made his debut for Essex in 2020 and has made nine first-class appearances for the county, along with playing 29 games in 50-over cricket and 24 matches in T20s during his career. Two of the T20 appearances were for Dhaka Dominators in the Bangladesh Premier League. title: Trump's Board of Peace unveils $2.45bn plan to begin Gaza's reconstruction
description: The figure was announced during a meeting of the group's board at the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
body: US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has announced a Gaza recovery plan worth $2.45 billion (£1.85 billion) during a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. The funding will be spread across 66 programmes over six months, and directed at housing, diesel generation and waste removal, among other needs. But the board admitted substantial donations were still needed, with $18bn pledged but only $280 million handed over so far. The board estimates full recovery and reconstruction will require about $71.4bn over the next decade. Jared Kushner, Gaza Executive Board member and Trump's son-in-law, conceded the project faced "different delays on different things, for whatever reason". "The goal of today was really just to show you that we're really fully committed to doing it," he told the meeting of board members and stakeholders. He was joined in New York by US envoy Steve Witkoff, who said the group had made "real progress" over the past year. "All of the hostages are home. There is a ceasefire, imperfect as it may be, but it still exists. Humanitarian efforts have achieved historic results, with billions of dollars donated and pledged to meet urgent needs and support the long work of recovery," Witkoff added. In addition to fundraising, the plan faces significant challenges including how to ensure security for those operating in Gaza, overhaul internal governance and find consensus between Israeli and Palestinians officials. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told a separate press conference on Wednesday that "a number of countries have stepped forward and pledged financial assistance" and the board was "looking for more that will participate in that". Former UK prime minister and board member Sir Tony Blair told the meeting: "The responsibility on us is huge" In August, a senior official on the Board of Peace, Nickolay Mladenov, criticised Israel's continuing air strikes on Gaza, as well as the actions of the Palestinian armed group Hamas. In August, Mladenov warned that a collapse of last October's ceasefire would be "a point of no return" for the region. At least 1,381 Palestinians, including 300 children, have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the US-brokered ceasefire began, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed in combat since the ceasefire and one contractor was killed in an "operational accident". The Board of Peace was created as part of Donald Trump's 20-point Gaza peace plan, which he unveiled alongside Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in September last year. Hamas agreed to return all 48 remaining hostages being held in Gaza in exchange for Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and Gaza detainees, and to the idea of handing over the governance of Gaza to Palestinian technocrats. In July, Hamas said it had accepted a disarmament plan for Gaza which will see it lay down its arms, provided Israel ends "all forms of aggression" and withdraws its forces from Gaza. But that was later rejected by Netanyahu, who said the military would stay in Gaza until Hamas is "genuinely" disarmed. The Board of Peace was originally thought to be an international organisation intended to bring peace to Gaza, but later expanded to include conflicts worldwide. title: Bentley unveils its first fully electric car
description: The SUVs will be built on a new production line in Crewe, which has been Bentley's base since 1946.
body: The Torcal will be built on a brand-new production line in Cheshire Bentley has unveiled its first fully electric car after investing £350m to upgrade its factory in Cheshire. The Torcal SUV will be built on a brand-new production line at the site, which has been the luxury carmaker's headquarters since 1946. Business secretary Jonathan Reynolds said the investment would "support 4,000 high-value local jobs in Crewe". The Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade said the Torcal would strengthen automotive supply chains, as Bentley is supplied by more than 700 businesses including 82 within a 50-mile radius of its base. The announcement comes as the UK motor industry is facing strong headwinds, with JLR recently announcing large-scale job cuts and manufacturers looking for new avenues to grow their businesses. Despite announcements of new electric models to future-proof the industry, there have been calls to slow the switch to a fully EV future. Bentley said the Torcal's 113kWh battery gave it a range of up to 375 miles (600km), adding that it could charge from 10% to 80% in less than 20 minutes using a 400kW charger. The company said the Torcal S model would also be its most powerful car yet with a top speed of 162mph, and the fastest-accelerating from standstill, reaching 60mph in 2.8 seconds. The standard Torcal model can travel at up to 155mph and takes 3.3 seconds to accelerate to 60mph. Materials like leather, wool and aluminium are used in the car's interior Dr Frank-Steffen Walliser, Bentley's chairman and chief executive, called the Torcal "one of the best Bentleys ever" and said it had been designed to combine luxury with electric technology. "The Torcal is a Bentley first and foremost, created by hand by people who care, using the best available materials and technology to blend heritage with cutting-edge innovation," he said. The new Bentley comes in an aluminium finish The new production line is inside one of the Crewe site's original factory buildings dating from 1938. It previously housed the company's machining shop and later its research and development workshop. It has been stripped and fitted with a new floor designed to allow autonomous guided vehicles to move cars through the production process. Reynolds described Bentley's £350m investment as "the third win in just seven days" for Britain's automotive industry following £500m announced by McLaren and £170m from Nissan. The government said it was investing £7.5bn to support a transition to electric vehicles, with plans to phase out new petrol and diesel cars from 2030.
