title: Itauma 'humiliated' but may never lose again - Hrgovic
description: Moses Itauma may never lose again if he can get over the "humiliation" of his IBF heavyweight title defeat, says Filip Hrgovic, who stunned the Briton in August.
body: Moses Itauma has only lost one of his 15 professional fights Moses Itauma may never lose again if he can get over the "humiliation" of his IBF heavyweight title defeat, says Filip Hrgovic, who stunned the Briton in August. The Croatian, 34, stopped Itauma, who had been the strong pre-fight favourite, in the ninth round of their meeting at the O2 Arena. The early signs suggested Itauma had the measure of his opponent, with Hrgovic touching the canvas in the second round and conceding that he was "outboxed" early on. Hrgovic took advantage when Itauma tired but stressed the 21-year-old southpaw is so skilful that he could go on to have a hugely succesful career if he learns from his loss. "He's really good. He's special. Very fast, very talented and he countered whatever I tried with his speed and timing," said Hrgovic. "I never was in the ring before with such a talented kid, with such a fast guy. You have some fast guys but they're small heavyweights. You can handle them with your power but this kid is fast and big. He's got great IQ and great talent. "I'm still kind of angry because he outboxed me. In my whole career, in 20 years of boxing, I was never outboxed in any sparring or any fight." While Hrgovic, who wants to unify the division, praised Itauma's boxing abilities, he suggested doubts remain over his mentality. "It was big shock for him, big humiliation, so maybe it's end of his career if he's not mentally tough. If he recovers from this loss, mentally, it will be hard for anyone to ever beat him again," Hrgovic added. "A lot of people after that kind of loss, they never come back. So, it will be a hard journey for him to come back. "You have to go through a ruthless, hard training camp. You need to go through hell to be mentally ready for this. I think he was physically ready but it's the mental part." title: Barrecore and Boom Cycle owner suddenly shuts studios
description: Common Bond has emailed customers announcing its locations were closed "until further notice".
body: The fitness company behind high-end exercise classes Barrecore, Boom Cycle, and Kobox has suddenly shut all its studios. Common Bond emailed customers announcing its locations, all of which are currently in London, were closed "until further notice". The firm describes itself as a wellness collective and charges £2,400 for 12 months of unlimited classes. It also runs Reformcore and Triyoga brands and said in August last year it had ten sites. Its website is no longer publicly accessible. The BBC has contacted Common Bond for comment. The email sent to customers on Wednesday seen by the BBC said: "We're sorry to let you know that all Common Bond studios are closed until further notice. "We sincerely apologise for the inconvenience and disruption this may cause . We understand this is frustrating, and we appreciate your patience while we work through this." Instructors have told the BBC they were told last week they would not be paid on time and that they only found out about the studios closures from the Wednesday email. One instructor said she and her colleagues were told their pay would be delayed on the day it was due on 14 August. She said: "In good faith, I continued to teach my classes without any news on when or if payment would be made. I have heard absolutely nothing since." The Wandsworth branch of Common Bond's London Barrecore locations It is not clear how many instructors and customers have been hit by the sudden decision to shut the studios down. Companies House filings for Common Bond show the company was incorporated in June last year, so has it has not yet published any accounts. The most recent filings show a director, Ben Allen, left the role last month. Gaspar Lipszyc, listed as a Belgian national living in Spain, is the only currently shown director of the company. Barrecore is a brand specialising in barre, a fitness discipline that combines pilates, ballet, and yoga. Barre is a low impact exercise and its popularity has soared in recent years as famous names including Pippa Middleton have praised its benefits. title: Man died of cardiac arrest on flight, inquest told
description: Geoff Kitchen died onboard a Singapore Airlines flight which experienced severe turbulence in 2024.
body: Linda and Geoff Kitchen were beginning a six-week holiday to Singapore, Indonesia and Australia when their flight experienced severe turbulence A British man who died on board a Singapore Airlines flight suffered a cardiac arrest after the plane was hit by severe turbulence, an inquest has been told. Geoff Kitchen, from Thornbury in South Gloucestershire, died on 21 May 2024 after the Boeing 777 plane travelling from London Heathrow to Singapore encountered a sudden drop in altitude near the south western region of Myanmar. The plane was later diverted to Bangkok, Thailand, where the 73-year-old was pronounced dead. Dr Peter Harrowing, assistant coroner for Avon, said: "I am satisfied that it was the physiological effect of the aircraft turbulence which precipitated the cardiac arrest and ultimately Geoff's demise." Harrowing reached the narrative conclusion into Kitchen's death at a hearing at Avon Coroners' Court earlier. He told the inquest Kitchen, who had a history of coronary artery disease, had also been "thrown from his seat and landed on an adjacent passenger" during the incident. Community condemn AI mural as 'insult' to artists 'Layers of Roman history' found during renovation Britain's oldest lido vows comeback after flood damage Kitchen, a retired insurance professional, had flown out of Heathrow for a six-week holiday to Singapore, Indonesia and Australia with his wife Linda. In a statement read to the inquest, Linda said her husband had been listening to a podcast before the plane experienced a "huge drop or lunge". She said she had started screaming and felt "incredible pain" as Kitchen had pressed her to the side, which caused injury to her back. She also suffered a head wound, which was "bleeding profusely". Kitchen was later moved to the front of the plane to be given CPR, but Linda, who sustained spinal fractures, said nobody told her he had died until two days later. Linda spent 10 days in hospital before she was airlifted back to Bristol, where she spent another week in hospital. Oxygen masks were deployed in the cabin during the incident An initial post-mortem examination held in Thailand found Kitchen had died from congestive heart failure. The inquest earlier was told he had undergone an operation to fit stents to his right coronary artery in April 2019. However, a review in October that year found he had returned to "normal exercise capacity", a statement from his GP said. Dr Edward Sheffield, who performed an additional post-mortem examination on Kitchen's body in Bristol, said his cause of death had been cardiac failure due to coronary artery atheroma and the physiological effects of turbulence. A report into the incident, which Harrowing partially read to the inquest, said 56 people had been seriously injured, 23 suffered minor injuries and one man - Kitchen - had died. "The aircraft was cruising at 37,000ft (11277.6m) when it was approaching the west coast of south-western Myanmar. "At 07:49 GMT, the aircraft flew past a waypoint when the aircraft experienced severe turbulence. "By 07:53, the aircraft had stabilised," the report said. The crew reported the severe turbulence and made a Mayday call at 08:01 with a request to divert to Bangkok. The plane landed there at 08:45 and was met by medical personnel. Linda was not told about her husband's death until two days later Linda launched legal action at the High Court against Singapore Airlines last month, seeking damages to help her access specialist support for her back. The head of Singapore Airlines, Goh Choon Phong, previously apologised for the "traumatic experience" for those onboard flight SQ321. He had also expressed his condolences to Kitchen's family. In a statement via her lawyers, Irwin Mitchell, Linda said her husband's death has been "absolutely devastating" for herself, the couple's two children and four grandchildren. "Losing Geoff was a crushing blow to the whole family as we all thought he would be around to see his grandchildren grow up," she said. Singapore Airlines have been approached for comment. title: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years in prison for sexual assault
description: In court, Miriam Haley said the assault had a "devastating effect on my life and sense of security that may never go away".
body: Harvey Weinstein in court in June 2026 Disgraced Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein has been sentenced to 15 years in prison, after a jury found him guilty last year of committing a criminal sexual act against a former assistant. In a victim impact statement in court, Miriam Haley said the assault had had a "devastating effect on my life and sense of security that may never go away". Appearing in court in a wheelchair, Weinstein denied the allegations but apologised to "anyone I may have hurt by my actions". Weinstein has already spent several years jailed in New York while he has faced three trials in New York over rape and abuse allegations. He has a separate conviction for sex crimes in Los Angeles. This is the second time he has been given a prison sentence in the Miriam Haley case. Weinstein was originally convicted and sentenced in the case in a 2020 trial, where he was also found guilty of raping actress Jessica Mann. But in 2024, New York's highest court overturned the convictions, ruling Weinstein did not get a fair trial. He was retried and convicted again last year on a single charge of a criminal sexual act against Haley. Weinstein, 74, is currently being held in a prison ward at New York's Bellevue Hospital for a series of ailments reported during his incarceration. Once the high-flying producer behind Miramax, the studio that produced hits like Shakespeare in Love, Weinstein fell from grace after the New York Times and the New Yorker revealed multiple women's allegations of sexual assault stretching back decades. The accusations against him sparked the #MeToo movement, but New York prosecutors have had to navigate a twisting path in securing convictions and sentences. The 2020 trial was for charges involving Haley and Mann. Haley testified that Weinstein had assaulted her in a bedroom in his Manhattan apartment in 2006. "I just thought, I have to stand up for myself. I have to stand up for the truth," she told the BBC of her decision to testify. In that trial, the jury also found him not guilty of assaulting Sokola and no verdict was reached on an additional charge of rape related to Mann. After Weinstein was retried last year, he was acquitted of forcibly performing oral sex on Sokola. The jury could not reach a verdict on a rape charge involving Mann and Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg pursued another trial on that charge. In May, the jury in the retrial deadlocked and the judge declared a mistrial. Meanwhile, Weinstein is awaiting a new sentence in California for his 2022 conviction of raping and sexually assaulting an actress in a hotel room in 2013. An appeals court denied Weinstein's request to overturn the California conviction, but ordered a resentencing. It found the judge who gave Weinstein his original 16-year prison term had considered the New York convictions that were later thrown out in determining the sentence. Weinstein has consistently denied the allegations against him, and has said in interviews he believes he will be proven innocent. As he sentenced Weinstein to a decade and a half in prison on Wednesday, Judge Curtis Farber criticised the former Hollywood mogul's stance. "You took what you wanted by force and you have never accepted responsibility," Farber said. title: Family tribute to 'devoted' mum and 'precious' children who died in fire
description: Elisha Brabin, 36, and her children, Leo, 16, Ellis, 8, and Prudence, 7, died in Bootle on Tuesday.
body: Elisha Brabin (pictured with Prudence), Ellis, Prudence and Leo died on Tuesday The family of a mother and three children who died in a house fire have said they are experiencing an "unimaginable" loss. Elisha Brabin, 36, and her children, Leo, 16, Ellis, 8, and Prudence, 7, died after a blaze "spread rapidly" inside a house on Stone Square in Bootle, Merseyside, in the early hours of Tuesday. Paying tribute, their relatives said they had been left "heartbroken" and the loss would be "felt forever". The statement added that "Elisha was a devoted and loving mother" and "our beautiful babies, Leo, Ellis and Prudence, were loved beyond measure". The family said they were "devastated by the loss of Elisha, Leo, Ellis and Prudence". "Elisha was our beloved daughter, wife, mother, sister, auntie, niece and cousin," they said. "She was a devoted and loving mother who lived for her children. They were her whole world, and she meant everything to us." The statement added: "Our beautiful babies, Leo, Ellis and Prudence, were loved beyond measure and brought so much joy, happiness and love to our family. "They filled our lives with laughter and precious memories that we will cherish forever. "The tragic loss of Elisha and our three precious children has left us heartbroken. They have all been taken from us far too soon. "The loss we are experiencing is unimaginable, and the impact on our family will be felt forever." The family asked for privacy whilst they grieved and supported one another, adding: "We would like to thank everyone for their kindness, support and understanding." Tributes, including flowers and teddy bears, have been laid at the scene Listen to the best of BBC Radio Merseyside on Sounds and follow BBC Merseyside on Facebook, external, X, external, and Instagram, external. title: The footballer who had a heart transplant - then became a World Cup winner
description: Martyn Jackson never thought he'd play football again when he had a heart transplant in 2024. Less than two years later, he was a World Cup winner with England.
body: England beat Spain 5-1 in the final of the Transplant World Cup in Frankfurt When Martyn Jackson walked off the pitch after Ramsbottom United's 2-1 win over Cheadle Town in October 2024, it never crossed his mind that one day he could be a World Cup winner. In fact, in the days after that match, his goal was just staying alive. Just a couple of days after the final whistle, Jackson started to feel unwell during the night. He went into hospital and was diagnosed with myocarditis, an inflammation of the heart usually caused by an infection. Within weeks, he was placed on the super urgent waiting list for a transplant. His life was saved when a donor heart became available, and on 28 November 2024, he had successful surgery at Wythenshawe Hospital in Greater Manchester. Fast forward to September 2026, and Jackson scored for England in their 5-1 win over Spain in the final of the Transplant Football World Cup. His team-mates and opponents were, like him, all recipients of a donor organ. This video can not be played England's win at the Transplant World Cup came three days before the start of Organ Donation Week "Obviously, when you've had a transplant, you don't think you're ever going to play again. That's what I thought anyway," Jackson tells BBC Sport. "I'll be forever grateful to my donor and the family for what they've given me. They've given me the gift of life and the opportunity to live my life to the fullest." Football at the Transplant World Cup is not quite the same as the game played at the Fifa World Cup. Instead, it reflects how delicate each player's body is having been through life-altering surgery. Matches are seven-a-side and played over 20-minute halves. Contact is "not as aggressive as I was used to", Jackson says. Having played 11-a-side football in the ninth tier of English football before his surgery, he became a game-changing new addition to the national transplant team when he joined up with the squad in January 2026. Jackson spent his youth career in the academy at Manchester United, before spells at Blackburn Rovers, Preston North End and Burnley. He eventually stopped pursuing a career as a professional and spent 13 years with clubs across the non-league pyramid. During his recovery, wife Lucy heard about the opportunity to join an England Transplant FC team on social media. Martyn Jackson won the Transplant World Cup less than two years after receiving a new heart Daley Cross, manager of the England team, said of Lucy's role: "She was just trying to do her best for him and trying to find a way to motivate him. "His wife did drop in the conversation that he used to play at Manchester United as a schoolboy. So that got our ears twitched instantly. "You could tell from him being on the pitch, even though he was so fresh into his journey, that he knew the football game and he would be such an incredible asset to us. "You can be in a dark place, at the time of diagnosis, through your treatment or even post-transplant. So to have us exist to help and inspire people means that we are getting some incredible footballers. "And that really is the power of it: to that transplant community or to the world, showing people that when you've had organ failure, your life isn't over. There is a chance for you, and you can go and resume and live your life." As the recipient of a donor heart, Jackson has to manage his exercise workload more carefully than his team-mates, many of whom have had kidney transplants, the most common transplant in the UK. His role in the side tends to involve 10-minute bursts, rather than playing for the duration of matches. Daley Cross manages the England Transplant team alongside his job as a youth worker Bayern Munich's Alphonso Davies was diagnosed with a mild form of myocarditis in 2022. He was sidelined for nearly five months, undergoing specialist cardiac monitoring, before returning to play. Jackson started to feel ill two days after Ramsbottom side's win over Cheadle, and his case became so severe that doctors had to fit his heart with a mechanical pump to keep him alive. "Of course it was extremely scary," he says, "but at that stage, when you are critically ill, there's not really much you can do about it. You have to accept it." The super urgent waiting list he was placed on is the highest priority of the three tiers of patients waiting for a new heart. Typically, only about four or five people are on the list at any one time in the UK. Dr Paul Callan, a consultant cardiologist at Wythenshawe Hospital's Heart and Lung Centre, worked with Jackson during his diagnosis and recovery. "Initially, we used to quote an average wait of seven days on the urgent transplant list," he says. "Now it's up to 14 days. Maybe 10% of patients who are put on the list get too poorly and have to be taken off the list." Martyn Jackson was playing for Ramsbottom United in the North West Counties Premier Division in October 2024 That increased waiting time is the result of a reduction in the numbers of organ donors in the UK, with a 9% drop recorded in 2026 compared to the same period last year. There are 8,700 people currently waiting for a donor organ, a figure that NHS Blood and Transplant say is an all-time high. This Organ Donation Week,, external which runs from 21-28 September, the NHS has launched an urgent response plan to address the decline. Jackson has yet to meet the family of the donor from which he received his new heart. He says he is considering reaching out to them around the two-year anniversary of his surgery. For him to make a recovery within that time frame, culminating in playing football in a Transplant World Cup, is "remarkable", according to Dr Callan. England beat six teams on their way to winning last Friday's final in Frankfurt, scoring 36 goals, but for every player at the tournament there is gratitude that they even have the opportunity to play

title: Iran's president tells Trump it will never 'bend the knee'
description: Masoud Pezeshkian's defiant speech to the UN comes after the US president threatened to "annihilate" Iran if a peace deal is not agreed soon.
body: President Masoud Pezeshkian has said Iran will never "bend the knee" after almost seven months of war with the US and Israel, but is ready for a diplomatic solution to the conflict. Responding to US President Donald Trump's threat to "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if a deal is not reached soon, he told the UN General Assembly: "The resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying." Pezeshkian also insisted any deal would have to include an end to the US blockade stopping Iranian ships from using a key Gulf waterway. "It cannot be the case that everyone benefits from the Strait of Hormuz while we are denied access," he said. There was no immediate comment from the US, whose delegation walked out of the chamber at the start of Pezeshkian's address. US and Iran hold first talks since June after Trump's 'annihilation' threat American power, AI and a walkout - key moments from Trump's UN speech UN experts say grounds to believe US committed war crimes in Iran strikes "The US president described us as terrorists. We have been the victims of terrorism," Iran's president told the UN in New York. He then held up a photo of the country's late Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed in a strike on his residence when the US and Israel launched a joint attack in late February. He also presented pictures of some of the more than 175 civilians, two thirds of them children, who Iranian authorities say were killed in missile strikes on a primary school in Minab and a sports complex in Lamerd that day. The US has denied striking Lamerd and said it is still investigating what happened in Minab. "Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed on our country. And we defended ourselves with utmost strength," Pezeshkian said. Iran retaliated for the massive US-Israeli air campaign by launching deadly missile and drone attacks on Israel and neighbouring Gulf Arab states which host US military bases. It also effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, by attacking commercial vessels in the Gulf, the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea. The US responded by imposing a blockade of Iranian ports and ships in April. In June, the US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade. Iran wants to retain some measure of control over the strait and collect fees from vessels that use it, which the US has rejected. This video can not be played Watch: Trump threatens to 'annihilate' Iran if no deal reached In his address to the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, Trump said he faced a "big decision" - either negotiate a deal that would allow Iranians to rebuild their country, or "annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly". Pezeshkian said the threat was "a sign of a bullying mentality". "[Trump] must know that the resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying. We will never bow our head or bend the knee," he said. But he added: "We are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations without accepting the language of force." Pezeshkian made clear that the US blockade would have to end as part of any deal. "It cannot be the case that everyone benefits from the Strait of Hormuz while we are denied access to shipping through this waterway," he said. He also reiterated that Iran would not give up its right to have a civilian nuclear programme and that it would not seek to develop nuclear weapons. "We say it clearly: no nuclear weapons and no limitations on peaceful nuclear technology." Trump argued in his speech that the war had prevented Iran from obtaining a nuclear bomb and demanded that its leaders "relinquish their nuclear ambitions". On Tuesday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and US envoy Steve Witkoff held indirect talks brokered by Qatari mediators on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. Witkoff said he hoped the discussions – the first since June – would "prove constructive and promising", adding that the mediators would continue their work. But Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baqai said the talks were "not anything new" and that Araghchi had maintained Iran's conditions, including the end of the US blockade and the release of frozen Iranian assets. title: Did El Niño turn Hurricane Polo into the most powerful storm of the season?
description: The BBC's Courtney Sargent explains how El Niño could have rapidly turned Hurricane Polo into one of the Pacific season's most powerful storms.
body: This video can not be played Hurricane Polo, a large storm off the coast of Mexico, has been downgraded to a category 4 hurricane but remains "very powerful", according to the US National Hurricane Center. The Pacific hurricane, one of the strongest of the season, was projected to head towards the coast of south-western Mexico bringing intense wind and rain, but was not expected to make landfall. The slow-moving storm is being fuelled by extremely warm waters caused by the El Niño climate phenomenon. The BBC's Courtney Sargent explains how El Niño caused one of the most powerful storms of the season in the Pacific Ocean. Read more about how the El Niño climate phenomenon is affecting the globes weather. Did El Niño turn Hurricane Polo into the most powerful storm of the season? title: Netherlands to return to Eurovision after 2026 boycott
description: The country did not participate in this year's contest but will return next year in Bulgaria.
body: The Netherlands last took part in Eurovision in 2025, when they were represented by Claude The Netherlands will return to the Eurovision Song Contest next year despite a boycott by the broadcaster that was previously in charge of the country's participation. Dutch network Avrotros withdrew in 2026 and said it would also not take part in 2027 because the competition could "no longer be considered neutral" given divisions over Israel's involvement and the Gaza war. The NPO, which oversees public broadcasting in the country, has now stepped in, saying coverage of the contest will be provided by broadcasting organisation NOS, while an independent panel will select the Dutch participant. Jurre Bosman, NPO's director of media, said: "It is important that, as a public broadcaster, we remain part of this unifying European event at this moment in particular." Israel's participation in the contest has become highly controversial, and five countries, including the Netherlands, boycotted this year's event. Eurovision organiser the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) has subsequently announced a number of changes, including to exclude any country involved in an armed conflict from hosting the competition. That means that, although Israel can still compete, the EBU would ask another country to host if it won. The EBU has also proposed changes to to the voting, saying politically motivated voting has become "persistent" and is widely seen as "deeply worrying". However, Avrotros said those changes did "not provide sufficient confidence that the independent and neutral character of the Eurovision Song Contest has been restored". In a statement on Wednesday, the NPO said the EBU has "taken significant steps regarding the rules" of the contest, and that the Netherlands will return. Acknowledging that the contest provokes "mixed feelings" in the Netherlands, the NPO said it had "explicitly asked the EBU to once again make the unifying character of the festival an important part of the event". The NPO also said the Dutch entrant would be chosen by "an independent team of experts" who would "carefully guide the process surrounding the act". Eurovision director Martin Green said in a statement: "We are delighted to welcome the Netherlands back to the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027. "We value the constructive conversations we have had with NPO and look forward to working together to reinforce the Contest as a place that truly reflects the spirit of 'United By Music'." Iceland, Spain, Ireland and Slovenia all pulled out of the 2026 contest in addition to the Netherlands. The 2027 contest will take place on 14 May in Burgas, after Bulgarian singer Dara won this year's contest with Bangaranga. Last month, it was announced that Canada will enter the contest for the first time. title: UK military jamming other nations' satellites to defend itself, BBC told
description: The head of the RAF says the UK faces "unprecedented threats" from adversaries in space, as a new unit is created to defend Britain's satellites.
body: It comes as the UK unveils a new unit dedicated to defending the UK's satellites in space - named the Space Effects Squadron The British military has been jamming or blocking satellites from other countries in order to defend itself from hostile threats, the BBC has been told. The RAF has been using a ground-based system for the past year, which a defence source said had already been used "to deter our adversaries". It is understood the system could be used to prevent a hostile nation's satellites from tracking the movement of the UK's nuclear armed submarines or other sensitive military operations, such as those involving special forces. It comes as the head of the RAF said the UK faced "unprecedented threats" from adversaries in space, coinciding with the creation of a new RAF unit set up to defend Britain's satellites. The Ministry of Defence (MoD) said the new Space Effects Squadron will be focused on "disrupting, degrading and denying hostile threats in space". In a speech on Wednesday, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said daily lives depend on satellites that power everyday technologies like mobile phones and banking apps, adding the loss of GPS would cost the UK economy £1.4bn a day. "Our dependency on space is precisely why it is increasingly under threat from our adversaries." he said. "We depend on them for everything from weather forecasts, energy supplies, and financial transactions to sat-navs, mobile phone connections, and Amazon deliveries," said Streeting, adding that the loss of "everyday conveniences would undermine our daily freedoms, and trust in our institutions." Speaking at the UK Space Conference, Streeting said that threat from Britain's adversaries was growing in "scale, speed and sophistication", adding that the "challenges in space increasingly mirror the geopolitics on Earth". A number of nations are believed to have similar ground-based systems against satellites. Last year the then head the UK's Space Command said Russia was trying to jam UK satellites with ground based systems "every week". The defence source described the UK's terrestrial electronic warfare capability as "world leading, and more". Last week US confirmed for the first time that it had also deployed an unspecified "weapon" in space to defend its own satellites. Both China and Russia condemned the move - warning of an arms race in space. However, Washington has already accused both Russian and China of developing their own space weapons - ranging from electronic jammers, lasers to blind other satellites and even projectiles that can be fired from satellites in orbit. Air Chief Marshal Sir Harvey Smyth said there were "more and more irresponsible and provocative actions" from the UK's adversaries. In May, the RAF tracked a series of "dangerous manoeuvres" by five Russian satellites moving close to two Finnish commercial satellites. The RAF's Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth said in June that a Russian satellite constellation had caused disruptions to GPS signals across Europe and Canada. The UK has a handful of military satellites in orbit for surveillance and military communications. But it works closely with the US Space Force - which has many more. In a separate speech at the space conference, ACM Smyth added that "unfortunately we are seeing more and more irresponsible and provocative actions from our adversaries". ACM Smyth warned that without satellites, some of the technologies people take for granted would be lost and would make every sector "less efficient, less prosperous and less secure". "Sat-nav systems would fail, congestion on our roads would be severe and our emergency services would take longer to help those in need," he said, adding that satellites are also needed to monitor the weather and the effects of climate change. title: Eriksen leaves Wolfsburg by mutual consent
description: Christian Eriksen leaves Wolfsburg by mutual consent, just over three months after collapsing during Denmark's friendly with Ukraine.
body: Christian Eriksen was fitted with an Implantable Cardioverter Defibrillator (ICD) in 2022 Christian Eriksen has left Wolfsburg by mutual consent, just over three months after collapsing during Denmark's friendly with Ukraine. The former Manchester United midfielder's contract with the German second-tier side had been scheduled to run until June 2027. Eriksen, 34, had previously suffered a cardiac arrest during Denmark's opening European Championship group match against Finland in Copenhagen in 2021. "At the moment, it is important for me to be close to my family in Denmark. I'm pleased that we were able to find a solution together," Eriksen said. "My time in Wolfsburg was marked by many highs and lows. I know that the club is now in good hands as it aims to make its way back to the Bundesliga, and I am convinced that a successful future lies ahead." Eriksen, who has not played since June, joined Wolfsburg as a free agent a year ago after leaving Manchester United and made 34 appearances for the club. The 151-cap international has previously played for Ajax, Tottenham, Inter Milan and Brentford. In a statement, Wolfsburg's managing director for sport, Dieter Hecking, said: "It was clear that the decision about his future had to be Christian's. "We wanted to give him that freedom in this particular situation and have now agreed to his request to terminate the contract. "Despite his short time here, he has left a lasting impression on his team-mates, our staff and the fans." title: When and how to see the Harvest Moon in 2026
description: September's full Moon will rise across on Saturday 26 September. The best viewing conditions currently look to be across southern and eastern parts of the UK.
body: September's full Moon will be visible in UK skies this weekend, just days after the autumn equinox. Known as the Harvest Moon, it will reach its fullest point at 17:49 BST on Saturday 26 September. At that time it will still be below the horizon for much of the UK, but it will rise shortly afterwards and appear almost completely full throughout Saturday evening. It gets its name from being the full Moon closest to the autumn equinox, which this year took place on Wednesday. September's full Moon is traditionally associated with the harvest, because historically, the additional moonlight after sunset was useful to farmers gathering crops. The Royal Observatory Greenwich also lists the Corn Moon as another common name, reflecting the crops traditionally harvested around this time of year. However, it does not always fall in September and if October's full Moon is closer to the autumn equinox, it takes the title instead. The 2025 Harvest Moon, seen here rising over the City of London, was on 7 October If you catch the Moon as it rises it may appear yellow, orange or even reddish. This is not a special feature of the Harvest Moon, but simply that when it lies low in the sky and is close to the horizon, its light has to travel through more of the Earth's atmosphere before reaching our eyes. More of the shorter blue wavelengths of light are scattered, allowing the yellows, oranges and reds to become more prominent. A pilot boat passes the rising Harvest Moon in 2021 off Swanpool Beach, Falmouth The current forecast suggests Saturday could bring some drier and brighter weather, particularly across parts of England. However, there is some cloud further west and rain for parts of Scotland and Northern Ireland by the evening. The best chance of clearer skies currently looks to be across some southern and eastern parts of the UK, while conditions are expected to be more changeable elsewhere. The exact times of the moonrise will vary across the UK but will be shortly after it reaches its fullest point. Keep up to date with the weather where you are online or on the BBC Weather app. Autumn equinox 2026: When was it and what happens now? title: Is Burnham right to blame Russia for spreading online disinformation?
description: BBC Verify examines Russian-linked operations spreading false information about the UK, Ukraine and other nations.
body: After Prime Minister Andy Burnham put Russia-linked disinformation campaigns under the spotlight, BBC Verify has been examining how these attempts to influence people's opinions work. We have tracked – and debunked – numerous online disinformation campaigns produced by Russia-linked groups that have attempted to shift public opinion on issues like the war with Ukraine, influence elections in the US and Germany, damage social cohesion and undermine trust in authorities or institutions. In his UN speech, Burnham said there was an "insidious campaign" being carried out by the Russian government to target people in the UK. Last year, a series of fake videos featuring British public sector workers appeared online. Among them was a 999 call operator in Preston named Aaron, who told BBC Verify he was shocked to find out his voice had been cloned with AI to create a fake video of him talking about the 2025 Polish presidential election. This video can not be played British 999 call handler's voice cloned by Russian network using AI Those videos are part of a major Russian-linked disinformation campaign known as Matryoshka, which BBC Verify and other research groups have been tracking. AI is used to create fake videos - sometimes dozens a day - which impersonate journalists and major news organisations like the BBC to push disinformation about Ukraine and Western countries onto people's social media feeds. But Aaron's case indicates ordinary British citizens could also be a target. In the run-up to the 2024 US presidential election, BBC Verify reported how there was a shift in focus from Ukraine to post fabricated videos about the US election. We are once again seeing early evidence of similar misleading videos ahead of November's US midterm elections. BBC Verify has previously exposed a large-scale disinformation campaign run by a former US police officer now based in Russia. With the help of AI, the operation created hundreds of fake local news websites in the UK, US, France and other Western countries with the aim of spreading completely made-up stories. A screenshot of a fake local news website produced by a Russia-linked disinformation operation One of these was a fake news website called the London Crier which falsely claimed that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had bought a mansion owned by King Charles at a bargain price. It was seen by hundreds of thousands of users on X and shared by an official Russian embassy account. We also found that a fake AI-narrated video on YouTube was the source of the bogus story. The platform removed it after we reported it. And in 2023, BBC Verify found a major propaganda operation involving bogus accounts on TikTok, which posted misleading videos in multiple languages - including English - generating millions of views, with the aim of influencing the views of users in several European countries about the war in Ukraine. TikTok removed more than 12,000 fake accounts involved in the operation, saying its investigation indicated that the accounts originated from Russia. Screenshots of two TikTok videos falsely accusing Ukraine's former defence minister Oleksii Reznikov and his daughter of buying a luxury villa and a car Another campaign was discovered during the 2019 UK general election campaign when a trove of confidential documents about a possible trade deal between the UK and US was posted by an anonymous user on the platform Reddit and later used by the Labour Party in its campaign. While the documents appeared to be genuine, Reddit later confirmed in a statement the leak "was part of a campaign that has been reported as originating from Russia". But there are questions about how widespread or effective some of these disinformation campaigns are in reality. While many of them appear to be extensive and organised, it is hard to determine how widely they have spread or how significant a role they have played in actually influencing people. Russia is also not alone in using industrial-scale disinformation campaigns which spread false information to further its own geopolitical aims, as other authoritarian governments like China, North Korea and Iran are also major players in online disinformation. BBC Verify has previously reported on a number of X accounts posting in support of Scottish independence, but whose location information indicated they originated from Iran. And, at the height of the Coronavirus pandemic, the BBC discovered a network of more than 1,200 faked or hijacked accounts on Facebook, Twitter and YouTube that posted pro-Chinese government and anti-US messages. There is evidence to suggest Western governments also engage in disinformation campaigns, although the scale of their operations are not always clear. An investigation by Reuters in 2024, external revealed that during the Covid pandemic, the US military ran a covert anti-vaccine influence operation to discredit China's Sinovac jab. And Meta has previously removed an influence campaign originating from France that targeted a number of countries in Africa, external. AI has also exacerbated the spread of disinformation, as images can now be more easily faked and videos misleadingly edited using text prompts. Text generation has also improved and can create plausible, authoritative and coherent sounding fake news reports. BBC Verify saw evidence of this during US-Israel war with Iran. While in the early weeks of the Russia-Ukraine conflict most of the disinformation published online consisted of old or misleading videos and inaccurate claims, we have seen a deluge of AI-generated images and videos since the Iran war began back in February of this year. Carl Miller, an author and founder of the Centre for the Analysis of Social Media at Demos, told BBC Verify that state-run influence operations "amplify and exploit existing grievances and fissures - making it really hard to work out exactly what sort of effect they might have". title: Ronaldo spurred on by 1,000 goals and Portugal glory
description: Cristiano Ronaldo contemplated retirement after the World Cup but wants to reach 1,000 career goals and help a new-look Portugal thrive before hanging up his boots.
body: Cristiano Ronaldo made his Portugal debut in 2003 and is set to win his 234th cap against Wales Cristiano Ronaldo considered retiring after the World Cup but says he opted to extend his glittering career as he believes he can help Portugal to further success - and reach a personal milestone of 1,000 career goals. The 41-year-old confirmed in the summer that the 2026 World Cup would be his last, although his long-term future remained uncertain. However, he has been included in Jorge Jesus' 25-man squad for Portugal's Nations League campaign, which begins against Wales in Lisbon on Thursday night. In the lead-up to the contest with Craig Bellamy's side, the Al-Nassr forward also targeted the 21 goals needed to reach that magical 1,000 mark. Asked if he thought about retiring from international duty after the World Cup, Ronaldo responded: "Yes, I did. "Of course, I'm always thinking on my decisions, my future, the present also. I'm a thinker, you have to think." The former Sporting, Manchester United, Real Madrid and Juventus player said: "I had a conversation with our president, with our coach. I still believe that I'm able to help the national team to reach what they want. "I think I can give to the national team my support, not only through the goals, but also outside of football." Ronaldo is a two-time Nations League winner with Portugal, and he said adding a third title was also an aim alongside his personal ambitions. "Both aims are important," he said. "One thousand goals, yes, and the national team. Winning the Nations League, the competition starts tomorrow [Thursday], it's a new age." Thursday, 24 September, 19:45 BST Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC One Wales, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Wales, Radio Cymru and 5 Live, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary. Young talents including Fabio Silva, Renato Veiga, Nuno Mendes, Joao Neves and Francisco Conceicao all feature in Portugal's squad for this international window. Ronaldo - who joked he will play on for another decade - says helping his country's newest talents was also a pivotal factor in his decision to continue to represent Portugal. "This is a new young generation. But for me the basic point is to be on the pitch to score the goals and to help the team win games," he said. "For me, the most important thing, I know what I am. I know what I do to be here, to have the success that I have. "I know why young kids love Cristiano, because they see me as an example, and I will continue to do that. Even when I am retired... in 10 years! "I'm happy with myself. It doesn't matter if I play tomorrow, if I rest the next game. For me, the most important thing is that I feel good." Contagious, confident - the rise of Lewis Koumas James had options - but Wrexham not among them This video can not be played Why did Cristiano Ronaldo continue Portugal career? Speaking at a news conference in Lisbon, Portugal boss Jesus described Ronaldo as a "symbol of Portugal and the national team". It came after the five-time Ballon d'Or winner addressed the criticism he has faced throughout his career - particularly during his time with some of the great clubs of England, Spain and Italy. "This [Portugal] is possibly where I have felt most cared," Ronaldo said. "From the fans, I also feel the Portuguese like me. "I do understand that some TV channels like to criticise me, they've tried to kill me with a shotgun, but I can still move away from it. "Anyway, I am used to it. For over 20 years I have been doing this, but my memories are with people who love me." Are fans now more invested in star names than clubs? title: Singer Michael Kiwanuka reveals he is recovering from a stroke
description: The award-winning musician says he faces a "tough journey ahead" after a "quite severe" brain injury.
body: Kiwanuka said he has had "a difficult few months I must say but it feels like I'm on my way there now" Award-winning singer-songwriter Michael Kiwanuka has revealed he has suffered a stroke and faces a "long, tough journey ahead" to recover. The 39-year-old from London, who won the Mercury Prize in 2020 and has been nominated for five Brit Awards, said in an Instagram post that the stroke occurred "a few months ago" and was caused "by a bleed in my brain brought on by high blood pressure". He added that "the brain injury I suffered was quite severe so there's a lot of rehab to be done", but told fans he will "look forward to seeing you all soon". Kiwanuka simultaneously announced the release of his fifth album, titled Fudge, which was recorded before the stroke. Kiwanuka performed on Glastonbury Festival's Pyramid Stage in 2024 "I'm very happy to be announcing to you my new album Fudge," his message said. "I'm especially happy because the last few months I've been battling some health problems which would heavily hinder and get in the way of me making music for the foreseeable future. A few months ago I suffered a stroke brought on by a bleed in my brain brought on by high blood pressure. "It's a long journey recovering from a stroke, which is why I missed some gigs recently out in the US, but I look forward to seeing you all soon. "I'm not sure when I'll be able to be back out on the road or what that will look like, the brain injury I suffered was quite severe so there's a lot of rehab to be done, it's a long, tough journey ahead but I'm fighting to get better. "It has been a difficult few months I must say but it feels like I'm on my way there now." He thanked "all the incredible NHS staff and every single medical professional who has helped care for me and continue to help and encourage me in my recovery", and his friends and family for their support. "This has definitely been one of the toughest challenges I've faced and I'll be happy to be on the other side of it when the time comes. Until then I wish you all well and look forward to seeing you further down the road." Fans and fellow artists sent well wishes, with BBC Radio 6 Music presenter Lauren Laverne replying: "So sorry to read this, Michael. What a time you must have had. Really glad you have good care and wishing you a full recovery asap. One day at a time. Xx." US singer Miguel wrote: "Man, take your time healing, you are needed brother." Radiohead guitarist Ed O'Brien posted: "Sending love to you Michael." Kiwanuka won the Mercury Prize for his self-titled third album in 2020 Kiwanuka first made his mark 15 years ago, being named the BBC's Sound of 2012, and has established himself as one of Britain's most acclaimed singers and songwriters. His first three albums were nominated for the prestigious Mercury Prize for best British or Irish album of the year. He won the trophy in 2020 with his third record, Kiwanuka. That album also earned him nominations for best male solo artist and album of the year at the Brits, and best rock album at the Grammy Awards. He is also known for the song Cold Little Heart, which was used as the theme tune for US TV drama Big Little Lies. But in July 2025 he cancelled all live shows on medical advice because of what was described as "continued illness". Fudge was originally scheduled to come out last year. Before it was postponed, an early review in Mojo Magazine described it as an "intimate" and "brooding" album, influence by Neil Young's On The Beach. title: We live with a 'heavy heart' knowing my brother's death was preventable
description: Lee Gannon died at the Royal Victoria Hospital in February 2022 after experiencing breathing problems at his home in Belfast.
body: Lee's father Colum and sister Colleen made four 999 calls after Lee experienced breathing problems The sister of a man who died after waiting hours for an ambulance has said his family lives every day with a "heavy heart" in the knowledge that his death was preventable. Lee Gannon died at the Royal Victoria Hospital in February 2022 after experiencing breathing problems at his home in Belfast. A post-mortem examination found he died from lobar pneumonia - a severe bacterial infection. The 25-year-old's family called an ambulance but the call was not deemed as a Category 1 emergency and Lee did not reach hospital for almost four hours after the initial 999 call. Delivering the inquest verdict, the coroner said the delay "materially contributed to his premature death". Colleen said her brother was "not just a name" or a number or a recorded call by the ambulance service but a much-loved brother and son who was kind, humorous and deeply cherished. "I stand here today with a heavy heart, I will struggle to find the words to express the pain and devastation that our family has endured." Colleen added that after Lee's death their mother died and said she can not explain the "pain" the effects the inquest had on her. "Five years on we are still here and we are still grieving. "Lee should still be here, our mum should still be here." She said she hopes her brother's death will "bring about change". At the inquest, she and her father Colum were told their family's actions, which included making four 999 calls and carrying out chest compressions, were the right thing to do. Lee Gannon died in February 2022 after experiencing breathing problems at his home in Belfast The coroner, Marie Dougan, said the initial 999 call made by the family should have been registered as a Category 1 - reserved for immediately life-threatening medical conditions - but it was not. There were two further missed opportunities to reassess and re-triage the case by ambulance operators when the family described Lee's deteriorating condition. After the fourth 999 call Lee was re-triaged as Category 1, but the coroner said by the time the paramedics arrived it was too late. "I find that the incorrect categorisation of the initial 999 call and the subsequent failures to re-triage the deceased resulted in a substantial delay in ambulance attendance and transfer to hospital," the coroner said. "That delay deprived the deceased of timely and appropriate assessment and treatment at the Royal Victoria Hospital for pneumonia and sepsis and materially contributed to his premature death." Delivering her findings, Dougan added this was not the first inquest where delays in ambulance response times featured and prolonged delays in handing over patients to Emergency Departments remained a problem across Northern Ireland. "The evidence before me demonstrated the significant effect which prolonged hospital handover delays can have upon the availability of ambulance resources to respond to patient in the community," Dougan said. She acknowledged that the Northern Ireland Ambulance Service (NIAS) was open throughout the inquest, had accepted fault and were committed to learning from his death. The court heard how Lee's mother Anne was devoted to her son and that he was known kindly as a mummy's boy who loved living in the family home. Dougan said while it was Anne's desire to understand what had happened to her son that night, it was a matter of great sadness that she hadn't survived to hear the findings. title: 150 homes damaged by Storm Babet flooding to be demolished
description: Residents in Brechin say they have been living in limbo since floods in 2023.
body: Some residents were rescued by boat when the South Esk breached flood defences in October 2023 A total of 150 homes in an Angus town which were devastated by Storm Babet almost three years ago are to be demolished. Hundreds of people who fled their homes when the South Esk breached flood defences in the River Street area of Brechin were unable to return for months and many properties remain empty. Councillors have approved plans to demolish 150 houses and flats, plus five garages, as well as changes to the river's flood defences that could cost about £8.2m. Residents said they had been living in limbo since the floods hit in October 2023. Dozens of storm-damaged houses could be demolished Council says Storm Babet repairs will exceed £4m Who pays the bills after the Storm Babet flooding? Storm Babet brought very strong winds and heavy rain across much of Scotland and north-east England. The Met Office recorded up eight inches (200mm) of rainfall in the wettest areas. Angus was one of the worst affected places. In Brechin, 60 households had to be rescued and many more went to evacuation centres in Montrose and Forfar. Betty Matheson said she has held off making alterations to her home since the flood Betty Matheson, 78, was forced out of her privately-rented home and was unable to return for several months while the house was gutted, rewired and restored. She said: "I think for all of us still living round here it's been like living in limbo. "There are things I would like to do to the house, but should I bother? "What is the point of doing something to the house and the house is going to be taken down? So there is this uncertainty all about it." She said she would miss the area, but knew her family would help her settle in a new place if needed. "I think it's a shame for Brechin itself," she told BBC Scotland. But she added: "I think I've known for a long time that I will have to move, but I am pragmatic about it." Angus Council has approved the demolition of properties in the River Street area Angus Council held a special meeting to consider options for the future of damaged homes, and the flood defences. Ahead of the meeting, councillor George Meechan said the local authority recognised how difficult the continuing uncertainty had been for residents. "Unfortunately, there is no simple solution that will meet everyone's needs in this area, and councillors must carefully consider the impact on wider Angus communities also affected by climate change," he said. Councillors have agreed to demolish a total of 150 homes, including 29 that are in private ownership. Local Brechin councillor and deputy provost, Jill Scott, said the council knew that not everyone would be happy with the decision. But she said it would "bring closure" for affected households. "With today's decision, the residents and council officers now have clarity in the next steps and while there is a lot of work to do, and there remain some risks in progressing this option, we can move forward together," she said. "I also want to stress that no-one is going to be made homeless by this decision. Our housing officers will support anyone into their next home, whether they are council tenants, private tenants or homeowners." Stella McIntosh's home is in the proposed demolition area Another affected resident said she wondered why Angus Council had taken so long to act since the storm. Stella McIntosh, 82, has lived in the home she owns on River Street for the past 45 years. The water reached shoulder-height in her house, but she has learned to live with the loss of irreplaceable belongings damaged or washed away in the flood. She said she believed her house could fall within the preferred option area for demolition. While her home was renovated after Storm Babet, other properties have remained empty, leaving the area like a "ghost town". "I just feel at my age I don't want to have to move again, but we're going to have absolutely no option," she added. John Cavanagh thinks the flood defences should be improved John Cavanagh, who lives behind River Street on Mitchell Drive, has concerns even though his home is not earmarked for demolition. He had to be taken by boat from his house during the storm. "This whole area was a pond - it was deep enough to take a motorboat fortunately," he said. "We were extremely lucky. I've got no explanation for why we didn't get water in the house at all." He has sympathy for those whose homes were damaged and is also worried that if there was a repeat of the floods the remaining houses could be affected. "Will the flood defences work next time, should they be adjusted?" he asked. "What's going to happen 50, 60, 100 years from now? We need to plan that. "Leaving things as they are clearly didn't work during the floods. If anything, some people will tell us the climate has worsened and we can expect more of these floods." Angus Council has proposed raising the height of the current flood wall. It said the outline cost was about £8.2m. title: Millions of lettuces ruined by UK aphid outbreak
description: Growers are facing losses of £10m, as 30 million heads of lettuce will be rendered unusable.
body: Millions of lettuces are set to be wasted as farmers are grappling with a record outbreak of aphids that has devastated the end of their growing season. Growers are facing losses of £10m, as 30 million heads of lettuce will be rendered unusable, according to the British Leafy Salads Association (BLSA). The organisation says that warm and dry weather has produced "ideal conditions" for the bugs, with as much as 30% of the UK crop between now and the end of October set to be wasted. Homegrown lettuce dominates the market in the summer and early autumn weeks before a transition that sees more imports filling shop shelves. But imported lettuces are now likely to be on the shelves in the UK a couple of weeks earlier than usual. Farms in many parts of England - the Midlands, East Anglia, the south-east, south and north-west - have been impacted by the outbreak. Speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live, BLSA spokesman Dieter Lloyd described the issue as "serious", while not affecting all of the UK crop. He said people have been eating salads from UK products "all summer" but added: "The issue though is serious, the aphids bloom in June and again in August/September." "What we're talking about here is the loss of the crop over the course of the last couple of weeks and the couple of weeks ahead." He said that "this is not all of the heads in the UK, but it's a significant percentage of it" and producers are "looking at not using 30 million heads of lettuce at the cost of £10m to the growers". Over the course of the season, UK growers produce around half a billion heads of lettuce. The outbreak could be set to cost growers £10million over the current four-week period Asked if weather is a factor that has contributed to the issues, Lloyd said that short-term weather patterns and regional variations do have an impact. "We had a problem with aphids last year, we've had a mild winter which traditionally might affect the aphid populations and then they do like warm weather." The National Farmers' Union said that they are looking to support growers and researchers amid the outbreak. Martin Emmett, the organisation's horticulture chairman, said: "This summer's warm and dry weather created a number of challenges for growers and the effects are still being felt, with rising levels of pests and disease now adding further pressure to farming businesses following an already difficult period. "While growers are working hard to tackle record high numbers of aphids, the NFU is supporting the work of grower groups, plant breeders and researchers." title: Badenoch registers gift of £8,177 for Murdoch meeting in Greece
description: The Murdochs' News Corp company paid for flights and accommodation for the Conservative leader and her husband to travel to Greece.
body: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has registered gifts worth £8,177 covering travel and accommodation for a meeting with media mogul Rupert Murdoch in Greece. Badenoch, along with her husband Hamish and shadow minister Alex Burghart, were flown to Athens on 24 August - with the costs paid for by the Murdoch family's News Corp UK organisation. Badenoch's spokesperson said: "Kemi was pleased to meet Rupert Murdoch and senior News Corp and News UK executives. "The visit has been declared in full in the usual way." The spokesperson added: "Kemi values serious engagement with Britain's major media organisations and the people who run them (including at the BBC) and will continue to make the case for a free and independent press." The figures were published, external in the latest register of members' financial interests, in which MPs must report gifts worth more than £300 within 28 days of receipt. In the latest list, Prime Minister Andy Burnham registered three tickets worth £677.34 for seats in the directors' lounge at Everton's first game of the Premier League season. In the record of her meeting with Murdoch, Badenoch lists the following gifts for her and her husband from News Corp UK: An outbound flight from Rome to Athens and a return flight to London, amounting to an estimated value of £4,000 Ground transportation and transfers costing £1,752.50 She describes the purpose of the visit as an "off-site meetings with Mr K R Murdoch and other senior executives from News Corp and News UK". Burghart, the Conservative shadow Northern Ireland secretary, also attended the meeting and has registered a gift of £4,088.97, covering flights, accommodation and transportation. The meeting took place shortly after Badenoch met Italian Prime Minister Georgia Meloni in Italy. Badenoch previously met Murdoch, along with other News Corp executives in 2022, when she was an international trade minister. Murdoch stepped down as News Corp chair in 2023 transitioning to the role of chairman emeritus. His son Lachlan became chair of the company, which owns UK media organisations including Virgin Radio, TalkSPORT, and the newspapers the Sun and the Times. UK politicians over the years have sought to develop good relationships with Murdoch and in 2011 Labour's Tony Blair became godfather to his daughter. Murdoch's publications have switched political allegiances throughout the decades, backing the Conservatives in the 1980s and early 90s and switching to Labour in 1997, before returning to the Conservatives in 2010. In 2024, the Times, Sunday Times and the Sun endorsed Sir Keir Starmer's Labour Party. title: Watch: How toxic smog from wildfires is making Indonesians sick
description: Around 175,000 people in Indonesia have suffered from respiratory illness since August.
body: This video can not be played Wildfires raging in Indonesia have produced toxic smog, causing around 175,000 people to suffer respiratory illnesses since August. The air quality in Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore has reached unhealthy levels as a result of the toxic haze. The BBC's Liza Tambunan explains the effects of the wildfires and how Indonesia is attempting to tackle them. Watch: How toxic smog from wildfires is making Indonesians sick. title: FA charges Cardiff's Bielik as police end inquiry
description: The Football Association charges Cardiff City defender Krystian Bielik over an altercation involving Portsmouth fans, but a police investigation has been concluded.
body: Cardiff defender Krystian Bielik was involved in an altercation with a Portsmouth fan before players became involved The Football Association has charged Cardiff City defender Krystian Bielik with misconduct over an altercation involving Portsmouth fans, but a police investigation has been concluded and they will take no further action over the incident. The flashpoint came during Cardiff's 2-0 Championship defeat at Portsmouth on Saturday, 5 September. The FA stated: "It's alleged that the player [Bielik] acted in an improper manner around the 71st minute of the match." The Poland international has been given until Friday, 25 September to respond to the FA charge. Hampshire Police were notified of the incident during the match and launched an investigation immediately afterwards, but this has been concluded. A police statement read: "Following an incident involving a Portsmouth FC supporter and a Cardiff player at Fratton Park on 5 September 2026, we have now concluded our investigation. "After speaking with the complainant and reviewing all available evidence, the matter has been resolved by way of an out-of-court disposal, agreed by all parties involved. As part of this resolution, an apology has been provided by the player. "The matter is now considered closed, and no further action will be taken in relation to this incident." Cardiff City have been asked to comment. Latest Portsmouth news, analysis and fan views Bielik was involved in a physical altercation with a fan as the 28-year-old went to retrieve a ball from the crowd late in the second half. Several Portsmouth supporters made gestures that indicated they believed the fan had been grabbed by the throat. Cardiff head coach Brian Barry-Murphy claimed afterwards that Bielik "got slapped in the face", while clips circulating on social media appeared to show the Poland international grabbing a young fan around his upper body. In the aftermath, another fan threw a ball at the head of Cardiff defender Perry Ng. Both supporters were ejected from the stadium. After the game, Portsmouth head coach John Mousinho apologised to Cardiff City's players. In the days that followed and having been shown the footage, Mousinho said he was "absolutely furious" at the position he says he was put in over the incident. title: Poland accuses Russian military helicopter of violating its airspace
description: Poland says the aircraft stayed in its skies for 42 seconds, forcing the Nato member to scramble its fighter jets.
body: Poland said a Russian military Mi-8 helicopter - like the one seen in this archive photo - stayed in Polish airspace for 42 seconds Poland has said a Russian military helicopter briefly violated its airspace, forcing the Nato member to scramble fighter jets while ground forces remained on alert. Its military said the Mi-8 aircraft had crossed from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad on Wednesday morning, penetrating Polish airspace to a depth of about 300 metres (328 yards) and staying for 42 seconds north of Braniewo. It said "the nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defence". Moscow did not comment immediately. Poland and other European Nato members have recently said Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine - Moscow denies this. Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly said Moscow does not plan to attack Nato states. By contrast, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said this month that it was Europe that was constantly talking about preparing for war, and he warned: "If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war [from that in Ukraine], and it will be very short." Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory, including the Crimea peninsula annexed in 2014. Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage - and Russia is the chief suspect In a statement, the Polish Army Operational Command said the brief incursion had happened at 11:08 (09:08 GMT), and the helicopter had been tracked by radar. Poland's air defence units were operating around the clock ready to "ensure the safety of Polish airspace", it added. A number of Russian drones and one unarmed Russian missile have landed in Poland since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine, which is not a member of Nato. Last week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk suggested Russia was planning drone and missile strikes against Poland and other countries on Nato's eastern flank. "In recent weeks, the Russian hybrid threat against Europeans... has intensified," he said. "The intent is to intimidate us and break our effort to support Ukraine. The result will be the exact opposite. We are not intimidated because we know that our security today and tomorrow is at stake in Ukraine." French President Emmanuel Macron said shortly afterwards that his country had been targeted by Russian hybrid attacks in the past few weeks, vowing that this would not be left "without a response". Macron said he had already ordered a plan to protect the country's critical infrastructure and defence industry sites. Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyberattacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary. These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary. There have recently been a number of suspicious fires and blasts at defence facilities in a number of European Nato members from Italy to Bulgaria to Estonia, with some of the affected countries blaming Russia. Earlier this month, Germany said Russia was responsible for August's drone attack at Leipzig airport - an accusation denied by Moscow as "absurd". And earlier this week, Lithuania's prime minister told the BBC that his country had already made evacuation plans in the face of threats from Russia, but added they would "not surrender" if attacked. Meanwhile in Ukraine, a Russian drone hit a passenger train near the border with Poland on 13 September shortly after former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson and top European security officials had passed through along the same line. Ukraine said the drone's target "could have been the diplomatic train", while the Russian military said only that it had struck "railway infrastructure". title: Man cautioned over Reform conference assaults
description: West Midlands Police is investigating a number of assaults after protests interrupted the Reform UK conference.
body: Nigel Farage's speech to the conference on 4 September was marked by protests A man has been given a caution by police as part of an investigation into assaults on protesters at the Reform UK party conference in Birmingham earlier this month. Footage appeared to show protesters being manhandled by audience members as they were thrown out. One woman had her hair pulled, and was was hit with a walking stick. West Midlands Police said it was investigating assaults on five people and two other men had been voluntarily interviewed, as inquiries continued. It said the man who was given a conditional caution had also volunteered for interview. The force has asked alleged victims and anyone with information to come forward. Activists disrupted the Reform leader, Nigel Farage, four times during his speech at the NEC on 4 September, before they were removed by security. A West Midlands Police spokesperson said: "Our investigation into a number of assaults that took place at the Reform UK national conference at the NEC continues. "One man has been given a conditional caution after being voluntarily interviewed as part of the investigation." Cautions are offered by police if they have enough evidence to convict and the person involved has admitted their part in a crime. Conditional cautions are the more severe of the two types of caution. Agreeing to a caution is an admission of guilt. People who agree to conditional cautions can be subject to certain terms, which can include a fine, reparations to the victim or rehabilitation. title: Uproar in France over award-winning author accused of using AI
description: Canadian-Haitian writer Thélyson Orélien has just been awarded the Prix du Roman Fnac for his first novel.
body: Thélyson Orélien has denied allegations he used AI in his work The French book scene is in uproar after a Canadian-Haitian author billed as a sensation was accused of using artificial intelligence (AI) to write his first novel. Thélyson Orélien, 38, has just been awarded the Prix du Roman Fnac – the first of the literary season's prizes – for C'était ça ou mourir (It was either that or die). He is also a finalist for the most prestigious annual French language awards, the Goncourt and the Renaudot, set to be issued soon. But on Tuesday a little-known group called Balance ton Claude (Denounce your Claude, in reference to Anthropic's AI assistant) claimed the book was "almost totally" written by AI - a charge the author denied. "We tested several passages, from different bits of the manuscript, to come up with the identical result: 100 percent AI," the group said on X. According to the group – whose membership is unclear – the detection was carried out by a programme called Pangram, which it said was "by far the most accurate", with an almost negligible chance of making a mistake. Orélien, who was born in Haiti and moved to Montreal in 2010, immediately denied the accusation. "I have always loved creation and literature. I can't see why I would feel compelled to use a machine," he told Libération newspaper. He said he was "compiling a dossier" with his editor to prove that he authentically wrote the book. "My traditions are Haitian and Caribbean. The images, the repetitions and the rhythms are the living word, they are my own," he said. The publishing house Grasset also came to his defence, saying the allegations "are atrociously injurious to a writer with an exceptional life-story" whose "work of creation is original and powerful." The novel tells the story of a teacher who flees gang violence in Haiti and his adventures before he finally makes it to Canada, where he re-discovers "the right to breathe without fear". The row recalls the controversy over Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir's The Serpent in the Grove, whose Commonwealth Short Story prize was initially withdrawn in July over allegations that it was written with generative AI. The prize was subsequently re-awarded, after the organisers said they were satisfied the writing was genuine. Critics of Pangram and other AI-detectors say they are unreliable – with different programmes often giving different results after analysing the same texts. Thélyson Orélien's book won the Prix du Roman Fnac this week These tools do not actually know who, or what, wrote a piece of text. Instead, they look for patterns commonly found in AI-generated writing, but those patterns can also appear in human work. Research has found that AI-detectors can wrongly flag human writing as AI-generated and miss text that was produced by artificial intelligence, particularly if it has been edited or paraphrased. Some also say that the programmes are built around the use of standardised language - English or French - and so cannot accurately interpret texts that use dialect from places like the Caribbean. But the writers behind Balance ton Claude said that Pangram had been shown to make a wrong call about an AI-generated text only one time in every 24,400. The latest detectors no longer compare text with text, to see if there has been plagiarism. Instead they analyse probabilities and statistics, to see if certain linguistic patterns betray the use of AI. With AI becoming increasingly normalised, the row over C'etait ça ou mourir will feed the debate over what mix of human and AI creativity is deemed acceptable – it being perfectly possible for writers to generate AI then adapt it, or conversely write an original text then ask AI to review it. Orélien was born in 1988 in the northern Haitian city of Gonaives. His first work – before leaving his homeland – consisted of mainly poetic texts, and later in Canada he worked as a journalist. The novel, described by his Canadian publisher as its biggest seller in 60 years, is due to be translated into around 20 languages. Orélien told Libération that the first draft of the book was written in 2019 – well before AI programmes to generate text became generally available.
