title: Charlotte Church accuses Ed Sheeran of choosing 'capitalism over doing the right thing'
description: Charlotte Church says Ed Sheeran chose capitalism over "doing the right thing".
body: Charlotte Church said Ed Sheeran had "chosen capitalism over doing the right thing" Charlotte Church has accused Ed Sheeran of choosing "consumerism and capitalism over doing the right thing", after Macklemore was dropped from his tour for making pro-Palestinian remarks on stage. Sheeran said the decision to drop Macklemore was made by his promoters, not him. The row has seen ticket prices drop and sales decline for the remaining US leg of his Loop Tour. On Saturday he apologised to fans for making "mistakes" as he opened his first show since the controversy. Sheeran has been approached for comment. Sheeran is one of the most successful songwriters of all time. He has sold more than 120 million records and spent more than 1,000 weeks on the US album charts. Church, who has taken part in pro-Palestinian demonstrations, told the audience at Charlotte Church's Pop Dungeon at Depot in Cardiff on Sunday - the day after Sheeran apologised - that the conflict had "massively changed" her. "Whilst he [Sheeran] has made millions and has an enormous following, he has an enormous platform to do real good in the world, he chose consumerism and capitalism over doing the right thing." She said she did not agree that "musicians shouldn't be involved in politics, politics is life". "Ed Sheeran, we're watching you," she added. Stadium owners put pressure on Sheeran and his promoters to drop Macklemore The controversy began on 4 September, when Macklemore, a long-time pro-Palestine activist, performed as the opening act atSheeran's concert at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. He told the audience: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine." The Thrift Shop rapper then performed a song dedicated to pro-Palestinian protesters at Columbia University. The lyrics are critical of Israel's military actions in Gaza following the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel. The following night, Macklemore referred to the death toll as a genocide, a claim that Israel rejects. In response, the Israeli American Council launched a petition demanding his removal from the tour, and the campaign group StopAntisemitism said the musician had ambushed fans with propaganda. Concert promoter Messina Touring Group said Macklemore was dropped because some venues - such as Kraft's Gillette Stadium - would cancel Sheeran's planned concerts if Macklemore remained on the bill. Kraft, who is Jewish, confirmed he banned the US rapper from performing at Gillette, accusing Macklemore of hate speech and antisemitic rhetoric. "I agree with Macklemore, too many lives have been lost and there has been too much suffering, but only sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas is not honest and only advances more divisiveness and hate," Kraft said. Macklemore was removed from Sheeran's tour on 14 September. Irish singer-songwriter Aaron Rowe, Danish band Lukas Graham, American singer-songwriter Finneas, and Irish folk band Beoga quit Sheeran's tour following Macklemore's departure. Finneas, the brother of pop star Billie Eilish, said artists should "not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed". Ed Sheeran told his Philadelphia audience on Saturday that he was "deeply worried" by the idea that venues would "pre-approve" content or performers At Sheeran's concert in Philadelphia on 20 September, the singer began by addressing the controversy, and spoke for nearly four minutes at the start of his set, saying he had made "mistakes" handling the fallout. "I never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about free speech and the most complex political issue on the planet," Sheeran said. He described the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks as "horrific" and called the situation in Gaza "unjustifiable". Sheeran told the crowd that while he was used to facing criticism for his music, "this week, the criticism was about something much more important, and I've had to take and make difficult decisions - and I am making mistakes - and I'm so, so sorry". This video can not be played "I cannot hide how I feel anymore": Ed Sheeran addresses Macklemore row at show He said he wanted to "address the question of where I stand in the situation in Israel and Palestine, and whether my doing this concert here tonight implies where I stand". "I have tried in my career not to be a political commentator of any kind, because I want my music and shows to be about unity, not division", he continued. "But this is a humanitarian issue, and I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore." Sheeran said what happened in Israel on 7 October was "horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain", and what was happening in Gaza was "catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate". "My heart has been broken by the scale of devastation and loss of civilian lives, of children's lives, and this systemic injustice we're seeing unfold in the West Bank cannot be overlooked." He said he was working out how to contribute in a way that would help "victims of these terrible times - and listening and learning, because I do not know enough". The British singer became emotional as he told the crowd his concert was "still a place where everyone is welcome, and everyone here can stand beside people that have opposing views". He said that he had not known "whether this tour would be carrying on" and "whether I even wanted to be an artist at all", but that he had returned to the stage because he was committed to his fans. Sheeran has been contacted for comment on Church's remarks. title: Two pilots eject and parachute out of RAF plane before crash
description: North Wales Police says the pilots of the RAF T2 Hawk aircraft are being treated for minor injuries.
body: This video can not be played North Wales Police says the pilots of the aircraft are being treated for minor injuries Two RAF pilots ejected and parachuted out of their plane before the training aircraft crashed. North Wales Police said the pilots of the RAF T2 Hawk aircraft were being treated for minor injuries following the incident in the Pencarnisiog area of Anglesey. The force said helicopters from the Coastguard and the Wales Air Ambulance were sent to the scene close to RAF Valley on the island. The pilots have been taken to Birmingham for treatment. The Ministry of Defence has been asked to comment. The two pilots were able to eject themselves before the plane crashed Moments captured from the scene The incident involved an RAF T2 Hawk aircraft flying out of RAF Valley Wreckage of the plane has been found The fire service arrive at the scene "Two pilots are being treated for what are thought to be minor injuries and at this stage there are no reports of any wider damage or injuries," North Wales Police said. "Please avoid the area until further notice." The two air ambulances which were at the scene of the Hawk T2 crash in Llanfaelog have both landed at the Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Birmingham, home of the Royal Centre for Defence Medicine (RCDM). The Royal Air Force said: "An incident involving an RAF T2 Hawk aircraft, flying out of RAF Valley. "An investigation is under way and we will not comment further at this time." One eyewitness told North Wales Live he had watched the aircraft take off before the crash. Pete Bennett said: "I knew straight away that it was in trouble – right on take-off there was an orange flame and as it accelerated it was basically on fire. "As it gained altitude the flame disappeared but it was clearly in trouble. "It climbed at an aggressive pitch… It pitched twice violently in the air and then there were two clear loud bangs. "The pilots ejected and both parachutes opened." The RAF plane crash happened near Pencarnisiog Defence Secretary Wes Streeting posted on X: "An investigation is under way. "My thoughts are first and foremost with the pilots. We will provide further updates in due course." Leader of Reform UK Wales Helen Jenner said: "I grew up in Bodorgan, just along the coast from Valley. "RAF Valley is part of the fabric of Anglesey. "It has trained generations of fast-jet pilots, and our island is proud to be home to the men and women who serve there." The Senedd member for Bangor Conwy Môn said the incident has left her "deeply concerned" and her thoughts were with the crew, their families and everyone at the base. Fighter pilots are trained at RAF Valley Fighter pilots are trained at RAF Valley and it is also a base for maritime and search and rescue operations. The MOD describes its No 4 Flying Training School as responsible for training the "next generation of world-class fighter pilots, external". It opened in February 1941 and became a staging post for US aircraft to help the war effort from 1943. The Prince of Wales was an RAF search and rescue pilot at the Holyhead base from 2010 to 2013 and lived on Anglesey with the Princess of Wales as newlyweds. He returned to the base in April to mark it 85th anniversary. Separately, a publicly-funded airport operated between Anglesey and Cardiff between 2007 and 2020. title: Urgent review after two migrant boats reach shore without being detected at sea
description: Twenty-six people are detained after the landings, but it is not known if others are being sought.
body: Migrants are usually brought to shore by Border Security Command or RNLI boats An urgent review has been ordered by the home secretary after two migrant boats arrived on beaches in Kent without being intercepted at sea. Shabana Mahmood told Border Security Command to carry out the review after vessels came ashore at Samphire Hoe, between Dover and Folkestone, on Tuesday, and near Folkestone on Monday. Twenty-one people were detained on Tuesday after the arrival at Samphire Hoe. Five people were also detained on Monday after the uncontrolled landing near Folkestone, the first undetected landing for a year. The Home Office has not said whether more people are being sought. Before Monday, no small boats had been officially recorded as arriving in the UK without an escort since 6 September 2025. Use all powers necessary on anti-migrant protests, home secretary tells police RNLI reviews security after volunteers targeted online Police must review anti-migrant protests, PM says Ports denied request to land 120 migrants in RNLI boats Hundreds of migrants enter UK after 10-day lull A government spokesperson said: "Border Security Command officers alongside Kent Police have been responding to an incident in Dover. "Twenty-one individuals have already been detained under a swift enforcement response. "There is a thorough investigation ongoing and it would be inappropriate to comment further." Officials said those who had been detained had been taken to Western Jet Foil for processing. Migrants crossing the Channel are usually brought to shore by Border Security Command or RNLI boats. On Tuesday, 154 migrants arrived in three boats, of which one was an uncontrolled landing. It takes the total of migrants to have arrived in the UK this year to 17,784. The total so far this year is down 44.7% compared with figures for 22 September 2025, at which point 32,188 migrants had arrived that year. title: Trump reveals millions of dollars' worth of share deals in big tech and AI
description: Stock in major firms such as Microsoft, Nvidia and SpaceX was bought and sold on behalf of the US president.
body: US President Donald Trump has disclosed millions of dollars' worth of stock market trades made during July, including in firms from Elon Musk's SpaceX to tech and AI giants such as Microsoft. According to official documents, between $6.5m (£4.8m) and $31m worth of stock in Microsoft was sold on behalf of Trump, while they show purchases of between $165,000 and $400,000. Across more than 1,000 trades, shares were bought and sold in AI company Nvidia and software firm Palantir, a contractor with the US defence department and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the filing shows. A White House spokesperson said Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third parties. The spokesperson told the BBC: "Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold. "There are no conflicts of interest." According to the filing, thousands of dollars' worth of stock was also bought and sold in SpaceX, the rocket, satellite and AI company led by Musk - who was once in charge of the US Department of Government Efficiency. SpaceX listed its shares on the US-based Nasdaq stock market in June. Its share price has fluctuated since then, sharply declining in July and August, but it is currently trading 14% higher than its stock market debut. Shares were also bought and sold in Tesla, Musk's electric vehicle-maker, on behalf of Trump. Trump has previously publicly disclosed thousands of stock market trades since he returned to the White House in January last year. title: Azerbaijan pardons Frenchman after EU lifts sanctions on Russian billionaire
description: Martin Ryan is pardoned months after he was jailed on charges of spying, but a second Frenchman remains in prison.
body: Martin Ryan was convicted of spying earlier this year - charges both he and France denied French national Martin Ryan has been pardoned and his release from prison ordered by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev after he was jailed on charges of spying. His release came hours after the EU agreed to lift sanctions on two Russian billionaires, prompting anger from Ukraine. Diplomats had indicated that France had pushed for an end to restrictions on one of the businessmen, Alisher Usmanov. Ryan, who denied espionage, is one of 20 people pardoned by Aliyev. However, a second Frenchman, Anass Derraz, remains in jail in Azerbaijan accused of accepting a Russian bribe. It was not clear what had led to pressure for sanctions on Russian-Uzbek billionaire Usmanov to be lifted - the EU also agreed to take Russian-Israeli oligarch Mikhail Fridman off its sanctions list. Slovakia is understood to have pressed for Usmanov's name to removed initially, and France then backed the move, highlighting national security concerns. Both men have been under EU embargo since the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and until now EU sanctions on more than 3,000 "individuals and entities" have had to be renewed every six months. The latest agreement extends the sanctions on the others for three years. Usmanov was cited by the EU in its 2022 listing, external as having "particularly close ties" to Russia's President Vladimir Putin, and of having "supported materially or financially and benefited from Russian decision-makers responsible for the annexation of Crimea and the destabilisation of Ukraine". The metals and mining billionaire denied this characterisation of him. He has also been sanctioned by the UK and US governments. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha bitterly criticised the EU decision to lift sanctions on the two men, complaining that Moscow was "celebrating, because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans". Latvia had initially opposed the move, but decided to abstain, announcing instead that it would impose its own measures on the two men. Foreign Minister Baiba Braže said it was "dangerous and sends completely the wrong signal at a time when Russia's behaviour is becoming more aggressive". Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said later that France's President Emmanuel Macron had agreed to start talks on Latvia's "accession to the French nuclear deterrence initiative". French relations with Azerbaijan have been poor in recent years, largely because of France's close relations with neighbouring Armenia. However, in May, Macron discussed developing ties with Aliyev, who later spoke of a "new era" in their relations. Under Aliyev's decree on Wednesday, Ryan is one of 20 people including Azerbaijanis and Turks given a pardon. Detained in December 2023, he was handed a 10-year jail term last March for espionage, charges denied by the French government. Prosecutors alleged he had co-operated with employees of France's security services in Baku and gathered information about Azerbaijan's relations with Turkey, Iran and Pakistan, as well as companies linked to Russia and China. "I did not spy. I am not a spy, and during the court case I tried to prove this," Ryan had told the court. Another man he went on trial with, Azad Mamedli, was given 12 years in jail. Mamedli was not among the 20 prisoners pardoned by Aliyev. title: The moment Antonelli knew he had been transformed as an F1 driver
description: Championship leader Kimi Antonelli tells BBC Sport how he is "still finding my way" in F1 after a 2024 crash "stayed in my head for a very long time".
body: Kimi Antonelli leads the drivers' championship by 81 points going into the Azerbaijan Grand Prix Kimi Antonelli says he knew from the first moment he drove this year's Mercedes that he would be transformed as a Formula 1 driver in 2026. The 20-year-old Italian, who is running away with the world championship in only his second season in F1, is reflecting on his breakthrough year in the sport in an exclusive interview with BBC Sport. A difficult debut season last year had left external expectations of Antonelli low at the start of 2026. But on a typically damp and cold January day at Silverstone, he already sensed that something special might be on the cards. "It was just a few laps in the wet," Antonelli says, "but I just felt better in the car, much better than I felt last year. Also the car felt well, but I just felt better mentally in the car. Less tense, more relaxed and more mature." Last year, he says, was "not great". "I was driving very tense most of the time, I wasn't able to extract the potential out of me," he says. "This year, it's a lot different. The mindset has been the biggest change." Fast forward eight months and the effects of that new headspace are plain to see. After 14 grands prix, and with either eight or nine remaining depending on the war in the Middle East, Antonelli is a massive 81 points clear of team-mate George Russell. Not only that, but he looks so in control. Always fast, always composed, a factor in every grand prix. Everyone knows the championship is basically over, barring some kind of dramatic misfortune. Even then, Antonelli says he is "still finding my way" in F1. The journey Antonelli has been on in the past two years is remarkable, and he says even he is "surprised" by the extent of his progress this year. He was comprehensively outperformed by Russell in 2025. So when it was obvious that Mercedes would start the new regulatory era with an advantage, it was the Briton who started the season as championship favourite. Russell duly won the opening race in Australia, but Antonelli was less than three seconds behind him at the flag. This, he says, was the second moment of realisation of what might be possible. "I had a big, big crash in FP3," Antonelli recalls. "But then thanks to the mechanics - who all throughout the season have done an incredible job, but on that specific occasion, it is a miracle - I was able to go back in the car and push again in the high speed and getting close to the limit. "The crash, definitely it compromised a little bit qualifying and the race because we couldn't set up properly the car. I mean, the car was still very quick. But it was not easy. "Still being able to stay close despite that, I was like, 'OK, you know, it's not going to be a walk in the park. It's going to be very tough', but I knew already that it was a different story compared to last year. "If it would have happened last year, I wouldn't have been able to overcome that." Antonelli climbs out of his Mercedes after crashing in first practice for the 2024 Italian Grand Prix at Monza Antonelli's first season in F1 was haunted by an incident that happened the first time he drove on a grand prix weekend. At the 2024 Italian Grand Prix, the day after they had formally announced Antonelli was the replacement for Ferrari-bound Lewis Hamilton, Mercedes gave him an outing in first practice at Monza. He was blindingly fast on his first flying lap - but then crashed heavily on his second. Team principal Toto Wolff played it down at the time, saying he was well aware there would be mistakes from Antonelli as he found his feet in F1. But behind the scenes the incident had had a big impact on the young man. "Monza stayed in my head for a very long time," Antonelli says. "I think all throughout last season, at least. Definitely that was a big thing that was kind of slowing me down. "This memory of being afraid to do a mistake, also because going through the difficult period (in the middle of 2025), this memory was even stronger in my head, if you know what I mean. "Because it was already a difficult period and I was like, 'If I even do a mistake or I crash, it's even worse.' "So yeah, it's been a thing that has been bothering me a lot last year. This year I was able to just put it behind." Doing so has involved a lot of work behind the scenes, analysing what happened in 2025, understanding what had gone well, what had not, and why, and what he could do to improve. "The mindset going into this season, it was mainly trying to be able to extract more out of my potential," Antonelli says. "Trying to, first of all, do a better job than previous year. But as well trying to put things more together. "The preparation that I did in pre-season was very, very intense. But it helped me a lot to arrive ready for this season. "Plus, I did a lot of work with my mental coach. Trying to get my head right, my thoughts right on understanding the goal, and understanding that the most important thing is to be ready and to stay present in the moment. "Not trying to think about final results or what would happen if I wouldn't achieve that. But just trying to be present and trying to do the best with what you can do in the moment." Antonelli crowd-surfs with joyful home fans after winning the Italian Grand Prix earlier this month Still, though, he admits to be "definitely surprised" at how much progress he has made. "I knew that I was going to be better than my first year," he says. "Obviously, because I think last year, towards the end of the season, I started to put things more together, starting to extract more performance. But still, it was still not great. "Whereas this year, it's a lot different. Also as well, with the first win, the first pole, it took a lot of weight off my shoulder." Antonelli has blossomed. Everything seems to be coming so easily to him. If he drops back in a race, he recovers seamless

title: Man Utd still £1bn in debt with £63.5m spent on new stadium
description: Manchester United's overall debt remains over £1bn despite Sir Jim Ratcliffe's extensive cost-cutting measures, with the club also confirming it has spent £63.5m buying land for their new stadium.
body: Manchester United are currently 12th in the Premier League Manchester United's overall debt remains over £1bn despite Sir Jim Ratcliffe's extensive cost-cutting measures, with the club also confirming it has spent £63.5m buying land for their new stadium. Amid a backdrop of fan protests and a disappointing start to the season that has left United 12th in the Premier League and already out of the EFL Cup, United have announced record revenues of £677.6m and a £22.6m operating profit despite not playing in Europe for the first time in a decade. This represents a huge shift from the £113.2m loss in 2023-24. However, while they have saved £8.5m of a projected £16.5m pay-off to axed boss Ruben Amorim after he accepted a job at AC Milan, other costs have increased. Net finance costs for the year were £69.6m, an increase of 228.3%. United put most of this down to a foreign exchange loss. According to football finance expert Kieran Maguire, this sum alone has now exceeded £1bn since the leveraged Glazer family buyout in 2005. Manchester United's new stadium will be the centre piece of a wider Old Trafford regeneration In addition, United also confirmed they spent £63.5m of an additional $125 (£94.14m) added to their historic debt during a summer refinancing move on land for their new stadium. The club has not explained what it has done with the remainder. The stadium itself is likely to cost in excess of £2bn. It means the club's overall debt, while reducing from £1.3bn at the end of December, is still over £1bn, made up of the historic debt, which now stands at £577.6m, the £111.4m outstanding on its revolving credit facility, and outstanding transfer fees, which club sources say represents approximated 75% of the £473m listed and being owed as 'trade and other payables'. This comes at a time when supporters are furious about what they believe to be chronic under investment in Michael Carrick's first team squad this summer. United spent £148m on three new signings - Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans - this summer. It was less than a third of the £458m Manchester City invested in their squad and lower even than newly promoted Ipswich. However, fans are angry there was no additional left-back purchased to provide competition for Luke Shaw, who has missed three matches due to injury already, or striking support for Benjamin Sesko, who missed pre-season as he recovered from a shin complaint that has already resurfaced. While United argue the additional funds were earmarked for their stadium, to be built 350 yards away from where Old Trafford stands, the loan itself is lodged within club accounts. "We are pleased to have secured record revenues," said chief executive Omar Berrada. "This demonstrates the underlying strength of our business, and shows the direct impact of the work we have been doing over the past two years. "While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we will continue to take a disciplined approach to ensure our finances remain sustainable. "With that financial sustainability in mind, we have strengthened both our men's and women's teams during the summer window and our men's team has seen the return of Champions League football to Old Trafford." United have also been criticised for a lack of investment in the Women's Super League squad, which is currently second bottom of the table with one point from three games. Ratcliffe previously argued the club had to take strong action to slash losses. Two lots of redundancies led to 450 people losing their jobs, while United have confirmed their latest set of salary costs have reduced by £11.3m to £302m. "This is primarily due to changes in the make-up of the men's first team squad, combined with savings associated with headcount reduction programs implemented over the previous two fiscal years," said the club. title: England players carrying World Cup scar - Saka
description: England winger Bukayo Saka says the team are still carrying the "scar" of their heartbreaking World Cup semi-final exit to Argentina.
body: Bukayo Saka started three of England's eight games at the World Cup England winger Bukayo Saka says the team are still carrying the "scar" of their heartbreaking World Cup semi-final exit to Argentina. Thomas Tuchel's team were on the verge of becoming the first England side to reach a men's World Cup final since 1966, but were stunned by two late Argentina goals as they fell to a 2-1 loss. A thrilling 6-4 victory over France in the bronze medal match gave the Three Lions their best World Cup finish in six decades, but the wait for their second trophy goes on. "Obviously, there is still a scar on us when you believed and everyone was so united and so confident we could do it," Saka said. "Not just us, but the whole country we felt. "You try to move on as soon as possible, but you know a scar is a scar, it decides to heal when it heals itself." England get an immediate reminder of what might have been as they host world champions Spain at Wembley on Saturday (19:45 BST) in the first of four Nations League matches over the next two weeks. "We are trying to draw a line under [the World Cup] now and focus on the new international season that we have coming up," Saka added. "We have got four massive, difficult group games to try and qualify us for the Nations League [knockouts] that we are really focused on." Meanwhile, Saka believes it is only a matter of time before his Arsenal team-mate Max Dowman, 16, earns a senior England call-up. "I think so," Saka said. "His talent is insane. It's up to him how far he is going to go in football. His talent is crazy." England Under-21 manager Lee Carsley concurred with Saka on Dowman's "amazing talent" but thinks the youngster staying with the under-19s during this international window is the best option. "He is more than capable of playing in the under-21s," Carsley said. "What I do think will happen with the age group he goes to is that he can play the minutes. "He can also have that time to consolidate where he is in his career and play with his friends again and take that little bit of pressure off him. "I have no doubt that Max is going to be with the under-21s. "That is something I am keen to have a conversation with him and his parents, on the way we see his pathway going, because he is an amazing talent and someone we are very lucky to have." title: Admiral insurance firm to cut 500 jobs in the UK
description: The proposals relate to Admiral's UK insurance business, and will affect about 5% of its workforce.
body: Admiral, which has its headquarters in Cardiff, said the job losses were part of its efforts to save £100m Insurer Admiral will cut 500 jobs in the UK to save £100m, it has announced. The proposals are related to Admiral's UK insurance business only, and will affect about 5% of its workforce. "We recognise this will be a difficult time for affected colleagues," said Alistair Hargreaves, Admiral Insurance UK's chief executive . While the Cardiff-based company uses artificial intelligence (AI) in its operations, adoption of AI is not believed to be responsible for these changes. Admiral said the job cuts would make the firm "faster and more efficient". Earlier this year, Admiral said it needed to save £100m, and has added the proposed redundancies are part of that cost-cutting effort. "These changes are aimed at making us faster and more efficient so we can continue to deliver great customer outcomes," said Hargreaves. Staff members who are affected will be offered "enhanced" redundancy payments and redeployment opportunities where possible. Hargreaves said Admiral was also "making a significant investment in meaningful support to help colleagues consider future options". title: Many hydrants lacking flow needed for firefighting needs, fire chiefs say
description: Inadequate water supplies are "affecting fire crews' ability" to respond to incidents, say fire chiefs.
body: National Fire Chiefs Council says half of UK fire services surveyed reported "frequently" encountering "insufficient flow" Fire hydrants in the UK often do not provide enough water flow for firefighting, fire chiefs have warned. A report published by the National Fire Chiefs Council (NFCC) claims that inadequate water supplies across the UK are impacting fire crews' "ability to respond effectively" and putting the public at risk. It carried out a survey of UK fire services which suggested that 81% have had to change their emergency response plans due to concerns over adequate water supplies. "The very least firefighters should be able to rely on is access to the water they need to protect people," said NFCC chairman Phil Garrigan. The report calls for firefighting water supplies to be recognised as a critical public safety requirement, for "greater accountability" for the water sector and for increased hydrant maintenance. Fire hydrants in the UK are access points that allow crews to access mains water when they arrive at the scene of a blaze. They are often marked by a yellow sign showing a capital "H" - there are hundreds of thousands across the UK. The NFCC warned that climate change, droughts and population growth are "increasing demand on an already stretched water network". It provided the example of West Midlands Fire Service, which experienced water pressure issues over several days during the major wildfire in Stourbridge last month. During the height of the blaze, it took 40 minutes to refill its water carrier due to reduced pressure - and crews had to rely on an additional high-volume pump for water supply. The report claims firefighters had to deal with water flow issues when responding to August's Stourbridge wildfire, which saw 19 residential homes destroyed "Firefighters cannot fight fires without water," said Mr Garrigan. "That sounds obvious, yet our evidence shows four in five fire and rescue services have had to change response plans because of concerns about firefighting water supplies," he said. "The demands on fire and rescue services are growing, with larger wildfires, extreme weather and increasingly complex risks." "As the task becomes more challenging, the very least firefighters should be able to rely on is access to the water they need to protect people and property." The NFCC's survey, conducted over summer and which received responses from 50% of UK fire services, found that half of fire services it heard from "frequently encounter insufficient flow". It also suggested that a third of water companies cannot increase water flow when needed. The NFCC said these factors have led to "workarounds", increased demand on resources and "reduced resilience" when responding to incidents. The organisation has called on water regulators to enforce measures on water providers regarding the provision of water for firefighting, and to implement "clear national standards" on fire hydrant repair and maintenance. It also urged the UK government to ensure that fire and rescue services are recognised as "key stakeholders" within the water sector. In response, Ofwat said it would consider the points raised in the NFCC's report and added that water companies do "have a duty to supply fire and rescue services to support firefighting". "We would expect water companies and fire services to work together to ensure this is the case," a spokesperson said. title: Watch: Why is the UK reviewing its Chagos Islands deal?
description: The UK is reviewing its deal to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, the defence secretary has said.
body: This video can not be played The UK is reviewing its deal to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, the defence secretary has said, after US President Donald Trump called it "terrible" at the UN General Assembly. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said "we have to" review the deal "because the United States doesn't support it". The original agreement would see the UK cede sovereignty of the territory to Mauritius and pay an average of £101m ($136m) per year to lease back a joint UK-US military base there, prized for its strategic location in the Indian Ocean. The BBC's diplomatic correspondent Caroline Hawley looks at why the government's agreement with Mauritius has stalled. Read more about Donald Trump's comments on Chagos Islands. title: Sandie Peggie says union did not take her case seriously
description: The nurse claims the Royal College of Nursing failed to properly support and advise her after she was suspended.
body: Sandie Peggie gave evidence at an employment tribunal in Dundee A nurse has told an employment tribunal she did not believe her union representative took her objections to sharing female changing rooms with a transgender colleague as seriously as she did. Sandie Peggie claims the Royal College of Nursing (RCN) failed to properly support and advise her after she was suspended over a complaint about her behaviour by Dr Beth Upton. The RCN disputes the claim. It is the second employment tribunal Peggie has brought over the dispute with Upton – a transgender woman who was born biologically male. Peggie partially won a claim for harassment against NHS Fife in December last year, but her other allegations of discrimination and victimisation were dismissed. The dispute began following a number of encounters between Peggie and Upton at the Victoria Hospital in Kirkcaldy towards the end of 2023. The nurse was suspended shortly afterwards and spoke to RCN representative Stuart Fraser. Peggie said Fraser "appeared pleasant", explained how long a disciplinary process would last and said she should treat the leave "as an extended holiday". She later told the tribunal: "After speaking with Stuart I got the impression he wasn't taking it as seriously as I was, or considering anything legal." Sandie Peggie's employment tribunal appeal to go ahead next year Sandie Peggie says 'I will not give up legal fight' in trans doctor row Asked by her lawyer Naomi Cunningham why she had felt the need to speak to her MP, Neale Hanvey, about the matter, Peggie replied: "I didn't feel comfortable that Stuart had taken it as serious complaint. "I thought he thought I'd been disciplined because I'd done something wrong." Peggie also said, after a meeting about her suspension, that she felt Fraser was "pushing" for her to change to another department against her wishes. Asked how she felt, she replied: "Not supported. I feel like people were taking the doctor's side rather than mine." The first tribunal, against NHS Fife and Dr Upton, became a high profile and controversial case. Peggie was backed by the campaign group Sex Matters, co-founded by Maya Forstater. The RCN's lawyer, David Hay KC, questioned Peggie about when she came to understand the phrase "gender critical". Peggie said it would have been "round about" the time she spoke to Forstater, which was shortly after she contacted her MP in January 2024. "I was made aware that because of what had happened in the changing area, I didn't believe biological men should be in women's changing spaces. "Being a sex realist was more or less the same as being gender critical." More stories from Edinburgh, Fife & East Hay highlighted that Peggie's case was funded by Sex Matters, and pointed to correspondence from the group that said the issues in the case were of "significant strategic importance". The lawyer asked Peggie: "My reading is that the strategy is Sex Matters' strategy, as opposed to being a particular strategy from you?" She added that speaking with Forstater led her to understand that she had a legal case "because of my beliefs". Turning to contact between Peggie and the RCN union, Hay said the first time Peggie had put in writing that she felt "failed from the outset" by the union was in March 2025. Prior to this, he said she had other opportunities to raise with her union representative that she was unhappy that the union had not offered her legal services. Peggie said: "I believe it [legal services] should have been offered." The tribunal, which is taking place in Dundee, continues. title: Orkney island welcomes first baby in more than three decades
description: Residents on North Ronaldsay toasted the birth of Duncan Wilder Thorstein Traill Suarez Ford with a dram of whisky last week.
body: Alice Traill Ford welcomed baby Duncan Wilder Thorstein Traill Suarez Ford in North Ronaldsay last week A baby has been born on Orkney's most northerly island for the first time in more than three decades. Parents Jorge Suarez and Alice Traill Ford welcomed baby Duncan Wilder Thorstein Traill Suarez Ford in North Ronaldsay last week. Islanders toasted the birth with a dram of whisky to celebrate the first newborn in the remote location since Thomas Brookman in August 1992. The family, who split their time between Costa Rica and Orkney and travelled more than 5,000 miles for the birth, said Duncan was born in a much-loved place. This video can not be played I wanted baby Duncan born into the energy of North Ronaldsay "North Ronaldsay has always been a very special place for me and I felt alive and free here every summer when I came up as a little girl," Alice told BBC Scotland News. "My intuition was telling me this was the right place for us so we spoke to the NHS to see if it would be possible. "We have this beautiful family home steeped in our history and ancestry so to be surrounded by that felt a very special introduction for him to come to Earth." North Ronaldsay is Orkney's northernmost island and is only accessible from Kirkwall on the main island via a 20-minute plane journey or a ferry, which takes two hours and 40 minutes. The island is famous for its seaweed-eating sheep, which are mostly confined to the shore by a 13-mile-long drystone wall that encircles the island. Alice's family still spend holidays at Holland House, which was built by her ancestors Baby Duncan was born in Holland House, which was built by Alice's ancestors - the Traill family - who bought the island in 1727. The house has been passed down through generations and is still owned by her family. Alice's grandfather, Duncan, was the former Laird of North Ronaldsay and provided the inspiration for her son's name. "I didn't know I was going to name him after Duncan when we arrived but I was sitting on the sofa and right in front of me was a collage of his pictures with my grandmother, so he has been very present with us," Alice said. "He was an incredible man, very kind and really strong and I felt like there would be no better name than his to carry on and continue his legacy in the world." The family will return to Costa Rica in November Historically when the Laird was on the island, a flag was flown at Holland House to inform the residents. So when baby Duncan was born at 04:05 on 15 September, Alice and Jorge followed the tradition to share the news. "Over the years we have found a lot of magical four-leaf clovers here and have kept them in a book," Alice said. "We stuck a four-leaf clover to a glass bottle, glued a Groatie Buckie to the lid then filled it with whisky and gave it to each of the islanders. "We raised the flag and everybody opened their whisky and shared a dram - a celebratory drink - together." A Groatie Buckie is a small, pale pink and white shell found on beaches across Orkney, which in local tradition brings good luck and fortune to the keeper. Alice and Jorge gave bottles of whisky with a four-leaf clover and Groatie Buckie glued to them to the islanders A flag was raised to tell the islanders baby Duncan had been born The family will return to Costa Rica in November, where the couple run a school. But Alice is certain her children will have the same opportunity to spend time in North Ronaldsay as she did growing up. "Duncan will absolutely be back every year," she said. "One of the things I want to give my children is the gift my mother gave us, bringing us to this island every summer, letting us run wild, explore the island and feel the connection to the community." title: Oasis add shows in Knebworth, Rome and Munich
description: The band says it is adding new dates after "phenomenal demand".
body: Brothers Liam (left) and Noel Gallagher reformed the band for a tour in 2025, having split up in 2009 Oasis have announced more dates for the second leg of their reunion tour in 2027. The band will now play six nights at Knebworth House in Hertfordshire, the 125,000-capacity venue where they staged two now legendary concerts in 1996. They have also added shows in Munich and Rome, while their Paris dates have been rescheduled because of planned railway engineering works. Tickets will not go on general sale. Instead, purchase links will be sent to fans who have already entered an online ballot. Oasis will now play 42 shows in 2027, one more than during the first leg of their reunion tour in 2025. The band had been due to play at the Stade de France in Paris on 23 and 24 July, but the first concert has been brought forward to 20 July. They have also added dates in Munich's Allianz Arena and at Rome's Stadio Olimpico, taking the total number of shows at each venue from two to three. Liam Gallagher played Knebworth with Oasis in 1996 and then returned as a solo artist in 2022 The band said standard ticket prices across the tour would be fixed at between £71.50 and £266.60. For the Knebworth shows, general admission tickets start at £170.50, while front-standing tickets cost from £203.50. If all six concerts sell out at full capacity, Oasis could sell 750,000 tickets at Knebworth, making it the world's fourth most-attended concert series at a single venue, behind Taylor Swift, Shakira and Coldplay. Announcing the new dates online, the band said the extra dates were added due to "phenomenal demand". This video can not be played Archive: Oasis set for 'biggest rock gig' of 1990s Knebworth has become known for heavy traffic before and after concerts, as a result efforts have been made to reduce congestion during the Oasis shows. Stevenage Borough Council said it was working with Hertfordshire County Council and highways officials on a "masterplan" to tackle potential problems. Ticketmaster has advised Oasis fans, external not to drive, and has arranged return coaches from 124 locations across England and Wales. Extra trains will run from Stevenage to London after the concerts, while stewards and lighting will be provided along the two-mile (3.2km) route between the station and Knebworth House. Saturday ticket holders will also have the option to pay extra to camp at the venue on the Friday and Saturday nights. Do you have a story suggestion for Beds, Herts or Bucks? Contact us below. title: Dramatic eviction of woman aged 87 highlights Spain's housing shortage
description: The tenant of the flat in Madrid, Maricarmen, was unable to pay the rent set by the firm which recently bought it.
body: Maricarmen had to leave the flat she had lived in for 70 years on Wednesday The dramatic eviction of an 87-year-old woman from the home in Madrid where she lived for seven decades has drawn attention to the depth of Spain's housing crisis. The tenant of the flat in the Retiro area of central Madrid, Maricarmen, was unable to pay the rent set by the investment firm that owns it. Maricarmen's father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent. However, the company that bought the property in 2018, Urbagestión, cited a legal glitch allowing it to raise her rent from €500 (£428; $572) to €2,650. It subsequently lowered the new rent to €1,650 but Maricarmen was still unable to pay it with her monthly pension of €1,350. Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts and the case has received increasing media attention. Supporters of Maricarmen camped outside the building on Tuesday night, joined by celebrities including Javier Bardem's brother, Carlos, and the singer Ana Belén, who read out the poem Desahucio (Eviction) by Rafael Alberti. Several hundred people, mostly youngsters, had gathered by the morning in a bid to prevent the eviction from taking place, chanting "Maricarmen stays". Some activists blocked the stairs inside the building. In a video posted on social media, a tearful Maricarmen thanked those who had come out to support her against "this cruel struggle by someone who wants to earn money". The hard men removing squatters in Spain 'Sometimes I want to cry': Eviction in a pandemic Police cordoned off a section of the street and removed people from the entrance to the building, including members of the media, striking some protesters with batons. A representative of tenants' organisation Sindicato de Inquilinas shouted at the police through a megaphone: "Think for 10 seconds about Maricarmen, who could be your own grandmother." "There is a police deployment as if this were a military operation," said Beatriz Duro, Maricarmen's lawyer. "This is the fourth time [they've tried to evict her] but the first time they've come right to the door of the property. It's completely disproportionate." In June, the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights called for the pensioner's eviction to be halted and for her to be offered affordable alternative accommodation. The local government said she had declined its offer of a place in an elderly care home. The central government said Urbagestión had refused its repeated attempts to negotiate Maricarmen's situation. The BBC has attempted to contact the company. Volunteers helped pack up Maricarmen's belongings Protesters had gathered outside the building on Tuesday under the slogan "Maricarmen is staying" Maricarmen emerged from the house in a wheelchair to greet her supporters Overcome with emotion at the gathering, the elderly woman broke into tears The possibility of a last-minute reprieve for Maricarmen appeared when an anonymous donor offered to pay most of her rent. However, Urbagestión reportedly rejected the offer and the eviction went ahead. "Today is a very sad day, a very dramatic day, when it's plain to see the effects of unbridled speculation, of not wanting to control the market, of putting out the red carpet for the vultures and the speculators," said Housing Minister Teresa Rodríguez. A shortage of available housing has been blamed for soaring rental costs in recent years, which have left millions of Spaniards struggling to find affordable homes. In Madrid, rentals have increased by more than 100% over the last decade, according to property site Idealista, with a 10% rise over the last year. The Socialist-led government of Pedro Sánchez has frequently targeted companies whose investment pushes up housing costs. In January, the prime minister said he aimed to "protect those who are most exposed to that speculation and that greed". However, some critics of the government say it needs to work harder to build new homes, and others warn that its rhetoric discourages many owners from placing their properties on the rental market. title: Ad break in Women's Champions League was unscheduled
description: Coverage of Arsenal's Women's Champions League opener also featured a dog on set, a vegetable platter and a rotating floor.
body: Disney+ won the broadcast rights for the Women's Champions League from the 2025-26 season for five years A three-minute advert break during a Women's Champions League game was not scheduled, Disney+ confirmed. Arsenal and HB Koge were drawing 0-0 in the second half on Tuesday when coverage was interrupted. It was one of several technical issues during the coverage, which fans said was "gimmicky" and "undermines" women's football. One guest was a dog with 137,000 Instagram followers. Disney confirmed it was an unintended interruption caused by a technical issue and understood the frustration caused. It was making steps to ensure it did not happen again. Arsenal won 1-0 in their first game of this season's competition thanks to a stoppage-time Mariona Caldentey penalty. Disney's coverage also featured a vegetable platter being served and a rotating floor. Alex Scott hosted the first show of the season, alongside former England forward Lianne Sanderson, content creators Alex Bailess and Tyra Mills, and a dog called Barley Boy. There was no explanation for his presence on set other than his Instagram following. It was the second season of the Women's Champions League to be broadcast on Disney+. Matches are produced by ESPN. New this season is "The Hangout", described by Disney as a live studio show billed as a "new match-day experience for fans, delivering pre-match build-up, half-time analysis and post-match reaction". In a media release before the first round of fixtures, Disney said: "The Hangout will combine expert analysis with fresh perspectives and fan engagement." However, the evening was marred by a series of technical issues – from players waiting to be interviewed but unable to hear questions from the studio, to a rotating floor that appeared to have a mind of its own. There were also camera shots with cushions blocking the view of Scott, and audio synchronisation problems. Italian reporter Roberto Perrone, in Milan for Inter Milan's match against Swedish side Hacken, also encountered audio problems. When the sound returned, viewers were shown a non-football-themed quiz, with questions ranging from types of pasta to Italy's biggest city. Alex Scott (centre) and Shebahn Aherne will alternate hosting duties throughout the competition. One fan wrote on X: "I think a lot of the problem with the debates in women's football broadcasting over analysis and punditry vs content creation and gimmicky fun, is that in men's football you can get both - and in different shows. "In women's football, you get one show, and so they try to do it all." Another fan wrote: "We want women's football to be taken seriously, yet coverage like this undermines that. Personality and fun have their place, but not at the expense of the football. "The game doesn't need gimmicks to make it interesting. Give the players, the competition and the football itself the same focus, analysis and respect we expect elsewhere in the sport. "Women's football is more than capable of being the main event." Megan Feringa, a journalist for the Athletic, said: "Watching Disney's coverage is like going in and out of a lucid dream. "Why is there a dog? Why is the couch spinning? Why do the adverts cut right into analysis?" Flo Lloyd-Hughes, a broadcaster and writer for the Cutback, said: "Why does women's football coverage always have to be so gimmicky? It's the Champions League, not Blue Peter. "Put some pundits who know about the teams in a studio, make sure the tech works and have a decent bit of time for build-up and analysis to contextualise everything." Last November concerns were raised over the professionalism and legitimacy of the Women's League Cup quarter-final and semi-final draw, which was conducted by social media influencer GK Barry. In the same month Sky Sports scrapped its new female-focused TikTok channel, Halo, after it faced a backlash online, with its posts described as "patronising" and "sexist". Disney+ coverage continues on Wednesday with Chelsea hosting Austria Wien at 20:00 BST. title: Dolly Parton's manager accuses her nephew of 'threats and intimidation'
description: Bryan Seaver, who announced Parton's death to the world, is accused of trying to extort her estate.
body: Dolly Parton died in August at the age of 80 Dolly Parton's management company has accused her nephew of "threats, intimidation, and coercion", revealing a bitter battle over the late star's legacy and business interests. The accusations against Bryan Seaver, who was Parton's head of security and was handpicked to announce her death last month, have been made public in US legal documents filed this week. The company that manages Parton's businesses and properties, She's Alive, is seeking a temporary civil restraining order against him. In court filings, She's Alive alleged that Seaver mounted "an obscene, deliberate and escalating campaign of threats", claiming he said he would ruin her empire if the estate did not pay him. He has denied the claims. In a statement to TMZ, external, he said that text messages and emails quoted in the court application had been taken out of context to make it look like he was threatening people. "Nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by," he said. "A lot of these messages are two guys having rage talk and crying on the phone together while we were grieving." Seaver, the son of Parton's sister Cassie, owns a company that provided the singer's security detail for the last 20 years of her life. Last week, he was fired by She's Alive as head of security for her properties. In a statement at the time, Seaver and his company said the dismissal was "unexpected" and "unexplained". They added: "We refuse to be intimidated by those whose actions we believe are being taken in bad faith and with the intent to profit from the life of someone who willingly gave so much." Bryan Seaver announced the news of his aunt's death to the world in August The request for a restraining order was filed in Nashville on Tuesday by She's Alive, which is run by Parton's longtime manager Danny Nozell. The court documents quoted a series of exchanges in which someone, identified by the estate as Seaver, threatened to destroy Parton's brand. In one, he's alleged to have said he would become "the hand of retribution for my entire family", according to the court documents. Another said: "I'm going to set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly's brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It's going to be great. Or [expletive] pay me." The papers also claimed that Seaver used his experience as a military contractor to intimidate employees. In an exchange with one of Parton's lawyers, he allegedly described himself as a "killer" and said that on the day his aunt died, he had sold $27m (£20m) in arms and ammunition to the Haitian police. "All I do is warfare... Everyone needs to be worried about what I might do," he was accused of saying, according to a copy of an email attached to the complaint. In his statement published on TMZ, Seaver said: "I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments. I am a security professional and I am a killer." But he denied making threats and said he had been "talking frankly in a private way with Danny who I thought was my friend". The messages have resulted in some employees and lawyers for Parton's trusts and estates resigning, according to the court documents. She's Alive has also had to hire private security for its employees, including at their homes, the filing states. The BBC has contacted Seaver and She's Alive for further comment. Previously, Seaver was known to the public for announcing his aunt's death in a video posted to her Instagram account on 25 August. Speaking in front of a black background, he was sombre and reflective as he introduced himself and shared the unexpected news. "This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago, before I fully absorbed it as a future reality," he said in the video. Seaver added that he had followed in his father Larry's footsteps in becoming Parton's head of security, a post he held for more than 20 years. Nozell started working for Parton in 2004, first as a tour consultant and later as her manager. In the 2019 Netflix film, Dolly Parton: Here I Am, he said his job was to transform her from a "heritage act" into a "superstar", and he took responsibility for reviving her international touring career. In a statement last month, he said the singer had "worked up until the day she died" on multiple projects, and envisioned a legacy that continued long beyond her death. "She loved seeing her dreams come to life, and loved knowing her work brought people joy," he said in the statement. "Ever the planner, Dolly worked with the team that she handpicked, for the past several years to build a project roadmap that will guide us for decades to come." The estate now faces a public tug of war over that legacy. title: Police worker jailed after death of boy in her care
description: Catherine Walker was the legal guardian of the nine-year-old boy, who was found unresponsive in his room.
body: Catherine Walker was the legal guardian of the nine-year-old boy A woman who worked at Nottinghamshire Police has been jailed after the death of a nine-year-old boy in her care. Catherine Walker, 47, was the legal guardian of the boy, who was found unresponsive in his bedroom in Warsop, Nottinghamshire, on 16 December 2024. Despite the efforts of paramedics and people at the scene, the boy died in hospital. The force said an investigation found "clear mistreatment of the boy over a prolonged period of time". Walker, of Appleton Street in Warsop, was jailed for six years at Nottingham Crown Court on Monday after pleading guilty to two counts of assault/ill-treat/neglect/abandon a child/young person to cause unnecessary suffering/injury. The force, which has not revealed what Walker's role was, said her former husband was the boy's primary carer and had been mainly responsible for his treatment. He died shortly after the boy's death, police added. Walker was sentenced at Nottingham Crown Court on Monday Officers investigating what had happened raised concerns about the conditions in the boy's bedroom, which police said "lacked any of the comforts seen elsewhere in the house". There were no blinds or curtains in the window, and an electric socket was "hanging dangerously off the wall". The bedroom had very little furniture, no radiator or door handle, and was fitted with a bathroom-style door lock on the outside, the force added. Walker claimed the room was being renovated, but police said further investigation "revealed this to be untrue". Officers also received evidence from other witnesses that showed "clear mistreatment of the boy over a prolonged period of time". After Walker's sentencing, Det Ch Insp Gail Routledge said: "This was one of the most upsetting cases I can remember. "This boy was very clearly mistreated for a significant period of time and was living in conditions that no child should have to endure. "It was always our case that this mistreatment was a deliberate choice by the defendant, rather than the result of neglectful parenting. "I am please she has now been held to account for her role in his death." title: OpenAI gives cyber defence tools to Ukraine
description: Ukraine will get access to OpenAI's advanced GPT 5.6 Sol model under the deal - a rival to Anthropic's Mythos and Fable
body: The tech giant OpenAI will share its AI cyber defence system Daybreak for free with the Ukraine government to help it protect civilian infrastructure, like hospitals and power plants, from cyber-attacks. According to the Computer Emergency Response Team of Ukraine (CERT-UA), the national cyber incident response team, Ukraine recorded nearly 6,000 attacks in 2025. Daybreak is able to quickly identify weaknesses in digital systems and help develop fixes. Under the deal, Ukraine will get access to OpenAI's advanced GPT 5.6 Sol model - a rival to Anthropic's Mythos and Fable. George Osborne, former UK chancellor and now Head of OpenAI for Countries, said: "Protecting civilian infrastructure means defending it against both physical and digital attacks, so people can continue to live, work and access essential services." Reacting to the news, Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat intelligence for the cybersecurity firm Sophos, said that Russian offensive cyber operations had been "a key component" of the Kremlin's aggression against Ukraine since 2014. "Any initiative that strengthens Ukraine's already highly capable, but heavily burdened, cyber defence efforts is a welcome development and could provide a valuable force multiplier," he said. Jamie MacColl, a senior research fellow specialising in cyber at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told the BBC western tech firms had been supporting Ukraine for some time - partly for altruistic reasons but also because they gain very valuable data and intelligence from an active conflict. "Given this, it's no surprise that OpenAI is now also providing defensive cyber security services" he said. He thought access to Daybreak would be useful, particularly given the volume of Russian cyber-attacks targeting the country. But he noted Ukraine already had access to AI tools provided by OpenAI's competitors, like Google. The cyber-abilities of the latest, most powerful AI models, called "frontier" models in AI jargon, can be a boon for cyber-defenders, but the same abilities can also be used for attack. Spotting weaknesses in systems, for example, is useful for defenders looking to block hackers, but also for attackers hunting for ways to infiltrate an organisation. Anthropic has tightly restricted access to its systems on the grounds that they are too powerful to fall into the wrong hands, but OpenAI has allowed some firms in Europe, as well as UK banks, to use its most advanced cyber models. The firm made the announcement alongside the UN General Assembly which is currently underway in New York. AI is firmly on the agenda there, and US tech bosses including OpenAI's Sam Altman and Anthropic's Dario Amodei are due to speak at the high-level gathering. United Nations Secretary General António Guterres called for the tech to be regulated in his final address, while US President Donald Trump says it should be renamed "super intelligence". Evidence suggests the technology is increasingly being used in the Russia-Ukraine conflict. In a report published earlier this month, Anthropic claimed that its Claude platform appeared to have been used by a group of Russian developers to build software for a swarm of so-called "kamikaze" drones designed for attacks in Ukraine. It said the group had activated virtual private networks - VPNs - in order to get around a geographical block put in place by the tech firm. Anthropic also claimed AI had been used in attempts to infiltrate the Ukrainian government, military and diplomatic services. Recently, around 100 US companies signed an open letter warning governments and institutions around the world that "the window is closing" to ensure cyber defences are robust enough to withstand AI-enabled cyber attacks. But it's not just bad actors deploying the tech that are of growing concern: in the summer, OpenAI revealed that a group of AI agents it had been testing had escaped from their controls, and secretly worked together to hack to another tech firm, Hugging Face. Anthropic, and Google subsequently revealed similar incidents. Additional reporting by Chris Vallance Google's Gemini AI hacked three companies in security test What is AI and how does it work? title: Police examine video of anti-migrant activist slashing dinghy with knife
description: Daniel Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, livestreamed a video of the alleged incident.
body: Police are looking into a video appearing to show anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas slashing at an inflatable boat with a knife in the English Channel. The boat had been carrying about 50 migrants who had launched from a beach in Normandy. They were picked up by two RNLI lifeboats once they had reached the UK search and rescue area and were taken to Dover for processing. Daniel Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, had been filming the transfer from a yellow speedboat while giving commentary to a live stream audience of more than 15,000 people. The video then shows him sailing up to the boat, taking out a small knife and start slashing at the side of the migrant boat. There were no migrants on board, but there was a French official from the coastguard vessel Abeille Liberté. As the Frenchman boarded the empty migrant boat mid-Channel Danny Tommo shouted "Right, you are on English territory. This is England. This is not France any more." Then he made a series of stabbing and slashing movements against the rubber side of the large inflatable boat. "Get off - get off," he shouted. "You've got time to get off the boat." It was not clear from the live stream if he did any damage to the boat. "We just wanted to make sure that boat was not taken back to France and used again," Tommo told his followers. Posting on X, campaign group Stand Up To Racism described the footage as "disgusting". Daniel Thomas, seen here in June, has been involved in organising anti-migrant protests There is no evidence that any boats that have been used by migrants to cross the English Channel have ever been taken back to France for reuse. Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary said: "We are aware of a video circulating online relating to damage being caused to a boat in the English Channel on the afternoon of 22 September, and we are conducting inquiries into the matter." title: Reform Wales deputy criticises colleague for claiming he had most support to be leader
description: Laura Anne Jones said James Evans was misleading in saying most Reform members had backed him.
body: James Evans defected from the Conservatives earlier this year Reform's new Welsh deputy leader Laura Anne Jones says a colleague was misleading when he said he had the most support to become party leader. James Evans claimed last week that he would not take part in the contest to be leader even though most of his party's Senedd members wanted him in the role. On Wednesday Jones told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast she did not recognise that to be the case and did not know why Evans said it. In response, Evans insisted he had "considerable support" but said it was time to "move on". Helen Jenner was elected as Reform's Welsh leader on Monday to replace Dan Thomas, who quit following his arrest on suspicion of assault and coercive or controlling behaviour. In a statement made after his arrest Thomas said he had "done nothing wrong". From punk to politics - the making of new Reform Wales leader Helen Jenner Laura Anne Jones elected Reform's deputy Welsh leader Jones was subsequently elected deputy leader, replacing the role Jenner previously held. Jones, Senedd member for Sir Fynwy Torfaen, said Jenner would be a "dynamic leader" and a "good choice the whole group can now get behind". "We've got a united front again," she said. Asked about Evans' claim that he had majority support, she said: "James says a lot of things. "It's not something that I recognise to be the case at the time. That's all I'm going to say. Helen has extremely strong backing here and everyone can easily get behind her." Pressed on whether she thought Evans had been misleading, she said: "It is, yes. Absolutely. I think the result speaks for itself. "James is a great politician. But on this, I don't know why he said what he did. The process is the process. There are a few stages to go from when he pulled out. "I don't really understand why he said that." Evans claimed he had majority support for the leader role at a hastily arranged press conference In response, Evans said in a statement he "had considerable support from colleagues", and was "grateful to everyone who encouraged me to stand". "Following discussions with my family, I made the decision not to put my name forward, so ultimately those numbers were never tested in a contest," he said. "Helen has now been elected leader, the process is over, and it's time to move on, get on with the job and give her my full support." Reform had not made the results of the votes for leader and deputy leader public. Although Jenner had confirmed that Senedd colleague Jason O'Connell had also sought to be leader, the party had not said who had run against Jones. Asked what she won by, Jones said she had not been allowed to "tell anything about the actual internal process, and it's not right to do so". She said: "What is important now is that we look forward, and we've got two strong women at the helm. We're firing on all cylinders. "It's been a crazy old week but we've come out of it stronger than ever." Evans called journalists to a press conference on the members' balcony at the Senedd last week, a day after ex-leader Thomas announced he would quit. Evans, Member of the Senedd (MS) for Brycheiniog Tawe Nedd, then announced that he would not stand in the contest and said he hoped the party "can unite behind a single candidate". "I had [the] majority of support in the group, but I do not think a competition at this time will be beneficial for anybody," he said. Both Jones and Evans are former Conservative MSs, with Jones the first to defect to Reform in the summer of 2025, before Evans joined the following February. When he was still a Conservative, Evans had criticised Jones for defecting to Reform, accusing her of having no "principles". Jones later shrugged off the comment, saying Evans had just been "playing the game". title: Tigray forces seize main airport in northern Ethiopia from police, residents tell the BBC
description: There are fears of a return to war in the northern region as tensions between the government and TPLF escalate.
body: The airport in Mekelle is usually guarded by members of Ethiopia's national police force Local forces in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray have seized control of the airport in the regional capital, Mekelle, from federal police, local residents have told the BBC. No flights are currently landing at the airport and Ethiopian Airlines said it had suspended flights to Mekelle and the cities of Shire and Axum because of what it called the "current situation" in Tigray. There have been escalating tensions this year between the government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray, fuelling fears of a return to civil war. On Sunday, the TPLF announced an alliance with six armed groups in Ethiopia to remove the government in Addis Ababa. A two-year war in Tigray ended in November 2022 - but both sides are now accusing each other of violating an African Union-mediated peace deal. It was one of the most-deadly conflicts this century, with the AU's mediator estimating some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine. Seven Ethiopian rebel groups form new alliance The flight suspension follows a series of reported drone strikes in Tigray. On Tuesday, a strike in the southern town of Alamata killed at least 14 people and injured 22 others, according to the Tigrayan authorities. The town's mayor, Mogos Shiferaw, told the BBC that more than five drones and one fighter jet had carried out more than 21 strikes beginning at around 03:30. "This caused a lot of psychological trauma in our city and our people were in a state of panic," he said. Mogos said all those killed and injured were civilians, accusing federal forces of targeting two secondary schools. He believed they were struck on suspicion that they were being used by Tigrayan forces. But the mayor said the schools, which had served as federal military bases during the civil war, were unoccupied as the academic year had not yet begun. The BBC has not independently verified the allegations and the government has not publicly commented. On Wednesday, the Tigray authorities accused Addis Ababa of launching an open invasion on the region's residents, urging people to support the regional forces and maintain unity. Meanwhile, the US State Department's Bureau of African Affairs has condemned a separate drone strike that it said took place on Monday, targeting a convoy of Catholic vehicles carrying food aid. It called for an investigation and urged all parties to resolve their differences through dialogue and take steps to prevent similar incidents. Both Addis Ababa and TPLF leaders have faced criticism over delays in implementing key provisions of the Pretoria Agreement, which formally ended the conflict in November 2022. In July, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed accused the TPLF of preparing for renewed conflict during an address to parliament. Just before the general election in May, the TPLF restored its pre-war administration, disbanding an interim one appointed by Abiy. There have also been reports that the TPLF has forcibly recruiting young men to join its forces. title: Netanyahu calls Macron's remarks on West Bank in UN speech 'grotesque'
description: Israel's PM denounces the French president after he appeared to downplay Hamas's activities in the occupied territory.
body: A French diplomatic source said there had been a "misinterpretation" of Emmanuel Macron's words Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has condemned French President Emmanuel Macron after he criticised Israel's actions in the occupied West Bank during his address to the UN General Assembly. "Look at what's happening in the West Bank, where day in, day out, we are seeing violations. And in the name of what? Hamas was never very active in the West Bank," Macron said in French, according to the UN's interpreter. Netanyahu called the remarks a "grotesque absurdity" and said members of the Palestinian armed group there "carry out attacks against Jews almost every day". There was no response from Macron's office, but one French diplomatic source said there had been a "misinterpretation". The source told the Jerusalem Post, external that the meaning of the French sentence spoken by the president, "Le Hamas n'a jamais sévi en Cisjordanie," was, "Hamas has never governed the West Bank." Macron also rejected US President Donald Trump's assertion that he had ended the war between Israel and Hamas in the Gaza Strip. Violence there has continued despite last October's ceasefire, including almost daily Israeli strikes, while humanitarian conditions remain dire "Some boast of a supposed peace. But that peace has not reopened humanitarian access for a single second," he said. "Are we simply to stand by and watch this spectacle that should shame us all?" After the address, the Israeli prime minister's office said in a statement: "The grotesque absurdity of Emmanuel Macron's statement is staggering." "On Sunday, the eve of [the Jewish holy day of] Yom Kippur, just two days ago, Netanel Shukrun - a French citizen and father of six - was murdered in his car by a Hamas terrorist in Judea and Samaria," it added, using a biblical term for the West Bank. "Hamas terrorists carry out attacks against Jews almost every day. They have murdered countless Israeli civilians in Judea and Samaria." The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, also denounced Macron's remarks as "out of touch with reality". Shukrun, 36, was shot dead when a Palestinian opened fire on a group of Israelis at a spring near the West Bank settlement of Neve Tzuf, according to Israeli police. The suspect was arrested later at a hospital in the city of Ramallah, they said. Hamas praised the attack but did not say it was behind it. The group - which is designated as a terrorist organisation by Israel, France and other countries - is a rival of the Fatah-dominated Palestinian Authority, which governs parts of the West Bank that are not under Israeli control. Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem - land Palestinians want, along with Gaza, for a hoped-for future state - during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them. The settlements are illegal under international law.
