title: From leaving Rangers to La Liga - Scotland is next step for Ure
description: Robbie Ure has made it all the way to Sevilla since failing to break through at Rangers and now a first Scotland cap awaits the striker, writes Tom English.
body: Robbie Ure played in Belgium and Sweden before his move to Spain Robbie Ure, cool and confident and 22 years old, played 90 minutes for Sevilla against Barcelona at the weekend; 90 minutes of being marked by Pau Cubarsi, man of the match in the World Cup final, 90 minutes of pitch-time with Rodri, player of the tournament, 90 minutes of breathing the same rarefied air as Lamine Yamal. Ure is a part of a new-ish wave of Scotland striker, uncapped but hopeful of making a debut on Saturday away to Slovenia in the Nations League. There is no Lyndon Dykes in Sebastien Pocognoli's squad and no George Hirst. Injury has ruled out Che Adams, Lawrence Shankland and Ross Stewart. Those five were all at the World Cup in the United States during the summer. Now, it's Ure alongside James Wilson of Hearts and Kieron Bowie of Sassuolo, who both have two caps, and Oli McBurnie of Hull, with the last of his 16 international appearances coming five years ago. There is an intriguing freshness to this and nowhere is that buzz more obvious than in the story of Ure, the boy who wanted to play for Rangers but couldn't force his way in, the young man who in his seven games for Sevilla since his move from IK Sirius in Sweden has already played against 12 of Spain's World Cup winning squad. Just over three years ago, Ure left Rangers as a teenager, his last forays with the senior team being one minute against St Mirren in November 2022 and another minute against Hibs in May 2023. Nations League: Slovenia v Scotland He is the poster boy in the Scottish FA's campaign to persuade clubs to give youth more of a chance. Ure wasn't given that opportunity in Glasgow and left for Anderlecht, then IK Sirius and now Sevilla, who paid £5.5m for him, plus another £2.5m in add-ons. He calls the past few months "busy" which is an understatement. He's operating at a different level now. Sevilla lost that Barcelona game 3-1 - he has yet to score for his new club - but this is an education he's receiving, a critical part of his development. "The first half, we were good," he says. "But as the game goes on, they wear you down. Raphinha at the moment. I mean…" This video can not be played 'I wasn't good enough for Rangers' - Ure There's a knowing smile there, an indication of the kind of class he is now witnessing. "I really enjoyed it," he adds. "But against these players, you give them one chance and most of the time it's a goal. For me, it was a really good experience. I'm only going to get better as a result of it." Ure is a Rangers boy - one that got away. Was it difficult having to leave? "Yeah, it was," he explains. "All I'd ever known was Rangers. Going in every single day since I was probably eight years old but it was something that I felt I had to do. "I felt like I wasn't good enough to play for Rangers at the time, which is normal for many 18-year-olds. It was nothing that affected my confidence. I would have loved to have stayed but I knew myself that I wasn't going to play, which I accepted. "At a club like Rangers, it's difficult for any 18-year-old to play. I needed a change of scenery and a fresh start, somewhere that I could go to play at a level that would be good enough for me at the time. Anderlecht provided that." Well-travelled Binks eager to make mark for Scotland McPake's 'colourful' journey from club-less to Scotland call-up in three years Belgium was the first step on his road to the Scotland team but Sweden was when it all started to happen. In 2025-26, he scored 11 goals in 30 games, a mere warm-up for what was to follow. Between April and July this year, Ure played 14 games for IK Sirius and scored 15 goals, including four in one game against Mjallby. "I was scoring near enough every game, so that was probably the happiest I've been," he says. "Every week I was scoring and we were top of the league. I was improving and that interest in me was getting bigger and bigger. "At a young age it's really important you're playing. I was playing 90 minutes every week, getting trust from the manager and from the club. I was given time as well. The day I scored the four goals, it was my first hat-trick. I felt like every time I shot it was going to be a goal. I've not had a feeling like that before in football. It was pretty special." Player pathway is a hot topic in Scottish football and Ure is an example of what can happen when a kid is given a proper chance. "Everyone's different," he says. "You have to give players patience and give them time to develop but the way to do that is, of course, playing minutes at a level where you can develop at. I couldn't find that level in Scotland, so I had to look elsewhere and I'm happy that I did that." The level he has found in Spain is stratospheric. No goals yet, but it's a savagely tough school. He will have his moment under Pocognoli in the coming weeks. Four games in quick succession - he will get his first cap and his first chance to shine on another stage. And he's earned it. title: US and Iran hold first talks since June after Trump's 'annihilation' threat
description: The talks are the first since a ceasefire collapsed in June, with the sides exchanging fire intermittently.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Trump threatens to 'annihilate' Iran if no deal reached Top Iranian and US officials have held talks at the UN in New York on a day when the US leader said he could "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if the conflict went unresolved. No breakthrough has been reported from the meeting mediated by Qatar and involving Iran's foreign minister and US President Donald Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff - the first since a June ceasefire unravelled. Witkoff said a round of discussions had been completed "that we hope will prove constructive and promising". Iran repeated its demand for the US to end its "acts of aggression". The US and Israel launched air strikes on Iran on 28 February. Iran responded by attacking Israel and US bases in the Gulf and Arab Gulf allies of the US - as well as blocking the Strait of Hormuz. Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to pass through the strait before the war and its closure has caused wild fluctuations of prices. It has also increased pressure on Trump to find a way of ending the conflict - particularly as the US heads to Congressional elections in November. In his address at the annual meeting of the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, Trump began by touting his accomplishments on the economy, immigration, the border and tackling violent crime - remarks that sounded more pitched to voters the US midterms than the diplomats in the hall. He spent much of his address justifying the war with Iran - a huge contrast with remarks earlier by UN Secretary General António Guterres, who warned global divisions were deepening and underscored the "interdependence" of the world's peoples. The US president argued that the conflict had prevented Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and demonstrated the value of what he described as peace through strength - ultimatums rather than deal-making or compromise. "Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?" he said. "Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell?" Trump said he believed an Iran deal, which has so far eluded him, would come right after November's elections. The remarks were indicative of his foreign-policy strategy of coercive diplomacy - threatening overwhelming force while keeping negotiations open. Trump later told reporters that American officials had had a "very productive" three-hour meeting with the Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the general assembly. Iran state TV confirmed that Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had met Witkoff. Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei, quoted by state broadcaster IRNA, later said negotiations took part through a Qatari mediator who communicated Tehran's conditions, including an end to the war on all fronts and to US "acts of aggression". The BBC asked Witkoff how the meetings had gone as he was leaving the UN building and he responded with a thumbs up. Witkoff later confirmed on X that the talks had been held "through the mediators, who shuttled between the two sides throughout the day". "They successfully completed a round of discussions that we hope will prove constructive and promising," Witkoff said. "The mediators will continue their work." Since the ceasefire collapsed, both sides have intermittently exchanged fire. Iran has attacked vessels it says have attempted to cross the Strait of Hormuz without authorisation. The US has attacked Iranian sites in the strait - as well as Iranian tankers off the country's coast. The US has also maintained a blockade of Iranian ports, causing a huge disruption to the Iranian economy. In an effort to force Tehran to agree a deal to end the conflict, President Trump has also threatened sanctions against any country that continues trading with Iran. But so far, there has been no indication of a change of course in Iran, which insists the US and Israel end their war, including against the Iran-backed Shia group Hezbollah in Lebanon which Israel has been attacking. Yemen's Houthis - also allied to Iran - have recently intesified attacks aimed at disrupting oil shipping from Saudi Arabia, promting an escalation of the conflict with the kingdom. title: Man's body found in river sparks IOPC inquiry
description: Police say they were chasing the man on foot in Stanstead Abbots in connection with two robberies.
body: Police said the man had been identified as wanted in connection with two robbery offences The death of a man who was being chased by police before he was found in the River Lea, is being investigated by an independent watchdog. Emergency services were called to the High Street and towpath in Stanstead Abbotts, Hertfordshire, on 14 September at about 13:20 BST. Officers said they pursued the man on foot after identifying him as being wanted in connection with two robberies. He was no longer in their line of sight when he entered the water. Hertfordshire Constabulary said it had referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), which subsequently decided to launch an investigation. "We are assisting the IOPC with its enquiries, and it would be inappropriate to comment further at this time", a police spokesperson said. An IOPC spokesperson said officers had attempted to stop the man on the High Street. The man was later found in the river and pronounced dead at the scene. The spokesperson added the investigation was in its "early stages" and that the man's family would be kept updated on its progress. Do you have a story suggestion for Beds, Herts or Bucks? title: Oompa Loompa, doompety done: Actor takes final bow
description: Rusty Goffe on working with his son and an AI-generated Gene Wilder in a new Willy Wonka TV show.
body: Rusty Goffe is playing an Oompa Loompa for the final time — 55 years after his debut in Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory An original Oompa Loompa actor from the 1971 film Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory has retired after reprising the role one final time. Rusty Goffe began his film career in the Gene Wilder movie, before later appearing in the original Star Wars, the Harry Potter films and Doctor Who. Last year, Netflix flew the 77-year-old from his home in Leighton Buzzard, Bedfordshire, to Brisbane, Australia, where he once again donned a green wig and overalls for the TV competition Wonka's The Golden Ticket. He said: "I started on Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory, and now Wonka's The Golden Ticket is my swan song. I've just ended my career on Willy Wonka. Isn't that wonderful?" Goffe (facing the camera on the left) appeared in the 1971 film based on Roald Dahl's book, which starred Gene Wilder as Willy Wonka The 1971 film was the first screen adaptation of the 1964 novel Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, written by Roald Dahl at his home in Great Missenden, Buckinghamshire. It followed Charlie Bucket, a child who is one of five winners who find "golden tickets" inside a Wonka bar and are invited to tour the mysterious chocolate factory run by the eccentric Willy Wonka. Filmed mainly in Munich, Germany, it featured 10 actors of restricted growth who played the Oompa Loompas - the factory's workers. Netflix bought the rights to Dahl's children's books from the author's family in 2021. Its new competition series sees 12 pairs of contestants compete for a cash prize inside a chocolate factory inspired by the original film. Johnny Depp played Wonka in director Tim Burton's 2005 version of the story, while Timothée Chalamet played him in 2023's "origin" movie, directed by Paul King. Goffe's son Ben also plays an Oompa Loompa in the Netflix show Goffe said returning to the world of Wonka more than half a century later felt "very surreal", although some things had changed. He said: "Fifty-five years ago, the costumer thought every little guy had the same size head with the same size wigs, so they pull it on, rake it on, glue it, whatever to make it stay on. "This time, they done their homework and the wigs were handmade, fitted just like a hat." There were other improvements too. The orange make-up could now be washed off with soap and water, the shoes were more comfortable and the chocolate river was no longer full of cigarette ends discarded by crew members. Contestants in Wonka's The Golden Ticket compete for a cash prize Goffe is not the only member of the original cast to feature in the series. Willy Wonka actor Gene Wilder "narrates" the show, explaining the various games to contestants. The actor died in 2016, but his voice has been recreated using AI, which has received some criticism, despite producers obtaining the consent of his estate and approval of his widow Karen B Wilder. Goffe described hearing his former co-star's voice on set as "magical". "I thought, sometimes, he was on the set behind me," he said. "It was perfect, because he is Willy Wonka, he really is. Working with him was excellent. He was a lovely guy. Nice, kind, funny. He was brilliant. "Gene Wilder is Willy Wonka. There's no other person that could do it." Gene Wilder's voice was recreated using AI in the new show, which Goffe said was "magical" The other Oompa Loompas on the Netflix set were new to the production and included performers of different genders and heights. Among them was his son, Ben Goffe, who has performed in Shakespeare in London's West End and has been working on a major film project in Spain. Having grown up watching the 1971 classic on video and DVD, Ben jumped at the opportunity to travel to Brisbane and perform alongside his father. Rusty described watching his son step on to the set in full costume as an emotional moment. He said: "I was so proud to have him next to me in Willy Wonka... my hero was with me." Goffe attends conventions for fans of the "Charlie" books and movies Despite appearing in many iconic films across his career, Rusty insists that none of them compare and "Wonka is magical". He continues to attend conventions around the world to meet fans of the original film. He said: "I've had a great career, the majority of it has been Willy Wonka." When asked directly if this series was his final bow, he laughed: "I think so, unless someone offers me a few bob to go back and do something else." Wonka's The Golden Ticket premieres on Netflix this week, with a two-part finale scheduled for 30 September. Do you have a story suggestion for Beds, Herts or Bucks? Contact us below. title: Hunting hidden gems - is there anywhere in the world left to scout?
description: Through live scouting and increasing data and footage, top clubs now have tabs on a large proportion of the world's talent.
body: Dario Osorio, 22, has won 25 caps for Chile and has featured twice for Crystal Palace since joining on loan this summer The world's biggest clubs were all aware of the teenage sensation turning heads for Universidad de Chile, the one dubbed his generation's Alexis Sanchez. "When we signed Dario Osorio, it was not because no-one knew about him," Kristian Kjaer, technical director at Midtjylland, tells BBC Sport. Osorio was on the radar of AC Milan, RB Leipzig, Salzburg and a number of other English and German clubs before he left Santiago for Denmark at the age of 19. It was a carefully considered pathway. After three seasons in Scandinavia, the winger joined Crystal Palace on loan this summer with a £24m option to buy which would make him the most expensive sale in Danish Superliga history. Midtjylland, where Brentford owner Matthew Benham was a majority stakeholder between 2014 and 2023, are renowned as one of the most innovative clubs in Europe for their use of analytics - from set-pieces to smart recruitment. "We work on both pathways," explains Kjaer. "We have subjective scouting, more classic video scouting, live scouting, a network, people we trust in the club and also our partners. And then we have the data scouting. "And Dario Osorio, we were aware of him long before we signed him." From feet-on-the-ground to the increasing availability of footage, data analytics and artificial intelligence, Premier League clubs - whether buying direct from source or tracking players like Osorio's progress - have a large proportion of the world's emerging talent covered. "That hidden gem kind of thing almost does not exist any more in football," says Kjaer. "Sometimes it does, but it's rare." Malick Yalcouye began his career at ASEC Mimosas, joining Brighton from IFK Goteburg two years ago and breaking into the first team this season following loan spells at Sturm Graz and Swansea "You would put this period as one of the most transformational in talent ID and recruitment," explains Sam Turner, head of operations at scouting and development platform Eyeball. Clubs can now obtain an incredible level of detail on players across the globe before they have even made a senior appearance. Eyeball, for example, was founded five years ago to focus on those predominantly aged 13 to 21. It is used by more than 60% of clubs in Europe's top five leagues, and a majority of Premier League sides, for access to more than 400,000 young players across 42 global markets from Europe to Africa and Latin America. Winger Malick Yalcouye, a new 20-year-old star at Brighton, was tracked on the system since developing at Ivorian side ASEC Mimosas, likewise Bazoumana Toure, who is now at Newcastle. The breadth of coverage is highlighted by other recent moves - Josue Caicedo left Ecuador's LDU Quito for Barcelona, Mustapha Nyassi swapped Gambia's Real de Banjul for Copenhagen and Nour Ashraf joined Leipzig from Egypt's ENPPI. "The availability of data and footage has prompted a change in methodology," says Turner. "That has brought a load of benefits in terms of data-led recruitment, time saving, cost saving." Eyeball takes north of 2,000 data points every match, typically from leading amateur clubs and elite academies who film and upload their fixtures. The result is a huge database allowing analysts to watch all of a player's progressive passes, for example, discover who covered the most distance or simply ask 'find me a player like Ashley Cole'. "There is always this human feel that can never be lost," adds Turner. "I like to think we have aided scouts and recruitment teams, supplemented them with the tools, data, information to be able to make more informed decisions on a more consistent basis." Data, says Midtjylland's Kjaer, is "extremely important because it gives you an objective tool you can lean towards" when complemented by years of decision-making experience. "We cannot just turn on the computer and it tell us who to sign and then we go sign them," he says. "We also need to know about the cultural background, the family background, to make sure they fit into our football club. "Of course, data has given us opportunities. We sign young. So the sample size will simply be smaller for us because if we are waiting until it's big enough, Brighton and Liverpool and Brentford and other guys, they will sign the player in front of us." Both Kjaer and Turner see Uzbekistan as one of the emerging talent markets, with 22-year-old Manchester City defender Abdukodir Khusanov among those to feature at the World Cup for the debutants this summer "We can find interesting players all around the world," explains Kjaer. "I like us to be open-minded. We are particular in the way we play and the way we sell. And therefore, we need to find these players who fit that style of play. "When you have done your due diligence and you feel certain, pull the trigger. The pace in decision-making is also a hidden gem." One country regularly mentioned is Uzbekistan, who played in their first World Cup this summer, while Turner says Azerbaijan is pioneering a national talent network and "very forward-thinking and motivated to progress the game domestically". Then there is Japan, which Turner calls a "guiding star" in youth development for a system which takes players from grassroots, to school and college football and then the professional game. Think Kaoru Mitoma's thesis on dribbling techniques. For European clubs, it makes identifying young Japanese prospects more complex. Latin America, too, remains a hotbed of talent. As former Midtjylland chairman Rasmus Ankersen, who has since worked for Brentford and Southampton, wrote in his book The Gold Mine Effect, a club such as Cruzeiro will reject 4,000 players under the age of 15 for every one they take in. title: 'Be comfortable in your own identity' - Agassi's advice to Raducanu
description: As Emma Raducanu plots a route back to the pinnacle of tennis, the Briton is taking inspiration from Andre Agassi's 2009 autobiography.
body: This video can not be played 'Don't judge the best of yourself by results' - Agassi's advice to Raducanu As Emma Raducanu plots a route back to the pinnacle of tennis, the Briton has been taking inspiration from Andre Agassi's 2009 autobiography. Five years have passed since Raducanu's remarkable US Open triumph, when at the age of 18 she became the first qualifier in the Open era to win a Grand Slam. American Agassi was a teenage prodigy himself and later claimed the first of his eight major singles titles at Wimbledon in 1992 aged 22. But between the peak years of his career, he had to overcome a challenging period when he went four years without a major and dropped to 141st in the world rankings. "I was especially intrigued by the passage where he got out of his slump in the late 1990s by creating his own training regimen and finding his way back to the top," Raducanu told Uniqlo. "It speaks in depth about his early successes and the lows he reached, perhaps as a result of them. "A lot of it was so relatable." Agassi said his hope was for his experiences to help other players going through similar periods in their own careers. "It's wonderful to hear that anybody can relate," Agassi told BBC Breakfast. "It was literally the hope that if one person read it and it gave them hope, some tools to understand that they're not alone, they can figure it out and get to a healthier place without having to direct their frustrations at the game of tennis, then it was a success for me. "So, hearing that 17 years later it can still impact somebody, especially in this game, it does make me feel good." Andre Agassi won his first Grand Slam title at Wimbledon in 1992 Raducanu reached a career-high ranking of 10 in July 2022, but the 23-year-old has slipped to 98th in the world. Her progress continues to be hampered by physical issues, and she most recently missed the US Open as she continues her recovery from a stress fracture in her lower right leg. A foot injury disrupted her pre-season training before she spent two-and-a-half months off court with a post-viral illness earlier this year. But Raducanu enjoyed one of the best weeks of her career at Queen's Club in June, reaching her biggest final since her triumph in New York five years ago. Agassi won all four of the sport's Grand Slams and claimed Olympic singles gold at the 1996 Games. Asked what advice he would give Raducanu, Agassi said: "I would encourage her to focus on being the best of herself on a daily basis, but don't judge that by results or thinking that somehow you have to be 100%. "You have to learn to be 100% of whatever percent you're at [and] be comfortable in your own identity inside of that - not what people say. "Back in my day, I could just put down the paper and not read it. Now it seems like it's harder for these youngsters to avoid." Keothavong 'can't fault' GB after BJK Cup loss to Czechs GB dominate Ecuador to reach Davis Cup Finals For Agassi, tennis was by no means a childhood passion. His father, keen for his son to become the very best, would introduce him to others as a future number one tennis player. That additional pressure, Agassi says, led him to play with "fear". It was not until he sank from world number one to 141st that he felt able to reconnect with the sport. Agassi, who created a foundation providing education for under-served children during that time, said: "I had more success from that point forward than I did playing out of fear. "The first thing I would advise a parent to think about is that it's not their life, it's their child. "You raise a child in their way and they'll never depart from it. You just have to find out what their way is." Agassi will captain Team USA in the Laver Cup at The O2 in London later this week, between 25-27 September. "Tennis is a hamster wheel of sorts - the fact that these guys make room in their schedule to play this incredible event tells you how great this event is," Agassi added. "We're obviously playing Team Europe, in Europe, so I don't know where the crowd is going to have their heart. "But I know one thing - they're going to see some spectacular tennis." title: Rare snails lay eggs during car journey to zoo
description: The zoo near Canterbury says glutinous snails started laying eggs on their way to Kent.
body: The glutinous snail was once widespread in the UK, but is now only found in one Welsh lake A rare snail found in just one lake in the UK started laying eggs on its six-hour journey from Wales to Kent, as a zoo joined a nationwide effort to save the species. Glutinous snails are no bigger than a fingertip and used to be widespread across UK water ways. It is thought habitat disruption and environmental changes reduced their population to such an extent that they are only now found in Llyn Tegid, a lake in Eryri National Park, also known as Snowdonia. Wingham Wildlife Park near Canterbury has taken some of the wild population to breed and release into the wild. Samantha Eden, assistant curator, said the zoo started with six snails and recently started a new colony. One single lake in Wales is their only known UK home Despite their slow reputation, the breeding efforts are off to a flying start, Eden said. "I brought 24 snails back from Wales at the start of July," she said. "It was a six hour drive, and by the time I'd arrived back at the park I had about 12 egg pods in the carry containers that we were using. They'd laid eggs literally whilst we were driving. "We started, with one of the ponds, with just six adult snails. We recently moved 130 babies out of that pond to start a new colony." Keepers say 130 babies were recently moved out of a pond to start a new colony Hannah Ellins, head of reptiles and invertebrates, said: "We do a lot of work with exotics, but it's cool being able to help our animals here." She added: "We'll keep breeding them and then hopefully we'll eventually then release them into the wild and help wild populations." The snails have had hundreds of babies in just two months The scheme is part of a wider national effort to protect the very rare species. Wingham Wildlife Park is joining Askham Bryan Wildlife Park in York and Longleat in Wiltshire, along with Dudley and Chester zoos, with the Freshwater Habitats Trust searching for suitable water bodies where the snails could eventually be released. title: 'Landing role on Thomas & Friends was crazy'
description: Ellie-Mae Siame, 14, says she was "in shock" but excited at being a part of the beloved series.
body: Ellie-Mae Siame, 14, is the voice of Nia in Thomas & Friends: Railway Stories Earlier this year, young actor Ellie-Mae Siame landed a role in a show about one of the world's most recognisable characters – Thomas the Tank Engine. The 14-year-old is the voice of Nia, the orange and black-coloured engine number 18 in Thomas & Friends: Railway Stories. A full-length YouTube special premiered on Thursday, which has already been viewed more than two million times, and it will be on Netflix from 30 September before a full series airs in 2027. "It was crazy to see how big Thomas the Tank Engine was – I knew it was big but not that big," Ellie-Mae told BBC Radio Stoke. The Stafford teenager said she was contacted by her agent and did a filmed audition for the show in January. She expected either not to hear back or be contacted to do a recall or a read-through – instead, she was offered the role of Nia straight away. Ellie-Mae said: "It's crazy to think they liked my voice that much and gave me the opportunity to be Nia that fast." A special episode of the new Thomas and Friends: Railway Stories series debuted on YouTube "When I found out I got Thomas the Tank Engine, it was a shock but it was also really exciting," she added. "It's opened such a big pathway – the doors to more opportunities and experiences." Ellie-Mae has been acting since she was five years old, first appearing as Maudie in the 2020 film Four Kids and It. Her credits since then have included Generation Z, His Dark Materials, Modern Love and My Week with Maisy, in which she starred alongside Dame Joanna Lumley. Ellie-Mae appeared alongside singer Cheryl in 2020 film Four Kids and It The teenager said she loved both screen and voice acting, but added: "I think voice acting is probably my favourite because I don't have to learn a script. "You get to change your voice a bit so it doesn't have to be your natural or your normal voice." Initially, she did not realise how big a deal Thomas the Tank Engine was because she was "more into princesses" than trains. But her parents' excitement, along with many others, showed her how beloved the franchise had become since it first arrived on TV screens in the 1980s, and in books for 40 years before that. Ellie-Mae starred alongside Dame Joanna Lumley in My Week with Maisy Ellie-Mae found the role particularly special as it meant combining her love of acting and singing – she can be heard on the programme's theme tune, for example. She described recording one of the songs for an episode as being one of her favourite memories, along with seeing Nia on screen for the first time. "I don't even know how to put it into words," she said. "It's such a big thing. Seeing how many people like Thomas the Tank Engine is crazy because I get to be a part of that. "I don't know how to explain it, it's such an exciting part of my life and definitely something I'll remember forever." title: White House to roll out the red carpet for historic Xi Jinping visit
description: Trump and Xi are expected to discuss a range of issues from trade to AI during the latter's multi-day visit to Washington.
body: US President Donald Trump will host Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week in Washington, with everything from AI to trade and Taiwan on the agenda for the leaders of the global superpowers. Xi is expected to be greeted personally by Trump at Andrews Air Force Base on Wednesday, followed by a White House welcoming ceremony on Thursday featuring a military flyover and nearly 500 military personnel. The trip marks Xi's first visit to the US in over a decade and his third meeting with Trump since the US president began his second term in office. Adding to the high-stakes state visit, a US-China trade agreement reached last year is set to expire in November. The trade truce - reached in October 2025 as Trump and Xi met in South Korea - saw Washington suspend steep tariff increases on Chinese goods while Beijing eased back from restricting rare earth exports critical for manufacturing. Experts said they will be watching for some sort of announcement around an extension of this agreement during the upcoming state visit. Xi's trip to Washington, which ends on Friday, will have plenty of pomp and pageantry, and includes lavish dinners, private tours and performances. David Sacks, a fellow for Asia studies at the Council on Foreign Relations, described the planned extravagant welcome by Trump as "really unprecedented". "From meeting Xi Jinping at Andrews Air Force Base to having a flyover for Xi as well, this is not something afforded to any US ally," Sacks said, "much less an adversary like China. "It's quite, quite stunning," he continued. Trump is expected to address several issues as he meets Xi, particularly on tariffs and trade. The US president has long criticised his country's trade deficit with China, which stands at more than $91bn (£68.2bn), according to the latest US Census Bureau data, external. Also, Chinese rare earth exports to the US are down, external despite the agreement last October. US and Chinese officials held trade talks on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday but failed to make meaningful progress ahead of the Xi visit, multiple sources told the BBC. The talks focused on finding areas of agreement around non-tariff trade issues and agricultural exports, according to sources familiar with White House thinking. US negotiators are expected to continue talks with Chinese counterparts in Washington on Wednesday after Xi's arrival. Rare look at the remote engine rooms powering China's AI ambitions Another likely talking point between Trump and Xi is artificial intelligence, a topic that David Firestein from the Bush China Foundation said has "climbed rapidly toward the top of the agenda" ahead of this visit. China and the US are competing in what has been described as an AI arms race. But after a series of recent high-profile security incidents involving the emergent technology, there has been growing pressure on the Trump administration to regulate AI and slow its development. Senator Bernie Sanders wrote on X this week: "For the sake of all humanity, Trump and Xi must negotiate a treaty NOW to pause AI and ban superintelligence before it's too late." Trump's former White House advisor Steve Bannon and some Republicans in Congress have also warned about dangers posed by AI. The president, who views the technology as vital to the US economy and a battleground in a global struggle for power, has been reluctant. He views defeating China in the AI race as a primary objective. "Whoever wins AI, wins," Trump has said. Firestein told the BBC he expects Trump and Xi to discuss ways for AI collaboration. On Sunday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met with his Chinese counterpart He Lifeng and said the two had "very successful" talks on trade and AI. This video can not be played Watch: Sanders calls for US and China to work together to ban AI superintelligence Experts who spoke to BBC said any major breakthroughs on AI or other issues are unlikely to occur during the many Trump-Xi meetings planned this week. Then there is Taiwan, which remains an ongoing diplomatic thorn. The US Congress has approved a multibillion-dollar arms sale to Taiwan that awaits Trump's signature. He has held off for now, viewing the move as a bargaining chip with China. China has long vowed to "reunify" with self-governing Taiwan and has not ruled out the use of force. Firestein said he expects Xi will be looking for Trump to either commit to extending the delay of the arms sale or somehow avoiding the sale altogether. Xi - like Trump - is also facing economic headwinds at home, and is expected to use this visit as an opportunity to discuss deepening US-China trade. However, that presents a potential political problem for Trump. Some members of his cabinet and his supporters view China with deep suspicion. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy issued a letter, external to Ford Motor Company in September, urging the company to cut ties with China due to national security concerns and protection of American jobs. Regardless of the clear hurdles that remain before any new US-China deals are inked, it is clear that Trump views personal contact with Xi as vital to the process. "Trump has made a decision that no matter what, we need to not have a confrontational relationship with China," Stephen Orlins, president at the National Committee on US-China Relations, said. "He believes that the more he and President Xi meet, the less confrontational that relationship will be," Orlins continued, "and he is right." title: Reports of violence against women in Gaza surge, UN agency finds
description: The UN Population Fund also says there has been a "severe escalation" in the number of early and forced marriages.
body: There has been a sharp rise in reports of violence against women and girls in the Gaza Strip, including early and forced marriage, according to a series of recent reports from the UN Population Fund (UNFPA). One report, which analyses data collected by 10 organisations, says, external the protracted crisis in war-torn Gaza has "created conditions in which women and girls face escalating risks of gender-based violence". It also warns that there has been a "severe escalation" in the number of early and forced marriage incidents in the second quarter of this year. Both are considered types of gender-based violence (GBV) by the UN. Another report presenting testimony from 230 women in crowded displacement camps in Gaza City and Khan Younis, external makes for a grim read, describing the violence they have experienced or witnessed. Some readers may find some of the details in this report distressing One displaced woman in a school-turned-shelter in Gaza highlights how rape victims are often married to their rapists to avoid shame and scandal. "When rape cases are discovered in schools, you find weddings and celebrations at the school the next day," she says. Another woman tells how last year, at the time of famine, "a man married off his 14-year-old daughter in exchange for two bags of flour so he and his [other] children could eat". Six women in different displacement camps shared stories of such exchanges - which would have been unthinkable before the conflict between Israel and Hamas began in 2023. Although data collection to establish actual figures remains tricky, in the second quarter of this year, the UNFPA says the number of reported cases of early and forced marriage had increased by 123% on the first quarter. Early or child marriage involved girls aged 12 to 17. "The trends are shocking," says Nestor Owomuhangi, the UNFPA representative to Palestine. He says that the extreme circumstances over the past three years - which have seen tens of thousands of people killed, mass destruction and multiple waves of displacement in Gaza - have broken down social structures, so "everything is eroded... there is no system". While food markets have reopened, many cannot afford the goods on offer, there is still extreme poverty and hunger with reliance on charitable handouts. Nearly all the population of more than two million Gazans have been driven from their homes, leaving most living in squalid tent camps or damaged buildings. Public services have largely collapsed, and Israeli air strikes have continued despite the ceasefire. About 1.2 million Palestinians in Gaza are living in tents or makeshift shelters Prior to the war, girls in Gaza outnumbered and outperformed boys at every level of education above primary school. Now, with prolonged school closures, many children have dropped out of education. For boys there is pressure to find informal work to help support their families, for girls there are heightened issues around safety. Living among strangers, without privacy, in a socially conservative society, there are complaints of heightened sexual harassment and abuse - many families see marrying their daughters as a way to protect them and preserve modesty. The UNFPA report - based on research carried out in late 2025 and early 2026 - reveals how girls orphaned during the war are especially vulnerable. One woman in a Gaza City camp interviewed for the report says she attended the wedding of two girls from her family, aged just 14 and 15. "Their uncles married them off very young. Do you know why? Because their father and mother were martyred, and their uncles wanted to get rid of the responsibility and expenses," the woman said. "By God, they don't understand what marriage or life is." The Women's Affairs Center in Gaza - a Palestinian NGO which works with the UNFPA - and other support groups have documented distressing cases of girls who have been married and suffered abuse, often becoming pregnant. They say that those in their early teens are much more likely to have miscarriages and underweight babies than adult women. "We see adolescent pregnancies going through the roof because of child marriage," says Owomuhangi. "A child who is at an age when the body is not fully developed to sustain another body, who is hungry, in unhygienic circumstances, who doesn't know how to take care of the infant, who doesn't even know how to take care of herself, the consequences of that pregnancy are always really, really bad." The UN and most humanitarian organisations categorise marriages of girls under 18 as early marriage. Even before the war, this was more common among Palestinians in Hamas-run Gaza than it was in the occupied West Bank, but it was declining. The law in Gaza allows exceptions to the minimum marital age of 17 with parental consent and authorisation by a judge. Court officials can approve marriage for those as young as 14 years and seven months old, although a local Sharia expert told us that "legal safeguards" had been removed when Islamic courts - which officiate over family matters for Muslims - were closed for a large part of the war. About 700,000 children missed formal in-person schooling for almost three years The BBC has been speaking to some families in which bereaved relatives were married. Zuhair, who is 25, says his uncles pushed him to marry a 16-year-old girl from his extended family after her father - her sole guardian - was killed in an Israeli air strike. Challenged on why he agreed to go ahead with the plan, he said: "One of the reasons that led me to marry her was that there was no one to take care of her. That's the first point." "If it were not for the war, she would still be a young girl spoiled by her father. She would be going to school," Zuhair adds. "She still has a child's mindset, not a mature mindset. She misses school, her family, friends. She even misses simply sitting at home." A couple says they allowed their 17-year-old son t

title: Open wounds and eyes that can't close - women warn about cheap bleph eyelid surgery
description: A concerning number of patients are reporting problems from treatment abroad, say doctors.
body: Nikita had stitches in her upper eyelids. This photo was taken seven days after her bleph procedure Warning: Graphic images and descriptions of surgery "Everyone made it out to be so easy, but my face felt like it was on fire and there was a horrible smell of burning skin," says Nikita Morgan, as she describes her eyelid surgery. She decided to get a blepharoplasty, or a "bleph", removing skin from just above the eyes - after seeing videos about it on social media. Even though she was given a local anaesthetic, Nikita felt extreme pain. Oculoplastic surgeons - doctors specialising in surgery around the eyes - say a concerning number of patients are reporting problems from cheap bleph surgery, typically carried out abroad. This video can not be played Watch: 'My eyelids split open and became infected - I was scared to sleep' They have told the BBC the demand for this procedure, which normally costs thousands of pounds in the UK, has increased as part of a wider aesthetic trend to tighten, smooth and lift the face. Surgeons say complications have been linked to clinics across mainland Europe, Africa and Asia, and, when they occur, the lack of aftercare puts a burden on the NHS. As well as Nikita, we have spoken to dozens of people who have experienced problems - including one woman who had to tape her eyes shut to sleep because too much eyelid skin had been removed, while another feared she was losing her sight. UK surgeons have also told us they have seen patients unable to close their eyes properly after treatment abroad. Nikita, from Dublin, wanted to make her eyes more defined, but could not afford upper eyelid surgery in Ireland that she was told would cost more than €4,000 (£3,400). Then the 31-year-old discovered on TikTok that she could get a bleph with Dutch company, Faceland for €750 (£650). She described its clinic in Düsseldorf as "like a conveyor belt, just one in, one out constantly". The company says it has performed more than 2,950 bleph procedures on UK patients at its clinics in the Netherlands, Germany and Switzerland since October 2024. It says it offers "safe and quality" treatments and told us "less than 1% of procedures have led to a complaint", although this does not include everyone who needed revision surgery. The majority of patients who spoke to the BBC about problems with their blephs had been to the company's clinics - but we do not know how many complications in total have occurred at Faceland. Nikita, who went for her bleph in November 2025, says she did not realise how invasive the procedure would be, believing it to be like "getting your lips or Botox done", she says. She was injected with local anaesthetic, but when the doctor began cutting delicate eyelid skin, she felt pain she had never experienced before. "I went into shell shock, it was horrible," Nikita says. "When she was stitching me I could feel the needle going through my skin." Nikita's eye before the bleph (L) and six days after the surgery (R) Faceland says all patients have consultations and sign consent forms before procedures, to ensure they are "well informed and well prepared". It added that Nikita's doctor had said Nikita was "very anxious and uncertain" during her procedure "which can influence the perception of pain". Within hours, a "traumatised" Nikita was boarding a plane home. Flying on the same day of surgery is not advised by medical experts as well as Faceland, but she saw lots of people doing it on social media. "I was struggling to see," says Nikita, "if I looked up, my stitches would bleed so it was like I was crying blood." She really regrets flying on the same day as her surgery and advises others not to. In the past three years, videos about blephs posted by UK social media accounts on four leading platforms were viewed nearly 150 million times, BBC analysis has found. This figure is five times greater than the previous three years. Many people report positive results in their posts, and a lot have been treated at Faceland. One woman told us her droopy eyelids had been restricting her vision and causing her headaches. She was not eligible for NHS treatment and could not afford to go private in the UK, but now she says, after going to Faceland, her issues have been resolved. The company's website claims it is changing the market by focusing on "affordable, accessible and high quality care". Treatments are carried out by accredited medical doctors who receive internal training by Faceland in surgical procedures, it says. Surgeons in the UK told us upper eyelid surgery typically takes about three hours, including preparation, surgery and post-operation care. But Faceland patients we have spoken to say they spent less than an hour at the clinics. Faceland says allowing practitioners to perform a higher volume of treatments helps significantly lower costs. Eight days after her Faceland bleph surgery, Laura, not her real name, made her first of four visits to A&E because her eyelid wounds had reopened. Her procedure at the company's Amsterdam clinic in June had seemingly gone smoothly, but problems began when she took her stitches out back home in the UK, something many patients do when they have treatment abroad. The crescent shaped cuts above her eyes which had been held together by the stitches came apart, exposing raw, red wounds which became infected. This should hardly ever happen if a practitioner has been properly trained, UK surgeons told us. The first time this happened, Laura, who is in her early 40s, says she called Faceland's emergency helpline several times, but could not get through. Desperate, she rushed to A&E. "When I closed my eyes for too long the tension would cause my wounds to open up again," she says. "I was scared to go to sleep and was in constant agony." title: RAF base prepares for threats at home and abroad
description: Combat first-aid training and weapons drills are being stepped up at the station in Lincolnshire.
body: Personnel have been taking part in chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear training A front-line RAF base has expanded training for all personnel to reflect evolving threats at home and abroad. RAF Coningsby, in Lincolnshire, is one of two quick reaction alert stations that protect UK airspace with combat-ready squadrons of Typhoon jets. Military leaders have raised the level of force protection training, which includes combat first aid, additional firearms drills and awareness of chemical, nuclear and biological hazards. Wing Cdr Ian Hart, who commands 29 Squadron, said the change in posture was "a recognition that the threat can come to us very, very easily in today's world". He added: "We need to be ready here and we need to refresh those drills and be ready to act on them should any of those threats actually become a reality for us." Wing Cdr Ian Hart says threats may emerge far closer to home than has previously been assumed The base is the first in the UK to introduce Module 2 Individual Readiness Training as its minimum standard. Hart said: "When we look at the unstable world and the threats we're facing, I think it just brings it home that actually we need to be ready wherever we are, all of the time." He explained how combat first aid training reflected threats such as drone strikes. "We've just finished our first aid training and when we talk about drones, if you look at what's going on in the Ukraine-Russia conflict, you see a lot of situations where you might be first on the scene, wherever you are. "That could be at Coningsby, it could be overseas." Warrant Officer Lee Hargreaves delivers the training The enhanced training is delivered by the Force Protection Training Flight, a specialist team staffed by members of the RAF Regiment. They are described by the service as "the unsung guardians". Warrant Officer Lee Hargreaves, who commands the flight, said the training was mandatory for all personnel, "from pilots through to chefs, HR specialists through to musicians". "Although they have a trade and a primary role to do, they still have to know the force protection skills so they can meet the requirement. "Pilots make up about 4% of the Royal Air Force. The other 96% is what makes that 4% happen." RAF personnel taking part in a live-fire weapons training session While RAF policy requires all personnel to hold Module 1 training as a minimum, Coningsby is the first RAF station in the UK to adopt Module 2 as standard. The approach is being rolled out more widely across the service. Listen to highlights from Lincolnshire on BBC Sounds, and watch the latest episode of Look North. title: 'Disabled artists need opportunities, not just access'
description: Artists say while access has improved at arts venues, more could be done to support their work.
body: Deaf artist Cathy Mager has created projections exploring sign language across Bristol Disabled artists are still being excluded from opportunities despite Bristol's reputation as an inclusive city, campaigners say. Deaf artist Cathy Mager, who set up Spectroscope in 2022 to create radical public installations by deaf and disabled people, said the city is lucky to have cultural institutions who value inclusion. "Most arts organisations are committed to accessibility but there's a difference between access and showing work by deaf and disabled people," she said. Jess Douek, a singer who has chronic pain, has won funding to create Bristol's first fully-accessible grassroots music venue so emerging disabled artists aren't "locked out of that rite of passage". Britain's oldest lido 'will reopen' after floods New cameras to cut school-run abuse in car-free zones Hovis workers' strike could disrupt bread deliveries Mager, who is deaf, started projecting images of British Sign Language (BSL) onto a neighbour's house during the pandemic, which led to similar projects being commissioned at the Arnolfini and Bristol Light Festival. Spectroscope provided an outlet for these installations and connected her with other disabled artists in the south west. Earlier this month, it hosted a gathering for artists at Ham Green House in Pill, and is soon launching an artist residency at East Quay in Watchet. "There are venues across the south west who are really interested in what we can do, but there's more that can be done definitely," Mager said. Spectroscope hosted Where We Land at Ham Green House in September to provide a collaborative space for disabled artists from across the south west "Bristol has always been open to difference; that's established in the culture of the city." Mager said she is particularly grateful to the Watershed, which has been "a leading institution for ensuring deaf and disabled people can find a home here". "There are lots of people doing great things in providing accessible spaces; perhaps there needs to be more disabled leadership," she said. Too often work by disabled artists is seen as a side project rather than something that can have a broad appeal, she added. "But we've shown that our work brings in audiences in a mainstream context." She also called for more funding to help with patchy transport in the region's rural areas, which can isolate disabled people. Raquel Meseguer Zafe has explored resting in public through her art projects Raquel Meseguer Zafe, a professional dancer from Easton, developed chronic pain in her late 20s. "I felt I was capable but was being excluded by the fact I can't be vertical all hours of the day that most people expect," she said. After years of working out how to live well with pain, she began exploring the idea of resting in public. In her project A Crash Course in Cloudspotting, audiences lay down together and listened to audio of disabled people's experiences. "I've been trying to advocate for a resting spaces network since 2018, where arts and cultural venues could provide resting spaces," she said. Raquel Meseguer Zafe said audiences become more open when resting horizontally Meseguer Zafe is currently working on Juliet and Romeo, an upcoming show at Bristol Old Vic, where there is a resting space. There will also be shows with BSL interpretation and audio descriptions. "The work being made by Bristol-based disabled artists is going all around the world," she said, thanks to "fearless" cultural institutions. She points to the Watershed and Arnolfini, who offer beanbags and yoga mats to lie down on during screenings and in the gallery space. But she says the success of disabled artists is at risk due to cuts to the government's Access to Work grants, which can remove barriers by paying for transport and support workers. "The potential for us to keep working as we're working is under threat," she said. Jess Douek has fibromyalgia which causes chronic pain but her band have designed a way of touring that works for them Jess Douek, the lead singer of alternative metal band Mallavora, lives with chronic pain caused by fibromyalgia. "Being a touring musician, everyone is stood up all the time, on stage, travelling long hours; the culture is roughing it - I realised early on that just wasn't going to be possible for me," she said. "I wasn't prepared to give up on music so wanted to find a way of doing things differently so I could forge a career for myself." Her band designed a way of touring that works for them, by hiring help and playing accessible venues that are welcoming to their disabled fans. Douek said her band broke the record for the number of wheelchairs at a fully-accessible gig at the Exchange in May. She said there are "amazing accessible venues in Bristol, but it's quite inconsistent". She has secured Arts Council funding and partnered with the Exchange to create Bristol's first fully-accessible grassroots music venue to showcase emerging bands in a smaller space. "I'm conscious that emerging disabled artists are locked out of that rite of passage," she said. Quarterly gigs, networking events and a talent pathway with festivals and booking agencies will launch in early 2027. title: Chris Mason: From inside the room, how Burnham survived first Trump meeting
description: Burnham seemed nervous at first, knowing how explosive these encounters with Trump can be, writes BBC political editor Chris Mason.
body: As I crouched between the cameras, determined to catch Donald Trump's eye and ask a question, I listened to a president seeking to be magnanimous. Remember, Trump can and does do warmth when he wants to, as well as acerbic. Prime Minister Andy Burnham, a mayor a matter of months ago, sat next to the most powerful man in the world. Put like that, it sounds believable when he said in advance he was looking forward to the meeting, but there must have been a jab of nerves too. Burnham did look a little nervous as us reporters trooped into the room, but then, for the most part, the compliments flowed from the president. The original plan was for journalists to be invited in at the beginning of the meeting, perhaps just minutes after the men had first met. Instead, we were kept waiting while the private talks took place, which came with the upside that they had more to say about each other and what they had discussed than would otherwise have been the case. Burnham knew, the world knows, how explosive these rolling, free wheeling, live on camera encounters with Trump can go. It is rollercoaster without a harness stuff. This video can not be played How did Trump and Burnham's first meeting unfold? Having got myself into the president's eyeline, I waited for the last syllable of Burnham's final word at the end of his opening remarks and I filled the brief silence with a question. Was the prime minister a man you can do business with, I asked the president, given your political differences? "I do, I think he's a natural business person. We've had a lot of discussions even before this meeting. We've spoken to each other numerous times on the phone. Yeah, I think so, I think so. He gets it. He understands what he has to do." The warmth was self evident. Perhaps the Downing Street nerves will have eased a bit. But how long would the questions keep going? This is the president's theatre and he decides how long the public performance lasts. On occasion they are way north of half an hour. This was a meeting on neutral territory, a windowless, non descript meeting room down a dingy corridor in the basement of the United Nations. This wasn't the Oval Office of the White House. Perhaps that dialled down the sense of occasion a notch. Nonetheless, for how long could the president maintain the bonhomie and sense of agreement? A question about immigration, potentially a point of friction, came and went without incident. So to did the Burnham government's decision, announced by the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who was in the room, to sanction settlements in the West Bank, a decision which infuriated Israel. But on the future of the Chagos islands, the president couldn't hide his view that Britain's decision to cede sovereignty of them to Mauritius and then rent back the military base on Diego Garcia was "terrible." Trump says he can do business with Burnham but criticises 'terrible' Chagos deal The president added: "I think the prime minister is going to be looking at [the deal]" and Burnham replied "yep". Later, it was my turn to do a short interview with the prime minister on behalf of all of the broadcasters. Burnham emphasised that the meeting was "very encouraging" and "we've established a good connection." But what about the Chagos deal? Would it change, I asked. Pointedly, he described it as a deal he had "inherited". "We've got to find a resolution, and so work will continue now…to see where that resolution might lead." In other words, it looks like it is going to change. Flashpoints down the track with Trump are near inevitable — barely any leader avoids them with this administration, and Burnham may want to lean into some, in time. And even those he doesn't might lean into him, Chagos possibly one of them. But outwardly Burnham has a relationship with the president he can now build on after this opening face to face conversation. What followed in the prime minister's remaining meetings at the UN were diplomacy by convention, not the wild ride with Trump he had just stepped off and survived. title: More than 170,000 respiratory cases recorded in haze-choked Indonesia
description: More than 40,000 of the cases – which range from mild coughs to pneumonia – involve toddlers.
body: More than 40,000 cases – which range from mild coughs to pneumonia – involve toddlers Some 175,000 people in Indonesia have suffered from respiratory illness since August, its health ministry said, as it continues to battle wildfires that have raged for weeks. More than 40,000 cases – which range from coughs to bronchitis and more serious conditions like pneumonia – involve toddlers. Forest fires have blanketed parts of the country as well as neighbouring Malaysia and Singapore in toxic smog, pushing air quality indices into "unhealthy" territory. Indonesia has deployed more than 54,000 officials and dozens of jets to the islands of Borneo and Sumatra for water bombing, but the vast territory and challenging peatland conditions make it hard to put out the fires, authorities say. "From the air to the ground, all forces continue to move," Indonesia's Cabinet Secretary Teddy Indra Wijaya said on Monday. "Everything is being done to extinguish the fires, reduce the impact of the smoke, and, most importantly, protect the public from the threat of forest and land fires." Indonesia regularly battles wildfires during its annual dry season, which usually runs from July through October. This year, however, the fires and haze have been turbocharged by a so-called "Godzilla" El Nino, which has fuelled extremely dry conditions. The independent forest monitoring platform Nusantara Atlas has detected around 734,000 hotspots across the country as of Wednesday - a figure that is more than 30% higher than that of 2019, one of Indonesia's worst wildfire seasons. Since January, at least 895,657 hectares of land – nearly six times the size of Greater London – have been burned. The wildfires have led to school closures and a surge in hospital admissions across Indonesia. The number of people suffering wildfire-related respiratory illnesses had more than doubled to 113,336 by 9 September, up from 50,891 on 1 September, according to figures from the health ministry. The toxic smog has also taken a toll on wildlife, including critically endangered orangutans. Late last month, an Indonesia-based wildlife foundation shared footage showing an orangutan writhing on the ground on a palm oil plantation in West Kalimantan, one of Indonesia's hardest-hit provinces. The great ape, which was discovered by a farmer, was rescued and given emergency treatment for hypoxia, but later died. This video can not be played Orangutans in danger as wildfires blaze through Borneo Indigenous and civil society groups in West Kalimantan filed a class action suit last week against the central government and local administrations, accusing them of deliberate negligence for failing to properly tackle the wildfires scorching the province. "This is a disaster that occurs every year. This recurring pattern proves our view that the defendants knew about the potential haze disaster and the risks of disaster from forest and land fires," the group's lawyer Glorio Sanen said in a statement at the time. Indonesia has carried out several rounds of cloud-seeding operations in recent weeks, some conducted together with members of Japan's Self-Defense Forces who arrived in Borneo earlier this month to help with firefighting efforts. Cloud seeding involves manipulating existing clouds, such as by dropping salt crystals or silver iodide into them, to help produce more rain. Meteorologists, however, are divided over the effectiveness of the practice. In the Malaysian state of Sarawak, one of the worst-affected areas outside Indonesia, authorities launched a five-day cloud-seeding operation earlier this month. Apart from tackling the ongoing haze, this exercise was aimed at boosting declining water levels at several hydropower dams ahead of a severe dry spell forecast for October. "October might be hotter and drier," Sarawak's Deputy Premier Douglas Uggah Embas told reporters. "We want to increase the water levels as much as possible while we still can." The haze has reached as far as parts of the Philippines, where local officials have urged residents to stay indoors as much as possible, and Singapore, where authorities have begun issuing daily haze advisories. title: Dozens of migrants taken to Dover after more than 30 hours at sea
description: Protesters had earlier gathered in Gosport after an initial report that the small boat would be brought further west.
body: Protesters gathered in the Hampshire town of Gosport Dozens of migrants who spent more than 30 hours at sea have been taken to Dover by water, the Conservative MP for Gosport has said. It comes after an earlier report that the boat would be brought to Gosport, prompting a gathering of protesters in the Hampshire town. The boat had left the Normandy coast on Monday morning. The French coastguard, who had shadowed the vessel, said about 60 migrants on the boat were in "precarious conditions" and refused help as they were "determined to take all risks to reach" the UK. British rescue boats were sent to collect the migrants on Tuesday, with the UK's Maritime and Coastguard Agency saying they would be transferred to Border Security Command. The French coastguard said migrants were on the boat for more than 33 hours. The Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI) said it was tasked by HM Coastguard with assisting just after 11:00 BST on Tuesday, when the crossing had been under way for 36 hours. The coastguard asked the RNLI to remove people from the dinghy "out of concern for their safety and their deteriorating health" before Border Force vessels arrived on the scene, the lifeboat service said. The Home Office initially said it was becoming "increasingly likely" the migrants would be taken to the Portsmouth area and acknowledged it would be "far from ideal", in a message shared by Caroline Dinenage, Conservative MP for Gosport. They said any decision to bring a vessel ashore there would only be taken "where operationally necessary and following careful consideration of all available options". Hundreds of protesters as well as police gathered near the marina in the Hampshire town on Tuesday evening after the initial reports. A number of men wearing black, several with face coverings, were at the front of the protesters. Some in the crowd were chanting "send them back". Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo, shared a YouTube livestream of the boat from the Channel. Thomas – a long-term campaigner against migrants – organised recent protests in Portsmouth and Dover. Around 19:00, Dame Caroline said she had been told that Border Force had intercepted the small boat and was taking those on board east to Dover by water. In a post on social media, the MP said: "This is a good result. All day I have been making the case to the Home Office that this boat should not disembark in Gosport." At about 20:30, the demonstrators left the Gosport protest. Later, Hampshire & Isle of Wight Constabulary said six people had been arrested in Gosport on Tuesday evening after protesters "became hostile towards officers". The government said: "The Border Security Command works around the clock to protect our border and will continue to detain, check and process every small boat arrival." The migrant dinghy appeared to have set off from close to the village of Vierville-sur-Mer, west of Bayeux. It is rare to see small boat crossings depart from so far west. Earlier this month, a dinghy which had launched from near Cherbourg in the Bay of the Seine - further west than boats normally depart - was brought ashore in Hampshire, triggering protests in Portsmouth. title: Will Trump's AI rebrand as 'super intelligence' catch on?
description: Some people close to the president have started to use the term but experts say it is unlikely to catch on.
body: This video can not be played US President Donald Trump says artificial intelligence (AI) makes the technology "sound fake" and wants it to be called "super intelligence" from now on. "Welcome to the new world of super intelligence - SI," Trump said during a wide-ranging speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday. While some people close to the president immediately started to use the term, experts have told the BBC that it is unlikely to gain widespread traction in the industry because it is typically used to refer to more advanced systems. The announcement is Trump's latest rebranding move after he had the names of Lake Ontario and the Gulf of Mexico changed on US maps and federal communications. "From this point forward, all of United States' documents, and hopefully the world's, will be changed to use the more accurate term 'super' as opposed to 'artificial'. So its 'super intelligence'," Trump said. In the past week, Trump asked his followers on social media to vote on other potential new names for AI including superior intelligence, extreme intelligence and supreme intelligence. After a series of polls on his Truth Social platform, super intelligence came out as the winner. The purpose of renaming AI - and whether it will be adopted by the technology industry - is unclear. AI refers to computer technology that allows machines to do tasks that usually require human thinking. Meanwhile, super intelligence has a specific meaning within the tech community. The term is often linked to the author and philosopher Nick Bostrom, who more than a decade ago defined the idea as an "intellect" that is superior to humans in all forms. It is still entirely hypothetical. The rebranding is "misleading", as super intelligence typically refers to a system that has the ability to improve by itself, said digital ethics lecturer Simon Coghlan from The University of Melbourne. "I doubt 'SI' will stick, in part because it exaggerates the current capacities of AI," he said. "A superintelligent system, if it came about, would be regarded by experts as the most consequential technology ever made," Coghlan said. National University of Singapore computer science lecturer Ben Leong said: "My guess is that professionals will want to save 'SI' for a higher level of AI, not so much to describe AI today. It doesn't feel like it's at that level yet." But some in Trump's circle have already started to use the new term. "The Super Intelligence (SI) President has spoken! The United States is and will remain the global leader in SI," US Chief Technology Officer Ethan Klein wrote on social media. While Trump's ambassador to the UN Michael Waltz later said: "If you didn't see the president's speech, it's now super intelligence. I think he's absolutely right." However, when asked for his thoughts on the new name, Canada's minister of AI Evan Solomon said: "Canadians are not enthusiastic, at all, about renaming things," in an apparent reference to Trump renaming Lake Ontario. American power, AI and a walkout - key moments from Trump's UN speech AI staff 'genuinely frightened' for humanity's future, ex-Anthropic researcher tells BBC It comes as top tech executives and researchers have in recent weeks called on the US government to regulate the industry over fears that AI could endanger humanity - concerns that Trump has dismissed as "a hoax". He has argued against regulating the technology and said the US cannot afford to give China - its key technology rival - an advantage, adding that whichever side "wins AI, wins". "We're leading now over China by a lot, and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way," Trump said. The US is not going to "stifle the growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution," he added. The government will "rein things in" if needed and will lead the sector responsibly, Trump said. Trump is set to meet his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping this week, with AI expected to be discussed by the leaders of the world's two biggest economies. title: 'Extremely dangerous' Hurricane Polo intensifies to rare category 5 storm
description: The storm's sudden intensification off the coast of Mexico is "truly remarkable", the US hurricane monitoring agency said.
body: Hurricane Polo has rapidly intensified off the coast of Mexico to become one of the most powerful storms of the season in the Pacific Ocean. A Hurricane Hunter aircraft, operated by the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), flew into the storm on Tuesday and recorded sustained wind speeds near 180 mph (285 km/h), with stronger gusts. NOAA's Miami-based National Hurricane Center called the storm "extremely dangerous" and said its intensification over 24 hours was "truly remarkable". The slow-moving storm is fuelling up on extremely warm waters caused by the El Niño climate phenomenon and is the season's third category 5 storm, the highest level on the Saffir-Simpson scale. The storm is predicted to skirt the coast of south-western Mexico, but is not expected to make landfall, a warning from NOAA said. As it slowly drifts northwest, Polo will drive torrential rainfall in parts of Mexico's south-west coast - which could lead to deadly flooding and mudslides, NOAA said. Rainfall totals of up to 6in (15cm) are forecast, with 8in possible in some areas. Residents have also been warned of large ocean swells and life-threatening surf conditions for the next few days. "So far, the information we have is that (Polo) will not make a direct landfall on the coast," Mexico's President Claudia Sheinbaum said on Tuesday, but she warned residents along the Pacific coast to be vigilant. Sheinbaum highlighted the states of Jalisco, Colima and Michoacan as being at risk. Data from the Hurricane Hunter aircraft indicated that Polo could still strengthen and would likely stay a category 5 storm for the next few days, because of what NOAA called a "very conducive" environment of extremely warm ocean waters feeding the storm. Members of the National Guard patrol a beach as Mexico prepares for Hurricane Polo Scientists monitoring the ocean temperatures say the current El Niño climate phenomenon is now the strongest on record. Daily sea surface temperatures in a key region of the central-eastern Pacific were 3.05C above average on 19 September - exceeding the previous record of 3.02C set during the very strong El Niño of 2015. Some longer-term measures of El Niño have not yet hit record levels but this is likely to change, with the peak not expected until later this year. Warmer ocean waters mean storms can pick up more energy, leading to higher wind speeds. El Niño is a naturally-occurring pattern, which happens about every two to seven years and tends to last for around a year. Trade winds that typically blow from east to west across the Pacific Ocean can weaken or even reverse, allowing warm water to spread eastwards. Heat is then released from the ocean into the atmosphere which can boost global temperatures and drive changes in weather patterns around the world.
