title: A new skyline of data centres is rising from the rolling plains of rural China
description: Potato farmers rub shoulders with rows of gleaming new data centres as Trump and Xi meet to discuss AI safety.
body: In the expansive grasslands of Inner Mongolia, farmers are picking plump potatoes alongside new neighbours: huge, rectangular blocks that will fuel China's AI platforms. Ulanqab, with its steppes and volcanoes, is an unlikely digital frontier. For years, it has been China's official "potato capital". But now its fields have also become construction sites for a slew of data centres, as Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping meet to discuss AI safety among other things. Hundreds of workers in yellow helmets carry heavy equipment into the building site as welding sparks fly off metal scaffolding. Above them huge cranes move with precision to build rooftops, while men balance on ladders to plaster brickwork. "This is China speed," jokes one worker. "An infrastructure maniac," is how he describes his country, laughing as he walks away. “There is one phase every year. This is the second phase," explains an electrical engineer. "There will be many more phases afterwards." Artifical intelligence sits at the heart of China's contest with the United States and the key to it is the computing power inside the data centres here. To the Chinese Communist Party, these buildings are critical for the country's economic and national security. Once finished, they will help drive its mission to embed AI across 90% of industries and society by 2030. This video can not be played Watch: Rare look at the remote data centres powering China's AI ambitions China's not just building the infrastructure. It's also creating a pool of talent: young engineers and researchers who now see their country as a place of opportunity, partly because tensions with the US and Trump's restrictions on immigration have soured the American dream. "Fewer students and researchers are heading to the US, and more are returning from the US to China. That is very clear," says Jack Zhang from the University of Science and Technology of China. He himself was recruited by a high-level programme after studying at Yale in the US, and Cambridge in the UK. "I wanted to take some of the AI work I was doing in the lab and apply it to human health and medicine. That requires more resources, more people and sometimes more government support, which can be difficult to access overseas." China's expanding AI capabilities are one reason why the US says it doesn't want to hit pause on its AI development, despite stark warnings from inside the industry that the technology was moving too fast. "Whoever wins AI, wins," President Trump said last week. The CEO of AI firm Anthropic, Dario Amodei, called for keeping the US-led ban on selling advanced chips and equipment to China, while warning that a Chinese lead would "pose grave danger for the US and the world". This is not what Xi will want to hear when he arrives in Washington on Wednesday. The state-run Global Times, which echoes Beijing, dismissed US fears as part of a "Cold War playbook" to "contain" China's rise. But China is not just focused on catching up to the US. It is also touting an alternate model. Xi himself is encouraging Chinese AI firms to develop more affordable, open-source models - which allow people, companies and countries to modify it as they wish. It also pits Chinese models against those in the US where developers including OpenAI and Anthropic use closed-model approaches, and their design elements are kept a secret. One reason Beijing is in favour of their approach is that it has worked well for them. By sharing the tech, Chinese AI firms have been able to innovate quickly. This has helped China overcome one of its biggest challenges: a lack of access to advanced chips, which would help unlock greater computing power. But Beijing also wants a bigger say in writing the rules that govern AI. Xi has repeatedly called for more regulation and a global framework for others to follow. With calls for AI safety growing, this week's summit at the White House is especially significant. Can the two sides collaborate on regulating AI? Is any talk of a slowdown even realistic? It certainly doesn't seem like that in places like Ulanqab, where China's AI ambitions are taking shape. China is building hundreds of data centres - for Huawei, ByteDance, DeepSeek - in sparsely-populated provinces: Ulanqab, Ningxia and Gansu in the north, Guizhou in the south-west. It has already built up vast renewable energy capacity - wind and solar - in these regions, land is cheaper and the weather cooler, so there is less demand for water. These potato farmers' new neighbours are at the heart of China’s AI race with the US This doesn't mean there are no concerns or downsides. China wants most of its data centres to be fuelled by green energy by 2030 - but some of its grid is still fed by coal power. Water supply remains a concern in the arid, dry parts of Inner Mongolia. Entire villages have been relocated, although it's hard to pin down the number or what compensation residents were offered. It's a topic few people will discuss because it can be dangerous to voice concerns too openly. "This big data has absolutely nothing to do with ordinary people," says one local, speaking anonymously off camera. "What benefits has it brought us?" He says few locals had found jobs there. Others told us of fears that their land would be taken and they would no longer be able to farm for a living. But there are optimists too, such as a man who told us his last name was Zhang, standing alongside potato pickers in a field near the data centres. “China is now at the forefront of the world," he says, adding that his children have managed to find jobs there. "It's not like the 1960s, when it was relatively backward. China is doing alright now. Whether in economic development or other areas, it is doing well." Zhang is optimistic about China's embrace of AI, and says his children have managed to find jobs in the new data centre

title: Council leaders wary of radical plan to redraw Scotland's local government map
description: Local politicians across Scotland are digesting plans for the biggest shake-up of the council system in 30 years.
body: The future of Scotland's 32 council system hangs in the balance Council leaders have been voicing their concerns about proposals for the biggest shake up of local government in 30 years. Some have warned Scottish government plans to potentially streamline the number of authorities from 32 to six will not save money. Others have questioned the potential impact on rural parts and the "absurd" timeline. Under proposals for a new two-tier system, external, the regional bodies would focus on major issues such as education and economic growth. Between 120 and 160 community authorities would also be created, contributing to local issues such as licensing and town centre improvements. Scotland's 32 councils could be cut to six under government plan The changes, which would fundamentally reshape a system that has existed since 1996, have now been shared with Holyrood's committees and council umbrella body Cosla ahead of a public consultation. The Scottish government argues that some of these councils are too large to be truly local but too small to be strategic. For almost 20 years there has been talk of councils working together more closely to share overheads and cut duplication - for instance sharing responsibility for road maintenance or back office functions. But less has happened than had originally been expected and the talk now is of a fundamental overhaul. Deputy First Minister Jenny Gilruth says the government wants to "empower communities" Deputy First Minister Jenny Gilruth has described the proposals as a "starting point" for reform. She said: "We need to ensure investment is focused on frontline delivery, with the right staff in the right roles to empower communities and deliver real improvements in public services." "Existing local government responsibilities could also be extended, including enhanced roles in economic development and business support so that individual areas can reflect local strengths and ambitions." The broad signals from the Scottish government at present seem to draw some inspiration from aspects of the two previous systems of local government in Scotland: Large regional councils - which existed from 1975 to 1996 - which had responsibility for major services like education. The old town councils - abolished in 1975 - which provided local services for distinct communities, sometimes of only a few thousand people. They worked together with county councils. There are no indications at present of the likely geographical boundaries of the new authorities. Nor is there any indication of just how they would be funded. Would the community bodies have tax raising powers of their own? Or would the existing funding system be amended? Inevitably this discussion may become intertwined with the question of replacing the council tax. So what do the current council leaders make of it? Perth and Kinross Council leader Eric Drysdale wants to ensure the local authority has a "strong voice" in the debate Perth and Kinross Council will be one of the first to fully debate the proposals on Wednesday. Council leader Eric Drysdale, told BBC Scotland News he wanted them to be "a starting point for discussion rather than any final decision". "That's why I believe it is vital to ensure that Perth and Kinross has a strong voice in the national conversation which is taking place about public service reform." Drysdale said the local authority already fulfilled many of the ambitions associated with public service reform through its partnership working, housing investment, employability support and collaboration with neighbouring authorities. He added: "We have valuable experience to contribute that other parts of Scotland could benefit from." Local authority workers help maintain roads But David Ross, leader of Fife Council, has questioned the very need for such fundamental structural reform - and does not think it will save money. He said it would be "much simpler and more effective" to maintain the status quo but allow local authorities to "merge if they wished" and to collaborate through city region and local growth deals. Ross proposed that they should also be trusted to develop local arrangements for "community empowerment". The council leader added: "Most local government services cannot simply be broken down into 'community areas' or they lose the economies of scale and operational efficiencies. "Anyone who went through the last local government reorganisation in 1995/96 knows the complexity and disruption of this process and if the first minister thinks there will be any financial savings from the process then he is sadly mistaken." Council services, such as bin collections, have come under pressure in recent years due to budget cuts Once actual proposals for the boundaries of the new regions and community bodies emerge, they may well prove controversial too. One senior figure within Scottish local government that he thought the idea of six regions was simply a starting point or negotiating position. He thought around 10 would be more realistic. Fundamental change costs money to begin with - any savings are achieved over the longer term. Another council leader, Brian Connolly, who heads up South Ayrshire Council, wants the costs of reorganisation to be met by the Scottish government. He said: "The merits or otherwise of a regional approach can be debated but it is essential that local views and decision-making are maintained, along with substantial transfer of powers." Connolly added the three Ayrshire councils already have a "strong history of working together". Most of councils' revenue funding is used for day-to-day costs like road maintenance Given their proximity and links it is possible that Edinburgh, the three Lothian councils and the Scottish Borders could be within the same region. But Euan Jardine, leader of Scottish Borders Council, said: "My biggest concern is rural Scotland. "The Borders is a huge rural area made up of towns, villages

title: We're growing jobs based on AI, not destroying them, says tech boss
description: One school even offers pupils a semiconductor qualification to help them get into the industry.
body: Newport has a long history of semiconductor production, which is booming due to the hardware requirements of artificial intelligence "I think there's a huge fear of AI taking away jobs. It's quite the opposite here," said Jutta Meier, who leads one of Wales' most successful semiconductor companies. In a vast metal building on the edge of the M4, scientists and engineers at IQE wear futuristic overalls as they create the chips that fuel the revolution in artificial intelligence (AI). "We are growing great jobs based on AI and supporting AI, quite the opposite from destroying jobs by AI," Meier said. The UK's AI minister Kanishka Narayan said Wales had to "reindustrialise itself" for an AI future, while also "supporting everyone who is affected" by changing technology. Jutta Meier has led IQE as its chips became a crucial component of the physical architecture of data centres Newport has established a cluster of semiconductor companies, with IQE in production since 1988 and the wider cluster is growing. An independent report for CSconnected, produced by Cardiff University's Welsh Economy Research Unit, found the south Wales compound semiconductor sector supported 3,140 jobs across Wales in 2025, up from 2,748 a year earlier, external, a 14% increase. Of those, 1,914 were direct jobs in the industry, concentrated around Newport and the wider M4 corridor. The report said average salaries in the sector were about £66,000. Office for National Statistics data estimated the median monthly pay in the UK in August was £2,657 - or £31,884 a year, external. Nearby Bassaleg School in Newport now offers a semiconductor qualification to students who are keen to join the industry. IQE has benefited from the recent boom in AI because its chips are part of the physical architecture of data centres. They are not connected to the algorithms that allow humans to interact with chatbots, but are found in the computer hardware that underpins the operation. "The last 18 months were quite bumpy," Meier admits, as IQE struggled for relevance with investors. Earlier this year its role in data centre computing power was acknowledged and its share price grew quickly, allowing the firm to clear debts and begin hiring more staff. The impact of AI on jobs has been evident recently with tech giant Oracle slashing 21,000 roles globally as it reshaped its business around the technology. Amazon and Facebook-owner Meta have also cut thousands of jobs in recent months as they invest heavily in AI. But Meier said: "We're really lucky to have a very dedicated workforce that stuck with us throughout this bumpy road. "Talent, for IQE, is one of the biggest assets that we have." Students at Bassaleg School in Newport are among the first in the UK to earn a semiconductor qualification Two miles from IQE, students at Bassaleg School are among the first in the UK to be offered a semiconductor qualification. Head teacher Victoria Lamb said it allowed students to learn about an industry that was "right on their doorstep". She said it was "important that we work with our community to offer pupils these kinds of opportunities". "It is really good fun," said 15-year-old Grace. "We are doing practical work, and before the course I used to think semiconductors were all on a computer." Grace said it was "pretty cool" to have the semiconductor industry in the city. Her classmate Evan, who counts soldering as a hobby, welcomed the chance to put the skills into practice in school. "I think semiconductors will play a big role in what I want to do," he said. "I want to go into the electro-mechanical side, making robots. And semiconductors play a massive role in making that possible." Evan said there were "so many different companies, especially around Newport" offering careers after leaving school. The students have support from semiconductor companies, with a cluster on their doorstep in Newport Kanishka Narayan, the UK government's AI minister, said Wales' "amazing heritage in manufacturing" needed to be applied to the growth in AI. "The biggest economic opportunity for us is how we create more manufacturing jobs here in Wales, re-industrialise ourselves, hark back to our heritage but for a more durable future and AI is going to be a big part of it," he told BBC Wales. The semiconductor cluster was "paying 40 to 50% higher wages" than many other sectors in the area, Narayan said. But he warned that the boom in AI-related jobs would come at a cost. "I think in all industrial change of the past, there have been some jobs created, some jobs lost. "The task for us as a society is to make sure that we're supporting everyone who is affected and creating opportunities for our kids, for their kids as well." One Welsh software company said AI had increased productivity, allowing it to hire more humans to focus on specialist tasks While the chips are powering the AI revolution, there are already examples in Wales where the technology is creating new roles and changing existing jobs. At TiqToq, a Welsh software engineering firm that helps companies to search for security flaws in its systems, the company said AI was initially viewed as a cost-saving opportunity. "But that's not been the story at all," said director Mike Beck. AI meant the work of its human engineers was now "much more efficient" and their use of AI to help stress-test their clients' software had led to "over 53% time saving" for employees. The pace allowed the company to hire more people, while AI became a key tool in completing tasks for clients. "What we've found is that the projects that our customers were looking to release next year, they'll now bring them forward to this year," Beck said, adding that engineers were now "focusing on the areas that require that extra human insight". Social worker Siân Palmer said AI transcription tools were taking away the burden of paperwork, and providing a more accurate record of meet

title: Trump threatens to 'annihilate' Iran in UN speech as officials meet on sidelines
description: In his speech, the US president pondered whether a peace deal would be agreed or whether he would have to take extreme action against Iran.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Trump threatens to 'annihilate' Iran if no deal reached President Donald Trump has told the United Nations General Assembly he faces a "big decision" on whether to strike Iran again or pursue a peace deal. A single member of Iran's delegation watched on during the president's speech on Tuesday in New York, in which he said he could "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if the conflict went unresolved. Before a standing-room-only audience, Trump also rejected "global government", vowed to broker peace between Russia and Ukraine and ensure the US wins the artificial intelligence race. His comments came on a day of high-level diplomacy. He has been meeting more than a dozen world leaders as wars in the Middle East and Ukraine test his foreign policy agenda. Live coverage of Trump at UN Trump began by touting his accomplishments on the economy, immigration, the border and tackling violent crime, in remarks that sounded more pitched to voters in November's US midterm elections than the diplomats in Manhattan. He spent much of his address justifying the war with Iran, which has spiked global oil prices while dragging down his approval ratings since the US and Israel launched the military action in February. Trump's tone contrasted with remarks earlier by UN Secretary General António Guterres, who warned global divisions were deepening and underscored the "interdependence" of the world's peoples. Trump also signed a deal with Denmark to beef up US military presence on Greenland The US president argued that the conflict had prevented Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and demonstrated the value of what he described as peace through strength - ultimatums rather than deal-making or compromise. "Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?" he said. "Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell?" Trump said he believed an Iran deal, which has so far eluded him, would come right after November's elections. The remarks were indicative of his foreign-policy strategy of coercive diplomacy - threatening overwhelming force while keeping negotiations open. Trump later told reporters that American officials had had a "very productive" three-hour meeting with the Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the general assembly. Iran state TV confirmed that Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had met US Special Envoy to the Middle East Steve Witkoff, although there was no comment from officials in Tehran. The BBC later asked Witkoff how the meeting had gone as he was leaving the UN building and he responded with a thumbs up. This video can not be played Watch: Moment Trump rebrands Artificial Intelligence to Super Intelligence In his speech, Trump once again predicted his diplomacy would end Russia's war in Ukraine, which has shown little sign of letting up as the two sides trade tit-for-tat missile and drone strikes deep into each other's territory. "We're working very closely with the leaders of Russia and Ukraine, and we will get that one done," he said. "It's going to happen, I think, more quickly than people understand." Trump also played down fears about AI, vowing that the US would not surrender its lead to China because of alarmism or what he described as a "globalist scheme" to control the technology. The US president argued artificial intelligence should instead be known as "super intelligence". "The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said. "It's not fake, it's actually amazing. But we have to be careful." On the sidelines of the general assembly on Tuesday, Trump signed an agreement with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland to beef up US military presence on the North Atlantic island. The deal reaffirms the sovereignty of Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark, but grants the US broad access to the island's airspace and territory. Britain's PM Andy Burnham held his first face-to-face meeting with Trump Trump has also been meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and leaders from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman. Earlier, Guterres gave his farewell speech as UN secretary general, urging unnamed superpowers to recognise "that their power isn't so super". "The fault lines in our world are widening," Guterres said, citing geopolitical rivalries, wars, climate change and artificial intelligence. By contrast, Trump criticised international institutions, accusing the UN of a "far-left agenda of globalist bureaucrats who nobody ever elected". The US president instead emphasised national sovereignty and "unmatched" American military power. "There is no global government," he said. He also warned that the US would not allow threats to establish themselves anywhere in the Western hemisphere. "If necessary, we will use our unmatched military might to secure the vital national interests of the United States," he said. Trump accused Cuba's communist government of cultivating ties to left-wing groups in the US, including the Communist Party USA, Antifa and the Democratic Socialists of America. The Cuban delegation also appeared to walk out of the assembly chamber as Trump turned his sights on them, referring to the island as a "failed state". title: How Ceuta, football and Israel are shaping Morocco's election
description: Young voters are being courted with football slogans, promises of jobs and anti-Israel rallying calls.
body: Moroccan voters will find candidates from 27 parties on the ballot Disillusioned young voters in Morocco were courted with viral football slogans, promises of one million jobs and anti-Israel rallying calls ahead of Wednesday's parliamentary elections. Yet, for many young Moroccans, politics remains deeply disconnected from reality. "I have no hope for this election. I'm ashamed of our political scene. It's a complete circus," Siham Azeroual, 32, an environmental activist who lives in the Atlas region, tells the BBC. The outcome of the vote will decide the make-up of the next government, just weeks after 60,000 people risked their lives to cross from the North African country to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta - a sign of the lack of opportunities many young people feel they have at home. Morocco operates as a constitutional monarchy where political parties compete for 395 seats in the House of Representatives, the legislative chamber. Yet executive power remains closely tied to the crown. King Mohammed VI, the 63-year-old monarch, appoints the prime minister from the political party that comes first in the election, but also presides over the Council of Ministers - the country's most important policy-making body. The current campaign also follows a wave of Gen Z protests that erupted in September 2025 over unemployment, healthcare and living costs. Demonstrators chanted slogans like "freedom, dignity, and social justice" which escalated to "get out Akhannouch", a reference to current Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch. More than 2,400 people faced prosecution following the unrest. Despite the crackdown, some young activists are choosing to enter the political arena. Some 60,000 people swam from Morocco to the Spanish territory of Ceuta in late July Hamza El Kharroubi, 29, was briefly arrested during the protests. He is now running for parliament with the little-known Environment and Sustainable Development Party, which has a green agenda. "As a young person, I don't have much hope. I joined this party because they wanted more Gen Z faces and they are allowing us to speak freely about our demands," El Kharroubi tells the BBC. He comes from Tetouan, just 34km (21 miles) from Fnideq beach, where the migration wave to Ceuta started in late July. Some 60,000 people crossed, both Moroccans and other nationalities. At least 100 people died in the largest migration surge to the enclave in recent history. "We want justice for the families of those who died crossing to Ceuta. We want compensation for their families," El Kharroubi says. He argues that the crossing was widely linked to economic hardship and unemployment. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates overall unemployment stood at 13% last year, while youth unemployment - between the ages of 15 and 24 - reached 37.3%. El Kharroubi says his goal is not to compete with established heavyweights - but securing a voice in parliament to build toward 2031. "As young people, we have to enter the parliament so by 2031 we have strong young politicians who can compete for a seat in the government." Morocco's FA president Fouzi Lekjaa is beloved by fans for helping put the Atlas Lions on the world football stage Fouzi Lekjaa, head of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation and a senior politician who works in the finance ministry, has emerged as the kingdom's newest political sensation - and a definite heavyweight. Credited with helping the Atlas Lions - as the national men's football team is known - become global contenders, Lekjaa joined the centrist Party of Authenticity and Modernity (Pam) in July. Videos of his campaign rallies have gone viral in the football-mad nation that is jointly hosting the next World Cup along with Spain and Portugal. The clips show crowds chanting "Sir" which means "Go" in Moroccan Arabic - the iconic catchphrase from Morocco's historic 2022 World Cup run, when it became the first Arab and African side to make it to the semi-finals. Lekjaa has promised to make Morocco sixth in the world in education and healthcare, to match the Fifa ranking of the men's football team. Pam is competing against 26 other parties, including Prime Minister Akhannouch's National Rally of Independents (RNI). In its bid for a second term, RNI has renewed a pledge to create one million job opportunities by 2031. Political expert Rachid Aourraz, from the Moroccan Institute for Policy Analysis (MIPA), remains sceptical about this promise. "The slogan 'one million jobs' has become an overused electoral slogan. There is also talk of raising the minimum wage, but what is proposed cannot withstand a structural inability to create stable net jobs," Aourraz tells the BBC. He adds that major parties "do not compete over an alternative model", but rather over how to implement public policies set by a royal vision. Huge pro-Palestinian protests often take place in Rabat Also seeking a political comeback is the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD) - using anti-Israeli sentiments to woo voters. Morocco normalised ties with Israel in December 2020 along with several other Arab countries, under the US-brokered Abraham Accords. Led by populist former Prime Minister Abdelilah Benkirane, the PJD is campaigning heavily on a promise to end diplomatic ties with Israel. He says the normalisation was a "mistake" made by his party which led the government between 2016 and 2021. Bilateral ties were hit during the Gaza war with weekly protests taking place in the capital, Rabat, against the Israeli diplomatic presence. During the conflict the Israeli liaison office was closed and direct flights between the two countries were suspended. Yet despite an outpouring of pro-Palestinian protests, with tens of thousands taking to the streets and setting ablaze the Israeli flag at the height of the war, it was announced earlier this month that Israel and Morocco had agreed to open full embassies in their resp

title: Evacuation plans over WW2 bomb cut to 300 homes
description: More than 300 households are likely to be evacuated on Wednesday, Cornwall Council says.
body: The planned cordon was revised from 1,400m to 755m, with an estimated 339 households set to be evacuated on Wednesday morning. More than 300 homes are set to be evacuated on Wednesday as experts continue to deal with a suspected unexploded bomb in a town, down from 1,300 homes in an earlier announcement. A 300m (984ft) exclusion zone is currently in place after the suspected 250lb (115kg) American World War Two device was found in water near Falmouth Docks on Monday. Cornwall Council said earlier the cordon was "expected to expand" to 1,400m (4,593ft) on Wednesday, with the possible evacuation of up to 1,309 homes, however, that was later revised to 755m (2,477ft), with an estimated 339 homes affected. Supt Ian Thompson, of Devon and Cornwall Police, urged those within the cordon to leave their homes by 09:00 BST. Cornwall Council said it had prepared reception centres and would provide support for people who needed help leaving their homes. The council has provided a link that gives all the postcodes of addresses that could be affected by the evacuation, external. Meanwhile rail operator GWR said train services between Falmouth Town and Falmouth Docks would be suspended from 08:45 BST on Wednesday. Cornwall Council released a map of the 755m (2,477ft) exclusion zone Thompson said the size of the cordon was determined by advice from military bomb disposal experts, with the evacuation of the area essential so specialists could proceed safely with the next stage of their works. He said police would be present in the area to speak directly with affected residents and to ensure they have the necessary support. "Our priority is public safety and protecting lives and it is important to note that our military colleagues will not be able to safely remove this device until they are reassured that the area has been evacuated." Devon and Cornwall Police said partner agencies continued "to assess the unexploded ordnance", stressing work was "ongoing to determine the safest and most appropriate course of action". Lt Cdr Ben Brown, commanding officer of the Royal Navy's Bravo Squadron bomb disposal team, added navy disposal experts were continuing to help police with the unexploded "air-dropped bomb". He said the team members were among "the most highly skilled and fearless personnel in the Royal Navy" and were "ready to protect the public". "We find these things around the country all the time. It's what we train for. We do this day in, day out," he said. Brown said there was "a whole plethora of planning" ongoing at the scene, with various different options on the table, including a possible controlled explosion. He said "every scenario" was "unique" and the ordnance was on the "larger side" of what the team usually dealt with, but was not as big as the ones discovered in Plymouth earlier in the year. GWR said no trains or replacement bus services would be able to operate between the two Falmouth stations, however, it said it expected that trains would still be operated between Truro and Falmouth Town. It added services would resume as soon as the device had been safely removed and the cordon lifted. Singer Will Keating was among residents affected in the area Police thanked the public for "continued patience and cooperation" and said emergency teams were working to resolve the situation "as safely and as quickly as possible". Three residential properties were evacuated on Monday as a precaution. Householders have been able to return home since but the public has still been urged to stay away from restricted zones. Falmouth Coastguard's Tom Bolt said a diver had come across the device and alerted the coastguard. "That basically informed us and we were able to let the MoD [Ministry of Defence] know and essentially they assessed the situation and confirmed it," he said. How an unexploded 'WW2 bomb' is disrupting life in Falmouth BBC Radio Cornwall: Need To Know Among the impacted residents was Falmouth-based singer Will Keating, who lives nearby. He said: "I couldn't get to my house because the road was cordoned-off. "I'm quite intrigued to find out a bit more about the bomb, where it's from and about the history of it. "I don't think I'm worried about it going off from where I am, but I'm just interested to hear how the story ends." Sophie Castle said she lives incredibly close to the area affected Nearby resident Sophie Castle said she was "slightly worried" about what might unfold next, adding her flat was "incredibly close to the situation". She said: "We haven't been told much. But, hopefully, things will be done in the proper way." Student Maisie Page arrived in Falmouth for university a week ago. She said it was "very nerve-wracking" to learn there was such a device "just down the road" while starting her first year. Tilly Ogilvie, who lives in student accommodation in the cordoned-off road, told BBC Radio Cornwall she was turned away from her home on Monday. She said: "They told me to go as far as I could but they weren't evacuating people." Bryony Mirfin said she has lived in the area for a long time Another resident Bryony Mirfin said the first she heard about the incident was on social media. She said: "I've lived here for a long time, so it reminded me of when the acetylene tanks were going off [in a fire] 20 years ago. "It's not even the first time it's happened." More news stories for Cornwall Listen to the latest news for Cornwall Beatrice Venner also lives in the student flats within the cordon. The second-year student said police had told her to "wait it out" as they were "waiting for information from the bomb disposal people". She said: "The bomb disposal people, it's their job... so hopefully they can dispose of the bomb." She added: "I'm from Devon, so this sort of thing happens in Plymouth quite a lot", referring to previous incidents there. Beatrice Venner was unable to return to her student

title: Trump says he would back ban on diesel exports
description: Republicans lawmakers have put pressure on the president to curb exports as diesel prices soar to record highs in the US.
body: US President Donald Trump has said he would back proposals to halt American diesel exports in a bid to ease prices for drivers at the pumps. His comments come after Republicans lawmakers put pressure on the president ahead of November's mid-term elections to curb exports, as diesel prices soar to record highs in the US. Speaking on the sidelines at the United Nations General Assembly, Trump suggested keeping domestic supplies inside the US could also ease broader petrol prices. "I've called for that too. I've said let's not send out the diesel. We make a lot of diesel. That could have a little bit of an effect on regular automobile gasoline," he said . US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed officials were assessing "whether a full or partial ban would work" without disrupting refinery capabilities. National average diesel prices surpassed $6.50 (£4.87) a gallon on Tuesday according to AAA data, a new high. The conflict in the Middle East has constrained global oil supplies, putting pressure on pump prices. The surge in the cost of diesel has sparked political urgency ahead of crucial mid-term elections on 3 November, with several Republicans pressing the administration to restrict the fuel's export to ease financial strain on voters. US Representative Ashley Hinson, a Republican running for Senate in Iowa, said on Monday that the state's consumers were "being squeezed and shouldn't have to foot the bill at the pump." In Alaska on Tuesday, Senator Dan Sullivan similarly urged for a "temporary pause of American diesel and exports" to rebuild domestic reserves. Adding to the global market volatility, Ukraine's targeting of Russian energy facilities has knocked out the country's refining capacity. "It is a serious hit on the Russians," Trump said during a meeting with Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky on Tuesday. "It's also a serious hit on the price of diesel." Trump confirmed he would discuss the strikes with the Ukrainian president, alongside broader efforts to negotiate an end to the conflict. "I think it's going to happen," he said. Kyiv has intensified drone attacks on Russian processing plants in recent months to choke off the Kremlin's primary source of war funding. Because Russia ranks among the world's leading diesel suppliers, reduced refining capacity – combined with Moscow's own strict export bans – has severely squeezed global reserves. While restricting US exports could offer short-term relief for American drivers, a ban may risk pushing up prices internationally. The US exports roughly 1.3 million barrels of diesel per day – nearly a quarter of its refining output. Cutting these shipments could put pressure on supplies for Western allies, including the UK and the Netherlands, which have relied on American fuel to cover deficits left by sanctions on Russian energy. title: Dolly Parton free book scheme to expand in London
description: The late singer's Imagination Library posts children a free book every month until they turn five.
body: Harriet Sedrick-Ugo says the books have given daughter Sienna more confidence Dolly Parton's Imagination Library, which posts children a free book every month until their fifth birthday, is to double the number of London boroughs it covers. The scheme, which runs in five boroughs, will expand to 10 boroughs. It comes a month after the country singer died at the age of 80. She set up the library in 1995 in tribute to her father, who could not read or write. Funded by the Postcode Lottery, the expansion of the scheme will make 157,000 children eligible. Harriet Sedrick-Ugo, from south London, said the monthly books had given her four-year-old daughter Sienna "a lot more confidence". "We read together every day and that's been made possible because we get a book once a month," she said. "She loves reading for pleasure because we have so many books at home from the Imagination Library." Sedrick-Ugo, an early years educator, said the expansion would take pressure off families. "Buying books can be quite expensive, so if they're going to be getting it for free, that would be something a lot of families can benefit from," she said. She added: "I think it's the kindest initiative ever and we are so very grateful to have something so meaningful gifted to us." The scheme is universal, meaning every child in a participating area can sign up regardless of their family's income. The Dollywood Foundation says more than seven million books have been delivered to children in the UK. Jeff Conyers, president of the Dollywood Foundation, said Parton always wanted more and more children to have access to books Jeff Conyers, president of the Dollywood Foundation, said Parton would have been "incredibly proud" to see it grow in the capital. "Dolly always wanted the Imagination Library to be something that lived on for generations into the future," he said. "She was constantly pushing us about how we get the Imagination Library to more and more children and more and more families." The announcement comes amid concern about how often young children are read to. Figures cited by the organisers suggest 41% of children aged four and under are read to frequently, down from 64% in 2012. Teachers have also reported that 28% of children starting reception cannot use books properly, with some trying to swipe or tap the pages as if they were a screen. Clara Govier, managing director of the Postcode Lottery, said: "Dolly understood the extraordinary power of something very simple: a child, a grown-up and a book." The expansion is being marked with a celebration at the British Library ahead of Give Like Dolly Day on 25 September. body: This video can not be played More than 20 young people in the UK were infected with a severe strain of meningitis B in March. Scientists say they have now discovered what made this particular strain so dangerous. The outbreak was traced back to a nightclub in Canterbury and is believed to have been transmitted between people by kissing, or sharing drinks and vapes. The BBC's Jim Reed looked at the findings. title: American power, AI and a walkout - key moments from Trump's UN speech
description: BBC correspondents who covered the president's address on Tuesday assess five key moments.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Trump threatens to 'annihilate' Iran if no deal reached US President Donald Trump returned to the stage at the United Nations on Tuesday, where he touted his administration's policies in front of world leaders and issued pointed threats to some of those gathered in the room. The lengthy speech was wide-ranging, covering the war in Iran, AI, Cuba and the role of America's military. The BBC's correspondents who covered the address have picked five key moments that stood out. By Sarah Smith, North America editor in the room The US president has no great respect for the United Nations – he accused it of imposing a far-left agenda – but he does relish the global platform it gives him. He used Tuesday's speech to tout his achievements, and claim the mantle of a peacemaker, at the same time as he issued a number of pointed threats. Iran might be annihilated, lethal strikes on small boats suspected of drug smuggling will continue and the Cuban regime may even be toppled. The clear message was: America is still prepared to use its military might wherever Trump thinks it might be required to secure its national interests. Trump said he was "reasserting American power" and flexed what he called the country's "unmatched military might". "The United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the Western Hemisphere," he said. Once again, Trump has made the full-throated assertion to the world of "America First". By Bernd Debusmann Jr, White House reporter in the room Trump took aim at one of the US's closest neighbours, Cuba, calling it "an absolutely failed state" and saying his administration has been pursuing "a fundamental change in the situation in Cuba". "It will fall," he said. The Cuban delegation walked out of the hall as Trump continued his remarks. Over the last year, the US president become more vocal in criticising Cuba's communist government. On Tuesday, he said it was under "enormous pressure" and "failing like never before". The US has not, however, provided a detailed picture of what it believes change will look like in Cuba. Cuba's foreign minister reacted angrily to Trump's comments and accused the US president of spreading "falsehoods". "The US government is incapable of accepting that Cuba is and has the right to be a full sovereign and independent country," Bruno Rodriguez wrote on X. This video can not be played Watch: Cuban delegation walks out during Trump's UN speech Trump says he can do business with Burnham but criticises 'terrible' Chagos deal Burnham expects to find 'common ground' with Trump in first meeting Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings By Khashayar Joneidi, BBC Persian correspondent in Washington Trump presented Iran with a stark choice at the UN General Assembly: reach an agreement with Washington and rebuild the country, or face the rapid "annihilation" of the Islamic Republic. He then again predicted that a deal to end the war would probably follow the US midterm elections in November. His remarks illustrated Trump's familiar strategy of coercive diplomacy - keeping negotiations open while also threatening overwhelming force. But his language blurred the distinction between destroying the political system and threatening Iran itself. International law experts have previously expressed concern at what they called "alarming rhetoric" used by US officials, including Trump himself, who has posted that the US might "obliterate" Iran's power plants. References on Tuesday to leaving "no chance of survival" and "no hope" for future generations will likely have stoked similar alarm. There is also an irony in delivering this warning at the United Nations, an organisation founded to save future generations from war. Yet the speech was not a declaration that diplomacy has failed. It was an attempt to define the terms of possible negotiations: the US remains prepared to make a deal, but only under the shadow of an existential threat. By Bernd Debusmann Jr, White House reporter in the room Trump also praised a new deal with Greenland under which he said the US would build two military bases in the Arctic territory. "We will have the complete ability to do what is necessary to defend the American continent and also Europe," he said of the deal, which he first announced on Friday. He added that it "very much enhances" the defence alliance Nato. The US, Denmark and Greenland held a joint signing ceremony at the UN shortly after Trump's address. Although Greenland is a semi-autonomous territory, it is part of the Kingdom of Denmark which primarily handles its foreign policy. Trump shakes hands with Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen before signing security agreement Trump administration officials are already hailing the agreement as enhancing US security at minimal cost - and with relationships intact. Denmark and Greenland's governments, however, will be hoping it ends the long-simmering disagreement that began when Trump threatened to take Greenland by force. That threat shook the Nato alliance and sorely tested the US-Danish relationship. Few clear details about the nature of the deal have been confirmed publicly, and given Trump had tried for months to purchase or annex the semi-autonomous territory, some analysts are viewing it as a quiet win for diplomacy. "The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said. "It's not fake, it's actually amazing. But we have to be careful." "Welcome to the new world of Super Intelligence - SI," he added. title: Trump says he can do business with Burnham but criticises 'terrible' Chagos deal
description: The UK has proposed handing the Chagos Islands to Mauritius and paying to lease back an important military base.
body: This video can not be played Burnham "gets it" says Trump, as the two leaders meet for first time US President Donald Trump has said Andy Burnham is a man he can do business with, after the two leaders met in person for the first time. Trump said UK-US relations are "more up now" that Burnham is in power, following their meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. Speaking to reporters, Burnham said he had "established a good connection" with Trump and they had "taken that further today" following discussions on issues such as trade and immigration. But the US president made clear his opposition to the UK's "terrible" deal to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius and pay to lease back a joint UK-US military base on the archipelago's largest island, Diego Garcia. Trump and Burnham met on Tuesday as they attended the United Nations for the annual gathering of world leaders. Following bilateral talks, Burnham sat alongside Trump and used his opening remarks to say: "You and I have established a good connection in our early discussions and we've taken that further today." The two men then faced questions shouted from the assembled press pack. Asked by the BBC if Burnham was a man he could do business with, Trump said: "Yeah I do, I think he's a natural businessperson, we've had a lot of discussions even before this meeting we've spoken to each other numerous times on the phone. "Yeah, I think so, he gets it, he understands what he has to do." Burnham later said he had explained to Trump that Britain has been in "too much turbulence" in recent times but it is time to "turn the story" about the country into a positive one. The US president added that the UK is a country with "great patriotism", and he thinks it is "waiting for good leadership, waiting for success". Relations between Sir Keir and Trump also began well before becoming increasingly strained earlier this year when the then-prime minister refused to permit the use of UK bases for the initial US-Israel strikes on Iran. Trump reiterated his criticism of the Chagos Islands deal and stressed how a joint UK-US military base on Diego Garcia is "strategically very important", particularly in relation to US operations in Iran. The agreement would see the UK cede sovereignty of the territory to Mauritius and pay an average of £101m ($136m) per year to lease back the military base - but in April the deal was paused indefinitely because Trump pulled his support. Speaking on Tuesday, Trump said: "I think the prime minister is going to be looking at [the deal]." The prime minister had spoken to his Mauritian counterpart, Navin Ramgoolam, ahead of his trip to New York. On Monday, he said the UK was "determined to secure the long-term operation of the base" and work "towards a resolution". Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, who has long been a critic of the deal, posted on X: "The Chagos deal is dead. Thank God." Burnham also referenced that his private discussions with Trump included the Falkland Islands, which have been the subject of comments by the president. Earlier this month, Trump hinted he would not come to the UK's aid in a potential future conflict with Argentina over the British overseas territory. He had previously said the US could revise its neutral position on the islands' sovereignty if the UK failed to increase defence spending. The Falklands, in the south-west Atlantic Ocean, remain the subject of a sovereignty dispute between Britain and Argentina, more than 40 years on from an armed conflict over the territory. One of the areas Burnham has been keen to focus on during his trip to the UN is artificial intelligence (AI). The prime minister met business leaders, including Apple's executive chairman Tim Cook, on Tuesday. He told them he wants a "single set of global principles and standards that are very much about unlocking the full potential whilst guarding against the risks". Burnham's approach could cause friction with Trump, with the president using his address to the UN General Assembly to say that the US "totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme" to control AI. Trump dubbed AI as "super intelligence" and said the US will "encourage it, not rein it in". Burnham later met European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, with the PM apologising for arriving around 10 minutes late due to his bilateral with Trump running over. Von der Leyen reassured the PM, saying: "These things are understandable." Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletter to keep up with the inner workings of Westminster and beyond. title: Lib Dems leave conference buoyed by Davey's message
description: Concerns over Sir Ed Davey's leadership were dampened by pledges at conference and his performance.
body: This was a more sombre, more serious, Sir Ed Davey. The stunts - from falling off paddleboards to hurtling down rollercoasters – were scaled back at this year's Liberal Democrat party conference. "This is the fight of our lives," he repeatedly told his party. The focus, much like his conference speech last year, was on Reform UK. But the announcement he'd held back for his speech was aimed at Conservative-leaning voters: tax cuts worth billions. And not just for lower income earners, but for those in the higher 40% rate of tax too. Part of the announcement – raising the amount you can earn before you pay income tax altogether – was the same policy Davey's bête noire, Reform UK, announced at their conference a couple of weeks ago. The dividing line he drew was over how it was paid for. Nigel Farage's party would reduce spending on benefits to fund the tax cut. The Lib Dem leader said he would pay for it through the economic growth he believes could be gained by rejoining the EU's Single Market and a customs union. Lib Dems vow to end 'computer says no' economy to boost growth Lib Dems call for one-to-one midwife care during childbirth Davey promises tax cuts for millions if UK rejoins EU single market By putting the European Union at the heart of how he would fund his tax cut, the Lib Dems couldn't be drawing a starker contrast with the Brexit-backing Reform UK and a Conservative Party also committed to cutting welfare. But the plan is speculative. The Lib Dems insist a deal with the EU could be negotiated within a year if the party was in government after the next election. Plenty of economic experts, including the official budget forecaster the OBR, believe the UK's economy could grow if the UK was in the Single Market. But as recent political history teaches us, negotiating a deal with the European Union is often more difficult than party leaders hope. And basing a tax cut on potential future economic growth is a risky business. There is also uncertainty over whether the Lib Dems' sums add up. The independent think tank, the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said the policy as set out in the press release would cost "much more" than the £17bn the Lib Dems have budgeted for. The party says the tax cut wouldn't come in until the fifth year after the next election. So even if the party got into power and successfully negotiated an EU deal, the tax cut could be eight years away. But the Lib Dem MPs I spoke to afterwards were less focused on these details than the message it sent to voters. Davey came into this conference facing criticism over his leadership from some MPs in private and others in his party in public worrying about the party's ambition and direction. For now those concerns have been dampened. "That was the speech a lot of us have been waiting for him to give," one Davey-sceptic MP told me afterwards. A small number are uncomfortable with the main policy from the party's conference being a tax cut that would most benefit the better off. One told me they would rather the focus had been wooing younger voters by tackling the amount graduates repay in student loans, an old bruise for the Lib Dems. But overall this speech, and this conference, was well received by the Lib Dem faithful. They are a party honing their messaging before the next general election. The strategy is primarily on those 27 seats where the Lib Dems came second in 2024. Most of them are held by the Conservatives and Davey's tax cuts are aimed at appealing to those voters. But already the attack from the Tories has been that the Lib Dems are "Labour's lapdog". That attack is in part because Davey has given his most explicit answer this week on not going into a coalition government with the Conservatives after the next general election. He's done the same for Reform UK. But he hasn't ruled out a pact with Labour. So that attack from the Conservatives will come again and again before the next election. But the Lib Dems leave their Brighton conference buoyed, with sights not just on retaining their record 72 seats won at the last election, but on winning some more. "I've got no ceiling on our ambitions," Davey said this week. He has already served in government once, in coalition with David Cameron's Conservatives. His eyes are on another stint in office. title: Jacks stars as England grind out win over Sri Lanka
description: Will Jacks' all-round efforts help England grind out an 89-run victory over Sri Lanka in the first one-day international at Chester-le-Street.
body: This video can not be played Highlights - Jacks stars for England as they beat Sri Lanka in first ODI First Metro Bank one-day international, Chester-le-Street England 265 (48.1 overs): Brook 67 (69); Colombage 3-44 Sri Lanka 176 (37 overs): Wellalage 45 (36); Jacks 5-22 England won by 89 runs Will Jacks' all-round efforts helped England grind out an 89-run victory over Sri Lanka in the first one-day international at Chester-le-Street to continue their quiet revival in white-ball cricket. Faced with a slow and low pitch, Jacks made 46 not out after 67 from Harry Brook and 44 from Joe Root, meaning England posted 265 despite being bowled out in 48.1 overs. That score appeared only par but a professional bowling performance limited Sri Lanka's scoring and found regular wickets. Jacks took the big wickets of Kusal Mendis and Charith Asalanka and then wrapped up the tail for career-best figures of 5-22. Sri Lanka, much improved in the field but far too timid with the bat, were bowled out for 176. England, who have now won 10 white-ball matches in a row against Sri Lanka this year, can seal a third ODI series win in a row with a game to spare on Thursday at Headingley. The three-match contest concludes on Sunday at The Oval - a match that brings down the curtain on one of the most topsy-turvy summers in recent memory. England fast bowler Wood retires from internationals India avoid shock defeat by Japan after controversial wide England go 1-0 up against Sri Lanka - as it happened This video can not be played Root, Buttler, Overton - Colombage's debut to remember for Sri Lanka This was not vintage England. For the first time since 2019 they did not hit a six batting first. Captain Brook and coach Brendon McCullum should not mind that, however. For too long, England have only been able to win when piling up big scores. Yes, they were dismissed for the 12th time since McCullum took charge of the white-ball sides last year and, as so often this summer, the quality of the opposition can be questioned. But Brook was the only batter to fall in a middle order collapse of 4-29 playing an aggressive shot. He sliced a drive to deep cover after batting in a restrained manner, while Sri Lanka's debutant leg-spinner Sachindu Colombage, who found a hint of turn to hit Root's off stump, had Jos Buttler lbw for 31 and bowled Overton with a googly for eight, was impressive. After the collapse, Jacks could have swung hard but batted responsibly to stretch out the innings from 211-7 in the 39th over. He took 18 runs from the 47th over and was primed to cut loose before Asitha Fernando, having dismissed opener Tom Banton for 10 with a bail-trimmer in the powerplay, found reverse swing to bowl Jofra Archer and Josh Tongue. Jacks' importance to England's white-ball sides is growing with every match. They will need bigger scores by the time the World Cup comes around in a year's time but, after beating Sri Lanka at the start of the year and toppling India in July, they are now primed to enter two months of white-ball cricket overseas on the back of another series win. This video can not be played Watch the best of Jacks' match-winning performance as England beat Sri Lanka With Adil Rashid out of this series with a hand injury, much of the attention was on Rehan Ahmed, who has a rare chance to press his case as England's leg-spinner. After being carelessly run-out for two, he dropped a caught-and-bowled chance in his first over and conceded 46 runs in seven overs. Those figures were harsh but he will hope for better before the series is out. Instead, it was Jacks who played the lead spinner's role with his off-spin, barely bowling a bad ball. Asalanka and Mendis were pinned attempting sweeps and Dunith Wellalage, who hit two sixes in a 36-ball 45 at number seven, was tempted to sky a catch to mid-on. When Fernando and Dilshan Madushanka followed, Jacks had the best figures by an England spinner since Vic Marks in 1984. England's total was also the lowest they have defended in a full ODI since July 2022 – before their dismal 2023 World Cup or their winless run at last year's Champions Trophy. Gus Atkinson bowled well for 1-25 in seven overs and Jamie Overton 2-21 in five. The seamers all bowled hard lengths and were rewarded. title: Ukraine anger as EU removes Russian oligarchs from sanctions list
description: Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman both have close ties to President Putin, and Kyiv said the move sent Moscow the wrong signals.
body: Usmanov is described as having particularly close ties to President Putin The European Union is to remove sanctions on two oligarchs imposed after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, according to reports, prompting anger in Ukraine. France had campaigned for Russian-Uzbek billionaire Alisher Usmanov to be taken off the list, citing "national security concerns". Luxembourg called for the removal of Russian-Israeli businessman Mikhail Fridman, who is suing the country for the release of frozen assets. Latvia initially opposed the deal but agreed to a compromise, part of which involved extending sanctions on nearly 3,000 other individuals and entities for three years. Ukrainian officials said the move was "unacceptable" and sent the wrong signal to Moscow. "Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans," Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said on X. He urged all EU member states to instead announce national sanctions on the two individuals. Latvia has already said it would do so. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov earlier welcomed the prospect of the two oligarchs being taken off the list, claiming the EU's sanctions were illegal and all Russians should be removed. Usmanov founded USM Holding company, an investment group that owns iron, steel and copper suppliers, and the Megafon telecommunications company. He has in the past had ties with the English Premier League clubs Arsenal and Everton. The EU froze his assets in 2022, describing him as "a pro-Kremlin oligarch with particularly close ties to Russian president Vladimir Putin". Usmanov said the decision was "unfair". It has been reported that France's initiative was linked to a prospective prisoner release deal with Azerbaijan. Fridman has avoided condemning Putin outright for the war in Ukraine Fridman, a Russian-Israeli citizen born in Ukraine, is the founder of the Alfa Group investment conglomerate, with key interests in energy and banking. The EU has described him as a top Russian financier and enabler of Putin's inner circle. Fridman himself said at the time of Russia's full-scale invasion that the conflict should end as soon as possible, but avoided outright condemnation of President Putin. His Russian-Latvian business partner Pyotr Aven was stripped of Latvia's highest civilian honour in 2022 for failing to condemn the invasion of Ukraine. This may have influenced Latvia's opposition to the move, vetoing it in a vote by EU ambassadors on Monday. However, on Tuesday it changed its vote to an abstention as a compromise was reached. The new deal involved extending sanctions on some remaining 2,600 individuals and entities to three years. Until now, sanctions had to be renewed every six months. Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs also announced that France had agreed to start talks with Latvia about joining a French nuclear deterrence initiative and strengthen its military presence in Latvia. Who are the mega-rich Russians facing sanctions? title: Booker Prize judges reveal shortlisted novels after selection 'tussle'
description: Past Booker winners Marlon James and Douglas Stuart are among the nominees for this year's award.
body: The Booker Prize 2026 judges are Rebecca Liu, Jarvis Cocker, Dame Mary Beard, Raymond Antrobus and Patricia Lockwood Past Booker Prize winners Marlon James and Douglas Stuart have been shortlisted for the prestigious literary award again, after a selection process that the judges described as "a tussle". Jamaican writer James is nominated this year for his latest novel The Disappearers; while Scottish author Stuart is shortlisted for John of John. This year's other contenders are award-winning US novelist Elizabeth Strout, and British authors M John Harrison, Luke Kennard and Rebecca Perry. But seven books that appeared on the longlist in July have been jettisoned, and Dame Mary Beard, who chaired the judging panel, said agreeing on the final six "has been, to put it mildly, hard work". Scroll down to find out more about this year's nominees. James previously won the Booker Prize in 2015 for A Brief History of Seven Killings, while Stuart won in 2020 for Shuggie Bain. Praising this year's entries, Dame Mary added: "English language fiction now is full of talent – talent old and talent new. "It's full of wit, seriousness, pleasure, challenge, discomfort and real brilliance, and I think we should be rewarding our novelists a lot more than we do." The other judges included former Booker Prize-shortlisted US novelist Patricia Lockwood, who said she discovered she was "bossier than I believed myself to be" when making the case for or against particular books in the judges' meetings. "I was sort of standing up a lot and tossing books across the room and being really active. I was like, 'Wow, yeah, I didn't know I had it in me'." Another judge, poet Raymond Antrobus, told reporters: "All of us individually had a different idea for a shortlist and then it was a tussle." Lockwood jokingly added: "A tussle, yeah. We wrestled like pigs in the mud!" Antrobus said the final choices are connected because they are books that "as well as having heart, also took risk". "These books, we truly believe, cannot be replicated by artificial intelligence. These are very human books for the way they talk about and navigate a lived experience." The judging line-up was completed by journalist, editor and critic Rebecca Liu and Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker, who said being on the selection panel was "a bit like being in a band". He said: "The way a band makes an appealing noise is by everybody combining, in a way, and if you don't like that then you have to go solo. "You get something that you couldn't get [alone] and no-one's in control of it and you make a good noise together. So I hope that's what this shortlist is, a nice noise." Cocker read some of the entries while on tour, and said he joined one judges' meeting online while wearing a dressing gown in a hotel room in Australia at 02:00 local time. "When you're on tour, it's quite dull when you're travelling so it was quite good to have something to read," he said. "I became known for being in those meetings wearing a towelling robe." The End of Everything by M John Harrison An unexplained catastrophe, and the arrival of mysterious alien beings, have turned British society upside down - and a man and his elderly aunt muddle through on the Kent coast. It's the author's first Booker nomination, and he'd be the oldest ever winner at 81. The judges said: "The End of Everything can be read as a thriller, a mystery, a satire, a dystopia, a road novel, a work of realism. The landscape may be bleak, the catastrophe may be immersive, yet there still were moments we found ourselves laughing aloud." The Disappearers by Marlon James This epic, visceral story revolves around a violent attack on eight gay men who had gathered to rehearse a queer play in Kingston, Jamaica, in 1988, and its aftermath. The New York Times called it "a masterpiece, the novel of the decade and possibly of the century thus far". The judges said: "A Jamaican epic from one of the most impactful Caribbean novelists today; readers will love the shifting register of the dialogue and poetic phrasings, often pierced through with sharp, double-edged humour." Black Bag by Luke Kennard An out-of work actor gets a new role - being locked in a black bag during psychology lectures for an entire term as a professor's experiment. The story unfolds into a humorous and poignant satire that makes sharp observations about the state of modern masculinity and creative life. The judges said: "In a wonderfully quirky campus novel, Kennard combines an absurd experiment with a moving story about human frailty, passion, confusion and identity. There's something for everyone here." May We Feed the King by Rebecca Perry A modern-day museum curator is commissioned to recreate a past scene in a historic palace, and becomes immersed in the world of the young, reluctant king whose life she uncovers. It is the debut novel by Perry, who is also a poet and a former competitive trampolinist. The judges said: "An affecting and lush jewel of a novel that moves between our present-day world to a medieval court and unsettles the idea that there's ever one universal historical truth." The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout Strout, a former Pulitzer Prize winner and double Booker nominee, tells the story of a high school history teacher in his 50s who feels adrift in modern America. When a secret emerges, he must face big questions about his relationships and life choices. The judges said: "A novel that engages with the deeply divisive politics of present-day America, without itself becoming divisive. This is the kind of book we need now: a calm antidote to contemporary events." John of John by Douglas Stuart The third novel by Stuart is about a fashion student who is drawn back to his home in a small, religious community in the Outer Hebrides in the mid-1990s. He and his father both nurse secrets. And both are called John. The

title: US to build two military bases in Greenland under new deal with Denmark
description: The defence deal signed at the UN General Assembly also re-affirms Denmark's sovereignty over its semi-autonomous Arctic territory.
body: US President Donald Trump signed the deal alongside Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen The US, Denmark and Greenland have signed a defence deal that allows Washington to build two new military bases in the Arctic territory, while reaffirming Copenhagen's sovereignty over it. At a signing ceremony at the UN General Assembly in New York, US President Donald Trump said "we will immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations". Danish PM Mette Frederiksen said the deal was "good for the US, Denmark and Greenland" and also for Europe and Nato, while Greenland's PM Jens-Frederik Nielsen said it was a "win-win-win". The three leaders then inked the deal, seemingly ending more than a year of tension over the Arctic territory. Trump had threatened to "take" the semi-autonomous Arctic territory over what he said were national security concerns, citing its strategic defence location and its mineral wealth. His rhetoric prompted outcry from Greenlanders, Danes and European leaders who issued a joint statement saying his words "undermine transatlantic relations and risk a dangerous downward spiral". The deal signed on Tuesday amends and updates a 1951 defence agreement between Denmark and the US. The new agreement says the US "shall be allowed to establish an additional Defence Area at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig" - referring to locations in Greenland's south and east. Narsarsuaq has deep-water access and a large runway which US military engineers were surveying last week, according to Danish media. The Mestersvig outpost is remote, far less developed, and used by a Danish naval dog sled unit. The "modalities and technical details" of the bases are yet to be confirmed, and according to the deal, must be mutually agreed by all parties. Washington currently operates its Pituffik Space Base in Greenland's north-west, and the new deal allows the US to "modernise and expand its activities" there. It also says that "no state that is not a member of Nato shall be allowed to establish its own manned or unmanned military installations in Greenland nor shall they be allowed a persistent presence of military forces in Greenland". Speaking at the signing ceremony, Trump said: "We going to have a tremendous relationship, a secure relationship." "This is tremendous for Europe and for the United States, for everybody, and for Greenland it's going to be incredible." Meanwhile, Frederiksen described the signing of the deal as a "milestone in our long-standing co-operation". "Seventy-five years ago we entered into an agreement about the defence of Greenland. Today, we're signing an even bigger and better agreement - a deal that can last forever." The Danish prime minister stressed that the agreement "respects sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark, as well as Greenland's right to self-determination". Jens-Frederik Nielsen said that "for Greenland, it is not only an agreement about us, it is [an] agreement with us. "It takes into account the people of Greenland, our rights, our livelihoods and the development of our country. "Greenland matters for North American security and for transatlantic security," he said, adding that the Nato had a key role to play in the North Atlantic in a changing security situation. The agreement also confirmed Greenland would remain in Nato if it were to gain independence from Denmark. The 1951 agreement already allowed the US to send as many troops as it wanted to Greenland. Washington already has more than 100 military personnel permanently stationed at its Pituffik base. Trump had tried for months to purchase or annex Greenland, arguing that it was vulnerable to adversaries, including Russia and China. He argued the Arctic island was an essential piece of his plan to build a futuristic "Golden Dome" defence system to protect the US against missile attacks. However the deal only mentions the project once, and contains no concrete proposal. The island has vast - and largely untapped - reserves of rare earth minerals, many of which are crucial for technologies including mobile phones and electric vehicles. Trump said last week that the new deal came with "no cost to the United States". A Nato spokesperson said shortly afterwards that the military alliance welcomed the deal, which would "help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region". title: Banned British player's £15m lawsuit against WTA dismissed
description: British player Tara Moore's legal bid for £15m in damages over a doping case which led to her being banned for four years is dismissed.
body: Tara Moore will be banned from playing until the start of the 2028 season British doubles player Tara Moore's legal bid for £15m ($20m) in damages from the Women's Tennis Association - over a doping case which led to her being banned for four years - has been dismissed by a United States court. Moore, 34, argued the WTA - the governing body of the women's tour - failed to warn players about the risk of eating contaminated meat at a tournament held in Colombia. But the United States District Court in New York has dismissed Moore's motion and directed to "close this matter". Moore, who has always denied intentionally doping, told BBC Sport after the ruling that the case has been a "nightmare". "It just shows how broken the anti-doping system is in tennis," Moore said. Keothavong 'can't fault' GB after BJK Cup loss to Czechs GB dominate Ecuador to reach Davis Cup Finals In April 2022, Moore tested positive for nandrolone and boldenone at a WTA 250 event in Bogota, with an independent tribunal ruling in December 2023 that contaminated meat was the source. Moore, who was Britain's leading women's doubles player at the time of the failed test, was found to bear "no fault or negligence", but the International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA) appealed against the decision. Last year, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) ruled in favour of the ITIA and Moore was banned until 2028. Moore then initiated proceedings with the American Arbitration Association, in which she claimed the WTA's "failure to warn against eating meat in Colombia was a direct cause of her positive test result and the harm that followed". The arbitrator supported the ruling made by Cas and dismissed the case against the WTA. In response, Moore filed a motion against the decision at the United States District Court in New York. Moore, who was ranked a career-high 77th in the world in 2022, claimed she was denied a fair hearing by the arbitrator. The motion detailed how Moore was seeking "no less than $20m in compensatory damages" after claiming the WTA "stayed silent in the face of a known and specific danger and then shifted the blame for its own negligence" to the player. On Friday, United States district judge Andrew Carter found Moore's challenge was "not justified" on a legal basis. The WTA and ITIA have been approached for comment.
