title: Plot targeting Manchester's Jewish community disrupted, say police
description: Two men were arrested in Manchester on Sunday, say counter-terror police.
body: Two suspects were detained in Manchester city centre on Sunday, police said Two men have been arrested over a suspected terrorist plot to target the Jewish community in Manchester ahead of Yom Kippur. The men, both in their 30s, were arrested on Sunday on the eve of Yom Kippur -considered to be the holiest day in the Jewish calendar, when thousands of British Jews were in synagogues already guarded with a heavy security and police presence. The men were detained on suspicion of offences under Section 41 of the Terrorism Act 2000, according to the Metropolitan Police, which is leading the investigation. Sources have told the BBC the suspected plot was "fairly imminent" and in the later stages of planning. Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans said police were aware the news would cause "further concern" to the Jewish community "especially given the significant High Holy day period". The two suspects remain in police custody after being taken to a London police station for questioning. Police said the investigation related to a "suspected terrorist plot to target the Jewish community in the Manchester area". "This has been a long-running proactive investigation which has led to the disruption of what we believe to be a plot to target the Jewish community in the Manchester area," said Evans. "Counter-terrorism policing (CTP) continue to focus our efforts on identifying and disrupting those who wish to cause harm in our communities. "Importantly, we do not believe there to be any ongoing threat to the public in relation to this matter, but as ever, we would ask that people remain vigilant and contact police with any concerns." Police went to a block of flats on Epworth Street in Liverpool following Sunday's arrests The two suspects were arrested on Newton Street in the Northern Quarter area of Manchester at 14:45 BST. Detectives have obtained warrants of further detention for both men, meaning they can remain in police custody until 27 September. Police confirmed searches at properties on Epworth Street in Liverpool and Lancaster Road in Salford had now been completed. Evans, who is the senior national co-ordinator for CTP, said: "We are acutely aware this news will cause further concern to the Jewish community, as well as the wider public, especially given the significant High Holy day period. "I want to reassure them we are working incredibly closely with colleagues in Greater Manchester Police and partners to ensure we're doing everything we can to keep them and the wider public safe. "And more broadly across the country, CTP is working with local police forces to provide protective security support and advice for areas with Jewish communities, and particularly during the High Holy Day period." Police have arrested two men, both in their 30s A spokesperson for the Community Security Trust, which coordinates security for Jewish communities in the UK, said the suspected plot was "utterly chilling coming so close to the anniversary of the terrorist attack at Heaton Park Synagogue last year". They added: "[This] is another reminder of the serious terrorist threat facing Jewish communities in this current time." title: Earl Spencer should pull Diana book from shelves, Piers Morgan says
description: The BBC understands the book's publisher, Penguin, will be amending the inaccuracy in future editions of the book.
body: This video can not be played Piers Morgan has called for Earl Spencer's book about Princess Diana to be pulled from the shelves over a factual error. Earl Spencer, Princess Diana's brother, apologised to Morgan for incorrectly describing him in the memoir as the editor of the Daily Mirror when the Mirror Group published "highly intrusive photographs of Princess Diana at the gym" in 1993. Speaking to the BBC, Morgan said he accepted the apology but that his lawyers would be "laying out that we want the offending pages to be removed from this book. And if that means they pulp the first edition, so be it". The BBC understands Penguin, the publishers of Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, will be amending this one point in future editions of the book. The photographs of Princess Diana mentioned in relation to Morgan in Earl Spencer's book were published by the Sunday Mirror on 7 November 1993. At the time, Morgan was working at The Sun and did not join the Mirror as its editor until 1995. Earl Spencer admitted "his assumption was incorrect" and "apologises to Mr Morgan for this error", a statement said. On his YouTube show, Piers Morgan Uncensored, Morgan read out a section of the book, in which Earl Spencer wrote: "They realised they were unable to be rude to the brother of the much-mourned princess… "The only one who sounded surly, as opposed to merely confused or embarrassed, was Piers Morgan of the Mirror, who snarled with annoyance before he hung up. "I assumed Morgan must be feeling particular guilt because, four years earlier, he and his Sunday Mirror counterpart had published photographs taken with hidden cameras by a gym owner. They were of Diana working out in a leotard. "This was such an intolerable invasion of her privacy that Diana instructed lawyers to sue the Mirror Group and to block further use of the images." A spokesperson for Princess Diana's brother said in a statement that "Earl Spencer's account of his conversation with Piers Morgan is accurate. Mr Morgan was surly and annoyed when Earl Spencer called personally to tell him that he was not welcome at his sister's funeral." The statement admitted the factual error, and said that "as an historian, accuracy is important to Earl Spencer. He therefore wishes to clarify that his assumption was incorrect. Earl Spencer apologises to Mr Morgan for this error." Speaking to the BBC, Morgan said: "He's a historian. He should want it removed from the shelves. Why, if you're doing this for historical record, would you want such a completely untrue series of claims over several pages about a public figure to still be in that book. "Now you've admitted it's untrue and apologised. He should pull the book." In a post on social media on Tuesday, Morgan said he was "pursuing legal action against him and his publisher Penguin to have the lies removed, and damages paid to the King's Trust". Key takeaways from BBC interview as Earl Spencer defends claims about King What we found in Earl Spencer's controversial Diana memoir Diana book row casts shadow over Prince Harry's events Swan Song, which contains a string of allegations including that King Charles said "we'll forget her soon enough" in the days after her death, has led to a war of words between the Earl and Buckingham Palace. The book claims the King, who was then the Prince of Wales, said "we'll forget her soon enough" during an argument over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in Princess Diana's funeral procession. In a strongly worded response, Buckingham Palace said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss". Separately on Tuesday, The Telegraph reported that Prince Harry is in talks to make a documentary about his mother, Diana. Earl Spencer's book also alludes to a "nephew" who wanted him to be in a documentary about Diana, which will further raise speculation about Harry's plans for the 30th anniversary of his mother's death next year. BBC News understands Prince Harry has discussed a number of possible projects to mark the anniversary and is still considering the most meaningful way to honour her legacy. title: Cyclist who dressed as man to avoid Taliban wins silver medal
description: Afghan cyclist Fariba Hashimi wins silver in the women's road race at the Asian Games, having fled oppression in her home country to pursue a sporting dream.
body: Hashimi fled Afghanistan in 2021 A female cyclist from Afghanistan who previously disguised herself as a man when chasing a career in the sport has won a silver medal at the Asian Games. Fariba Hashimi fled her country after the Taliban returned to power in 2021. She says she trained in disguise out of necessity before then in an effort to avoid being attacked, in a country where women's rights are heavily restricted. She earned her medal in the women's road race near Nagoya in Japan on Tuesday. The 23-year-old's achievement follows her seventh-place finish in the women's individual time trial on Sunday. Describing her medal as "something special", Hashimi hopes it can inspire other women in Afghanistan to follow their dreams. "I was born inside a country where the women who dream are getting attacked, and I'm really happy that I have fought against that," she said. "I hope that the next generation will come here and represent their country without any fear." Banned from football at home, Afghan women's team reunite 8,000 miles away King meets women's cricket team that is not allowed to exist Hashimi followed her sister Yulduz, also an international cyclist, into the sport at the age of 15, despite danger in their home province of Faryab. "I always dressed as a man to go to training, wearing two or three different masks so ‌people ⁠would not recognise or attack me," Hashimi previously told Reuters., external Hashimi said she would have to avoid stones being thrown at her whilst riding her bike. Hashimi now lives and trains in Italy thanks to help from the Italian former world champion Alessandra Cappellotto. Looking back at life in Afghanistan, Hashimi said the Taliban "took away our freedom". "This silver medal can show a lot of resilience from Afghan women, and I'm really happy," she said. "I'm not alone, I know that behind me millions of women, from many countries, have the same dream and they are standing with me." Hashimi and her sister competed at the 2024 Paris Olympics and are now setting their sights on the 2028 Los Angeles Games. "I never want to give up," Hashimi said, "and hopefully we can see [what can happen] again in Los Angeles." title: Top South African policeman charged with sexual offences
description: Shadrack Sibiya, who has made no comment, is alleged to have groomed a 16-year-old and raped an 18-year-old.
body: Lt Gen Shadrack Sibiya, seen here giving evidence at an inquiry into police corruption, made no comment in court One of South Africa's highest ranking police officers has been charged with sexual offences at a brief appearance at a court north-west of Johannesburg. The charges relate to allegations that Lt Gen Shadrack Sibiya sexually groomed a 16-year-old girl and raped an 18-year-old woman. He is also facing a charge of trafficking, which could mean that others may be arrested in relation to this case. The suspended deputy police commissioner, who was detained on Monday, has made no comment. The 59-year-old is due to appear in court again on 29 September for a bail application. Prosecutors are expected to oppose bail. The state has also requested that the court change the prison where Sibiya will be held in the meantime as there are indications of a potential escape plan, national broadcaster SABC is reporting. The case comes as the police service is in the spotlight at a major public inquiry over allegations of corruption and collusion with criminals. The inquiry, known as the Madlanga Commission, began last September and has heard accusations that Sibiya received a gift of 20 impalas from an alleged criminal kingpin in exchange for a police contract. title: Reform UK MSPs jeered as they walk out of Scottish independence debate at Holyrood
description: The party's leader in Scotland, Malcolm Offord, describes the debate as an insult and a waste of time.
body: This video can not be played Reform UK Scotland leader Malcolm Offord leads his party's MSPs out of the chamber Reform MSPs have walked out of the Holyrood chamber in protest against a debate about Scottish independence. The party's Scottish leader Malcolm Offord, who had tried to have the debate cancelled because it related to non-devolved matters, described it as an insult and a waste of time. He then led his MSPs out of the chamber, to jeers from the rest of the parliament. It came after First Minister John Swinney tabled a non-binding motion asserting Scotland's right to decide its constitutional future - which passed with support from Labour and the Greens. Look back at the debate on Scotland's right to decide on independence Reform MSPs storm out of Scottish independence debate at Holyrood Scotland has right to decide constitutional future, new Scottish Labour leader says Offord told MSPs: "This debate is an insult to the Scottish electorate who expect politicians to deal with serious issues in their communities." Announcing that he would withdraw his amendment and leave the chamber, Offord said: "We did not come into this parliament to waste our time on vanity projects." Scottish Greens co-leader Ross Greer quipped that he hoped a nearby pub had extra staff on this afternoon, adding: "They may be busy." Presiding Officer Kenneth Gibson described Reform's "antics" as "a gross discourtesy to all members of the chamber". Earlier, Swinney told parliament that his motion was a "vital question to debate". title: Davey promises tax cuts for millions if UK rejoins EU single market
description: The Lib Dem leader vows to raise tax thresholds if he becomes PM, in a speech to his party conference.
body: The Liberal Democrats will fight the next general election on a promise to cut taxes for millions of workers, Sir Ed Davey has said in a speech to his party conference. The Lib Dem leader said that if he gained power, he would raise the annual tax-free personal allowance to £15,000. He would also raise the 40p income tax threshold from £50,270 to £56,000, in a £17bn package funded by the economic boost he says would come from the UK rejoining the EU single market and customs union. He claimed the plan would mean a £680 cut for "most taxpayers" but it would not come into full effect until the fifth year of a Lib Dem government - potentially up to eight years away. The announcement was greeted with sustained applause by Lib Dem MPs and activists in the Brighton conference centre. The £12,570 income tax allowance was frozen by the Conservatives in 2021, resulting in more people being dragged into paying the tax, and Labour has so far resisted calls from trade unions and some of its MPs to unfreeze it. The Lib Dems said they would raise the threshold to £15,000 a year, and increase the starting point for paying employee National Insurance (NI) to the same level. At their conference earlier this month, Reform UK promised to increase the income tax personal allowance to £15,000 within 100 days if they won power. Sir Ed told the Lib Dem faithful "the difference between us and Reform" is that "their tax cut is paid for through cruelty." He said "Reform's figures show they'd pay for it by ripping £22bn of crucial support away from disabled people." Explaining his pledge to raise the 40p income tax threshold, Sir Ed argued that more and more people were being dragged into a tax bracket that had originally been intended for higher earners. "A tax band designed for stockbrokers is now holding back teachers and nurses" he said, adding: "That's not fair, it's not right." Under the Lib Dem plan, based on research by think tank Frontier Economics, external, the economic boost from rejoining the single market would allow the party to spend £17bn on tax cuts by the end of the next Parliament. The party says it would unfreeze personal allowances in the second year of a Lib Dem government, allowing them to rise with inflation, before bringing in big tax cuts in year five when the economic benefits of closer trading with the EU had kicked in. However, the move would depend on the party being able to negotiate a closer trading arrangement with the EU in just 12 months. Stuart Adam, of the Institute for Fiscal Studies think tank, told BBC Verify the Lib Dem package would cost "much more" than the £17bn quoted by the party. Reform has estimated that its policy, to raise the starting threshold to £15,000 just for income tax, would cost £21bn by the fifth year. The Lib Dems say their policy would be funded by an extra £27bn from its plans for a "growth and defence pact" with the EU. Sir Ed has been under pressure this week to set out bolder policies, with his party languishing in fourth or fifth place in national opinion polls. He began his speech with a sombre and punchy attack on Reform UK leader Nigel Farage. He stopped short of calling Reform fascists, but drew a link between the fascists in Britain in the 1930s with what he called "thugs, in black shirts and balaclavas" in reference to the protests in Dover and Portsmouth in recent weeks. "This is a far-right movement that is given oxygen, and heat, and fuel by politicians and parties who claim to be serious contenders to lead our country," said the Lib Dem leader. The solution, he said, was "community politics" that he argued was the hallmark of the Lib Dems. "It will take more than a manifesto. It will take a movement, rooted in decency, fairness and community. British values. Liberal values," he said. Repositioning the Lib Dems as a tax cutting party is aimed at appealing to voters they are targeting in traditional Tory heartlands. And Sir Ed used his speech to attack Tory leader Kemi Badenoch over her policy shifts on climate change and human rights law. "Millions of decent, moderate Conservative voters are getting her message, and they're turning away – increasingly, to us," he told the audience in Brighton. He took a swipe at Prime Minister Andy Burnham for failing to commit to rejoining the EU single market, something the Lib Dems say they would do in their first year in government. Lib Dem sources refused to say whether the income tax plan would be a condition of joining a coalition government with Labour or another party, saying the party's aim was to get as many MPs as possible. Sir Ed has ruled out a coalition with Reform UK, and dismissed suggestions he could do a deal with the Conservatives, as his party did in 2010. The Lib Dem leader also addressed the potential threat posed by AI in his speech, saying that "handled badly, it concentrates more power in fewer hands than at any point in human history." He said Burnham's AI partnership with US president Donald Trump "doesn't come close to meeting the scale of this threat" and called for "a global treaty to press pause on super-intelligent AI now". He proposed "a new International AI Safety Agency - like we have for nuclear - to stop anyone from developing this technology recklessly." title: 'We screwed up': Doordash admits underpaying New York workers
description: The food delivery giant will pay a $131.5m settlement following a city probe into wage violations.
body: DoorDash has agreed to pay a $131.5m (£99m) settlement to New York City regulators after the food delivery giant admitted failing to compensate thousands of workers correctly or on time. "Simply put, we screwed up," DoorDash said. "Our mistakes meant some Dashers were underpaid or paid late." The agreement with the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection follows a city investigation into wage violations, with a significant share of the payout addressing how DoorDash calculates compensation for the time delivery drivers spend waiting for orders. The settlement marks another chapter in an ongoing battle between so-called gig economy platforms and municipal leaders. The likes of Uber Eats and Grubhub have repeatedly clashed with city officials over tipping laws, minimum wages and data-sharing requirements. The majority of DoorDash's settlement - $83m - is to resolve a disagreement over how to calculate pay for the time workers spend online between deliveries. Pay for idle time between orders is a major industry flashpoint. Traditionally, apps only paid drivers during active deliveries but New York's rules require compensation for all time logged into the app. San Francisco-based DoorDash blamed "complex" changes to the minimum wage in New York state introduced in 2023. Under the landmark minimum pay standard for app-based delivery workers, wages differ depending on the county, tipping and how many people work for the employer. DoorDash also cited technical glitches and multi-stop delivery routes for causing the firm to underpay workers or delay wages. The company said: "While these mistakes weren't intentional, that doesn't make them okay." DoorDash said local workers earn roughly $30 per active hour on average. It said it has now patched the software bugs responsible for the mistakes. The business said the errors hit roughly 264,000 workers, though it insisted the issues affected under 1% of overall local transactions. Systemic errors caused around $6.6m wages to never reach workers at all, and another $5.7m arrived days or weeks late. title: 'Looksmaxxing' influencer Clavicular charged with rape in Massachusetts
description: Authorities allege Braden Peters drugged a woman before assaulting her in May. He denies the charges.
body: "Clavicular", whose real name is Braden Peters, has become a key figure in the "looksmaxxing" community. The online influencer Clavicular, whose real name is Braden Peters, has been charged with rape, providing liquor to a person under the legal US drinking age, and drugging someone for sexual intercourse, court records show. The alleged offences occurred in May 2025, according to the charges filed in the state of Massachusetts. A spokesperson for Peters told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, that the charges are "bogus" and that the influencer has yet to be served with an arrest warrant. Peters is facing a civil lawsuit filed by a woman earlier this year who alleged that he had served her several rounds of vodka and had nonconsensual sex with her at his parents' home on Cape Cod. The woman said she was a minor at the time and also accused him of injecting her with a non-FDA approved substance. He denied the allegations. The criminal charges filed this month do not identify the alleged victim. Clavicular is known for his role in an online movement called "looksmaxxing", centred on maximising physical attractiveness. His online account has amassed a large following, where he streams the lengths to which he goes to achieve physical perfection. Peters has spoken openly about methods such as "bone smashing", which involves hitting his jawline with a hammer or other objects to get a more chiselled look. Despite courting controversies for his "looksmaxxing" protocols, Peters has translated his online fame into broader cultural recognition. In June, he walked the runway at a fashion week show in Paris. Peters has also had brushes with the law. He was charged earlier this year in Florida after he filmed himself shooting at what appeared to be a dead alligator, for which he pleaded no contest to unlawfully discharging a firearm in public. In March, he was arrested in Florida on suspicion of battery charges after authorities suspected him of instigating a fight between two women. Authorities later said in July they did not intend to file charges. After the Massachusetts charges became public, Peters posted a video on X that appeared to show his accuser, as well as a handwritten note. "Happens to all successful young men, people try to come for your money," he wrote. title: 'I have never felt heat like that' - a survivor on watching 33 cellmates die in Nigeria
description: The BBC goes inside the prison where prisoners were trapped in stifling, cramped conditions.
body: Usman Muhammad survived but 33 others died in the cell and four others died later in hospital Usman Muhammad pauses by the entrance to a tiny Nigerian prison cell and leans his forehead against the wall unable to speak. The day before he had been trapped inside the stifling room, measuring roughly 6m (19.7ft) by 3m (9.8ft), with more than 50 other prisoners. Thirty-three of his cellmates died in the cramped conditions in the prison in Minna, the capital of Nigeria's Niger state - and four died later in hospital. The mass deaths caused an outcry and sparked protests, including attacks on public buildings, as relatives and locals demanded answers. Federal officials had initially blamed the deaths on a diphtheria outbreak but exactly what happened is now the subject of an investigation. "I have never felt heat like that in my life. When we touched each other's bodies, it felt like fire burning," Muhammad tells the BBC once he is able to gather his thoughts. When he was locked inside, there was standing room only amid humidity levels of more than 90%, which in some circumstances can be dangerous to human health as it prevents the natural cooling mechanism of sweat drying on the skin. The temperature outside was above 25C and the only ventilation came from a small, high-up window. "One of us fainted and we started knocking at the [cell] door. When [a guard] came we asked him for water. He looked at the guy that fainted and closed the door. That's how they started dying one after the other," Muhammad says. Like the others who had been detained, the young man, in his 20s, is an artisanal miner, eking out a living searching for precious metals at mine sites. The federal government has tried to crack down on this alleged illegal activity as it says it costs the country revenue, damages the environment and can be linked to wider criminal activity. Officers from the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) had arrested a large group of miners near Minna last Tuesday and Wednesday. The prisoners were held at its detention centre in the city, but the NSCDC has not shared either the names or the number of those it was holding. This video can not be played The BBC's Madina Maishanu shows the conditions inside the cell where so many died As the hours inside the cell wore on, the heat and dehydration became unbearable and Muhammad says some of the detainees began drinking their own urine and collecting sweat from their bodies to try to stay alive. He describes seeing people in distress and struggling to breathe. "People were calling for help, some were already very weak." But no-one came to help, he and others allege. "While in the cell, we were shouting and telling them that people were dying," another survivor Adamu Isah told the Reuters news agency. "We tried to break down the door when they refused to open it… At one point, a security officer came to the door. "We were shouting and telling him that people were dying, but he said it wasn't his problem if people died." Finally, on Thursday, the cell door was opened and the guards saw the dead bodies. The NSCDC has not directly responded to the accusations of neglect and maltreatment but has said that 24 of its personnel are now in custody in connection with the deaths, including its suspended Niger state commandant Suberu Aniviye. "The people who were killed are not flies. How can this go unlooked? We will get to the bottom of this," Niger state Governor Umaru Bago told the BBC. The only air coming into the cell was from a small window high up on the wall As the organisation involved is a federal body rather than a force under his jurisdiction, such as the police, the governor is unable to exert direct influence but he welcomes the investigation that has been ordered by the government in capital, Abuja. A 10-member committee has now been set-up to determine exactly what happened. It has two weeks to establish the causes of the deaths and identify who was responsible and can recommend legal action against anyone found culpable. No officer, regardless of rank, would be protected and any attempt to obstruct the investigation would be taken seriously, Interior Minister Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo said. As he leaves the cell after talking to the BBC, Muhammad says he hopes that by speaking out he can help find justice and bring some closure to this traumatic event. title: Ella Langley's Choosin' Texas becomes longest-running number one in US chart history
description: The country smash racks up it 23rd week in the US charts, breaking a record set by Mariah Carey.
body: Ella Langley's country smash Choosin' Texas has overtaken Mariah Carey's All I Want for Christmas Is You to become the longest-running number one single in US chart history. Released last October, the bittersweet song details Langley's suspicions that her boyfriend is about to run off with another woman. It topped the US Billboard chart for the first time in February, and has now spent 23 weeks at number one., external Choosin' Texas also rose to pole position on the UK singles chart at the start of September, where it replaced Sam Fender and Olivia Dean's Rein Me In. That song had also spent 23 weeks at number one, making it the UK's longest-running chart-topper. The immovability of both songs has raised questions about stagnation in the charts, and whether streaming services are doing enough to promote new music. Langley won seven trophies at this year's Academy of Country Music Awards Langley's song was written at a writing retreat in 2024, with assistance from country star Miranda Lambert. Unexpectedly, it started with a discussion about a pet kangaroo Lambert had once owned. "She told me the story about how she got pulled over [by the police] with a kangaroo in the passenger seat and a dog in the back," Langley explained. The officer was so surprised that she didn't issue a ticket. Langley responded to Lambert, saying the cop must have known she was from Texas, given the chaos unfolding in the car. That prompted the lyric, "She's from Texas, I can tell." Over the next 30 minutes, the writers (who also included Luke Dick and Joybeth Taylor) cooked up a story about a woman in Tennessee, who realises her partner's heart still belongs to Texas... and to another girl. First previewed on stage in February 2025, Langley said she instantly knew it would become the first single from her sophomore album, Dandelion. "We loved that song, but I don't think I could ever have imagined what's happening with it right now," the singer told Billboard magazine. "Every day I wake up and it's doing something that I didn't even know was a goal I could have had. It's crazy, it's nuts." Its success helped the 27-year-old, who is actually from Alabama, sweep the Academy of Country Music Awards in May. She won in all seven categories in which she was nominated, including female artist of the year, artist songwriter of the year, and both single and song of the year, for Choosin' Texas. It is now one of only two songs to surpass 20 weeks at number one on the US charts - with the other being Mariah Carey's perennial Christmas smash All I Want for Christmas Is You. But the records for long-running hits have been tumbling ever since streaming became a mainstream phenomenon. For 23 years, Carey's own One Sweet Day, a duet with Boyz II Men, held the title, notching up 16 weeks at number one. Daddy Yankee and Luis Fonsi's Despacito remix, featuring Justin Bieber, tied the record in 2017; then Lil Nas X's Old Town Road surpassed it the following year, eventually spending 19 weeks at the top. All I Want for Christmas Is You eventually overtook that, thanks to its habit of returning to the charts every December. But critics say that streaming services are increasingly encouraging listeners to play the same playlists of familiar songs over and over again, creating a bottleneck that makes it harder for new music to break through. In 2022, a report by the UK's Competition and Markets Authority, external found that more than 60% of streams were of music recorded by only the top 0.4% of artists. title: I was close to joining Liverpool in 2016 - Mbappe
description: Kylian Mbappe says his mum was a "big fan" of Jurgen Klopp and wanted her son to move to Merseyside.
body: Kylian Mbappe (right) is France's all-time leading goalscorer Kylian Mbappe has revealed how "close" he came to joining Liverpool in 2016, saying he went against the advice of his mother who "fell in love" with Anfield. The France and Real Madrid striker said the Reds tried to sign him at 18, while he was playing for Monaco in Ligue 1. Former Liverpool boss Jurgen Klopp said the club laid on a private jet and food for Mbappe and his family in an attempt to sign him, before he eventually joined Paris St-Germain. Speaking to the Athletic, Mbappe said his mum was a "big fan" of Klopp and wanted her son to move to Merseyside. "I was close to [joining] Liverpool. The favourite destination for my mum was Liverpool. She wanted me to go there," he said. "I didn't listen because I wanted to play in my city, Paris. I didn't want to leave my country before I was someone. "But yes, my mum was always saying, 'Liverpool - you're going to be there, playing at Anfield, it's going to be insane for you'." Mbappe, now 27, said his mother went out to Liverpool for the "first step" of the negotiation. "She went to the city, the stadium, she met the people. She was like, 'it's a wonderful club, everybody's so kind, it's a family club, a big club', said Mbappe. "She went to Anfield and fell in love with it. She watched a few games alone, to feel the atmosphere, because she wanted to imagine me in this stadium." Klopp, who spoke about the possible move on Magenta TV as a pundit at the 2026 World Cup, explained how a flight was taken from Blackpool to Nice in France, where "the entire Mbappe family boarded a private jet with five rooms or something". "We really went all out. Then we flew around in a circle, talked with the family, ate good food," Klopp said. He said they had not wanted to be seen having talks - but the meeting proved fruitless. "We flew in a circle. It was fantastic. And then he went to Paris," Klopp added. "It's a funny story," said Mbappe. "But in the end, I took the decision to go to PSG because for me, born and raised in Paris, there was no better feeling than to show I could be a star in my hometown." Mbappe later joined PSG on loan, in a deal including an option for the move to become permanent for 180m euros (£165.7m). He went on to spend seven years in Paris, becoming the club's record scorer before leaving for Real Madrid in 2024. title: Watch: Trump floats rebranding artificial intelligence as super intelligence
description: "The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said told the UN. "It's not fake, it's actually amazing."
body: This video can not be played Donald Trump has a penchant for branding and in his speech he gave artificial intelligence a new name: super intelligence. "The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said. "It's not fake, it's actually amazing. But we have to be careful," he added. "Welcome to the new world of super intelligence - SI," he went on to say. Trump has previously argued that whoever wins AI, wins, and he is firmly against regulation. But that puts him at odds with many here. The question is whether the slow pace of diplomacy can keep up with AI’s rapid development. title: Juvenile murder sentence rule doesn't breach human rights, says Supreme Court
description: The top court rejects an appeal for a minimum term review from a man who was sentenced after turning 18.
body: Jesse Quaye (left) and Ayomindy Bile were sentenced to serve a minimum of 15 years for murder Scrapping a law that could have shortened a man's prison sentence because he committed murder as a child was not a breach of human rights, the Supreme Court has ruled. Jesse Quaye, then 17, and Ayomindy Bile, then 15, murdered Connor Barrett in Hemsby, Norfolk in 2014 - leading to both being jailed for life with a minimum term of 15 years. But a later change in the law meant Quaye could not ask for a review of that minimum term, because he had turned 18 before he was sentenced. The Supreme Court's decision to reject his appeal ends the legal battle over juvenile life sentences in the UK courts - but the case could potentially be reopened at the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg. Connor Barrett, 21, died after he was attacked by Quaye and Ayomindy Bile when they turned up uninvited at a birthday party to assault another attendee. Their trial heard that the pair had brought knives with them and that their victim died in front of his family, including his younger brother. After their conviction, Quaye, by then 18, and Bile were jailed at Her Majesty's pleasure - the legal term for a life sentence given to child killers. Under long-standing legal principles, a juvenile who is sentenced to murder can ask for their minimum term to be reconsidered once they have served half of that time. Connor Barrett was killed while defending another party-goer That policy and other juvenile sentencing laws take into account evidence that some serious offenders rehabilitate in their 20s as they mature. However, Parliament voted in 2022 to block juvenile killers from seeking a review if they had been sentenced after they had turned 18. The new law meant Quaye could no longer ask for a review of his minimum term and the 29-year-old remains in prison, prompting him to mount a legal challenge. Lawyers for Quaye had argued that his treatment amounted to a breach of the ban on arbitrary detention, retrospective punishment and discrimination based on age in the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR). In 2024, two High Court judges ruled that Quaye's treatment breached those safeguards - but the Court of Appeal later reversed that decision. In their ruling on Tuesday, the five Supreme Court judges said the law had long differentiated between child and adult killers, and that the trial judge had correctly and fairly decided on a minimum term. They concluded the ECHR did not compel the UK government to consider reducing Quaye's minimum term. The Supreme Court resolves disputes over what the law means in the UK "The judgement is one of social policy, involving questions of moral and political judgement, which is the province of the legislature [Parliament]," they said. "Moreover, drawing a bright line distinction based on being 18 at the date of conviction or sentence is a recognised feature of sentencing and the criminal justice system." Simon Creighton, a leading sentencing law solicitor who represented Quaye, said the case had raised two basic questions of fairness. "When people receive these particular sentences, they were told that the sentence meant they would have a review," he said. "To be told a decade later that was no longer the case is one aspect of the unfairness. "We all know about the lengthy delays in the criminal courts at the moment. And it really is purely arbitrary whether your case is going to come up for trial before you've turned 18 or not. "To make a decision about what the sentence means, based on something that's so arbitrary and out of people's control, feels like a major injustice." Creighton said there was a "strong prospect" of asking the European court in Strasbourg to review the outcome. In general, such cases can take years to be heard and the court only considers appeals when it thinks the courts in the UK have not fully resolved human rights questions. title: Inquest opens into 'Putney Pusher' suspect's death
description: Nicholas Brandram, who was suspected of pushing a woman into the path of a bus, was found dead last week.
body: Nicholas Brandram was under police investigation over the 2017 incident A man suspected of knocking a woman into the path of a bus on Putney Bridge was found dead by his brother-in-law after missing a family meal, his inquest has heard. Nicholas Brandram, 44, was discovered at his home in Chiswick on 15 September, West London Coroner's Court was told. He had been arrested in June on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm in relation to the incident of May 2017, when a woman was shoved into the road by a jogger. His family say he was not involved. Opening and adjourning the inquest, West London coroner Melanie Lee said she had been told of a referral to the Independent Office of Police Conduct and was suspending the inquest pending the outcome of its inquiry. The coroner offered her "sincere condolences" to Brandram's family, in particular his sisters Sophie Voelcker and Alexia Hicks who were at the hearing in Fulham. The court heard that Brandram's brother-in-law used a spare key provided by a neighbour and found the married banker in an upstairs room. Paramedics attended but despite their resuscitation efforts he was pronounced dead just before 21:00 BST. The police did not view his death as suspicious or as having any third-party involvement, the inquest was told. Brandram's family have insisted he was not the jogger, referred to as the Putney Pusher in media coverage at the time, and blame the Met Police's handling of the case for his death. They said last week that he "took his own life after months of immense pressure caused by a Metropolitan Police investigation", and there was no forensic evidence linking the banker to the incident. The force said it recognised the "strain that being subject to a police investigation" could cause. title: Autopsy shows Hayden Panettiere died from a drug overdose
description: The death of the child star - who had fentanyl, Xanax, a muscle relaxant and antipsychotic medication in her system - was ruled an accident.
body: Child star Hayden Panettiere died from the toxic effects of fentanyl, Xanax and several other drugs in her system, according to an autopsy completed by the Greenville County Coroner's Office in South Carolina. The coroner's office said Panettiere's death was an accident and that no signs of trauma were discovered that would have contributed to her death. Panettiere died last month at the age of 36 after she was found unresponsive at a South Carolina residence. The star of US TV shows Heroes and Nashville had spoken openly about her struggles with substance abuse. The coroner's office also found methocarbamol - a prescription muscle relaxant - and quetiapine - an antipsychotic medication that is used to treat certain mental health conditions. Drugs at their fingertips, intense pressure: Why child stars fall into addiction Fentanyl is a synthetic opioid that has killed hundreds of thousands of Americans over the past five years alone. The coroner's office said emergency responders had "initiated advanced cardiac life support measures; however, resuscitation efforts were unsuccessful". The US Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) was reportedly joining the local police department's investigation into the child star's death. Panettiere's ex-boyfriend, Brian Hickerson - who has admitted to abusing her - and his brother Zack were with Panettiere when emergency services came, according to a police report from the day she died. Just months before her death, Panettiere published a memoir where she discussed at length her issues with addiction and postpartum depression. title: GB out of BJK Cup as Kartal & Boulter beaten by Czechs
description: Sonay Kartal and Katie Boulter lose their singles matches as Great Britain are beaten by a strong Czech Republic side in the Billie Jean King Cup quarter-finals.
body: Katie Boulter was Britain's highest ranked player as the world number 54 Sonay Kartal and Katie Boulter lost their respective singles matches as Great Britain were beaten by a strong Czech Republic side in the Billie Jean King Cup quarter-finals. Anne Keothavong's team headed into the tie as underdogs, with all five Czech players placed higher in the singles rankings than any of the British squad. Sonay Kartal produced a gritty performance as she returned to tennis after six months out with a lower back injury, but fell to a narrow 7-6 (7-2) 4-6 6-4 defeat in a marathon three-hour encounter with Marie Bouzkova. Boulter could do little to get Britain back into the best-of-three tie as she was outplayed 6-2 7-6 (7-3) by Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova. It was a second successive loss for Boulter at the hands of a Czech player, coming just three weeks after a 58-minute demolition by Karolina Muchova at the US Open. It is the first time since 2023 that Britain have failed to reach the semi-finals at the Billie Jean King Cup and their wait for a maiden title will go on for another year. The Czech Republic, who are 11-time winners of the tournament and the only team boasting two top-10 players at the Finals, will face either Kazakhstan or Spain in Friday's semi-finals. Playing her first match since retiring injured in the fourth round at Indian Wells in March, Kartal started well and struck early against world number 26 Bouzkova. However, she was broken back immediately and Bouzkova dominated the tie-break to take the opener. The Briton broke early in the second set and held on to force a decider, but her first double fault of the match handed Bouzkova a break for a 4-2 lead. Kartal delayed defeat by saving three match points and breaking back, but Bouzkova restored her lead immediately to clinch victory after exactly three hours on court to put the Czechs in front. With Noskova and Muchova - this year's Wimbledon finalists - in the Czech squad, it was always going to be a uphill battle for number one Boulter. Two double faults in the first game saw Boulter drop serve early and world number six Noskova steamrolled her way through the opening four games before wrapping up the set. Boulter improved in the second set and threatened to force a decider, but she was unable to create a single break point and Noskova took control of the tie-break to send her nation into the semi-finals. title: Four people die in Bootle house fire
description: Another person was taken to hospital following the "intense fire which spread very rapidly", says fire chief.
body: Fire crews were called to the scene at 03:45 BST after receiving a 999 call Four people have died and a fifth has been taken to hospital with burns after a house fire on Merseyside. Six fire engines were at the scene at the height of the blaze at the semi-detached property in Stone Square in Bootle, Sefton, at 03:45 BST. Eight firefighters searched the house where they discovered four people in an upstairs bedroom, showing no signs of life, Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service said. Another casualty, who was outside the property when crews arrived, was taken to hospital. Officers from Merseyside Police are also at the scene and a joint investigation with the fire service into the cause of the blaze is under way. The North West Ambulance Service's hazardous area response team also attended the scene of the fire and confirmed the four fatalities. Chief Fire Officer Nick Searle confirmed the "intense fire [had] spread very rapidly". The street was cordoned off by police and, earlier, fire officers could be seen knocking on neighbours' doors. One said: "I heard shouting in the early hours but I just thought someone was having an argument, then I came downstairs and saw all the fire engines." Emergency services remain at the scene as investigations continue Another local resident, who did not want to be named, said: "We all came out on the front and we could see smoke coming over from the houses. "The sirens woke me up and there were fire engines in the street." The fire service said the main blaze had been extinguished with crews damping down the area. The fifth casualty was outside the house when fire crews arrived Kevin Longshaw, area manager for Manchester Fire and Rescue Service, said: "This is a devastating incident, and our thoughts are very much with the family and friends of those who have lost their lives and been injured. "We will work closely with relevant colleagues to ascertain the cause of the fire, but in the immediate term, we again extend our sincere condolences to those affected by this tragic incident." title: Call of Duty's Activision to make next Halo game as Xbox cuts more jobs
description: The news comes as part of a "reset" announced by Xbox in July, with 3,600 planned job losses overall.
body: Xbox is cutting hundreds of jobs and making sweeping changes to the production of its flagship Halo franchise, as its company-wide "reset" continues. Its latest reductions, forming part of a wave of ongoing layoffs, will impact staff at the studio which currently makes Halo - with Call of Duty publisher Activision to take on development of any future games. Jez Corden of Windows Central said the change was a "dramatic move", while gaming analyst Christopher Dring said it raised questions over whether it could help revive what was once Xbox's "crown jewel". It comes as questions also mount over the future of other notable Xbox studios, including Cambridge-based game developer Ninja Theory. Xbox chief executive Asha Sharma said in July the Bafta-winning studio behind the Hellblade games would be spun off, alongside four others, amid its dramatic downsizing. But Matt Booty, chief content officer at Xbox, wrote in a blog post on Tuesday, external that attempts to find a buyer for the studio had failed - with "two separate agreements" falling through. He said Ninja Theory would now enter into consultation with employees on a proposed closure, though potential buyout talks are continuing. Of the four other affected companies, three have now returned to management, while consultation for Arcane remains "under way", Booty added. Xbox's announcement of a further 268 cut jobs comes after Sharma revealed in July that the company was "beginning the most significant restructure in Xbox history". It saw 1,600 jobs cut immediately, amid 3,600 planned losses overall. The company says it is three quarters of the way through its planned restructure. Sharma said, external at the time that the Microsoft's gaming division had not been "healthy" and while platforms like its subscription plan Game Pass had "created meaningful value", they had not grown quickly enough. In an interview with the BBC in August, she also pointed to the "crisis" in rising computing prices and hardware costs as another external pressure on the company. Ninja Theory has won several awards for its Hellblade series, including Best British Game at the BAFTA Game Awards Halo has been a hallmark of the Xbox brand since Microsoft's first entry into the console market in 2001, helping establish the firm as a major player in the industry. Xbox said on Tuesday that Halo Studios, which recently released Halo: Campaign Evolved in July, would continue to support the game's community and work on existing games, as opposed to focusing on any new release. Christopher Dring, editor-in-chief and co-founder of The Game Business, said the military sci-fi shooter was once Xbox's "crown jewel" but that hadn't been the case "for more than a decade". "Halo was once to Xbox what Mario is to Nintendo," said Corden, "but years of mismanagement have eroded that". Dring said bringing Halo under Activision's leadership "makes sense", though the company would be "mindful not to lose what makes Halo unique". "For Halo, our goal is clear: make the greatest Halo game ever, worthy of its universe and legacy, while staying true to what made players love it in the first place" said Rob Kostich, Activision's president. "We have already begun assembling a purpose-built team, unique in capability and talent, ready and excited to deliver this next chapter with the community." As well as leading any new Halo game development, Xbox said Activision's remit would expand to manage the World's Edge studio, home to the Age of Empires franchise, as well as the studio Rare and its series Sea of Thieves. The PlayStation rival also confirmed consolidations of some of its current companies - saying Elder Scroll-makers Bethesda would "expand its remit" to include Fallout New Vegas-makers Obsidian, and combining the studios behind Forza Horizon and Fable. title: Laura Anne Jones is Reform's new deputy Welsh leader
description: She fills the vacancy left by Helen Jenner becoming leader on Monday.
body: Laura Anne Jones is an MS for Sir Fynwy Torfaen Laura Anne Jones is Reform's new deputy leader in Wales, the party has announced. The post was vacated after the previous deputy Helen Jenner took the party's Senedd leadership on Tuesday. In a statement, Jones said: "We've made a fantastic start here in the Senedd, giving a voice to the voiceless and standing up for Wales' left-behind communities." Reform has said there was an election. It has not announced any rivals and has denied she was appointed. Jones was suspended from the Senedd in November 2025 after she used a racial slur to describe Chinese people in a Whatsapp chat. She apologised and denied she was racist. Jenner became party leader after her predecessor Dan Thomas quit last week, following his arrest on suspicion of assault and coercive or controlling behaviour. Thomas is on police bail pending further enquiries, and denies doing anything wrong. Reform said Jones was elected by her colleagues on Monday morning. The party did not say in its initial statement whether anyone stood against Jones. A spokesperson, asked if any other MSs were interested, said there was an election that followed group rules and that she was not appointed. Laura Anne Jones is a former Conservative who defected to Reform in the summer of 2025. At the time she was the highest profile defection the party had achieved in Wales, unveiled in a shock press conference at the Royal Welsh Show that riled her former Tory colleagues. Jones won re-election on Reform's list in Sir Fynwy Torfaen last May - she is the party's rural affairs spokesperson. Jones was suspended from the Senedd for two weeks in November 2025 after it emerged she had used a racial slur to describe Chinese people in a Whatsapp chat. She later said she was "genuinely sorry" for using the slur in August 2023 and denied she was racist. The MS also courted controversy when she said rival parties had "entertained" the idea of children self-identifying as cats. Jones was accused of misinformation but said the matter had been raised with her by parents. Jenner was elected by Reform MSs in a meeting on Monday, and was unveiled by UK party leader Nigel Farage on the Senedd steps. Farage said Jenner, who had been a member of UKIP before joining Reform's predecessor the Brexit Party, was "a determined campaigner". title: Tim Westwood charged with two more sexual offences
description: The alleged sexual offences date back to 1991 and 2004.
body: Former BBC Radio 1 and Capital Xtra DJ Tim Westwood has been charged with two more offences, the Metropolitan Police has said. The charges are an alleged indecent assault against a teenage girl aged 16 to 17 in Hammersmith and Fulham in 1991 and the alleged sexual assault of an 18-year-old woman in Wandsworth in 2004. These charges are in addition to those brought against Westwood, 68, in October 2025 relating to seven women, which include four counts of rape. Westwood has previously denied multiple sex offences, including rape and sexual assault, and pleaded not guilty to earlier charges last December. Westwood is now facing a total of 17 charges involving nine women. Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy, from the Metropolitan Police Service, said: "The women who have made reports have placed their trust in us, and we remain committed to providing them with all available support. "Independent support is also available through Rape Crisis via its 24/7 Rape and Sexual Abuse Support Line." Catherine P Baccas, deputy chief crown prosecutor in the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) London, said: "Today the Crown Prosecution Service has authorised two further charges of sexual assault and indecent assault against Tim Westwood. "Mr Westwood is already charged with nine counts of indecent assault, two counts of sexual assault and four counts of rape in relation to reported non-recent offences between 1983 and 2016 involving seven women. "These new charges, following an investigation by the Metropolitan Police, relate to separate reports of non-recent offences in 1991 and 2004 involving two additional women. "Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring these additional charges to court and that it is in the public interest to pursue further criminal proceedings. "The Crown Prosecution Service reminds everyone that criminal proceedings are active, and the defendant has the right to a fair trial." Westwood is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court at a future date in relation to the two additional charges, the Met Police said. A trial relating to the original 15 charges is scheduled to begin at Southwark Crown Court on 25 January 2027. title: Student who accidentally overdosed on paracetamol learns to walk and talk again
description: Riley Lubas took two over-the counter medicines without realising they both contained paracetamol.
body: Riley spent six weeks at King's College Hospital in London before moving back to an ICU in Newport The parents of a student who suffered organ failure and nearly died after accidentally overdosing on paracetamol have spoken of the distress it caused and said they have "no idea how it happened so quickly". Riley Lubas, 20, came down with a bad cold in March 2025 in his first year at university, and took two over-the counter medicines without realising they both contained paracetamol. After being placed on life support and enduring weeks in hospital, he went on to make a miraculous recovery, and has even relearned how to walk and talk. The Royal College of General Practitioners Cymru Wales, external advised people to always "read the label carefully" and seek advice from a GP before taking medication. Riley was studying creative media at the University of Bath when he got hit with a springtime cold which he described as feeling "pretty non-eventful". "People get freshers flu or colds all the time in first year, so I got two medicines," he said. "I didn't realise at the time that both had paracetamol in them." A paracetamol overdose can cause severe liver and kidney damage, according to the NHS, external, with early symptoms often including nausea or vomiting and stomach. Riley decided to phone for help when his stomach started hurting. Tests at Bath's Royal United Hospital discovered that his liver was struggling. His parents, Chris, 40 and Kate Lubas, 39, raced from Newport to be with their son. Chris, a company director, said doctors were initially concerned it was hepatitis, external. "Hours later, at half one in the morning, I got a call from the ICU staff at the hospital saying we had to get there immediately," he added. "All they could say at the time was they were doing everything they could." Riley's parents received a call from the ICU staff at the hospital telling them to get there immediately His parents were told Riley was heading towards liver failure, and they watched as his condition deteriorated to the point where he was delirious and hallucinating. "By 6pm that night, he was sedated and on life support and dialysis and in multiple organ failure," said Chris. "The staff there were able to finally tell us how bad it had gotten." Riley's brain fluid had left the hospital staff "concerned" and his lungs and kidneys had also stopped working. "We were so distressed and had no idea how this could have happened so quickly," Chris added. By now Riley's condition had become so bad, he was transferred to London's King's College Hospital which has a specialist ICU init. His parents were asked about his paracetamol intake, and they were able to find the two medications and work out what had happened. Chris said: "It didn't necessarily help with a solution, but it was good to know the cause at last." Riley bought the medicine as "people get freshers flu or colds all the time in the first year" While Riley waited for a liver transplant, doctors began to notice improvements in his health, despite his parents initially being told the damage could be "irreversible". "They spotted some improvement in the liver," said Chris. "We watched Riley's situation closely for a couple of days, and he continued to improve, until he was taken off dialysis and life support just a week later." Riley had to relearn how to walk and talk, spending a total of six weeks at King's College Hospital, before moving to an ICU in Newport. "We were amazed to see his improvement,' said Chris. "He'd had a tracheostomy, external, so he needed to learn how to speak again, and because of how many organs shut down, had to relearn walking too. "But just seeing him up and alive again was unbelievable." Chris said there was "no exact answer" that explains his recovery, but doctors think his health and age played a part. Riley has now recovered and is back working in a pub as a bartender. His parents have done a 31 miles (50km) hike across the Gower Peninsula to raise money for King's College ICU and raise awareness for paracetamol overdose. Riley said it was "mad how quickly it all escalated". He added: "Because I was already sick, when my stomach hurt I just assumed I'd caught a stomach bug, so I didn't notice the pain in my liver specifically. "I'm just so grateful that I was able to come out the other end alright." In the UK, an estimated 6,300 tonnes of paracetamol are sold annually The Office for National Statistics latest figures, external show there were 27 deaths registered in Wales in 2024 that mentioned any paracetamol on the death certificate. Dr. Will Mackintosh, a GP and chairman of RCGP Cymru Wales, said accidental paracetamol overdose in young people was "a fairly rare occurrence", but there was a small risk if some inadvertently takes two products containing paracetamol at the same time. Mackintosh said pressures placed on young people who are working and studying, in particular, can lead to them taking as much over the counter to "keep going when they're ill". "Particularly things like viral illnesses, while they're not serious, it's important to get enough rest as well," he added. Mackintosh said he felt rest was sometimes "downplayed" in favour of taking medicine that will get you back to normal as quickly as possible. "For a lot of these illnesses, you need some time to rest and allow them to run their course as well as taking over the counter medicine," he added. He said local community pharmacies are "very cautious" about selling large amounts of medication, so they will "often place restrictions on the amount of paracetamol that can be sold". He said GPs had also become more aware of the risk a paracetamol overdose can have on older patients who, in particular, have low body weight. "When these things happen, the symptoms can be very severe and the risks are high, so we want to minimise this to as few case

title: Who will start for England at Euro 2028? BBC Sport's predictions
description: As England prepare to face world champions Spain on Saturday, BBC Sport's experts predict who will be starting for the Three Lions at Euro 2028.
body: Who do you think will be England's starters for Euro 2028? Less than two months after Spain were celebrating their World Cup triumph, the next major tournament cycle begins. From 9 June 2028, the European Championship will be hosted by England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland - and the path to the finals starts now. England host Spain on Saturday in their Nations League opener and, while the competition doesn't offer a direct qualification route, it does provide a secondary route for teams who don't qualify automatically. Despite being co-hosts of Euro 2028, Thomas Tuchel's men are not guaranteed a spot in the tournament - with all hosts having to earn their place. But, assuming England will qualify for the tournament, who do you think will be in the side for the opener in the summer of 2028? We have asked some BBC Sport experts for their predictions and want you to pick your team using the selector at the bottom of the page. Will England boss Tuchel 'embrace the chaos'? Just a couple of changes from the World Cup. Jordan Pickford will be 34 by the time Euro 2028 starts so no problem there for goalkeeper, although James Trafford will mount a serious challenge. I would pick Trent Alexander-Arnold at right-back but I am still not convinced Tuchel trusts him even though he has handed him an England recall. On that basis I have selected Tino Livramento, if he can stay fit, although I still hope Tuchel puts doubts about Alexander-Arnold out of his mind. If Everton's Jarrad Branthwaite can steer clear of injury – if – then I think Tuchel could partner him with Marc Guehi in the centre of defence, with Nico O'Reilly staying on the left. Personal preference persuades me to pick Adam Wharton ahead of Elliot Anderson – who I do rate very highly – with Declan Rice a no-brainer. Tuchel could go either way but I believe Wharton can win that fight between now and then, despite missing out on that final squad. Of course there will be claims for Cole Palmer, Morgan Rogers and even Morgan Gibbs-White, but Jude Bellingham ended any arguments, such as they were, about his class and place in the team with a brilliant World Cup. Where would you play them? I'm banking on Harry Kane having one more major tournament in him, even though he will be pushing 35 – and let's face it, who else is there? Bukayo Saka is another certain pick in my opinion, but I believe Liverpool's Rio Ngumoha will develop as such a rate he will be an England regular by 2028, so he gets the nod on the left. This is largely the same team that was viewed as England's first choice at the World Cup, apart from Morgan Rogers (although I think it will be a close call between him and Anthony Gordon). It's a team packed with players who will all be in their peak years and at the moment, it's hard to see anyone coming out of the team in the next two years. On the bench, however, England will have some fresh options with the likes of Rio Ngumoha, Alex Scott, Lewis Miley and even Max Dowman likely to be pushing for a spot in the squad. But when you consider that England have reached a World Cup semi-final and a European Championship final in the past two years it does suggest that this group of players are close and there is nothing there to be ripped up. And the fact England would be playing on home soil has to increase their chances of finally getting the job done. I would not be surprised to see James Trafford and Dean Henderson given opportunities in goal but it may be that by the tournament it is still his experience that gives Jordan Pickford the edge. Maybe it would be different if the other two were playing for teams challenging for the major honours. I expect Tino Livramento, Lewis Hall and Ben White to be staking a claim in the full-back positions. And obviously Morgan Rogers, Cole Palmer, perhaps Morgan Gibbs-White and maybe by then Max Dowman will be close to the starting line-up. But I don't think the 11 I've named above would be too far away from the reality. When Euro 2028 kicks off on 9 June in two years' time, England captain Harry Kane will be 34 years and 317 days old and knowing his levels of desire, he will be determined to lead England for that tournament on home soil. Barring injury then I can see him still leading the line for his country and I would also back Jordan Pickford still to be in goal too. In fact if you look at the current squad then it's hard to see who would not be around as this group of players continue to grow together for England. Ezri Konsa would be the only other 30-something which is why my starting XI has a very familiar feel to it. I would back Max Dowman to be part of the England squad for 2028 but in terms of a starter my only area of uncertainty is at right-back. There have been nine different players to have started in that position since September 2024. I wouldn't rule out Archie Gray to force his way into contention. Like Nico O'Reilly I could see another midfielder adapting into that position on the right. I saw him play there as Spurs captain recently and he has the quality, temperament and leadership qualities to step up to senior international level. Starting with the goalkeeper, I think Jordan Pickford will still be the England number one but James Trafford after a couple more seasons of Premier League football will be pushing him close. It was a very tight call for Adam Wharton or Myles Lewis-Skelly in the middle of the pitch but with Tuchel still likely to be in charge I think he will go for the more physical Lewis-Skelly as his number six. Jarrad Branthwaite could be the key physical centre-back and as a left footer will bring balance to the defence but this pick could also go to Levi Colwill. Max Dowman will be 18 years old by the time the next Euros comes around and will likely be in the squad and could be challenging Saka while Brian Madjo looks to be the next bright natural

title: Neutral venues and no 'away' fans - how Israel v Republic of Ireland became so contentious
description: BBC Sport explores the backdrop to the Republic of Ireland's matches against Israel, amid fraught tensions between the nations.
body: Israel have not played a fixture on home soil for three years, since the beginning of the Gaza war, and have used Hungary as a home base for 10 fixtures in that time An elite-level European football match will be played on Sunday at a neutral stadium, with no 'away' fans, and reduced television coverage. That the match is even taking place had been in doubt - one side had to vote on a motion confirming whether or not they would participate amid significant opposition from fans, pundits and politicians. But the vote confirmed the fixture would go ahead, and now the Republic of Ireland will travel to Debrecen, Hungary, for a Uefa Nations League 'away' match against Israel, played against a backdrop of ongoing and increasingly volatile disagreement between the two countries about Israel's military offensive in Gaza. And on 4 October, the Republic of Ireland will face the same opponents in a 'home' match in Backa Topola - a small town in Serbia. No tickets have been sold to Irish fans for either fixture, and Irish public broadcaster RTE will air a stripped-back version of match coverage, with no commentators, pundits, or half-time analysis. So how did a Uefa Nations League match become one of the most contentious fixtures in football? As soon as the Republic of Ireland were placed with Israel - plus Austria and Kosovo - at the Nations League draw in February, the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) faced calls from some to boycott the matches because of Israel's military action in Gaza. In May a friendly match the Republic of Ireland played against Qatar in Dublin was twice interrupted after fans threw tennis balls onto the pitch featuring the Palestinian flag. The FAI eventually took a vote of its delegates in July, in which 75 members voted to play the matches and 32 voted to boycott. Not playing the matches could have harmed Irish football in the long-run, the FAI said, amid the possibility of Uefa sanctions for refusing to fulfil the fixtures and the potential loss of millions of euros in income. As well as curtailing its coverage, RTE will not take advertising or sponsorship income from the matches, saying it will only "meet its contractual obligations" to broadcast the fixtures. No tickets are being sold to Irish fans for either the 'home' or 'away' matches, with a small allocation available for Israeli fans for the first fixture, which has been the case at multiple previous Israel home games held in Hungary. Fans of Irish Premier Division club Bohemians are among those who have protested against Ireland playing against Israel Hungary has been deemed a suitable host nation for Israel matches because the two nations enjoy stronger diplomatic ties than those between Israel and many other European nations, and it has been willing to provide the necessary policing and security arrangements for matches to operate smoothly. The FAI decided in the summer to play its 'home' fixture against Israel at a neutral stadium, citing "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil". Reports have claimed the FAI was concerned protests could prevent the match from taking place in Dublin. The FAI gave no official reason for the selection of Backa Topola, but choosing a venue in Serbia - in a town so remote - in theory renders security management easier and reduces the possibility of protest. In 2025, Serbian foreign minister Marko Duric described Israel as one of Serbia's "closest friends and strategic partners". Serbia has also purchased military equipment, including drones and missiles, from Israel in recent years. The decision to play in neutral stadiums has not curtailed opposition. Fans of various Irish clubs have demonstrated against the matches during domestic fixtures in recent weeks, and on Monday more than 160 Irish athletes signed an open letter by the Irish Sport for Palestine group urging a boycott. The signatories include boxer Tyrone McKenna and former European champion athlete Ciara Mageean. FAI CEO David Courrell said last week Uefa had rejected a request for the teams to be kept apart in future draws, director of football John Martin described the games as a "very uncomfortable situation for everyone". Manager Heimer Hallgrimsson, meanwhile, said playing the match did not constitute legitimisation of Israel's "genocide". "We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," Hallgrimmson said. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel." In response, the Israel Football Association accused Hallgrimsson of "ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity". The Republic of Ireland faced Israel in Women's EuroBasket qualifiers last autumn and earlier this year after "extensive deliberations". The Republic of Ireland has been among the European countries to most keenly show support for Palestinians since the start of Israel's military offensive in Gaza in October 2023. More than 73,000 people have been killed in Israeli attacks, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations (UN). In May 2024, alongside Spain and Norway, Ireland officially recognised a Palestinian state, and later that year joined South Africa's Gaza genocide case against Israel in the International Court of Justice. The country has also boycotted Eurovision since 2025 because of Israel's ongoing participation in the song contest, was the first EU country to ban goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank, and has issued travel bans for Israeli government ministers. On Monday, Irish foreign minister Helen McEntee said: "Ireland's view is clear - international law is being breached. We are seeing an attempt to erase a population." Israel has criticised Ireland's standpoint and claims its actions in Gaza constitute self-defence, after the armed Palestinian group

title: Veteran BBC Africa correspondent Mark Doyle dies aged 67
description: Doyle was best known for reporting on African conflicts in the 1990s and 2000s, notably in Rwanda and Sierra Leone.
body: British journalist Mark Doyle, best known for his reporting on conflicts in Africa in the 1990s and 2000s, has died aged 67 after a short illness. After living in Africa, he joined the BBC in 1986. Doyle became East Africa correspondent in 1993 and made his mark covering the Rwandan genocide a year later. As West Africa correspondent from 1997 to 2002, he reported on Sierra Leone's brutal civil war and aftermath of Liberia's conflict. Following Doyle's death, BBC foreign editor Paul Danahar said he was a "legendary figure", as well as a" brilliant, brave, empathetic reporter". The BBC's Andrew Harding, who worked with Doyle, paid tribute to his former colleague in a 2015 article, published to mark his departure from the national broadcaster. In the piece Fergal Keane, another prominent BBC correspondent in Africa, recalled their stint in Rwanda in 1994. "He stayed longer than any of us," Keane said of Doyle. "Those who were in that awful place at that awful time will know what Mark Doyle gave for the cause of truth and for the BBC." In the same article Sir David Richards, who headed British forces struggling to stop Sierra Leone's civil war in 2000, also praised Doyle. Sir David said his reporting helped convince the UK government of the need for a robust intervention. "Hence the saving of thousands of Sierra Leonean lives that would otherwise have been at huge risk," he said. In 2004 Doyle won first prize in the UN Correspondents Association/UN Foundation Awards for his coverage of post-war Liberia. He became BBC World Affairs correspondent before retiring from the BBC in 2015. The man admired by presidents and warlords Go to BBCAfrica.com, external for more news from the African continent.
