title: Sri Lanka court convicts 15 men over deadly Easter Sunday bombings
description: Three churches and three luxury hotels were targeted in the 2019 attacks which killed 270.
body: Dozens of police and commandos were deployed to the courtroom before the verdicts were announced Sri Lanka's High Court has convicted 15 men who had been charged with plotting the 2019 Easter Sunday bomb attacks that killed 270 people and injured more than 500. Those found guilty include Naufer Moulavi, who prosecutors said masterminded the suicide bombings. Nine other men were acquitted. The co-ordinated blasts at three churches and three luxury hotels were the deadliest in Sri Lanka since the end of its civil war in 2009. Forty-five foreigners were among the dead. All the bombers who carried out the attacks died in the blasts. Investigators have previously blamed the bombings on Islamist extremists, and the 25 men indicted were from Sri Lanka's Muslim minority. One died in custody. The court session was adjourned before sentencing. The accused, who had been charged with more than 23,000 offences, were handcuffed in pairs and brought to the High Court in the capital Colombo in two prison buses. Most of those killed were Sri Lankans, many of whom were children. They included celebrity chef Shantha Mayadunne and her daughter, an entire young family of five, at least eight members of staff from the hotels targeted and five members of the same family from the western Sri Lankan city of Negombo. The foreigners who died included 11 Indians, eight Britons and five Americans. Among the dead there were also citizens of Australia, Bangladesh, China, Denmark, Japan, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and Turkey. Three of Danish billionaire Anders Holch Povlsen's children died in the attack on the Shangri-La hotel, while the family had been holidaying there. In the wake of the attacks, Sri Lankan authorities pointed to a "major intelligence lapse". Its parliament heard that a tip-off from India about the attacks was not properly shared with the authorities. In 2023, the Supreme Court ordered former president Maithripala Sirisena to pay millions in compensation to the victims of the bombings, after finding him responsible for national security failures that led to the attacks. Last month, two former senior officials were sentenced to death for criminal negligence that led to the bombings. Death sentences are usually commuted to life in prison in Sri Lanka due to a decades-old moratorium on executions. For years, Sri Lankans have held regular demonstrations demanding justice for the victims of the Easter attacks. The verdict comes as a separate investigation into former intelligence chief Suresh Sallay is under way. Sallay is accused of orchestrating the bombings with Islamist extremists. The allegations echo those aired in a 2023 documentary by British broadcaster Channel 4, which heard whistleblower testimony claiming the attacks were allowed to happen to boost the popularity of the Rajapaksa family, which long dominated Sri Lankan politics. Sallay, who was arrested in February, denies the allegations. Former president Gotabaya Rajapaksa, who was elected months after the 2019 attacks, with a campaign of tackling Islamist extremism has also denied the allegations. Rajapaksa, who has been banned from leaving the country, has asked the court to prevent his potential arrest in connection with the ongoing investigations. title: Lindsay Clancy's lawyer asks judge to investigate juror and check his phone
description: The attorney wants the court to look at the juror's mobile phone use and answers on questionnaires.
body: Lindsay Clancy attorney Kevin Reddington made several attempts to convince the judge not to declare a mistrial The defence lawyer for a Massachusetts mother accused of murdering her three children has asked a judge to investigate a juror in the case. The proceedings against Lindsay Clancy ended in a mistrial and acrimony this month after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict. Her attorney, Kevin Reddington, wants the court to probe mobile phone use by "Juror Doe" during deliberations as well as a questionnaire he filled out. A lawyer for Michael Desronvil, the lone juror who wanted to find Clancy guilty, said the latest defence motion was a "Looney Tunes" attack on his client for doing his civic duty. Desronvil has said there was "enough proof that she [Clancy] knew exactly what she was doing". This video can not be played Watch: Patrick Clancy says he forgives his ex-wife, Lindsay Warning: This article contains distressing details The juror forewoman has claimed in a media interview that Desronvil had expressed reasonable doubt about Clancy's guilt, which would require him to find her not guilty. He denies this. Clancy has not denied killing her three children, Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, eight months, at the family's Massachusetts home. Her attorneys argued she was not guilty by reason of insanity, that she was struggling with postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors said Clancy made a calculated decision to send her husband out of the house on an errand so she could strangle her children. In his motion filed on Friday, Reddington asked the court to look at calls and texts that "Juror Doe" made between 08:00 and 16:30 local time during all the days the jury deliberated. Cora, five, Callan, eight months, and Dawson, three He also asked the court to examine the truthfulness of the answers the juror gave during the jury selection process, as well as his responses to prospective juror questionnaires. In a separate motion, Reddington also asked for the case against Clancy to be dismissed. Prosecutors have yet to say whether they will retry her. Facing a backlash for refusing to acquit Clancy, Desronvil has hired an attorney to represent him. The lawyer, Edward Paltzik, said in a statement on X that the "disgusting" defence motion was an attack on the US constitutional right to a fair trial. "If the new normal is that jurors are going to face brutal reprisals for disagreeing with a defense attorney, you can kiss the Sixth Amendment goodbye," he wrote. Desronvil (seen here in a photo provided by his lawyer) has said he had no doubt about Clancy's guilt Several jurors have said after the trial ended that they were ultimately divided 11-1 in favour of finding Clancy not criminally responsible. Desronvil said last week that he had no doubt about her guilt. "As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence presented," he said in a statement to the BBC's US partner CBS News. The jury forewoman, a retired fifth-grade teacher, said in an interview with NBC that Desronvil had admitted he had reasonable doubt, but refused to find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity. title: Pollock left money on table to stay at Saints - Hearn
description: Henry Pollock turned down rival offers worth much more than his Northampton extension, which will earn him over £400,000 a year, says adviser Eddie Hearn.
body: Henry Pollock (right) celebrates June's Prem final win over Exeter with Northampton team-mates Rory Hutchinson and Fin Smith Henry Pollock turned down rival offers worth hundreds of thousands of pounds more than his extension to stay at boyhood club Northampton, says Eddie Hearn. Hearn, whose Matchroom promotional empire is centred on boxing, darts and snooker, has been working as Pollock's adviser since March. Pollock, 21, has agreed a new deal with Saints that extends his terms to summer 2028 and is worth more than £400,000 a year. "There were a couple of domestic offers – a couple of Prem offers - and international offers as well," said Hearn of Pollock's options during his renegotiation. "We had a very, very straight conversation. I said to him, 'be honest, do you want to go?' And he went, 'no, I really don't want to go'. And that was it. "He knew the numbers, but ultimately he just wanted to stay at the club. "He left a lot of money on the table to stay with Northampton. But it wasn't even a tough decision for him." Hearn says that some of Pollock's suitors were offering "well in excess of seven figures". This video can not be played Eddie Hearn on Henry Pollock's decision to stay at Northampton The £1m mark was where Hearn valued Pollock's annual salary prospects in an interview with the Daily Telegraph interview in August., external Hearn acknowledges that his client's new deal "didn't quite get to the number" that was targeted. The headline basic figure Pollock has accepted does not account for a signing bonus and various payments he receives for off-pitch work. And Hearn says that Pollock's endorsement deals have carried him comfortably over £1m in total annual earnings. "Everybody from major financial institutions to household brands to performance brands to nutritional brands to wellness brands… I mean, there isn't really a sector that hasn't hasn't approached us about Henry Pollock," said Hearn. Pollock is keen to explore the possibility of representing Great Britain in rugby sevens at the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles. GB's qualification is far from certain after the programme went part-time and the team slipped from the top tier of the international circuit. The back row's new deal does not include the sort of dedicated time to train up for sevens that France captain Antoine Dupont took before Paris 2024, but the prospect has been raised with Saints. "Our principal obligation is to perform for Northampton and to help them win championships," said Hearn. "Part of the arrangement allows him to look at those kind of opportunities, but only with a sensible conversation with the club." Pollock was ringside at a sold-out Croke Park in Dublin for Katie Taylor's farewell fight earlier this month Pollock's ability to maximise his on-pitch earnings in England is restricted by a £6.4m salary cap for Prem clubs. Each team is allowed one player whose salary is exempt from the calculations; however, players who move between top-tier teams can only qualify for such marquee status after two years with their new side. Hearn would scrap the cap entirely. "Let the players earn," he said. "All they hear about is salary caps or one star player per team - marquee names or whatever you want to call it. You don't want that. "You want to say to a young player, 'hey, come to rugby, you can be a superstar and you can earn a fortune'. "You could have lost Pollock and it would have been a disaster for English rugby." The salary cap is designed to make the Prem sustainable and competitive, with similar systems in place in most major American sports. Players such as Pollock can supplement club earnings with a central England contract, worth about £150,000 a year, or one-off Test match fees. Still, some England players, such as Jack Willis, Kyle Sinckler and Sam Simmonds, have left for France's Top 14 where a salary cap of 11m euros (£9.4m) offers scope for greater earnings. Hearn's current stable of rugby stars is only two strong. Bath and Scotland fly-half Finn Russell is similarly represented by Matchroom in off-pitch matters and advised by Hearn. However, Hearn has ambitions to become more deeply involved in the staging and promotion of the game. He is set to meet with Prem Rugby chief executive Simon Massie-Taylor in Monaco in the coming weeks to discuss ideas. "We haven't really touched the surface in terms of what we could do in the sport," said Hearn. "All I've done is done a few deals with Henry, he's come to a couple of fights and I've done a couple of Zoom calls [with journalists]. "That just shows you the buzz that can be created with a little bit of hype and perception. "But hype and perception are nothing without substance. The sport and the brand is the substance and it's significant in rugby. "Look at what Matchroom has done elsewhere. Boxing was dead, darts was non-existent, snooker was stuck in the air. We don't fail. Our track record is second to none. "If we went into rugby, it would be a stroll in the park for me. It's a huge global sport steeped in history with fantastic values and tradition that just needs to be just turbo-charged." title: Sir Sean Connery's family plans new filmmaking centre in Edinburgh
description: It will be named after the James Bond actor, who worked as a milkman in the Scottish capital before becoming a Hollywood star.
body: The NFTS Sean Connery Institute will be based in the centre of Sir Sean's hometown of Edinburgh The family of Sir Sean Connery has announced plans for a new filmmaking centre in Edinburgh. It will be named after the James Bond actor, who worked as a milkman in the Scottish capital before becoming a Hollywood star. His children say they want it to provide training for the next generation of Scotland's film and TV talent and help them build lasting careers. They said their father "understood that while talent may be distributed equally, opportunity is not, and that those who demonstrate determination and endeavour should have the chance to fulfill their potential". They have unveiled plans to open the NFTS Sean Connery Institute in Edinburgh city centre within the next 18 months. Sir Sean Connery appeared in seven James Bond films It is the product of a partnership between the Sean Connery Foundation and the National Film and Television School (NTFS). It would be a new, permanent home for the NTFS, which would deliver training, as well screenings, masterclasses and events. Sir Sean's children said their father was "immensely proud" of his Scottish roots and he would be pleased they were deepening their relationship with Edinburgh. They said: "Our father believed deeply in fairness, hard work, and supporting talented people in need." And they added: "We are proud to make this long-term commitment in his name and in keeping with the values he held dear." NTFS director, Jon Wardle, said: "Together with the Sean Connery Foundation, we have an extraordinary opportunity to build on Sean's legacy and his deep connection to Scotland by creating a genuine pathway into and through the Scottish screen industry." The Sean Connery Foundation was set up in 2022 to support emerging Scottish talent Sir Sean was born in Edinburgh 1930 went on to play Bond in six films. He also appeared in Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade and The Hunt for Red October. He won an Oscar in 1988 for his performance as Jim Malone in The Untouchables. In October 2020 Sir Sean died peacefully in his sleep in the Bahamas, having been "unwell for some time", his son said. The Sean Connery Foundation was set up in late 2022 with the aim of supporting emerging Scottish talent primarily in film-making and golf. It has worked with the NTFS since 2023 on the Sean Connery Talent Lab - an intensive year-long development programme bringing together emerging Scottish writers, directors, producers, cinematographers and editors. Jason Connery (front) with the Sean Connery Talent Lab's year two cohort Sir Sean's son Jason is also the co-owner of First Stage Studio a film studio based in Edinburgh's Port of Leith. The studio has homed multiple productions including Edinburgh set Netflix show Department Q. What stories would you like BBC News to cover from Edinburgh, Fife and the east of Scotland? title: Why is the Bab al-Mandab Strait so important?
description: The BBC's Frank Gardner explains why the narrow waterway is key to oil transportation and the world economy.
body: This video can not be played Thousands of refugees have fled Yemen in recent days after Iran-backed Houthis seized territory along the country's Red Sea coastline, including near the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule. Now, following a Saudi request, the UK has said it will deploy a military aircraft to help refuel Saudi Arabian fighter jets taking part in "purely defensive" missions. The BBC's Frank Gardner has this analysis. Read more on the crisis in Yemen. Why is the Bab al-Mandab Strait so important? Video, 00:01:17Why is the Bab al-Mandab Strait so important? Up Next. title: Developing El Niño becomes strongest on record weeks before expected peak
description: Scientists say the developing El Niño is now the strongest on record with weather impacts already being felt around the world.
body: Wildfires fuelled by El Niño are affecting around 12.5 million people across Indonesia, according to the country's health ministry. The developing El Niño climate phenomenon is now the strongest on record, according to scientists monitoring Pacific Ocean temperatures. Daily sea surface temperatures in a key region of the central-eastern Pacific were 3.05C above average on 19 September - exceeding the previous record of 3.02C set during the very strong El Niño of 2015. Some longer-term measures of El Niño have not yet hit record levels but this is likely to change, with the peak not expected until later this year. El Niño can cause major shifts in weather patterns around the world, with the Met Office saying many of the expected impacts are already being felt. El Niño set to be 'strongest in living memory', says Met Office What is El Niño and why could it mean record temperatures? El Niño is a naturally-occurring pattern, which happens about every two to seven years and tends to last for around a year. Trade winds that typically blow from east to west across the Pacific Ocean can weaken or even reverse, allowing warm water to spread eastwards. Heat is then released from the ocean into the atmosphere which can boost global temperatures and drive changes in weather patterns around the world. Forecasters track the development of El Niño by watching temperatures in a key region of the Pacific Ocean. When these are consistently 0.5C above normal, an El Niño is declared. There are different ways of measuring the strength of El Niño, however. The records that have now been broken relate to daily measurements of sea surface temperature compared with the long term historical average. This is called the Oceanic Niño Index (ONI). Many scientists - including forecasters in the USA and Australia - also consider an alternative measure known as the Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI). This measures how warm the key El Niño region is relative to the rest of the tropical oceans, meaning it takes into account the background warming caused by climate change. By the RONI index the current El Niño is not yet a record-breaker - but it is likely that more announcements will follow in the coming weeks. Professor Adam Scaife, Head of Long Range Prediction at the Met Office, said: "We have been signalling for months that the developing El Niño will be an unprecedented event. "The fact that it has already exceeded previous records – with several weeks to go before it peaks later this year – shows the enormity of this El Niño." Every El Niño is different, therefore impacts on global weather patterns are not guaranteed. And the unprecedented strength of this El Niño does not necessarily mean it will have unprecedented impacts on the weather. Professor Scaife said: "Scientists are still assessing whether the impacts will be in proportion to its magnitude, but we are already seeing expected effects worldwide." El Niño increases the odds of storms and floods in some regions and of drought and wildfires in others. This video can not be played Watch: How does El Niño affect world weather? El Niño years tend to bring below-average monsoon rainfall in India, which is already being reflected in this year's data. Statistics from the India Meteorological Department show that, until 22 September the southwest monsoon had brought 15% less rain than normal. Another typical impact of El Niño is reduced hurricane activity in the Atlantic due to changes in wind patterns high in the atmosphere. So far in 2026 there have been no Atlantic hurricanes, setting a new record for the latest date without a hurricane forming since satellite monitoring of storms began. Other possible effects - some of which are already being felt - include the increased risk of floods in coastal parts of Ecuador, Peru and the southern USA, and the enhanced threat of drought and wildfires in Brazil, Australia and Indonesia. These weather impacts can have significant knock on effects for on crop yields, food security and economies around the globe. The UK is thousands of miles from the tropical Pacific and so the effects of El Niño tend to be less clear-cut than in other regions. However, it does bring the increased chance of wet and stormy conditions across north-west Europe during the late autumn and early winter. A forecast released by the Met Office this autumn stated that there were already "signals for increased rainfall and storminess in autumn here in the UK", especially into November and December. The winter of 2015 and 2016, which coincided with a very strong El Niño, brought a succession of major storms delivering what experts at the time described as the most extreme flooding on record. In addition to storminess, El Niño can also be associated with UK cold spells in the late winter - but the link is not a strong one and the past evidence is mixed. The so-called Big Freeze of winter 2009/2010 was, at the time, the coldest in three decades - and this coincided with an El Niño. However, 2006/2007 was also an El Niño winter and that was unseasonably warm. As this unprecedented El Niño approaches its likely peak towards the end of 2026, scientists will continue to monitor its development - and its impact on weather around the world. title: 'Lego-type blocks' anger woman who was fenced in
description: Helene Ball had won a legal dispute with Derbyshire County Council over access to her garden gate.
body: Helene Ball, who has lived in her home since 1967, stood between two concrete blocks that have been laid on grass near the rear access to her home A council has placed two "concrete Lego-type" blocks at the rear access to the home of an 81-year-old just one week after she won a legal wrangle over access. Retired teacher Helene Ball won a three-year battle against Derbyshire County Council after it fenced off a 98cm gated gap between her garden and a council car park in April 2023. As well as being fenced in, dozens of concrete blocks were laid on the access road leading to the car park, off Cavendish Road in Matlock, after it was put on the market. After a first-tier tribunal ruled in Ball's favour on 27 August, she said the council was "a law unto themselves" after two new concrete blocks were laid at the rear of her home. The BBC understands the two additional blocks were to protect the grassed area and trees from unauthorised parking and damage once the car park entrance is opened. The council has acknowledged it was "unreasonable" to erect the original green fence at the heart of the dispute, adding it had "apologised for any distress caused". A right of way has now been established, while the council has been ordered by the courts to pay £50,000 costs and to ensure Ball's access is not impeded again. These two concrete blocks were placed on to the grass after Ball won her legal dispute The other blocks on the roadside were put in place as part of the county council's preparations to comply with the judgement, pending the full details being issued. This will likely involve opening the entrance to the car park so that Ball, of George Road in Matlock, can drive and walk to the rear of her garden. However, Ball said the placement of the additional blocks, to provide a direct pathway from her gate to the road, made her feel "very annoyed". "It appears to me that if I deviated from that path, that I would be trespassing. "At 81 years of age, I clearly need guiding out of my back gate to the access road," she said. "[Upon seeing them] I felt a mixture of anger and then wanting to laugh at how petty they are. "I don't think there's any length this council won't go to. I'm very annoyed. These two blocks were not here." The access road to Cavendish Road car park, which is currently for sale and provides rear access to Ball's home Concrete blocks line the road to the car park As well as being left "exhausted" by the dispute, Ball said her victory had brought unexpected media coverage around the world. "It's popped up in Argentina in Spanish, in the United States, in the Netherlands," she said. "I'm 81. I've had a very busy life. And all I want to do is sit in my little house at the top of the road and live the remaining years in peace." While she says she is not happy about the widespread coverage, she admitted it had been humorous and helped her with stress. "I've actually been nicknamed 'Gangsta Granny' by someone online. So many humorous comments I've had to laugh," she said. "I also had a wonderful card from a lady in Essex, who I don't know, who just sent me a beautiful message of support." This is the fence that started the three-year legal dispute A spokesperson said the authority was in the process of negotiating access when legal proceedings were initiated. "It would not be appropriate to comment further on matters that have been considered by the court other than that the council has a duty to safeguard its legal interests in public assets, including land that it owns and manages on behalf of residents," they said. "Where issues arise concerning council-owned land or access rights, the council has a responsibility to consider the matter carefully and, where appropriate, defend any action. "Its actions are always guided by its statutory duties." title: What is the White House press pool and why is it in a row with Trump?
description: The White House press pool is at the centre of a major row between President Donald Trump and TV networks. What is it?
body: A network boycott affected live TV coverage of Trump's ribbon-cutting event at the White House When Donald Trump unveiled a helipad at the White House on Monday, his remarks were barely audible in live footage of the event. This was due to a row over an institution that rarely makes the news – the White House Press pool. Yet it is at the heart of relations between the US president and the media, and this dispute could have constitutional implications. Coverage of upcoming presidential engagements, which include the UN General Assembly in New York, could be affected. It is a group of news organisations that combine resources to follow presidents wherever they are - in the Oval Office, at state dinners, on Air Force One or on holiday. There are separate pools for TV, photographers and print and radio outlets, as well as a "new media" category. Material from the TV pool feed is shared between its members - CNN, ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC - to save on costs and space. The pool is always on standby in case an event requires the president to speak to the nation. The latest row began on Friday, when Trump said he was banning three outlets - CNN, Politico and MS NOW - from the White House, accusing them of spreading "fake news" and "fictions and lies" about his team. A day later, reporters from those organisations found that their entry badges to the White House had been disabled. On Monday, all the major US TV networks decided to pull out of White House pool duties - in effect boycotting presidential events. That afternoon came the first test of this post-pool era - the new helipad at the White House. With no pool cameras present, much of the media did not carry any pictures and for those that did, there was no microphone to clearly pick up the president's remarks. But there were no such problems at Trump's meeting later that day with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, because it was not dependent on pool cameras and lots of media were there. This video can not be played Watch: Mamdani says press allowed at event with Trump regardless of "critique" Fox News Washington bureau chief Bryan Boughton, who currently holds the rotating role covering the White House, wrote in an email seen by the BBC that "effective today, the TV pool will not be covering events designated as pool coverage" of President Trump. In a joint statement, the five networks said: "The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. "No administration should restrict a news organisation because it objects to its reporting." The First Amendment of the US Constitution protects speech and press freedoms. It forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press - language that courts have traditionally interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage. CNN, Politico and MS NOW have filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration to "defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports". A hearing is scheduled for Wednesday. In a joint statement on Monday, they said: "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting. "Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference." Trump's speech to the United Nations on Tuesday will be unaffected by the boycott because it will be carried by outlets which are not part of the pool. But the president's movements to and from his various New York events, which are usually filmed, could be subject to the blackout. The TV network rotate coverage of White House events Responding to news of the lawsuit, Trump called the outlets "Third Rate Clowns" and "Crooked and Corrupt Press" that "trivialise and demean" his achievements. "Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown 'sources,' shouldn't be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform. He added that his team would file an appeal. Meanwhile the White House has launched Trump TV, a 24/7 stream on YouTube. Its description reads: "Watch the Trump Administration's biggest moments all in one place." So far, the channel has primarily consisted of replays of previous Trump speeches and rallies. For now, the White House media slot has remained vacant and instead the conservative TV outlet, Real America's Voice, was listed as "secondary" crew on Trump's trip to New York. Unlike the traditional pool, however, that outlet is under no obligation to share material with others and has operated unilaterally for its audience. In February, the White House announced it was taking control of the press pool which has access to Trump and had for more than a century been managed by the White House Correspondents' Association. The same month, the administration moved to bar Associated Press reporters and photographers from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because of the outlet's usage of the term "Gulf of Mexico" instead of "Gulf of America". AP filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing. There have been a few instances of other administrations attempting to limit certain outlets' access. The Obama administration tried to exclude Fox News from participating in a press pool interview with an administration official in 2009. But after pushback from the other four networks in the pool, Fox News was granted access. Unlike with Trump's exclusion of CNN, MS NOW and Politico, the Obama administration did not try to bar Fox News from all pool coverage, just one specific interview. title: Mikel Arteta agrees new deal with champions Arsenal
description: Mikel Arteta agrees an improved new contract with Premier League champions Arsenal.
body: Arteta was appointed Arsenal boss in December 2019 Mikel Arteta has agreed an improved new contract with Premier League champions Arsenal. The Spaniard's current deal expires at the end of this season but talks over a new contract have been ongoing for a number of months. BBC Sport reported earlier this month that an agreement between all parties was close. And it is now understood that Arteta has reached a final agreement with the Gunners to extend his stay at the club. There is no confirmation over the length of his new contract but it is set to take him into at least his 10th year at the club following his arrival in December 2019. The new contract will also include a sharp pay increase from his current salary of £10m per year plus an additional £5m in bonuses. Speaking about his contract talks, Arteta said last week: "They [the fans] don't have to worry about any of that because I want to be here. I'm extremely happy and I feel very grateful to work with the people I work with." Latest Arsenal news, analysis and fan views Ask about Arsenal - what do you want to know? title: British man missing after diving into Lake Como to rescue teenager
description: The man had jumped in to save a father and son in difficulty in the water, local officials say.
body: File photo of Dongo, where the boating trip set off, on Lake Como Italian authorities are searching for a British man who went missing after diving into Lake Como to rescue a teenager. The local coastguard said the man, in his late thirties, had been attempting to rescue two people - a father and his 16-year-old son - who were in distress in the water near the lake's western shore on Monday afternoon, local officials said. The man, who was friends with the family, had been on a boating trip with them at the time, the coastguard said. The father and son were later rescued by a passing boat, but the man has not been seen again. The UK Foreign Office said: "We are supporting the family of a British national missing in Italy and are in contact with the local authorities." A helicopter, divers and boat units from the fire department, coastguard and state police have been drafted into the search. As the lake's depth can reach more than 250m in the search area, rescuers were also preparing to deploy two underwater robots to scan the lake bed where the lake becomes too deep for divers, the Italian Coast Guard said in a statement. The alarm was first raised around 13:30 local time (12:30 BST) on Monday, when the man noticed his friend and the boy experiencing difficulty swimming and jumped in to help them. The teenager's mother, who had remained on the boat with her younger son, called the emergency services when she saw the man sinking beneath the surface. The father and son were transferred to a coastguard boat that had responded to the call and were given medical treatment after suffering from the onset of hypothermia, officials said. The mother and younger son, who were at this point adrift around 600m from shore, were then brought back to land. The coastguard earlier said that it had been the father who had jumped in to save the boy and the 37-year-old man, before revising its statement of events. Lake Como, around 30 miles north of Milan, is a popular tourist hotspot, with more than 78,000 foreign visitors in 2024, local chamber of commerce research shows. However, water temperatures there can start to fall from September onward. title: Sir Jim Ratcliffe suspends production at key UK plants blaming high gas prices
description: Ineos said natural gas in the UK is twelve times more expensive than in the US.
body: Sir Jim said Ineos was being 'forced' to pause production at the three plants Billionaire Sir Jim Ratcliffe's industrial giant Ineos is pausing production at its three plants in Hull, blaming high UK gas prices. The firm said gas prices in the UK are twelve times higher than in the US, and eight times more expensive than the coal-based processes used by Chinese competitors. Sir Jim said: "We are being forced to mothball some of the most efficient plants in Europe, but with gas prices now 12 times the level in the US and 8 times that of China, we just cannot compete." The facilities produce raw materials used to make pharmaceuticals, clothing, cosmetics, detergents, construction materials and military explosives in the UK and Europe. Gas is a key ingredient in production. Ineos said the move will affect up to 1,000 of its staff, of whom 245 work directly at the site. But the BBC understands workers across the sites will be kept on while Ineos tries to buy liquefied natural gas (LNG) directly from the US at lower prices - which could take up to a year - or waits for gas prices to go down. Billionaire Man United owner says he has lost confidence in the UK Ineos is asking governments in the UK and the EU — where most of its products are exported to — to put in tariff protections against Chinese products. One plant makes acetic acid, which is used in vinegar, paint and glue. Another makes acetic anhydride, a key ingredient of aspirin, and the third makes ethyl acetate, which is used as a solvent and for decaffeinating tea and coffee. He said the current government's energy policy was "economic vandalism on an industrial scale". The wholesale price of natural gas — used for heating homes and generating electricity — has almost doubled in the UK and Europe since July. The disruption of supplies of oil and gas through the Strait of Hormuz following the US-Israel war in Iran has pushed up prices around the world. Ineos says that its plants in Humberside are "among the most efficient in the world", producing materials with half the carbon footprint of US rivals, and only one eighth the footprint of Chinese equivalents. Two plants are already shut and a third will stop production in the coming days, the company said. It's the second time in less than a week that Sir Jim, who also owns a large stake in Manchester United, has heavily criticised government policy. He told BBC News last week that he has lost confidence in the UK, describing the country as "on the slide", which he blamed on high taxes and high immigration. Sir Jim, whose wealth is estimated to be around £15bn, has prompted controversy in the past with his comments on immigration. He was a supporter of Brexit but has been a tax resident in Monaco since 2020. The Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade said it would be a "concerning time for workers in Saltend and their families". A spokesperson said: "We've taken bold action to support our chemicals industry including £350 million for strategically important chemicals producers, which will be available on a co-investment basis. "We've also put trade measures in place on foreign chemicals imports and are tackling high electricity costs via our Supercharger and British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme to keep our chemicals sector competitive." How has the increased cost of gas affected your home or business? title: First person to face UK prosecution for Rwanda genocide appears in court
description: Dr Vincent Brown was charged following a seven year British investigation into the 1994 killings.
body: A 65-year-old doctor has appeared in court, the first person in the UK to be charged over the genocide in Rwanda in 1994. Dr Vincent Brown, formerly Dr Vincent Bajinya, who is in custody, confirmed his name and address from the dock at Westminster Magistrates' Court. He was charged following a seven year British investigation into the killings. He was told he faced a charge of conduct ancillary to genocide and six offences of conduct ancillary to murder, as a crime against humanity. The case was passed to the Old Bailey for a hearing on 9 October. A bail application will be considered later on Tuesday. The 1994 killings in Rwanda lasted 100 days, during which Hutu extremists carried out a campaign of slaughter against Tutsis and other moderate Hutus. The charges against Brown relate to an alleged slaughter in the Rugenge district of Kigali between 6 April and 13 April in 1994. Brown is accused of "killing, directing or encouraging" the deaths of members of the Tutsi ethnic group, as well as intending to destroy the group "as a whole or in part." Prosecutors said he was being charged with genocide under the 2001 International Criminal Court Act and the alleged killings were "part of a widespread or systematic attack, directed against a civilian population, with knowledge of the attack." Three members of the same house were allegedly murdered, along with a taxi driver, a mother and her young son. The alleged victims were Dominique Mukurarinda, Immaculee Mukankusi, Gerasi Rurangirwa, Leandre Mbogoye, Charlotte Kamaguja and Olivier Tuyishime. Brown is a medical doctor who qualified in Rwanda in the 1980s. He later became head of the country's Department of Family Health in Kigali and lived in a suburb there with his wife and young son. In 2006 he was worked at Praxis, a London-based charity which helps refugees from places like Rwanda. He has also served on the Refugee Nurses Task Force, which was set up in 2003 to advise the UK government. Senior police officers have previously stressed the UK should not be a safe haven for alleged war criminals, and investigators have been trained in international war crimes legislation. Sam Blom-Cooper, a barrister for Brown, told the court his client denied the allegations and was intent on going in front of a jury to clear the "stains of these appalling allegations." He said the defendant had hoped for, longed for, and prayed for the best part of 20 years, for this day." "These are appalling crimes, terrible murders committed in 1994 but this is the beginning of the end for Dr Brown." Inquiries continue into other alleged genocide offences in Rwanda. title: PM to warn EU chief of 'damage' posed by Made in Europe scheme
description: The prime minister says he will raise his concerns when the meets the European Commission President in New York.
body: The prime minister was speaking to reporters as he headed to New York for a meeting of the UN General Assembly Andy Burnham has warned of the "collateral damage" posed by the EU's Made In Europe rules, ahead of a meeting later with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen during a UN summit in New York. The proposals aim to curb the presence of Chinese companies in the EU by giving manufacturers inside the bloc priority for public contracts and subsidies. Speaking on the flight to the US, Burnham also declined to rule out committing to rejoining the EU in Labour's next manifesto, saying it was an issue "for another day". He said his "immediate priority" was to rebuild the relationship with the EU and reach "practical agreement that will further boost the British economy". The Made In Europe scheme - formally called the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) - is yet to be finalised, but the UK government is concerned that plans to favour EU companies could harm British manufacturing. Burnham said it could "affect British industry and supply chains" and that he would raise his concerns with von der Leyen during a meeting that is expected to take place on Tuesday at the UN's annual summit. "We have considerable support among the member states for the position we are taking, because Europe's argument is not with us," he added. "We both suffer the same effects as other countries, particularly steel and the issue it raises for the steel industry in Europe and in Britain. "We are making the argument 'we are not your enemies here… we are not the problem'. Made in Europe is dealing with a different problem. "We are making the argument that 'let's avoid collateral damage'." Tensions over the Made in Europe policy have reportedly further delayed this year's planned EU-UK summit, which had already been postponed in the wake of Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as prime minister in July. Burnham expects to find 'common ground' with Trump in first meeting Watch: What to expect from the UN General Assembly Ten years on, Brexit's economic impact is becoming clearer Burnham told reporters his own speech to the UN General Assembly later would reflect on the decade since the Brexit vote and the "turbulence comes when outside actors seek to manipulate, to distort facts, influence the British democratic process". "Going into the next decade, we need to be clear-eyed about that and become stronger and more on the front foot about challenging that," he said. Asked if he would rule out making a pledge to rejoin the EU at the next general election, Burnham said: "Our focus at the moment is on a UK-EU summit which we hope will take place later this year. "My immediate priority is to build on the good work that Keir [Starmer] did in rebuilding bridges, because those bridges were broken in the early part of this decade." He added: "What we have got to do is now go to the next level in terms of reaching practical agreement that will further boost the British economy, and those issues are the substance of the summit alongside EU requests around youth mobility." He said questions about rejoining the EU were for "another day". Speaking at the Liberal Democrat conference in Brighton on Monday, the EU's new ambassador to the UK was asked whether the UK could rejoin the EU or be granted associate membership. Jukka Salovaara said: "The doors are open but it's very much up to the UK public to identify and decide on its level of ambition when it comes to deepening cooperation with the EU." Last September, Burnham said he would like to see the UK back in the EU in his lifetime. Earlier this year, he said Brexit had been "damaging" but "the last thing we should do right now is re-run those arguments". The EU has recently suggested Canada could become the bloc's first "associate member". Asked if this could be an option for the UK, Burnham said: "The European Union made it clear that that wasn't open to us." title: Man admits causing the death of his son in hotel fall
description: The two-year-old boy fell from the window of a hotel in Cyprus in July, a Paphos court hears.
body: The man was allowed to return to the UK for his child's funeral on condition that he flew back to Cyprus to attend court A British man has pleaded guilty to causing the death of his two-year-old son who fell from a hotel window in Cyprus. The father, from Essex, admitted a charge of causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act at a court in Paphos on Tuesday. The boy fell from the fourth floor of the King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort in Chlorakas on 12 July, the Times had previously reported. A further hearing will take place on 5 October when the prosecutor will set out the facts of the case and the defence will present mitigation, a court official confirmed. The defendant's name was not given during the hearing. The boy fell from the fourth floor of the King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort in Chlorakas on 12 July The man was allowed to return to the UK for his child's funeral, on condition that he flew back to Cyprus last week in order for the plea hearing to take place. His lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, said he would ask the court to lift travel restrictions so that his client can return to the UK to be with his wife and daughter until the next hearing. Paphos district court was told in July that the boy fell through an open window when his father was holding him around his waist and swinging him from side to side. The father decided to plead guilty to avoid a long trial and spare his family reliving the child's death in court, Alexandrou said. A long trial would mean that the man was "again a victim of this tragedy", the lawyer told the Associated Press after Tuesday's hearing. "The most important thing for him is to return to his family," he said. The maximum sentence for the charge was four years in prison, but Alexandrou said the court should take previous cases into account where defendants had been fined or received a suspended sentence. title: NHS maternity data lost during routine IT work
description: Police are notified of the data incident and officers are assessing its impact.
body: Nottingham University Hospitals (NUH) NHS Trust, which runs City Hospital, said records were accidentally overwritten due to "human error" A trust at the centre of the largest maternity scandal in NHS history has revealed it lost historical data during routine IT work, with police now assessing its impact. Maternity records of women and babies who received care between September 2011 and November 2022 were overwritten during work at Nottingham University Hospitals (NUH) NHS Trust. Information has been restored since the "human error" on 18 August, but the trust has not been able to restore the history showing who viewed maternity records during this period. A police probe last year into a missing data file containing the details of hundreds of maternity cases found it was most likely deleted "intentionally or maliciously". Nottinghamshire Police has been notified of the data incident and is assessing whether there has been any impact on Operation Perth - the investigation into deaths and injuries related to maternity care at Nottingham City Hospital and Queen's Medical Centre, the main two hospitals run by the trust. Deputy Chief Constable Rob Griffin, gold commander for Operation Perth, said: "At present, no crime has been identified. We have received a report from the individual concerned and have spoken with them. "Further assessment is ongoing, and we are awaiting analysis of the digital process that was used. "In relation to recovery, we are awaiting a copy of the database, before any further attempts can be made. We anticipate receiving this during the course of the week. "The overall impact on Operation Perth remains under assessment and we will be in a better position to provide a fuller update once the outstanding analysis and recovery work has been completed. "I appreciate that this update may cause concern for families, and I would encourage anyone with questions or concerns to contact Operation Perth, where the team will be happy to provide support and, where possible, further information." The records were lost during "routine technical work", the trust said Maternity services at NUH were under the spotlight again following the landmark review, published in June, that found more than 500 mothers and babies suffered potentially avoidable harm or died due to "deeply embedded systemic failures". Officials at NUH said the latest error occurred while a copy of a radiotherapy database was being created. A setting that should have been changed, before a set of pre-written computer instructions was run, was "missed" and the process was carried out on a maternity database instead, causing records to be overwritten. The trust has restored clinical information, including notes, observations and test results, but has been unable to restore a complete history of who viewed records. It means "in most cases", the trust may be unable to confirm whether a maternity record was viewed by a particular person between September 2011 and November 2022. Information about current maternity patients has not been affected and no patient information was "accessed or used inappropriately" after the incident, NUH added. The trust said the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) was notified and that it had taken steps to improve its technical processes to prevent a similar incident. Andy Callow, chief digital and information officer at NUH, said: "I am sorry for the concern and distress this incident may cause to women and families affected. "On 18 August 2026, a human error during a routine technical process resulted in a maternity records database being unintentionally overwritten. We took immediate action to investigate the incident and recover the affected information." A statement from the Nottingham Maternity Family Group - which represents many of those affected by the wider scandal - said the incident was "extremely unnerving". "Families who have already endured preventable harm, injury and bereavement should not also have to worry about the security of the records of their experiences," it said. "The ability to trust NHS professionals to look after both patients and their data is paramount, but far too many Nottingham families feel that the NUH has fallen short of this. "With each new incident, the trauma of what we have faced is compounded and the confidence and trust we have in the trust is further eroded." The group added it was pleased the ICO and police were investigating the latest data loss to see whether any criminal offences may have occurred, why the data was deleted and whether patients' rights and privacy were unlawfully compromised. title: 'Our disbelief at release of killer who is now on the run' - victim's family
description: Francesca Kelly says her family were not told her brother's killer had been released from prison until after he absconded.
body: Francesca Kelly says they were only told her brother's killer had been released from prison after he absconded The sister of a man whose killer has been on the run for eight days has said her family had no idea he had been released from prison to attend his father's funeral until after he absconded. Gary Anderson and his brother Sean were jailed for life in 2023 for the murder of Karol Kelly in Londonderry in 2018. Anderson was freed from Maghaberry prison for two hours last Monday after a court sitting the previous day overturned a decision by the Northern Ireland Prison Service (NIPS) not to release him. Francesca Kelly said the failings had been "at the highest level" and she wanted to raise these face-to-face with the Justice Minister Naomi Long. Gary Anderson, who is serving a 15-year sentence for the murder of Karol Kelly, remains on the run Speaking for the first time since Anderson went on the run, Francesca said her family were only told about his release from prison in a phone call just before 14:00 BST on Monday, hours after it had happened, and after he had gone missing. "At that stage the prisoner had already absconded for a few hours, so we weren't aware at all of any application for compassionate leave," she told BBC News NI. "There was initially a sense of disbelief. "I felt that maybe he would go missing for a few hours but eventually hand himself in. "We certainly didn't think we would be sitting one week and a day later with him still at large." Karol Kelly was stabbed to death in Londonderry in 2018 She said the past eight days had taken a heavy toll on her family, describing it as "exhausting". "You work hard to move forward in your life," she said. "You work hard to ensure the loved ones still here are okay and can move forward in their lives. "But the trauma, it sits quietly within each and every one of us and it only takes one slight trigger, and you're right back to that night, you're right back to that graveside, you're right back to that courtroom - and that's a very difficult place to be." Francesca said the justice system had let a lot of people down, including Karol's five children, the wider family and the jury at the trial who listened to "thorough, onerous and sometimes difficult evidence". "It has also let down those brave witnesses who took the stand to ensure that they could share what they'd seen and experienced that night," she said. "So yes, that is all the justice system has let all of us down, because their one job was to ensure that the sentence imposed by Judge Babington was adhered to, and it has not." Asked if she had a message for Anderson, Francesca said the family had decided they were "not going to give energy to either him or that". "But for me personally, I just find there's a big difference between being free and having freedom," she said. "And I don't think a life where you're constantly looking over your shoulder, where you're living on your nerves, where you're not able to integrate in society or with those you love, I don't call that being free." She said she believed that in time, Anderson would be "returned to his cell". "And I trust that once the consequences of this situation are laid bare, this may not have seemed like as good an idea." Naomi Long addressed the assembly on Monday about the circumstances surrounding Gary Anderson's compassionate temporary release The justice minister has apologised to the Kelly family and agreed to meet them to hear their concerns. The circumstances surrounding Anderson's release have sparked a political row in Northern Ireland, with Long denying on Monday that she had misled the assembly over the matter. She has now ordered an independent review into what happened and said she understood why it would be distressing for Karol Kelly's family that one of his killers remains on the run. A day before the funeral last Monday, a judge granted Anderson a two-hour compassionate temporary release (CTR) from Maghaberry Prison to attend. It came after the application was originally denied by prison officials. His brother Sean had also applied for compassionate leave from a different prison, Magilligan, but the decision to deny that application was upheld by the judge. The funeral service took place at St Mary's Church in the Creggan area of Derry last Monday morning. Anderson was not given permission to attend cremation in Letterkenny, County Donegal, in the Republic of Ireland that afternoon. At some stage on Monday morning, he absconded from his court-approved civilian chaperone. Court documents show that the chaperone appointed by the court to accompany Anderson during his father's funeral is a relative of the prisoner. He is identified in court documents as an uncle; there is no suggestion of wrongdoing on his part. Policing and justice expert Danny Shaw described it as a "very unusual situation". "I can't remember, certainly in the UK, ever there being a situation like that where someone's been allowed out for a funeral without a prison officer or police officer in close attendance," he said. Questions were raised over the granting of Anderson's compassionate temporary release (CTR) following the publication of the full 15-page judgement from the judicial review of the Prison Service's decision. The judgment found that the decision to refuse Anderson's request was based on inaccurate information about the risk he posed. The decision had been taken by the duty governor at Maghaberry Prison. In his judgment, Mr Justice Rooney found that an internal assessment of Anderson's likelihood of reoffending had been recorded at a higher level than the score held on the Prison Service's internal system. title: The 'selfless decision' that saved our boy's life
description: Ollie is still thriving and happy 10 years after receiving a liver transplant from 17-year-old Miriam.
body: The family first met in 2020 and have continued to meet up over the years The family of a teenage organ donor say it has been a "true honour" to watch the little boy who received her liver thrive 10 years on. Miriam Lee, 17, from Kettering, Northamptonshire, died from sudden cardiac arrest in 2016. Her liver was given to 11-month-old Ollie Jolliff, from Poole, Dorset, who urgently needed a transplant due to a genetic condition. Ollie's brother Kieran died from the same condition at the age of four. Their mother Hannah said they received word of a possible donor for Ollie on what would have been Kieran's 10th birthday. Miriam's parents, Nicola and David, said: "It has been a true honour to see Ollie grow up. It's helped us with our grief, that something positive has come out of something awful." Their story comes as health officials urge the public to sign the NHS Organ Donor Register amid a decline in donations. Family consent rates have fallen from 67% in 2020/21 to 57% last year, according to NHS Blood and Transplant (NHSBT). Miriam died after a sudden cardiac arrest at the age of 17. She had signed the organ donor register before her death Miriam's parents said their daughter's death had come "completely out of the blue" but they knew they had to honour her wishes of being an organ donor. "She was a very caring person," Nicola said. "Miriam had registered on the Organ Donor Register when she was registering to give blood and as a part of the process, she had also told us her wishes. So, we knew we had to honour them." The teenager donated her kidneys, liver, pancreas, eyes and tissue, saving the lives of four people and giving sight to two more, her family said. "She wanted to offer everything she could and positively impact as many lives as possible," Nicola added. "When we heard from Hannah and Mike and learned that Miriam's liver had gone to tiny Ollie, it was such an emotional moment. "It has been a true honour to see Ollie grow up." He was "living because of Miriam", she said. Miriam's "selfless decision" saved Ollie's life, his family said Ollie's mother Hannah said that a transplant had not been an option for his brother Kieran and he had spent most of his young life in hospital. Ollie was tested at birth and diagnosed with a metabolic condition which caused toxic amounts of ammonia in his blood. He was given medication while he waited for a new liver. "It's 10 years this year since Ollie received his transplant and he's doing so well – he's going into his last year of primary school, he's got passions and interests and he's living his life like any other 10-year-old boy," Hannah said. "Ollie knows he's got a special liver, and he knows that Miriam is the special girl who gave it to him. We're so aware of how different things could have been had Miriam and her family not made the decision to donate. "It was a difficult and completely selfless decision, and we are so grateful to them." She also urged people to consider what their decision would be and to confirm it on the NHS Organ Donor Register. The two families have met several times since Ollie's transplant 10 years ago There are currently 8,700 people waiting for an organ transplant, according to NHS Blood and Transplant (NHSBT). However, it added that fewer families had consented for their loved ones' organs to be donated, and there had been a reduction in the number of eligible donors. Anthony Clarkson, director of organ and tissue donation and transplantation at NHSBT, said: "We are facing one of the most challenging periods for organ donation in over a decade. "The sharp decline in donors and the rising number of people waiting for a transplant need urgent action." Do you have a story suggestion for Northamptonshire? Contact us below. title: To Kill A Mockingbird first edition found in Oxfam shop
description: The copy of Harper Lee's seminal 1960 work was discovered in a box of American books given to the charity.
body: The book has since been acquired by the British Library and will join its national collection A rare first edition of the novel To Kill A Mockingbird has been found among items donated to Oxfam, according to the charity. The copy of Harper Lee's seminal 1960 work was discovered in a box of American books given to the charity's bookshop in Portobello Road, west London. It has since been acquired by the British Library and will join its national collection. Shop manager Olivia Haysman-Walker, who identified the copy as being a first US edition, said the book could easily have been missed. "There were lots of books to work through in the donation, but we recognised To Kill A Mockingbird and thought it was worth taking a closer look." She added: "We realised quite quickly that we had something really special. "The dust jacket showed its age, and although it was worn around the edges, the pages inside were in beautiful condition. "It's amazing to think that this book has passed through our Oxfam bookshop and into the national collection at the British Library. "It really has been quite a journey, and it's a lovely reminder, during Second Hand September, of the kind of treasures that can be hiding among the shelves and donations in our shops." Second Hand September is Oxfam's annual campaign encouraging people to buy second-hand. The dust jacket "showed its age" but the pages inside were in "beautiful condition", Olivia Haysman-Walker said Lee's Pulitzer Prize-winning book tells the story of lawyer Atticus Finch as he defends Tom Robinson, a black man wrongly accused of raping a white woman. Her story of racial injustice and childhood innocence, set in Alabama in 1934, has sold more than 40 million copies around the world and has been translated into 40 languages. The US novelist, who was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, died in 2016 at the age of 89. title: From punk to politics - the making of new Reform Wales leader Helen Jenner
description: Who is Reform's new Welsh leader, former English teacher Helen Jenner?
body: Helen Jenner was previously deputy leader of Reform Wales Helen Jenner, the new leader of Reform Wales, got a taster session for the top job on Tuesday, with a confident performance quizzing Plaid Cymru First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth in the Senedd. The Bangor Conwy Môn MS took over after her predecessor Dan Thomas quit as leader following an arrest on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour. He says he has done nothing wrong. As an ex-teacher, Jenner reckons she has no fears appearing before politicians in Cardiff Bay. Over the summer she told the BBC Walescast podcast it was "nothing compared to year 11 last lesson on a Friday". "You can't get a more discerning audience than a class of teenagers," she said. There's a smattering of showbiz glitz in Jenner's background. She taught English at the Brit School for the performing arts in south London, where Adele and Amy Winehouse studied. Her pupils included Britain's Got Talent semi-finalist Harrison Pettman. Reform not suspending former leader arrested on suspicion of assault, says chief whip Reform defector reveals she voted Remain in Brexit vote and wants Welsh independence Born in Neath, where her mother is from, Jenner moved to Anglesey aged two where she learned Welsh at school. She studied English literature at Bangor University. With bright, pink hair, she was more focused on singing in a "very punk, rocky type" band called The Mephs, short for Mephistophelean Engines of Pleasure. It is not, one suspects, the sort of name dreamt up by someone planning a future career in Welsh politics. Indeed, she says politics was not something she was into then. "My dad banging on about the European Union constantly," she said. Her father, who's from Liverpool, had joined UKIP. Then Jenner saw Nigel Farage on television. "It was seeing him, and then watching his YouTube clips in the European Parliament and everything: I've never seen anybody so animated," said Jenner. "I felt he was really principled and I suddenly thought 'oh, I actually care about politics now'." She became a fellow UKIP member and stood for Nigel Farage's next party, the Brexit Party at the 2019 UK general election. Married with two children, Jenner describes herself as a "proud British person" but "first and foremost" a "very proud Welsh person". Reform is by far the biggest opposition party Cardiff Bay has seen, albeit with its seat tally dropping to 33 after a defection to Plaid Cymru last week. After a tumultuous week for Reform, Jenner's first job is damage limitation. Her second, longer-term task, is convincing Welsh voters that Reform is more than Nigel Farage's party in Wales and has the makings of the next Welsh government. title: Can you take the 'London' out of London Fashion Week?
description: An initiative to show that LFW is "bigger than London" launched this year - but will it make a difference?
body: As London Fashion Week comes to a close, an initiative has launched to help talent from outside the capital to get into the industry The curtain might have fallen on London Fashion Week (LFW) - but bosses hope the runway of the future will start to look a bit different. Fashion Britain is the British Fashion Council's initiative to open up access to talent outside of London - so how do you shift the focus away from the traditional centre of that world? The council told BBC Newsbeat it has been working with LFW on a series of pop-up events in England, Wales and Scotland to show this year's event was "bigger than London". Northern Ireland wasn't included as a location for this year's initiative - but will be included next year, the council said. A recent House of Commons report, external found that more than half (51%) of the creative industries' economic output was generated in London in 2022. However, it did report that there are "clusters of creative industries" across the country, which included cities like Manchester and Leeds. "A lot of people think in order to make it big, you have come to this big city because it has the schools here," says Charles Jeffrey, founder and creative director of international fashion label Loverboy. "But actually, there is so much amazing education that happens in different places," the Scottish designer tells Newsbeat. "I first started [in] a tiny studio in Dalston [in east London] and we were having to use fabrics from these cheap fabric shops that you would probably only really get in London because of the rag trade," he recalls. "Now a lot of them have gone and what made London a capital city for fashion has been taken away, so you're probably better getting your fabrics from a little fabric shop in Manchester - it's probably ten times cheaper." Charles Jeffrey says there is more than one way into the fashion industry Jeffrey supported Fashion Britain this year, with the aim of opening doors in the industry for creatives outside of London, but how feasible will that be? Birmingham City University graduate Imarnie Bennett knows a bit about the struggle. She travelled to the capital to showcase her project with fellow BCU fashion graduates to an audience at Somerset House. "London is such a big city, it's really well known and there are lots of opportunities," says the 22-year-old. "You hear Birmingham and it's a bit like, 'will they get us the same opportunities as London?', but I feel like Birmingham is becoming more noticed for what we do." Bennett says you can harness the power of being different. "Even colours, some cities are brighter and warmer than others, so it changes people's perspectives on things," she says. Yet fellow designer Sean Pajarillo says he is hopeful about job opportunities because of how the technology and fashion industry is moving. "The merging of industries is what's going to create new opportunities for someone in the future," says the 25-year-old. Birmingham City University (BCU) Fashion Design graduate Sean Pajarillo says he feels positive about opportunities in the industry - despite not living in London Natalie Potter is network director at the British Fashion Council, and says the Fashion Britain initiative is "about recognising that British fashion is bigger than London". Potter says that in the run up to LFW there were events in London, Bristol, Manchester, Liverpool, Newcastle, Edinburgh, Dundee and Cardiff. But what happens after the catwalk leaves town? Potter says the aim of Fashion Britain is that it will connect talent to "the infrastructure and opportunities that they need to grow". "So working with the big global businesses that we do across the country to make sure that they've got routes to retail, to give them active mentorship," she explains. Potter says this will happen "locally and regionally". Designer Priya Ahluwalia says practical help can go a long way to opening doors for people This is something that British designer Priya Ahluwalia believes is vital. "I do think there is a genuine issue with London being seen as the centre of the universe in terms of fashion," she says. "There is incredible talent from all over the UK, some of the best designers have come from the north, come from Wales, Scotland". Ahluwalia spoke to Newsbeat after showcasing her archive at Westfield Stratford City shopping centre as part of Fashion Week. The designer explained how practical help is important in helping talent access the industry. "Whether we decentralise or not, London is still going to be the centre of UK fashion. "There needs to also be support for people to be able to travel to London, show up in London", Ahluwalia says. For Jeffrey, formal training isn't the only way into the fashion world. "Sometimes having a university degree does kind of put your foot in the door - but honestly, I really think it's just about the work and work ethic."
