title: Spain battles climate change on several fronts
description: A summer of wildfires and heatwaves underlines the threats to the country's economy.
body: Farmer Juan Ángel Izquierdo says it is hard not to worry about wildfires In a small green meadow in the Gredos mountains, west of Madrid, a couple of dozen cows belonging to Juan Ángel Izquierdo and his family are grazing. The only noise is the gentle clang of the bells around the animals' necks. This would be an idyllic scene were it not for the blackened pine and oak trees all around, the legacy of a devastating recent wildfire. "It was immense, I've never seen anything like it," says Izquierdo, whose family have been farming here for 200 years. The fire, in late July, merged with two others, burning a total of around 80,000 hectares (200,000 acres), making it the biggest blaze Spain has ever registered. It consumed more than two-thirds of Izquierdo's land and killed 12 of his 85 cows. Another eight animals had to be put down because of their injuries. All the hay he had gathered to feed his cows in the winter was also burned. "For us farmers, the summers are becoming more and more worrying, because they are getting hotter," he says. "It rains less, the wet season ends earlier and the autumn starts much later." For farmers, such conditions are synonymous with fires. "If you don't think about the wildfires too much, you feel okay," Izquierdo says. "But when a fire starts in a nearby village you start wondering – 'and what if we're next?'." Wildfires are one of several symptoms of climate change which in recent years have had a substantial impact on Spain's economy, as well as contributing to shocking human tragedies. World Weather Attribution, an international research organisation, found that the extreme conditions that drove record-breaking fires in Spain and Portugal in 2025 were 40 times more likely, external to happen due to the warming climate. "The ultimate reason for the greater frequency and intensity of these kinds of fires has to be attributed to the increase in greenhouse gases caused mainly by the generalised use of fossil fuels," said Ernesto Rodríguez Camino, president of the Spanish Meteorology Association. The Socialist Prime Minister, Pedro Sánchez, has described the fires in dramatic terms, placing Spain in the front line of an environmental crisis. "The climate emergency kills," he said in July, during a visit to the southern province of Almería where a wildfire claimed 15 lives. Research found that extreme heat and resulting fires in Spain were now 40 times more likely This year, around 300,000 hectares of land have been burned in Spain, according to the European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS), approximately half the total affected in the entire European Union. In the last 40 years, damage caused by Spanish fires each year has exceeded 200,000 hectares on eight occasions – three of those since 2022. 'This landscape is completely charred': Inside the village at epicentre of Spain's wildfires 'It's a hell of a situation': Spain grapples with devastating wildfires Farming insurance association Agroseguro estimated that 16,000 hectares of crops had been destroyed by mid-August this year, a major blow for Spain's agri-food industry, which contributes 9% of the country's GDP. The local authorities in Castilla y León, the region most heavily affected by this year's massive fire near Madrid, are offering compensation – between €5,500 ($6,300; £4,700) and €25,000 ($29,000; £21,000) to each farmer – depending on the damage suffered. But Izquierdo estimates that this will cover less than half of his losses. For decades, Spain's warm climate has been a boon for one of its other biggest industries - tourism. Sun-drenched resorts along the Mediterranean coast, and in the Balearic and Canary Islands, have driven the country's growth as a tourist hub. This year, close to 100 million foreigners are expected to come to Spain, making it the second most-visited country in the world, just behind France. Yet there are signs that the heat is becoming too much for some travellers. A study by researchers at Madrid's Rey Juan Carlos University found that it can as a deterrent to potential visitors., external "When there is a heatwave, the number of overnight stays drops in the destinations that we've studied, and there is also a drop in arrivals from some of Spain's biggest markets," says María Dolores Sánchez, an economist who co-authored the report. "Tourism represents 13% of Spain's GDP, so this could have repercussions in the medium term when it comes to Spain's competitivity." The city of Toledo, near Madrid, saw temperatures soar above 40C on numerous days this summer The medieval city of Toledo is on the plains of Castilla-La Mancha, far from Spain's coastline, but its rich history and winding streets have made it a popular destination for those seeking an alternative to the country's beaches and bars. However, this summer tested their tolerance of heat, with the country registering a record-breaking 61 days of heatwaves that continued into early September. Toledo repeatedly saw temperatures in excess of 40C. "It's quite difficult to do the tours in the summer," says guide Diego Esteban, of the company Visit Toledo. "We need to adapt, whether it is those of us who work in the tourism industry or the locals." When leading tours in the summer months, Esteban makes sure that there are frequent stops, drinking water is provided and that the itineraries include plenty of shade. However, he would like to see more shade and drinking fountains available. He says the heat has started to change the timing of the tourist season, bringing many more visitors during the cooler months of spring and autumn. Warmer summers have also encouraged the so-called "coolcation" trend, whereby Spanish travellers seek out cooler areas to spend their holidays, typically in the north of the country. Another consequence of Spain's warming climate has been drought. In 2

title: No regular contact with pair held in Iran, family say
description: Craig and Lindsay Foreman's family say they were promised contact after they ended hunger strikes.
body: The pair were arrested in Iran in January 2025 A British couple who have been detained in Iran for more than 20 months have not had regular contact restored with their family, despite assurances, their family say. Lindsay and Craig Foreman, who were sentenced to 10 years in jail over espionage charges which they deny, were promised family contact after they ended hunger strikes, but there had not been regular calls since, they said. The family of the couple, who are from East Sussex, is calling for an urgent meeting with Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband to discuss what action can be taken. The Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) said the couple's welfare was its "top priority" and officials had been working to provide assistance. It said this included the ambassador visiting the pair in prison and facilitating calls with their family back in the UK. The couple began hunger strikes earlier this year, after claiming that prison authorities had began to prevent them from speaking to their families. The hunger strikes lasted 93 and 84 days respectively. The family is now calling for the government to provide regular consular visits and implement a focused strategy to secure the couple's release. A spokesperson for the family says a British consular visit is planned for 5 October, which they say will be just the second visit of 2026. They said the length of time it took to arrange the meeting, particularly following the hunger strikes, was "extremely concerning". The FCDO said the family met with Middle East Minister Stephen Doughty and the UK's envoy for complex consular detentions Alistair Burt in August. A spokesperson for the office said Doughty "set out how unjustified and appalling we consider Lindsay and Craig's incarceration to be, and the action that the UK Government is taking to try and secure their release". Joe Bennett, Lindsay's son, joined the couple for the final five days of their hunger strike Joe Bennett, Lindsay's son, said: "I understand perfectly well that the British government cannot simply tell the Iranian authorities what to do. I have never expected that. "What I do expect is for our government to stand up for its citizens, to challenge what is happening and to keep pushing when commitments are made and then not honoured. "Mum and Craig brought their hunger strikes to an end believing things would improve. Regular calls were supposed to be part of that. "Instead, we are once again in a position where we are waiting, trying to understand what is happening from a distance and being given another date further down the road. That cannot just become normal." Bennett, who is from Folkestone, in Kent, says he wants a meeting with Miliband to understand what is being done to bring the couple back to Britain. "After everything Mum and Craig have been through, it is reasonable for us to ask whether every possible avenue is genuinely being explored and whether this case is being treated with the urgency it deserves," he added. Bennett said he wanted Miliband to hear the case "directly from the family". "After more than 600 days, I do not think that is too much to ask," he added. title: At least 11 injured in shooting at Turkish high school
description: Footage appears to show a male in the area carrying a firearm, while officials say the attacker has been captured.
body: A photo of the school where the attack took place, taken in 2022 At least 11 people have been injured in a shooting outside a high school in Turkey after an attacker opened fire before fleeing the scene. The incident happened at the Inci Uzmez Vocational and Technical Anatolian High School in Turkey's western province of Manisa at about 08:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Tuesday. The attacker has since been detained, according to the local governor's office. Local media reported that two of the victims taken to hospital were in critical conditions. CCTV footage posted online appeared to show a male on a street near the school carrying a firearm, with other clips apparently showing him fleeing still carrying the weapon. The motive behind the attack was not immediately clear. It has been reported in Turkish media that the gunman is a 15-year-old student, though that has not been officially confirmed. In a statement, Turkey's education ministry said the incident had "deeply saddened our nation, and our educational community in particular". It said that three national investigators from the ministry had been sent to Manisa. title: England fast bowler Wood retires from internationals
description: England fast bowler Mark Wood announces his retirement from international cricket with immediate effect.
body: Mark Wood is a two-time World Cup winner and one of the fastest bowlers of his generation England fast bowler Mark Wood has announced his retirement from international cricket with immediate effect. The 36-year-old, who is one of the fastest bowlers to ever play for England, has been blighted by injuries throughout his career. The Durham paceman only returned to action in the first Ashes Test in Perth in November after 15 months out with an elbow injury followed by knee surgery. However, he bowled just 11 overs before suffering swelling in the same left knee and subsequently flew home for treatment. He has not played for England since. "Although this may not come as a surprise given the past year, it just feels like a natural time at the end of my contract," Wood said in a statement on social media. "I've always tried to be resilient and come back from injury to prove people wrong and show everyone what I can do. Unfortunately, this time I lost the battle. "On medical advice, Test cricket and 50-over cricket are not possible, so the England dream has slowly been ground out of me over the last year. "Playing for England has been the greatest honour I could have ever wished for and a dream come true." Wood added that he hopes to continue playing cricket in some capacity. Wood took 119 wickets in 38 Tests after making his debut in 2015, and that summer he helped win back the Ashes on home soil. However, he has suffered a string of ankle, knee and elbow injuries during his career. In a bid to limit the stress on his body, he lengthened his run-up in 2018, and that did allow him to play key roles in some of England's biggest successes in recent years. The altered run-up did not impact his pace and he was part of the team that lifted the 2019 50-over World Cup, where he took 18 wickets. He was also in the squad that won the T20 World Cup in 2022, but missed the end stages of the tournament with a calf problem. In white-ball cricket, Wood retires as England's sixth-highest wicket-taker in men's T20s with 54 from 38 matches, and he took 80 scalps in 70 one-day internationals. Wood played a key role in helping England come from 2-0 down in the 2023 Ashes, with his return to the team - and blistering spells of bowling - helping them level the series. "It's been a privilege to watch the latter part of a great career," said Rob Key, managing director of England men's cricket. "To have been a point of difference in Ashes series wins, two World Cup wins, and to have thrilled crowds every time he got the ball in his hand is something very few players achieve. He can look back with enormous pride on a career very well spent." Anyone who has ever played cricket at any level will have tried to bowl fast. The dream is to be able to hurtle the ball down at irresistible speed: batters flinching, stumps flying. Mark Wood lived that dream. Few who have played for England, or any country, know what it is like to bowl with Wood's speed. The sight of Wood flying in, bowling himself off his feet - literally, on many occasions - was one of the most thrilling in the game. He captured the imagination of supporters not only with his raw pace, but his personality. Wood engaged with supporters and never took himself too seriously. It seemed he always remembered that cricket is supposed to be fun. Naturally, there will be the nagging doubt of what might have been had his career not been so badly hit by injuries. The human body is not designed to bowl fast and the rigours of the job hit Wood worse than most. But, when the stars aligned, it was electrifying. A demolition of West Indies in St Lucia in 2019, complete with a remodelled, longer run-up, showed what Wood would be capable of in the latter part of his career. He was one of the few England players to emerge with credit from the awful Ashes tour of 2021-22 and his entrance to the return series in 2023 was unforgettable. Held back until the third Test, when England were already 2-0 down, Wood bowled at the speed of light at Headingley. In one of the great Ashes spells, Wood knocked over Usman Khawaja with a 95mph thunderbolt. At the end of the Test, in a nail-biting run chase, Wood was at the crease with Chris Woakes to see England over the line. Woakes was another held back until the third Test and, without these great friends performing the way they did that summer, England would have been soundly beaten. Wood has been a multi-format performer for England. He was in the XI on the unforgettable day at Lord's when the World Cup was won in 2019, coming out to bat with Ben Stokes despite carrying an injury. Wood was also in the squad when England lifted the T20 World Cup in 2022. He is one of a handful of England players to have won both World Cups and the Ashes, having been part of the last England team to regain the urn in 2015. With Wood gone, the only remaining England player in Test cricket to have tasted Ashes glory is Joe Root. There was no last hurrah in Australia. A long recovery from elbow and knee injuries did not produce the pace England were craving down under. Wood could only play in the first Test in Perth and said last month he was "ashamed" at what happened. His retirement confirms the end of an era in English pace bowling. First Stuart Broad, then James Anderson, followed by Woakes and Wood into retirement. Throw in the all-round talent of Stokes, and England have lost 1,871 Test wickets in less than three years. title: Unexpected UK borrowing surge adds to pre-Budget pressure on chancellor
description: Borrowing was higher than expected in August as inflation piles pressure on the government ahead of the Budget.
body: An unexpected surge in government borrowing in August, driven by persistently higher inflation, has added to pressure on Chancellor John Healey as he prepares to deliver his first Budget at the end of October. Borrowing - the difference between tax receipts and government spending - was £18.3bn in August, almost a fifth higher than the year before, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said. That figure was £3.5bn more than official forecasters expected. Inflation rose to its highest rate in five months in August in the UK, driven up by higher petrol and diesel prices. Although tax receipts were higher in August compared with a year ago, spending on public services, benefits, and other costs grew more as the pace of price rises increased. The interest the government is paying on its debt rose to £8.8bn, its highest August level since records began in 1997. The cost of servicing that debt comes as the government is under pressure to spend more on defence and cost-of-living support to households, said Martin Beck, chief economist at WPI Strategy. He said it was important not to "overinterpret a single month given the volatility in the numbers", but added that there were some "concerning elements". He said the cost of paying the interest on government debt is likely to rise in the coming months. While the figures were an "unwelcome setback", he said the government tends to look at the OBR's medium-term fiscal forecast - so what it expects for the public finances three years into the future. "But even there, the chancellor's got problems," he said. "The cost of that interest has gone up. That's going to feed through into more borrowing." The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) warned that spending on debt interest is "a worryingly large share of overall government spending and has been pushed up" since the last official forecasts from the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR). Research economist Nick Ridpath said: "Both higher borrowing costs and higher inflation make life harder for a chancellor who is looking to bring down borrowing and to spend more on government priorities." About a quarter of the interest paid on UK public sector debt is linked to the Retail Prices Index, a measure of inflation which tends to be a higher rate than the Consumer Prices Index measure used to calculate the UK's headline rate. Ruth Gregory, deputy chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said it is a "dismal backdrop for the autumn Budget, with the government once again borrowing more than expected". She said the figures raise the likelihood of many of Prime Minister Andy Burnham's policy ambitions being "reined in or delayed to avoid big tax hikes and/or a backlash in the markets". Gregory also warned that, with the economy weakening, the government is likely to continue borrowing more than expected. Emma Reynolds, chief secretary to the Treasury, said that the UK has "huge potential" for economic growth, but only with "fiscal discipline" from the government. "At a time when debt interest costs billions of pounds that could otherwise be spent on improving lives, we must always know where the money is coming from to pay for public services," she said. She added that the government is committed to its fiscal rules "with a buffer against uncertainty". However, Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said the Labour government had "lost control of the public finances" by overshooting the OBR's forecasts. "Only the Conservatives will make the tough choices on welfare and public spending to get Britain's finances under control," he said. Economists think the chancellor may have to find £15bn, perhaps through tax rises, to do this and meet the government's self-imposed spending rules. Inflation - the pace of price rises - has been above target, and putting pressure on the UK economy. Consumer price inflation rose to its highest rate in five months in the year to August, running at 3.1%, pushed up in part by the fallout from the US-Israel war in Iran. title: Businesses struggle to profit as fuel prices soar
description: Fuel prices across the West have risen to nearly £2 per litre amid ongoing conflict in the Middle East.
body: The cost of filling up a vehicle has soared as the conflict in the Middle East continued to disrupt global oil supplies Businesses across the West of England say they are struggling to make a profit as petrol prices soar to nearly £2 per litre. Disruptions around critical shipping lanes like the Strait of Hormuz have tightened global oil supplies amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. Retailers facing higher wholesale prices for fuel deliveries are given the choice of passing this increase onto the customer, or forfeiting their profitable margins. Pieter-Jon Allis, owner of Stroud Taxi in Gloucestershire, said he faced "continual pressure to lowball" his prices in order to retain customers and still stay afloat. Child rail fares a 'birth lottery', say parent Plans for city centre loop bus and one-hour ticket Football prescribed to tackle mental health issues Petrol prices across the region vary, but rural areas are more expensive due to higher transport costs, lower sales volumes, and a lack of local competition. Filling up your tank in Bristol would currently set you back an average of £1.70 per litre, while some petrol stations in Hullavington in Wiltshire are charging £2.40. Elsewhere, a petrol station in Upton Noble, Somerset, has increased their prices to £1.86, and another near Whaddon will cost you £1.96 per litre. "Obviously it's a concern because our chief business cost on a day-to-day basis is fuel. I think we're headed for pretty tough times ahead," Allis said. He added at least 50% of the calls he receives are requests for quotes, as customers compare his pricing with other services, such as Uber. "We're under a continual pressure to lowball ourselves and do prices we were doing 15 years ago, even though fuel prices are at an all time high," he said. "It's just a complete nightmare in that respect." Susannah Moffat, who runs Ledbury Road Services in Tewkesbury, Gloucestershire, said "the last thing we want is to lose more trade" by putting the prices up. "The only thing we can do is keep cutting our margin, time and time again, to try and keep the price increases to a minimum," she said. Moffat said the petrol station was now "relying" on income from shop sales instead. "It's a difficult business to be in at the moment. Seems like there's no end in sight really, but hopefully it won't be forever," she added. Freewheelers Blood Bike charity say they may have to reduce the number of callouts if fuel prices continue to rise Meanwhile, volunteer blood bike charity Freewheelers, which supports the NHS by delivering lifesaving medical products, said they are "sucking up the impact in our reserves". The organisation covers an operational distance of more than 220,000 miles per year across Bristol, Somerset, Bath and west Wiltshire. "We've spent £17,000 on fuel per year over the last couple of years," said Chris MacDonald, chair of the Bristol branch. "This current year it's heading towards £22,000, so it's a significant jump." The charity relies solely on public fundraising, and said if fuel prices continue to rise, they would have to reduce the number of "low priority" callouts. "But we're not there yet. We can sustain the current situation for a while by digging into our reserves," MacDonald assured. title: Pollock signs new Northampton deal in excess of £400K
description: Henry Pollock has brought an end to his contract stand-off with Northampton, saying it was ultimately "a very easy decision" to sign an extension.
body: Henry Pollock came through the academy at Northampton, initially joining up with the club aged 13 Henry Pollock has brought an end to his contract stand-off with Northampton, saying it was ultimately "a very easy decision" to sign an extension with the defending Prem champions. "I am very, very happy to sign here," Pollock told BBC Radio Northampton. "I have been here my whole career so it made sense for me to stay on the journey with such a young group of players, who are so ambitious. "It was a very easy decision in the end." The 21-year-old, whose profile has exploded over the past two seasons after appearing for England and the British and Irish Lions, had been talked up as a "seven-figure player" during negotiations by his advisor Eddie Hearn. However, the boxing promoter's valuation was never likely to be met at Northampton or elsewhere in the Prem, given Saints' star-studded line-up, the league's £6.4m squad salary cap and rules over players moving between clubs. The exact level of Pollock's pay increase is unclear. While some sources have valued his new contract at £400,000 a year, others involved in the deal say the figure is higher. It is certainly short of Scotland playmaker Finn Russell, who, as Bath's marquee player, is on the league's most lucrative package, worth about £1m a year. Pollock's pay puts him well ahead of most of his contemporaries in the Prem however. His new deal is comfortably ahead of the average annual salary in the league (£191,000), the average earned by someone in his 20-22 age bracket (£106,000) and with his level of international experience (£224,000), as revealed by the latest league payroll data, covering the 2024-25 campaign., external Only 4% of Prem players that season were paid in excess of £400,000 a year. Pollock's previous contract, signed in December 2024, is understood to have been worth about £150,000. Northampton say his new deal is a "multi-year" agreement that keeps him at the club beyond the expiry of his previous contract in summer 2027. Pollock was part of a Saints team that beat Georgian club side Black Lion 93-10 in a pre-season friendly on Friday "I don't create it, my team do," said Pollock of the speculation that has surrounded his future over the past seven weeks. "It is one of those things that you have to take in your stride, but I am happy it is all done and I can focus on the rugby." Asked about the possibility of Saints becoming the first side since Saracens in 2019 to successfully defend their English title, Pollock was bullish. "We have the squad depth and the belief in this group that we can do it," he said. "Let's see, hopefully we can create some magic along the way. Let's write a new story." Pollock, who was instrumental in Northampton's run to the title last season, insisted last week that he was still open to offers, raising the possibility of a move abroad or even to another sport. However, remaining at Northampton, for whom he made his league debut in November 2023, always seemed the most likely option. After winning an age-grade world title with England's under-20s at the end of that season, Pollock returned to Franklin's Gardens and established himself as a first-team regular. Follow Northampton Saints on BBC Sounds Saints news and views from BBC Radio Northampton Subscribe and listen for everything you love about the Saints His pace, energy and on-pitch persona propelled him into the public consciousness and into contention for international honours. He made his Test debut off the bench against Wales, scoring two tries, in March 2025 and was a bolter pick for the Lions squad only two months later. His try-scoring feats through Saints' run to the Champions Cup final, complete with pre-planned celebrations, earned him a spot on the eight-strong shortlist for the continental competition's player of the year. He has appeared in each of England's past 12 Tests, albeit with his only start coming in a 42-21 defeat by Ireland in February. "Over the last few years, everyone has seen the quality he brings on the pitch and the speed of his rise through the game – but just as importantly, he's a young man of outstanding character," said Northampton's director of rugby Phil Dowson. "What's most exciting is that there's still so much more to come from him. Henry is incredibly ambitious and constantly looking for ways to improve. He understands that individual success comes from contributing to a successful team, and he's already taken on leadership responsibilities within the squad despite his age. "People sometimes underestimate how intelligent he is as a rugby player. When we sit down to review performances, he's often identified the same things we were going to discuss before we've even raised them. His understanding of the game is excellent, and that gives him a huge platform to keep progressing. "He's become an important figure not just for Saints, but for the wider game. He inspires young supporters, brings excitement to rugby, and understands that everything off the pitch is built on performing consistently on it. We're excited to see what he can achieve over the coming years." title: Major US outlets boycott shared Trump coverage in protest at media ban
description: Regular coverage of the president has been disrupted after he banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House.
body: Trump's comments at a ribbon-cutting ceremony on Monday were streamed by the White House but were inaudible Major US television networks suspended their pooled coverage of President Donald Trump on Monday in response to CNN, Politico and MS NOW being barred from the White House. Trump announced the ban on Friday as he accused the organisations of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration. The companies said their reporters were denied access to the building on Saturday. The three US outlets have since said they will sue the Trump administration in a bid to "defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports". Shortly after, the White House launched its own streaming channel, Trump TV, which operates a 24/7 feed of clips of the president. Several other US outlets have also announced that they would not participate in coverage of pooled events, with some, including the New York Times and Washington Post, saying they would not share still images from Trump events on Monday. It meant there was no network TV footage of Trump boarding Air Force One or arriving in New York to attend the UN general assembly. Trump also took part in a ribbon-cutting ceremony for the new Marine One helipad on the White House South Lawn. The event was streamed on the White House site but his comments were inaudible. The president did later appear on television following a meeting with the Mayor of New York Zohran Mamdani. He told the president that all members of the media would be welcome at the press conference. Trump said: "It's interesting because, they said they were going to boycott me, but they never boycott me, so I wasn't very worried about that. Look at all that press." The pool involves media organisations sharing material to save on costs and space when broadcasting presidential events to the American public. Fox News Washington bureau chief Bryan Boughton, who currently holds a rotating role helping to organise media TV crews covering the White House, wrote in an email seen by the BBC that "effective today, the TV pool will not be covering designated as pool coverage" of Trump. The message said the move followed the White House "preventing" CNN from fulfilling its pool duties for Trump's trip to New York and that "there will be no replacement pool put in place". The three media organisations banned from the White House filed a lawsuit on Monday in US District Court in Washington. A joint statement announcing the legal action said: "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting. "Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference." title: Sri Lankan court to deliver verdict on deadly Easter bombings
description: Co-ordinated suicide attacks killed 270 people across several churches and hotels in Colombo in 2019.
body: For years, families of the victims have held regular demonstrations demanding accountability after the attacks A Sri Lankan court is set to rule on Naufer Moulavi, who is accused of masterminding the Easter bomb attacks that killed 270 people and injured more than 500 in 2019. Twenty-three others will also receive verdicts for their involvement in planning and carrying out the co-ordinated suicide bombings. The attacks on several locations including several churches holding Easter mass and three luxury hotels was the deadliest attack Sri Lanka had seen since the end of its civil war in 2009. The associates and relatives of nine suicide bombers are among those facing more than 23,000 charges, including murder, conspiracy to commit terrorism and possessing firearms. The prosecution had named Moulavi as the main organiser of the attacks, and had submitted what they said was a voluntary confession to the court where he had admitted his role. The court accepted the confession. However, Moulavi later told the three-judge bench hearing the case that he was not shown what he was signing and rejected the allegations against him. More than 2,300 people gave evidence for the prosecution. There were also 2,076 pieces of evidence, including explosives, swords and firearms. In the wake of the attacks, Sri Lankan authorities pointed to a "major intelligence lapse". Its parliament heard that a tip-off from India about the attacks was not properly shared with the authorities. In 2023, the Supreme Court ordered former president Maithripala Sirisena to pay millions in compensation to the victims of the bombings, after finding him responsible for national security failures that led to the attacks. Last month, two former senior officials were sentenced to death for criminal negligence that led to the bombings. Death sentences are usually commuted to life in prison in Sri Lanka due to a decades-old moratorium on executions. For years, Sri Lankans have held regular demonstrations demanding justice for the victims of the Easter attacks. The verdict on Tuesday comes as a separate investigation on former intelligence chief Suresh Sallay is under way. Sallay is accused of orchestrating the bombings with Islamist extremists. The allegations echo those aired in a 2023 documentary by British broadcaster Channel 4, which heard whistleblower testimony claiming the attacks were allowed to happen to boost the popularity of the Rajapaksa family, which long dominated Sri Lankan politics. Sallay, who was arrested in February, denies the allegations. Former president Gotabaya Rajapaksa, who was elected months after the 2019 attacks, with a campaign of tackling Islamist extremism has also denied the allegations. Rajapaksa, who has been banned from leaving the country, has asked the court to prevent his potential arrest in connection with the ongoing investigations. title: 'Alarming' - does WSL have a homegrown problem?
description: The London City Lionesses raised eyebrows with no English players in their starting line-up against Manchester United, but is there a wider trend?
body: Hannah Hampton and Lauren James are two players that have established themselves in the England starting XI under Sarina Wiegman (centre) When London City Lionesses beat Manchester United on the opening night of the 2025-26 season, it suggested times were changing in the English women's game. For some, that had become clear about an hour before kick-off in Bromley when the team news revealed a starting XI without any English players - the first time a Women's Super League side had done so on the first day of the season. Two days later it happened again, when Scotland striker Kirsty Hanson was the only British player to start for Tottenham in their win over West Ham. Both instances speak to the increasing ability of WSL clubs to attract top talents from across the globe, creating a league many now view as the world's best. But, with the Women's Champions League returning this week, is what's good for the WSL good for homegrown players, and by extension the home nations? Or is it, as The Guardian's Tom Garry puts it, "alarming" for the hopes of the home nations? Arsenal v HB Koge, Women's Champions League Tuesday, 22 September, 20:00 BST Listen to BBC Radio 5 Live commentary and follow text updates of the matches featuring English teams on the BBC Sport website as the Women's Champions League returns Ten years ago when current champions Manchester City last won the WSL title, they did so with an all-British starting line-up. In 2018, the WSL went fully professional, the subsequent success of the Lionesses in the 2020s rapidly grew the game's audience and revenues have increased accordingly. As a result, clubs have expanded their scouting pool and been able to attract players from a wider variety of nationalities - with transfer fees exploding since the turn of the decade. Over recent windows, WSL clubs have recruited heavily from Germany and Sweden, while two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas exchanged the trophies of Barcelona for big-spending London City this summer. The proliferation of players from Japan and Australia also highlights the WSL's attractiveness for those at the top of the game as those clubs with the deepest pockets pack their squads with players from across the globe. "Our league has grown significantly and attracted world class athletes from all over the world," says Birmingham City manager Amy Merricks. "Unfortunately that blocks some of the pathways for the youngsters coming through. "We need [this] talent in our league because our league is growing, but at the same time we have got to try and address this issue." Looking at the proportion of homegrown players (English, Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish) to start 11 or more matches, half of a WSL season, the data shows a steady decline over the past three seasons to under a third. The first three weeks of 2026-27 have offered a bump on last season, but that can partly be attributed to the WSL's expansion from 12 teams to 14 teams and the greater proportion of homegrown talent in the promoted trio of Birmingham City, Crystal Palace and Charlton Athletic. It is a downward trend that is not mirrored across other major European leagues. For 2025-26, 61% of those to start half or more of Premiere Ligue matches in France were French, 63% of those in Frauen Bundesliga games were German, and 69% of Liga F players in Spain were Spanish. And, while WSL managers say they appreciate the importance of cultivating homegrown talent, the reality of the job ensures it is not their first priority. "The club has a responsibility to raise young players, give our own talents possibilities to be in the squad and compete every week," says Manchester City boss Andree Jeglertz. "But when it comes to team selection, I always need to pick the team that gives us the best chance of winning the game. If that contains eight young and promising English players or zero, I don't care. I just want to win the game." Ellen White and Ben Haines discuss homegrown WSL players on the Women's Football Weekly Superstar-led London City live up to hype as Man Utd suffer It feels like a crossroads has been reached between clubs wanting to be competitive, the WSL continuing to grow, and the need to regenerate an England squad that has not changed much over the past three major tournaments. After all, England are the two-time European champions but seven of the team that started against Spain in June also played in the Euro 2022 final against Germany - while two of the remaining starters in this year's game were on the bench four years ago. Sarina Wiegman's side were outclassed in Majorca, losing 4-0 to miss out on automatic qualification for the 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil. They must now navigate two rounds of play-off matches, starting against Greece next month. Discussions on England's future is pertinent given the biennial Women's Under-20s World Cup is ongoing in Poland. Last Thursday, Lydia Bedford's young side were dismissed 3-0 from the last 16 by Nigeria, albeit with the caveat a number of players such as US-based Erica Meg Parkinson and Laila Harbert were not released by their clubs to play. Nevertheless, in 2022 and 2024, like the other home nations, they did not even qualify. It is a far cry from the class of 2018 where the likes of Alessia Russo, Lauren Hemp and Georgia Stanway led the Lionesses to third place in the Under-20s World Cup, setting the tone for the incredible subsequent success. Wiegman has handed debuts to 21 players since her arrival in September 2021, but only Lauren James, Hannah Hampton and Lucia Kendall have become established starters. When England kick off in Crete on Friday, 5 October (20:00 BST), it is likely to be the same faces once again. title: Why is Monaco staging a sprint race? F1 Q&A
description: BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions before the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.
body: Overtaking is almost impossible at Monaco in normal racing circumstances Formula 1 has a rare Saturday race this weekend for the Azerbaijan Grand Prix. Kimi Antonelli goes into round 15 of the season with an imposing 81-point lead in the drivers' championship over Mercedes team-mate George Russell. BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions before the event in Baku. What are your thoughts on having a sprint race next year at Monaco? I was very surprised to see that on the calendar, given that the race has so little chance of overtaking - Graham F1 to have 10 sprint races in 2027, including Monaco Formula 1 announced the 2027 calendar last week, with the number of sprint events increased from six to 10, and one of them Monaco. This has proved controversial with some fans. Why pick the worst track on the calendar for overtaking to have two races in one weekend, some have wondered. What's the point of having two boring races; isn't one enough? The thinking behind it, though, is less about the races than about qualifying, and how making Monaco a sprint could mix up the weekend. Monaco qualifying is renowned as one of the highlights of the season. In that case, surely two great qualifying sessions is better than one? It was also pointed out by F1 that it gives the chance of two different grid orders and therefore more variability. There is another factor to consider, too. Monaco is one of the most demanding tracks on the calendar, and it is renowned as somewhere drivers have to build up to the limit progressively so they can become confident with knowing how the car will behave when they get there. Get that wrong, push too hard too soon, and the chances of an accident are considerably higher. So asking the drivers to go straight into a qualifying after a single practice session is a really difficult challenge. It is likely to mean more mistakes, more action, more drama, and therefore more entertainment. The same goes for grand prix qualifying. Yes, by then the drivers will have done a sprint race. But there are always changes made to the cars for qualifying, so again the drivers will be going in blind to some degree. Yes, the sprint is likely to be a procession. How could it be anything else? But it adds an extra degree of jeopardy to the whole weekend. Do you think F1 might consider the F2 approach for the virtual safety car, where drivers cannot pit under a VSC but can pit under a full safety car? As a regular viewer of both series, I think this works well in F2 and is another way to solve the jeopardy a short VSC period brings to a race. - Caroline The VSC was discussed at the so-called FIA sporting advisory committee last week, but sources say no consensus emerged there as to potential changes. It was also on the agenda for the F1 Commission meeting on Monday but there were no significant developments. Lando Norris, who lost victory in Madrid by the VSC timing, said after the race that the drivers had previously discussed with the FIA the idea that the VSC should be out for a minimum of a lap so this sort of thing could not happen. But every potential 'solution' comes with consequences. In that case, F1 might end up with a full lap of VSC just to recover a bit of debris. The VSC was introduced so that relatively small-scale incidents could be dealt with without the lengthy disruption of a full safety car. It's accepted that the safety car affords possibilities to gain and lose out, so why should the VSC not do the same? The argument is that, generally, these even out over the season, although the Norris case in Madrid had particularly dramatic consequences. Antonelli benefited from this one, for example, but has lost out in other scenarios this year. For example, when the VSC gifted Lewis Hamilton the lead in Barcelona, even if that was rendered moot by Antonelli's subsequent retirement. This video can not be played Verstappen easily beats 100 racers in a go-kart Why did Mercedes put George Russell on a two-stop strategy in the Spanish Grand Prix when the race has the longest pit lane of the season? George was the only driver out of the top 15 finishers on a two-stop and did this decision cost him a podium finish? - Richard Mercedes were a bit stuck when the virtual safety car was deployed on lap 14 in Madrid. The team had split the drivers' tyre strategies - Kimi Antonelli took the conventional strategy and started on the mediums, Russell had gone for the hards. With overtaking so difficult in Madrid, it was always likely that one option would turn out to be sub-optimal. The timing of the VSC was very unfortunate for those who started on hard tyres because it coincided with the pit-stop window for those on mediums. Mercedes had two choices - stay out, or pit and change tyre compound, as drivers are obligated to use two compounds during a dry grand prix. Charles Leclerc, who also started on hards and was running immediately ahead of Russell, stayed out. Mercedes pitted in the hope of trying to beat Leclerc. Whichever tyre Russell chose was unlikely to make it to the end, so Mercedes knew at that point they would almost certainly have to stop again. The hard tyre was comfortably the best race tyre in Madrid, and on his mediums Russell did not have the pace to narrow the gap to Leclerc to less than it takes to do a pit stop. So there was nothing to lose by pitting again. Team boss Toto Wolff said: "He said the tyres were not in a great shape, the mediums. We didn't think they would go to the end. (We thought) the better opportunity was not to hang out and wait for a red, but to change the tyres and get on with it." Russell said: "Maybe I could have stayed out with Leclerc but I would have still finished behind him. Maybe I could have not pitted on to the hard again but everything I would have done would have brought us to the same position." title: How fields of Fermanagh helped Daisy Edgar-Jones prepare for her latest film
description: The actor, whose mum is from County Down, recalls long childhood summers in Northern Ireland.
body: Daisy Edgar-Jones stars as Elinor Dashwood in Sense and Sensibility Actor Daisy Edgar-Jones is no stranger to Ireland, having spent five months in the country filming hit drama Normal People which was released in 2020. But it was actually fields in County Fermanagh, where some of her family live, that helped her prepare for the role of beloved character Elinor Dashwood in Jane Austen's Sense and Sensibility, some 20 years before. Her mother is from County Down and Edgar-Jones spent her childhood roaming fields in Northern Ireland. "I remember big long summers when I was very young in Fermanagh in the fields which definitely helped with my Sense and Sensibility journey because I was doing a lot of the similar wandering around, with not much to do, under the big sky and I love being here," she told BBC News NI. "I always feel so welcome and the people are incredible." Sense and Sensibility was published in 1811 and has been adapted many times, but the 1995 adaptation starring Kate Winslet, Emma Thompson, Alan Rickman and Hugh Grant is perhaps the best known. The Austen novel centres around a relatable story of sisterhood and romance, mainly between Elinor Dashwood (Edgar-Jones) and Marianne (Esmé Creed-Miles). The Dashwood family is left penniless after the death of their father and the two older sisters are in search of a husband as they are forced to leave their home and move to the modest Barton Cottage. The film was made by production companies Focus Features and Working Title. Caitriona Balfe features alongside Edgar-Jones in the new adaptation Edgar-Jones is surrounded by Irish actors in the film, with Irish star Caitriona Balfe playing her mother Mrs Dashwood, Fiona Shaw as Mrs Jennings and Hamnet's Bodhi Rae Breathnach, who plays the Dashwoods' youngest sister, Margaret. Balfe has often appeared on screens in recent years, mostly in her roles in Outlander and Belfast, alongside Jamie Dornan. The County Monaghan actress, who grew up in a family of seven in the village of Tydavnet, said starring in the film reminded her of her own childhood. "There was a lot of that sisterly dynamic that I recognised," said Balfe. "This is one of the beautiful things about this film is watching the richness of this family. One of the words that kept coming to me was the resilience of them - even though they were destitute financially, what you see when they go to Barton is actually this blossoming, because they have each other. She said it was an "amazing" time in Ireland for art. "I'm so proud to be Irish and it's such an amazing time in Ireland right now for all the incredible art that is being produced here and to be able to bring this film here is really special," she said. Balfe said she speaks with her husband about moving back to Ireland "all the time". "You never know, it might be in the future." Sense and Sensibility is in cinemas from 25 September. title: Chelsea struggles to Villa bench - Garnacho faces defining season
description: Alejandro Garnacho joined Aston Villa on loan from Chelsea with a view to kick-starting his career, but his early weeks in the Midlands have been a struggle.
body: Alejandro Garnacho cost Chelsea £40m from Manchester United last year Just like last season, questions are being asked about Alejandro Garnacho. Two months after joining from Chelsea on an initial loan, the winger has yet to convince Aston Villa boss Unai Emery of his worth. The Argentina forward has played just 31 minutes for Villa, spread across three substitute appearances. A 15-minute outing against Hull is the most time he has spent on the pitch in a game. Garnacho has been an unused substitute for Villa's past four matches , watching from the bench again as they won 3-2 at Tottenham on Saturday. One goal and four assists in 24 Premier League games for Chelsea last term fell below what the Blues expected from their £40m recruit from Manchester United, so he was allowed to move on. This campaign is only a month old, but 22-year-old Garnacho could be at a crossroads at Villa Park already. This video can not be played Highlights: Villa survive late Spurs scare for first PL win of the season Emery likes to ease new players into his teams. Youri Tielemans did not start a Premier League game until November 2023 after joining in the summer, but became an integral part of Emery's machine. Only Joao Gomes, out of 10 new summer signings, started Villa's opening Premier League game. Just two - Zion Suzuki and Nicolas Jackson - started the next. Garnacho's situation feels extreme though, having been left on the bench for the Carabao Cup win at Coventry when Emery made seven changes. Academy product George Hemmings, who joined Villa from Forest as a teenager, has started the season well to earn Emery's full trust and start ahead of Garnacho. Ibrahim Mbaye, a £47m arrival from Paris St-Germain, made his first Villa start in the 3-1 victory at Coventry and is also preferred to Garnacho for now. A facial injury in early August hampered Garnacho's pre-season and meant he missed the Super Cup defeat by Paris St-Germain, adding to the complications. Emery needs his players to understand their roles and his methods before having full faith in them and he expects Garnacho to catch up. "Continue working. Work, work, train, work," Emery said when asked about Garnacho's absence from the pitch. "When he can have minutes to play, try to play well. He is progressing, but we have players in front of him now. "George is playing fantastic. Alysson is also understanding things well and is giving us things I want. [Ibrahim] Mbaye also responded well. "We want a competitive team and players to compete in the style we have. Garnacho is a little bit behind because of some circumstances we had in pre-season. It is time to be patient for the time he needs." Garnacho, who first made his name as a livewire teenager, has shown in the past he can torment defences at Premier League level. He spoke about needing time to adapt to a "different club and a different place" at Chelsea. A further season of struggle would be a significant setback. Emery is clearly yet to be convinced by what he sees in training, despite being a long-term Garnacho admirer. Villa wanted more pace in their side and Crysencio Summerville was considered before he moved to Saudi Arabia's Al-Hilal. Chelsea's £117m signing of Morgan Rogers from Villa left a gap for Emery to fill and Garnacho was available. A positive relationship between the clubs allowed for easy discussions. Striker Jackson also joined from Chelsea for a Villa club record £65m and there have been eight deals between the clubs in the past four years. Alejandro Garnacho suffered a facial injury against BG Pathum on Aston Villa's pre-season tour in Thailand Garnacho did not train with Xabi Alonso's Chelsea squad before leaving for Villa Park in July. Roma were interested in the winger, but their loan offer did not suit Chelsea. Instead, Villa's deal gives the Blues the chance to make their money back after last year's outlay. There is an obligation to buy tied into the loan that is believed to relate to appearances, and it is expected to be achievable - but that does not guarantee anything. For instance, Harvey Elliott would have triggered a move worth £35m if he made just 10 Premier League appearances last season. As it turned out, the Liverpool loanee - now at Valencia - was used just four times by Villa in the top flight. Emery did not feel the 23-year-old was good enough and made up his mind not to sign Elliott permanently just a couple of months into the season. It raised the question for some within the game about whether a loan at Villa should be viewed with caution, and whether other players' careers could be derailed in the way Elliott experienced. It was accepted that Elliott's options this summer were not as extensive following his season at Villa Park. Time will tell whether Garnacho faces the same struggles, having experienced his career stalling over the past two years. He made his Manchester United debut aged 17 and was part of Argentina's Copa America‑winning squad in 2024, but has not added to his eight international caps since November of that year. The Madrid-born attacker also won the Premier League's goal of the season award in 2023-24 for his overhead kick against Everton while playing for United, but his output for Chelsea was disappointing. Emery is waiting to see Garnacho fulfil his full potential at Villa, but the winger will have to wait until he gains the coach's trust, and then take his chance. title: Texas ICE shooting leaves Venezuelan DoorDash driver with bullet in his back, says lawyer
description: The delivery driver was transferred from a hospital to a detention centre, his lawyer tells US media.
body: This video can not be played Watch: 'I am frustrated' - Protestors take to the streets after Austin ICE shooting A Venezuelan DoorDash delivery driver who was shot by ICE agents was transferred from hospital to a detention centre with a bullet still in his back, his lawyer has told US media. The shooting of Wilber Rafael Garcés Perez, 28, triggered protests in Austin, Texas, on Sunday. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said in a statement to the BBC it was investigating the shooting of a man in the Texan capital who had entered the country illegally. It was unclear what led to the shooting with the local mayor and police demanding an investigation. It comes months after a man in Houston was shot dead by an ICE officer. Wilber Rafael Garcés Perez was shot and injured by an ICE officer Attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch told CBS that Garcés Perez called his wife while "yelling in pain" in hospital. She told National Public Radio he was in ICE custody. The Trump administration has ramped up immigration enforcement efforts and arrests during Trump's second term, sparking unrest across several US cities. The administration has defended its policies and the agency's controversial tactics as necessary for public safety and to enact Trump's campaign promise to secure the border and carry out mass deportations. The shooting in Austin on Sunday occurred just before 1300 local time, although details remain scarce. Dozens of protesters, some waving the flags of Mexico and Guatemala, gathered at the scene carrying signs demanding that ICE leave Austin. Local television outlets showed the demonstrators gathering across the street from ​a blue Toyota Corolla that ⁠sustained damage to the passenger-side door, as ICE agents stood nearby, Reuters news agency reported. Mayor Kirk Watson, a Democrat, said that Austinites have a right to know what happened and "a right to feel safe in their city" during a media briefing on Sunday. "They should know the truth," he said, adding that he is pleased that the city will also be involved in the investigation. He added that ICE operations have surged in Austin in recent weeks. ICE has faced intense scrutiny after a number of deadly shootings, including the death of Houston resident Lorenzo Salgado Araujo. Salgado Araujo had not been a target of an ICE investigation, but was shot during an ICE traffic stop, according to DHS. Texas Congressman Greg Casar, a Democrat, has demanded a full and immediate independent investigation into the latest shooting and the release of body camera footage. He also demanded "accountability for any ICE officer who broke the law". Activists say that the administration has violated due process as it carries out the crackdown. Democrats have demanded reforms at the agency, including requiring immigration enforcement agents to wear body cameras and not conceal their faces. Earlier this month the US Department of Justice charged an ICE agent with lying about the non-fatal shooting of a Venezuelan migrant in Minnesota - a rare instance in which the current justice department accused a federal agent of breaking the law on the job. Earlier this week, Florida lawmaker Maria Elvira Salazar, a Republican who has spoken out against the immigration crackdown, released an advert criticising the targeting and detaining of individuals who have no criminal record. Salazar appeared on the CBS programme Face the Nation on Sunday and said that she has since spoken to the president, and believes he will keep the country on the right track. "He gets it more than anybody," she said. What is ICE and what powers do its agents have to use force? title: Divers spend six hours clearing river of waste
description: Divers from the Northampton Scuba School team up with other local organisations for a clean-up.
body: A team of divers from Northampton Scuba School with their haul from the River Nene A team of divers from Northampton Scuba School arranged a six-hour clean-up of the River Nene in Northampton. They collected two old shopping trolleys, a milk churn, a number of car tyres, an old bike, a drill and charger. The event on Saturday 19 September was organised alongside Northampton Active and Northampton Rowing Club, with the aim of clearing as much rubbish from the river as possible. Organisers at Northampton Scuba School said they are committed to removing waste from the River Nene on a regular basis and plan to return in the coming months. A diver from Northampton Scuba School removes a large piece of wood from the River Nene during a six-hour clean-up Team members received a safety briefing before starting A spokesperson for Northampton Scuba School said: "It was an amazing day and a brilliant example of what can be achieved through teamwork, support and a shared commitment to our local environment. We are incredibly proud of everyone who took part and are looking forward to continuing this important work." The clean-up team was loaned two canoes from Northampton Active, which were used to support the divers. The Northampton Canoe and Kayak Club also provided a ladder to help divers get in and out of the water safely. Anyone not diving was invited to join the litter-picking team along the riverbank, where waste was also collected. Organisers said the amount of waste collected shows that there's a lot of work to do, and the team will now support regular dives throughout the year. title: Rising fuel prices 'cost tow truck business £10k'
description: A business says fuel duty will need to be cut by 30p to 50p per litre to help.
body: Oliver du Feu said fuel duty would need to be cut by up to 50p per litre to help manage costs. Rising fuel prices are hitting businesses, with the owner of a vehicle breakdown service saying prices had cost his business between £9,000 and £11,000. Oliver du Feu said it had a "big impact" because trucks, which held between 80 and 120 litres of diesel, were filled up every two days. It comes as a proposition to lower fuel duty - currently about 65p per litre - by 10p per litre between October and December was withdrawn. Jersey's treasury minister said there would be "targeted measures" in the government's budget to help people with the cost of living. Treasury Minister Alan Maclean said cutting fuel duty would be a "blunt tool" Fuel prices have continued to rise since the outbreak of the United States' war with Iran in February. Du Feu said fuel duty would need to be reduced by 30p to 50p per litre to help businesses manage costs. He said he expected prices to keep rising and, while his business had absorbed higher costs so far, he might have to charge customers more. Treasury Minister Alan Maclean said duty cuts were a "blunt tool" and largely helped wealthier people. Carl Walker, from the Jersey Consumer Council, said there was a "misconception" that fuel prices only impacted people who drove. "Of everything that we consume in this island, 97% is imported. "It needs fuel to get here and it needs fuel to be delivered... ultimately it will hit consumers in their pockets, even if they're literally buying a litre of milk in the shop." The Jersey Consumer Council said the number of people using its fuel and food price comparison website had more than doubled since last year. In the UK, the cost of petrol and diesel is the highest it has been since 2022. More news stories for Jersey Listen to the latest news for Jersey The government is set to publish a proposed budget by the end of September before it is debated in December. Deputy Lucy Stephenson said she withdrew her proposition to cut fuel duty following "constructive discussions" with Maclean. Maclean said he could not discuss budget measures as they were being developed. He said it was "possible" people might feel worried that there would be no relief before next year. He said: "Of course things are much more expensive than they were three years ago, but we've seen the pace of increases reduce slightly, which is encouraging. "The first quarter of next year is going to be where people are likely to feel the greatest pressure, and that's what we're focusing on." The director of ATF Fuels in Jersey, Jon Best, said: "Wholesale fuel prices have reached their highest level in four months. "While the Channel Islands are geographically distant from the Middle East, they are not insulated from the global energy market. "Fuel is traded in an international marketplace, meaning disruptions to supply, production, or distribution anywhere in the world can have a direct effect on local wholesale costs." title: Apple Music to open concert venue in Battersea
description: The tech giant has built its own concert hall, but says its not in competition with small venues.
body: The venue will inhabit the north side of the former power station, with views overlooking the Thames The US tech giant Apple is to open a new, state-of-the-art concert hall in London, situated underneath its UK headquarters at Battersea Power Station. The 600-capacity venue will host one-off shows by major recording artists and new bands, all of which will be filmed and broadcast live online. Apple Music's vice president, Oliver Schusser, told BBC News the facility, which is expected to open in the coming weeks, contained "more cameras and speakers than any venue of its size, anywhere in the world". It comes as London's live music scene faces huge pressure, with 45 venues closing in the capital last year alone. It's a reflection of a national trend: Between 2020 and 2025, as the cost of living increased and people made post-Covid lifestyle changes, about 400 of Britain's clubs closed. The rate in London is higher than the rest of the country, so the arrival of a deep-pocketed tech company could give independent venue owners cause for concern. But Schusser said its new venture was not trying to steal customers. "We're not trying to be in the live business. We're not trying to compete with anyone. "We're going to run the venue like a venue, with tickets and everything, but the sole purpose for us is to do great work with artists, to connect artists with fans, and to broadcast the content on Apple Music. "We have really no interest in trying to be in the way of anyone else, and that's one of the main reasons it's a smaller space." The venue has been designed so that artists can configure the stage for everything from huge televisual productions to intimate acoustic sets Artists will arrive on stage after walking past photos of previous Apple Music concerts The venue, known as Apple Music Hall, marks the company's return to London, nine years after it scrapped the popular iTunes Festival, which saw acts like Lady Gaga, Elton John, Britney Spears and Adele play free concerts at venues such as Koko and The Roundhouse. Culture secretary Lisa Nandy welcomed the development, calling it "a huge vote of confidence in the UK as a global creative powerhouse" and "a signal of just how strong our creative sectors really are". Details of the opening act are expected to be announced soon. Lady Gaga launched her third album, Artpop, at the iTunes Festival in London's Roundhouse in 2013 BBC News got an early look at the venue as the finishing touches were being made in early September. It's a small, intimate space, with fluted vaults and brick-lined walls that echo the Art Deco architecture of the former power station. But echo itself won't be an issue -even the bricks have been specially selected to absorb reflected sounds. The stage is 38-foot long, and can be configured for both "in the round" and more traditional front-facing shows, while the dressing rooms are kitted out with en-suite showers and dedicated costume storage areas. The facility also contains new studios for Apple Music's radio stations, which will move from their current home in King's Cross, and dedicated rooms for DJ mixes, writing camps and band rehearsals. The whole building is wired for video and audio, meaning artists can walk in, record a podcast, appear on a radio show, and live-stream a gig in the same day. Apple's hope is that creating bespoke content will help to distinguish its service from competitors like Spotify and Amazon Music. The effort comes after legendary music mogul Jimmy Iovine said music streaming services were "minutes away from being obsolete", because they don't foster a connection between the listener and the music. "It's one dimensional. It's an ATM machine," said Iovine, who has worked with everyone from Bruce Springsteen to Tupac Shakur, in an interview this February. "The artists want to communicate with their fans, period. That's what they want. "Not for philanthropic reasons, but this is what TikTok does. That's what Instagram does." Dressing rooms and green rooms have been designed to fit with the aesthetic of Battersea Power Station Schusser, who has been at Apple for 21 years (including the period from 2014-2018 when Iovine was a creative consultant) agreed. "We want our music services not just to be an anonymous place on the internet where you press a button and music starts playing. "For most artists, it's kind of sad in streaming. There's nothing for them to do. The music gets delivered by the labels, and then it's a bunch of playlists. "But [fans] want to have a chance to meet the artists, know more about the artists, understand why they made an album the way they made it." Schusser said Apple also hoped to promote new and upcoming bands who might otherwise struggle to make headway, as people's listening habits stagnate. "It's one of the biggest opportunities and challenges we have in the music business right now. "There are too many artists who rely on [their back] catalogue. Catalogue music is great, but we need to make sure we have a new era of catalogue music in 10, 20, years from now." Night-time economy in alarming state - association End of hedonism? title: Iran must stop arming Houthis in Yemen, G7 says ahead of UN General Assembly
description: The G7 also condemns "in the strongest terms" Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, saying that the escalation in fighting in Yemen jeopardises global energy security.
body: Iran must "end its arming of and support" for the Houthis in Yemen, the foreign ministers of G7 nations have said in a joint statement. The G7 also condemned "in the strongest terms" Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, adding that the recent escalation in fighting against Saudi-backed forces in Yemen represented a threat to regional and global energy security. Thousands of refugees have fled Yemen in recent days after the Iran-backed group seized territory along the country's Red Sea coastline, including near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a critical shipping route for global trade. The statement comes ahead of the annual UN General Assembly in New York, where senior Iranian officials are due to speak. "We call on the Houthis to immediately cease all military actions, all threats and attacks against civilian shipping, and to return to the political process in good faith," said the foreign ministers of the UK, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States. It went on: "Their reprehensible actions constitute a dangerous pattern of escalation that risks further exacerbating the conflict, undermining international trade and creating global economic instability." "Looking forward, we will continue to support the legitimate Government of Yemen and reaffirm our strong commitment to the unity, sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity of Yemen," the ministers said. Their statement was issued following a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. Yemenis flee across Red Sea as Houthis and Saudi-backed forces escalate war Houthis say they targeted Saudi capital with ballistic missiles Meanwhile, at least six people were killed in Saudi strikes on the strategic Yemeni city of Mokha, the AFP news agency reported, citing Houthi-affiliated media. Two children and a woman were among the dead, while eight others were injured in the attack on the city, which the Houthis seized from pro-government forces earlier this month. Saudi Arabia, which backs the internationally recognised government of Yemen, has not yet commented on the reported strikes. The UN estimates that in all, more than 120,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the sudden surge in fighting along Yemen's Red Sea coast. Earlier this month, the Houthis, who had already seized most of the populated parts of Yemen, took control of Bab al-Mandab, a narrow, maritime chokepoint where the southern Red Sea flows into the Gulf of Aden and the wider Indian Ocean. This video can not be played Watch: Inside a camp for Yemeni refugees in Djibouti Saudi Arabia has retaliated with hundreds of air strikes in the region. The Houthis have also launched hundreds of drones and missiles at cities and infrastructure in south-western Saudi Arabia, including the capital city, Riyadh. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the UK will provide "defensive air-to-air refuelling" support for Saudi Arabia, involving a single British aircraft, a Voyager, based out of RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus. Burnham said the announcement followed a request from Saudi Arabia for "military support", which he agreed to on the advice of Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband. A diplomatic source told AFP that France has pledged support as well, and says is ready to work on "securing" Saudi energy infrastructure via a "strictly defensive approach". Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has also requested military support from President Donald Trump, US media reported. Trump has wavered for weeks over whether to act on a Saudi request for help in fighting the Houthis, the New York Times reported on Monday. The US president had earlier told Fox News that he was in "deciding mode" as he considered options for the next steps in the war against Iran. On Sunday, US embassies across the Middle East issued new security alerts as fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed coalition in Yemen intensified. The Houthis declare themselves to be part of the Iranian-led "axis of resistance" against Israel, the US and the wider West - along with armed group such as Hamas and Lebanon's Hezbollah movement. Tehran has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and says it only supports them politically. title: Outrage in India over viral video of teen molested and her friend beaten
description: Three minors were arrested after videos capturing the assault went viral in India, sparking anger.
body: The incident which took place on Saturday has sparked outrage and anger A video showing a teenaged girl being sexually assaulted and her male friend beaten by a group of men in India's Bihar state has sparked widespread outrage. The school students, both minors, were stopped in Jamui district on 19 September. Footage shared widely online shows them surrounded and repeatedly pleading to be allowed to leave. The boy is seen being slapped and pulled by his collar, while the girl is touched inappropriately and, in another clip, carried away by a man as the boy tries to intervene. Three accused, also minors, have been arrested in connection with the assault. A special investigation team has been set up to catch the other suspects. The disturbing footage has prompted anger over the harassment of the two teenagers and renewed a wider debate about the safety of women and girls in Bihar, as well as questions over the response of state authorities. The outrage intensified after Bihar minister Shravan Kumar said that "sporadic incidents keep happening" and that the government was keeping a watch on them. "The world is not entirely free of crime," he said, adding that those responsible would not be allowed to escape and would face strict action. Umesh Kushwaha, of the governing Janata Dal (United), also faced criticism after referring to such cases as "isolated incidents" and contrasting the government's record with that of the previous RJD administration. Kushwaha later said his remarks had been "distorted and misrepresented" and promised action against those responsible. Police said the incident took place around 19:00 local time [13:30 GMT] on Saturday, but it came to light on Monday after the video of the assault went viral. The teenagers, both students of 10th standard, attended the same coaching institute and had gone to the area to take photographs after their classes, according to police. Jamui police chief Bishwajeet Dayal said neither of them had initially reported the incident - officers began investigating after the video circulated widely online and traced the pair using the registration number of a vehicle visible in the footage. Their statements were subsequently recorded and a case was registered following a written complaint from the girl. A case has been registered under India's stringent Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, or Pocso. Police have also invoked sections of India's criminal code covering assault or criminal force against a woman with intent to outrage her modesty, assault or criminal force with intent to disrobe, and acts carried out with a common intention. Senior police officer KS Anupam said three minors had been arrested and that investigators had established the involvement of two other people. Police have also begun action against 32 social media accounts accused of circulating footage in which the teenagers could be identified, she added. The shocking nature of the assault has provoked outrage online, with many social media users expressing horror and questioning why a group of men believed they had the right to confront two teenagers for being together. Some characterised the incident as an extreme form of "moral policing", while others tagged Bihar police and demanded strict action against the harassers. Shreyasi Singh, a Bihar minister and legislator from Jamui, told NDTV news channel, external the incident had brought "shame to society". Singh, a former international-level sport shooter, said women in Bihar were advancing in many areas but concerns about their safety persisted. She called for the remaining suspects to be arrested quickly and for strict action against those responsible. Opposition leaders, meanwhile, have seized on the case to question the state government's record on women's safety. Rahul Gandhi, MP and senior leader of India's main opposition Congress party, described the footage as "deeply disturbing" and said the incident reflected a patriarchal "belief that men could police a girl's body, movements and choices". "This is not culture. It is patriarchy," Gandhi wrote on X (formerly Twitter). Tejashwi Yadav, the opposition leader in Bihar, said the incident had left him "deeply ashamed" and accused the government of failing to ensure the safety of women and girls in the state. Members of Bihar's governing coalition have rejected the opposition's wider criticism of the state's law-and-order record and said those responsible for the attack would face strict action. India's National Commission for Women has also intervened, calling for all those involved to be identified and arrested and for an impartial investigation. The commission has asked for a report from Bihar police and urged authorities to prevent further sharing of the video clips to protect the girl's identity and privacy. The Bihar State Women's Commission has also sought information from district authorities about the action being taken in the case.
