title: Watch: Ukraine's race to counter a new type of Russian drone
description: Russian attacks on Ukraine are becoming even more devastating than before due to new jet-powered drones, which are much harder to shoot down.
body: This video can not be played Russian attacks on Ukraine are becoming more devastating than before because of their new jet-powered drones, which are harder to shoot down. Russia launched nearly 3,000 of these new drones in August alone and while Kyiv has used missiles and fighter jets to fight against them, it is proving too expensive. Ukraine is now in a race to develop low-cost weapons that can counter them. The BBC's Abdujalil Abdurasulov spoke with Ukrainian air defence units about how they are fighting against this new threat. title: 'Terrifying' 101-acre data centre plans would be 'heartbreaking', campaigners warn
description: Campaigners fear the proposed Canolfan Ddata Menai plans would ruin the landscape.
body: Emma Lewandowicz says the sheer size and environmental impact of the proposed data centre is "terrifying" A proposed data centre spanning 101 acres would have a "heartbreaking" effect on the landscape and wildlife, campaigners have warned. Developers want to build the new centre between Caernarfon and Y Felinheli in Gwynedd, saying it could create more than 900 jobs during construction and a further 200 permanent roles. But nearly 15,000 people signed a petition in opposition to the plans, with local campaigners saying the proposed development was too big and would lead to noise pollution and ruin the landscape. A spokesperson for Canolfan Ddata Menai said it would "transform and revitalise the long-derelict" site and offer significant employment, with plans currently out for public consultation. Data centres are buildings full of powerful computers used to run digital services, from online banking to movie streaming. The UK government classifies them as critical national infrastructure and, according to recent Senedd research, "most jobs in the UK" are now reliant on them. Planning documents show the proposed centre would include five main buildings for storing data with the highest of them standing at 30m (98ft). But campaigners have raised concerns about water usage, the effect on the environment and how many jobs would go to local residents. I used to live in a quiet area - now a data centre overlooks my garden A backlash over data centres is another threat to the AI juggernaut More than 100 people attended a public meeting on Saturday with many raising concerns. Among those opposing the plans is Emyr Davies, whose house lies not far from where the boundary of the site would be, should it be approved. "Visually it would have a massive effect, not just for us here in Caernarfon but also in Anglesey, and it would change the views of Snowdonia forevermore," he said. "It's going to be horrific for the locals, not just visually but also we're worried about the noise." Planning documents refer to a study showing the noise would affect people within a 2.5-mile (4km) radius. Davies said he would even consider selling his house if plans were approved. "I wouldn't want to bring my three children up next to this industrial estate," he said. Emyr Davies' house is not far from the boundary of the proposed site Campaigners have also raised concerns about water usage by the centre, with details showing on average it would use around 700,000 litres a day, although that figure could be nearer to 12 million litres a day at its maximum. Developers said this figure was the "higher maximum-use scenario that is stated as a necessary requirement of the environmental assessment". It added no water would be taken from the Menai Strait and no warm cooling water would be discharged into it. But campaigners have warned the sheer size of the development would destroy the local landscape, with submitted plans showing the centre would span beyond the existing old disused Ferodo site - the planned location of the new data centre. "I'm not against every type of development at Ferodo," said councillor Gwion Emyr. "We need something there and it's been empty for over 20 years. "There are advantages and disadvantages, but jobs can't come at the expense of the local community." The proposed data centre would be built on an industrial site that has remained vacant for years Emma Lewandowicz also lives locally and said the proposed development would be "heartbreaking". "It's really terrifying just to see the sheer size of it and the environmental impact, it's not just necessarily the noise but the effect on the community," she said. "It's easy to ignore it when it's not on your doorstep but these things, they sort of crop up when you're not looking. "I've got a little boy and I feel like it would tear our futures apart... I know they're promising jobs and that always sounds promising on the surface but beneath all that it's just really heartbreaking." In Case You Missed It: Why a hospital park and ride could be replaced by a data centre A proposal to build a data centre on a Cardiff hospital park-and-ride has sparked debate. As demand for AI grows, who benefits and what are the trade-offs? There are currently 568 data centres listed in the UK, according to the data centre map, external. Research suggests that number is set to increase by almost a fifth with nine proposed in Wales. A Senedd Research document, external recently outlined the opportunities that data centres could bring, including "jobs, investment, skills development and support for innovation". But it also noted the "significant resource and policy questions they raise", including electricity demand, grid capacity, water use, land requirements, biodiversity and impacts on local communities. Ofgem said the amount of electricity being requested by data centre projects seeking to connect to the grid had risen from 41GW to 125GW in the past year, reflecting a sharp increase in demand. Water UK, the trade association for the UK's water industry, estimated, external that data centres used approximately 6.6 million litres of water each day - the equivalent used by 20,000 average homes. By some analyses, the UK is already the third-largest nation for data centres behind the US and Germany. A spokesperson for Canolfan Ddata Menai said it understood locals' concerns about the scale of the development and wanted discussion to be based on accurate information. "The proposed data centre would transform a long-derelict industrial site that has remained vacant for years, addressing contamination and safety issues through private investment," the spokesperson said. "The design has been developed to minimise visual impact through building materials, landscaping and layout." title: Soaring fuel costs hit small businesses
description: It comes as fuel prices reach their highest since 2022, driven by conflict in the Middle East.
body: Noel Lewis, who runs a haulage company in Worcestershire, says he is facing more than £1,200 a week in extra fuel costs Small businesses are bearing the brunt of rising fuel prices, the owner of a haulage company has said. Noel Lewis, who runs Lewis Light Haulage & Storage in Stourport-on-Severn, Worcestershire, said he was having to absorb thousands of pounds a month in extra costs due to the price of fuel. His comments come as fuel prices - driven by conflict in the Middle East - reach their highest point since 2022, with diesel averaging at £1.92 per litre according to the RAC. A Treasury spokesperson said the government continued "to protect the British people and businesses from this crisis". "This means drivers benefit from the extension of the 5p fuel duty cut, with diesel 11p per litre cheaper until the end of the year than it would have been compared to plans inherited from the previous government," they added. Hauliers would also benefit from a 12-month road tax "holiday", the spokesperson said. With six vehicles run by his company, Lewis said he was now facing around £1,200 in extra fuel costs per week. Smaller businesses like his, he said, were now struggling to compete with larger firms with "bigger buying power on their fuel". "They have the economies of scale working in their favour [...] if you put your prices up somebody might come in and be able to suffer that cost for a few weeks, just to knock you out the game," he said. The price of diesel is nearly £2 a litre in Telford, Shropshire Lewis explained that he and his wife had been forced to take wage cuts in order to keep money in the business and avoid passing price increases onto customers. "With businesses, you want to keep custom coming back to you so you do not want to put your prices too high," he said. According to the RAC, the cost of filling up a vehicle is now at a similar level to when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The US-Israel war with Iran has severely disrupted the production and transportation of oil across the region, with the effects felt worldwide. It is not just businesses being impacted - individual drivers are also seeing soaring prices at the pumps. Susan Parkes from Telford drives a diesel car and said the prices she pays had become "extortionate." "We went on holiday and we had to put in an extra £20 in the tank which, brought us up to about £120," Parkes added "You have to cut your cloth accordingly. Where you are used to having a treat, you have got to think about your meals and shopping [because of money spent on fuel]." Susan Parkes said the price of diesel had become "extortionate" Katie Woollacott, also from Telford, said she used an app to find the cheapest fuel and often drove outside the town to find lower prices. "Personally, I would rather travel about 20 minutes to 30 minutes going either towards Birmingham or Whitchurch, because it's like 20p cheaper," she said. "I stopped to refill the other day and it cost me about almost £70 for my 1.6 litre Mini, so it's definitely a jump as I do not normally spend over 50. A government spokesperson said they would "tackle the cost of living to make life's essentials affordable again and bring back hope", and pointed towards the Fuel Finder service which uses data to help drivers find the cheapest fuel near them. title: Winter support planned for vulnerable residents
description: People could be eligible for awards of between £150 to £250, depending on their circumstances.
body: Those applying for the financial help must live in the Tandridge District Council area A Surrey council is poised to set aside £150,000 to support its most vulnerable residents through the winter months. Tandridge District Council plans to run its winter support scheme for another year, giving eligible residents money to help with essentials and bills. Councillors on the strategy and resources committee are due to consider the proposals this week, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service. "Each past scheme has helped nearly 500 households," a report issued ahead of Thursday's meeting says. Those applying for the support must be a householder aged 16 or over, have their primary residence in the Tandridge District Council area and be struggling to meet their essential short-term needs. Several categories of residents will be prioritised for aid, including those with dependent children, those with disabilities, pensioners, carers, those at risk of homelessness and victims of domestic abuse. Council officers will assess any application for support and decide on each case based on "local economic factors and arrangements in place with other agencies". The report adds the scheme will be fully funded by Tandridge District Council using allocated funds. Applications would open on 9 November if the renewed programme is approved. "Awards will not normally exceed £150 for households without children and £250 for households containing children," the report adds. title: Traffic chaos in Perthshire villages after Google Maps glitch
description: The issue saw vehicles leave the A9 and travel through the Perthshire villages of Ballinluig, Tulliemet and Guay.
body: Drivers were diverted off the A9 and on to the unclassified 163 road A Google Maps glitch has caused chaos after traffic was mistakenly diverted from the A9 to a single-track road between Dunkeld and Pitlochry. The issue - which was first noticed on Friday - saw vehicles, including campervans, leave the trunk road and travel through the Perthshire villages of Ballinluig, Tulliemet and Guay. On Saturday Transport Scotland posted on X on that Google Maps was falsely reporting the A9 as closed and was recommending an "inconvenient alternate route" when it remained open. The problem now appears to be resolved but local residents said the inaccurate information left them worried and, in some cases, unable to leave their homes. "People were just doing as Google said but the excessive speed was unbelievable," Joanne Boyne, who lives in Guay, told BBC Scotland News. "Traffic was going in both directions so when cars came to a section where nobody could pass, everyone had to reverse." She said the U163 road is a single-track road with no designated passing places. The winding and narrow nature of the road and the overgrown trees and bushes make it unsafe to drive fast. But over the weekend, she saw campervans, a large coach and cars with trailers - one towing a boat - all drive down it, some at speeds as fast as 40mph. "We were really worried about trying to get to potential appointments or if there was an emergency," Boyne said. The bumper-to-bumper traffic meant there would have been no space for an ambulance or fire engine to get past if something was to happen, which was a serious concern in the community. Boyne's parents live about three miles away from her in Tulliemet. "My parents live on the road and they have not been able to leave their house since Friday - even to go for a walk - because it has been too dangerous," she said. The drive from her house to her parents' house would normally take her about 10 minutes but, when she went to check on them at the weekend, it took her almost 45 minutes to get there. Joanne added that she struggled to get to work at about 07:50 on Monday as there were three cars waiting to turn onto the road from the A9, which is unusual. Residents, who live next to the road, struggled to leave Joanne Boyne said the traffic impacted her commute to work on Monday morning Laura Hansler, from the A9 Dual Action campaign group, said the bug was fixed after a member of the group contacted the Google Maps team in London. But she said problems appear on Google Maps now and again but she did not know what causes them. Laura added that Google Maps had previously shown incorrect speed limits on sections of the trunk road. "It is not an old diversion that was never cancelled, it is one of these daft diversions that make no sense," she said. "Sometimes it will tell you the road is closed because there has been a collision but sometimes Google Maps acts up for no reason." Google has been contacted for comment. Large vehicles were seen driving along the narrow single-track road Laura said people who drive on the A9 tend to use a satnav as a safety feature to avoid collisions and roadworks. She added many of the diversion routes are unsuitable for large vehicles and volumes of traffic. "People are using them proactively and on the A9 when someone sees a diversion, they automatically presume it is because something has happened," she said. "If these maps are not updated, it will cause an accident, which was my biggest fear at the weekend. "It was just out of hand." Laura said she had been in touch with Transport Scotland and the Scottish government on several occasions about the issue. But Transport Scotland told her it did not have a direct relationship or feed to satellite navigation providers, such as Google. The campaign group is now seeking further response from the government on the problem and calling for action to be taken to prevent future incidents. title: Inside Scotland's wildcat HQ - 'It's like Big Brother for cats'
description: The Saving Wildcats partnership is keeping an eye on the latest wildcats being bred in captivity for release into the Cairngorms.
body: From behind a giant bank of screens in a small windowless room, Estelle Morgan, animal team leader from the Saving Wildcats partnership, is keeping an eye on the latest wildcats being bred in captivity for release into the Cairngorms. "It's like Big Brother for cats", she says of the 72 cameras being used to watch over the animals in their enclosures. They are assessing whether they're healthy and have the behavioural potential to survive in the wild. "We want to know what the cats are actually doing," she says. Estelle Morgan monitors the wildcats via 72 cameras in the Cairngorms "What are they like without us there? she adds. "Are they able to climb? Are they able to pounce? Can they navigate complex structures? Are they active at natural times?" This year they were even able to capture on camera for the first time a wildcat giving birth. It is quite a surveillance programme - but it has to be. They don't want the cats to become comfortable around people and contact is kept to an absolute minimum. They are also assessing the cats' behaviour ahead of being released: "If we've got some cats which are quite bold does that mean they're more likely to go near roads in the wild, or venture closer to a farm or to human settlements," she says. For the first time this year, Saving Wildcats were able to observe a wildcat having its kittens Saving Wildcats has been successful in reintroducing 46 wildcats into the flats and foothills of the Cairngorms. Those wildcats have successfully reproduced and the team working on the project are aware of at least 20 wild-born litters to released females since 2024. There are now plans to reintroduce wildcat populations into other areas in Scotland. The Cairngorm project has had "an enormous amount of success, but it is only the first step," says NatureScot species project manager Dr Martin Gaywood. Now he says they need to think big: "Wildcat conservation is really complex. It has all sorts of threats and issues and in order to restore wildcats to the whole of Scotland we need to plan long term and we need to plan at a big scale." Dr Gaywood is optimistic that with careful planning the translocation of wildcats into other parts of Scotland could happen within years: "It would be great maybe within the next five years to start at least one new project, you never know maybe two," he says. Helen Senn said climate incidents had the potential to have an impact on the wildcat conservation programme As well as identifying new release sites, the national strategy will prioritise restoring and reconnecting wildcat habitats to allow the expansion of their range. In the areas chosen for the eventual translocation of wildcat populations there will be additional microchipping, neutering and vaccination of pet and feral cats to reduce interbreeding. Dr Helen Senn, head of conservation and science at the Royal Zoological Society of Scotland (RZSS), says climate change is one of the reasons why is it important to identify other areas in which wildcat populations can be reintroduced. "We have had some really big climate incidents here in the Strath over the last couple of years. "We've had some major storms and flooding incidents. We've also had, unfortunately, a very significant forest fire in the north of the release area and all of these have the potential to impact the population". She adds: "The way to be resilient to risk is to have larger population sizes and to have populations present in multiple areas". Louise Hughes leads the team that tracks the wildcats as they establish their new territories In 2018, scientists warned that the Scottish wildcat population was functionally extinct. They are classed as critically endangered so even once released the wildcats that now roam the Cairngorms are still carefully monitored. A network of trail cameras - up to 100 at any one time - captures their movements. The wildcats are also fitted with collars which drop off after around seven to nine months in the wild which emit a signal for a short period of time every day. Louise Hughes, who is operations manager for the Saving Wildcats partnership, explains that the information they are gathering is invaluable, although not always easy to pick up. She says the wildcats establishing their new territories: "Might be down a hole, they might be in a tree root, they might have gone for a wander over the mountains." But the data can help the scientists learn more about the cats' movements and hunting behaviour. It can also help them understand the habitat the wildcats are using. The project has released 46 wildcats into the foothills of the Cairngorms Scottish Land and Estates has been supportive of the Scottish Wildcat Conservation Action Plan. Several estates have been actively helping: providing release sites, monitoring the wildcats, recording sightings. Lots of the information being gathered does come from public sightings. Louise takes me to the territory on which one wildcat that was recently captured on camera: "The cat that lives in this territory, Sully, is an amazing cat. She was released in 2024 and she has been captured on video swimming across the River Spey." Wildcats, she says, "never cease to surprise us." Estelle Morgan points out that wildcats were once widespread throughout the UK. The work they are doing in the Cairngorms will help inform releases elsewhere in Scotland. She says the only native cat found in the wild in Britain "deserves to be here, they're part of the landscape." title: Drivers rethink spending as fuel prices climb
description: Drivers and firms in the West Midlands say rising prices are hitting budgets and forcing cutbacks.
body: This video can not be played Motorists are facing higher costs at the pump as global oil prices rise Soaring fuel prices are forcing motorists to cut back on everyday spending and adding tens of thousands of pounds a week to business costs, with petrol at its highest level since November 2022. Drivers say they are changing their spending habits to cope with rising costs at the pump, while businesses warn higher fuel bills are placing increasing pressure on their finances. Petrol prices rose to an average of 161.3p per litre between July and August, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), the highest level recorded since November 2022, when Russia's invasion of Ukraine pushed up global energy costs. Diesel is also expected to top £2 per litre in the coming days. Among those feeling the impact is Arvander Pabla in Willenhall, in the West Midlands, who drives a lot every day and says rising fuel costs have forced him to make cutbacks elsewhere. "I do nearly 70, 75 miles per day, and it has really affected me price wise, because it has nearly gone double," he said. To create more room in his budget for fuel, he said he had reduced spending on takeaways and eating out, and was considering replacing his car with a more fuel-efficient vehicle. Arvander Pabla said rising fuel prices had forced him to cut spending elsewhere. Motorist Sue Willis said the rising cost of filling up was becoming increasingly difficult for households to absorb. "It's absolutely ridiculous, how we are expected to keep paying for it, I don't know," she said. "How people are coping as families I don't know, I really don't know." Sue Willis said the cost of filling up was putting pressure on household budgets. At a petrol station in Willenhall, fuel retailer Shailesh Parekh said rising wholesale costs were affecting both businesses and customers. Parekh, director of Midland Motor Fuels Ltd, which operates seven petrol stations across the region, said: "We certainly don't have any control over it, we just have to try and mitigate as much as we can the price increases. "We do so by filling our tanks up when the prices are going up or delaying the purchase of fuel when prices are going down. "Most people have a budget for how much fuel they have per week so as prices go up, the number of litres that are sold, drops." Fuel retailer Shailesh Parekh said customers were buying fewer litres as prices rise The increase comes as conflict in the Middle East continues to disrupt global oil supplies. The price of a barrel of oil has risen to about $91, compared with $73 before hostilities began earlier this year. Overall, motor fuel prices increased by 23% compared with August last year. Rising fuel costs are also contributing to inflation, increasing pressure on the prices of other goods and services. Among the businesses most exposed are haulage firms. BJS Haulage, based in the West Midlands, employs more than 1,100 people and operates 140 trucks and 350 vans. The company said fuel represents about a third of its costs and has increased expenditure by about £40,000 a week. Sales director David McWilliams said: "It is a cost we try and pass on to our customers but our customers are under their own cost constraints at the moment. "I think only the government can intervene now, whether it's a VAT reduction. "Horrifyingly we're hearing of the fuel levy getting increased in the next budget, that would just be disastrous for this industry." BJS Haulage sales director David McWilliams said only government intervention could ease pressure on the industry. The rising costs have prompted renewed political debate over fuel duty. The government has postponed a planned increase in fuel duty until the end of December, while Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey has called for an immediate 10p-a-litre cut until Christmas, arguing motorists need support with the cost of living. title: Watch: What to expect from the UN General Assembly
description: The BBC’s Sarah Smith outlines which world leaders Trump is set to meet and the key topics expected on the agenda.
body: This video can not be played World leaders have descended on New York for this year's UN General Assembly. The 81st High-Level Week brings together nearly 130 leaders under the theme, “Restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations that delivers for all.” The BBC’s Sarah Smith outlines who US President Donald Trump is set to meet and the key topics expected to be on the agenda. title: Watch: Six-year-old girl from China sets new Rubik's Cube world record
description: Lian Yunzhi broke the women's world record twice in three days at World Cube Association competitions.
body: This video can not be played A young girl has broken the women's world record for the 3x3x3 Rubik's Cube twice in three days at the World Cube Association. At age six, Lian Yunzhi has become the only female cuber in the world to have an average time under 4.5 seconds. She first broke the record with an average of 4.52 seconds and then 4.27 seconds at competitions in Wuhan and Guangzhou, China. The young competitor from Sichuan Province has mastered more than 1,300 Rubik's Cube solving algorithms after vigorous training that involved spending two to three hours a day on the cube over the past year. title: Canadian province sues OpenAI over Tumbler Ridge school shooting
description: British Columbia has accused the company of failing to report the shooter's troubling interactions with ChatGPT to law enforcement.
body: A Canadian province is suing OpenAI over its alleged failure to notify authorities about concerning user interactions on ChatGPT prior to the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting. The company has previously apologised for not flagging Jessie Van Rootselaar's account to law enforcement before the 18-year-old killed eight people, including six children, in February. British Columbia attorney general Niki Sharma said the lawsuit, filed to a US federal court on Monday, raised questions about "the responsibilities of technology companies when they become aware of credible threats of serious violence". Families of those killed or injured in the shooting have filed separate lawsuits against OpenAI. Media reports revealed that Van Rootselaar's ChatGPT activity was flagged by OpenAI's safety team for references to gun violence months before the attack, but the company did not alert local authorities. In April, OpenAI's chief executive Sam Altman apologised to the families of the victims. "I am deeply sorry that we did not alert law enforcement," Altman wrote in an open letter. The BBC has requested comment from OpenAI regarding the latest lawsuit. "To date, OpenAI has not taken meaningful steps to address the concerns raised by survivors, families and the Tumbler Ridge community," Sharma said in a statement. "The company still has an opportunity to demonstrate accountability by strengthening safeguards, improving transparency and taking concrete action to help prevent similar tragedies in the future." Speaking to reporters on Monday, Sharma said she had not read the contents of the OpenAI chats. "We have asked OpenAI to disclose these chats. They have refused. We should all be asking them: Why?" she said, according to CBC, external. Sharma said the lawsuit was filed in California, as the alleged decision not to report the shooter's ChatGPT account occurred in that US state, according to AFP. Sharma told reporters that any financial damages won by the province would go towards rebuilding the secondary school. title: Burnham expects to find 'common ground' with Trump in first meeting
description: In New York, the prime minister will also deliver a speech to the UN General Assembly expected to be focused on AI.
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham and his wife, Marie-France Van Heel, board the aircraft taking them to New York Andy Burnham said he expects to find "common ground" with Donald Trump at the pair's first face-to-face meeting on Tuesday. The prime minister and US president are in New York City for the annual gathering of world leaders at the United Nations. The two men have spoken by phone twice since Burnham became prime minister in July, with Downing Street saying those calls established a "productive relationship". "We've found a connection. So, I will go with where I feel it's right, to meet him where he is at, and search for that common ground, which I'm sure we'll find," the prime minister told reporters on his flight to the US, adding "I'm looking forward to it." Burnham says he told Trump UK will be pragmatic about North Sea oil Burnham says he's not embarrassed about hoax message exchange Asked about the state of the relationship between the UK and US, the prime minister said he believes it is "as strong as it's ever been". Burnham has travelled to New York with his wife, Marie-France Van Heel, for a day of diplomacy and a speech to the UN General Assembly, which is expected to focus on the opportunities and dangers associated with artificial intelligence (AI). He said: "I will be making the case for closer international co-operation on AI, a just and lasting peace in Ukraine, and renewed efforts to bring an end to the conflict in the Middle East because what happens abroad impacts each and every one of us at home." The prime minister will also announce the start of work on a new AI and Autonomy partnership between the UK and the US, focused on protecting critical national infrastructure using AI tech. Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey is expected to criticise this plan at the final day of his party's conference, saying it "doesn't come close to meeting the scale of the threat" and "only risks making us more dependent on a Trump administration in the pocket of the tech bros". He will also call for a global pause on superintelligent AI and propose a new International AI Safety Agency. His criticisms come after a series of stark warnings from the AI industry about the technology's possible dangers. For a new British prime minister, the first meeting with a US president has always been a pivotal encounter, but officials are well aware of the added jeopardy of a public appearance alongside the most unpredictable president in American history. In advance of the meeting, the UK revealed that the UK and the US have, for the first time, fired an American torpedo from a British undersea drone in a military exercise. The torpedo, described as "heavyweight" by UK officials, is "designed to sink ships and deep diving submarines", Downing Street said. It was launched in UK waters last week from a 12-metre long undersea drone called Excalibur, made in Plymouth. It is the first time either the UK or the US have launched a torpedo from an uncrewed underwater vessel, rather than a crewed submarine, and is seen as a breakthrough in attempts to protect vital infrastructure such as deep sea data cables. "Our work together already shows what can be achieved when our two countries combine our expertise and innovation," the prime minister said. Burnham was also asked by reporters about the UK government seeking to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius and pay to lease back the joint US-UK military base on Diego Garcia. It was confirmed in April that the deal had been paused indefinitely because of Trump pulling his support. Burnham spoke to the Mauritian prime minister, Navin Ramgoolam, on Monday. He was asked by reporters to outline what he had told Ramgoolam, whether he supported the deal and if he had a plan to convince Trump to back it. Burnham replied: "I said that we remain determined to secure the long-term operation of the base, which is crucial to our security and that of our allies. "The assurance I gave was I will work towards a resolution, at the moment we don't have that, but I gave an assurance that I would commit to working towards one." title: Lithuania ready to 'fight back' but has evacuation plans in face of Russia threats, PM tells BBC
description: Sinkevičius told BBC Newsnight Lithuanians feel "constantly threatened" by Moscow, but the nation was prepared to "fight back" if attacked.
body: This video can not be played ‘We will fight back’ if Russia attacks, Lithuanian PM says Lithuania's prime minister has told the BBC his country has made evacuation plans in the face of threats from Russia, but added they "will not surrender" if attacked. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius told Newsnight that Lithuanians feel "constantly threatened" by Russia, in part because of drones entering the nation's airspace. He told Newsnight if his country was attacked, "we will fight back... we will engage". But he said there were plans for a "variety of scenarios" and used an example of getting elderly citizens out of cities "smoothly" and avoiding traffic jams. Lithuania, a Nato member, shares a land border with the Russian enclave of Kaliningad. "We're thinking about a variety of scenarios, not all of them are being discussed very much publicly," Sinkevičius told the BBC. "We face concrete threats, not on a daily basis, but we're experiencing them and it's a true reality for us." Sinkevičius also said the UK needed a "shift in the mindset" in terms of its approach to defence, but noted that Lithuania was "closer to the border and closer to [the] threat". It comes just a week after Nato fighter pilots shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace. Though the origins of the drone have not been confirmed, Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas told Newshour that it came from the direction of Belarus, Lithuania's neighbour and a key Russian ally. The UK's Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "Thanks to the swift and professional actions of Lithuanian and Italian forces, Nato once again demonstrated our readiness to protect our airspace. "We stand united, around the clock, in defence of every inch of Nato territory." Moscow did not comment on the incident. Military drone incursions have become increasingly common across Europe since the beginning of Russia's full-scale of invasion of Ukraine. Residents in Lithuania's capital Vilnius were also forced to take shelter in May after a drone alert was triggered, briefly grounding flights and rail travel. Nato jets have scrambled multiple times to shoot down stray Ukrainian drones that have crossed into fellow Baltic countries Estonia and Latvia this year. Ukraine has blamed the stray drones on Russian electronic warfare, technology designed to change the flight paths of Ukrainian drones. Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia all joined Nato in 2004, becoming signatories to the Article 5 provision that states "an armed attack against one NATO member shall be considered an attack against all members". War may be coming. Are we psychologically ready? title: The Papers: 'Air traffic out of control' and 'RAF to help Saudis'
description: A second glitch this month in the national air traffic system and the PM's first major foreign policy move lead the papers.
body: British air traffic is "out of control", writes the Metro, after a second glitch to the control system this month grounded "thousands" of flights. Now, it says airline chiefs are calling for the boss of the National Air Traffic Services (Nats) to be sacked. Transport secretary Heidi Alexander has called the outage "deeply frustrating". Also on the Metro's front page, "Cindy's agony" as Presley Gerber, son of supermodel Cindy Crawford, has died aged 27. The lead story for the Telegraph is Prime Minister Andy Burnham's decision to send "RAF to help Saudis" against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen. The PM said he had agreed to give refuelling support to Saudi jets on advice from Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband. The Times also leads with "military aid for Saudis", quoting Burnham as saying that getting oil flowing will help the cost of living. This is his "first big foreign policy intervention", the paper notes. Also on its front page, The Times reports that most inmates freed as part of the early release scheme will not be given a tag before their release. The paper says the Probation Service does not have capacity to fit monitoring tags before releases begin on 1 October and that released inmates will instead be tagged "once in the community". The Guardian too has British support for Saudi Arabia as its top story. It also notes the PM has said he will use his first meeting with US President Donald Trump to urge him to end the conflict in Iran. In domestic news, Martha's Rule, which allows patients, staff and relatives to request a review of their care, is being expanded across all A&Es in England. The Independent echoes several other fronts with Burnham's announcement about aid to Saudi Arabia, which comes as he prepares to meet Trump at the UN in New York City. The paper also carries a striking image of a burning building following a Russian attack on Zaporizhzhia on Monday. In other NHS news, the Daily Mirror reports that the health service "needs 55,000 more nurses". A "damning" report found that the shortfall is double the advertised vacancies, "putting patients at risk". Like several of Tuesday's papers, it also previews the upcoming season of the Celebrity Traitors, due to start on 1 October. On the front page of the Sun is a call for a retrial for nurse Lucy Letby by a doctor who originally accused her. Now, Dr John Gibbs tells the paper he is "not sure of guilt". Letby is serving 15 whole life sentences after she was convicted of the murder of seven babies and the attempted murder of seven others. The Daily Mail says there is a "new small boat farce" after it reports a dinghy carrying "up to seven migrants" landed unintercepted near Folkestone, Kent. It reports five of the occupants were apprehended "only after a GB News producer alerted the authorities". The UK has fired a torpedo from an undersea drone in what The i Paper says is a "new warning to Putin". This was the first test of the "XV Excalibur" drone, it adds. The Financial Times reports that "Kremlin-aided forgers moved $7bn through global banks". The Kremlin-backed fintech company "tricked its way" into Standard Chartered, Citigroup and other international banks in a case of "old-fashioned money laundering". In an exclusive for the Daily Express, leader of the Conservatives Kemi Badenoch tells the paper "more freedom [is] given to new arrivals in Britain than British citizens." She was pictured with residents of Piddington, who have voted to leave the UK in a symbolic referendum to protest the government housing migrants nearby. "Racing done for!" laments the Daily Star as the head of Betfred, Fred Done, says he "won't sponsor the Derby if bet shop tax rises". The Star says his sponsorship warning applies to racing's five Classics. Sign up for our morning newsletter and get BBC News in your inbox. title: Autumn equinox 2026: When is it and what happens?
description: In the northern hemisphere, the September equinox marks the start of astronomical autumn.
body: Astronomical autumn begins this week, with the autumn equinox taking place in the early hours of Wednesday. The equinox will occur at 01:06 BST on 23 September, according to Royal Museums Greenwich. It is a precise moment in time when the Sun crosses the celestial equator and neither hemisphere is tilted towards or away from the Sun, meaning day and night are roughly equal in length across the world. And while the equinox itself cannot be seen, the day has cultural and spiritual significance for some people. Gatherings take place at sites including Stonehenge, where people come together to mark the occasion and watch the Sun rise. Many people, including druids and pagans, gather at Stonehenge to take part in a autumn equinox celebration The word "equinox" comes from Latin and means equal night. At the equinox, the daylight measurement is taken from the point when the centre of the Sun is at the horizon, and is 12 hours sunrise to sunset and 12 hours sunset to sunrise. However, it is the top edge of the Sun which is visible first at sunrise and last at sunset. Because of light refraction - light being bent by the atmosphere - there is still light for a time when the Sun is not directly visible. This adds extra time to daylight hours. In autumn, this means that the time when day and night are actually equal happens after the equinox. This is known as the "equilux", which means equal light. This year, that happens in the UK on Friday 25 or Saturday 26 September, depending on your latitude. Although the equinox happens at the same moment everywhere, the change in hours of daylight is not the same across the UK. The further north you go, the bigger the difference between the long days of summer and the short days of winter. That means places in northern Scotland are losing daylight more quickly at this time of year than parts of southern England. Around the autumn equinox, the change is particularly noticeable as sunrise gets later and sunset earlier. Sunrises like this one in Dunbar, East Lothian, will will get progressively later as autumn continues The autumn equinox may mark the start of astronomical autumn, but it does not necessarily mean there will be a sudden change in the weather. As the Sun gets lower in the sky and the days shorten, temperatures generally fall as we head further into autumn. So far this September, UK mean temperatures have been above average overall, according to the Met Office. There is still some warmth in the forecast this week, particularly in the south-east of England, before rain moves across the UK on Wednesday, followed by fresher conditions on Thursday. Towards the end of September, changeable weather is expected, with temperatures likely to remain slightly above average overall. However, clearer and cooler nights could bring some fog and even frost in places. title: Schools not ready for AI and 'crying out' for government guidance, report warns
description: Author Sir Anthony Seldon says AI needs to be addressed with the same urgency as a war or epidemic.
body: Schools are "crying out" for guidance from government on how pupils and teachers can use AI safely and effectively, a new report has warned. Sir Anthony Seldon, former head teacher and author on AI in education, says the technology is being used more and more frequently, but that its introduction has been "chaotic and anarchic". His report calls for the government to roll out a national framework for adopting AI in education in England, including training teachers on how to use it, which schools should use to develop their own "AI strategies" by September next year. The government says its changes to the curriculum in England will give children digital skills and help them spot disinformation. Sir Anthony's report, co-authored with venture capitalist Tim Bunting, says schools have not been prepared for AI's arrival. Sir Anthony co-founded the group AI in Education, which was set up in 2023 to help educational institutions navigate AI safely. His report argues that getting a grip of AI requires the same level of national urgency as wars and epidemics, and requires a taskforce modelled on the one which helped to roll out the Covid vaccine. Sir Anthony Seldon's report says "standing still is not an option" on AI The report recommends a 10-point plan for AI in education in England, including: The prime minister delivering a landmark speech to set out the importance of aligning education with how AI is used in the real world Schools and colleges developing their own AI strategies, and having Ofsted assess their implementation as part of its inspections A mass information campaign to set out the opportunities and risks of AI Using AI to transform the way schools and colleges collect and use data to track pupil progress Reforming assessments into a "two-lane" system of both exams and a "continuous evaluation of a student's understanding" using AI The report says its poll of young people suggests many of those who responded thought AI was making education less important in their lives, with some saying it could eventually replace teachers and make universities "useless". "Put simply, education has not kept pace with how – and how much – young people are already using AI, and that gap is starting to show up as a loss of perceived value in the institution itself," the report says. A spokesperson for the Department for Education says ministers take the "significant opportunities and challenges" of AI "incredibly seriously". As well as refreshing the curriculum in England, they say they are building new AI tutoring tools and introducing new vocational routes to get children into successful careers. Some schools have already embedded AI into the curriculum. Benjamin Barker, principal at King's Leadership Academy in Liverpool, says he wants his students to learn how to use tools safely, while also developing their critical thinking skills. Student Emma, 12, says she uses AI for her robotics projects, as well as proof-reading her English homework, and believes more students should be taught how to use it responsibly. "AI is coming into the future. It's getting more advanced," she says. "There's no way we're going to completely pull back from it. So I think that we should use it to be better people." AI has entered the classroom - but is it the solution for overworked teachers? title: New right to bereavement leave to cover step and half relatives
description: The new law will also cover foster, kinship care and adoptive relationships, as well as early pregnancy loss.
body: A new legal right to unpaid time off work after suffering a bereavement will cover step and half relatives, as well as foster, kinship care and adoptive relationships, the government has said. From April next year, employees in Great Britain who lose a spouse, partner, parent, adult child or sibling will be entitled to up to two weeks' unpaid leave. The government had already confirmed the new rights will also apply to parents who experience a miscarriage before 24 weeks of pregnancy. Previously only parents who have lost a child aged under 18 or stillborn from 24 weeks had a legal right to bereavement leave. The Employment Rights Act, which became law in December 2025, introduced a new legal right to unpaid leave for employees who have suffered a bereavement, including pregnancy loss, from the first day in a job. 'I went back after 3 days': Calls for miscarriage bereavement leave How will the changes to workers' rights affect you? Following a consultation, the government has now set out exactly who the new right will apply to. It said including step, half, adoptive, foster and kinship care relationships – where family or friends take care of a child when their parents are not able to - would "bring the UK's laws into the 21st century". Welcoming the move, the chief executive of the Kinship charity, Lucy Peake, said: "Kinship families grieve the loss of a loved one just like any other family, and this right to take time off work will help ensure they are treated fairly alongside other bereaved families." Meanwhile, the right also covers women and their partners who experience a pregnancy loss, including miscarriage, terminations and unsuccessful IVF embryo transfers. It will also apply to the other biological parent, or intended parents in a surrogacy arrangement. Employees will be able to take the leave flexibly within 56 weeks of the loss, rather than as a full block. The CBI, which represents UK businesses, said many employers already provide compassionate leave in these circumstances and it would engage with the government and unions to ensure the details work in practice. However, the government said "there needs to be a safety net beyond this discretion". Minister for the Future of Work, Kate Dearden, said: "No one should have to fight for time to grieve. "These changes back people going through some of the hardest moments of life, whoever they are and wherever they work." Miscarriage UK described the announcement as "an important step in recognising pregnancy loss as a bereavement". Chief Executive Vicki Robinson said she hoped it would "provide a baseline for employers to go further", with the charity calling for bereavement leave to be paid. Bereavement support charity Sue Ryder has also called for the right to paid leave, saying bereavement can have a significant financial impact. title: Scientists discover why Kent meningitis outbreak was so severe
description: The bacteria responsible picked up some new genetic material, say experts.
body: Scientists say they have discovered why the bacteria responsible for the UK's worst outbreak of meningitis B in Kent earlier this year proved so dangerous. More than 20 young people, mostly students, were infected in the March outbreak, linked to a Canterbury nightclub. All needed hospital treatment, while nine ended up in intensive care and two died. Experts at the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) and the University of Oxford, who have looked at the DNA of the bacterium, external, say it picked up some genetic material from other bugs found naturally in the throats of some people. This exchange created a new strain or variant that then spread between clubbers and caused severe illness. Experts stress the meningitis vaccine currently being offered to more than a million young people starting university protects against it. "This investigation shows just how quickly and dramatically these bacteria can change," says Dr Charlene Rodrigues, consultant in Pathogen Genomics at UKHSA. "The fact this outbreak variant was able to spread to so many young people was due to the social environment, a place where lots of close social mixing takes place." Speaking exclusively to the BBC, she said bacteria are known to undergo changes like this, known as horizontal gene transfer. Such changes can make infections more severe, and may mean they get past the immune system because people haven't encountered them before. These events, while rare and unpredictable, could happen again, so experts "should not take their eye off the ball", she added. Scientists say speed and severity of the Kent outbreak was very unusual. It was described as "unprecedented" and "explosive" at the time, with so many infections happening in one place and over a very short period. Two people died - a 21-year-old University of Kent student and Juliette Kenny, a sixth-form pupil at Queen Elizabeth's Grammar School in Faversham. The outbreak is thought to have started in a nightclub called Club Chemistry in the city centre, which was popular with university students. It's likely one person brought the infection in with them, and then it spread that evening. Meningitis is passed through close contact - including kissing and sharing drinks or vapes. Dr Rodrigues suspects the very same genetic changes that made the strain so dangerous may also explain why the outbreak was short-lived and did not continue to spread. People were generally too sick to be silent carriers who can pass it on unknowingly to others. Following the Kent outbreak, a one-off menB vaccination programme was launched to protect young people heading to university this autumn. In July, the Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation (JCVI) also recommended that teenagers should be offered the jab on the NHS around the age of 15, with catch-up programmes for those who would otherwise miss out. title: The Inquiry
description: Italy was once known for political instability, so how did that change?
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations World Service,·24 Sep 2026,·24 mins Available for over a year Italy has long been associated with political instability, with governments on average lasting just over a year. Current Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has broken that pattern. Her government has become the longest continuously serving administration in post-war Italian history, surpassing the previous record for a single uninterrupted period in office. Meloni has presented the stability of her own right-wing coalition as one of her government’s major achievements. A general election must take place next year. As that approaches, she faces fresh challenges, including the emergence of new opposition on the right. Meanwhile, the current government’s longevity record raises a bigger question about whether Italy has entered a new era of political stability, and what has made that possible. So how did Italian politics become stable? title: I couldn't cook when I left home – but these easy £2.50 recipes became my go-to
description: Former culinary-challenged students share four low cost meals they think everyone can master.
body: Mia says she saved £20 a week on her grocery shop when she started cooking from scratch When Mia Jones left her home in Anglesey to go to university in London, she couldn't cook "whatsoever" - but quickly realised this had to change. "I couldn't live off pasta for the rest of my life," she says - and all the ready meals and pot noodles were starting to add up. "I'd be spending £45 a week on food," says the 22-year-old. "That wasn't viable." So she started buying fresh ingredients. "Then I realised, 'Oh, I need to learn how to cook now'." She started following social media videos for tips and recipes, swapping out foods she didn't like. Mia says learning how to cook "made me realise I could function on my own" While there were some early disasters it was not long before Mia was proud to say she could cook. "It made me realise I could function on my own and live on my own", she says. "[First year] me would not be able to believe it all". What's more, Mia cut her weekly shop by £20 - and found she had more energy. "I was feeling a lot more awake in my lectures, which was very useful," she says. After finishing her masters degree she now shares her recipes online, hoping to help other students in the same position she was in. Rumella Dasgupta asks what dishes you should be able to cook when you leave home for the first time Mia and other once culinary-challenged students have shared the signature dishes they learned that were cheap, easy - and most importantly tasty. All of the recipes can be made by stocking up a starter store cupboard for under £13. Then each meal uses additional ingredients for under £2.50 - which make several portions perfect for the next day or popping in the freezer. We asked retail tracking platform Assosia to find the rough cost of standard sized packs of ingredients using the average pre-promotion price across Tesco, Sainsbury's, Asda & Morrisons on 11 September 2026. Mia's first recipe is a chickpea curry: "It's very cheap and very nutritious," she says. This article contains content provided by TikTok. "It's a 10 minute recipe, it's easily customisable [with tofu or chicken] and really useful for a weeknight dinner." Mia says she'll add chilli oil if she's feeling fancy. Like Mia, Jayda Otuo-Mensah "didn't really cook" before going to university. The physiotherapy student wanted to know how to make healthy food while spending around 40 hours a week on placement in hospitals. "It's a lot easier when you're cooking because you know exactly what's going in," she says. "I can have a chicken burger and it's really healthy because of the way I cooked it." Jayda says she learned to cook by following TikTok videos After "a lot of trial and error" following TikTok videos, the 20-year-old Coventry University student felt confident enough to film herself cooking. Now she buys staples, and while she tries to stick to a weekly meal plan she mostly cooks what she is feeling. One of the meals Jayda makes the most is tacos. "It's a great meal to learn; it's quick and affordable," she says. This article contains content provided by TikTok. Rob Medhurst credits the student staple of spaghetti bolognese as being his springboard onto greater dishes. "It's very affordable and it's easy," says the 25-year-old graduate of Nottingham Trent University. "I know some people love the art of cooking but personally I don't," says Rob "I quickly learned meal prepping and batch cooking was the best way for me," he says. "I know some people love the art of cooking but personally I don't." Rob has found the simple spag bol a versatile recipe: "You can just adapt a couple of things for chilli or lots of burritos." He says he's made the same recipe so many times he describes it as "muscle memory". When making this you can also add extras such as grated cheese Chef and cookbook author Claire Thompson remembers her daughter Grace leaving home to go to university, and wondering: "Can she really cook?" She sent Grace off with three crates of supplies, which her daughter described as being "stocked for the apocalypse just in case anything went awry". Chef and cookbook author Claire Thompson says there is an essential store cupboard of items everyone needs to make quick and easy meals But for Claire there are certain essentials everyone should consider stocking up on when leaving home. "I think spices are a really good thing to start getting your head around," she told the BBC World Service's The Food Chain podcast. "They deliver lots and lots of flavour for not very much money, and they last well in your store cupboard," she says. "Adding a jar of chickpeas to a tomato sauce and adding that [to] your pasta, you're boosting really good levels of protein and bringing nutrients to a really pretty cheap dish really." title: Martha's Rule rolled out at every A&E department in England
description: The rule is named after 13-year-old Martha Mills, whose family's concerns about her care were not listened to before her death.
body: The rule is named after Martha Mills, who died aged 13 at King's College Hospital in London in 2021 The NHS is expanding Martha's Rule to all hospital emergency departments in England to help patients and families challenge staff and seek second opinions about their care if they want. It is named after Martha Mills, who died aged 13 at King's College Hospital in London in 2021 after developing blood poisoning or sepsis. Her family's concerns were not listened to, which later prompted her parents, Merope and Paul, to change that culture by creating the rule. Patients, loved ones and staff in A&E units will be able to call a dedicated phone number to trigger an urgent review if a patient's condition is deteriorating and they are concerned this is not being listened to. The nationwide expansion starts now and should be complete by March 2028, following a successful trial at seven trusts. It is already being rolled out across all inpatient wards. In 2022 a coroner ruled, external Martha would probably have survived if she had been transferred earlier to intensive care and given appropriate treatment. She was in hospital after a bike accident left her with serious injuries to her pancreas. During a family holiday, she had skidded on some sand while cycling and fell heavily onto the handlebars. After a few weeks, she developed an infection and then signs of sepsis - when the body's response to an infection is overwhelming and ends up injuring its own tissues and organs - but this was not managed properly. Prof Aidan Fowler, national director of patient safety at NHS England, said the expansion of Martha's Rule would give families and NHS staff "a critical new lifeline" to help improve care and save more lives. Staff can themselves ask for a review from a different team if they are concerned the appropriate action is not being taken. During the eight-month pilot at the seven trusts, 69 calls were made to dedicated Martha's Rule phone numbers, including some calls relating to acute deterioration following an urgent clinical review. In some cases, it led to a patient having immediate surgery or being transferred to intensive care. Prof Fowler said: "Early testing has shown that Martha's Rule can work well in busy A&Es and builds on the evidence from our adult and children's wards, where thousands of calls have been made by patients, families and staff to date, with many leading to changes in treatment and potentially life-saving interventions." Health minister Baroness Merron said the initiative was part of "wider efforts to put patient safety at the heart of the NHS." Patients and their families can check with their local hospital or NHS trust where Martha's Rule is available by visiting the trust's website or asking hospital staff. Scotland is beginning to use Martha's Rule and Northern Ireland is considering using it, while Wales has a similar scheme called Call4Concern. title: Why a Bollywood celebrity manager's 2020 death case has been reopened
description: Disha Salian's father insists her death was not suicide or an accident, but that she was gang-raped and murdered.
body: Disha Salian was Bollywood actor Sushant Singh Rajput's manager On 4 June 2020, as a deadly wave of Covid-19 swept through India, celebrity manager Disha Salian asked her father Satish Salian to call a police helpline to check if it was safe for her to travel. She was excited about an advertising campaign she was going to shoot and showed her parents a photo of the cheque she had received as advance remuneration. As she walked out of the door, she told her parents that she would be back in two days. It was the last time the Salians saw their 28-year-old daughter alive. On the intervening night of 8 and 9 June, Satish Salian was called by the police to a hospital where he learnt that his only child was dead. Police said she had fallen from the 12th floor of a building in the western city of Mumbai. Disha's friends at the hospital said she had been drinking alcohol and fell accidentally. Police later said their investigation had shown that her death was a suicide. But earlier this month, the Bombay High Court ordered the federal police - the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) - to reopen the case and reinvestigate Disha's death. The court order came after a petition filed last year by Satish Salian, who had insisted from the start that his daughter's death was not a suicide or an accident and alleged that she was gang-raped and murdered. His allegations that some senior police officers had destroyed evidence and created a false story of suicide to protect some ministers and influential politicians who had a role in the alleged crime has made it one of India's most discussed deaths in recent years. In the order, external on 2 September, Judges Sarang V Kotwal and Ranjitsinha Raja Bhonsale criticised the police and said there were "too many glaring discrepancies" in their investigation, which was carried out in two phases over more than six years. The judges insisted that they were not holding "a mini trial" but said "the investigation carried out by the police raises more questions than it answers". Satish Salian (centre) has been fighting for six years to get justice for his daughter Disha They pointed out the unexplained delay in police paperwork, that no blood had been found at the spot where the body had fallen and said that the injuries mentioned in the post-mortem report did not seem consistent with a fall. "We find this difficult to accept," they wrote. One of the biggest criticisms from the court was that the police had only investigated it as a case of suspicious or unnatural death and not registered an FIR (First Information Report) - a document police have to prepare when they receive information about a crime. Satish Salian's accusations are only allegations so far, but they have formed the basis of a new investigation by the CBI, which last week registered an FIR based on a written complaint from him. The BBC has reviewed this FIR and read through the court order in the case. Summarising Satish Salian's allegations, the court order said that at the time of her death, Disha was working with Kwan Entertainment - a celebrity management company - and represented Bollywood actor Sushant Singh Rajput. "She got to know about some objectionable activities of the powerful people. She gave that information to Rajput, who innocently divulged that to others. Ultimately that information reached back those people and she was murdered to silence her," it added. Rajput mourned her death in an Instagram story. "It's such devastating news. My deepest condolences to Disha's family and friends. May your soul rest in peace," he wrote. In the initial days, Disha's death went largely unnoticed until less than a week later, Rajput himself was found dead in his home. Police also ruled his death to be a case of suicide, saying he had mental health issues for which he was under treatment. But weeks later, his actress girlfriend Rhea Chakraborty was arrested following accusations from Rajput's father that she had contributed to his suicide. He also denied that his son had any mental health issues. Following outrage, Sushant's case was also handed over to the CBI which, last year, closed the case, saying he had indeed died by suicide and that neither Chakraborty nor her family had a role in his death. In the FIR Satish Salian has registered with the CBI, he has alleged that the deaths of Disha and Rajput are linked. Actor Sushant Singh Rajput was found dead in his home less than a week after his manager Disha Salian's death Disha, he says, shared with the actor "incriminating and objectionable information concerning alleged drug trafficking, child abuse and other unlawful activities" involving a former minister and some others and the two intended to hold a press conference to bring it into the public domain. "In order to prevent that and protect the persons involved, a well-orchestrated criminal conspiracy was hatched. The victim was gang raped and murdered, and thereafter evidence was suppressed /fabricated and a false story of suicide was created to cover up the crimes and shield the accused." In its order, the court said that registration of the FIR "does not imply any finding of guilt against anyone" and that no-one shall be treated as an accused unless the investigating officer finds "sufficient grounds to raise reasonable suspicion against them". But as the FIR names some of the state's top politicians, police officers and Bollywood actors, the case has dominated headlines in India amid allegations of misuse of political power, denials and claims of political vendetta. title: The simple skincare routine for teens that actually works - and five expert tips
description: From popping spots to getting enough sleep, experts share their advice on the best way to look after teenage skin.
body: More than 80% of 13- to 18-year-olds experience acne during their teenage years Social media is driving the trend for "flawless complexions" and complex "glass skin" routines in teenagers, with many prioritising advice from influencers in Get Ready With Me (GRWM) videos over professionals. But do teens really need a multi-step skincare routine? For consultant dermatologist Dr Jonathan Kentley, the most concerning influence social media is having is the "relentless images of unrealistic beauty standards". "I've seen thousands of patients and I've never seen anyone with 'glass skin'. I don't think it exists, and it's just these over-filtered images that make children think that this is achievable when it's not." Visible pores, blackheads, blemishes, pigmentation, redness and scarring are all very normal for teenage skin, says Dr Kentley. But he adds that everyone's normal is different: "I don't think there's anything that is really abnormal." This video can not be played Is our skin care routine actually making it worse? More than 80% of 13- to 18-year-olds experience acne during their teenage years. Dr Zainab Laftah, a consultant dermatologist, explains that most of the so-called problems you encounter during puberty are related to testosterone, which drives rises in oil production and acne. Boys can experience more of these problems, but girls have testosterone as well so get many of the same symptoms. "This, together with blocked hair follicles and inflammation, leads to blackheads, whiteheads and inflamed spots," Dr Laftah says. "Acne is very, very common and it's normal and treatable." Salicylic acid, a common active ingredient that penetrates into oil-filled pores to help clear the buildup of sebum and dead skin cells "can be particularly helpful for teenagers with oily or acne-prone skin" says Dr Laftah, warning that unnecessary or excessive use may cause dryness and irritation. If you're suffering from severe acne or a severe skin problem, Dr Kentley advises getting help from your GP or a dermatologist rather than engaging with people on social media on how to manage it. Social media is fuelling the trend for "flawless complexions" and multi-step "glass skin" routines So, how best to look after teenage skin? Experts Dr Zainab Laftah and Dr Jonathan Kentley share their five top tips: Keep your skincare routine simple You need three basics: a gentle cleanser, a fragrance-free moisturiser and a broad-spectrum sunscreen of SPF 30 or higher. That's it. More skincare products aren't necessarily better A complicated routine with frequent exfoliations or strong acids can irritate young skin. Remember the skin barrier is still developing and it can result in damage. Dr Kently says he's seen an exponential rise in a condition called perioral dermatitis in teens, which is related to the overuse of ingredients that strip skin barriers like exfoliating hydroxy acids and retinoids. Dr Laftah adds: "Teens are increasingly adopting adult-style routines with numerous serums, toners, masks and actives. These actives are likely to result in skin barrier compromise and lead to more skin issues." Getting enough sleep and a balanced diet is important Raised cortisol through diets high in white carbohydrates and sugar as well as a lack of sleep have been linked to breakouts. Dr Laftah is a supporter of getting a good night's sleep. "We know that a lack of sleep increases cortisol levels, which is a stress hormone that can lead to acne breakouts." While Dr Kentley says a diet that is high in carbohydrate foods, like white rice and pasta, high sugar diets and whey protein found in protein shakes have all been linked in studies to acne flare-ups. But he makes the point that everyone's skin is individual and that "some people may find that other things flare up their skin". Don't pick or pop your spots The risk is that you can increase the inflammation by pushing the content deeper into the skin, which can result in scarring and discolouration. Dr Laftah says she's a fan of the pimple hydrocolloid star patches as a social media hack. "They work by absorbing fluid from superficial spots while creating a protective barrier that discourages picking," she explains. See a GP or dermatologist If you have persistent painful cystic or scarring acne, seek medical advice, as often prescription-grade treatment is needed. A lot of the so-called "problems" during teenage years are related to androgens, a hormone which, although present in girls, is more prevalent in boys. "So male skin can sometimes be a little bit more oily and potentially have some more spots, and often you're getting to grips with the concept of facial hair and shaving, and that can introduce irritation," explains Dr Kentley. "If you're not shaving properly you can develop quite a lot of folliculitis which is a bit of a crossover from acne. So you can cause quite a lot of damage to the skin barrier, a lot of inflammation." Here are Dr Kentley's top tips for shaving to protect skin: Shave after showering so that the skin is hot, has been steamed and prepared for a shave Use a shaving brush to lift the hairs off the skin Shave with something lubricating like shaving foam or shower gel Always shave in the direction of travel of the hairs Cosmeticorexia: How girls are falling down a skincare rabbit hole Italy investigates Sephora and Benefit over marketing skincare to children I went for a full body MOT and the results came as a shock Watch our pick of standout clips from across the BBC Airlines criticise air traffic control as second glitch causes more disruption UK to provide Saudi Arabia with 'defensive' military support, says Burnham Yemenis flee across Red Sea as Houthis and Saudi-backed forces escalate war Teenager's organ donation saves five lives after her death What food items should you stock up on in case of an emergency?

title: Flights at major US airports delayed after cable cut by construction workers
description: The cable had been repaired and airports are resuming normal operations, the US transportation secretary says.
body: Flights resumed at New York's LaGuardia Airport and other airports Monday evening after the disruption Hundreds of flights have been delayed at major airports in the US after construction workers accidentally cut a cable needed for air traffic control. Ground stops and delays were issued on Monday afternoon for airports in New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Massachusetts. Hours later, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the cable had been repaired and airports would resume normal operations, though delays were still expected. The major east coast disruption came ahead of the UN General Assembly (UNGA) in New York City on Tuesday, which is expected to be attended by scores of world leaders arriving into New York-area airports. That includes UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who managed to board his flight before the delays began and was expected to arrive on time. The delays happened after the damaged cable impacted the Terminal Radar Approach Control system, which is used to guide planes during takeoff and landing, transport officials said. New Jersey public transportation agency NJ Transit told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, that its construction workers had accidentally severed the line and that markers had been wrongly placed at the digging site. The BBC has reached out to NJ Transit for comment. Duffy earlier said the damage was caused by workers from Amtrak, the US national operator of intercity railroad service, who were doing the construction work. This "caused a telecom outage" which forced the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to ground flights, Duffy posted on X. An Amtrak spokesperson said in a statement, reported by US media, that the incident involved a NJ Transit contractor. Telecommunications company Verizon, which owns the cable, also said it was not responsible. The severed cable was actually a backup network, and the error was only discovered after the primary circuit failed, according to the head of the FAA, Bryan Bedford. Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey - one of the three major airports that services New York City - was the most heavily impacted by today's air traffic control disruptions, according to flight-tracking website FlightAware. It reported that 267 departing flights were delayed today, while a further 257 flights destined for Newark were also delayed. John F Kennedy International Airport and LaGuardia Airport, both in New York, were also affected, as was Philadelphia International Airport. One passenger, Douglas Tewnion, said he boarded a flight to New York from Edinburgh and that his plane had been diverted to Boston, Massachusetts instead. He told the BBC that, two hours after his flight was due into New York, he and the other passengers were still "sitting on the same plane, on the tarmac at Boston with no information". Though "everyone is in good spirits", Tewnion said "it's just a pain" to see two more hours waiting added onto a lengthy flight.
