title: 'My army dream was ended by childhood eye surgery'
description: Some 114,000 Army application were rejected on medical grounds in the past five years, Freedom of Information figures show.
body: Lewis Jackson has been blocked from joining the British Army on medical grounds Lewis Jackson cannot remember a time when he did not want to join the army and continue a family tradition of military service going back to World War One. That dream was shattered, though, when his application was rejected on medical grounds. "Serving my country has always been a dream of mine and I never considered that I'd do anything else," said the 21-year-old. Jackson, from Cirencester, was turned down by the Army because he had cataract surgery at the age of three. A Ministry of Defence (MoD) spokesperson said: "Service in the Armed Forces is physically demanding, so it's right that we have sensible health and recruitment policies which maintain operational effectiveness but don't unnecessarily exclude people." The BBC has spoken to potential recruits and professionals who question whether the rules are too strict while some applicants said they had been prevented from joining because of medical conditions they regard as minor or no longer relevant. Jackson spent his teens in the cadets, preparing himself for a career in the Army Jackson spent his teenage years in the Army Cadets where he was recognised in his unit as the best shot. He applied to join the Army Reserve, motivated by a desire to "give back" to a country which he said had given him "so much", but he was rejected. "It's very frustrating, especially when you know that you are fit and healthy and you haven't even been given the opportunity to fail," he said. There were 108,020 applications to the British Army Regular Forces in the year leading up to September 2025. Separate figures obtained under a Freedom of Information (FOI) request to the Ministry of Defence (MoD) showed more than 114,000 applications to the Army were rejected on medical grounds in the past five years. Psychiatry, eye and musculoskeletal conditions were some of the most common reasons for rejection. An MOD spokesperson said: "The majority of these figures cover years before the substantial changes the government has made to remove over 100 outdated and unnecessary recruitment policies." Jackson was the top shot in his cadet force The figures come against a backdrop of wider recruitment challenges for the armed forces. Latest UK defence personnel report figures showed the military remained at about six percent below its full-time trained strength target with a shortfall of 8,460 personnel. Jackson said he had appealed against the rejection, providing a range of supporting evidence, including a note from a consultant ophthalmic surgeon who said his vision was now "excellent in both eyes" and "everything was stable". But although his vision now meets the standard, he is ineligible because medical entry rules mean applicants who have had lens replacement surgery are considered "unfit" as they need "the visual function to be able to perform their role safely and effectively". He has been told he is "permanently medically unfit to serve". Jackson said: "We are missing out on young men and women who are passionate about serving but instead are pursuing different careers. "I think it is ludicrous. If you're fit, you should be able to join." One of Jackson's relatives was awarded a medal for bravery during World War One GP and Labour MP for Stroud Dr Simon Opher said there needed to be a "more sensible approach" to medical screening. "If a health condition is stable and it's not affecting someone's functional ability, then there's no reason to exclude that person," he said. "We have to get that balance right between what's happened in the past and what would actually affect an armed forces personnel in their day-to-day duties." The MoD sets out the medical standards in a document known as the Joint Service Publication (JSP) 950 Medical Policy. In 2024, it reviewed recruitment policies, including removing a ban on applicants with asthma and severe acne. But for 20-year-old Ben Smith those changes have made little difference as his application was rejected because of ongoing use of an inhaler. Ben Smith wanted to follow in the footsteps of his father Smith, from Blandford Forum, Dorset, wanted to join the Royal Air Force (RAF) but asthma has prevented him from doing so. "There is nothing more I wanted to do in the world," he said. "I'd led 250 cadets on parades and then, for all of that to come crashing down when I didn't have a back-up plan, it was horrible." After rising through the cadet ranks, Smith studied military protective services at college and dedicated himself to reaching the fitness standards required for service. "I was proud," he said. "I was lifting double my body weight in the gym and my bleep test scores were constantly improving." Smith uses an inhaler to treat asthma but he said it did not affect his fitness Inspired by other family members who had served in the armed forces, he applied to join the RAF, hoping to train as either aircrew or a mechanic. However, his application was rejected because he uses an inhaler. Smith's appeal included a letter from his GP which said he had an "unlimited exercise tolerance". The letter said: "He is a fit and active young man with a strong ambition to join." The review said: "All candidates, irrespective of role, need to be a minimum of 12 months treatment, symptom and medication-free." For Smith, the decision brought his life-long ambition to an end. "The dream has ended," he said. "I've been told no. I don't know what to do with myself." Lt Col Stuart Crawford said the military must "relax its medical policies" Prof Neil Greenberg, president of the Society of Occupational Medicine, said: "The military has to have strict standards of physical and psychological health. "It requires people to go all around the globe, often at short notice, and to put up with environments that really are quite unpleasant. "It is vital that soldiers can perform to a v

title: Expectant mothers face 'nightmare' over Daisy Hill service suspension plan
description: The Southern Trust has not been able to recruit enough consultant obstetricians.
body: Carol McGahon, who is 30 weeks pregnant, says her journey time will now double for her nearest services Mothers waiting to give birth at Daisy Hill have described Monday's announcement that maternity services may be suspended at the hospital, as "a kick in the teeth". It was reported that no babies will be delivered at the Newry hospital if plans for a temporary suspension of services go ahead amid "significant" workforce pressures. The Southern Trust has not been able to recruit consultant obstetricians to fill vacancies and it is preparing to temporarily move inpatient maternity services to Craigavon Area Hospital. While Health Minister Robbie Butler said the move is not final, it is a serious problem for those expecting - like Carol McGahon who, at 30 weeks pregnant, described the move as "a nightmare". Eimear McVerry, who is due to give birth in about six months time, was born at Daisy Hill herself Living in Kilkeel she told BBC News NI that the change of location for her, which is around 45 minutes away, means "more travelling, more time off work and a bit more anxiety-inducing". "It's a bit of a kick in the teeth for such a lovely hospital because I have enjoyed coming here. All the staff are lovely, the maternity unit is fab, so I'll be sad to see that happen." She said the time it will take for her to get to Craigavon Area Hospital will nearly double. "I had a few scans there and it's like an hour and a half away," she said. "We had to circle parking for like 40 minutes before we even got in.This is actually a bit of a nightmare. This is going to change things." Regarding the location of Daisy Hill she said: "It's bad even travelling that much, if in an emergency, and I had complications with my other delivery, so I'd be a bit fearful of having to travel that far." Like her mother before her, Eimear McVerry was hoping to give birth at Daisy Hill. Some 28 weeks pregnant and just home from Australia, she called the move "bit inconvenient" due to the fact she was only 15 minutes down the road from Daisy Hill. "It's a bit disappointing, and I had been happy so far, but this is now the first that I have heard of it. "It's kind of just shocking really. You get used to the staff and all you're seeing and then go to a completely new place you know nothing about," she said. Her mother Jolene said the hospital "has been here a lifetime, everybody you know had their kids here". "It is just so disappointing to know that you have to go to Craigavon, which is quite a distance", she said, "especially for mums going into labour or if they go into unexpected labour, premature labour or anything like that." Claire Boyle was visibly upset when she heard the news Claire Boyle is expecting a third child and her first two children were born in Daisy Hill. "I don't know where this leaves me. Craigavon is crazy far from me now, so it's a bit of a disaster, not good to hear." Her first reaction to hearing the news was "probably panic", she said, "because I had such good experiences with my first two and there's great staff. "I live in Ballynahinch direction, I have other options but not great options. Daisy Hill would be my best option," she added. This isn't the first time Daisy Hill has had issues and been forced to close part of its services. In 2022 emergency general surgery was forced to be temporarily withdrawn due to, what the trust said was an "ongoing recruitment challenge". It to re-allocated services to Craigavon. It lost the surgery permanently in January 2024. In June 2023 changes to services saw a reduction in more than 100 beds as well as losing its stroke and some inpatient services. BBC News NI understands that Daisy Hill Hospital's maternity unit has become reliant on locum and temporary staff. The trust said it "cannot run a safe maternity service without the required medical cover and unfortunately that is a position that the trust is having to plan for at this moment in time". It is thought ante and postnatal clinics will continue in Newry but alternative arrangements will be made for women due to have their babies in Daisy Hill from November. Trust chief executive Steve Spoerry said the health minister had asked the wider Northern Ireland health system to explore what support might be available to help maintain the service in Newry in the longer term. He told BBC Evening Extra the service "would more likely than not" move from Daisy Hill. In the last year, 4,481 babies were born within the Southern Trust's two maternity services: 1,713 at Daisy Hill Hospital and 2,768 at Craigavon Area Hospital. Clodagh Corrigan, a Daisy Hill consultant who is deputy chair of the British Medical Association in Northern Ireland, said "there is a major workforce crisis across many of our specialities in Northern Ireland" and it services have "reached a crunch-point. "There has been a complete failure of workforce planning by the department of health over over many, many years," said Corrigan, citing South West Acute Hospital in Enniskillen and Causeway Hospital in Coleraine as a examples of other facilities experiencing difficulties. Speaking to BBC Radio Ulster's Talkback programme, Corrigan said sustained warnings from the health sector "have not been listened to". She said "we see staff leaving in their droves to cross the border, which is not far from Daisy Hill, to work in the Republic, where they get better terms and conditions, better pay, better service to give and a much nicer work-life balance". In the last year, 1,713 babies were born at Daisy Hill Hospital The Director of the Royal College of Midwives in Northern Ireland, Dr Dale Spence, said: "When maternity units like Daisy Hill are forced to suspend services because there aren't enough staff, it should ring alarm bells. "Unless we tackle the urgent workforce crisis, services will continue to be disrupted, putting further strain on an already stretched m

title: I'd rather pay thousands on a holiday: Meet the pensioners spending the kids' inheritance
description: The phenomenon sees retirees spend all their money on enjoying life to the full.
body: Sarah and Geoff Moorhouse have the blessing of their daughter Poppy to spend all their money Happily retired, Sarah Moorhouse is using her private pension "to go places and do nice things at the drop of a hat". While other retirees with a decent monthly pension income may choose to build up an inheritance for their children, Sarah, 64, and her husband Geoff are opting to spend their money on living life to the max. "We like going to Scotland," says Sarah, a retired school administrator. "We've been down to Cambridgeshire, which was lovely. We go up to the Lake District quite regularly to a holiday cottage, and we're planning to go to Norfolk." The couple, who live in the Yorkshire Dales, go on holiday four or five times a year, spending hundreds of pounds each time because, in Sarah's view, "you only have one opportunity at life". They did recently sell their vintage Sunbeam Alpine sports car. But only so they could replace it with a more modern, sporty two-seater convertible, a Mazda MX-5. "I'm of an age where I'm going to friends' and acquaintances' funerals, and I think you just need to live life and enjoy it while you can, because it's a very precious commodity," says Sarah. Sarah and Geoff are part of a global personal finance phenomenon that has been dubbed "skiing", which stands for spending the kids' inheritance. It is challenging the notion that assets will get handed down to the next generation. One in seven UK parents of children of all ages (15%) now plan to prioritise enjoying their money in their retirement over leaving an inheritance, according to a March report, external by pension provider Standard Life. And in the US, the number of people expecting to get an inheritance from their parents dropped to 20% last year, from 25% in 2024, according to a study, external by financial services firm Northwestern Mutual. Sarah and Geoff have two adult daughters. One of them, Poppy, tells the BBC that she couldn't be happier that her parents are out and about having fun. She firmly rejects the notion that she and her sister should expect an inheritance. "To me that's wild. It never even crossed my mind that I'll get money when my mum and dad die. I'd so much rather them do what they want to do." Mike Ambery, retirement and savings director at Standard Life, believes that the move towards skiing in the UK has been driven by the disappearance of final-salary pensions, which provide guaranteed monthly pension payments that last for as long as the retiree lives. Instead, more people in the UK now have what are called defined contribution pension pots, which can run out. Ambery argues that it's easier to be generous with a legacy if you know your retirement income will last as long as you need it. He also points to pensioners wanting to simply enjoy themselves after a life of working. "It's just having a little bit of indulgence to enjoy life. Let's face it, working life can be very hard for some people." Not all retirees are well off, of course. In the UK, 16% of pensioners live in poverty, , externalaccording to the Joseph Rowntree Foundation charity. The figure for the US is 15.4%, newly released data shows., external But at the same time, UK pensioners have seen their disposable income, excluding housing costs, increase by more than that of non-pensioners over the last three decades, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies think tank, external. Some 69% of retirees in the UK have a private pension in addition to their state one, official figures show., external In the US 56% of pensioners, external have a private pension. Karen Green, 60, says she has been very upfront with her children. "I have been quite explicit to say there is unlikely to be a legacy because I'm anticipating spending it all." Karen Green has warned her children that there might not be any money left for them to inherit Originally from Berkshire, Karen has lived in Provence in the south of France for the past 11 years, and spends more than £10,000 a year on holidays. "This year, I'm going to a yoga retreat. I did one in March in Morocco," she says. "Then in October into November I'm going to Vietnam and Laos to do a little bit of a tour." She describes herself as semi-retired, as she tops up her private pension by still doing some business consultancy work, the job she used to do full-time. When it comes to how much money she has per month, she says that her income is the same as when she was working full-time. In addition to her pension and income from her part-time work, she gains 40% of her funds from renting out a property. But Karen insists she's not "crazy with money" and likes "to get a deal". Like Sarah Moorhouse she won't get her UK state pension until she is 67. That's currently a standard £12,547.60 a year for people who reached the state pension age after April 2016, but it is due to go up next year. As a comparison, retirees in the US get state payments known as social security retirement benefits. The maximum annual amount starting from the "full retirement age" of 67 is $49,824 (£36,993)., external However, people can choose to take a lower payment, external from the age of 62. Matthew Loveless, a vice president at Northwestern Mutual, based in Ohio, says retirees need to be upfront with their adult children, some of whom might be expecting an inheritance that they intend to rely on. Back in Yorkshire, Sarah is planning her next holiday. "I've worked hard all my life and I think I deserve to have a bit of free time and to be able to do nice things." title: Vet prescription fees capped under rule changes
description: Vets must also tell clients if cheaper medicine is available online as part of the rule updates which surgeries have the coming months to bring in.
body: Written prescription fees from vets will be capped at £21 as part of a raft of changes that practices will be legally required to bring in over the coming months. Vets must also tell clients if cheaper medicine is available online, write price estimates ahead of treatment, and publish price lists for services as part of the rule updates. The official competition watchdog has brought the measures into force after its investigation into the sector found prices had been rising at nearly twice the rate of inflation. However, critics say the measures will hit independent vets hardest and will benefit the six firms that own more than two-thirds of practices. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) made its remedies for the sector legally binding as of Tuesday and vets have up to 12 months to bring all the changes in. As well as capping prescription fees, other changes include: Vet practices must publish a "comprehensive" price list for standard services – including consultations, common procedures, and cremation options A written estimate must be provided in advance for any treatment expected to cost £500 or more, including aftercare costs, plus an itemised bill. Emergencies are the only exception to this Vet businesses must make clear whether they are part of a group or an independent business To help pet owners compare local practices, price and ownership information will be made available through the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons' "Find a Vet" service, which will share the data with third-party comparison sites. The timelines for when vets need to bring in the fixes depends on the exact regulation and the group's size. The CMA sets it out here., external "The changes that are being required are changes that will help inform pet owners about prices," said CMA panel chair Martin Coleman. Cate Titterton believes vets will have to put up prices for things like consultations and surgeries However, Cate Titterton, the owner of an independent vet service in Saltburn, told BBC Your Voice the changes will make trips to the vets more expensive for customers. "Veterinary practices still have to have a pharmacy that is fully stocked, so if we're not making that tiny profit on the drugs, we're going to have to make some profit elsewhere. "So, things like services, consultations, surgeries – unfortunately, those prices are very, very likely to have to go up." She believes there is "one clear winner" from this - larger vet groups and the corporates. British Veterinary Association President Dr Rob Williams said veterinary practices were already largely working to the CMA's remedies, including the orders relating to complaints handling, price estimates for routine procedures and prescription costs. "We've been clear with the CMA throughout its investigation that it must ensure its remedies do not disproportionately impact smaller, independent practices and we've pushed back where we've had concerns," Williams said. Clive Di Giorgio says he was quoted thousands of pounds for cancer treatment his dog Louis didn't need One person hoping to see a cheaper more transparent market for vet services is Clive Di Giorgio, who got in touch with BBC Your Voice. He says he was quoted thousands of pounds for treatment after a vet told him that a rash on his dog Louis' back was "definitely" a sign of cancer. However, after going to a different vet surgery, he says he was told Louis' rash was not cancerous. A treatment of steroids, antibiotics, and a spray cleared up the rash in two weeks, Clive says. "You just don't feel as if when you go to the vets now they're interested in the animal," he says. "You feel as if all the interest is how much money they can basically squeeze from you." How have vet charges affected you? Do you welcome the changes? title: Manchester to host world leaders at G20 summit in 2027
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was pleased he would be welcoming US President Donald Trump to the city.
body: Manchester Central has held major events in the past, from rock concerts to political party conferences World leaders, including Donald Trump, will head to Manchester next year for the G20 leaders' summit. Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who is the former mayor of Greater Manchester, said he was "really pleased" he would be welcoming the US president to the city. The G20 summit, an annual gathering of the world's biggest economies, will take place on 27 and 28 November 2027 at the Manchester Central Convention Centre. It will be the largest summit ever held in the city. Manchester was chosen earlier this year, prior to Burnham becoming prime minister. Downing Street said preparations will now step up, with hundreds of local people expected to be involved. In June, as it looked likely Burnham would become prime minister, Trump called him "the mayor of a town". Burnham told reporters that in the first phone call between the pair, he told the president: "Manchester isn't 'some town'…this is Manchester". He said the "right thing to do" was to laugh about it and "move beyond it". When he was mayor, Burnham told the Manchester Evening News, external that he "wouldn't welcome" a visit from the American president. But on his way to New York, where he will meet Trump for the first time on Tuesday, he said "politicians say things throughout their career, but now the important thing is to focus on the moment you are in". Speaking to the BBC, Councillor Garry Bridges, the new leader of Manchester City Council, said an event like this would have been "unthinkable a couple of years ago" and that he hoped it would change Trump's perception of Manchester. The UK has hosted the G20 before, in 2009 in London. The cost of the security operation at the time was estimated at £7.2m. As well as the summit in Manchester, there will be events across the country next year as the UK takes on the G20 presidency. The presidency is currently held by the United States, with this year's summit taking place in Miami in December. The G20 brings together 19 of the world's largest economies, plus representatives from the European Union and the African Union. It represents about two-thirds of the world's entire population and more than 85% of the world's wealth. The annual event was first set up in 1999 with the aim of promoting financial stability and cooperation. title: Being run over by pitch roller was 'terrifying' - Townsend
description: Townsend says he was lucky to only escape from under the roller with a few "bumps and bruises".
body: Andros Townsend moved to Thailand in 2025 when he joined Kanchanaburi Power Former England winger Andros Townsend has described the moment he was run over by a pitch roller in Thailand as "terrifying". The 35‑year‑old former Tottenham, Luton and Crystal Palace forward, now with PT Prachuap in Thai League 1, was warming up for a match in Pattani on Saturday when a member of staff appeared to lose control of a heavy pitch roller. Townsend's left leg briefly got stuck under the vehicle, but he was unhurt. He came off the bench late on in a 3-0 win. Speaking about the incident for the first time on Piers Morgan's Football Uncensored, Townsend said he was lucky to only escape from under the roller with a few "bumps and bruises". "Every time I see it, I'm cringing, I'm in disbelief," he said. "It's horrible to watch back and to see what could have been, thankfully I was fortunate I did manage to fall onto the floor at the right time, so nothing snapped as the roller went over me." Townsend run over by pitch roller in Thailand Townsend, who won 13 caps for England, said that he did think it was strange to see two rollers either side of the pitch during the warm-up. "I remember thinking to myself, 'I've never seen that before in my career, what are they doing?' But we got called to warm-up. Didn't think anything of it," he said. "The next I saw him was when I was literally underneath him and thankfully no serious damage. A couple of bumps and bruises but managed to walk away unscathed, luckily." Townsend, who has had numerous setbacks with injuries during his career, said the roller incident was "definitley not going to stop me from continuing". "They (his team-mates) were very surprised that I continued the warm-up. They were telling me to go to the doctor," he said. "It was quite heavy, but I was able to kind of lift [it], force it off me. So when it was completely on me, I was getting crushed a little bit. "I was able to get my left arm up and relieve some of the pressure, and then I was able to get my team-mates around me who were able to lift it, and I was able to squeeze out but at that moment where it was crushing my left leg, it was quite terrifying, I must say." Townsend was concerned his ankle and left knee, which have both been operated on, would be damaged in the incident. He said: "I thought, either my left ankle was going to snap or my left knee is going to snap. I thought I was done. I was very fortunate that I was able to hobble away and recover within a few minutes." The midfielder made light of the incident on Instagram, referencing one of his recent posts in which he compared a sun-drenched Thai away trip with previous visits to Stoke's Bet365 Stadium. He wrote: "It turns out Stoke away wasn't so bad after all." title: 'We're inundated' - Glasgow's struggle to house the homeless
description: Scott Crean has been homeless for the last year - and since Christmas has been staying in a hotel room in Glasgow.
body: Scott Crean has been staying in a hotel room since Christmas Scott Crean is living out of a suitcase. He's been homeless for the last year - and since Christmas has been staying in a hotel room in Glasgow. In September 2025, the 37-year-old was among a record number people who were stuck in temporary accommodation in Glasgow and across Scotland. Now the latest figures are set to be released amid fears that the problem is continuing to get worse. Scott says he has been "in limbo" after being made redundant from his job at a charity shop and then made homeless after a family breakdown – all within the space of a few weeks last year. "It's as if I'm stuck in a time I can't get out of... It's the waiting game that I can't stand," he said. Scott lives in a basic room in Glasgow's Trongate Scott showed us around his hotel room near the city's Trongate. It's a basic room with a queen-sized bed, sink and small shower room. His clothes and personal effects are dotted round the cramped space, which is paid straight from his Universal Credit. "Granted, it's nice... but I want my own home. The idea of living in a hotel doesn't live up to the hype," he said. "At the end of the day, it's not somewhere I can decorate or call my own. It's living out of a suitcase. I don't feel comfortable here. "Even through I've got a roof over my head, I want to be in my own home, paying my own rent, paying my electricity, paying my way." Scott said he accepted an offer of a home in the Sandyhills area two weeks ago, but had not yet been told when he could view the property. "It's frustrating, needing an answer and not getting it. Doesn't matter how many times you email or call, the council won't get back to you. "At the same time, I count myself lucky that I have this place." Scott also volunteers at a nearby shelter run by Homeless Project Scotland, which is itself under threat of closure due to a rise in crime near its premises. Four homeless deaths in Scotland a week, data suggests Record high number of homeless people in temporary housing Three years ago, Glasgow City Council declared a housing emergency. It followed the example set by Edinburgh, where a housing shortage saw even worse pressure on homelessness services and temporary accommodation. Since 2023, the strain on housing services in Scotland's biggest city has steadily grown. According to the latest data, last September saw Glasgow record its highest ever total of households in temporary homeless accommodation, at 4,332. That included a record number of children - 3,225. While the number of new applications to be made homeless fell between March and September last year, the number of open cases - people stuck in the system waiting to be housed - also hit a record high at 6,734. The figures covering the period until March 2026, which will be published today, are not expected to show much improvement. Social care worker Samantha Lyle said cases loads were "extremely high" Samantha Lyle has been employed by the city's health and social care partnership as a social care worker for five years. She works within its enhanced outreach support team, and said they were "absolutely inundated" with demand. We met her at the Simon Community Hub in Argyle Street, a one-stop-shop for homelessness and addiction support run by the charity and partly funded by the local authorities. There was a small queue of homeless applicants, some of whom were from overseas. "I think with leave to remain and the refugees, the hub is a focal point so we could have hundreds through the doors," said Lyle. "But I think in general terms the homelessness services are extremely busy, a lot busier... Case loads are extremely high and there are a lot more complexities with those presenting as homeless." Several councils in Scotland have announced a housing emergency due to social housing shortages Her job is also about problem-solving. In one of the hub's booths, a woman discussed her situation with Lyle. The woman, who has mental health problems and was living in Edinburgh, was given a tenancy in Glasgow in January - but something has gone wrong. "She's come in, basically saying that men are coming in and threatening her," Lyle said. "They are banging on her door, assaulting her, entering her flat without her permission. "This is what we could call 'cuckooing' - the tenancy or the flat has been overrun by unknown individuals for many reasons. Lyle said that a lot of people the service worked with could not maintain a tenancy or independent living. "For us, a lot of it is down to a lack of services that mean we'd be able to house people with complex needs," she said. Ricky Bell succeeded Susan Aitken as leader of Glasgow City Council Ricky Bell, the new leader of Glasgow City Council, said they needed to "start acting as though this is an emergency - and that means doing things slightly differently". During his campaign to run the council, Bell said he believed Glasgow was "carrying the burden" of the UK's policy on housing refugees. In 2023, council officers told the BBC that Glasgow's housing emergency had been exacerbated by attempts by the Home Office to clear the backlog of people awaiting asylum decisions. Some applications were streamlined, meaning a higher number of claimants were given leave to remain. They were asked to leave their Home Office-provided accommodation and presented to local homelessness services. Between April and September 2025, almost half of Glasgow's homeless applications came from those with refugee or leave to remain status. "That's causing a real problem for us in terms of how we cope with that significant increase in the volume of people that are coming," said Bell. "We don't have the infrastructure. title: Israel FA accuses Hallgrimsson of 'ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity'
description: The Israel FA accuse Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson of "ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity" in comments made last week.
body: Hallgrimsson's side is due to play Israel twice The Israel FA has accused Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson of "ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity" in comments made last week. During his squad announcement for the upcoming Nations League games which include two fixtures against Israel on 27 September and 4 October, Hallgrimsson said: "We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide. We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel," when the subject of keeping his players focused on the games was raised. On Monday, Israel's football body hit back on those comments on social media, saying: "We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way. "Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by @IrelandFootball team coach. We're not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we're playing against the coach who embodies them." The Football Association of Ireland has not responded to the Israel FA's comments, with a protest also taking place at the Republic of Ireland team's hotel on Monday evening as pressure to boycott the fixtures continues to build. The armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza. The United Nations believes the retaliation has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians. Israel has regularly denied committing genocide or war crimes and has said its actions in Gaza have been justified as a means of self-defence. More than 160 Irish sportspeople have signed an open letter by the Irish Sport for Palestine Group to urge a boycott of the games against Israel. The Republic of Ireland are due to play Israel on 27 September in Hungary before the reverse fixture in Serbia on 4 October. The letter states that the FAI, Uefa and the Irish government should have intervened before this stage, but there is still time to "show the power of sport to unite". Sportspeople such as Olympian Ciara Mageean, former Republic of Ireland footballer Louise Quinn, ex-Ireland rugby fly-half Tony Ward - who boycotted an Irish rugby tour of South Africa - and boxers Tyrone McKenna and Eric Donovan have signed the letter. Also included in the 160 plus names are GAA's Padraig O'Hora, Joe Brolly, Colm O'Rourke, Michael Darragh Macauley, Philly McMahon, Valerie Mulcahy and Rena Buckley, as well as para-athlete Alan Dineen and ultimate frisbee's Stephen Jones, who both boycotted fixtures against Israel earlier this year. "This is a significant moment and with this moment you have an opportunity to do the right thing," the letter states. "Putting on the Irish jersey and representing your country means something. But the Ireland we want represented is the one that remembers its roots in anti-colonial and anti-imperial resistance, which Irish sport played a large part of. "This moment symbolises something deeper, it is bigger than sport. But in a way this IS sport. "Not playing the game would be the most sporting thing you could do. Through your leadership and courage, it would show the power of sport to unite, remind us of the shared values that connect us all, and have an impact far beyond the game." Uefa rejected request to keep Republic of Ireland and Israel separate - FAI Republic of Ireland braced for testing Nations League Hallgrimsson spoke to players individually about Israel games In July, the FAI's General Assembly endorsed a motion for the Republic of Ireland to go ahead with their upcoming Nations League fixtures against Israel with 75 votes to 32 against and three abstentions from the 114 delegates. The FAI had previously said boycotting the games would cause "significant and lasting harm" to Irish football as well as leading to a potential loss of 10.3m euros (£9m). The fixture has caused much controversy with Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson adding that he spoke to players in his squad individually about the prospect of facing Israel, and "none of us feel comfortable playing in these games". The Nations League games mark the Republic of Ireland's first competitive action since their World Cup play-off semi-final heartbreak against the Czech Republic in March. Since the penalty shootout loss in Prague, they have played four friendlies, beating Grenada and Qatar and drawing with North Macedonia and Canada. title: Bishop of Lincoln resigns amid sex assault inquiry
description: The Right Reverend Stephen Conway remains under investigation following a "safeguarding complaint".
body: Stephen Conway, Bishop of Lincoln, has resigned amid an ongoing investigation into sexual assault allegation The Bishop of Lincoln, the Right Reverend Stephen Conway, has resigned amid an ongoing investigation into an allegation of sexual assault. It follows his arrest in February. Conway's resignation, which will formally come into effect on 1 October, was confirmed in a statement from the Church of England. "The complaint process is ongoing. Clergy remain subject to church disciplinary procedures following resignation or retirement," it said. Conway had been suspended from ministry in February when a "safeguarding complaint" was made. At the time, Lincolnshire Police said the arrest was part of an "ongoing investigation following an allegation that a man was sexually assaulted between 2018 and 2025". Following Conway's resignation, the Church said Dr Nicholas Chamberlain, the Bishop of Grantham, would continue as Acting Bishop of Lincoln until a permanent replacement is chosen. title: UK to provide Saudi Arabia with 'defensive' military support, says Burnham
description: The prime minister says "defensive air-to-air refuelling" is to be provided following a request from Saudi Arabia, after it faced attacks from the Houthis in Yemen.
body: A single British aircraft, an RAF Voyager, is believed to be involved in the operation. Andy Burnham has said the UK will provide "defensive air-to-air refuelling" support for Saudi Arabia, in response to attacks the country has faced from the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen. It is understood this is likely to begin in the coming days and will involve a single British aircraft, a Voyager, based out of RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus. The prime minister said it follows a request from Saudi Arabia for "military support", which he agreed to on the advice of Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband. Government officials said the offer is "time limited" and likely, in the first instance, to last "for weeks". Houthi militants are locked in a civil war with Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia. In recent days, the Houthis in Yemen say they have carried out drone and ballistic missile attacks on the Saudi capital Riyadh, as well as energy sites on the country's Red Sea coast. Defensive support is described by UK officials as that which aides Saudi air force jets shooting down incoming Houthi missiles and drones. Speaking to reporters travelling with him on the way to the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Burnham linked cost of living pressures to the decision. "I go back to the point I made about cost-of-living pressures and acting to secure the interests of Britain and the wider region," he said. "Because of course Saudi Arabia has been experiencing attacks, is looking at potential further disruption, and we need to keep those pathways open, and hence our agreement to the request." Shipping routes through the Red Sea are a vital artery of the world economy. The Houthis recently seized control of the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island, a gateway to the Red Sea - a key shipping route used by Saudi Arabia. In a BBC interview last week, Nato Secretary-General Mark Rutte hinted that European support for Saudi Arabia was likely. He said: "I would not be surprised if some phone calls were taking place between European allies, 'hey, how are we going to deal with this?'. "Let's see what happens, and if Nato can help, we will always be helpful." Energy Minister Martin McCluskey last week told MPs that the UK was "providing air defence support" to Saudi Arabia through the defence partnership that they have, although would not be drawn on questions of operational military activity. In January 2024, the UK joined the US in launching air strikes against Houthi targets across Yemen. Then-Prime Minister Rishi Sunak said the UK "acted in self-defence" following the Houthis' targeting of ships, including a Royal Navy warship. He also said the strikes were "necessary, proportionate, and targeted" to protect lives and commercial shipping. Further joint air strikes from the UK and US followed in 2024, external. title: Driver jailed after killing 'devoted' mum while fleeing police
description: Lydia La Polla's life was "needlessly cut short, not far from her 25th wedding anniversary", the judge said.
body: Michael Connors, 28, admitted causing death by dangerous driving A dangerous driver has been jailed for 13 years after causing the death of a "devoted" mum while he fled police. Michael Connors went on the run to Ireland after killing Lydia La Polla, 47, in Wrexham in March 2025. He was extradited on an international arrest warrant. Connors, 28, had been driving at 71mph in a 20mph zone seconds before the crash, which also seriously injured the victim's husband Robert La Polla, 44, and a 16-year-old girl who was a passenger in the car driven by the defendant. Judge Simon Mills told Mold Crown Court that Lydia's "excellent life was needlessly cut short at the age of 47, not far from her 25th wedding anniversary". Connors did not have insurance or a driving licence when he killed Lydia La Polla Judge Mills said Connors, who was driving a silver Mercedes, fled the scene in a "cowardly fashion". "If the defendant has any sense of decency at all, he will carry the weight of what he did until the end of his days," he said. Judge Mills said Connors should not have been driving the vehicle, as he did not have insurance or a driving licence. He added: "We don't know whether you were under the influence of cannabis or not. I don't assume you were although four wraps of it were found in the vehicle." Connors, who was on licence from jail at the time of the crash, had driven across two junctions in two "highly dangerous" manoeuvres. Judge Mills said it was "simply by chance" that "more people were not killed" as a result of his "dangerous" and "completely selfish actions". Prosecutor David Mainstone said on 24 March 2025, a police officer spotted the Mercedes and decided to follow it. Lydia La Polla had been driving a Toyota Yaris when the Mercedes ploughed into the passenger side, causing it to become airborne, roll over and hit a wall. The Mercedes was still travelling at 63mph at the time of the crash and three passengers were inside. Connors' DNA was found on an airbag and his fingerprint on a can of Red Bull. In a victim impact statement read out to the court, Robert La Polla said the death of his wife had left him with a "profound sense of loss". "My life will never be the same again," he wrote. "To say I am heartbroken is an understatement. "Lydia was a wonderful mother to our children and they absolutely adored her. It breaks my heart to know that their mother won't be there for their weddings, and she won't be there to see them grow up and have children of their own. "Our close family unit has been shattered into a thousand pieces, and it will never be the same again without Lydia." Connors, of Landen Road, Ballyfermot, Dublin, admitted causing death by dangerous driving. He also pleaded guilty to causing serious injury by dangerous driving. As well as his prison sentence, he received an eight-year driving ban with an extended re-test, to run after his release from prison. Mainstone said Connors had a record for 64 offences, including nine dangerous driving allegations in Ireland. He had nine offences for being uninsured and, in 2021, in Britain, had been sentenced to six years for conspiracy to burgle. Jane Miller, defending, said: "The defendant appears genuine in his remorse. He's had time to reflect upon his conduct." title: Arrests as migrant boat reaches UK unintercepted
description: Five people have been detained and an investigation launched, the Home Office says.
body: People in life jackets were pictured being taken in to Dover's border security command compound in a separate incident Five people have been detained and sent to border security command after a migrant boat reached Kent without being intercepted. The dinghy made it to shore at Folkestone on Monday morning. The Home Office says an investigation has begun. All on the boat are believed to have been accounted for. The thousands of migrants who cross the Channel are usually brought to shore by border security command or RNLI boats but this one is thought to have slipped through undetected. No small boat arrivals to the UK coast without an escort have been officially recorded since 6 September, 2025. Kent Police said it became aware of the incident at about 09:25 BST on Monday. "Patrols attended and five people were detained and passed to border security command officers," the force said. The Home Office called the incident "isolated and rare". It said: "Officers responded quickly, detaining five individuals. There is an ongoing investigation and it would be inappropriate to comment further." Also on Monday, people in life jackets were pictured being taken into the border security command compound in Dover. Other migrant dinghies were also believed to be in the Channel, with French lifeboat and navy vessels tracking one as far west as Normandy. Some 17,480 migrants have arrived after crossing the Channel by boat so far this year, including 5,011 since Andy Burnham became Prime Minister. The 2026 total is down 46% on this time last year. title: Settling old scores with royals drives Spencer's book, but Diana steals focus
description: What more revelations are going to appear now the full details of his Diana book are published?
body: Earl Spencer talked about his memoir of Diana with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg A slanging match doesn't usually do either side much good. Unless you're selling books, when a controversy can be extremely helpful. Earl Spencer's book about his sister, Diana, has had six days of public accusations and counter-claims, with extensive news coverage. So perhaps it's not surprising that even before it's officially published, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister is racing up the Amazon best-seller chart. It's likely to be the most significant royal book since Prince Harry's startling 2023 memoir, Spare, and Andrew Lownie's 2025 book Entitled, which doomed Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's reputation. Key takeaways from BBC interview as Earl Spencer defends claims about King 'I'm telling the truth': Earl Spencer defends Diana book claims about Charles in BBC interview Bitter row over Diana book brings back unhappy times for royals The coverage has been driven by a simple question: should we believe Earl Spencer's claims about the King's callousness after Diana's death? Or should we believe the unusually robust denial from Buckingham Palace? But when you read further through the book, there's a more complicated story being told. Earl Spencer is the brother watching events unfolding in the strange and ultimately doomed life of his sister, who has stepped from being his childhood companion to become one of the most famous women in the world. He describes a kind of grief and irritation as Diana becomes public property and then royal property, which irks him even more, disliking the "nonsense of fawning" around the monarchy. It's a stark reminder that Diana was only just 20 years old when she married - becoming a global superstar - and was dead 16 years later. Earl Spencer depicts her as a caring, generous character who was haunted by self-doubt, dogged by eating disorders, lacking in warmth from her new royal family and then ultimately dragged down by the tabloid media. "She craved acceptance, admiration, kindness, and - perhaps above all - love," writes Charles Spencer about Diana. "She got stuck into gritty, controversial, but crucial causes partly because she had a fine, natural social conscience, but also to assuage nagging feelings of worthlessness." And with a memoir like this it will be the extra details that will fascinate people. The stepmother to Diana and Charles, Raine Spencer, is painted in an unflattering light, and Diana is described as getting so angry once that she pushed Raine down the staircase at their home in Althorp. "Raine fortunately landed flush on her buttocks, rather than on bone, and got up, leaving the saloon without a backwards glance," he writes. It was in response, says the book, to Raine telling Diana: "I have always felt so very sorry for the Prince of Wales, marrying someone quite as stupid as you." There's not a single mention of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, even though she was talked about in the TV interviews We're told that a "nephew" wanted Earl Spencer to be in a documentary about Diana, which will raise speculation about Prince Harry's plans for his mother's 30th anniversary next year The book recounts that she disliked Dodi Fayed's father, Mohammed Fayed, accusing him of crudely groping her Diana's preferences included the soap opera Crossroads and the music of David Bowie. She'd watched The Sound of Music 16 times and the paper she read was the Daily Mail Earl Spencer and the then-Prince Charles opening a memorial to Diana in 2004 Earl Spencer will ultimately be remembered by the passionate eulogy he delivered at Diana's funeral in Westminster Abbey. He reveals how he had pretended to have lost his copy of his speech at the rehearsal, so no one could hear it in advance and try to tone down his stinging criticism of the press and the royals. After the hounding of Diana by the paparazzi, he says he personally rang tabloid newspaper editors to disinvite them from the Abbey funeral, after their invitations had already been sent out. She was buried on an island in the Spencers' Althorp estate, rather than a graveyard - and the book describes how a bishop was brought to consecrate the ground to make it possible. Much of the interest in this book has been driven by its settling of old scores with the Royal Family. It can feel like medieval barons jousting. References to King Charles are almost all negative, including the suggestion that he was jealous of his wife's public popularity. The book reports a conversation in which it's claimed the then-Prince Charles complained: "I mean, I'm 43,' he said, 'and I employ fifty people' – he was flushed in the face now – 'but my parents insist on treating me like – like a child!'" The King is portrayed as resentful, with a "senior courtier" reporting an alleged comment by the late Queen: "He even resented it when I taught him the alphabet." There's a bizarre account of discussions in the Royal Family about whether the then-Prince Charles's ears should have been pinned back. And there's the allegation that Diana had said the King was in love with his valet, which the author himself says seemed improbable. What comes across is how close the Spencers were to the royals - but without being friends. Charles and Diana Spencer went to the same children's parties as the young royals. The royals are depicted as the type of children who come round, break your toys and then disappear, in what might be an extended metaphor for how he saw Diana's story. There's also a story about a teenage Prince Andrew smirking in a church service because the priest used the word "womb". title: Watch: Police raid organised crime targets in Teeside
description: Cleveland Police carried out one of their biggest raids in years, following the A66 crash that left two officers dead.
body: This video can not be played Cleveland Police have carried out one of their biggest raids on organised crime targets in years. About 130 officers were involved in the operation which saw 17 people arrested in the Middlesborough area. The raids are part of a response to a crash on the nearby A66 last month, which resulted in the death of two officers in a police pursuit. The BBC's Stuart Whincup was with the police as they carried out the arrests. Read more about the raids in this story. Watch: Police raid organised crime targets in Teeside. title: Infantino says he is open to Fifa reform
description: Fifa president Gianni Infantino has proposed an external review of the governance of world football's governing body.
body: Gianni Infantino was first elected as Fifa president in 2016 Fifa president Gianni Infantino has proposed an external review of how world football's governing body operates, and says he is open to reform. In a letter sent to members of the Fifa Council and all of its national associations, Infantino said the process would "recommend potential improvements". Before a meeting of the Council next month, Infantino says he is also suggesting a consultation on "how Fifa's decision-making can be further strengthened". This would include proposals on the role of the president, as well as "practical ways to strengthen transparency, participation and accountability in major strategic initiatives". Infantino has come under increasing pressure over his aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal. That would have involved selling stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors, and it sparked a major backlash. In what appears to be a conciliatory gesture, Infantino writes: "Over recent weeks, I have taken time to listen before writing to you." He then insists that the FFE plan "did not involve relinquishing Fifa's control or authority over sporting decisions. Obviously!" His letter adds: "The proposal entered the public domain before Fifa's planned institutional process had been completed and before it could be presented in full to the Council and the member associations. I recognise that, without the full context, this caused concern and created the impression that decisions had already been taken. They had not." Infantino also claims that "democratic processes, independence and sporting authority were never for sale. They are not for sale and never will be". He states he remains "fully committed to leading Fifa and confident in what we can achieve together". Infantino's letter comes after Uefa and Concacaf - the confederations for Europe and North America, Central America and the Caribbean - demanded Fifa pays $10m to all 211 members from its cash reserves. FFE would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights of all Fifa competitions, including World Cups, with 21% sold off to a private investment company. Infantino claims that the collapse of FFE "does not diminish our ambition or our responsibility to invest more of Fifa's success back into football. "We will continue to explore sustainable ways to grow Fifa's resources and expand development and solidarity support for every member association. What changes is not the ambition, but the strength of the process through which major ideas are developed, tested and decided. "The progress we have made over the past decade gives us a strong foundation for the future. It also gives us the confidence to examine whether our governance remains suited to the scale and complexity of the decisions ahead." Earlier this month, Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt, a Fifa vice-president, told Infantino to release all documents relating to his controversial plan. The 56-year-old Swiss-Italian Fifa leader will stand for election for a fourth time in March 2027, with his opponents having until 18 November to find an alternative candidate. Last month, European football's governing body Uefa began preparing criminal legal proceedings against Infantino at courts in the US over the FFE plan, demanding the release of all documents. Fifa hit back and accused Uefa of a "smear campaign against it and its leadership" in a challenge to the litigation. title: 'Real fear Littler could walk away' - darts would be loser in booing row
description: Could Luke Littler walk away from darts completely if the booing he has suffered at European tournaments continues?
body: This video can not be played Why does Luke Littler keep getting booed? At just 19, Luke Littler has won almost every major trophy in darts. He is a multi-millionaire with lucrative sponsorship deals and his own TV show. But has his rapid rise turned some against him? This past weekend the teenager was once again subjected to boos and whistles from sections of the crowd as he took to the stage at the World Series of Darts in Amsterdam. What is surprising though is that it came as 'The Nuke' was on a quest to complete a darts clean sweep by becoming the first player to win all 10 major televised tournaments in a calendar year. Littler suggested afterwards that, if the booing continues, he will not attend events held in the Netherlands. But Samuel Gill, editor of Dartnews.com, suggests Littler's future in the sport could be at stake. "There's a real fear that within a few years he'll just turn around and walk away from the sport," Gill told BBC Sport. "So, I think for fans, 'Don't bite the hand that feeds you'. If people keep taunting him and don't want him to win, he might end up just walking away and not bothering anymore." Amsterdam was the latest tournament where Littler has faced what some might describe as an overly hostile reaction from fans. A vibrant pantomime-style atmosphere is part and parcel of the darts experience and Dutch and German crowds are amongs the most raucous - but it is clear Littler believes he has been unfairly targeted. The referee stopped the match during his narrow win against Nathan Aspinall in the last-16 on Saturday to warn the hostile crowd about its behaviour, before play resumed. It followed Littler also being booed during his win against home favourite Danny Noppert on Friday. The teenager's quarter-final defeat to Jonny Clayton ended Littler's quest for the clean sweep, but the Warrington native clearly felt fans had been unduly harsh towards him. Littler has now withdrawn from a series of upcoming events. "Just no point in me travelling, wasting my time while I'm getting booed," said Littler. Littler has also been jeered at numerous events in the UK. His phenomenal rise saw him reach the PDC World Darts Championship aged just 16 in his debut year as a professional. He captured the title the following year and the trophies, sponsorship deals and six-figure winners' cheques have continued to flow. But increasingly so have whistles and boos during his performances. "I don't think people expected him to reach the heights that he has so quickly," Gill said. The darts journalist - who became aware of Littler when the sport star was 14 - says this level of attention is not just unique to the British player. "Michael van Gerwen was the same for a long time when he dominated the sport. He barely lost a game in about five years, and he was hoovering up titles for fun and it was similar," said Gill. "Everyone wanted to boo him and even me as a viewer before I got into this role, growing up watching Van Gerwen, I wanted him to lose because it's something different for the sport every single week." Currently ranked number one in the world, Littler is so far ahead of his closest rivals that he already has the advantage of only having to play in selective tournaments. His boycott threat could end up being a blow to tournament organisers. "They don't like him because he's that good. And he's got a bit of swagger to him," said Karl Holden secretary of St Helen's Darts Academy - where Littler honed his skills from the age of nine. "Luke's got a bit of a character to him. For me, he's the ultimate professional. He might give a little bit of the large sometimes, but you need that, otherwise darts would be totally boring." This video can not be played How the teenager became a dart sensation It seems remarkable that the future of Littler's career in the sport is even being debated. More so when you consider his age and the fact he only turned professional two years ago. However, Gill believes that Littler's rapid haul of trophies, coupled with the huge amounts of money now in the sport, could result in the teenager leaving in the next "four to five years" should the boos and whistles continue. Gill believes Littler's impact on the darting world is immeasurable. Tickets to events featuring him are often sold out, applications to darting academies are reported to be at an all-time high and the Briton has transcended the sport. Gill therefore feels that, if Littler was to walk away, the sport would be the real loser. "He's the one who is bringing this sport to a completely different level. Nowadays, he is back-page news wherever you go," Gill said. "He might just decide 'I just want a quiet life now and just live off his money'." Littler has barely known anything other than winning. His challenged now is maintaining that victorious streak while keeping fans - whose interest helps fund his prize money - happy. Tricky when some are paying with the hope of seeing him lose. "If he was on that stage, everybody liked him and he just threw darts, I think I'd get bored of watching him," Holden said. title: Drunk council leader accused of drinking bottle of gin and vowing to 'wipe out' Plaid Cymru quits
description: Steve Hunt apologised and blamed "personal" reasons for his behaviour and "banter".
body: Steve Hunt will continue to serve as an independent councillor in his constituency A council leader who fell over while drunk after allegations he drank a "whole bottle of gin" and then threatened to "wipe out" the Welsh party Plaid Cymru has quit. Steve Hunt, from Neath Port Talbot Council, said he "should have exercised better judgement" after becoming "intoxicated" at a Welsh Local Government Association conference. Hunt said he was a strong supporter of the Welsh language, but admitted saying he wanted to "wipe out" Plaid Cymru politically as "banter". He denied drinking a bottle of gin. Hunt will continue to serve as an independent councillor, but a council spokesperson said a new leader would be appointed on 14 October. A source who attended the conference told the Local Democracy Reporting Service the independent councillor for the Crynant, Onllwyn and Seven Sisters ward was loudly bragging about drinking heavily. Hunt said the comment about Plaid Cymru "should be understood in the context of political banter and disagreement at the end of a long evening, rather than as a threat or anything other than a political statement". The councillor also said there were "personal circumstances" that contributed to his behaviour which were "relevant". His role as council leader had carried a "significant level of pressure and responsibility", he said, and he saw the event as an opportunity to "switch off" from those pressures. "Regrettably, I drank far beyond what was sensible," he said. Hunt said it did not excuse his behaviour and that he apologised to the Plaid Cymru group leader the following morning. Hunt has led the council's Independent and Plaid Cymru coalition since local elections took place in 2022. It was the first time in Neath Port Talbot's history that the Labour Party lost control of the council. Following his decision to step down, Hunt said he had done what he believed was in the "best interests" of the council and residents and communities that it represents. "I will continue to serve as an Independent councillor and will continue to work for the residents and communities I represent," he said. title: Paramount settles lawsuit with US states, helping clear way for $110bn merger with Warner Bros
description: Paramount has reached a settlement with the US states in a lawsuit challenging its $110bn merger with Warner Bros
body: A coalition of states led by California had challenged the deal, raising concerns over competition across film and television. Paramount Skydance has settled a lawsuit with dozens of US states, removing a major hurdle to its $110bn (£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery. California Attorney General Rob Bonta told a news conference that state officials agreed to terms after securing commitments to protect competition across film and television, and broadcasting. Still, "the settlement is not a vote of support for this merger," Bonta said. "I don't think these two companies should merge." Paramount chief executive David Ellison hailed the resolution, saying: "Our shared aim was an outcome that best serves consumers, workers and - most importantly -the creative community so vital to the art of visual storytelling." In a statement, Ellison said that now the state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America concerns had been addressed, "we have complete clearance for this merger and look forward to putting these commitments into action". Ellison had previously threatened to move studio operations out of California. The settlement will help boost film production in the US, Bonta said, adding that under the agreement, Paramount must release at least 30 films each year. Bonta stressed the agreement guarantees a massive boost to domestic output, "$300m to $1.5bn more, at minimum, for film and TV production right here in our country". "Importantly, that is the baseline. That is the minimum," Bonta said, noting that production commitments could surge by up to 700% if Congress passes a federal film tax credit. Under the deal's initial terms, Paramount must ensure 20% of all film production takes place in the US for the first two years, rising over 30% over the following three years. While mergers typically lead to corporate overlap and redundancies, Bonta maintained that it would be a "job creator" that will put people back to work across the industry. title: Atletico hit back at Mourinho over referee complaints
description: Atletico Madrid hit back at Jose Mourinho after he complained about the refereeing in the Madrid derby.
body: Mourinho arrived at his news conference with screenshots of incidents he believed should have resulted in red cards for Atletico Atletico Madrid have hit back at Jose Mourinho after the Real Madrid boss arrived at his post-derby news conference on Sunday carrying printouts of screenshots displaying two incidents he believed should have resulted in red cards for Atletico. Mourinho accused the officials of making key errors after Real were beaten 2-1 by Atletico, claiming the hosts should have been handed two red cards in the first half. On Monday, Atletico posted twice on their X account, the first being a video showing a sheet of paper coming out of a printer with the words #StopAcosoArbitralYA, meaning "stop referee harassment now". A second post showed a picture of Mourinho at the news conference with the same message. The response from Atletico, whose team are coached by Diego Simeone, received two million views on X within two hours of it being posted. Atletico often use their social media accounts to respond to rivals, repeatedly posting on X this summer to ridicule Barcelona over their pursuit of Atletico's talisman Julian Alvarez. Alongside Mourinho's post‑match claims, the match report published on Real's website said that the derby loss was decided because of "dreadful refereeing", external by Ortiz Arias. The posts has more than two million views on X Mourinho's side had defender Dean Huijsen sent off early in the second half, when the game was goalless, for pulling down Atletico's Giuliano Simeone just inside the penalty area. The match outcome was Real's second defeat of the season, having lost 1-0 to Real Betis earlier in September. "We can skip the press conference because the story of the match is right here," Mourinho said as he showed media the printed images on sheets of A4 paper on Sunday. "Those were two clear red cards. Given the difficulties we faced afterwards playing 11 against 10, we can only imagine what 50 minutes of 11 against nine would have been like. "So I'll just have to limit myself to hugging my players, who gave it their all and played a first half, showed great class and character, setting us up perfectly to win the second half." Simeone, when asked to respond to Mourinho's refereeing rant, said he was always respectful of everyone else's opinions. "I understand that we're in a privileged position with a lot of public scrutiny, as coaches, and whether it's Mourinho, [Barcelona manager Hansi] Flick, [Real Betis boss Manuel] Pellegrini, me, or anyone else, we need to be careful about what we say," he said. "We have to know how to respect others, the referees, our colleagues. And when someone crosses that line of respect, it's not right - you can't cross that line." title: First UK charges brought over 1994 Rwanda genocide
description: Dr Vincent Brown, formerly Dr Vincent Bajinya, 65, will appear at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Tuesday charged with seven offences.
body: The Metropolitan Police said the charges follow "a complex and extensive seven-year investigation" A Rwandan man, who has been living in north London, has become the first person charged in the UK with offences relating to the 1994 Rwanda genocide, the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) has said. Dr Vincent Brown, formerly Dr Vincent Bajinya, 65, has been charged with one offence of conduct ancillary to genocide and six offences of conduct ancillary to murder as a crime against humanity. Frank Ferguson, head of the CPS's Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division, said Brown "is alleged to have directed and incited acts of murder and genocide carried out by others". Brown will appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Tuesday. Ferguson said the decision to charge Brown was made "after reviewing a file of evidence submitted by the War Crimes Team at the Metropolitan Police". "We concluded that our legal test for bringing criminal charges had been met," he added. The War Crimes Team began their investigation in September 2019 after a formal request from the Rwandan government to investigate people allegedly involved in a genocide in the Rugenge district of Kigali in April 1994. Over the course of 100 days in 1994, an estimated 800,000 ethnic Tutsis and politically moderate Hutus people were killed in Rwanda by Hutu extremists. They were targeting members of the minority Tutsi community, as well as their political opponents, irrespective of their ethnic origin. The mainly Tutsi forces who took power following the genocide were alleged to have killed thousands of Hutu people in Rwanda in retaliation. The Metropolitan Police said the charges against Brown follow "a complex and extensive seven-year investigation". Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said: "This case demonstrates the UK is not a safe haven for individuals suspected of committing international crimes. "The War Crimes Teams remains committed to ensuring those suspected of involvement in genocide and other atrocity crimes are held accountable through due legal process. "A number of other investigations remain ongoing into other individuals in the UK for similar offences related to the genocide in Rwanda." title: Scotland call for Montgomery as Tierney & McLean drop out
description: Blackburn Rovers midfielder Kristi Montgomery gets a first call-up for Scotland as Kieran Tierney and Kenny McLean drop out of the Nations League squad.
body: Montgomery made his Scotland Under-21 debut last year Kristi Montgomery has been given a first call-up for Scotland after Kieran Tierney and Kenny McLean dropped out of the Nations League squad. The Blackburn Rovers midfielder has been promoted from the under-21s by new head coach Sebastien Pocognoli for the games against Slovenia (twice), Switzerland and North Macedonia. The 22-year-old has started all eight Championship matches for Tony Mowbray's side this season. Celtic defender Tierney and Norwich midfielder McLean have 119 international caps between them, while experienced trio Scott McTominay, Che Adams and Lawrence Shankland were unavailable before Pocognoli made his picks. Montgomery is the eighth uncapped player in the 27-strong group, joining Luke Graham, Robbie Ure, Luis Binks, Colby Donovan, Jon McCracken, Josh McPake and Stephen Welsh. Oli McBurnie, Scott Bain, Kieron Bowie, Josh Doig, Lennon Miller and James Wilson were recalled and Napoli midfielder Billy Gilmour returns after missing the World Cup through injury. Dominic Hyam, Lyndon Dykes, George Hirst, Grant Hanley, Anthony Ralston and Ross Stewart are among those overlooked by Pocognoli, with Manchester United teenager Tyler Fletcher in the under-21s after taking Gilmour's place in the USA. title: F1 reduces maximum distance of races by 15km
description: F1 announces the maximum race distance for grands prix will be reduced by 15km from 305km to 290km for the 2027 season.
body: New rules will cover F1 races delayed or disrupted by rain or incidents from 2027 Formula 1 has announced the maximum race distance for grands prix will be reduced by 15km from 305km (189.5 miles) to 290km (180.2 miles) for the 2027 season. Grands prix are limited to a maximum of two hours of racing, but when there are interruptions caused by rain or accidents, a "hard stop time" will replace the current maximum three-hour duration to finish the event. This will allow for greater flexibility to complete disrupted races. A statement from governing body the FIA said: "These changes were introduced to ensure that the spectators have the best possible chance to enjoy a full race if disruptions occur." The hard stop time will vary from race to race, depending on local conditions. At night races, for example, there will be more flexibility to allow the race to run later than at a daytime race when there is a relatively early sunset. The reduction in race distance has been introduced because the ratio of internal combustion to electrical power is changing from 53-47 this year to 58-42 next year, before becoming 60-40 in 2028. This means that the cars will use more fuel, and that became a concern when it emerged that some teams wanted to carry their chassis over into next year to save money. As the fuel tank is within the chassis and therefore its size could not be changed, this meant those teams might not have been able to finish grands prix with their existing fuel tanks. Another change agreed at a meeting of the F1 Commission, a rule-making body composed of the teams, the FIA and commercial rights holder F1, was to introduce "greater flexibility to extend free practice sessions should they be interrupted". Under current rules, the clock does not stop in practice sessions in the event of a red flag caused by an incident, unlike in qualifying and races when the competition is suspended. title: Invitation for men to 'experience hot flushes'
description: A MenoVest will allow people at an event in Hull to experience one of the symptoms of the menopause.
body: A common symptom of the menopause is a hot flush Partners of women going through the menopause are being invited to experience one of the symptoms at a forthcoming support event. At the Menopaus'ull Support Network event in Hull next month, health group Over The Bloody Moon will be taking one of its MenoVests, allowing people to experience a hot flush – one of the symptoms of the menopause. Sarah Weichardt, who co-manages the project, said: "We're particularly interested in getting men along to come and experience the MenoVest, just so that they can understand what women go through." The event will be at Princes Quay shopping centre on 17 October, from 10:30 until 14:30 BST. "It's not just a hot flush, it's what the hot flush brings with it," said Weichardt. "So it could be panic, it could be anxiety. It's experiencing it all at the same time." She said she hoped the vest would give people a "better understanding of what women are going through". "The more people we can get to experience it, the better," she added. Treatment for the menopause can include HRT patches The menopause describes the end of a woman's reproductive years, and often happens at about the age of 50. The period leading up to this is called the perimenopause, which is when many women notice their periods becoming unpredictable. Other symptoms can include mood shifts, difficulty sleeping, and discomfort during sex. Weichardt said her organisation had a banner with nearly 40 symptoms on it. Many women "don't necessarily know that they're going into the menopause or they're perimenopausal" until they see the banner – and then they sometimes have a "lightbulb moment", she said. Once women have "accepted it and are happy" they are menopausal or peri-menopausal, they can seek the support they need, she added. There is also a Menopaus'ull Support Network event in Beverley on 10 October between 10:30 and 13:30 BST at the Toll Gavel Church.
