title: First look at The Other Bennet Sister Christmas special revealed
description: Filming wrapped on the BBC Christmas special in October, as fans eagerly await its return.
body: The series finale saw Mary Bennet, played by Ella Bruccoleri, agree to marry Tom Hayward, played by Donal Finn The first image from The Other Bennet Sister Christmas special has been revealed, teasing a romantic picnic scene. Inspired by Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, the first series was filmed largely in Wales and attracted 7.3 million UK viewers in its first four weeks. The series finale saw Mary Bennet, played by Ella Bruccoleri, agree to marry Tom Hayward, played by Donal Finn. Filming wrapped on the BBC three-part Christmas special at the end of October, as fans eagerly await its return. The first series focused on Mary, the couple's seemingly unremarkable middle daughter as she navigates the societal pressures of Regency England. It was primarily filmed in south Wales, at locations including Merthyr Mawr in Bridgend county, the Gower peninsula, and Brecon, in Powys. The Christmas special has been produced by Cardiff-based Bad Wolf, and filming took place over the summer, primarily in Wales. Gavin & Stacey's Ruth Jones will return to the hit show as Mrs Bennet, who she previously described as "often quite cruel" to her daughter Mary. Other returning cast members include Ted Lasso's Tanya Reynolds as Caroline Bingley and Laurie Davidson as Mr Ryder. Also resuming their roles are Varada Sethu as Ann Baxter, Poppy Gilbert as Lizzie Darcy, Maddie Close as Jane Bingley, Grace Hogg-Robinson as Lydia Wickham, Molly Wright as Kitty Buncock and Anna Fenton-Garvey as Charlotte Collins. Nerys Amber-Stocks, best known for appearing in Out There and Mammoth, joins the cast as Mary's housemaid Lucy. The show's producer Edoardo Ferretti announced to fans on social media that the special had finished filming at the end of October. He posted a short but sweet message on Instagram, saying: "And yet another wrap! Every time emotional, every time proud. This one is going to be so special!" The first series was filmed largely in Wales and attracted 7.3 million UK viewers in its first four weeks Little has been shared about the plot of the upcoming Christmas special, however, the BBC has teased: "With marriage comes a new identity and the question remains: who will Mary become as Mrs Hayward?" The three additional episodes, announced in June, will run for 30 minutes each and continue to be based on storylines from the original novel by Janice Hadlow. It has been written by screenwriter Sarah Quintrell, with Asim Abbasi returning to direct the special. It will air in the UK on BBC iPlayer and BBC One, while in the US and Canada, it will also be available on BritBox. Sony Pictures Television will distribute The Other Bennet Sister internationally. title: Man charged with causing death by dangerous driving over crash that killed 6
description: Four members of the same family and a married couple on a motorbike died in the 2024 collision.
body: Shannen Morgan, Shane Roller and their daughters Rubie and Lillie died in the collision with husband and wife Christopher and Janine Barton A man has been charged with causing death by dangerous driving over a crash that killed six people, including two children. Shannen Morgan and Shane Roller died along with two of their daughters, nine-year-old Rubie, and Lillie, four, when the family's car collided with a motorbike on the A61 between Barnsley and Wakefield on 21 July 2024. Husband and wife Christopher and Janine Barton, from Barnsley, who were both travelling on the motorcycle, also died in the crash. Christopher Cockell, 50, is due to appear at Leeds Magistrates' Court in October charged with six counts of causing death by dangerous driving. An inquest previously heard that the silver Ford Focus being driven by Mr Roller, 33, collided head on with the BMW motorcycle being driven by Mr Barton, 56, at about 15:50 BST between Staincross and Newmillerdam. Wakefield Coroner's Court heard the collision happened as the motorcycle was overtaking another vehicle on the single-carriageway road, which had a 50mph (80 km/h) speed limit. Coroner's support officer Phil Marr told the hearing: "As a result of a head-on impact, the car was spun to the side of the road, where it caught fire. "It was not possible to release any of the occupants and all four were pronounced dead by paramedics at the scene." Floral tributes were left at the scene of the collision on the A61 Marr said a pathologist concluded Mr Barton's provisional cause of death was due to head and chest injuries. He said Mrs Barton was "thrown onto the adjacent golf course" in the collision, with her death due to chest injuries. Ms Morgan and van driver Mr Roller, who lived in Athersley, Barnsley, had another daughter, aged 11, who was not with them at the time of the crash. An online fundraising page, set up by a family friend in the wake of the tragedy, raised more than £400,000 for her. In a social media post at the time, Mr Roller's father, Graham, paid tribute to the couple, who he described as an "amazing" mum and dad. "Shane wasn't just a son but an amazing father and he had a heart of gold," he wrote. "Shannen, our daughter-in-law, was funny and was also an amazing mum and they thought the world of their little family." The A61 was closed while forensic teams inspected the scene Co-head teachers of Athersley North Primary School, which Rubie and Lillie had attended, said the girls had been "a delight to teach". In a statement, Clare Storr and Kirsty Wordsworth, said: "The girls were a credit to their parents, who were always incredibly supportive and who will also be greatly missed." Mr and Mrs Barton, 48, who had lived in Barnsley, had recently celebrated their 25th wedding anniversary. In a tribute issued via West Yorkshire Police in 2024, their son described his parents as "a loving, caring mum and dad who always put me before everything else". A spokesperson for West Yorkshire Police said Cockell had been summoned following an investigation by the force's Major Collision Enquiry Team and would appear before magistrates on 28 October. Cockell, of Gresford Close, Woolley Grange, had already been facing a charge of failing to stop at the scene of a collision. title: Two pilot whales dead after mass stranding
description: Attempts to refloat the whales off the Northumberland coast are unsuccessful due to the tides.
body: The pod contained about 40 pilot whales Two pilot whales have died after a distressed pod was spotted off the Northumberland coast. British Divers Marine Life Rescue (BDMLR) said it had been alerted to a group of about 40 whales near to the shore at Amble at 15:00 BST on Sunday. It said the whales had been "behaving in a distressed manner typically seen prior to a stranding event". Due to the tides, attempts to refloat the animals had been unsuccessful, the charity said, and rescue teams were forced to withdraw. Whales are highly social mammals and are well known for stranding in groups because they travel in large, close-knit communities which rely on constant communication. There are a range of theories for why beachings occur. Some experts say the animals can become disorientated after following fish they hunt to the shore. Others believe that one individual can mistakenly lead whole groups to shore. The BDMLR said it was not the same pod of whales which was herded out of the River Thames at the weekend as the distance between the locations was further than the species could swim in 24 hours. Local boats were launched with medics on board to try to herd the whales offshore to stop them from stranding. But the animals remained tightly packed around one of the largest, which was lying motionless on its side. The teams were stood down after losing the light on Sunday. Earlier on Monday, the BDMLR said about a dozen had been stranded on Coquet Island around rocky terrain. On investigation, six animals were found - five ashore and one afloat. Two of the stranded whales were confirmed to have died, the BDMLR said. Due to the tides and limited access to the island, attempts to refloat the live animals were not possible and the teams withdrew once again. The BDMLR said it would remain along the coast, ready to provide care and attempt to refloat those which were healthy enough. The RSPB said its staff from nearby Coquet Island were continuing to support the BDMLR's response to the incident. "This is a distressing situation and our thoughts are with all those involved in the response," a spokesperson said. title: Repeated air traffic control failures leave us in worrying territory
description: The question is whether all of these incidents were isolated and unavoidable, or whether they point to something more systemic.
body: To have one air traffic control failure in a fortnight may be regarded as a misfortune, to have two looks like carelessness. The UK's air traffic services provider is coming in for a wave of criticism at the moment, so where is it all leading? The incident at the National Air Traffic Services (Nats) main control centre in Swanwick earlier this month was extremely serious. It caused more than 2,000 flight cancellations over two days, affecting hundreds of thousands of passengers. Some were left sleeping on airport floors, others were stranded in foreign airports. Monday's failure at the Prestwick centre, which looks after air traffic in Scotland, northern England and northern Ireland was not as dramatic. But according to the aviation analytics company Cirium, it still led to about 150 flights being cancelled and many other delays affecting tens of thousands of travellers. The first failure this month was attributed to a previously undetected software flaw, which had an impact due to a very specific set of circumstances combining in a millisecond. Today's issue was blamed on a "connectivity issue" specific to the system used in Scotland. The two, Nats says, were unrelated. But this is becoming worryingly familiar territory. In August 2023, on a bank holiday weekend, a problem with a single aircraft's flight plan caused a key system at Swanwick to break down, leading to cancellations and delays that affected 700,000 passengers. Two years later, a smaller "radar-related issue" disrupted air traffic for four hours, and led to the cancellation of 150 flights. The question is whether all of these incidents were isolated and unavoidable, or whether they point to something more systemic. Airlines criticise air traffic control as second glitch causes more disruption UK flight delays continue after issue with air traffic control in Scotland is fixed There is no question that the job Nats has to do is fiendishly complicated, looking after some of the busiest airspace in Europe - including the approaches to Heathrow and Gatwick - which means handling up to 8,000 flights a day. Visiting the Swanwick centre, it's hard not to be impressed by the sheer scale of the place, where hundreds of staff sit behind an array of large radar screens, calmly making sense of what looks to the untrained eye like utter chaos. But these controllers need reliable equipment, and the concern is that they aren't getting it. Steve Heapy, chief executive of Jet2 made the point: "It is simply not good enough for this critical national infrastructure to keep letting customers down." Easyjet said the latest incident "calls into question the resilience of Nats' systems and demonstrates the need for firm actions to prevent these repeated failures." A Nats spokesperson, apologising for the latest issue, said technology "can and sometimes does fail. Our job is minimising disruption where possible." They continued: "What isn't acceptable is any incident where safety is compromised - this is always our first priority." Sources say that behind the scenes, airlines are "furious" that disruption keeps on happening, and that they have to bear the costs of refunding passengers and looking after those who are affected by delays. There are deep concerns that not enough resources are being put into ensuring the air traffic control system has the resilience it needs. Some have gone further. Ryanair, for example, has repeatedly called for the Nats chief executive Martin Rolfe to resign, or failing that for the Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander to remove him from his post. But although Alexander has described the disruption in early September as "completely unacceptable", there seems little appetite to force through a change of leadership at Nats. The government has asked the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) to carry out an independent review of the first incident from this month, which is expected to take six months to complete. Action is unlikely before the CAA's report appears, and today's events do not appear to have changed that. Meanwhile, Rolfe made it clear on Friday that he has no plans to resign. He emphasised that in systems of such complexity, obscure faults are extremely hard to prevent. "We spent so much time making sure they work that anything that does happen of this nature is, by its very nature, going to be incredibly complicated and probably difficult to understand at the time," he said. Nevertheless, it is clear that impatience with the Nats failures is growing, both among the airlines that pay for air traffic services and among passengers who bear the brunt when systems do not work as they should. title: London Fashion Week 2026: The five trends we'll see in spring
description: As London Fashion Week comes to a close, here are the biggest trends for your wardrobe.
body: Alexander McQueen made a historic return to London Fashion Week after 25 years, staging a homecoming show that fused severe tailoring with dark romanticism This London Fashion Week has been about return and renewal - as two of Britain's biggest designers showcased their spring/summer 2027 designs. The first was Alexander McQueen, which as a brand moved to London after 25 years of showing in Paris - something Laura Weir, CEO of the British Fashion Council, told the BBC was "quite a big deal for us". Creative director Seán McGirr brought the brand back to its roots, with a runway of devil horns, lace corsets and chainmail skull dresses. Mulberry was the second designer to make its big return, this time after a nine-year absence, with Christopher Kane's debut collection centring around the brand's Baywater bag, while going big on leather in the form of coats, skirts and loafers. Weir says the "big mission" for her and her team this season was to "re-platform London Fashion Week as not only a home for British design, but an engine for creativity and commercial growth". Here are some of the major trends to come out of London Fashion Week 2026: Rejecting "quiet luxury" uniforms, Chopova Lowena, Sinead Gorey, and Conner Ives led London Fashion Week's embrace of the "messy girl" aesthetic by championing deliberate chaos, pairing intentionally undone tailoring and messy updos "The number one trend for this season is messy girl," says Elektra Kotsoni, deputy director for Vogue Business and Vogue Runway, whose team predicts the trends ahead of each season. She tells the BBC: "We're going to be having a messy girl summer" and says "it's a reaction to the clean girl and quite luxury aesthetics that took over our Instagram feeds," last year. Kotsoni says as "the world is quite messy" this form of dressing is a sign of "resilience" and rebellion. She says if you are looking to replicate this trend, mix pastel colours, dreamy florals, and tactile materials to form "unexpected clashes" that "look really messy". This form of what Kotsoni calls "crazy styling" was on display at London Fashion Week - with the noisy clashes at Chopova Lowena, Sinead Gorey and Conner Ives. Erdem, Yuhan Wang, and Bora Aksu channelled a "gardencore" vibe, trading quiet luxury for unpolished, allotment-ready chaos - pairing parkas and structured trench outerwear with kitchen-garden details According to Kotsoni - gardening is officially cool in the fashion world. A new twist on the cottage-core looks that emerged post-pandemic, instead of gingham, wicker bags and sourdough starters, it's all about looking like you're fresh from planting seeds or operating a lawnmower. "There are lots of gardening appropriate silhouettes on the runways," she says, including aprons, waterproof materials and trench coats. It started with Spanish fashion house Loewe launching a watering can-shaped handbag a couple of months ago and has now translated on the runway with Erdem, Yuhan Wang and Bora Aksu. Kotsoni says "fashion is always a reflection of what's happening in the world" and likes how designers have been able to "take an interest like gardening and present it as something" tangible in a fashion show. Dujancourt's free-spirited aesthetic, organic draping, trailing ribbons, and delicately hitched slip skirts Whilst some designers have been taking cues from the great outdoors - others have been inspired by film. Another key trend identified by Kotsoni's team is the idea of the modern goddess - a take on the styles of Ancient Greece and a nod to Christopher Nolan's hit film The Odyssey this summer. Kotsoni says the items to look out for are "draped garments, breezy materials and lots of bohemian and flowy silhouettes". Pauline Dujancourt's London Fashion Week show epitomised this style - focusing on maximum volume and billowing fabrics. Kotsoni says these looks are in opposition to how guests themselves have been dressing at this fashion week, suggesting a turning of the tide. "Everybody has been dressed really minimalist in a specific quiet luxury way and I think people are tired of that," she notes. Mulberry, Justin Cassin, Enny Atelier and Vin + Omi all featured orange in thier shows Whether your preference is melon, tangerine, ginger or coral - orange appears to be the big colour trend for next year. Kotsoni says she is hedging her bets on whether a shade of orange will be Pantone's colour of the year for 2027 as it has already been making its way into celebrity styling (it's not too late to replicate Kylie Jenner and Timothée Chalamet's matching neon outfits , externalat the Marty Supreme premiere for Halloween) and on the runway. Mulberry, Justin Cassin, Enny Atelier and Vin + Omi all featured orange in their London shows and presentations over the last couple of days. A school sports hall is transformed into a ballet stage for Edeline Lee's latest collection which drew inspiration from the intense discipline, repetition, and physical toll of classical dance Ever the fashion muse, Chalamet is once again at the centre of another trend for 2027 - ballet. After he said "no one cares" about the discipline in May this year, Kotsoni says she "thinks it's interesting" that it's now being forged as a clear trend for next year. Edeline Lee put on a striking show in London - complete with models taking to the runway en pointe in a transformed school sports hall. "Ballet is very much in fashion," she says, noting that this month's Vogue Italia has La Scala's principle dancer Roberto Bolle on the cover, whilst Royal Ballet dancer Francesca Hayward has recently been modelling for Armani and Chanel. "Ballet flats are massive and still will be [next year] and small silhouettes for shoes are going to be prevalent next season," Kotsoni adds - encouraging fans of the style to seek out items in charity and vintage shops if they want to replicate the look.

title: I've got no ceiling on Lib Dem ambitions, says leader Ed Davey
description: The Lib Dem leader also backed the controversial Jackdaw gas field, which the government is expected to approve.
body: Sir Ed Davey and Lib Dem MPs visited a wind farm off the south coast of England Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey has insisted he is not just aiming to be a junior partner in a coalition government, saying: "I am a candidate to be prime minister." He also backed the controversial Jackdaw gas field, which the government is expected to green light later this month, saying it had "passed the climate test" and was compatible with a transition to renewables. Sir Ed has faced criticism from some in his party that he lacks ambition and the vision needed to cut through in a crowded political field. He acknowledged the "frustration" felt by some of his MPs that the party was not making a bigger impact - and vowed to set out bold policies in his conference speech on Tuesday. Sir Ed led the Lib Dems to a record 72 MPs at the 2024 election, making big gains at the expense of the Conservatives in southern England, but the party has since slipped to fourth or fifth in national opinion polls, behind Labour, the Tories, the Greens and Reform UK. Despite this, the Lib Dem leader claimed his party had an "historic opportunity to do far better than anyone imagines at the moment" at the next general election. "Because the right wing is split," he said, "and fragmented like it's never happened before in over 200 years of British parliamentary elections. "If we take that opportunity, and I believe we're showing how we can, we'll be a massive force in the next parliament." Asked if he wanted to be the kingmaker in the next government, providing support for a party falling short of the 326 MPs needed for a majority, Sir Ed said: "I've got no ceiling on our ambitions. "I'm a candidate to be prime minister, but what we need to do is make sure that we build on that [election success], area by area, constituency by constituency." He made clear he will not go into a coalition government with Reform UK and has dismissed suggestions he could do a deal with the Conservatives. "We've got a moral responsibility to stop Nigel Farage - and indeed stop Kemi Badenoch giving the keys to No 10 to Nigel Farage - I think there could be that sort of coalition on the right and we've got to stop that," he told the BBC. Asked if he would form a coalition with Labour, he said he did not deal in "hypotheticals". He said he wanted the Lib Dems to win support across the UK, but the BBC has been told his party's strategy is focused on the 27 seats where they came second in 2024. Of those 27, 20 are held by the Conservatives. Controversial Jackdaw gas field set to be approved in weeks, sources say Lib Dems sleepwalking to irrelevance under Davey, says council leader Lib Dems call for one-to-one midwife care during childbirth Sir Ed was speaking just before he headed out to visit the wind farm off the coast of Brighton, which he said he had signed off on when he was energy secretary in the Conservative-Lib Dem coalition government a decade ago. He set out why supporting Jackdaw was not in conflict with his party's stance on tackling climate change, saying: "We're going to need gas for a long, long time as part of our transition, and when I was secretary of state for climate change, I always thought that we were going to need gas, and [Jackdaw] has passed the climate change test." Sir Ed explained the alternative was shipping in liquified natural gas (LNG) from across the globe, which would be more problematic than using gas from the North Sea, about 150 miles northeast of Aberdeen. "There's a lot of energy produced in both putting the gas into liquid and then taking it out into gas," he said. "The carbon footprint of that is far bigger, a lot more damaging for our climate, so this way, not only is it better for the climate, but also tax revenues come to the Exchequer." However, he told the BBC "the jury is very much out" on the Rosebank oil field, not least because that may not pass the same test on reducing carbon emissions. And he insisted the Lib Dems were still committed to a transition away from oil and gas, for the climate and also to lower people's energy bills. "Thanks to President Trump's mad war in Iran, people are paying far higher," he said. "We are paying far higher for that fossil fuel energy, and you've seen over the years how fossil fuels, oil and gas, can be extremely expensive. "So, the way to get energy bills down, get the economy growing, is to be less dependent on fossil fuels and we want to be." title: Seventeen arrested in Teesside police raids
description: The raids across Teesside follow the A66 crash which killed two police officers and five men.
body: About 130 officers were involved in the raids across parts of Teesside Police have carried out a series of early morning raids targeting those suspected of being involved in organised crime. Cleveland Police said 17 people had been arrested during the operation - involving about 130 officers including some from the National Crime Agency - across South Bank, Grangetown and Eston, near Middlesbrough, on Monday. It is part of a high-profile response to a crash on the nearby A66 last month which came at the end of a police pursuit and left two officers dead. Five men died also died when their Volkswagen Passat went the wrong way down the road and hit a Cleveland Police armed response vehicle heading in the opposite direction. The force said Monday's raids had seen people arrested on suspicion of various offences including drugs and assault. A convoy of about a dozen vans started the operation shortly after 08:00 BST, with roads temporarily blocked by patrol cars. Officers used battering rams to force entry to several properties as parents walked past with their children on the school run. Cleveland Police said much of the information behind the raids had come from the local community Assistant Chief Constable Mark Hall said public support after the crash had been ''absolutely phenomenal". "It's clear criminality of any sort is not welcome on these estates and we are here to tell those people we've heard their concerns and we will act," he said. Officers PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, along with all five occupants of the Passat died at the scene of the A66 crash. Cleveland's Police and Crime Commissioner Matt Storey said it was important for people to see officers on the streets targeting those responsible for crime. He said: "This makes people more reassured about what is really going in their communities. They see people arrested, charged and taken off the streets. "It shows the public good work is happening, despite the problems we have." Follow BBC Tees on X,, external Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external. title: Was Neville right to call out Man Utd for a 'lack of effort'?
description: Was Gary Neville right to call out Manchester United for a "lack of effort" in their 1-1 draw at Fulham on Sunday?
body: Gary Neville started for Sky Sports as a pundit and co-commentator in 2011 "I've watched Manchester United since the age of five and that's the worst 15 minutes I've ever seen. Absolutely pathetic." Gary Neville did not hold back in his criticism of the Manchester United's performance during Sky Sports' coverage of Sunday's 1-1 draw at Fulham. The players had just laboured through the opening period of the second half, culminating in a Lisandro Martinez own goal gifting the home side the lead. "I've never seen such a lack of effort," Neville added. "What must Michael Carrick be thinking?" Neville played 602 games for United over a 19-year career, winning everything the club game had to offer. So his criticism comes from a qualified position. This season's out-of-possession stats would appear to back it up too, with the Red Devils ranking 16th for distance covered, and 17th for total number of sprints. But does that tell the whole story? How did United play under Carrick when they were winning games towards the end of last season? And, as Neville makes the headlines, what does this say about his influence in the media around Manchester United? This video can not be played Cunha's late strike denies Fulham first league win of the season United's dismal running and sprinting stats made for stark reading in the wake of Neville's criticism. After all, the former right-back had directly questioned a lack of effort, and referred to the players as "mannequins". He said United - and Fulham - were walking too much during the game. In the Premier League this season only four teams have covered less distance than the Red Devils, and just three teams have produced fewer sprints. It comes alongside United's joint-worst start to a Premier League season, with four points from five games. So is this down to the running and the effort? Let's take a look at the second half of last season, after Carrick had been appointed as manager. Between 17 January and the end of the season, United picked up more points than any other team - 39 points from 17 games. Yet only four teams ran less than United, and only two clubs had fewer sprints. There is no material difference in the running stats, but United were returning 2.29 points per game compared to the 0.8 this season. Something is clearly different, but it does not appear to be linked to this particular stat because barely anything has changed - apart from the results. Maybe this United squad simply does not have runners. Then there is the comparison to rival teams. Manchester City have won all five Premier League matches, but have covered less distance than United. Enzo Maresca's squad have also recorded the lowest number of sprints in the division. Brighton, one of the most exciting teams in the league this season and the top goalscorers, are one place above United for sprints. Maybe United's problem is tactical rather than a simple case of not running enough? Neville setting the media agenda when it comes to United is not a new thing. The former England international has called out the team's shortcomings on many occasions. Look back to December 2021, and a poor first-half performance against a struggling Newcastle side which saw Ralf Rangnick's side trail 1-0 at the break. "They're a bunch of whinge-bags," Neville said at half-time on Sky Sports. "I'll not go into names but they're whinging at each other, arms up in the air complaining about everything. "There's no pressing, no urgency, the basics of the game." Edinson Cavani rescued a point at St James Park, but Neville's comments had already made the headlines. You only need to look at how the post-match coverage went after the Fulham draw. Neville's remarks were put to Carrick at full-time. The United manager said fitness levels of his players were not an issue. But the die was cast. "Neville: That was the worst ever", read the back page of Monday's Daily Telegraph. "15 minutes of shame", was the lead for the sports section of the Daily Star. "United boss keeps calm after Neville Ful blast," said the Daily Express. It was picked up across online media, and discussed at length on radio talk shows - including across the BBC, as evidenced by this piece. This video can not be played Carrick impressed Man Utd 'kept belief' to earn draw at Fulham When Neville criticises his former club, it carries weight. In January, with Ruben Amorim under pressure for poor results, the Portuguese said that "if people cannot handle the Gary Nevilles and the criticisms of everything, we need to change the club". Amorim was dismissed the following day. There always seems to be a strong influence in the media related to the dominant team of a previous era. For example throughout the 1990s and 2000s, former Liverpool stars such as Alan Hansen, Mark Lawrenson and Phil Thompson dominated a lot of the conversation. It stands to reason that now members of the all-conquering United squad will have a leading role in the media. But for Neville, it is bigger than anyone apart from Gary Lineker and his Goalhanger production company. How Lineker and Neville became rival media moguls Neville calls Man Utd 'pathetic' - but Carrick maintains belief 'I've asked for forgiveness' - Eckert and Southampton braced for Spygate verdict "When does Sky wonder if they are paying a lot of money in wages to train their next competitor?" It is a question posed by Richard Gillis, who hosts the Unofficial Partner sports business podcast. While Neville started out in the media as a pundit with Sky Sports, the 51-year-old is now one of the biggest players in a rapidly changing industry. title: Scotland's 32 councils could be cut to six under government plan
description: Between six and 10 regional bodies would replace local authorities under proposals submitted by ministers.
body: Scotland's 32 councils could be replaced by as few as six regional authorities under proposals published by the government. Under the reforms, external, the regional bodies would focus on major issues such as education and economic growth. They would also be responsible for supporting between 120 and 160 community authorities, which would oversee some local issues. The proposals have been shared with Holyrood's committees and council umbrella body Cosla ahead of a public consultation. Scotland's councils face budget shortfalls. How bad is it in your area? How will Swinney 'rewire' local government and public services? The proposals suggest that the regional bodies would be given powers over larger planning decisions, education and economic development. They would also oversee the delivery of key services such as waste management, cleaning and early learning. The smaller community authorities would contribute to local planning decisions, town centre regeneration, licensing and the historic environment. Separate set-ups for Scotland's islands would also be required, according to the paper. Councillors would be elected to the existing wards across Scotland and serve on both the local and regional authorities. However, the document suggests the increased time commitment may require a boost in pay. The proposals do not outline how the reforms would be financed. Scotland's current council set-up, with 32 local authorities, was introduced by the UK government in 1996. Before then, the country had a two-tier system of nine regional councils and 53 district councils. Deputy First Minister Jenny Gilruth said: "We need to ensure investment is focused on frontline delivery, with the right staff in the right roles to empower communities and deliver real improvements in public services." She added: "Existing local government responsibilities could also be extended, including enhanced roles in economic development and business support so that individual areas can reflect local strengths and ambitions. "These proposals are intended to provide a starting point to facilitate debate and discussion as we work to deliver reforms that strengthen public services and improve outcomes for the people and communities we serve." Scottish Labour local government spokesman Joe Fagan said: "The Scottish government must not blunder into another reorganisation. "Any reforms must be made in partnership with local government and backed up with fair funding for local services." Earlier this month, First Minister John Swinney announced plans to cut the number of health boards in Scotland from 14 to 2. He described the reforms, designed to cut costs and improve efficiency, as "the most significant structural reform of our NHS in the devolution era". Separate plans are also being considered for the three island groups - Shetland, Orkney, and the Western Isles. title: Airlines criticise air traffic control as second glitch causes more disruption
description: EasyJet says the latest incident "once again calls into question the resilience" of the system.
body: Airlines have criticised the UK's air traffic control system after a second technical problem in two weeks caused major disruption to UK flights EasyJet said Monday's incident "once again calls into question the resilience" of how the service works, while Wizz Air said there was a "national confidence crisis" in National Air Traffic Services (Nats), which runs the UK's air traffic. The technical problem at Prestwick in Ayrshire caused disruption at airports across Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England, delaying dozens of flights. Nats said a "connectivity issue" was to blame for the disruption, and that it had "nothing to do" with a separate software defect at Swanwick that led to the cancellation of 2,000 flights earlier in September. The underlying issue causing Monday's disruption has since been resolved, with Nats saying it was running at "full capacity" although officials warned of knock-on effects. A spokesperson said they were now "focused on working with our customers to recover their residual delays and help get their operations back to normal". According to aviation analytics company Cirium, as of 13:45 BST, at least 200 flights had been cancelled or did not fly on Monday. This includes 100 flights scheduled to arrive in the UK and 99 that were due to depart from the UK. Easyjet was the worst affected airline, with 47 of its 670 scheduled departures cancelled, while British Airways has seen 11 cancellations from its 513 scheduled departures. The UK Civil Aviation Authority said passengers who had flights disrupted were "unlikely" to be entitled to compensation. It said the technical issue is "likely to be considered the result of 'extraordinary circumstances' under passenger rights rules", meaning that "although passengers should be looked after by airlines, they are unlikely to be entitled to compensation for delays or cancellations that were directly caused by the incident". Industry representative body Airlines UK said both passengers and airlines "deserve better" service after "yet another Nats failure". Managing director of Wizz Air UK, Yvonne Moynihan, called for "urgent reform" of Nats, adding that she did not have confidence in its current leadership. When asked by BBC Radio 4's World at One programme whether Nats chief Martin Rolfe should resign, Moynihan said: "We need to look at the leadership at the top. But more than that, what are the board of directors doing?" Jet2 boss Steve Heapy called for "urgent and accountable" action to bolster the UK's air traffic control infrastructure. Ryanair reiterated its calls for Rolfe to resign, saying he had failed to deliver" either a reliable system or an effective back-up". The latest outage affected 140 of the airline's flights and 25,000 passengers. British Airways said "yet another technical fault with Nats" was "disappointing". Airlines criticise air traffic control after second glitch this month causes more disruption A Nats spokesperson apologised for the disruption, saying: "In the real world, we accept technology can and sometimes does fail. Our job is minimising disruption where possible. "What isn't acceptable is any incident where safety is compromised - this is always our first priority." They added that it was working to return air traffic to normal as quickly as possible and urged passengers to check their flight status with their airline. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander acknowledged the problems with flights were "deeply frustrating" for passengers. Steve Davies, 74, told the BBC he was "cheesed off with air traffic control" as technical issues with its systems seemed to be "happening a lot". He and his wife Sadie became stuck at Birmingham airport after being told to disembark their easyJet flight to Edinburgh on Monday morning. Nicole McCloskey, from Kilmarnock, had been due to go to Disneyland Paris with her family before their flight was cancelled. She told the BBC her family got a message to say the flight was delayed while they were travelling to Glasgow airport, but only found out it had been grounded altogether once they arrived. Nicole said they have been rebooked on another flight on later on Monday and were hopeful "it's sorted in time". Nicole McCloskey and her daughters have had their flight to Disneyland cancelled This is the second failure at Nats, the company that looks after UK airspace, in less than a fortnight. Not much is known about what happened on this occasion, except that there was a technical failure at Nats' control centre in Prestwick. Nats has two main centres. The first, at Swanwick in Hampshire, looks after airspace in the southern part of the UK, including the approaches to Heathrow and Gatwick. Nats says the latest failure at Prestwick was different - Prestwick in Ayrshire looks after traffic across northern England, Scotland and Northern Ireland, catering for about 42% of the UK's air traffic. The Swanwick incident last month affected hundreds of thousands of passengers, with some sleeping on airport floors or getting stuck overseas earlier this month. That disruption was much more severe as it affected intercontinental and long-haul travel via UK airspace. Nats said in a report last week that the software glitch happened "in the space of a millisecond" leading to the system producing corrupted data. However, the fact that the UK's air traffic control system has suffered two significant issues in a short space of time has attracted a great deal of criticism, and the pressure on Nats boss Martin Rolfe - who insisted last week he would not resign - is only likely to mount. Rolfe told the BBC at the time he would not resign, saying the software defect was "very, very obscure". "My job is to make sure that we have this happen as infrequently as possible," he said. title: Two arrested over major fire at Kent hotel
description: A 38-year-old man and 21-year-old woman were arrested on suspicion of arson, police say.
body: The fire service said the blaze was believed to have started in the basement Two people have been arrested on suspicion of arson after a fire at a seaside hotel which led to hundreds of people being evacuated. Kent Police said a 38-year-old man and 21-year-old woman were held after the blaze at the Grand Burstin Hotel in Folkestone on Saturday. The fire broke out at the hotel in Marine Parade in the early hours and about 280 people were evacuated from the building. A total of 90 people were relocated from neighbouring Pavilion Court in Marine Terrace following concerns raised by safety inspectors, Folkestone and Hythe District Council said. The pair who were arrested have been released while inquiries continue, a police spokesperson said. Police say road closures remain in place for investigation work following the blaze, which started at about 01:20 BST. The blaze is being treated as suspicious and police are appealing for witnesses. Britannia Hotels Group, which runs the Grand Burstin, said at the weekend it was fully cooperating with police and supporting the investigation. The group said engineers and building inspectors had been at the site to carry out structural assessments, and its team was working to assist guests. Twenty six fire engines were sent to the hotel and Kent Fire and Rescue Service said it was believed the fire had started in the basement of the building. The council has been working to arrange alternative housing for affected residents while the hotel undergoes assessments and any required works to make it safe. Kent Police said the fire at the Grand Burstin Hotel was being treated as suspicious On Saturday, a welfare centre was set up for hotel residents. Other businesses, including nearby pub The Harbour Inn, also opened their doors to those affected. Ross Honeycombe, who was staying at the hotel with his family, described how they were woken by fire alarms at about 01:00, adding: "We looked out and there was smoke billowing from the underground car park. "Later we started hearing explosions." A resident at Pavilion Court, John Dighton, said he "grabbed stuff for a couple of days" and was staying at a nearby hotel. He said the worst thing was not knowing how long they would be away from their homes. title: Council leader found guilty of fraud and tax evasion
description: Jason Zadrozny, leader of Ashfield District Council in Nottinghamshire, is convicted of 13 offences.
body: Jason Zadrozny was found guilty of nine counts of fraud and four counts of tax evasion Ashfield District Council leader Jason Zadrozny has been found guilty of fraud and tax evasion. Zadrozny, of Stanton Hill, was accused of setting up a fake heritage group to defraud Nottinghamshire County Council out of thousands of pounds. Prosecutors also alleged he failed to pay tax on four rental properties. The 46-year-old, who served as an Ashfield Independents councillor on the county council, was found guilty of nine counts of fraud and four counts of tax evasion. The verdicts came after a jury at Northampton Crown Court had deliberated for nearly 11 hours. Zadrozny was told by the judge he will be sentenced on 27 November, and was "at risk of an immediate custodial sentence". Thanking jury members for their "care and attention" during the trial, judge David Herbert KC added the council leader would be given unconditional bail until his sentencing hearing. Zadrozny denied any wrongdoing at Northampton Crown Court During the trial, jurors were told Zadrozny had set up the Ashfield Heritage Society in 2018 before applying for funding from Nottinghamshire County Council, which he then transferred into his personal account. This included £7,500, requested three days after setting up a bank account for the society, which Zadrozny - who was a county councillor at the time - claimed was "to support heritage projects in Ashfield". The council issued the funds and they were sent directly to Zadrozny, who deposited them in the account, before withdrawing them in cash in March. Prosecutors alleged part of the money was used to buy a house with friends. They said the fraud came to light in March 2021, when Catherine Mason, who was hoping to stand for election in Ashfield, was looking into the council's expenditure and investigated the setting up of the heritage society. The county council launched an investigation and subsequently passed the details on to the police. Zadrozny denied the offences and told the trial all the funds he had received were spent on the community. He told jurors he gave the cash from the Ashfield Heritage Society to Tony Brewer - a former Ashfield District Council chairman who died from Covid in 2020 - to carry out the repair and maintenance of war memorials in the area. The defendant told jurors his paperwork for funding applications was "terrible", adding: "I wouldn't be sitting in the dock if I filled it out much more clearly." He also said the wrong address on the application form for the heritage society was "clearly an error" and he cannot remember why he wrote it down. Jurors found him not guilty of three of the 12 counts of fraud. Addressing Zadrozny, the judge said: "You have been convicted by the jury. Please understand in my mind is an immediate custodial sentence, given the nature of these offences. The breach of trust element makes them particularly serious. "Please don't think because the sentencing is not today that it won't be an immediate custodial sentence." A spokesperson for Ashfield District Council said the authority was aware of the verdict. "The council will now follow the appropriate legal and democratic processes," they said. "We will continue to deliver our services and undertake our responsibilities for residents, businesses and communities." title: Merz vows to keep coalition together for Germany's 'democratic future'
description: The chancellor has come under increasing pressure after resounding state election defeats, but says the results "go far beyond my own person"
body: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz says he will keep his ruling coalition together for the sake of his country's "democratic future", following resounding defeats for his party in two state elections. "We are determined to live up to the historic challenges our country is facing," Merz said, referring to the coalition between his Christian Democratic Unionist (CDU) party and the Social Democratic Party (SPD). Merz's position has come under mounting pressure after Sunday's election results. In the north-eastern Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won the most votes, with the CDU failing even to reach the threshold to stay in the state parliament. Meanwhile in Berlin, the CDU came second to the hard-left Die Linke party, with the AfD also making significant gains. Speaking at the news conference on Monday, Merz described the result in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern as "a heavy blow" for the centre-left CDU. "This election is a profound turning point. It is a dramatic, unprecedented result for the CDU in Germany," he acknowledged. Merz said there had been no discussion about his own position since the results and pushed back against the idea that his low popularity ratings alone were behind the election defeats. "I know that I as an individual played a role in these state elections," Merz said, before adding: "But the reasons for the results go far beyond just me." "We are witnessing a profound transformation of Germany's political party system, as is happening in many other countries around the world." There have been rumours Merz, who has only been in power for 16 months, could be replaced mid-term in a so-called chancellor swap due to his poor approval ratings. Asked earlier on Monday how long Merz has left in office, the AfD's co-leader Alice Weidel told the BBC: "Pretty soon, he's going to leave." This video can not be played AfD co-leader Alice Weidel predicts Friedrich Merz will be out of government soon The two elections took place on Sunday, a fortnight after the CDU saw its vote halved in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD won a major victory. In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the CDU fell short of a 5% threshold to enter parliament, underperforming against what had already been projected to be the party's worst ever result in the area. Merz earlier conceded that this result was "a disaster". While the AfD won the most votes in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, it was far short of a majority and is unlikely to govern as other parties may refuse to work with it. Some branches of the party are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence, a designation it strongly rejects. But its anti-immigration, Germany first, and Russian-friendly agenda has found fertile ground in the country's former communist east. In Berlin, the CDU's defeat means Die Linke, which won the most votes, could now take power in a coalition. title: Yemenis flee across Red Sea as Houthis and Saudi-backed forces escalate war
description: The BBC's Frank Gardner speaks to some of those who have fled the war by crossing the Red Sea to Djibouti
body: This video can not be played Watch: Inside a camp for Yemeni refugees in Djibouti Ibrahim Issa, 50, is from the Yemeni coastal town of Dhubab, right on the front lines of the war between Yemen's Houthis and the Saudi-backed pro-government forces fighting them. Today he sits, surrounded by his family, on a tarpaulin spread over a sandy floor inside a vast open-sided warehouse at Markazi camp in Obock, northern Djibouti, packed with Yemeni families who have fled by boat across the narrow Bab al-Mandab strait. After their sea crossing, Yemeni refugees have made their way by truck and on foot to this camp, jointly administered by the government and the UN. "How could I just sit there when my kids are screaming and shaking in terror?" says Ibrahim Issa. "When the sound of the planes start, and the kids hear the planes, they begin shouting and screaming. As parents it is our responsibility, what can you do when you see this? That is why we fled, to save them." Saudi Arabia issues first air raid alerts for Riyadh since Houthis escalated attacks Lightning Houthi advance in Yemen may bring dangerous new dimension to Iran war Ibrahim Issa escaped on his fishing boat with family and several goats As a fisherman, Ibrahim Issa already owned a boat large enough to bring out his family from Yemen. He even brought several of the family's goats which I can now see nibbling at scraps nearby, foraging amidst the discarded canisters of cooking gas and empty plastic bottles. Some families have been able to bring small bundles of possessions with them from Yemen – one family has even brought a "jeraak", a tall metal shisha pipe – but others have arrived, exhausted, in just the clothes they left in. In just the last few days more than 3,000 refugees have arrived here from Yemen, many entire families. The UN estimates that in all, more than 120,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the sudden surge in fighting along Yemen's Red Sea coast. This month, the country's Houthis, who had already seized most of the populated parts of Yemen years ago, made a lightning dash down the coast towards Bab al-Mandab, the narrow, maritime chokepoint where the southern Red Sea flows into the Gulf of Aden and the wider Indian Ocean. Saudi Arabia, which backs the internationally recognised UN-recognised government of Yemen, has responded with hundreds of air strikes along the flat, coastal plain where the Houthis are now digging in. The Houthis have also launched hundreds of drones and missiles at cities and infrastructure in south-western Saudi Arabia. "We don't care which side it is that's attacking," is the message I got loud and clear in Arabic from everyone here I spoke to. "It's the bombs falling all around us that have caused us to flee." Djibouti, a tiny former French colony that sits just across the water from Yemen, has made it clear it has no intention of involving itself in the war between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government. And yet Djibouti is one of the most militarised nations in Africa. Since 2003, the US has run a huge multinational base here, Camp Lemonnier, once home to the French Foreign Legion. China too has a major base here, its largest military presence on the Indian Ocean and recently upgraded. Back in Markazi camp, one of those I spoke to is Qassim Abraham Abssy. Once also a fisherman, his identity card shows him to be 100 years old. "What led us to come here?" he asks rhetorically. "It was the planes. The sounds of the planes, boom! That's what made us flee, for the sake of our children. It burns ours hearts. We don't know which side they are from. They are bombing everywhere, because the Houthis are everywhere, in the mountains, in the roads. A plane comes, bombs everywhere." More than 120,000 Yemenis are estimated to have been displaced by the sudden surge in fighting Outside in the blazing 37C heat, close to the neat lines of tents supplied by the UN refugee agency, UNHCR, I met Mohammed Abdullarim from Aden, a 63-year-old former tour guide old enough to have been born when Aden was still a British protectorate. Unlike the new arrivals, Mohammed has been here since 2015. He fled to Djibouti soon after the fighting first flared up between the Houthis and the government of the now-ousted President Abdrabbuh Mansour Hadi. He has been at the camp ever since but suddenly, as we were talking, the sadness of what is happening to his country overwhelmed him and he turned his head away, choking back tears. "Most of the people here are in the worst condition, inside the tents here. I am very touched, I'm crying for these people, for my people, for their suffering. I want our voices to be heard by the NGOs and the Djibouti government. And I'm thankful to them for accepting us." How long will they have to stay here? That depends, of course, on the fighting. Yemen has been wracked by a horrific civil war that has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced millions since 2014. A shaky, UN-brokered 2022 truce between the Saudis and the Houthis has broken down spectacularly in recent months, with the two sides trading missiles, drones and air strikes. "We are willing to go back in peace if peace returns to our country," says Aisha Abdulkadir Mohammed Yemen's war may be a remote one to most people but the effect of choking off Saudi Arabia's oil exports through the Bab al-Mandab strait are well publicised. But as ever, it is often the human cost that goes unnoticed. Sitting beside his wife on their tarpaulin, amid the cacophony all around them, Qassim Abssy the fisherman is wary of leaving the safety of Djibouti: "If the war continues then we're not going back because we have peace here." His wife, Aisha Abdulkadir Mohammed, agrees. "We are willing to go back in peace if peace returns to our country, and we are praying to God that peace does return. All we need is peace, even for our children's future, they get safety first,

title: Driver, 20, jailed after dashcam filmed 'horrific' head-on crash which left victim with PTSD
description: Martin Howells was left unable to work for 10 months after Ethan Loveridge crashed into him.
body: This video can not be played Head on collision captured on dash cam A 20-year-old man who lost control of his car and crashed head-on into another driver has been jailed. Ethan Loveridge, from Llanbradach, Caerphilly county, seriously injured Martin Howells in the "horrific" crash in August 2024. Howells, 50, suffered suffered eight broken ribs, a broken nose, a detached bicep, injury to his left shoulder and a rotator cuff, and nerve damage to his neck and shoulder. He was off work for 10 months. Dashcam footage showed Loveridge's Kia Sorento clip another car on the A468 in Caerphilly before hitting Howells' car. At Newport Crown Court, Loveridge admitted causing serious injury by dangerous driving and a string of drugs offences and jailed for five years. "It was a horrific crash that has changed my life forever," Howells said. Loveridge's car ended up on its side, while Howells remained injured inside his vehicle as passers-by attempted to help him. In a victim personal statement read to the jury, Paul Hewitt, prosecuting, said: "It was a horrific crash and it changed my life forever. "I had 18 months of physical therapy. "My injuries left me with weakness in my arms and I am unable to lift anything above shoulder height, which I will live with for the rest of my life." He said difficulties with his fingers had prevented him from playing guitar, which he described as something he loved. "I have been diagnosed with PTSD and underwent eight months of psychological therapy," he said. Howells said his grandson was born six weeks after the crash, but he was unable to fully enjoy his arrival because of his injuries. He said he was unable to sleep properly and would wake during the night thinking about what could have happened. Ethan Loveridge pleaded guilty to multiple charges Loveridge was also sentenced for drug offences after he and his then partner Elise Humphreys, 21, were stopped in a Ford Mondeo on 26 June 2025. They were seen discarding items from the car and a search found cannabis and cash. Their phones were seized and messages revealed they had been involved in supplying cocaine and cannabis for six months. A search of Loveridge's property found 810g of cannabis worth £8,000. Loveridge later pleaded guilty to causing serious injury by dangerous driving, possession with intent to supply a class B drug, being concerned in the supply of class A and B drugs, and possession of criminal property. Recorder John Philpotts said: "You are well aware of the potential consequences of a head on collision of the sort you caused. "In fact you are fortunate there was no fatality in this case." Humphreys was given a 12-month community order, a 15-day rehabilitation activity requirement and a six-month trail monitoring requirement. Loveridge was sentenced to five years in prison and disqualified from driving for four years. title: Millions urged to evacuate as powerful Typhoon Dujuan hits Japan
description: The country's meteorological agency had warned of an "imminent threat to life," but this has now been downgraded in most areas.
body: Almost two million people are under evacuation orders in Japan as Typhoon Dujuan batters a number of the country's prefectures. Japan's Meteorological Agency had warned of an "imminent threat to life", but several warnings have now been downgraded, with the danger to life warning remaining in place in Oshima Town. Strong winds caused power cuts for more than 50,000 people, while hundreds of flights have been cancelled and rail services have been suspended. Dujuan has had sustained winds of 130km/h (80.8mph) and gusts of 194 km/h. It is the latest in a series of storms in the Pacific, made more intense by the "super El Niño", which has warmed the ocean, fuelling the formation of storms. Pedestrians caught in the rain at the Shibuya crossing in Tokyo The level three warnings, for heavy rain, and the level four warnings, for landslides have now been either downgraded or lifted by the Japan Meteorological Agency in most areas. The level four warnings remain in Shinagawa Ward, Toshima Village, and Niijima Village. Authorities have advised the public to pay attention to weather information. Dujuan, which is Japan's 25th typhoon of the year, has hit in the midst of a five-day holiday and forced the cancellation of several events. Concerts scheduled for Monday at the Rock in Japan music festival have been cancelled, while the Tokyo Game Show, a video game convention, has also cancelled Monday's programme. Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has reportedly delayed her trip to the United States this week to monitor the effects of the typhoon. She had been due in New York on Tuesday to meet with US President Donald Trump and speak at the UN General Assembly. Passengers waiting for updates at Haneda Airport The Yokosuka City Fire Department told the BBC that a woman who lived in the house, aged in her 60s, may have been swept away and is believed to have been buried alive. Separately, Sodegaura City Fire Department in Chiba prefecture told the BBC a man in his 50s was rescued after getting trapped while working to clear debris at a landslide site. The department said the worker fell into a bamboo thicket, along with some heavy machinery. He was then taken to hospital. Firefighters in Kanagawa prefecture said they received a call from a man who reported his house had been crushed by a landslide. A woman struggles with her umbrella outside Shinjuku station Some research suggests that Japan has become more exposed to destructive storms, but climate change is not thought to be increasing the number of these storms globally, and could even make them less common in some regions. As temperatures rise, typhoons that do form are likely to become more intense on average, however. Warmer ocean waters mean storms can pick up more energy, leading to higher wind speeds. And because a warmer atmosphere can hold more moisture, these storms could also bring heavier rainfall. A satellite view shows Typhoon Dujuan approaching Japan This year, El Niño - the natural weather phenomenon bringing warmer water to parts of the tropical Pacific - is another factor. El Niño doesn't have a clear effect on the total number of typhoons, but it can affect where typhoons form, their strength and which countries they hit. Some El Niño events may expose Japan to stronger typhoons, for example. The typhoon is continuing to travel along the country's Pacific coast, heading north. The extent of the damage today may not be known until Tuesday. title: Cate Blanchett asks theatre audience to stop filming during show
description: The A-list actress is the latest star to ask fans to put their phones away during performances.
body: The actress is appearing at London's National Theatre in Electra/Persona A-list actress Cate Blanchett has become the latest star to make a plea for theatre audiences to put their phones away during performances. The Australian film and stage actor and producer was appearing at London's National Theatre in Electra/Persona. During the curtain call on Friday, Blanchett said: "There are few places on this planet where we can simply be together and be present. "I understand you like filming the curtain call – and it is kind of flattering in a way – but for anyone who is filming the show, please don't, because it spoils it for the next group of people who come in and are present with us. So thank you very much." The two-time Oscar winner's words were greeted with cheers and clapping from the audience. One audience member explained what had happened earlier in the performance, saying that the filming took place between two acts: "I was there on Friday, so just to clarify what happened: after the first act, while they were changing and preparing for the second, latecomers were being let in, the staff were cleaning the stage, and the cast were doing their makeup on stage. "Cate noticed someone recording during that break. She came towards the front of the stage and gestured "no, no, no" with her finger for them to stop. She also mentioned it to the audience at the very end before they left," the theatre-goer wrote on Instagram, external. "The person wasn't filming the actual performance, but the interval between the two acts while the cast were still on stage. To be fair, people do this quite often and the staff usually don't say anything. It was my third time seeing the play, and I've seen people film during that break every time. Friday was simply the first time I saw Cate notice it herself, just after she had finished doing her makeup." Electra/Persona is a new play written and directed by Benedict Andrews that combines the Sophocles tragedy Electra with Ingmar Bergman's film Persona. The play, which is on until 10 October, sees Blanchett sharing the roles of Electra/Elisabeth and Clytemnestra/Alma with her co-star Nina Hoss, determined by a coin toss live on stage every night ahead of each performance. Rosamund Pike calls out audience member for texting during show Loud eaters and phones nearly spoiled my cinema trip - and it's not just me Actors rage at World Cup fans on phones Many theatres, like cinemas, ask audiences to switch off their mobile phones during performances. Rosamund Pike called out an audience member for texting during an emotional moment from her performance in West End play Inter Alia earlier this year, saying: "When I feel that and see it, it's hard." Cynthia Erivo interrupted her recent performance of Dracula after spotting an audience member filming. And Andrew Scott halted his "to be or not to be" soliloquy in Hamlet, a few years back, after someone started using a laptop. Other stars including Daniel Craig, Hugh Jackman and Patti LuPone have all made similar criticisms, while Lesley Manville told BBC Radio 4 earlier this year that she found it "insulting" when punters took photos, even of curtain calls. title: Man guilty of murdering partner in frenzied flat attack
description: Alexander Brennan, 54, killed Brodie MacGregor, 23, at her flat in Glasgow's Springburn on 26 August 2024.
body: Brodie MacGregor was found dead in her home on Elmvale Street in Springburn on 26 August 2024 A man who attacked his partner with broken glass bottles has been found guilty of murder. Alexander Brennan, 54, killed Brodie MacGregor, 23, at her flat in Glasgow's Springburn on 26 August 2024. A post-mortem examination found MacGregor suffered a total of 78 injuries to her head and body after she was repeatedly punched, slapped and struck with glass bottles and a microwave plate. Brennan was convicted and jailed for a minimum of 22 years following a trial at the High Court in Glasgow. This story contains details which some readers may find distressing. Judge Lord Scott told the killer he had left a child without a mother. He said: "You brutally murdered a woman who offered no serious physical threat to you. "A doctor described her injuries as ones seen in high velocity impacts or falling from a building. "As she lay there for around an hour, conscious or unconscious, you took no steps to seek medical assistance which would have offered a slight chance that she would survive. "You showed complete disregard to whether she lived or died." The judge told Brennan he had showed 'complete disregard' for MacGregor The court previously heard Brennan had fallen out with MacGregor when he travelled from Stirling to her home in Glasgow, at about 01:35 on the day of the murder. MacGregor dialled 999 at about 04:35, where she was heard to say on the call: "You attacked me". Officers showed up at the property but MacGregor told them the call was a mistake and she was safe in Brennan's company. CCTV later showed the pair separately leaving the flat and walking in the surrounding area before returning. About 09:41, footage showed Brennan putting his blood stained trousers in a clothing bin near MacGregor's flat. He called 999 at about 09:55 and told the call handler he did not think MacGregor was breathing. Brennan did not respond to the handler when he was asked what happened. Emergency services arrived at the scene and the door lock was forced open. Witnesses found MacGregor lying face down on the living room floor, surrounded by fragments of broken glass bottles. Det Sgt David White told the court: "It looks like her mouth has been severed completely. "Her face more or less was hanging off." The court heard there was blood in the living room, including on the ceiling. White added: "This was one that stood out for me and will stay with me forever." MacGregor was pronounced dead at the scene at 10:15. After the attack, Brennan got on a train to Camelon, in the Falkirk area, where he visited the home of friend Robert McCallum. McCallum's then partner Tina Marie Hatton, 46, told jurors Brennan had "blood all over him" and she cleaned him up. When she asked what had happened Brennan replied he "couldn't stop" and he was "done". Hatton added he had injuries to his hands and above his eyebrow. The blood stained jumper was seized from a washing machine and the trousers were recovered from the clothing bin. The blood on the garments was found to have come from MacGregor. More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland Dr Julie McAdam, 54, told the court MacGregor's cause of death was "extensive facial injuries" She said a post-mortem examination found the victim had suffered a series of "blunt force injuries, bruises, abrasions and lacerations". MacGregor was described as having two "bilateral black eyes", which McAdam said was seen in "high velocity injuries, people in road traffic injuries or seriously assaulted". The trial was also told MacGregor had swallowed a lot of blood which filled her lungs and airways. McAdam added MacGregor would have been alive for an hour after suffering her injuries and could have survived had medical assistance been sought sooner. Brian McConnachie KC, defending, stated after the verdict: "As far as events are concerned, he has very little recollection. "As I understand it, he has some recollection of an argument taking place but has unable through proceedings to accept total responsibility for what took place." It was revealed that Brennan has previous convictions for assaults which include to injury. Det Supt Lynsey Watters said: "My thoughts remain with Brodie's family and friends as they continue to come to terms with what happened. "No verdict can bring her back, but I hope this sentence will bring them come comfort. "Brennan now faces the consequences of his reprehensible actions." She added violence against women and girls was "an absolute priority" for Police Scotland. title: Celtic can't sack manager O'Neill, says Lambert
description: Martin O'Neill leaving Celtic would not surprise Paul Lambert, but the former club captain would be "shocked and disappointed" if the veteran manager was to be sacked.
body: While Celtic are two points clear at the top of the Premiership, Martin O'Neill has said he will consider his future Martin O'Neill leaving Celtic would not surprise Paul Lambert, but the former club captain would be "shocked and disappointed" if the manager was to be sacked. The 74-year-old said he would use the international break to take stock following back-to-back defeats by Rangers. Those Old Firm setbacks came either side of a home loss to Ferencvaros in the Europa League, while there was a shock Champions League collapse to LASK in August, with a 4-0 aggregate lead surrendered. "I will reflect on the games," said O'Neill, who was made permanent manager for a second time in the summer after two stints as interim boss last season resulted in a league and Scottish Cup double. O'Neill, who won another seven trophies with Celtic from 2000-05, when Lambert was playing, added: "I'm not immune from criticism. Absolutely and utterly far from it. "I think there's every reason to ask 'can you turn this round? Can you change the whole thing?' I have to kind of look at the bigger picture at this minute." Lambert insists O'Neill is Celtic's best manager since the great Jock Stein, but the 57-year-old added: "It wouldn't surprise me if he left. I don't think he needs it. "I'd be shocked and disappointed if Celtic sacked him. "I think they give him the option, if that's what's on his mind, if he did want to walk away. "He's got enough credit in the bank. It wasn't that long ago people were shouting for a statue for him, so I don't think you can go from one extreme to the other. "If he wants to go, then he goes himself." 'It might be time to wrap it up' - O'Neill ponders Celtic future after defeat Rangers look like they know where they want to go - Celtic just look lost O'Neill steadied the Celtic ship twice last term following the departures of Brendan Rodgers and Wilfried Nancy. "They were hanging on by a thread and he turned that around," is how former Ipswich Town and Norwich City manager Lambert described the impact of his former boss. "There was only one person who could rescue Celtic last season and he did that. "I'd bet any money that he hasn't changed anything from how he was then." Lambert was critical of individual performances in the defeats by Rangers as well as the remarks of defender Cameron Carter-Vickers, who spoke of playing "too random" and "getting a script and sticking to it". "The players need to take responsibility," he told BBC Radio Scotland. "I watched the game and dear oh dear... "That was cringeworthy, the stuff from Carter-Vickers. I thought 'hang on, you're not making a movie'. "Solve the problem yourselves. When something is not going right, you look to rectify it, you don't look to a manager to say 'do this or do that'. "I thought that was bang out of order, coming from someone who's been a decent player for Celtic." title: Watch: Patrick Clancy says he forgives his ex-wife, Lindsay
description: The ex-husband of a US mother accused of murdering their three children has said he would have been "eaten up inside forever" had he not forgiven her.
body: This video can not be played In an interview with CBS, the BBC's US news partner, Patrick Clancy, the ex-husband of a US mother accused of murdering their three children, has said he would have been "eaten up inside forever" had he not forgiven her for their deaths. Clancy also said he did the best he could as his then-wife Lindsay Clancy struggled with mental illness in the months leading up to the day she strangled their children. The Clancy trial was declared a mistrial earlier this month after the jury said it could not reach a unanimous verdict. Watch: Patrick Clancy says he forgives his ex-wife, Lindsay. title: How is Scotland squad shaping up for Pocognoli debut?
description: Sebastien Pocognoli's faces his first test as Scotland head coach against Slovenia on Saturday, but how are his squad shaping up for his debut?
body: Billy Gilmour (left) scored for Napoli against Fiorentina Sometimes luck can be the difference between success and failure as a manager and Sebastien Pocognoli appears to have it with him for his first Scotland squad - at least before a ball is kicked. Scott McTominay was obviously a notable miss from the new head coach's original selection, the 29-year-old Napoli midfielder having to undergo what he described as minor heart surgery that should only keep him sidelined for a few weeks. Rangers' Lawrence Shankland and Torino's Che Adams are also absentees from the frontline options through injury. But, of the 28 players named in Pocognoli's extended squad for Scotland's opening four Nations League fixtures, none have so far pulled out through injury. So how are they shaping up after their latest round of club games? Pocognoli Facetime helps Miller over summer of discontent Xhaka under investigation over Covid-19 certificate Scottish Football Podcast: Belief is back for Rangers as Celtic in turmoil The goalkeeping position was a problem for some time under predecessor Steve Clarke, exacerbated by 84-cap Craig Gordon coming to the end of his career and with playing time often limited for the alternatives. But current first-choice Angus Gunn is now a regular starter with San Jose Earthquakes after his summer switch from Nottingham Forest. Scott Bain is also performing well for Falkirk, while Jon McCracken has helped Bradford City to the top of League One after his move from Dundee, making Rangers' Liam Kelly the only goalkeeper not playing for his club. The absence of Shankland and Adams gave Pocognoli the opportunity to bring in some fresh blood among the forwards, and the recalled Oli McBurnie continues to start for Hull City on their return to the Premier League. Meanwhile, Robbie Ure was back in the starting line-up for new club Sevilla as they lost 3-1 to La Liga leaders Barcelona on Saturday, while James Wilson has cemented a first-team place since returning to Heart of Midlothian from his loan to Tottenham Hotspur. In saying that, striker Kieron Bowie and wingers Findlay Curtis and Ben Gannon-Doak had to make do with being substitutes over the weekend for Sassuolo, Rangers and Bournemouth respectively. John McGinn (centre) set up Aston Villa's third goal against Tottenham Hotspur While 20-year-old Gannon-Doak's continued lack of minutes is not ideal considering he has proved to be a key provider of pace to Scotland's play, club-mate Ryan Christie will have received a boost by being handed only his second start of the season, albeit the midfielder came off after 75 minutes of a 1-0 home defeat by Liverpool. Indeed, all seven of Pocognoli's central midfield options started at the weekend. That includes Lennon Miller in Udinese's 1-0 home defeat by Cagliari. Also in Serie A, Billy Gilmour scored only his second senior goal with a fine strike in Napoli's 1-1 draw at Fiorentina, as well as being named man of the match. Meanwhile, Lewis Ferguson is back starting every game as Bologna captain, including their 1-1 draw with Torino. For visitors Torino, Nathan Patterson made his second appearance as a substitute since his loan move from Everton as right-back continues to be a problem area for Scotland. Aaron Hickey also had to make do with coming off the bench in Brentford's fine 3-0 win over Chelsea. Colby Donovan did start again for Celtic, albeit as the Scottish champions suffered a third straight defeat, while all three left-backs - Donovan's club-mate Kieran Tierney, Tottenham Hotspur's Andy Robertson and Sassuolo's Josh Doig suffered losses after starting. Only Scott McKenna - an unused sub as Croatian league leaders Dinamo Zagreb beat Lokomotiva - did not play in his club side's latest game among Pocognoli's defensive options. With Gilmour the only weekend goalscorer and Robertson and Aston Villa midfielder John McGinn providing an assist each in Spurs' 3-2 defeat, Pocognoli could look to that experienced trio to provide the creative spark for the Nations League matches starting away to Slovenia on Saturday.
