title: Best not to underestimate us - GB plan BJK Cup upset against all-star Czechs
description: Great Britain face the Czech Republic at the Billie Jean King Cup Finals on Tuesday - and know full well the size of the challenge facing them.
body: Great Britain play the Czech Republic in the BJK Cup on Tuesday from 10:00 BST - live on the BBC "It's best not to underestimate us," says a defiant Harriet Dart. But Great Britain's Billie Jean King Cup squad know full well the enormity of the challenge that awaits them. On Tuesday, the tight-knit British team - Dart, Katie Boulter, Sonay Kartal, Mika Stojsavljevic and Jodie Burrage - take on the Czech Republic in their BJK Cup quarter-final in Shenzhen, China. GB have reached the semi-finals in three of the past four seasons, but in the Czechs they face the 11-time champions and an eye-watering line-up - the only team boasting two top-10 players at the Finals tournament. In Linda Noskova and Karolina Muchova, they have the current Wimbledon champion and her beaten opponent from this summer's all-Czech final. While Marie Bouzkova has not yet hit such heights in reaching a major final, the 28-year-old has won two WTA titles this year, including on the Nottingham grass, and team-mate Sara Bejlek, 20, has enjoyed a breakthrough season featuring a first title and victories against the likes of Aryna Sabalenka and Madison Keys. In doubles, Bouzkova and Noskova teamed up to triumph in Cincinnati in August, though Katerina Siniakova is likely to feature in the BJK Cup as the current top-ranked women's doubles player with 12 Grand Slams to her name. All five members of the Czech team are ranked higher in the singles rankings than any of the British squad. "I think naturally we are definite underdogs," Boulter, the current world number 54, told BBC Sport. "We are the ones that are going to have to make something happen, something special. But that being said, a lot of pressure is on them, and we've seen in this tournament before that people can make upsets, and I think that's what we'll be looking to do. "I think we have no pressure ourselves, and we're just going to go out there with no expectations." The tie will be shown on the BBC Sport website and app and on BBC iPlayer, with coverage beginning from 10:00 BST. Billie Jean King Cup: Czech Republic v Great Britain Coverage from 10:00 BST on BBC Sport website and app and BBC iPlayer By her own reckoning, the 2026 season has brought "an improvement" for Boulter, winning her fourth WTA title in Ostrava and beating new world number one Elena Rybakina at Queen's in a year in which the Kazakh won the Australian and US Open crowns. But the British number one has repeatedly come unstuck against Czech players. Boulter lost 6-3 7-5 to Muchova in Miami back in March but fell to a more emphatic defeat to her in the US Open second round earlier this month, winning just one game in a "bad day at the office". She faced Noskova in Cincinnati in August and lost 6-3 6-3, but Boulter can take confidence from the fact she beat the Czech in straight sets in Osaka in October 2025. "They are both incredible players, both extremely good at what they do," Boulter, 30, said. "They have been in places that I've never been before. So I think for me, it's about taking it to them. "Their base level is so high, you can't play the same way that you would normally play if you were to play someone ranked a lot lower. "I think you have to give them respect, but also play the ball that's coming at you at the same time. That's my challenge, to focus on the ball coming at me and try and impose my own game. "I think there are ways I'm going to try and win points, and that's through what I'm doing, not what they're doing." Dart, who lost 6-2 6-2 to Bouzkova in the US Open second round, said: "I think even though the match-up on paper here is pretty rough for us, at the same time I know how well this team can play. "We have strong belief within ourselves and within our own team that we can do well in this competition." Sonay Kartal and Katie Boulter return to the GB squad having missed the win over Australia in April Great Britain qualified for Shenzhen - their fourth BJK Cup Finals in five years - by shocking Australia in Melbourne in April. Boulter and Kartal were among a list of absentees from that squad - including Emma Raducanu, who is again missing through injury - but the pair's return to the line-up strengthens captain Anne Keothavong's side. Should they pull off an upset and beat the Czechs, GB would next play the winner of the quarter-final between Kazakhstan - who are without Rybakina - and Spain on Friday. "I think pressure is a privilege, isn't it? I think whoever you're drawn against in this competition, particularly when you've made it through to the Finals, there are no easy matches," said Keothavong. "We've seen over the years how people are able to rise to the occasion when they represent their nation. I've seen it from the players here beside me. title: Katya Adler: Merz's political crisis threatens Germany's obsession with stability
description: Political shifts in Germany are being watched closely in Europe and beyond, Katya Adler writes.
body: The German chancellor's political future hangs in the balance after bruising election defeats Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz is a political record-breaker. The problem for him is these records are overwhelmingly negative and he is at risk of losing his job over them. The problem for the EU and for Europe more broadly is this has a destabilising effect far further afield. At a paltry 13%, Merz's popularity rating is the lowest for any German chancellor since polling began. German voters' ardour for him started lower and fell faster than any of his predecessors. The former corporate lawyer is perceived by many to be arrogant and out of touch with their problems. He has only been in government for 16 months but under his chairmanship, Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Unionist (CDU) party has suffered three very poor showings in regional elections over the last couple of weeks. The state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern broke another record on Sunday according to preliminary results: Merz's conservative CDU party did not even reach the 5% threshold to enter the regional parliament. Conversely, the anti-immigration, nationalist right Alternative for Germany (AfD) - a political party Merz had promised to slash support for when he was running for CDU leadership - has performed spectacularly well. It became the biggest political faction in two out of those three recent state elections and broke another record: they have a chance at governing in one of those states, Saxony Anhalt, despite the German authorities labelling them in part anti-democratic and far-right extremist. The AfD also tops opinion polls nationally, a particularly sensitive issue for Germany after its Nazi past. The AfD, led by Tino Chrupalla and Alice Weidel, has surged in national opinion polls The party rejects the far-right label. Its German name, Alternative fuer Deutschland, means Alternative for Germany. That is exactly what they say voters now want. Following this month's regional election surge in success for the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, plus its gains in Berlin - where the victors were the hard left Die Linke party - AfD co-leader Alice Weidel said on Monday that her party had effectively replaced the center-right CDU as Germany's true Volkspartei, or catch-all people's party. The AfD accuses Merz of failing to fulfil his key election promises to improve the spluttering German economy - once seen as the financial engine of Europe - and to find workable solutions to voter fears about immigration and security on their streets. High time for political change, says the AfD. Merz's position as German chancellor certainly looks wobbly. There have been rumours for weeks of a brewing palace coup, where he would be replaced by a more popular CDU politician. Possible candidate names are swirling but no individual will stick out his or her neck in public until they know they have the backing of the party. I have reported on Germany for decades. This is a stability-obsessed country. This kind of political upheaval is deeply unusual. Even if Merz stays in post, his political clout and credibility, his room for manoeuvre inside a fractious coalition government, will be restricted. Looking uncharacteristically forlorn on Sunday evening, Merz jumped to make a televised address even before the regional election results were confirmed. He would press ahead with tax, welfare and economic reforms to bring about prosperity, he said. "Backbone, steadfastness and patience" were required. This video can not be played Why Merz is staying on as German chancellor after election 'disaster' But German patience is running thin. Voters in Germany, as across much of Europe, have repeatedly elected traditional parties of the centre-left, such as Germany's SPD party, or centre-right, like the CDU, since World War Two - but increasingly they feel let-down and frustrated as they fear for their economic future. Voter resentment really started to mount after the financial crisis of 2007/8, when these traditional parties were seen bailing out big banks, while families felt their savings and living standards dropped. Then came the 2015 migration crisis, when more than one million refugees and other migrants arrived by people-smuggler boats across the Mediterranean and made their way across Europe, often by foot, trying to settle in wealthier countries like Germany and Sweden. Germany took in one million people. Integration into German society has been mixed and Germans have been shocked and scared by a number of headline-making attacks by migrants over the years, some with a history of mental illness, others linked by the German authorities to Islamist extremist groups or ideology. In December, for example, police said they arrested five individuals suspected of plotting a Christmas market attack in Munich "based on an Islamist motive". Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has had another scarring effect. Germans pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe. The loss of access to cheap Russian energy that German car factories and other industries relied on, plus Donald Trump's trade tariffs and aggressive economic competition from China, have had a heavy toll on this country's export-driven economy. As the AfD squeezes the CDU on the right, the left wing Die Linke party attracts voters elsewhere Germany is Europe's, and therefore the eurozone currency's, largest economy. It is the world's largest single donor to Ukraine right now and it is the biggest net payer into the EU budget. When Germany's finances are in trouble and the country turns inward because of a political crisis, the knock-on effect beyond its borders can be considerable. Under financial pressure, Merz has been pushing hard, along with a group of other wealthier EU countries to slash their contributions to the bloc's budget, for example. This comes

title: How will clubs train during three-week international break?
description: BBC Sport looks at how clubs are planning to deal with the extended three-week international break.
body: Keith Andrews will give his remaining Brentford players the week off before they return to the training ground on Saturday The first international break of the season is under way - and this one is longer than fans will have become accustomed to. For the first time, the Premier League and the Championship will come to a halt for three weeks rather than the usual two. Football fans tend not to love international breaks, but this change has been done with good intentions. It merges the four games played in the old September and October breaks into one slot. So the domestic game stops for three weeks, rather than four weeks across two windows. Club football is actually getting a week back. But for players not on international duty, three weeks is a long time for finely tuned athletes not to play competitively. So how are clubs going to deal with this change? Here's how different teams plan to balance the international break. Most squads in the Premier League these days are packed with international players, and Brentford are no different. Most of the Bees' squad are away, with about 12 players - including Callum Wilson and Igor Thiago - left at their training facility, including five who are coming back from injury. Brentford have a longer break than almost every other team, given they hosted Chelsea on Friday evening. Boss Keith Andrews has given his first-team players a week off with individual training programmes to follow. Those players will not have restrictions on leaving the country, but it is unlikely long-haul flights would be sanctioned. The squad will reconvene on Saturday, 26 September to begin training again, before playing a behind-closed-doors game against another English club on the weekend of 3 October. That friendly could potentially give the likes of Nathan Collins and Sepp van den Berg a chance to return to action, with the rest of the squad made up of under-21 players. The second international break will look very different, with the Bees playing Brighton on Sunday, 8 November and back in action against Everton on Saturday, 21 November. Players may be given the odd day off, but in general it will be a normal training programme with no friendly before the usual preparation for the fixture against the Toffees. Liverpool, meanwhile, will carry on training with the small number of players that remain, with a few days off. Manager Andoni Iraola says he will be left with "no more than three days probably to prepare" for the home game with Manchester City on 11 October. Aston Villa have a very different international break planned. Unai Emery will return to former club Sevilla, where he won the Europa League three times on the bounce. Sevilla and Villa will face off in the 15th edition of the Antonio Puerta Trophy on Friday, 2 October. The game is played in memory of the 22-year-old Sevilla wing-back, who died on 28 August 2007 after having multiple cardiac arrests on the pitch during a La Liga game against Getafe. Tony Mowbray was appointed Blackburn Rovers manager for a second time in June While Premier League teams see their squads decimated by international call-ups, it is not quite as dramatic in the Championship. Many clubs will only have a handful, such as Blackburn Rovers with just four call-ups. For Rovers boss Tony Mowbray this break will be a positive for a couple of reasons. Mowbray has had to contend with an injury crisis in the early part of the season, with more than 10 players ruled out in the opening weeks. The break gives Rovers the chance to ease some of those players back into action, such as Gady Beyuku and Moussa Baradji who recently made their comebacks, and others close to a return like Scott Wharton. After the trip to Portsmouth on Saturday, Rovers headed back to Lancashire and will have a few days on the training ground this week. After such a busy start to the campaign, with league fixtures and the Carabao Cup, it also gives Mowbray - who returned to the club in the summer - a chance to properly work with his players. But it will not all be training. Mowbray intends to give the players a few days off from the end of the week. Players such as Yuri Ribeiro will be able to return home to Portugal, if they so wish. The cycle will then be repeated the following week, training the first half with a short break over the weekend. Then for week three, it is back to the usual pre-match routine before the home game against Cardiff. Mowbray is also looking to find a Premier League or League One team to play in a behind-closed-doors friendly. It will help those returning from injury to get minutes in the bank, and keep other members of the squad ticking over. In the two-week break in November, players may still get a short spell off while matches are more likely to be in-house affairs with teams made up of senior and under-21 players. The three-week international break might have posed a unique situation for a couple of clubs, whereby they could have a full squad and no games to play. League One carries on playing unless clubs get three call-ups which meet the EFL's criteria, then a postponement can be requested. Only four of the 12 matches have survived on each of the two weekends. Yet many clubs prepared in advance by scheduling Football League Trophy fixtures during these three weeks. Clubs tend to rotate in this competition anyway, so the games still go ahead even if league games are postponed. Twelve teams will play two trophy ties, with 10 clubs playing once. That left just Leyton Orient and Reading at risk at not having a game to play. Both have only had one league match called off, so will not have all three weeks vacant. title: Fourteen people linked to evidential activity at time of Omagh bomb, inquiry told
description: Twenty-nine people, including a woman pregnant with twins, died in the bombing in the County Tyrone town on 15 August 1998 - the biggest single atrocity in the Troubles.
body: The bombing exploded during a busy Saturday in Omagh, County Tyrone in 1998 Fourteen people have been linked to evidential activity in the days leading up to and on the day of the Omagh bombing, the inquiry into the explosion has heard. Twenty-nine people, including a woman pregnant with twins, died in the bombing in the County Tyrone town on 15 August 1998 - the biggest single atrocity in the Troubles. It came less than three months after the people of Northern Ireland had voted yes to the Good Friday Agreement. The inquiry, which opened last year with 14 days of testimony from bereaved families and survivors, was established to determine if the bombing could have been prevented by UK state authorities. Paul Greaney KC outlined the "working hypothesis" of the inquiry when it resumed its latest phase on Monday. In 2009, a judge ruled that four men - Michael McKevitt, Liam Campbell, Colm Murphy and Seamus Daly were all liable for the Omagh bomb. A fifth man, Seamus McKenna, was acquitted in the civil action and later died in a roofing accident in 2013. In a statement to the inquiry, sitting at Bradford Court in Belfast, Greaney named McKenna, Daly and Murphy as among the 14 people linked to evidential activity. Greaney told the inquiry: "The evidence suggests Colm Murphy sat like a spider in the centre of the web of the plan to detonate a bomb in Omagh." Referring to the civil case, Greaney said that the fact that McKenna "was not found liable is not an outcome which binds this inquiry". "Our working hypothesis is that, contrary to that finding, he played a key role," he said. The use of telecommunications is a key part of the evidence in front of the inquiry and some of the most frequently referred to mobile phones have been assigned colours for ease of following their links. The inquiry heard how it was "likely" that the Vauxhall Cavalier car used in the bombing was "stolen to order" in the days before the bombing. Evidence was outlined that on 14 August 1998, the day before the bombing, a "test run" of the journey to the bomb site was carried out in a Volkswagen Golf car. This video can not be played The principal objective of this chapter of the inquiry is to understand how the bombing was carried out and by whom. Among the witnesses this week will be a senior garda officer who is expected to provide initial evidence about the theft of the car used in the explosion. It was stolen in Carrickmacross, County Monaghan, two days before the explosion. The inquiry was established to determine if the bombing could have been prevented by UK state authorities. The third phase is expected to last about four weeks. The Omagh bomb exploded on 15 August 1998, killing 29 people including a woman pregnant with twins. More than 200 people were injured in the blast. No-one has ever been convicted of the atrocity. The bomb devastated Omagh town centre in August 1998 Three days after the attack, the Real IRA released a statement claiming responsibility for the explosion. It apologised to "civilian" victims and said its targets had been commercial. No-one has been convicted of carrying out the murders by a criminal court. In 2009, Michael McKevitt, Liam Campbell, Colm Murphy and Seamus Daly were all ordered to pay a total of £1.6m in damages to the relatives, but appeals against the ruling delayed the compensation process. title: Google hit with €403m fine by Irish data watchdog over GDPR violations
description: The penalty follows an inquiry launched into the tech giant six years ago, following complaints from several European consumer rights organisations.
body: Google say they have improved data protection practices in recent years Google has been fined €403m (£345m) by the Republic of Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC) over its handling of location data. The penalty - one of the largest of its kind imposed by the Irish watchdog authority - followed an inquiry launched into the tech giant six years ago, following complaints from several European consumer rights organisations. On Monday the DPC said its investigation found Google had processed data in a manner that was not "lawful", "fair" or "transparent". The inquiry concerned Google's processing of location data in three specific features - Web & App Activity, Location History and Location Accuracy between 25 May 2018 to 4 February 2020. Location data is any kind of data which can be used to infer a person's location. It can "reveal a significant amount of information about an individual, including information that is inherently private", said DPC deputy commissioner Graham Doyle in a statement released on Monday. The report said Google's practices "infringed" General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) - legislation that came into effect on 25 May, 2018, creating strict data privacy and security law within the European Union (EU). Doyle added: "The GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) provides a high level of protection of personal data throughout the EEA (European Economic Area), and requires that the processing of personal data must be carried out in a lawful, fair and transparent manner." He continued: "As a result of Google's failures... individuals could have been unaware that their location was being used to, for example, influence them with ads or to infer their interests, and could lose control over their personal data. "The retention of users' location data for longer than necessary aggravated this loss of control." In addition to being fined, Google has also been ordered to bring its data processing into compliance within six months. In a statement, Google said: "This case centres around historical policies that have since been updated. From 2019 onwards, we've significantly evolved our practices and launched robust tools that make managing location data simple." They also said they have made data protection improvements in recent years, including "industry-first auto-delete controls", which enables all users to "set your account to automatically delete your data on a rolling three, 18, or 36-month basis". Other measures to safeguard personal data have also been introduced, they said, such as "simple ads management", which allows you "to turn off personalized ads entirely", and "increased transparency", including "consolidated detailed information about our location data practices and account settings". title: Xhaka under investigation over Covid-19 certificate
description: Switzerland captain Granit Xhaka is being investigated over an issue with his Covid-19 vaccination certificate.
body: Granit Xhaka captained Switzerland at the World Cup earlier this year Switzerland captain Granit Xhaka is under investigation by Swiss prosecutors over allegations he obtained a forged Covid-19 vaccination certificate. The 33-year-old is alleged to have obtained the certificate in 2022, when it was a requirement in Switzerland for some travel abroad. The public prosecutor's office of the city of Lucerne confirmed the investigation was under way to determine whether any criminal behaviour took place in obtaining a "false or forged" certificate. The Sunderland midfielder, who was playing for Arsenal at the time, posted a statement on social media on Monday saying he had a "mistrust" towards the vaccine and had been "influenced by worries and uncertainty". He said: "In this troubled state of mind I acquired a vaccine certificate, instead of clarifying my unanswered questions in the proper way. "Today I see clearly, that this way was not correct. It was a mistake. I'm sorry. "I take responsibility for this decision, will engage with the process of establishing the facts and fully co-operate with the relevant authorities." The Swiss office of public health confirmed that while there was never a general legal requirement to obtain or hold such a certificate, it was needed for access to various activities, venues and travel, meaning that participation was restricted for anyone who did not possess one. These measures in Switzerland were in place until spring 2022. After that point, Covid-19 certificates continued to be issued, primarily to enable members of the public to meet entry requirements when travelling abroad. The Swiss Football Association said Xhaka, the country's record appearance holder with 152 caps, had withdrawn from the Swiss camp for their upcoming Nations League matches against Scotland, North Macedonia and Slovenia following his statement. It added the decision to withdraw had been made jointly by the player and management and that they would discuss Xhaka's future with the team after the international window. Switzerland have away fixtures against North Macedonia and Scotland on 26 and 29 September, before facing Slovenia and North Macedonia at home in early October. Sunderland boss Regis le Bris refused to comment on the allegations following the Black Cats' defeat at Manchester City on Sunday. "It is not my area to speak about those problems or situations," he said. "My area is football. About football, he is really good." Xhaka captained Switzerland at the World Cup earlier this year, where they were knocked out in the quarter-finals by eventual runners-up Argentina. title: British Museum bans visitors from photographing Bayeux Tapestry
description: Visitors stopping to take pictures of the 68m medieval embroidery were holding up others, prompting the rule change.
body: The British Museum has banned visitors from taking photographs of the Bayeux Tapestry over concerns that they were taking too long to view the historic work. Curators had initially allowed photos to be taken but reversed that decision after long queues delayed ticket-holders from accessing the exhibition. The medieval embroidery, which is on display in Britain for the first time, depicts the events leading up to the Norman conquest of England and the Battle of Hastings in 1066. Visitors are being allowed into the sold-out exhibit in groups every 40 minutes and told to keep moving along the 68m (230ft) work in one direction. But people stopping to take photographs along the way was restricting that flow and delaying later visitors. A British Museum spokeswoman said: "There has been enormous interest in viewing the tapestry, and our priority is to ensure that all visitors have the best experience possible. "In order to do this, we have made the decision to restrict photography while people are moving along the length of the tapestry." The 11th Century artwork - which is not a tapestry and was actually embroidered in England - is currently on loan from its home in Normandy, France, and will be displayed in London until July 2027. British Museum bosses decided that the embroidery would be displayed in a single, straight line, unlike the horseshoe-shaped gallery in which it is displayed in Bayeux. The loan was confirmed following a Franco-British summit in 2025, following years of planning between the two countries. Under the agreement, the British Museum is funding the costs of move while insurance is provided by the UK government. The artefact was carefully packed in a climate-controlled crate and was given a police escort along the unprecedented 350-mile (560km) journey from its home to central London. Some would-be visitors have criticised the high price of tickets - as much as three times what it costs to see the Bayeux Tapestry in France - to cover the museum's expenses. Tickets for the exhibition are sold out until 31 December but more are expected to go on sale in October. Alternately, a full-scale replica of the Bayeux Tapestry is available to see for free in Tewkesbury Abbey in Gloucestershire and at Reading Museum. title: 'Other generations just buried it' - Youths share their mental health concerns
description: The BBC's Catherine Burns spoke to some young mental health ambassadors who called for an increase in mental health support.
body: This video can not be played Accusations that those growing up today are a snowflake generation are wrong, the head of an independent review into mental health, ADHD and autism has said. Prof Peter Fonagy told the BBC that there had been a real rise in mental distress among children and young people, with anxiety, depression, self-harm and eating disorders the most common. His review was ordered nine months ago by Wes Streeting after the then-health secretary claimed in an interview that young people were over-diagnosed and "written off". The BBC's Catherine Burns spoke to some young mental health ambassadors who echoed the report's findings and called for an increase in mental health support. title: US strikes on alleged drug boats could be crimes against humanity, says UN
description: A report says the attacks, of which there have been at least 68, were not self-defence.
body: The report comes two days after the US military released these pictures of an attack on alleged traffickers in the Caribbean A UN report has concluded that recent US airstrikes on vessels allegedly trafficking drugs breached international law and could constitute crimes against humanity. The report by Special Rapporteur Ben Saul said since September last year there had been at least 68 US strikes in the Caribbean and Pacific, outside US territorial waters, which killed more than 220 people. Saul said that even if targets could be identified as members of designated terrorist groups, they had not staged an armed attack on the US which would trigger a right to self-defence under international law. The report comes two days after the US military said it killed four people in a strike on a vessel in the Caribbean. "Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narco-trafficking. The operation killed four narco-terrorists," Southcom, which commands US forces in the region, said in a statement about the latest attack, which was accompanied by a grainy video. But in a briefing note released by the UN Human Rights Council on Monday, Saul said that "such attacks amount to serial extrajudicial killings in violation of the right to life, being unjustified in national or personal self-defence or under international humanitarian law, the international law of the sea, narcotics suppression conventions, or international counter-terrorism law". "There are reasonable grounds to believe that the reported 68 attacks that killed 223 people constituted crimes against humanity of murder under customary international law," Saul concluded. BBC News has contacted the White House and State Department for a response to the report. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has previously said the overall operation is aimed at removing "narco-terrorists from our hemisphere" and securing the US from "the drugs that are killing our people". The US military launched the operation, known as "Southern Spear", in early September. However, officials have not offered definitive evidence that the vessels targeted are involved in trafficking. Since the beginning, experts have questioned the legality of the strikes, which initially drew strong criticism from Latin American leaders whose citizens have been targeted. However, Nicolás Maduro, who was the Venezuelan leader at the time and opposed the strikes, was seized by US forces in a dramatic and highly controversial night-time raid on the capital Caracas at the beginning of this year. Another outspoken critic of Operation Southern Spear, Colombia's left-wing president at the time, Gustavo Petro, stood down in August after a Trump-backed candidate won June's presidential election. title: Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac buy historic Wrexham football pub
description: The Turf is a regular feature on the Welcome to Wrexham Disney documentary series.
body: Wrexham's Hollywood co-owners Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac have bought The Turf pub to "protect its future" Wrexham's Hollywood co-owners Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac have bought the pub next door to the football club's Racecourse home ground to "protect the future of the club". Wrexham AFC was founded at the then-named Turf Hotel in October 1864 and is the oldest football club in Wales. A club statement announcing the purchase from Admiral Taverns said it hoped to "help protect the historic pub" by "incorporating the club, the Racecourse Ground and The Turf under a single ownership". The pub and its landlord, Wayne Jones, have become regular features on the award-winning "Welcome to Wrexham" Disney documentary series, and Jones described the buy as "great news for all Wrexham fans". Celebrities have been spotted visiting The Turf since Reynolds and Mac took over the club in 2021, including Paul Rudd, Channing Tatum and Will Ferrell. Prince William even pulled a pint behind the bar with Mac to mark St David's Day in 2024. This video can not be played Prince William pulled a pint at the Turf pub alongside Rob Mac The club statement continued: "The acquisition allows for the preservation of the history and traditions of the historic public house that is inexorably linked to the Racecourse Ground and Wrexham AFC Football Club since its foundation in 1864. "This will include opportunities to enhance the current fan zone and other fan-related activities in the area next to The Turf on the Mold Road. "The acquisition of The Turf is a continuation of the strategy to protect the future of the club and its interests by ring fencing key areas related to the life of the club." Channing Tatum and Ryan Reynolds dropped by the Deadpool sculpture at the Turf pub in Febuary last year "The Turf Tavern, as it was then, predates the club and records suggest that the club itself was founded in the pub," said Jones, who has been landlord of The Turf for the past 20 years." "It has played a key part of the club's history ever since, with the players changing in the pub before running out onto the Racecourse Ground as recently as the 1940s. "It continues to be a focal point for fans on matchdays and non-matchdays," Jones added. Jones will continue running the pub as part of the purchase deal, and said he was looking forward to bringing its "unique mix of history, atmosphere and sometimes Hollywood stardust" to the next generation of Wrexham fans and locals alike. The club said the purchase of The Turf pub will allow for "further investment into the fan experience in and around matchdays" The Racecourse Ground staged its first Wales fixture in March 1877 and is the world's oldest football stadium still hosting international matches. Eric Allyn, on behalf of minority investors the Allyn family, said: "Ever since we invested in Wrexham AFC through Red Dragon Ventures in 2024, the town, the community and the football club have become a second home. "By bringing The Turf into the group, we are securing the long-term future of the pub and with it preserving its history and that of the club." title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico to file lawsuit against Trump's White House ban
description: The US media outlets say they are defending "the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes".
body: Trump announced the ban on Friday, accusing the organisations of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration CNN, Politico and MS NOW have said they will sue the Trump administration after the three US media outlets were barred from the White House. President Donald Trump announced the ban on Friday, accusing the three organisations of writing "fiction or lies" about his government. The companies said their reporters were denied access and had their badges seized when attempting to access the building on Saturday. In a joint statement on Monday, they said they were pursuing legal action to "protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes". The First Amendment forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press - language that courts have traditionally interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage. "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting," the CNN, Politico and MS NOW statement continued. "Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference." BBC News has asked the White House for comment. Announcing the ban last week, Trump did not mention specific stories or reporting that prompted the move, but later said "it's really just cumulative stories over the last few years". The US president added that there "may be others to join them". When later asked by a reporter what he meant by this, Trump responded: "Others to come in terms of fake news? Well, you know, the New York Times is fake news, the Washington Post is fake news." CNN - one of only five US news outlets in the White House press pool for live television - was originally slated to cover Trump's trip to the UN General Assembly in New York on Monday and Tuesday. But the pool slot has remained vacant and instead the staunchly conservative TV outlet, Real America's Voice, was listed as "secondary" crew on the trip. The pool acts as a representative for the media, sharing material with other outlets to save on finance and space when covering presidential events. In February, the White House announced it was taking control of the press pool which has access to Trump and had for more than a century been managed by the White House Correspondents' Association. The same month, the administration moved to bar Associated Press (AP) reporters and photographers from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because of the outlet's usage of the term "Gulf of Mexico" instead of "Gulf of America". AP swiftly filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing. Trump has been frequently critical of news organisations and his administration has launched legal action against a series of outlets, including the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal, and the BBC. Some of the lawsuits have resulted in media organisations agreeing to pay multimillion dollar settlements. Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is ongoing. title: Southport killer accused of throwing boiling water mixed with sugar at prison officer
description: Axel Rudakubana is accused of grievous bodily harm and two other assaults of prison officers while serving a life sentence.
body: Axel Rudakubana appeared at the court hearing wearing a pale grey and blue tracksuit top Southport killer Axel Rudakubana has appeared in court accused of throwing boiling water mixed with sugar at a prison officer. The 20-year-old is charged with the attempted grievous bodily harm of a prison officer at HMP Belmarsh, having allegedly thrown the boiling mix through the hatch in his cell door on 8 May last year. He is also charged with two other assaults of prison officers, as well as possession of a knife or other offensive weapon while in prison. Rudakubana, who is serving a life sentence for murdering three children at a dance class in Southport in July 2024, appeared via video link at Westminster Magistrates' Court wearing a pale grey and blue tracksuit top. He spoke only to confirm that he could hear the chief magistrate, and to give his name and date of birth. He rested his head on his left hand throughout the hearing. Prosecutor Catherine Pattinson told the court that prompt medical attention prevented the prison officer Rudakubana is alleged to have attacked on 8 May from suffering any lasting injury. The prosecution also accused him of threatening to soak a female officer outside his cell if she did not pass him a newspaper on 6 May 2025, then throwing an "unknown liquid" at her through his door hatch. Then, on 28 October last year, he allegedly punched a male prison officer in the face. The prosecution said the officer was trying to establish whether Rudakubana had taken his medication at the time. The offensive weapon charge relates to sharpened stone shards that the prosecution say had seemingly been prised from the floor of the defendant's cell. They were found stuck to the under side of a shelving unit in his cell. Pattinson told the court that "when questioned by a prison officer, he said that he was keeping them for self-defence". Rudakubana, who appeared from Broadmoor secure psychiatric hospital, was not asked to enter pleas during the hearing on Monday. He was remanded into custody to appear at the Old Bailey on 19 October. He is currently serving out a life sentence over his deadly attack on a Taylor Swift dance class in July 2024, in which he murdered nine-year-old Alice da Silva Aguiar, six-year-old Bebe King, and Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven. Rudakubana was also convicted of the attempted murder of eight other children and two adults during the attack. title: Helen Jenner announced by Nigel Farage as new leader of Reform in Wales
description: Farage said it had been untenable for former leader Dan Thomas to continue after his arrest last week.
body: Farage described Jenner as a "determined campaigner" on the steps of Wales' parliament Nigel Farage has announced Helen Jenner as the new leader of Reform in Wales, replacing Dan Thomas after his arrest on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour. Speaking on the steps of the Senedd in Cardiff on Monday, Farage said: "I've known Helen for many, many years. She is a determined campaigner." Farage said he was sorry for former leader Thomas's "personal difficulties", but said it had been untenable for him to continue. "We could have done without this bump in the road," he said. Jenner, who served as Thomas's deputy alongside her role as Senedd member for Bangor Conwy Môn, said it was an honour to be elected to the top job. A leadership vote was held by Reform's 33 Senedd members on Monday morning, in which BBC Wales understands Jenner's colleague Jason O'Connell stood against her. O'Connell had not been expected to stand. Speaking to reporters outside the Senedd, Farage said there would be a vote for a new Welsh deputy leader to replace Jenner on Tuesday. Dan Thomas had steered Reform to its best-ever result in a Senedd election in May, becoming the second-largest party in Wales Jenner had been interim leader and favourite to replace Thomas, with sources telling BBC Wales that "very senior" Reform figures had backed her. Thomas stepped down on 15 September after he was arrested on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour. He was bailed pending further enquiries, and denies doing anything wrong. He was not on the steps of the Senedd for Jenner's unveiling as leader, but he remains a Reform MS after chief whip Llŷr Powell said he had not considered removing the whip from him. After he stepped down, Thomas had been among the Reform Senedd members who met in Cardiff Bay last week to discuss their next steps, with a party official from London attending to oversee proceedings. title: BBC removes 11 Mitchell and Webb comedy sketches from iPlayer
description: The corporation said it had included "the ones that still work today and not the ones that don't."
body: The BBC has removed nearly a dozen comedy sketches from That Mitchell and Webb Look after deciding they no longer "work today". The Bafta-winning comedy, starring David Mitchell and Robert Webb, originally ran for four seasons between 2006 and 2010. The show recently returned to the BBC's iPlayer to mark its 20th anniversary. But 11 old sketches, including one that reportedly showed the comedy duo satirising racism while in blackface, have now been cut. A BBC spokesman said in a statement: "This is a 20-year-old sketch show; in consultation with the programme makers, we have included the ones that still work today and not the ones that don't." The Times reported, external the removed material included scenes featuring war re-enactors in blackface, a sketch about a contestant on a makeover show wearing a burka and a "tribe" living in a garden centre. BBC news has asked Mitchell and Webb - who rose to prominence on the Channel 4 sitcom Peep Show - for a comment. That Mitchell and Webb Look grew out of a similar radio show titled That Mitchell and Webb Sound, which began on Radio 4 in 2003, and went on to win the Bafta for best comedy programme in 2007. Defending the double act, fellow comedian Dom Joly, of Trigger Happy TV, questioned the BBC's "censorship" of itself. Joly told The Times: "I totally get it if the BBC is putting out something really racist, which is laughing at and encouraging other people to feel that it's OK to do that. "But it's so clear that Mitchell and Webb are not doing that. Their intent was not to be racist." Jimmy Mulville, the co-founder of Hat Trick Productions which makes Have I Got News For You, told the same newspaper he could understand the corporation's predicament. "The BBC are in an impossible position," he said. He added that producers had "to be careful", though, "that this is not the thin end of a wedge where we cut things out". Mitchell and Webb are not the first comedians to have had their work edited or removed in recent years, as societal attitudes have shifted. Some artists themselves also began reassessing their work in the aftermath of the Black Lives Matter movement. Matt Lucas and David Walliams' hit show Little Britain was removed from iPlayer, Netflix and BritBox in 2020, after objections resurfaced about some of their characters portraying people from different ethnic backgrounds. At the time, both the BBC and Britbox noted how "times have changed" since the Little Britain first aired in the early noughties. The show is now back on iPlayer but, like Mitchell and Webb, some sketches have been removed. title: Countryside buses resurging in England after years of decline - check your local figures
description: A rise in bus miles with council funding might be starting to reverse the reduction in services.
body: Wiltshire Connect is a demand responsive service - one of the ways some councils are tackling a lack of transport in rural areas Council-funded rural buses described as a "lifeline" by some are enjoying a resurgence after years of decline and new laws are giving authorities more power. Does this mean buses are back in business? Government data shows council support for local buses is rising. With the exception of London, 17% of bus miles travelled across England were supported financially by government. That's down from almost a quarter in 2010, with bigger drops in rural areas, but it is up from a pre-pandemic low of 13% in 2019-20. However, fewer of us have been catching the bus. Journeys per person in England stood at 88 in 2010 and that number was down to 63 by 2024-25. Numbers dropped sharply during the pandemic and a recent rise has not returned them to pre-Covid levels. Figures for 2024-25 show the councils providing the most support to their bus networks tended to be in rural areas. The charity Bus Users UK described supported bus services as "fundamental to social inclusion" and "a lifeline, not a choice" for many. "Without them, people can become isolated and less able to participate fully in their communities," a spokesperson said. Wiltshire is one of those rural areas. The council is one of those across the country attempting to tackle this using DRT - demand responsive transport. West raises thousands for Nepalese flood victims Charity shop helps to 'bankroll' village carnival Solar farm to be built near M4 despite concerns It is a type of on-demand service that passengers book in advance when it is needed and the bus route changes depending on where people need to go. In 2021, the Department for Transport provided £20m to 15 local authorities in England to trial DRT via the Rural Mobility Fund. The Wiltshire Connect service has been rolled out in different areas across the county. It has 13 minibuses operating across three zones and first launched in 2023. There have been 250,000 journeys since, a spokesperson for Wiltshire Connect said. Martin Smith, from Wiltshire Council, said he sees DRT as the future Councillor Martin Smith, the cabinet member for transport in Wiltshire, explained it has been more "affordable" for the council. "If we weren't doing this we'd be trying to subsidise a lot of rural bus routes taking very, very few people from place to place and here we have a solution where it's a couple of buses which move around the area all the time," he said. People book via an app or over the phone and the cost is the same as an ordinary bus service. Passengers have the option to be picked up from various spots close to them and travel to areas within a certain zone. The council still subsidises other services, which are contributing to their supported mileage rather than the DRT. It was expected at first that older people would mostly use DRT but the council said it had found younger people "piling in there". Smith said: "If we can get the younger generation used to using public transport then they will continue to do that potentially through their adult lives." Wiltshire Connect driver James said passengers "love it" One passenger, Cat Jones, and her family started using the service when they moved from London to Wiltshire. They had not needed a car at their previous home and they said the buses were a "lifesaver". She said: "In Wiltshire, you sometimes need more flexible transport than the scheduled buses allow and that's what Wiltshire Connect is. "Everybody is smiling. You feel plugged into the community." James, who is a Wiltshire Connect driver, said: "They [the passengers] love it. "It's a service that has helped so many people be able to get out. "I think some of them feel quite trapped, especially in the smaller villages." This video can not be played How can rural bus services be improved? Bus Users UK has described the overall mileage increase as "encouraging". A spokesperson said: "It shows targeted investment can work but mileage alone does not tell the full story. "A bus service is only useful if it enables people to make the journeys that matter - whether that is getting to work, attending a hospital appointment, accessing education or staying connected with friends and family." It emphasised that the decline before the pandemic was down to local council budget cuts forcing them to "abandon" routes. It said that to get people confident in using the bus again, long-term funding for networks "that people could rely" on was needed. The Campaign for Better Transport said that the publication of a national bus strategy in 2021 had made "the value of buses more explicitly understood and authorities have had the option to step in and plug gaps in provision thanks to dedicated government funding". Silviya Barrett, of Campaign for Better Transport, said: "It is great news that these services are now increasing but overall bus provision is still at a lower level than in 2010 and our mapping shows that many areas still do not have the bus service they need." The Local Government Association has a similar view. It described the recent investment in services as "good" but said it also wanted to see "sustained levels of funding" to encourage people to use buses. The government announced more funding last year as well as the Bus Services Act which gives local authorities more power over the buses in their area. It is not just rural council-backed services that have shrunk. The miles on the buses - for commercial routes too - have been slowly dropping since 2010. There has been a drop of about 22% since 2010. It is back on the rise but has yet to reach the same levels as pre-Covid. Commercial bus miles decreased by a quarter between 2010 and 2025. title: Why Cardiff is set to win race to host Fury-Joshua
description: Why Cardiff is set to beat competition from London and New York to host the long-awaited fight between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua.
body: Anthony Joshua's fight against Tyson Fury is set to be held in Cardiff The long-awaited heavyweight fight between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua is expected to take place at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on Friday, 11 December. While BBC Sport understands final details are still being hammered out between Netflix, Saudi Arabian organisers Sela and both fighters' camps, Cardiff has firmly emerged as the frontrunner, with an official announcement expected this week. It marks another dramatic twist in a saga that, only weeks ago, appeared destined for New York. A date at Madison Square Garden was so close to completion that plans were already being drawn up for a Manhattan news conference. Instead, after Joshua and promoter Eddie Hearn refused to budge on their contractual right to stage the fight on British soil, the Welsh capital has taken centre stage. BBC Sport takes a look at how Cardiff became the leading candidate to host what would arguably be the biggest event in British boxing in the 21st Century. Wembley Stadium was long assumed to be the natural home for a meeting between the two defining British heavyweights of their generation. However, the path to making the fight was complicated by Joshua and Fury having signed separate agreements with Sela rather than a joint contract. Joshua's deal explicitly stipulated that the bout must take place in the United Kingdom, whereas Fury's contained no such restriction. That distinction proved critical when organisers and broadcast partner Netflix began lobbying to move the show to the United States. Hearn acknowledged that virtually every other party involved preferred New York, with Matchroom even exploring what compensation would be required to waive the UK clause. For a moment, that stand-off threatened to scupper the entire event. Fury publicly accused Joshua of stalling and briefly floated the prospect of a trilogy fight with Oleksandr Usyk. But once Fury relented, organisers needed to find a British venue capable of satisfying the broadcast demands without leaving fans exposed to the British winter. Cardiff, almost by process of elimination, became the answer. Cardiff's Principality Stadium has a retractable roof The fight had initially been discussed for November but, with negotiations over the venue dragging on, it now looks set for December. Staging an open-air stadium fight in the UK at that time carries immense risk. While Wembley offers unmatched prestige, exposing tens of thousands of fans and a massive international broadcast operation to potentially freezing temperatures, wind and rain was deemed unacceptable. Moving the event indoors to an arena like London's O2 would eliminate weather risks, but at the cost of sacrificing tens of thousands of ticket sales. The Principality Stadium's retractable roof allows organisers to capture the immense scale, atmosphere and gate revenue of a stadium show while offering full protection from the elements. The venue's official seated capacity is just under 74,000, but boxing configurations allow for even larger crowds. Joshua has already proven he can sell out the venue, having defended his WBA and IBF titles there against Carlos Takam in front of nearly 80,000 fans in 2017 before adding the WBO belt against Joseph Parker five months later. We want Fury v Joshua at Wembley - London mayor Fury says he is looking for new opponent, calls out Usyk 'Bring it on' - Cardiff businesses react to Fury vs Joshua rumours Perhaps the most difficult hurdle has been aligning the event with Netflix's preference to broadcast during prime-time hours in the United States. A projected UK ring walk of about 01:00 GMT - 20:00 on the US east coast - created a logistical headache for London. Wembley operates under a strict 23:00 event curfew. While Mayor of London Sadiq Khan offered his support and Wembley officials were open to discussions, securing the necessary approvals from Brent Council and local safety advisory groups for a 01:00 start presented an administrative hurdle. Cardiff offers a far smoother path. The Welsh Rugby Union, which owns and operates the Principality Stadium, previously indicated it would be delighted to host the fight and confirmed a late-night finish would not be a dealbreaker. While early-hours finishes still require extensive coordination around transport, policing and crowd management in the city centre, the venue already holds a clear precedent for late-night boxing. In 2007, Joe Calzaghe's super-middleweight unification victory over Mikkel Kessler did not start until 02:00 local time to satisfy American television network Showtime. For all the delays and frustrations that have plagued this rivalry over the past decade, Fury against Joshua remains the pinnacle of domestic boxing. Downgrading to an indoor arena would diminish the magnitude of the occasion. Crucially, taking the fight to America would have deprived domestic fans of a generational spectacle. British supporters have driven the commercial value of this rivalry for years, filling stadiums for both fighters' respective careers and following every collapsed negotiation. Staging the bout on home soil serves as a long-overdue reward for that loyalty, even if both men are now former world heavyweight champions. A stadium fight of this magnitude dominates the national conversation in a way a 04:00 New York or Las Vegas broadcast simply cannot, and local amateur boxing clubs could see a surge in interest when the country's biggest stars compete on home soil. Wales also has history of staging a huge fight between two British heavyweights: In 1993, Lennox Lewis defended his WBC title against Frank Bruno at Cardiff Arms Park - the venue that the Principality Stadium replaced. When the demands surrounding the event are broken down, Cardiff's emergence becomes easier to understand. Boxing schedule and results 2026 Watch every Born to Brawl episode Notific

title: Tories pledge to bring back tax-free shopping for tourists
description: The party says scrapping the scheme in 2021 left the UK less competitive than European destinations.
body: Tory leader Kemi Badenoch (left) and shadow culture secretary Rebecca Paul visited Bicester Village, a designer outlet shopping centre popular with tourists, to promote the policy The Conservative Party has pledged to bring back tax-free shopping for tourists from outside the European Union. The Tories said the decision to scrap the scheme in 2021 left the UK less competitive than European destinations. Leader Kemi Badenoch, who was a Treasury minister when the tax relief was abolished, said businesses were being "let down by a tax policy that is chasing their customers away". But Labour accused the party of "a spectacular U-turn". The VAT Retail Export Scheme - which allowed overseas visitors to get a VAT refund on items they had bought in Great Britain and took home in their luggage - was scrapped for non-EU visitors under the previous Conservative government in 2021, while it was also not extended for EU visitors. At the time, Badenoch said it was "a costly relief which does not benefit the whole of GB equally". However, the Conservatives have now set out plans to restore VAT refunds for eligible visitors from outside the EU. The party said that if evidence confirms the scheme "pays its way", this would be extended to visitors from the EU by the end of the next Parliament. It said the cost of reintroducing the scheme would be offset by cracking down on "NHS health tourism", including more consistent charging of patients ineligible for free treatment, minimum recovery targets for debts and requiring full repayment of debts before visa applications or renewals will be considered. The remaining costs would be funded from a package of savings set out by the Tories last year. Reinstate VAT-free tourist shopping, businesses say Bring back duty-free perk to boost London - mayor The party also argued the move would benefit shops, hotels, restaurants and the wider tourism industry. It pointed to research by the Centre for Economics and Business Research (Cebr), which suggested fully restoring tax-free shopping for tourists could attract up to 2.35 million extra visitors and generate £4.1bn in extra spending. The report from earlier this month also estimated that for every £1 of VAT refunded, this could generate £1.54 in other taxes. Badenoch said: "We have iconic retailers, inventive designers and brilliant manufacturers, but they are being let down by a tax policy that is chasing their customers away. "Holidaymakers are choosing rival cities in other countries for the simple reason that it saves them money." Businesses have long called for tax-free shopping for tourists to be reintroduced, arguing they are at a disadvantage to other European countries. EU countries offer VAT refunds for non-EU visitors, while other European countries such as Switzerland have similar schemes. Helen Dickinson, chief executive at the British Retail Consortium, said: "Introducing a modern tax-free shopping scheme would help attract more international spending to the UK, supporting high streets, jobs and investment in towns and cities across the country. "Done properly, it would boost economic growth and deliver a net benefit to the Exchequer." However, a Labour spokesperson said: "Kemi Badenoch used to say tax-free shopping was a costly giveaway and now she's trying to sell it as an economic miracle. "If they really think it's such a great idea, they should explain why they scrapped it in the first place and how they'd pay for bringing it back." title: Three arrested in South Africa over one of nine women's body finds
description: The body of Jabulile Ntimba was the ninth to be found recently in an area east of Johannesburg.
body: Jabulile Ntimba's body was found by a road last Thursday Three suspects have been detained in South Africa in connection with the murder of a woman in an area east of Johannesburg – the last of nine recent cases in that region that has shone a spotlight on the level of violence against women in the country. Under pressure to solve the spate of murders which has involved victims' bodies being dumped on a roadside, police have described the arrests of the three – a man and two women - as a "breakthrough". Referring to all nine cases, acting police chief Lt Gen Puleng Dimpane said her officers were "working tirelessly to bring those responsible to justice". The three suspects are due in court on Monday morning. Their case relates to the death of Jabulile Ntimba, whose half-naked body was found wrapped in a sheet in Dawn Park last Thursday. Several of the recent victims were discovered partially clothed and with injuries, but police have stressed that they have not established whether all the deaths are connected or whether a serial killer is responsible. Addressing journalists on Monday, deputy police chief Lt Gen Tebello Mosikili said that "a team of analysts are working hard to see if there are links to all these cases" but the killing of Ntimba "appears to be an indication of a murder that stemmed from a relationship... this includes... a possible love triangle". South Africa has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence in the world. It also has a very high murder rate and though officials statistics do not identify the gender of the victims, a recent estimate from the country's Human Rights Commission indicated that, on average, six women were murdered every day between April and June this year. The recent grim discoveries have sparked a national outcry about the scale of the problem and increased the feeling of insecurity for many women. title: What are my rights if my flight is cancelled or delayed?
description: Flights are affected again owing to air traffic control problems, so what are your rights if you're affected?
body: Flights in Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England have been affected by air traffic control issues – the second major disruption at UK airports in a few weeks. When a flight is cancelled or delayed, passengers affected have various rights, such as a refund or an alternative flight at no extra cost. However, these can vary depending on which carrier you are flying with and from where. Extra compensation is payable only when an airline is at fault, which is not the case with air traffic control problems. Here's what it means for you. Under UK law, airlines have a duty to look after you when flights are delayed or cancelled. The reason for the delay or cancellation does not matter. So anyone affected by the air transport delays will be eligible. That includes providing meals and accommodation, if necessary, and getting you to your destination. The airline should organise putting you on an alternative flight at no extra cost. Additional losses, such as unused accommodation, might require a claim to a credit card provider, if that was the payment option used. After that, a claim may need to go to your travel insurance provider, but there is no standard definition of what is covered. It may require a close look at the details of the policy to see what is covered and in which circumstances. Passengers are also being urged to heed travel advice from the UK government, external, as this can also affect travel insurance rights. UK law generally applies to your flight if you are flying from a UK airport on any airline, arriving at a UK airport on an EU or UK airline, or arriving at an airport in the EU on a UK airline. If your flight was coming into the UK on a non-UK or EU airline, then you should check the terms and conditions of your booking. If your flight is covered by UK law, your airline must let you choose between either getting a refund or being booked on to an alternative flight. That's regardless of how far in advance the cancellation was made. You can get your money back for any part of the ticket you have not used. So, if you booked a return flight and the outbound leg is cancelled, you can get the full cost of the return ticket refunded. If you still want to travel, your airline must find you an alternative flight. If another airline is flying to your destination significantly sooner, or there are other suitable modes of transport, then you have a right to be booked on to that alternative transport instead. How do I renew my UK passport and what is the 10-year rule?, external Three things you can do to stop EU border checks at the airport costing you If you are stuck abroad or at the airport because of a flight cancellation, airlines covered by UK legislation must also provide you with other assistance. a reasonable amount of food and drink (often in the form of vouchers) a way for you to communicate (often by refunding the cost of calls) free accommodation, if you have to stay overnight to fly the next day transport to and from the accommodation If your airline is unable to arrange assistance, you have the right to organise this yourself and claim back the cost later. The Civil Aviation Authority advises people to keep receipts and not spend more than necessary. Civil Aviation Authority: Delays and cancellations, external You are entitled to the same assistance as for a cancellation if your flight is delayed by more than two hours for a short-haul flight, three hours for a medium-haul, or four hours for a long-haul. If you are delayed by more than five hours and no longer want to travel, you can get a full refund. If you booked a package holiday with a company that is an ABTA member and your flight is cancelled, you are entitled to a suitable alternative flight or a full refund. ABTA: What are your rights?, external Disruption caused by "extraordinary circumstances" – which includes things like air traffic control issues, bad weather, strikes by airport staff, or conflict – does not entitle you to extra compensation. However, in other circumstances, when it is considered to be the airline's fault, you have a number of rights, external if your flight is covered under UK law. What you are entitled to depends on what caused the cancellation and how much notice you are given. If your flight is cancelled with less than two weeks' notice, you may be able to claim compensation based on the timings of the alternative flight you are offered. The amount you are entitled to also depends on how far you were travelling: for flights under 1,500km, such as Glasgow to Amsterdam, you can claim up to £220 per person for flights of 1,500km to 3,500km, such as East Midlands to Marrakesh, you can claim up to £350 per person for flights over 3,500km, such as London to New York, you can claim up to £520 per person Airlines will not refund you for loss of earnings. Travel insurance policies will not usually cover loss of earnings either. If you think you're going to be late back at work because of flight delays, you have a responsibility to let your employer know, legal experts say. You should agree with your employer how to deal with the absence – for example, by using annual leave or taking unpaid leave. Employers have no legal obligation to pay employees who are absent in this situation, experts say, unless it is stated in their contract. Have your travel plans been disrupted? Share your experience. title: Chris Martin joins busker for impromptu duet
description: Busker Hanny Junee says he did not realise who had joined him in Trafalgar Square until afterwards.
body: This video can not be played Chris Martin surprises Trafalgar Square busker with impromptu duet Coldplay singer Chris Martin joined a busker in central London for an impromptu duet. Hanny Junee was getting ready to sing Coldplay's hit Viva la Vida to a small audience in Trafalgar Square when the star joined him by the microphone and started singing along. But Junee said he did not realise who he was. He told the BBC: "I thought: 'This guy has amazing energy, nice vibe and a really good voice, he sounds really similar to Chris Martin.' "But I thought: 'Come on, Hanny, don't be ridiculous, of course it's not him, Chris Martin doesn't roam the streets of London.' Then he finished a verse and the next thing I know he's gone. It was magical." Junee added: "Afterwards some people came up to me and told me it really was Chris Martin. "It was amazing, it was like we connected purely through music, not fame." Speaking about Friday's duet, the full-time busker from South Korea said he had given his audience of about 20 a choice between Viva la Vida and a song by The Script. More hands went up for Viva la Vida, he said. A Coldplay fan himself, Junee said he could not believe what happened. He said he usually spent his days busking around Covent Garden, the London Eye and Trafalgar Square. Chris Martin, pictured in BBC Radio 2's Piano Room in 2024, has surprised his fans before It is not the first time Martin has surprised fans. In August 2025, he played an impromptu gig at a small pub in West Yorkshire, and in June 2022, he performed a song at a pub near Bath for a couple about to get married. title: Inside Djibouti refugee camp for thousands fleeing Houthi advance in Yemen
description: Fighting on Yemen's west coast has prompted thousands of people to flee by boat across the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
body: This video can not be played Fighting on Yemen's west coast has prompted thousands of people to flee by boat across the Bab al-Mandab Strait to Djibouti over the last ten days. The BBC's Frank Gardner visited a refugee camp in Obock, a small port town where officials are preparing for the arrival of up to 10,000 refugees. The UN International Organisation for Migration said people were ​travelling on overcrowded boats and arriving with very limited food and water. The crossings were sparked by an offensive by the Iran-backed Houthi movement to take control of a key island and seize the strategically important port of Mokha. title: Edwards signs short-term deal with Red Roses
description: Shaun Edwards has started a short-term coaching consultancy role with England women.
body: Edwards (left) has been approached by the Rugby Football Union in the past about a role with England's men's team, without ever being brought on board Shaun Edwards has started a short-term coaching consultancy role with England women. It is understood the 59-year-old will work with current Red Roses defence coach Sarah Hunter for the rest of their WXV Global Series matches, starting with New Zealand at Allianz Stadium on Saturday. The news comes after England's 39-Test winning streak ended with a 26-26 draw against Canada last weekend. Englishman Edwards is one of the most decorated coaches in rugby union. He recently left his role as France men's defence coach, where he won three Six Nations titles. He has never previously worked for England's men or women. His playing career in rugby league saw him win 36 caps for Great Britain before coaching success with London Wasps and Wales and a six-year stint with France. This video can not be played Watch highlights: England 26-26 Canada On the appointment of Edwards, England head coach John Mitchell said: "Since his time with France ended, we have had a conversation about our game, and he expressed an interest in working in an international women's set-up for the first time. "He has a huge amount of respect for the Red Roses and what we stand for; he sees it as a privilege to join our environment. "His coaching credentials are exceptional and his experience at the highest level of the game speaks for itself. "Defensively, Sarah Hunter is relishing the opportunity to learn from him, alongside the rest of our coaching group, as we head into another exciting Test match against New Zealand." Last week, Edwards expressed his desire to return to coaching and be a part of next year's men's Six Nations. "I'm def­in­itely open to offers now, until I sort out a full-time role," he told the Daily Mail., external "I'm a proud Englishman and everybody loves to represent their country, don't they? I'm no different." title: Calvin Harris recognised for 1.6m world record DJ set crowd
description: An estimated 1.6m people attended the Dumfries DJ's set in Sao Paulo in Brazil earlier this year.
body: Harris has been recognised by Guinness World Records on a number of occasions Scottish DJ Calvin Harris has been celebrating writing his name into the record books after performing for an estimated 1.6m people in Sao Paulo earlier this year. The musician from Dumfries received recognition from Guinness World Records (GWR) for the largest attendance for a DJ set by a single artist. He took to social media to highlight the award for what he described as a "truly insane day" which he said could only have happened in Brazil. GWR said it had been reported that his headline appearance had forced the closure of the Rua da Consolação with some fans fainting in the heat. This article contains content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. You may want to read Meta’s Instagram cookie policy, external and privacy policy, external before accepting. To view this content choose ‘accept and continue’. Harris has already been recognised for a number of other records in the past. In 2014, GWR presented him with a certificate for most top 10 hits on the UK singles chart from one album for 18 Months which produced no fewer than nine. It also lists him as the highest paid DJ in one year for his earnings between June 2015 and 2016. GWR said Harris had turned Sao Paulo into "one massive street party" by climbing on board a carnival float for his performance on 8 February 2026. Wearing a Brazilian football shirt with the name Calvinho on the back he worked his way through a setlist featuring many of his biggest hits. The record book also noted that a similar-sized crowd attended Madonna's free concert on Copacabana Beach in May 2024 during her Celebration Tour. title: World Gurning Championship winners crowned
description: The World Gurning Championship is held annually in the small Cumbrian town of Egremont.
body: Will Mellor came second in the men's competition Actor Will Mellor has come a surprise second in the World Gurning Championships, pipped to the main prize by local man Ged Eccles who had come close but never before won. Part of the annual Egremont Crab Fair in Cumbria, which began in 1267, the gurning competition has been a fixture since the 1500s. Competitors are judged on their ability to pull the ugliest or most grotesque face. The Hollyoaks and Mr Bates vs The Post Office star won second place in the men's competition after attending as part of a programme he was filming. Eccles said he felt "ecstatic" to have finally won the men's competition. It was his first victory since becoming the junior champion in 1985. He came second in 2023 and was third in 2016 and 2009 and said he believed he had won this year because of the extra practice he had put in. Ged Eccles won this year's world championships "I practise in front of a mirror for maybe three to four hours a day," he said. "I've been doing that since the end of May." He said he did this to loosen up his neck, cheekbone and jaw bone muscles in order to get his lip on to his nose. "And that's what I did," he said. Eccles said he hoped to defend his title next year and that he planned to continue gurning "until the day I can't do it anymore". One of the event's organisers, Dan Nixon, said it was good to see Eccles finally win. He said there were about 50 entrants to the men's, women's and junior versions of the competition and that up to 800 people had attended. "I think everyone in Egremont takes part in the Crab Fair in some way," he said. Claire Lister is a seasoned winner, Dan Nixon said Local woman Claire Lister won the women's competition again after losing her crown last year. The nine-time champion said: "I'm absolutely delighted to have won again, I'm really proud and it still feels just as special every time. "It's just a bit of fun and keeps the Egremont Crab Fair tradition going." Lister said she does not train or practise for the competition but just turns up on the day and gives it her best. "I think after doing it for so many years it just comes naturally to me now," she said. Nixon described her as "a seasoned winner". The competition's organising committee have already started planning next year's event which will be its 760th. "We're very much hoping that it's going to be a really, really big spectacular," he said.
