title: D-Day veteran who survived capture dies aged 101
description: Kenneth Hay was an "extraordinary gentleman whose remarkable life will never be forgotten", the British Normandy Memorial says.
body: Normandy veteran Kenneth Hay was an "extraordinary gentleman", the British Normandy Memorial said Normandy veteran Kenneth Hay, who survived being captured just weeks after D-Day and spent years educating children about World War Two, has died aged 101. Hay, from Upminster in east London, served in the 4th Dorset Infantry Regiment. He was captured a month after the allied invasion of northern France and survived a 1,000-mile (1,609km) forced march in eastern Europe until he was liberated by US forces. His death was announced on Sunday by the British Normandy Memorial, for which he was an ambassador. The organisation said he was an "extraordinary gentleman whose remarkable life will never be forgotten". In its statement on social media, the British Normandy Memorial added: "His passion for education was unwavering. "The countless schoolchildren whose lives he touched with his stories of courage and resilience nicknamed him 'Grandad Ken'. "We extend our most sincere condolences to Ken's sons Chris and Jeremy, all the Hay family and his very many friends." Hay, pictured in 2025 at the British Normandy Memorial in Ver-sur-Mer, France, served in the 4th Dorset Infantry Regiment D-Day, on 6 June 1944, saw British, American and Canadian troops storm beaches along the Normandy coastline to begin the liberation of France from Nazi occupation. Hay had landed at Courseulles-sur-Mer just days after and was captured by the German 12th SS Panzer Division during a night patrol on 7-8 July. He was taken to Zabrze in Poland, where he was put to work as a prisoner of war in a coal mine. Speaking of the capture in 2024, Hay recalled his first feelings were of "dread" and "fear". "We went out on night patrol, was supposed to be doing a blow up of a self-propelled gun in no man's land, but in fact, it was behind their lines," he said. "So they let us through and then very unfriendly, they sealed it and wouldn't let us back, so we had a battle. "We had 30 [that] went out on our patrol, 16 including my brother, who was a corporal, got back, five of us got captured and then presumably nine got killed." As the Russians approached, the prisoners were marched to a new location, approximately 1,000 miles away, during which many of them died. During the three-month march, Hay said he once "lay down to die" after it became too painful to continue, but two friends turned back for him and lifted him with an "arm around each shoulder". This video can not be played 'Most people see names, I see faces' says Normandy veteran Kenneth Hay Eventually they were liberated by American troops and Hay returned to the UK, via Reims, on 4 May 1945. Recalling the moment he made it to his mother's house in Barking, he said: "They came running down the road to greet me." After the war, he was appointed an MBE for services to the community and received the Legion d'Honneur, France's highest order of merit. Hay regularly visited British schools to share stories of the war and answer questions, saying he believed it was his "duty to pass it on". title: Flights in UK delayed by 'technical issue' with air traffic control in Scotland
description: Engineers are investigating the issue at the Prestwick Centre which handles air traffic control across Scotland and the north of England.
body: Edinburgh is one of the airports affected by the incident A "technical issue" with air traffic control in Scotland is causing delays to flights in the UK. The national air traffic service (Nats) said engineers had been called in to deal with the issue at the Prestwick Centre in South Ayrshire which handles air traffic control across Scotland and the north of England. The service said the issue was not related to a software defect that led to the cancellation of 2,000 flights across the UK earlier this month. Passengers have taken to social media to confirm they are experiencing delays at Glasgow, Prestwick and Edinburgh airports. Dundee and Benbecula airports have also confirmed flights are impacted. A spokesperson for Edinburgh Airport said: "We are experiencing some delays due to the Nats issue at Prestwick Centre. "We are monitoring the situation closely and are working with Nats as they work to resolve the issue." A spokesperson for Ryanair said they had been notified of a Nats "equipment failure" affecting airspace above Scotland and northern England. They said it was impacting flights to and from the UK and Ireland. A Nats spokesperson said: "Our engineers are continuing to investigate the issue at our Prestwick centre in Scotland. "Airports south of Manchester are broadly unaffected, however flights heading north and flights departing Scottish airports are currently subject to some delay." The spokesperson apologised for the disruption and urged passengers to check with their airline for more information. Lewis Fraser from Inverness is onboard a flight stuck on the runway at Glasgow Airport. He told BBC News: "We boarded the flight as normal but were immediately told we were delayed. "The latest update was around half an hour ago to say we might be waiting another hour and 45 minutes. Some passengers have left the plane in the last few minutes." He is travelling to Heathrow to get a connecting flight to Chicago but said making his connection seemed "unlikely". Have you been affected by the disruption to flights? title: Gavin and Stacey co-stars support Strictly debut, says Melanie Walters
description: Walters, best known for playing Gwen West in the BBC comedy, is partnered with professional Aljaz Skorjanec.
body: Melanie Walters and Aljaz Skorjanec performed together for the first time on Saturday's show Actor Melanie Walters has said her Gavin and Stacey co-stars have been "hugely supportive" of her Strictly Come Dancing debut, with Joanna Page "very excited" for her to take to the ballroom floor. The screen and stage star, 64, best known for playing Gwen West in the BBC comedy, is partnered with professional Aljaz Skorjanec, 36, in the new series of the dance programme. Walters said being paired with Skorjanec was a "dream come true" after the pair performed together for the first time at Saturday's launch show. She said her Gavin and Stacey co-stars had sent her "lovely messages, especially from Jo [Page], who's just very excited". When asked if she would be bringing any of her character from the comedy onto the ballroom floor, she added: "I've got no idea, this is Aljaz's department. "I've got no idea what's going to happen on that ballroom." Walters told the Press Association it was "mind-boggling" to be asked to join the series and that it was "a bit out of my comfort zone". "I've not been one for doing panel shows or quiz shows or anything," she said. Melanie Walters said her Gavin and Stacey co-stars had been very supportive "So, it's now me, Melanie Walters, which is not what I'm used to putting out there, because I'm quite a private person. I just thought, 'no, let's tick that box'. "And basically, I really want to learn to dance properly. Always have. "Getting weekly masterclasses. You couldn't ask for anything better." Walters starred in Gavin and Stacey from its launch in 2007 and reprised her role for a 2024 Christmas special. Her television work also includes roles in Coronation Street, Beyond Paradise, Being Human, Hollyoaks, Biff And Chip, and Doc Martin, while her film credits include Submarine, Resistance, High Tide and Save The Cinema. On stage, she has appeared in productions such as The Importance Of Being Earnest, Blood Brothers, Twelfth Night, Educating Rita and What's New Pussycat?. She also recently appeared in two series of the BBC's crime mystery series Death Valley. title: Lib Dems demand action over increase in child birth injuries
description: Sir Ed Davey pledged to spend £600m a year on maternity services if the Lib Dems were in government.
body: Health spokesperson Helen Morgan met parents and babies to discuss maternity care The government must not ignore a "national safety scandal" in maternity services, Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey has said, as figures suggest life-altering childbirth injuries in England have reached record levels. Lib Dem analysis of NHS figures showed the number of women suffering potentially life-threatening levels of blood loss is the highest ever recorded in England. Three in every 100 women suffered serious tearing injuries requiring emergency surgery in the first half of this year, something Sir Ed said was a "devastating indictment of our NHS maternity services". The government is expected to publish a new national maternity and neonatal action plan by the end of the year. Speaking to BBC Breakfast at the Lib Dem annual conference in Brighton, Davey pledged to spend £600m a year on maternity services if in government. He said £1.3bn a year was currently being spent on "failure" through negligence compensation payouts for poor maternity services, but said this investment should go towards prevention instead. Calling for more senior midwives and consultants, he said: "Our current maternity staff are run ragged - they're massively overstretched. "That's the best way, all the evidence shows, to make sure maternity units are safe," he added. "It is a scandal at the moment - we've seen inquiry after inquiry. So many women are suffering injuries at birth and we're seeing the loss of babies too; it is a tragedy as well as a scandal." He said ministers "cannot turn a blind eye to this national safety scandal" and mothers "deserve safe, compassionate care". The party pointed to Care Quality Commission (CQC) survey data showing one-in-10 women, about 54,000, were left alone during late stages of labour or childbirth last year, which the Lib Dems said was due to lack of training and staff shortages. More than 8,000 women had postpartum haemorrhages with blood loss of more than 1.5l since the start of this year, more than double the number over the equivalent period in 2021, the party's analysis of NHS figures suggests. Rates of major haemorrhage peaked between April and June this year, while 32.7 women per thousand needed emergency treatment. The rate of third or fourth degree vaginal tears during childbirth has risen by 29% in the last five years, according to the analysis. The Lib Dem health spokesperson Helen Morgan, who successfully campaigned for an independent maternity commissioner to drive improvements, said reports on previous maternity scandals were "gathering dust". "Years after the Shrewsbury and Telford scandal which devastated my community - my neighbours and friends - women continue to suffer," she said. "This must be the moment we say 'enough'." A review in 2022 found catastrophic failures at Shrewsbury and Telford NHS Trust (SaTH) over 20 years may have led to the deaths of more than 200 babies. The trust apologised and said it had already put in measures to prevent a repeat. A Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) spokesperson said the review to be published later this year will bring together the recommendations from the Baroness Amos, Donna Ockenden, and Lady Justice Thirlwall inquiries, set clear priorities and hold the system to account for delivering improved outcomes. "Every woman deserves safe maternity care and the new health secretary has made this issue a personal priority," they said. "Through the National Maternity and Neonatal Taskforce that she is chairing, this government will deliver the reforms needed to ensure the very highest standards of safety and care for every mother and baby." England's first statutory Maternity and Neonatal Commissioner will be appointed to ensure the voices of women, babies and families are at the heart of national policy making. The DHSC is also extending Martha's Rule to every maternity and neonatal ward to ensure that any reports of deterioration from patients or their families are acted upon, and has invested £187m since April 2025 to address critical safety risks in the maternity and neonatal estate. A Labour Party spokesperson said: "Ed Davey was part of the coalition government that tore up the national standards for maternity services that Yvette Cooper is now having to restore. "He never raised any objections to that decision at the time, and he has never apologised since. Until he does so, his words on this issue will ring hollow." "We have grown really fast under my leadership , with record number of MPs and running more councils," he said. "When you have a bigger party you can't please everyone all the time." title: Public confidence 'damaged' by on-the-run killer case, says Long
description: Gary Anderson remains at large a week after he absconded while attending his father's funeral in Derry.
body: Naomi Long says is to speak in the Assembly on Monday about the circumstances surrounding on-the-run killer Gary Anderson's compassionate temporary release from Maghaberry Prison Public confidence in the justice system has been "damaged" by the circumstances surrounding the temporary release from prison of convicted murderer Gary Anderson, Justice Minister Naomi Long has said. Anderson, who is one of two brothers jailed for life in 2023 for the 2018 murder of Karol Kelly in Londonderry, remains at large a week after he absconded while attending his father's funeral in Derry last Monday. Naomi Long, who is to meet the murder victim's family, is ordering an independent review into the circumstances surrounding Anderson's release from Maghaberry Prison. That happened after a court overturned a decision by the prison service to refuse him permission to attend the funeral. A day before the funeral last Monday, a judge granted Anderson a two-hour compassionate temporary release (CTR) from Maghaberry Prison to attend it. The funeral service took place at St Mary's Church in the Creggan area of Derry last Monday morning. Anderson was not given permission to attend cremation in Letterkenny, County Donegal, in the Republic of Ireland that afternoon. At some stage on Monday morning, he absconded from his court-approved civilian chaperone. Gary Anderson, who is serving a 15-year sentence for the murder of Karol Kelly, remains on the run CTR can be granted to prisoners when a family member has died or is seriously ill, but the decision to release them takes into account the circumstances of the case and any risks involved. Questions have been raised over the granting of Anderson's CTR following the publication of the full 15-page judgement from the judicial review into the Prison Service's decision., external The judgement found that the decision to refuse Anderson's request was based on inaccurate information about the risk he posed. The decision had been taken by the duty governor at Maghaberry Prison. In his judgement, Mr Justice Rooney found that an internal assessment of Anderson's likelihood of reoffending had been recorded at a higher level than the score held on the Prison Service's internal system. A legal representative for the Prison Service told the court that the increased score had come from a colleague rather than the duty governor's personal knowledge. When the system was checked, Anderson's score was 27, indicating a medium likelihood of reoffending, rather than 32, which had been recorded as a high likelihood in the decision letter. The judge found that the duty governor "clearly took account of this incorrect information" when assessing the risks and considering whether the decision was proportionate. He invited the duty governor to reconsider the decision, but that offer was declined. The judge described the decision not to review it as "somewhat surprising" and he granted Anderson temporary release subject to a number of conditions, finding that the Prison Service's decision was "flawed" and had taken into account "irrelevant and incorrect factors". The judge said the failure to secure and take account of the correct risk assessment was unlawful. Speaking to BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme on Monday, Long said a procedural failing by the Departmental Solicitor's Office (DSO), meant prison officials were not told that a judge had offered them the chance to reconsider their decision not to release Anderson. Long said that the DSO had acknowledged a "procedural failing on their part" and this was "not communicated at any stage". "We have identified that that offer was not passed on to the decision-makers within Prison Service at that time and so we have only become aware of it when the full judgement was actually published and we were then able to refer to the transcripts. "I'm setting up a completely independent review because our understanding would be that it would be for our legal advisors from the department, the Departmental Solicitor's Office (DSO) to come back to us and there was contact between Northern Ireland Prison Service and our solicitor during this period but it didn't include any reflection that the judge was offering an opportunity to reconsider or re-evaluate or provide additional information and that's absolutely key. "It's a normal process when it goes to court that the judge may ask for more information, may ask for more clarity and that offer was not made to Prison Service and therefore we were in a situation where it rested in the hands of the judge and the judge in good faith made the decision based on the information that he had." Speaking on Monday, Long apologised to the family of Karol Kelly and acknowledged the impact Gary Anderson's release and subsequent absconding from prison has had. She said she was "desperately sorry that they have been put through this trauma as a result of whatever has happened" and said she was commissioning and independent review. "Whatever miscommunication, whatever poor information, they should not have been subjected to this ongoing trauma and distress, and I can only apologise genuinely for that. "I will be meeting them, obviously subject to their wishes. I received a letter last week from Mark H Durkan, and I wrote back and said that I would be happy to meet with the family at their earliest convenience, and hopefully that will be able to happen soon. "I don't want them to be drawn into this, I don't want them to feel any further distress." Long has said all relevant facts must be established and carefully considered and is to update MLAs on Monday about the case. "I am concerned enough about this case and I think it's important to say by the impact that it has had on the Kelly family and they are first and foremost in mind at the moment," she said. title: Palmer set to withdraw from England squad after recall
description: Chelsea forward Cole Palmer is set to withdraw from England's squad for the upcoming Nations League matches because of a minor injury.
body: Cole Palmer has two goals and two assists in the Premier League this season Chelsea forward Cole Palmer is set to withdraw from England's squad for the upcoming Nations League matches because of a minor injury. The 24-year-old had been recalled by manager Thomas Tuchel having been controversially left out of the Three Lions' squad for the World Cup. Tuchel previously said Palmer had a "point to prove" and needed "to step up" to "keep his shirt and justify the nomination". However, the Blues forward will now miss the extended international break in which England play four games. The Three Lions face World Cup winners Spain at Wembley on Saturday, 26 September, then travel to the Czech Republic (29 September) and Croatia (3 October) before hosting the Czechs on 6 October. Palmer's withdrawal comes after he played the full game for Chelsea in their 3-0 defeat at Brentford on Friday. Following a summer off after missing out on World Cup selection, he has started six of Chelsea's seven games and played the full 90 minutes in five of them - scoring four goals and providing two assists. Palmer was hampered by a recurring groin injury in 2025-26, which former Chelsea manager Enzo Maresca - who is now boss at Manchester City - said did not make sense. Palmer last played for England in their 1-0 friendly defeat by Japan in March. title: Seven Ethiopian rebel groups form new alliance
description: The groups have been active in Ethiopia's most populous regions for years and now say they will work together.
body: There have been renewed tensions in the northern Tigray region Several of the rebel groups which have been fighting the Ethiopian authorities in different parts of the country have announced they have formed an alliance to remove the government in Addis Ababa. The alliance brings together the Fano militia in Amhara, the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and four other smaller groupings in a coalition named Alliance for Survival. The seven groups accuse Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government of presiding over "war, genocide, mass destruction, and utter poverty", claiming Ethiopia is at risk of disintegration. Federal authorities have not yet responded. Ethiopia has faced years of armed conflict in Oromia and Amhara, the most populous states in the country. There have also been renewed tensions in the northern Tigray region, where a two-year civil war left hundreds of thousands dead and displaced millions. An African-Union peace deal ended that war in 2022, but there have been fears of a return to a full-scale conflict, with both sides accusing each other of violating that agreement. Besides Oromia, Amhara and Tigray, the new alliance also includes groups based in three other regions - Ogaden, Afar and Benishangul-Gumuz – making up a half of Ethiopia's 12 regional states. Amhara's Fano group fought alongside federal forces during the Tigray war. It however turned against the federal government in an armed insurgency less than a year after the war ended, after refusing government orders to disarm. The government has been fighting the OLA since 2018. The announcement of the Alliance for Survival coalition comes months after reports of an alleged alliance between TPLF and neighbouring Eritrea. Abiy responded by saying he had faith in Ethiopia's "defensive capabilities". "Even if others were added, we do not have an iota of fear regarding Ethiopia's sovereignty," he told lawmakers in July. The country held a general election in June, with Abiy's Prosperity Party retaining its overwhelming parliamentary majority, despite the poll being overshadowed by conflict, accusations of repression and little participation by opposition parties. The Fano and OLA rebel groups rejected the election and its results. The Tigray region and its six million inhabitants were completely excluded from the poll. title: Sydney policeman allegedly disguised himself as Uber Eats rider before murders
description: Beaumont Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to the 2024 murder of his ex-partner and his new boyfriend.
body: Luke Davies (left) and Jesse Baird were allegedly murdered by Beaumont Lamarre-Condon in Feburary 2024 A former police officer accused of using his work gun to kill a Sydney couple was driven by a "jealous infatuation" with his ex, a court has heard. Beaumont Lamarre-Condon, 31, has pleaded not guilty to two charges of domestic violence-related murder and one of aggravated break and enter. Prosecutors allege Lamarre-Condon shot his ex-partner, 26-year-old TV presenter Jesse Baird, and Baird's new partner Luke Davies, a 29-year-old Qantas flight attendant, at a home in the Sydney suburb of Paddington in 2024. The couple's bodies were found in a rural area 200km away, hidden in surfboard bags. The trial is expected to run for three months. In his opening address on Monday, prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC described how Lamarre-Condon had developed an "obsessive and jealous infatuation" with Baird after a brief romantic relationship. It manifested itself in a "range of compulsive behaviour", Hatfield said, which escalated when Baird ended all contact in November 2023. The barrister said Lamarre-Condon used a friend's phone to message Baird and claim he had cancer, stalked his ex-lover, and tampered with his car in the weeks after their break-up. Beaumont Lamarre-Condon is accused of murdering his former partner, Jesse Baird, and Baird's new boyfriend Luke Davies On the day of the alleged murders, Lamarre-Condon had set his alarm for 04.30 local time, Hatfield claimed, and sent a text to a friend which read: "I'll try to call you tonight and update you... there's no sign I'm doing it". Lamarre-Condon then switched to a burner phone, picked up a rental car and waited outside Baird's home for three hours dressed as an Uber driver, the prosecution alleged. He had previously bought a surfboard bag to dispose of Baird's body, Hatfield said. After entering Baird's home with a key he had previously obtained, Lamarre-Condon shot Baird in the kitchen and then killed Davies in the bedroom as he was trying to call emergency services for help, the court was told. Hatfield said that the accused had planned Baird's murder, and killed Davies so as to "eliminate him as a witness". In the hours and days after the alleged killings, Lamarre-Condon tried to cover up the murder, Hatfield said, including sending messages from Baird's mobile phone. The aggravated break and enter charge that Lamarre-Condon is facing refers to an incident in August 2023 where it's alleged he broke into Baird's home and stole his phone and wallet. Hatfield also told the court that Lamarre-Condon had earlier offered to plead guilty to a single charge of manslaughter relating to Baird's death but this was rejected. Police were first alerted to the alleged murders after bloodied items belonging to Baird and Davies were found in a bin in Sydney's south. Later that week, Lamarre-Condon handed himself in to a police station and was charged. Eight days after the alleged killings took place, authorities found the couple's bodies. Lamarre-Condon was sacked by New South Wales Police in the weeks after he was charged with the alleged murders. Before the opening address on Monday, a 15-member jury was selected, with the judge, Justice Natalie Adams, explaining that three extra people were chosen - a jury is typically made up of 12 people - as a contingency for sickness and other unforeseen circumstances. title: Temperatures forecast to hit 25C but heatwave chances fall
description: While temperatures are expected to rise this week, it won't be warm enough to be classed as an official heatwave.
body: It is set to turn warmer across the United Kingdom over the next few days, with temperatures peaking around 25C (77F). Widely, however, temperatures will climb into the low 20s Celsius, which is around five degrees higher than the average for late September. It will also stay mostly dry with some sunny spells, though rain is likely at times across northern and western parts of the UK. The warmth is likely to last for much of the week across England and Wales while it gets a bit cooler in Scotland and Northern Ireland. High pressure is building across the UK and this means the weather will become more settled with brighter conditions. After a chilly start on Monday morning, with sunshine and light winds across much of England and Wales, temperatures will climb into the low 20s. Even with more cloud in Scotland and Northern Ireland, it will turn warmer with highs also reaching 18 to 22C. It will also start to feel more humid again. That more humid air combined with light winds across England and Wales into Tuesday means it will start off rather misty and foggy with areas of low cloud for some. Once the sun has broken through though, it will feel warmer still. Temperatures could peak at around 24 or 25C in south-east England, but reach the low 20s Celsius in many other parts of England, Wales, Northern Ireland and Eastern Scotland. The highest temperature though will be determined by how much the cloud breaks allowing the strong September sunshine through. 2026 has already been a record-breaking year for the number of days above 25C, with last week exceeding the record of 89 days set in 1959. Temperatures will rise across the UK on Tuesday and while turning less warm on Wednesday, the warmth will remain especially in south-east England. At the start of the week, high pressure will largely block rain-bearing weather systems from crossing the UK. However, some rain is possible on Tuesday as a weather front moves into western Scotland and the west of Northern Ireland. This will become more substantial by Wednesday, stretching across Scotland, Northern Ireland, Wales and western areas of England, as high pressure is nudged a bit further east. It will also turn a bit cooler here with temperatures back to around the average of 14 to 18C. Drier and warmer conditions will likely persist in east and south-east England with temperatures once again reaching the mid-20s Celsius. While temperatures may go down by a few degrees for the end of the week, it will still be warmer than average with temperatures in the high teens to low 20s. The settled, drier weather will also likely last in southern and eastern England too with little rain for places continuing to experience drought conditions. The warmer spell of weather this week will not meet the criteria to become a heatwave. The Met Office defines this as temperatures reaching 26 to 28C - dependent on location - for three consecutive days. With temperatures expected to be more like 20-25C, it will fall short of the threshold. However, these temperatures are notably warm for late September and it could therefore feel like summer has made a return. Warm spells at the end of September are fairly usual as the UK can still get hot air transported from southern Europe or North Africa with any southerly airflow. The last week of September also looks like it will be slightly warmer than average overall across the UK, despite being less warm than this week. The forecast further ahead and into October is more uncertain but signs are it could start to feel more like autumn with wetter and windier weather becoming more dominant. title: 'No surprises' as results emerge in Russian parliamentary election
description: Preliminary results suggest that Kremlin-backed United Russia is on course to retain its constitutional majority.
body: This video can not be played Preliminary results from Russia's elections suggest that the party backed by President Vladimir Putin, United Russia, will maintain its grip on parliament. The outcome comes as no surprise, according to the BBC's Russia editor, Steve Rosenberg, who has been following the elections from Moscow. The vote comes after more than four and a half years of war against Ukraine, a conflict which has seen huge battlefield losses for the Russian army and sparked economic hardship. The only anti-war party, Yabloko, was removed the ballot in the run-up to polling day – although some candidates remained in some constituencies. title: 'Far from their best' to 'a joy to watch' - ranking Premier League teams' start to season
description: Five matches into the league season, which teams in the Premier League have impressed so far and who have disappointed?
body: Manchester City striker Erling Haaland (left) and Manchester United defender Harry Maguire There is now a three-week international break with no Premier League games until 10 October. We are five matches into the league season and there is a long way to go in the campaign, but which teams have impressed so far and who have disappointed? You can have your say in the comments at the bottom of the page. Arsenal: Solid start to their title defence until they were ripped apart by Brighton having survived a penalty scare at Sunderland. 7 Aston Villa: Signs they are beginning to move in the right direction after losing so many key players during the transfer window. 6 Bournemouth: If games lasted 80 minutes the Cherries would be near the top of the table. Need to cut out conceding so late. 6 Brentford: Demolished Spurs and Chelsea without fuss during a highly impressive unbeaten start. Can they keep it up and challenge for Europe? 8 Brighton: Kings of entertainment after hitting 16 goals in five top-flight games, including three against champions Arsenal. A joy to watch. 9 Chelsea: After a strong start under Xabi Alonso, the Blues have lost two of their past three - and were picked apart by Brentford. Are they really moving in the right direction? 6 Coventry City: You could hear the sighs of relief in the away end at Nottingham Forest on Saturday. Will Frank Lampard's side kick on after that win? 6 Crystal Palace: Room for improvement after one win and three defeats. 5 Everton: Despite a transfer window to forget, David Moyes has made the Toffees hard to beat. 6 Fulham: Decent draws against Liverpool and Manchester United but need a win. Ipswich (away) followed by Hull (home), Coventry (away) and Crystal Palace (home) offer hope when they return from the international break. 5 Hull City: To have eight points from a tough opening five fixtures is an excellent return, including beating Manchester United and drawing with Aston Villa and Chelsea. 8 Ipswich Town: Defensively vulnerable but two late winners, against Sunderland and Crystal Palace, have earned them six points and shown their fighting spirit. 5 Leeds United: Fifth in the league, unbeaten and with the joint-best defensive record. They showed what they are capable of with a superb 4-1 win over Newcastle. 7 Liverpool: Unbeaten but have been far from their best. Three clean sheets in their past three games, but more is expected from Andoni Iraola's side. 6 Manchester City: Five league games, five victories. Managed to win at Manchester United despite going down to 10 men midway through the first half. With Erling Haaland already top scorer, City fans will expect a real push to win the league. 9 Manchester United: Disappointing performances to lose at Hull and draw at a Fulham side who were bottom of the league. Their only win so far came against Ipswich and they were denied a victory at Everton by a late equaliser. 4 Newcastle United: A mixed bag under new manager Matthias Jaissle. They impressed in a draw against Liverpool, won comfortably at Tottenham, but were also terrible in a loss at Leeds, although they responded well to beat Hull. 6 Nottingham Forest: Their best results have come away, drawing at Liverpool and winning at Aston Villa. But their home form will be a huge worry - yet to score a goal and with only one point from three matches at the City Ground. 5 Sunderland: After coming seventh in 2025-26, Sunderland fans will have wanted a better start to this season. The Black Cats gave good accounts of themselves against Arsenal and Manchester City, but lost both matches. 5 Tottenham Hotspur: After spending more than £300m in the summer, Spurs have been poor, failing to score in their opening four league matches. title: Chiefs back in business as star QBs go down - five things from NFL week two
description: Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs look back to their best but Caleb Williams and Jayden Daniels suffer serious injuries. Here's what you need to know from week two in the NFL.
body: Caleb Williams (l) and Jayden Daniels (r) suffered serious injuries while Patrick Mahomes looked back to his best in week two After a feast of points in week one, defences hit back in week two of the NFL. The Chicago Bears came crashing back down to earth after a flying start - and they suffered one of the two worrying injuries to two of the league's top young quarterbacks. The Kansas City Chiefs were back doing what they do best but the Baltimore Ravens were surprisingly beaten, while two games were settled in overtime and one decided with just nine seconds on the clock. Here's our pick from Sunday's week two action. Allen stars as Bills open new stadium in style The Chicago Bears hope Caleb Williams' hamstring injury is not as bad as first feared The Chicago Bears scored 59 points last week but just three this time in an ugly 9-3 home loss to the Vikings, as Minnesota won their seventh straight game at Soldier Field. The 56-point drop-off is the second most in NFL history as the Bears saw two touchdowns lost with a dropped catch and a fumble, had a field goal blocked but worst of all lost their star quarterback Caleb Williams. The first pick of the 2024 draft was carried off the field in the fourth quarter looking in serious pain, but initial reports are that his hamstring injury may not be as serious as first feared. Jayden Daniels was the second pick of that 2024 draft behind Williams and he left Washington's defeat at Dallas with a serious injury to the same elbow he dislocated last season. Daniels, who seems certain to be out for some time, would still have struggled to keep up with Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott who threw four touchdowns in their 37-20 victory. Prescott surpassed Tony Romo's team record of 248 touchdown passes by taking his tally to 249. Patrick Mahomes showed no signs of his surgically repaired knee troubling him as he recorded his most passing yards for three years The Kansas City Chiefs gave another ominous sign that they were back in business with a 33-30 overtime win over the Indianapolis Colts. Winning tight games was a hallmark of the Patrick Mahomes dynasty during three recent Super Bowl wins, so there was a familiar feeling when Harrison Butker kicked the winning field goal right at the death. Mahomes threw three touchdowns and his 382 passing yards was his most for three years. Travis Kelce had 101 yards and a touchdown and summer signing Kenneth Walker had another huge game. The Super Bowl MVP had 178 total yards and was crucial in overtime to help overcome a strong challenge from Daniel Jones and the Colts - who may have lost their first two games but look to have plenty to build on. The Green Bay Packers also triumphed in overtime by erasing a 10-point deficit in the fourth quarter against the New York Jets to win 20-17 - and snap a six-game losing streak. Super Bowl champions Seattle look the real deal again after beating the Arizona Cardinals 31-7 for a 12th straight win. Drew Lock showed he is no ordinary back-up quarterback with three touchdown passes to Jaxon Smith-Njigba, including an 82 yarder that is the longest of the talented receiver's career. The Seahawks lost Walker to the Chiefs but have retained a remarkable 17 of 22 starters and 44 of their 53-man roster from last season's title win. That consistency should see them go close again, but they'll face a rejuvenated San Francisco 49ers in their division, who are also 2-0 after beating the Miami Dolphins 35-15. Showing no signs of jet leg from their victory over the Los Angeles Rams in Australia, the Niners scored touchdowns on their first five possessions to blow Miami away - Christian McCaffrey scored twice, George Kittle also found the end zone and Brock Purdy accounted for three scores. With the 49ers having their defensive stars back from injury Kyle Shanahan's squad look the total package once again. The Cincinnati Bengals also look more well rounded this season after winning a 20-6 battle in Houston, thanks to an early touchdown of the season contender catch from Ja'Marr Chase. We expect fireworks from Chase and Joe Burrow, but having a defence capable of keeping CJ Stroud out of the end zone, and sacking him four times in a road game is the biggest reason for optimism among Bengals fans. The Philadelphia Eagles were on the ropes against the Tennessee Titans until Jalen Hurts threw the winning touchdown pass to Darius Cooper with just nine seconds left in the game. Although not as impressive overall as other 2-0 sides, that ability to win games at the death is a familiar trait with Philly - and will make them dangerous all season again. The New Orleans Saints just fell short after a monster comeback in Detroit last week, but went one better this week by upsetting Lamar Jackson's Baltimore Ravens 24-17 in their home opener. Tyler Shough bundled over in a big crowd for a slightly controversial touchdown given the ball was largely unsighted, before two-time MVP Jackson then threw a late interception when trying to salvage the game. The Saints may just surprise a few more teams this season. Surprising everyone right now are the Las Vegas Raiders, who sit on 2-0 after winning 26-14 at the hapless Chargers. The Chargers have lost by double digits to two of last season's biggest strugglers and with away games at Buffalo and Seattle, things look likely to get much worse. DeShaun Watson threw a fourth quarter touchdown as the Cleveland Browns also sprung an upset win on the road in Tampa Bay, with a weather delay meaning they had to wait an extra two hours to seal the deal. Perhaps the biggest surprise so far though is just how bad the Atlanta Falcons are. They were beaten 34-3 by the Carolina Panthers to become just the fourth team since 1978 to fail to get into an opponents red zone in their first two games. title: Lindsay Clancy's ex-husband explains why he forgave her over children's killings
description: The husband of the US mother who strangled her three young children discusses his grief in an interview with CBS News.
body: This video can not be played 'It's painful to see,' Patrick Clancy says about online hate Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of attempted suicide Patrick Clancy, the ex-husband of a US mother accused of murdering their three children, has said he would have been "eaten up inside forever" had he not forgiven her for their deaths. In an interview with CBS, he also said he did the best he could as his then-wife Lindsay Clancy struggled with mental illness in the months leading up to the day she strangled their children. Lindsay has not disputed that she killed them but her lawyers argued she should not be held legally responsible because she was suffering from severe mental illness. A judge declared a mistrial in the case earlier this month after the jury said it could not reach a unanimous verdict on whether she was guilty of murder. The prosecution had alleged that on 24 January 2023, Clancy intentionally strangled all of her children - Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, eight months - in their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home. Clancy, now 36, was then left paralysed after jumping from a second-floor window. She attended the trial in a wheelchair. Lindsay Clancy's team said she had postpartum psychosis after birth Patrick Clancy testified during the trial about his ex-wife's declining mental health after giving birth. Clancy's team said she had postpartum psychosis, a rare condition in which postpartum women can experience mania, depression or a mixture of both. "I didn't know how to manage a postpartum illness. I think mental illness has this ability to be tragically deceptive," he told CBS, the BBC's US news partner. It was her mental health that led to Patrick Clancy deciding later to forgive her. "I saw headlines that said, you know, 'Killer Mom', and 'Baby Murderer', 'Monster'. And none of them were accurate," he said in the interview. "I believe that it was her mental illness that caused that. So I shared those words. And I think when it comes to forgiveness, I also felt that if I didn't get there, I would be eaten up inside forever." Asked if he felt he had failed in some way in this period leading up to the killings, he said: "I think I did the best I could with what I had at the time. And I live with the outcome. I live with it every day." Living with his grief in the weeks after the tragedy became a struggle and he admitted having suicidal thoughts. "I didn't think I would live to see my 35th birthday. And I was completely fine with it," he said. This video can not be played Watch: Patrick Clancy's new wife describes him as "selfless father" During the seven week trial, Patrick was singled out online for wild vitriol and cover-up accusations. There were claims he was to blame for the murders in some way. Thrust into the limelight, tabloids snapped photos of him travelling and with his new wife Rachel Danis. The 36-year-old said the speculation was "deeply harmful to the legacy of my children. It is a huge distraction from what really matters here, which is perinatal mental health". It was also "painful to see" for him personally. "And it makes it difficult to be in public and it's possible that some of those people after seeing lie after lie after lie, they start to believe it and that's what we're left with," he said. The intense scrutiny prompted him to move from Duxbury to New York City in a bid to seek anonymity. Now he is starting a family with Danis and looking forward to telling his future children about their siblings. "I think every parent can agree, you have different relationships with your kids, but they're all your kids. And I can't wait to tell them about their brothers and sister." The mistrial leaves the case unresolved. Prosecutors have not said whether they will seek a retrial. The next court hearing is scheduled for 29 September at Plymouth Superior Court in Massachusetts. If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide, external. A list of UK organisations that can help is available here. title: US and China discuss AI safety plan ahead of Trump-Xi summit
description: Top US and Chinese officials held talks in New York on Sunday ahead of a Trump-Xi summit this week.
body: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met China's Vice Premier He Lifeng Top US and Chinese officials have discussed creating a new "notification mechanism" for AI incidents that could affect national security, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told reporters on Sunday. Bessent made the comments after what he called "successful" talks with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York. The meeting came as US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping are due to hold a summit in Washington later this week. AI has come under intense scrutiny in recent days after researchers warned of the potential risks posed by the technology and some of the industry's most high profile figures called for developers to take a more cautious approach. "We think that, just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world is very important," Bessent told reporters after the talks. He said the meeting also covered other topics, including plans to "operationalise" a process to identify potential tariff cuts on goods called the Board of Trade. A truce in the tariffs war between the world's two biggest economies is due to expire on 10 November. The BBC has contacted the Chinese embassy in the US for comment. Chinese state news agency Xinhua said the two sides had "candid, in-depth and constructive exchanges on key economic and trade issues", noting that they had discussed AI. Bessent said in a post on X on Sunday that the talks "help lay the groundwork for President Trump to advance America's economic interests and deliver results for the American people." The US and China are locked in a race to dominate the AI and technology industries. In recent days Washington has faced calls to slow down the development of AI over fears abouts its potential negative impact on humanity. Trump has largely dismissed those concerns, arguing that there are sufficient policies around AI and that the US cannot lose its edge to China. He said earlier this month "whoever wins in AI, wins." title: Presley Gerber, Cindy Crawford's son, dies aged 27
description: His family asked for privacy during a "very difficult and painful time" following the model's death.
body: Presley Gerber became a model like his mother and sister Presley Gerber, the son of supermodel Cindy Crawford, has died at the age of 27. Gerber, a model, passed away at a rehab facility on Sunday, according to records filed by the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner. The cause of death was not listed. Allie Jenkins, a representative for Crawford and her husband Rande Gerber, told the BBC's US news partner CBS: "The family is asking for privacy during this very difficult and painful time." Gerber had been a model like his mother and younger sister Kaia, making his runway debut for Italian label Moschino aged just 16. He went on to model for brands including Burberry, Dolce & Gabbana, and Bottega Veneta. His father Rande Gerber, a well-known businessman, co-founded the Casamigos tequila brand with George Clooney. In recent years, Gerber had spoken openly about his mental health challenges and drug use. In 2023, he told the Studio 22 podcast: "Having struggled with mental health, depression and some other things that come along with that, I think that whether I help one person or a hundred people get out of that place that I was in at one point in my life, that's all I need to do." And in this month's American Vogue, Kaia discussed her brother's struggles with addiction. She said: "When something like that happens in a family, it kind of levels everyone. "I think that's also why I started to self-identify as the easy one and never wanted to ask for help." title: 'I've asked for forgiveness' - Eckert and Southampton braced for Spygate verdict
description: As Southampton manager Tonda Eckert awaits the FA hearing into his 'Spygate' misconduct conduct charge BBC sports editor Dan Roan speaks to him and club chief executive Phil Parsons on what happens next.
body: This video can not be played I've asked for forgiveness and apologised publicly - Eckert More than four months since the Spygate scandal erupted, Southampton manager Tonda Eckert's wait to discover his fate for authorising an espionage campaign is almost over. In the coming days, a decisive Football Association hearing will take place, after the German coach was charged with misconduct in July. Spying on three clubs has already cost Southampton the chance of promotion to the Premier League (worth £200m), after they were expelled from the Championship play-off final. An EFL panel also docked the club four points for this season. Now Eckert could be banned. As the club prepared for the latest twist in the saga, BBC Sport spoke exclusively to both Eckert and Southampton chief executive Phil Parsons, who - in his first interview on the case - insists any further punishment would be "really tough to take". But how are the club and their coach dealing with the prospect of more turmoil? What is at stake? And why have Southampton given a permanent role to the intern who was caught spying on Middlesbrough in May? "I would lie if I say that the summer has just been easy. Of course, if you care deeply about your profession, about the football club, there's nothing that prepares you for that. There just isn't." Eckert speaks slowly and with an intense gaze when asked to reflect on being at the centre of one of the biggest controversies in English football history. The 33-year-old apologised in June after an EFL independent disciplinary commission found he had orchestrated a "contrived and determined plan" to spy on Oxford United, Ipswich Town, then Middlesbrough before the play-off semi-final. Having insisted he was unaware it breached EFL rules, and that the spying had no impact on performances, Eckert was backed by Southampton. His team have made an encouraging start to the new season. Without the four-point deduction, they would be fourth in the table, rather than 13th. "We've talked a lot over the summer of how we want to go through that process of addressing everything, giving everyone the chance to put questions out that are still there, to put out what they feel and have gone through, and then also close the door and move on," he says. "Because the reality is it's a new season. We have big ambitions as a football club, and in order to reach them, we need to move on." That is easier said than done, with Eckert in limbo while he awaits the outcome of the FA's disciplinary process. "I've had the chance to sit down and just talk the FA through everything that happened," he says. "And now it's up to them to make a decision. I don't really have any emotions towards that." So does he feel the FA has listened to him during its investigation? "That was my impression," he says. "We sat for almost four hours, so it's been quite a long conversation." When asked whether he feels the club has been punished enough, and if a suspension for him would be excessive, Eckert chooses his words carefully. "It's been a big, big punishment," he says. "Absolutely unheard of in the history of sports. "And it's tough for me to say that because it concerns me. I'm judging on myself, not an outside situation. But I've asked for forgiveness for what I've done. I've apologised publicly. "I think the punishment has been very hard on the club for the last season. And to go into a new season on minus four. And the rest is not for me to decide." Southampton owner will not sack head coach Eckert This video can not be played We don't know what the FA will hand out - Parsons Parsons is more forthright on whether the club has been punished enough. "We don't know what the FA will actually hand out," he says. "It could be a long ban. It could be a short ban. It could be a suspended sentence. "What we hope as a club is they actually recognise where we are at the moment, and what we've already been through, because I think it has to be taken into account. I really feel like we've taken enough. We've been hurt. I think it's one of the largest sanctions ever when it comes to football, or even sporting, history. "This isn't just about the club, this is about people. We lose money not being in the Premier League, but [local] businesses lose money. We had to spend a huge amount on legal fees, and it really impacts the club even further. We don't want to be seen as a victim of this. We need to get on. We've had our cards dealt." When it is put to Parsons that the EFL's punishments applied to the club - rather than Eckert himself - he says: "I think it's impossible to sanction the manager without the club getting hurt even more." The most recent precedent for this case came at the 2024 Olympics women's tournament, when Fifa banned Bev Priestman - Canada's head coach - from all football for a year, after opponents New Zealand were spied on. Parsons insists "the Canadian case is very different" but if Eckert , who is only contracted until the end of the season, is also banned, how long would it have to be for the club to look elsewhere for a new coach? "We don't know," he says, firmly denying having approached other coaches in case Eckert has to leave. Parsons also says the club may appeal if the ruling goes against them. "We can't worry about something we can't control at the moment," he says. "We have to deal with it when we get there but we're hoping that they look at it sensibly." Parsons says the club's ownership "want" to back Eckert. "We've been through an entire transfer window when it comes to recruiting players for Tonda, and that's another challenge. title: 'Constant bombardment' - fans shown 65,000 junk food ads at World Cup
description: New data shows fans were shown more than 28 hours of adverts for unhealthy food and drinks during World Cup matches this summer.
body: This summer's World Cup featured ads promoting an official beverage partner (Coca-Cola), official snack food partner (Lay's), and an official quick-service restaurant sponsor (McDonald's) Football fans were shown a "constant bombardment" of advertisements promoting junk food and drinks during matches at the 2026 Fifa World Cup, according to a new study. Researchers at the University of Bristol and University of Oxford created an AI tool to analyse ads which were visible to television viewers during live play in the tournament's 104 matches, mostly displayed on pitchside advertising boards and around stadiums in the USA, Canada, and Mexico. They found that logos and products for brands that produce junk food and drinks - defined by the UK government as being high in fat, salt or sugar - were displayed 65,722 times in total. And the study also found that those adverts were visible for 28.1 hours' time across the tournament, or just over 16% of the total time that matches were being played. The ads were all shown on the international feed of matches during play - meaning they were visible to every viewer in every country broadcasting matches - and do not include ads shown during pre-match coverage, half-time commercial breaks, or the controversial in-match hydration breaks. The model used by the researchers estimated that there were an average of 576 visible ads for junk food and drink shown during each individual match. Coca-Cola had the highest number (21,893), followed by McDonald's (13,915), Powerade (12,777), and Lay's - the crisps manufacturer known as Walkers in the UK - (12,087). All four brands are official partners of world football governing body Fifa, with the Powerade energy drink owned by the Coca-Cola company. In response to the findings, Fifa argued that the vast majority of its revenue is put back into football, including on projects promoting health and wellbeing in which thousands of people participate. A Fifa spokesperson said: "Fifa works with a broad, global portfolio of partners, all of which are subject to its governance and compliance frameworks. "Fifa's social impact campaigns, including Be Active, delivered messages of unity, inclusion, health and friendship to audiences on an unprecedented scale throughout the World Cup". BBC Sport also contacted Coca Cola, McDonald's and PepsiCo - which owns Lay's - but did not receive a reply. The report also analysed other forms of "potentially harmful" advertising, and found that junk food and drink promotion was far more prevalent. Junk food and drink logos were recorded around seven times more often than those for alcohol and prediction market brands, 10 times more often than those of gambling firms, and almost 25 times more often than cryptocurrency. "Repeatedly connecting unhealthy food and drink brands with football, excitement and national identity can make these brands familiar and normalise their consumption," the researchers argue. McDonald's advertisements were displayed frequently throughout Spain's victory over Argentina in the World Cup final Since October 2025, foods such as burgers, chips, crisps and drinks with added sugar have been included in a ban on junk food advertising on TV before 9pm in the UK. But because the advertising shown during matches appears on hoardings, and is at an international event, it falls outside the legislation. That means viewers seeing ads for burgers, crisps and fizzy drinks during the hours they are theoretically banned, and calls have grown for a more global approach. "It is definitely a loophole," Greg Fell, president of the Association of Directors of Public Health, told BBC Sport. "There is acres of evidence demonstrating that governments around the world are legislating very hard at the moment to limit advertising of junk food. "It requires worldwide collaboration because obesity is a problem everywhere. Advertising is one of the key mechanisms by which harm from obesity happens. "Obesity is almost the new tobacco - there isn't much difference with the methods the tobacco industry used before they were excluded from advertising. "A lot of this is targeted at children, because these companies want to grow their markets, and children are the future market." The UK government recently announced sweeping changes to school dinner rules, banning deep-fried food and increasing the inclusion of fruit, vegetables, fibre and wholegrains, in attempt to tackle childhood obesity. According to the NHS, data from 2024 showed that 15% of children in the UK were obese, and 26% were overweight. "We are facing a global crisis of childhood obesity and diet-related disease, yet the world's biggest sporting event is saturated with marketing for unhealthy food and drinks", said Dr Elisa Becker, one of the report's co-authors. "Sport should be part of the solution to poor health – not one of the world's most powerful advertising platforms for the products driving it." title: Portrait of George Mitchell will not be removed from Hillsborough Castle
description: The picture will remain as part of the castle's "important story" in the peace process".
body: The portrait is on display in Lady Grey's study A portrait of former US Senator George Mitchell on display at Hillsborough Castle, Northern Ireland's official residence of the Royal family, will remain in place as part of the castle's "important story" in the peace process. The former US envoy played a key role in the 1998 Good Friday Agreement, external, which ended decades of violence in Northern Ireland. In 2026, a number of institutions had severed ties with George Mitchell over his links with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. It followed the release of millions of files relating to Epstein by the US Department of Justice, including further references to an earlier claim George Mitchell had sex with Epstein victim, Virginia Giuffre. A bust of Mitchell was removed from Queen's University Belfast last year Mitchell has previously said allegations contained in released documents are false, saying "I have never met, spoken with or had any contact with Ms. Giuffre." As a result of the files, the US-Ireland Alliance said the George J Mitchell Scholarship Program would no longer bear his name. Queen's University Belfast also removed a £35,000 bust from its grounds. BBC News NI has been told there are no plans to move a portrait of Mitchell from Hillsborough Castle, which is also the UK's official residence of the Secretary of State. It is on display in Lady Grey's study, a room open to the public for guided tours which features a number of figures from the Northern Ireland peace process. The study features a number of figures from the Northern Ireland peace process Portraits of high-profile figures are displayed, including former prime ministers, taoisigh (Irish prime ministers), US presidents, secretaries of state and local politicians. The space often hosted small one-to one discussions or bilateral talks during the peace negotiations. The room is described as a "calm, cosy place for contemplation" by the independent charity which looks after six royal sites and palaces. The Historic Royal Palaces has the responsibility for the curation of exhibitions and art hanging at Hillsborough Castle. The Royal Household is not involved in the process. The charity has told BBC News NI there are no immediate plans to change the display. "The 'Preparing the Peace' display is the means through which we share the story of the peace process, and the role that the castle played in negotiations, with our visitors. "The display is situated in a room at the castle where many important negotiations and bilateral talks between the individuals involved took place. "It does not seek to promote or endorse the contribution of any one individual and the works on display have been selected solely because the sitters featured attended peace talks at Hillsborough Castle. "We maintain that the castle's role in the peace process is an important story to share, and we will continue to do so." Hillsborough Castle is the official residence of the Royal family and the UK's official residence of the Secretary of State in NI In response to a question from BBC News NI about whether there has been any consideration of the portrait's place, a Northern Ireland Office spokesperson said the running of the castle is not their responsibility. "In March 2017, the Northern Ireland Office (NIO) granted Historic Royal Palaces a 25-year lease to manage Hillsborough Castle and Gardens. NIO Ministers have use of the castle, but responsibility for its day-to-day running, including the collections and art on display, rests with Historic Royal Palaces." In 2019, a court document contained claims that Virginia Giuffre had been directed to have sex with a number of high-profile people, including former US Senator George Mitchell. Mitchell has previously said the allegation contained in the released documents is false. "I have never met, spoken with or had any contact with Ms. Giuffre." The latest release of documents indicated a continued relationship between Mitchell and Epstein, following Epstein's first conviction. Earlier this year, Mitchell's spokesperson said "he never met, spoken to or had any contact with Giuffre or any underage women". A spokesperson said Mitchell "profoundly regrets ever having known Jeffrey Epstein and condemns, without reservation, the horrific harm Epstein inflicted on so many women". The spokesperson added that he did not observe, suspect or have any knowledge of Epstein engaging in "illegal or inappropriate conduct with underage women". Epstein, a well-connected financier and convicted sex offender, was found dead by suicide in 2019 while awaiting a trial on sex trafficking charges. Trafficking victim Virginia Giuffre took her own life at the age of 41. Being named or pictured in the Epstein files is not an indication of wrongdoing. Many of those identified in other releases have denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein. title: Quadruple amputee enters the Big Brother house
description: Charlotte lost her arms and legs to meningitis as a toddler and is now a contestant on Big Brother.
body: Charlotte Nott, 18, from Oxford, lost her arms and legs to meningitis as a toddler Charlotte Nott has never let anything hold her back. The student, from Oxford, is a quadruple amputee, having lost the lower parts of her arms and legs to meningitis when she was just two years old. Now 18, Charlotte is a contestant in the latest series of Big Brother, something she has dreamed about for most of her life. Her dad, Alex, told BBC Radio Oxford he was anxious about her appearance on the show, but said there had never been much point telling his daughter not to do something she had her sights on. That resilience was on full display within seconds of Charlotte's arrival on the show. During the launch, her shoe broke as she stepped out to be introduced, and she had to remove her prosthetic legs on stage before entering the house. "Maybe it was my fate to walk in with no legs," she told the diary room. "Maybe that was just what was meant to happen." She added that she was used to going without her prosthetics at home. "When I'm at home, I have my legs off all the time," she said. "When I'm cooking, I have my legs off. I like to be four foot. I like to be tiny, like a little tiny doll." Alex said the moment had summed up his daughter's unstoppable nature perfectly. Charlotte applied for the show earlier this year - the first time she had been old enough to enter - and made it through a process her dad said involved around 50,000 applicants. "She's wanted to go in there since she was about five or six," he said. "I think she used to watch it religiously with her mum." Charlotte had applied without telling her dad and had already completed several interviews with producers before he found out. He admitted he had struggled to come to terms with her decision to apply. "I thought she was on a wind-up to start with," he said. "She was dead serious. I've been in bits for about three months." But Alex said there was little point trying to stand in her way. Charlotte, pictured as a child, lost the lower parts of her arms and legs to meningitis at the age of two "You try telling someone like Charlotte that she's not allowed to do something," he said. "We've gone her whole life trying to tell her that she can't do stuff, and she's just taken on that mantle." Since she turned 16, he said she had taken charge of every decision relating to her own care and prosthetics. Alex said his daughter had the resilience to handle whatever reaction she received from the public. "Every day is a struggle for her, more than for anybody else," he said. "But she's got skin as thick as a rhino's. I take my hat off to her." Charlotte said she expected viewers watching her around the clock to be surprised by how ordinary her daily life actually was. Charlotte's dad said she had wanted to go in the Big Brother house since she was young Watch the latest episode of South Today Listen to the latest news from Oxfordshire "People are surprised at anything I do, even normal things like cooking, doing my makeup, getting dressed," she said. "They're probably going to be surprised at the most normal things for me." Asked what she would do with the prize money if she won, Charlotte said her prosthetic legs cost around £25,000 each. "I probably would put a lot of it into savings," she said. "My prosthetic legs are about £25,000 per leg, so probably put half in savings and then the other half... just go on a nice holiday, just kind of spend it." Caroline Hughes, senior support services Manager for Meningitis Research Foundation, said the long term consequences of the disease "remain widely misunderstood". "Every day, we support people navigating the physical, emotional and practical challenges that can follow a meningitis diagnosis," she said. "That's why it is so powerful to see people like Charlotte sharing their experience on a platform like Big Brother. "By speaking so openly about her story, she is helping bring greater understanding of the long-term impact meningitis can have, while also enabling others affected by the disease to feel seen, heard and less alone." The 23rd series of Big Brother began on 13 September and will last 54 days, making it the longest series since 2017. ITV said the series had been "reimagined as a house of surprises" and viewers could expect "ambitious tasks, high-stakes nominations and dramatic live evictions". title: University staff begin five-week strike on day one of new term
description: UCU members at the university will not take part in lectures, seminars or tutorials until the end of October.
body: UCU staff voted in June for the five week industrial action Lecturers at the University of Dundee are beginning an unprecedented five-week strike over the threat of compulsory redundancies. Members of the UCU union will not take part in lectures, seminars or tutorials until after 23 October. The vote for "last resort" industrial action was the latest move in a long-running dispute which started almost two years ago when the university announced a £30m deficit. Since then, 675 jobs have been lost through voluntary redundancy, and the university has received bailouts of £40m from the Scottish government and £22m from the Scottish Funding Council. The university said it "anticipates the majority of classes will run as normal" from Monday and that it would seek to minimise the impact of strike action on students. UCU staff at Dundee University went on strike for three weeks last year The latest of wave of cuts was announced in June proposing to close 187 posts, however that figure fell to 154 job losses by August. Since the announcement, UCU bosses said there had been 149 applications for voluntary redundancies, which should now rule out the need for compulsory redundancies. Dr. Melissa D'Ascenzio, co-president of the Dundee UCU branch told BBC News: "None of our members want to go on strike for five weeks, this is absolutely last resort that we've come to. "The university is still refusing to remove the threat of compulsory redundancy. "There has been no attempt from the university to try to find common ground and try to avoid five weeks of disruption." Dundee UCU will stage five weeks of strike action from 21 September Lecturers previously went on strike for three weeks in February last year. Two voluntary severance schemes have now run at the institution, with previous rounds focused on professional services staff who work alongside academics. But the latest round of redundancies over the summer was aimed at lecturers and researchers. Union officials said they were keen to highlight the impact of previous cuts to student services and the student experience. BBC News understands that while lecturers are not required to notify the university in advance of taking strike action, some academics told students during freshers week that their classes might not be on. Iain Ellis, co-president said, "New and returning students will be impacted at the start of term, which is hugely regretful, but we're also clear that university management cutting more jobs and more staff leaving will have a major and long-term impact on students' education and the university." Tom Christisen, president of the students' association (DUSA), said he recognised that the action could have a significant impact on students. He said, "At the same time, we recognise why staff have reached this point. The prospect of compulsory redundancy has created significant uncertainty for colleagues about their jobs and futures at Dundee. "Our responsibility is to stand up for students throughout this period, while continuing to press the university to address the circumstances that have led to industrial action. UCU members at the campus are already working to contract, refusing to carry out "extra" unpaid tasks, such as attending weekend open days. This is unlikely to stop unless the dispute is resolved. It does not currently include a marking or assessment boycott. In previous strikes, a "no-detriment" policy was applied to prevent students being penalised and removing untaught topics from assessments. UCU officials told the BBC they would expect this to apply again now. More than 100 people lobbied the university's governing body, which was meeting at the Bonar Hall A spokesman for the university said: "We recognise the right of trade union members to take industrial action and will strive to work constructively with the University and College Union during the dispute. At the same time, the university will seek to minimise the effects of strike action on students, particularly at a time when they are starting the new academic year. "We anticipate the majority of classes, student contact time, and other activity across the university will proceed as normal. Any impacts will most likely be varied across different areas of the university, reflecting UCU membership." UCU members are now striking each weekday for over a month, as the university refuses to rule out compulsory redundancies. A Scottish government spokesperson said: "Industrial action is in no-one's best interests – least of all students' – so while the Scottish government cannot intervene directly, we encourage universities and trades unions to engage constructively and seek resolution to these disputes."
