title: Oxford grooming gang survivors tell BBC 'hundreds' of abusers still free
description: Men who sexually abused them as underage girls are still walking around the city, they say.
body: This video can not be played Watch: 'I see my abusers in the supermarket' - survivors of Oxford gang tell of ongoing torment Warning: This story contains details of sexual violence Survivors of an Oxford grooming gang say they still see men who sexually abused them, and who have not been brought to justice, walking around the city. "A shop, a petrol station, a restaurant - everywhere you can imagine - you'll see a man that's done something," one survivor, Sarah, tells BBC Panorama. Sarah and two other survivors believe "hundreds" of perpetrators are still free. An ex-police detective who led the initial investigation into grooming gangs in Oxford agrees. It is the first time that Sarah (whose name we have changed) and one of the other women have spoken out publicly about what they were subjected to. Sarah says she was sexually abused and plied with heroin from the age of 11. More than two decades later, three men were found guilty of abusing her after she testified against them in court. They were jailed for between five and 24 years in 2020. But it was too little, too late for Sarah, who has battled drug addiction for most her life and has spent time in jail. "I think they should stay in there forever, because obviously they've taken my life," she says. Chloe, another survivor whose name we have changed, says she also sees some of her abusers in her local area. Like many survivors, she chose not to go through a police investigation. "It's difficult because this is where I live, it's where I grew up. There is a few of them that I've seen a few times, even just in the supermarket, driving around," she explains. She feels "sick, cold" when she sees them, she says. Sarah, whose image is blurred to protect her identity, said the gang had "taken her life" A third woman, Rachel - again, whose name we have changed - was abused between the ages of 12 to 15 and says many of those men are still free. She was a key witness in the first trial of Oxford grooming gang members, in 2013, when seven men were convicted. That trial revealed the grooming, trafficking and rape of six girls over an eight year-period in the city. But subsequent prosecutions have identified many more victims, and it was estimated in 2015 that more than 370 children were affected. Rachel says, for years, police did not believe her when she told them what was happening to her. She and the other women say the investigations have not gone far enough. Thames Valley Police works tirelessly to investigate offenders involved in these horrific crimes and bring them to justice, a spokesperson said. "It is never too late to come forward", the spokesperson continued, and the force will listen and do everything it can to support victims, survivors and their families. Panorama - Grooming Gangs: Why Were We Ignored? For years, organised gangs of abusers, mostly of Pakistani heritage, preyed on girls in Oxford while authorities looked the other way. Panorama examines the devastating legacy for three survivors. Watch now on iPlayer or on BBC One at 20:00 BST. Gangs of men were found to have sexually exploited and abused underage girls in several towns and cities - including Rotherham, Rochdale and Telford, as well as Oxford - between the 1990s and 2010s. Oxford was one of the places where most of the perpetrators were identified as older men of Pakistani heritage. In some cases, such as in Rotherham, police were accused of hesitating to act out of fear of being seen as racist. But in Oxford a serious case review found no evidence that this had been a factor. Now, the government has launched a national inquiry to address why vulnerable children were not protected in England and Wales - including whether attitudes to the girls or the ethnicity of the perpetrators contributed to the failings. Sarah says the cigarettes she was given by her groomers were laced with heroin. "My addiction through my whole life now has resulted from them giving us those cigarettes," she says. She agreed not to take drugs before speaking to Panorama and received support from her case worker. Sarah says the men who gave her the cigarettes - and alcohol - then told her she was in debt and needed to have sex with them in order to pay them back. "They're like, 'well you know, you owe me this money now, so you're going to have to do this'," she says. "They used to say 'drink this, drink that' to the point where I'm throwing up and sick. Having to be in them houses and feeling trapped. They used to just lock us in. "Then before you know it, there's one, two, six, seven people turning up. You're just outnumbered, basically." Rachel, from the age of 12, also found herself in a cycle of sexual abuse and drug addiction. She was trafficked to other towns and cities where men paid the gang for sex with her. Rachel says she was not believed for years and that investigations have not gone far enough A police officer even tried to take advantage of her in Oxford, she says, but she never reported the incident. "I was put in the back of a police van on the Cowley Road and there was two male officers and one of them said, 'Well, we know what you're about.'" He then asked her to perform oral sex on him, she says. Despite a total of 21 men now having been convicted in connection with the Oxford grooming gang, Rachel says there are many perpetrators who have never faced consequences. "There are a lot of people out there who have been involved in this to some degree or another, that have just been allowed to get on with their lives that were involved in the sexual abuse of children." Many of the girls were targeted in the Cowley area of the city, pictured here in 2015 As one of the hidden victims of the Oxford grooming gang, none of Chloe's abusers have faced justice for the crimes committed against her. title: Baby bank helping more parents in full-time work
description: The couple who run the bank say they are in "desperate need" of baby formula as demand is so high.
body: Kavita and Karvinder Dhillon say more people in full-time work are using their baby bank A Birmingham baby bank says it is helping a growing number of people in full-time work who are struggling to afford essentials for their children. Kavita Kaur Dhillon and her husband Karvinder run the Handsworth Baby and Family Bank on Soho Road, which provides free items including nappies, baby formula, clothes and toys. The couple said the majority of people they first helped were from low-income households, but they were now seeing more working families needing support with everyday costs. "We don't need any more clothing, it's the everyday essentials, formula, nappies, wipes, toiletries," said Kavita. Karvinder said demand had shifted in recent years. "Before, we mainly needed nappies," he said. "As the daily cost of living has gone up, people need help with more day-to-day things." The couple said they were currently in desperate need of baby formula and often had only a handful of tubs left in stock. "Just because you dress nice, or drive a nice car, doesn't mean you don't need help," Kavita said. "Nobody knows people's circumstances. People can judge, but the reality is people are struggling." The bank provides free essentials including nappies, clothing, toys and baby formula The bank, which operates from inside the couple's Dhillons Boutique store, has been helping families since 2024. Kavita believed sharing a space with the shop helped remove some of the stigma that can come with asking for support. "You go out of our shop and people think you have purchased something, but in fact you've just used our baby bank," she said. She described it as a "warm and welcoming space" and said demand had continued to grow since it opened. For the couple, supporting families remains the most rewarding part of the project. "For me it is fulfilling, knowing I've been able to support or help someone else be okay and smile," Kavita said. She urged anyone who was struggling not to suffer in silence. "It's nothing to be ashamed of or to be scared of. There's no shame in asking for help." title: UK should 'team up' with Canada in new Europe alliance, Canadian minister tells BBC
description: It comes after European Commission President proposed "opening the door" for Canada to become an associate member of the EU.
body: The UK should "team up" with a proposed economic alliance between Canada and Europe, Canadian Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne has said. "This is all about the substance, to build an alliance of the future," he told the BBC. "The world has changed. America has changed. So we need to change." Champagne also gave a frank assessment of the Canada-US trade war after a deal collapsed last month, saying the country had "stood up for our industries, our workers, our country" by imposing tariffs. His comments come after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed "opening the door" to an associate EU membership for Canada, an unprecedented move for the bloc. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's visit to address the European Union in Strasbourg, shortly after von der Leyen's proposal was made, was "to build the alliance of the future", Champagne said. Carney, the former Governor of the Bank of England, has previously talked about an alliance of "middle powers" working together on economic growth, resilience and security. Speaking to the BBC, Champagne said the UK and Canada had shared values. "We need to look at partnership in a different way, and the great thing is that when you look at Canada, and I would say the United Kingdom, we share the same values. We are very aligned in our vision of the world. Why don't we team up?" he said. "We are independent and sovereign, but we are stronger together." After his return to the White House last year, US President Donald Trump imposed sweeping global tariffs, including on long-standing trade allies such as the UK. While the UK renegotiated a trade deal with the US in June last year, the new Canada-EU alliance does raise questions for the UK's post Brexit positioning with Europe, as well as its position with the US, after some changes of presidential rhetoric over the Falklands and Irish unity in recent weeks. Carney met Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Liverpool in the middle of his trip to Brussels and Strasbourg last week, while Champagne attended a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin on Friday, alongside the Chancellor John Healey. The developing discussions around closer ties between the EU and Canada come as Canada remains locked in an escalating trade war with the US, with both sides imposing tit-for-tat tariffs after talks broke down at the last moment in August. President Trump has also threatened further tariffs on the EU if the associate membership plan proved "hostile" to the US, calling the idea laughable and labelling Canada a "terrible trading partner". Champagne said the trade war was not a conflict chosen by Canada. "We responded because at some stage you have to say 'Enough is enough'. No one can infringe on our economic sovereignty… the world took notice," he said. The minister said Canada does not seek escalation after its "measured, targeted and strategic… dollar for dollar, tariff for tariff" response, and the country would "reengage at the right time" with its southern neighbour. Affected industries would be supported "as long as it takes and whatever it takes", he added. Champagne argued that Canada's strong fiscal position helped underpin its resilience, and the dispute with the US provided a "golden opportunity" to diversify. This is the backdrop to the promise of an "alliance of the future" between Canada and the EU, and the idea of "teaming up" with the UK too. Carney's new love-in with EU has everything to do with Trump What could EU associate member status mean for Canada? Burnham will meet Trump for the first time this week, in New York at the UN General Assembly. Last year, after his election, Carney invited King Charles to open the Canadian Parliament in Ottawa, a move widely seen as a rebuff to Trump's repeated suggestion that Commonwealth Canada could become part of the US. The detail of the offer made by the EU to negotiate "associate membership" for Canada is yet to be formalised. Champagne said this was "a moment of great opportunities" and to strengthen the existing relationship between Canada and the EU. Carney last week pointed to Canadian membership of EU university, scientific research, AI and defence funding schemes, as well as for young Canadians and Europeans to "cross the ocean and be able to study and live". He said Canada could supply critical minerals and gas and would seek access to European advanced technologies. It is understood that both Canada and the EU see the opportunity for a process for like-minded nations which might not ever be full members, for example Australia. title: Young people aren't snowflakes - mental distress is rising, says head of official review
description: Speaking exclusively to the BBC, Prof Fonagy says being young is much harder now than it was.
body: Accusations that the young are a snowflake generation are wrong, the head of an independent review into mental health, ADHD and autism has told the BBC. Prof Peter Fonagy said in an exclusive interview that there had been a real rise in mental distress among children and young people, with anxiety, depression, self-harm and eating disorders the most common. He said it was "harder to be young" now given the economic and employment uncertainty young people face, coupled with the challenges presented by social media. His review was ordered nine months ago by Wes Streeting after the then-health secretary claimed in an interview that young people were over-diagnosed and "written off". It is likely to feed into government policies on everything from NHS services and benefits to support for young people who are not in education, employment or training. Fonagy said he chose to speak to the BBC ahead of the publication, which is expected later this week, because he was concerned the debate around ADHD and autism would "obscure" the wider issue of mental health. Some have argued greater awareness and misattributing normal life stresses to mental illness were factors in the increase in cases. Fonagy said his personal battle with mental health when he was young was a driving factor in his desire to help young people. He experienced suicidal thoughts as a teenager after moving to London from Hungary without his parents. But he says he was fortunate to get therapy from a local service that "saved his life". "It's harder to be young now," the 74-year-old said, adding that his review "dismisses the idea of a snowflake generation". "I'm in awe of the way they have adjusted to an environment that is far more difficult than I ever had to face." He said economic and employment uncertainty, as well as the pressures of social media, had created a "very toxic" environment for young people. "They are a generation that has real serious challenges that I would not wish to have had when I was their age. "Adults have let them down. We're the first generation that probably collectively feels we had a better life than our children will have. "So, to the person who says it's a snowflake generation, just try living 24 hours as a 16-year-old." Prof Peter Fonagy believes the youth of today face a much more challenging childhood than previous generations More than 100 experts and families with experience of mental health problems have worked on the review with Fonagy, a clinical psychologist and adviser to NHS England. He said it will conclude that the rise in mental health problems since the 1990s was real, with about one in four 16 to 24-year-olds now struggling. The data on this is contested as some sources rely on self-reporting, while sceptics argue greater awareness and reduced stigma around mental health mean more people are coming forward. Some have also questioned whether society was now over-medicalising distress in people's lives – giving people diagnoses when what they are facing is temporary stress that they should learn to cope with. Last year, the BBC found that many GPs had concerns about over-diagnosis and felt normal life stresses were being over-medicalised. Child mental health crisis: Is better resilience the solution? Teen mental health: When to seek help and what parents can do Fonagy, however, is adamant that what young people are experiencing represents a real rise in mental health problems. But he also accepted that greater awareness was leading to more people seeking medical help. The trend is affecting both boys and girls, but becomes particularly pronounced in girls from about the age of 12. Sexual aggression from boys was a big concern, he said, but added that the expectations society placed on girls and young women was a factor. "It's very difficult to be a young woman now in secondary school." Fonagy said young people were struggling with a range of different conditions from eating disorders and anxiety "that's so powerful people avoid going to school", through to depression that was "so strong people cannot sleep at night and lose their appetite and feel their life is not worth living". His report will say these problems were exacerbated by the pandemic because of the disruption it caused to their lives. Young people the BBC spoke to who have struggled with their mental health say it is important that the government acts on the findings of Fonagy's report when it comes out. "It's all very well having this flashy report, but it's useless if they don't put that into practice," Omari, 22, said. He had a tough time at school, but said his teachers did not listen. "I made an attempt on my life because I was really struggling with bullying. I was 15. "Suddenly, when I did end up in hospital, they all wanted to care. But it's like you're a bit too little, too late here." Others expressed concern about their futures. Mattea, 17, is in temporary social housing and has struggled with anxiety and depression. "I don't know what's going to happen to my life," she said, adding that she felt like adults had let her down. "No one's going to come and sort my life out for me. I have to do it on my own." Mattea feels let down and is concerned about her future Fonagy said the support being provided to young people needed to be improved. The NHS, he said, was simply "not fit for purpose". He said too many people were being left on waiting lists, pointing to figures that show one in three people referred to mental health services were still waiting for help after a year. There were some positives steps being taken, he said, including the rollout of mental health teams to work closely with schools. However, he said tackling the problem will require action across society – in education, employment, housing and families themselves. title: What will 'greatest captain' bring to Bellamy's Wales?
description: The return of former captain Ashley Williams to the Wales coaching team excites boss Craig Bellamy before their Nations League fixtures.
body: Ashley Williams made his Wales debut in 2008 Wales go into their Nations League openers aiming to shut out Cristiano Ronaldo and Erling Haaland. With that kind of challenge, Craig Bellamy's squad might need all the defensive help they can get for games against Portugal, Denmark and Norway. Cue Ashley Williams, the centre-back described by Bellamy as Wales' "greatest captain" of the modern era. Williams was skipper as Wales reached the semi-finals of Euro 2016 against Ronaldo and Portugal, the peak of an international career that earned him 86 caps, wearing the armband for more than half of those appearances. Now 42, the former Everton and Swansea City defender will not be adding to those appearances. Instead, he will form part of a new-look Bellamy backroom team that the Football Association of Wales (FAW) hopes will add a missing ingredient in the bid to reach Euro 2028. Bellamy says Williams, and fellow new coach Alan Sheehan, will help provide "a different dynamic". But what exactly will they bring? Colwill's 'surreal' Ronaldo and Haaland ambition Wilson major Wales injury concern for Nations League With Bellamy losing two key assistants just weeks after it seemed the Wales boss himself would walk away from the job amid interest from Burnley, Williams' arrival was something of a surprise. His coaching experience has been limited to informal roles and fans are accustomed to seeing the much-admired ex-captain in the Match of the Day studio. Sheehan, too, was not an expected announcement, with the former Leeds, Leicester and Luton full-back out of work since November 2025 when he was sacked by Swansea City following a relatively unsuccessful seven-month stint. They replace James Rowberry, who has opted to focus on his role with Mark Robins at Stoke City, and Piet Cremers, a man whose analytical work Bellamy said meant "everything" but left to join Belgium's Club NXT in July. Cremers spent time under Pep Guardiola at Manchester City and worked with Bellamy and Vincent Kompany during their successful period at Burnley. He was often the person Bellamy turned to mid-match, but Bellamy says he was already keen to take on more of the tasks that Cremers performed. "I loved this summer interviewing people, seeing who could add to us," said the 47-year-old, who has seen former Wales midfielder and now Tottenham assistant Andrew Crofts remain part of the setup. "It freshens you up, gives you a different eye. Different strengths coming in means a different dynamic to how you work, which leaves me quite excited." This video can not be played Craig Bellamy on Match of the Day pundit Ashley Williams joining Wales staff The obvious strength Williams brings is his personality. Past team-mates for club and country will queue up to attest to his character as a player and a person. With Bellamy's Wales a young side, it mirrors the role the more experienced Williams played while on the field. As senior to the likes of Gareth Bale and Aaron Ramsey, he was a leader among equals. "I played underneath Ash as a captain, and he was a great leader in the dressing room and led by example in the way he conducted himself on and off the pitch," says Euro 2016 colleague Sam Vokes. "He can be someone who speaks from experience and [will] go into that dressing room and immediately command respect. "Portugal and Denmark away, he has played in those environments. "He will be able to speak to the lads that are going out in those environments because he led by example, and led in the trenches many times." Bellamy agrees, having retained a friendship with the former Swansea skipper after sharing a dressing room with Wales. "In my time he's been our greatest captain," says Bellamy. "Some ex-players with a certain presence can really add something, but also his knowledge of the game is really high, his football IQ is really high." Craig Bellamy and Ashley Williams first played together for Wales under John Toshack Wales might need it at the back. The appointments come against the backdrop of Wales' failure to reach the World Cup and the beginnings of criticism around the side's openness. "He'll bring some unique skills, particularly when you play Nations League A games when you have to defend a lot," said FAW chief football officer Dave Adams of Williams' appointment on the Feast of Football podcast. "Some of the dark arts of defending, he'll bring some interesting things for the players to think about." There is the thought that Williams would also be prepared to challenge Bellamy's thinking – seen as healthy part of a management team. But while Bellamy says he is keen to lean on Williams' defensive know-how, it will still be the former Liverpool, Manchester City and Newcastle forward's managerial message. "With his position, sometimes it's easier coming from a player who's been in there," said Bellamy - a former Wales captain himself. "Now, I'll lead a lot on the information, but it's nice for me to be able to ask 'What would you see with this? If you played there, how did you feel when I asked you to do that? Is that possible? Is that not possible?' I believe he'll be a huge asset to me." Sheehan's appointment also suggested a more defensive focus. The former Republic of Ireland Under-21 international was seen to have a pragmatic style at Swansea. But it appears Wales will look to benefit from the 40-year-old's eye for set-piece work, something he has also been responsible for during previous coaching roles at Luton and Southampton. "We really want someone who is in tune with restarts and set-pieces," added Adams. "In these sorts of games they could be the factor that give us a chance to win the game, because they are going to be very hard games to play in. "We realise the importance of attacking and defending set-pieces in these next six games, and feel Alan and [goalkeeping coach] Martyn Margets

title: Watch: Dramatic moment a cargo ship crashes into another vessel
description: Verified footage appears to show a cargo ship colliding with a fishing boat near Singapore, with investigators still working to establish exactly when and how the crash happened.
body: This video can not be played Two videos circulating on social media appear to show the moment a cargo ship crashes into a fishing vessel, with dramatic footage capturing the impact. BBC Verify authenticated the clips, identified the ships involved and traced the collision to waters near Singapore, with evidence suggesting it likely happened on 17 September. It remains unclear is whether anyone was injured or killed and why the collision occurred. Watch: Dramatic moment a cargo ship crashes into another vessel. title: The Papers: 'Russia to test Nato pact' and 'Labour eye tax raid'
description: Potential threats from Russia to Nato and speculation over Labour's tax plans ahead of the Budget lead Monday's papers.
body: The Guardian reports that European intelligence officials are raising the possibility of an imminent Russian attack on Nato territory, with one telling the paper it could happen within "months not years". The paper also carries comments from Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who has said intelligence reports suggest it would be part of Moscow's efforts to test whether Article 5 - which holds that Nato members will come to the defence of an ally under attack - is "more theoretical than practical". The "flames of war" are pictured on the front page of the Financial Times following Ukraine's latest drone attack on Moscow, described by the city's mayor as the largest attack to date on the Russian capital. The FT also reports that big tech firms have issued up to $300bn in "guarantees to back debt for AI data centres and chips" in the past year, but are "recording little of that exposure on their balance sheets." The Daily Telegraph, like several of Monday's papers, leads with speculation Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Chancellor John Healey are eyeing up a "tax raid" in the upcoming Budget. The paper reports they are reviewing proposals to raise Capital Gains Tax to 45% in order to increase the personal allowance on income tax. The latest set of German state elections also make the front page, as the paper notes Chancellor Friedrich Merz is on course for a "humiliating double defeat". More than half of Labour MPs have a greater number of disability benefit claimants than their majorities in their respective constituencies, according to analysis by the Times, which says they are at risk of a backlash from their constituents over possible cuts to Personal Independence Payments at the Budget. The Daily Mail leads with a pledge from Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch to restore tax-free shopping for tourists in the UK, reversing a post-Brexit rule. The Mail agrees with her as it campaigns to "scrap the tourist tax". The Daily Express also quotes Badenoch, who is urging the government to end the "hammering" of Britain's shops and pubs. Metro carries comments made by Earl Spencer in a BBC interview ahead of his book launch. The earl has denied siding with the Duke of Sussex over his brother, the Prince of Wales. Former England footballer Andros Townsend has avoided serious injury after being run over by a pitch roller during the warm-up for a league match in Thailand, the Daily Star reports. The paper also pictures singer Ed Sheeran, who became emotional while addressing crowds at his first concert since the decision to drop a support act for making pro-Palestinian comments. "We women are all at risk from men" reads the headline of the i Paper, summarising comments from Women and Equalities Minister Bridget Philipson. Her comments follow concerns from female villagers about living near proposed housing for asylum seekers in Piddington. The Independent highlights its Climate 100 - the "changemakers and innovators helping turn the time on our climate crisis". Among them are activist Erin Brockovich and Prince William. title: Nvidia boss rejects AI extinction fears as 'doomsday narratives'
description: Jensen Huang's comments come after warnings from AI researchers that the technology could lead to human extinction.
body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has described warnings that AI could lead to humanity's extinction by the next decade as "doomsday narratives". "2030 is not going to be the end of the world. There is 0% chance that's going to be the end of the world", Huang said in an interview with CBS News, the BBC's US partner. Huang added: "Scaring people is unnecessary. It is irresponsible." Warnings from researchers in recent weeks about potential risks posed by the technology escalated the debate about AI safety, with some industry executives calling for a slowdown in developing models. His remarks follow claims posted on social media by former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon that AI developers believe the technology "could kill us all by the end of the decade". Coxon's concerns sparked debate about the technology's risks, including calls by top executives like Anthropic boss Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman urging for AI's development to slow down. Huang said that such predictions are "not grounded in science", adding that it is in Nvidia's best interest to ensure the industry builds its products responsibly. "Our company's success is directly connected to the safe deployment of products and services," he said. "If we don't continue to do that, our value would be diminished." Huang suggested AI firms talking about a "slow down" could be seeking liability protections for harms their products may cause. "Go and read between the lines," he said. "They're actually not asking for more laws. They're asking to be relieved of the laws we do have, and I think that that's a problem." Not all AI workers think the tech could kill everyone OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they? Nvidia is a key player in the industry, developing cutting edge computer chips that are crucial for making AI models. The firm's most powerful chips face restrictions in China due to measures imposed by both Washington and Beijing. US export controls aim to slow China's military and AI progress, while Chinese regulations are designed to encourage reliance on domestically produced technology. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng held talks in New York on Sunday as they try to strike deals on AI, tariffs and critical minerals. The meeting came as President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping are due to hold a summit in Washington later this week. Last week, Huang appeared at a UK summit hosted by King Charles, who warned tech leaders of the "existential dangers" of AI. "The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world," the King told the group. In the US, President Donald Trump has downplayed concerns about AI's risks. Trump made a surprise phone call to Huang while the Nvidia boss was speaking on stage at a tech conference in Los Angeles on 14 September. During the call, Trump criticised calls to slow the pace of AI development and dismissed fears as a "hoax". title: Russia's elections had few surprises - but how the Kremlin uses the results is far from clear
description: Vladimir Putin will likely use the result to claim most Russians back the so-called special military operation in Ukraine, writes the BBC's Steve Rosenberg.
body: Russian President Vladimir Putin recently ruled out another wave of mobilisation for the Ukraine war Many things about Russia are hard to predict. The result of this election wasn't one of them. In a political system tightly controlled by the Kremlin, the party of power – United Russia – had been widely expected to maintain its grip on parliament. There was no upset. No surprises. No other party came close. Preliminary results suggest that United Russia is on course to retain its constitutional majority in the State Duma. And that's after more than four and a half years of war against Ukraine, which have resulted in huge battlefield losses for the Russian army, sparked economic hardship, as well as petrol shortages due to Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil facilities. It appears that those parties which have crossed the 5% threshold and made it into the new Duma are the same ones that were in the last parliament. And that Duma was fully behind the Kremlin and the so-called special military operation. Members of a local electoral commission empty a ballot box before counting votes One party that didn't make it into parliament was Yabloko. Yabloko had been the only anti-war party allowed to run in this election. But just 12 days after being registered it was removed from the ballot by the Supreme Court. That seemed to be a sign of Kremlin concern that Yabloko's pro-peace message was gaining too much traction with the public. The party isn't surprised that the new Duma looks like being as compliant as the previous one. "What other result can there be if there were 10 parties on the ballot and they all support the policies of [Russian President Vladimir] Putin?" Yabloko party chairman Nikolai Rybakov tells me. "I don't think the Duma will change. They'll vote 100% for the policies of Putin just like they did." Although Yabloko had been struck off the party list, around 100 of its candidates remained in individual constituency races, although the party continued to face sustained pressure. "Some of our candidates, who should have been running, are in jail, many were barred from running and some of our election observers weren't registered and were unable to keep an eye on the voting," Nikolai says. Members of an electoral commission count votes after polls close at a polling station in Belgorod, Russia Ahead of the final day of this three-day election, Ukraine had launched a large-scale drone attack on the Moscow area. The city's oil refinery was hit. At a polling station near the oil refinery, I spoke to voters about the attack. Here, too, there was little surprise at what had transpired. More than four and a half years into Russia's war on Ukraine, Muscovites had grown used to their city periodically becoming a front line. Instead of astonishment, there was quiet resignation. "People in the Donbas, as well as in Bryansk, and Belgorod near the Ukrainian border, hear this kind of thing every day," says a voter called Viktor, who has exited the polling station. "They just get on with their lives." If the outcome of this election was predictable, what happens next is less clear. The Kremlin will likely use the result to claim that most Russians have rallied behind the president, and to justify future policies and subsequent decisions on the war. President Putin recently ruled out another wave of mobilisation. "There is no scenario today that would require it," he declared. Not today. But what about tomorrow? Despite official denials, in Russian society there remains deep anxiety over the possibility of a new mobilisation. At the very least, the Kremlin is likely to treat the election result as a "mandate from the people" to continue the war. War may be coming. Are we psychologically ready? title: Brigitte Bardot's ballet flats and diamond rings to be sold at auction
description: Many of the film star's personal items, on sale in Paris, are priced at under €100.
body: Personal possessions of late actress Brigitte Bardot – from Repetto ballet flats and diamond rings to her copy of the Kama Sutra – are being sold at auction on Monday with proceeds going to her animal charity. Fans of the iconic figure, who died last December at the age of 91, have been coming en masse to contemplate the nearly 300 lots on display at the Drouot sale rooms in central Paris. The items are from Bardot's two homes in Saint-Tropez as well as her Paris flat, parts of which are recreated in the display. "Each item on sale bears the trace of an encounter, an involvement, a moment of happiness, a stage of her life. They tell the story of the woman as well as the legend," said her secretary for many years, Frank Guillou. Bardot is seen today as one of the most important female personalities of the late 20th century. As a model and actress from the 1950s, she became an emblem of modern femininity and the sexual revolution before later taking up the cause of animal rights. But later in life she was also criticised for making homophobic slurs and was fined multiple times for inciting racial hatred. The items are from Bardot's homes, including this one in Saint-Tropez Monday's auction is a chance to acquire everyday objects that were once her intimate belongings. Along with furniture, clothing and religious statuary, kitchen utensils, Le Creuset pans and cigarette lighters are on offer. Other highlights include the manual typewriter she used to write her correspondence and autobiography, jewellery, and classical guitars. Two of Bardot's guitars are on sale in the auction on Monday Her Peugeot bicycle is on sale, as are two pairs of leather Repetto ballet flats. A trained ballerina, Bardot helped popularise the Repetto brand after asking the company to make her a version for everyday use. The sale also features a large selection of portraits of the star, some erotic. "Brigitte used to say that she didn't want to have to look at her mug all day, so they weren't up on the walls - but she did keep them, either because she knew the artists or because the pictures meant something to her. They were all gifts," said Guillou. Black leather ballet flats are among Bardot's clothes and shoes in the auction The typewriter Bardot used to write her autobiography and Guerlain perfume will be auctioned Most lots have starting prices of under €100 (£86), but bidding is expected to push these up considerably, according to Cecile Dupuis of the auction-house Millon, which is running the sale. "[The sale] is for all those people who still live with her memory and who keep her cause alive. They are animal lovers and Brigitte Bardot lovers at the same time. The room will be full of all these fans," she said. Many items on sale reveal her adoration of animals, including a large selection of cuddly toys and collars that belonged to her dogs. "Brigitte could not live without animals around her. When one of them died, she was totally wiped out with grief. They were all buried according to a strict protocol in the gardens, and their photographs had pride of place in her homes," said Guillou. When she died in December, Bardot's estate was divided between her Foundation and her only son Nicolas-Jacques Charrier - who also benefits from the sale. title: Jailed teacher convicted of sexual abuse secretly released early in Indonesia, BBC finds
description: Undercover footage recorded by the BBC reveals he has been released after serving less than half his sentence.
body: This video can not be played Watch: BBC tracks down abusive teacher secretly released early An Indonesian teacher convicted of sexually assaulting a student at an Islamic boarding school has been secretly released from prison early, a BBC Eye investigation has found. Moch Subchi Azal Tsani or Bechi, as he is known, is the son of an influential Islamic religious leader. His trial sent shockwaves through Indonesia, a Muslim-majority country where millions of parents send their children to Islamic boarding schools. He was arrested in 2022 at his father's school in East Java where he had taught, after a 15-hour siege involving nearly 1,000 riot police - his family's supporters had gathered in large numbers to prevent his arrest. He was sentenced to seven years in prison later that year. The government withdrew the school's operating licence, but then President Joko Widodo intervened to keep the school open, arguing that the case involved an individual rather than the institution. But our investigation has uncovered further allegations against Bechi, 46, and evidence suggesting that the school and the family attempted to suppress them. Bechi's release comes as the National Commission on Violence against Women warns of an "emergency" of sexual violence in Islamic boarding schools. It says the power of religious leaders is shielding these schools from oversight and repercussions, while discouraging students from reporting abuse. Bechi was recorded at an event earlier this year by BBC reporters who were undercover Of the several female students who alleged abuse and rape against Bechi, only one pursued a legal case that led to him being convicted. Her identity has never been made public. Prosecutors sought the maximum sentence – 16 years – for rape, but the court found Bechi not guilty of rape, and convicted him for the lesser charge of sexual assault. Undercover footage recorded by the BBC now reveals that he has been released after serving less than half his sentence. Two ex-students expose sexual abuse by teachers at Islamic boarding schools in Indonesia Bechi would have been eligible for parole around March 2027, or would have been released at the end of his sentence in 2029. Indonesia's Ministry of Immigration and Corrections told the BBC that Bechi was released in August 2025 because of "sentence remissions granted to him in accordance with applicable regulations". The ministry said it could not say why his sentence was reduced. Ira Puspitasari was another student who testified at the trial, but her allegations didn't lead to separate charges. She waived her legal right to anonymity to speak publicly about this for the first time. "I was treated as his slave. I was held captive, raped, beaten," she says. "I can never forget what he said to me: 'Don't you realise you're just my slave?'" After watching the undercover footage of Bechi smiling and greeting supporters at an event in March, she tears up and says: "It's like nothing ever happened." Ira told the BBC she was raped and sexually abused by him for more than four years, from the time she was 15 years old. She said she tried to run away but Bechi's private security guards tracked her down, kidnapped her and took her to a secluded hut, where Bechi tortured and raped her. She said she was then expelled from the school. She said she reported all of this to the police but was then intimidated into withdrawing her police report. She shared an audio recording of Bechi's mother telling her to say that "nothing had happened". Ira is speaking publicly for the first time about her allegations against Bechi In January this year, after hearing that Bechi may have been released early, BBC undercover reporters attended an annual prayer event at the Shiddiqiyyah Islamic boarding school in East Java. The reporters saw Bechi wearing a mask and sitting beside his father. Just before he appeared on stage, filming and photography was prohibited, a marked difference from previous years. Then in March, BBC reporters again captured Bechi on hidden camera at another prayer event for Eid at his family home located in the same compound as the school. The BBC sought comment from Bechi, his mother and the Shiddiqiyyah school but there has been no response. The students who testified, including the girl he was convicted of sexually assaulting, were placed under witness protection and Indonesian law requires them to be informed of Bechi's release. But they were not informed, Ira and another former student who testified told the BBC. They were stunned by the undercover footage of Bechi because they believed he was still in prison. The ministry said that victims need not be informed because Bechi remains on parole, but the witness protection agency disputed this, saying the victims must still be informed. Ayu Masuroh says she was never abused by Bechi but she started investigating the allegations of abuse against him after hearing about them from schoolmates. She lives close to the school and says she is frightened about Bechi being out of prison. "He hates me. His supporters have threatened to kill me many times. I will never feel safe here. I don't feel safe living in Indonesia." Speaking publicly for the first time, she told the BBC she collected testimonies from at least 10 other female students, all of whom alleged that they were sexually assaulted or raped by Bechi. According to her, some said Bechi told them they were "chosen", and one of them said Bechi raped her after calling her for a "personal interview". These accounts were part of the closed-door trial, which alleged years of abuse at the school, according to court records seen by the BBC. title: Watch: BBC tracks down abusive teacher secretly released early
description: BBC Eye has discovered a teacher who was imprisoned for sexually assaulting a student in Indonesia has been secretly released early.
body: This video can not be played BBC Eye has discovered a teacher who was imprisoned for sexually assaulting a student in Indonesia has been secretly released early. Other students have also made allegations against Mochamad Subchi Azal Tsani, known as Bechi, including Ira, who says he raped and sexually abused her for years. The BBC put the allegations to Bechi - he did not respond. The Ministry of Immigration and Correction said he was given early parole due to legal sentence reductions. title: Smart beds and motion sensors - is this the future of dementia care?
description: Jyoti and Bharat Patel are testing dementia technology including sensors in socks, their bed and around the house.
body: Jyoti and Bharat Patel are "super testers" of dementia technology in an NHS trial There are sensors in every room of Jyoti and Bharat Patel's home. Their movements and habits are monitored constantly. But this doesn't worry them, in fact it gives them peace of mind. Jyoti was diagnosed with dementia five years ago, and they are now part of an NHS trial using high-tech devices to help patients live at home safely. The couple, who are in their 70s, are one of more than 250 families participating in the project by the UK Dementia Research Institute (UK DRI). The hope is that the technology could be extended more widely across the health service, to reduce preventable trips to hospital and give families peace of mind. Bharat and Jyoti travelled all over the world as professional magicians Bharat and Jyoti met at a magic show in 1977 and became a double act, with their career leading them to meet King Charles and Princess Anne as well as a host of celebrities. In 2019, Bharat started noticing that Jyoti was making uncharacteristic mistakes on stage. "Normally she used to set my stage up and everything was perfect, but I saw something I was looking for and it wasn't there, so I thought something is wrong," he said. They went to a private health specialist who diagnosed Jyoti with Alzheimer's in 2021. Jyoti says when she went out, if she did not look around her, she would find that she was lost. "I didn't know it [was] dementia but I knew it was something which [was] unusual," Bharat says. The couple sleep on a smart mattress that tracks Jyoti's heart rate and breathing In 2023, they were approached by the team at UK Dementia Research Institute and Imperial College London to take part in the trial, which is funded by the medical research charity LifeArc. Their house in west London is now fitted with different sensors, which are connected via the internet, that send data back to a dedicated team of doctors, nurses and other clinical specialists. The team then uses the information to better understand how the person is managing their daily routine, identify early signs of changing health and care needs with the hope that they can maintain independence for longer. Door sensors detect if someone leaves in the middle of the night, movement is monitored to check for signs of a fall, while kitchen appliances are fitted with sensors to check whether Jyoti has eaten and is sticking to her daily routine. The couple sleep on a "smart mattress" to track sleep disturbances and Jyoti's heart and breathing rates, which can spot early signs of an infection. Alongside this trial, Jyoti is also testing out smart socks and a special watch that also contain sensors to monitor her body temperature and keep track of any long-term changes in her gait - indicating frailty. Costs are expected to be about £2,000 a year, mainly to cover the monitoring and paying healthcare staff to analyse the data. If rolled out more widely that could be a significant amount of money with almost a million people living with dementia in the UK. But Sarah Daniels, health and social care lead at the UK Dementia Research Institute, says the cost is no more than a couple of weeks in a care home. The main aim, she says, is to give earlier signals to health and social care professionals. "Earlier signals means earlier intervention, which means we can head potential complications of an infection, potential challenges around care, we can head that off before it becomes a crisis," says Daniels. Devices around the home pick up movement and alert care staff if needed None of the devices record sound or video, protecting the individual's privacy, however, some people may feel nervous about the amount of data they are allowing other people to access. Daniels argues that by enhancing the level of information you provide to your GP, it enables them to make better decisions about your care. The number of people with dementia in the UK is expected to climb by another 40% by 2040, so the hope is to extend it more widely across the health service. Dr Jeremy Isaacs, national clinical director for dementia and older people's mental health at NHS England, said the health service would be closely monitoring the trial and said the research built on NHS programmes which were already supporting people to remain more independent in their own homes. While some people might feel uneasy about having all these sensors in their home, Bharat says they give him greater "peace of mind". "Even if it can cut down my worries by 5 or 10%, then it helps me and it will help other people too," he says. title: Will you get £13,000 a year when you stop working? Here's how to check
description: How to find out how much state pension you're likely to receive - and what you can do about it now.
body: It may well be decades away, but do you know how much money you will get when you stop working? The current state pension is soon likely to top £13,000 a year. Yet one in eight people surveyed by the UK tax authority have never checked how much money they are forecast to receive. Here's how to find out, and what you can do now to boost it. If you're working, it is highly likely you're contributing to the state pension - paid by the government when you hit pension age in your late 60s. the flat-rate state pension - for those who reached state pension age after April 2016 - is £241.30 a week (£12,547.60 a year) the old basic state pension - for those who reached state pension age before April 2016 - is £184.90 a week (£9,614.80 a year) Many people on the old basic state pension may receive a top-up called the additional state pension. Most pensioners have other income, primarily from pension savings built up over their career. The state pension goes up each year in line with the highest of either inflation, wage increases, or 2.5%. So next April, the flat-rate state pension is expected to go above £13,000. Workers pay National Insurance (NI) contributions. In general, you need 35 years of qualifying contributions to get a full state pension. You may have gaps in your NI record if, for example, you have lived abroad. If you've taken time away from work to care for children or family members, then you get NI credits if you receive child benefit or carer's allowance. It's possible to boost your contribution history with voluntary payments. Since April 2025, you have only been able to make payments for the previous six years. That's one reason why it is important to check your state pension forecast well before you retire, experts say. You can see what you are forecast to receive: By downloading the HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) app, external Using the official online state pension forecast webpage, external To get a state pension, you will need to prove your identity using official photo ID. Importantly, never click on a link sent in an unsolicited email or text message, even if it looks official, as it could be a scam. For more general information about tax and pensions, HMRC has launched a Tax Confident website, external. And the government-funded, independent Money Helper website has a free retirement guidance tool, external to walk you through the options. The most common reason for not checking a state pension forecast was feeling that retirement was still too far away to think about, a recent survey of 5,000 consumers by HMRC found. Losing track of pension pots from previous jobs, and concerns about how career breaks might affect their entitlement, were also frequent responses. People aged 45-54 were the most likely to have never checked. "Whether retirement is decades away or just around the corner, I'd encourage everyone to check their forecast and see if there's anything they can do now to boost their entitlement later," says Myrtle Lloyd, HMRC's chief customer officer. title: What food items should you stock up on in case of an emergency?
description: Extreme weather may be changing the way we need to shop, with the UK government urging people to stock up on canned goods.
body: Extreme weather may be changing the way we need to shop. Earlier this month, the UK government urged people to add a few more long-life products into their food basket - just in case the food supply chain is interrupted. Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle told the Guardian the powerful natural climate phenomenon El Niño would lead to "more extreme storms in this country". Climate change, along with cyber-attacks, disease outbreaks and conflicts can all put a strain on the process that eventually gets food into our shops and homes. This video can not be played Watch: The food items to keep in your cupboard Prof Richard Wilding, an expert in supply chain strategy, tells me not to be "overly worried" as global shipping professionals are adapting all the time but to be prepared to buy different products if needed. "Things that were in supermarkets and seen as relatively abundant may all of a sudden be in shortage," he adds. So how easy is it to stock up and what are the things to avoid? A staple item for those looking to stock up on supplies is tinned oily fish - including salmon, mackerel and brine Senior nutrition scientist Dr Sammie Gill, from British Nutrition Foundation, says you should prioritise certain food groups: Complex carbohydrates such as wheat biscuits, wholegrain cereals, crackers and breads plus oats, rice and pasta Proteins such as canned chickpeas, lentils, kidney beans, unsalted nuts, peanut butter and canned oily fish such as tuna, mackerel and sardines Rebecca McManamon, a consultant dietitian, lists the following essentials: Tinned fruit as you can drink its juice for added fluids, vitamins and fibre Pickled foods such as vegetables and eggs Both experts also recommend keeping long-life milk found in the non-refridgerated aisle for protein, calcium and as a source of fluid Gill says look out for salt and sugar content when buying tinned items: Avoid items tinned in brine or syrups, water is the healthiest option Avoid instant noodles and tinned soup due to high salt content Avoid breakfast cereals and snack bars with added sugars and limited nutrients Choose tinned fish over tinned meats such as sausages, hot dogs or corned beef as they are often processed and high in salt and saturated fat Limit sweet treats such as biscuits and chocolates as they have a high sugar content And what about making the essentials taste nice? McManamon says stock up on nuts as a sweet alternative but be aware that they may have a shorter shelf life. She also recommends keeping dried herbs, spices and salt available as, she says, tinned food can be slightly bland. Make basics taste a bit nicer with peanut butter and pickled veg, say experts You should aim to take in about 1,500-2,500ml of fluid a day, whatever the weather, says McManamon. This can obviously come from bottled water, but also from what she describes as fluid rich tinned foods if supplies are short. For those worried about whether tinned food is as nutritious as fresh food, Dr Gill says it absolutely can be used as part of a healthy diet. "There is little difference nutritionally between canned and fresh food in terms of macronutrients, like carbohydrates, protein, fats, and fibre, as well as fat-soluble vitamins, like vitamin A and E, and minerals," she says. It may not be as good for other vitamins, such as B and C, because the canning process has been found to decrease vitamin levels, but Gill offers assurances that these foods can still be a "useful source" of vitamins. title: Union calls for halt to graded Ofsted inspections over health concerns
description: The National Association of Head Teachers says inspections in England may pose a "risk to life" for school leaders.
body: England's biggest school leaders' union has called for a halt to graded Ofsted inspections, saying they could pose a "risk to life" for school staff. The National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT) said the change to inspections, rolled out nationally just under a year ago, had been severely harmful to school leaders' welfare. It said schools should instead be rated using short narrative reports that set out their strengths and areas they could improve. Ofsted said it had worked closely with unions and parents to develop the new report card inspection system, and would continue to grade schools. Ofsted, England's schools' inspectorate, introduced the report card system to replace its previous one or two-word judgements last November, following the death of head teacher Ruth Perry, who took her own life after Ofsted downgraded her school from "outstanding" to "inadequate". An inquest ruled that an Ofsted inspection had contributed to her death in January 2023. That led to a change in how Ofsted assessed schools, bringing in report cards designed to grade schools on several areas, rather than focusing on one overall grade for the whole school. Example of an Ofsted inspection report card But the new system faced criticism from when it was first proposed, with Perry's sister, Prof Julia Waters, saying it appeared to be "a rehash of the discredited and dangerous system it is meant to replace". The NAHT issued a claim with the High Court for a judicial review over the changes, arguing there had not been adequate consultation on the new report cards before they were introduced, but that was rejected. Nearly a year after it was fully rolled out, the NAHT says evidence from its members suggests the new system is having a detrimental impact on school leaders' mental health. Testimonies seen by the BBC suggest head teachers are being left "overwhelmed" and "anxious", with the pressure caused by the inspections described as "intolerable". Although the system had been changed with the intention of lowering the burden on school leaders, the testimonies say the inspection and assessment process had become "higher stakes than ever before". Amanda Hulme, head teacher at Claypool Primary School in Bolton, said a recent inspection at her school had been "easily the most stressful experience" of her career. "It was definitely damaging to my health and really quite distressing," she said. "I couldn't sleep and it led to my blood pressure and pulse rate increasing. "The effect on my team has also been significant, with some colleagues no longer wanting to pursue headship, and another teacher considering leaving the profession entirely." Head teacher Amanda Hulme says she found the new inspection system "much worse" than the previous one The NAHT says it has shared examples with Education Secretary Lucy Powell of some of the "damaging experiences" it says its members have faced. Speaking to LBC earlier this month, Powell said she took head teacher wellbeing "incredibly seriously" and that the system of accountability needed to be "supportive and understanding. "I'll continue the work that I do with head teachers, head teacher representatives and others to make sure that we get this Ofsted framework, but also the culture and the whole regime, right," she added. The NAHT said the results of a recent survey of its members suggested that the majority who responded felt that inspections had worsened in the past 12 months. The union is now calling for inspections to pause to allow for a "fundamental review of how inspection works", drawing on examples from other nations. In Wales, the inspectorate Estyn has removed judgements such as "excellent" and "good" from its reports, instead summarising findings by highlighting a school's strengths and areas for improvement. Northern Ireland's Education and Training Inspectorate (ETI) also uses narrative reports without grades. Scotland's His Majesty's Inspectorate of Education (HIME) does use grades, but there has been a recent consultation on their use. NAHT general secretary Paul Whiteman said: "The clear theme emerging across all the feedback we have received is that this Ofsted framework is even more stressful than the one that preceded it. "It poses a real and present danger to the well-being and mental health of school leaders and teachers, possibly even a risk to life." He said he welcomed the new education secretary's focus on teacher wellbeing, adding: "Really fundamental changes to inspection are needed, and we stand ready to work with the new government to achieve that." Responding, Ofsted said it has worked closely with teaching unions over the past three years, to deliver significant reforms and reduce unnecessary pressure on teachers. "Ofsted exists to raise standards for children and to provide clear reporting to parents," a spokesperson said. "We will continue to engage closely with trades unions – but we will also continue to grade schools." title: Specialist courts for rape cases to be rolled out across England and Wales
description: Funding will allow victims to view proceedings remotely and give evidence from a separate room via video link, the government says.
body: Specialist courts to handle cases of rape and other sexual offences will be introduced across England and Wales over the next two years, the prime minister has announced. Each crown court will have at least one courtroom especially set up to hear such cases, while victims will be able to view proceedings remotely and give evidence from a separate room via video link. Victims will also be provided with private entrances and waiting rooms to separate them from defendants, though it is understood this will be dependent on the architecture of each building. Rape Crisis England and Wales said this was a "significant step forward" and addressed several reforms it had been requesting for many years. "Taken together, they reflect the urgency of ensuring that courts are fit for purpose and properly meet the needs of victims and survivors, which is crucial to securing justice," said the charity's chief executive, Ciara Bergman. Under the new measures, expected to cost around £23m from the Ministry of Justice's budget, court staff will be given "trauma-informed training" and a single person of contact will be assigned to each survivor. From next month, trials will be given a fixed date rather than placed on floating lists in what Prime Minister Andy Burnham said was an effort to "rebalance the scales of justice and put victims first". The government said the changes follow Labour MP Charlotte Nichols showing "immense strength and bravery" in speaking publicly about being raped and calling for changes to the justice system. Nichols waived her automatic right to anonymity in March when she made a Commons speech and described having to wait more than 1,000 days to go to court. Earlier this year, the government announced that rape victims would be given access to specialist legal advice throughout the criminal justice process. MP reveals rape ordeal during court reform debate Delays to my rapist's trial left me terrified, survivor tells BBC Rape victims to get specialised legal advice in courts 'Rape victims failed by court delays' say charity Woman dropped sex assault case after court delays Labour promised in its 2024 manifesto to halve violence against women and girls within a decade. "For too long, victims of rape and serious sexual offences have felt let down by our justice system," Burnham said. "Prosecution rates for rape remain shamefully low, with many victims waiting years for justice. This is not good enough." The changes were "long overdue" and would make a "significant difference" but focusing on prosecution alone would not be enough, he added. "So as well as ensuring victims get justice, we will step up action to prevent these horrific crimes from happening in the first place," the prime minister said. Nichols spoke publicly for the first time about being raped when she accused the then Justice Secretary, David Lammy, of using crime victims as a "cudgel" to push through his reforms of the legal system. She was criticising the Courts and Tribunals Bill's plans to limit jury trials to cases with a likely prison sentence of three years or more. She said she had waited 1,088 days to go to court, with every day being "agony" and the "trauma" made worse by her role in public life. Her attacker, she said, was acquitted at crown court but subsequently ordered to pay compensation after she won a civil case against him. "It is because I have been raped that I am as passionate as I am about what it means for a justice system to be truly victim-focused," she said. "It is because I have endured every indignity that our broken criminal justice system could mete out that I care what kind of reform will actually deliver justice for survivors and victims of crime more widely." Responding to news of the specialist courts being rolled out, the Conservatives said tackling delays to criminal rape trials was "long overdue" and they pushed Labour to commit to scrapping plans to restrict jury trials. "The fact that victims have been withdrawing their cases because they have taken too long has been a disgrace," said shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy. "Labour need to get courts sitting throughout the year, end the delays and clear the backlog – not undermine our right to a trial by jury." Last year another charity, the Salford Survivor Project, said victims of rape and sexual assault were being "failed by the system" as court backlogs reached a record high. The long delays for cases to go to trial were having a serious impact on victims' mental health, it said. Also last year, a woman who says she was sexually assaulted by a taxi driver on her 21st birthday told BBC News she had dropped the case because of court delays. She reported the alleged incident in early 2022 and gave evidence in court in December 2023 but the case was adjourned until September 2024 when the judge fell ill. "I made the decision, even though I hate the statement, to drop the case," she said. "I couldn't let this hurt me further." The Crown Prosecution Service said that, without her testimony, the case had been dropped because of insufficient evidence. If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line website. title: Workers came across human remains – and unearthed a mass grave of 572 people
description: Workers in northern Sri Lanka accidentally uncovered the country's largest mass grave – and reopened wounds from its civil war.
body: Jeyaruby Jeyabalan was 12 when her father, Kandaiah Jayapalan, disappeared When a mass grave was unearthed in northern Sri Lanka last February, it was not by design. Workers were digging to extend a cremation ground in the Chemmani area of the Jaffna region when they suddenly discovered human remains, prompting an investigation. By August, archaeologists had completed the third phase of the excavation at the site, during which they found the skeletal remains of 572 people, including children and infants. Among the dead were artefacts from their lives – bangles, a school bag, a milk bottle. It is believed to be the largest mass grave site ever uncovered in Sri Lanka. There had been whispers of its existence before - a soldier on trial for the rape and murder of a young woman during the country's devastating civil war, had spoken about a mass grave which contained hundreds of bodies. Rights groups said they were disappeared civilians But there was no proof - until now. And while the discovery is devastating, it has offered hope to people like Jeyaruby Jeyabalan, whose father was among thousands of people who disappeared during the decades-long war. Jeyabalan and families like his hope that answers about what happened to their loved ones lie among the bodies. Many Tamils believe the grave holds the victims of extrajudicial killings carried out during the civil war. They are calling for an investigation – and for justice. But the excavation process at Chemmani has moved slowly, testing the patience of families searching for answers about their disappeared loved ones. The discovery of hundreds of remains near a previously identified mass grave has fuelled anger among the Tamils, who have long-demanded a thorough inquiry into disappearances. Many fear the mass grave will eventually fade from public attention because of a lack of political will to pursue the truth – and so the grave has become a rallying point for renewed protests in Sri Lanka's north. Sri Lanka, particularly the Tamil-dominated north and east, suffered decades of conflict. The war, which lasted from 1983 to 2009, divided the island-nation along ethnic lines. Tamil Tiger rebels fought for an independent state in the north-east of the country due to what they called systematic discrimination by the Sinhalese-dominated government. The conflict lasted 26 years and the fighting killed an estimated 100,000 people. It also left about 23,000 – mostly Tamils – missing. Both the security forces and Tamil Tigers are accused of atrocities and crimes. A baby's bottle was among the personal items uncovered at the grave site. In 1995, after a bloody conflict, the Sri Lankan army wrested control of the Jaffna Peninsula from the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE). It was seen as a key turning point in the war, which ended with the defeat of the Tigers in 2009. As they extended control in the late 1990s, the entire Chemmani region became part of a high-security zone and was dotted with army camps, check points and security posts. There was an army camp in Chemmani close to the cemetery as well. Some at that time described the Jaffna region as an "open prison" - and the security forces were accused of causing the disappearance of thousands of civilians, something Sri Lankan governments have always denied. "I was 12 years old when my father was picked up by the Sri Lankan army at a checkpoint close to Chemmani area in September 1996. We still don't know what happened to him," Jeyaruby Jayapalan, who now lives in Jaffna, tells the BBC. She recalls how, after learning of his disappearance, the family panicked and visited military camps and police stations across Jaffna in a desperate search for information without any luck. He never came back. Her father, Kandaiah Jayapalan, was a government employee who also ran a roadside café not far from Chemmani. "I went to Chemmani mass grave with many others hoping that I will find some answers. But we didn't find any material evidence. We want a detailed forensic analysis of the human remains," says Jeyaruby. Two weeks before Kandaiah Jayapalan vanished, an 18-year-old Tamil school girl, Krishanthi Kumaraswamy, disappeared in the same area. In 1998, a court in Colombo sentenced five soldiers to death for the rape and murder of Kumaraswamy and for killing three of her family members. The case drew global attention at that time. Their bodies were later found buried in Chemmani area. It is among the most infamous cases from the conflict – and the grave currently under investigation is within 100 metres of the remains of Kumaraswamy and others were found. In a startling court testimony, one of the convicted soldiers, Somaratne Rajapakse, alleged that between 300 and 400 people who had been killed in the mid-1990s were buried in Chemmani. His claim led to the first excavation at Chemmani a year later, during which investigators unearthed more than 10 human skeletons. Human rights activists believed those remains were linked to people who had disappeared during the civil war, but there was little judicial follow-up. Activists say that because the war with the Tamil rebels was ongoing, the then government didn't pursue the investigation and did not explain why. The discovery of another mass grave in the same area has revived calls for accountability. Map of Sri Lanka showing location of Chemmani "Preliminary inspections suggest this was not a normal burial site and not consistent with ordinary Hindu burial practices," says Gehan Gunatilleke, a commissioner with Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka, which conducted inspections at Chemmani last year. Activists and experts say that while a few dozen bodies appeared to have been formally buried, the vast majority told a different story. Most of the human remains were found without clothing, packed tightly together and, in some cases, stacked on top of others. title: Man, 82, dies after beach fight with 76-year-old over sunlounger in Greece
description: One eyewitness said the scene was so chaotic that screaming could be heard from the other end of the beach.
body: The incident occurred on in Vouliagmeni beach near Athens on Sunday An 82-year-old man has died after getting into a fight with a man in his 70s over a sunlounger on a beach in Greece, local media is reporting. Witnesses say a disagreement over the use of the loungers at Vouliagmeni beach, near Athens, escalated into a violent fight, which then further spiralled to involve other people. One eyewitness told the Kathimerini newspaper that the scene was so chaotic, the screaming could be heard from the other end of the beach. The younger man, who was 76, has reportedly been arrested. A 21-year-old woman who was with him was also detained but later released. Witnesses told Ta Nea daily newspaper that she had a bloodied and swollen face. During the fight, the 82-year-old collapsed. According to various reports, he received CPR and a defibrillator was used on him before an ambulance arrived. The man was taken to hospital where he later died. Another witness said that the victim seemed to be waiting for other people and had reserved a sunlounger, which appeared to be the cause of the initial disagreement. Authorities are investigating what led to the physical altercation and what caused the man's death. title: Smith wins World Series of Darts Finals as Littler run ends
description: England's Ross Smith shocks Wales' Gerwyn Price to win World Series of Darts Finals as Luke Littler's clean-sweep dream ends in last eight in Amsterdam.
body: Finals winner Smith lost in the first round of his only two other appearances in this season's World Series of Darts Englishman Ross Smith won the final six legs to produce a shock 11-5 victory over two-time former winner Gerwyn Price in the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam. It was just a second major title for the 37-year-old, whose only previous success at this level of the PDC World Tour came at the European Championship in 2022. But the world number 14 overpowered his loftier opponent with a barrage of 180s, hitting 11 maximums, compared to Welshman Price's five, to finish a deserved winner. It was a fitting finale to a tournament of shocks that saw world champion Luke Littler lose in the quarter-finals and miss out on his quest to claim a clean sweep of the major PDC titles in 2026. Littler could boycott Dutch events over booing Littler seals dramatic final-leg win over Aspinall Thousands at darts audition to take on Luke Littler "Honestly, I am made up with the win. I am just so happy," said Smith, who suffered first-round exits in New Zealand and Australia in his only two other appearances in the 2026 World Series. "You are playing Gerwyn Price - one of the best players in the world. You have got to up your game." Smith beat Northern Ireland's Josh Rock 10-7 in the last eight and Dutch hope Gian van Veen 11-8 in the semi-finals to give himself a shot at the £100,000 winner's prize. Price, meanwhile, made it past England's James Wade in the quarter-finals before beating compatriot Jonny Clayton - Littler's conqueror - in the last four. The 2020 and 2022 winner won back-to-back legs to make it 5-5 against Smith in the final but was hanging on as his opponent continued to score heavily albeit with a lower checkout success. Smith, however, was far more clinical after the interval, winning the next three legs, including back-to-back checkouts of 127 and 123. The checkouts cooled but Smith won a succession of scrappy legs to seal victory as Price's game deserted him. Earlier, Littler's bid for a clean sweep of all major PDC titles in 2026 was ended by a 10-4 defeat by Clayton in the quarter-finals. The world number one had followed his World Championship triumph at Alexandra Palace in January by winning titles at the World Masters, UK Open, Premier League, World Cup of Darts and World Matchplay. But after threatening to boycott events in the Netherlands after being roundly booed by the crowd during his last-16 win over Nathan Aspinall, the Warrington-based player failed to produce his best darts against Clayton.
