title: Illegal off-road vehicles to be seized on the spot as police warn of 'long walk home'
description: With damage to protected habitats reportedly rising, police have powers to seize illegal off-roading vehicles on the spot.
body: TikTok accounts linked to one group of off-roaders showed images and videos of damage being caused to ancient peatlands Police say off-road drivers causing anti-social behaviour or damage to protected habitats will have their vehicles seized "on the spot". PC Eryl Lloyd, of North Wales Police's rural crime team, said new powers allowed officers to take vehicles without notice, and warned offending drivers: "It's a long walk home." Both the force and Natural Resources Wales (NRW) said damage caused by off-roading incidents and other anti-social behaviour was on the rise. In August, three men who caused "irreversible" harm to the Berwyn Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) in 4x4s were convicted after videos of them causing the damage were shared on TikTok. Off-roaders caught damaging protected site after posting videos to TikTok John Robinson, Michael Williams and Joseph Hodgson were part of a seven-vehicle convoy which drove from Liverpool to the Berwyn range, an area of moorland in northeast Wales, where they caused "serious damage" to the peat and bog habitat. Robinson and Williams were fined more than £2,000 each and disqualified from driving for two months. Hodgson was ordered to pay £1,000 compensation for damaging the SSSI, as well as costs, and was also banned from entering the Berwyn SSSI for three years. PC Eryl Lloyd – who is seconded to NRW – said his team had "definitely seen an increase in off-roading incidents". As well as 4x4 vehicles and motorbikes, "we're getting a lot more reports about e-bikes, which also cause the same amount of damage as motorbikes" he added. This video can not be played Illegal off roaders, caught by their own footage, were prosecuted in August Under the Crime and Policing Act 2026, introduced earlier this year, police have new powers to tackle the problem. "Previously, we had to give a warning for incidents of anti-social behaviour, careless driving. "Now we can just seize the vehicles there on the spot. "We will use these new powers and we will be seizing vehicles on the spot as well." Although the reason for a rise in off-roading incidents is unknown, Lloyd believed it was "to do with social media" and people sharing locations. He added: "They come from all over the UK. We are very close to the northwest of England. But we've seen people travelling from the Midlands, even London as well." While social media may have contributed to a rise in off-road incidents, Lloyd also said: "We've had incidents over the summer in Newborough Forest, Newborough Beach [Anglesey], where social media has exploded. "And the amount of people coming to wild-camp, and causing anti-social behaviour from that, from illegal fires to barbecues… so it's been a busy summer." Both Kirsty Roberts of NRW and PC Eryl Lloyd are seeing a rise in incidents On the Berwyn Range, damage which led to the convictions of drivers last month included the wearing away of hundreds of years worth of peat growth. Kirsty Roberts, of NRW, said: "On this specific occasion we're talking about peatlands, which are really slow-growing habitats. "So in this particular scenario we had a depth of 40cm (15in) worth of peat, which equates to around 400 years worth of peat depth and peat growth. "And so, to see this area naturally recover, we just wouldn't see it in our lifetime." Damage caused by off-road vehicles to peatlands and vegetation also impact wildlife, including ground-nesting birds, she said. Without intervention to avoid further degradation, she warned: "We're not going to be able to reverse that biodiversity curve." As well as a rise in 4x4 and e-bike incidents, she said "general anti-social behaviour" was also increasing, including use of barbecues and "a lot of waste being dumped on protected sites", adding: "It's happening on areas that are really fragile." Lord Newborough is "gutted" by the damage, and says more resources are needed Lord Newborough, of the Rhug Estate in Denbighshire, owns the Berwyn land damaged by the off-roaders convicted last month. He said areas of the estate had been opened up "for the public to enjoy", but "the mountain is very precious and we've tried to protect that and be good custodians for many years". He agreed that damage to important habitats caused by off-road vehicles was becoming more frequent. "I feel gutted basically because this is damage that has happened in recent years." Under the Countryside and Rights of Way Act, a fifth of Wales is classed as "access land" including areas where land owners have agreed the public have a right of entry on foot. "I'm pretty old myself, so I grew up respecting the mountains and not seeing the encroachment that we've got by the public now. "So, yes it hurts me and it hurts, the fact that the damage has been done. "We monitor the bird life on the mountain every year and we know that certain precious nests are being damaged wilfully, and this isn't really the way ahead." title: Human extinction fears make me want to flee AI and live on an island
description: People share their anxieties following recent headlines over concerns about AI advancement.
body: James Downs is a mental health campaigner who shares his own experience of anorexia, depressions and anxiety to educate others Since headlines broke about claims AI advancement could lead to human extinction, James Downs has felt his anxiety rising. "It makes me almost feel powerless. Like, what can I do as an individual?" said the mental health campaigner from Cardiff. This sense of fear has led him to check his phone for more news. "And the more you look at it the more your attention's drawn to the negative or scary things and the worse and worse it can seem," said the 37-year-old. Earlier this month, a top safety researcher at Anthropic warned AI was advancing so quickly he believed there was a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade. Then computer scientist and Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton, known as the "Godfather of AI", told the BBC that the claim was "not unreasonable", external. On Tuesday, amid rising public concerns about the risks, the boss of ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said people should have more faith in AI firms to keep the tech safe. James says connecting with friends and doing something positive for the environment helps him feel good during anxious times James, who is in recovery after being diagnosed with anorexia, anxiety and depression as a teenager, said the recent headlines about AI have added another layer of worry to ongoing concerns such as the climate crisis, the cost of living crisis, conflict around the world and nuclear threat. "I can't escape this background anxiety about the future - will I be OK? Will the planet be OK? Will my finances be okay? All of these different, multi-layered things which go from the big existential things, like what if it wipes us all out, to the day-to-day things." He said it could lead to a sense of helplessness. "It kind of makes me want to give up trying to make a positive change in the world, or makes me just want to run away, be a nomad or something, go and live on an island somewhere with no technology, but that's not a sustainable solution either." Psychotherapist Lucy Theo says her clients often bring up their anxieties over AI during therapy Lucy Theo, a psychotherapist from Bonvilston, Vale of Glamorgan, said clients had been bringing up the recent news about AI in therapy. "It's kind of intensifying people's nervous systems which are already kind of stretched post Covid," she said. She said for a long time clients had been talking about their fears over what AI could mean for things like privacy and job security and the latest headlines had advanced that conversation. "It kind of intensifies a general feeling of lack of stability," she said. "Fear of death is a very common fear and it can cross into that sense of 'who am I? What's my path? How are things going to be for me at the end of my life'?" Luke (left) says he treats news about AI advancement with a scepticism On an overcast Friday at Barry Island, Vale of Glamorgan, people's reaction ranged from sceptical to concerned. Chelsea Brown, 31, and her husband Luke Brown, 32, were out for a walk with their newborn. "I'm nervous but also suspicious as leaders of AI companies say things when it suits them," said Luke, who works in tech. "That may be me trying to feel more comfortable about it, but I am sceptical because they do say things that either boost their stock or suit their agenda." But he said by using AI at work he had seen how quickly it had progressed. "It does scare me but the way I cope with it is I look at the news with a sense of scepticism," he said. Chelsea, who works in marketing, said she feared what the speed of progress would mean for their new baby and four-year-old. "I've got quite a lot of anxiety about it, we talk about it quite a lot... it's terrifying," she said. "I really hope regulations come in a lot quicker than they did for social media. I don't know why the regulatory process is so slow." Susan Harvey has found recent reports "quite scary" Susan Harvey, a grandmother to five, said she was out for a walk to clear her head and escape the news. "It is quite scary," she said. "The stories sound extreme and I worry for my grandchildren. I think everything is out of control." She too described feeling powerless, but did have some optimism. "I do think things are changing, people are becoming more 'let's stand up against this and do something'," she said. The Royal College of Psychiatrists said AI's rapid development could "understandably cause anxiety for some people". Its chair Prof Alka Ahuja said: "As with any major technological change, people may feel uncertain about what the future holds and what it could mean for their lives." He advised limiting exposure to alarmist content, discussing any concerns with trusted friends or family and seeking help from a GP if anxiety begins to affect daily life, wellbeing or relationships. Neil Ingham says there are some simple steps that can help top manage anxiety over world events Neil Ingham, executive director for Samaritans Cymru, said: "These headlines affect everybody and they can create anxiety and can make people feel like they don't have control." He said there were steps people could take to reduce their anxiety. Curate your social media feeds: "We can choose who we follow, who we don't follow, what types of trusted news sources we choose to get our news from and who we choose to maybe ignore and mute," said Neil. "We can also choose what alerts pop up on our phone." Think about what time of day you consume news: "If your phone is next to your bed when you wake up you're going to pick up your phone, and if the start of your day is reading about big global news stories or a story about AI you're not really giving yourself a chance to settle into the day," said Neil. "Similarly, at the end of the day, if the last thing we do before we go to sleep is read ab

title: Mourinho prints out 'red card' incidents after Real lose derby
description: Real Madrid manager Jose Mourinho prints out screenshots displaying two incidents he believes should have resulted in Atletico Madrid dismissals.
body: Where did he find a printer? Mourinho arrived at his news conference with screenshots of incidents he believed were red cards for the hosts Real Madrid manager Jose Mourinho arrived at his post-match news conference carrying an A4 sheet of printed paper with screenshots displaying two incidents he believed should have resulted in Atletico Madrid dismissals. Mourinho accused the officials of making key errors after Real Madrid were beaten 2-1 by Atletico Madrid, claiming the hosts should have been handed two red cards in the first half. It was Real Madrid's second defeat of the season, having lost 1-0 to Real Betis earlier in September. "We can skip the press conference because the story of the match is right here," Mourinho said as he showed media the printed images. "Those were two clear red cards. Given the difficulties we faced afterwards playing 11 against 10, we can only imagine what 50 minutes of 11 against nine would have been like. "So I'll just have to limit myself to hugging my players, who gave it their all and played a first half, showed great class and character, setting us up perfectly to win the second half." Diego Simeone, in contrast, was ecstatic with the result and when asked to respond to Mourinho's refereeing rant, said he was always respectful of everyone else's opinions. "I understand that we're in a privileged position with a lot of public scrutiny, as coaches, and whether it's Mourinho, [Hansi] Flick, [Manuel] Pellegrini, me, or anyone else, we need to be careful about what we say," he said. "We have to know how to respect others, the referees, our colleagues and we all lose out. And when someone crosses that line of respect, it's not right - you can't cross that line." Mourinho argued the two first-half decisions had a significant impact on the match, insisting his team had shown character despite the circumstances. The first incident Mourinho referenced involved Real's Jude Bellingham and Atleti's Cristian Romero in the 37th minute, when both players challenged for a loose ball and the clash ended with Bellingham being shown a yellow card. At the time, Mourinho pleaded with the referee for a red card to be shown to the Argentina international for dangerous foul play, because replays showed Romero made contact with his studs on Bellingham's knee. Bellingham's yellow card was retracted after a video assistant referee review and Romero was given a yellow. The second was for a challenge by Atletico's Lee Kang-in on Fede Valverde, which Mourinho believed should have been a straight red card. The Portuguese also questioned the appointment of the match officials, saying he wanted to believe the decisions were mistakes rather than deliberate. "I want to believe they are simply mistakes, just as a coach makes mistakes, just as a player makes mistakes," he said. Despite the defeat, Mourinho said he had no complaints about his players' commitment and praised their performance, particularly in the first half. "I liked my team as a unit. Even in the first half I really liked them, and in the second half it was obviously very difficult to get the ball and to stop Atleti's possession. I liked their pride, I liked their determination, and it's a good feeling for me to not be disappointed in my players". Mourinho also addressed the dismissal of Dean Huijsen, which awarded Atletico a penalty, admitting he had not yet watched the VAR replay. The defeat leaves Real Madrid fourth in the league standings, with Atletico second - five points behind league leaders Barcelona. Yet Mourinho was keen to stress that there was still a long way to go in the season. "Under normal circumstances, it's not about how it starts, it's about how it ends," he said. Atletico manager Simeone rejected the suggestion the result would be overshadowed by the refereeing debate, saying his team had controlled the contest. "The match I watched was an intense one, where I think we controlled it at all times," the Argentine said. "We faced an opponent with incredible transitions and extraordinary players who obviously play for their team and do so very well. We controlled almost all the transitions they could have had." Simeone described the derby as an intense match and praised his players' defensive organisation and collective effort against a Real Madrid side featuring several dangerous attacking players. "I think we controlled the match at all times, through our teamwork, our defence, our collective effort, our group dynamics, and our play. Looking for where we could hurt them, which we knew was on the right side." La Liga will resume on Friday 9 October following the international break. title: Neville calls Man Utd 'pathetic' - but Carrick maintains belief
description: Gary Neville calls Manchester United "pathetic", but boss Michael Carrick maintains belief after salvaging draw at Fulham.
body: This video can not be played Carrick impressed Man Utd 'kept belief' to earn draw at Fulham Gary Neville took a deep breath after Lisandro Martinez's own goal put Fulham ahead just over an hour into what had been a laboured Manchester United performance, and delivered his verdict. The former United skipper is never short of a scathing word, but even by his standards, this was brutal. "I've watched Manchester United since the age of five and that's the worst 15 minutes I've ever seen," he said. "Absolutely pathetic. "I've never seen such a lack of effort. What must [Michael] Carrick be thinking?" For context, Neville was part of the United side beaten 3-1 by Sunday's opponents Fulham at Old Trafford in October 2003. In recent memory they have also lost 7-0 at Liverpool and 6-1 at home twice, to Tottenham and Manchester City. Neville's words came after a poor quarter of an hour from the start of the second half to Martinez's moment of ill fortune, before United went on to snatch a 1-1 draw thanks to Matheus Cunha's deflected strike in the 89th minute. It seemed an extreme reaction. But in a week when United lost the Manchester derby to a City side reduced to 10 men midway through the first half, then against Brighton for the first time in more than 50 years were beaten at home after giving away a two-goal lead, frustration among the fanbase is high. Questions over fitness were first raised during pre-season when midfielder Youri Tielemans revealed United were not prioritising running. While Cunha did not exactly agree with Neville in his post-match interview with Sky Sports, his comments will have fuelled more debate around the issue. "At the beginning of the second half they put in more energy than us," said the Brazilian. "We cannot accept this." Unsurprisingly, Carrick had a different take. He used the way his side tried to pressure the home team in the latter stages, leading to Cunha's equaliser, as evidence his squad is fit enough. "The way we finished the game, actually, it didn't look like that. We finished the game really strong actually, and kept pushing. I don't think that's an issue, no," he said. This video can not be played Cunha's late strike denies Fulham first league win of the season Cunha also mentioned the "noise" around United when he spoke to BBC Match of the Day. Neville is a significant part of that noise, either directly or through his growing media empire. Carrick has previously said he can shut it out. It cannot be quite so easy though when United fans - who usually back their team through disappointment - followed up chants on Wednesday in disgust at the Brighton debacle by here booing Carrick's decision to take off popular England midfielder Kobbie Mainoo 11 minutes from time. "There's always going to be certain reactions when you're making changes," said Carrick. "I've spoken to Kobbie after the game and he's absolutely fine. "I understand at times when we are chasing the game, everyone's a little bit emotional. The supporters are, as well they should be, desperate for us to do the right thing. "But I don't take any negatives or offence to it. I think we've just got to try and keep doing the right things to get back into the game. "The supporters were unbelievable today, I have to say, all the way through, and stuck with the boys and supported them. At least we've given them something small at the end to take from it, and I'm sure there's more to come." And that is the key point. A draw at Fulham is "something small" considering the home side started the game at the foot of the Premier League - and have now swapped places with Tottenham. Five points from five games leaves United 12th, an incredible 10 points behind pacesetters Manchester City already. Their £70m summer signing Carlos Baleba is still to make his debut, and long-term injury victim Matthijs de Ligt was not involved at all, even though both were part of the squad that travelled south on Saturday. Striker Benjamin Sesko also missed the game after suffering a recurrence of the shin problem against Brighton that he was troubled by for an extended period last season before submitting to a recovery programme that ruled him out for more than three months. Carrick says "at this point" the extent of the damage is unknown. This would all be pretty underwhelming were it not for the ticketing issues instigated by the club's touting crackdown that has annoyed so many in the fanbase. On Wednesday, United will release their full-year financial results to 30 June, around which the full extent of their current debt will be revealed. Then there is the general debate about the wisdom of new stadium, which is set to cost in excess of £2bn, with planning permission potentially submitted with the main Old Trafford masterplan, which is earmarked for late 2027 or early 2028. Little wonder, after leading United back to the Champions League so unexpectedly last season, Carrick is presiding over a club whose supporters feel deflated, even if he does not recognise that. "It's still a big season ahead," he said. "It's a long season and you're going to have spells through a season. That's part of the journey. "It's not a sprint, it's a long effort. "I'm not playing it down, you know. We wanted more points, so I'm not saying everything's great. I understand the frustration. We wanted to be better and we wanted to do other things. "But deflation is certainly not what we have within the club and within the group. The players didn't have that on the pitch today and that's what will carry us through the season without a doubt." title: What have we learned from the Premier League so far?
description: BBC Sport takes a look at the opening weeks of the Premier League season as a long international break arrives.
body: Brighton's 3-0 win over Arsenal could have a big impact on both teams' seasons The Premier League takes a near three-week break as we enter a four-game international window. So, what have we learned from the opening five matches of the season? BBC Sport takes a look. This video can not be played Highlights: Brilliant Brighton batter Arsenal in shock first defeat as champions Premier League champions Arsenal were looking fairly unstoppable in the opening weeks of the season. A win over Brighton on Saturday would have given the Gunners a club-record equalling eighth consecutive win in all competitions to start the season. But that all ended with a 3-0 loss at Amex Stadium on Saturday. The Gunners had not lost a league game by more than one goal, let alone three, since October 2024. It was their heaviest defeat in the league since May 2023 when they lost 3-0 to the same opposition. "That's not going to take away what the team has done and the boys have done in the last six or seven weeks since coming back from the World Cup," said boss Mikel Arteta. "What we've done, the way we've competed and the amount of games we've won has been remarkable - but this is a big lesson for all of us to understand what it takes to win at this level." Brighton humbling 'a big lesson' for Arsenal - Arteta This video can not be played Man City come out on top in eight goal thriller against Sunderland Many wondered if Manchester City would experience a post-Pep Guardiola slump when the legendary boss left after a decade. Things did not start too well under Enzo Maresca, with the Community Shield defeat by Arsenal. But they have won all five games in the Premier League - and seven in a row in all competitions - after Sunday's entertaining 5-3 win over Sunderland. That takes them three points clear of Arsenal. "In the press conference before the game, I said I expect a very tough game," said Maresca. "Then we also conceded two or three goals but we have learned a lot in these eight weeks and this is good." Perfect 24 hours as Man City put pressure on Arsenal This video can not be played Brentford stay unbeaten as they put three past Chelsea Brighton and Brentford, two clubs who have never won a major trophy, have continued to impress this season. Fabian Hurzeler's Brighton enjoyed that 3-0 win over Arsenal to see them sit third in the table, only two points behind the Gunners. Brighton have won at home against the reigning Premier League champions in each of the last three seasons. Star player Pascal Gross laughed and said "no" when BBC Sport asked him if Albion were in the title race. But stranger things have happened... Meanwhile, just one point below them in the table are Keith Andrews' Brentford. Many tipped the Bees to struggle after the departure of Thomas Frank last summer but if anything they improved under their former set-piece coach Andrews. And their start to this season - unbeaten after five games and fourth in the table - is showing he is no one-season wonder as a manager. They go into the break on the back of their most impressive result, a 3-0 home win over Chelsea. Leeds, impressing again under boss Daniel Farke, are also on nine points and in a potential Champions League place. Andoni Iraola's Liverpool and Everton are just below them on goal difference. From near oblivion to Europe - Brighton celebrate 125th anniversary in style This video can not be played Cunha's late strike denies Fulham first league win of the season Seven years apart, United did the same thing twice hoping for different results - appointing a club legend who last managed in Britain in the Championship after a good start as caretaker boss. In 2019 it was Ole Gunnar Solskjaer and this time it was Michael Carrick. But this season, after Carrick having a summer to work on his team, the Red Devils have only won once in the league. Their five points after five league games is their joint fewest at this stage of a Premier League season. They go into the international break on the back of a 1-1 draw against Fulham, and even needed a late deflected Matheus Cunha strike to stop the Cottagers winning their first game all season. After the Lisandro Martinez own goal that give Fulham the lead, ex-United captain Gary Neville said on Sky Sports: "I've watched Manchester United since the age of five and that's the worst 15 minutes I've ever seen. "Absolutely pathetic. I've never seen such a lack of effort." United's owners will have almost three weeks to stew on this before they host fellow underachievers Tottenham (more on them soon) on 10 October. This video can not be played Coventry defeat Forest for first win since Prem return In 2024 and 2025, the three promoted teams went straight back down - mostly with really low points tallies too. But that streak came to an end last year when Sunderland finished seventh to qualify for Europe and Leeds came 14th. Only Burnley went down. And the early weeks of this season indicate we could be in for a similar situation. Hull City are eighth after five games, with their 2-1 loss to Newcastle their first defeat. Ipswich are 11th. And Coventry, after losing the first four games without scoring, beat Nottingham Forest 1-0 and only sit in the drop zone on goal difference. A Coventry win 25 years in the making This video can not be played Highlights: Villa survive late Spurs scare for first PL win of the season Tottenham finished 17th the last two seasons, their lowest two finishes since being in the second tier in 1977-78. But expectations were raised after a summer of big spending - with Spurs splashing out £302m as well as making two high-profile loan signings. Defence and midfield in particular were overhauled, with new wingers too. But they are left with one senior striker in Dominic Solanke, who has only scored 12 Premier League goals in over two years at the club. "I feel they have overpaid for every player

title: Sister of Pakistan's ex-PM Imran Khan arrested
description: Aleema Khanum is accused of mobilising her brother’s supporters ahead of country-wide protests.
body: Aleema Khanum, pictured in January 2025 outside Adiala jail, speaking to the media after her brother's jail sentence The sister of Pakistan's imprisoned former prime minister, Imran Khan, has been arrested ahead of next week's protests held in his support, his Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party has said. Aleema Khanum was detained in the eastern city of Lahore on Sunday afternoon, PTI officials said, calling it an "illegal detention". Her son is demanding her return. The order for Khanum's arrest, which came from Lahore's deputy commissioner, alleged that she was mobilising Imran Khan's supporters "through social media and public meetings". It added that she will be detained for 30 days. Khanum is a vocal critic of her brother's detention, regularly speaking to his supporters and the media. A police official confirmed Khanum's arrest to the BBC. According to the order, she will be taken to Kot Lakhpat jail in Lahore. Earlier in the day, her family said they had had "no contact or news of her whereabouts". "We demand the government immediately disclose her whereabouts and ensure her safe return," Khanum's son Shahrez Khan wrote on X. Many have linked her arrest to the protests that have been organised across the country on 27 September, when demonstrators plan to march to the Pakistani capital, Islamabad. The arrest order said Khanum had been mobilising people to "create law and order situations" and "raising/chanting objectionable slogans amongst the general public against the Government." Streets in Islamabad are already lined with shipping containers, ready to safeguard the city's government buildings. Local media has reported Pakistan's interior minister as saying that the protests harm the country and that the government will do everything they can to stop them. Khan has been detained since 2023, when he was sentenced to three years in prison for not declaring money earned from selling gifts he had received while in office. He has faced charges in over 100 cases, ranging from leaking state secrets to selling state gifts - all of which he has decried as politically motivated. Last year, the cricket star-turned-politician was jailed for 14 years in a land corruption case - the longest sentence he has received. While in prison, his health has being deteriorating, and last month Khan had to visit a hospital for an examination. title: Middlesex beat Leicestershire to win One-Day Cup
description: Middlesex claim their first silverware in a decade as they beat Leicestershire in a thrilling One-Day Cup final.
body: Middlesex lifted their first white-ball trophy since 2008 Metro Bank Men's One-Day Cup final, Trent Bridge Middlesex 231 (49.5 overs): Higgins 100, Duke 55; Holland 5-36 Leicestershire 200 (44.2 overs): Kelly 103; Roland-Jones 3-27, Helm 3-32 Middlesex win by 31 runs Middlesex claimed their first silverware in a decade as they fought back from a tricky start to beat Leicestershire in a thrilling One-Day Cup final at Trent Bridge. Having been put into bat by Leicestershire captain Stephen Eskinazi, Ryan Higgins' magnificent hundred dug Middlesex out of a hole and helped them reach 231 before being bowled out in the final over of their innings. Higgins, 31, struck nine fours in his 115-ball knock after his team had slumped to 71-5 in the 22nd over, putting on 135 with on-loan Yorkshire wicketkeeper Harry Duke (55) for the sixth wicket. Ian Holland returned his second-best List-A figures of 5-36 for the Foxes, while England all-rounder Rehan Ahmed took 3-55. In reply, Leicestershire too lost early wickets as former England seamer Toby Roland-Jones bowled 10 overs straight through in a fine opening spell of 3-27. Leicestershire were indebted to the efforts of New Zealand international Nick Kelly, who reached a glorious century of his own off 103 deliveries and appeared to be taking his side to victory. However, the game swung again in the over after Kelly reached his hundred as the left-hander heaved Tom Helm to Higgins on the mid-wicket fence to leave Leicestershire eight down. And that proved the decisive moment as Helm dismissed Ajaz Patel and Tom Scriven skied Naavya Sharma straight up, with captain Ben Geddes taking the winning catch. Middlesex's most recent success was the County Championship in 2016, and they had not won a white-ball trophy since lifting the T20 Blast in 2008. Ryan Higgins' hundred was crucial in Middlesex's total of 231 Middlesex had to overcome adversity more than once in Nottingham as they ended their long wait for a trophy. They faced the most difficult batting conditions of the day in the opening hour and many teams would have crumbled at 71-5. The sixth-wicket partnership between Higgins and Duke was a game-defining one as they fought back and gave their bowlers something to work with. It was Higgins' first List-A hundred and it will live long in the memory for Middlesex supporters fortunate enough to watch it as he displayed character, graft and no shortage of skill. Roland-Jones is a legendary figure at the club and he showed exactly why with a near-immaculate spell, taking the key scalps of Rishi Patel and Ahmed. Sharma is Middlesex's leading wicket-taker in this competition and the 21-year-old too impressed with the ball, making the breakthrough as he found Eskinazi's outside edge, pinning Hamza Shaikh lbw and then returning to take the final wicket. With Kelly in full flow, heads never went down and they showed all the composure of a team that have only lost once in this format all season. The wicket of Nick Kelly (right) was the decisive moment for Middlesex Off the back of their 27-point deduction in the County Championship, Leicestershire's team talk is more than likely to have been straightforward. And they started like a team with a point to prove after Eskinazi won the toss, backed by a vocal travelling support. Holland set the tone with the new ball, nicking off Nathan Fernandes and Max Holden cheaply before Tom Scriven took two wickets of his own, including a fine catch by wicketkeeper Ben Cox to remove Josh De Caires (26). Incredibly Cox caught the first five wickets to fall. Middlesex fought back through Higgins and Duke, and the Foxes will perhaps look back on that partnership as an opportunity that slipped away. Rishi Patel and Eskinazi got the chase off to a bright start, but three wickets for just three runs stalled their momentum and similarly to Middlesex's innings, Leicestershire found themselves five wickets down in the 70s. Ahmed will regret his decision not to review after being given out lbw off Roland-Jones, with replays showing it would have missed leg stump. Much as Higgins revived Middlesex, Kelly breathed new life into the Leicestershire chase with his defiant knock, which featured 10 fours and three sixes. The Kiwi left-hander was being serenaded from the stands as the runs required ticked away, but he had to drag himself from the middle with 44 runs still needed. Those fans continued to sing until the end, but were left disappointed as their team fell short. title: German Chancellor Merz calls state election a 'disaster' for his party but vows to stay on
description: Exit polls show damaging losses for Merz's centre-right CDU party in the states of Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.
body: Merz delivered a statement shortly after exit polls were announced from Berlin and Mecklenburg- Vorpommern Embattled German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has vowed to stay on despite exit polls in two local elections suggesting damaging defeats for his centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party. In the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the party was projected to only just scrape into parliament, while the AfD was on track to win the most votes. Merz called the result "a disaster" for his party. In Berlin, the ruling CDU was also expected to be beaten by Die Linke (The Left). Merz is under mounting pressure, with poor approval ratings and rumours he could even be replaced mid-term in a so-called chancellor swap. Votes took place on Sunday, a fortnight after the CDU saw its vote halved as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a major victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt. Echoing comments he made after that defeat, Merz told reporters on Sunday that he would forge ahead with his coalition government's plans to push through a package of economic, tax and welfare reforms. "The reforms have to come," he insisted. "I am taking on this responsibility, because I want to move our country forward". "I would even go so far as to say that these reforms are the antidote to the authoritarian poison that, with the fascination of authoritarianism, is penetrating ever deeper into our society," Merz added. As the projected results came up on the screen at the CDU's election night gathering in Berlin, there were no cheers or celebration. This is a party that knows it's in trouble. Friedrich Merz is going on the offensive, quickly declaring he is going nowhere. He has long coveted the top job in German politics and likely won't give it up easily. Polls for both states closed at 18:00 local time (17:00 BST), with a final result expected in the coming hours. According to public broadcaster ZDF, the AfD was projected to take 38% of the vote share in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. It was followed in second place by the centre-left SPD, on 36%. However, the AfD is unlikely to govern in the state as other parties refuse to work with it. For Berlin, the broadcaster put the CDU on 20% of the vote share when polls closed, behind Die Linke on nearly 26%. Prior to Sunday's elections, there had been intense speculation in Germany that Merz could be replaced unless his party's political fortunes improved. Earlier this week, the leaders of eight German states backed Merz, who has only held the post for 16 months. While his backers have argued that many of the problems the nation faces are inherited, Merz himself is deeply unpopular. The former corporate lawyer's tack to the right on issues like immigration has failed to erode AfD support while also alienating people further to the left. title: Last-minute Cunha goal saves Man Utd from another defeat - who rated highest at Fulham?
description: Last minute Cunha goal saves Man Utd from another defeat - who rated highest at Fulham?
body: Manchester United's Marcus Rashford tries to beat Fulham pair Timothy Castagne and Josh King at Craven Cottage Matheus Cunha's deflected last-minute equaliser spared Manchester United more misery after Lisandro Martinez's own goal had threatened to give Fulham victory at Craven Cottage. Here's how I rated the players and you can see how you scored them below. What do BBC Sport's player ratings mean? Cunha rescues point for Man Utd at Fulham Bernd Leno: On his toes to make an early save from Lisandro Martinez and scrambling when Matheus Cunha's effort looped on to a post. Denied Bryan Mbeumo with full-length save. 7 Timothy Castagne: Booked for bringing Marcus Rashford down as Manchester United broke in the second half. 6 David Affengruber: Excellent defence-splitting pass to release Josh King, but he couldn't finish. Exceptionally fortunate to escape after being outwitted by Cunha close to the goalline but stepped in to take the ball off Mbeumo as he looked to counter. 7 Calvin Bassey: Not the easiest game positionally as Manchester United played without an orthodox centre-forward. Got forward to create Fulham's goal. 7 Antonee Robinson: Pushed into advanced areas in the inside forward position, which caused the visitors a defensive issue. 7 Sander Berge (Off, Larsson 76): Shot from the edge of the area turned away by Senne Lammens. 7 Shea Charles: Midfield partnership with Berge was key in protecting the Fulham defence when the visitors had extended spells of possession around the home area. Passing let him down on occasion. 6 Oscar Bobb (off Kevin, 70): Rolled an effort just wide of the post and probably should have done better. 6 Josh King (off Andersen, 79): Always looking to get on the ball and threaten. Took a good save from Lammens to deny him at the far post and his shot across goal was going in without the visitors' keeper kicking it away. Blotted his copybook by getting booked for diving. 8 Alex Iwobi (off Palacios, 70): Also tried to exploit the inside left channel when Fulham went forward. Low cross almost created a chance for Gonzalo Garcia and another deep one did for King. 7 Gonzalo Garcia (off Muniz, 79): Half a stride away from having a tap-in from an Iwobi cross from the left. 6 Palacios (on 70, Iwobi): Kept Fulham ticking over. 6 Kevin (on 70, Bobb): Settled in well. 6 Larsson (on 76, Berge): 6 Muniz (on 79, Garcia): 6 Andersen (on 79, King): 6 Subs not used: Lecomte, Manuel Angel, Sessegnon, Smith Rowe. Senne Lammens: Key first-half saves to keep Manchester United level and came out bravely at Iwobi's feet to prevent another Fulham chance. Distribution could have been better and he didn't cover himself in glory with the Fulham goal. 6 Diogo Dalot: Tidy spin and dash into space to create a chance for Rashford but had too much work to do defensively as he lacked cover far too often. 6 Harry Maguire: Used his experience to draw a foul out of King as United tried to deal with Fulham pressure near their own goal. 7 Lisandro Martinez: Well-struck half-volley drew an excellent save out of Leno. He did eventually find the net - at the wrong end. 5 Luke Shaw (off Dorgu, 83): Returned from a three-match absence. Carrick's side are far more balanced when he is there. 7 Youri Tielemans: Wasted an excellent opportunity when he got no power behind his effort as he ran on to Rashford's short pass. 5 Kobbie Mainoo (off 79, Mount): Usual tidy game in possession without making the key passes. Never looks flustered. 7 Bryan Mbeumo: A lot of strong runs but, like many Man Utd forwards, nowhere near his best. Tough ask, but did he give Dalot enough defensive support? 6 Bruno Fernandes: Low shot against the post from Cunha cut-back but once more not at last season's levels. 6 Marcus Rashford (off 76, Zirkzee): Tried to set up Tielemans with a short pass but the Belgian couldn't finish. An attempt of his own before the break was saved by Leno and another, better opportunity flew way over the bar. 6 Matheus Cunha: Again started in the number nine role he doesn't seem suited to but created an excellent opportunity for Fernandes. Deflected shot hit the post and spun wide. Probably the visitors' most dangerous forward. 7 Zirkzee (on 76, Rashford): 6 Mount (on 79, Mainoo): 6 Dorgu (on 83, Shaw): 7 Subs not used: Darlow, Mazraoui, Mount, Yoro, Andrey Santos, Baleba, Lacey. title: Danny Dyer and Becky Hill join water industry protest
description: Activists are calling for the water industry to be returned to public ownership.
body: Danny Dyer and his daughter Dani Dyer joined a protest calling for public ownership of water companies in Leysdown Actor Danny Dyer, his daughter Dani Dyer and singer Becky Hill have attended a protest in Kent demanding public ownership of the water industry. Activists from Surfers Against Sewage descended on Leysdown on Sunday after 315,000 signed a petition calling for the water industry to be returned to public ownership. Rivals and EastEnders star Dyer, who has been running a caravan park on Isle of Sheppey as part of a new TV series, told the BBC: "Sometimes when you look out to the sea, you can smell the twang in the air." Water UK said that "no sewage spill is ever acceptable", while Southern Water said it was committed to reducing storm overflows. Dyer said that the quality of the water was "a disgrace". "It's a very dangerous thing," he told the BBC. Meanwhile Hill said that she loved swimming in the open water but found it "disgusting" to find human waste in the sea. She said that she was campaigning for her family and other families for a cleaner sea. "We can stand up and make a difference," she added. Singer Becky Hill said that she would like to see improved water quality in the sea Ed Acteson, co-founder of the protest organisers SOS Whitstable, said: "The public has had enough of being asked to accept polluted waterways, failing infrastructure and rising bills. "Water is an essential public service, not a vehicle for private profit. "We want an industry run in the interests of people and the environment, with its income reinvested in the system rather than extracted from it." Meanwhile Cliff Roney, a GMB activist who has worked in the water industry for more than 40 years, said: "I have seen this industry at its very best and now at its very worst. "If the industry is not brought back into public ownership quickly, we are heading towards a national catastrophe." Water UK said it was working to end sewage spills "as fast as we physically can". "That's why we are tripling investment over the next five years to halve spills from storm overflows and upgrade the capacity of 1,700 wastewater treatment works," a spokesperson said. "This is part of a record £104bn investment programme – the largest in the industry's history – to stop sewage entering our rivers and seas, secure our water supplies and support economic growth." Southern Water's director for environment and innovation, Nick Mills, said its 10-year, £1.5bn Clean Rivers and Seas Plan was "already starting to make a difference". "In Whitstable, we're harnessing both AI and nature-based solutions, and we're investing £90m in improvements to Swalecliffe Wastewater Treatment Works. Together, these measures will dramatically reduce storm overflows in the area." According to Defra's Bathing Water Quality site, the most recent classification for Leysdown is rated good, based on samples taken from 2022 to 2025. There have been no pollution incidents reported there, the website states. Follow BBC Kent on Facebook, external, on X, external, on Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Kent on Sounds. title: Burnham hails Greenland deal ahead of expected first Trump meeting
description: While Burnham praised the agreement, Lib Dem leader Ed Davey called it a "pretend" victory for Trump.
body: Andy Burnham has hailed a deal between Denmark and the US to "strengthen security in the Arctic" after the two countries resolved a months-long feud over Greenland. The UK prime minister and his Danish counterpart Mette Frederiksen "welcomed the US's commitment to the region" in a call on Sunday morning, Downing Street said. Nato previously said the agreement would help stabilise the region, as Trump declared Denmark would grant the US "permanent control over security, and all other needs" in the semi-autonomous Danish territory in the Arctic. Burnham's comments come as he is expected to meet Trump for the first time at the UN General Assembly (UNGA) in New York this week. Nato welcomes Greenland deal as Trump says it will give US 'permanent security control' The agreement comes after months of threats by Trump to "take" Greenland over national security concerns, citing its strategic location for defence purposes as well as its mineral wealth. No text of the agreement has been released, but Trump said in a Truth Social post the deal came with "no cost to the United States" and meant it could "do what is necessary" to "secure and defend the security of Greenland". He said it included a rule that no US adversary could maintain a military presence in Greenland or "make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval". In a readout of Sunday's phone call, a No 10 spokesperson said Burnham and Frederiksen "welcomed the US's commitment to the region and underlined the strategic and shared importance of the High North for Euro-Atlantic security". The spokesperson added: "The Prime Minister congratulated Prime Minister Frederiksen and the Kingdom of Denmark on negotiating a deal benefiting the US, Greenland and Denmark, and said he would pass on his congratulations to President Trump." While Burnham praised the agreement, Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey called it a "pretend" victory and a near carbon copy of the existing agreement. Greenlanders protested against Trump's ambitions for the territory in the country's capital, Nuuk, earlier this year "Donald Trump is trying to claim he's got a success in Greenland, but actually, all he's got is almost a carbon copy of the agreement that's persisted since the 1950s," he said at a Q&A with members at party conference. "So let Donald Trump try to pretend he's had a victory. The truth is, Europe, Nato, countries like Canada stood up to him and won." Trump had tried for months to purchase or annex the semi-autonomous territory, arguing that it was vulnerable to adversaries, including Russia and China. In the wake of the deal, Frederiksen said she was "pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement" for all three parties, which was expected to be signed at the UN General Assembly next week. The deal "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" while also recognising "the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination", she said in a joint statement with Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen. The agreement would still need to go through "the necessary parliamentary procedures to enter into force" once signed, the statement noted. Burnham has spoken with Trump at least twice since entering Downing Street and No 10 said he intends to use the UNGA to "drive forward work on issues that matter to people at home" including the cost of living and the war in Ukraine. Why does Trump want Greenland and what could it mean for Nato and the EU? title: Kelsey Parker welcomes baby after 'devastating' stillbirth last year
description: The widow of The Wanted singer Tom Parker has given birth after last year announcing the "devastating" loss of a stillborn baby.
body: Kelsey Parker attended the VIP screening of Disney's Moana at Leicester Square in July Kelsey Parker, the widow of The Wanted singer Tom Parker, has welcomed a baby after last year announcing a "devastating" stillbirth. The podcaster and author, 35, had two children with British boy band star Tom Parker before he died in 2022, aged 33, after being diagnosed with terminal brain cancer. She is now in a relationship with Will Lindsay and last June revealed the "earth-shattering news" that they had lost their baby Phoenix. On Sunday, a post on her Instagram account showed a photo of a newborn baby's arm next to a pink sign with the word River. "Welcome to the world, River. Our little bit of hope," the caption said. Celebrities including The Saturdays singer Rochelle Humes, TV presenter Susanna Reid and reality TV star Holly Hagan-Blyth have congratulated Kelsey Parker on social media. "Congratulations angel," Rochelle Humes wrote. "Oh my goodness – this is so wonderful – welcome River," Susanna Reid said. Hagan-Blyth commented "I am SO happy for you xxxx". Kelsey Parker's Instagram bio says "turning life's hardest moments into hope". Last year she posted a poem online after the loss of her stillborn baby. It was called Born Sleeping, Forever Loved, and began "the world grew quiet as you arrived, So loved, so longed for, yet not alive. Our precious boy, our angel light, Born with wings, took silent flight". Kelsey (right), pictured here in 2016, married her former partner Tom Parker (left) in July 2018 In 2023, she published a book titled With And Without You, about the first year after the death of her former partner Tom. The couple married in 2018 and had a daughter, Aurelia Rose, and a son, Bodhi. In a post after his death she wrote "thank you to everyone who has supported in his care throughout, he fought until the very end. I'm forever proud of you". Her latest pregnancy was announced in May in an Instagram post that said "somehow, through all the heartbreak, it feels like Tom and Phoenix have sent us another little gift from heaven, our little rainbow baby". title: Impressive defence seals solid start at Liverpool for Iraola
description: Liverpool are looking good defensively but Andoni Iraola needs more from his attackers after a hard-fought win at Bournemouth.
body: Liverpool have kept three consecutive clean sheets in the Premier League for the first time since September 2024. It was third time lucky for Alexander Isak after a wayward first-half effort and a second-half cross that ballooned over the bar to much amusement from the home crowd, but Liverpool's win at Bournemouth was built as much on their increasingly solid defence. The Swedish forward took his fourth goal this season well and the chants of "Isak's a Red" from the travelling supporters, long after the final whistle, told you all you needed to know. Yet it is the lack of goals Liverpool are conceding that really deserves highlighting. They were far from perfect on Andoni Iraola's Cherries return but were solid defensively. His side have now kept three consecutive clean sheets in the Premier League - the first time Liverpool have done so since September 2024 - and did not give up an xG of more than 0.76 in any of those. For all the talk of a front three who all cost in excess of £100m, Liverpool are becoming a harder side to beat under Iraola. "The more times they play together, the more solid the defensive line becomes," said Iraola, whose side remain unbeaten in all competitions. "Virgil [van Dijk], Jeremy [Jacquet], Ronald [Araujo] and Milos [Kerkez] - they're getting the connections and becoming more solid." Two reliable campaigners, goalkeeper Alisson and centre-back Van Dijk, were superb, with Alisson making a great first-half save to deny Evanilson. But arguably the biggest positive of Liverpool's campaign so far has been the emergence of Jacquet. "I think he has showed a lot of good things so far this season. Still so young, a lot to learn and a lot to give. Let's keep it going," said Van Dijk. Jacquet, 21, has started every Premier League game since making the £60m move from Rennes in the summer and is poised to make his France debut over the international break after getting the call-up from boss Zinedine Zidane. "I'm happy for him as he also received his first international call-up. He's also very young and adapted really well to the Premier League," said Iraola. "The first games, he was physically feeling the change of rhythm and I had to substitute him. "Today has been a step forward. He looked solid until the end. I think he's in a good place physically and I hope he can continue his development." Iraola was business-like on his return to Bournemouth, saying pre-match the time for talks would be after the game. He cut a frustrated figure for much of the match as Liverpool struggled to get a hold on the game but they improved after the break and deserved the win, according to Iraola, who held true to his word. After his post-match news conference, Iraola spent time talking about San Sebastian with some of the local journalists, who travelled there with Bournemouth earlier in the week for their Europa League bow. With nine points from a possible 15 in the Premier League and wins at Anfield in the Champions League and Carabao Cup, Iraola has had a largely positive start to life at Liverpool. The 44-year-old is the first manager to remain unbeaten in his first five league games in charge of Liverpool - winning two and drawing three - since Joe Fagan in September 1983. "Overall, we have definitely improved since the first games," he said. "Some of the things we still need to improve. I'm happy that it is the third league clean sheet in the row. "Today is a difficult game - you never play comfortable here, Bournemouth does not allow you to play comfortably, they put you under pressure and you have to adapt and you have to win these kind of games." The need to adapt and find ways to win games was stressed after last week's goalless draw against Fulham - but Iraola's side are learning. "We we still have to get ready because the schedule we have now is very difficult," he said. "I think we play against the top four teams and then in between there is Champions League and Chelsea in the Carabao Cup, every two or three days. So we have to be ready because this month after the break is very demanding for us." After the international break, Iraola will also need more from his attackers. Cody Gakpo was impressive again but Florian Wirtz struggled, while Bradley Barcola is still awaiting his first goal or assist for Liverpool. "It was a slow start but after the first phase Florian helped us to improve and I am much happier with his performance in the second half," said Iraola. On Isak, he said: "A striker's job is like this. He had a couple of crosses that he did not hit properly or control but in the end he has to help us to be closer to the box, to play in the opposition's half and have more meaningful possession. "And then if the team is playing there, he will receive rewards in terms of goal." Latest Liverpool news, analysis and fan views Ask about Liverpool - what do you want to know? title: Perfect 24 hours for Maresca as Man City put pressure on Arsenal
description: Manchester City head into the international break in a jubilant mood after enjoying the perfect 24 hours this weekend.
body: Manchester City are three points clear at the top of the Premier League heading into the international break Manchester City head into the international break in a jubilant mood after enjoying the perfect 24 hours this weekend. City saw champions Arsenal thumped 3-0 by Brighton on Saturday and they capitalised the following day by beating Sunderland 5-3 in a thriller at Etihad Stadium. Manager Enzo Maresca said before Sunday's game this was his side's "toughest" test of the season so far, but the end result cements an ideal start to his role at City, where he faced the unenviable task of replacing Pep Guardiola in the summer. The knives were being sharpened on Maresca after a Community Shield humbling by Mikel Arteta's Gunners in August but City have responded in superb fashion with seven straight victories in all competitions. "To be honest, I prefer to win 1-0 than 5-3 but I expected a very difficult game," said Maresca. "I knew how they good are, off the ball very aggressive and on the ball they have different weapons, set-pieces and [Brian] Brobbey. "I know it was a difficult game but [I'm] happy because we found a way to win the game and the good thing also is that these seven official games we played, they are all different, we experienced different things. "In the last one with 10 men and today was a complicated one - the Bournemouth one we were losing 1-0 so also a chance to learn from the game." Hat-trick hero Brobbey on losing side - player ratings for Man City v Sunderland Man City battle past Sunderland in eight-goal thriller Arsenal's stunning loss on the south coast opened the door for City and they took full advantage. They are the only side in England's top four divisions with a 100% winning record intact, going three points clear at the top of the Premier League. Such has been the brilliant start that Maresca becomes only the sixth Premier League manager to win his first five games in charge at a club after Carlo Ancelotti, Craig Shakespeare, Maurizio Sarri and Ole Gunnar Solskjaer. The other name? Predecessor Guardiola when he took over at City in 2016. On the pitch there were plenty of positives to take too, including the return to form of Antoine Semenyo with two goals and an assist, Rayan Cherki's delightful performance and Enzo Fernandez scoring his first goal for the club. Meanwhile, striker Erling Haaland's late effort means the Norwegian ticked off Sunderland from his scoring list - he has now netted against all 25 Premier League teams he has faced. It means City have put pressure on Arsenal in the early stages of the campaign, with the Gunners previously being tipped as heavy favourites to retain their crown. City, though, will undergo a stern examination upon their return to action after the three-week international hiatus, facing a trip to unbeaten Liverpool on Sunday, 11 October. Former Reds midfielder Charlie Adam described it as a "brilliant start to the season" for City, adding on BBC Radio 5 Live: "A lot to work on but [positive] to score five goals at home and have shown that level of performance. "With Arsenal losing on Saturday, [City] could have gone into the break top of the table and they have done that today." Before facing the Black Cats, City had only conceded two goals in their first four Premier League games. On Sunday, they ended up shipping three in 90 minutes and the way the side lost control will be of some concern to Maresca. Sunderland striker Brobbey ran captain Ruben Dias ragged all game and managed the rare feat of scoring a Premier League hat-trick and ending up on the losing side - the Dutchman becoming just the sixth player to achieve that unwanted statistic. Regis le Bris' side could have scored more and their expected goals (xG) of 4.25 was the most by any visiting side on record at Etihad Stadium in a Premier League game. Maresca said: "I am always concerned, always trying to see what we can do better. For sure, two of the three goals we conceded were too easy. "The second coming from a quick [Granit] Xhaka free-kick and that cannot happen. The third goal comes from another free-kick, too easy in that way. "We concede more chances but we scored five, created [more] and could score two or three more." Adam said: "Maresca will be delighted in terms of how it has gone, the new players coming in and how he has adapted to being the Manchester City manager. "In terms of things to improve on, they can't go through a season playing like that, they need to be able to control spaces at times, instead of getting dragged everywhere man against man." He added for Marseca this will provide a "real positive feeling" and that City "can go into this international break with real pride". title: Rangers look like they know where they want to go - Celtic just look lost
description: Tom English reflects on the first Old Firm league game of the season, in which Rangers repeated their League Cup win over Celtic.
body: Ryan Naderi's goal was enough to give Rangers victory At the end, every fibre of Derek McInnes' being must have wanted to have one of those Steven Gerrard moments, a scream of delight and relief into a Celtic Park camera lens, a human reaction to a significant victory on hostile terrain. McInnes, though, showed little emotion. He shook hands with a now beleaguered Martin O'Neill and pretty much got out of there. Later, the first words he uttered on radio were about not going "overboard" after back-to-back wins against their city rivals. "Just three points." he said. "Three points closer to Celtic." That's true, of course, but it was also the first time a Rangers manager has won his first two games against Celtic since Graeme Souness in 1986. McInnes was 15 years old at the time. So there was historical context but also deep relevance in the here and now. Rangers were good, and clearly deserving of the win, but they didn't quite hit the levels of ruthlessness of a week ago at Ibrox. They can be better and yet they won as comfortably as it's possible to win when the margin at the end is just a single goal. Their superiority would have been better reflected had they won by two. Naderi goal gives Rangers second derby win over Celtic in week 'It might be time to wrap it up' - O'Neill ponders Celtic future after defeat Rangers flip narrative as McInnes makes mark Watch: Scott Brown & Andy Halliday discuss Old Firm game on YouTube O'Neill said there was "not much between the sides" but nobody was really buying that, Celtic folk chief among them. The Celtic manager has problems and they're mounting game-by-game. His team is physically weak and mentally substandard. They have lost the elan they had in a few games in early season. They were out-played, out-muscled and out-coached. Again. O'Neill has time to pause now, time to reassess. Time, perhaps, to question whether he's got the answers to the myriad ills of his team. He doesn't have robust players in midfield because his board has not delivered them. He doesn't have the kind of wingers the club had when Daizen Maeda, Liel Abada, the still unfit Jota and Nicolas Kuhn were knocking around. In Yang Hyun-jun's absence - and week on week he appears to be spoken about as an absent world beater - James Forrest is the best winger they have. So says former captain Scott Brown, who knows Celtic players. Forrest is 35-years-old. This video can not be played 'M8 motorway between teams' - Halliday Neither does O'Neill, at present, have good instincts. Starting Sebastian Tounekti at Ibrox last week was an odd call and he changed it at half-time. Going with Sam Johnstone in goal at Rangers back-fired. Giving Luke McCowan his first start of the season on Sunday was another curious decision that didn't work. The midfielder was off the pace and never came out for the second half. O'Neill's famed ability to problem-solve and inspire has deserted him, for now. When set against the newfound organisation and vigour of this Rangers set-up then Celtic look jaded. Their supporters are being cast into a scenario that none of them want to be a part of - wondering aloud, or just quietly, if the icon still has it in him. He sounds like he does. If that is the case then he needs more from his assistants - or just better ones. From board level to coaching and playing, the whole operation looks humdrum and in need of a mighty shake. It's as if the 5-1 Champions League disintegration against LASK has removed not just confidence but heart and soul. There was little gumption at Ibrox in the 3-0 League Cup loss, there was only a brief early reaction against Ferencvaros in the Europa League before another beating, and now there's a third poor loss in a row and a fourth inside a month. This video can not be played O'Neill on back-to-back defeats by Rangers How quickly things turn. A few short weeks ago, as Rangers exited Europe to the sound of booing, McInnes didn't hold back when assessing the problems in his team. Not a possession team, not a pressing team, not a counter-attacking team, he said. They were also too young and too inexperienced, a collection of individuals but not a unit - no identity, no discernible style of play. What were weaknesses then are, in the blink of an eye, strengths now. Callowness has become youthful excellence. For the second straight week, Olwethu Makhanya was the most dominant and classy defender on the pitch. He's 22. For the second straight week the hardest-working and most effective attacking player was Ryan Naderi. He's 23. Dan Neil and Nico Raskin, aged 24 and 25, were once again hugely influential in the middle of the park. Neil looked fairly ordinary not that long ago. Now he's growing fast as Rangers captain. The oldest Rangers player from the start was James Penrice, who is 27. Celtic had six guys who were older than him in their team. The average age of the line-ups was 26.7 versus 24.4. McInnes has moulded them all into a group of players who have, against Celtic, shown maturity and togetherness. He has really hit on something. This video can not be played 'We’ve come a long way from Jablonec' Certain things stood out. At half-time, Rangers were not just ahead thanks to Naderi's goal, they were winning battles all over the pitch, just as they had done last Sunday. They were winning aerial duels by 67.6% to 32.4%, they had eight shots to Celtic's one, six on target to Celtic's zero. Camilo Duran had eight touches of the ball, Kevin Kelsy had 13 and Naderi 23. All the individual match-ups were more or less Rangers victories. Even when Celtic's club record-signing Kasper Hogh came on, not a lot changed. Rangers had more chances in the second half. Hogh got no service again, but he's beginning to look like a player so devoid of belief that even if service did come

title: Kuenssberg: I asked Earl Spencer who we should believe - him or the King?
description: Princess Diana's brother has caused a storm with his new memoir - the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg describes how she put his claims to the test.
body: Laura Kuenssberg met Earl Spencer at Althorp, the ancestral home on the grounds of which Diana is buried When I arrived at Althorp on Thursday to speak to Charles, Earl Spencer, only a handful of people were in evidence in the vast stately home, where Princess Diana had once tapdanced in the hall and rollerskated in the cavernous library. It was only hours after Buckingham Palace had sent out its blistering statement in response to the explosive claims made in a new book by Earl Spencer. From the particularly English peace of this grand countryside setting, Diana's brother had provoked a storm. That Palace statement, questioning Earl Spencer's account of the days after his sister's death, was a total contrast to its normal "never explain, never complain" mantra. But it meant that as we sat down, with oil paintings of Earl Spencer's aristocratic ancestors staring down at our TV lights, the interview was not just about his recollections of his sister. It had become about whether the earl, or the King himself, was telling the truth. As we asked Earl Spencer: which Charles are we meant to believe? This video can not be played 'There was a lightness in his tone', says Earl Spencer about Charles' reaction to Diana's death That's why it was so important to test Earl Spencer's claims. Was he really sure that the then-Prince Charles had sounded "giddy" after his former wife had died on that terrible night in 1997? Both men, after all, were in a moment of profound shock. Did the earl, a historian and former journalist himself, have evidence of another of his memories, that Charles had "hissed" at him that the world would "forget her soon enough"? Why does he, the uncle of William and Harry, think the world needs to hear his version of events from all those years ago? Earl Spencer was resolute; strong in his conviction that his version of events needed to be told as a matter of record. And he recounted his memories of his conversations with the King in meticulous detail, noting carefully in our discussion that the Palace had not explicitly denied his claims, instead choosing to question his judgement. Key takeaways from BBC interview as Earl Spencer defends claims about King Harry and Meghan's media treatment echoes what happened to Diana, Earl Spencer tells BBC There is deep unhappiness and frustration in Buckingham Palace at what Earl Spencer has put into the public domain. Their strongly worded statement tells you everything you need to know about how upset they are. "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss," it said. Bear in mind that the two Charleses have had a difficult relationship for decades. Even before either of them was born, the Spencers and the Windsors, two aristocratic families, had years of splits and spats. In the past 48 hours, allies on either side have lined up to back the two different accounts, with acolytes of the King suggesting he would never have said such things. Others emerged to back Spencer. There is no way of being completely sure what exactly happened. There hasn't been an explicit denial, but the Palace has objected in very strong terms to how Earl Spencer has presented the past. But speaking to Diana's brother for about half an hour, I felt he seemed entirely sure in his own mind. His book is carefully constructed to give his account, as well as pay tribute to his sister's life as the 30th anniversary of her death approaches. Princess Diana: My Sister's Story Watch the full interview with Laura Kuenssberg. After we had spoken, we walked down to the lake on the estate where, on a wooded island, Diana was laid to rest. It's a place where, Earl Spencer told me, she could be safe from intrusion, and is marked as a burial place with a huge stone urn. We passed the little green rowing boat he uses to go to the island to visit her, and walked to what he calls The Temple. It's an 18th Century building that now bears her name and includes a quote from her and another from his famous eulogy to her. It's a line he now says was specifically intended to be a riposte to the other Charles' suggestion that she would quickly be forgotten: Diana "will never be extinguished from our minds". Earl Spencer told me he was not being "vengeful" and that he was not trying to damage the monarchy - even saying there was more he knew about the King that he could relate but had chosen not to. But by speaking out so boldly, publishing his book, serialising it in the papers, and speaking to us, the earl was not just paying a moving tribute to his sister, but stirring up the long-running contest for control of Diana's memory. This video can not be played Watch: 'You never get over it': Earl Spencer's emotional tribute to late sister Diana In the closing moments of our interview, Earl Spencer revealed himself not to be a public figure trying to settle old scores or correct myths about his incredibly famous sister. When I asked how much he missed her, he welled up, and nearly three decades on, the tears still came. He said he missed her every day. "The thing with sibling loss? You never get over it," he said. Charles Spencer was a young man when his sister died at 36 in the most awful circumstances. He joked about crying as a 62-year-old man at the end of a TV interview in which he'd discussed the monarchy and also made claims about the King that he was well aware would stir up controversy around the world. In the normally hidden world of Althorp, the grief of a brother was still plainly on display – what happened to Princess Diana is not all in the past. title: No criminality in death of three sisters who died in sea
description: An investigation by Sussex Police into the deaths off the coast of Brighton has concluded.
body: The three sisters, here as teenagers with their father, died in the sea. From left to right, Jane Adetoro, Joseph, Christina Walters and Rebecca Walters A police investigation into the deaths of three sisters in the sea off the coast of Brighton has concluded, with no evidence found of criminality or third-party involvement. The bodies of Jane Adetoro, 36, Christina Walters, 32, and Rebecca Walters, 31, were recovered from the water near Black Rock on 13 May. A post-mortem examination found that all three women died by drowning, Sussex Police said. An inquest will aim to establish the facts of where, when and how the sisters died, the force added. The police investigation found that the sisters were dropped off by a taxi in Madeira Drive at about 22:20 BST on 12 May. No evidence was found to suggest that they visited any nightclubs or local businesses in the area at the time, police said. Up to the point of discovery of their bodies, there was "no evidence the women came to harm by any individuals", the force added. Ch Supt Adam Hays said: "From the outset of this complex and challenging investigation, we have been acutely aware of the speculation surrounding this incident, the public's unanswered questions and their desire for answers. "Our priority throughout has been uncovering the truth for the loved ones of Jane, Rebecca and Christina, because at this incident's core there has always been a grieving family coming to terms with an unthinkable tragedy and loss. "However, our inquiries have now concluded, pending any new information coming to light." The bodies of the three sisters were recovered off Brighton beach in the early hours of 13 May An inquest opened into the deaths in May at Brighton & Hove Coroner's Court and is set to continue early October. The father of the sisters, who were all living together in Greenford, London, formally identified their bodies. In a moving tribute, their father previously said that "no words can truly describe the pain of losing three daughters in the prime of their lives". He described the three as "my joy, my strength, and the beautiful light that filled our family with happiness and love".
