title: Key takeaways from BBC interview as Earl Spencer defends claims about King
description: Earl Spencer speaks to the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg ahead of the publication of his book about his sister Diana, Princess of Wales.
body: Earl Spencer has told the BBC writing his book about sister Princess Diana, which has made headlines for its criticism of King Charles, was his "duty...as an eyewitness to history". In an interview with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg ahead of the memoir's release on Tuesday, Earl Spencer said he wanted "to put things down once and for all that were true". Among claims made in Swan Song: Diana, My Sister about the King, who was then the Prince of Wales, was that he said "we'll forget her soon enough" during an argument over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in Diana's funeral procession. In a strongly worded response, Buckingham Palace said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss". Here are the key moments from Earl Spencer's interview, which include his first account of how he was told about Diana's death and criticism of press coverage of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex. Earl Spencer was in South Africa when Princess Diana died in a Paris car crash in the early hours of 31 August 1997, along with close friend Dodi Fayed and the driver of the car. He told the BBC he got a call in the middle of the night from his sister Lady Jane Fellowes, who said Princess Diana had been in a crash but "it's not too serious". But then he "kept getting more and more distressing calls" from his sister. "And then my sister Jane said, 'I'm afraid she's died.' It started... as a little prang, and then it became a broken leg, perhaps a head injury, and then death." Describing the hours after her death, Earl Spencer said he took a call at his home in Cape Town from Prince Charles, who told him how he broke the news to Princes William and Harry at Balmoral Castle. "I felt there was a sort of giddy tone," he told the BBC. "I'd had a lot of calls that day from people who cared, who were stunned... and I just felt there was a lightness in his tone about Diana's death that really jarred with me." In his book, Earl Spencer compares his tone to like a "lottery winner" and says he suspects the prince's reaction was based on how this event would free him to marry the woman he loved, his future wife Queen Camilla. When asked by Kuenssberg if he could be sure that is what Prince Charles was thinking, Earl Spencer said: "I cannot be sure, I'm saying that's what I assume from the tone is a possibility." Princess Diana: My Sister's Story. The full interview with Laura Kuenssberg is available on BBC iPlayer and will be broadcast on BBC One at 18:30 BST on Sunday Earl Spencer told the BBC he had been discussing funeral arrangements with a palace official, who said it had been agreed Princes William and Harry should walk behind their mother's coffin. Unhappy, he said he told the official it is not what his sister would have wanted, before the conversation came to an end. Soon after, the earl says he took a call from Prince Charles, who asked him about his opposition to it. "I said, 'Well, of course not, sir, she wouldn't want it'. And then he said, 'Well, I walked behind Lord Mountbatten's coffin.' And I said, 'Yes, but you were 30 and he wasn't your mother'." He then claims Charles went "ballistic... and ranted for a while" about the Spencer's sense of duty not being adequate enough before "he said 'We'll forget her [Diana] soon enough'." "I really was so stunned and after a stunned silence I said 'I can not believe you just said that' and I hung up on him", the earl told Kuenssberg during his sit down interview at his Althorp estate. Princes William and Harry walked in the procession behind their mother's coffin Responding to the Palace's statement pushing back on the story, Earl Spencer said: "I can tell you here and now, those are exactly the words he said. "I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage in my life. "I was hyper-alert to what he was saying, and those are precisely the words he said. And I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. "I don't hear him saying he didn't say that." The earl said he told "close friends and family" about the "monstrous" comment. When asked if people should believe him or the King, he said: "Well, I'm telling the truth... what else would have made me hang up on the King that day?" On what Princes William and Harry might think of the comments being brought up nearly 30 years later, he added the words "will not be a surprise" to the brothers. He also said his renowned funeral eulogy, in which he said his sister's qualities would never be "extinguished from our minds", was a "direct rebuttal" of the prince's comments. Talking about his motivations for writing the book, Earl Spencer, aged 62, said it was his "duty... as an eyewitness to history" and as someone in the "final season of my life" with his parents dying in their sixties. "I'm aware of mortality and I wanted to just put things down once and for all that were true," the historian and journalist explained. "This is not a threat, it's a fact, I know lots of things about the King which I chose not to include in the book because they were not relevant." When put to him that the statement sounded like a threat when it involved potentially damaging information, he said: "No, not at all a threat, it's just the reality." Kuenssberg questioned why he included an account of a conversation in which his sister told him Prince Charles was in love with his valet - a claim Earl Spencer said was improbable - and asked if he was motivated in including some of these allegations to create interest to sell the book. "It's in the context of a conversation where Diana is telling me that her marriage is over," the earl replied. "It's a brother

title: Watch: Earl Spencer says he felt Charles had 'giddy tone' during call after Diana's death

body: This video can not be played Earl Spencer has said he felt there was a "lightness" in the tone of the then-Prince Charles during a phone call following the death of his sister, Diana, Princess of Wales. In an interview with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg, he said he took a call at his home in Cape Town from Charles, who told him how he had broken the news to Princes William and Harry at Balmoral Castle. "I felt there was a sort of giddy tone," Earl Spencer told the BBC. "I'd had a lot of calls that day from people who cared, who were stunned... and I just felt there was a lightness in his tone about Diana's death that really jarred with me." Buckingham Palace released a rare statement on Wednesday in response to claims made by Earl Spencer in his book Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, which is due to be published on Tuesday. It said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss". title: Watch: Emotional Earl Spencer says he misses sister Diana every day
description: "This is my swan song too. I'm not here to bang on about Diana, this is my final word, celebration of her", Earl Spencer told presenter Laura Kuenssberg.
body: This video can not be played Earl Spencer, brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, said he misses his sister every day during an interview with the BBC. "That's the thing with sibling loss, you never get over it," he told Laura Kuenssberg. His book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, is due to be published on Tuesday and is expected to be highly critical of the Royal Family. He said one of the reasons the book is called Swan Song is because it is his "sign off" as Diana's brother and "final take on the situation". "This is my swan song too. I'm not here to bang on about Diana, this is my final word, celebration of her," he added. The full interview, Princess Diana: My Sister's Story, is available on BBC iPlayer and will be broadcast on BBC One at 18:30 BST on Sunday. title: Lib Dems sleepwalking to irrelevance under Davey, says council leader
description: Devon County Council leader Julian Brazil tells the BBC Ed Davey is not the right person to lead the party.
body: Julian Brazil is leader of Devon County Council A Liberal Democrat council leader has said the party is "sleepwalking into irrelevance" and questioned whether Sir Ed Davey was the right leader. Julian Brazil, the leader of Devon County Council, told the BBC the party was "lacking ambition" and "not saying the things that people can relate to". Asked whether Sir Ed was the right leader for the party, Brazil said "I wish he was" but "all the evidence is no". A Lib Dem spokesperson said the party was in "an incredibly strong position" under Sir Ed's leadership because he was focused on the "issues that really matter" such as the cost of living and the health service. "Under Ed's leadership we had our best result for a century, and achieved a record breaking streak of remarkable local election results," they added. "We are the most united party in Westminster and with Ed as leader we will stop Reform and the Conservatives and change our country after a decade of failing governments." Sir Ed led the party to record 72 MPs in the 2024 general election, but it has slipped to fourth or fifth in national opinion polls, behind the Greens and Reform UK. Brazil told the BBC the Lib Dems had "allowed other parties to go steaming past us," adding that "something has to change within the party if we're going to move to the next level and it's not happening at the moment". He added: "I think there is a fantastic opportunity now for us to be right in the middle of politics and we don't seem to be. We seem to be peripheral. "We're lacking ambition, we're lacking courage of our convictions. We're not saying the things that people can relate to." He said the party was asking people to "vote for us because we're not somebody else". Brazil became the leader of Devon County Council in May last year after the Lib Dems overtook the Tories to become the largest party, but without overall control. His comments are echoed privately by some Lib Dem MPs, as they gather for their annual conference in Brighton. In an essay, written ahead of the conference, South Cotswolds MP Roz Savage asked: "Why are we as a party struggling for relevance at precisely the moment when so many people feel powerless?" She urged the party to rediscover its "insurgent spirit" rather than being the "polite custodians of a system that leaves people feeling powerless". Sir Ed, who was elected leader in 2020, told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg he shared the "frustration" of some of his MPs that they could not bring about "real change," blaming the UK's political system. But he insisted the party was gaining ground in council elections. "It's the most successful period that we've had," he said. "But outside elections, in terms of changing the law, which is what my MPs rightly want to do, and they're a very talented bunch, and they've actually had more success than all the other smaller parties, but they want to have more." Sir Ed was asked directly about Brazil's complaints during a conference Q+A session on Sunday. "I have know Julian for many years and he is good councillor," he said. "In Devon the party doing better than it has for decades - six MPs and local councils all across the area and in parts of Devon we are showing how to beat Reform. "I'm really proud of what we have been doing in Devon." Sir Ed got a vote of confidence from former coalition cabinet colleague Sir Vince Cable, who told a fringe meeting that he was the most successful leader in the party's history and "you can't argue with success". Speaking at another fringe meeting, pollster Luke Tryl said the Lib Dems were not cutting through nationally and needed a more compelling message. The executive director of More in Common said it was possible the party could take more seats in traditional Tory heartlands at the next election, potentially putting Sir Ed in a position to be deputy prime minister in a Labour-led government. But the risk for the party, he added, was the Tories saying "if you vote Lib Dem you will get Labour". title: Justice minister 'deeply concerned' over temporary release of convicted killer
description: Gary Anderson was released on Monday from Maghaberry Prison to attend the funeral of his father but absconded and remains at large.
body: The department of justice said minister Naomi Long "remains deeply concerned surrounding compassionate temporary release of Gary Anderson and his subsequent absconding" The justice minister remains "deeply concerned" about the circumstances surrounding the temporary release of a convicted murderer. The NI Prison Service (NIPS) refused Gary Anderson permission to attend his father's funeral but that decision was quashed by the courts. Anderson was released on Monday from Maghaberry Prison to attend the funeral but absconded and remains at large. He is one of two brothers jailed for life in 2023 for the 2018 murder of Karol Kelly in Londonderry. The court service has now published the full 15 page judgement from the judicial review. It reveals the decision to refuse Anderson's request to attend the funeral was taken by the duty governor at Maghaberry Prison. But the judge found that that decision "was based upon inaccurate information which was material to the key issue of the potential risks posed by the applicant". "The information which was considered was also materially disadvantageous to the applicant." That's a reference to an internal assessment of the likelihood of Anderson reoffending, which was wrongly recorded at a higher level than recorded in the internal system. A legal representative for the prison service admitted to the court that "information containing an increased score came, not from the duty governor's personal knowledge, but from a colleague. When the system was checked, the score was sitting at 27 (medium likelihood) and not 32 (high likelihood) as stated in the decision letter." The judge, Mr Justice Rooney, found "the duty governor clearly took account of this incorrect information when making his own risk assessment and when conducting a proportionality assessment". He invited the duty governor to review the decision but that offer was declined, in a move the judge described as "somewhat surprising". Gary Anderson, who is serving a 15-year sentence for the murder of Karol Kelly, remains on the run In a statement, the Justice department said that "this opportunity was not communicated by legal representatives to those within NIPS who held responsibility for the decision". "Updates provided to NIPS following the hearing, including legal readouts, did not indicate such an opportunity had been offered." Mr Justice Rooney granted Anderson temporary release with a number of conditions attached after finding that the prison service's decision was "flawed" and took into account "irrelevant and incorrect factors". He added "the failure to secure and take account of the correct risk assessment is unlawful". The department said Minister Naomi Long "remains deeply concerned surrounding compassionate temporary release of Gary Anderson and his subsequent absconding". Following a review of the case, further information emerged regarding the handling of the case. "As soon as the minister was made aware of these issues, she instructed the director general of the Northern Ireland Prison Service to undertake an urgent investigation into these matters." "The minister is clear that it is important that all relevant facts are established and considered carefully, and she intends to update the assembly at the earliest opportunity as to the actions she will be taking to ensure that this happens." UUP leader Jon Burrows called the judgement "damning" Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) leader, Jon Burrows described the judgement as "damning" adding "it exposes catastrophic and inexplicable failures in senior decision-making, procedure and record-keeping at Maghaberry Prison". "The substantive decision to refuse Gary Anderson compassionate temporary release was, in my view, clearly correct. His subsequent absconding has only underlined the serious risk he presented. "However, that decision was catastrophically undermined by incorrect information, missing records and an extraordinary refusal to reconsider it when the court provided an opportunity to do so. "This was not a minor administrative error. The incorrect information went directly to the assessment of the risk posed by a convicted murderer and was expressly relied upon in refusing his release. "The decision collapsed because it relied upon materially incorrect information, the assessment supposedly supporting it could not be produced and the duty governor refused the opportunity to reconsider. "The family of Karol Kelly and the wider public deserve the full truth, urgent accountability and firm action to ensure that this can never happen again." title: Top Gear star Richard Hammond thanks emergency crews 20 years on from crash
description: Richard Hammond was seriously injured in a jet dragster crash at Elvington in September 2006.
body: In his post on Instagram, Hammond, pictured in 2023, thanked all those involved in saving him Former Top Gear presenter Richard Hammond has thanked emergency services for their help on the 20th anniversary of the crash in which he was nearly killed. Hammond was seriously injured in September 2006 when the 320mph (515km/h) jet-powered Vampire dragster he was driving veered off the track at Elvington airfield, near York, during filming for the BBC show. In an Instagram post, Hammond said he wanted to thank the members of the staff who rescued him and supported him following the accident "from the bottom of my heart". In the post, he spoke of the events of that day and said he would be "forever grateful" to all those who helped him in the aftermath of the crash. He wrote: "Twenty years ago today, I came to an abrupt stop upside down in a Yorkshire field, convinced I was about to die." He said he recalled having pulled the lever to release the car's parachute before trying to steer it away from disaster, "but disaster was, it seemed, my fate". "Having done everything I could to avert it, I gave myself over to that fate," he said. Richard Hammond crashed in a jet-powered dragster at Elvington airfield near York in September 2006 A front tyre had blown on the car and Hammond said in his post that he did not scream during the ensuing crash. He explained that while "it wasn't frightening", it had "simply occurred to me that the next thing on my to do list was to die". The Top Gear star spent two weeks in a coma after the crash and returned to the show in early 2007. In 2023, he spoke of how he believed his memory may have been affected by the accident. In his post on social media marking the anniversary of the crash, Hammond said: "I am only here today to note this anniversary and write these words because of the work of the many people involved in rescuing me from the shattered car, flying me to hospital and treating me there." Hammond, pictured with Clarkson (centre) and May (right) presented Top Gear until 2015 Hammond went on to name members of the Yorkshire Air Ambulance and aftercare teams who helped him, saying he would be "forever grateful" to them. He said he would not have had the lucky career breaks, amazing adventures around the world and two of the "happiest, kindest, most wonderfully talented and loving daughters" if he had not been helped that day. "Thank you all from the bottom of my heart," he added. Hammond was also injured in a serious crash during a practice run for an electric car race 11 years later in Switzerland in June 2017, when his vehicle left the road, tumbled down a hillside and burst into flames close to a house. After leaving Top Gear with co-hosts Jeremy Clarkson and James May in 2015, the trio reunited for The Grand Tour, which they presented until 2024. title: Trump says his planned triumphal arch will double as a military complex to store ammunition
description: Trump said the updated plans were at the request of the US military and for national security purposes.
body: This video can not be played A look at the design plans for Trump's triumphal arch as proposed in April US President Donald Trump has said his proposed triumphal arch will double as a complex to store military equipment, complete with the ability to deploy snipers and drones. In a Sunday morning post, Trump said he is updating the plans at the "strong request" of the US military and for "national security purposes". The "top grade" military complex and arch will "house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage", he said. He did not provide details on construction plans or timing, and it's not clear if he needs further approval for the facility. "There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform. He added that out of "the 59 top cities and Capitals", Washington DC is "the only one in the world that does not have a triumphal arch", without specifying what those cities are. Construction on Trump's 250-foot arch, planned for a site across the Potomac River from Washington DC just outside the Arlington National Cemetery, was expected to begin this month. A rendering of the design from earlier this year includes a golden, winged Lady Liberty on the top of the arch, flanked by two gold eagles, and with the phrases "One Nation Under God" and "Liberty and Justice for All" inscribed in gold on either side of the structure. It will stand 250-feet (76m) from its base to the top of the golden lady statue. At that height, the structure would dwarf the 99-foot Lincoln Memorial nearby and be half as high as the Washington Monument. Plans for the arch from earlier this year feature a golden, winged Lady Liberty on the top, flanked by two gold eagles. The BBC has contacted the Department of Defence for more information on the updated plans. Trump has pursued a number of construction projects during his second term to revamp the US capital, including a gilded makeover of the Oval Office, constructing a White House ballroom estimated to cost around $400m, paving over the White House Rose Garden, and renovating the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. The triumphal arch is one of the biggest projects Trump has set his sights on. title: Man rearrested after missing mum's remains found
description: The remains of mother-of-three Joanne Sheen were found almost seven years after she went missing.
body: Joanne Sheen was reported missing by her family in February 2020 A 56-year-old man has been rearrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder and further arrested on suspicion of murder after human remains were identified as a missing mother-of-three. Joanne Sheen, then aged 44, was last seen when she travelled from Fareham to Southampton with a friend on 5 December 2019. Metropolitan Police officers were called to Padstow Walk in Feltham, London, on 12 August after bones were found in shrubland damaged by a fire a week earlier. The man, from Southampton, first arrested in 2020, has been released on conditional bail. Another man, also 56 and from Southampton, was released on bail after being arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder. The human remains were found at Padstow Walk in Feltham, south-west London Sheen's disappearance sparked a major police investigation, which the force said led to more than 4,000 lines of inquiry, more than 300 statements taken and detailed searches at more than 10 addresses carried out using numerous vessels. Sheen was reported missing by her family in February 2020, two months after she was last seen. An investigation led to a number of arrests on suspicion of conspiracy to murder in 2020, but no-one was charged and the case remained unsolved. Officers previously said she had no fixed address and did not own a vehicle or hold a bank account. The area damaged by the fire was cordoned off after the remains were found by a member of the public London Fire Brigade attended a fire at Bedfont Pits on 5 August that damaged about two hectares of shrubland. The Metropolitan Police said human remains were found by a member of the public at the site near Bedfont Lakes Country Park a week later. Detectives in London handed the investigation over to Hampshire Police after the remains were identified as those of Sheen. title: Homes evacuated over fears fire at seaside hotel weakened building's structure
description: Residents living near Folkestone’s Grand Burstin Hotel relocated after safety inspectors' concerns.
body: Kent Police said the fire at the Grand Burstin Hotel was being treated as suspicious Residents living near to a fire-damaged seaside hotel in Folkestone have been evacuated over safety fears that the intensity of the basement blaze weakened the building's structure, the council has said. The blaze broke out at the Grand Burstin Hotel in Marine Parade in the early hours of Saturday, with about 280 people evacuated. Folkestone and Hythe District Council said 90 people were relocated from Pavilion Court in Marine Terrace following concerns raised by safety inspectors. Kent Police said the blaze was being treated as suspicious and has appealed for witnesses. The fire service said the blaze was believed to have started in the basement A council spokesperson said the Pavilion Court residents had been given hotel accommodation in the town, adding that it was "working to arrange alternative housing for all affected residents while the Grand Burstin undergoes further assessments and any required works to make it safe". In a statement, Britannia Hotels Group, which runs the Grand Burstin, said it was "fully cooperating with Kent Police and supporting their investigation into the circumstances surrounding the fire". It added: "We remain in close contact with all relevant authorities and will provide any assistance or information required as their enquiries continue. "In the meantime, the safety and wellbeing of our guests and team members remains our priority." A total of 26 fire engines were sent to the hotel at about 01:05 BST on Saturday, Kent Fire & Rescue Service said, adding: "It's believed the fire started in the basement of the property." On Sunday, a fire service spokesperson said the firefighting operation had ended, and the scene had been handed over to Kent Police. Station manager Lawrence Pater said the "very severe" fire had raised concerns about the structural integrity of the building and that the fire service was seeking advice from inspectors. Folkestone & Hythe District Council set up a welfare centre at the Three Hills Sports Park for hotel residents evacuated on Saturday. Other local businesses, including nearby pub The Harbour Inn, also opened their doors to those affected. John Dighton said he was told to leave his Pavilion Court flat on Saturday evening Speaking to the BBC, John Dighton, who was evacuated from Pavilion Court, said he was told to leave his flat at about 19:00 on Saturday. The 50-year-old said: "We don't know how long we will be out for but we have grabbed stuff for a couple of days. "The worst thing is the not knowing. We are at a hotel over the road from the flats." Ross Honeycomb, 39, was staying at the hotel with his family and told the BBC on Saturday how they were woken by fire alarms at about 01:00. He said: "I thought I was dreaming, it was horrifying. "We looked out and there was smoke billowing from the underground car park. Later we started hearing explosions." Kevin Crawford, 91, and his wife Kathleen, 82, said they had booked in for a two-week stay at the hotel. The couple, from London, told the BBC that they were in their room on the sixth floor when they heard a fire alarm. "We saw the fire but we thought the fire brigade had it under control," said Kevin. "We managed to sleep through it. At the time, we didn't realise how bad the fire was." The council's chief executive, Susan Priest, said on Saturday: "The extent of support of organisations, including Three Hills, Morrisons and the Salvation Army, has been amazing and helped to ensure that visitors and residents were looked after, supported and had food and hot drinks. "This was an extremely difficult day, firstly for the hotel guests and this evening for our residents who have had to move out of their homes." title: Billionaire Man United owner loses moral high ground after tax exile, Labour chair says
description: The billionaire businessman told the BBC he has lost confidence in the UK due to a combination of high taxes and high immigration.
body: The Labour Party chair has said Sir Jim Ratcliffe loses "the moral high ground" by making statements about the UK while living in tax exile. Speaking to Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Bridget Phillipson said she would take the billionaire businessman's comments that the UK was "on the slide" with a "pinch of salt". Sir Jim, the founder of petrochemical giant Ineos and Manchester United's co-owner, told the BBC he has lost confidence in the UK due to a combination of high taxes and high immigration. He has been a tax resident in Monaco since 2020 and said "things would have to get better" in the UK for him to return. When questioned over the remarks, Phillipson said Sir Jim loses "the moral high ground" by "making these kinds of pronouncements while choosing to make decisions, that he is within his rights to make, to become a tax exile". Pushed on whether it bothers her that people who create jobs and pay a lot of tax were leaving the UK, the minister said she was "optimistic about our country's prospects". Other high profile billionaires have left the UK, including including steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal and most recently the UK's third biggest taxpayer, hedge-fund boss Chris Rokos. But, Philipson argued the country was in a good position ahead of the Budget next month, and Andy Burnham has shown a "sense of hope and optimism whilst recognising that many families are still struggling and there is more to do." "Of course, there are challenges, including big international headwinds, but I fundamentally believe that we are in a strong position going into this budget because of the decisions taken over the last two years, and I believe our country's best days lie ahead of us," she said. Philipson declined to speculate over whether there would be tax rises in the Budget on 28 October, and said the government remained committed to being disciplined about its spending rules. Billionaire Man United owner says he has lost confidence in the UK UK's third-biggest taxpayer to leave for Greece Sir Jim, whose wealth is estimated to be about £15bn, also criticised the government for failing to invest further in North Sea oil and gas, claiming it amounted to "insanity". "You would expect [the government] to exploit our natural resources and we're clearly not doing that. We're shutting it down. "If you tax everybody to death, they're all going to leave. And that's what's happening," he added. Sir Jim's company, Ineos, operates the Forties pipeline which transports about 30% of the UK's North Sea oil. The government spokesperson said that oil and gas would play an important role in the UK "for decades to come", but they added: "The transition to homegrown clean power is the only way to deliver energy and financial security for families and businesses." title: Lib Dems vow to end 'computer says no' economy to boost growth
description: Deputy leader Daisy Cooper also proposes a Growth and Defence Partnership with the EU in a speech to her party conference.
body: Deputy leader Daisy Cooper says she has a plan for growth Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper has warned the UK's economic growth is being held back by a "computer says no" approach. She unveiled a 30-page growth plan aimed at removing barriers to business as part of her speech to the Lib Dem conference in Brighton. Cooper, who is also the party's Treasury spokesperson, said too many ideas, start-ups and research started in Britain but ended up being taken overseas. She also outlined a new Growth and Defence Partnership with the EU to reverse the economic damage of Brexit, that she claimed is currently costing the UK £90bn a year in lost tax revenue. Speaking on stage in Brighton, she said: "We build brilliant start-ups, and watch too many leave to scale somewhere else. We produce world-class research, and too little of it becomes a British product." "Britain has the potential," she went on. "The system holds it back. The computer says no. "This plan tears down the barriers to investment, to innovation, and to skills." Cooper called for the creation of a digital one-stop-shop service for businesses and investors, combining tax, regulatory, legal, Companies House, and general business services. Creating this within a new Department for Growth would simplify red tape and help small and medium-sized businesses compete and grow, she said. Cooper said a new Growth and Defence Partnership with the EU, would be the "single biggest growth lever we could pull" by deepening ties with Europe. "It could turbo-charge our economy and start to reverse the economic damage of Brexit which is currently costing us £90bn a year in lost tax revenue," she said. "In power, we will strike the deal on the single market, we will strike the deal on a customs union, we will strike the deal on defence." She claimed the Lib Dems would say "what no other party dares to say" that Britain "belongs at the heart of Europe, and we will take her there." Before becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham said he would like to see the UK rejoin the EU in his lifetime but he respected the result of the 2016 referendum and had no plans to "re-run" Brexit arguments. On Friday, Chancellor John Healey met EU ministers and asked them to let the UK into its Made in Europe scheme, aimed at protecting industries from unfair Chinese competition. Healey also pushed for closer UK-EU partnerships on tech, defence, and manufacturing at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin the same day, as Burnham held his first official meeting with Taoiseach (Irish prime minister) Micheál Martin in No 10 North. Seeking to differentiate the Liberal Democrats from rival parties, she said her party would avoid "more punishing tax hikes from Labour or painful spending cuts by the Conservatives and Reform UK". She attacked Healey for his speech earlier this month, which "contained no vision, no ideas, and absolutely no mention of Europe". Cooper also attacked Reform and the Conservatives for being "locked in a race to the bottom without a single credible costing between them". She highlighted how the new Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith had helped to deliver and defend the Liz Truss mini-budget, which she said "crashed the pound, it spiked your mortgage, it cost the country billions", and Nigel Farage defended the move. "But the worst could be yet to come: Farage is modelling himself on Trump," she said. "A President who has used the presidency to enrich himself, dismantled anti-corruption safeguards and pardoned crypto criminals. "We cannot allow that kind of politics to take hold in our country -- We cannot afford to allow Nigel Farage to win the keys to No 10 or let the Tories put him there." title: Chiltern Railways renationalised after 30 years
description: It joins Great British Railways as part of government plans to save money and improve services.
body: Chiltern Railways, which was privatised in 1996, has become part of the Great British Railways Chiltern Railways has been brought into public ownership after 30 years as a private company. It is the 10th rail company now under the Great British Railways (GBR), the government's programme of public ownership, which it says will save money and improve services. Chiltern Railways, which was privatised in 1996, operates services from London Marylebone to Buckinghamshire, Oxfordshire and Warwickshire, as well as destinations in the West Midlands. The government said the transfer into public ownership would tackle overcrowding by introducing 25 additional daily services from December. The start of the first day of public ownership saw some disruption, with Chiltern warning the line between Birmingham and Marylebone, external was "expected to be much busier" due to the late notice of the West Coast Main Line closure affecting services at London Euston. The operator said it would run more trains than usual between the stations with significantly enhanced capacity. The Department for Transport (DfT) said the additional weekday services under GBR would provide 10,000 extra seats. They would include half hourly services during weekdays on the Chiltern Main Line between London and Birmingham, as well as more weekend services. Rail minister Lord Peter Hendy met staff at Marylebone Station on Thursday alongside the first Chiltern train in the GBR livery. "The most difficult thing on Chiltern is that it's shorter capacity and those extra trains and those extra seats will make a real difference to people travelling on this line up here from Marylebone every day," he said. Rail minister Lord Peter Hendy said the government hoped to "build a railway the country can trust and rely on" The rollout of the new trains would also improve accessibility and provide better Wi-Fi on board, the rail operator said. From Sunday, passengers whose train had been cancelled can use another operator's service two hours either side of their train to get to their destination at no extra cost, it added. Chiltern's interim managing director Tony Baxter said: "Sunday is a significant milestone for Chiltern Railways and we look forward to working together with the wider rail industry to deliver a better railway for everyone in Great Britain." The aim is for GBR to operate all passenger services by the end of 2027. Great Western Railway's services will be the next operator to be brought into public ownership, on 13 December. Lord Henry said: "Every transfer into public ownership gives us the chance to tackle the bread-and-butter issues people care about – more frequent, comfortable trains that turn up on time. "As we set up Great British Railways (GBR), we're putting passengers first. "It will not happen overnight, but we will build a railway the country can trust and rely on and that will create growth, jobs and homes." title: MP calls for Yorkshire to get its own parliament
description: Harrogate Lib Dem MP Tom Gordon says Yorkshire devolution should go further than elected mayors.
body: Harrogate and Knaresborough Lib Dem MP Tom Gordon would like to see devolution go further A Liberal Democrat MP has called on Prime Minister Andy Burnham to go further with his devolution plans and give Yorkshire its own parliament. Harrogate and Knaresborough MP Tom Gordon said too much power was currently in the hands of elected mayors and a Yorkshire parliament would better reflect the region. Burnham has recently set out plans to give elected mayors more power over planning and tackling fly-tipping and said he would give them a share of income tax and business rates. But Gordon told BBC Politics North he believed that giving more money and powers to four separate Yorkshire mayoralties actually deepened divides in the county and a Yorkshire parliament would be "a good thing". Yorkshire currently has three Labour mayors - Oliver Coppard for South Yorkshire, Tracy Brabin for West Yorkshire and David Skaith for York and North Yorkshire - as well as Luke Campbell, the Reform UK mayor of Hull and East Yorkshire. The MP said if Wales, Scotland and London could have a parliament, then so should Yorkshire Gordon said Yorkshire had a population larger than Scotland and an economy larger than Wales, and, as such, it should have a parliament with a broader spectrum of views represented, rather than so much power resting with the four elected mayors. The Lib Dem said that while people had been told the recent local government reorganisation in North Yorkshire would "simplify" the situation, he believed that was not the case. "We've ended up with a new North Yorkshire Council at a higher tier and a Harrogate town council below it, so we've ended up with two tiers. In fact, there's a third tier when you throw in the regional mayor," he said. "So we've ended up with more tiers, but those powers have been moved upwards rather than down to people. "I think we owe it to have everyone have a seat at that table, not just all that power put in one person's hands." Gordon said he believed a Yorkshire parliament was the way forward "if it's good enough for Scotland, if it's good enough for Wales, if it's good enough for London". "We should have a model where we have broader people elected to it who can feed in all those issues into a Yorkshire-wide parliament. That, to me, is only a good thing," he said. The idea of a Yorkshire parliament has previously been advocated by the Yorkshire Party. Since 2014, the party has argued that it would create a more "engaged, democratic society". Meanwhile, when devolution deals were first being discussed, a proposal was put forward for one mayor for all of Yorkshire. The so-called "One Yorkshire" plan was backed by 18 of the region's 20 local councils, while Sheffield and Rotherham opted for a separate South Yorkshire solution. However, the then Conservative Communities Secretary James Brokenshire rejected the proposal and said the plan did "not meet our criteria". Deals were later done for the four counties within Yorkshire In a speech earlier this year, Burnham said decision-making needed to be "pushed to regions and local communities", adding that it would see "good growth in every postcode". David Skaith says Yorkshire's mayors work "collectively" Responding to Gordon's comments, Skaith said the Greater Manchester and Liverpool City Region, which has had devolved powers for longer, had worked "really well". But Skaith also said he believed that all views were represented within the current system. "It's not just four mayors who sit in Yorkshire, all our combined authorities are made up of those local authorities as well," he said. "So, I'm not making decisions sat in York and North Yorkshire on my own. It's in partnership with the two local authorities." Skaith pointed to the so-called "White Rose Agreement", signed by himself and the mayors of South and West Yorkshire, pledging to work closer on things like transport. “Rail is a classic case - Northern Powerhouse Rail - where we got particularly the working around York station and the wider area of North Yorkshire," he said. "We have got that collective buy-in as to what we want for Yorkshire for rail. "That's why we've got so far with government, because we work collectively as mayors, because we know our transport is so interconnected." When he was prime minister, David Cameron, together with Chancellor George Osborne, previously introduced "devolution deals". Successive Conservative governments have extended those deals and powers for regional mayors. However, York Conservative councillor Chris Steward warned that a parliament for Yorkshire would be "an absurd, costly and bureaucratic nonsense". "I am a proud Yorkshireman, having lived here all my life," he said. "But while it is a county for so much - from the scenery to county cricket to all the things making it famous - as we saw in the discussions about devolution, it is not a functional economic geography and politics viewed across the region would not work. "People do not want yet another layer of politicians and the related expenses." Reform UK has been approached for comment. title: Ed Davey calls for immediate 10p cut to fuel duty
description: Sir Ed blamed Donald Trump's war with Iran for damaging the UK economy and pushing fuel prices up.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey calls for immediate action on fuel costs Sir Ed Davey is calling on the government to immediately cut fuel duty by 10p a litre until Christmas as part of a package of policies aimed at cutting the cost of living. The Liberal Democrat leader is also urging the government to scrap a permanent increase in fuel duty which is set to take effect in January. Fuel duty was frozen under the Conservatives in March 2022 and Sir Keir Starmer's government continued the freeze, deciding in May to push back a planned 3p increase in September until the end of this year. The Lib Dems claim cutting 10p from fuel duty now would mean fuel would drop by 12p per litre at the pump. Sir Ed claimed drivers should be supported and a temporary three-month fuel duty cut would pay for itself by stimulating the economy. "Petrol and diesel prices are higher than they've been for a long time because of Trump's mad war with Iran, and people need help now," he said. The policy would cost about £2bn, he said, adding: "It's a three-month package, a temporary package, but if you look at the extra money the government will get through the energy profits levy, from gas taxes, from VAT and fuel duty, it's self-funding." In a speech to his party's conference on Tuesday, Sir Ed will make further calls to cut the bus fare cap from £3 to £1, and reduce rail fares by 10%. He will also call for VAT to be dropped from public charging points for electric vehicles and a review of network costs the Lib Dems have labelled unfair. Chancellor John Healey is under pressure to raise taxes or cut spending at his Budget next month, amid soaring government borrowing costs. Asked about Sir Ed's call for a fuel duty cut, Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson told Laura Kuenssberg: "I'm sure John Healey will be open to any and all suggestions ahead of the budget but actually this is an area where the Labour government has taken action on fuel duty already. "Whilst I recognise what the Lib Dems have to say on this topic, this is the element of politics about it - they've got their conference, they're making their pitch, good luck to them." title: Family shares hidden cost of cancer care
description: Maya, 13, from Hythe in Kent, was diagnosed with neuroblastoma when she was three.
body: The family of Maya, 13, from Hythe, say they have faced an increased financial burden while they care for her after she was diagnosed with neuroblastoma The parents of a teenage girl with a rare form of childhood cancer say the hidden costs of caring for their daughter have left them in fear of losing their home. Maya, 13, from Hythe in Kent, was diagnosed with neuroblastoma at three years old, but relapsed in 2023 having been in remission for five years. Her mother, Dellanie, said the pressure of paying a mortgage and bills whilst she and her husband, Terry, are working less to care for Maya is continuing to take its toll on their family of five. Dellanie, an NHS nurse, said: "Whilst your child is poorly and you are fighting for her life, the bills don't stop coming." She added: "My husband has lost his income as he is caring for Maya, and these days you need two people working just to keep your head above water. "It has been very, very difficult but our aim has always been to to look after our child as well as each other. "I always put a brave face on - of course I'm hurting, but I can't be in the corner crying." Maya, who her mother described as a "larger than life person" who loves animals and music, was first diagnosed with neuroblastoma near her adrenal gland when she was three-years-old. Dellanie says Maya is a "larger than life person" who loves animals and music Neuroblastoma is a rare cancer which mainly affects children under five-years-old and around 100 children are diagnosed with it a year in the UK, according to Cancer Research UK. After initially going into remission, Maya's neuroblastoma returned three years ago, and has since been cared for by specialist teams including at the Royal Marsden hospital in London, and Great Ormond Street Hospital. In 2025, during a clinical trial of CAR T-cell therapy, a technique currently used to treat some types of leukaemia and lymphoma, Maya developed a brain injury which Dellanie said left her "profoundly disabled". Her disability meant Terry had to leave his job to care for Maya full time, while Dellanie reduced her working hours to care for her, and support her husband. Dellanie said: "I just have to be grateful for what we have got. "At the moment, Maya is a fighter and there is so much fight in her." Charity Young Lives vs Cancer says families of children with cancer face average extra costs of around £700 a month, and an average loss of income of about £6,000 per household. Sonia Malik, the charity's associate policy director, said: "We find people are having to dip into savings, and most of these costs are immediate. "It impacts the whole family and their lives are thrown into chaos. "The financial stress should be the last thing families have to think about." Malik said that some support is available for cancer patients and their carers, such as financial support from charities, disability benefits and carer's allowance, but it can take time for families to receive benefits support. title: Townsend run over by pitch roller in Thailand
description: Former England winger Andros Townsend jokes that playing Stoke away "wasn't so bad after all" following a bizarre incident before a game in Thailand.
body: Andros Townsend moved to Thailand in 2025 when he joined Kanchanaburi Power Former England winger Andros Townsend joked that playing Stoke away "wasn't so bad after all" following a bizarre incident in Thailand in which he was run over by a pitch roller. The 35-year-old former Tottenham, Luton and Crystal Palace forward plays for PT Prachuap in Thai League 1. Townsend was warming up before a match at Pattani on Saturday when a member of staff appeared to lose control of a heavy pitch roller. Townsend's left leg briefly got stuck under the vehicle, but he was unhurt. He came off the bench late on in a 3-0 win., external Townsend, who won 13 caps for England, made light of the incident on Instagram, referencing one of his recent posts in which he compared a sun-drenched Thai away trip with previous visits to Stoke's Bet365 Stadium. He wrote:, external "It turns out Stoke away wasn't so bad after all. Swipe to see why." title: Littler could boycott Dutch events over booing
description: Luke Littler threatens a boycott of playing in the Netherlands after being booed and whistled at the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam.
body: Littler has won back-to-back PDC World Championship titles World champion Luke Littler has threatened to stop playing in the Netherlands after being booed and whistled at during the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam. The referee stopped the match during his narrow win against Nathan Aspinall in the last eight on Saturday to warn the hostile crowd about its behaviour, before play resumed. It followed Littler also being booed during his win against home favourite Danny Noppert on Friday. Littler has faced similar treatment in Germany and has stopped playing in European Tour events in the country. Asked if he was prepared to take a similar stance for Dutch events, the 19-year-old told Online Darts: "100%." Littler, who is expected to play at the European Championship in Dortmund in October, added: "With the Germans, I haven't been for a long time, we will have to see in Dortmund whether it changes or stays the same. "If the Dutch stay like this, then I'm not going to do any Euro tours over there. There's just no point in me travelling, wasting my time whilst I'm getting booed. "I just want to play my darts, obviously sign autographs. "The past two nights, I've done nothing, I've just walked off stage and not thanked anyone. There's no point thanking everyone when they are booing me." Littler was also booed during a win over Rob Cross at the PDC World Championship in December. After the match, he said: "I'm not bothered [by the booing]. Really not bothered. You guys pay for tickets and you pay for my prize so thanks for booing me." title: German elections under way which could decide fate of Chancellor Merz
description: The chancellor is facing intense political pressure which will increase if his party struggles in Sunday's polls.
body: Local elections are taking place in two German states on Sunday which could increase the political pressure on Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Opinion polls in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommerm suggest Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) is at risk of damaging defeats, which would raise further questions about the chancellor's future. These latest elections come after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won a major victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt two weeks ago, while the CDU saw its vote halved. There has been speculation in Germany that Merz could be replaced as chancellor mid-term unless the CDU's political fortunes improve. He has said he will carry on but is facing poor approval ratings amid rumours of a so-called chancellor swap, though his challengers are "still hesitating", writes German news site Tagesschau, external. According to the polls, Merz's conservatives could lose power in Berlin as it tussles with Die Linke (The Left) over first place. Meanwhile in the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the CDU has only just been hovering above the 5% threshold needed for a party to enter the state parliament. It could spell their worst ever result in a state election. How did it come to this after just 16 months in power? Friedrich Merz is having to answer for the tumbling popularity of his own party, while the political force that he aimed to counter - the AfD - continues its rise. Some branches of the AfD are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence, a designation it strongly rejects. But its anti-immigration, Russian-friendly, Germany-first agenda has found fertile ground in the country's former communist east. The AfD is hoping to build on its recent landslide win in Saxony-Anhalt by topping the polls in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. However, the centre-left SPD has staged a late comeback to be in contention for the top spot through its lead candidate, Manuela Schwesig. Currently the state premier, Schwesig is trying to sweep up the anti-AfD vote as she bills herself as the "Die Frau gegen Blau" - "Woman against Blue", the AfD's party colours. But her local popularity belies the far poorer fortunes of her national party which is locked in a loveless coalition with Merz's CDU. Reinhart thinks the chancellor is out of touch with the German public In a queue for a campaign event in the city of Neubrandenburg, AfD supporter Reinhart tells us that the traditional parties are being washed away. "Not only in Germany. In Italy, in France, in Great Britain. Everywhere the traditional parties go down." He smiles when asked what he thinks of Merz, saying: "Oh well everyone thinks the same about him. "He is arrogant, out of touch, not on the same level as the general public." Merz's backers argue that the chancellor has had a tough time with global events and that a lot of the problems the nation faces are ones he has inherited. But whatever faith people had in his ability to fix those problems, it is apparently ebbing away - and, the brutal truth is, it can be hard to find voters who like him. The former corporate lawyer's tack to the right on issues like immigration has failed to erode AfD support while also alienating people further to the left. His blunt communication style has also caused irritation, such as his dismissal of "work-life balance", telling Germans they need to work more and take less sick leave. Supporters would argue he is a man who is ready to administer the medicine the nation needs, even if people do not like the taste of it. But the country's long-stuttering economy, high energy costs and fraught debates about immigration are feeding a sense of national gloom. Earlier this week, the leaders of eight German states backed Merz and said restorting trust in the CDU lay in "listening ​and taking political action, not in debates ​over personnel". But while no one within his party has openly challenged Merz for the top job, murmurings of discontent have grown louder. Martin Rohloff, the CDU candidate for Neubrandenburg, thinks Merz does not have the "Fingerspitzengefühl, the feeling for the small persons". Rohloff believes there are people with "better feelings" towards the public than the chancellor "Maybe he wants the right things," muses Rohloff, but "he cannot communicate well". Asked if Merz should go, he says it is not an easy question but: "If I have to answer yes or no, I would say yes. There are other people who maybe have better feelings for the public." Merz has vowed to carry on as his coalition government aims to push through a package of economic, tax and welfare reforms that are finally due before parliament this autumn. But Sunday's vote brings a danger for the chancellor - that he is already out of time. The chancellor is reportedly due to meet senior party figures in Berlin on Sunday evening having already cancelled a planned trip next week to New York, in an apparent effort to contain the crisis. A staunch backer of Ukraine, the fall of Friedrich Merz would trigger further instability in a continent already rocked by warnings of increased Russian aggression. How significant are AfD's historic gains for Germany and the rest of Europe? title: 'Beat the Aussies' - new England coach Fleming's key aim
description: New Test coach Stephen Fleming says he shares English cricket’s “obsession” with the Ashes and arrives with the goal to “beat the Aussies”.
body: This video can not be played England job one of the most prestigious in cricket - Fleming New Test coach Stephen Fleming said he shared English cricket's "obsession" with the Ashes and arrives with the goal to "beat the Aussies". Fleming was speaking to the media for the first time since being appointed in July and ahead of taking charge for the tour of South Africa in December. Like his predecessor Brendon McCullum, Fleming is from New Zealand, the "little cousin" to Australia, in his words. The next Ashes series is in the UK next summer, when England will look to defeat the Australians for the first time since 2015 and avenge a dismal 4-1 defeat down under last winter. Asked if England are too obsessed with beating Australia, Fleming told BBC Sport: "No, because I have an obsession with it as well. New Zealand has an obsession with it, we love it. "We want to beat the Aussies. We're heavily linked to England performances. We have a deep desire to beat Australia in everything, as the little cousin. We are linked, and I'm incredibly excited about being part of it. "You don't think you're ever going to get that opportunity. To have that opportunity and be part of it, I can't wait. "I want to be my best self and have a team that represents itself in the best possible way. I've got a vision of that and it's aspirational. It will be brilliant." Listen to the full Stephen Fleming interview on the TMS podcast Fleming on England discipline, Stokes, late arrival and coaching styles Fleming, the former New Zealand captain, did not taste victory in any of the 14 Tests he played against Australia. He succeeds his former team-mate McCullum, who was sacked as Test coach earlier this summer, but remains as boss of the white-ball team. England won only two of McCullum's final 10 Tests in charge, including the hammering in Australia. Part of the criticism of England under McCullum and former captain Ben Stokes was their inability to adapt to the changing situations of Test cricket, as well as a lack of attention to detail. Fleming is a great friend of McCullum – the pair are business partners. He described the difference between the two as being: "I'll bet on the favourite and he'll bet on the longest odds possible." On whether a Test team should have a brand or style, Fleming said: "I don't think so. The greatest thing for a team to do is to be able to play conditions and situations. "I'd love people to say we are well-planned, there's a discipline and a really strong basic structure to what we're doing, but there's also a bit of flair." Stephen Fleming, left, and Brendon McCullum, right, played 32 Tests together between 2004 and 2008 The final months of McCullum's reign were dogged by late-night drinking controversies, which continued after England changed the Test coach. On Friday, Derbyshire Police announced they had closed an investigation involving England pace bowler Brydon Carse following allegations of an assault last month. Though Carse will face no action from the police, he now faces an investigation from the Cricket Regulator. He remains available for England selection, albeit has not been part of a squad in any format since the Derby incident. "There are standards," said Fleming. "We pick on runs and wickets primarily, but I think it's foolish not to also say there are standards that need to be set. "You need to behave in accordance with your position. We're in a very privileged position, and it's understanding that privilege and what goes along with it. It can't be convenient. You can't be when it suits you to do the right things, then when you don't want it to suit you, not. "You've got to live it every day. If we can create something when you want to live it every day and better, then that's really powerful." Fleming was at Old Trafford for England's defeat of Sri Lanka in the third T20 on Saturday. Earlier in the week he visited a number of counties and met Stokes during Durham's draw against Worcestershire. Stokes abruptly retired from international cricket in July and has a previous relationship with Fleming from their time together with Chennai Super Kings at the Indian Premier League. But Fleming said he had too much "respect" for Stokes' decision to attempt to coax him out of retirement. "He was in a great space, really happy, enjoying his time with Durham," said Fleming. "He's got a good winter planned with the family and is very much at peace with his decision. When a player makes that decision to retire, I respect that decision 100%. "To try to turn that around and question that is wrong. I know how much goes into that type of decision, and I respect that." Almost two months after being appointed Test coach, Stephen Fleming outlined what the England team may look like under his stewardship. He was calm, measured and authoritative, perhaps showing he is exactly the sort of leader England need after a chaotic period on and off the pitch. There were also signs of Fleming's character and sense of humour. He joked he has a "stress fracture of the left ear" after all the phone calls he has had with those connected with the England team, then laughed about occasionally turning up in fancy dress to relax the environment of his Chennai Super Kings team. Most revealing was the description of his relationship with Brendon McCullum – "I'll bet on the favourite and he'll bet on the longest odds possible". There were plenty of times during McCullum's reign as Test coach where those long-odds bets were placed, while Fleming seems much more likely to play the percentages. The two are great friends, which should help with a split-coaching dynamic that has not always served England well in the past. "Big brother" was one way the Fleming-McCullum dynamic was referred to, and there was a sense that England now have a grown-up in charge

title: New £1m grant to help groups protect green spaces
description: The cash can be used by local communities to protect threatened green spaces and wildlife sites.
body: The grant from the Summerfield Charitable Trust aims to help protect woodland and green spaces A £1m fund has been set up to help local communities protect threatened green spaces. The Summerfield Charitable Trust said the money would help groups buy and safeguard local woodlands and wildlife sites when they come up for sale. It is part of a new initiative from the Gloucestershire Nature and Climate Fund and the Gloucestershire Local Nature Partnership. "We need an initiative like this now more than ever," said Diane Hill, chair of the Gloucestershire Nature and Climate Fund. "Once an important green space is lost, it can be lost for good." Under pressure council 'seeking second bailout' Granddad, 82, to take on 10k as part of family team Fans line street for EMF star's final farewell Hill said: "We know there are people across Gloucestershire who desperately want to protect woodland or wildlife sites in their community but when that land comes up for sale, they simply don't have the time or resources to compete with a private buyer. "This funding means we can help them when it really matters. "We can provide money to act quickly, bring in the legal and ecological expertise they need." Recent examples of communities taking action to protect land include Daisybank, Lott Meadow and Southcourt Green, in Cheltenham, as well as Juniper Hill Field and Heavens Valley in Stroud. Another was Rodborough Fields, near Stroud, where a public campaign to protect the woodland from development led to it being brought into community ownership. John Bloxsom, chair of the Rodborough Fields and Frome Banks Preservation Group, said: "It's good news that a fund like this has been set up." The group successfully bought nine acres of Rodborough Fields thanks to a Crowdfunding campaign that raised £200,000 but now the future of a further 30 acres is uncertain after it was put on the market this summer. Bloxsom said that their latest bid had been rejected in favour of a rival bid from an unknown party, which was "causing concern in the community". Rodborough Fields Preservation Group said it wanted to maintain the area's biodiversity Angela France, one of the directors at Daisybank CIC, which helped to saved the field in Cheltenham from development last year, said she was "delighted" to hear about the new fund. "Local green spaces are so important to us now," she said. "I see more and more local communities getting together to protect them." She said since buying the land, the group had organised litter picking, butterfly counts and an ecological survey in order to plan how best to maintain the field so that local wildlife could thrive. A community event is also organised for 24 October to gather views on the future of the field. The new fund has also been designed to contribute to nature recovery across the county, while addressing unequal access to nature. David Owen, chair of trustees at The Summerfield Charitable Trust, said the initiative "has the potential to create a lasting legacy for nature, communities and future generations across Gloucestershire". He added: "Through this investment, we hope to enable communities to act quickly when opportunities arise, protect important natural assets and create benefits for wildlife, health and wellbeing that will endure for many years to come." title: Wembley welcomes 'rabid' college football fans
description: Wembley hosted its first American college football game on Saturday, but did the event meet expectations?
body: Tate Nagy of Kansas scored the opening touchdown with a 72-yard punt return It wasn't even gameday in London but the rivalry had already begun. Fans of the Kansas Jayhawks and Arizona State Sun Devils gathered at a pre-game party in Waterloo on Friday. Kansas fans shouted their rallying cry "Rock Chalk, Jayhawk", while their rivals replied with "ASU, ASU". After hosting 42 NFL games since 2007, this was London's introduction to a different kind of American football and a different kind of fandom. Wembley hosted its first American college football game on Saturday, with 46,523 fans attending the inaugural Union Jack Classic (UJC). UJC organisers vowed to create an authentic college gameday in London, and they began with tailgate parties. Fans enjoy food, drink and music for hours before the game, and they are far bigger for college games than in the NFL. One American fan told BBC Sport she prefers the tailgate to the game itself. The main tailgate at Wembley opened at 10am - seven hours before kick-off - with Kansas City rapper Tech N9ne helping to entertain the crowd. Arizona State alumni held their own party, with nearly 2,000 fans packed in, while ASU's marching band and cheerleaders performed on stage. But the wildest party was on Wembley Way, where Fox Sports had an outdoor studio for its live pre-game show. It was surrounded by fans and the Fox crew kept trying to stoke the rivalry, while the Kansas and ASU bands battled it out on Wembley Way and on the pitch before kick-off. This video can not be played American college football comes to London The pageantry and passion of college football is what makes it different. NFL fans often choose their team, whereas college teams tend to be passed down through families. "You feel a loyalty to your lineage," said Kansas fan Hannah, who added that college football fans are not just fanatical but "rabid". BBC Sport spoke to families at Wembley who have had multiple generations attend the same school and alumni who now live all over the US but travel thousands of miles to watch their alma mater. Current ASU student Sophie said her family "bleeds maroon and gold". Her friend Amelia has ASU merchandise all over the house. She just got a car that's maroon too. About 15,000 fans travelled from the US for Saturday's game - 9,000 rooting for ASU and 6,000 Kansas. College games in the US rarely have away fans but, with both teams having a sizable contingent at Wembley, as well as playing at a neutral venue, some visitors said the atmosphere was like a play-off game. The Arizona State Sun Devils went into Saturday's game as favourites Fans from 35 countries bought tickets and, as with NFL games in London, they represented several teams, not just those playing. Neutrals wore NFL jerseys and college jerseys, of bigger schools such as Oklahoma, Miami and Texas. There were even some British university jerseys. More than 100 universities in the UK have American football teams, and UJC organisers targeted those players, partly because, as students, they often find college football more relatable than the NFL. They formed partnerships with the British American Football Association, British Universities and Colleges Sport and the Jacksonville Jaguars to establish links with the grassroots game in the UK. The UJC has helped to train more than 1,050 British coaches and referees this year, some of whom were at Saturday's game. Cambridge University player Alex said it has been "cool" to learn the stories of Kansas and ASU and he would probably go to more college games in future "if they're teams we can rally behind". Jaren Hamilton made the game's best play with a 100-yard kick-off return at the start of the second half to help ASU to a 17-7 lead After planning for an attendance of 60,000, Wembley was about half full at 46,523, with some ticketholders moved to the bottom tier to keep the top tier empty. Although there were some big plays, the game was not as entertaining as anticipated as ASU claimed a 24-17 win that flattered Kansas. Music acts played throughout the game and there was a light show in the third quarter. It gave UK fans a flavour of college football, but it lacked the pomp and circumstance of regular games in the US. There were fewer band members and cheerleaders than normal, and the crowd was not as loud as during ASU home games – they averaged 54,000 last season. Both teams took 105 players (or student-athletes), 90% of which did not have a passport before this trip. Many fans and members of the coaches' families also visited London for the first time, and ASU head coach Kenny Dillingham said they had "an experience they will remember for the rest of their lives". Kansas head coach Lance Leipold added that the hospitality was outstanding, while the hotel and practice facility "was a win". Both teams are part of the Big 12 Conference, whose commissioner Brett Yormark said: "It exceeded my expectations, from the crowd to the logistics to how the local community has embraced us. It's been fantastic, so we want more." UJC organisers have signed an exclusive multi-year deal with Wembley, and Yormark says other Big 12 colleges are interested in playing in London. Big 12 teams also played two games in Dublin over the past 13 months, and the conference could expand to another international market. Yormark said: "There's not a two-week period where I don't get a call to say 'take some of your product to this country or that country', so we're exploring that right now." He said there will be an announcement about next year's London game "within the next month or two". That will give UK fans plenty of time to swot up on the next two teams who will make their presence known across the pond. Tailgate parties, marching bands... and Ted Lasso? title: 'You never quite know what you're going to pull out'
description: The group is marking a decade of fishing everything from an inflatable doll to a Nintendo out of the harbour.
body: Volunteers are celebrating a decade of cleaning up Bristol Harbour A voluntary clean-up group is marking a decade of finding unusual items in Bristol Harbour, ranging from an inflatable doll to a Nintendo Switch. Clean Up Bristol Harbour was launched in September 2016 in a bid to remove plastic pollution from in and around Bristol's waterways. The group has fished out some unusual items from the harbour in the past 10 years, including a message in a bottle containing a note in Spanish, a kettle, tennis balls, glasses and single shoes as well as the inflatable doll and Nintendo Switch. "You never quite know what you're going to pull out of Bristol Harbour," said founder and Bristol resident Chloe Juyon. Volunteers have fished out a whole range of unusual items from the harbour over the years "Some of the things we've found over the years have definitely made us laugh but there is a serious point behind it. "So much floating rubbish simply can't be reached from the harbourside. "Getting volunteers onto the water was always a big part of what I wanted Clean Up Bristol Harbour to become." However, the future of the project remains uncertain because funding was coming to an end, Juyon said. Volunteers found a Marathon-branded chocolate wrapper Juyon founded the group after she was struck by the amount of rubbish floating around her boat while she was coxing on the River Avon at high tide. The group has since been taken on by adventure sports centre All Aboard Watersports. During recorded monitoring between 2021 and 2023, some 236 volunteers removed more than 880kg (1940lb) of waste from Bristol Harbour with almost 390kg (859lbs) sent for recycling. Nipple tattooist 'frustrated' by online censorship Dealer jailed for firearms and drug offences 'Helping people with music is my mission' Much of the rubbish includes everyday waste, such as plastic packaging, bottles, cans, polystyrene and takeaway rubbish. But over the years, volunteers have fished out some unusual items, such as a Nespresso capsules, alcohol bottles, plastic cones, clothing - including thermals still in their packaging - and even a packet of butcher's tripe mix. One particularly unusual find was a Marathon-branded chocolate wrapper - the UK name for Snickers until 1990 - found during a clean-up several years ago. Reflecting on the anniversary, Juyon said: "There were just five of us at that first clean-up in 2016. "I stepped away from running the project several years ago, so seeing it reach its tenth birthday is quite amazing. "For me, it really demonstrates the power of community." To mark the 10th anniversary, the group will hold a community clean-up event later to mark World Cleanup Day., external Members of the public can take part in a self-guided litter pick from 10:00 to 12:00 BST, either on foot around the harbourside or using their own craft. With its current funding coming to an end, All Aboard Watersports has launched a Crowdfunder bid aiming to raise an initial £5,000 to help continue the project. Charley Peak-Payne, from All Aboard Watersports, said having a clean harbour has had a positive impact on people who use the harbourside for waters sports and boating. "The direct effect it has had on wildlife has been a gradual but noticeable change," he said. "The water that they are swimming in is considerably cleaner - to the point that we are now running swimming events in the harbour too, something that due to pollution would never have happened 10 years ago."
