title: JLR suppliers call for shift to aerospace
description: Suppliers tell the government that Britain's manufacturing future lies beyond car production.
body: JLR suppliers say skills and factories could be redirected into aerospace and defence Major Jaguar Land Rover suppliers have urged the government to help automotive manufacturers move into aerospace and defence, warning that large-scale car production in the UK faces long-term decline. In an open letter to the prime minister, chancellor and West Midlands Mayor Richard Parker, industry leaders argued Britain's automotive supply chain was "not in decline" but "in the wrong market". The intervention comes nearly a fortnight after JLR announced plans to cut 4,000 jobs. The Treasury said it recognised the uncertainty facing workers and was supporting the automotive sector through grants, lower energy costs and investment in electric vehicle production. JLR has its global headquarters in Coventry and plants in Solihull, Wolverhampton and Halewood. Signatories to the letter said the redundancies were "the first visible crack" in a UK automotive supply chain supporting about 183,000 manufacturing jobs. David Roberts said large-scale car production in the UK faced long-term decline The group, which includes Coventry-based Evtec, Solihull-based Artifex and the Confederation of British Metal Forming, said suppliers faced rising energy costs, growing overseas competition and increasing pressure from vehicle manufacturers sourcing components abroad. David Roberts, chairman of Evtec, said manufacturers believed high-volume car production in the UK was entering a decade of decline. Speaking on BBC Politics Midlands, he said: "We want to take action today rather than wait for that to happen." Roberts argued there was a "very big opportunity" for manufacturers to redirect skills, factories and investment into the UK's expanding aerospace and defence sectors. The letter said automotive suppliers already possessed many of the capabilities needed to support aircraft, defence equipment and military vehicles, but warned firms needed help to make the transition. "The capacity exists. The people exist. What is missing is the bridge," it said. The open letter calls for support to help automotive firms enter aerospace and defence The manufacturers called for lower industrial energy costs, support to help firms qualify for aerospace and defence contracts, and a West Midlands programme to accelerate the shift into those sectors. The letter was signed by executives representing businesses with more than 8,600 direct employees, alongside the Confederation of British Metal Forming, which represents about 75,000 workers. According to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, Chinese-owned brands accounted for about 15% of new car registrations in the UK in 2025 and 2026. The suppliers argued that competitors overseas benefited from lower energy costs, greater automation and, in some cases, government subsidies. A Treasury spokesperson said Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds had met JLR and trade union representatives following the redundancy announcement and pointed to government backing for electric vehicle production through the £2.5bn DRIVE35 programme. The government said manufacturers were also expected to benefit from measures to reduce industrial electricity costs and support investment in the sector. title: An arrest, a defection and a new leader - how Reform's 'challenging' week unfolded
description: How an extraordinary seven days that rocked the party unfolded.
body: Dan Thomas made his last appearance as Reform Wales leader on the BBC's Politics Wales "It's been challenging but we've come through it," said Reform's chief whip in the Senedd, Llŷr Powell, as he reflected on the past seven days. The week began with the party's leader in Wales being arrested on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour. Dan Thomas said he had been "released without charge" and had "done nothing wrong". Confirmation of his arrest was swiftly followed by news of a Reform Senedd member's defection to Plaid Cymru. This is the story of how that "challenging" week unfolded. Politician who switched from Reform to Plaid 'lied about her beliefs', says Richard Tice Last Sunday morning, Thomas was at the BBC's offices in Cardiff to appear as a guest on the Politics Wales programme. Later that day, he was arrested before being released on bail. Journalists got wind of the arrest on Monday evening, which is also when senior Reform figures in Wales began to find out. A few people at Reform HQ in London, including Nigel Farage, had already been told. Helen Jenner filled in for Dan Thomas at First Minister's Questions and is expected to replace Thomas On Tuesday morning, Reform Members of the Senedd (MSs) gathered for their weekly group meeting. With the "rumour mill going wild" there was "confusion" within the group. Dan Thomas was not present, and the MSs were not given the full picture, but they were warned that the party faced "a tough few days". It was soon announced that Thomas would not take his usual spot in the chamber for First Minister's Questions and would be replaced by his deputy, Helen Jenner. At that point Reform said his absence was due to "personal reasons". But as time went on it became clear that the story was about to break. A legal letter sent to media organisations by a Reform barrister would not be enough to block the reporting of Thomas's arrest. BBC Wales and others had secured confirmation that Thomas had been arrested and so the party needed to act. That's when Thomas sent a WhatsApp message to his party's MSs explaining the situation. Some of them were in the chamber at the time. In his media statement Thomas said he was standing down as leader. He remains a Reform MS for Casnewydd Islwyn. Sarah Cooper-Lesadd's defection emerged soon after Dan Thomas stood down as leader Then came the next bombshell as it emerged that Reform MS for Pen-y-bont Bro Morgannwg Sarah Cooper-Lesadd was defecting to Plaid Cymru. Reform only found out about it after BBC Wales asked the party for a response to the story. Moments earlier she had been sitting on the Reform benches and had been due to speak for the party in the chamber. Most of Plaid Cymru's MSs - including some government ministers - were only told about the defection plan at their group meeting earlier in the day. The defection needed the group's approval and some Plaid MSs wanted assurances that Cooper-Lesadd fully understood what it meant to be a Plaid Cymru member. The defection was approved with the necessary two thirds majority. But it wasn't backed by everyone. At a hastily arranged news conference in the Senedd, Cooper-Lesadd said her switch to Plaid followed "a period of reflection and deliberation" and that she had found "the right political home". The move was completely unconnected to Dan Thomas's arrest. Neither Cooper-Lesadd nor Plaid will say how or when the talks over the defection began, only that the process had gone on for "a while" and she had been on a "journey". The defection, just four months on from May's Senedd election, has raised fresh questions about the electoral process where voters were required to back a party rather than an individual. Jess Blair, from the Electoral Reform Society, said that while defections were "nothing new" there was more of an "accountability gap" given the Welsh voting system. "When this electoral system was put in place a review mechanism was also built into that process and what we need now is to really see that review take place," she said. By Wednesday, Reform's focus was on appointing a new leader. A party official from London came to explain the process to MSs, and Dan Thomas was also at that meeting. As is the case when a new leader is needed, various names were being discussed. James Evans was seen as one obvious contender. When it was announced that he would make a media statement reporters scrambled to hear what he had to say. "Having consulted with my family...I will not be putting my name forward," he said, despite "a majority" of the party's MSs backing him to take over. By Thursday morning it was looking increasingly likely that Helen Jenner would be the next leader. While Reform UK bosses in London have not had any formal input to the process, sources say there have been "signals" that Jenner - a Farage ally since the UKIP days - would be seen as a good choice in HQ. Confirmation of Jenner's appointment is expected as soon as Monday. "I feel we're more united than ever," said Llŷr Powell. "For us it's a new start next week and that's what we're building on." Politics Wales is on BBC1 Wales at 10:00 BST on Sunday 20 September and iPlayer. title: When did grey squirrels start posing a threat to reds?
description: A pair of grey squirrels was reportedly brought to the United Kingdom by a Cheshire banker in 1876.
body: Grey squirrels, native to North America, carry a virus which is deadly to red squirrels Endangered red squirrel populations have plummeted from about 3.5 million to less than 300,000 in the UK, with their grey-haired rivals continuing to thrive. But when exactly did the squirrel stand-off begin and how bad has the situation become? In England, the situation is particularly dire for reds. The Woodland Trust reckons there are only 39,000 of them left, while the Save Our Reds campaign thinks just 15,000 remain, including in conservation areas such as Formby on Merseyside. In May the group warned that red squirrels, which "still cling on" in parts of northern England, could disappear entirely within 25 years. In stark contrast, since their introduction from North America in the 19th Century, greys have thrived at the expense of their distant cousins, which compete for habitats and carry lethal viruses. The first verifiable importation of greys, external is widely understood to have come 150 years ago, when a Victorian banker named Thomas V. Brocklehurst is said to have released a pair of greys into Henbury Park, near Macclesfield in Cheshire, that he had brought back from a business trip to the United States. The rest, they say, is history and nobody back then would have realised the unintended lasting consequences of his actions. According to Graham Paskett from the Red Squirrel Survival Trust, there are now between 2.5 million and 2.7 million greys in the UK. A petition earlier this year calling for urgent action to conserve red squirrels attracted more than 75,000 signatures Jackie Foott, from the British Red Squirrel conservation group, told the BBC that reds and greys cannot coexist in the same location and that to protect the reds you have to "get rid of the greys - we realised that a while ago". She explained: "The grey squirrel is a pest, non-native, invasive species. "People don't realise just how much damage they are doing to trees, crops and properties - they cause at least £40m damage to forests and forestry services each year." But why can reds and greys not live cheek by jowl? "Greys outcompete reds for habitat and food - they don't actually physically attack them but they do bother them," said Foott. "Secondly, greys have squirrel pox - it doesn't affect them but they transmit it to red squirrels and it's fatal for them. It's a horrible disease and causes them ulcers and blindness." So what solutions are available? "Fertility control isn't available now - and has the effect of affecting other species, including reds," said Foott. "Gene therapy is probably at least 10 years away. "For now, the only way is lethal control - by shooting or trapping." The collapse of the native red squirrel population over the past 150 years Paskett, though, thinks there could be an effective additional way to control grey squirrel numbers within the next five years. He said the Red Squirrel Survival Trust was jointly funding a field trial by the government's Animal and Plant Health Agency. Beginning "later this year or early next year" Paskett said his organisation had "developed the means to deliver oral contraceptives to grey squirrels using a 'hopper' which sees the squirrel lift up a lid" to access them. Because greys typically weigh 500g - approximately twice that of reds, only they can access the contraceptive. If the field trial is successful, Paskett hopes landowners and forest rangers will be able to sign up to the scheme. For now, though, Foott said shooting and trapping were the main options. However, she said: "The reintroduction of pine martens can help. Because they are a native species in the UK, they evolved together with red squirrels. "They do eat red squirrels but the reds know to quickly get out of their way and will send out the alarm signal to the rest of the colony. "The greys are a little bit stupid and will say 'hello, I haven't seen you before' and the pine marten will get them!" When asked about the grey squirrels' UK origin story, Foott said: "Nobody really knows - there are several records but it doesn't really matter." So why were greys imported in the first place? Foott said: "Somebody said 'Wouldn't they look cute running around my garden?' More than a century later, she said experienced British Red Squirrel volunteers were now working with farmers and landowners to control grey squirrel populations near red colonies. In May, a spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said the government was protecting endangered red squirrels by tackling the threat of non-native grey squirrels. title: Families missing out on NHS money for healthy food
description: Figures show as few as 64% of eligible families are claiming NHS money to buy milk, fruit and veg.
body: NHS money is available to help families on the lowest incomes with young children to pay for healthy food and milk Charities are warning that thousands of low income families are missing out on money they are eligible to claim to buy fresh fruit, vegetables, and milk. Families earning less than £400 a week are entitled to weekly NHS Health Start payments including pregnant women and those with children under four years old who are entitled to £4.65 a week. Figures found take-up of the scheme is as low as 64% in some parts of the North East and Cumbria. Newcastle-based charity Feeding Britain said hikes in food prices meant "every layer of protection possible" was needed for families on the lowest incomes. The government has been approached for comment. Amelia, from Sunderland, has a two-year-old son and does not qualify for the scheme, but said she understood the struggle families face. "It's expensive to feed the whole family. It's getting ridiculous really. It's not just food, it's the nappies and wipes and days out." She said she tries to batch cook to save money and eat the same meals as her son. Amy, a working mother with a toddler, said: "He was on formula and it was expensive for the tins. They never had offers or promotions." She said she often eats less so her son can have more food. Amelia from Sunderland said food prices were "ridiculous" Families with a baby under 12 months old can claim £9.30 a week as part of the NHS Health Start scheme. However, figures suggest thousands of eligible families have not enrolled. The latest NHS figures on the take-up are from 2022. Redcar and Cleveland Council had the highest enrolment - 87% of entitled families were claiming the weekly payments. In the former Eden Council area, only 64% of those eligible were enrolled and in the former Copeland Council area, take-up was 68%. In Sunderland and Stockton, 81% of eligible families were enrolled. Take-up was lower in Newcastle and Middlesbrough, where just 77% of those entitled to payments received them. Across the region that meant 6,149 eligible families were missing out. Penny Walters works for the charity Feeding Britain and said the value of the healthy start scheme was "worthless" Penny Walters works for Feeding Britain which supports some of the most deprived families in the North East. She said Healthy Start payments were not increasing in line with inflation. "£4.65 - what can you buy with that?" she said. "If you've got a baby you get £9.30 and you can buy one tin of formula with that. "But how many tins have you got to go through a week with a baby? It's worthless." She said professionals were still finding stark levels of poverty in the region, including a malnourished baby admitted to hospital in Newcastle. "The only thing the mam could afford to give the baby was sugar water," she said. "That's not right. We're not in Dickensian England. Where was the support? Why is this happening?" Director of Feeding Britain, Andrew Forsey, wants the Healthy Start scheme to have an auto-enrollment system Several national charities are calling for the Healthy Start scheme to be updated, including Sustain, The Food Foundation, and Feeding Britain. Newcastle-based Feeding Britain director Andrew Forsey said: "Given the increases in food prices that are coming our way in the months ahead we need every layer of protection possible for families on the lowest incomes." He said the government should make Healthy Start an auto-enrollment scheme for eligible families. "The government can use the data and the technology at its disposal to register parents automatically, just to lift some of the burden off parents' shoulders," he said. Labour MP for South Shields, Emma Lewell, said she had been campaigning to try and ensure the allocated money does not return to the Treasury if unclaimed. "It just feels like such a no brainer," she said. "The money is there, the government have it, it's not going to the people who need it and there's things we can do to make sure it does, but they're not being done. Charities are also calling on the Department for Health and Social Care to release updated figures on enrollment on the scheme. The NHS stopped publishing data in January 2023 due to an inaccuracy that was discovered and this has not since been rectified. It means charities and local authorities cannot track who might be missing out. The department has been approached for comment. title: Two killed in 'massive' Ukrainian drone attack on Moscow region, says Russia
description: An oil refinery was also reportedly hit in Moscow, and flights were suspended at two capital airports.
body: Plumes of smoke rise from fires at an oil refinery in Moscow after reports of an overnight Ukrainian drone attack At least two people have been killed and six injured in a "massive" overnight Ukrainian drone attack on the Moscow region, Governor Andrei Vorobyev has said. Vorobyev said 249 drones had been shot down, and he reported fires in several residential houses. A local warehouse was also ablaze. In the capital Moscow, an oil refinery was damaged, and flight restrictions were in place at two airports. Earlier, a Ukraine official said seven people, including two children, were killed in Russian attacks in the Kyiv and Sumy regions on Saturday. Russia and Ukraine have recently intensified their strikes, targeting energy-generating and transport facilities, as well as major logistics hubs. In a post on Telegram on Sunday, Vorobyev said a 44-year-old woman was killed in Sofyino after a drone hit a three-storey residential building. Another five people - including two children - were injured, he said. In the Orekhovo-Zuevo district, an elderly man died after a private house was hit, the regional governor said. Videos have emerged on social media purportedly showing explosions in the night skies in the Moscow region, and of a burning warehouse. The footage has not been verified by the BBC. Meanwhile, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said a drone struck a building near one of the capital's boulevards and a facility at an oil refinery was damaged. He said on social media that 450 drones heading for Moscow had been shot down in what he called an "unprecedented attack". Sheremetyevo - Moscow's biggest airport - warned passengers about "temporary restrictions" in place, while at the capital's Vnukovo airport all arrivals and departures were halted. In Ukraine, a mother and her two small children, a boy and a girl, were killed in Saturday's Russian attack in the city of Fastiv, Kyiv regional head Tymur Tkachenko said. He added that several private houses were also damaged. In the north-eastern Sumy region, four people were killed when a Russian drone hit the car they were travelling in, top local official Oleh Hryhorov said. Both Russia and Ukraine have continued to hit energy infrastructure targets in the past week, despite US President Donald Trump claiming on social media that the two sides had agreed not to. Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. title: Will the three-week break put more pressure on managers?
description: So far this season two coaches have lost their jobs, but plenty of others will be looking over their shoulders heading into the new, extended international break.
body: Fulham coach Alvaro Arbeloa and Manchester United boss Michael Carrick have endured difficult starts to the season Three weeks is a long time in football - especially if you are a manager struggling for results. So far this season two coaches have lost their jobs - Paul Heckingbottom at Preston North End and Michael Duff at Wycombe Wanderers. But plenty of others will be looking over their shoulders heading into the new, extended international break. That includes the managers of Fulham and Manchester United, who on Sunday meet at Craven Cottage in the final fixture before players jet off around the world with their countries. It will all be pretty new to Alvaro Arbeloa, appointed as Fulham's manager in the summer after taking charge of just 28 games as Real Madrid boss in the second half of last season. But with no wins and three defeats in his first four Premier League matches, and speculation of unrest among the squad due to players' social media activity, the pressure is already on Arbeloa. Likewise Michael Carrick at Old Trafford, especially after the 3-2 EFL Cup exit to Brighton on Wednesday. It was the first time United had led at home by two goals and lost since they were beaten 3-2 by Tottenham in 1976, half a century ago. Coming on the back of the 1-0 loss to 10-man Manchester City, and with their only victories this season against Ipswich Town and Sabah, Carrick needs results. But they are not the only managers who might have cause for concern. Over the past 10 years, it has been rare for a Premier League manager to be replaced this early in the campaign. Even more so in the international break. But could it be different this year? The first break is longer, three weeks rather than two, and comes later. The September slot used to come at the start of the month when clubs had only played three league fixtures. In the past 10 years only two managers - Watford's Javi Gracia in 2019 and Nottingham Forest's Nuno Espirito Santo last year - moved on during this break. What about the October stoppage? Again, only two managers have previously lost their jobs during the same period - Francesco Guidolin at Swansea in 2016, and Xisco Munoz at Watford in 2021. This suggests clubs do not tend to use an international break to change manager. It is, though, far more likely to happen in November, with six bosses replaced in the past 10 years. That does not mean managers are safe, though. The changes simply were not made during the breaks. In the past 10 campaigns, nine coaches had left their jobs by the time the second international break came along - which is where we are in the number of games. With no manager to move on yet, could it come in the next three weeks? Former Stoke, West Brom and Middlesbrough boss Tony Pulis explains when the pressure can build for a football manager. With the first international break upon us, rumblings around certain clubs that have started the season poorly have surfaced. In my time, the October/November international breaks, the pause just after the Christmas period, and then early March would be the three sticking points for any manager who was struggling with results. Why these breaks are used for clubs to make changes is plain to see. The pause in the season gives football clubs the chance to appoint a new manager with time for them to settle into their new role, to take stock of the surroundings, staff and time to prepare for their first game in charge. After Christmas, usually the first game is an FA Cup match, which again gives the new boss a chance close up to see what they have to work with. First impressions can be a vital starting point, so again the manager has time to prepare and deliver their principles to the lads. Personally, I've joined quite a few of my clubs midway through seasons, and have left a few clubs going the other way, but I do honestly believe that those international breaks, for the reasons I've given, definitely heighten the chances of struggling managers getting the sack. I don't see this September break as a flashing light, it is too early in the season, but from then on in, the dates I have mentioned really do come into play. But this early international break doesn't help any managers. Whether your team is winning or losing, on both accounts, it's a nightmare. If you're winning you want to keep playing, and yet if you've started badly as a manager you want more time to put it right. Players travelling and the chance of injuries at such an early stage of the season is completely bonkers in my opinion. Roberto de Zerbi's Tottenham are yet to win a Premier League game this season While the evidence suggests things have to get pretty bad for a club to change manager early in the season, a few bosses are feeling the heat. There are ways of losing games of course, but I don't see the trip to Fulham as being 'make or break' for Carrick in the sense of his job. Carrick says it would be "ridiculous" to think that way - and I agree. He got enough credit in the bank last season by steering Manchester United into the Champions League to ride out a poor start to the season. I think the issue is United generate so much debate that a loss at Craven Cottage, which would be United's first since 2009, against a team that has only one point and is bottom of the table, would lead to numerous external inquests - which in turn puts a laser focus on the club when they resume their campaign against Tottenham on 10 October. It is unclear exactly how much danger Arbeloa is in, but there appears to be some substance to reports of disgruntlement among elements of Fulham's squad early in the campaign. His significant tactical changes since replacing Marco Silva have left the Cottagers vulnerable at the back, although they produced a more solid display in a goalless draw away to Liverpool last weekend. title: Artist, 94, thrilled by House of Commons exhibition
description: Eric Fawley says that the chance to have his artwork displayed has made him "very happy".
body: Eric Fawley said he had been drawing since he was five years old A 94-year-old man with dementia said he was "very happy" to be given the opportunity to have his artwork exhibited in the House of Commons. Eric Fawley, from Blackpool, has produced hundreds of drawings since arriving at Greenbanks Care Home in Watford, Hertfordshire, over a year ago, after a fire at his home. His drawings and paintings depict the world around him, as well as his former bosses at BT. Nirmala Singhvi, the lifestyle coordinator at the home, said: "Eric's story offers a warm and thoughtful look at creativity in later life, as well as the individuality and imagination that remain after a dementia diagnosis." Fawley's work is due to go on display in the Upper Waiting Hall at the Houses of Parliament in October. The exhibition was facilitated by the Watford Labour MP Matt Turmaine after he saw Fawley's work at the care home. This is one of the few drawings Fawley has produced in colour, as he prefers to sketch in black and white Fawley said he began creating artworks from an early age, encouraged by his mother, a violinist, and his father, a gifted amateur painter. His family were unable to support his ambition to attend art school. He left school at the age of 14 and worked in a variety of jobs, including electrical work for the famous Blackpool illuminations, before going on to become a Post Office engineer with BT. Singhvi ensures Fawley's artwork is framed and displayed for residents and staff at the care home Fawley relocated to London, after he married his wife Olive, and he continued to work for the telecoms company. From there, he rose through the ranks of the company, taking charge of an office where his portraits and keenly observed caricatures of colleagues were prominently displayed. Fawley said he enjoyed "sending up colleagues" and that they "secretly used to like it". When drawing someone, he said it was important to start with their hair. "If the hair is wrong, then everything is wrong," he added. Fawley's sketches of former colleagues at BT won him several art competitions. One of Fawley's wartime sketches features his sister, Charlotte, who regularly visits him at the care home Since moving to Greenbanks in March last year, Fawley has continued to sketch. He said being creative helped to focus his mind and "ensures that every day is different". He has held exhibitions across Essex and also performed a ceremonial ribbon-cutting at an exhibition at Harlow Library. Staff at the care home are "super proud of him" and are "excited" to see his artwork gain wider recognition, with Fawley challenging perceptions of what people can achieve in care. title: Watch: Diana's brother says press has 'cancerous influence' on Harry and Meghan's lives
description: Earl Spencer says that he can see echoes of Princess Diana's treatment from the press in the way Harry and Meghan are scrutinised.
body: This video can not be played Earl Spencer has told the BBC that there are similarities between the way his sister Diana, Princess of Wales and the Duke and Duchess of Sussex have been treated by the press. He said Princess Diana was "brought low" by press criticism of her and that it is a "pity" to see echoes of that in Harry and Meghan's lives now. He added that people should learn from Princess Diana's example, and that for anyone being "destroyed daily" by the tabloid press, it must be a "cancerous influence" on their lives. The full interview with Laura Kuenssberg, Princess Diana: My Sister's Story, will be available on iPlayer from 16:00 and broadcast on BBC One at 18:30 BST on Sunday. title: Watch: Fans cheer as Ed Sheeran speaks out over Macklemore controversy at show
description: Ed Sheeran told the crowd he had made mistakes after Macklemore was dropped from his tour for making pro-Palestinian remarks.
body: This video can not be played Ed Sheeran told his fans that he had made mistakes after Macklemore was dropped for making pro-Palestinian remarks on stage this month. Earlier, pro-Palestinian protesters had gathered near the stadium to express solidarity with Macklemore. The British singer's backing band and opening acts boycotted the event – leaving Sheeran alone on stage to address the crowd. "I have tried in my career not to be a political commentator of any kind, because I want my music and shows to be about unity, not division," Sheeran said. "But this is a humanitarian issue, and I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore." The BBC's Carl Nasman was at the concert. title: Harry and Meghan's media treatment echoes what happened to Diana, Earl Spencer tells BBC
description: Princess Diana's brother says she was "really brought low by all that criticism" and he saw her in "tears of despair".
body: This video can not be played Diana's brother says Harry and Meghan face 'cancerous' press like his sister Earl Spencer has told the BBC the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's treatment at the hands of the media has "echoes" of what happened to his sister Diana, Princess of Wales. He described press coverage of Prince Harry and Meghan as a "cancerous influence in their life" and said it would be "beholden on people to learn from Diana's example". The Sussexes, who recently returned to the UK from California six years after stepping back from royal duties, have been repeatedly critical of the media. It comes after the BBC reported on Friday how Earl Spencer says he was "telling the truth" when he claimed King Charles said people would forget Diana "soon enough" in a phone call in the days after her death. Bitter row over Diana book brings back unhappy times for royals Speaking to Laura Kuenssberg at his Althorp estate, Earl Spencer was asked if he believed Diana would "identify" with the scrutiny the Duke and Duchess of Sussex face. "If you look at an article in a tabloid about Diana or the couple that you were mentioning, Harry and Meghan, you know, they can be really, really unpleasant," he replied. "And I think it would be really beholden on people to learn from Diana's example. "I'm not here to speak for Harry and Meghan, but for anyone who's being destroyed in this way daily, it must be such a cancerous influence in their life." He said he saw Diana's "tears of despair" when describing the impact of media coverage on her, adding she was "very, very sensitive to criticism". Earl Spencer said his sister - who married the then-Prince Charles in 1981 - was "really brought low by all that criticism", describing it as a "pity" to see "echoes of that now" in the treatment of his nephew Prince Harry and wife Meghan. He also said he thought there was a media perception that he was "on Harry's side" but insisted: "I'm on my deceased sister's sons' side, both of them and if either of them wanted anything, then I'd be equally there for them." Princess Diana was subject to huge press interest right up until her death in a car crash in Paris on 31 August 1997. In the eulogy he delivered at her funeral, Earl Spencer accused the media of being on a "permanent quest...to bring her down" and said newspapers had been threatened by her "genuine goodness". Princess Diana: My Sister's Story. The full interview with Laura Kuenssberg will be on BBC iPlayer on Sunday from 16:00 BST and on BBC One at 18:30 BST His comments about the Sussexes come just weeks after the pair returned to the UK. They have long been critical of their treatment by the British press as well as the support they received from the Royal Family prior to their decision to leave the UK. Speaking in the couple's 2021 interview with Oprah Winfrey, Prince Harry accused the tabloid media of having created a "toxic environment" of "control and fear". Meghan, meanwhile, said in the couple's 2022 Netflix series that "no matter how hard I tried, no matter how good I was, no matter what I did, they [the media] were still going to find a way to destroy me". In July this year, Prince Harry and six others including Liz Hurley and Sir Elton John lost a privacy case against the publisher of the Daily Mail, and may face a legal bill of up to £34.5m. In separate, earlier legal battles, the Duke of Sussex beat the Mirror Group in court, and the News Group out of court, forcing a settlement, damages, payout and apology. Harry and Meghan seen during a visit to Australia earlier this year Earl Spencer's interview with the BBC was his first since the Palace issued a strongly-worded response to his claims about King Charles. That statement said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss". Earl Spencer, in comments first reported on Friday, reacted to it by saying: "Well, is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?" He added: "I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage of my life. "I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said and I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. I don't hear him saying he didn't say that." Pressed on whether he had evidence to back up the claim, he said he told family and friends at the time what had been said "because it was so monstrous". In his response to the Palace disputing his account, Earl Spencer, who shares his first name with the King, said: "They've sort of smudged that one, haven't they? They've said that recollections may vary." When asked which Charles the public was meant to believe, he said: "I'm telling the truth." Earl Spencer's book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, is due to be published next week and is expected to be highly critical of the Royal Family. In further extracts published on Thursday, he claimed how the King "sounded giddily elated" when he called him after Diana's death, alleging Charles sounded like a "lottery winner". description: Some Ed Sheeran fans say they are excited to enjoy music and are not there for politics after Macklemore was dropped from the tour for making pro-Palestinian comments.
body: This video can not be played Concertgoers filing into Ed Sheeran's concert on Saturday night had mixed emotions about seeing him perform without opening acts or his support band, after Macklemore was dropped for making pro-Palestinian remarks. Nearby, protesters gathered to express support for the American rapper and urge Sheeran to address the controversy. title: Everything we know about the Ed Sheeran and Macklemore controversy
description: The show in Philadelphia comes after rapper Macklemore was dropped from Ed Sheeran's tour over pro-Palestinian comments.
body: This video can not be played "I cannot hide how I feel anymore": Ed Sheeran addresses Macklemore row at show British singer Ed Sheeran has performed his first show since facing backlash over a controversial decision to drop rapper Macklemore from his tour. The decision - which Sheeran said was made by his promoter, not by himself - stemmed from pro-Palestinian comments Macklemore made on stage earlier this month. Sheeran addressed the controversy and spoke for nearly four minutes at the start of his set in Philadelphia on Saturday, saying he had made "mistakes" handling the fallout. "I have tried in my career not to be a political commentator of any kind, because I want my music and shows to be about unity, not division; about humanity, not politics. But this is a humanitarian issue, and I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore." Sheeran described the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks as "horrific", and also called the situation in Gaza "unjustifiable" in his first in-person remarks on the matter since the controversy erupted. The ongoing saga from Macklemore's comments and subsequent removal from the tour led Sheeran's support acts to drop out, and fans to express frustration. Here's what to know about the story. This video can not be played Ed Sheeran's tour in 'damage control mode' after Macklemore backlash While performing as the opening act for Sheeran at a concert in early September in New Jersey, Macklemore said: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine." The Thrift Shop rapper then performed a song dedicated to pro-Palestinian protesters at Columbia University. The lyrics are critical of Israel's military actions in Gaza following the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel. The following night, Macklemore referred to the death toll as a genocide, a claim that Israel rejects. In response, the Israeli American Council launched a petition demanding his removal from the tour, and the campaign group StopAntisemitism said the musician had ambushed fans with propaganda. Pop star Pink, who is Jewish, reposted an anti-Macklemore meme and then her own message, explaining her criticism of the rapper's comments. Macklemore then posted on Instagram that the media attention "surrounding Pink and what I said" had caused billionaire stadium owner Robert Kraft to call Sheeran. "Ed told me that Kraft said I would not be allowed to perform in his stadium," Macklemore wrote of Kraft, who also owns the New England Patriots American football team. Ed Sheeran and Macklemore performing together on stage in 2014 Concert promoter Messina Touring Group said Macklemore was dropped because some venues - such as Kraft's Gillette Stadium - would cancel Sheeran's planned concerts if Macklemore remained on the bill. Kraft, who is Jewish, confirmed he banned the US rapper from performing at Gillette, accusing Macklemore of hate speech and antisemitic rhetoric. "I agree with Macklemore, too many lives have been lost and there has been too much suffering, but only sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas is not honest and only advances more divisiveness and hate," Kraft said. Macklemore was removed from Sheeran's tour on 14 September. The rapper said in a lengthy Instagram statement that after a week of "difficult conversations" with Sheeran that ultimately ended "in a place of fundamental disagreement", he was dropped from the lineup. Sheeran said the call was made by Messina Touring Group. The Bad Habits and Shape of You singer said he respected "Macklemore's strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes", adding that while he doesn't use his own platform for politics, that "doesn't mean I don't care" or "support causes in my own, personal way". In his statement, Macklemore said he empathised with the difficult position Sheeran was in but criticised the English singer for not taking a stance. "Taking a side can cost you. Money, brand deals, sponsorships, festivals, private shows, relationships and access. I've lost all of those things. But there is no neutral position between the oppressor and the oppressed," he wrote. The rapper, who in 2014 apologised for a costume he wore on stage which critics said was anti-Semitic, also addressed the accusations of antisemitism, writing that "one of the most effective ways to enforce silence has been to weaponize the accusation of antisemitism". American musician Macklemore has been removed from Sheeran's tour Sheeran fans and ticket holders are torn about the situation. Some have said that without all the supporting acts, the show is no longer what they paid for. A woman who spoke to the BBC on her way inside the stadium on Saturday said she bought tickets on the resale market after someone put them up for sale. "Music is music, I'm not here for politics... We have sympathies for the Palestinians... no one should have to go through war," she said, adding that she did not think other bands dropping out would impact the show. Damien Given, who is from Northern Ireland and has tickets to Saturday's show, told the BBC that he felt that Macklemore was treated "very, very wrong" and thought Sheeran was not being transparent with fans. Given said that Sheeran can't suddenly say he's not political because he had previously voiced support for Ukraine after Russia invaded the country. But another fan named Patti Ann told the BBC that Sheeran was in a "no-win situation". "I back [Sheeran] 100% for his decision," she said. "I feel like he has an obligation and a contract with his venues, and sometimes, financially, you can't get out of those types of things." title: Ed Sheeran admits 'mistakes' as he addresses Macklemore controversy at Philadelphia show
description: The mega-star spoke about Israel and Gaza at his first concert since rapper Macklemore was removed from his tour.
body: This video can not be played "I cannot hide how I feel anymore": Ed Sheeran addresses Macklemore row at show Singer Ed Sheeran has apologised to fans for making "mistakes", as he opened a solo show in Philadelphia by addressing the controversy that has engulfed his tour. The star responded to the fallout over rapper Macklemore being dropped from the tour for making pro-Palestinian remarks on stage earlier in September. "I never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about free speech and the most complex political issue on the planet," he said at Saturday's show. He described the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks as "horrific" and called the situation in Gaza "unjustifiable" in his first in-person remarks since the controversy began. Several artists left the tour and the price of tickets dropped and sales declined for the remaining US leg of his Loop Tour due to the controversy. The singer has said the decision to drop Macklemore was made by his promoters, not him. "My concerts have always been a safe space for everyone," he said at the start of Saturday's show, adding that he is committed to his fans and that is why he returned to the stage. "Now, I want to address the question of where I stand in the situation in Israel and Palestine, and whether my doing this concert here tonight implies where I stand," he said. "I have tried in my career not to be a political commentator of any kind, because I want my music and shows to be about unity, not division; about humanity, not politics. But this is a humanitarian issue, and I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore." Sheeran said what happened in Israel during the 7 October 2023 attacks was "horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain". He added: "What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate. My heart has been broken by the scale of of devastation and loss of civilian lives, of children's lives, and this systemic injustice we're seeing unfold in the West Bank cannot be overlooked." He said he is trying "to work out how to make a contribution that helps victims of these terrible times and listening and learning, because I do not know enough". This video can not be played Watch: Concertgoers and pro-Palestinian activists arrive at Ed Sheeran concert Getting emotional, Sheeran told concertgoers: "I am honestly so grateful that you're here tonight with me. "This concert is still a place where everyone is welcome and everyone here can stand beside people that have opposing views." The singer said he took issue with the idea that venues would "preapprove" content or performers, which received applause from the audience. Sheeran then closed his statement by saying that he hoped his concert could be a place where everyone could gather irrespective of their beliefs. Sheeran's remaining tour dates are scheduled with shows set throughout North and South America. While the mega-star's previous tour was among the highest-grossing of all time, some ticket prices for this show dropped to $32 (£24). Fans also reported being able to get ticket refunds, though Ticketmaster and concert promoter Messina Touring Group did not confirm they were being reimbursed. Some protesters waved flags outside the venue, but the concert proceeded largely unfettered. Ed Sheeran and Macklemore: How a tour spiraled into controversy Fans filtered in ahead of the show, which began almost three hours later than planned Of the handful of attendees who stopped to talk to the BBC, there was a sentiment of determination to enjoy an evening of music while at the same time supporting freedom of speech. One married couple, who paid $450 (£335) per ticket, said that they respect Macklemore's right to speak freely. Another group of two ladies, who told us they got a "deal" for Saturday's concert after prices dropped, said that they support a free Palestine and at the same time love Sheeran's music. Finally, one family let their two young teenage daughters, Victoria, 15, and Sadie,13, be interviewed. When we asked what they thought of the controversy and Macklemore's removal, they replied "Who is Macklemore?". One protestor, who gave his name as Cooper, told the BBC that he came out "to support the struggle for" the Palestinian people. "We need more people like Macklemore and other artists who have a voice, who have a public platform, to be able to speak on behalf of the Palestinian people and their struggle for liberation, especially in the United States," he said. Cooper said that a best-case scenario at the concert would be an apology from Sheeran, but he was not optimistic. There was a small protest ahead of Saturday's concert The controversy began in early September, when Macklemore performed a song dedicated to pro-Palestinian protestors, and referred to "genocide" in Gaza, a description Israel rejects. The rapper also said criticism of Israel was not intended as criticism of "my Jewish brothers and sisters". Messina Touring Group said Macklemore was dropped because some venues - such Gillette Stadium in Boston, Massachusetts - would refuse to let the concerts take place if he performed. Billionaire Robert Kraft who owns Gillette Stadium and the American football team the New England Patriots, confirmed he had banned Macklemore from performing during the British singer's forthcoming shows. Kraft, who is Jewish, accused the US rapper of hate speech and said he was "only sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas". Meanwhile, support acts including Irish singer-songwriter Aaron Rowe and Danish musician Lukas Graham and his backing band Beoga quit the tour in solidarity with Macklemore. The artists argued his removal represented a chilling effect on free speech. title: The Papers: 'Gaslit by the King' and 'McCann suspect's book plot'
description: Earl Spencer's memoir and plans for the chief Madeleine McCann suspect to write a book lead Sunday's papers.
body: Claims made by Earl Spencer about King Charles III's comments following the death of Diana, Princess of Wales continue to feature on some of Sunday's front pages, ahead of the publication of the earl's book about his sister. "It's not every day you get gaslit by the King," is the headline of the Mail on Sunday after Buckingham Palace released a statement saying that fraternal grief could "colour memory". The "furious" earl has denied claims he is writing the memoir for money and has said Diana would be "cheering from the rafters" at the book. The Sunday Times carries comments from unnamed friends of the King who the paper says have called Earl Spencer a "hypocrite" who is "peddling Diana's privacy". They refer to the "much-married" earl as getting out his "crested carving knives". Beneath that story on the front page, a cartoon of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor reading Earl Spencer's book shows the former prince asking "how dare he embarrass the King! That's my job!" There is "fury" over plans for a suspect in the disappearance of Madeline McCann to write a tell-all book, according to the Sunday Mirror. Convicted rapist Christian Brueckner, who was released from prison in Germany last year after serving an unrelated sentence, "wants to cash in on the mystery with his side of the story", the paper says. The Sunday Telegraph quotes Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch as saying the "PM 'fiddles as Putin threatens to burn Europe'." Also on its front page, the Telegraph has been told by friends of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor that he is "living in limbo" over the police inquiry into his relationship with convicted paedophile Jeffrey Epstein. "Kangaroo" is the headline of the Sun on Sunday as it reports footballer-turned-pundit Wayne Rooney is "in advanced talks" to join the cast of I'm a Celebrity Get Me Out of Here. Top Boy actor Nkechi Simms poses on the front of the Observer, telling of her "quest to retrieve her care files". The headline reads "Careless: how the state stopped me learning the story of my childhood". Pharmacies are failing on AI diet pill checks, writes Sunday People. It shares an AI-manipulated image of one of its reporters who has visibly increased her BMI using AI to demonstrate the ease of how people "cheat BMI review". Former Premier League player Neil "Razor" Ruddock tells the Daily Star that modern "footie needs more hard men". The paper also carries a photo of Earl Spencer with the caption "I'm not bitter." And the Sunday Express reports on a "flood" of illegal knives into the UK. Campaigners tell the paper that the 2,729 blades entering the country in the first half of the year "could be just the tip of the iceberg". title: 'People forget we exist': Why older LGBTQ+ community fears losing identity
description: A report suggests older LGBTQ+ people experience more social isolation than their heterosexual peers.
body: Mindy says people often presume she is straight because of her age As a 75-year-old lesbian, Mindy Meleyal has lived through every major milestone in the modern LGBT rights movement, from the start of decriminalisation in 1967 to the first same-sex marriages in 2014. But now she says this important part of her identity is frequently overlooked due to her age. She's part of England's older LGBTQ+ community, which a new report suggests often experiences poorer health, more limited finances and greater social isolation than the wider older population. The report, from the Centre for Ageing Better, says without specialist support, this growing demographic could be forced "back into the closet" when accessing care, warning they may even delay getting the care they need because of concerns about homophobia. Adam Porter, a housing development manager from the LGBT Foundation charity, says he regularly meets older members of the community in exactly that situation. "It's very common for people to hide things if they have a carer visiting their home, for example hiding their wedding photos or taking down a trans flag," he says. "In the case of someone moving into a care environment, that means hiding who they are in their own home, for what could be the rest of their life." He says he has been "horrified" by some of the stories he has heard meeting older LGBTQ+ people, including some who have had carers offer to "pray for them" regarding their sexuality. Porter is part of the team behind Kindred House, a first-of-its-kind LGBTQ+ social housing scheme for over-55s, set to open in Manchester next year. An artist's impression of what Kindred House will look like when it opens The scheme, a joint project with the local council, will provide 80 self-contained apartments and communal areas available to the local community. The majority of residents will be LGBTQ+. The Kindred House scheme is what's known as extra-care housing, which means residents live independently, but there is a 24/7 care team available for those who need extra help, and all staff will receive specialist training around LGBTQ+ inclusion. Porter says he hopes the scheme will "trigger some conversations" about how to best support older LGBTQ+ people in the challenges they face. Mindy and her wife Linda have been together for more than 30 years, but says they're often mistaken for sisters. "She's 18 inches taller than me, I've got a Yorkshire accent and she's got a Northern Irish accent," Mindy says. "I think it's pretty obvious we weren't brought up in the same building." She believes part of that is often down to people presuming she is straight because of her age. "There are different tribes of people in every age group, but when you get older, people start clumping you together with other stereotypes," she says. After divorcing her husband and coming out as lesbian, Mindy co-founded a lesbian commune in Hull before moving to Manchester On one occasion, while Mindy was in hospital after a stroke, a nurse referred to Linda as Mindy's husband. She said it was not only "insulting", but made her consider what sort of training the staff might have had. The Spotlight on Ageing report says these sort of experiences can also have an impact on the support people receive. Sarah Wilkinson, research and analysis manager at the Centre for Ageing Better, says after a "lifetime of homophobia and transphobia", older LGBTQ+ people now face the "additional, and overlapping, challenge of ageism". The report, external says older LGBTQ+ people are less likely to have children - someone born in 1950 would have been in their 50s by the time same-sex couples could legally adopt - and that they are more likely to be estranged from their families when compared to their heterosexual counterparts. The report also found more than half of gay and bisexual men aged 65 and above live alone, compared with less than a quarter of heterosexual men. Bisexual women aged 50 to 64 are twice as likely as their heterosexual peers to live alone. It also suggests that only half of gay and bisexual men aged 50 and above definitely agree they would have someone to help them if they needed, 14 percentage points lower than heterosexual men of the same age. Norman Goodman, 75, came out as bisexual in his late 60s after the death of his wife Marilyn. The couple never had children, and Norman now has no immediate family nearby to help him with things like hospital visits or housework. He says his support system comes in the form of his partner Tony, and a group of friends and neighbours he refers to as his "chosen family". "I'm lucky, I've got great friends and great neighbours, and I know I can knock on somebody's door day or night and I could get help," he says. Norman came out as bisexual when he was in his 60s and says he relies on "chosen family" to support him But despite having their support while he's relatively independent, Norman says he worries about the prospect of facing discrimination if he needs more formal care as he ages. "Hopefully I will maintain and look after myself the best I can, but I've heard horror stories of gay people in nursing homes being treated terribly," he says. "I think nurses, doctors, carers should all be trained on how to look after LGBT people." It's the reason behind schemes like Manchester's Kindred House, which are not unusual in other parts of the world. There are similar projects in Spain, Sweden, Germany, the US and Canada, but in the UK they are few and far between. In 2021, the UK's first LGBTQ+ retirement home, Tonic, opened in London with 19 apartments for private rental or shared ownership. The scheme attracted so much attention, later this year it is set to feature in a Netflix documentary telling the story of one of its first residents, Chek Min-Ong. title: Sex and dating for the sandwich generation - Sharon Horgan on her latest comedy Youth
description: "It's really weird watching yourself age on screen because that's not fun," Horgan reveals.
body: Casual sex. Relationships. Parenting. Sharon Horgan has already seen us through several life stages via hit comedy dramas such as Pulling, Catastrophe and Motherland. Now, with her latest show Youth, Horgan puts the spotlight on 50-something women, imbued with her trademark tightly balanced mix of hilarity and pathos. The HBO Max series sees Horgan's character, Alex, gamely attempting to juggle a stressful publishing career while looking after a teenage son and elderly parents. She's part of the so-called sandwich generation, those in midlife who have to juggle caring responsibilities for old and young while often working, too. And that's not all - Alex is also back in the dating game following a divorce. I'm curious to know how much of Youth is based on Horgan's own experience. The star is divorced and has two daughters. "We've all got kids who are kind of adults now and parents who are getting older and ailing in some cases. There is a chunk of my life in there, an… autobiographical element for sure. But the good thing about writing autofiction is that no one really knows which bits are real and which bits aren't, I guess, except the people [in it]!" The hit writer, producer and actress mulled over the idea for Youth before going on to make Apple TV's Bad Sisters, coming back to it after the dark comedy ended. The 56-year-old says she was keen to "write about this particular time in a woman's life... through the lens of a mother of a son". Horgan wanted the story to be "post-divorce and "menopause adjacent". "And I wanted it to be a comedy, you know? Because there's a lot that's very funny about our bodies failing!" But it's not just her comedy chops that have gained her a loyal following - a big factor in Horgan's success over the last 20 years or so is the authenticity she brings to her work. "I spent a lot of time trying to make it as real and as accurate as possible and trying to put in my faults as a parent and mistakes as a woman, my own sort of anxieties and insecurities," she says. "I try to put all that in there… and hope that's a universal feeling because it's really madly important to me that women, especially, watch it and see themselves reflected back." She says that Youth "felt like the next stage on" from her popular sitcom Catastrophe. The series, which first aired in 2015 on Channel 4, followed the lives of 40-somethings Sharon and Rob (played by Horgan and Rob Delaney), a couple who got together suddenly after their brief transatlantic fling resulted in pregnancy. "This [show] feels part of the same trajectory, almost, which was fun and really helpful when it came to trying to figure out what the tone was, although I hope it's kind of doing its own thing," Hogan explains. There are new issues to concern ourselves with in mid-life and, as you'd expect, Horgan doesn't shy away from embarrassing situations or mildly unhealthy preoccupations. Her protagonist - who is 50 - has a slight obsession with sagging skin, which will no doubt strike a chord with many. "It's really weird watching yourself age on screen because that's not fun," she reveals. Horgan says she wanted to offer "an honest depiction of someone having a complicated relationship with ageing". She adds that she herself has now formed "a better relationship" with getting older. "I think it's OK to age any way you want to age. And we're insecure about it for a reason. And that's because it's shoved down our necks that we need to look a certain way, especially within the entertainment industry and in magazines. And women who age really well are celebrated just for that. And that is annoying." Alex (Sharon Horgan) and Ruari (Aran Murphy) have a close but fractious relationship When it comes to sex, she says "you just have different insecurities" when you're a bit older. "You think about angles, you think about the shapes you make and how to be sexy as an older woman. And, you, know, lighting comes into it! But I also have friends who are incredibly free with their bodies and feel like this is a whole new era and they're embracing it. "I know that I will get there," she continues. "But I wanted to show a middle-aged woman having a complicated relationship with her body but still putting herself out there because... she wants to find someone to grow old with." Sherwood star Sharlene Whyte, who plays Horgan's boss and best friend Sam, says we need to see older women's stories on screen. "We should see more of it - women who are later on in age, who have been privileged to get here later on, who are still killing it and are still beautiful and sexy and funny," she says. "But I think women in their 50s are more visible (now)... and there's more (acting) work for women in later life." Sharlene Whyte (right) plays Alex's boss and best friend Sam Despite the two lead characters being 50-something women, Whyte describes Youth as "an inter-generational watch". That's probably due to a prominent Gen Z storyline involving Alex's son, Ruari, played by 19-year-old Aran Murphy (Cillian Murphy's son. And yes, as you might expect, he's very good). Ruari has a difficult relationship with his feckless father - Alex's ex-husband (Owen McDonnell) - and in one poignant scene, describes how confusing it is to find your way as a young man in today's world. "Having good people around you is so important, and it's not always easy to have that," Murphy muses. "So, for someone like Ruari, when you don't have the foundation of friends and stuff, you look to the (wrong) kinds of people... and oftentimes, you'll be left out on your ass with the wrong answers." title: Cultural treasures are being destroyed by war, and people want justice
description: A cauldron of conflicts is bubbling across the world, with cultural monuments being destroyed. These people are fighting against it.
body: Cultural treasures are being destroyed by war, and people want justice August was a brutal month for Ukraine. Russian aerial attacks increased significantly, launching thousands of drones. Kyiv was intensely bombarded, as were the southern cities of Mykolaiv and Odesa. Amid the destruction and loss of life, Odesa reported damage to six Unesco-protected sites, including the salmon-pink 19th Century Alexandru Sturdza House. It raised again the question of why it is so hard to hold actors accountable for the destruction of buildings and objects with real cultural significance. In the last month alone, Ukraine's Ministry of Culture reported that 148 cultural heritage sites were recorded as damaged or destroyed, including in Odesa. Several Ukrainian activist groups have tried to get accountability by lodging complaints with the International Criminal Court (ICC) against Russia over cultural destruction and looting, but no indictments have been issued. Bijan Rouhani, a senior researcher at the Endangered Archaeology in the Middle East and North Africa project, says that the legal framework may be strong on paper but in practice it almost inevitably falls short. "No state actor has ever been tried for this offence. The obstacle is no longer evidence. We have satellite imagery, remote sensing and monitoring teams. The obstacle is jurisdiction and political will." Looking at the cauldron of conflicts convulsing the world, the question is ever more pressing as to whether effective action is possible to stop the damage being done or ensure accountability when it does. The conflict in Ukraine is just one of the panoply of wars in recent years that have revealed once again the disastrous impact of conflict on cultural heritage. Tareq Abu Dayyeh sells craftwork, souvenirs and antiquities in Gaza. The Great Omari Mosque features on many of the items he sells. It represents the very identity of Gaza - charting its history through the building's many manifestations from ancient pagan temple to Byzantine church to Seventh Century mosque to Crusader Cathedral and then back to being a mosque. The Great Omari Mosque was all but destroyed in an Israeli strike in 2023. The Israeli military said the strike was targeting Hamas. The Great Omari Mosque in Gaza was largely destroyed in an Israeli strike in 2023 Now Dayyeh says his heart is broken every time he sees the ruins. "When your past is destroyed, you have no present." The war in Gaza has claimed tens of thousands of lives and an estimated 200,000 buildings have been damaged or destroyed by Israeli bombardment. But despite the overwhelming death and devastation, such cultural losses run deep. This is a sentiment expressed throughout history by people living through war. In Sudan, Lebanon, Yemen and Iran, the alarm has been raised time and time again. More than 100 sites in Iran are reported to have been damaged during the aerial war launched by the US and Israel back in February. They include the Unesco-listed Golestan Palace in the capital, Tehran, and Naqsh-e Jahan Square in Isfahan. The civil war in Sudan has further imperilled one of the ancient wonders of the world - the Meroe Pyramids, built during the flourishing civilisation of the Kingdom of Kush. Unesco, which designated Meroe as a World Heritage Site in 2011, has warned that the fighting has halted all preservation work there, leaving the fragile ancient structures prey to erosion from the encroaching sand and vegetation. In response to the massive destruction of World War Two, the first-ever international treaty exclusively dedicated to protecting cultural heritage during armed conflict was adopted in The Hague in 1954. It applies to monuments and architecture, but also works of art and books, requiring states to safeguard and respect cultural property and refrain from any actions that might endanger it. Since the Hague Convention, there have been several additional moves to strengthen protective measures for cultural heritage. A Second Protocol to the Convention in 1999 said that any site that has been placed under enhanced protection due to its immense cultural significance must not be made a military target even if it is being used in such a way as to have become a 'military objective' - unless there is no other feasible way of ending its use in that way. When the International Criminal Court was established in The Hague in 2002, part of its remit was to bring accountability for deliberate attacks in war against buildings of religious, artistic and educational value as well as historical monuments, which had been defined as war crimes. But this has been a complex and difficult task. So far, only one case has been successfully brought at the ICC. Ahmad al-Faqi al-Mahdi was a jihadist militant leader in Mali who was found guilty of directing attacks that destroyed mausoleums and a mosque in Timbuktu. He was sentenced to nine years in prison. Ahmed al-Faqi al-Mahdi remains the only person successful prosecuted for this by the ICC Rouhani says that without the full backing of the major powers and a genuine commitment to international law and its enforcement, the world will simply keep watching the same devastating pattern repeat itself. "For most governments, heritage is a secondary concern, unless it becomes useful for propaganda," Rouhani says. "The Hague Convention requires states to build protection into their military rules and to respect cultural property abroad as well as at home. Looking at the scale of damage in recent conflicts, it is difficult to conclude that these obligations are taken seriously." In conflicts from Ukraine to Iran to Gaza, where schools and hospitals are seen as permissible military targets by combatants, how likely is it that a museum or pile of ancient stones, however freighted with beauty and history and memory, will be spared? title: Mum's viral barefoot race sparks debate over India's education crisis
description: Unprepared and in flip-flops, the 47-year-old widow ran 3km to try secure her daughter's future.
body: Rambai Ranveer took on a 3km sprint, hoping to win enough prize money to buy books for her daughter Despite having no training, or even a pair of running shoes, Ramabai Ranveer sprinted barefoot to victory in her first-ever race in August. The 47-year-old widow had entered a 3km (1.86-mile) community run with a single goal: winning the prize money to help pay for her two daughters' education. When she crossed the finish line first, Ramabai from Maharashtra in western India was delighted. The 3,000-rupee ($31; £23) prize would help her buy books and study materials for her daughters. It was not much money. It would not come close to covering the cost of higher education in India, or even a course at the coaching centre where one of her daughters is preparing for a government recruitment examination. But videos of her barefoot run spread rapidly on social media and in newspapers, striking a nerve as India's education system faces unusual scrutiny. "Is it glory or a source of shame for us as a society?" one social media user remarked. Soon, a woman who had never imagined becoming a runner was being held up as a symbol of something much bigger: the extraordinary lengths some Indian families go to in the hope that education will give their children a better life. For Ramabai, the decision to run was simple. "My elder daughter came to me early in the morning and said, 'Mummy, I want to take part in a running race'," she told BBC News Marathi from her home in Beed district. Ramabai has been her family's sole breadwinner since her husband's death in 2012 "I asked her where it was and she said it was nearby. She told me that if she won the prize money, it would help with her education." Her younger daughter, Arati, lives in Nanded and was struggling to afford books. "I couldn't send her money to buy books and because of that she didn't speak to me on the phone for eight days," Ramabai said. "So I decided I had to run and win the race." When her slippers kept slipping off, she removed them, gathered her sari and ran barefoot, pulling ahead to win the women's 30-60 category. Her elder daughter, Pooja, also won a prize after finishing second in her age group. But she reserved her praise for her mother, describing her as courageous. Against women aged 30 to 60, Ramabai raced to victory in a saree and flip-flops despite no preparation Ramabai has been the family's sole provider since her husband died in 2012. "I did whatever work I could find," she said. "I picked soybeans and chickpeas in other people's fields. I also collected turmeric, processed it and sold it." She left school when she was 13. Her daughters, she says, should have the opportunities she never had. "I believe that as long as I am alive, I should do everything I can to give my daughters a good education." That aspiration is shared by millions of Indian families. But getting a child through the education system and into a secure career can involve years of preparation, intense competition and, for many families, considerable expense. One of Ramabai's daughters is preparing for police recruitment and the other for the civil services - two fiercely competitive routes into the security and social status associated with a coveted and secure government job. Ramabai's elder daughter Pooja (l) is training for police recruitment at the school where her mother works as a cook Millions of young Indians spend years preparing for such examinations, often paying for coaching and study materials. But faith in the system has been shaken by repeated allegations of question-paper leaks and other irregularities. The controversies have fed a wider sense of frustration among young Indians over education, jobs and the increasingly uncertain promise of a secure future. That frustration has also fuelled student-led protests and youth movements demanding changes to India's education system. For families such as Ramabai's, education is something they make sacrifices for every day. After her husband's death, she took whatever work she could find. She now cooks at the coaching centre where one of her daughters prepares for police recruitment. Ramabai's run also drew the attention of authorities. Earlier this month, Chief Justice of India Surya Kant directed local officials to provide her with financial assistance of 50,000 rupees. But Sukhadeo Thorat, a former chairman of the University Grants Commission, says the family's story points to broader structural challenges. "If a woman is compelled to struggle so hard for her daughters' education, it shows that government education schemes are not reaching people adequately," he said. "Both the central and state governments run a variety of schemes. The problem is that implementation remains weak." For Ramabai, though, the debate is secondary. What matters most is ensuring her daughters have a better future. "I don't want them to go through the hardships I have faced," she said. "I don't want them to struggle through mud or travel under the scorching sun and rain. Whatever I have suffered, I don't want my daughters to suffer the same." Additional reporting by Laignee Barron. title: Maddy Cusack 'more than a number on a shirt' as anniversary falls during inquest delay
description: The third anniversary of Maddy Cusack's death falls during a pause in the footballer's inquest.
body: Maddy Cusack's family say her inquest paints a "one dimensional" picture of the footballer Sitting on a bench dedicated to her memory, Maddy Cusack's sister and cousin fondly remember her as their sunshine and someone with a real sense of fun. Olivia Cusack says her big sister was the person "I looked up to my whole life", while for Emily Reilly, her cousin Maddy's the one who "used to get us in trouble with my dad". But as they come to remember the former Sheffield United footballer on the third anniversary of her death, they're still waiting for answers. An inquest examining what happened to Maddy Cusack, who was 27 when she was found unconscious at her home in Derbyshire, started in June and should've finished in July. But it has been paused for months while her former club Sheffield United looks for documents linked to her medical records. It means her family will have to wait until at least December to hear more evidence, a wait Olivia describes as "extremely overwhelming". "It is very emotional and you can find yourself frustrated at times," she tells BBC Newsbeat. Emily and Maddy always planned to spend their birthdays together Maddy's inquest had already been delayed twice when the coroner adjourned it after a little under two weeks in July. Evidence, including testimony from her mum, heard how Maddy had struggled with her mental health before she died on 20 September 2023 and had problems with Sheffield United coach Jonathan Morgan. Morgan told the inquest he had "no concerns" about their relationship and that "things have not been portrayed factually or correctly with how she was feeling". While Maddy's relationships and wellbeing were scrutinised, Olivia says she felt Maddy herself, and who she was away from the pitch, was overlooked. "It dawned on me that when people were asked questions about Maddy and to share what she was like as a person, they were all very similar answers and quite focused on the football side of her," she says. "People don't seem to know her like we did - of course they don't. "But I wanted to introduce a different side of Maddy. "I wanted them to know more than the number on the back of her shirt or the colours that she wore on the football pitch." Olivia and Emily often come to Maddy's memorial bench in Scargill Park in West Hallam, Derbyshire, which is where they all grew up. With both of their birthdays at the end of October, Emily says they'd always planned to spend them together, but "now I just come here". "She used to get us in trouble with my dad when we were younger," she says. "It was always her idea then I'd take the blame for it." In an inquest focusing on darker times in her life, it's this side of Maddy that her family thinks has got lost. Olivia, along with other members of Maddy's family, has campaigned tirelessly since her sister's death, setting up a foundation in her name to support aspiring female footballers. "The foundation keeps me going," she says. "It's been a real lifeline to be able to continue her story." On Saturday, she organised a walk from Bramall Lane, Sheffield United's ground, to near Derby where Maddy lived - a distance of almost 30 miles. "The aim with the walk is just to do her proud," Olivia says. "Maddy would love that we were all challenging ourselves." Olivia says her big sister was the person "I looked up to my whole life" An external report ordered by Sheffield United shortly after Maddy's death cleared the club of wrongdoing. A second report from the Football Association, commissioned in early 2024, won't be published until her inquest concludes. In December, the family will return to Chesterfield Coroner's Court to hear more evidence about the circumstances around Maddy's death. "She will only ever remain a part of this life if we keep saying her name and keep remembering her," Olivia says. "And as painful as that can be on days where you want to forget and you just want to stay in bed all day and not face the world, I try and make a conscious effort to keep saying her name and keep her living alongside us ultimately."
