title: Not all AI workers think the tech could kill everyone
description: In text exchanges and conversations, multiple people who have worked for leading companies are sceptical of the warnings.
body: Not all employees of major firms working on artificial intelligence (AI) think the technology spells doom for humanity. In text exchanges and conversations, multiple people who have worked for companies including OpenAI, Meta and DeepMind were sceptical of the idea that unchecked AI development would lead to tools that could kill people en masse. "Lol", "Haaaaaa" and "Bringing the luls" were among the reactions the BBC received to a recent flurry of high-profile warnings by some people in the industry. While these fears go back decades, claims made last week by Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic employee, went viral and were echoed by others in the sector who urged a slowdown in development. The idea that a future AI tool or agent, an AI bot that is programmed to operate somewhat autonomously, could endanger people has been supported online by employees of Anthropic, as well as OpenAI, Deepmind and Elon Musk, who has an AI startup called xAI. All of the workers who spoke with the BBC did so on condition of anonymity as they were not permitted to speak to the press. Their identities are known to the BBC. "My first thought was, 'That guy?'" said a former OpenAI employee who knew of Coxon when they both worked at the company. The person, who now works at another AI company, said their amusement at the new moment of existential AI fears largely stemmed from how little detail had been provided by its proponents to defend the notion that all of human life was at stake. The claims are "always vague", the person said, adding that when they sound specific, they tend toward major jumps in reasoning or hypothetical circumstances. Coxon has said a group of AI agents, based on AI models that do not currently exist, could decide to create and then aim a biological weapon, but he did not detail how exactly that would take place. This video can not be played 'There is a possibility of human extinction,' former Anthropic employee says about AI Rishub Jain, who this summer founded the AI safety research firm Sampura Research after spending seven years at DeepMind, told the BBC that the current tone among many people working in AI with regard to fresh fears had "definitely been a little jokey". "People have been talking about this idea for many years now, so people in AI companies didn't just wake up last week thinking 'Oh no, AI is going to kill everyone,'" Jain said. "If this was all new, it would be a different tone." Colin Fraser, a data scientist at Meta, wrote on social media last week that there was no real evidence that AI models would inevitably pursue a goal leading to human death. While Fraser's explanation was technical and specific, he hit a light-hearted note to summarise it: "LLMs [large language models] won't wipe out humanity because they just don't have that dog in them." The phrase "that dog in them" is common slang that usually denotes a fierce drive. Despite the jokes, AI workers and researchers have shared concerns about the genuine, immediate risks posed by the technology they are developing. "The conversation among experts has been much more nuanced, but essentially everyone agrees there are a wide variety of risks that are all important to consider and mitigate," Jain said. Such risks include preventing users and hackers from forcing an AI tool's guardrails to fail. And there are growing ethical concerns about AI tools being much more widely adopted in military settings. Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they? Uncontrolled AI could lead to 'silicon species' rivalling humans, warns Microsoft Why some experts increasingly fear AI will take over Questions mount over what an AI 'slowdown' would look like These problems and topics have taken on a new sense of urgency in AI circles after OpenAI lost control of certain new AI models, which went rogue during a security test and hacked the Hugging Face startup. Jain said there was now more agreement in AI circles that "actual near-term harms" needed to be better understood. There is even growing agreement that evaluators from AI safety research organisations should be brought into major AI labs in order to evaluate new models, something Anthropic boss Dario Amodei and OpenAI boss Sam Altman have both said they intend to do. More than 100 people working in AI on Friday signed a letter, external supporting the move, insisting that outside evaluators needed to be "meaningfully independent". This video can not be played Watch: AI creations could ‘compete’ with humans for resources, says Microsoft's head of AI Numerous AI employees the BBC spoke with noted that they had yet to learn of any such safety researchers being embedded in an AI lab. Anthropic announced on Friday that it would bring in AI evaluators from Faculty, external, an AI company owned by Accenture. Accenture and Anthropic are also business partners, external, with Accenture having previously agreed to help Anthropic expand the use of Claude among businesses. Anthropic did not say when evaluators would arrive at the company. A spokesman for Faculty declined to comment when asked about timing. Neither Anthropic or OpenAI responded to a BBC request for comment regarding when they planned to bring in outside evaluators. The OpenAI-Hugging Face incident has been widely treated as a "wake-up call" for the AI industry as well as companies, industries and governments who may have online systems vulnerable to AI hacking. But even Hugging Face, a company of 200 employees which is now set to be acquired by Nvidia for almost $13bn, has taken a droll tone over the already infamous incident. In a security file that was briefly available, external on the Hugging Face website, the platform wrote "A note to AI agents". title: 'I don't even know if my parents are alive' - the war heroes jailed 25 years ago
description: The children of key politicians jailed 25 years ago without a trace in Eritrea want answers.
body: Aster Yohannes and Petros Solomon fought in Eritrea's war of independence Hanna Petros Solomon breaks down in tears as she recalls how she and her siblings effectively became orphans 25 years ago when their father was arrested in Eritrea and jailed without trial. Their mother was subsequently detained - and no-one has heard from either of them - or of them - since. "He had a towel on his shoulders like a sportsman," she tells the BBC about the last time she saw her father when she was 10 years old, and he had gone out for a jog. "He used to work out every morning." Her parents met when they both fought in the long liberation war that saw Eritrea gain independence from Ethiopia in 1993. Her father Petros Solomon had been one of the senior leaders during the war and is regarded by many as a national hero for his critical role. After independence, he had served as defence minister, then foreign minister and had been heading the fisheries ministry when his troubles began. That was in May 2001 when he and 14 other high-profile politicians signed an open letter to President Isaias Afewerki calling for the implementation of a constitution that was ratified after independence and demanding national elections. They became known as the G-15. Isaias, the leader of the Eritrean People's Liberation Front (EPLF) which had fought against Ethiopia, did not take the criticism well. As foreign minister, Petros Solomon met then-US President Bill Clinton and his wife Hillary Unbeknown to Hanna, her father had been dismissed as a minister, though he still went out early to get some exercise each day. It was not until a few days after 9/11 - when the world was distracted by the al-Qaeda attacks on the US - that the country was to discover the full extent of Isais's displeasure in what became a watershed moment in Eritrea's history. In the early hours of 18 September, the security forces positioned themselves outside the homes of 11 senior government officials in the capital, Asmara, on the president's orders. Petros was picked up by security agents as he left in his tracksuit. The family had no idea what had happened to him. Hanna and her three siblings went to stay with their paternal grandmother as their mother, Aster Yohannes, was away studying in the US. It was only some days after Petros had disappeared that things became clearer, says Hanna about the painful memories. "My classmates told me that my father sold out his country. "That is when I understood how serious the situation was, and how people framed my dad and his colleagues who fought for the independence of their country. I was hurt." In the US, Aster was shell-shocked by what had happened - and was in a very bad way. She asked government officials if they could issue the children with passports - but they refused, telling her to come home. After agonising about the situation for two years and reportedly receiving assurances from government officials, she packed her bags to return. Hanna and her siblings desperately wanted her back - but they were also worried. "I told her on the phone: 'What if they arrest you?'" Hanna remembers. "She insisted nothing would happen to her, saying: 'I haven't done anything wrong, and am only coming to raise my children.'" Hanna says she learned later that President Isaias himself had promised Aster that she would be safe. But while the family waited at Asmara International Airport on 11 December 2003, she failed to emerge through arrivals with the other passengers. Their hopes began to wilt along with the flowers they had brought: "It was a long, long wait. Eventually we gave up and went back home. "First we called to the US, friends and relatives told us they saw her off at the airport." Then ominously an official called from the airport asking Aster to collect her luggage. That is when they realised she had arrived in the country but would not be coming home. All pleas and requests for information fell on deaf ears in the months that followed. Instead Hanna's grandmother was warned by authorities to stop inquiring. The family later heard that Aster was being held in the infamous jail known as Karshelli in the heart of Asmara. Hanna's father is believed to be detained, with the others arrested on 18 and 19 September 2001, in the remote, hostile and highly secretive prison known as Ela-Ero, located in eastern lowlands north-east of Asmara. Accused of treason, none of them has ever been brought to trial or allowed to see their relatives. At around the same time, the government also shut down all the fledgling independent newspapers and detained their editors and journalists - also believed to be imprisoned in Ela-Ero. The Eritrean government - including its embassy in the UK - has not responded to the BBC's request for comment regarding the whereabouts of the prisoners or whether or not they are alive. Hanna, like many thousands of young Eritreans fleeing conscription and in search of better opportunities, left the country - travelling secretively over the border without a passport. Now 35 years old, she is married and lives in the US, working as a trauma specialist - but still feels traumatised herself by how she lost her parents. As she stares at old pictures of her parents, she worries her memories will fade of the happy times before their arrest - the laughter, the family gatherings, the birthday parties: "My dad always wanted to gather people in the house, they were good days." Hanna often looks at old photos - this one shows her with her parents - and worries about her memories fading She also hankers after her mother's "unmatched" egg and potato sandwiches. On trips down to the coast when her father was the minister of fisheries, Hanna remembers him organising singing competitions in the car: "He would ask us to sing one by one and whoever won would get a present." title: Our head teacher was an abuser. We joined forces to get justice - now we're married
description: Students spent years collecting evidence against their Indonesian principal, before falling in love.
body: Zia and Yusron were both star pupils at a boarding school in Lombok Warning: This story contains details of sexual assault The voice on the end of the phone made Yusron Azzahidi's stomach lurch. He had rung his sister's number after she had texted, urgently asking him to call. But this was not her on the line - it was Yusron's former head teacher. He was in Yusron's family home. "I knew. I knew exactly what he wanted to talk about," Yusron says. Ahmad Imanuddin Sumar, known to his students as "Abah" ["father"], had a reputation to uphold. He was the widely respected leader of an Islamic boarding school on the Indonesian island of Lombok. And Abah had discovered that Yusron and his old school friends had been collating testimony from several students who say he sexually assaulted them. This video can not be played Listen: Ahmad Imanuddin Sumar pleads with former student Yusron to keep quiet about sex abuse claims Sexual abuse in Islamic boarding schools has been described as a national emergency by Indonesia's National Commission on Violence Against Women. But many cases never reach the courts because the victims are persuaded to withdraw their allegations, or are pressured into staying quiet, legal experts say. And now Abah was on the phone to Yusron, making exactly that kind of demand. "Cover the shame of your teacher. Everyone makes mistakes, my child," he sobbed. What he did not realise was that Yusron was recording his every word. World of Secrets: Catching My Teacher When a dark secret emerges at the heart of their school in Indonesia, former students turn detective to seek the truth. The full story with be available in subsequent episodes of World of Secrets Catching My Teacher Watch the full investigation on iPlayer from 0001 Monday 21 September. If you are outside the UK, you will be able watch on YouTube Yusron began investigating Abah a year previously, sparked by a revelation one night by his former classmate Ziadatur Rahmah. They had both been star pupils at Lombok's Abu Barokat school. Now they were at university - Yusron in the capital Jakarta, and Ziadatur in Cairo, Egypt - and had begun reminiscing over the phone about their school days. One night Ziadatur, known to her friends as Zia, told Yusron that Abah had sexually assaulted her when she was 16. She had needed to go to the toilet during class and Abah had intercepted her in the school gardens and asked her to accompany him to his house which was on the premises. Once inside, he had told her he loved her, she told Yusron. "He pulled me down so I was sitting on his lap… Then he started kissing me… He was stroking and touching my body," she later told the BBC World Service, too, explaining that he told her to do the same to him. Luckily, she said, one of his children began banging on the locked front door. Abah signalled to her to leave and she bolted out the back. But the effect was devastating. "I felt very dirty, ruined, and I was lost." Yusron, when he heard Zia's account, was unsure what to do. Their school had inculcated them with the motto: "Sami'na wa ata'na" ["We hear, and we obey"]. Yusron, photographed here at boarding school, had always looked up to his head teacher But he also could not stop thinking about it. So he suggested that he and Zia, together with her school friends Wanda Hamidah and Mahima Eka, gather corroborating evidence to support her testimony. And slowly, as they spoke to their old classmates, other recollections emerged - the friends sharing their findings with each other on WhatsApp. The most significant was from a friend of Wanda's. She recalled seeing a younger girl crying in the school bathroom during their final year, late at night. And that Abah had come looking for her, red-faced and panting. This girl, Sukma Rohana, was still at the school. She told the BBC about her ordeal. Sukma says Abah tried to rape her When Sukma was 17, Abah had asked her to join him for new year's prayers, she told us. When she entered Abah's house, he had covered her mouth and told her to lie down, she said, before he stripped below the waist. "He kept talking, saying he couldn't control himself any more," Sukma said. "He was feeling me up through my knickers… He tried to rape me." And then, she said, she had found the strength to kick him hard in the stomach and took the opportunity to flee. As she ran, she said she had looked back to see his torch seeking her out. As evidence like this emerged, Yusron would co-ordinate it - following up with calls to the students making the allegations, and keeping painstaking notes. He typed up a seven-page document outlining the alleged abuse of Sukma, Zia and four other former students. Wanda organised a meeting with representatives from the Nahdlatul Wathan Diniyah Islamiyah (NWDI) - the powerful organisation that ran their school and hundreds of others, and which was also funding some of the students' studies in Cairo. The meeting went well, the friends told us - the NWDI representatives had said they would help them take the case to the police. But three weeks later, when Yusron received that ominous text from his sister - calling back to find Abah on the end of the phone in Yusron's family home - it became clear the NWDI had passed on Yusron's written documents to him. "If this is leaked to the media… I'll be destroyed," Abah can be heard saying on Yusron's recording of him. He pleads with Yusron to lie for him, giving him a series of cover stories he can use to retract his evidence document. He then called Zia and exerted similar pressure. Like Yusron, she recorded the call. In it, Abah admits he abused her but pleads with her to stay silent. Ahmad Abah Sumar, known to his students as "Abah", asked Zia and Sukma to keep their experiences quiet Sukma, for her part, told us she was called to Abah's house to discover two police officers and an NWDI lawyer waiting for her. T

title: 'I'm often stopped on the street for confessions' - Retiring bishop reflects on a life at the heart of the community
description: Bishop Donal McKeown has no regrets about choosing a religious life, but "would have loved to have been married".
body: Donal McKeown has spent the past quarter of a century as a bishop The outgoing Catholic Bishop of Derry believes one of the biggest challenges of retirement will be getting used to his phone "not ringing so often". Donal McKeown has spent the past quarter of a century as a bishop, but on Sunday he will say his final Mass as head of the diocese after 12 years. Bishop Michael Router will then be installed at St Eugene's Cathedral. As he prepares to retire, Bishop McKeown has been reflecting on being part of being part of important moments in history and as well as being stopped on the street for confessions. Ordained in his native Randalstown, County Antrim, in 1977, McKeown became Bishop of Down and Connor in 2001 and Bishop of Derry in 2014. He has become one of the best-known faces of the Catholic Church in Ireland. At the age of 76, McKeown is now preparing for a life away from being a church leader. "A bishop friend who retired told me it took three years for the tiredness to leave his body," McKeown told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme. "I am ready to start adjusting to a new way of life. "As bishop, my day is full of meetings, events, a lot of timings and places I need to be. "Retirement does bring with it a relief not to be in charge anymore, but I also now have to get a sense of who I am away from being in a position of leadership." Bishop McKeown and Pope Leo XIV met at the Vatican in Rome, in April of this year McKeown plans to stay in the area, a place he describes as "marvellous, with wonderful, welcoming people." "In many ways, the high points have been the low points," he said. "When it comes to difficult times, like the death of Lyra McKee, or big funerals of people like John Hume, Martin McGuinness, Seamus Heaney and plenty of others, the city is remarkably good at coming together. "It's the strength of the community that is able to respond to difficult times and that applies to the rural parishes too." He added that his "biggest joy has been being able to work with people". "I like walking the streets of Derry and I am often stopped by people asking for prayers and confessions." The Catholic Diocese of Derry spans 51 parishes across almost all of County Londonderry, parts of County Tyrone and a very small area across the River Bann in County Antrim. It also covers parts of County Donegal in the Republic of Ireland. Amidst concerns over too many dioceses in Ireland, The Vatican has been considering a potential cross-border merger of the dioceses of Derry and its neighbour in the Republic of Ireland, Raphoe. Church leaders, including McKeown, have in the past expressed concerns and pushed for a delay McKeown said the prospect has not "gone off the table" in Rome, but he believes any final decision remains some time off. "It's possible Derry and Raphoe may be asked to work together in the future. "I have made clear to the Vatican it would need a major civic reorganisation, one diocese is registered as a charity in Dublin, the other in Belfast, who would be in charge? "But I can also see on the map, there's really nowhere else that Raphoe can go other than with Derry in terms of the border that it shares." Bishop McKeown (centre) on his ordination as a bishop at St Peter's Cathedral in Belfast in 2001, pictured with Bishop Patrick Walsh (right) and Bishop Anthony Farquhar (left) Canon law states that diocesan bishops are expected to hand in their resignation when they turn 75. McKeown, who is also chair of the Council for Catholic Maintained Schools (CCMS), admits keeping up the energy needed for leadership at 76, is not easy. "It is different to what it was 20 years ago," he added. "I am much more relaxed now and grateful to have the pressure of decision making off my shoulders. "I've always done a lot of sport, five-a-side football, GAA (Gaelic Athletic Association), and marathons and I am glad [to] have good health at this stage of my life." Bishop McKeown with his parents, James and Rose on his ordination to the priesthood in 1977 in Randalstown Retirement can bring with it reflection on life choices, but McKeown is at peace with his religious path. "I am very happy with the choices I made and my vocation in life," he said. "I would have loved to have been married. "I think I wouldn't have been a bad husband, bad daddy or grandfather but that was not my vocation and I'm perfectly happy with that. "I have made mistakes, but I have been blessed to be a priest and a bishop over the past 49 years." He added that he hoped he had "done some good and laid some foundations for others to build on". "We just pass on the baton to someone else. "I look back only with gratitude." title: The deadly new drugs reshaping Scotland's fight against addiction
description: Experts warn potent new substances are making an already deadly crisis more dangerous.
body: Nitazenes are a class of synthetic opioids often sold as heroin Efforts to bring down Scotland's sky-high rate of drug deaths are being frustrated by the arrival of hundreds of powerful new synthetic substances that experts warn are making the deadly drugs crisis even more dangerous. In the past three years, there has been an explosion in the supply of new synthetic cannabinoids and opioids, transforming the illicit drugs trade and increasing the risk of fatal overdoses. Annual figures to be released on Wednesday are expected to show a rise in the number of drug-related deaths in Scotland, which already has an unenviable record as the drugs death capital of Europe. "The illicit drug supply in Scotland is getting more and more dangerous," said Dr Lorna Nisbet of Dundee University's Leverhulme Research Centre for Forensic Science. Forensic scientist Lorna Nisbet says the illicit drug supply in Scotland is getting more dangerous Unlike heroin or cocaine, which are derived from cultivated plants, many of the new substances are manufactured in clandestine laboratories. They include synthetic opioids such as nitazenes and orphines, some of which are hundreds of times more potent than heroin. Police say organised crime groups are increasingly mixing the substances with existing drugs to maximise their profits. "I think it's shameful behaviour that we're seeing from these organised crime groups," Supt Niven Bull, of Police Scotland, said. "They are profiting from people's misery." On average, a new psychoactive substance emerged every week in 2025, according to the European Union Drugs Agency (EUDA)., external The agency says tighter controls imposed by China and the Taliban's ban on poppy cultivation in Afghanistan have pushed production closer to consumer markets. That includes Scotland, where police have raided two suspected nitazene factories in the past 14 months, making five arrests in total. In July 2025, officers discovered an alleged illicit drugs laboratory in Patna, Ayrshire, leading to the arrest of three people. Deputy Chief Constable Jane Connors later described it as the UK's first suspected nitazene laboratory. BBC News can also reveal that two men, aged 43 and 56, were arrested in February this year after police searched a unit in Loanhead, Midlothian, as part of an investigation into another suspected synthetic opioid lab. In 2024, nitazenes were implicated in 76 drug-related deaths in Scotland, according to official figures, external, more than three times the number of the previous year. "These drugs are extremely dangerous, and it's pretty rapid for us to be able to keep up as scientists," says Dr Nisbet, whose laboratory is soon set to take on an expanded role as Scotland's national drug testing facility. The changing nature of the supply also creates challenges for lawmakers who are in a race to identify and ban dangerous new substances before they can spread legally and cause havoc. "New and harmful substances continue to be created to circumvent legal controls," EUDA points out. While control of illicit drugs is reserved to Westminster under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971, responsibility for public health, policing and prosecutions is devolved to the Scottish government and its agencies. Gareth Balmer says this is a frightening new landscape On the front line of the battle to save lives, charity workers say they are seeing the devastating impact of the new synthetic opioids first-hand. In the woods at Glenbarr on the Kintyre peninsula, staff from the drug, alcohol and mental health charity With You are trying to treat trauma in a group designed to help former drug and alcohol users reconnect with nature. Gareth Balmer, the charity's national harm reduction lead, says nitazenes and other synthetic opioids are now appearing across the drug supply, from benzodiazepine (street Valium) pills and cannabinoids, known as spice, to cocaine and heroin. "This is a frightening new landscape," he said. "I don't think drugs have ever been as risky or as dangerous as they are now." The result is that some users are experiencing unexpected and sometimes catastrophic overdoses. "Some of these substances are so potent that a grain would be enough to take somebody over," Balmer warned, adding that access to naloxone, which can reverse the effects of an opioid overdose, is now more important than ever. The figures behind Scotland's drug death toll Scottish drug deaths fall but remain worst in Europe Bull said Police Scotland was taking a twin-track approach, promising to "relentlessly pursue" dealers while also recognising that many drug users need help. In 2025, officers seized about £80m worth of street drugs. So far this year that figure has already reached £78m. "Hundreds of individuals have been arrested, and many people are serving custodial sentences," Bull said. But he added that the force also wanted to help users "to make better life choices". "If we come across people who are suffering from addiction, who are in a low point in their life, then we will look to help support them and we'll look to refer them to the relevant agency," he said. Prof Niamh Nic Daeid says her team will be able to provide near real-time information to drug-using communities Prof Niamh Nic Daeid, director of Dundee University's Leverhulme laboratory, said its expanded role as a national drug testing and research centre would make a difference too. On one hand, she said, her team will be able to provide near real-time information to drug-using communities, allowing them to make safer and more informed choices. On the other, the research will help to inform government policy. "Drugs are changing all the time," she said. "Part of the establishment of this facility is to have a research capability that will enable us to try to keep up. "If we don't know what substances are present in the samples, how can we provide the right advice?" Vick

title: Carrick has faith in VAR despite derby error
description: Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick still has faith in VAR despite the derby blunder that cost his side in their home defeat by Manchester City
body: The VAR failed to spot Enzo Fernandez (left, on ground) in an offside position and clearly interfering with play as Manchester City scored their winning goal at Manchester United Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick says he still has faith in the video assistant referee - but added that the apology for the error that led to their defeat in the Manchester derby does not mean much. Referee's body Pro Ref issued a formal apology to United within three hours of the end of Manchester City's 1-0 victory at Old Trafford. Neither VAR Matt Donohue nor his assistant Blake Antrobus have been selected for games this weekend after failing to spot City midfielder Enzo Fernandez clearly in an offside position and interfering with play before Erling Haaland's matchwinner for City. Carrick was livid after the game, saying it was a "worrying" interpretation of the rules. And before his side's Premier League trip to Fulham on Sunday, the United boss was asked if he still had faith in VAR. "One-off things can happen," he said. "At the time it was a pretty big one, we know that. I don't think I need to go over that. But yes, I've got faith in it. It's the system we work towards and that we use." Referee's chief Howard Webb has been heavily criticised over general officiating standards in the game. Analysing the incident on 'Match Officials Mic'd Up', Webb said he was "really disappointed" with the outcome, stating the officials had been too focused on a potential offside against Haaland and had failed to assess Fernandez's position. Webb has spoken to United about the situation in an effort to be more accountable. "The apology doesn't mean an awful lot," said Carrick. "I can appreciate and respect them putting their hands up and saying we got that wrong - it does happen. We just have to deal with it. "Maybe we get one or two decisions on the law of averages or whatever but that one had a huge impact on the game and that's why it was particularly tough." Leny Yoro has made 69 appearances for Manchester United Carrick has backed central defender Leny Yoro despite his disappointing performance in the 3-2 Carabao Cup defeat by Brighton on Wednesday. Yoro was linked with Real Madrid, Paris St-Germain and Liverpool when he joined United from Lille as an 18-year-old in July 2024. The £52.2m fee underlined the faith United's recruitment department had in Yoro's potential. So far though, it has been unfulfilled. The 20-year-old has featured in 55 Premier League games, but 25 of those have been as a substitute. His only starts this term have been against Sabah FK in the Champions League and Brighton, when his positioning was called into question as the visitors became the first side to win at Old Trafford after trailing by two goals for over 50 years. "I've got no worries for Leny," said Carrick. "He's got a fantastic future ahead of him. "There's no cut off point. Some players find when they're 18 that they are at a level where they can really perform. Sometimes it's 22, 23, 24 when you see players start developing. "What we've got to be careful of, and I certainly won't do, is making knee-jerk decisions on certain players just because of one game or one half or one moment in a game. We've got a lot of belief in Leny." title: Littler seals dramatic final-leg win over Aspinall
description: World champion Luke Littler beats Nathan Aspinall 10-9 to reach the last eight of the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam.
body: Luke Littler (left) said he and Nathan Aspinall "bring the best out of each other" in his post-match interview World champion Luke Littler beat Nathan Aspinall in a dramatic finale to reach the last eight of the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam. Littler, 19, trailed 9-8 in a best-of-19 contest that had been close throughout and he held throw in the 18th leg to force a decider. Needing to break Aspinall's throw to win, Littler started the leg with his seventh 180 of the match and checked out 58 for a match-clinching 12-darter. The two Englishmen had been involved in a World Matchplay classic in July, when Littler threw a nine-darter in the opening leg of an 11-8 victory. "The pace of the game suits us both, we're good friends and we bring the best out of each other," said Littler, who has a chance to complete a clean sweep of the PDC's premier events in 2026. "I only played well in the last session [from 6-6 onwards]. In the first two sessions, I didn't feel confident but I managed to get it to 6-6 and I was very good in the third." The world number one will meet former Premier League champion Jonny Clayton in the quarter-finals on Sunday. Clayton beat Japan's Motomu Sakai 10-8 and is one of two Welshmen in the last eight, with Gerwyn Price also progressing courtesy of a 10-5 win against Canada's Jim Long. England's James Wade was the other winner in Saturday's evening session, defeating Wessel Nijman of the Netherlands, and will face Price next. Littler survives scare to progress in Amsterdam Champion Van Gerwen loses in first round to Gurney Earlier on Saturday, world number two Luke Humphries lost the deciding leg of his last-16 match against Dirk van Duijvenbode. Van Duijvenbode's next opponent will be fellow Dutchman Gian van Veen, who was beaten by Littler in January's World Championship final. England's Ross Smith and Northern Ireland's Josh Rock also won their last-16 ties to complete the quarter-final line-up. The tournament concludes on Sunday, with the quarter-finals taking place from 12:00 BST and the semi-finals and final being played during the evening session (18:00 BST). title: Strictly returns with new hosting trio as celebrities find out dance pairings
description: Emma Willis, Josh Widdicombe and Johannes Radebe take over from long-running presenting duo Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman.
body: Strictly Come Dancing has returned to the small screen for its 24th series, in a new era for the show as it moves forward with a revamped presenting line up. Broadcaster Emma Willis, comedian Josh Widdicombe and former Strictly professional Johannes Radebe made their presenting debut on Saturday, taking over from long-running hosting duo Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman, who left the show last year. A fresh cohort of famous faces – including actress Melanie Walters and former England footballer Shaun Wright-Phillips – also stepped onto the ballroom floor for the first time. During the launch show, it was revealed which professional dancers they were paired with. Stepping out onto the ballroom floor after a huge all-cast opening dance routine, Willis said presenting Strictly was a "genuine honour". "Josh, you've got moves," proclaimed Radebe, a former professional on the show. While Widdicombe added that it was "a little bit overwhelming" but he was "delighted" to be there. In a first for the show, celebrity and pro pairings were revealed via three dance routines. It functioned as a musical chairs of sorts, in which the contestants switched partners until the music was paused, and a couple was announced. Here is a list of the pairings in full: Actress Lacey Turner and Vito Coppola Reality TV star Dani Dyer and Nikita Kuzmin Hair stylist to the stars Chris Appleton and Amy Dowden Australian singer and actress Delta Goodrem and Kai Widdrington DJ and social media personality Cach Mercer and Maddie Ingoldsby TV and radio presenter Will Best and Dianne Buswell Paralympian Dame Sarah Storey and Julian Caillon Actress Jaime Winstone and Carlos Gu TV and stage actress Bethany Antonia and Nancy Xu Former England footballer Shaun Wright-Phillips and Alexis Warr Presenter and author Graeme Hall and Lauren Oakley Actor Lawrence Robb and Jowita Przystał Skeleton athlete Tabby Stoecker and Mark Karmalita YouTuber John Nellis and Katya Jones TV and stage actress Melanie Walters and Aljaž Škorjanec One pair who won't need to get to know each other are reality TV star Dani Dyer and Nikita Kuzmin. Dyer is back to compete for a second time, having withdrawn from last year's series due to a fractured ankle. "I'm just over the moon. I'm so, so happy," she said after the pairing, while Kuzmin added that he had "tears of joy" in his eyes. Meanwhile, actress Bethany Antonia and professional Nancy Xu became the third two-woman couple to compete in the show. In a poignant moment, Antonia revealed that watching boxer Nicola Adams and Katya Jones performing together in Strictly's 2020 series was a "big part of my coming out journey". Among the other pairings were EastEnders actress Lacey Turner and Vito Coppola, former Paralympian Dame Sarah Storey and Julian Caillon, and Shaun Wright-Phillips and Alexis Warr. Also back on the dancefloor for a final spin was reigning Strictly champion, former Lionness Karen Carney. Clad in the same diamante-encrusted football shirt, Carney recreated the Jive that first marked her out as a contender of her series, alongside dance partner Carlos Gu. "I absolutely feel like I'm at home," Carney told Willis after the routine, as she paid tribute to her pro partner. In 13 weeks time, she'll have to surrender that glitterball trophy to a new victor. Reigning champion Karen Carney returned to perform her week one Jive with pro partner Carlos Gu And it is not just presenters and celebrities navigating the ballroom for the first time: Aleksandra Isaeva, Cristian Priori, Lethabo Monametsi, Maddie Ingoldsby, and Mark Karmalita are the five new professionals joining the Strictly cast this series. They hail from the UK, Canada, Italy, South Africa and Ukraine. The five made a high-impact entrance, performing a searing routine that kicked off on top of an enormous encaged disco ball. Strictly's five new professional dancers gave a high-octane debut performance Saturday's show was a more paired back role for Craig Revel Horwood and his fellow judges - Motsi Mabuse, Shirley Ballas and Anton Du Beke - who featured less. But there was still time for resident villain Horwood to direct a jibe at broadcaster Will Best's hip action: "Call in the paramedics darling, dislocation - my goodness." And some other traditions remain intact. Once all the dance routines were wrapped, the pairings announced, and the chats in the "Clauditorium" concluded, it was time for the show's three new hosts to bid farewell with the customary order to "staaart dancing!" title: Trump says US will form 'AI Force' and appoint an artificial intelligence tsar
description: The president said his administration "will not in any way hinder or stifle the growth" amid amid warnings about the emergent technology.
body: US President Donald Trump has announced that he will form an "AI Force" and appoint an artificial intelligence tsar amid warnings about the emergent technology. In a social media post on Saturday, he said his administration "will not in any way hinder or stifle the growth" of the industry, and pushed back against calls to slow down the development of AI until better safeguards are put in place. His post came as a slew of warnings about the potential dangers of AI have spurred calls for coordinated action on the technology's development. Trump offered no details or a timeline for his plan. Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings "AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25% of our Country's GDP," he said on social media, adding that he wants the US to continue leading China in AI. AI now sits at the heart of the US-China rivalry as the world's two largest economies seek to gain an edge in advanced tech, and it is expected to be discussed when Trump meets President Xi Jinping next week. Meanwhile, Trump said his administration would use the existing criminal and civil justice system to target any bad actors using the AI. He also repeated comments that criticism and concerns around the potential dangers of AI are a "hoax". This video can not be played Watch: Cyber Correspondent Joe Tidy considers if could AI wipe out humanity, and how it might do it Claims by current and former researchers that the tech will endanger humanity - with one suggesting there is a greater than 10% chance of it "killing all humans" - have raised alarm bells in recent weeks. Major AI companies have been racing to develop better systems, including creating what they call super intelligence - theoretical tech which is smarter than humans. AI titans Anthropic, OpenAI and Google - the tech companies behind Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini, respectively - have also disclosed instances of security breaches or incidents in which their chatbots were used for "malicious activity". Anthropic head Dario Amodei recently called for AI development to slow down and proposed industry-wide deceleration and regulation, as well as independent monitoring of AI model development. Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk of xAI have both said they agree with his recommendations. Jack Clark, co-founder of Anthropic, told BBC that a "kill switch" that can be checked by a third party may need to be mandatory for the industry. The warnings have prompted US lawmakers to propose legislation around the technology but Altman suggested this week that Washington has struggled to keep pace with the new tech and how to regulate it. He said people should have more faith in AI firms to keep it safe. "The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it's the right thing and we feel the magnitude of this," Altman told a conference in San Francisco. In the UK, MPs across parties and peers have identified human rights risks posed by artificial intelligence and have argued that existing laws are ill-equipped to address the technology's rapid growth. The Joint Committee on Human Rights (JCHR) has published a report calling for a new bill on AI to "address the scale and seriousness" of such threats. title: Tens of thousands of fridge freezers left at docks as household collections suspended
description: A recycling firm collapsed in 2025, leaving the appliances in limbo until a takeover is complete.
body: The closure of the Newport site is thought to have taken away about 30% of the fridge recycling capacity in the UK People have reported storing broken fridges and freezers in their gardens for months because some council collections have been suspended. It follows the closure of specialist treatment facilities and a wider shortage of capacity to process cooling appliances, the Local Government Authority (LGA) said. Recycling company Unimetals, which had dozens of sites in the UK, filed for liquidation in 2025 leaving tens of thousands of fridge freezers at Newport Docks. The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said it was working to manage the capacity shortages. Almost a quarter of Welsh councils say they have suspended household collections of fridge-freezers due to a shortage of space at disposal sites. Cardiff is one of these and Lee Young, who lives in the city, has been trying to get rid of his broken fridge-freezer for two months. "I tried to take it to the recycling centre in July but was told it wasn't accepted. Someone said the council would collect it, but they won't either." It has been sitting in his back garden ever since and he does not know when council collections will resume. Lee Young has repurposed his old fridge freezer for plant storage overnight until he can get rid of it Lee said he was also confused by the different policies in neighbouring councils. "If I lived in Barry or Penarth (Vale of Glamorgan) they would be able to collect it from the kerb. I don't know why I can't in Cardiff." The Welsh Local Government Association has been asked why some councils are still able to carry out the collections while others are not. Michael Enea, a campaigner in Newport who blogs about fly-tipping, said he often saw the old appliances at the side of the road and thinks this could now get worse. "I think there'll be a lot of people in local communities where they don't have the ability to dispose of their fridges and freezers, who will end up literally dumping them in the street. "We see it quite a lot in Newport and right over Wales." Michael Enea has seen fridge freezers fly-tipped around Newport in recent months The LGA said it had identified dozens of councils across Wales and England that had been forced to stop or restrict collections, with more expected to follow suit. Oxfordshire County Council has urged the UK government to reopen the Newport plant to help with the "crisis". Associated British Ports, which took over the running of the Newport site, said it was "in discussions with third parties" about the future of the site and materials. A spokesperson added: "In the interim, the material is being managed responsibly as part of the site's transition and will be transferred to another specialist recycling operation in due course." APB said appliances will be transferred to another specialist recycling operation in due course Dr David Santillo, a research scientist at Greenpeace, said it was possible that some of the fridges and freezers at Newport Docks still contained "some of the most harmful chemicals" such as hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs). HFCs are mainly used in air conditioning, industrial chillers and fridges, but are also powerful greenhouse gases. Chemicals such as isobutane, pentane and ammonia can also be found in commercial-type fridges, Dr Santillo added. "None of these chemicals are benign. They all have the potential for harmful effects, or they can be toxic if they leak," he said. Santillo said some older chemicals could have a "much wider impact" on the environment and leaving appliances out for long periods had the potential to produce "toxic smoke" if a fire breaks out. Dr David Santillo has urged the UK government to improve the recycling capacity for appliances Santillo said the recycling of fridges and freezers was a national issue and he urged the UK government to "step in and find a solution". Defra said it appreciated the "challenges" facing local authorities, and was working to manage the impact of treatment capacity shortages. It added: "This includes allowing the storage of fridge and cooling equipment on temporary sites provided certain conditions set out by the Environment Agency are met." Regulator Natural Resources Wales said it was "aware of the pressures" affecting operators across the UK. It added that it was providing "regulatory flexibility" to help manage temporary storage pressures and would "continue to support efforts across the sector to restore treatment capacity and minimise disruption". The Welsh government said it was working with NRW, local authorities and the UK government to "manage the situation and support a return to normal capacity." title: Matthew Rhys' sister 'so proud of him' after historic Emmy wins
description: Rhys, from Cardiff, became the first person to win two lead acting Emmy prizes in one night.
body: Matthew Rhys's sister Rachel was there with him at the Emmy Awards for his historic double win The sister of Hollywood actor Matthew Rhys said her family had been "pinching ourselves all week" following his historic Emmy success. Rhys became the first person to win two lead acting Emmy prizes in one night, after he was named best lead actor in a limited series for the psychological thriller The Beast In Me, and best lead actor in a comedy for his role in Widow's Bay. His older sister Rachel Evans, who accompanied Rhys to the ceremony in Los Angeles, said she was starstruck seeing Hollywood royalty at the event, and revealed that she and her brother called their parents afterwards, who were sat at home in their dressing gowns. "I think we just all giggled for a long time." Rhys, who grew up in Cardiff, made history at the Emmy Awards, becoming the first person to win two lead acting prizes in one night Speaking to Lucy Owen on BBC Radio Wales, Evans said watching Rhys win the awards was "an experience I will never ever forget or probably match". She said that as the "bossy" older sister, she told him that morning that he needed to prepare, adding: "If you win, you cannot wing it." "We're so proud of him," she said. She also recalled the emotional moment when he thanked her during one of his acceptance speeches, calling her "the brains of the outfit". Rachel and Matthew as children Evans described the moment he won as "insane". "Keri [Russell, Rhys' partner] and I just looked at each other and we just could not believe it. "Matthew's described it as surreal and it just really was." Evans said that Russell "loves to celebrate him and she's his biggest supporter", and was "just cheering, whooping, hands in the air" after his award wins. This video can not be played "Luck and timing": Matthew Rhys on his historic Emmy Awards double win Evans said that she saw many Hollywood stars that evening, and was starstruck by Harrison Ford. "I'm a bit nervous about these things. I was just happy gaping and remembering things," she said. Despite attending multiple after-parties that evening, Evans said they made sure to video call their parents who were sat at home in their dressing gowns. "They were so far away, but they were so proud of him, as we all are... and they were pleased that I was there with him really." Evans told Owen that she unexpectedly burst into tears while watching his Emmy awards being engraved, saying that was the moment it "sank in". Matthew Rhys' sister Rachel celebrates his Emmy success Rachel Evans joins Lucy to look back on a proud week for the family. Evans told Owen that the response back in Wales had been "overwhelming". "We were just thrilled by the response when we woke up in the morning from home. It was just everything we could wish for," she said. In his acceptance speech, Rhys paid tribute to the "great and good people of Wales, who were as much a nurturer as anyone else". "We are a small but mighty nation," he said, ending his speech with "diolch yn fawr iawn", which means "thank you very much" in Welsh. Evans said her brother has lived abroad for 25 years, but Wales "is absolutely in his heart and is his home", adding that he was "really keen to speak to everybody" the day after his wins. "Wales had been so supportive of his career all along and had really cheered him on," she added. title: Hear'Say, 'Snake' & Tony Blair: A Coventry win 25 years in the making
description: Coventry City's win over Nottingham Forest - thanks to Jay Dasilva's goal - was a victory which was over 25 years in the making following some dark days for the Sky Blues.
body: Jay Dasilva's goal was Coventry's first since Mustapha Hadji netted in a 3-2 defeat by Aston Villa on 5 May 2001 Hear'Say were top of the pops, a mobile phone game called 'Snake' was all the rage and Tony Blair was Prime Minister. Wind the clock back to April 2001 and things looked rather different. It was also the last time Coventry City tasted victory in English football's top flight. That came courtesy of a 1-0 win over Sunderland - John Hartson heading in the winner for Gordon Strachan's side in front of 20,946 fans at Highfield Road. Much has happened in the life of Coventry since that moment 9,287 days ago. A rollercoaster journey might be understating it. They were relegated at the end of the 2000-01 campaign and would spend the next 11 seasons in the second tier before dropping down to League One in 2012. Then followed a particularly dark and turbulent period in the club's history featuring points deductions and a stint in administration. Having left Highfield Road in 2005 they became embroiled in a bitter dispute over the Ricoh Arena in 2013 and its rent. The nadir, arguably, was when they were forced to play matches away from Coventry, at Northampton Town, before later plummeting down to the fourth tier for the first time in 59 years in 2017. Doubtless there were those packed into the Bridgford Stand at the City Ground on Saturday who were present during those years of Sky Blue hell. So the explosion of emotion at the full-time whistle - after Jay Dasilva's goal settled matters - felt like Sky Blue heaven. "It's been a tough opening for us, so those first Premier League points feel great," Coventry boss Frank Lampard told BBC Radio 5 Live. "I thought the players were brilliant. The fight, work ethic and togetherness but also the tactical side of it. They dug and fought for each other which is what you need to win a Premier League game." This video can not be played Coventry defeat Forest for first win since Prem return Coventry had been stranded on 99 Premier League wins for over a quarter of a century before this victory ticked them over to three figures at long last. Lampard hopes this victory could be a key staging post in a campaign where avoiding relegation will be the main aim. "It's really important for some of the players," he told BBC Match of the Day. "For many of them it is their debut in the Premier League, they haven't been here before and they need to feel like they belong and play like that." Lampard acknowledged his players must have thick skins to come through the slog of a Premier League season. The fact this victory came off the back of a 5-0 drubbing at home to Brighton makes it all the more rewarding for the Coventry boss. "There are lots of things we can learn and sometimes this year we may take those hits, it's a reality for teams that get to the Premier League," added Lampard. "It's important we overcome them in terms of how we take it on board and stay together. "It is easy to point in different directions when you lose but the group's really strong, really together, there'll have a good feeling from this one. But we'll keep our feet on the ground because it is one win, but it was needed for us." title: Premier League fans and players honour Noah Woods
description: Everton and Ipswich supporters and players pay tribute to the three-year-old, who died this week.
body: Ipswich and Everton fans stood to applaud in Noah's memory as a picture of him was shown on the big screen A tribute to three-year-old Noah Woods was shown on the big screen ahead of the Everton vs Ipswich Town Premier League match, while players wore black armbands in his memory. The toddler became separated from a relative after visiting a playground in Merriam Close, Brantham, on Tuesday afternoon, Suffolk Police said. About 1,300 members of the public joined a search to find Noah, who police said was non-verbal, partially deaf and had been undergoing an assessment for autism. Met Police divers recovered his body from a lake, known locally as Decoy Pond, on Wednesday afternoon and Suffolk Police said his death was not being treated as suspicious. Ipswich Town defender Leif Davis donated £2,000 to a fundraising appeal set up in aid of Noah Woods's family Three minutes into the game, won 1-0 by the home side, both sets of supporters stood to applaud in memory of Noah, Everton said in a post on X, external. Town defender Leif Davis donated £2,000 to the fundraising appeal set up to support Noah's family and captain Dara O'Shea and goalkeeper Christian Walton were among the club delegation who laid flowers at the playground where he went missing. On Thursday, Noah's father Rhys Woods paid tribute to his son in a message shared on a community Facebook group. He wrote: "There are no words to describe the pain of this loss, we are all absolutely heartbroken, Noah was the sweetest and most innocent little boy, with nothing but love to give, and we are going to miss him so very much." Noah Woods was at a playground with a relative before he went missing Suffolk Police said on Thursday that the body of the child recovered by police divers had been formally identified as Noah, subject to confirmation at formal inquest proceedings. The force said police still have a number of inquiries to complete before submitting a file for the coroner. Meanwhile, a fundraising page set up by Good Dads Club, a community of fathers based in nearby Colchester, had received more than £100,000 in donations from a total of more than 6,000 supporters by Saturday evening. title: Olid's Man Utd take big step forward after 'intense week'
description: A week ago, the picture at Manchester United looked bleak. Then on Saturday, victory was snatched away from them at Arsenal. But have we seen signs of improvement from Eva Olid's side?
body: Swedish midfielder Julia Zigiotti joined United from Bayern Munich last year A week ago, the picture for Manchester United looked a lot bleaker than it did at the full-time whistle on Saturday. Regardless of the stoppage-time equaliser they conceded at Arsenal's Emirates Stadium, United's performance marked a major sign of progress. Defeats in their opening two matches, including a 5-0 thrashing by Chelsea, meant the list of questions for new manager Eva Olid seemed endless. United were disorganised, lacking in identity and were wide open at the back as their new era under Olid began in disappointing fashion. Those early displays did little to fill supporters with confidence, and Olid faced criticism for her decisions despite being in the job just a matter of weeks. However, a gutsy defensive display against Arsenal delivered a well-earned 1-1 draw and they were only denied victory by a 95th-minute leveller. While United's wait for a first Women's Super League win of the season continues, this performance suggested there may not be quite the cause for concern many suspected. Arsenal earn point with late leveller against Man Utd Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed Olid, 41, took over as manager in the summer, joining from Hearts, and promised to implement a new attacking style of play that focused heavily on possession. However, in their opening two games, United had just two shots on target and less than 40% possession in both matches. In the second of those games, they suffered the five-goal humbling at home by Chelsea. Few expected them to come away with anything against an Arsenal team who many tipped to win the title before the season kicked off, albeit they have struggled to score goals efficiently. Olid knew it would be a test but said on Friday she wanted her players to believe in themselves, show confidence, and to go back to the defensive roots they knew and built so well under her predecessor Marc Skinner. "It has been an intense week because there were a lot of emotions from players and staff. Nobody wants to lose 5-0," said Olid. "We grew as a team. The first day after losing 5-0 is not easy for anyone. We spoke and said we needed energy this week and a positive mindset. "The focus was the defensive shape. It's trying to get them more confidence." Olid ultimately wants her United team to dominate the ball and create more chances in front of goal, but this time they delivered on her plea to be defensively solid. They looked well organised in an even first half in which United midfielder Simi Awujo stood out, while Andrea Medina tracked back effectively. They won more duels than Arsenal, put in more tackles and completed more interceptions than their opponents - but still had only 40% of possession. Former England midfielder Izzy Christiansen told Sky Sports: "Manchester United have done a terrific job defensively. Overall, it's just been solid. "It looks so much better. The addition of Awujo has added some running power and they look so much freer in the final third." Arsenal's pressure grew in an edgy second half, but United held on for as long as they could and were unfortunate to concede with seconds left on the clock. They had led from midway through the half, after Julia Zigiotti seized on a mistake from Georgia Stanway. Smilla Holmberg's late volley denied United the spoils, but Olid saw foundations she could build on. "I think the attacking will come," she said. "If you implement a new style of play, you need time. "That effort, that intensity, can never be missed. We deserved three points for the hard work and the effort. "Of course, we need to create more chances. That is why I'm here. We need time, but today is the minimum that we have to deliver. I hope we can improve the attacking side." Manchester United lost their opening two matches of the season The biggest question is whether United really can build on this performance. They were already a difficult team to break down under Skinner but came up short in previous big games against WSL title rivals. In three Women's FA Cup finals, United won once against Tottenham, falling to higher-placed Chelsea on the other two occasions. Four years have passed since they won a game at Emirates Stadium against Arsenal, and their heavy defeat by Chelsea last week showed the gap to the elite still remains. Olid was brought in to transform their style by implementing an attacking philosophy that the club hope will deliver them long-term success. Patience was already beginning to wane after their demoralising early defeats, so conversations took place and they had to revert back to what they already knew. The result of that is significant progress from last week, but is it progress for the long term? "We are a team who need to press high, but at the same time we want to be better with the ball," Olid said on Sky Sports. "We lose simple passes and we cannot recognise the free player. Those things need to improve. It will come, I'm sure. "But we need to keep this [defensive structure], then from there, little by little, be an attacking team, create more chances, score more goals. "I cannot pretend it's happening in four weeks, but I'm sure it will come." title: Celtic win 'changes game' - but can they reverse Rangers' derby dominance?
description: Former Celtic captain Scott Brown believes a win for the Scottish champions against Rangers on Sunday "changes the game" after a turbulent week for Martin O'Neill's side.
body: Celtic and Rangers meet for the second Sunday in a row Former Celtic captain Scott Brown believes a win for the Scottish champions against Rangers on Sunday "changes the game" after a turbulent week for Martin O'Neill's side. Rangers triumphed 3-0 at home in last Sunday's Old Firm League Cup quarter-final before Celtic opened their Europa League campaign with a 3-1 defeat at home by Ferencvaros on Thursday. However, Celtic's early season domestic form has them going into Sunday's match in the east end of Glasgow - which like last week will have no visiting supporters in attendance - with a five-point advantage over their Ibrox rivals. "If Celtic win and they're eight points clear, it changes the game," Brown said on BBC Scotland's YouTube channel. "Can [Rangers] go to Celtic Park and do they exact same thing as last week? "Celtic now have had a week to understand how that game went. They are going to have to make sure that they match that energy but also match that willingness to go and win the match." Celtic seek spark as Rangers aim for further derby joy Scottish Premiership: Celtic v Rangers Listen on Sportsound, highlights on Sportscene 20/9/26 from 11:00 BST (radio), 19:15 (TV) Brown was impressed by Rangers manager Derek McInnes' change of approach in the season's first derby, change to a 3-5-2 shape and going man for man with Celtic's front three. "They went after Celtic from the get go," Brown said. "They looked like they wanted the win more. For him to change his tactics, nobody expected him to do that. That is a very, very good manager to pick that out." Brown also pondered Celtic's tactical plan. "Martin O'Neill when he was manager [from 2000-05], loved a 3-5-2 and it was fantastic to watch," said the former Scotland captain. "He had two big guys up front. That was an unbelievable team. He's not got those players that probably can be suited to a 3-5-2." This video can not be played Hogh needs a 'big game performance' With Yang Hyun-jun still on Asian Games duty with South Korea, Sebastian Tounekti and James Forrest have both been used on Celtic's left flank. But Brown believes the club's problems go beyond that. "Rangers got in their face, they blocked Callum McGregor off and as soon as you block Callum McGregor off and you man-mark Cal, it's hard for anyone else to go and dictate. "That's when you need a [Benjamin] Nygren to drop under, a [Mika] Baur to go and drop under and them do their job as well. You can't always keep looking at Cal to do everything." And Brown believes who starts best could be crucial. "Rangers were up for the fight," he added on Sportsound. "The first 15 minutes, it should be a battle. If you can go and win that battle, you can get the ball down. "Celtic started very, very slow last week. They need to go back to basics, make sure they've got the fight, make sure they've got the hunger because they've got the talent - I know they've got the talent. "You cannot have just one of those days against your biggest rivals, ever." title: Brighton humbling 'a big lesson' for Arsenal - Arteta
description: An uncharacteristic performance from Arsenal saw the Gunners ship three goals in the defeat to Brighton - but could the loss be the "big lesson" they needed?
body: This video can not be played Highlights: Brilliant Brighton batter Arsenal in shock first defeat as champions An uncharacteristic performance from Arsenal saw them ship three goals at Brighton - but boss Mikel Arteta believes their first Premier League defeat this season could prove a "big lesson". The defending champions have been tipped by many to retain the title they won last season for the first time in 22 years. An impressive seven-match winning start to this campaign in all competitions - nine in successive league games dating back to April - backed up that belief. But Arsenal were humbled on the south coast as a well-drilled and clinical Brighton outfit beat them comfortably 3-0 to go third in the table. Arteta, whose side did not lose by more than a single goal in the top flight last term, acknowledged the Seagulls "deserved" the success and there were lessons the Gunners needed to take heading into the international break. The manner of the defeat - Arsenal's heaviest in a season where they were the reigning top-flight champions since 1989 - will also offer hope to their title rivals that they are not invincible. Arsenal handed first loss by brilliant Brighton Since taking charge in 2019, Arteta has made a point of reiterating how much he values physicality and the demands he puts on his side to win duels. But against Brighton, Arsenal were dominated all over the pitch and lost challenges which they would usually be expected to win. Arteta said he was "extremely disappointed" as his side were "very far" from doing the basics he expected, with uncertainty in defence, a loss of midfield control and lack of attacking creativity. Asked why they were below par, the Spaniard added: "Well, the first one because Brighton they were really good, and they had another bite, and at the times it was better. "There are a lot of moments when the ball is 50-50 and it changes hands and most of the time it was for them. "Sometimes there were some technical errors very much involved that opened us up in a really difficult way, but that's something to learn." He was quick to remind the media in his news conference after the game that it was still a good start to the season. The Gunners had 15 players at the World Cup which meant that a large part of the squad joined up for pre-season later than the rest of their team-mates. "That's not going to take away what the team has done and the boys have done in the last six or seven weeks since coming back from the World Cup," added Arteta. "What we've done and the way we've competed and the amount of games we've won has been remarkable, but this is a big lesson for all of us to understand what it takes to win at this level." Arsenal lost their first game of the Premier League season against Brighton Brighton are currently the Premier League's top scorers with 16 goals - hitting eight of them in the past week - and could have had more against an Arsenal side who pride themselves on keeping clean sheets. The Gunners conceded the fewest goals of any side last season and just one got past David Raya in their first four league games before Saturday's defeat. "It should have been more, the chances Brighton created, they were that good," said former Newcastle striker Alan Shearer on BBC Radio 5 Live. "They absolutely battered Arsenal. How many times have we said that recently? From start to finish today Brighton were magnificent, every single one of them played their part. "They were strong, they were fit, they went after Arsenal. They had no fear and it worked brilliantly for them, it should have been six or seven goals." The Gunners were 2-0 down at the break and have not recovered to win from such a position in a league game since March 2008 at Bolton. "Every time Brighton chased down the ball, they got it absolutely spot on. They did it as a team, they didn't do it individually," added Shearer. "They thought, 'we respect Arsenal but we're not going to give them any space to play'. "The organisation was great and that just doesn't happen on it's own and you've got to give [manager] Fabian Hurzeler credit for that." Arsenal spent around £200m in the summer transfer window in a bid to strengthen the squad to challenge for more honours, and Arteta was asked if they needed reminding how tough the Premier League can be. He said: "I think they knew, I think we knew how tough it was going to be today, and the first thing that we had discussed was about the first part. "If you don't get out of that first part as winners, it will be extremely difficult to dominate the game and to have any probability of winning the game. "We knew that, but that's again credit to them for what they've done because they've overcome us and they had another edge than we did. "And that's something that at this level it's extremely important to respect and to understand before anything else." Former Premier League defender Curtis Davies believed the Gunners could put the result and display down to a "blip". "Their form this season has so far been good, this has been a really shocking performance," he said on 5 Live. "That defence today was nowhere near what it's used to being. The disappointment will be a set-piece goal conceded, Arsenal will have a real long look at themselves. "They didn't lay a glove on Brighton, and didn't make anything of their attacking situations." title: 'Greater things to come,' says Mitchell after England winning run ends
description: Head coach John Mitchell says England's thrilling draw with Canada will inspire "greater things to come" from the world champions despite the result ending their record-breaking winning streak.
body: This video can not be played Watch highlights: England 26-26 Canada Head coach John Mitchell believes England's thrilling draw with Canada will inspire "greater things to come" from the world champions despite the result ending their record-breaking winning streak. England had won their past 39 Tests before Saturday's fixture. Canada, who had lost their 13 previous meetings with the Red Roses on English soil, held England to a 26-26 draw in a nail-biting, physical battle at Exeter's Sandy Park. It was only the second game domestically or internationally for England's players this season and, for Mitchell, one result is not justification to tear up the playbook. Instead, he views it as a building block towards future success. "It was just a matter of scoring across the white line," Mitchell said. "We were applying huge pressure. We just didn't convert." Avoiding defeat means the Red Roses have extended their unbeaten run to 40 matches, a record they will hope to extend with WXV Global Series games against New Zealand, two more fixtures against Canada and another against the United States still to come. This video can not be played Watch: England coach John Mitchell on draw with Canada Mitchell said: "There was such good stuff in there. I'm very patient because we're just starting and we're still alive in this Test series. "I'm a realist. There will be greater things come as a result of this. There's a greater purpose and one Test match is not going to take us away from our purpose." For the opening 10 minutes, the match followed the script of last year's World Cup final between the two sides, with Canada breaking the deadlock and England immediately hitting back. But unlike last September, when they roared on to win 33-13, the Red Roses could not maintain control, with the two teams never separated by more than one try and England unable to convert 20 minutes of sustained pressure into the crucial score. While acknowledging England would have to review their "game management", captain Meg Jones hailed the spectacle the two sides delivered. "It was definitely tit for tat and definitely a game of momentum swinging," said centre Jones. "It was two good teams going at each other. "It was an amazing contest and competitive as we imagined. This is the first Test. We get another two shots at it [against Canada]." Echoing Jones' defiance before October trips to Toronto and Ottawa, Mitchell added: "We're in a Test series. It's 1-1. That's it." England's 39-game winning run started under former head coach Simon Middleton, who, after the World Cup final defeat in 2022, led the Red Roses to a Women's Six Nations Grand Slam in 2023. Mitchell then took charge midway through the 2023 WXV1 campaign and had won every game until this one. England beat Scotland in the World Cup quarter-finals last September to claim their 31st straight Test win, surpassing their own record winning streak across both men's and women's international rugby union, which was set in 2022. World Cup glory, another Women's Six Nations title and victory over Australia last weekend extended that record further. "It's not necessarily something we speak about as a group; it's something that's just been there," Jones said of the winning run. "We're very process-driven, so the outcome tends to look after itself." title: Davey says Lib Dems are 'firewall against Farage' as conference begins
description: Lib Dem leader Ed Davey claimed the party was aiming to beat its 2024 record of 72 MPs in any snap election.
body: This video can not be played Ed Davey says the Lib Dems have "a historic opportunity to win many more seats and a moral responsibility to stop Reform" Sir Ed Davey said the Liberal Democrats are "a firewall against Nigel Farage and Reform" as the party's conference began in Brighton. The Lib Dem leader sought to strike a combative stance as he faced down some criticism from MPs, including one who said publicly that they felt the party was struggling for relevance. On the first day of the autumn conference, Sir Ed warned an "unholy alliance" between Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch and Farage could turn the UK into a "Trump satellite state". Addressing speculation about a possible snap election, he said the party was ready to fight and would build its so-called orange wall even higher by winning more than its 2024 record of 72 MPs. Sir Ed's attention-grabbing stunts helped raise the party's profile ahead of the last election, but recent polling showed 43% of respondents were unclear what the Liberal Democrats stand for, with just over half describing them as "weak". In an essay, external written ahead of conference, South Cotswolds MP Roz Savage asked: "Why are we as a party struggling for relevance at precisely the moment when so many people feel powerless?" She urged the party to rediscover its "insurgent spirit" rather than being the "polite custodians of a system that leaves people feeling powerless". Asked about her comments, Sir Ed said: "No, I heard Roz [Savage], and I really value her, but I think she's wrong on that. "If you look at our election results up and down the country, we now run more councils than the Conservatives." He added: "Listen, MPs get elected and they get frustrated because they can't change the world. "I'm afraid that's the political system. I've been used to it for a little while and people are learning about that frustration." Speaking on the pebbles of Brighton Beach, Sir Ed told reporters the Liberal Democrats would fight to stop a Reform government. "One of the things that makes us unique is that we are a firewall against Nigel Farage and Reform," he said. "Many of the seats he needs to get himself into No 10 are seats that we will defend and indeed win - and we are also able to take seats off the Conservatives, because I really fear that Kemi Badenoch will give the keys to No 10 to Nigel Farage, so we have got to stop the Conservatives as well. "We have got an historic opportunity to win many more seats and a moral responsibility to stop Reform." He added a manifesto working group had already been set up in case of an early election "so we'll be ready if it comes early, but, you know, it still could be up to three years away". Sir Ed insisted his party has a "distinctive position" in British politics, and will use the four-day conference to position it to take on the challenge from Reform as well as its typical rivals the Conservatives, talking up their focus on the NHS and goal of re-joining the EU single market and customs union. The Lib Dem leader highlighted how six former Conservative cabinet ministers were among 25 Tories to have defected to Reform in the last two years, claiming they were now competing with each other to see who can divide the country more, rather than looking to fix the country's problems. "An unholy alliance between Farage and Badenoch is the only way either can get into power," he said. "Together, they want to turn Britain into a Trump satellite state which would trash our NHS, turn our communities against each other, cause untold damage to our environment, and trample over traditional British values of fairness, tolerance, and decency. "A bigger Orange Wall is the only thing that can stand between Britain and this dangerous experiment, and we will not let them pass." Davey also attacked the Labour government as having no plan for growth, failing to support families struggling with the cost of living and taxing small businesses "to the brink". Ahead of a speech to party members, Davey urged Liberal Democrats not to look away from injustice or "human dignity under attack" but to fight back.
