title: 'Our flat has been for sale for four years': Why is the market so weak?
description: James Schaife and his partner are among the many Londoners struggling to sell their flat.
body: James and his partner have been unable to sell their one-bedroom flat in London and say they are on the verge of bankruptcy In 2015, thousands of people queued overnight in the rain to reserve and buy studio apartments selling for under £200,000 in Hounslow, west London. It's in stark contrast to today's appetite for flats, with property portals reporting a slump in sales. But why, when the country is in a housing crisis with a desperate need for affordable homes, are flats now struggling to sell? According to the property site Zoopla, 88% of flats listed for sale in inner London on its website in 2025 did not find a buyer within six months. The company also says the gap between the value of a flat and a house is the widest it has been for 30 years. Executive director Richard Donnell points to post-pandemic social changes with "people looking for space, prioritising houses, working from home". He also points to higher mortgage rates, people concerned about "all the costs and liabilities of owning a property" including service charges and ground rents. In September, nearly all the major mortgage lenders in the UK announced increases in the cost of home loans. Donnell says flats in inner London are struggling in particular as they are more expensive, the service charges are higher, and "there's greater complexity - it's highly likely it's a bigger building, maybe more of a complex building, so less are selling within six months". This is a message echoed by property platform Rightmove, which says as of August, only 50% of flats listed for sale nationally successfully find a buyer, compared to 65% of houses. Nationally, as of August, the average price for a flat is down 2% from 12 months prior. That is the largest drop seen over the period by any type of property. Compared with August 2021, flats have only risen in price by 4% nationally, the least of all property types. Colleen Babcock, Rightmove's head of partner marketing, says London faces additional challenges because its market is heavily weighted towards flats, and "affordability more broadly remains a key challenge". She points to higher borrowing costs, increased stamp duty costs, and the limitations of the Lifetime ISA in higher-priced areas, which mean both first-time buyers and home-movers in London can face additional hurdles when buying a home. Flats aren't becoming unsellable for one single reason. Higher borrowing costs, service charges, leasehold and shared ownership complications have made them more expensive and complicated to own, damaging their reputation. James Schaife, 36, says he and his partner are "on the verge of bankruptcy" after struggling to sell their one-bedroom north London flat for the past four years. He bought a 35% share of the £585,000 flat - run by Newlon Housing Trust - in 2017, but after his partner got a new job, James moved out of London in 2022 and relocated north, putting the flat on the market. Within an initial "nomination period" - a set window of time where the association has the exclusive right to find an eligible buyer - the flat generated next to no interest. The housing association gave them permission to sell it on the open market - but James claims they have been "forced to use a narrow selection of valuers chosen by Newlon", despite estate agents telling him the flat has been overvalued. They have been forced to rent out the property with a special "consent-to-let" agreement with their housing association - although this is due to expire imminently and James claims Newlon will not renew it. James said the situation has affected their plans to start a family, pushing them back to an age "where it's probably unlikely that we'll have children". "It's just ruined our lives." A spokesperson for Newlon Housing Trust said that "this is not a picture we recognise", adding that they were bound by "strict rules about resales to protect the public purse". The spokesperson said that "strict rules to limit subletting... prevent the risk of people profiting by letting subsidised affordable housing". "As is well reported, the sales market is flat. The saleability of a home at any time is subject to variation in the property market, which we have no control over, and is part of the risk taken on by anyone who buys a home." Sophie Bishener is unable to move to a bigger property as her building needs a second wave of fire safety repairs Some flat-owners living in homes with building safety concerns have also found their properties impossible to sell. It may be a more extreme example, but many find themselves in this position. As of July 2026, there are 4,697 residential buildings 11m and over in height being monitored due to unsafe cladding, external, but work still isn't complete on 61% of them. Sophie Bishener, leaseholder and campaigner with the End our Cladding Scandal group, said that flats with unsafe cladding left unremediated were like "prisons", and this is having a "devastating" impact on people's lives. She bought her one-bedroom flat in Hertfordshire in 2017 but nine years later, now with a young family, she is unable to move to a bigger property as her building needs a second wave of fire safety repairs. "Being trapped means that you can't move on with your life." She points out that even buildings which have been remediated are affected by a market that is "so distrusting" at the moment. "If you're in a position where you can get to market, there are so many hurdles... management packs costing hundreds of pounds, conveyancing solicitors not willing to take on buildings covered by the Building Safety Act." Sophie thinks there should be a building safety register, "where you've got all the buildings noted, and we know what they're made of" to help boost buyer confidence. title: The man who would be king - the rise and fall of 'the next Prince Naseem'
description: Touted as the king to Naseem Hamed's prince, Daniel Teasdale's story is instead a cautionary tale.
body: Daniel Teasdale, pictured, was tipped for the top from an early age Boxer Daniel Teasdale was hailed as the heir to the legendary Prince Naseem Hamed, but his promise never materialised into fame, fortune and films. "He's better than Naz at the same age," said trainer Brendan Ingle. Hamed had won his first world title aged 21. Teasdale was still a teenager. Ingle, from his gym in Sheffield, moulded the careers of a conveyor belt of world-beaters and title winners. He guided both of the fighters from childhood. Before super-middleweight Teasdale's first professional bout, the Rotherham fighter had been featured in national newspapers, books and was being documented by photographers and film-makers. He won a succession of national titles, establishing himself as the next contender to emerge from the Ingle gym. Photographer Simon Roberts travelled to the Ingle gym in 1997 hoping to photograph Hamed. "Brendan said 'don't worry about Naz, start photographing that kid in the corner. He's going to be bigger than Naz'. That was Daniel," Roberts said. Roberts began to follow the young sensation, hoping to capture his rise on camera. Teasdale's early promise earned him plenty of headlines and column inches Filmmaker Stuart Mitchell had a similar brief. "We were selling the documentary as 'who's the next Prince Naseem?'," says Mitchell. He recalls Teasdale being the subject of similar headlines in national newspapers, and later accompanying him to an event gathering together the best British prospects from every sport for the new Millennium. Attention on Ingle's latest protégé was more than just hype. "He was like Oscar de la Hoya," recalls former stablemate Amer Khan. "Teasdale was exceptional as a junior, he was stopping everyone." Teasdale learnt both ballet and gymnastics to develop his footwork and skills in the ring and was seemingly set for stardom. "I was very teachable, could talk, had the looks and could box," says Teasdale, who took up the sport aged six. Prince Naseem's star quality brought plenty of media attention to the Ingle gym and its fighters The bitterness of Hamed's split from trainer Ingle in 1998 has been well-documented, with both sides seemingly losing. "Brendan lost the focus with the up-and-comers," Teasdale says. He followed Naz in leaving the gym, linking up with one of its greatest exports, three-time world title challenger Herol 'Bomber' Graham. The exit was said to have been spearheaded by Teasdale's father who "essentially gave up his career" to help his son fulfil his potential, Roberts says. It was funded by a businessman with no prior experience in boxing, but a thirst to be part of Teasdale's rise to the top. Teasdale remembers Graham's influence as "a breath of fresh air", but the presence of others was less helpful. "People started to try and feed off Daniel," says Roberts. "I photographed [Mike] Tyson and Lennox [Lewis], I have seen all of this stuff before." Mitchell was also filming future Olympic bronze medallist Darren Sutherland when he arrived at the Ingle gym from Ireland. "Daniel was probably more talented than Darren, the trouble with Daniel was he was always being wooed," reveals Mitchell. Teasdale's tag as the next Prince Naseem also hung heavy. "I was like catnip for cats, everybody wanted a piece," Teasdale explains. While the career of some talented prospects is carefully nurtured, Teasdale may not have been as well protected. "To some extent Daniel was used because he was seen as a big potential and was a good scalp for somebody who wanted to get through the ranks," Roberts says. Different trainers, managers and promoters followed, but Teasdale admits instability harmed his progress. His debut had been a disaster - abandoned due to rioting in the crowd - while the following year he received death threats before a bout. Despite undeniable talent, those early misfortunes could now be seen as an omen of what was to come. Daniel with his then trainer Glyn Rhodes in 2004 following death threats. He won the fight After filming Teasdale across five years, Mitchell shelved his documentary when commissioners lost interest. He too lost faith after a training session in Graham's garage. "It felt very small and I didn't think this was going anywhere," he says bluntly. Many have since raised doubts over whether the "pretty boy" was made for a career getting punched in the face. "Everybody has a weakness and mine was women," Teasdale confesses. "I lost the edge and my focus wasn't where it should be." He walked away from the sport in 2005 after he was stopped in the first round of a light-heavyweight contest - his first professional defeat. He returned in 2010 and reunited with Ingle, winning his one and only comeback fight. Teasdale and Ingle reunited ahead of his brief comeback in 2010 "After that I just gave it up, I thought 'I'm not going to be second best to the first me," says Teasdale, whose professional career ended after just five fights over a seven-year period. "At 27 I should have been a world champion defending my title." Roberts continued to photograph Teasdale. "There were a lot of unfortunate circumstances with him which meant he didn't fulfil his potential," Roberts says. "There was a lot of bad advice and a lot of people wanting something from him, and not necessarily for the good." Mitchell did some "soul searching" over his role in Teasdale's journey. "There was so much clamour around him - then it just evaporated," he recalls. "That must be very difficult to deal with when expectations are that you are going to be a successful and famous boxer." Teasdale says "everything went up in the air" as a professional, in contrast to the stability of his early years. Bad management played a part in not fulfilling his potential, but he admits "living for other people's dreams and ambitions." Teasdale looks back on h

title: Hummingbird hawk moths and ivy bees: The insects thriving as temperatures rise
description: Hummingbird hawk moths - often mistaken for small birds - are being spotted in the West Midlands.
body: The hummingbird hawk moth hovers as it feeds from flowers, much like its feathered namesake As parts of the West Midlands baked in warmer temperatures this summer, species once considered unusual in the region, such as hummingbird hawk moths, ivy bees and the wasp spider have been spotted in growing numbers. The hummingbird hawk moth, known for its furry grey body, orange hindwings and long proboscis, migrates to the UK from southern Europe and north Africa in the summer months. James Benwell, from the Birmingham and Black Country Wildlife Trust, said 2026 was a "record year" for sightings of the species, which was often mistaken for a small bird. The moth, which can be seen hovering over flowers, has wings that beat about 80 times per second, external, according to Benwell. "They've had a really good year this year," he said. "Normally they would come in small numbers. We'd normally hear of a few maybe. But this year, we've seen loads of records of them. "They're absolutely amazing but I somehow haven't seen one this year, so I'm jealous of anybody else that has." The moth migrates to the UK from southern Europe and north Africa in the summer months Ivy bees, which feed mainly on the nectar of ivy flowers, had also become more prevalent in the Midlands, Benwell said, adding they were easy to find on buildings. The bees, first recorded in the UK in 2001, are slowly spreading north, after first being recorded in the region in Stourbridge in 2015. "There's nothing that distinguishes them from other bees really, they're not that kind of attention-grabbing species, but, you know, were you to look for them, go to ivy and you'll see them," Benwell said. The ivy bee was first recorded on British shores in 2001 Other insects that had seen an increase in their numbers locally included the clouded yellow butterfly, a European migratory species known to have "peak" years during unusually hot summers. "Most individuals are unable to survive the British winter, but if temperatures continue to rise as a result of climate change, we may well see them becoming permanent residents," Benwell said. "There's numerous species that we could point out that weren't here 20 years ago... and now they're quite abundant." The clouded yellow butterfly was a regular visitor to Britain and Ireland, the Butterfly Conservation said Others once more commonly associated with southern England have also spread further north. The trust said the hornet hoverfly, with yellow markings that mimic a hornet to protect against predators, although it cannot sting, had become really common after it was first recorded in Birmingham and the Black Country in 2004. Another species, the cricket bat spider, which gets its name from its cricket bat-like markings, has also become more common in grassland since it was first spotted in the region in 2019. The sightings come as one of the UK's largest spider species, the wasp spider, was spotted in the Midlands as warmer temperatures pushed it more than 100 miles away from its usual habitat. The spider has recently been recorded in Worcestershire, alongside sightings in Herefordshire and Warwickshire, said the Worcestershire Wildlife Trust. The wasp spider is known for its distinctive yellow, black and white stripes Rosemary Winnall, from the Wyre Forest Study Group, which maps the wildlife and ecology of the forest in Worcestershire, said the arrival of the wasp spider was to be celebrated. She said the group was always on the lookout for new arrivals and had already recorded the willow emerald damselfly, the southern oak bush cricket and the purple emperor butterfly, as more species travelled north. "The impressive western conifer seed bug is here as is the box bug," she added. Hot weather had also benefited butterflies that loved sunshine, such as the holly blue and the pearl-bordered fritillary, which the Butterfly Conservation charity, external said was once "very widespread" but had rapidly declined in recent decades. However, despite an increase in some species appearing in the region, there were others whose numbers were dwindling. "The once-common small tortoiseshell butterfly is now rarely seen for example, and there are far fewer records of the two-spot ladybird," Winnall explained. "We are encouraging folk to record the common species of today as they may be the rarities of the future." title: 'Fast, furious and dangerous' - a city's quad bike menace
description: Videos show groups of riders weaving through busy city centre traffic in Birmingham.
body: This video can not be played Several videos showed riders around the Stephenson Street area of the city Sitting in his Birmingham city centre apartment, one resident says he can often hear them before he sees them. The sound of revving engines is followed by groups of quad bikes and off-road motorcycles weaving through traffic, performing wheelies and riding through some of the busiest streets in the city. "It's only a matter of time until something serious happens," he said. Videos shared on social media over recent months have captured groups of riders travelling through areas including Hurst Street, Bristol Road and Corporation Street, often with faces covered and no visible number plates. One video filmed by the resident showed a pedestrian narrowly avoiding being struck as a group rode through the city centre. "I've watched them and they go through red lights, they just totally ignore the red lights," he said. "People still cross when the pedestrian lights are green, but they don't even slow down to check. "They're zigzagging in the middle of cars. No number-plates. It's bad because nobody sees any action happening and it's only a matter of time until something serious happens." Residents say groups of riders have become a familiar sight in the city centre The resident, who did not want to reveal their name, said the groups were not a daily occurrence but had become a familiar sight over the past year. "The one I filmed the other day was at six o'clock and they were coming back around at nine," he said. "It goes on for hours by the look of it." Birmingham-based content creator GB Street Stories has also encountered and filmed riders in the city. "It might just be a hobby or for fun for them, but they have absolutely no right to put other people's lives at risk or damage public property," he said. "I've personally witnessed them breaking traffic laws, driving down the wrong side of the road and speeding straight through stop signs at tram tracks without pausing even for a second. "Riding in this manner is extremely dangerous and puts both their own lives and the safety of everyone else in serious jeopardy." Residents say riders have been seen performing wheelies in busy parts of Birmingham city centre Residents say the issue is not solely about road safety. The noise created by the bikes is also a source of frustration, particularly in busy pedestrian areas. "For people in and around the city, not just residents but visitors too, if you've got young children walking around, you don't want to hear all that," the resident said. "It's fast, furious and dangerous." Witnesses said some riders ignored red lights and weaved through moving traffic The riders have also been seen by street wardens working across Birmingham city centre. A spokesperson for Colmore and Southside Business Improvement Districts said wardens had, on occasion, witnessed groups of riders while carrying out patrols and had shared information with relevant agencies where appropriate. The organisation said wardens did not have powers to stop or detain individuals, but continued to work alongside partners including West Midlands Police and Birmingham City Council. Residents say concerns extend beyond road safety to noise and disruption The issue is not unique to Birmingham. Cleveland Police has used drones in efforts to tackle off-road bikes, while Metropolitan Police officers have deployed electric bikes to pursue riders through areas difficult to access with patrol cars. Elsewhere, new measures allowing police to order people to remove face coverings have been introduced in Nottingham and are due to be introduced in Stafford, as authorities look at different ways of tackling anti-social behaviour. West Midlands Police said it was aware of the issues in Birmingham city centre. "We are aware of concerns around the use of e-scooters and off-road bikes being ridden antisocially in the city centre," a spokesperson said. "Officers are working to crack down on their use locally and, as a result, we are encouraging the public to report any incidents to us. "If a rider is caught using any type of off-road motorbike or quad bike and causing a nuisance to others, they are liable to prosecution, and the vehicle will be seized." Most quad bikes cannot legally be ridden on public road Vehicles used on roads must be registered, taxed and insured Riders must hold the appropriate driving licence Police can seize vehicles being used illegally or antisocially Riders causing a nuisance can be prosecuted (Source: Department for Transport), external Tell us which stories we should cover in Birmingham and the Black Country Follow BBC Birmingham on BBC Sounds, Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. title: RNLI video receives 'pure hatred' after anti-migrant protests
description: Elizabeth Evans, who shared a video of an RNLI training exercise, says the comments were "really, really bad".
body: Elizabeth Evans said people "spread hatred" in the Facebook comments A woman who shared an RNLI video on social media says she has received "pure hatred" following anti-migrant protests in England. Councillor Elizabeth Evans, who represents Aberaeron and Aberarth in Ceredigion, shared a video on Facebook which showed New Quay's RNLI lifeboat leaving the station on a training day. According to Evans, the post - which attracted 30,000 views - drew comments of hatred, some of which she described as "really, really bad". It comes after RNLI volunteers in Portsmouth were targeted by protesters following the charity's role in helping to bring migrants on a small boat to shore earlier this month. The RNLI said it existed "to save lives at sea". Evans said she was "really shocked" by the reaction to the video. "I couldn't believe it," she said. "And it wasn't a few. It took me a good half hour to get rid of those comments, just one after the other. With that thread of hatred." Describing the comments, Evans continued: "The comment thread was 'traitors', 'taxis for migrants', they were some of the politest ones." She said one of the comments was suggestive of violence, adding: "I don't want to go on because I don't want to give those comments oxygen but they were really, really bad." Evans said she deleted the comments but was subsequently criticised for "shutting down discussion". "I wasn't shutting down discussion because there was no discussion available to be had," she said. "I was shutting down hatred." The video showed an RNLI lifeboat leave the station at New Quay Peter Sparkes, chief executive of the RNLI, said recent events had "generated deliberate misinformation and a misunderstanding about the RNLI". "Our mission, and our tasking is to rescue those women, children and men in danger of drowning. "Anyone rescued from a small boat by the RNLI is immediately handed over to the UK's immigration authorities. "Illegal immigration is a political issue; the RNLI exists to save lives at sea." Small boat protest explained: How a Channel crossing sparked unrest Track UK's latest migration numbers - net migration, visas, asylum and small boats A total of 16,513 people arrived in the UK in small boats in the year to 1 September, 43% lower than the same period the previous year. UK net migration has meanwhile dropped to its lowest level outside of the Covid pandemic since 2012. Evans said social media platforms should do more to crackdown on online abuse and urged the UK government to help. "They need to enforce through legislation that these companies have an absolute responsibility to make sure that they keep their users safe but also, that it's not used as a platform for hatred… We must not allow it to be normalised," said Evans. The UK government said those who dedicated themselves to the service of others should be able to do their work without fear of harassment or abuse online, adding that Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy expected social media companies to be more proactive and rigorous in removing harmful content. A spokesperson for Meta, which owns several social media platforms including Facebook, said "no one should be subjected to abuse of any kind" adding that it removes harmful content when it finds it. title: The man who's been walking around the world for 28 years
description: The BBC heads to Belgium as the adventurer from Hull nears the end of his 28-year expedition.
body: Karl Bushby, right, with the BBC's Kevin Shoesmith as they approach Mons, Belgium Adventurer Karl Bushby has been walking around the world for 28 years and now the end of his journey is in sight. I have been writing about him for most of that time, but although we have spoken frequently and exchanged hundreds of emails we have never met. We are in the village of Havré and I am joining Karl on a five-mile (8km) stretch to Mons. It is part of the final march to Calais, from where he plans to swim across the English Channel in October. Dressed in shorts and a T-shirt which bears evidence of a roadside repair, Karl - sporting a grey beard - appears in the car park of a Belgian railway station. He is pushing a trolley laden with camping equipment and other essentials. Karl set off from Chile, heading back home to Hull, with two self-imposed rules: he cannot use transport to advance and he cannot return to the UK until the walk is complete. Karl arrives in Mons as his adventure nears its end Sweat is seeping through his T-shirt, forming wing-like patches over his shoulder blades. The former paratrooper set off in November 1998, expecting his walk back to his childhood home, where his mother still lives, to take about 12 years. Some 28 years on, he is still going, with visa restrictions, the 2008 financial crash which cost him sponsors, Covid-19 and geopolitics having slowed his progress. The 57-year-old has covered more than 30,000 miles (more than 48,000km) and a swim across the English Channel now beckons after Channel Tunnel bosses vetoed his request for access to a service tunnel. Karl ducks into a shop and comes out with a bottle of water, flinging it under a bungee cord attached to his trolley, which he had made in Nicaragua early in the adventure. The Beast, as he calls it, is his lifeline. Karl battling through ice as he crosses the Bering Strait to cross into Russia in 2006 We maintain a fast pace. In 30C heat, I am finding it hard to keep up, with Karl showing no sign of fatigue, despite having trekked 10 miles before lunch. We talk about how he crossed the frozen Bering Strait in 2006 with French adventurer Dimitri Kieffer and his 186-mile swim across the Caspian Sea. Discussing his crossing of the Darién Gap, which links Colombia and Panama, Karl says: "You're having to push through a dense jungle. "You've got these river systems and lots of swamps. Laid over the top of that you've got the fact that it's a warzone." Faced with the threat of kidnap, Karl sought to look as though he was homeless. "Homeless people are pretty much invisible, nobody pays attention to them, so that was our intent. "I did not want to be the blond-haired, blue-eyed gringo with the latest North Face equipment. "I dyed my hair and skin and reduced my clothing to tatters. I carried my stuff in sacks." Karl pictured in Chile at the start of his adventure A woman peers out of a window and looks bemused at the sight of two men and a trolley. Karl invites me to push The Beast for a short while. The black fabric tape covering the handle is worn and peeling. With each passing mile, our conversation becomes more philosophical. I ask him what the biggest lessons have been on the walk. "Tenacity is emperor," he replies. Karl struggles to weave The Beast past a row of parked cars. "These towns can be fun assault courses," he sighs. Returning to the question, he adds: "Coming from a military background, you don't necessarily see the best in people, so it has really been an eye-opener. "From day one, I have been received with open arms from the rest of the world." Karl says he has been out to prove to himself and others what he can do Karl talks about the "kindness of strangers", noting how one family in Chile became "almost like a second family". "They were driving out for eight hours at a time to find me and feed me on the side of the road," he recalls. I reach into my rucksack and retrieve a letter from Karl's mother, Angela Bushby. Also in the bag are packets of his favourite sweets. "Mother remembers," he laughs, selecting the caramel wafers. The pair last met in 2015. "You're still her little boy, aren't you?" I ask. "Apparently so," says Karl. "A very happy little boy with all that chocolate." In the letter, Angela asks if he really must swim the Channel. Both mother and son know the answer. And then comes a line that speaks volumes. "You used to think you were useless. Well, you have proven you're not," Angela has written. I have always known Karl to be self-deprecating, but this leaps from the page. Angela Bushby writes a note to her son, which I handed to him on his approach into Mons He tells me he never felt as fit as his fellow comrades during his Army days. Karl, whose father served in the SAS, says the Army helped build his confidence, but the "damage was done" in his early childhood, with undiagnosed dyslexia making him a target for bullies. "I had no confidence," he says. "I was an underachiever. My dyslexia was not identified until my last year in school." Karl, though, has never doubted he could finish his journey. "There is definitely this sense of wanting to prove myself," he says. "To myself and others. We're talking about doing something other people couldn't even dream of doing." Karl in Colombia in 2001, when he was three years into his trek home For years, Karl has been relaxed about the end date. Not now. There is a real urgency. "It's definitely time to call it a day," he says. "I don't want to keep this going for much longer." We reach Mons and the impressive Grand-Place, where several young people, recognising him from his Instagram account, make a beeline for him. "Oh my God, you are a legend," one excited young man tells Karl. Karl says he is now recognised everywhere because of social media Does the future scare Karl? "Yes," he admits. "One day I'm going to wake up in my mother's house – 57 years old with noth

title: Bluebird at centre of new legal dispute
description: The claim for nearly £150,000 revolves around whether items provided were donated or not.
body: The restored Bluebird ran on Coniston Water earlier this year Donald Campbell's Bluebird is at the centre of a legal battle worth nearly £150,000. Paul Kinghan is seeking £147,162 from the museum which houses the world-famous hydroplane – the Ruskin Museum in Coniston. He said this was the value of the items and cash he had provided to the museum in recent years which had not been repaid. But museum director Tracey Hodgson said everything Kinghan had provided to the museum had been given as donations. Kinghan's claim, issued through a statutory demand, centres upon three engines he bought for the museum as part of its plans to run Bluebird in the Lake District earlier this year. Two of the engines ended up being sold with Kinghan giving the proceeds of the sales to the Ruskin Museum. The museum still owns the third engine. Kinghan said the engines, as well other items and services he had supplied, had been delivered with the understanding that those running the museum were the "right people to be the trustees of the boat". But he said he now wanted his money back because he felt "deceived and let down". "They weren't the people they told me they were," he said. "I was misled". But Hodgson said: "You cannot just donate something and then ask for it back. That's the whole point of a donation." She said the museum had documentation for everything Kinghan had provided and that the forms did not offer any stipulations for the items and services provided. Hodgson said Kinghan's claim had been passed on to the museum's legal representatives, and that it was up him whether to pursue it further in court. Campbell, pictured here at Coniston Water in November 1966, was killed two months later The museum had previously faced a long-running legal dispute with the Tyneside engineer Bill Smith who recovered and restored Bluebird. Smith went on to stake a claim in its ownership, which was disputed by Campbell's daughter, Gina Campbell, and the museum. Smith eventually walked away and handed the hydroplane to the Ruskin Museum. Crowds lined Coniston's streets when Bluebird was handed over to the Ruskin Museum in 2024 Bluebird was recovered from Coniston Water in 2001 after its pilot was killed in a crash in 1967. Donald Campbell died aged 45 when the hydroplane flipped into the air and disintegrated as he attempted a water speed record. title: 'I will be a WWE champion': Meet the young wrestlers dreaming big
description: With a new generation of talent setting their sights on some of wrestling's biggest stages, could Northern Ireland produce its next big star?
body: Among those hoping to make it to the top is 16-year-old Eva For many wrestling fans growing up meant watching stars like The Rock, Stone Cold Steve Austin and John Cena on television. But for anyone who dreamed of following in their footsteps, making it into the industry could feel a world away. Now, those involved in the sport say opportunities are growing closer to home, giving aspiring wrestlers a chance to train, perform and begin building a career. With a new generation setting their sights on some of the sport's biggest stages, could Northern Ireland produce the next big wrestling star? Among those hoping to make it to the top is 16-year-old Eva, who only began training in January. A lifelong wrestling fan, she grew up watching WWE with her family. Discovering she could train locally turned something she watched on television into a realistic ambition. "The reason I joined is because it's so local, it was a great opportunity because I always wanted to do something like this," she said. Eva hopes to study performing arts after leaving school, which she believes could help develop the character and performance side of her wrestling. Eva's wrestling ambitions stretch well beyond Northern Ireland She also points to Irish WWE star Becky Lynch as an inspiration, saying her success gives her "hope and motivation" that where someone comes from does not have to limit them. Despite being only months into her wrestling journey, she has already set herself the biggest possible target. "In the future I will be a WWE champion," she said. Eva is one of a growing number of people turning an interest in wrestling into action by stepping into the ring. And she isn't on her own, with one coach saying the number of people interested in the sport has "grown exponentially" in recent years. Five years ago, the number of people training in professional wrestling across Northern Ireland was believed to be in the 30s. Today it is more than 150. Amira Blair moved to London to pursue her dream For Lisburn's Amira Blair, who appeared in the ring at Wembley Stadium last month, the route into wrestling looked very different when she was growing up. She first dreamed of becoming a wrestler at the age of 11, but pursuing it as a career from Northern Ireland seemed a very distant prospect. "I never thought this was a goal that you could have. It seemed like something on the TV you see Americans doing," she said. Blair is now a full-time professional wrestler, but growing it was such a "niche thing" that she did not feel able to talk about her ambition with others. Following that dream also meant moving from Northern Ireland to London - a decision some people struggled to understand. "They thought I was just losing the plot and why would I not go get a normal job with stability," she added. "Why am I moving to London on a whim and pursuing something that's just so out there?" She says the industry has also changed significantly for women, going "from having three minutes of time in matches to getting main events". Damien Corvin opened a professional wrestling academy in Larne last year Damien Corvin believes the gap between starting out in Northern Ireland and building a career is beginning to narrow. He is a full-time professional wrestler and head coach at the Relentless Pro Wrestling Academy in Larne. Corvin says aspiring wrestlers no longer necessarily have to move away to turn wrestling into a career: "It's very, very possible to be a full-time pro wrestler, for this to be your full-time job while still living in Northern Ireland. "You can travel the world as an independent pro wrestler." Corvin has done that himself, wrestling in India, France and Switzerland, as well as across the UK and Ireland. He says the opportunities available to those starting out in Northern Ireland have improved significantly in recent years. "We're giving these guys a platform to try out new characters, to try out new moves, to see what works, and get them in front of an audience," he said. "Just watching them get that little bit better every single week is amazing as a coach, but it also leads me to have high hopes for the future of what we can do in Northern Ireland wrestling." Dylan says he would sleep outside if it meant he could wrestle full time Carrickfergus man Dylan Todd, known in the ring as DD Crooks, is among those hoping to turn wrestling into a career. Growing up, he was more interested in drama and skateboarding than traditional sports and despite being a wrestling fan, did not realise it was something he could pursue locally. He says being around wrestlers who have progressed in the industry makes it feel much more achievable. "When you see those guys doing it and you're like, 'well, it wasn't long ago they were probably in my position'," he said. Dylan believes the "immense" talent currently coming through across the island of Ireland could lead to more wrestlers making their mark in the ring. "I'd sleep outside if it meant getting a job wrestling one day. Honestly, it's my dream job," he added. title: Winless Villa and Spurs face telling early showdown
description: Aston Villa and Tottenham are winless in the Premier League - and both in need of inspiration as they prepare to face each other on Saturday.
body: Aston Villa have lost three of their opening four Premier League games More than half a billion spent between them, for just three points and one goal. Tottenham and Aston Villa are in need of Premier League inspiration. It is not a surprise that a summer of change at both clubs has failed to bring immediate results - but they need to ignite their season. They meet at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Saturday as the past two Europa League winners but sitting in the bottom four of the early Premier League table. With 10 new players, and six key sales - including Morgan Rogers and Ollie Watkins - Unai Emery is shaping a new Villa team. Tottenham also added 10 players for more than £300m but goodwill is in short supply after two years of relegation battles. Victory is paramount for both teams. At VIlla, Emery has credit in the bank after turning them from a team floundering in mid-table to Europa League winners - qualifying for Europe every season since his arrival, and getting them back into the Champions League this year. This term there is a different remit, to be successful while integrating 10 new players - having spent more than £250m - following the summer exits. Emery conceded he did not know exactly why Villa lost control during last Saturday's defeat by Nottingham Forest - but knows he was unable to make a significant impact from the touchline with all the new players still fitting in to their new set-up. He can look frantic in his technical area during games, but has an impressive ability to decompress immediately and speak to the players calmly by the time he has returned to the dressing room. Emery remains confident Villa will improve yet is relying on John McGinn and Tyrone Mings, as two of the senior players, to help him and the squad through a difficult patch. It is a reason why both played in Wednesday's Carabao Cup win at Coventry rather than being rested. Captain McGinn has previously described learning Emery's methods as doing "a lot of homework". That may be why Aaron Wan-Bissaka has struggled in his opening three games as he tries to adapt quickly - the same too for other new signings perhaps overthinking their roles. An extended three-week break follows Saturday's match. But the head coach will not get the much-needed time on the training ground with his squad, as many go on international duty. "This break is crazy because it's three weeks," Emery said. "I don't like to be three weeks but we must accept it. "We are not going to have the players we want. [Johan] Manzambi played the first two matches with us and Saturday the third and then he goes with the national team. "Back with us, we must again try to join him with us in our structure and his mind will maybe be confused. "We don't want to use the international break as an excuse. "Saturday is very important as we lack points but we continue in our process trying to work as well as possible." Manzambi, brought in from Freiburg, and £47m winger Ibrahim Mbaye, who has moved from Paris St-Germain. made their debuts last weekend, coming off the bench against Forest, and are set to form part of a new attack. Nicolas Jackson, signed from Chelsea in August, will start on Saturday after coming off the bench at the CBS Arena as Emery gets close to his preferred line-up, with Villa looking to click after notching just one point in their opening four games. This video can not be played Tottenham's wait for league goal continues after Everton draw Only Villa, with 3.39, have a worse xG in the Premier League so far this season than Spurs' 3.45. Alysson's header in the 2-1 defeat by Forest was their first goal in the Premier League this term, with Spurs still searching for theirs. Both are still worse than bottom club Coventry, who are pointless and goalless, but have an xG of 4.21. Villa have had the lowest number of shots in the Premier League with 33, compared to Tottenham's 51, while their six on target is also the worst in the top flight followed by Spurs' 12. Only Hull have had fewer touches in the box (47) than Villa's 62. Yet Villa's defence must still be wary of struggling Spurs despite the hosts' lack of goals. Matty Cash is available after recovering from a muscle problem but fellow defenders Pau Torres and Ian Maatsen are out for a match in which Villa can expect to face pressure. Only Manchester United, Arsenal, Brighton and Liverpool have made more passes in the final third than Tottenham (617), who have the highest successful pass completion rate, at 81.4%. Villa's tally of 32 crosses, the lowest in the league, is half as many as Tottenham have managed. It has been 407 minutes since Spurs last scored in the Premier League. They have failed to score in four successive Premier League matches - the first time that has happened since September 2006. Their stalemate with Everton was their first goalless draw at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in the Premier League after 140 games. But despite both sides' struggle for goals, history does not point to a 0-0 draw. None of the past 22 Premier League meetings between Spurs (15 wins) and Aston Villa (seven) have been drawn. As Villa rebuild, they might hope a match against opponents struggling for wins might be the chance to kick-start their season. But they cannot afford to be lulled into a false sense of security. title: A village familiar with tragedy mourns Noah Woods
description: "This is a community that knows tragedy and has had to contend with tragedy in recent years," says rector.
body: Noah Woods' family said he was "the sweetest and most innocent little boy" who will be "missed forever" When three-year-old Noah Woods disappeared, hundreds came together in the hope of bringing him home. It was at about 15:00 BST on Tuesday when he became separated from a relative while at a playground in Brantham, Suffolk. The following day the news came that nobody wanted to hear: a child's body had been recovered from a nearby pond. At least 1,300 people helped to try to find him, coming together in hope then grief. It is not the first time this village of about 2,600 people has been hit by tragedy. Just how does a community come to terms with such a loss? Tributes have been left next to the playground in Brantham where Noah was playing before he disappeared In July 2024, Anita Rose, 57, who lived in Brantham, was taking her dog Bruce for a morning walk when she was attacked. She died three days later. It would be three months before her killer Roy Barclay - a violent offender and one of the county's most wanted criminals - was arrested and charged with her murder. The large police and media presence that descended on Brantham on Tuesday as the search for missing Noah grew, will have brought back painful memories for the village's residents. Helicopters, dog units and members of the public began scouring the area, close to the River Stour on the Suffolk-Essex border. Noah was non-verbal and partially deaf, which added complications to the search efforts. Noah's father Rhys Woods, from nearby East Bergholt, Suffolk, praised those who joined the search. "The compassion shown by all of you will never be forgotten by us, and brought us comfort and strength at the darkest time of our lives." Reflecting after Noah's death, the Reverend Chris Willis, rector of St Michael's Church, in Brantham, said: "This is a community that knows tragedy and has had to contend with tragedy in recent years. "All I can say, unequivocally, is this is a community that has been amazingly positive. It has dealt with the pain of loss and I have no doubt we'll pull together. "There was a love shown that was my first impression, and I hope and believe we'll see that continue." More than 1,000 people from as far as Birmingham and Hampshire turned up to help find Noah James Cartlidge, the MP for South Suffolk, was standing with the volunteers when the police delivered the news of his death. "That was pretty hard to watch to be honest because they were in deep grief. And that will remain the case," he said. "I've been many times to Brantham and always get the feeling it is a strong community. "There's history, there's community, and there is strength. And they showed it with the terrible case with Anita Rose. And they will show it now, and they are showing it now, the way they've responded." Mal Bridgeman, the chairman of Brantham Parish Council, said he was not sure the community could ever come to terms with the events of the past week. "I think that Noah will live in the memory of everybody," he said. "As time goes on, the emotions will quieten down. People will come to terms with it but I think people will just come to terms with it in their own time." It was a view echoed by the parish council's clerk, Sarah Keys, who said: "People were really hopeful and they felt empowered and really wanted to help. "So I think finding out that they weren't able to do that anymore was just completely devastating. "Not the outcome we wanted, but it has really restored your faith in community and in people and in, well, Brantham." Supt Tom Pearse delivered updates to volunteers at Brantham Leisure Centre during the search Canon Yvonne Tulloch founded the charity Ataloss after the death of her husband in 2008. As chief executive, she campaigns for more support for those navigating grief. She said that as a society, we are not good at acknowledging grief - preferring to convince ourselves that we will live until old age; because of this, emotions can be suppressed and come to the fore following high-profile cases. "We assume it's next of kin who will be the grievers and, while that is correct, it is not the whole picture. "There are these ripples, there will be people who will grieve who we wouldn't assume would be doing so. "Because we've been so poor at understanding grief, what can happen even more is when there is a tragedy that is near to us it makes us think it could have been us - particularly when it involves a child and you're a parent who can relate to it." Tulloch added this can be "confusing" because those removed from a tragedy can feel they do not have a right to grieve. She said: "Those who helped with the search have done so because they felt helpless. Equally there will be those who did not help and feel they should have done more. "In most cases people will have made their decision for sensible reasons and you have to release yourself from guilt and realise you did the best you could." For the family, there is a balance between appreciating the community support, but not being overwhelmed by it, she said. "The important thing is not to isolate the family because you do not know what to say. "People fear saying the wrong thing, but it takes nothing more than acknowledging somebody and saying, 'I'm so sorry, I just want you to know I care'. "It can mean even more coming from a stranger." Annie Owen, who volunteers at Ipswich and East Suffolk Samaritans, said that in the modern world, the overload of information can anaesthetise people to many tragedies. "But for this pure innocent child, there is nowhere to put our reactions or our grief," she said. Owen said it was important that people do not "beat themselves up" over what they did or did not do. title: Google's Gemini AI hacked three companies in security test
description: The AI model accessed the internet and guessed credentials to three websites, a Google official told the BBC.
body: Google's AI model Gemini autonomously hacked into three companies during a test of its cyber-security capabilities, the company has said, in what is thought to be the first known case of it carrying out such an act. Gemini found "public information online and guessed credentials to access websites it thought were part of the test", a Google official told the BBC, noting that in each instance "the model stopped". The affected companies have been informed about the breach. It comes after renewed public scrutiny over the pace of AI development, with some tech firms calling for a slowdown as they raise concerns over its potential threat to humanity - though not all companies agree. The hacks first reported by the Wall Street Journal, occurred in May during a test conducted by an independent company that carries out cyber-security evaluations. Heather Adkins, vice president of Security Engineering at Google, told the BBC in a statement: "We ensured the three entities were made aware, and we worked with our training partner on the changes they've now made to their testing processes." She added: "These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly." Other AI systems have recently reported similar instances of breaches. In July, Anthropic's Claude escaped its test environment to hack three organisations on its own just days after OpenAI said its models had carried out cyber-attacks against several "publicly available services". As public debate continues to grow over the safety of developing the tech, so too does conversation around regulation. Both Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang and OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman are expected to attend a White House state dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping next Friday. Altman will then brief the UN Security Council next week. On Friday, Huang told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, "we should go as fast as we can" with AI development. title: Saudi Arabia issues first air raid alerts for Riyadh since Houthis escalated attacks
description: Residents later received the all-clear after explosions were reported in the capital.
body: Residents in Saudi Arabia's Riyadh have been given the all-clear after air raid alerts were issued and explosions were reported in the capital. It was the first time alerts have been issued in Riyadh since the Houthis increased their attacks and declared a "maritime embargo" on the Saudis in July. The Saudi Civil Defence sent alerts for the capital and several other regions late on Friday night and Saturday morning (local time) as the Kingdom's conflict with the Iran-backed Houthis continued to escalate. Journalists from Reuters and AFP reported hearing explosions in the capital, but authorities have since said the danger has passed. Residents were urged to avoid gathering in crowds. The Houthis recently seized control of the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island, a gateway to a key shipping route used by the Gulf state to export to Asia and Europe. The Iran-backed group's military spokesman said the naval blockade was in retaliation for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled north-western Yemen. Saudi vessels have relied on that stretch of the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz. Last week, the Houthis attacked several Saudi oil facilities with drones and missiles, causing fires which led to operations being temporarily halted. The attacks on Saudi oil assets have directly impacted global energy markets and the price of petrol and diesel in many countries has sharply risen in recent weeks, compounding already elevated costs caused by the blockades of the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the country's de facto ruler, has personally asked US President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News, the BBC's US media partner. Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, offering instead to assist with intelligence and targeting support, the sources said. A senior Trump administration official told the BBC: "We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen government regarding regional stability." Earlier this week, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said the Houthis had launched drones and missiles at Saudi Arabia in retaliation for more than 450 Saudi air strikes on their territory over the past week. The United Nations Security Council held an emergency meeting on Tuesday, during which both Yemen's government and Saudi Arabia called for more decisive action against the Houthis, who they accused of choking the Bab al-Mandab Strait as a way of applying economic pressure. Council members agreed that freedom of navigation in the Red Sea must be maintained to prevent disruption to global supply chains. Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule. The fighting has reportedly left more than 150,000 people dead and triggered one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, with more than 22 million people in need of some form of aid, according to the UN. Additional reporting by Tabby Wilson. title: Parents could lose benefits or face prison for child's crimes, minister says
description: The reforms to Parenting Orders could also see parents losing benefits, Jake Richards MP told the Times.
body: Parents could lose their benefits or face prison sentences for their children's crimes under reforms to the youth justice system, a minister has said. Youth Justice Minister Jake Richards told the Times newspaper the system "should hold parents to account in a proportionate way for ensuring that they play their role in keeping communities safe". His comments come after the government set out plans in May to strengthen and expand Parenting Orders, which can currently compel parents or guardians to address their child's behaviour by attending counselling sessions or face fines. Richards said prison sentences would only apply "in the most extreme cases" and would be up to judges' discretion. He described the proposed changes as part of a "carrot-and-stick" approach. "Parenting orders are going to make sure that parents are more involved in the process by which we try to turn around young offenders," Richards told the Times. "Yes, that will have some stick. It could be custodial, or docking benefits - ultimately it will be up to a judge. But we want them to be more involved and that comes with responsibilities as well." Critics of the proposals say engaging with parents on a voluntary basis is generally more effective. When the government white paper was announced in May, then Justice Secretary David Lammy said that strengthening parenting orders would mean "there are real consequences for parents and carers who wilfully fail to support efforts to address their children's behaviour." He told BBC Breakfast at the time that if a parent was struggling, then the "judge can intervene to make sure that the young person is getting the support that they need and the parent is doing the best that they can". He also said he expected the power to jail parents to be used "very, very rarely". Courts are currently required to consider issuing a Parenting Order where a child under 16 has been convicted of an offence. They can also consider an order for 16 and 17 year olds if they believe this would help prevent further offences. However, government statistics show the use of parenting orders has declined in recent years, from more than 1,000 orders in 2009/10 to just 33 in 2022/23. The government's youth justice reform plans come after Phase One of the Southport Inquiry report found "catastrophic" failures by the parents of the Southport killer and various agencies meant clear chances to prevent the 2024 child murders were missed. title: Could AI wipe out humans and how might it do it?
description: Cyber Correspondent Joe Tidy looks at some of the scenarios being imagined and assesses how likely they are.
body: This video can not be played Recent AI (artificial intelligence) safety concerns have been fuelled by stark warnings from AI scientists about the growing risks of the technology going rogue. Some of the most pessimistic predictions warn that there is a greater than 10% chance that AI could wipe out all humans in the next 10 years. Many of the apocalyptic messages come from observers of the AI world known as 'AI Doomers' - but the big question many are asking, is how these Doomers think AI could actually bring an end to mankind. Cyber Correspondent Joe Tidy looks at some of the scenarios being imagined and assesses how likely they are. Could AI wipe out humans and how might it do it? title: The Papers: 'Monstrous words' and 'Russia to ramp up war'
description: The fallout from Earl Spencer's book about Princess Diana leads most papers on Saturday.
body: Many of Saturday's papers continue their coverage of the fallout from Earl Spencer's book about his sister Diana, Princess of Wales. In an interview with the BBC, Earl Spencer said he was telling the truth about the nature of a phone call he had after his sister's death with the then Prince Charles. In excerpts published by the Daily Mail, the earl claimed King Charles III told him "we'll forget her soon enough", but Buckingham Palace said in a statement that fraternal grief could "colour memory". The Mail says Earl Spencer hit back at the King in a "defiant" interview. The Daily Star also leads with Earl Spencer's interview with Laura Kuenssberg. "Monstrous", is the paper's one-word headline in reference to how the earl characterised the King's words. The Sun says the earl has been branded a "hypocrite", reporting that in a 1998 interview he claimed he would "never profit from my sister's life" but now "rakes in [a] fortune" from her death. The Daily Express leads with claims from author Tom Bower that the earl is "undoubtedly" working with his nephew, the Duke of Sussex, to "damage" King Charles. The paper dubs the alleged pairing the "Spencer alliance". The front page of the Times carries a photo of Earl Spencer, captioned "I don't hear denial from the King". It also reports that the Treasury is considering lowering the "mansion tax" threshold to £1.5m ahead of next month's Budget, citing unnamed government sources. The paper says if Chancellor John Healey announces the change, thousands more homes will be hit by the tax. "Russia prepares to ramp up war" is the main headline on the front page of the Daily Telegraph. It says Western intelligence officials believe Russian President Vladimir Putin is "laying the ground for a 'stealth mobilisation' over this weekend, in which thousands of Russians could be drafted". According to the i Paper, the British Army "secretly relaxed security checks", claiming this led to "letting in far-right extremists who backed Russia" over the course of two years. Leading the Guardian is an investigation revealing that "sensitive" police data is being held on a "vulnerable" cloud platform. New Great British Bake Off presenter Nigella Lawson is also on the front page alongside a chocolate cake, as she says "eating is my superpower." The founder of Betfred "attacks high taxes" in Britain in the Financial Times's lead story. Fred Done, who according to the paper is "Britain's biggest taxpayer", says at aged 83 he is "too old" to leave the country for tax purposes as others have done. "My dear friend Ann" is the headline of the Daily Mirror, as Strictly Come Dancing judge Craig Revel Horwood describes the late politician as "an amazing human being, and brave." He tells the paper he spoke to her six days before her death. Sign up for our morning newsletter and get BBC News in your inbox. title: Kerry Kennedy: 'It would be a tragedy' if Kennedy Center is demolished
description: The BBC’s Caitríona Perry spoke to the late president's niece, as protesters gathered at the venue to condemn demolition threats.
body: This video can not be played The BBC's Caitríona Perry spoke to Kerry Kennedy, the niece of late president John F Kennedy, about demolition threats to the performance centre named after him. A US federal judge ruled the Trump administration must give 30 days' notice before any "demolition" occurs to the Kennedy Center, as President Donald Trump warned the Washington DC performing arts venue could be "ripped down". The order comes after Trump was photographed onboard Air Force One looking at a poster with a headline that appeared to tout the demolition of the site. Protesters also gathered at the venue on Friday to demonstrate against demolition threats. Kerry Kennedy: 'It would be a tragedy' if Kennedy Center is demolished. title: I found love at an Irish matchmaking festival - and I want others to do the same
description: Mary Timby flew to Ireland on a whim last year and met her boyfriend at a matchmaking festival.
body: This video can not be played "It was very serendipitous" - Mary and Jason on finding love in Ireland Mary Timby was fed up with dating apps when she booked a trip to Ireland on a whim last summer - from the comfort of her Colorado couch. The spur-of-the-moment trip was unlike her: Timby, 39, is a self-described "total planner". But she'd always wanted to visit Ireland, and she found herself exhausted by the local dating scene while navigating a career transition. And then she remembered a few throwaway lines from a comedy series about a matchmaking festival in Ireland. So she looked it up - and not only was the Lisdoonvarna Matchmaking Festival real, it was also taking place during the entire month of September, when she was scheduled to visit. Now, a little more than a year later, Timby is reaping the benefits of that uncharacteristic last-minute decision: She's become a viral star. She's found love with an Irishman she met at a pub called The Matchmaker. And she's even started a new business venture - bringing others to Lisdoonvarna who hope to follow in her footsteps. Timby and Jason Mangan, 38, from County Clare, Ireland, are pursuing a transatlantic romance "It's really about enjoying County Clare, enjoying the festival, and, if you meet someone, you do - and that's what happened with us," says Timby, smiling at her partner, Jason Mangan, sitting beside her. They're speaking from the windswept coastal cottage they rented together for the summer in his native County Clare - about 20 miles (32 km) southwest of Lisdoonvarna, the site of their first fortuitous meeting. From the outset, Timby's inaugural Ireland trip seemed to take on a life of its own. She filmed a short video on the plane before her flight took off, telling her approximately 300 TikTok followers that she was heading on an off-the-cuff trip to an Irish matchmaking festival - and didn't "know what's going to happen". Timby then "turned my phone on airplane mode, then spent about eight hours on the flight (and) woke up at Shannon Airport," she says. When she turned on her phone, "it was blowing up". A group of friends had texted her. "They said, 'Mary, your video is going viral,'" she says. "I didn't even have notifications on for social media." She rented a manual transmission car - horrified to find the gear stick on the left side of the driver's seat - and set off through County Clare to her accommodation at an Irish family's home. Then she headed to Lisdoonvarna, where she saw firsthand that the festival is a whole-town, month-long celebration of conversation and dancing, rather than a line of singles waiting to be set up by a sage local matchmaker. Colorado woman Mary Timby, 39, visited Ireland's Aran Islands with her new beau That's changed since the festival's origins 170 years ago, when bachelor farmers and moneyed visitors would flock to the spa town of Lisdoonvarna to bathe in its mineral-rich waters and socialise. Generations of matchmakers would ply their trade to set up successful marriages, and word spread. Now, while the town's year-round residents number fewer than 1,000, that number swells up to 80,000 each September as revellers descend upon Lisdoonvarna from around the world. Third-generation matchmaker Willie Daly still holds court at his nearby home and at festival events, and Timby even visited him during her trip - when he put her on the phone to random men whose accents she struggled to understand. But the real magic of contemporary Lisdoonvarna lies in the town's overflowing streets and pubs - as Timby soon found out. Her first night in town was "a little slow," she admits - and Timby was tired and jet-lagged. She retired to her room and spent the next day sightseeing, but the Irish woman running her accommodation convinced her to try Lisdoonvarna again that night. "My AirBnB host said, 'You should go back tonight, because I heard that the younger folks come out at night,'" laughs Timby. So she did - and found herself dancing and drinking pints at The Matchmaker Bar in the centre of town. That's when a "handsome Irishman" approached her. "I went over and introduced myself, and... conversation just flowed," says Mangan, 38, from Ennis, County Clare, about 22 miles southeast of Lisdoonvarna. He'd been to the festival before and was well-acquainted with its cultural significance, remembering his grandparents making the journey decades earlier for the dancing. "Unfortunately, I didn't have much time on my hands, because I was turning back to Ennis," says Mangan, designated driver that night for a group of friends. "So I got her name, and I said, 'Oh, sure, I might see you around.' "It was a very short interaction, to be honest with you." The couple first met at Lisdoonvarna's Matchmaker Bar during the annual festival He didn't leave it at that, though; Mangan found Timby on Instagram and followed up with a message inviting her out. "It was short and sweet, and it was really genuine, too," says Timby - and she took him up on the offer. What followed was a series of whirlwind dates - lunches, dinners, sightseeing and shopping trips. Timby extended her time in Ireland and documented much of it for her newfound following - but she didn't reveal anything about her new beau. They wanted to save the burgeoning romance for themselves. When Timby eventually had to fly home, there were "tears at the airport" - but they decided to keep the relationship going. "It was very tough to say goodbye," Timby says. "It was very tough to start a long-distance relationship, but it ended up being a really good opportunity for us to sort of slow things down a bit." They kept talking daily, Mangan impatiently waiting for Timby to wake up seven hours behind him in Colorado.
