title: Tata Sons: India's corporate crown braces for upheaval amid boardroom revolt
description: The Tata boardroom battle has intensified over a re-appointment of its chairman and a diktat to go public.
body: Noel Tata (l) and N Chandrasekaran (r) are at the centre of the feud This week, the board of Tata Sons - one of India's oldest conglomerates and owner of iconic British brands such as Jaguar Land Rover and Tetley Tea - defied its largest shareholder, Tata Trusts, by reappointing N Chandrasekaran as chairman and backing a public listing of the holding company. Tata Trusts, which owns 66% of Tata Sons called the decision "illegal" under its articles of association and also opposed the listing, setting the stage for a period of prolonged upheaval and possibly a protracted legal drama at Bombay House, the headquarters of the 158-year-old company. For the Tatas, who are no strangers to boardroom battles, a cloud of uncertainty now prevails at multiple levels. The resolution to reappoint Chandrasekharan, while approved by the board, could be defeated at the company's Annual General Meeting as Tata Trusts is likely to vote against it, putting a question mark over his future. The meeting has to take place before 31 December as per reports, after the previous one was adjourned for lack of quorum, but no new date has yet been announced. "The Nomination and Remuneration Committee (NRC) of the Board of Tata Sons which reappointed him has no power to take this decision. They can only make a recommendation. Also, their decision flies against the governance code of the company that requires executives to step down from active roles at 65. These are serious lapses," Nitin Potdar, a prominent Mumbai-based corporate lawyer told the BBC. Chandrasekharan, who got a five-year extension, will turn 65 in 2028. Tata Group stocks first soared and then crashed as the tensions mounted, reflecting hope and uncertainty about leadership and business continuity amid several high-stakes but loss-making bets by Chandrasekharan in sectors like semiconductors and airlines. But beyond the leadership tussle, the bigger question to contend with is the group's public listing, "which now looks increasingly inevitable", Nirmalya Kumar, who previously headed strategy at Tata Sons, told the BBC. Bombay House, the Tata Group head office in Mumbai In 2022, India's central bank, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), classified Tata Sons as an "upper layer non-banking financial company" because of its systemic importance and investment activities. This created a listing obligation on the group. Tata Sons sought to get out of this classification by repaying their debt and arguing that they do not borrow directly from the public markets. But after sitting on its application for over two years, the RBI rejected the company's bid to get out of the framework earlier this month, pushing the group closer to a stock market debut. In a statement, Tata Trusts reiterated its long-held opposition to going public and said "all available options and not a listing alone" are being explored even though its trustees are no longer unanimous in their position on the matter. Potdar says the regulator has no power to force any company to go public and the issue will almost certainly be legally challenged by Tata Trusts. The RBI meanwhile has pre-emptively, external approached the courts seeking to be heard first in any matter related to the ‌listing. The issue has sharply divided opinion among corporate pundits. Many in the group, including the late Ratan Tata and veteran director NA Soonawala, have long argued strongly for keeping the group private. A publicly held Tata Sons could significantly reduce the control and special rights the Tata Trusts wield over the group. They say the Tatas have a unique operating structure where the majority shareholder is a charity which uses dividends received from commercial arms to fund hospitals, universities and research. A listing, they say, will destroy its character by making it accountable to outside shareholders whose focus would be financial returns. "A new group of shareholders might say, 'Don't declare dividends; we need to reinvest this money in the companies.' What happens then? The first casualty will be the hospitals they run," said Potdar. Opponents of the initial public offering (IPO) also worry that bringing in public investors will weaken the group's internal support function to rescue distressed businesses and expose the company to quarterly performance pressures. Moreover the timing is another crucial factor. "The group currently faces large financial commitments from recently formed subsidiary companies, including Air India, investments in long gestation projects, and losses in newer ventures," Soonawala wrote, external in a piece for Times of India. "The current situation in the case of Air India would be an acid test. All these would need to be disclosed fully in an IPO prospectus. Consolidated financial statements – reflecting subsidiary losses and borrowings – may not present an especially attractive picture to sophisticated investors, pointing to wrong timing for an IPO at the present time." Many, including Potdar, also argue that globally, industrial foundations are being protected as sources of patient capital - money that can be committed for years to fund long-gestation projects and social goals. By forcing the Tatas to list, India is going the other way. Tata Group officially regained control of the national carrier Air India in 2022 But supporters of a listing say it would bring much-needed transparency and accountability to a group that is systemically important to India. "There should be tougher scrutiny of their capital-allocation decisions being so central to the Indian business ecosystem. Everybody wants complete control over their empire and the freedom to take capricious decisions, but that is not a good thing for the organisation," said Kumar. Collectively, listed Tata companies including Tata Motors and TCS have a market capitalisation of more than $260bn and influence over 17.7 million retail shareholders, pension funds, insurers and mut

title: Billionaire Man United owner says he has lost confidence in the UK
description: Ineos founder Sir Jim Ratcliffe tells the BBC he thinks the country is "on the slide" and calls for more investment in the North Sea.
body: This video can not be played Sir Jim Ratcliffe says the UK economy is "on the slide" One of Britain's richest people, Sir Jim Ratcliffe, says he has lost confidence in the UK, describing the country as "on the slide". The founder of petrochemical giant Ineos, who also owns a large stake in Manchester United, said the UK was in decline due to a combination of high taxes and high immigration. He told the BBC failing to invest further in North Sea oil and gas amounted to "insanity" and warned gas storage was so low that the UK could "run out of gas" if there was a cold snap this winter. In response to the billionaire's criticism, the government said it was working to deliver growth and that business investment had increased in the last two years. A spokesperson said they did not foresee any problems with gas supply: "We have a diverse energy mix and are confident in our security of supply." Sir Jim, whose wealth is estimated to be around £15bn, has prompted controversy in the past with his comments on immigration. He was a supporter of Brexit but has been a tax resident in Monaco since 2020. The businessman's UK exit has been followed by other high-profile billionaires, including steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal and most recently hedge-fund boss Chris Rokos. Sir Jim said the politics of envy was driving people away from the UK. "In America they applaud people who create wealth," he said. "Unfortunately the UK has got a bit of a green eye towards wealth at the moment." He said for him to return to the UK "things would have to get better". Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will take a "pragmatic approach" to oil and gas, but one of the biggest decisions facing the government, whether to give the go-ahead to further development of the oil and gas fields at Rosebank and Jackdaw, is still waiting to be resolved. Sir Jim criticised the hesitation and suggested high taxes on North Sea operators were threatening the sector's viability. Tax on energy company profits is being reformed, but won't be fully implemented until 2030. Ineos operates the Forties pipeline which transports about 30% of the UK's North Sea oil. "You would expect [the government] to exploit our natural resources and we're clearly not doing that. We're shutting it down. "If you tax everybody to death, they're all going to leave. And that's what's happening." Recent climate data combined with record heatwaves have given weight to the argument against further exploitation of fossil fuels. However, political pressure has grown on the government to proceed with Rosebank and Jackdaw to support UK jobs, tax revenues and boost energy security. Sir Jim backed those calls, saying it was "absurd" to import more energy than necessary. The government spokesperson said that oil and gas would play an important role in the UK "for decades to come", but they added: "The transition to homegrown clean power is the only way to deliver energy and financial security for families and businesses." Ineos has invested in the EU's first carbon capture project in Denmark Sir Jim warned that low gas storage levels in Europe posed a risk to the UK in the months ahead. "If we have a really sharp cold spell, then there is conceivably the possibility that we'll run out of gas and have to switch industry off... our storage is not full," he said. The UK does not typically store a great deal of gas, relying instead on LNG (liquidfied natural gas) and gas imports from Europe. Energy specialist consultancy Cornwall Insight said that current gas storage levels in the EU were at about 69%, when typically they would be at 85% at this time of the year. However, Adam Bell of consultancy Stonehaven, said supplies were unlikely to run short. "We are down compared to where we normally would be but not what I'd regard as catastrophic," he said. "The physical risk of running out of gas is relatively low, especially if Jackdaw gets the go ahead." He said the main source of uncertainty was policy in the US, which supplies LNG to the UK. Sir Jim was speaking in Denmark at the launch of the EU's first carbon capture and storage system (CCS). Ineos has invested in the scheme which is being subsidised by the Danish government and the EU. He said he had hoped to develop CCS in the UK but there had not been enough government support. The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) said the government had committed £21.7bn for CCS projects over 25 years, however, no projects are yet operational in the UK. At the project in Esbjerg in the south west of Denmark, carbon captured from around the country arrives in huge zeppelin-like tanks before being pumped into a ship called Carbon Destroyer 1. It is then pumped into a depleted oil field nearly 200 miles off shore. Critics say CCS is expensive, money that could be better used to invest in renewables rather than supporting continued fossil fuel use. Sir Jim's critique of the UK is not limited to energy and tax policy. He said the country had at one time been "a fantastic place". "We had the greatest empire in the world. We were a great people. We won two world wars," he said. But he said immigration and welfare spending were both currently too high and that politicians had proved reluctant to tackle either. "Nobody's tough enough to deal with the immigration problem. Nobody's tough enough to deal with the benefits problem. But somebody needs to do it," he said. Earlier this year he caused controversy by saying the UK had been "colonised by immigrants". He later offered an apology for "offending some people". You can listen to the full interview here on the Big Boss Interview podcast with Simon Jack. title: Earl Spencer's Diana book opens old wounds royals would rather forget
description: Many of the Royal Family's current troubles can be traced back to the aftermath of the then Princess of Wales' death.
body: The legacy of the shocking death of Diana, Princess of Wales, is still the rawest of wounds for the royals, as demonstrated by the no-holds-barred memoir from her brother Earl Spencer. It might be almost 30 years ago, but Buckingham Palace's unusually angry rebuttal to the book's allegations of a callous response to his ex-wife's death from the then Prince Charles shows how much this still matters. That late summer in 1997 was a moment when the Royal Family looked out of touch, lacking in empathy for Diana's loss, and at peril of losing public support, as people laid siege to the palaces with flowers. While the royals dealt with their own private grief, they were also facing a reputational disaster, at risk of becoming the focus of public dismay at the sudden death of the "People's Princess" in a car crash in Paris. An outpouring of public grief saw flowers laid outside palaces and Diana's homes "It was a very febrile mood. Everyone was taken by surprise by the strength of feeling, and the strength to which the Royal Family was unpopular. The palaces were deemed to have treated Diana badly," recalls royal author Valentine Low. Low was inside Westminster Abbey for Diana's funeral and vividly remembers the public response to the electrifying speech made by Earl Spencer. "I heard this noise. I couldn't quite make out what it was, and then I worked out it was the crowd outside the abbey, who'd been listening on the speakers," he says. "That noise appeared to come through the stone walls of the abbey and it was the most extraordinary thing - as people then started to applaud inside the abbey. It was so astounding, in front of Charles and all of the Royal Family." 'I'm telling the truth': Earl Spencer defends Diana book claims about Charles in BBC interview A volatile public mood followed Diana's death, with the late Queen Elizabeth eventually having to respond with a live televised address paying tribute to the princess and acknowledging how difficult it can be to articulate grief. "We have all been trying in our different ways to cope. It is not easy to express a sense of loss, since the initial shock is often succeeded by a mixture of other feelings: disbelief, incomprehension, anger - and concern for those who remain," said the late Queen. A fresh-faced new prime minister, Tony Blair, was said to have been a modernising influence on sending such a direct message - an intervention later depicted in the movie, The Queen, starring Helen Mirren. There was disagreement about whether it was right for the princes to walk behind Diana's coffin So many of the current tensions in the royal world can be traced back to the trauma of those events. The death of a mother at such a young age was inevitably a huge shaping influence on her sons - and it can feel as though those unresolved tensions are still playing out. In the Duke of Sussex's memoir Spare, Diana's absence is a huge presence, his sense of loss unabated. There is still a graphic sense of his distress at walking behind her coffin, with Prince Harry mentioning Earl Spencer's opposition. "Mummy's brother, Uncle Charles, raised hell. 'You can't make these boys walk behind their mother's coffin! It's barbaric'," wrote Harry. Harry's accusation that the interests of the institution of the monarchy had been put above the happiness of individuals has been part of the narrative that saw him stepping down as a working royal and remaining at loggerheads with his brother, Prince William. There was a wave of applause from outside Westminster Abbey when Earl Spencer finished his eulogy The disputes that followed Diana's death, within the family and between in-laws, are still being aired loudly in Earl Spencer's book - Swan Song: Diana, My Sister - and in the global news coverage it has triggered. It opens up old questions about King Charles's character, his treatment of the young princess and his relationship with the now Queen Camilla. On social media, Diana's fans are believing Earl Spencer's version of events, says Prof Pauline Maclaran. She says the royals remain "highly vulnerable" to anything that evokes the story of a "beautiful princess whose life was cut short in such tragic and ambiguous circumstances". Royal commentator Jenny Bond described it as a "fantastically hostile, absolutely rude book... it's a very unpleasant portrayal of a man - but it's his memory of it, and who knows who's right?" Prince William was 15 and Prince Harry just 12 at their mother's funeral At issue is Earl Spencer's account of a conversation with the then Prince Charles after the death of Diana, with the prince accused of telling Earl Spencer: "We'll forget her soon enough." He is accused of sounding "giddily elated" and like a "lottery winner" after the news of her death. Buckingham Palace hit back with a response, which although dressed in courtier-like politeness, was essentially saying the conversation had never happened like that. The King was said to be "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways that others do not recognise". Anyone who has lost someone knows how feelings can run high, people can hear different things about the same conversations - and families can fall out, or come together, in the wake of a death. Psychotherapist Nick Hatter says he doesn't have a view on which version of events is correct, but he says that during traumatic events memories can be "distorted". A phone call doesn't have any of the visual clues or body language to give a fuller picture, he adds. Hatter says there can be very different and unpredictable responses to grief, including a condition known as "bereavement mania" where someone can seem inappropriately hyper or even euphoric after the loss of a loved one. title: Is it cool to wear M&S clothes now?
description: The retailer hosted its first-ever London Fashion Week show this week, celebrating 100 years of producing clothing.
body: M&S show during London Fashion Week September 2026 "I'm the first person to be like, 'It's from M&S, you need to get on to it,'" Farron Clark, a 26-year-old brand strategist tells me. She says it's officially cool to buy your clothes from the high street retailer now. According to Clark and others on social media, Marks and Spencer is becoming the hot place to shop for women under 35, while also keeping its core older audience happy too. "For a long time M&S had this fusty reputation - it was less valued by younger people," says Chioma Nnadi, head of editorial content at British Vogue, who tells the BBC there is now a "fresh energy around the brand". And accompanying that fresh energy is a new marketing strategy, which includes hosting its first-ever London Fashion Week show on Friday, featuring a collection of outfits inspired by the brand's archive. So how is M&S attracting and retaining a younger generation of shoppers in a highly competitive market? The BBC went to the catwalk show and spoke to experts to find out. Speaking ahead of the event at the Design Museum, the company's head of womenswear design, Lisa Illis, says they wanted to do this because of the "immediacy of seeing something and being able to own it and wear it, rather than waiting six months". For many, M&S is more synonymous with pig-shaped sweets than cutting-edge fashion, but its runway of 43 womenswear and 10 menswear looks did a lot to persuade people that the latter is where its true talent lie. Normally Fashion Week is about seeing what you'll be wearing six months from now, but this runway was full of colder weather fits, from opulent faux fur jackets and wrist cuffs, to satin jumpsuits and dresses in rich tones of navy, burgundy and brown. The catwalk featured a diverse range of models in age, size and gender, demonstrating the brand's desire to cater to a wide market. But there was certainly a concerted effort to attract the eye of younger shoppers with a fashion-forward approach to Christmas party staples like sequinned dresses, tasselled skirts and see-through lace tops. Womenswear and menswear collections at London Fashion Week are inspired by the M&S archive The retailer has been focusing on "newer styles and relevant trends" to attract younger customers, says Illis. But she says that this has been achieved without compromising on quality which is what keeps M&S's core audience on board. "They have created a modern version of everything we know and love - cashmere staples, knitwear and the lingerie department," says Nnadi. Clark agrees that M&S has been nailing "funnel neck [styles] and barrel jeans, which are filtering down from high fashion". M&S has perhaps been fortunate to rebrand at a time when consumer habits are changing, as young shoppers consider buying capsule wardrobes - a smaller number of staple pieces that can be styled in a variety of ways. Clark notes that the idea of wear-it-once fast fashion has declined as people "are looking for [foundational pieces] to rotate". This is something Perrie Sian, one of Britain's biggest fashion influencers, has also noticed. The 34-year-old tells the BBC: "The real height of fast fashion is behind us". "As a group we've changed our shopping habits and M&S slots into that," she says. "In my content and with lots of other creators we're showing people how to wear things in multiple ways, how to look after them." She added that she is noticing "people are willing to spend a little bit more" on wardrobe staples and items that "wash well and are made of cotton, not acrylic or polyester". During the Covid pandemic M&S struggled, but returned to growth in 2022-2023, with its fashion, home and beauty market share reaching 9.6%. This again increased in 2023-2024 to 10%, and 10.5% in 2024-2025. But the business took a big hit in 2025 due to a cyber attack, which left shoppers unable to use its website and app and affected stock in stores too. It means M&S's market share on fashion, home and beauty now sits at 10.2%, external for 2025-26. Nnadi says M&S has been investing heavily in its retail spaces in recent years, focusing on "accessible luxury" with stores that feel "welcoming, new and fresh". And that's something Clark has noticed too. "Getting an iced coffee and having a walk around M&S with my friends is the perfect Saturday," she says. "My generation do so much sitting on our phones, so an in-person experience becomes a bit of an activity." According to Sian, M&S has also taken "more risks" recently, which has helped it "create viral moments", including hosting a pit-lane fashion show at this year's F1 British Grand Prix and collaborating with British designers and creators. "I'm seeing on Instagram or TikTok somebody say, 'Oh my goodness, this faux leather jacket is from M&S and it looks like it's £500 from the runway.' "And what am I doing? I'm hop, skip, jumping into my car and getting straight to my local M&S to hunt it down," Sian jokes. "They have embraced young designers like Marco Capaldo, the founder and creative director of 16Arlington," adds Nnadi. "And the Aries collab was genius and unexpected - it's a brand that has a lot of fashion kudos and is very British in its aesthetic but represents a younger vision of what British cool looks like," she says. Clark agrees the brand has "homed in on experts in their craft, rather than partnering with a million different people" like other fashion brands have made the mistake of doing. She notes their recent partnership with Stormzy's stylist Melissa Holbrook-Akposoe, who goes by Melissa's Wardrobe on social media, as "adding credibility" for younger shoppers. title: Grim discoveries of murdered women spark fear in South Africa
description: Dineo Motapane is one of nine recent victims whose deaths have left a nation traumatised over the level of violence against women.
body: This video can not be played 'We are dying': Aunt of murdered woman pleads for action on femicide "What we are going to do, I have no idea," sobs Nokwanda Matshikiza, reflecting on the murder of her niece Dineo Motapane. "But something must give." "For us, for all the other women. How many other bodies will be found before something happens?" Nokwanda is speaking to the BBC from the family home near South Africa's main city, Johannesburg, just two days after relatives identified Dineo's body. The 38-year-old mother-of-two was last seen alive last Sunday. Her battered body, partly burned, found later in the residential region of Ekurhuleni. Nokwanda weeps as she describes how the family will have to face, at some point, the grim task of telling Dineo's daughter of her death. "How do you explain that your parent was brutally murdered, dumped in a field, and just left there, discarded like a piece of rubbish. "There's no coming to peace with it," she adds. "It's something that you can never reconcile yourself with, that you can never get over." Dineo's death this week has come amid a series of comparable incidents in Ekurhuleni – her body one of three discovered there this week. In total, nine bodies of murdered women have been found in similar circumstances in the region since July. The problem has always been there but this spate of grim discoveries has once again sparked a national outcry about the scale of violence against women in the country – which has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence in the world. Dineo Motapane's body was "discarded like a piece of rubbish", her aunt said Themba Kekana is also living in shock at the death of a loved one. His sister, Itumeleng, was one of the first to disappear in Ekurhuleni. The 32-year-old shopkeeper's body was found in July, 17 days after she was last seen alive. Her body was badly bruised, partially clothed and dumped on a bridge. "We are devastated with grief," says Themba, wet eyes shining. "I look at my sister's young daughter and my eyes fill with tears, I know there is no way that I can ever take this pain away from her. "No family should have to deal with what we are faced with." Only one arrest has been made in connection with the murders – and that was two days after the first body was discovered on 15 July. Nobody has been detained following the murders of Itumeleng or Dineo or the other six Ekurhuleni women. Itumeleng Kekana's killing has left her young daughter without a mother Most of the victims were young, in their 20s or 30s, and almost all had suffered extreme violence before their deaths. Police have said they are not sure if they are hunting a serial killer. It is possible the cases are not linked. Either way, what has happened in this residential district east of South Africa's biggest city has traumatised the nation, shining a spotlight on a situation that many believe is a crisis. South Africa's police issue detailed crime statistics every quarter, which show that during the last quarter – between April and June this year - 5,427 people were murdered. The official data does not distinguish between the genders of the victims, but this week the country's Human Rights Commission released figures showing that 569 women had been killed in that period (six a day on average), with another 1,052 who faced attempted murder. Many women - already feeling unsafe - have been left reeling by recent events. And it has put pressure on the government, less than a year after ministers acknowledged the scale of the issue and declared gender-based violence a national disaster. Announcing the move last November, Minister of Social Development Nokuzola Sisisi Tolashe said treating the issue as a national disaster would help the government tackle the crisis. It followed weeks of protests, culminating in a "Women's Shut Down" march as South Africa hosted the G20 summit. This week has seen a chorus of calls for things to go further. Rights group Amnesty International said an important first step towards protecting South Africa's women was to recognise femicide as a separate crime. "Every day that femicide remains unrecognised as a crime is a failure to confront the targeted killing of women," said Amnesty's country director Shenilla Mohamed in a statement. "It is time to call it what it is: Femicide. "Femicide is a gender-motivated crime. It is the killing of a woman because she is a woman." Amnesty says femicide is criminalised as a specific crime in 33 countries, including Gabon and Morocco in Africa. It argues that making that change in South Africa could help focus on the scale of the issue. "It would compel the state to confront their failure to protect women and girls from violence," says Mohamed. "You cannot fix what you are not tracking." Almost everyone in South Africa agrees more needs to be done. President Cyril Ramaphosa this week pledged to leave "no stone unturned" in investigating the crimes in Ekurhuleni, adding: "As a nation, we must stand up for the rights, safety and dignity of women and girls." Activists held a demonstration when South Africa hosted G20 leaders last year Lebogang Ramofoko, an advocate for gender and social justice, said the levels of violence against women in the country were symptomatic of a much bigger problem – a lack of regard for humanity. "The bodies of black women have been treated as disposable in this country for time in memorial, passed down from colonisation through to apartheid," she tells the BBC, referring to the legalised system of racism that was in place until 1994. "What we see happening to women is testimony to legacies of violence from those systems whose traumas were never addressed. "This is not to say black men are inherently violent, but in systems where violence was meted out against them for decades, historically black women were the people that that violence would be taken out on -

title: A four-minute warning isn't enough: Russia's new relentless missile tactics exhaust Kyiv residents
description: Increasingly frequent and ferocious attacks on the Ukrainian capital have left many on edge.
body: Daria left her apartment in Kyiv this summer after Russia's attacks on the city intensified For much of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Daria was not afraid of the shelling. Even on nights of heavy bombardment, the 27-year-old could sleep through the explosions in her apartment in Kyiv. Like many Ukrainians, she relied on the "two-wall rule": staying safe by keeping two walls between herself and the outside world. But this year that has changed. In recent months, Russia has scaled up the intensity and frequency of its attacks against the Ukrainian capital. In the first 10 days of July alone, the Russians launched dozens of ballistic missiles in three major attacks, killing nearly 60 civilians, according to official figures. Similar large scale attacks took place in August and September. A BBC Verify analysis of government figures found Kyiv is now suffering more daily air raid alerts than at any time since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. It was during an attack one night in May that Daria realised she no longer felt safe in her home. She and her boyfriend were in the corridor of their ninth-floor apartment, watching a boxing match, as explosions went off around them, the blast waves causing the windows to repeatedly slam open and shut. When the fight ended, "there was no longer anything to distract me," Daria says. "That's when I realised I was really scared." At first, she thought she would start using a nearby bomb shelter during attacks. But in June, when a young mother was killed running to a shelter in Kyiv, Daria decided she needed to leave the city altogether. She returned to her family's country house, 30km (18.6 miles) away in Romankiv, and now spends a total of four hours a day commuting to and from Kyiv, where she works in the defence sector. A photo from the State Emergency Service shows the impact of a Russian strike in July Daria's experience is far from unique. Residents in Kyiv who say they had got used to Russia's missile and drone strikes have told the BBC World Service the renewed intensity of the attacks is making them rethink how they live their lives. Previously, Ukraine's air-defence network and military intelligence gave residents a degree of predictability. Large-scale attacks could often be detected in advance, allowing people to spend the night in shelters, leave the city or take other precautions. But since the summer, Russia has changed its tactics. It has relied less on aircraft, whose movements can be spotted ahead of time, and more on ballistic missiles that travel at tremendous speed and provide little warning. Air-raid alerts sometimes begin only moments before impact, or even simultaneously with the first explosions. Daria can see her nearest shelter from the window of her apartment, which she still rents. Even so, it takes around 10 minutes to reach it. During a ballistic attack, she might have just four minutes' warning or less, she says. She decided to leave Kyiv in June after holidaying abroad this summer and seeing people living "normal" lives. Since then, she has only spent one night in Kyiv. Ballistic missiles are difficult to detect in advance Yet, for many, leaving is not an option. Sixty-two-year-old Olha Vlasova lives on the seventh floor of a high-rise apartment block with her 98-year-old mother, Nadia Tsybina. Despite her age, Nadia remains intensely engaged with the world. From her bed she follows events in Ukraine and abroad, discussing everything from US President Donald Trump's policies, to anti-corruption protests in Kyiv, and the Epstein files. She's also learned that she can often tell, simply by listening, whether a Russian missile or drone has been intercepted or has reached its target. This summer, she says she has heard fewer interceptions. "It's upsetting when there's nothing to shoot them down with," Nadia says. "I can hear them firing with whatever they've got, rifles, machine guns." Nadia, 98, continues to follow world events closely from her bed Olha has taken to placing a mattress by the window to protect her and her mother from flying glass With Nadia confined to her bed, she and Olha cannot go to a shelter, however serious an attack is. Instead, as soon as an air-raid siren sounds, Olha covers her mother with a blanket, pushes a mattress into their window frame, and then hides in a wardrobe which puts two walls between her and outside. Nadia places a pillow over her head to protect her face from flying glass. Once in her wardrobe, Olha will often stay awake watching the news all night. "They come in, they bomb us," Nadia says. "You haven't even had time to fall asleep, and there's another alert. They come again, they shoot them down again. And it goes on all night. "People don't sleep, and then they walk around like zombies." The new academic year in Kyiv began with many students attending classes in shelters as an air raid alert was in effect in the morning An increase in daytime attacks means life in Kyiv is now interrupted by air raid sirens day and night. At the beginning of September, when children returned to school after the summer break, there were dozens of air raid alerts, followed by explosions and fires. According to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko, two children were injured in attacks on 31 August. As a result, many children stayed at home, while others spent hours in the basements of schools and kindergartens. Commuters in Kyiv have become accustomed to long wait times as the metro is disrupted. When the sirens sound, it also affects businesses and transport. Shopping centres close and above-ground metro stations suspend operations, often severing public transport links between Kyiv's Left and Right Banks, on either side of the Dnieper River, for hours at a time. New metro operating rules during air raid alerts are being introduced in an attempt to improve the situation. For Olha, it has meant seeing less of

title: Temperatures could peak at 26C as summerlike warmth returns next week
description: After a changeable week, drier and warmer conditions will dominate for some next week, but with little rain for those who need it.
body: Temperatures could peak at 26C next week as late summer warmth returns to parts of the UK. Southern areas will experience the highest temperatures, but most locations will be warmer than normal for late September. Warmth could last all week for some in England and Wales, but it might only be a short-lived boost for Scotland and Northern Ireland. The high pressure, which is responsible for the warmth, will also mean little rain for places continuing to experience drought conditions. The changeable conditions that have dominated the past week will continue into the weekend, with blustery winds coming in off the Atlantic and gales for some western coasts and hills. While Saturday will become a day of sunshine and passing showers for many, in southern parts of England and Wales a weather front draped across the area will mean mostly cloudy conditions and rain or drizzle at times, especially in the south-west. Despite the cloud, it will feel warm and humid due to the south-westerly winds dragging in warm and moist air from the mid-Atlantic. Over the coming days the jet stream will buckle to the north of the UK allowing high pressure to build The much more autumnal look to the weather charts at the moment is down to a particularly brisk and straight jet stream roaring through the skies across the Atlantic. It has meant rain-bearing areas of lower pressure to the north of the UK, high pressure to the south and stronger winds in between, creating the changeable conditions. However, as the jet stream starts to buckle through the second half of the weekend the weather will slowly being to calm down. On Sunday, early rain in the far north and south of the UK should move away to leave most parts dry with sunny spells by the afternoon. Strong winds in north-east Scotland should ease too. While it will feel pleasant in the sunshine, temperatures will be close to the seasonal average of 15-21 Celsius. Into the start of next week, high pressure will build across the UK more widely at first. Other than early rain in Scotland and northern England, most places will see increasing amounts of sunshine breaking through during the day. Temperatures will lift by a degree or so compared to Sunday and humidity levels will creep up too. That more humid air paired with light winds across England and Wales into Tuesday means some will start off rather misty and foggy. Once the sun has broken through though, it will feel like late summer warmth has returned. Temperatures could peak at around 25 or 26 Celsius in south-east England, but reach the low 20s in many other parts of England, Wales, Northern Ireland and Eastern Scotland. 2026 has already been a record-breaking year for the number of days above 25C, with last week exceeding the record of 89 days set in 1959. A weather front moving into western Scotland is likely to bring some rain and could be the focus for a developing low pressure system that will bring more widespread rain midweek across the northern half of the UK. Temperatures lift across the UK early in the week As high pressure holds on across the south, many will stay largely dry and warm here through the rest of the week. While many may enjoy the warm weather, it is not good news for declining reservoir and water storage levels. While recent rain has been welcome, it has been well short of what is required to break the drought across most of England and Wales. By Friday morning Leconfield, East Yorkshire had only received 11% of its normal September rainfall, and Durham just 14% - both well below the 50-60% that would be typical by now. Some forecasts do show the potential for rain returning more widely from late week and into next, but others hint at continuing high pressure and potentially even warmer air. title: 'Our industry is still male dominated, but things are changing'
description: There has been an increase in the number of women studying for engineering degrees in NI.
body: Lorraine O'Neill first joined Powerscreen in County Tyrone back in 1994 There has been a significant increase in the number of women studying for engineering degrees in Northern Ireland, new figures show. Over the last 10 years the number of female students studying Mechanical Engineering at Queen's University has increased by 40%, while at Ulster University the number studying engineering has almost doubled over the past decade. But employment figures also show that the engineering and wider manufacturing industries in Northern Ireland are still male dominated. Now a group of women working in the engineering industry in Mid Ulster are raising awareness about the opportunities for women in the sector. Lorraine O'Neill is one of them. When she first joined one of County Tyrone's largest manufacturing firms back in 1994, there were less than 10 women working there. Now the company employs more than 300 females across Northern Ireland. "Yes there are still gender stereotypes in this industry, but we've come a long way since I first started out", she said. Powerscreen is one of the companies that pioneered the concept of mobile screening "When I joined more than 30 years ago, there were no females in the senior management team at all, but today 50% of our senior leadership team are female." O'Neill is currently Senior Logistics Manager at Powerscreen, a global manufacturer of equipment used in the quarrying, mining and construction industries. She wants to encourage more women to aim for senior leadership roles in manufacturing and engineering sector. She said: "I love my job, I help ship our machinery all over the world and no day is the same. "A lot of people have a picture in their head about engineering and manufacturing jobs but they don't understand there are so many different opportunities from logistics, to finance to procurement. She added: "Things are changing and seeing women in senior roles really helps." Powerscreen has celebrated 60 years in business by open its factory doors to the local community, including local schools Tyrone is known for its cluster of engineering and manufacturing firms and today more than 40% of the world's mobile crushing and screening equipment is made in the Mid Ulster area. Founded as Ulster Plant Ltd in 1966, Powerscreen pioneered the concept of mobile screening. Over the following decades, the business grew from a local engineering firm into a global brand. It was acquired by Terex Corporation in 1999 but continued to retain its roots in County Tyrone. As it celebrates its 60th year in business, together with its parent company Terex, they are looking at how their workforce has changed and diversified. Sneha Saji isn engineering graduate who has recently joined Powerscreen Recent graduate Sneha Saji has been working at Powerscreen as a manufacturing engineer for a number of months. She said: "Before starting my engineering degree, I probably did have an idea in my head that this industry was primarily for men, but doing internships and seeing women in senior engineering roles really did inspire me. "It can be daunting if you're in certain departments that might be male dominated, but I would say just give it a shot, don't let the stereotypes put you off, ask plenty of questions and don't be afraid to make mistakes." Amelia McCormack has been with Powerscreen for seven years Amelia McCormack has been with Powerscreen for seven years and now works as a senior logistics co-ordinator. She joined the company through an apprenticeship. The "earn while you learn" element attracted her and she has "never looked back". She said it is a "hands on, fast paced" job. "I am really proud to be a woman working in this industry, showing that things have changed, but it's fair to say that there is still work to do." Figures show that women hold approximately 11% of engineering roles in Northern Ireland and make up about 23% of its manufacturing workforce. Juliana Early is a professor at the School of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering at Queen's University. She believes the increase of women studying Engineering centred degrees is a sign that things are changing. She said: "Having worked at Queen's for the past 23 years, I have seen first-hand the sustained commitment to increasing participation of women in the engineering sector. "This growth reflects changing perceptions of the opportunities afforded by engineering and the success of targeted efforts to ensure that talented women see the sector as a place where they can thrive." Rachel Pattison has worked as an engineer in Northern Ireland for 16 years. She believes the key to more gender diversity is getting young women interested in science, technology, engineering and maths (STEM) at an early age. She said: "I was always good at maths and physics at school and had very supportive parents, so I never thought that engineering and manufacturing was something that I wouldn't be able to do." Pattison credits that to being surrounded by encouraging teachers and because of that the idea that it might be a male-centred workforce was not off-putting. In 2024, while maths and physics were among the most popular subjects studied at A-level by boys they were not in the top five most popular subjects taken by girls. According to the Department for the Economy's (DfE) women in STEM taskforce, only one in five STEM jobs are filled by women in Northern Ireland. Rachel Pattison has worked as an engineer in Northern Ireland for 16 years Pattison is now head of operations for Tierco Healthcare, a company that designs specialists seats for hospitals and care facilities. She believes changing perceptions for young women will continue to impact the statistics. "There's no arguing the employment statistics show there's still along way to go in terms of female representation in the industry, but it's about shining a light on those women al

title: Daisy Edgar-Jones: I try and bury my emotion when it comes to love
description: In real life the actress says she is just like the character she's playing in Sense and Sensibility.
body: Daisy Edgar-Jones has been well cast in her new film. She plays Elinor, the rational elder sister in Sense and Sensibility, opposite the younger, more romantic sister Marianne. Speaking to the BBC, Edgar-Jones says that in her personal life, she really is like her character. "When it comes to love, I think I am very much more Elinor in every sort of way," she says. "I definitely lead a lot with my head and try and push aside, bury my emotion." But she notes that one of the joys of the film is seeing Elinor learn to enjoy a "wilder, passionate side" of herself. "And I feel like I learnt to do that too," she says. Best known for starring in hit TV series Normal People with Paul Mescal, Edgar-Jones, 28, is now taking on a lead role in the latest adaptation of Jane Austen's book. Ahead of its release, she’s been talking to me about whether we really need another Sense and Sensibility film (spoiler: yes. “The more the merrier, in my opinion.”) She also told me why young people today can still see themselves in Jane Austen's stories - and gave me her take on whether her friend and former co-star Mescal should be the next James Bond. Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles in a scene from Sense and Sensibility The new film, directed by Georgia Oakley, follows the Dashwood sisters as they navigate their way through love, loss and societal expectations, following the death of their father. It's a classic adaptation of Austen's novel, rather than a more contemporary take. When I meet Edgar-Jones at a hotel in central London, I ask her whether there was ever a temptation to make it more "2026". "It does feel very much like it's honouring the period," she agrees, "but I think there's a freshness to the filmmaking that I think is really beautiful". She is starring alongside Esmé Creed-Miles, 26, who plays her sister Marianne. Together, the two sisters' different approaches to life are characterised as "sense" (Elinor) and "sensibility" (Marianne). Creed-Miles is also well cast, it seems. "I'm more like Marianne [than Elinor], yeah, which is annoying sometimes," she laughs. Daisy Edgar-Jones stars as Elinor in Sense and Sensibility Sense and Sensibility has been adapted for screen countless times before - including the hit 1995 film starring Emma Thompson and Kate Winslet. Edgar-Jones loves that version (“one of my favourite films of all time”) but also feels there's room to tell Austen’s classic tale again. "Her stories are something that fascinate us still today,” she says. It was also easy for her and Creed-Mills to build the sisterly rapport on screen, as they previously worked together as teenagers on the 2018 film Pond Life. “We had a real laugh," Creed-Mills says of their time on that film. "We would have sleepovers every night and watch Love Island." For Edgar-Jones, the theme of sisterhood is something that stuck with her from Sense and Sensibility - despite her being an only child in real life. “I've heard a lot of people say that after watching the film, it either makes them want a sister or to ring up their sister and say like, ‘Hey, I love you,’ and I think that's really special. It's the part of the film I'm most proud of.” Esmé Creed-Miles and Daisy Edgar-Jones play two sisters in Sense & Sensibility Jane Austen seems to be everywhere right now. Last year marked the 250th anniversary of her birth and, in recent years, we've enjoyed two BBC TV series, Miss Austen and The Other Bennet Sister, the West End's Clueless musical (based on the cult 90s teen film adaptation of Emma), and Ava Pickett's modern stage adaptation of Emma. There's also a new adaptation of Pride and Prejudice written by Dolly Alderton and starring Emma Corrin coming to Netflix. For Edgar-Jones, the themes in Austen's books are just as revelant today. "She has an incredible way of articulating the female experience," she says. "Her ruminations on love, on romance, on sisterly love, on family dynamics, on interpersonal social dynamics - she's such a talent." Daisy Edgar-Jones takes a selfie with a fan at the world premiere for Sense and Sensibility in London earlier this week Austen also wrote about the sort of dating behaviour that people complain about on TikTok (like situationships and ghosting), before terms like that had even been invented. Does that help Gen Z audiences relate to her, I ask? "We still have the same human heart as we did 200 years ago. Our capacity to love and feel heartbreak, and that early first love feeling, is something that we all experience in various ways. "And so yes, I think definitely the trials and tribulations of the two women [Elinor and Marianne] as they navigate life, love and all that becomes as you grow up, definitely is so relatable to all generations." "These women are very relatable," agrees Creed-Mills. "I don't know if seeing a movie is going to fix everything, but it might make you feel a little bit less alone in some of the things you're feeling." Daisy Edgar-Jones and Paul Mescal's breakout roles were in Normal People, which came out in 2020 Edgar-Jones shot to fame during the pandemic with her role in Normal People. Based on Sally Rooney's novel, the BBC Three drama charted the on-off relationship of teenagers Marianne and Connell, played by Edgar-Jones and Paul Mescal. The pair have remained close (a few years ago, Edgar-Jones told me Mescal was "one of my all-time best friends") - and both are now successful actors. Edgar-Jones has since starred in Twisters and Where The Crawdads Sing, while Mescal was in Gladiator II, Hamnet and will be in the Beatles films. Recently, Page Six claimed Mescal was on the audition list to be the next James Bond, external. So, is he really in the running? Edgar-Jones didn’t give too much away. “I don’t know, but I think there’s nothing Paul can’t do,” she says. “So I would be there. Wow, that’s cool.” Sense and Sensibility is out

title: Hodgkinson powers to Athlos win in speed suit
description: Keely Hodgkinson powers to victory in a full-body speed suit before being presented with a Tiffany & Co crown as Athlos makes its London debut.
body: This video can not be played 'Speed meeting style' - Hogkinson charges ahead to win Athlos 800m Keely Hodgkinson powered to victory in a custom-made full-body speed suit before being presented with a Tiffany & Co crown as Athlos made its London debut. Hodgkinson was greeted by loud cheers as she emerged on to a stage and revealed the all-black aerodynamic outfit at the third staging of the all-female athletics meet. The 24-year-old ensured she ended a mixed year with a dominant 800m victory in front of a sellout home crowd at StoneX Stadium, bursting clear on the back straight and crossing the line in one minute 56.40 seconds. Speaking about the outfit, Hodgkinson told BBC Sport: "This has been like a year in the making. It's a mixture of fashion and speed and science all coming together for maybe the future of athletics. "It was a real honour for them to choose me to put this out first. We weren't sure when we were going to wear it. "But an all-women's event that's all about the glitz and the glamour and putting eyes on women, a bit of a moment, I think was the perfect way to finish the season." Created by Alexis Ohanian, Reddit co-founder and husband of tennis' 23-time Grand Slam singles champion Serena Williams, Athlos was staging a meet for the first time outside of New York. In addition to the silver Tiffany crown awarded to winners instead of medals, a top prize of $65,000 (£48,500) was on offer in each event. The single-night meet included seven disciplines, each featuring six athletes, with money on offer for each position from a total event prize pot of $1.05m (£790,500). American sprint stars Gabby Thomas and Sha'Carri Richardson were among the champions amid a party atmosphere which featured a live track-side DJ. This video can not be played Hodgkinson shows off her dance moves at Athlos The athletes had arrived on a red carpet in north London but Hodgkinson saved her starring moment for the main event. The eye-catching speed suit, reminiscent of that worn by Cathy Freeman in winning Olympic 400m gold in 2000, featured an open back and a hood with a ponytail opening - the latter, she said, was non-negotiable - while colour-changing 3D-printed nodes reduced drag in key areas. Paired with dark sunglasses and Nike's latest carbon-plated spikes, it helped Hodgkinson achieve her first victory since the London Diamond League in July. It has been a year of record-breaking highs and frustrating setbacks for the Olympic champion. An indoor season in which she landed her first world 800m title and smashed a 24-year world record heightened expectations that she would take down the sport's longest-standing mark outdoors. But a nasty fall suffered on a post-session cool down run in July, and a recurrence of the hamstring injury which kept her out of action for much of 2025 at the European Championships, conspired to hinder her progress. While still improving her British record this summer, Hodgkinson finished second to breakout Swiss star Audrey Werro at both the European Championships and inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship. However, with Swiss athlete Valentina Rosamilia finishing more than two seconds behind, she ended the season with a smile on her face and a crown on her head as she danced on stage with the night's other winners. This video can not be played Dramatic sprint finish - Hunter Bell second in Athlos mile Training partner Georgia Hunter Bell was pipped to victory in the mile by Poland's Klaudia Kazimierska. Diamond League champion Kazimierska, who denied Hunter Bell in her bid to win a fourth major title of 2026 at last week's World Athletics Ultimate Championship, squeezed past on the inside to edge the Briton in four minutes 19.43 seconds. That close finish left Ohanian in disbelief as he watched trackside alongside tennis great Williams and their children, with famous athletes and celebrities also present. Former world champion Richardson stormed to victory in the 100m in 10.80 seconds, as Britons Imani-Lara Lansiquot (11.35) and Daryll Neita (11.36) placed fourth and fifth respectively. Olympic 200m champion Thomas took victory in the final race of the night, winning the 200m in 22.13 seconds, while Dominican Olympic champion Marileidy Paulino overhauled Norway's Henriette Jaeger to win the 400m in 48.73 seconds. There were also wins for Americans Alaysha Johnson in the 100m hurdles and Alyssa Jones in the long jump. This video can not be played What is the athletics event Athlos? Ohanian has been clear about his eventual intention to make Athlos a global season-long league. Athlos was supposed to expand to a two-day event in 2026, but the New York meeting scheduled for 2 October was cancelled following consultation with the athletes at the end of a long season. Instead, Ohanian now hopes to align Athlos within the global athletics calendar from next year. How that will work remains to be seen. The Diamond League, athletics' premier season-long series, runs from May until September, while the introduction of the Ultimate Championship - joining the Olympics and the World Championships on the calendar - means every season will now feature a global competition of some description. American Masai Russell, who broke the 100m hurdles world record last month, was among the late Athlos withdrawals following last week's Ultimate, organised by the sport's governing body and offering record prize pot of $10m. It achieved just that, with some of the world's top female athletes going head-to-head in competitive even

title: US and Denmark reach deal over Greenland after Trump annexation threats
description: Trump said the agreement will give the US "permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland", though specifics haven't been confirmed by Danish officials.
body: The US and Denmark have announced a deal on Greenland's security, resolving a diplomatic dispute sparked by President Donald Trump's threats to seize the territory by force. Trump said the agreement would grant the US "permanent control over security, and all other needs". Denmark's Prime Minister said the deal "strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" but did not address specifics in the agreement that Trump mentioned in a social media post. The deal comes after months of threats by Trump to "take" Greenland over national security concerns, citing its strategic location for defence purposes and its mineral wealth. Trump, in a post on Truth Social, said the deal comes with "no cost to the United States" and will grant the US the ability to "to do what is necessary" to "secure and defend the security of Greenland". He said it includes a rule that no US adversary can maintain a military presence in Greenland or "make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval". Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen confirmed that the agreement will be signed at the United Nations General Assembly next week. She said the agreement "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" while also "at the same time recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination". She added that the deal still needs approval from legislators, and "will have to go through the necessary parliamentary procedures to enter into force". Chairman of the Greenland Government Jens-Frederik Nielsen said in a statement announcing the deal that it "is gratifying that we are about to enter into an agreement that ensures and strengthens the security" of Greenland, Denmark and the US. "The agreement recognises Greenland's interests and our place in international co-operation. It is for the benefit of us all," he said. Trump had tried for months to purchase or annex the mineral-rich Danish territory, arguing that it is vulnerable to adversaries, including Russia and China. He even threatened military action in Greenland, prompting an outcry from Danes and other Nato countries. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called it a "historic deal" and a "huge win for the United States and the American people". "This deal permanently and completely addresses our national security concerns in Greenland," he said in a statement. No text of the agreement has been released. The BBC has reached out to the Danish Embassy and the White House. However, an unnamed US State Department official outlined the deal without providing specifics. Among the agreed provisions is one stating the deal would not expire even if Greenland became an independent country in the future. The official added that under the deal, the US has unilateral power to build additional military structures with no approval needed from Greenland or Denmark. It includes "permanent access, basing and overflights rights," the official said. It also bans non-Nato countries from building bases in Greenland, and "bans adversaries from making investments in Greenland that could threaten the United States". The official added that under the current status quo, adversaries have been allowed to invest in Greenland's "sensitive sectors without investment screening". The official specifically referenced Russia and China, saying it blocks them from deploying troops or making investments in "sensitive sectors". Without the official text being released, it is unclear how exactly the deal differs from a 1951 agreement with Denmark, under which the US can send as many troops as it wants to Greenland. The US already has more than 100 military personnel permanently stationed at its Pituffik base in the north-western tip of the territory. Trump says Greenland is essential for his plan to build a Golden Dome defence system, designed to protect the US against missile attacks from Russia and China, and that European allies could co-operate in this endeavor. The island has vast - and largely untapped - reserves of rare earth minerals, many of which are crucial for technologies including mobile phones and electric vehicles. title: Chelsea miss Joao Pedro... and can't stop conceding goals
description: Chelsea's problem was defending, but with Joao Pedro ruled out through injury, scoring goals has also become an issue.
body: This video can not be played Brentford stay unbeaten as they put three past Chelsea Chelsea's problem was once again defending. But with striker Joao Pedro ruled out through injury, scoring goals also became an issue at Brentford on Friday. The Brazilian striker's absence with a knee injury disrupted new manager Xabi Alonso's previously free-scoring attack, which featured Cole Palmer and club record £117m signing Morgan Rogers. Danny Welbeck replaced the forward, but was unable to make an impact. At Brentford, it was an even contest until Jaidon Anthony gave the hosts a 61st-minute lead - then Chelsea collapsed to a 3-0 defeat. Early on this season, Chelsea were outscoring teams through the individual brilliance of their attack. Not now. And they have conceded 12 goals, more than any other side in the Premier League, albeit having played a game more than every other team. Alonso is only the sixth manager to concede two or more goals in each of his first five Premier League matches in charge. There is one conclusion to draw from that statistic: It is becoming increasingly urgent for Alonso to stop Chelsea from conceding. Some of his team's problems are inherited, but the new manager has not built any kind of tactical coherence in the opening weeks of the campaign. Alonso has experimented with different systems, giving 11 debuts, including two on Friday - one for midfielder Mahdi Nicoll-Jazuli, the first 16-year-old to play for Chelsea in the Premier League, and one for new signing Jordan Henderson, 36, against his former club. Ultimately, it was a tale of Chelsea's attack not firing, and the team then falling apart after Brentford got their noses in front. With the extended international break coming up, they have three weeks to stew on this latest defeat. Superb Brentford beat Chelsea to maintain unbeaten start A weight off Igor Thiago's shoulders - Brentford v Chelsea ratings Chelsea signed a striker from Brighton for the second successive summer, bringing in Welbeck to reunite him with Joao Pedro and provide support in attack. Welbeck, 35, was tidy in possession but, with little service, managed only 17 touches before being substituted in the 71st minute. Unlike Joao Pedro, who is capable of creating chances for himself, Welbeck found it difficult to influence the game in the same way. Joao Pedro came into the weekend with the most goal involvements in the Premier League, having scored three and provided three assists in four appearances this season. His impact extends beyond goals and assists, with the Brazilian linking well with Palmer and Rogers. Against Brentford, however, Rogers arguably produced his quietest performance since arriving from Aston Villa in the summer. Rogers eventually moved up front with fellow striker Emmanuel Emegha sidelined through injury and still waiting to make his Chelsea debut. Before Brentford's opener, it was a closely contested match that appeared likely to be decided by the first goal. Chelsea, however, made victory a certainty for the hosts with a dramatic collapse. Alonso has not managed to cure Chelsea's set-piece weaknesses. They have conceded 23 goals from set-pieces since the start of last season - no Premier League side has let in more. And Anthony's simple header from a corner took this season's total to five. Set-piece defending was an area Chelsea sought to address when they appointed Bernardo Cueva from Brentford two years ago. This summer, he was replaced by another highly regarded specialist in Austin MacPhee. Asked about Chelsea's defending from set-pieces, stand-in captain Levi Colwill told Sky Sports: "Not good enough. At times we have been bullied in the box and we definitely need to improve. "We have full trust in our set-piece coach and are still adjusting to new ideas, but we need to improve as a team." Like many of his predecessors, Alonso has been attempting to instil a stronger competitive edge within his squad and improve the mentality of his players. That issue has often been linked to the relatively young age profile of the squad, but Chelsea fielded their oldest starting XI since May 2023. Henderson, in making his debut on Friday, lined up alongside fellow over-30s Welbeck and goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez. "I would say that we have dropped our consistency and our competitive mentality in the second half. We know that small details can be decisive," Alonso said after Brentford added two late goals. It is also fair to say Alonso is still experimenting with systems and personnel, and has yet to settle on a style of play that gives his side control throughout a match. "It's not about looking for excuses," the Spaniard told Sky Sports. "We need to look at each other and know that we have to work and improve because there is still a long way to go." After the initial excitement - and victories - provided by Alonso's attacking football, Chelsea head into the international break with serious questions to answer. title: Trump signs sweeping Russia sanctions bill
description: The bill is named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, a staunch advocate of aid for Ukraine.
body: US President Donald Trump has signed a sweeping sanctions bill, taking aim at Russia's economy by punishing major purchasers of its oil and gas. The bill, passed by the US House of Representatives earlier this week, gives Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas – most significantly China and India. At Trump's behest, the bill also extends to Iran's energy and weapons sectors. The bill is named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, one of Ukraine's staunchest defenders in Washington before his death on 11 July. The 48-page bill, formally titled the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, includes exceptions for countries that import less than 15% of their natural gas from Russia and are working to lessen their dependency. Additionally, the bill includes sanctions against Russian President Vladimir Putin, senior figures within the Russian government as well as banks and other financial institutions and Russia's "shadow fleet" of tankers used to circumvent existing sanctions. Senator Richard Blumenthal, a New York Democrat, previously described the legislation as "scorching sanctions" which would "throttle Putin's war machine". Data from the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, or CREA, shows that China accounted for 50% of Russian crude exports between December 2022 and August 2026, followed by India at 37%. Turkey and the European Union each accounted for 5% during the same time period, although Russian energy exports to the EU have been decreasing. Senator Graham had long sought to push the Trump administration to do more to punish Russia for the war that followed its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The bill also had the support of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who praised its passage by the House of Representatives earlier this week. "It is symbolic that the US House of Representatives' passage of Lindsey Graham's sanctions bill took place on the night of yet another Russian attack on Ukraine involving ballistic missiles, other missiles, and drones," Zelensky wrote on Telegram on 17 September. Graham, 71, died on 11 July of an "aortic dissection" caused by cardiovascular disease shortly after returning from a trip to Kyiv. "He died doing the work he was born to do," Trump said at the time. Prior to his death, he was widely considered one of Ukraine's fiercest allies on Capitol Hill, at a time when Republicans were bitterly divided over the extent of US involvement abroad and the amount of aid being given to Ukraine.
