title: 'Not an easy inbox' for new Scottish Labour leader
description: Anas Sarwar's replacement will be named later and has big challenges set out already.
body: Michael Marra (left) and Joe Fagan are the last two standing in the Scottish Labour leadership race There's an old joke involving someone asking for directions, and the reply comes: "Well, if I were you, I wouldn't start from here." And that's probably the (unhelpful) advice a lot of people would give the next Scottish Labour leader. It's a job that will go to one of two MSPs this weekend - Michael Marra or Joe Fagan. The victor will inherit a party that had a historically bad result in May's Scottish Parliament election. They will lead a group of just 17 MSPs. That makes them the joint second largest party at Holyrood, tied with Reform UK, but there remains a gulf between Labour and their SNP rivals. Scottish Labour leader Anas Sarwar speaks to the press following his defeat in the Holyrood election in May Anas Sarwar fell well short of his goal to become First Minister of Scotland, and swapped Holyrood for the House of Lords shortly afterwards. It has been revealed during the contest to find Sarwar's successor that the party's membership has slumped to around 11,000. You can see why it's a less-than-ideal starting point. So what are the challenges facing the next leader? And what – if anything – can they do to get the Scottish Labour show back on the road? We asked the pollster Mark Diffley to spell out some of the issues that Marra or Fagan will have to tackle. He didn't mince his words: "The party has become a bit of an irrelevance, and I think that is the biggest hurdle that they face going forward. "The vast majority of people don't really know either of the candidates and, worryingly for them, don't know that the contest is going on". Marra and Fagan have appeared together at events to meet their Labour members but many people were unaware the contest was happening So what does the pollster think the winner needs to do? Diffley spells out three priorities: become relevant, develop a relationship with the prime minister (who he says is currently popular in Scotland) and spell out appealing policies. Some aspects of that will be easier than others. One senior party insider agreed with much of Mark Diffley's analysis, warning "it's not an easy inbox". They told me there's a need to change approach, and Labour might look to learn from a rival party – the Scottish Greens. The Green strategy has been to get their policies taken on by the SNP. You'll often hear the Greens talk about Scottish government decisions and essentially say: 'that was our idea'. And Labour, this insider argues, should be taking the same approach. There could be offers to back SNP budgets in return for more public control of buses or higher wages for care workers, for example. At future elections, Labour could then have tangible "wins" to point at. It would be a change in approach from a party that tended to oppose or abstain on budgets in the last parliament. Andy Burnham has been criticised for his lack of presence in Scotland It's a view shared by another party figure, who called for a constant "SNP bad" approach to be ditched, saying "the electorate rejected that wholesale". They added that Scottish Labour had to be "far more considerate about where we pick our battles", and said that they should approach SNP policies, like cutting the number of health boards, constructively. And that's not the only pressing issue the new leader may have to address. While many think Andy Burnham has had a good start as prime minister, there is concern within Scottish Labour about some aspects of Number 10's approach north of the border. Some told me they believe the prime minister should have made more visits to Scotland. And another said Downing Street had been "a bit all over the shop" when it came to a second independence referendum. And that brings us to an age old area that could prove tricky for the next leader: the constitution. Andy Burnham seemed to set hares running last week in the Commons when he suggested there was a scenario where a second Scottish independence referendum could be on the table. His spokesperson quickly rowed back on the comments, but SNP figures couldn't believe their luck when the door seemed to be opened (even just slightly) to a second vote. It's an issue that the new leader of Scottish Labour will have to engage with. Both candidates have, at times in this contest, seemed to struggle to articulate exactly where Scottish Labour stands on the question of a second referendum. Perhaps one area where the new leader may have a slightly easier time is managing their group of MSPs. It would be a bit of a mean joke to say this is easy when there's not that many of them - but there's an element of truth here for Scottish Labour. This hasn't been a particularly ill-tempered contest, and there aren't vast ideological differences between Joe Fagan and Michael Marra. Scotcast: The Scottish Labour leadership interviews Michael Marra and Joe Fagan are vying to succeed Anas Sarwar as Scottish Labour leader. They talk to David Wallace Lockhart about their party’s failures, the route to indyref2 and guilty pleasures. The loser in the contest is unlikely to make life particularly difficult for the winner. Although it's important to note that this contest hasn't been a bed of roses, with Monica Lennon labelling the party "quite nasty" when she failed to make the final leadership ballot. But the overall state of Scottish Labour, and its pattern of decline at Holyrood, will be the most pressing concern for the winner. The party is in a hole, and getting out of it will fall to either Joe Fagan or Michael Marra. Getting this movement to a more positive destination is possible, but it looks like a gruelling task. Perhaps they wouldn't want to start from here, but they don't get a say in that. Meet the men applying for the 'hardest job in British politics' Lenno

title: When a beloved tree began withering away, locals suspected a killer in their midst
description: A neighbourhood’s fight to save a cherished ginkgo pits them against an unlikely foe.
body: Every summer, Seoul turns a deep green, growing dense and lush under humid skies. But this year, one tree was visibly suffering. "Green leaves were falling to the ground, which shouldn't happen at that time of year," recalls Jung, who lives near the streetside ginkgo in Buam-dong, a largely residential neighbourhood in the north of Seoul. The tree is beloved by locals, who believe it has occupied its spot for more than 100 years. So Jung couldn't ignore what she was seeing. With each passing day, her curiosity turned to concern. A rotting carpet of familiar fan-shaped leaves soon surrounded the tree, a sight so alarming Jung and her neighbours formed a crew of amateur detectives to solve the mystery: what was ailing their hardy ginkgo? The whodunnit engrossed Buam-dong and piqued the country's interest, making national headlines. But the attention unsettled Jung, who spearheaded the campaign but has since requested anonymity - we are using a pseudonym. "Imagine a grandfather who silently embraces you every day, listens to you, and has always been strong and full of life," she says. "Suddenly, he begins to die. "How heartbreaking would that be?" So began one community's fight to save a cherished symbol of their neighbourhood. Their unlikely enemy, who they believe plotted a surreptitious attack, was a museum built to honour a pioneering, nature-loving Korean artist. As summer went by, the ginkgo's branches started to turn bare and brown Tucked between two mountains, Buam-dong is recommended by travellers and locals for its picturesque views, art galleries and cosy cafes - an escape from Seoul's bustle. Because of its proximity to the Blue House, the president's official residence, urban development has been restricted, allowing the neighbourhood to retain its quaint charm. In a place where you usually find ginkgo trees in private gardens or untamed forests, this one is special, Jung says, because it flourished on the side of the road. To her, it's "Grandpa Ginkgo". "I pass this tree whenever I come home. I would say, 'Grandpa, I'm home.' Or 'Grandpa, I'm heading out now'." Jung only moved here four years ago, but the grand old tree was the first thing she noticed, and she grew to love it. "It was the only tree in the neighbourhood that belongs to everyone." To Park Jeon-hee, who has lived here for nearly all his 74 years, the ginkgo is his "oldest friend". It's the same for 10-year-old Kim On, who walks past it everyday on his way to school. It has stood since before he was born, Kim says, and "thinking it might fall down makes me sad". Buam-dong is popular among people looking for an escape from Seoul's busy centre So it wasn't surprising that Jung found ready allies in the community who had also noticed the ginkgo's withering leaves. They soon became suspicious of 10 white plastic funnels peeping out from behind the trunk. Jung had initially assumed they were providing nutrients, but then began to wonder if something more sinister was at play. She and her neighbours sieved through security camera footage from a nearby house, until they found something odd: one morning in late April, the camera had recorded two men wearing white gloves and crouching over the base of the tree with a drill. Were these men installing the funnels? Jung and the others couldn't exactly tell from the footage. But then they remembered something the local council had told them: a museum had previously asked landowners in the area for permission to remove the tree. The Whanki Museum had apparently claimed that its outer brick wall, which sits inches from the ginkgo, was under strain from the tree's roots. The residents soon suspected the funnels contained some kind of herbicide that was slowly killing the tree - a suspicion also shared by arborists who came to examine it. And they believed the Whanki Museum was behind it all. On the very day they saw the footage, a group of Buam-dong residents stormed into the museum, accompanied by four police officers. When confronted, an employee "basically admitted" the museum had done something to the tree, Jung and her neighbour alleged. "Once they had said it, there was really no taking it back," the neighbour told the BBC. The museum has neither publicly confirmed nor denied injecting herbicide into the tree, and has not responded to the BBC's questions. But it did publish a statement in May, saying the wall of its compound was "collapsing because of the ginkgo's roots". It said it had sent letters to more than 40 property owners "requesting a solution". There was no response, the museum said, so its staff "attempted to resolve the situation". It did not explain what they had done. A local council representative told the BBC that an inspection last year found "no meaningful connection" between the ginkgo tree and damage to the museum wall. If there had been an issue, "we would have taken appropriate action and informed the relevant parties," the official added. The residents, who still believe the Whanki Museum had the funnels installed, want them to reveal what was in them, so experts can treat the ginkgo. They have filed a police report against the museum's director. Officials say police are investigating the case, but police declined to share more information when contacted by the BBC. Residents allege that the Whanki Museum has poisoned the ginkgo tree Opened in 1992, the museum is dedicated to the late Kim Whanki, a celebrated painter and abstract artist, known by many as the "Picasso of Korea". On the museum website, architect Woo Kyusung explains he wanted to create a space for Kim's works "that would complement the elements of the nature - the moon, mountains, clouds, rocks and trees - that were so important to his art". In fact, Kim wrote essays under the pen name Su-wha, which translates to "conversation with trees". The irony is not lost on Bua

title: Arsenal open to Dowman loan in right circumstances
description: Arsenal are open to allowing teenage prodigy Max Dowman to leave the club on loan this term if it aids his development.
body: Max Dowman is the youngest player to ever start a game for Arsenal Arsenal are open to allowing teenage prodigy Max Dowman to leave the club on loan this term if it aids his development. Last season, the 16-year-old set two records, as the youngest player to score in Premier League history and for the Gunners. However, while he is yet to feature in the English top flight this term, he marked his first appearance of the season with two goals in Arsenal's 4-2 win at Ipswich in the Carabao Cup on Tuesday. And while his manager Mikel Arteta stressed that he is keen to keep the youngster involved in his senior squad, he said the club will evaluate what is best for Dowman at regular intervals. "We will evaluate every six months where we are and what is the best thing for him to do and then make the right decision," Arteta said. "It depends on a lot of factors. What he needs, and what the team needs as well, the availability we have in the squad, the minutes that he is playing and the qualities of those minutes. "We have to be open, but now the focus is to be here and to impact the team." Dowman, who completed his GCSEs in the summer, will be eligible to make a loan move when he turns 17 on 31 December. The winter transfer window is scheduled to open the following day, with League One side Luton's manager Jack Wilshere, the former Arsenal midfielder, believed to have expressed an interest in taking the youngster on loan. "We haven't really listened to any of the possibilities because we were crystal clear that we wanted to have Max in the squad, that we wanted him to be part of the pre-season and then start to see where we are from there," Arteta added. What are the Premier League rules for academy players? Dowman featured 13 times for Arsenal last term as they ended their 22-year wait to win the Premier League. And with Arteta keen to protect the teenager, he was guarded around whether it may be too early to send Dowman out on loan. "There have been many cases of that age when they have gone out and been successful and others not," Arteta added. "In my particular case, I was 17 when I went to Paris [St-Germain]. It depends on the atmosphere that you find there, and how much the coach believes in you as to whether you go there just to be part of a squad or play minutes. "Which country, it depends. But now he is in a good place, let's keep him here." Starting by defeating Manchester City in the Community Shield, the Gunners have won all seven of their domestic and European fixtures this term. And Dowman will hope that his performance against the Tractor Boys puts him into Arteta's thinking for Saturday's Premier League trip to Brighton. "The best way to knock on the door is to do it on the pitch, not in the office," added Arteta when asked about Dowman's prospects of featuring against the Seagulls. "Then you just leave out the arguments. When a player delivers constantly on the pitch, every single day in training, that's the best way, that's the best signal for the manager. That's the best signal for his team-mates, too. "And what Max did the other day, alongside all the other players as well that haven't played many minutes this season, was really impressive." title: Littler survives scare to progress at World Series Finals
description: World number one Luke Littler survives a first-round scare to overcome Danny Noppert in a thrilling World Series of Darts Finals match in Amsterdam.
body: Luke Littler is the back-to-back world champion World number one Luke Littler survived a first-round scare to overcome Danny Noppert in a thrilling World Series of Darts Finals match in Amsterdam. The 19-year-old, seeking his second World Series Finals victory after 2024, recently whitewashed the Dutchman, who is a former UK Open champion, 6-0 on his way to winning the Czech Darts Open. There would be no repeat here as Noppert won three straight legs to take a 3-1 lead. Having levelled the match at 3-3, Littler turned to the crowd and tapped his ears in response to boos. Despite the teenager then busting his score, Noppert failed to take advantage and retake the lead. With the score 4-4, Littler let out a passionate roar towards the crowd after a wonderful 95 checkout, with Noppert left on 46. The finish brought him within one leg of victory, which he comfortably secured. Littler will now face fellow Englishman Nathan Aspinall, who defeated Raymond Smith 6-4. Wales' Gerwyn Price beat Brody Klinge 6-4 to progress, but was made to work after taking control at 5-0. Klinge avoided a whitewash and then grew in confidence, turning what once looked like a thrashing into a one-leg deficit. However, Price comfortably closed out the match and will now face Jim Long. Motomu Sakai beat England's Callan Rydz 6-5 to progress, while James Wade overcame Damon Heta 6-5. Wales' Jonny Clayton will face Sakai after he beat Maik Kuivenhoven 6-3. Defending champion Michael van Gerwen fell to a 6-5 defeat by Daryl Gurney on Thursday, while world number two Luke Humphries will face Dirk van Duijvenbode after emerging victorious against Wattimena. title: Train passengers could be overcharged by new pay-as-you-go scheme, council warns
description: Flintshire council said Transport for Wales' new system charges all users an adult fare.
body: Pay-as-you-go has expanded to stations in north Wales A council has warned that Transport for Wales' (TfW) pay-as-you-go system could leave some rail passengers paying more - as it charges all users an adult fare. TfW recently launched a social media campaign to promote the payment system's availability to passengers on the 27-mile (44 km) Wrexham-Bidston Borderlands Line. A TikTok advert for the scheme tells viewers it offers passengers TfW's "best value fare". But Flintshire council said there had been no explanation that children, families and pensioners, who all qualified for concessionary fares, would be charged full adult price. TfW said it was "actively reviewing" how to communicate alternative ticketing options to customers. The pay-as-you-go scheme allows customers to use a tap-in and tap-out process using a contactless debit card or smartphone device without needing to buy tickets in advance for adult single journeys. Alasdair Ibbotson, a councillor for Penyffordd, first raised the concern that passengers were being overcharged by the system in July. He told a council meeting that signage around stations did not explain that concessionary travel would not be supported. Ibbotson criticised the messaging that pay-as-you-go offers the "best value fares" as it was possible for some passengers to pay less through concessionary travel. "The tap‑and‑go machines can only charge full‑fare adult tickets," he said. "If you are eligible to travel on a child ticket or at a reduced rate because you have a railcard you will not be charged the correct fare for your journey. "You will be overcharged. So the notion that this is the best value fare is categorically untrue." A screenshot of TfW's latest advert on TikTok, promoting pay-as-you-go on the Wrexham-Bidston line He told the meeting there had been small print on station banners that stated the value claim was compared to equivalent TfW tickets – but the system only measured against a full adult fare. However, he claimed the social adverts gave no indication that tap-and-go fares were not the cheapest for everyone. The council has now warned rail passengers to check whether a cheaper travel option is available to them before using pay-as-you-go. Glyn Banks, cabinet member for waste and transportation, said it was a "convenient option", but it was "important" that passengers understood it was not always the cheapest choice. He said people could save money by buying tickets in advance, using travel passes or railcards, and that pay-as-you-go did not support railcard discounts, child, family or return tickets. "We've asked TfW to make it clearer for passengers when travelling as tap and go calculates the standard adult single fare for your tapped journey," he said. "We hope this issue can be addressed as soon as possible to ensure passengers are not disadvantaged." The council's chief executive Neil Cockerton had also written to TfW asking for new signage to be installed at stations, in order to inform passengers that they may be able to access cheaper tickets through other payment methods. TfW said it was committed to making rail travel "as simple, convenient, and affordable as possible" for customers. A spokesperson said: "While railcard and concessionary discounts are not yet supported via pay as you go, advice on alternative ticketing options is available on our website, at stations and through customer channels. "We are actively reviewing how we communicate this to customers." TfW said it was exploring a pilot to allow eligible railcards to be linked to pay-as-you-go accounts, and hoped to introduce child fares in future, but said further development was needed. The spokesperson said: "Free concessionary travel and family or group offers are not in scope for our pay-as-you-go offering. The latter position is aligned with that of most other pay as you go schemes nationwide. "We remain focused on making rail travel easier, more flexible, and better value." The rail company said further details on improvements to its pay-as-you-go scheme would be announced in due course. title: Trump says he is banning CNN and Politico from White House
description: The US president has had a tense and fiery relationship with the US media throughout his political career.
body: Trump has taken an aggressive approach to the White House press corps since returning to office last year. US President Donald Trump has announced that he is "immediately" banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, the latest twist in his fraught relationship with media outlets. In a post on Truth Social on Friday, Trump said that the outlets "constantly write or report fiction or lies" about his administration, although he provided no examples. Trump later called it a "very simple ban", but did not explain how it would work. It is unclear whether employees of those outlets would be prevented from entering the White House grounds. CNN swiftly slammed the move as an "illegal assault" on American press freedoms. The move by Trump is likely to be met with legal challenges. Reporters from both Politico and CNN were still on the White House grounds shortly after the announcement was made. A crew from CNN was also travelling with Vice-President JD Vance to and from an event in Iowa. In a statement, the network called a potential ban illegal and said it "stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting." "We have a right under the US Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government," the CNN statement said. "Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally-protected right." The BBC has contacted Politico and MS NOW, formerly MSNBC, which have not released statements. In his post Trump said: "Media outlets shouldn't be able to constantly write or report fiction and lies when they're covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration or the United States of America. Other news outlets to follow." The post did not mention specific stories or reporting that led to the move. Asked about the ban in the Oval Office, Trump said that there was "no reason" for the announcement being made on Friday afternoon. "It's really just cumulative stories over the last few years," he said. "You get sick of it." Trump added that there "may be others to join them", but did not name any specific news outlets. He also acknowledged that legal challenges may follow his announcement. "I think it's good to point it out, whether it survives or doesn't," he added. "To be honest with you, I don't think that a court should allow fake news to be written day after day after day." Since returning to office in January 2025, Trump and administration officials have repeatedly clashed with members of the White House press corps. In February, the White House announced that it was taking control of the press pool which has access to Trump and had for more than a century been managed by the White House Correspondent's Association. The same month, the administration moved to bar Associated Press (AP) reporters and photographers from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because of the outlet's usage of the term "Gulf of Mexico" instead of "Gulf of America". The Associated Press swiftly filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing. The president often clashes with reporters in the Oval Office on Air Force One and during White House events, often referring to them as "fake news" and "rude". In his first term, Trump also banned CNN correspondent Jim Acosta from the White House, although they restored his credentials after CNN sued. The announcement was immediately criticised by leading advocacy organisations for freedom of the press. In a statement on Friday afternoon, the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University said that "with so many courts having ruled against him on exactly this point, you'd think President Trump would have learned this lesson by now". "If President Trump means to expel these news organizations from the White House press pool, his action is doubly unconstitutional because the press pool is a 'public forum' under the First Amendment, which means the president can't exclude journalists from it on the basis of their viewpoints," the institute's executive director, Jameel Jaffer, said. A major group that provides legal services to the media - the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press - said it expects Trump's ban to be quickly struck down by the courts because it is "flatly unconstitutional". "The First Amendment is clear that once the White House invites in some journalists, it can't ban others because it doesn't like their reporting," said the group's president Bruce Brown, calling the potential ban "textbook viewpoint discrimination." The Freedom of the Press Foundation also said it was illegal, adding: "It's also hard to imagine a dumber move." Trump "has been retaliating against the press for years, but it hasn't helped him," it said, saying "these outrageous attacks only demonstrate how scared he is of an informed public". Trump has pursued legal action against a number of US and international news outlets, including the Wall Street Journal, the New York Times and the BBC. Some of the lawsuits have resulted in media organisations agreeing to pay multimillion dollar settlements. Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is ongoing. title: A weight off Igor Thiago's shoulders - Brentford v Chelsea ratings
description: Brentford climb to third in the Premier League with a 2-0 victory over Chelsea - here are BBC Sport's player ratings.
body: Igor Thiago scored his first Premier League goal of the season Brentford climbed to third in the Premier League with an impressive 3-0 victory over Chelsea. Goals from Jaidon Anthony, Igor Thiago and substitute Fabio Carvalho secured the three points as Chelsea's winless league run extended to three matches. Here's how I rated the players and you can see how you scored them below. What do BBC Sport's player ratings mean? Caoimhin Kelleher: An accomplished display, although he was never required to make any outstanding saves. 6 Michael Kayode: Played a couple of sloppy passes and rarely ventured forward. 6 Kristoffer Ajer: A sizeable presence at the back despite coming under significant pressure from crosses in open play and from set-pieces. 7 Jannik Schuster: The young defender excelled in his own box but looked nervous in possession on a few occasions, including an overhit backpass that could have led to an own goal. He then set up the winner. 7 Keane Lewis-Potter: A poor clearance led to a Neto chance in the 10th minute, but he was impressive on the counter-attack. That perhaps owed something to his experience of learning the left-back role after previously playing as an attacker. 6 Yehor Yarmoliuk: On his 100th appearance, he threatened with a powerful long-range effort in the 37th minute and created Brentford's best chance shortly after half-time. 7 Vitaly Janelt: Did just enough to halt a Cole Palmer dribble early on, although he risked conceding a penalty. He provided a physical presence in midfield, with a potential Germany debut on the horizon under new manager Jurgen Klopp. 7 Mikkel Damsgaard: The Dane was not at his usual level from set-pieces or with his shooting from distance until he delivered an incredible whipped corner that led to the opening goal. 6 Kevin Schade: The in-form forward produced several pressure-relieving dribbles and had a shot blocked in the first half. Played a part in the final two goals. 7 Igor Thiago: The Brazil international was on a four-game goalless run before kick-off and worked hard but struggled in front of goal. He eventually delivered with a late strike to seal victory and his celebration looked like a weight then lifted off his shoulders, along with his Brentford shirt. 7 Jaidon Anthony: After a quiet first half, he missed his side's best chance early in the second half but responded well to score the opener. 7 Mamadou Sangare (on 72, Yarmoliuk): Did his combative duties well. 7 Aaron Hickey (on 72, Kayode): A steady presence. 6 El Hadji Malick Diouf (on 81, Lewis-Potter): N/A Dango Ouattara (on 81, Anthony): N/A Fabio Carvalho (on 87, Damsgaard): Ghosted in nicely to add a goal late on in a very short spell on the pitch. 7 Subs not used: Ballcombe, Henry, Wilson, Frederick Emiliano Martinez: The Argentine did not face any clear chances or difficult set-pieces in the first half. There was little he could do about Brentford's opener. 6 Wesley Fofana: The Frenchman was a physical presence at the back and dealt well enough with Brentford's long balls but was taken off for Josh Acheampong in the 72nd minute. 6 Maxence Lacroix: He coped well with Igor Thiago for most of the match, winning the majority of his duels, but he gave the ball away for Brentford's second goal and he missed a clear chance in the dying moments. 4 Levi Colwill: A quiet match by his high standards after being left out of the England squad. 6 Pedro Neto: His well-struck effort was saved in the 10th minute. He was lively throughout, linking up well in attack and stretching Brentford with his pace. 6 Jordan Henderson: There were no signs of rust. After receiving some early boos, he settled into the game and looked a vocal leader on the pitch. He also put some good corners into the box. 7 Valentin Barco: On his first Premier League start, the Argentine impressed defensively and was more ambitious with his passing than Henderson. 6 Pep Chavarria: Produced some dangerous crosses and was tidy in possession. A largely positive display despite one piece of naive defending in the first half that led to a free-kick. 7 Cole Palmer: Undoubtedly Chelsea's best player on the night, with much of their attacking play going through him. However, he was unable to produce the decisive moment he craved, with a free-kick comfortably saved and few other clear opportunities. He also worked hard defensively. 7 Danny Welbeck: On his first Premier League start for Chelsea, the 35-year-old created a chance for Neto but did not do enough to compensate for the absence of injured striker Joao Pedro. His 72nd minute withdrawal said a lot. 5 Morgan Rogers: Had a dangerous effort blocked in the penalty area just before half-time. The club-record £117m signing could also have done more to win the header at the back post for Brentford's opener. He ended the match playing up front as a striker. 5 Josh Acheampong (on 72, Fofana): It was unclear why Acheampong came on when he did and, as a young defender, didn't make much impact in these circumstances. 6 Geovany Quenda (on 72, Welbeck): Impressively got on the ball often and tried to make something happen for Chelsea but without any results. 6 Estevao Willian (on 87, Neto): N/A Mahdi Nicoll-Jazuli (on 87, Barco): N/A Subs not used: Penders, Gusto, Hato, Lavia, Gittens Rate players out of 10 for this game. The rater will close 30 minutes after the final whistle. You must be signed in to a BBC account to play. After the opportunity to rate players has closed, the score displayed represents the average from all the submissions by BBC Sport users. title: Nottingham attacks family condemn police promotion
description: Police say the process consisted of an application form, a people panel and external advisors.
body: Rob Griffin was appointed substantively into the role of deputy chief constable, Nottinghamshire Police said The father of a student who was stabbed to death in the Nottingham attacks has criticised a move by Nottinghamshire Police to promote the senior officer who led the investigation. Grace O'Malley-Kumar, Barnaby Webber and Ian Coates were stabbed on 13 June 2023 by Valdo Calocane, leading to a public inquiry. Rob Griffin, of Nottinghamshire Police, was temporary deputy chief constable from 29 April 2025 and was appointed substantively into the role following a selection process in August, the force said. Sanjoy Kumar, Grace's dad, told the BBC on Friday: "I think this is completely wrong." Police say the process consisted of an application form, a people panel and external advisors. Griffin has previously been described by Barnaby's mother Emma Webber as having "blood on his hands", following the force's failure to detain Calocane, who had been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020, after an arrest warrant was issued in September 2022. Barnaby Webber, Grace O'Malley-Kumar and Ian Coates were stabbed to death by Valdo Calocane on 13 June 2023 Kumar told the BBC Griffin had a "long history" with the Nottingham Inquiry, external, adding: "He also initially was going to go with a statement that the Nottinghamshire Police could not do any more to actually prevent the attacks, which we found really offensive when he admitted at the inquiry that a lot more could've been done. "Furthermore, he didn't let us know about the professional standards investigations that were taking place." Kumar said families would have expected people appointed in senior police roles, such as the deputy chief constable, to have "candour and integrity". "We clearly felt that lacking in this case," he added. He said he wanted to ask the secretary of state responsible for policing in the UK and the policing minister "what on earth is going on here?" He added: "This is not someone who is reliable, this is someone who misled victims in a horrific situation. "This is a person who lacked candour and integrity from our point of view. Why was he appointed to this role and made substantive from an active role? "I think this is completely wrong, and the message it gives out to people in the country is that this government does nothing but reward failure." We'll crumble when inquiry ends, says victim's mum Former police chief turns down senior review job What we learned from the Nottingham attacks public inquiry A spokesperson for Nottinghamshire Police said: "Rob Griffin was temporary deputy chief constable of Nottinghamshire Police from 29 April 2025 and was appointed substantively into the role following a selection process on 13 August 2026. "The selection process took place between 6 July 2026, when the position was advertised, and 13 August 2026, when the process was completed. "This process consisted of an application form, a people panel, which involved representatives from our support networks, staff associations, and members from external stakeholders, including Independent Advisory Groups and the Youth Commission, and an executive interview, which included two independent panel members." title: McIlroy in mix heading into weekend at Wentworth
description: Rory McIlroy stays in contention with a five-under 67 to sit four strokes behind second-round leader Ryan Gerard at the BMW PGA Championship at Wentworth.
body: Rory McIlroy is second in the Race to Dubai standings BMW PGA Championship - round two -12 R Gerard (US); -10 A Scott (Aus), F Celli (Ita); -9 M Elvira (Spa), A Rai (Eng) Selected others: -8 R Fox (NZ), R Fisher (Eng), R McIlroy (NI), I Elvira (Spa), JJ Spaun (US); -7 M Wallace (Eng); -6 S Straka (Aut), A Noren (Swe); -5 L Aberg (Swe), V Hovland (Nor); -4 D Law (Sco), R MacIntyre (Sco), S Lowry (Ire), M Fitzpatrick (Eng); -3 J Rose (Eng) Rory McIlroy stayed in contention with a five-under 67 to sit four strokes behind second-round leader Ryan Gerard at the BMW PGA Championship at Wentworth. The Northern Irishman made three birdies in his opening five holes and recovered from dropped shots on the eighth and 16th by picking up four strokes on the back nine, including birdies on the 17th and 18th holes. Reigning Masters champion McIlroy's hopes of winning a record-equalling eighth Race to Dubai title were also buoyed by the withdrawal of Patrick Reed after nine holes. The American, who currently leads the standings on the DP World Tour, had been well placed after the first round but was forced to retire through injury while nine-over par for Friday's round. "Unfortunately he's pulled out this week, which gives me an opportunity to try to claw back some ground that I lost last week in Ireland," said McIlroy, who is at eight under overall. "This weekend is a big weekend for me to pick up a few points and make the race even tighter going into these last few weeks. I'm in a great spot heading into the weekend." Gerard made five birdies and an eagle in a flawless round of 65 to leave him two shots clear of Australia's Adam Scott and Italian Filippo Celli, who are at 10 under. US PGA Championship winner Aaron Rai, who played alongside McIlroy and Open champion Ryan Fox in a marquee group, also enjoyed a birdie-birdie finish as he signed for a 69. The Englishman, who had shared the lead overnight, was at nine under alongside Spain's Manuel Elvira, with McIlroy and Fox among a quintet of players a further shot back. Five-time major champion Brooks Koepka was among the big names to miss the cut at one over. Englishman Tommy Fleetwood will also miss the weekend after a 74 left him at three over, while Spain's Jon Rahm endured another day to forget, following up a six-over-par 78 on Thursday with a 77 to end 138th and last of all those to finish on Friday. title: Is the Kennedy Center losing 'hundreds of millions of dollars'?
description: Records in 2024 show the venue had a surplus of millions of dollars once contributions and grants had been factored in.
body: This video can not be played US President Donald Trump has claimed the Kennedy Center in Washington DC has been losing "tens of millions of dollars, even hundreds of millions of dollars" for years. Trump, who wants his name on the famous performing arts venue, was photographed onboard Air Force One looking at a poster with a headline that appeared to tout the demolition of the site. Federal audit records for 2024 show that, despite having "an operating deficit", it had a surplus of millions of dollars - as Aisha Sembhi explains. Design by Mesut Ersöz and Henry Esterson. title: Driver who killed woman celebrating 60th jailed
description: Donna Brighton was thrown into the road through the open window of a taxi, a court hears.
body: Donna Brighton died after the taxi she was travelling in was involved in a crash A speeding driver has been jailed for two years after he caused the death of a passenger in a taxi when he crashed into the vehicle in Leicester. Thomas Goulty killed grandmother Donna Brighton when she was thrown from the taxi through an open window in Glenfield Road on 16 September 2023. Brother and sister Steve and Andrea Sidsaff, who were also passengers in the back of the taxi, were seriously injured in the collision, Leicester Crown Court heard. On Friday, Goulty, 36, of Aikman Avenue, Leicester, was sentenced after admitting causing Brighton's death and causing serious injuries to the other passengers by careless driving. The court heard Goulty drank two lagers before he drove his silver Vauxhall Astra at 64mph in a residential 30mph limit area before crashing into 69-year-old Sarwar Mohammad's Peugeot Expert Tepee taxi. Mohammad, of Willow Brook Road in Leicester, who had been driving the taxi and admitted the same offences, was handed a six-month prison sentence, suspended for two years, and told he must do 100 hours of unpaid work. Prosecutor Steven Bailey told the court Brighton did not know the Sidsaffs, who had come to Leicester for the Radio 2 in the Park music festival, but they shared a taxi because they were going in the same direction. Brighton, who was from the city, had been out with her friends celebrating her 60th birthday. Bailey said the collision happened as a result of the "combined bad driving of Thomas Goulty and Sarwar Mohammad", while the taxi was making a right turn towards Westfield Road across the central reservation of the dual carriageway. Goulty had been out in the city and sent someone a message minutes before the crash saying he was "just out having a couple of beers", and in a roadside test immediately after the crash tested positive for alcohol in his breath, but later assessments could not conclude that he was over the driving limit. Bailey said Goulty's speed was "excessive", up to 64mph (102km/h) on approach and 55mph at the point of impact. "He had left himself little or no calculation time and any braking was far too late," he said. "He drove too quickly for the road and its conditions, about twice the speed limit, having taken alcohol and in the dark." The sentencing hearing took place at Leicester Crown Court on Friday Bailey told the court it seemed Brighton was helping Mohammad with directions as to where to turn and when to turn when he "allowed himself to become distracted". The court heard he was driving lawfully at 25mph in the 30mph zone before he slowed to 8mph to carry out the right-hand turn, but Bailey said "crucially he did not come to a stop fully" and "did not maximise his chances of avoiding the collision". Brighton "was thrown out of the taxi through the open window into the road", Bailey said, and suffered fatal head and chest injuries, while the other two passengers suffered serious injuries, including several fractured bones. Barristers for both defendants told the court they are remorseful about what happened. Sentencing the defendants, Recorder Jacob Hallam KC said: "You took Donna Brighton's life, and the people who loved her are still paying the price of that today, and you caused the Sidsaffs, as I have said, terrible injuries." Goulty has been disqualified from driving for five years and must take an extended retest, while Mohammad was disqualified for two years but will not need to take an extended retest. title: 'We simply don't know' - JP Morgan struggling to forecast oil prices due to Trump's war with Iran
description: The bank said it "assumed" there would be economic red lines, like oil at $100 a barrel, that the US would be unwilling the cross.
body: Investment banking giant JP Morgan has said it is struggling to predict how oil prices will be impacted by the US-Iran war, telling investors in a rare note that "we simply don't know how to model the endgame". The bank said it assumed at the start of the conflict that there would be "economic red lines" that the Trump administration would be unwilling to cross, and therefore it believed a deal would have been struck to open up the Strait of Hormuz shipping lane back in June. It said such red lines included oil prices rising above $100 a barrel, inflation reaching 4%, gasoline topping $5 a gallon and rates on 10-year government borrowing hitting 5%. "The market is on edge," analysts said. JP Morgan is a huge name in the financial world, so for the investment bank to admit its experts are grappling with working out the economic impact of the US-Iran conflict reflects the tricky nature of trying to predict President Donald Trump's next moves. An oil and gas industry source told the BBC it was "unusual" for such a high-profile investment firm to issue such a note, but added it was a "reflection on the state of play", given the uncertainties around the conflict. Investors often make investment decisions on inflation expectations and the price of oil is a major factor in prices rising across the world, given the commodity's widespread use and humanity's dependence on it. While gasoline remains below $5 and inflation has also not reached 4%, oil prices have surged back above $100 in recent weeks and the interest rate - known as a yield - on government bonds, which are issued in order for the US to borrow money from financial markets, has ticked over 5%. "Six months later [since the war began], many of those lines have been crossed, yet the exit strategy is less clear, not more," said the commodities research team at JP Morgan in note. "For the first time since the start of the Iran conflict, we don't have a baseline view. We simply don't know how to model the endgame." How Trump and the oil markets move in sync: A tango in five charts US borrowing costs hit fresh highs over inflation fears US President Donald Trump said last week he did not think the Iran war would end until after November's midterm elections in the US. "Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward," Trump told reporters last week. "I think it's going to take a little bit longer than the midterm." High oil prices have been behind the rising cost of living in the US and around the world, with fuel and energy prices surging ahead of the colder months. The US central bank, the Federal Reserve, raised interest rates this week for the first time in more than three years and signaled they could be increased further this year and into 2027 in an effort to slow rising prices. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said the move was because "inflation is too high and has been for too long", though Trump disagreed with the decision. In JP Morgan's note, analysts said it estimated the "fair value" for oil in September would be around $90 a barrel, despite it trading above $100. But it said "the market is pricing in the risk" of more disruption to trade. Analysts cited further risks to oil supply in the Middle East, with Yemen's Houthis, which are backed by Iran, seizing an area at the mouth of the waterway in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which is another key international shipping route. The conflict between Russia and Ukraine also continues to have an impact. Analysts said with "no clear signals" of the war de-escalating, the assumption that global oil supply disruption was temporary is "becoming increasingly difficult to sustain". title: Met PC denies charge over pregnant woman's death
description: Mariam Ahmed died after a Met Police car collided with hers at 50mph in Eltham, south-east London.
body: The crash happened in October 2024 A Metropolitan Police officer accused of causing the death of a pregnant woman by dangerous driving has denied the charge. Mariam Ahmed, 38, died after her Volkswagen Polo was involved in a high-speed collision on Eltham Road in Eltham, south-east London, on 17 October 2024. Her unborn child could not be saved. PC Chris Johnson, 56, pleaded not guilty at the Old Bailey to causing her death by dangerous driving. Former PC Danny Tomkins, 35, denied dangerous driving before the crash took place. The court heard that both officers, who were on duty in separate vehicles as part of a "pre-planned deployment", drove at more than 70mph in a 30mph zone and overtook traffic on the wrong side of the road for around 130m. Johnson, who was driving the police vehicle involved in the collision, was allegedly travelling at about 50mph at the point of impact, prosecutor Louise Oakley KC said. Tomkins, whose vehicle was not involved in the collision, overtook Ahmed at 78mph shortly before the crash, prosecutors say. Flowers were laid near the scene after the crash The charges followed an investigation by the Independent Office for Police Conduct after a mandatory referral from the Met Police. Ahmed was travelling in the same direction on the same road as the officers and had indicated to turn off before the collision, prosecutors say. The force has said Johnson is attached to the Met's Taskforce. Tomkins was attached to the same unit at the time of the crash, but has since left the police. The two men have been granted unconditional bail and will next appear at the Old Bailey for a case management hearing on 8 January. A trial date was set for 7 June. title: Watch: Voting under way in Russian election tightly controlled by Kremlin
description: Russia's parliamentary elections are under way, the first since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
body: This video can not be played Russia's parliamentary elections are under way, the first since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ruling party United Russia, which is backed by President Vladimir Putin, is expected to be the biggest party in parliament. Critics say the election is neither free nor fair, with all ten parties on the ballot either backing - or not openly challenging - the policies of Putin and the war in Ukraine. The only anti-war party, Yabloko, was removed the ballot in the run-up to polling day – although some candidates remain in some constituencies. The Kremlin will likely to claim the results show public backing for both the president and the war. Voting takes place from 18 to 20 September, with no surprise wins expected. The BBC's Steve Rosenberg looks at how or the elections will or will not affect the political landscape in Russia. Watch: Voting under way in Russian election tightly controlled by Kremlin. title: North Korean anthem played for South Korea at Asian Games
description: Organisers have apologised for playing the North Korean national anthem for the South Korean men's hockey team at the Asian Games in Japan.
body: This video can not be played North Korean anthem blunder for South Korea at Asian Games Organisers have apologised for playing the North Korean national anthem for the South Korean men's hockey team at the Asian Games in Japan. South Korea, who thrashed Bangladesh 5-0, looked confused as the incorrect national anthem was played. South Korea's Yonhap news agency reported that Bangladesh's national anthem followed before South Korea's actual anthem was played. A stadium announcer did apologise for the mistake. "This is a really serious problem. When we protested, they said, 'We're sorry. It wasn't that it wasn't prepared; there was a mistake on the part of those responsible for playing it'," South Korea coach Min Tae-seok said. "But this is something that simply should never happen." North Korea's national anthem, along with other symbols of the secretive state, are banned in South Korea. The two countries are still technically at war, after the 1950-53 conflict between the two ended without a peace treaty. The build-up to the Asian Games, which officially starts on Saturday, has already seen complaints from teams about the quality and amount of accommodation. A member of the South Korea basketball team posted a video of a leaking pipe and soaked floor in his room, with the caption: "Please help me." Some teams were also stranded at the airport for up to six hours when they landed this week. Field hockey at the Asian Games started on Friday and runs until 3 October. title: Warren Buffett steps down after six decades at Berkshire - 'Father Time always wins'
description: Since taking control in 1965, Buffett grew a struggling textile mill into a global conglomerate.
body: Howard Buffett's main duty as chairman will be guarding the firm's "culture and values." Warren Buffett has stepped down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, handing over leadership to his son Howard in the final chapter of a long-planned transition at the US business giant. At 96, the world-famous investor will move into an advisory role as chairman emeritus and remain on the company board to offer his "judgement and perspective", according to a letter to shareholders, external. The decision comes nine months after Buffett passed the chief executive role to Greg Abel, with his son, Howard, who has been a director since 1993, taking over non-executive board duties. Known as the "Oracle of Omaha," Buffett built one of the most successful investment track records in modern history. He took control of Berkshire Hathaway in 1965 when it was a struggling New England textile mill and turned it into a $1.1 trillion (£822b), global conglomerate. Today, the business owns a wide range of well-known brands including GEICO car insurance, Dairy Queen, and BNSF railway system. It also owns large stakes in companies like Apple and Coca-Cola – a brand close to Buffett's heart, as he famously drinks five cans a day. Buffett has made his mark through "value investing" – a strategy focused on finding companies with solid fundamentals, buying them at fair prices, and holding them for decades. His annual letters to shareholders and festival-like annual meetings turned him into a leading mentor across the financial world. Despite his retirement from the top board post, the change is considered an orderly passing of the baton rather than a sudden shock. "The timing is right to complete the transition," Buffett wrote, noting he had recently celebrated his 96th birthday and the first birthday of one of his great-grandchildren, who is "moving a bit faster" than he is. The company assured investors that day-to-day operations will remain steady. While Greg Abel manages corporate strategy and capital decisions, Howard Buffett's main duty as chairman will be guarding the firm's "culture and values". A former farmer, philanthropist, and sheriff, the younger Buffett brings more than three decades of board experience to the role. Buffett concluded his letter by saying it had been the "privilege of a lifetime" to serve as chairman, but acknowledged that in the end, "Father Time always wins". title: Ryanair boss Michael O'Leary apologises over 'high-fare rapists' remarks
description: O'Leary described his choice of language as "careless" and said "it won't happen again".
body: O'Leary had previously refused to apologise to a rape crisis centre which criticised him for the comments Ryanair chief executive Michael O'Leary has said he is "truly sorry" for describing rival airlines as "high-fare rapists". He had previously refused to apologise to a rape crisis centre which criticised him for the comments. O'Leary had made the remark earlier this month while talking to journalists ahead of Ryanair's yearly meeting with shareholders. Following the comments, the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre (DRCC) wrote to him asking for an apology, in a letter seen by the BBC. O'Leary had originally said that some people were "desperate to get to Ryanair's low fares because they can't afford to fly with the high-fare rapists around Europe". He subsequently defended his choice of words when asked by a reporter from the Press Association whether the language was appropriate. "British Airways, Lufthansa, and everybody else's high fares, I'll happily offend them on a regular basis," he had added. Asked whether it would offend sexual assault victims, he said rape was "a terrible crime". In a video posted on Friday, O'Leary said that, over the last ten days, he had had "conversations with family and friends, both inside and outside Ryanair". "I have come to realise however that the word that I used so carelessly has caused considerable upset and offence to a wide number of people, especially to victims and survivors. "I want to apologise, sincerely and unreservedly, to those people, especially to the survivors." O'Leary described his choice of language as "careless", and said "it won't happen again". "I will try to learn from this mistake, and do better in future." Following O'Leary's first comments, the DRCC's chief executive Rachel Morrogh had written to O'Leary accusing him of trying to get a headline with his comments. She said the DRCC had received calls from rape victims who were "upset and distressed because of what you said". She offered O'Leary training on the impact of sexual violence and urged him to apologise. "I can't imagine you would ever use the term so flippantly again if you truly understood [what] it was like to survive rape," she wrote. In response, O'Leary had said: "I am quite clear that no remarks of mine could possibly trivialise the heinous crime of rape." He added that as he had not "trivialised the heinous crime of rape" he would "not be issuing any apology or accepting your offer of training". It was not the first time O'Leary had offended people while talking about his business. In 2004, he reportedly called the owners of Stansted Airport "a bunch of overcharging rapists", external in a row over airport charges. He has also previously called some of his own staff "lazy bastards" and once said to passengers looking for a refund "we don't want to hear your sob stories". In June, he said the airline would "reluctantly" stop charging parents to sit next to children after a watchdog investigation was opened, but insisted its previous policy complied with laws. title: Men lose appeal for harrassing BBC journalist over A Very British Cult documentary
description: Kristofer Deichler, Jatinder Kamra and Sukhraj Singh were given community service and restraining orders for their harassment of Catrin Nye.
body: From left to right: Kristofer Deichler, Jatinder Kamra, and Sukhraj Singh Three men have lost their appeal for harassing BBC journalist Catrin Nye, who presented the podcast series and documentary, A Very British Cult. Kristofer Deichler, 47, Jatinder Kamra, 46 and Sukhraj Singh, were sentenced for harassment after visiting her home where she lived with her partner and children, first in a group in August 2024, and then again as the three of them in September 2024. "We accept she was terrified by the unexpected attendance" at her home, said Judge Pounder at Snaresbrook Crown Court, adding there was "heightened concern" as her children were also home. All three men are members of Lighthouse, which was investigated for the 2023 documentary and podcast fronted by Nye. Three men sentenced for harassing BBC journalist over A Very British Cult documentary Three men guilty of harassing BBC journalist over A Very British Cult documentary The men were attempting to overturn their convictions from February, when they were each sentenced to 200 hours of community service and given restraining orders banning them from contacting or approaching Nye or her partner for 10 years. They were also banned from entering the London borough where the couple live for a decade. A year after the initial broadcast of the BBC programmes about the organisation, the Lighthouse group began a campaign of peaceful, and legal, protests outside BBC offices in London, against Nye and the BBC. "While there were elements of peaceful protest and freedom of expression, their conduct, as we have already identified, was not proportionate to the proper exercise of those rights and went beyond what was acceptable and indeed became criminal", the judge said. After an interaction with Nye in July 2024, Kamra gave evidence that he was "dissatisfied" and that questions he had for Nye were still not answered. The group decided to visit her home address, which they found using a private investigator and said that they had looked up BBC guidance of doorstepping. "The appellants therefore appreciated that there was a line which their conduct must not cross", said Pounder. "What happened descended into bullying and oppressive conduct", he added, deeming that the behaviour of the three men was not reasonable. During the first visit to Nye's home address on 29 August, the group had distributed leaflets they had printed to Nye's neighbours. The judge said the contents were "not confined to criticism of journalism". "They identified her to those living in the immediate neighbourhood and associated her with serious allegations concerning racism, dishonesty and the concealment of child sexual abuse by family members," he explained. "That is materially different from distributing critical literature outside the headquarters of a public broadcaster." The court heard Kamra later returned to the property to post a handwritten letter saying "we will be back", which "materially reinforced" Nye's concerns, Pounder said. Deichler, Kamra and Singh visited her property again a week later, on 5 September, before they were later arrested. The three men maintained that they were performing citizen journalism and were at her property to obtain a doorstep interview, as part of their own documentary, and that they were acting in the public interest. Judge Pounder accepted that they saw themselves as citizen journalists, but underlined their behaviour was not reasonable, as he pointed to their "deliberate acquisition of a private address, attendance of home, distribution of inflammatory literature, indication return visit and subsequent return". Giving evidence for the second time, from behind a curtain, Nye told the court of her fear when the three accused went to her property. It was "extremely" distressing, Nye said. Their actions had resulted in Nye installing CCTV, panic alarms, direct lines with the police and carrying rape alarms, the court heard. The three men had also claimed that their attendance outside Nye's home was an expression of their religious beliefs. Pounder said there was no doubt that their views were "sincerely held", telling them that it had been concluded that a prayer they said outside her door was "an incidental part of their attendance at the address". The Bible they wanted to give her, Pounder said could have been posted to her via the BBC. On top of their original convictions, the judge has ordered the three men to each pay an additional £1,000. title: Uefa & Concacaf demand Fifa pays $10m to all 211 members
description: Uefa and Concacaf issue a joint statement calling on Fifa to pay $10m from its cash reserves to each of the 211 member associations.
body: Gianni Infantino was first elected as Fifa president in 2016 Uefa and Concacaf have written to Gianni Infantino calling on Fifa to pay at least $10m (£7.5m) from its cash reserves to each of the 211 member associations. It is the latest chapter in the war of words between the governing bodies, in response to Fifa president Gianni Infantino's aborted private equity proposal. Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights of all competitions, including World Cups, with 21% sold off to an investment company. The idea was scrapped after four days following widespread opposition from national associations. The letter, seen by BBC Sport, was signed by Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin and his Concacaf counterpart Victor Montagliani. It outlines that "Fifa is on course to close 2023-26 with reserves of approximately $6bn (£4.5bn)" which is "considerably more than is required" through to the 2030 men's World Cup. It said that Fifa should "make at least $10m available to each of its 211 member associations over the 2027-30 cycle" which should be used "for investment in infrastructure and football development". This "one-off release of reserves" would come at a cost of $2.11bn (£1.57bn), and would be in addition to the regular funding in the cycle. When the controversial plan was revealed in the days following the World Cup final, Infantino told members they would receive $40m (£30m) if they backed it. Infantino set a deadline of 19 September for federations to accept his plans if they want to access an initial $20m (£15m). In the letter, Ceferin and Montagliani said analysis carried out on Fifa's published financial statements and budgets raised doubts that the FFE proposal was "necessary to deliver greater resources". It added that the analysis was "deliberately conservative" and a larger distribution from the reserves should be considered by the Fifa Council once the financial position at year-end is known. An "independent review" of Fifa's finances should be commissioned, it added, with "full access to the underlying figures and assumptions". "Fifa currently holds billions of dollars in accumulated reserves," it read. "These resources belong to football and exist to serve the game and its 211 member associations. "Prudence should not prevent a careful examination of whether a portion could responsibly be released to the extent those reserves exceed Fifa's foreseeable needs. "Releasing part of these reserves would demonstrate that member associations should not have to choose between development and good governance; between investment and integrity; or between financial support and the ability to consider proposals on their merits. "Development is an institutional responsibility of Fifa – not a matter of individual discretion." Another letter, also seen by BBC Sport, has been sent to the presidents of the other confederations - Asia, Africa, South America and Oceania - asking them to support the motion. The news comes a day after Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt sent a letter to Infantino and Fifa secretary general Mattias Grafstrom demanding that all documents relating to the controversial FFE plan were released. Hewitt, a Fifa vice-president, said that the Fifa Council should also receive a written explanation for the cancelled suspension of United States forward Folarin Balogun at the World Cup. Infantino was told he should make all documents available before the next Fifa Council meeting, which is on 15 October. Infantino, 56, will stand for election for a fourth time in March, with his opponents having until 18 November to find an alternative candidate. title: Man admits to killing woman in Londonderry, court hears
description: Ciaran Edward Murray, 30, of Malvern Terrace in Derry is charged with the murder of a 65-year-old Spanish national in 2024.
body: The body of Montserrat Martorell was discovered in a flat in Harvey Street on 24 August 2024 A man has admitted to killing a woman who was found dead in a ground-floor flat after a blaze at the property more than two years ago, a court has heard. Ciaran Edward Murray, 30, of Malvern Terrace in the Waterside area of Londonderry, is charged with the murder of 65-year-old Spanish national Montserrat Martorell. Her body was discovered in a flat in the Harvey Street area of Derry on 24 August 2024. Appearing via video link before Belfast Crown Court on Friday, when the charge of murder was put to him, the 30-year-old replied: "Not guilty, but guilty to manslaughter." Following this, prosecution lawyer told the court that his instructions were to proceed with the murder case. A defence lawyer said a psychologist was due to examine the accused in late October. They added that the defence had been instructed by the accused "at this first opportunity, to apologise to the family of the deceased for his actions". Prosecution counsel Simon Reid KC said that, in light of the defence seeking a report from a clinical psychologist, he would have a clinical psychologist for the prosecution on standby once the defence report was delivered. Mr Justice Fowler said he would list the case for November for an update on progress with the medical report. title: 'I'm telling the truth': Earl Spencer defends Diana book claims about Charles in BBC interview
description: Princess Diana's brother tells the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg that "we'll forget her soon enough" were "exactly" the words used by the then-Prince of Wales.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Earl Spencer says he's 'telling the truth' about what Charles said after Diana died Princess Diana's brother has told the BBC exclusively that he is "telling the truth" about a phone call with King Charles in the days after his sister's death. Earl Spencer claims in a new book the then-Prince of Wales said "we'll forget her soon enough" during an argument over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in Diana's funeral procession. In a strongly worded response, Buckingham Palace said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss". But in his first interview since, Earl Spencer said: "I can tell you here and now, those are exactly the words he said." Earl Spencer spoke to the BBC's Laura Kuennsberg from his Althorp estate in Northamptonshire Reacting to the rare statement from the Palace, Earl Spencer said: "Well, is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?" Speaking to the BBC at his Althorp estate, he added: "I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage of my life. "I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said and I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. I don't hear him saying he didn't say that." Pressed on whether he had evidence to back up the claim, he said he told family and friends at the time what had been said "because it was so monstrous". In response to the Palace disputing his account, Earl Spencer, who shares his first name with the King, said: "They've sort of smudged that one, haven't they? They've said that recollections may vary." When asked which Charles the public was meant to believe, he said: "I'm telling the truth." Buckingham Palace declined to give a response to Earl Spencer's fresh comments. The remarks may bring a renewed focus to the war of words between the Palace and the King's former brother-in-law. Princes William and Harry, then aged 15 and 12, walked behind their mother's coffin alongside Earl Spencer and their father In excerpts of his book published by the Daily Mail, Earl Spencer claims the phone call took place after he insisted Diana would not have wanted the young princes to walk in the procession. In his BBC interview, he says the King "went ballistic" and "ranted for a while", accusing his family of not having an adequate sense of duty. "And then he stopped and I thought, oh now, now he's gonna pull himself together and say something more appropriate," Earl Spencer said. "And then, he said, 'we'll forget her soon enough'." He said he couldn't say exactly what went through his mind at that moment as he was "just so stunned", adding: "I just, after a stunned silence, I said, I cannot believe you just said that. And I hung up on him." Diana is buried at the Spencer family's Althorp estate Earl Spencer's book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, is due to be published next week and is expected to be highly critical of the Royal Family. In further extracts published on Thursday, he claimed how the King "sounded giddily elated" when he called him after Diana's death in a car crash in Paris on 31 August 1997, alleging Charles sounded like a "lottery winner". Earl Spencer recounts being alerted to the crash by a phone call from his sister Jane in the middle of the night at his home in Cape Town, South Africa. A call from Charles was among those that followed, and he alleges: "Unlike my other callers, who were stunned, barely able to articulate their condolences and offers of help, he sounded giddily elated - like a lottery winner, I remember thinking at the time." The death of Diana, a hugely popular figure, created a volatile atmosphere in the country at the time, with the royals accused of failing to show feeling and empathy, and seeming to be out of touch with the public mood. Earl Spencer's emotional and defiant speech at her funeral added to that cloud of grievance hanging over Diana's death at the age of 36. Prince Harry has previously said that walking behind his mother's coffin aged 12 was something no child "should be asked to do". In 2017, he told the BBC he didn't "have an opinion whether that was right or wrong", but "looking back on it", he was glad to have been part of the day. The full interview with Laura Kuenssberg will be on BBC iPlayer on Sunday from 16:00 BST and on BBC One at 18:30 BST. title: Brother didn't match description of 'Putney pusher', suspect's sisters tell BBC
description: Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Nicholas Brandram's sisters accused the Metropolitan Police of being "negligent and reckless".
body: This video can not be played The sisters of the man suspected of being the so-called "Putney pusher" have told the BBC their brother was innocent, and the police showed "no urgency" to clear his name. Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Nicholas Brandram's sisters accused the Metropolitan Police of being "negligent and reckless". Brandram was found dead on Tuesday evening and his family said he "took his own life after months of immense pressure" caused by the investigation. Brandram's sisters Alexia Hicks and Sophie Voelcker told Today presenter Justin Webb their brother's mental health deteriorated after his arrest and questioned why the police were not able to carry out DNA tests that could have proved his innocence. title: Man in court charged with murder over Armadale shooting
description: Billy Watson was pronounced dead after police were called to a property in the West Lothian town on Saturday morning.
body: Billy Watson died in Armadale on Saturday A man has appeared in court charged with murdering another man who was shot dead in West Lothian. Police were called to a property on Harestanes Road in Armadale at about 11:50 on Saturday. Billy Watson, 35, was found injured and died at the scene. Frank McCarthy, 57, appeared at Livingston Sheriff Court on Friday, charged with murder and attempting to defeat the ends of justice. He made no plea and was remanded in custody. A 29-year-old man and 44-year-old man have also been arrested in connection with the incident. Police Scotland said inquiries were ongoing. Police were called to the property on Saturday Detectives previously said they were also investigating whether a nearby car fire in Netherhouses and a fire at a derelict house on Wotherspoon Crescent on Saturday were linked to the incident. Uniformed officers were seen in the Netherhouses area where the car was set ablaze. A cordon was also put in place on Wotherspoon Crescent. The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service said nobody was injured in the fires. title: 'Get in' - woman joins police chase by giving officer a lift in Nissan Micra
description: The suspect reverse-rammed a police car and crashed into parked cars while trying to escape.
body: This video can not be played Police officer given lift by driver in Nissan Micra mid-chase A driver came to the aid of a police officer who was chasing a suspect on foot - telling him to "get in" after stopping her Nissan Micra and offering him a lift. The officer had been pursuing Jacob Roberts, 25, who had reverse-rammed a police car twice and crashed into parked cars and a building while trying to escape. Roberts sped away from officers who had smelled cannabis coming from his van, with the chase seeing him drive in an erratic manner, failing to stop at multiple junctions, mounting pavements and putting pedestrians at risk. The driver helped PC Kerswell catch up to Roberts, who was arrested and later jailed for one year and two months for a number of driving offences. While fleeing from police in his white van, Roberts had driven into a dead-end street in Abercwmboi, Rhondda Cynon Taf, where he ditched the car and tried to escape officers on foot. Police bodycam footage captured the moment the officer then runs to a red Nissan Micra driven by an un-named female driver and tells her: "I need a lift." "Get in," the woman replies. As she gave chase the woman is heard asking the officer to direct her, saying: "Where to?" The officer is seen jumping out of the car after spotting the suspect and takes out his taser and arrests him. During a search officers found two cannabis cigarettes on him. Roberts, from Mountain Ash, was jailed for one year and two months for dangerous driving and disqualified from driving for three years. He was sentenced at Merthyr Tydfil Crown Court on 16 September, where he pleaded guilty to dangerous driving, driving whilst disqualified, driving without insurance, failure to stop after a road accident, criminal damage to property, and possession of controlled Class B drugs. Kerswell said: "Roberts was already banned from driving when he committed these offences - he showed complete disregard for all other road users, including pedestrians. "I hope it acts as a deterrent for others who think of driving dangerously. "It's lucky that no one was seriously injured during this pursuit. We hope this sentence will give Roberts time to reflect on his actions." title: Ex-Brookside star who fled after fraud trial arrested in Spain
description: Philip Foster was already serving a jail sentence for conspiracy to defraud, as of last year.
body: Philip Foster played Christian Wright in the Merseyside TV soap A former TV soap actor has been arrested in Spain after skipping bail before his trial for a £13.6 million fraud that conned would-be models. Philip Foster, 51, who played Christian Wright in the Liverpool soap, is wanted and must serve an eight-and-a-half year jail sentence after being convicted of fraud and money laundering last year. He ran an operation involving sham modelling agencies that exploited the dreams of aspiring young models and their parents for more than eight years. The National Crime Agency (NCA) said that after jumping bail, Foster was convicted and sentenced in his absence at Sheffield Crown Court in February 2025. He was arrested by officers on Thursday in Alicante. Extradition proceedings to return him to the UK are now under way, the NCA said. A National Trading Standards (NTS) investigation found that more than 6,000 victims parted with large sums of money on the false promise of securing paid modelling work in the fraud that Foster ran from his base in Marbella. He used a network of associates in England to run a string of sham agencies and photography studios in cities including London, Manchester, Leeds, Bristol, Coventry and Nottingham which was uncovered after a six-year NTS investigation. The victims were duped into thinking that a model agency was interested in them, with emails telling them they had potential after they responded to a local photographic studio and social media advertising campaign. They were told they had to buy their portfolio photographs from the studio in order to join an agency and become an agency model. Some of them used credit deals arranged by the fraudsters or expensive payday loans to make the upfront payment. In return, the victims got poor quality digital photographs that stood no real chance of landing them professional jobs and most did not get paid modelling work. Foster bought high-end watches and cars with his share of the proceeds while many victims told NTS investigators they had been left financially and emotionally devastated, and felt humiliated and betrayed.
