title: Why an American football game played the Canadian national anthem
description: The field in Buffalo was decked out with the flags of both countries, as tensions simmer and a trade war escalates.
body: This video can not be played Watch: In a border city stadium, American NFL fans sing Canada’s anthem with gusto There are no Canadian teams in the NFL - but there are millions of fans. At the Buffalo Bills game in New York on Thursday night, plenty of Canadians wore the team's trademark red, white and blue while drinking beside their pick-up trucks, which were parked to tailgate - a very American pre-game tradition. The Bills' stadium is only 112 miles (180 km) from Toronto - about a two and a half hour drive for fans - and right across Lake Ontario, which President Donald Trump has sought to rename Lake America. So it was no surprise that many Canadians arrived long before kick-off to soak up the atmosphere and enjoy the sights of the new Highmark Stadium for their team 's home opener against the Detroit Lions. What was unusual was that their national anthem rang out through the stadium. The field was decked out with both the stars and stripes of the US flag and the maple leaf of the Canadian one, and the 1990s Canadian band The Barenaked Ladies belted out Oh Canada! in front of a massive crowd. There was a fireworks display for the team's home opener at their new stadium The Barenaked Ladies belted out Oh Canada! in front of a massive crowd It was an emotional moment for many of the Canadian fans, who said they felt an extremely warm welcome even if their country's mood has recently grown more frosty towards the US. "I've always felt welcome here," said Ben Kerr, from Bradford, Ontario. "I think it's a nice acknowledgement," he added. "I appreciate that the Bills are doing that for Canada." The relationship between the two countries, which began to sour when US President Donald Trump returned to office and made repeated calls to annex Canada, has frayed further with an escalating tit-for-tat tariff showdown. Prime Minister Mark Carney has said Canada, which shares the world's longest undefended border with the US, is "at war" with its southern neighbour over trade. Trump has called Canada "nasty" and "entitled". The Bills' new home, Highmark Stadium, cost $2.2bn to build Both sides are feeling the economic impact, with Canadian industries reeling from tariffs and Canadians boycotting travel and spending in the US. The ongoing tensions made the decision to travel to Buffalo a little more complicated for Kerr. "I try to spend as little money as possible in the US," he told the BBC. "Buy our food in Canada, buy our beer in Canada, bring it across and drink it here. We're not big in supporting the American economy in this trade war." Canadians dream of Europe as Carney floats longshot plan for living and working in EU Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America EU chief backs plan for Canada to become 'associate member' Many Americans at the game expressed their own frustrations with the escalating trade war, and the way it has divided the two neighbours. For Drew Grier, an American who lives eight minutes from the stadium, "the anthem playing tonight is a core part of who we are as a border city". At a Buffalo Sabres playoff ice hockey game in April, a microphone died while the Canadian anthem was being sung and the audience's voices filled in. "You sang the Canadian anthem because it needed to happen," Grier said. Canadian Blake Parnham recalled that moment: "I was sobbing watching the game at home because I felt so vindicated, that Buffalo is different." He couldn't make it to Buffalo for the Bills home opener, but he enjoyed it from his elaborately decorated backyard in Keswick, Ontario. Grier said that singing the Canadian anthem tonight is "not that polarising of a thing". "If anyone is polarising it, it's coming from those outside here, because those of us here, we love Canada," he said. But some thought it was a step too far. "The only acceptable reason to sing that anthem would be if they were playing a Canadian team, but they don't play any Canadian teams," posted one fan on social media. "I don't think it's really necessary," said David Waring, who attended Thursday's game. Blake Parnham's Bills-themed backyard in Keswick, Ontario Many Canadians are boycotting the US, so this is where they're travelling instead In the end, it may all come down to simple economics. The Bills' new home, Highmark Stadium, cost $2.2bn to build. While the population of western New York is a little over 1.5 million, the nearby Toronto and Hamilton greater metro areas is home to more than 8 million. Simply put, the team needs Canadian fans. Gavin Kemp, who has run the NFL-Canada office for eight years, told the BBC that Canada's relationship to the NFL was "extremely important". Asked why the Bills chose this year to play the Canadian anthem, Kemp said the team was "leaning into one of their biggest parts of their market". Canada boasts nearly 15 million NFL fans – about one-third of the country's population, and roughly 10-15% of Bills season ticket holders are Canadian, according to the team. "Sports really transcends all of this," Kemp said. "All this politics is kind of secondary to the fact that your team is doing fantastic right now." Carol Breed, a die-hard Lions fan, took her family to the first home game of the season last weekend Even American fans who traditionally cheer for other teams found themselves siding with the Bills. Carol Breed, who backs the Detroit Lions, considered travelling to Highmark Stadium from her home in Battle Creek, Michigan, after she heard they would play the Canadian national anthem. "I love our country's relationship with Canada," the 74-year-old told the BBC, adding that in Michigan the country is viewed more as a "relative". "I just hate what Trump has done to the partnership." She wasn't able to watch the game in person, but has found other ways to scratch her O'Canada itch. A couple of weeks ago, Breed embarked on t

title: Gabriel, 15, in Barcelona amid speculation over future
description: Man Utd youngster JJ Gabriel travels to Barcelona as some of Europe's biggest clubs continue to vie for his signature.
body: JJ Gabriel has told Manchester United he wants to leave Manchester United youngster JJ Gabriel has travelled to Barcelona as some of Europe's biggest clubs continue to vie for his signature. The 15-year-old has told United he wants to cancel his registration with immediate effect. BBC Sport reported on Thursday that Real Madrid have a firm interest in the forward, and Bayern Munich, Paris St-Germain and Barcelona are also known to be keen. It is understood Gabriel left the UK on Thursday and went to France, but is now in Barcelona. If United hold on to the Londoner's registration, it would stop him moving to another English club until the end of the season. But if he obtains an European Union passport through either his father - a former Republic of Ireland international - or mother, who has Greek-Cypriot heritage, he could join a club in he EU when he turns 16 on 6 October. What next for Gabriel and Man Utd? Gabriel has not trained at United since scoring a hat-trick on his Uefa Youth League debut on 10 September. Tournament rules prevent him from playing for a side other than United in this season's competition. Sources close to Gabriel were furious the club did not register him for their Champions League opener with Sabah FK, which Michael Carrick's side won 4-0. Carrick was again asked about Gabriel on Friday at his news conference to preview Sunday's Premier League match against Fulham. "He's a young boy, JJ, and I think it's important we don't play anything out here," he said. "With the exposure and scrutiny and everything, you got to be careful and be sensible and think of him as much as anything. "The situation will work itself out, whatever way it's going to work itself out. Making sure he's OK is the important thing." Gabriel scored in his first two Premier League 2 outings for United this season but will not be involved against Brentford at Leigh Sports Village on Friday. title: Harry Potter and the goblet of no booze
description: The proposal to allow alcohol and music at the event sparks concerns among people living nearby.
body: The real-world, non-alcoholic version of Butterbeer is a popular drink at Harry Potter-themed events Organisers of a Harry Potter-themed event have failed to conjure up a licence to sell booze after the plan was turned down amid residents' complaints - and a politician's swipe that "normal men" would not drink the fare on offer. Forestry England wanted people to have mulled wine and Irish cream hot chocolate as they made their way around an illuminations trail at Cannock Chase Forest in Staffordshire, set to run from October. The bid was turned down by Cannock Chase District Council which received more than 75 objections, plus the jibe - during a licensing hearing - from a Reform UK councillor. The applicant had told the hearing that it would ensure there was no adverse impact for neighbours. Permission was also sought to play music along parts of the designated route lined with illuminated features depicting scenes from the Harry Potter franchise. But as the suitability was thrashed out by the council's licensing sub committee and ultimately rejected, member John Parkes questioned the sort of drinks that would be sold, claiming "normal men" would not partake of such beverages. The branded, non-alcoholic drink Butterbeer was unaffected by the ruling. Parkes described Butterbeer as "horrendous". The event is set to run between 1 October and 3 January Jon Payne from Forestry England told members at Wednesday's meeting: "It's very much a family-orientated event. "The amount of alcohol consumption is very small, served from limited outlets in the forest, and not available throughout the site." One resident who objected to the application said people should not be encouraged to "drive to an event, have a drink and then drive home", claiming it could put children in danger. "We don't need Harry Potter, it's already a magical place," she added of the event's location. "We're not trying to be killjoys but the woods can be challenging at night – it's dark and it's dense. "Add alcohol and the risks multiply. Must we tell our children that every event we do should be soaked in alcohol?" The licensing application proposed to sell alcohol and play music between 15:30 and 22:30 while the event was taking place. Another resident raised concerns about those timings, describing the evening as a period when people expected "to enjoy peace and quiet". "Residents are concerned about lights shining into bedrooms and repeated vehicle noise," he added. "They have experienced problems at previous events including noise, parking problems, and anti-social behaviour." Emily Sewell, from event producers Culture Creative Limited, said background music would be used in "limited areas" of the site. She added that, in the company's experience, one in five visitors drank alcohol at these events. The committee's chair Maureen Freeman, Labour, said the panel was "not minded to grant the licence as requested". This news was gathered by the Local Democracy Reporting Service which covers councils and other public service organisations. title: No Norrie as GB bid for Davis Cup Finals spot
description: Cameron Norrie will miss Great Britain's Davis Cup tie with Ecuador this weekend, with qualification for November's eight-team finals on the line.
body: Great Britain have not reached the Davis Cup Finals for the past three years Cameron Norrie will miss Great Britain's Davis Cup tie with Ecuador this weekend, with qualification for November's eight-team finals on the line. British number two Norrie felt pain in his arm during a practice session and will be replaced in Saturday's singles by world number 95 Toby Samuel. "He wasn't able to accelerate on the ball like he wanted to," Davis Cup captain Leon Smith told BBC Sport. "It's nothing major, but there's still a lot of tennis to be played this year and with that in mind, we had to make the difficult decision to replace him." Great Britain have not reached the knockout stage of the competition since 2023, and they will have to do so this time with an inexperienced team. Jack Draper has ended his difficult season early, while Jan Choinski and Jacob Fearnley are both unavailable with injury. It means Samuel will make his Davis Cup debut against Andres Andrade in Saturday's first match, with British number one Arthur Fery following against Alvaro Guillen Meza. Both of Ecuador's singles players are outside the world's top 200, but Fery's only previous appearance for his country was in Poland last September. Asked if he was concerned about the lack of experience, Smith said: "I'm not sure it concerns me, but it is obviously a factor. "Neal [Skupski] is in the team, Cam is staying with the team. I've had 16 years at this so I can hopefully help a little bit. "But you want them to experience this. You have to start somewhere and I have a lot of confidence in Arthur, Toby and our doubles team. "If they can put out the level of tennis we've seen over the course of the summer and before that, they'll give themselves a good opportunity." British number seven Harry Wendelken, who is at a career-high world ranking of 175, was at the Copper Box as a practice partner and has been added to the team in Norrie's absence. World number one Henry Patten will team up with new US Open champion Neal Skupski for Sunday's doubles, which precedes two reverse singles. Davis Cup: Great Britain v Ecuador Coverage from 13:00 BST on 19 September and 12:00 BST on 20 September In July, Fery played on Wimbledon's Centre Court in a men's singles semi-final, but this will be the first time he has played for his country as the British number one. He lost in the first round of the US Open in August but reached the Winston-Salem final in the build-up to the final Grand Slam of the season. "I'm aware of the role I have as the number one player and I am representing my country, so there's always a little more responsibility," Fery told BBC Sport. "But at the same time I've been able to deal with high-pressure situations a lot of times this year and I feel like I've done a great job with them. Tomorrow isn't going to be any different to that. "I think there's no shying away from it - if I want to do great things in tennis and push on, be top 20 or top 10, I have to take this responsibility on. "I'm ready to do that and represent my country. It's something new but something that I feel comes with the player I'm becoming." Great Britain beat Norway 4-0 in the first qualifying round in February and are trying to reach the quarter-finals for the first time since 2023. Ecuador may be the underdogs, but they were in the same role when they beat Australia comprehensively in February. And they have won, famously, on British soil before. Ecuador beat a British team that contained Tim Henman and Greg Rusedski 3-2 on Wimbledon's Court One in July 2000. The seven winners of this weekend's qualifying ties will join three-time defending champions Italy in the final eight stage in Bologna from 24 to 29 November. "We've missed not being at that stage and it's up to us now to take that opportunity," Smith added. "We have a good opportunity. It's never ever straightforward, despite what people might look at in the rankings - just ask Australia what happened in February. "We're on it, we've got a good team, and we'd be thrilled to get to the finals." title: Tenko and Doc Martin actress Stephanie Cole dies aged 84
description: She was best known for playing the character Dr Beatrice Mason in the 1980s BBC wartime TV drama
body: The actress Stephanie Cole, known for roles in Tenko, Open All Hours and Doc Martin, has died aged 84. A statement from her agent John Grant, issued on behalf of her family, confirmed the actress had been living with Alzheimer's for several years. "Stephanie was an extraordinary talent whose long and distinguished career included many iconic performances in theatre and television," the statement read. "She brought joy to millions through her many much-loved roles in sitcom and drama. She will also be remembered for her tireless work supporting mental health charities." Cole's credits included a role opposite Suranne Jones in Gentleman Jack Cole appeared opposite David Jason once again in the 2010s reboot Still Open All Hours Solihul-born Cole, who trained at Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, enjoyed a lengthy career that spanned TV, radio and film. She was perhaps best known for playing the character Dr Beatrice Mason in the 1980s BBC wartime TV drama Tenko. The series chronicled the lives of British women in Singapore after the Japanese invasion and their consequent confinement in a Japanese prisoner of war camp. Cole, in her breakout role, played a doctor who struggled to look after the health of the women, opposite Ann Bell and Claire Oberman. During this same period, Cole also played the moody Mrs Delphine Featherstone, aka "The Black Widow", opposite Ronnie Barker in Open All Hours. She would go on to win the award for best TV comedy actress for her part as the sharp-tongued photojournalist Diana Trent in Waiting For God. But she cited her earlier performance as Muriel in Alan Bennett's monologue Soldiering On, alongside Maggie Smith and Julie Walters, as one of her proudest moments. Her stage highlight, by her account, was in a West End production of A Passionate Woman. Cole also played Roy Cropper's mother in ITV soap Coronation Street for two years from 2011 Cole (pictured alongside co-star Ann Bell) was perhaps best known for the 1970s series Tenko Cole also played the aunt of Martin Clunes's titular character in the ITV medical drama Doc Martin. Her other notable roles included Keeping Mum, Waiting for God and Cabin Pressure. She also appeared in Coronation Street as Roy Cropper's mother Sylvia Goodwin, which won her another comedy prize, in her 70s, at the 2012 British Sopa Awards. Cole reprised her earlier role opposite David Jason in the 2010s reboot Still Open All Hours, and also appeared alongside Suranne Jones in Gentleman Jack. The actress's stage work in Driving Miss Daisy and King Lear at Bristol Old Vic. Her last major TV role was appearing opposite Greg Davis in his BBC comedy series The Cleaner in 2021. title: Russian hybrid attacks against Europe intensifying, says Macron
description: The French president says he has tasked the government with protecting critical infrastructure and defence industry sites.
body: French President Emmanuel Macron has warned that the threat of hybrid attacks by Russia against Europe and France has intensified. In a news conference at the Elysee Palace, Macron said he had ordered a plan to protect critical infrastructure and defence industry sites in the face of this threat. He said France had been targeted by Russian hybrid attacks in the past few weeks which would not be left "without a response". A growing number of European leaders have warned that Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine. War may be coming. Are we psychologically ready? Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyberattacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary. These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary. The French president was speaking to journalists after meeting party leaders to discuss the security impact of the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine. Macron mentioned last month's drone attack on Leipzig airport in Germany, blamed on Russia, and remarks by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk suggesting Russia was planning drone and missile strikes against Poland and other countries on Nato's eastern flank. "In recent weeks, the Russian hybrid threat against Europeans and against France has intensified," he said. "The intent is to intimidate us and break our effort to support Ukraine. The result will be the exact opposite. We are not intimidated because we know that our security today and tomorrow is at stake in Ukraine." On Thursday Tusk told Polish MPs that Russian plans included strikes by drones and missiles on countries supporting Ukraine. He said there was a "real risk" of such strikes on the territory of Nato countries, with Moscow then claiming that they were "accidental", in an attempt to split the alliance. Last Sunday, a Russian drone hit a passenger train near the Ukraine-Poland border shortly after former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson and top European security officials had passed through along the same line. Ukraine said all the passengers had been evacuated just minutes before the strike at Yahodyn, which hit the train's engine. Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly said Russia does not plan to attack Europe, but Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov warned European nations against sending troops to Ukraine, which would be seen by Russia as a declaration of war. "If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war, and it will be very short," he said. This video can not be played Macron also addressed the energy situation, saying that the government had been tasked with protecting critical infrastructure and the "most sensitive" defence industry and technology sites against drone and cyberattacks. He also announced that France would call a meeting of the G7 to discuss energy and raise the question of gas stocks with the European Commission. "In the coming weeks, we will have a G7 meeting devoted to these energy issues, both to strengthen cooperation and to avoid unnecessary tensions between the G7 countries and our main partners," Macron said. "It will also be an opportunity to consider options for a possible release or unlocking of strategic reserves." German airport drone-bomb: Could Russia be involved? Hand of Moscow? title: Flight chaos caused by software defect in space of a millisecond, report says
description: The failure led to more than 2,000 flights being cancelled and hundreds of thousands of passengers affected.
body: Thousands of passengers were delayed by the NATS outage An air traffic control failure that sparked widespread travel chaos earlier this month was caused by a "software defect" affecting the system underpinning UK air space management, the national air traffic service Nats has said. The problem happened "in the space of a millisecond", Nats said, leading to the system producing corrupted data. The failure led to more than 2,000 flights being cancelled and hundreds of thousands of passengers affected, with some sleeping on airport floors or getting stuck overseas. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander called the disruption "completely unacceptable", while industry body Airlines UK is writing to Nats to demand immediate compensation for costs incurred. The incident prompted questions over the resilience of Nats' systems, and some airlines questioned the position of its chief executive Martin Rolfe. There has also been anger from passengers about how much support they got from airlines, and about the fact that they are unlikely to be entitled to compensation because the regulator judges the situation was extraordinary circumstances. In an initial report, external, Nats said the software defect meant air traffic controllers had reduced information available, so restrictions were put in place to limit air traffic to maintain safety. The defect occurred at 10:00am on 8 September, but it did not become apparent this was a serious problem for another two and a half hours. The system restart did not start until just after 3:15pm, and restrictions on UK airspace were not lifted until 7:30pm. Flights in and out of the UK's main airports were affected, including Heathrow, Gatwick, Luton and Glasgow. The disruption took days to completely resolve because of the number of planes and crew left out of place. Martin Rolfe apologised to those affected by the disruption. "It's our job to get people where they want to go, quickly and without delay and we are devastated when that goes wrong," he said. "However, our primary role is to keep our skies safe, and everyone who flies through them. At no point last week was safety in question." Reacting to the Nats report, the transport secretary described the disruption as "completely unacceptable" and "frustrating" for passengers, airlines and airports. "It's clear we need to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos," Alexander said, adding that a Civil Aviation Authority review was underway. This is the third national air traffic incident in the past three years. In 2023, a computer shutdown over the August bank holiday weekend caused chaos for 700,000 passengers. There was another, smaller Nats outage in 2025, which caused 150 cancellations. Tim Alderslade, chief executive of Airlines UK, said: "Once again, it is passengers who have suffered and airlines who have picked up the pieces - and the tab - of an ATC [Air Traffic Control] system failure, while Nats itself faces no real consequences." He added that passengers deserved "commitment and proof that the system is being fixed". Alderslade also said Airlines UK was writing to NATS "to demand immediate compensation for the costs incurred and a credible plan to improve resilience." Addie Kitson was hit with almost £100 in unexpected costs when her flight back from China was diverted to Stockholm Addie Kitson, 26, had been on holiday in China when her flight home was diverted to Sweden. "I thought I landed fine" she told the BBC, "but then they went: 'Welcome to Stockholm' and I went: 'Ooh, that's not London'". After being told about the issues affecting UK airspace, passengers were kept on the plane for a few hours, and then spent 19 hours inside Stockholm airport. Addie ended up with nearly £100 in unexpected costs after having to buy refreshments, adaptors and to pay for Wi-Fi to work. "I got one £11 food voucher that didn't even cover the cost of a sandwich in Stockholm airport", Addie said. Addie questioned the rules around compensation, saying there had been multiple air traffic outages. "It doesn't seem that extraordinary," she said. Were you affected by this air traffic control failure? title: Teenager jailed for life over ambush murder
description: Sulaiman Tajzai travelled from Leeds to London, where he stabbed his victim with a kitchen knife.
body: Sulaiman Tajzai admitted murder and possessing a knife A teenager who travelled more than 150 miles from Leeds to London to stab a man has been jailed for at least 25 years for his murder. Sulaiman Tajzai, 18, ambushed shop worker Farmanullah Sherzad outside the 26-year-old's home in Westminster on 27 March, stabbing him at least 10 times. Sentencing him at the Old Bailey to a life term, Judge Angela Rafferty KC said he had held a grudge against Sherzad "based on a false suggestion of misconduct" and had been "effectively stalking him down like prey". Describing the attack as "exceptionally violent", she told Tajzai: "It is not said on your behalf, nor could it be, that you had any justifiable or excusable grievance against this man." The court heard that Tajzai, an Afghan asylum seeker, wrongly believed Sherzad belonged to the Taliban, which had kidnapped his father and was suspected of killing him. The court was also told Sherzad had been arrested in Leeds in October over an allegation involving a woman known to Tajzai. He told officers he had been invited to the address and was in a relationship with her, and police later said no further action would be taken. In January, Tajzai travelled to London and carried out reconnaissance near Sherzad's Abbey Orchard Street home and his workplace, the court heard. On 27 March he armed himself with a kitchen knife and took a train south, arriving at King's Cross station in a face mask, distinctive jacket and dark gloves. CCTV tracked him across the capital to Abbey Orchard Street, where he waited for Sherzad to cycle home from work at about 22:00 GMT. Farmanullah Sherzad's family said they were "deeply shocked and angered" by the circumstances of his death Prosecutor Lisa Wilding KC said Tajzai had given his age as 14 when he arrived in the UK in August 2022 and claimed asylum the following year. In mitigation for her client, who admitted murder and possessing a knife, Frida Hussain KC said he had post-traumatic stress disorder after exposure to violence in his village and the deaths of relatives. Sherzad's family described him as "kind, gentle and free-spirited", a keen cricketer who often worked six or seven days a week. In a statement, they said they were "deeply shocked and angered by the circumstances surrounding his death". title: Will England boss Tuchel 'embrace the chaos'?
description: After the World Cup, England boss Thomas Tuchel wanted greater control. Two months on, he is keen to "embrace the chaos" after naming his squad for the upcoming Nations League fixtures.
body: This video can not be played Tuchel recalls Palmer and Alexander-Arnold to England squad England manager Thomas Tuchel left the United States in July pining for greater control. At his first squad announcement since the World Cup on Friday, the German spoke of "embracing the chaos". Is it possible to have controlled chaos? It seems Tuchel is ready to find out. England's third-placed finish in the US was the nation's best performance at the World Cup since 1966. But the memories of the team's semi-final loss to Argentina linger. In the aftermath of the heartbreaking defeat, Tuchel pointed to his team's inability to find control having taken the lead via Anthony Gordon's opener as a key factor behind his side's late collapse. Fast-forward two months, however, and the messaging is rather different ahead of the four upcoming Nations League games. "Football is about adapting to situations and football without any control is sometimes hard to digest for a coach, if you look at the 6-4 against France [in the World Cup bronze-medal match]," said Tuchel. "But people talk about it like it's one of their nicest experiences ever, to watch a football match, so maybe I have to compromise in my wish for control, for a little bit more chaos, embrace the chaos, and maybe it brings out the best." Tuchel recalls Alexander-Arnold and Palmer with warning Mixed signals? Or maybe it is just a sign that Tuchel wants his side to become more unpredictable in their search for success. Because that is what the best teams do - mix it up when required. Despite Tuchel's remarks, his latest squad for the fixtures against Spain, the Czech Republic and Croatia rather contradicts any thoughts of a havoc-rich approach. The return of Trent Alexander-Arnold and Cole Palmer, two of English football's most technically gifted players, screams control. So do the call-ups of Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott and Newcastle left-back Lewis Hall, who are both extremely adept in possession of the ball. Of course, there is certainly a balance to be struck. That would be Tuchel's ideal scenario. Rio Ngumoha's first senior call-up will certainly add an air of unpredictability to Tuchel's options. The Liverpool winger, 18, has had an exciting start to the season, catching the eye with his invention and trickery down both flanks for Andoni Iraola's side. That Tuchel revealed Fulham attacker Josh King is also close to earning his first senior call-up provides further indication the England manager wants to reinvigorate his forward line ahead of the forthcoming Nations League campaign and beyond. Yet, we shouldn't expect Tuchel to completely let go of the handbrake just yet. In response to a question as to whether his team can replicate the fast-paced approach of a Premier League team but harnessed with a greater control, Tuchel responded: "That would be the wish, that we become for 10 minutes a little bit more like Spain, here and there. "The more I reflect on it, it's maybe more buying into our strengths and play more minutes like we played the second half against Croatia, and more minutes like we played the first half against France, and buying into these strengths, because I think we get a lot of value out of it, we get a lot of connection to the fans, this is what the Premier League reflects. "We are maybe not the most economical team to play football but this is maybe also a characteristic of the Premier League. The Premier League is not a very economical league, you have to play. "You need to max out every single match otherwise you cannot compete for the title so this is something more beautiful. But this is where we are, where I am in my mindset and I think where the players are, so it's still a bit ambiguous." But while Tuchel may not have total clarity with regards to whether control or chaos is the way forward, he showed no hint of confusion over who he believes his best players are. Tuchel refuted assertions his decision to recall Palmer and Alexander-Arnold was an admission he'd got his World Cup squad wrong. Indeed, Tuchel has hinted he would have picked a vastly similar squad for the upcoming games to the one he selected for the US had all his options been available. "Before we did the nomination in the last month, I thought we had more of a continuation of the World Cup squad but then a lot of members of our World Cup squad - Reece [James], Dan [Burn], Dean [Henderson, [John] Stones, [Jordan] Henderson, Djed Spence - can't be with us due to injuries, so it is not like a full continuation. "These players were crucial for us in building the brotherhood, in building the spirit and taking care of the mentality that took us the long way in the tournament. We will not negotiate on that, we will not give in on that. "So other players will step up, this is basically how I see this camp. "My mindset at the moment is not to change too much within the formations." England host World Cup winners Spain at Wembley on Saturday, 26 September then travel to the Czech Republic (Tuesday, 29 September) and Croatia (Saturday, 3 October) before the Czechs visit on Tuesday, 6 October. title: Woman detained indefinitely for stabbing two boys
description: The victims were found with non life-threatening injuries after police raided a flat in Friskney.
body: Officers found two boys with stab injuries when they raided a flat in Friskney A woman who stabbed two 10-year-old boys has been detained indefinitely in a psychiatric hospital. Armed police found the injured boys after forcing their way into a flat in Friskney in November 2022 following a stand-off lasting several hours. Ann Marie McEvoy, 45, of Church Walk, Colchester, was tasered and arrested. In July, she pleaded guilty to two counts of attempted murder. On Friday, she was sentenced to a hospital order under the Mental Health Act at Lincoln Crown Court. The boys were treated in hospital for non life-threatening injuries. McEvoy was seen holding a large knife prior to her arrest, the court heard. Dr Tim Rogers, a consultant forensic psychiatrist, told the latest hearing the offences would not have happened had McEvoy been mentally well. McEvoy suffered from schizoaffective disorder, the expert said, adding it was clear she needed treatment, potentially for the remainder of her life. Judge Simon Hirst said he was satisfied the best way to protect the public was to impose a hospital order. Doctors and the Secretary of State will decide if and when she can be released. Addressing McEvoy, Hirst said: "Your need for treatment is likely to be significantly longer than a prison sentence. "It is necessary to protect the public and it is not possible to say for how long that will be." McEvoy was previously deemed unfit to stand trial and was made the subject of a hospital order in September 2024 after a jury found she was responsible for stabbing the boys. The Crown Prosecution Service chose to resume criminal proceedings against McEvoy in March this year after her condition improved in hospital. She was deemed fit enough to enter her pleas. Mark Knowles, defending, said McEvoy had entered guilty pleas because she not want to subject the boys to the ordeal of a trial. Impact statements from both boys were read out in court. One of them described how he suffered a punctured lung and was rushed to hospital for surgery on his neck. The other boy said he had only just started feeling better. Hirst also made a restraining order which prevents McEvoy contacting the children. Listen to highlights from Lincolnshire on BBC Sounds, watch the latest episode of Look North. title: 'Not a catastrophe' - Carrick dismisses Man Utd job fears
description: Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick says there is no point wasting any time worrying if his job is under threat.
body: Michael Carrick has won 14 out of 23 games since taking charge at Manchester United in January 2026 Manchester United boss Michael Carrick says it would be "ridiculous" to start thinking how long he has left in the job after "two or three" bad results. His side visit Fulham on Sunday after an awful week. After United lost at home to a Manchester City side reduced to 10 men after 23 minutes, Brighton became the first side to come from two goals down to win at Old Trafford in 50 years in their Carabao Cup tie. United supporters responded to the midweek setback with boos and by chanting against their team. Carrick said in the aftermath he was "not bothered" by the pressure - a sentiment he reinforced as he spoke to the media before the Fulham trip. "I know the club, I know the role, I know what's expected here in terms of playing to a certain standard and achieving certain things on the pitch," he added. "In terms of future and ownership and how long I've got in the job, that's totally not in my thinking. It's ridiculous to think that way in the position I'm in, that's just not on the radar. "It's two or three games. It's two or three games too many because I really hate losing, but that doesn't mean the world caves in. In some minds it does, it can't for us." There has been no sense from senior figures inside United that Carrick's position is under threat. They are more focused on the perceived under performance of so many players given the 12 games out of 17 that were won under the 45-year-old over the second half of last season. By contrast, they have two victories from six games so far, against newly promoted Ipswich - when they had to come from behind - and Azerbaijan champions Sabah FK in the Champions League. "It's not a catastrophe or a disaster," said Carrick. "It's not the end of the world." Yet it is the measure of the noise around a club of United's size that is often feels that way. Carrick accepted issues at Old Trafford are frequently amplified, so they look to be bigger than they actually are. Despite this, he loves his job - and the club he served with such distinction as a player, and began his coaching career. "There's great feelings, and there's obviously disappointments, and sometimes the smaller disappointments lead to being a little bit bigger," he added. "It's just part of coping and being at this great football club. "I wouldn't want to be anywhere else, genuinely. "It's the best place for me to be, in part because of the times when it's maybe not going to plan. Sometimes they are best times to work your way through, to find out a few things and come out an awful lot stronger." Externally, the inquests have tended to focus around recruitment - or lack of it, specifically at left-back - United's finances and debt levels, Carrick's relative inexperience and, other than assistant boss Steve Holland, that of his coaches. "It's not a blame game," said Carrick, who revealed Luke Shaw and new signing Carlos Baleba "have a chance" of being fit for the Craven Cottage meeting. "We all search for things to look at and point at, or whatever reason it may be and find a blame. Blame me. No problem. I will take the responsibility. "But it's not about blaming people. It's about us, it's about us finding solutions and being better. That's as a whole football club." title: Teen who piloted Channel boat with 165 migrants jailed
description: Chan Mathok Atak has been sentenced to two years and three months in prison after piloting the boat.
body: The dinghy carried 165 migrants across the English Channel on 23 July A teenager who piloted a dinghy carrying a then-record 165 migrants across the English Channel to the UK has been sentenced to two years and three months in prison. Chan Mathok Atak, 19, from South Sudan, admitted endangering others during a sea crossing on 23 July. Prosecutors at Canterbury Crown Court said Atak created a risk of death or serious personal injury to others on board the boat. At the time, the so-called "mega dinghy" set a record for the largest number of migrants brought over on a small boat in recent years. That figure has since been surpassed with 230 people on board a vessel in August. At Canterbury Crown Court on Friday, Judge Sarah Counsell said the offence was so serious "only an immediate custodial sentence can be justified". She warned Atak that as a foreign national he was liable in principle to automatic deportation once he completed his sentence. James Harrison, prosecuting, told the court the boat Atak was piloting was 12.8ft (3.9m) wide and 46.9ft (14.3m) long, a similar length to a standard bus. The boat had travelled between Calais and the UK and was deflating when it was picked up by border force vessels. Chan Mathok Atak admitted endangering others during a sea crossing The dinghy, which had 31 children on board with the youngest aged 14, had two outboard engines but one was not working, the court heard. The National Crime Agency (NCA) said the boat was "severely overcrowded", had limited food, drinking water, and medication, and had been at sea for almost 24 hours. The quality of the lifejackets on board was also "completely inadequate" and the fire risk was "considerable" due to how close batteries were to fuel cans, the NCA added. Harrison said just before the boat was intercepted, Atak moved away from the engine into another part of the vessel and took off his jacket. This video can not be played Atak was seen piloting the boat during 90 minutes of aerial footage He said this was an attempt to not to be identified as the helmsman. However, Atak was seen during 90 minutes of aerial footage to be piloting the vessel using its one remaining functioning engine while wearing a black jacket with an "Italia" logo on it, the court heard. Footage also showed one person "constantly pumping" to try to re-inflate the rigid-hulled inflatable boat. Harrison said: "There's no evidence to suggest that the defendant had any training or experience of conducting this type of navigation. "The size of the vessel and the number of people on board presented an obvious danger. The vessel would have been unstable because of it deflating." Harrison said the risks of the crossing "would have been apparent to Atak". In an interview, Atak said he paid €200 euros (£172) to a gang for the crossing but denied he was the helmsman. NCA senior investigating officer John Turner said: "Atak was unimaginably reckless and his actions could have easily resulted in many deaths had this boat not been intercepted. "Not only did he place the lives of 165 migrants in severe peril, this flimsy vessel was entirely unsuitable for crossing one of the world's busiest shipping lanes." Endangerment at sea was made a new offence this year to target those alleged to have steered small boats over the Channel. Anna Turley, Minister for Border Security and Asylum, described Atak as an "evil criminal". "He joins 16 other pilots sentenced in just three months for endangering lives with flimsy, overcrowded dinghies," she said. "This is a stark reminder of the ruthless acts used by smuggling gangs to exploit desperate people for profit, but today shows there is nowhere for them to hide." The court heard Atak moved away from the engine and took off his jacket to avoid being identified as the helmsman Defending him, barrister Audrey Mogan said there was "not a single shred of evidence" to suggest Atak had "anything to do with the number of people on the vessel, the state of the dinghy, or the fact that there were no life jackets or that the jackets were inadequate, or the lack of safety equipment or flares". "The idea that he had anything to do with the state of the boat and its overcrowding just flies in the face of reason," she added. Mogan described Atak as someone who had "escaped the horrors of South Sudan", where he saw people being shot and having their throats cut, and militia setting fire to a neighbourhood. title: Live forever: Unheard Oasis recordings to be sold
description: The hidden tapes have been in the possession of a former sound engineer's family for 20 years.
body: The recordings were made by a former front-of-house sound engineer in the 1990s Oasis fans are set for a Wonderwall experience when they get the chance to bid for unheard recordings of the Supersonic boys at their peak. The archive includes recordings of 63 live shows, soundchecks and more than 100 hours of rehearsals from the band's rise and rise in the 1990s. The lots, which also include original setlists, tour itineraries, a band-played Epiphone guitar and an Oasis tour parka, will be offered for sale on 3 October in Evesham, Worcestershire. The collection, known as The Desk Tapes, has been in the possession of Owain Richards for 20 years, after his dad, a former front-of-house sound engineer joined the band's crew during their heyday. "Dad labelled everything, recorded everything and backed it all up to cassette, over and over," he said. "I grew up listening to these recordings. Oasis were part of the family as much as they were part of the culture." The previously unheard Oasis recordings will go on sale next month Littleton Auctions is handling sale and say the tapes, recorded directly from the sound desk, form the only master archive of their kind. Also among the items due to go under the hammer is a pair of Adidas Kegler Super Ostrich trainers gifted to Noel Gallagher. Only 100 pairs were produced in 2000 to mark the 100th anniversary of Adidas founder Adi Dassler. The unheard archive includes recordings of 63 live shows Ben Homer, managing director of Littleton Auctions, described it as "one of the most exciting collections" the auction house had brought to market. The sale will take place online and in person with bidders, who are required to register in advance and pay a deposit, hoping they won't be looking back in anger on the day. title: Football club apologises for United 93 shirt advert
description: Oxford United apologises for the image, which features the call sign of one of the planes used in the 9/11 attacks.
body: Oxford United's new clothing range has been withdrawn from sale A football club has apologised after it published images of a new clothing line with "United 93" printed on the back - the call sign of one of the aircraft hijacked on 9/11. The clothing was supposed to make reference to Oxford United's founding year of 1893. However, it said it had been released "without understanding of the historical context and associations". United Airlines Flight 93 crashed in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, killing all 44 people on board after being hijacked on 11 September 2001. A docudrama film titled United 93 was made about the tragedy and released in 2006. Oxford United was founded in 1893 as an amateur club called Headington and now plays in League One - the third tier of the English football pyramid. In a statement, the club said its Campus Clothing range had been withdrawn and it "sincerely apologised" for the error. "It should not have reached the point of sale and we take full responsibility for not undertaking proper due diligence," it said. "We have removed the collection with immediate effect and are reviewing our approval processes to ensure nothing like this happens again." The 9/11 attacks saw 19 Al Qaeda members hijack four commercial passenger planes in the US. Two of them were flown into the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center in New York City, resulting in them both collapsing. Another plane struck the Pentagon, near Washington DC, while the fourth plane - United 93 - crashed in rural Pennsylvania. It was believed to be destined for the US Capitol Building, also in Washington DC. The attacks killed 2,977 people and injured tens of thousands more. title: New sighting of missing Lillia, 13
description: Lillia went missing from Bolton last week and has not been seen by her family since.
body: This video can not be played Sighting of missing Bolton girl Lillia, last seen in a McDonalds in Piccadilly in Manchester. Police have received fresh CCTV of a girl who has been missing from home for a week. Lillia, 13, from Bolton, was last seen by her family last Friday, but was seen later that evening in Manchester's Picadilly bus station, and at the Trafford Centre the following day. Officers who have been handing out hundreds of leaflets to try to locate Lillia have now released new footage of her at a McDonald's restaurant in Piccadilly from Sunday at about 20:20 BST. Greater Manchester Police Ch Spt Int Helen Critchley said: "Officers are making every effort to locate Lillia, and our team have been working through hours of CCTV footage and exploring every avenue to try and find her." At a press conference on Thursday, Critchley issued an appeal on behalf of Lillia's mother Jessica, saying: "Lillia, if you see this appeal, please know your family love you, miss you and just want to know that you are safe. "You are not in any trouble, they simply want you to come home." Lillia's mother Jessica sat beside police as her statement was read out Lillia was seen boarding a 247 bus from the Trafford Centre on Saturday, heading in the direction of Altrincham, but it was not known where she got off. Critchley said the McDonalds sighting was the last confirmed sighting of her, adding: "Our investigation currently covers the whole of Greater Manchester with officers across the force being asked to support our enquiries. "We are also mindful that Lillia could have travelled outside of the Manchester area and are keeping an open mind regarding this possibility." Police describe Lillia as about 5ft 5in tall with light brown hair and glasses The force wants to hear from anyone who may have relevant CCTV or doorbell footage, or who has had any contact with Lillia since she was reported missing. The teenager is described as slim, about 5ft 5in (1.67m) with light brown hair and glasses, and was last seen wearing a black zip-up hooded top, light blue baggy jeans, and a black Nike backpack. Lillia was reported missing from Bolton on Friday 11 September. Critchley added: "If you have any information that could help us find Lillia, I would urge you to come forward. Her family just want her home. Please report any information, no matter how small." title: Resident Evil: The video game adaptation with a lot to prove
description: The video game adaptation is a hit with critics, but director Zach Cregger says the fan response surprised him.
body: Zach Cregger's Resident Evil follows Bryan - a courier having a very, very bad day at work One of the hottest horror directors on the planet adapting the world's most popular scary video game series? On paper Zach Cregger and Resident Evil are the perfect unholy alliance. The film-maker was widely praised for his original, imaginative work on horror hits Weapons and Barbarian and is a long-time fan of the video game series. But in the lead-up to the film’s release, Cregger’s spent a lot of time defending himself against complaints he’s cashing in on the Resident Evil name. Speaking to BBC Newsbeat, the director says he was "not prepared" for what came his way. The original Resident Evil game was a smash-hit when it came out in 1996 First launched in 1996 on the original Sony PlayStation by Japanese developer Capcom, Resident Evil was a sensation. Rather than casting players as super-powered characters, as was the case with most video games in the 90s, it forced them to survive with limited resources. Thanks to smart reinventions and remakes, the series has managed to stay relevant, selling a total of 213 million copies since its debut. Some of its characters are among the most well-known in video games, and there are whole communities dedicated to discussing the lore of their universe. Cregger's Resident Evil follows the story of Bryan, an original character played by Austin Abrams who worked with the director on Weapons. He's a courier who agrees to deliver a package to a hospital in Raccoon City - a key location from the games. As Bryan makes his way to the drop-off, it becomes apparent he is caught in the middle of some sort of viral outbreak, with the infected becoming monstrous creatures. When the first trailer appeared online, many users swamped comment sections to complain about what they'd seen. Where were the beloved characters? The familiar monsters? Cregger says he had little interest in simply retelling the story of the Resident Evil games, but that didn't seem to calm some fans. "I think I was naive," he says. "I think I was expecting people to be excited to see a Resident Evil movie that felt in the spirit of the games. "What I was trying to do is make a movie that really honoured the experience of playing them." Zach Cregger impressed horror fans with his previous films, Weapons and Barbarian According to most reviews, Cregger has achieved what he set out to do. In its three-star review, NME , externalasked whether it was "the first great horror movie game adaptation". "For a large chunk of the film's runtime, the answer is a resounding yes," wrote reviewer Jordan Bassett, who said Bryan's encounters become repetitive as the film wears on. Doug Jamieson, of The Jam Report, external, awarded four stars and said Cregger "understands adaptation as translation rather than imitation". In an eight out of 10 review, Looper, external critic Alastair Ryder wrote: "Zach Cregger has done the best job I've seen of translating the experience of playing a video game and making it feel cinematic." The verdict from fans remains to be seen, but Resident Evil looks to be on track to have a successful opening weekend at the box office. It follows recent video game adaptations such as the Minecraft and Super Mario Bros films, which were poorly reviewed but hugely popular. Zach Cregger and Austin Abrams reunited after working together on Weapons This isn't the first adaptation of Resident Evil, which was brought to cinema screens in 2002 - the first of six films overseen by writer-director Paul WS Anderson. His wife, Milla Jovovich, starred in each one, and while they have grown a cult following they were never a hit with critics. A 2021 "reboot" heavily based on the games and a 2022 Netflix series also failed to impress. The live-action rights to Resident Evil are owned by German production company Constantin Film - a fact fans have blamed for the perceived low quality of previous adaptations. Reports online suggest the company's agreement with Capcom prevents Constantin from setting its films in the same timeline as the games. Cregger told Newsbeat he'd had no contact with the game developer while working on the film. "Nobody from Capcom ever reached out to me, ever, in any way," he said. Constantin Film declined to comment, but BBC Newsbeat has been told there was co-ordination between the developer and the film's producers behind the scenes. Cregger says it's "probably" impossible to please everyone, but it was never his intention to recreate the game on-screen. "If I had delivered a faithful retelling of one of the stories in the games, I feel like those people would probably be upset with me for that too," he says. "Because I would have messed it up somehow, inevitably. "So all I can do is just tell the story that I think is going to be the very best story. "If somebody's going to have a problem that it doesn't do exactly what they had in their mind of what a Resident Evil movie is, I can't say anything to that." title: British Steel plan lacks credibility, MPs say
description: A committee report says the government has not set out how British Steel will become profitable.
body: British Steel was taken into public ownership in July after years of uncertainty over its future The government has no credible plan for the future of British Steel, MPs have claimed. A report by the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) said the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (DBIST) had not set out how British Steel, which runs its main plant in Scunthorpe and has operations in Teeside, would become profitable. MPs warned steel tariffs could drive firms out of business or to move abroad. A spokesperson for DBIST said it welcomed the report and would review the recommendations, adding securing the long-term future of the UK steel sector "was in the national interest". A 26-page report, external, published on Friday, said the government was unable to provide clear estimates of how much the overall nationalisation could cost. It had projected costs to reach £642m by 30 June this year, but the government later said it had only been £555m. In April last year, the government passed an emergency bill to take control of British Steel amid reports the then-owner Jingye was planning to switch off two blast furnaces in Scunthorpe. The Steel Industry (Nationalisation) Bill became law in July, taking the company into public ownership. The government then published its steel strategy in March this year, which included an ambition for 50% of steel used in the UK to be made in Britain. The strategy confirmed electric arc furnaces as the future of British steelmaking, replacing traditional blast furnaces, which resulted in job losses at steelworks including Port Talbot. It also highlighted concerns that British Steel's 4,052 workers face uncertainty and the steel strategy is still vague about when the 50% target would be achieved. The report said: "Without a credible long-term plan, uncertainty and costs for workers, industry and taxpayers will continue to increase." The report also shared concerns the new tariff regime, made in a bid to boost British Steel production and usage, could cause smaller businesses to go bust. From July, Britain lowered the tariff-free quota level for steel importers by 51% in order to stop the UK becoming a "global dumping ground". It also doubled import taxes on steel coming into the UK above certain levels from 25% to 50%. However, firms said that some steels that they need would be affected by the tariffs, but are not able to be bought from the UK. The PAC said: "This risks steel manufacturers having to pay tariffs on types of steel that they cannot avoid importing. "There is a risk that businesses reliant on these products will face higher costs, which could result in smaller firms going out of business or companies moving production overseas." The PAC said the government needed to set up a "formal route" for steel companies to raise concerns about the new tariff regime. The DBIST spokesperson said: "Taxpayer value for money remains a central consideration in our assessment of the future of the site and we are also backing the communities that rely on it through our steel strategy to build a sustainable, competitive and decarbonised steel sector for the years ahead." title: Ronaldo named in Jesus' first Portugal squad
description: Cristiano Ronaldo is named in the first squad selected by new Portugal coach Jorge Jesus for their upcoming Nations League games.
body: Ronaldo has scored 146 goals in 233 appearances for Portugal Cristiano Ronaldo has been named in the first squad selected by new Portugal coach Jorge Jesus, ending speculation the 41-year-old could retire from international football. Ronaldo refused to confirm whether he would continue to play for his country after Portugal's World Cup round-of-16 defeat by eventual winners Spain in July. But the Al-Nassr forward is part of a 25-man group chosen for Portugal's four Nations League games between 24 September and 4 October. Jesus has replaced Roberto Martinez, who stepped down as Portugal coach after their World Cup exit. The 72-year-old was Ronaldo's club boss last season, when the pair helped Al-Nassr win the Saudi Pro League for the first time in seven years. The former Manchester United Real Madrid forward, who announced that this summer's World Cup would be his last, was in tears after Portugal's World Cup exit. When asked if he would keep playing for his country, he said: "I will meet the family and take decisions with a calm head." This sparked speculation he could follow his great rival Lionel Messi and retire from international football. Ronaldo will turn 42 before next summer's Nations League finals and will be 43 by Euro 2028. The oldest player in the history of the Euros is Ronaldo's former Portugal team-mate Pepe, who was 41 and 130 days for his last game at Euro 2024. Manchester United pair Diogo Dalot and Bruno Fernandes are also in the squad, along with Ruben Dias (Manchester City) and Pedro Neto (Chelsea). Portugal are at home to Wales on 24 September (19:45 BST) and away to Norway three days later. They then play in Denmark on 1 October and return home to host Norway on 4 October. title: Economy minister accuses SoS of 'mischief making' in social media exchange
description: Dr Caoimhe Archibald posted on X about a new one-off electricity bill reduction, which Sir Chris Bryant reposted saying the UK government funded it.
body: Dr Caoimhe Archibald posted on X about a new one-off electricity bill reduction which Sir Chris Bryant reposted, saying the UK government funded it Economy Minister Dr Caoimhe Archibald has questioned whether the secretary of state is "mischief making" after a social media exchange around energy payments. The Sinn Féin MLA posted on X, external about a new one-off electricity bill reduction announced on Thursday, which Sir Chris Bryant, reposted, external saying: "I'm really glad that the UK government is funding this." Archibald said she was "bemused and surprised" at his "intervention on social media". A UK government spokesperson said the funding for the Household Electricity Discount Scheme was provided through the prime minister's "commitment to remove VAT and some levies from electricity bills". "As I have set out, the British government initially didn't intend that this support would apply here, we had to make the case for that, we then had to design a scheme," Archibald told BBC Radio Ulster's Talkback programme. She described what Sir Chris said as "a little bit condescending". "Frankly I'm not sure what the secretary of state was up to, mischief making? I don't know. But I think that question would be better posed to him." The minister said she has not been in touch with the secretary of state personally since the online exchange, but said she will continue to focus on finding a way forward in budget negotiations. Households across Northern Ireland will get the one-off £63 reduction in electricity bills from next month and it will be applied automatically without the need for an application. The schemes are being funded by the UK government. Bank payment customers will have their bills automatically reduced while pay-as-you-go customers will receive £63 in credit when they top up their meter. The only complication for pay-as-you-go customers is they should not buy more than £112 of credit if they want to get the discount all in one go. That is because meters are set up to take a maximum payment of £175. Top ups over this value means the £63 payment will be split over a subsequent top up. In announcing the scheme, Archibald said the money would "provide some help for families as winter kicks in and energy bills rise". She said the money would "provide some help for families as winter kicks in and energy bills rise". Her department agreed the NI scheme with the government and will deliver it to consumers. A UK government spokesperson added that the scheme will "provide families in Northern Ireland with some breathing room on bills this winter". Archibald said the money would "provide some help for families as winter kicks in and energy bills rise" Speaking to Talkback on Friday, Archibald said: "People here rightly would expect that if support is being put in place for people in respect of their bills in Britain that it absolutely should be put in place for people here also. "We have made the case, we have delivered the scheme. "It is tax payers from here that are contributing to that and I think if there are going to be interventions in cost of living support then it has to apply here. "Ultimately the British government are the ones with the levers with the ability to make the interventions that we really need to see in terms of cost of living. "Ultimately I'm not sure the tone of the engagement from the secretary of state was particularly helpful," Archibald said. title: Tuchel recalls Alexander-Arnold and Palmer with warning
description: England boss Thomas Tuchel recalls Trent Alexander-Arnold and Cole Palmer but says players have to "perform".
body: This video can not be played Tuchel recalls Palmer and Alexander-Arnold to England squad England head coach Thomas Tuchel says "the door is always open" after recalling Trent Alexander-Arnold and Cole Palmer to his first squad since the World Cup - but has warned players they have to "perform". Tuchel controversially left Real Madrid right-back Alexander-Arnold and Chelsea forward Palmer out of his squad for the summer tournament in North America. Both return for four Nations League games during an extended international break after this weekend's club fixtures. Alexander-Arnold, 27, won the most recent of his 34 England caps when he came on as a substitute in a 1-0 win against Andorra in June 2025. He has made five appearances, including three starts, for Real Madrid so far this season, registering one assist. Palmer, 24, last played for England in a 1-0 friendly defeat by Japan in March. He has scored four goals and provided two assists in six games this season. "They had a good start to the season," said Tuchel, who has again omitted Manchester City's Phil Foden. "They never did something wrong. We just chose different players. "So now it is a new competition. Some players, some positions, have more injuries. Some have less injuries. Cole has his starts that he always had but he has his numbers back - he has his assists back, he has decisive goals back - so that is why he is in the squad. "I think he has a point to prove, and the same goes for Trent. He was never off the list. He was never non-selectable for us, and it is his chance to show, come to camp and be the best version of himself." Alexander-Arnold played in midfield in Real's Champions League win over Inter Milan earlier this month, but Tuchel said he had picked the former Liverpool player as a full-back. "He had a good start in two positions for Real Madrid and he comes as a right-back for us," he said. On his trust in Alexander Arnold, Tuchel said: "[He needs to] perform, that's just what it is. It is a competition and I understand the question because he was not with us at the World Cup. We trusted other players. "I still stick with this decision and it is now time to fight for his place. He always said he is up for a fight, he always said he is up to fight for his place - especially for England - so it is on him to prove and he is more than welcome in camp. "We have a long camp and I am sure he will show up." Tuchel said the onus was now on players to impress in the international set-up. "It is one thing to be nominated, like with Cole, and getting your ticket back in the squad but it's another thing to perform for England," he said. "Cole needs to step up when he comes and he needs to show these kind of numbers to get his place, keep his shirt and justify the nomination." England host World Cup winners Spain at Wembley on Saturday, 26 September, then travel to Czech Republic (Tuesday, 29 September) and Croatia (Saturday, 3 October) before the Czechs visit on Tuesday, 6 October. Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott and Liverpool winger Rio Ngumoha, who were both in the Three Lions' pre-World Cup squad, both feature again. Dominic Calvert-Lewin, whose three top-flight goals so far this season have helped Leeds United go third in the Premier League, is also included. Tuchel has also picked Newcastle United left-back Lewis Hall, Everton centre-back Jarrad Branthwaite, Arsenal's Myles Lewis-Skelly, who can play at left-back or in midfield, and Brighton keeper Jason Steele. Dean Henderson, Jordan Henderson, Reece James, Djed Spence and John Stones, who were all in the World Cup squad, miss out, with Tuchel saying they were not selected because of injuries. Along with Foden, other notable absentees are Nottingham Forest's Morgan Gibbs-White, Crystal Palace's Adam Wharton and Manchester United's Harry Maguire. The Three Lions took a 1-0 lead but conceded two late goals, with former England captain Wayne Rooney saying the team "crumbled" and became "too passive", which he said started from "the manager and the decisions he made". Though England missed out on their first men's World Cup final in 60 years, they beat France 6-4 in an thrilling bronze-medal match to finish third. "The more I reflect on it, it's maybe more buying into our strengths and playing more minutes like we played in the second half against Croatia and the first half against France," said Tuchel. "Buying into these strengths because we get a lot of value out of it. We get a lot of connection to the fans. This is what the Premier League reflects. "Football is about adapting to situations, and football without any control is sometimes hard to digest for a coach if you look at the 6-4 against France - but people talk about it like it's one of their most nicest experiences ever. title: Michael Sheen's 'constructive' meeting with first minister over toxic dumping claims
description: Michael Sheen said his meeting with the first minister was "early days but that's really encouraging".
body: Michael Sheen said his meeting with the first minister was "early days but that's really encouraging" Hollywood actor Michael Sheen said he had a "constructive" meeting with First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth over toxic dumping claims raised in his BBC documentary. Buried with Michael Sheen explores toxic chemical dumping in 14 sites in Wales and England. Sheen initially said an offer to meet the first minister "was not taken up" before the documentary was broadcast in August. On Thursday, the Welsh actor said he met the first minister, speaking about how they could move forward adding it was "early days but that's really encouraging". Speaking on Instagram, external, he said "I've just come from a meeting with the first minister. "Talking about how we can move forward and address all the issues that Buried [the documentary] raised around the toxic dumping, and that was really constructive. "So early days but that's really encouraging." In the UK Parliament last week, Sheen urged MPs to back a national testing programme for historic toxic dumps to make sure sites were safe, after high levels of cancer-causing chemicals - known as PCBs - were found in soil samples and in the blood of people living near sites linked to chemical giant Monsanto. Sheen interviewed farming consultant turned campaigner Douglas Gowan shortly before his death, who had spent decades warning that communities were at risk of toxic chemicals. The actor later teamed up with investigative journalists Lucy Taylor and Dan Ashby who had inherited all of the campaigner's documents and research. They set about testing 14 sites in Wales and north west England where it was thought Monsanto had been dumping PCBs, and found elevated levels at all but one. Sheen appeared before the Welsh Affairs Committee alongside investigative journalists Lucy Taylor and Dan Ashby, who co-presented the BBC series, Buried with Michael Sheen Susan Smith, who worked at Monsanto in Wrexham, said her happy memories of working there have been replaced with fears following the documentary. Susan and her husband Geraint's home, which they have lived in for 53 years, is separated from the decommissioned Ruabon chemical works by a thin tree line. Geraint was diagnosed with prostate cancer 13 years ago before more recently developing skin cancer, while Susan developed breast cancer when she was 38. While they admit they are not certain that Monsanto was responsible, the documentary has made them question the possible impact of the factory on their family's health. Susan worked as a secretary for four years when she was 19, then returned once for temporary cover and another time to overhaul a failing system. "Most of my time was spent in the telex office next to the warehouse. We used to send delivery notes, instructions, requests on little pieces of ticker tape through a machine to other Monsanto offices," she said. "We had a small glass hatch that the instructions would be passed through and it was never closed because people were passing things through so often. As a result dust and powders and all sorts would blow through and coat the desks, the paper, even our sandwiches." Susan said she wasn't given a "safety briefing, protective clothing or anything" and office staff never knew they were at risk. Susan had her blood tested by the documentary team and while the PCB levels in her blood were not deemed high, the fact there is no safe level of PCB and the lack of accountability from Eastman – the US company which now owns what was once Monsanto – has left her with unanswered questions. The couple have joined the Monsanto Contamination Action Group – which was set up for people in Wrexham who live in communities affected by historic industrial waste dumping. Eastman was approached for comment. title: Police begin operation to move migrants from Ceuta beaches
description: Police reportedly fired into the air on Friday morning as they struggled to contain crowds jostling to secure a place at the tented site.
body: Migrants in Ceuta push Spanish Civil Guard members as they are transferred to a camp Police have begun moving hundreds of migrants in Ceuta to a new tented site in the port area of the Spanish territory in north Africa. Officers struggled to contain crowds of people jostling to secure a place at the site after weeks of living on the beaches. Shots could be heard, with reports that police fired into the air. Several hundred migrants have now reached the camp, which has a capacity for 1,700 people. Most of the 72,000 migrants who breached the border from Morocco in July have returned, but it is believed that more than 13,000 remain in the enclave. The operation began at about 07:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Friday, with more than 3,000 migrants being transferred, according to the Spanish government-owned news agency Efe. During the process, some migrants broke through the cordon along the designated 2km (1.2 mile) route to the port. Video shows young men running in the darkness as police tried to maintain control. More than 170 police officers have been deployed, including drone technicians, Efe reported. It added that the situation was later "brought under control quickly", and the operation was able to continue. The operation is part of the government's attempt to concentrate the migrants in facilities where they can be identified and cared for while their administrative status is individually determined. More than 3,000 migrants being transferred on Friday, according to Spanish media The chaotic scenes will do little to dampen opposition criticism in Spain of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who has faced strong criticism over his handling of the crisis. Since the migrant influx, residents of the 18.5 sq km (7.2 sq miles) territory have expressed safety concerns. Some have destroyed shelters and blocked aid being supplied to the migrants. Ceuta's Mayor Juan Jesus Vivas told lawmakers in the European Parliament earlier this month that the migrants had turned Ceuta into a "pressure cooker". "The city is completely different than it was before this event, Ceutans have lost their joy and their lifestyles have been completely shaken up," the conservative mayor said. The opposition also accused Sánchez of knowing about the influx of migrants in advance. Sánchez has insisted that it was impossible to predict, but according to government documents, its intelligence services had warned of social media calls for a mass migrant crossing into Ceuta the day before the events happened. Ester Muñoz of the conservative People's Party said the government was "directly responsible for the invasion of Ceuta and for those who died". Pedro Sánchez denies knowing about the migrant rush in advance The incident has also created diplomatic headaches for Sánchez. The prime minister is at odds with Italy, with the two countries earlier this week extending temporary border controls imposed on each other. He is also trying to maintain his bilateral relationship with Morocco. The influx of migrants in late July came after Spain's Supreme Court ruled that migrants stopped at sea while trying to reach Ceuta cannot be summarily returned to Morocco. After the ruling, some social media accounts spread misinformation and offered to help migrants cross the Spanish border for hundreds of pounds. Thousands of people then flooded across the border fence and swam around the ocean barriers. At least 100 people died during the crossing, according to local authorities.
