title: Tailgate parties, marching bands... and Ted Lasso? Wembley hosts US college game
description: Wembley will host its first American college football game on Saturday and one of Kansas' most famous fans could be among the 60,000 crowd.
body: Both Kansas and Arizona State have a 1-1 record this season The NFL has been playing in London since 2007 but now a different kind of American football is coming to the capital of England. American college football games were being played abroad long before the NFL headed overseas, in countries as diverse as Cuba, Japan and Tanzania. But this Saturday the UK will host just its second college football game, and it will be a far bigger event than the first at Crystal Palace in 1988. About 2,500 fans were there that day, whereas 60,000 will be at Wembley to watch the Kansas Jayhawks face the Arizona State Sun Devils (17:00 BST). The inaugural Union Jack Classic (UJC) will feature marching bands, spirit squads and tailgate parties outside the stadium - and Ted Lasso actor Jason Sudeikis might be there too. This video can not be played Why is American college football coming to the UK? The UJC chief executive is entrepreneur Brian Dubiski. He and a business partner both played college football, with the latter then working with the NFL in London. And while chatting over a few beers, they asked themselves why no-one had taken college football back to England, especially since Wembley's first NFL game in 2007. After mulling the idea over for a few years, they decided to do it themselves and managed to book a date at English football's national stadium. Then they had to find the teams. Brett Yormark, commissioner of the Big 12 Conference, is "bullish" about building its global appeal and was keen to be involved. So two Big 12 teams committed to the trip. Founded in 1890, the University of Kansas (KU) has one of the oldest college teams and wants to expand its brand, while the game coincides with Arizona State (ASU) opening a London campus this month. Before this trip, most of their players did not own a passport so both teams also wanted to give them a cultural experience they will never forget. What is the Union Jack Classic and who is in it? The Kansas Jayhawks marching band usually plays in front of 32,000 fans at their home stadium Virtually all NFL players come via the US college system, and in many parts of America, college football is more popular than the NFL. College games often have bigger crowds - eight of the world's 10 biggest stadiums are for college football, all holding more than 100,000. The fans are also more passionate as support is often passed down from one generation to another, and multiple generations attend the same school. Kansas player Calvin Clements, for example, is a fifth-generation Jayhawk. Actor Paul Rudd is also a Jayhawk, while lifelong fan Jason Sudeikis grew up in Kansas and frequently weaves KU references into his work. "They're very spirited, and you get the tribalism, so it's the closest thing we have to European football fanbases," Dubiski told BBC Sport. Both the NFL and college football have tailgate parties, where fans gather in the car park and eat and drink for hours before the game. But college football fans chant during games, which feature marching bands and spirit squads - made up of cheerleaders, dancers and mascots. "We want the game to showcase what we think is one of the greatest sports in America," said Yormark. "There's something special about college football - the pageantry, the traditions, the fandom. It's dynamic - there's a lot of energy and passion. It truly is an experience." The Union Jack Classic has become the British American Football Association's first national league sponsor since 1992 and has subsidised more than 750 coaching and officiating qualifications in the UK, plus held clinics for more than 400 coaches According to the NFL, 14 million people in the UK identify as fans of America's biggest sports league. UJC organisers have tried to tap into that fanbase and the UK infrastructure the NFL has built, but also appeal to younger fans. It formed partnerships with the British American Football Association (Bafa), British Universities and Colleges Sport (BUCS), and the Jacksonville Jaguars, who host an annual NFL game at Wembley. About 60,000 tickets have been sold and 15,000 fans are travelling from the US, with student sections to help create the typical college gameday atmosphere. "We're really pleased with that in year one," said Dubiski. "We never expected to sell the stadium out, and 60,000 is higher than the average Big 12 attendance." Dubiski agreed an exclusive multi-year deal with Wembley and is already working on games in the next three years. He might expand to other European cities and bring basketball games too. More than 54,000 fans watched ASU beat Morgan State 70-7 in their season opener two weeks ago Yormark believes a positive experience for fans and players would constitute success, plus an exciting game. Former NFL quarterback Robert Griffin III, now a college football analyst with Fox Sports, agrees that "we've got to bring excitement". "The way to encourage fandom is to create moments, so I'm happy the two teams coming over know how to score points - and score them in bunches," he said. Griffin also believes college football could ultimately be more successful overseas than the NFL. "The fandom around college football is better, it just is," he added. "It's more similar to world football so there's a better opportunity to connect, also because there's more teams. In the NFL there's 32, but in college football there's 400 you can fall in love with. "And if you want to be a real NFL fan, you have to be a college football fan because that's the feeder system into the league and you get to watch these guys develop." Fox Sports' Big Noon Kick-Off show is nationally televised in the US Griffin will be at Wembley as part of Fox's team for their flagship pre-game show, which has gone overseas for the first time, with coverage starting two hours before kick-off. "They'll be set up right outside Wembley,"

title: From depression after Chelsea injury to playing non-league at 37
description: Sam Hutchinson is getting ready to play for Farnham Town in the second qualifying round of the FA Cup - 19 years after making his Chelsea debut under Jose Mourinho.
body: Sam Hutchinson (back row, third from left) lines up for Chelsea before a friendly against Paris St-Germain in New York in July 2012 Sam Hutchinson played under both Jose Mourinho and Carlo Ancelotti at Chelsea, set up a goal for Frank Lampard, and was in Munich on the historic night they won the Champions League for the first time in 2012. His time at Chelsea, however, was "filled with regret and what might have been" after a chronic knee injury so nearly ended his career before it had properly started. A product of Chelsea's youth system, Hutchinson was a promising defender on the fringes of the first team when he was diagnosed with a chondral defect (a hole in his right knee) after suffering a serious injury during a reserve game at Aston Villa. Having joined Chelsea as a seven-year-old, made his first-team debut at 17 under Mourinho and captained England at Under-19s level, Hutchinson took the gut-wrenching decision to retire at the age of 21 in 2010 after struggling to recover. A period of depression followed for the young player, who had been identified by Mourinho as a bright prospect. "I had already played for the first team and Mourinho had said some encouraging things about me in interviews," he says. "Then the injury happened and everything fell apart. I was just a kid. "After I retired I was in a bad place with dark thoughts." Hutchinson sought help for his depression. "Unless you get help, you never know how bad you are," he tells BBC Sport. "Even telling this story, it's like therapy. "It's like the old saying - a problem shared is a problem halved. That's true about mental health. If you're suffering in silence, it's not going to help." After receiving treatment at the Priory, and with his damaged knee finally fixed, Hutchinson came out of retirement in December 2011 to re-sign for Chelsea. More injuries followed but despite being limited to six senior Chelsea appearances, he has gone on to have a fulfilling career. Hutchinson played 200-plus games in the Championship, most notably for Sheffield Wednesday, where fans remember him fondly. In addition to overseas spells in the Netherlands with Vitesse Arnhem and in Cyprus with Pafos, he has also turned out for Nottingham Forest, Reading and AFC Wimbledon. Sixteen years after fearing his career was over for good, the father-of-three is still playing the game he loves at the age of 37. This summer Hutchinson signed a two-year contract with non-league Farnham Town - after surviving a major health scare. Hutchinson (back left) with team-mates Didier Drogba, Ryan Bertrand and Gary Cahill at Chelsea's Champions League parade in 2012 Monday, 26 May 2025. A date etched in the memories of AFC Wimbledon fans after their side won promotion to League One by beating Walsall at Wembley in the play-off final. It was Hutchinson's winner at Grimsby three weeks earlier that ensured the Dons made the play-offs. He did not know it at the time but the defender-turned-midfielder would not start another game for 11 months after scoring at Blundell Park. "Throughout the first half my chest was getting increasingly tighter and I was in so much pain," recalls Hutchinson about that game at Grimsby. "I felt dizzy and my hands started sweating. "I was rapidly going downhill but then our centre-back won a great header, the keeper tipped it on to the bar, and it dropped down to me to tap over the line." While AFC Wimbledon's travelling fans celebrated the goal wildly, Hutchinson felt so unwell his only thoughts were finishing the game and making it home to his wife and three children. It would be several days, however, before he returned to the family home in Ascot. On the journey back to London, his condition deteriorated to such an extent that a decision was taken to divert the team coach to a hospital in Nottingham so he could receive treatment. After tests Hutchinson was quickly transferred to a nearby cardiac unit. "I was put me in the back of an ambulance and I remember hearing the blues and twos," he recalls. "My blood levels had spiked so much, I was in a really bad way. A couple of the paramedics knew who I was because I had played for Nottingham Forest a few years earlier. "They said: 'You can thank us later for saving your life.' I was told I'd had a heart attack." Hutchinson spent the next five days in hospital and had successful heart surgery. "A branch of an artery was blocked 75%. I had an angiogram, external and had a stent put in by a specialist. The one thing that the professor - who had looked after both Tom Lockyer and Christian Eriksen – said was my situation was nothing like theirs. "It was a blockage and it was all fixed, there was no need for a defibrillator to be fitted." John Terry, his former Chelsea team-mate, was among those who reached out to Hutchinson during his recovery, while the player was well enough to visit Wembley to watch AFC Wimbledon win promotion. A month later the Dons announced he had signed a one-year contract extension after being given the all-clear to train again. However, Hutchinson was limited to just a handful of appearances in 2025-26 and in May - 12 months after that game at Grimsby - it was announced he would be leaving at the age of 36. "Sam played a pivotal role in getting us over the line, not only with that iconic goal at Grimsby but his performances leading up to that," said an AFC Wimbledon statement, external announcing his departue. Some may have decided it was the perfect time to retire from playing after what he had been through. Hutchinson, though, had other ideas. title: Johnny Marr guitars sell for almost £4m at auction
description: One instrument was used on the The Smiths' debut album and also appeared on the cover of Oasis's debut single.
body: Johnny Marr's guitar collection includes instruments used with The Smiths and on his forthcoming solo album Guitars owned by The Smiths musician Johnny Marr have sold for almost £4m at auction. The instruments, which were used during his time with The Smiths and on his forthcoming solo album, went under the hammer as part of Christie's Marr's Guitars: The Johnny Marr Collection sale. The sale lasted for more than five hours and included buyers from 34 countries, fetching £3,649,280 - more than three times its estimated value. Marr said: "The auction has been a great experience and has exceeded all my expectations. I'd like to thank everyone who made bids and special thanks to Christie's for making it so memorable." The sale included 10 guitars as well as amplifiers and gold discs Marr's 1982 Rickenbacker 330 Jetglo sold for £358,400 after attracting a bidding battle lasting more than five minutes. The guitar was used throughout the recording of The Smiths' debut album and on the band's early tours. It can be heard on songs including This Charming Man, Still Ill and What Difference Does It Make? The instrument also featured on the cover of Oasis's debut single Supersonic. Marr had lent it to Noel Gallagher during early recording sessions for Oasis' album Definitely Maybe. A second guitar, Marr's 1960 Cherry Red Gibson ES-355, sold for £204,800. The instrument inspired him to write the music for The Smiths' 1984 single Heaven Knows I'm Miserable Now and its B-side Girl Afraid. Johnny Marr played the Gibson guitar in early TV appearances with The Smiths, including this performance on The Tube It was bought for him in 1983 by Sire Records founder Seymour Stein after Marr joked that The Smiths would sign to the label if he bought him a new guitar. The auction comes ahead of the release of Marr's first studio album in four years, The Age Of Everything, which is due out on 2 October. Marr was guitarist and co-songwriter for The Smiths alongside singer Morrissey. The Manchester band released four studio albums before splitting in 1987 and became one of the defining groups of the British indie music scene. This video can not be played Johnny Marr auctions guitars - including one on Oasis album cover The sale also saw 100% of the hammer price of 31 lots, which included 10 guitars, donated to two charities: The Guide Dogs for the Blind Association and The National Autistic Society. Amelia Walker from Christie's said the sale prices reflected Marr's "groundbreaking and unparalleled musical influence". She said: "It has been an absolute honour to work with him and to share these amazing instruments and their stories with so many fans, collectors and fellow musicians around the world. "We are also delighted to have been able to support Johnny in raising valuable funds for his chosen charities." title: How the race they said women couldn't run took centre stage
description: After making its debut at the 1928 Olympics, the women's 800m was cut from the programme. Now, it's often billed as the must-see event of major athletics championships. So, how did we get here?
body: Audrey Werro has come just 0.42 seconds shy of breaking the long-standing women's 800m record For 32 years, the women's 800m was absent from the Olympics, with its competitors deemed too frail. Now, it is one of the most hotly anticipated events on the track. This extraordinary story starts at the 1928 Olympic Games, which represented a huge - if temporary - step forward for women's sports. The Amsterdam Games were the first to allow women to compete in track and field events. Five women's events were added to the programme - the 100m, high jump, discus, 400m hurdles and, controversially at the time, 800m. The progress, however, was temporary. German athlete Karoline Lina Radke, external became the first woman to win Olympic gold in the 800m - but she would also be the last for another 32 years. The event was removed from the Games after reports - later proven to be false - claimed competitors suffered extreme exhaustion after the race, and the International Olympic Committee decided women were too frail to compete, external over the two-lap distance. Fast forward almost 100 years and the event now gets headline status at major events. In recent times, it's been the battle between Britain's Olympic 800m champion Keely Hodgkinson and the Swiss European champion Audrey Werro that has captivated fans. So how did the 800m become the 'one to watch'? BBC Sport spoke to the women who helped shape the race to find out. It was the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, and Ann Brightwell (nee Packer) had just crossed the finish line of the women's 800m to take gold - and set a new world record. In doing so, Brightwell became the first British woman to win an Olympic gold on the track, in a time of two minutes 01.1 seconds. She told BBC Sport: "My husband, who was my fiance then, said to me, 'you don't realise what you've done'. "I didn't give it a thought at the time… but now I realise I played a very small part in women running longer distances." But the controversy hadn't completely gone away. Brightwell knew all about the claims that had seen women unable to compete for 32 years after the 800m was removed from the Olympics. Brightwell adds: "Men weren't happy about women competing in these very high profile events…we were considered too frail and too delicate. "And they took it upon themselves to make it look really bad. They were saying women were collapsing on the way round. But it was all a lie." After 1928, women's middle-distance shrunk into the shadows for the next few decades. The 800m was finally reintroduced to the Olympic programme in 1960 and, four years later, the then-22-year-old Brightwell went to her first Olympics, fitting training around her job as a teacher. "Many people in my era either had to take unpaid leave or resign, or they got sacked because they were trying to juggle their sports with their career," she said. "My school was very tolerant towards what I was doing, so I was fortunate." Ann Brightwell (nee Packer) crosses the finish line. The 1964 Olympics was just the third Games with the women's 800m included on the athletics programme Going out for a run around the local streets or countryside - which seems so commonplace today - was unusual in the era Brightwell was competing. "If I just felt like an easy run, I would run around my village, around the streets… people commented on it or tooted their horns. And it was funny looking back, but it never troubled me," the now 84-year-old told BBC Sport. Brightwell's 800m time of 2:01.1 stood for almost three years, before Australian Judy Pollock broke that with a new time of 2:01 flat in 1967. The next target was to go under two minutes. "Records are great and medals are the best, but when you break a barrier it's a fantastic feeling," said Christina Boxer-Cahill (nee Boxer). It was at the 1979 European Cup final in Turin that Boxer-Cahill looked up at the clock and realised she'd gone under two minutes. She added: "I knew this would probably be my last chance, because there were other girls in Britain trying to do it." In 1971, Germany's Hildegard Falck, external had become the first woman to break the two-minute barrier. Eight years later, it was the 22-year-old Boxer-Cahill who became the first British woman to do so, in a time of one minute 59.05 seconds. "It's a bit like when Roger Bannister broke four minutes for the mile. Once he'd done it everybody did it because you see what's possible," Boxer-Cahill, who is now 69 years old, told BBC Sport. "I just think I'm so fortunate that I was in a sport where everybody accepted that you have men and women's races in the Olympics." Boxer-Cahill won gold for England in the 1500m at the 1982 Commonwealth Games From 1971 to 1983, the women's 800m world record would be broken six times. But the 1983 record stands to this day. It belongs to Czech athlete Jarmila Kratochvilova, who ran a time of one minute 53.28 seconds at a meeting in Munich. Kratochvilova's record has been questioned, with claims it was assisted by her country's doping regime that existed at the time, something she has strenuously denied. In 2017, European Athletics proposed wiping out records set before 2005 - sending a strong signal that records set before then were disputable. Several Soviet satellite states - including East Germany - are known to have been operating state-sponsored doping programmes throughout the 1980s. At the 1988 Seoul Olympics, Boxer-Cahill finished fourth in the 1500m, behind a Russian athlete who was later banned for doping. Boxer-Cahill said: "I was running during that Eastern Bloc era when, you know, they've looked back and some of the performances, there's sort of a cloud over it. "I'd just have loved to have been on that rostrum. I wish the Eastern Bloc system hadn't been there, but that's what it was. "Politics in sport, when

title: Costume exhibition celebrates 50 years of city's 'spaceship-like' theatre
description: To mark the anniversary of the seven-sided theatre constructed from tubular steel, some archive costumes go on display.
body: One of the costumes from a performance of The Skriker at the Royal Exhange Theatre Fifty years ago, the Royal Exchange Theatre in Manchester opened its doors for its first production of Richard Brinsley Sheridan's The Rivals. It was September 1976, and the seven-sided theatre constructed from tubular steel in the heart of the city was described by some as something from out of space. "It sits almost like a spaceship inside this extraordinary great Victorian Hall with all the pillars so already you have this tension," said Selina Cartmell, the theatre's creative director. "They created a theatre of 750 seats in the round, a democratic arena where the alchemy between actor and audience is at its most purest form and they've created something that still feels fresh today." In the five decades since the theatre opened in St Ann's Square, some of the world's most famous actors have performed at the theatre. The exhibition at the Royal Exchange Theatre, pictured, will celebrate "50 years of storytelling through costume, craft and performance" Hugh Grant in 1986 and Bob Hoskins and Helen Mirren in 1981 are just some of the acting talent to have graced its stage. In 2004, long before Spiderman, Andrew Garfield was in Cares, while Maxime Peake appeared more recently in 2015 and the following year Don Warrington swapped Death in Paradise to play King Lear. To mark its 50th anniversary, some of the costumes worn by those acting greats are on display. The Mythic Reinvention exhibition, which is free, includes just a small fraction of the theatre's collection. There are more than 25,000 costumes and other items kept in its archive and all the outfits for its performances are made in-house. It aims to provide an exclusive insight into the inner workings of the theatre's costume department from the artists who created some of the Royal Exchange's most iconic shows. Christopher Gable, Patricia Routledge and James Maxwell pictured on stage in The Rivals in 1976 The exhibition has been curated by award-winning designer Leslie Travers. "To think there are so many pieces of costume here from so many productions," he said. "I think Manchester should be incredibly proud of this building because the costume-making is world famous. "It's amazing that these costumes, some of them are 50 years old but they look brand new. They've been so well looked after." He added: "It's a big auditorium but it's incredibly intimate so the material selection has to be really considered because you get to look at the costumes close up." The Royal Exchange Theatre is situated in Manchester city centre Cartmell said the exhibition would "give audiences a never-seen-before look into what makes the Royal Exchange such a special place". "It will be a chance to celebrate every individual who has helped create and shape this beloved theatre as we look to our future." Mythic Reinvention: An exhibition celebrating 50 Years of Costume and Craft is open until 15 November. title: Odyssey painting goes on show at city art gallery
description: The work by Turner is on loan from the National Gallery and forms part of a new exhibition in York.
body: The famous Turner painting is on loan from the National Gallery A famous painting depicting a scene from Homer's Odyssey has gone on display at York Art Gallery. The J.M.W. Turner creation, on loan from the National Gallery and forming part of a new exhibition, shows Ulysses, also known as Odysseus, sailing from the island where Polyphemus, a one-eyed giant, had held him and his men captive. Following the recent success of the new Christopher Nolan film based on the epic poem, curators said they hoped there would be renewed interest in artists' interpretations of Homer's work. The painting is one of more than 100 works to go on display as part of Turner, Wedgwood & Beyond: Inspired by Flaxman, which opens at the gallery on Friday. The exhibition looks at work by John Flaxman, a York-born artist, on the 200th anniversary of his death, as well as the artists he inspired. Senior curator Dr Beatrice Bertram said: "Flaxman may not be a household name these days, but what we hope to do within this show is to really redress him and give him some time in the light again. "In his time, he was internationally renowned for his sculptures and his designs, particularly his illustrations of Homer's Iliad and Odyssey." John Flaxman was known for his sculptures and designs According to the show's curators, elements of Flaxman's sketches can be seen in Turner's painting called Ulysses Deriding Polyphemus – Homer's Odyssey, including outlines of horses in the sunset and the shadow of a cyclops. The works are shown side by side on the gallery wall, inviting visitors to compare them. Co-curator Richard Johns, from the University of York, said the exhibition had not been planned around the release of the film, but was rather a "happy accident". "It wasn't actually something we had in mind when we were developing the exhibition, or even when we asked the National Gallery if they would lend this painting," he explained. "The interest in the Odyssey as a poem has increased enormously as a result of the success of the film. "I hope it will encourage people who've seen the film or have a renewed interest in Homer to come and see what artists in the 18th and 19th Century made of Homer's poetry, just as we've seen how an artist like Christopher Nolan in the 21st Century interprets those same ideas." The exhibition will be on display until 17 January 2027. Listen to highlights from North Yorkshire on BBC Sounds, catch up with the latest episode of Look North. title: Forced adoption records could 'unlock' missing histories
description: A campaigner says church records could reveal the hidden history of forced-adoption homes.
body: Diana Defries was sent by her family to Nazareth House in Southampton in 1974, when she was 16 years old A woman whose baby was taken from her in a forced adoption aged 16 has said important questions about the UK's mother-and-baby homes remain unanswered, including how many children were buried in unmarked graves. Diana Defries, who successfully campaigned for a state apology for forced adoptions, said greater access to records could help families understand what happened in the homes. And historian Dr Michael Lambert, from Lancaster University, argued that archives held privately by religious congregations could help "unlock" important pieces of history. Defries, originally from London, was sent by her family to Nazareth House in Southampton in 1974 after becoming pregnant. "I remember the feeling of walking into somewhere that would change me," she said. The home, run by the Catholic Sisters of Nazareth, received funding from Southampton social services, as well as fees paid by the families of women who stayed there. The mother-and-baby wing opened in 1960 and by the time it closed in 1985, local media reported it had housed 1,552 women and girls. Unmarked graves of children who died in Nazareth Houses, which were then mostly a network of residential care facilities and orphanages run by the Sisters of Nazareth, and in similar institutions operated by other religious orders, have been found in the UK. Sister Anna Maria Doolan, safeguarding lead for the Sisters of Nazareth, said the order welcomed and supported the government's apology for forced adoptions. Diana Defries said she felt records held by those who ran the mother-and-baby homes were "protected" In a statement, Doolan said: "Requests to access information regarding former residents are welcome in line with the archive access policy. "However, the records are sometimes, sadly, incomplete as the guidelines for keeping records pre-1980 were very different to today's requirements." After giving birth in hospital and returning to the home, Defries said she was discouraged from holding her baby to prevent her from bonding. It was only on the train to the adoption agency in London, accompanied by her mother, that she said she was able to really hold her daughter. "I didn't want to let her go," she said. "I kept holding on to the idea that they'd see the truth - they'd realise this was their grandchild, and they'd relent." She then recalls a woman from the agency wearing a white coat, a stethoscope and a pearl necklace appearing and taking her daughter. "This woman carried [my daughter] away, turned around and said 'say bye-bye' and waved her little hand at me," she said, "As if this was the most banal thing." Next week, she was back in school. "And I have never felt so broken in my entire life." The former site of Southampton's Nazareth House is now occupied by several blocks of flats Defries met her daughter again in 1992 when she was 18. "When you first meet the person you lost, there is grief as well as joy, as well of a sense of expectation," she said. Later, she became the chair of the Movement for an Adoption Apology, which campaigned for the UK government to apologise for forced adoptions. That was delivered in July by then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer. It came with a promise of £4m to assist in funding a national online resource, led by charity CoramBAAF , externalwith the Archives and Records Association, to help people find out where adoption records are held. Defries believes the apology, and funding, will help. Through requests to the Sisters of Nazareth, she has tried to get her own records, and received a redacted copy of a register that showed she was at the home. But she has also requested administrative files and financial records, to get a better understanding of how the home operated. She said the order told her they had been obliged by law to destroy many of the other records she asked for. Diana Defries chaired a successful campaign for a state apology for forced adoptions She still believes they may exist, and that privately held records like those could help people understand their experiences, or could hold clues to other potential injustices - not only in homes run by the Sisters of Nazareth, but in similar institutions across the UK. "What hasn't yet been explored here is all the babies who died in the homes, and were buried in unmarked graves, and the women who suffered birth injuries that weren't repaired, and the women who died," she said. "And the different things that have gone on that are not being explored because they're yet to be properly recognised," she said. "And the records are hidden, or protected." The Sisters of Nazareth allow requests for both remote enquiries and on-site research, but visits must be approved by the congregation and are supervised. There are further restrictions around accessing material containing personal information, that is business-sensitive, or has not yet been appraised, according to the congregation's access policy. Dr Michael Lambert is a historian at Lancaster University who has investigated mother-and-baby homes. He supported the campaign for an adoption apology by providing evidence from his own research. Some of that research was carried out with access to the records granted by the relevant diocese. Dr Michael Lambert argued that greater access to privately held records could help build a fuller understanding of the history of mother-and-baby homes in the UK Lambert said they indicated many more infant deaths in a Church of England home than had previously been revealed. He argued it was impossible to know what records were and were not held by a particular congregation or order if they controlled who could see them. title: Thames Water rescue deal should be rejected - MPs
description: A report on the future of Thames Water, urging the government to take action, has been published.
body: Thames Water serves 16 millions customers across London and the Thames Valley A cross-party committee of MPs has urged the government to reject a £10bn takeover proposal from Thames Water's creditors. The UK's biggest water company owes roughly £20bn and has been working with creditors and government officials. A report by the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (EFRA) Committee has now said the government should consider placing it into special administration, a form of temporary nationalisation. A Thames Water spokesperson said it needed to be "recapitalised and put on a firm financial footing". Fears that the firm, which serves 16 million customers, could collapse first emerged three years ago. The committee said a takeover plan by a consortium of more than 100 of its creditors did not have "the interests of the public, the company or the environment at heart". The plan was seen as the final realistic option to avoid a special administration regime, after a previous deal with a US private equity giant collapsed. Creditors, who collectively own about £17bn of Thames Water's debt, were previously warned by former environment secretary Emma Reynolds their plan did not go far enough to protect customers or the environment. The new report said Thames Water, alongside other "poor-performing" water companies, was in a "doom loop" of fines for poor performance leaving it with less money to invest in improvements. It warned the company would "likely accrue" more than £900m in penalties over the next five years. The committee said laws needed to change to allow the government to trigger a special administration on performance grounds alone. It also warned the top priority for the bidders, called London & Valley Water, was to "extract immediate value from Thames Water, not steer it to long-term success". Alistair Carmichael, chairman of the committee, said: "We believe Thames Water can be turned around, but not by giving the keys back to the people who have been joy riding in the family car. "The government should reject offers from the company's creditors in return for relief from fines for pollution and poor service." Carmichael said "liabilities that the government will face in the short-term" could be recouped by a future sale of Thames Water once its finances and performance are back on track. He added: "The chaos of another Thames Water-style saga must not be repeated." Watch the latest episode of South Today Listen to the latest news from Oxfordshire A spokesman for London & Valley Water said: "This group of investors has never been in control of the company and has never received a dividend from Thames Water. "They have stepped in to fund a significant revenue shortfall to ensure Thames Water's record capital investment programme can continue without disruption." He added: "Our enhanced proposal will address all feedback from Ofwat and ministers and is the fastest route to fix Thames Water's complex problems." A Thames Water spokesperson said: "Turning Thames Water around will take a decade and require significant and sustained investment, but we are already making progress and this is a different business from the one it was two years ago." They added: "Anything that delays the recapitalisation risks slowing the turnaround, disrupting investment and increasing the cost of delivering the improvements our customers and the environment need." title: Fenced-in woman, 81, wins three-year access fight
description: Derbyshire County Council shut off a gap, which had been used by a family since 1967.
body: Helene Ball said the council had tried to bully her An 81-year-old has won a three-year battle against a council that fenced across a gap in her garden wall her family had used as access for decades. Helene Ball - a resident of George Road in Matlock, Derbyshire, since 1967 - took legal action after Derbyshire County Council cemented a metal fence panel blocking the 98cm gated gap between her garden and a council car park in April 2023. A first-tier tribunal has ruled in Ball's favour over the dispute, after she proved use of the gate since the 1960s. A right of way has now been established, while the council has been ordered by the courts to pay £50,000 costs and to ensure her access is not impeded again. Ball, a retired teacher, told the Local Democracy Reporting Service: "I have taught nine, 10 and 11-year-olds all my life, but I never expected the council to act so babyish, they have been spitting their dummies out of the pram and it has been beyond childish. "They did everything they could to bully me. They tried to put us off but they messed with the wrong ones. "At my age you don't know how many years you have left, and this has given me three years-plus of stress but now we have proven they blocked our rights." Concrete blocks have been placed to allow Ball access to her property While the fence panel was removed within a year, vehicle access had been blocked throughout the whole legal battle as the Cavendish Road car park has been on the market for sale as a small housing development. A route through the site for Ball has now been created by the council using concrete blocks. The court ruling from Judge Robert Brown said that hired legal representation from the council was "surprisingly combative" and found parts of the legal representation for the council "totally irrelevant" and "most unhelpful". The council refused to comment on or provide the cost of the legal challenge. title: Nebula image wins Royal Observatory competition
description: Ali Alobaidly is named Astronomy Photographer of the Year for his image of the Shark Nebula.
body: The winning image was captured in Jahra Governorate, Kuwait The Royal Observatory Greenwich has announced the winner of its Astronomy Photographer of the Year competition for an image of the Shark Nebula. The dark nebula is made from interstellar dust dense enough to block starlight and is 650 light years away. Steve Marsh, one of the judges and art editor at BBC Sky at Night Magazine, said the image by Ali Alobaidly showed "flawless presentation, pin-sharp details and dynamic contrast". He added: "The Shark Nebula is already a striking object, but when it is resolved to the point where even detail-rich distant galaxies can be seen through it, you know you're looking at something very special." Alobaidly, who won £10,000 for winning the competition overall, said he hoped to use his photographs "to make astronomy more accessible, engaging and meaningful through science communication and education", and described the award as a "tremendous honour". For the 2026 competition there were almost 4,000 entries from 66 countries. Alobaidly's entry, taken in Kuwait, was entered in the Stars and Nebulae category. Mineral Moon by Nikolaos Strimpoulis aged 15 won for ZWO Young Astronomy Photographer of the Year Nikolaos Strimpoulis, 15, won for ZWO Young Astronomy Photographer of the Year for his image Mineral Moon, taken in Palaio Faliro, Athens, Greece. The close-up image of the Moon's surface includes dark areas known as maria and bright areas known as the highlands. The orange and blue colours on the lunar surface are caused by iron and titanium deposits and it was for that reason that the image was given its title. Marsh said: "Many of us start our astrophotography journey with the Moon – some of us stay there forever! But often we don't delve deep into the subtle colours of its mineral deposits until much later. This amazing young astrophotographer has achieved perfectly developed colouring in this photograph." Dr Greg Brown, astronomer at the Royal Observatory Greenwich, said the entries from the 18th year of the competition demonstrated "skill and innovation" coupled with improvements in technology. Stefano Pellegrini won the Skyscapes category for his entry Botswana Star Trail Tom Williams won in the Planets, Comets and Asteroids category for his image taken in Trowbridge, Wiltshire Max Inwood won in the People and Space category for his image taken in California Radoslav Sviretsov won the Aurorae category for his image taken of the Northern Lights in Iceland An exhibition of the winning and highly commended images will be on display at the National Maritime Museum, London from 18 September. title: Moving from Newcastle to Liverpool easy decision - Isak
description: Striker Alexander Isak says Liverpool's ambition and determination to sign him was a big part of why he joined the club.
body: This video can not be played 'It feels like things are getting better and better' - Alexander Isak Alexander Isak says joining Liverpool last summer was an "easy decision". The Sweden striker arrived from Newcastle on transfer deadline day in September 2025 for a British record transfer fee of £125m. "[Liverpool] is a massive club, and everything about the club made it pretty clear," he told BBC Sport's The Football Interview. "And the club's ambition and the club's will to get me in as well. It was a big part of it." Isak missed pre-season last summer and trained at his former club Real Sociedad amid uncertainty around his Newcastle future, saying promises made to him there had been "broken". However, he struggled for goals in his first season at Anfield before a leg break ruled him out from December to April. This season the 26-year-old has already matched last season's tally of three Premier League goals, after only four games. Asked if there was ever a point last season when he regretted the move, Isak replied: "No, never. I would never think like that." He added: "[The leg break] was tough. Anyone who had a long injury would know. But on the other hand, when you're in a good place and when you feel good, you don't really tend to look back because it doesn't really benefit you. "So I'm just looking forward and feel really optimistic and excited about the season, and what it can bring to us." Over the summer, Isak made his World Cup bow for Sweden after managing just 1,032 minutes for Liverpool over 22 appearances last season. He scored once and assisted three goals for Graham Potter's side before they were knocked out by France in the last 32. "Playing for your country in a World Cup is a dream of most people," said Isak. "With the injuries last season, the World Cup was perfect. I had that period where I could play and gain rhythm and form. "And, on top of that, it was a massive experience, so that was perfect to do and come back here for pre-season and to start the season." This video can not be played 'He's a humble guy' - Isak praises team-mate Gakpo New Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola, who replaced Arne Slot in the summer, has told Isak that he wants him to defend from the front as it is an "attacking weapon" for Liverpool. "He asks me to be part of the defending but to defend in positions where, when we win the ball, we can counter quickly and get the ball forward to the offensive line," said Isak. "He said 'score goals', but he wants me to defend. The way we defend - we defend to score goals so defending, in the end, is an attacking weapon." Under Iraola, Liverpool are aiming to implement a front-foot and aggressive style of football. They have made the most sprints in the Premier League this season. "He came with his football - the way he wants to play and the high intensity which I think will benefit me, the club and the way the club wants to play football," added Isak. On the style of football since Iraola joined, Isak says: "I think that's what the team needs. It's not just about getting the ball to me, it's about getting the ball forward and to all of the offensive players quickly. "I think that will benefit the team. I think if we can do that then we should score more goals." And Isak, who has 60 Premier League goals to his name, is determined to help bring silverware to Liverpool this year but insisted he is not someone who sets personal targets. His most prolific Premier League season came with Newcastle in 2024-25 when he scored 23 goals. "Everyone knows that success for this club is winning trophies," said Isak. "I want to score every game. Everyone is different. Some like to set targets and some don't. I'm the one that doesn't." More dropped points at Anfield - is it too early for Liverpool to worry? title: Harry Styles funds free coffee at two London cafes
description: The singer funded free coffees for customers at Kaffeine's two central London cafes on Saturday.
body: Owner Peter Dore-Smith said his coffee shops were a "favourite" of Harry Styles Harry Styles bought coffees for all of the visitors to his "favourite" London coffee shop to celebrate the extension of his record-breaking Together, Together tour. The singer funded free coffees for all of the customers at Kaffeine's two central London cafes on Saturday through promoter Live Nation. Owner Peter Dore-Smith said he was not allowed to promote the free drinks on social media, but could tell customers that they had been bought by Together, Together, the name of the artist's tour. Last week Styles announced three additional dates at Wembley Stadium on 25, 27 and 28 August 2027. Customers were told their drinks had been paid for by Together, Together Dore-Smith said he was told by Live Nation that his company was chosen as Styles' "favourite coffee shop", but the free drinks could not be promoted beforehand. The owner said Styles covered the usual Saturday takings at both sites on Eastcastle Street and Great Titchfield Street and also added a buffer to ensure all drinks could be paid for. Dore-Smith said that the star had visited his Eastcastle Street coffee shop "a couple of years ago", and that they put his song lyrics on their blackboard during his last concerts in London. On the day of the giveaway, Dore-Smith said they placed posters in the window and put Together, Together tour stickers provided by the promoter on every cup of coffee they sold. Styles' music played in the shops and staff wore ties to "dress up" like the artist, who often performs wearing the accessory. "We put extra staff on, and on the day people just rocked up as normal," Dore-Smith said. When customers asked why their drink was free, his staff told them "because Harry Styles is buying everyone's coffee today," he said. He added: "I know they've done it with a florist before, and I think they've done it with an ice cream parlour before." Live Nation declined to comment. title: 'Don't be silly' over Falklands and Irish unity, top Tory tells Trump
description: Shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat says the US president's recent comments were aimed at US voters, in a BBC interview.
body: Tom Tugendhat was appointed Tory shadow foreign secretary earlier this month The shadow foreign secretary has told Donald Trump "don't be silly" over his comments on the UK's sovereignty of the Falkland Islands and Irish reunification. Conservative MP Tom Tugendhat said the US president was trying to appeal to voters at home by making comments about the British overseas territory in the Atlantic Ocean and saying he would "love" to see a united Ireland. Trump has said America's position on the Falklands is "one of many" under review, and hinted he would not help the UK in any potential future conflict with Argentina. And the US president said on a visit to Ireland last week that Irish reunification was "going to happen eventually" and it would be a "great thing". Britain and Argentina still dispute the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands, four decades on from an armed conflict there which the UK won. Argentina's president heightened tensions with the UK over the Falkland Islands earlier this month, saying in a presidential address that "winds of change" favoured his country's claim to the islands. He warned he will impose economic sanctions on firms which exploit oil nearby. In response, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the UK's position on the islands was "unwavering", and they would remain British as "that is the overwhelming position of the Islanders." And Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has hit back strongly over the issue, insisting "the Falkland Islands are British" and that Britain's continued connection with them "is of vital importance". But Tugendhat, the Tory MP for Tonbridge in Kent who Badenoch appointed her shadow foreign secretary in a reshuffle earlier this month, has suggested Trump does not mean it. "What he's doing is he's bumping his gums on some issues that he thinks are supportive to various electoral issues for himself at home," he told Nick Robinson on Political Thinking. "He's got elections coming up in November, he knows he's got votes to win. "Is it helpful to us? No. But this is his politics, not ours. So sometimes we have to say something and sometimes we have to go, 'come on mate, don't be silly'." Political Thinking with Nick Robinson Nick Robinson has a conversation with, not an interrogation of, the people who shape our political thinking about what shaped theirs. Tugendhat explained that Britain's military capability in the Falklands is radically different from in 1982, when the UK and Argentina fought for 74 days over the territory, with the UK Foreign Office not negotiating to give the islands up in recent years. And asked about Trump saying he would "love to see" Irish reunification on a recent trip there, Tugendhat branded this "plain old electioneering," ahead of US mid-term elections in November. "Is he going to do anything about it? No," he added. Elsewhere in his interview, Tugendhat revealed he had received no confirmation from China that the country's sanctions against him had been dropped. This is despite then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer announcing they had been in January. He said he would only visit China, whose communist regime he has long criticised, if there was something relevant and worth discussing - but he feels talks can be held elsewhere at the moment. He also said Miliband should have waited rather than showing "weakness" after the UK sanctioned illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. And he ruled out bringing Britain back into the European Union if in government, despite his close personal ties to the continent including his French wife who was influential in the recent Bayeux Tapestry exchange. Having run against Badenoch for Tory leader in 2022, he praised her performance as leader so far - saying her hoping to be Britain's next prime minister was a weight off his own shoulders. title: Twenty women had breasts removed unnecessarily during cancer treatment, NHS trust admits
description: The women were among hundreds who were harmed by their treatment at County Durham health trust.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Denise (pictured), Pam and other women describe how they were failed Twenty women underwent mastectomies unnecessarily while being treated for breast cancer, an NHS trust in north-east England has told the BBC. They were among hundreds of patients who came to harm during treatment at the breast unit of the County Durham and Darlington Foundation Trust (CDDFT). The admission comes in the wake of revelations about serious failures in the unit, as reported by the BBC last year. Steve Russell, who has recently taken over as CDDFT's chief executive, says he apologises "unreservedly" for the harm the trust caused. "There are no words I could use to convey how personally distressed I am," he says. "What happened was utterly unacceptable." This video can not be played Watch: Steve Russell offers an apology to women affected by CDDFT failures Dozens of affected women and their families contacted us following our earlier reporting. Patients described the shock they had felt on being told a mastectomy (the removal of all or part of a breast) could have been avoided, as well as the psychological and physical pain that many still live with. We also met former patients who have come together to support each other and call for a public inquiry. CDDFT is now carrying out an internal review of breast cancer cases between January 2023 and February 2025, alongside the cases of 640 former patients who contacted a dedicated helpline. Of 514 cases reviewed by the trust so far, 315 patients have been found to have suffered harm, including 77 who were significantly harmed. One patient is known to have died. Cases have also been identified where cancer diagnoses were missed or delayed. Some of these patients subsequently saw their cancer spread, says Russell. The BBC understands a decision is imminent on whether to extend the scope of the review, and look at cases dating back to 2015. This could mean the re-opening of up to 10,000 medical records. The National Crime Agency says it is now working with Durham Police to investigate allegations by former patients and determine if any criminal offences have taken place. Breast Cancer Scandal: Exposing The Harm BBC health correspondent Sharon Barbour investigates a deepening breast cancer scandal in County Durham and hears from women whose mastectomies were unnecessary. Watch on BBC iPlayer now or on BBC NE & Cumbria at 19:30 on Friday 18 October Denise Howarth is one of several women who have now been told by the NHS that their breast was removed unnecessarily. "I was just in shock, then ended up in tears on the phone," says the 51-year-old from Consett, County Durham. Denise had been diagnosed with grade 1 (slow growing) cancer in 2023 after discovering a lump in her breast. She initially underwent a lumpectomy, then a mastectomy, as well as eight rounds of chemotherapy and radiotherapy. The call she received from the NHS in September 2025 was quickly followed by a letter from CDDFT. It said that Denise could have been offered a second lumpectomy rather than full breast removal, but acknowledged the option had never been discussed with her. She says the apology was "all good and well" but will not bring her breast back. Jo (not her real name) contacted the trust's helpline about a mastectomy she had undergone in 2021. The former NHS worker says she was told, in a phone call earlier this year, that the procedure could have been avoided. Jo says the trust's mistakes were "absolutely unforgivable" Jo says she had trusted the people she considered colleagues to do the best for her. "You go to work to do your best, don't you?" she says. "So why would I think that anybody else wouldn't?" She now says she feels "mutilated" by what happened to her, and feels the mistakes made by the trust were "absolutely unforgivable". The consultant overseeing Jo and Denise's care was Mr Amir Bhatti, who was CDDFT's clinical lead for breast services from 2013-24. He has now been suspended from carrying out clinical practice but is still employed by the trust on full pay. Last year, we reported that nearly £6m had been paid by the trust over six years to breast cancer diagnostic clinics and surgery companies run privately by Bhatti. Concern about this arrangement was raised in a 2025 review into the running of the trust, external, carried out by governance specialist Mary Aubrey, She said outsourcing patient appointments had created financial incentives which were potentially "a risk to clinical standards". Payment per service is not uncommon in healthcare, Russell argues, although he tells us the trust has now ended this arrangement for breast cancer services. "We recognise there was a conflict of interest that wasn't managed properly," he says. Pam says she felt "butchered" by her breast removal operation Pam Brown from Durham was an NHS patient who underwent a mastectomy in 2022 at Spire Hospital in Washington, where one of the outsourced private clinics was based. As with Denise and Jo, Pam does not know who carried out her operation. Bhatti was the consultant overseeing the care of all three women. As far as Pam knows, her mastectomy was necessary. But the scars left behind - both physical and psychological - have deeply affected her. We have shown photographs of Pam's scarring to Liz O'Riordan, a former breast cancer surgeon. She describes them as "awful" and says she has never seen anything like it: "That's not acceptable at all. I'd have brought her back for revision surgery." Concerns were also raised last year in a report by the Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) that breast cancer cases had not been discussed properly in multi-disciplinary team meetings (MDTs). These meetings are designed to ensure treatment plans are reviewed and challenged by surgeons, radiologists, pathologists and cancer specialists - before major decisions, such as mastectomies, are made. title: UK's 'dismal' Eurovision song choices to be examined by MPs
description: It comes after the UK's entry Look Mum No Computer came last in May's final, scoring just one point.
body: Sam Battle, performing as Look Mum No Computer, finished in last place at the 2026 Eurovision Song Contest with one point for his song "Eins, Zwei, Drei" The UK's "dismal" record in selecting songs and acts for Eurovision is to be scrutinised by MPs. In May, Look Mum No Computer came last with one point. In 2023 Mae Muller finished second from bottom and in 2021 James Newman came last - this time with "nul points". The act that represents the UK is selected by the BBC, sometimes with a record label or music management company. The chair of the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport committee, Dame Caroline Dinenage, said: "We want to get to the bottom of who chooses our entrant, on what basis and whether our dismal record of achievement in recent years [Sam Ryder to one side] is the result of bad song choice, weak performance... or something else". James Newman came last with song Embers, scoring "nul points" in 2021 It's expected that figures from the BBC, as well as music industry experts, will be called to give evidence to the committee of cross-party MPs at a hearing that will be held "over the coming months". The committee is also likely to receive relevant written submissions. Although the UK has, over the years, produced some of the world's most successful artists, that kind of success has rarely been repeated at Eurovision. Over the past 15 years, the UK has only come higher than 15th place on one occasion - when Sam Ryder came second with his song Space Man in 2022. He was beaten by Ukraine's Kalush Orchestra. And next year's event, being held in Burgas in Bulgaria, will mark 30 years since the UK last won the contest, when Katrina and the Waves scored 227 points with their song Love Shine A Light. Many countries choose their entry through a publicly televised selection process. The last time this was done in the UK was with the show Eurovision: You Decide in 2019. Michael Rice was selected, but went on to come last at the contest in Tel Aviv, Israel. Success story Sam Ryder finished second at Eurovision 2022... ... while Katrina and the Waves were the last UK act to win Eurovision, in 1997 The MPs' hearing will be part of the committee's State of Play inquiry, where members of the public or others can request an evidence session to be held into a particular subject that interests or concerns them. Dame Caroline told BBC News: "This application interested us because of the UK's reputation for scoring 'nul points', coming bottom, or close to bottom in recent years at Eurovision, despite having world-class song writers and musicians." The Eurovision final has consistently been one of the UK's most popular music events, with millions staying up late to watch the final result. No time frame for the select committee hearing has been set yet, but once all the evidence has been examined, it's expected that the committee may produce a short report containing recommendations to the BBC. title: Japan raises interest rate to new 31-year high to curb rising prices
description: Central banks around the world have hiked rates as high energy prices are pushing up inflation.
body: The Bank of Japan has been raising the rate since 2024, when it stood at minus 0.1% Japan's central bank has raised its main interest rate to a fresh 31-year high as it continues to move away from decades of ultra-low borrowing costs and as the country faces increasing economic pressures. On Friday, the Bank of Japan (BOJ) increased the rate to 1.25% from 1% - a level not seen since 1995. It comes as major central banks around the world are hiking rates as higher energy prices caused by the Iran war are helping to push up inflation. On Wednesday, the US Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate for the first time in over three years, while the European Central Bank also increased its borrowing costs earlier this month. The BOJ has been raising the rate since 2024, when it stood at minus 0.1%. It has now hiked rates six times in the last two and a half years. Since then the bank has been steadily putting up the rate as it tries to reach a level similar to other major economies. When a central bank raises rates, the country's currency usually becomes stronger as it makes the it more attractive to traders. Japan is facing several economic challenges including a persistently weak yen, rising prices and a shrinking workforce. Official figures published on Friday ahead of the BOJ announcement showed that inflation eased slightly last month. Core inflation fell to 1.7% in August from 1.8% the previous month but remains close to the bank's 2% target level. While Japan's inflation rate is not high by international standards, rising prices are a relatively new development in the economy. Until recently the country had experienced very low inflation or deflation - falling prices - for around three decades. Global oil and gas prices have risen this year as the Iran war caused major disruptions to shipments through the key Strait of Hormuz shipping route. Japan is particularly vulnerable to those supply interruptions as it is heavily reliant on energy from the Middle East. The country's currency has also been under pressure in recent months. In August, Tokyo and Washington confirmed that they had jointly intervened to halt a slide in the yen after it fell to a fresh 40-year low. The coordinated intervention was the first since 2011, when both countries took action together to weaken the yen after the devastating earthquake and tsunami that hit eastern Japan. Both Japan's Ministry of Finance and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said at the time that they would not hesitate to conduct more joint interventions in the future. Bessent has also been ramping up pressure on the BOJ to raise interest rates to help support the yen, calling on its Governor Kazuo Ueda to "do the right thing". title: British woman rescued in Malawi shootout that left four suspected kidnappers dead
description: Police exchanged fire with the suspected kidnappers, who were armed with an AK-47 rifle and a pistol.
body: Nusrat Osman was taken to hospital for treatment after the rescue A British woman who was kidnapped in Malawi nearly a week ago has been rescued in a police operation that left four suspected kidnappers dead and a senior police chief wounded. Nusrat Osman, 47, was freed on Thursday during an operation on the outskirts of the southern city of Blantyre, police said. Officers exchanged gunfire with the suspected kidnappers, who police said were armed with an AK-47 rifle and a pistol. "The criminals got shot and were rushed to the hospital where they succumbed to the injuries," the Malawi Police Service said in a statement. Deputy Inspector General of Police Noel Kayira, who was involved in the operation, also sustained gunshot injuries and is being treated in hospital. The police statement said he was in a stable condition. Osman was reunited with her family following the rescue and was also taken to hospital for treatment, and for physical and mental health assessments, local media reported. Police have not identified the four suspected kidnappers who were killed and have not provided further details about how officers located the group. Osman was abducted by four unidentified men in Blantyre's Mount Pleasant neighbourhood on 11 September. Police said she had been driving home when the men blocked her vehicle, forced her into another car and drove away. Her disappearance prompted a major search operation, with authorities offering a reward of 30 million Malawian kwacha ($17,000; £12,500) for information leading to her rescue and the arrest and conviction of those responsible. Osman, who is from Leicester in the UK, has lived in Malawi for several years and works for an auditing firm. She is married and has two young children. The UK Foreign Office earlier told the BBC that it was aware of reports that a British national had been abducted in Malawi and was in touch with local authorities. The case had puzzled investigators because police said there had been no known ransom demand or communication from the kidnappers following her disappearance. Her family had made emotional public appeals for her safe return, describing the disappearance as deeply distressing and urging anyone with information to contact police. The kidnapping also caused concern among Malawi's business community and British nationals living in the southern African country, where abductions of foreign nationals are relatively uncommon. Police have not disclosed a possible motive or said whether they believe other people were involved. They said investigations were continuing to establish the full circumstances surrounding the kidnapping and the subsequent rescue operation. Authorities have urged the public to remain calm while the investigation continues. Go to BBCAfrica.com, external for more news from the African continent. title: See tiny organisms on show in microscopic video competition
description: The winning video features tiny hair-like structures, called cilia, in the airways of a child with a rare genetic disease.
body: This video can not be played Nikon's annual Small World In Motion competition is open to anyone around the world with an interest in film or time-lapse photography through a microscope. This year's winning video was magnified to 100 times in size, and featured tiny hair-like structures, called cilia, in the airways of a child with a rare genetic disease. It was submitted by Dr Ning Xu, a researcher at Tsinghua University in China, who used a series of complicated light waves to illuminate different parts of the sample in colour. Runners up in the competition included videos of a roundworm encountering a single-celled organism and microscopic jellyfish larvae suspended in droplets of water. Clips of bioluminescent algae and a tiny sea slug were among the highly commended. See tiny organisms on show in microscopic video competition. title: Why US plan to sell F-35 warplanes to Saudi Arabia is controversial
description: Saudi Arabia has lobbied the US for years to buy F35s, the world's most advanced fighter jet.
body: President Trump and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in the Oval Office President Donald Trump's administration says it has approved the sale of nearly 50 F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia in a policy shift for the US that has raised concerns from some members of Congress. Saudi Arabia has sought for years to buy the world's most advanced warplane, equipped with stealth technology that allows it to evade enemy detection. Washington had resisted, partly because it supplies F-35s to its ally Israel, which is guaranteed under US law to receive top-of-the-range American weapons compared with those its regional neighbours can access. Congress has 30 days to scrutinise or attempt to block the $24bn (£17.8bn) sale to Riyadh, which is the largest customer for US weapons. A US Air Force F-35 Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois, a Democrat, opposed the sale on Thursday. He warned "it could put the crown jewels of American military technology within reach of the Chinese Communist Party". Other Democratic lawmakers and some American defence officials have raised similar concerns about giving F-35s to Saudi Arabia. They said Riyadh might share the sensitive technology with China under a security partnership between the two countries. The state department said in announcing the deal on Thursday that it would support US "foreign policy and national security objectives". It said the deal would improve "the security of a major non-Nato ally that is a force for political stability and economic progress in the Gulf region". "The proposed ⁠sale of this equipment and support will not alter the military ⁠balance in the region," the state department added. Trump has a close relationship with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who visited the White House last November. The two also met in May last year in Riyadh, where a $142bn arms sale was sealed – described by the White House as the "largest defence sales agreement in history". The latest proposed sale announced to Saudi Arabia would include 48 F-35s, which are built by the arms company Lockheed Martin. This would place the country on a level with Israel, which currently has a fleet of 50 jets. However, Israel's ministry of foreign affairs announced in May, external that it would procure another F-35 squadron. This deal would double the size of Israel's F-35 fleet to 100, according to the Jerusalem Post, external. Just one of Lockheed Martin's F-35A jets costs about $82.5m. Congress has previously questioned arms deals with Riyadh after the murder of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi in 2018. Former US President Joe Biden's administration considered supplying F-35s to Saudi Arabia if Riyadh would normalise its ⁠relations with Israel, but that diplomatic effort faltered. The proposed sale comes as the Saudis are engaged in fighting with the Houthis, an Iran-backed armed group that controls much of western Yemen. The Houthis have recently seized control of swathes of Yemen's Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed pro-government forces. The Saudi crown prince has personally pressed Trump to take military action against the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News, the BBC's US media partner. But Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, the sources said. title: Zara Larsson criticises White House for using her song in deportation video
description: The White House removed Larsson's Midnight Sun from one of its reels after the artist called the clip "dehumanising".
body: Larsson accuses the White House of using her song to promote "dehumanising" messages Swedish pop star Zara Larsson has condemned the White House for using one of her most recognisable songs in a social media reel. The clip used Larsson's Midnight Sun in a video appearing to show immigration enforcement raids. The song has since been removed from the post, but the video is still visible on the White House's TikTok feed. The video is captioned "never ending deportations", riffing on Larsson's lyrics "never-ending midnight sun". In a three-minute reaction video posted on social media, Larsson described the clip as "dehumanising", joining a growing list of singers, including Sabrina Carpenter and Ariana Grande, who have told the Trump administration to not use their music. The BBC has contacted the White House for comment. The reel splices together multiple videos of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, as well as other US law enforcement personnel, handcuffing men and putting them into vehicles. Larsson reposted part of the original clip, which then cuts to a selfie video of her using her fingers to hold an 'L' shape against her forehead. In the reaction video that has already clocked up more than 4.2 million views on TikTok, she tells her followers the White House video is "so dehumanising". Larsson continues: "These people in this video – they're real people." "The vast majority of these people who are undocumented are regular people with jobs and they're just trying to have a better future". "It's so crazy how everything is so memefied and so 'ha-ha-ha'," she says, accusing the White House of using her song to sow "division", despite the lyrics reflecting a connection between people and nature, according to Larsson. Earlier this year, Larsson condemned a video of President Donald Trump dancing at various events overlayed with her hit Lush Life. White House social media accounts have been forced to remove various songs from their feed following interventions from artists. Taylor Swift's seasonal track August disappeared from a reel shared by the Trump administration in August, while one of Olivia Rodrigo's songs vanished from a video after the singer condemned its use for what she called "hateful propaganda". Sabrina Carpenter and Ariana Grande have also warned the Trump administration in separate incidents to not use their music in social media content after the White House posted videos featuring their songs. title: US fans with Ed Sheeran tickets left 'torn' over Macklemore controversy
description: With Sheeran's next gig this weekend, some ticket holders said they were in two minds about going.
body: This video can not be played Ed Sheeran's tour in 'damage control mode' after Macklemore backlash The snowballing controversy over pro-Palestinian rapper Macklemore being dropped as a support act for Ed Sheeran has plunged the tour into crisis and left concert-goers in the middle of the fraught Israel-Gaza debate. Fans who spoke to the BBC - including those who have tickets to see Sheeran's next show - have been split since Macklemore was dropped from the Loop Tour this week after his "free Palestine" protest on stage. All of Sheeran's opening acts have since quit in solidarity. "I'm still torn," Damien Given told the BBC on whether he would attend Sheeran's show on Saturday, calling the artist's response disingenuous. Another fan called it a "no-win situation". Since the controversy blew up earlier this week, ticket prices, external for his remaining shows in the US, Mexico and South America have dropped, as calls for boycotts spread. Sheeran has responded, saying he's been "appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine", but would not be drawn into a political debate. He argued that "those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum" and stressed he was not responsible for Macklemore being removed from the tour. Still, the backlash has come from all sides. Some are upset Sheeran's tour is continuing without all the listed acts and they want refunds. It's no longer the show they paid for, they said. Given, who is from Northern Ireland, said he's felt in two minds over the tickets he has on Saturday to see the show in Philadelphia. It will mark Sheeran's first time back on stage since the controversy spiralled. Given said he's felt that Macklemore was treated "very, very wrong" and thought Sheeran was not being transparent with fans. "[Sheeran] said he was in support of Ukraine when the Ukraine-Russia war started," said Given. "You can't just say now suddenly, 'I'm not political.'" Damien Given and his wife, Kellie, danced to one of Sheeran's songs at their wedding But he explained the poignant connection he's felt to Sheeran's music that has drawn him to Saturday's show. The singer's hit Thinking Out Loud was the first dance at Given's wedding. "When she danced," Given, 52, said, recalling the moment with his bride, "the first words of the song were, 'When your legs don't work like they used to before.'" His wife, Kellie, had been diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and could barely walk. She died four years later, in 2024. Given said if it wasn't for "that connection, I would absolutely" not be attending, but "I'm probably leaning towards going". Fellow fan Patti Ann has felt less conflicted over the backlash and instead said Sheeran was in a "no-win situation". "I back [Sheeran] 100% for his decision," she said. "I feel like he has an obligation and a contract with his venues, and sometimes, financially, you can't get out of those types of things." Ann, who has been a Sheeran fan for years, said she thinks a concert venue is not the place for politics. Believe what you want, she said, "just don't press it on me". She still plans to attend his show in Atlanta, Georgia, in October. Heather Park is worried some shows might be cancelled Matt Jaye, a Jewish-American from Florida, said he was outraged watching Macklemore's comments on a New Jersey stage earlier this month in support of Palestine. He contacted Ticketmaster and asked for a refund for tickets he has to Sheeran's November show in Tampa, Florida. His request was denied, which he said was "pretty upsetting". His mood changed, though, after Macklemore was removed from Sheeran's line-up. "I'm not in favour of a one-sided presentation of things from an artist," Jaye, 48, said. "That's not why I'm going to the concert." Jaye said he believed Sheeran bore some culpability for Macklemore's pro-Palestinian protest. "If [Sheeran's] saying that he's apolitical, I would expect him to maintain those same standards for the artists that he's bringing on," he said. "I don't think he handled it in the best way possible." He added that he would have liked Sheeran to issue an apology to the Jewish community for making part of his audience "very uncomfortable". Some fans are worried what will become of the tour by the time Sheeran is set to play in their city. Heather Park, who has tickets this weekend, said she's worried some shows might be cancelled. "My main thing was to go see Ed Sheeran," she said. "Macklemore was just a bonus." While Park, 49, believes Macklemore's ouster was unfair and a violation of free speech, she said she's mostly unbothered by the drama and prefers to separate the artist from the art. "I still like the music," she says.
