title: Sunshine to return to parts of UK with warmer and drier weather on way
description: High pressure over the UK next week will bring a break from the wet and windy weather so far this month.
body: Don't pack away your summer clothes just yet as warmer and drier weather could be set to return to the UK next week. Temperatures could reach as high as 25C in parts of England and Wales - several degrees above the average for the time of year. Forecasts for early next week show an area of high pressure building near the UK. This will largely block Atlantic weather systems, which often bring wind and rain, from reaching the country. North-west Scotland will see some rain but these systems are not expected to push across the rest of the UK, so this would mean drier weather with lighter winds and higher daytime temperatures for most. The last few weeks have been very changeable with rain and strong winds in most parts of the UK. Despite this, the whole of Wales and most of England are still in drought. After stronger south-westerly winds are due to blow cloud and outbreaks of rain across from the west on Friday, the weather will start to settle down over the weekend. The northern half of the UK will see a return to sunshine and blustery showers on Saturday, with most of the showers being in Scotland. The southern half of the UK is likely to be more cloudy and have a muggy feel with the chance of light rain and drizzle. A photo shared by a BBC Weather Watcher At least seven months of relentless rain needed to end drought, research shows This rain will clear to the south on Sunday and most places will then be dry with sunny spells. West to north-west winds will still be strong in Scotland. Temperatures will peak around 22C in southern England on Sunday - nothing out of the ordinary for the time of year. But as we go into the working week, an area of high pressure will arrive, bringing drier weather, lighter winds, and some sunshine, which for much of the country could last throughout the week. While there will still be the chance of catching the odd shower, most places will be dry. Rain-bearing bands of cloud coming in from the Atlantic will be restricted to north-west Scotland. The past week has felt quite chilly but temperatures next week are forecast to reach 20C in Scotland and Northern Ireland, and as high as 25C in England and Wales. This is some way off the UK's September temperature record, though, which stands at 35.6C, set in 1906 at Bawtry in South Yorkshire. An area of high pressure will block Atlantic weather fronts from reaching most of the UK Autumn is often a time of wild swings in the weather. This upcoming quieter spell in the UK is not influenced by the record-breaking Pacific Ocean warming from El Niño, but there could be impacts later in the autumn. The Met Office long range forecast shows a higher degree of confidence that deeper areas of low pressure will affect the UK in November, potentially bringing stormy weather. This is consistent with weather patterns during El Niño events at this time of year. But no two El Niños are the same - so, while it may increase the chance of certain types of weather occurring, this is not guaranteed. Keep up to date with the forecast where you are on the BBC Weather website and app. Stormy autumn, cold winter - how might El Niño affect the UK weather? title: Not just 'Nice Guy Eddie': Lib Dems eager for leader to show radical side at party conference
description: There is a sizeable group of Lib Dem MPs who openly question whether the party's problem is with its leader, while others support his stance.
body: Discontent bubbles not far from the surface as the Liberal Democrats gather for their conference this weekend. Two years on from their best ever general election result, conversations with those on the party's frontbench, its MPs, and backroom staff reveal a frustration at what many see as a failure to capitalise on that success. Polling by YouGov in the build up to the conference highlighted the Lib Dems "have seen no real growth in support since the last general election" and if anything have slipped back. "We lack the ability to say something new or interesting," said one senior Lib Dem MP. "There is no energy, no excitement." A frontbencher said: "With the possible exception of our position on Trump, you could characterise most of our press lines as 'a Lib Dem spokesperson said, steady on now, gently does it'." Others describe the party's approach as "boring" and are spooked by the rise of the Green Party under Zack Polanski. The party's leadership are aware of the anger. They insist this conference will be a "gear shift". Daisy Cooper, the deputy leader, told me it would be "a gloves-off kind of conference". "You'll see a bit of fighting talk," she said. Some of the caution until now has been deliberate. The party's leadership met over the last few months and discussed whether to copy Polanski's punchy, social media-focused style but decided it wouldn't appeal to the well-heeled areas of southern England that form the Lib Dem heartlands. Those involved in that decision point to Polanski's recent struggles and feel vindicated. But at all levels of the party there is an acknowledgement they lag behind other parties on grabbing attention on social media, highlighted by Andy Burnham's "social first" approach. The party has only recently rolled out training for its MPs on making social videos, something senior figures despair at. "When we have a success we're very good at getting a leaflet sent out to supporters straight away," one senior MP said. "But we don't do that for socials." Digital and social media will be a focus of at least 17 fringe events at conference, as the party tries to improve its online communications. But others worry that social media is just the medium and the problem is with the message. One MP raised the majority of voters (52% according to YouGov,) who view the party as "weak" in recent polling; and the tendency to say it's unclear what the party stands for (43% believing the party was weak, to 18% thinking it was strong). "We need to become bolder and more radical," a senior MP added. "We need to be angry on behalf of our constituents." Another Lib Dem MP said: "We are stuck fighting the guerilla politics of local campaigning. There is no broader articulation of what a vision for Liberal Britain is." Even those most loyal to Davey admit the party was struggling to offer a clear and coherent message. The Lib Dems' success at the last general election was, the party's own strategists believe, because voters wanted to remove the Conservatives and the Lib Dems benefitted from that anti-Tory sentiment. "We haven't yet answered why people should vote for us rather than against the Tories," admitted one senior advisor. In public, Lib Dem MPs are often coy about the possibility of a coalition government with Labour after the election. In private, there are no such reservations. In an election many think could produce a hung parliament with no party in overall majority, the Lib Dem ambition is to be kingmakers to block a Reform government. "If you're a serious political party you exist to be in government," the same senior adviser said. Lib Dem strategists are confident they can retain most of the 72 seats they won in 2024. Their sights now are on the 27 others where they came second, most of which were won by the Conservatives. The party made gains in the May local elections in England The party's leadership characterise the last two years since the general election as "stage one" when a largely new intake of MPs bedded into their constituencies. "Stage two is winning the air war and describing exactly what Liberal Britain looks like. You'll see a lot of that at conference," said Cooper. Of her boss, party leader Sir Ed, she said: "He's not just nice guy Eddie. I think you're going to see him being a bit more gritty because he's a real fighter." She added Davey saw the battle with Reform UK as the "fight of our lives". Critics within the party point out that promise of fighting talk to take on Reform UK accompanied the last Lib Dem conference. Yet little has changed in the party's national standings. Join EU migration pact to tackle small boats, says Ed Davey Change voting system before next election, Davey urges Burnham Lib Dems offer alternative to extremes of Reform and Greens, Davey says There is a sizeable group of Lib Dem MPs, and members of its frontbench, who openly question whether their problem is not with the message, nor the strategy, but with Davey, the leader. "I think he's holding us back," said one of the party's spokespeople who is planning a tilt at the leadership if a race is triggered. "The atmosphere is ripe for a leadership challenge," another MP, talking of the frustrations in the party, said. "But we don't have a Wes Streeting," they added, referring to Labour's defence secretary whose challenge to Sir Keir Starmer undermined his leadership. "There is a lack of an ambitious, young alternative putting themselves out there to show a different way." Davey's supporters in the party point to his experience of government and insist there is no one better to replace him. They also dismiss national polling as the way to measure the Lib Dem's standing. "I'd like to be on more than 10% [in national opinion polls]," one frontbencher loyal to Davey said. title: Badenoch says she is bringing in lawyers to challenge government after Tory-run council's 94% tax hike
description: A row is growing over Wandsworth Council's rise, which the local authority is blaming on government funding cuts.
body: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has said she has brought in lawyers to challenge the government over local funding cuts, after a record council tax rise in one of her party's flagship local authorities. She told BBC Newsnight the proposed 94% hike in Wandsworth, a south-west London borough run by the Tories, was "outrageous". Badenoch said the Conservative Party had "instructed lawyers" to explore if an £84m-a-year government funding cut, which Wandsworth Council has blamed for the increase, can be blocked. The government has insisted it needs to reform the "outdated" council funding system to move money to where it is most needed. Wandsworth has long had one of the lowest council tax rates in the country, with an average Band D property currently paying just over £1,000, compared to above £2,000 in an increasing number of London boroughs. But this would nearly double with the planned £958 rise - half of which is set by the council and the other half the mayor of London. There has been heavy criticism since the move was announced in a council meeting on Tuesday. A final decision is to be made early next year. Commenting for the first time on the row, Badenoch accused ministers of seemingly "taking money from areas that don't vote Labour and giving it to places that do vote Labour". "I think it is outrageous that Wandsworth Council is having to put up council tax. "But they're not doing it because they want to. It is because the government has taken away 40% of their funding. "So we have actually instructed lawyers, as the Conservative Party, to see if we can challenge the government on this decision." Kemi Badenoch on BBC Newsnight Watch the full interview on a range of topics on Newsnight's new primetime Friday evening edition. 19:00 BST on BBC Two Pressed by presenter Matt Chorley on how the rise will still mean Wandsworth's council tax is lower than many councils across the country, Badenoch said it would still worry some families. "I think if you suddenly have a nearly 100% increase in your council tax, you would be extremely worried. Families have budgets," she said. "Just because on average it's lower than somewhere else doesn't mean that people are going to be able to afford it." She refused to say what alternative rate of increase she would propose, but questioned why a 40% cut was being imposed on the council when "Andy Burnham has not found 40% of anything to cut" himself. She also defended her record as local government minister when the Tories were in Downing Street, despite Conservative governments having slashed some council grants. Other London councils including Westminster, Richmond and Kensington and Chelsea are considering joining Wandsworth in using the Sustainable Communities Act to challenge government funding cuts. As a result of the central government cuts, the usual cap of 5% annual council tax rises was lifted for all these councils as well as Windsor and Maidenhead in Berkshire. Wandsworth Council's Tory deputy leader said on Tuesday: "Higher council tax will not be easy or welcome. We do not regard it as fair and will continue to challenge the government by every possible means." Leader of the opposition, Labour councillor Simon Hogg, said: "It's outrageous, it is stunning. People who don't know how to run the council panicking and making you pay the price. "This increase is unfair, it's unnecessary and we oppose it." However, the PoliticsHome website reported, external that three Labour MPs in Wandsworth - Rosena Allin-Khan, Fleur Anderson and Marsha de Cordova - have refused to back the council's appeal to the government to stop the funding cuts. The three Labour MPs claimed the council "was in a strong financial position" before the Tories took over at the May elections earlier this year. In a statement when the council tax rise was announced, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said: "Local authorities decide the level of council tax they wish to set, but we are clear that in doing so they should put taxpayers first. "We're fixing an outdated funding system so funding goes where need is greatest, while protecting councils through the transition and ensuring no area faces a cliff edge." title: Leaden, stale, disheartening - where do Celtic & O'Neill go from here?
description: After another defeat, keeping the faith is surely becoming more testing for Celtic's fans, writes Tom English.
body: To Celtic fans it might seem like sacrilege to doubt Martin O'Neill's capacity to get them through whatever it is they're going through right now - a slump or something deeper - but keeping the faith is surely becoming testing. After their shellacking at Ibrox on Sunday, Celtic's response against Ferencvaros was another heavy defeat and three more goals conceded. More absent-minded stuff in the midfield, more loose defending, more negativity and lack of accuracy on the ball, no great grasp of the basics of pass and move, not enough intensity, not enough work-rate, not enough of anything that you need to give yourself a chance. At times, as it meandered along at 3-1 to Ferencvaros, Celtic tried to stage some kind of gallop but their attempts were from distance, hopeful efforts rather than anything built on the back of coherence and pressing and speed. Celtic at their best - in the finest days under Ange Postecoglou - were all about aggression and ingenuity, about dynamism and risk-taking, about pace and belief and pulling defenders into places where they did not want to be. This is a poor imitation. Fragile Celtic beaten by Ferencvaros in Europa League opener Celtic are 'little bit broken' - but is change of shape 'worth risking'? Reaction, analysis & have your say on Celtic's defeat Things can turn quickly in Scottish football. The second act of this season's Old Firm show on Sunday is still a hard one to call, partly because it's at Celtic Park and also because there surely has to be some kind of response from O'Neill's team to their pitiful fate at Ibrox last weekend. Their fans will be worried, though. Five goals given up against LASK, a desperate experience at Ibrox - and now this. In moments on Thursday, some of their football was reminiscent of darker days - the failures of Cluj and Copenhagen in 2019 and 2020, when Bayo and Bolingoli were in the building; Sparta Prague in 2020, when Klimala and Ajeti, Duffy and Laxalt were in the team. It was all very Legia Warsaw, very Salzburg, very Maribor. The energy levels were low, the booing was loud and the feeling of a side with no answers was unmissable. In the aftermath, O'Neill spoke about frustration, failure and psychological damage, how low moments like these hit you hard and test your resolve. He promised to "get ourselves together" for Rangers on Sunday but his tone was flat and a touch tired. He outlined some of the ways in which Celtic were deficient on the night but didn't talk with the spirit of a man who had answers. In many ways his post-match comments mirrored his team's performance - leaden, stale, disheartening. O'Neill has fixed many problems over the years, not just in his first trophy-laden spell but in his return to chaos last season. He restored order and confidence, two things that have been lost. The force of his personality gave Celtic fight. They were not always pretty to watch but they were ferociously hard to beat. Nobody managed it on the title run-in. That kind of never-say-die only seems like yesterday, but in other ways it feels like an awfully long time ago. They had a decent start against Ferencvaros, then conceded a soft goal. They hauled themselves back into it with a little glimpse of quality, but then fell back into destructive ways. Safe passes, little zeal, only a modicum of fire and emotion. The goal they conceded just before the break was the type of goal that poor sides give away. Hesitancy in the first instance to fight for the loose ball, weakness in the second instance when trying to prevent the cross and then defensive disorganisation and bewilderment in the end. Celtic had 62.5% possession in the opening half but trailed 2-1. Camilo Duran, playing through the middle ahead of Kasper Hogh, had eight touches of the ball. Duran was in his favoured position but offered little. A player who showed such zest and love of his new life in Glasgow only a few short weeks ago is looking a shadow of himself. Hogh, with goals against Manchester City (two), Atletico Madrid, Inter Milan, Sporting, Porto, Jagiellonia and Olympiacos (three) for Bodo Glimt, has morphed into an awkward looking centre-forward with a poor first touch and no chances to feed on. He has now scored in just one of his eight games as a Celtic player. O'Neill has so far failed to get the best out of a player the club paid £11m for. This video can not be played Callum McGregor, the great totem, is looking a little lost. O'Neill has all the nous in the world to arrest this, but he needs to do it quickly. It has to be said, he doesn't look or sound all that convincing. The way things are going for Celtic you could almost have guaranteed a goal for Daniel Arzani, their former player who came and went in a blur of nothingness. To add salt, it was a magnificent strike after a counter-attack that exposed Celtic in the most embarrassing way. There was more order in the Keystone Cops. Arzani appeared in acres of space on the left, Colby Donovan having over-committed to attack and now busting a gut in a forlorn attempt to recover. Arzani had patience and precision. He whipped his shot into the top corner. Easy. O'Neill needs some amount of solutions in the coming days. Football is weird. He might find them, but his team is lacking ideas, conviction, composure, physical and psychological heft, creativity, ruthlessness and stomach for a fight. The manager, himself, looks like he's lacking in any inspiration. He's bounced back from challenging situations in his football past and you almost become attuned to him doing so again, but there is a lot to fix here. McGregor says the team is a little bit broken at the moment. Rangers might be licking their lips at the prospect of facing a wounded animal. Beware the backlash and all of that, but they have an opportunity to land another blow. Sunday will tell us much about the way of things betwee

title: 'Complete despair': Afghan female medical students fear being sent home from Pakistan
description: Since 2023, hundreds of thousands of Afghans have been deported from Pakistan and over two million have left.
body: Women in Afghanistan can no longer study beyond primary school level Nooria, which is not her real name, still remembers one of the moments that made her want to be a doctor. It was back home in a village in Afghanistan, where she was born. A 13-year-old boy there became sick and died because of appendicitis. "He was completely healthy, but the road was blocked and he died on the way. There are multiple incidents just like this." "That and the potential I saw in myself, I thought I can be a doctor for them, I can help." She fears that dream could now be over and that she could be sent back to Afghanistan. That would be the end of any chance at a career for Nooria who, as a woman, is barred from studying or working by Afghanistan's Taliban government. Earlier this month, Pakistan's Medical and Dental Council - the medical education regulator - issued a letter to all medical and dental colleges across the country saying that students from Afghanistan studying in their colleges must return to their home country. Failure to follow the directive, it said, would be "viewed seriously" and may lead to regulatory action. A temporary stay order from the Lahore High Court stopped students in Punjab, such as Nooria, from being deported immediately until the next hearing, scheduled for Friday. There is no certainty that the stay will continue. Since 2023, hundreds of thousands of Afghans have been deported from Pakistan and over two million have left according to the UN. These numbers increased as the relationship between Pakistan and Afghanistan dramatically deteriorated in the last year. Pakistan has accused Afghanistan's Taliban government of harbouring militant groups, which it denies. The announcement from the medical council was met with a strong reaction. Amnesty International called the decision "patently discriminatory and arbitrary" and said that "Pakistan has obligations under international human rights law to uphold the right to education without discrimination on the basis of national origin." Several of Pakistan's former envoys to Afghanistan also urged the council to reconsider; one called it "shocking" and "a question of humanity, compassion and Pakistan's own moral responsibility". The council told the BBC that they can give no further comment while the court case continues, but their lawyer has told the BBC that none of the Afghan students were registered with PMDC. The students say that this is the responsibility of their colleges, not them; a notification issued by the PMDC earlier this year, external directs colleges to ensure that students are registered. Afghan refugees have been packing up and leaving Pakistan in large numbers The medical and dental students the BBC has spoken to say they do not see how the relationship between the two countries should affect their ability to study. For Nooria, this stings even more because she says it took a lot for her to get here. She first began studying at Kabul University, but as the Taliban forces approached the city, she left. She was offered what she thought at the time was a lifeline: the opportunity to study medicine in Pakistan on a scholarship. Now a final year student at a medical university in Lahore, she says she has given everything to the course. "I was studying, day and night. I couldn't sleep because there was so much pressure and knowledge that I had accumulated in my mind. I got used to it a bit, but I have compromised a lot. My relationships, talking to my family, spending time with my friends. I think I haven't lived for these years, I have only studied for my dream." So when she heard about the letter, Nooria was in shock. She's still nervous about the repercussions of speaking out, which is why she asked we don't reveal her name. "We knocked on every door, our teachers, organisations, anyone we thought could help us. We are under so much pressure that we have completely forgotten about our studies, we don't know what will happen to us." Final year students like Nooria have their last exams in just a few months. Said Mubin, another final year student in Punjab, is in the same position. "I was in complete despair, my mind was blank. It was like a panic situation because they were giving us very short time to evacuate the (accommodation), the college," he says. Other students have also brought cases across the country, but different directives have been issued, adding to the confusion. Some students told the BBC that they have finished their exams but not completed the practical training - known as a 'House Job' - to complete their medical education. Women were banned from Afghan medical training centres by the Taliban government in 2024 Without completing their degrees, both Mubin, Nooria and many other medical and dental students the BBC spoke to, fear that none of their credits will be recognised by another institution. "It means you have to start from zero, from your first year," Mubin says. Both Nooria and Mubin have valid student visas, seen by the BBC. The PMDC did not provide the BBC with the number of students they believe are affected, but Anayatullah Momand, a spokesperson for the Afghan medical students, has said that they estimate it's approximately 1,000 medical and dental students, 65% of whom have visa holders. Some are still waiting for a visa, but Momand said that 15% have had their visas cancelled or have not yet applied for one. While the medical council's letter makes no distinction between students with the right documents, Pakistan's Ministry for Foreign Affair's spokesman did. "Our policy is that those Afghan students who are in Pakistan on a valid visa and registered for a valid course will continue and complete his or her education," said Sajjad Haider Khan during a recorded press conference at the ministry. title: From -17 points to dream European start for Bournemouth
description: Bournemouth started a League Two season on -17 points in 2008, now they have made a dream start in European competition.
body: Adam Smith captained Bournemouth on their European bow after making his debut for the club in League One 'From -17 to Europe', read a flag in the away end at at the Anoeta Stadium. As Bournemouth embarked on the first European campaign in the club's 127-year history, it served as a reminder of just how far they have come. But a 2-1 victory at Real Sociedad in their Europa League opener shows they are not ready to stop there. It is now 11 years since the Cherries were first promoted to the Premier League, meaning there is now a generation of supporters who will view top-flight football as the norm. From that perspective then, qualifying and playing in Europe might simply appear the next logical step for a well-run and ambitious club. "It's a brilliant win in our first European game. It's brilliant for the club and the 2,000 fans from Bournemouth," manager Marco Rose told TNT Sports. Yet for the vast majority of fans celebrating a famous victory on Thursday, the whole thing still seems surreal. Just 18 years ago, the club was on the brink. A 10-point deduction for entering administration resulted in their relegation to League Two. To even stay in the Football League for the 2008-09 season, they had to accept a 17-point deduction and agree not to appeal against the decision after it was ruled that, as they had been unable to agree a Company Voluntary Arrangement, they had not met their terms for exiting administration. Thoughts of a £100m-rated midfielder picking out a Brazil winger to head Bournemouth to victory in Europe was the stuff of fantasy as the Dorset club battled for survival. But that now is Bournemouth's reality with Alex Scott swaggering around San Sebastian, showing why there is such a clammer for his signature among top Premier League clubs, and Rayan providing another example of why the Cherries will demand every penny of a reported £130m release clause to let him go. Bournemouth have nothing to compare it to but this was a proper European away performance. Up against a Real Sociedad side led by a World Cup-winning forward in Mikel Oyarzabal and who beat Atletico Madrid to win the Copa del Rey last season, they were dominant for 45 minutes. They suffocated Sociedad with their relentlessness off the ball, winning the ball back high up the pitch time and again and showing the quality on the ball to create chances - even when the defence was set. But there is an edge to the Basque side and, poor as they had been, that they came out fighting after the break was no surprise. The adrenaline-fueled exuberance of Rose's side in the first half appeared to catch up with them in the second, but their desire to compete never wavered. Bournemouth are not known for their defensive resilience and, as Sociedad ramped up the pressure as the game wore on, thoughts might have turned to leads surrendered in each of their first four Premier League games. But the Cherries, aided by the sharp reflexes of Djordje Petrovic in goal, held on to secure a famous win. "It was very intense and tough," Rose told TNT Sports. "Brilliant first half in everything. The way we won balls and the possession high up. In the second half, we needed to suffer because we were not so sharp." Speaking on BBC Radio Solent, former Cherries full-back Charlie Daniels added: "It is a big occasion. A big moment for the club, and they should be applauded for it." Bournemouth hold on to win at Sociedad on European bow Cherries fans hail historic day in San Sebastian Bournemouth's incredible rise can be traced back to the appointment of Eddie Howe in January 2009. The former boss guided the Cherries to safety, finishing nine points clear of the relegation zone despite that 17-point deduction. A mere six and a half years later, Howe - back for his second spell as manager - had taken a transformed Bournemouth to the Premier League. It was fitting then, that on this latest milestone night for the club, the team was led out by a man involved during Howe's first stint. Adam Smith joined Bournemouth on loan during the 2010-11 campaign, returned on a permanent deal in 2014 and has been at the club ever since, with approaching 400 league appearances to his name. "Adam has been with the club for so long," Daniels said. "Dedicated himself to the club, and it's such a proud moment, not only for him, but for his family, his team-mates and old team-mates to see how he's grown - not only as a player but as a man as well. "To lead out the Cherries on this historical night is fantastic." Smith also made history of his own, becoming, at 35 years and 141 days, the oldest English outfielder to make their debut in major European competition since Ipswich's Reginald Pickett in 1962. The club captain will appreciate more than most what a special night this was for Bournemouth. Things have been far from straightforward for the club, even in recent years, with relegation in 2020 and, since re-establishing themselves in the top-flight, the seemingly annual battle to replace players picked off by Europe's top clubs. Even qualifying for Europe was not enough to keep hold of manager Andoni Iraola, who returns to the Vitality Stadium with his new club Liverpool on Sunday. That pattern is unlikely to stop anytime soon but, while there is the prospect of more nights like this one, Bournemouth supporters won't be complaining. They've seen enough to know that these are the good times. title: 'This is our company': Nigerians show off oil wealth after share-buying frenzy
description: Many Nigerians buy their first ever shares - in the oil refinery owned by Africa's richest man, Aliko Dangote.
body: Aliko Dangote wanted all Nigerians to get involved in the share offer Every Nigerian is now an oil magnate. At least that is what the social media memes would have you believe as investor fever hits the country. Nigerians have been eager to have a piece of the energy business that was built up by the country's – and continent's – richest man: Aliko Dangote. More than four billion shares in his giant oil refinery – representing just over 3% of the company - went on the market on Monday in Africa's biggest-ever sale of its kind. The minimum purchase was 10 shares for about $4 (£3) and despite this only representing a miniscule portion of the firm, many are now celebrating and joking about their new-found (part-)owner status. One popular social media video has a Nigerian narrating how he stopped a speeding Dangote company lorry driver, telling him not to be reckless with company property. Other memes show investors trying to phone up Dangote to discuss business matters. And the term "Yangote" – a pun in the Hausa language essentially meaning "we all have a share now" - has been trending on social media. On the first day of the Initial Public Offering (IPO), investment apps crashed as they could not handle the high demand. The Bamboo trading platform crashed as so many people tried to buy the shares Bamboo, which runs one of the most popular investor tools here, later apologised, saying: "We know we let you down." Public affairs analyst Jamil Ubah said he had rarely seen Nigerians as excited about something as this. He argued that it fed the dream that it could lead to greater riches for a population that is often battling to make ends meet. "I think the hope for the common man is that his money will grow into something big, and don't forget this is coming at a time when many are struggling as the economy is not doing great," he told the BBC. Dangote wanted this to be "the people's IPO" with drivers, cooks, cleaners and servants having the chance to be part of something big. And they took him at his word. Twenty-five-year-old clothes seller Idris Lawal Musa made his first-ever stock exchange purchase and told the BBC he was happy after investing 21,000 naira ($16; £12) in 40 shares. "It is no longer Dangote but 'Yangote', the company belongs to us now," he said while laughing. But he may make a quick sale. "I am a trader by profession and when I see that the shares have increased in price I will sell," he noted. Newspaper adverts encouraged people to invest in the refinery The popularity also reflects a growing investment culture among younger Nigerians who have embraced mobile trading platforms, cryptocurrencies and digital savings products. But fear of missing out may have also pushed some to get into the investment business. In the build-up to the IPO, social media platforms were awash with financial conversations. People shared subscription guides, debated valuation metrics and encouraged friends and family to participate. But amid the frenzy, experts have warned that there are risks – shares can go down in value, as well as up, meaning people could lose some, or all, of their investment. Financial analyst Shuaib Uwais said prospective investors should avoid thinking of the IPO as a guaranteed route to wealth. He urged people to consider a number of factors that could impact the refinery's future performance, including disruptions to crude oil supply, operational challenges, regulatory changes and fluctuations in demand for refined petroleum products. "If for any reason the company experiences difficulty in sourcing its raw materials, there could be challenges," he told the BBC. Nevertheless, the IPO has given people the chance to be part of this home-grown success story. Dangote's sprawling refinery on the outskirts of Lagos, which began operating two years ago and now processes around 700,000 barrels of crude a day, has transformed the fortunes of Nigeria's oil sector. Until recently, Africa's largest crude oil producer had no refining capacity and had to import the finished product. Now the Dangote refinery is feeding much of the domestic demand. But for Dangote, the share offer is about raising cash to fund the growth of the business, something that the country's mini-magnates may now be able to get behind. title: War may be coming. Are we psychologically ready?
description: The military and government say the risk of conflict is growing, but we may not be mentally ready for it
body: War may be coming. Are we psychologically ready? If the UK suddenly found itself at war, would you know what to do? Do you know what would be expected of you? The Government wants us all to start preparing for severe disruption to our lives. It wants us to stockpile canned food and drinking water, strengthen our civic resilience, and plan for the possibility of war. Work has begun on the government's so-called "war book", which hasn't been updated in decades. The UK's most senior soldier has sounded the alarm. The Chief of the Defence Staff Sir Richard Knighton this week said the threat from Russia meant Britain was living through the "most dangerous" period of his 35-year career in the armed forces. But what is the threat? In 1940 the danger of a German invasion of the UK was very real. But the chances of Russian tanks rolling up Whitehall are surely negligible. "It's not the tanks you need to worry about," says historian Margaret MacMillan, author of War: How Conflict Shaped Us. "It's the cutting of cables on the ocean floor. It's the hacking into systems on which so many things depend. The possibility for asymmetric war, for cyber war, is growing by leaps and bounds." But are we ready? After 80 years without war on our own soil, are we, as a society, psychologically prepared for it? Are we ready to approve large increases in defence spending, and for the sacrifices that that might entail in other areas of our national life? Or does the threat seem too far-fetched to be real? "I think we have become used to the idea that peace is the normal state of affairs, that it's going to last," says McMillan. "So no, I don't think we are psychologically prepared… but I do think that we are beginning to recognise that war is something that is closer to us than we'd like to think". Archive film footage showing Britons in 1913 enjoying days at the races or watching the cricket contrasts sharply with what followed during the horrors of World War One. The summer before World War One has come to symbolise a lack of readiness for war "In a sense it's now a bit like those Edwardian summers before 1914, when there was a lot of talk of war but the notion of actually going to war seemed so far-fetched as to be beyond belief and I think that's where we are at the moment," says retired British General Sir Richard Shirreff, a former Deputy Supreme Allied Commander Europe. Europe has not always been so war-averse. In 1914, recruitment stations were flooded with volunteers eager to serve their country. In Britain, that generation was raised on heroic tales of empire-building, in which war was one glorious cavalry charge, leading to swift victory and everyone home by Christmas. But the experience of what came to be known as the Great War seared itself into the popular consciousness and survives in our collective imagination. One in eight of the men who enlisted in the UK left their bones in the fields of Flanders and France, Mesopotamia and Gallipoli. The survivors carved their unspeakable grief into the landscape with the erection of thousands of war memorials. The pain of it touched every community in the land. The horrors of the war touched every part of society That conflict, says Margaret MacMillan, changed fundamentally the way Europe thought about war. "The experience of the First World War showed just how dreadful modern war is… And the idea that war could be glamorous never really came back after that." Europeans, and especially Western Europe's leadership elites, have succumbed to a decades-long "crisis of disbelief", argues Andrew Michta, a Polish-born American academic who is professor of strategic studies at the Hamilton School, University of Florida. He argues that the UK, in common with many European nations, has very low levels of psychological preparedness, and that authorities are not being candid about the looming threats. "The Germans have totally disarmed during the last 30 years. The UK is also largely disarmed and, most importantly, mentally. There is no readiness for what's happening because the policy elites are not addressing their publics in a way that would honestly state the gravity of the situation," Michta says. When the Soviet Union collapsed in the early 1990s, many European countries began a decades-long winding down of military preparedness, dramatically cutting defence spending, in the belief that the threat from Russia had disappeared. Michta singles out Germany's heavy reliance on Russian energy via the Nord Stream gas pipelines - which transported huge quantities of gas from Russia to Germany under the Baltic Sea - in what he sees as the mistaken belief that Berlin could manage its relationship with Moscow via political and economic means. "So you've lived through 20 years of appeasement in Europe driven by the elites' lack of willingness or courage… to articulate how the situation was changing and how rapidly." General Sir Richard Shirreff argues that Russia's initial invasion of Ukraine in 2014 was the real turning point, the moment Russia revealed itself as a tenacious threat to western security. "The reality is that Russia believes it's been at war with Nato since 2014. Not a conventional war, but a war designed to undermine the integrity of target states or alliances. "I would never take the Russians for granted. It would not be beyond the realms of possibility for them to try to unhinge Nato by, for example, attempting to take over Spitsbergen [in the Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard] or something else indirect. "So that's what we need to be prepared for". Richard Knighton says this moment is freighted with danger Mounting calls for increases in defence spending are rooted in a belief that the best way to prevent a war is to be ready - psychologically and militarily - to fight one. Not everyone agrees. The belief that we are under threat is key, says psychologist Jim Orford,

title: The Papers: 'Giddy King' and 'war of words' over Earl Spencer book
description: Most papers feature the latest from the royal feud on the second day of Diana's brother Earl Spencer's book being serialised in the Daily Mail.
body: Further allegations made in Earl Spencer's new book are in several of today's papers. The Daily Star headlines on King Charles being allegedly "giddily elated like a lottery winner" when he him called about Diana's death, her brother, Earl Spencer, claimed in the book. Buckingham Palace has strongly pushed back against the credibility of the book, saying: "His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss." The Daily Mirror splashes on a "war of words" and "Earl's astonishing claims" after excerpts were released. In the memoir, Earl Spencer claims Diana considered taking her own life, but that "her love for her sons stopped her", the Daily Mirror reports. The Daily Mail, which has published exclusive excerpts from Earl Spencer's upcoming memoir, says the late Queen "dramatically offered to restore Princess Diana's royal title on the day of her funeral", according to the book. The book Swan Song: Diana, My Sister is "so raw and revealing" it has "sparked a bitter war of words" between the King and Diana's brother, the paper says. King Charles's former communications chief has come out in defence of his old boss saying the then-prince "was absolutely emphatic that we were to respect Diana's memory", according to the Daily Express. The Times also headlines on Earl Spencer's claims. Spencer's latest allegations include him suggesting King Charles's reaction to Diana's death was to think "how this event might free him to marry the woman he loved", the Times includes. Buckingham Palace is "on the defensive", the i Paper reports. The latest allegations will "escalate the row" with the Palace, the i Paper says. The Sun asks "why is he doing this to the King now?" after royal insiders questioned the "motives of Earl Spencer's vicious attack on the King", according to the paper. Following the release of excerpts from Spencer's new book, a source told the Sun that a "grief-stricken Charles fought for his ex-wife to have a royal funeral", the paper says. "It's keep calm and carry on" says the Metro readers today as Kate, the Princess of Wales, is pictured happily playing shinty while on a trip to Scotland with Prince William. As claims from Spencer's book came to light, the King Charles, 77, was busy hosting an AI summit, the paper reports. Tourism bosses have warned owners of holiday cottages will be forced to sell amid the government's plans to tax tourist rentals as second homes rather than as a businesses, the Daily Telegraph reports. Labour is considering the plans ahead of the Budget next month, the paper says. The Bank of England has warned that interest rates could rise during the Middle East energy crisis, the Financial Times reports. The Independent leads with an image of Nicholas Brandram, whose family has insisted he was not the so-called "Putney pusher" and have blamed the Metropolitan Police for his death. Elsewhere, the paper reports on Reform UK planning "tax breaks for crypto investors". And the UK Prime Minister has said that Britain must fully commit to reaching net zero by 2050, the Guardian reports. The paper describes Burnham's comments as his "strongest yet on the issue". title: New wild cat species discovered - with only one known living member
description: A spotted wildcat long mistaken for relatives has been identified as a new species in Bolivia.
body: The only known living member of the species is in a wildlife sanctuary in Bolivia A spotted cat from the forests of Bolivia has been confirmed as a new species. The small feline, about the size of a domestic moggy, went under the radar because it was confused with other wild cats that share similar spots and stripes. But DNA studies show the cat is actually in a class of its own, highlighting how much remains unknown about some of the world's most elusive mammals. Scientists hope the discovery will draw attention to the conservation of tiger cats, a group of small wild cats found in South and Central America that receives far less public attention than their larger cousins like lions, leopards and tigers. The cat has been given the nickname Tigrino Tiger cats are small, spotted wild cats found across Central and South America, from Costa Rica to Bolivia and Argentina. They look remarkably similar and even experts can struggle to tell them apart. "It's an amazing result that we have a new species for the world, which is the Leopardus tilcayo," said Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz of Universidad Mayor de San Andres in La Paz, Bolivia. "It's amazing that there are still new species waiting to be discovered: we don't have to go to a volcano, an island, or deep into the sea." The oncilla, or northern tiger cat, looks remarkably similar Only one confirmed member of the species is known - a cat living in a rescue sanctuary in Bolivia - but scientists believe others exist. It was this 10-year-old cat, nicknamed 'Tigrino', that set scientists on the path to discovery. Bolivian scientist Dr Nogales-Ascarrunz was volunteering at the sanctuary when she noticed the cat looked unusual. It had been found in the forest by a local resident, who initially thought it was a domestic kitten. As it grew older, however, it became clear that it did not behave like a house cat. Dr Nogales-Ascarrunz had heard of other sightings of small wild cats in the dense forests of the country's Yungas region, but these had not been investigated by scientists. To solve the mystery, she joined forces with other researchers from around the world to investigate the family history of tiger cats, using DNA from living animals and museum specimens. "There's so few records or pictures, no individual in a museum, so it was hiding because nobody was looking," said Eduardo Eizirik, a conservation geneticist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil. The study, published in Current Biology, external, uncovered further surprises, suggesting there are five rather than three tiger cat species, including the newly described Tilcaya cat (Leopardus tilcayo) of Bolivia. Bolivia has dense forest that supports thousands of rare plant and animals However, identifying the species is only the first step. Co-researcher Dr Caroline Sartor, of the Wildlife Conservation Research Unit at the University of Oxford, said the discovery was important for conservation because it is impossible to protect a species if we don't know what it is or where it lives. "These are animals similar in size to a domestic cat, so you might think we would know them all by now, but this discovery shows how much biodiversity is still to be uncovered in some of the less-studied regions of the world," she said. Tiger cat species are considered vulnerable to extinction because of deforestation, habitat loss and illegal hunting, although the new species is missing from previous assessments. The new discovery suggests the world's cat family - all domestic and wild cats, big and small - will expand from 41 known species to 44 or 45 The discovery could also have wider implications for the world's cat family. Both wild and domestic cats belong to the biological family Felidae, which includes every living cat species from tiny house pets to massive tigers. There are officially 41 species recognised but the new discovery, and the finding that there may be several species of tiger cat, brings the number to 44 or more. Andrew Kitchener, an expert in mammals at National Museums, Scotland, who was not involved with the research, says the small spotted South American cats known as tiger cats have been a "taxonomic nightmare". "These cats are confusing because they look so similar and there are few specimens in museums, so even now we are still learning how to tell them apart as genetics reveal more species," he said. title: Early Bowie music available to stream for first time
description: Previously unheard material from the start of the artist's career has been released for the first time.
body: Ten years ago Alec Palao was casually flicking through a collection of old records when he noticed some faint pencil markings that were enough to draw a gasp. "Davie Jones," it read. What he had found was musical gold: five unreleased songs by a young David Bowie, filed away under his birth name. From Friday, those tracks, plus another five unreleased songs that came Palao's way after the initial discovery, will be available to buy and stream. "They are probably the most visceral, raw you'll ever hear the man," said Palao, a music historian and archivist. For the music industry, David Bowie is big business. He entered the mainstream with his 1969 single, Space Oddity, and went on to achieve 11 number one albums. He died in 2016, but remains one of Britain's most recognisable cultural icons. Six of the previously unreleased tracks from the new collection will be available on vinyl, tapping into Bowie's popularity in that format specifically. In 2022, Bowie was named the best-selling vinyl artist of the 21st century by Music Week, ahead of The Beatles. "It's just a fascinating window into London in 1965 and its possibilities," said Palao. In the early sixties, Bowie was a teenager, performing as Davie Jones at London clubs and dreaming of stardom. Many of the tracks he recorded in that period are either little known or lost to time. But his first professional producer, Shel Talmy, had kept a recording from 1965 among his collection of material by other artists he had worked with: The Kinks; The Who; Manfred Mann; The Easybeats. In 1965 Bowie made an appearance on the BBC show 'Gad Zooks Its All happening' but caused controversy with his long hair. It was within Talmy's collection that Palao came across the valuable 12-inch acetate. That material and the five other previously unheard tunes, as well as demos and remastered songs, form part of a new, posthumous album called The Shel Talmy Recordings. A limited edition vinyl will be sold at Record Store Day and HMV outlets. In 2022, David Bowie's estate sold the publishing rights to decades of the singer's work to Warner Music Group. For this new material, Palao, along with Talmy Enterprises Incorporated, licensed the album to Warner, and it will be released by the company's subsidiary, Parlophone. Royalties will be paid to Bowie's estate by Warner. "I think it's wonderful that people can get to hear the early Davie Jones music," said Dana Gillespie, an early collaborator of Bowie's. She met him after a performance at the Marquee Club in London when Bowie was 17. "They're songs that don't really sound like David but it's him trying to find his voice. He was experimenting." Gillespie became close friends with Bowie, eventually working with him on his "Ziggy Stardust" album. Talmy worked with both artists and Bowie's song "Andy Warhol", on his fourth studio album, was originally written for Gillespie. "He was very driven," remembered Gillespie, who is still touring and making music at the age of 77. "Some time in the sixties, he asked me to come and visit his parents. We were in his little house in Bromley, and when his parents left the room he turned to me and said: 'Whatever it takes, I want to get out of here.' And he did," she said. It is a decade since Palao found the recordings. Since then, it has been a long process to bring them to market. The result is an album that he says is "absolutely pure rock 'n' roll". "If you're looking for clues as to what he was to become, there's maybe less of that," said Palao, "but objectively speaking, I feel it's important stuff." Gillespie is excited by one song in particular. "There was a famous café called the Gioconda in Denmark Street where I often used to go with David," she said, recalling the centre of musical life in London in the 1960s. "One day when I was sitting there, David rushed in and took me by the hand. He said: 'You have to hear this'. "He ran with me around the corner and squeezed us into a small listening booth. I had one speaker and he had the other, and he played me 'I Pity The Fool'." A remastered version of the song can be heard in the new album. For music historians, fans of Bowie, and those who were there, the new album is another chance to reconnect with an enduring cultural icon. "David always wanted to be a big star," said Gillespie. "I'm so happy that his early stuff hasn't been forgotten." title: Why we bought our first home with a 100% mortgage - despite the risks
description: The share of UK mortgages with smaller deposits is the highest it's been since 2008. The BBC spoke to borrowers about how they manage the risks.
body: The couple are aware of the risks that come with their no-deposit mortgage Until last year, Conroy, 32, and his partner Amber, 28, saw little prospect of owning their own home. They were renting in central Manchester where they work and could not afford to save up for a deposit. Then they came across a relatively niche, and some experts say riskier, type of mortgage that offered a solution. The Track Record mortgage from Skipton Building Society covers 100% of the value of a property, with the borrower paying nothing upfront. Borrowers must meet strict eligibility checks and pay a higher interest rate - in Conroy and Amber's case 5.33% fixed for five years - but they were happy to do this. And in August they bought a four-bed home for £242,000 in Swinton on the edge of Manchester. "I don't think it's dawned on us it's really ours," says Conroy, a video editor. According to the Bank of England, the share of UK mortgages with deposits worth less than 10% of the property's value is currently the highest it has been since 2008, external when such loans were widely available. The average deposit for first-time buyers is currently around 20%. It comes as lenders such as Lloyds, Santander, Skipton and Yorkshire Building Society have launched a raft of new mortgage deals over the last few years covering upwards of 95% of the value of a property, and in some cases as much as 100%. They say they want to help first-time buyers get on the housing ladder as property prices continue to rise and while saving for a deposit remains a struggle. But these loans tend to charge higher rates, aren't available for all types of property or borrower, and come with risks customers should be aware of. Conroy and Amber thought they would be renting for the foreseeable future Conroy and Amber, a solicitor, have a 25-year loan with monthly repayments of £1,500 - roughly what they were paying in rent. He says they feel comfortable with the higher cost because they "earn quite well" and expect their salaries to rise. But he is aware there is a greater risk of falling into negative equity with a no- or low-deposit mortgage. That is when the value of a property falls below the value of the loan still owed on it - leaving the borrower with potentially painful costs if they suddenly have to sell. Conroy says they plan to overpay their mortgage for the first five years to build up more equity in their home. "There is always the element of a gamble with the property market," he says. "But I have researched the area we moved to and don't think house prices are going to drop." Twenty-seven-year-old Bronya and her partner George, 29, also used a low-deposit mortgage to buy their four-bedroom house in Rhuddlan, North Wales in August. Lloyds lent them £258,000 - roughly 98% of the property's value - over a 33-year term and they only had to put down £5,000 as a deposit. The couple pay an interest rate of 5.89%, fixed for five years, equating to monthly repayments of £1,400 - about the same as what they paid to rent a one-bed flat before. Bronya and George bought their first home this year with a roughly 2% deposit Bronya, a civil servant, says they could have put down a bigger deposit but wanted to use their savings for a renovation project costing upwards of £20,000. They are aware of the risks of negative equity but believe the refurbishment will boost the value of their home. "We also plan to stay here our whole lives," George adds, explaining that they are prepared to ride out any dips in the property market. The couple are renovating their home Widespread uptake of low-deposit mortgages by borrowers who could not afford them was seen as a major factor in the 2008 global financial crisis. But today's deals have much stronger affordability checks and do not pose the same risks, says David Hollingworth, associate director at brokers L&C Mortgages. Borrowers of Skipton's zero-deposit mortgage, for example, have to prove they have kept up with their rent for at least 12 consecutive months and credit payments for the last six months. And Lloyds won't issue one of its £5,000 deposit mortgages for new-build properties and shared ownership homes. Hollingworth says lenders are recognising that some people have "good affordability but may be struggling to save for a deposit while paying a rent and dealing with cost of living pressures". Following a recent rule change, he adds, lenders are also offering more "flex" on how much someone can borrow as long as it's within their means. Nevertheless, he urges borrowers to use common sense. "Think carefully - what do monthly payments look like? Are you aware that interest rates could go up?" Are you buying your first home? How have you managed it? title: The virtual worlds where robots are trained
description: Training systems that allow robots to negotiate the real world are getting more sophisticated.
body: This video can not be played Freddo the robot in action at Vsim Freddo the robot walks across the office and takes a plastic bottled offered by a staff member. Given that a robot recently beat Usain Bolt's 100m sprint record, it's not the most startling achievement. But the speed by which Freddo has been trained to walk, recognise the bottle and grasp it is impressive. It took just a few minutes to develop those skills and upload them to Freddo. His developers say rival systems could take days to attain such skills. I'm at Vsim, a British start-up based in Cambridge. Founders Michelle Lu and Kier Storey hope one day their software will control robots that can navigate and do useful tasks in the home and workplace. But there's a long way to go. "It's a weird situation with robotics because actually the stuff that we find as humans to be incredibly difficult, like gymnastics, you can get robots to do reasonably well. The stuff that humans are really good at, like fine dexterity, is really hard in robots," Storey says. Vsim founders Michelle Lu and Kier Storey Freddo's skills were honed in a virtual environment, where a task can be performed in a computer simulation millions of times. Once the optimum solution (known as a policy) is found, it can be uploaded and used by the hardware - in this case Freddo. Such virtual simulations are a common way to train robots. Tech giant Nvidia has a system called Isaac Sim which works that way - Lu and Storey both worked on an early version of it. In 2022 they decided to set up Vsim, to build the their own training system environment and other tools. As they were starting from scratch Lu and Storey could optimise the software to exploit the powerful computer chips used in AI, known as graphics processing units or GPUs. "The underlying algorithms that we were using for most of these robotic simulations they hark back to the 1970s and 1980s, but those algorithms are not really brilliant fits for GPUs," Storey says. Within months they realised their system could work much faster than anything they had seen before. "Eighteen months in and we actually have a completely functional, super high-performance simulator," says Lu. The software is so efficient that it can run on the hardware carried by Freddo. That means the robot can run tens of thousand of simulations while it is moving around. "It can look about a second, or so, ahead into the future for 20,000 different kind of combinations of things that might happen," Storey explains. And that would be vital for a robot moving around an unstructured environment like the average home. "Things outside of the robot's control, like humans, animals or even other robots, could do things that require a change of strategy. These unexpected events could happen very quickly and the robot needs to be able to quickly adapt to ensure its actions remain safe and on-mission," Lu says. Robot training systems use virtual environments where tasks are practised Vsim is a start-up with 10 engineers working on its tech. Nvidia is at the other end of the industry. It dominates the market for computer chips used for AI and has a leading robotics software division, with hundreds of engineers. It does not build robots, instead it has a suite of software designed to let organisations train and control robots. That includes virtual simulation training systems and a so-called world model, external, called Cosmos, which gives a robot an understanding of the physics of the real world and how its environment might change as it moves around. But even with the powerful computer resources available to Nvidia, the software only gives a rudimentary understanding of the real world. "Manipulation, - where I just grab a bottle, that's not too hard. The problem is when you start doing long-horizon tasks, where I say: 'I want you to take the bottle and I want you to fill it up and I want you to go pour'," says Spencer Huang, director of product for robotics at Nvidia. But he's confident that good progress is being made. This year Nvidia has started using AI agents to help build virtual environments to train robots and validate whether the solutions from training work or not. "When we talk about creating the [virtual] world and actually scanning it in - a lot of that is actually manual labour. "We're just throwing agents at it... it's basically given us a huge workforce," Huang says. Simulation is not the only method for training robots. They can also be trained by watching human or video demonstrations. Rika Antonova has spent more than a decade working in robotics Rika Antonova has been working in the field of robotics since 2015 and is currently an associate professor at the Department of Computer Science and Technology at the University of Cambridge. Her research is focused on, external developing software and hardware that can aid robots to learn complex behaviour. Antonova works with a training system called MuJoCo, owned by Google's DeepMind since 2021. It's open-source software, which means researchers can use it for free, and are allowed to tinker with the code. "It is very, very user-friendly. So for research groups or for small start-ups, that's useful," she says. She says that Vsim's approach - very fast simulation - is promising. "If you have a very, very fast simulator, then you can simulate hundreds of millions of samples in that few seconds that your robot is thinking about how to adjust its motion, and then you can change the motion almost in real time," she says. But those simulated environments are still rough approximations of the real world, which limits what can be trained. "There are certain things that are hard to model in simulation, like highly deformable objects and cutting," she says. It's a challenge that Nvidia and Lu and Storey at Vsim are working on. title: Healey to ask EU finance ministers to let UK into 'Made in Europe' industry scheme
description: The chancellor wants the Made in Europe programme to deepen ties with the UK "rather than erecting new barriers".
body: John Healey is meeting EU finance ministers on Friday The chancellor is to warn the European Union (EU) not to lock the UK out of its scheme to protect industries from unfair Chinese competition. John Healey will push for closer UK-EU partnerships on tech, defence, and manufacturing at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin on Friday. But he will call on the EU to design its "Made in Europe" programme in a way that deepens ties with the UK "rather than erecting new barriers", Treasury sources told the BBC. Officials said Healey will tell European finance ministers it is important to "learn lessons" after talks collapsed last year for Britain to join an EU defence loans scheme. That dispute centred on how much money the UK would pay to join. The "Made in Europe" policy, officially called the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), is currently being considered by the bloc and aims to protect EU manufacturing with restrictions on goods from outside countries. There is concern in government the scheme could lock British firms out of European supply chains. Treasury officials said Healey wanted to reduce the economic impact of Brexit and build closer ties with the EU, but not at any cost to the UK. Healey said: "The next chapter of Britain's growth story will be written in more places. "To me, closer ties with the EU means British businesses – wherever they are based across the UK – get better access to both the supply chains and the customers they need to grow." Healey will use the meeting in Dublin to focus on tech firms, defence companies, and manufacturing. "The chancellor wants to make sure nothing holds them back," a Treasury source said. It comes after a reset summit with the EU was delayed after Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as prime minister. Treasury sources now expect that to take place in November. Healey's meeting in Dublin comes after it emerged earlier this week that he is in discussions about joining a global investment bank aimed at raising more money for defence spending. He is considering a bid to join the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB), not long after his predecessor Rachel Reeves rejected the idea. Canada has been leading efforts to establish the bank, which supporters say would enable governments to borrow at lower costs to increase military spending. Paying for the UK's growing defence commitments is one of Healey's biggest headaches as he prepares for the Budget in October and next year's spending review. title: Rapist police officer was first arrested and released 17 years ago
description: Police officer Campbell Petrie was convicted of raping two women at the High Court in Glasgow.
body: Campbell Petrie was found guilty of nine charges against two women A former police sergeant convicted of rape was first arrested 17 years ago following a complaint from one of his victims. Campbell Petrie, 50, is facing a lengthy jail sentence after being found guilty of sex offences and violence against two women between 2006 and 2022. Police Scotland told BBC News that one of the women, who he met through his job, made a complaint of threatening behaviour against Petrie in 2009. He was arrested and held in a police station for five hours, but no further action was taken because of a lack of evidence. Petrie remained a serving officer until another woman made an allegation of rape against him in October 2023, prompting an investigation by specialist sexual crime officers. He was arrested, charged and suspended in December 2023, and retired from the force two years later. Petrie denied the allegations but was convicted of nine charges after a trial at the High Court in Glasgow. Police officer guilty of series of rapes and sex attacks over 17 years The case has appalled workers at Rape Crisis Scotland, which supports survivors of sexual violence. The organisation's external affairs manager, Nicola Love, said: "It does stick in the throat that someone like that is allowed to leave the force on their own terms, instead of as a result of what they've done. "We know perpetrators come from all walks of life, and that does include the police force, but it provokes an intense reaction because these people have a duty to protect us. "There's an expectation that they keep us safe, and this flies in the face of that." Petrie was found guilty of indecently assaulting one of the women while she was asleep and on various occasions between 2006 and 2009. He was convicted of raping the second woman on multiple occasions between 2011 and 2014. A trial found he assaulted both women to the danger of their lives by grabbing their throats and restricting their breathing. Petrie remained a serving officer with Police Scotland until October 2023 Petrie's conviction means that three serving or former Police Scotland officers have been exposed as rapists this year. In July, Cameron Ross was jailed for ten years for raping two women and subjecting a third to a campaign of abuse. Three weeks later, a BBC Disclosure investigation revealed that Alan Greer - a police officer who took his own life in May - was a violent rapist who had attacked and attempted to murder women over at least 14 years. Further BBC Scotland inquiries established that Greer had passed vetting checks to join Strathclyde Police in 2009, despite having two reports of criminal behaviour against women on his record. At least 15 potential victims of Greer have been identified so far and the National Police Chiefs Council (NPCC) has been brought in to carry out an independent investigation. Under its terms of reference, published this week, the NPCC will try to identify whether his crimes could have been discovered any earlier. PC Alan Greer was exposed as a violent rapist who attacked a number of women over a 15-year period The Petrie case has raised fresh questions over background checks on police in Scotland. In 2023, all UK forces carried out a "historic data wash" following the crimes of Met officers Wayne Couzens, who abducted and murdered Sarah Everard, and serial rapist David Carrick. Officers and staff were checked against the national police data base to identify whether they had a criminal past which had been missed. Police Scotland's deputy chief constable Bex Smith told BBC Scotland: "In 2009 Campbell Petrie was arrested and questioned in connection with a complaint of threatening behaviour, however, the case did not proceed due to insufficient evidence. "The independent historic data wash, carried out by UK policing between March and July 2023, interrogated the Police National Database and did not identify any unknown information on Petrie. "The checks carried out by Police Scotland went further than UK forces and included robust interrogation of both the vulnerable person's database and intelligence system." UK police forces carried out a "historic data wash" following the crimes David Carrick and Wayne Couzens In total, 23,822 Police Scotland officers, staff and volunteers were checked during that process. Concerns were raised about just eight individuals, with a civilian member of staff facing a criminal investigation. In the wake of Petrie's conviction and the Greer case, the Inspectorate of Constabulary in Scotland (HMICS) said they were "deeply concerned" about vetting at the force. The chief inspector of constabulary, Craig Naylor, said: "HMICS have previously scrutinised Police Scotland's arrangements for vetting, misconduct and the management of officers subject to allegations of wrongdoing, and have made a number of recommendations for improvement. "We have recently raised concern with both Police Scotland and the Scottish Police Authority about a lack of progress in relation to the vetting of officers within Police Scotland, including the effectiveness of a historic data wash exercise and the associated assurance around these issues." Justice secretary Neil Gray said Petrie's crimes were "extremely disturbing" Strengthening vetting procedures is a key aim of the Police (Ethics, Conduct and Scrutiny) (Scotland) Act passed by the Scottish Parliament in January 2025. The intention is that all officers will now undergo a career-long, structured regime of on-going vetting. Scotland's justice secretary Neil Gray described Petrie's case as "extremely disturbing" and his abuse of his position of trust as "abhorrent." He said: "Police officers are rightly expected to uphold the highest standards of integrity, which is why we have strengthened vetting through legislation and Police Scotland have been clear there is an ongoing programme of work to re-vet all officers." The new law

title: 'Just the beginning' - Samba, 17, steals Man City show
description: Floyd Samba's scintillating debut stole the show at Etihad Stadium but also took the headlines away from another high-profile teenager in Manchester.
body: Floyd Samba's brother Tyrone is also a Manchester City player Floyd Samba's scintillating first-team debut not only stole the show at Etihad Stadium on Thursday but also snatched all the headlines away from another high-profile teenager in Manchester. Website articles, social media posts and column inches have been filled this week with the news that highly rated 15-year-old forward JJ Gabriel is on the verge of leaving Manchester United. But that particular saga will be overshadowed in Friday's football cuttings by 17-year-old Samba's stunning bow on the professional stage, scoring twice in Manchester City's 5-0 Carabao Cup third-round thrashing of Norwich City. Samba was prolific in City's under-18 side last season and those impressive performances led to him being promoted to the first-team set-up by new manager Enzo Maresca this summer. The show of faith is already being repaid. "I knew there would be an opportunity to get some minutes for the first time with the first team," Samba told BBC Radio 5 Live. "To get a debut like that is mind-blowing. "I couldn't believe it myself - but that is just the beginning, I have got a big career ahead of me. It was a great debut. "I spoke to all of them [first-team players], they have all been brilliant with me - before the game, giving me advice like 'play your game, be you' - those words have given me confidence and helped me score those two goals today." Samba with debut double as Man City thrash Norwich The youngster joined City's academy at under-nine level and he really started to make a name for himself last term. Samba scored 24 goals and provided 10 assists in an eye-catching first full season with the under-18s, including curling home a stunning free-kick to help City win the FA Youth Cup final against rivals Manchester United in May. On his debut, Samba played the entire 90 minutes and fully grasped his opportunity. With City struggling for openings, Samba broke the deadlock by flicking home a header - he celebrated by blowing a kiss in the direction of family and friends in the stands, before curling in a delightful second later in the game. Samba was afforded a generous ovation towards the end of the game when being deservedly named man of the match. "[I'm] satisfied not just for the goals but for the performance too," said manager Maresca. "I asked him in the last three, four days - when I decided to play him as nine - he said he never played there. He is not a nine for sure, but he was good. "He is young, full of energy, strong, can finish, can set [players up]. He made some good decisions in the first half. I am happy but they are young and we have to go slowly, slowly. "Hopefully we can give him more chances." Christopher Samba (left) played for Blackburn in the Premier League between 2007-12 The Samba surname will be familiar to those of a certain age who have followed the Premier League. Floyd is the son of former Blackburn and QPR defender Christopher, who played 171 top-flight matches for those two sides, as well as a further 12 in the Championship with Aston Villa. The City forward is the younger of two brothers at the club, with Tyrone also involved in the youth team, and will now be aiming to play more first-team minutes after an exciting debut. As a fleet-footed forward, Floyd could not be more of a different player to his dad Christopher, who was a no-nonsense towering centre-back. "Coming from under-21s to first-team training, that is a big jump," added Samba. "The sessions are more tiring, you have to run more - they demand more of you and you have to cope with it." Former Norwich striker Chris Sutton added on BBC Radio 5 Live: "Absolutely brilliant moment for Floyd. His dad was in the stadium and will be extremely proud. It's the journey, he has been nurtured at Man City, got his moment and what a night for him. "He has given Enzo Maresca a bit of food for thought moving forward. Of course, he is not going to play ahead of Erling Haaland but it is a great evening for him and good for his development. "Maresca can think he can trust him a little bit more."
