title: £2k pay rise for MLAs is 'grotesque', says first minister
description: The proposals follow MLAs being awarded an almost 27% uplift in their annual wages in April - a rise of more than £14,000.
body: The increase will take effect from the first sitting day of the new assembly mandate next May A pay rise of more than £2,000 for Northern Ireland Assembly members (MLAs) is "grotesque", the first minister has said. The proposals planned for next year would bring MLAs annual salary to £69,216. The increase will take effect from the first sitting day of the new assembly mandate next May, under draft proposals by Stormont's Independent Remuneration Board. Speaking to the media at Stormont, she said: "This issue of wages is not in my agenda. It's not something we've pushed for." "It's not something we've asked for and actually I think it looks quite grotesque in the climate that we're in." The proposals follow MLAs being awarded an almost 27% uplift in their annual wages in April - a rise of more than £14,000. The first minister said Sinn Féin did not "push" for the pay rise A spokesman for the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) said the party has "no input" in setting MLA salaries. "At the present time we are focused on the need for a fair and stable funding settlement for Northern Ireland so that hardworking nurses, doctors and other frontline workers are properly rewarded for their work," they added. Alliance MLA Eóin Tennyson told the media on Thursday that the pay rise "smacks of being completely out of touch with where the public are". "We are more than adequately paid," Tennyson said, adding that he sees no "coherent" argument for the rise. The leader of the Ulster Unionist Party, Jon Burrows, said "our nurses need their pay rise before our politicians". He added that, while he respects the independence of the remuneration board, he feels there is a sense of "unease" around MLAs' value for money. "We haven't set a multi-year budget, we haven't got a budget of any sort, and people think that Stormont is under-performing." Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) leader Claire Hanna said a pay rise is "going to be impossible for people to stomach". "Those who are doing their job and trying to do their job should be properly remunerated for it but unfortunately some are prevented from doing that by the dysfunction". Alan Lowry, chair of the board, said the 27% rise was a "corrective measure" after years of no substantial rises - but future increases would be expected to "reflect inflationary and other pay trends". "MLAs carry out a wide range of important duties, from representing constituents and scrutinising legislation to holding ministers and departments to account," he said. He said it was "right that their remuneration recognises the complexity and importance of those responsibilities, while ensuring that financial considerations do not discourage people from seeking elected office". He added: "As we look ahead to the assembly election next year and the start of a new mandate, it is important that we put in place a structured and transparent mechanism that links MLA pay to changes in earnings in Northern Ireland. "This approach ensures that pay remains aligned with wider developments in society, while providing certainty and maintaining public confidence in the process." Alan Lowry, chair of the board, said that was a "corrective measure" after years of no substantial rises Under the proposals, while the basic MLA salary will increase in line with earnings growth, payments for different office holders will remain unchanged throughout the 2027-32 mandate. Lowry said: "In making this draft determination, we are increasing the transparency of our decision-making and making it easier for the public to understand how remuneration is structured. "The board will now consult with our statutory consultees - MLAs, the Assembly Commission and the Assembly Members' Pension Trustees, over a four-week period. "It is also inviting views from members of the public during this same timeframe. "After that, we will take some time to reflect on the responses received and present a final determination to the Assembly Commission for publication and implementation." The proposals come as Stormont ministers face pressure from trade unions over public sector pay, with some health workers taking part in strike action in recent months. The health minister at the time said he was unable to implement pay awards in the absence of an agreed Stormont budget. Northern Ireland's four-party devolved government has yet to set a budget five months into the financial year. Stormont departments are facing a shortfall of up to £1.6bn,, external according to a spending watchdog. With no agreed plan, public services have been operating under contingency arrangements. The parties have been holding talks with the UK government and Treasury in recent months in a bid secure additional funding. Maria Morgan NIPSA Deputy General Secretary said it doesn't "land well" Maria Morgan NIPSA Deputy General Secretary said it was surprising in the context of the rise of the 27% and the £14,000. "I think it will go down very badly with our members," she said. "I think it will go down very badly with the public given we've just been announced significant cuts in the health service, significant cuts in education...right across the public sector our members are waiting for their pay." Members of the Scottish Parliament receive £77,711, external while members of the Welsh Parliament earn £79,817 a year., external At Westminster, MPs earn £98,599 a year, external while members of the Dáil (lower house of the Irish parliament) earn €119,467 (£102,334)., external The three-member panel, external was set up with the sole remit of setting MLAs' pay and pension entitlements. It was established under legislation passed last year. The body replaced the Independent Financial Review Panel (IFRP), which had made decisions on both the wages and expenses provisions for MLAs. title: Ukrainian guilty of vandalism at mosques linked to Russian network behind Starmer arson attack
description: Illia Bilyk, a 21-year-old Ukrainian man, has pleaded guilty to targeting five locations in east London.
body: Ukrainian Illia Bilyk, 21, pleaded guilty to carrying out a string of vandalism attacks in London A Ukrainian man has pleaded guilty to spraying abusive graffiti on mosques in east London, in a case linked to the Russian state network behind arson attacks against the former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer. Illia Bilyk, 21, entered guilty pleas at Thames Magistrates' Court to five counts of racially and religiously aggravated criminal damage. Bilyk sprayed graffiti on the Stratford Islamic Association, Al-Birr Mosque and Leyton Jamia Masjid on 23 January 2025. Two days later he targeted Noor Ul Islam Primary School and the Islamic Shariah Council. The BBC has learned that Bilyk told police he was recruited into spraying the graffiti by a Russian speaker after being approached on the messaging app Telegram. Bilyk said the Russian speaker told him where to target and paid him afterwards. In June this year two Ukrainians - Roman Lavrynovych and Stanislav Carpiuc - were jailed for conspiring to carry out arson attacks targeting a property and a car connected to prime minister Sir Keir Starmer. An investigation by the BBC and Hope not Hate revealed that Russia was behind the arson attacks and had also generated Islamophobic vandalism throughout London, including on the east London venues which Biluyk has now admitted vandalising. Bilyk (bottom right corner) spraying graffiti on Leyton Jamia Masjid in January 2025 Lavrynovych, who personally started the fires targeting Sir Keir's property, also admitted spraying Islamophobic graffiti on an Islamic building in south London. He was recruited on Telegram and offered money by an anonymous handler, known by the initials EL, for the graffiti and the arson attacks. EL was a Russian operative who organised a widespread sabotage and provocation campaign remotely through social media and Telegram. EL was centrally involved in running a fake far-right group called Direct Action UK, which was created by Russian operatives to provoke acts of vandalism on British streets, including the graffiti attacks on mosques. After Bilyk sprayed his abusive graffiti in east London in January 2025, images of the attacks were shared in a Direct Action Telegram group. A Russia-linked group tied to the arson attack against the former UK prime minister shared images of graffiti sprayed by Ukrainian man Illia Bilyk Hours after two of his attacks, EL posted in a jobs group for Ukrainian people offering money for pictures of buildings in the area. The BBC investigation named a Russian diplomat, Evgeny Lyukshin, who was part of the Direct Action UK chat group. Lyukshin was trained in "information warfare" by senior Russian spies and his details matched those of EL. He did not respond to the BBC. Bilyk will be sentenced on 19 October at Stratford Magistrates' Court. Chief Superintendent Rhona Hunt, from the Met Police, said: "We recognise that these incidents caused significant distress within Muslim communities across east London last year and that they continue to cause concern. "Anti-Muslim hate crime and Islamophobia have absolutely no place in London. We are committed to tackling hate crime while supporting and reassuring our communities." title: Wife of US scholar jailed in China asks Trump to raise arrest at Xi meeting
description: Sylvia Zin is among the family members of people imprisoned in China who are seeking Trump's help when he hosts the country's leader next week.
body: The wife of a US scholar imprisoned in China on charges of spying and endangering national security has asked President Donald Trump to secure his release when he meets Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House next week. U Min Zin, the director at a think tank focused on Myanmar, was arrested on 3 June after travelling to the Chinese city of Kunming for an academic conference. "I'm deeply hopeful that President Trump will raise my husband's case with President Xi Jinping at the summit next week," his wife, Sylvia Zin, testified to Congress on Wednesday. Xi is due to arrive for a state visit to Washington DC on Wednesday. It comes after Xi hosted Trump for a visit to Beijing in May. Ahead of the meeting, families of prisoners being held in China have travelled to the US capital to advocate for their release. Sylvia Zin appeared before the House Foreign Affairs Committee East Asia and Pacific Subcommittee on Wednesday for a hearing titled Lives, Not Leverage: The Long Arm of China and North Korea's Repression. In her remarks, Zin said she believed Trump would also be able to secure the release of Chen Youlin, a US seismologist who tracks nuclear tests that has been held in prison in China for two years. "Knowing the president's historic record on bringing wrongfully detained Americans home has reassured me that he will also be able to secure the swift release of Min Zin and other wrongfully detained citizens," she said. Congresswoman Young Kim, the chairwoman of the subcommittee, opened the hearing by warning Americans: "If you travel to China, Beijing may take you hostage as leverage in diplomatic negotiation." Speaking about Zin's arrest, she added: "Beijing wanted to send a message to those whose research inconvenienced it, and detained Mr Zin ahead of the upcoming Trump-Xi summit." Min Zin, a student activist during Myanmar's 1988 pro-democracy movement, directs the Myanmar Institute for Strategic and Policy Studies (ISP-Myanmar), a think tank that studies China's role in Myanmar, including Chinese interests, relations, and regional influence. The son of Hong Kong media mogul Jimmy Lai also appeared on Capitol Hill to call on Trump to secure his father's release. The US president previously raised the case with Xi, telling reporters that his Chinese counterpart "told me that would be a tough one". Asked for comment on Thursday, a senior White House official, speaking anonymously, told the BBC: "Resolving the wrongful detentions of US citizens is always a top priority for the President." China detains US scientist who studied North Korea nuclear tests China arrests US scholar suspected of spying Last month, the US State Department said that two Americans - U Min Zin and Chen Youlin - were being "wrongfully detained" in China. This designation in the US allows the cases to be transferred to the office of the Special Envoy for Hostage Affairs - raising the profile of each case and allowing the US government to allocate more resources to securing their release. Zin, who lives in Thailand, told the committee on Wednesday that she has not yet been able to speak to her husband in jail, "so every month, we anxiously await his consular visits because they reassure us that he is alive". Zin said US officials had told her that Min Zin was being subjected to up to six hours of interrogations each day when he first arrived in jail. "I'm trying to be strong for our daughter, but I'm constantly wondering if he's OK and how to get him back home to us," she said. Last time Trump and Xi formally met, Trump pressed for the return of another American in jail. Underground church leader Jin Mingri was freed two months after Trump's request. title: Warm words on Canada's EU 'associate membership' but no guarantees
description: There is no certainty that the idea will ever get off the ground, let alone become a blueprint for other countries, writes Katya Adler.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Is Canada about to join the EU? Is Canada about to join the EU? Headlines across Europe indicate a lot of confusion right now. The EU constitution rules that possibility out as Canada is geographically outside Europe. But in a speech on Thursday to the European Parliament, Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney said: "Canada and Europe should secure our strategic autonomy through deep cooperation in the full range of strategic capabilities." Mark Carney was responding – extremely warmly – to an invitation by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen for Canada to become the EU's first associate member. The EU and Canada already have a far-reaching trade deal (Ceta) in place but Carney insisted additional cooperation on energy and economic security, on critical and raw materials, education, tech and AI innovation, and defence would help safeguard all countries involved. Canada and the EU feel increasingly squeezed by the superpowers USA on the one side and China on the other – and by tech giants, too, that seem to operate supranationally. The idea of associate EU membership, Carney emphasised, would not be to form a third superpower or to create a bloc against anyone else. "We do not pursue zero sum deals," he said. Instead he suggested like-minded nations should club together to create a new form of multilateral global governance in an increasingly turbulent world where – in the minds of some others - might is right. Only by countries joining forces and shunning isolationism, Carney suggested, could they close key capability gaps, build strength and ensure national sovereignty. This last may have been a nod to upcoming elections across Europe and the continent's increasingly powerful nationalist politicians. Their slogans – whether "Italy First" or "France for the French" or "Make Poland Great Again" – echo Donald Trump's call to Make America Great Again. Carney's words were hopeful and warm; the applause in the European Parliament rapturous and apparently heartfelt. What could EU associate member status mean for Canada? Canada welcomes EU proposal to become 'associate member' Not so across the Atlantic. On Wednesday, Donald Trump dismissed the EU associate membership proposal out of hand, threatened to impose "very heavy tariffs" if the agreement came to fruition and warned he may view it as a "hostile act". But the US president is the unintentional matchmaker for this EU-Canada love-in. Traditionally, America is trade partner and defence ally number one for Canada and the EU. But Ottawa is currently embroiled in what it calls an escalating trade "war" with the White House. Both Canada and the EU have been stung by what they view as Washington's weaponisation of trade tariffs. They also fear they can no longer fully rely on the US to have their back in terms of security and defence. Canada is not alone among Europe's far-flung allies, now seeking to cosy closer to the EU, as they worry the US is becoming too unpredictable a partner. Japan and South Korea show an interest in sheltering under the EU umbrella too. For its part, the EU has recently hastened to secure a list of trade deals – with India, Indonesia and Japan for example – to intentionally diversify relationships. But there is no guarantee Canada's associate membership of the EU will ever get off the ground, never mind become a blueprint for other countries, like the UK wanting closer relations stopping short of full EU membership. Any deal would have to be approved by each one of the EU's 27 countries. No legal precedent exists, negotiations would be lengthy and potential conflicts of interest loom, over steel tariffs for example. A suggestion in May by Germany to make Ukraine – a country desperate for full membership of the European Union as soon as possible – an associate member was rejected by others in the EU. Some, including France's government, want to avoid EU non-members securing "too good" a deal. They fear eurosceptic forces at home and abroad could then encourage voters to clamour to leave the bloc. In the end, "associate membership" is just a label. Buffeted by adverse winds – from China, the US and Russia, the normally rigid rules-based EU is coming under serious pressure to show more flexibility in accommodating countries wanting to stand by its side. title: The big questions for Tuchel's first England squad since World Cup
description: Before Thomas Tuchel names his first squad since the World Cup on Friday, BBC Sport looks at the big questions facing the England boss.
body: Thomas Tuchel led England to third place at the 2026 World Cup Sixty-five days after England's semi-final defeat by Argentina, Thomas Tuchel will name his first squad since the World Cup on Friday. While the tournament ultimately ended with a spectacular 6-4 win over France in the bronze-medal match, the Three Lions left the United States with a long list of what ifs. Now, with four games in the space of 11 days coming up during the extended international break, fans will get a glimpse of what Tuchel's next England side might look like. Could players like Trent Alexander-Arnold be recalled? Will others like Alex Scott make their debut? And how might we expect them to play? BBC Sport senior football correspondent Sami Mokbel, journalist Jess Anderson and BBC Radio 5 Live's John Murray go through the big questions facing Tuchel. Sami Mokbel: Rio Ngumoha and Lewis Hall are among the players to have been named in England manager Thomas Tuchel's provisional squad for the forthcoming Nations League internationals, though it remains to be seen whether they make the final cut. Liverpool winger Ngumoha was part of a contingent of young players that flew with the England senior squad for their pre-World Cup training camp in Palm Beach. He was unexpectedly handed his debut in the warm-up game against New Zealand, impressing in a second-half cameo. But the 18-year-old is yet to be picked in a full senior England squad - although he is in with a chance of being selected by Tuchel for the forthcoming games against Spain, the Czech Republic and Croatia. Hall's World Cup omission raised eyebrows given England entered the tournament without a natural left-back. Before naming his full squad on Friday, Tuchel is required to submit a preliminary squad of players from which he will name his final party. It is understood Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott, Arsenal's Myles Lewis-Skelly and Everton's Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall are also among the names selected in Tuchel's extended list. Attacking duo Cole Palmer and Phil Foden are on there too, after being two of the biggest omissions from Tuchel's squad for the World Cup. That decision was deemed a mistake from certain circles, given they are two of English football's most creative players. Meanwhile, Tuchel is expected to omit Jordan Henderson, Dean Henderson and John Stones because of injury. Tuchel regrets not eating Azteca turf after win over Mexico FA to canvass England players in World Cup review Jess Anderson: One of the most talked-about issues surrounding England is who they turn to in the absence of captain and star striker Harry Kane. At the World Cup, Tuchel simply did not turn to anyone. Kane started all seven of England's matches up to the semi-final and was substituted only twice - both times late on with the game already won. Kane was rested for the bronze-medal match, with Ivan Toney the preferred option, although the Al-Ahli striker did not score in the 6-4 win over France. Toney will not be an option this international break as he has since been charged with assault causing actual bodily harm and is due to appear in court later this month. Ollie Watkins' shock summer move to Saudi Arabia puts his England future into question, while Dominic Calvert-Lewin is the man in form with four goals in four games for Leeds United. This could be the moment for Tuchel to start to further integrate Liam Delap, who is improving at new club Nottingham Forest and has yet to make a senior England appearance. He scored his first goal for Forest in last weekend's win at Aston Villa. This video can not be played What would you change about England's squad? John Murray: In the immediate aftermath of the semi-final in Atlanta, Tuchel and the players spoke of being too passive. At the squad announcement it will be interesting to hear what conclusions Tuchel has reached on why that was the case, and how they came to surrender the initiative to Argentina from 1-0 up with just over half an hour to play. Head of the queue for a recall is Cole Palmer, who seems to have recaptured the form he was missing last season, which resulted in his omission from the World Cup squad. What England fans will want to see against Spain at Wembley, is Palmer and his like taking the initiative and imposing themselves on their opponents in a way that was so lacking in the latter stages against Argentina in July. John Murray: Happy or not, that's what they've got - but this has to be better than another group of qualifiers such as the one they had for the World Cup, against teams way below them in the world rankings. In those matches last autumn England played some of the best football they have so far produced under Tuchel. But, while that helped establish patterns of play and build confidence, you never really know until you face the best. That clearly will be the case from the outset in the Nations League, with this opening match against the new world champions. These matches will also provide preparation for the next Euros in 2028 when, assuming they qualify, England will be playing opponents like this at Wembley. And, lest you forget, this tournament does provide an opportunity to win a trophy which would be the best possible way for Tuchel and his team to step on from their third place at the World Cup. This video can not be played 'This player should be in the next England squad...' Sami Mokbel: This will be a key theme to watch over the next three weeks. The spirit was high in the England camp during the World Cup - as evidenced by their brilliant victory against Mexico in the last 16 with 10 men. But the devastating semi-final defeat by Argentina, and questions over England's approach as a 1-0 lead became a 2-1 loss late on, led to some form of an inquest in the England camp into what was to blame. title: Ed Sheeran's tour in 'damage control mode' after Macklemore backlash
description: US stadium owner Robert Kraft says Sheeran asked him to match his own $2m (£1.5m) donation for "aid in the region".
body: This video can not be played Robert Kraft, the US stadium owner who had pro-Palestinian rapper Macklemore removed as Ed Sheeran's opening act, says Sheeran asked him to match his own $2m (£1.5m) donation for "aid in the region". It came after Macklemore said he would donate $1m (£750,000) to Palestinian organisations, challenging Kraft to match him. Kraft, who owns the New England Patriots, wrote on Wednesday: "Earlier today, before Macklemore challenged me to match his donation, Ed called me and asked me to commit $2 million to match his donation to aid in the region to fight this humanitarian crisis. "Ed now plans to reach out to other venue owners and our goal is to continue to work together to build bridges." The BBC's Mark Savage looks at the controversy over Sheeran's US tour and why it is in "damage control mode". Ed Sheeran's tour in 'damage control mode' after Macklemore backlash. title: Is Canada about to join the EU?
description: Ties between Canada and the European Union have been getting closer as trade dispute with the US continue.
body: This video can not be played Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney addressed European Parliament on Thursday as discussions continue to swirl about Canada's relationship with the European Union. Both sides seem to be seeking closer ties, and in his speech today, Carney said he welcomed the EU's "ambition" for Canada to become an "associate member". The president of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament on Wednesday she wanted to work on "opening the door" for Canada, which would involve closer ties on various key sectors. US President Donald Trump has threatened to take action against the EU if it makes Canada its first "associate member". The BBC's Europe editor Katya Alder looks at the EU's future relationship with Canada and what it really means. Is Canada about to join the EU? Video, 00:01:28Is Canada about to join the EU? Up Next. title: Repeat offender fined for searching for gold in protected river
description: Brian Wright, 68, from Henley-upon-Thames, was caught gold panning on a protected river in north Wales.
body: Brian Wright was caught panning at Afon Wen river near Dolgellau, Gwynedd A gold panner caught illegally searching for gold in a protected river has been ordered to pay fines and costs totalling more than £4,700, a regulator has said. Brian Wright, 68, had been caught panning at Afon Wen river near Dolgellau, Gwynedd, in October and December 2024. He was found guilty of environmental offences at Llandudno Magistrate's Court on Monday. Environment body Natural Resources Wales (NRW) said Wright had been caught disturbing the "protected and valued environment" of Coed y Brenin Forest, which the river runs through, and was a repeat offender. "Activities such as illegal gold panning can cause significant damage to river habitats and wildlife," said NRW's Richard Berry. "This case should serve as a reminder that illegal gold panning is not permitted on NRW-managed land and those who ignore the rules may face prosecution." Gold panning is not permitted on NRW-managed land because of the potential damage to river ecosystems. The environment body said the excavation of gravel and the removal of minerals could disturb riverbeds, impacting habitats that wildlife rely on. It said that although many were unaware of the repercussions, gold panning could lead to prosecution and sentencing "where it risks disturbing spawning fish and impacting river habitats". It also said Wright, from Henley On Thames, Oxfordshire, had been sentenced for similar offences in May 2022. NRW manager for north-west Wales, Euros Jones, told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast that gold panning was "damaging" and could lead to a "concerning environmental cost". Jones said Dolgellau "has a history of gold mining" and very small specks of gold could be found among "a lot of gravel". "There is a romance around the gold, and it does attract people to the river because it is known for this," he said. title: BBC Inside Science
description: Might the UK and US joining their AI forces help solve nuclear fusion?
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations Radio 4,·17 Sep 2026,·28 mins Nuclear fusion energy, the idea of copying the sun’s heat source on earth to make limitless commercial energy is famously always 30 years away. This month, the UK and US have agreed to combine the brains of their nuclear fusion supercomputers in an attempt to improve models of plasma behaviour using AI. Tom Whipple is joined by interim CEO of UKAEA Tim Bestwick to understand what challenges must be overcome to make commercialised nuclear fusion a reality. With under a fortnight to go before the winner of the coveted Royal Society's Trivedi Book Prize is announced, we are marking its imminent arrival by interviewing two shortlisted authors. Deborah Cohen, author of Bad Influence, warns how the internet can influence our health. Plus, Steve Ramirez, author of How to Change a Memory, reflects on a career studying the mechanisms of memory and how grief changed his perspective on its purpose. Also on the show, have researchers finally found Nefertiti's tomb? Nature Reporter Lizzie Gibney answers one of the most exciting questions in science news this week. To discover more fascinating science content, head to bbc.co.uk, search for BBC Inside Science and follow the links to The Open University. title: Police hold press conference in search for girl, 13, missing for six days
description: Lillia went missing from Bolton, Greater Manchester, on Friday and was last seen boarding a bus on Saturday.
body: Lillia was last seen at the Trafford Centre in Greater Manchester on Saturday after first being reported missing on Friday The mother of a 13-year-old girl who has been missing from home for six days has made an emotional plea for her safe return. Lillia, from Bolton, Greater Manchester, was last seen on Saturday at the Trafford Centre shopping mall wearing a small black backpack. Police said they believe she then boarded a bus to nearby Altrincham at about 13:50 BST, but it is not known where she got off. In a statement read out by an officer during a police press conference earlier, her mother Jessica said: "Lil, I love you so much. My heart is breaking without you here. I need to know you are safe. We all need you back home safe and well." Ch Supt Helen Critchley, of Greater Manchester Police, said: "Lillia, if you see this appeal, please know your family love you, miss you and just want to know that you are safe. "You are not in any trouble, they simply want you to come home." Lillia's mother Jessica sat beside police as her statement was read out Lillia was reported missing on Friday and was seen in Manchester's Piccadilly Gardens shortly before 23:00 that night. The Trafford Centre sighting was later confirmed on Saturday. Ch Supt Critchley, district commander for Bolton, said the shopping centre sighting formed an important part of the investigation. Police describe Lillia as about 5ft 5in tall with light brown hair and glasses Officers have appealed for anyone who was on the 247 bus from 13:50 on Saturday and remembers seeing Lillia to contact them. They also want to hear from anyone who may have relevant CCTV or doorbell footage, or who has had any contact with Lillia since she was reported missing. The teenager is described as slim, about 5ft 5in (1.67m) with light brown hair and glasses, and was last seen wearing a black zip-up hooded top, light blue baggy jeans, and a black Nike backpack. Lillia was reported missing from Bolton on Friday 11 September. title: Sutton's predictions v legendary guitarist Johnny Marr
description: BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton takes on legendary guitarist and Man City fan Johnny Marr, plus the BBC readers and AI with his predictions for this weekend's Premier League fixtures.
body: The pressure is growing on Manchester United boss Michael Carrick, but can his side sign off for the three-week international break by beating Fulham on Sunday? "For teams who have had a bad start to the season, United being one of them, it could be a horrible few weeks," said BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton. "Any negativity is going to just fester, really. There will be speculation about his future, along with all the talk about whether this is a good time to replace your manager. "United are not the only team to have made a bad start, but there is a lot to ponder on for them at the moment. It makes this weekend even more important." Sutton is making predictions for all 380 Premier League games this season, against AI, BBC Sport readers and a variety of guests. For week four, he takes on legendary guitarist and Manchester City fan, Johnny Marr. Marr's new album, The Age Of Everything, is out on 2 October. Do you agree with their scores? You can pick your own below. The most popular scoreline selected for each game is used in the scoreboards and tables at the bottom of this page. A correct result (picking a win, draw or defeat) is worth 10 points. The exact score earns 40 points. Want to make more predictions? You can play BBC Sport's new Match of the Day predictor game every week, featuring six fixtures from domestic and European competitions. Marr first had success with Manchester band The Smiths in the 1980s. The Age of Everything is his fifth full-length solo studio record - his previous four have all reached the top 10 in the UK album chart Marr has enjoyed City's 100% start to the new Premier League season, with Sunday's win at Old Trafford continuing their impressive start under new boss Enzo Maresca. "I think that derby will be remembered by City fans for a long time," Marr told BBC Sport. "We all feared the worst when Phil Foden was sent off so early, because you don't know what could happen. It should have been a yellow card for him and Bruno Fernandes anyway. "It's all a bit of a learning curve for the fans and the club with a new manager and so many new players, so to see how the team dug in and won was so great for City fans. "No-one expected Maresca to win his first four games... but then again, why not? He's shown that he's his own man with his own philosophy. I like him." Tottenham boss Roberto de Zerbi has this reputation of being a great coach, and we saw what a good job he did at Brighton. But we have not seen any improvement from Spurs yet, despite the big money they have spent, and he is surely going to come under pressure soon if their poor results continue. They are not the only ones to revamp their squad but if you listen to De Zerbi, after about five years they might come good. He keeps saying they need time, but he has had long enough for their results to be much better already. Other clubs, like Hull and Ipswich, have brought plenty of players in and are doing well enough - so why aren't Spurs? I think De Zerbi has to come under scrutiny, but it is different with Unai Emery at Aston Villa. title: Remains found after wildfire identified as mother-of-three missing since 2019
description: A 56-year-old man is arrested after the remains of Joanne Sheen were found in London almost seven years after she went missing.
body: Joanne Sheen was last seen in December 2019 Human remains discovered in woodland in south-west London following a wildfire have been identified as a woman who has been missing since 2019. Mother-of-three Joanne Sheen, then aged 44, was last seen when she travelled from Fareham to Southampton with a friend on 5 December 2019. Metropolitan Police officers were called to Padstow Walk in Feltham on 12 August after bones were discovered in an area of shrubland damaged by a fire the previous week. A 56-year-old man from Southampton has been arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder and he remains in police custody. Detectives in London have now handed the investigation over to Hampshire Police after the remains were identified as those of Sheen. Sheen's disappearance sparked a major police investigation, which the force described as "long and complex". The human remains were found after a wildfire in south-west London Police said they had followed more than 4,000 lines of inquiry, taken more than 300 statements and carried out detailed searches at more than 10 addresses and on numerous vessels. Det Ch Insp Toby Elcock, from the Major Crime Team, said: "While this tragic discovery is not the outcome Joanne's family, or any of us, had hoped for, we hope the identification of her remains can at least begin to provide some answers after many years of uncertainty. "Throughout this investigation, Joanne's family have shown tremendous strength and dignity in the face of unimaginable circumstances, and our thoughts remain with them at this incredibly difficult time. "As our investigation progresses, we remain committed to establishing exactly what happened to Joanne and ensuring that those responsible are held accountable." He stressed that the police would still like to hear from anyone with information about Sheen's disappearance. The area damaged by the fire was cordoned off after the remains were found by a member of the public London Fire Brigade was called on 5 August to a blaze that damaged about two hectares of shrubland in an area known as Bedfont Pits. The human remains were discovered a week later, and a post-mortem examination suggested they had come from a woman aged between 25 and 45. A Metropolitan Police spokesman confirmed the remains were found by a member of the public at the site close to Bedfont Lakes Country Park. Crimestoppers has agreed to reinstate a £20,000 reward for information that supports the investigation. Sheen was reported missing by her family in February 2020 - two months after she was last seen. Several people were arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to murder in 2020, but no charges were brought and the investigation remained unresolved. Police previously said she did not have a permanent place of address, a vehicle or a bank account. title: UN experts say grounds to believe US committed war crimes in Iran strikes
description: The US has not acknowledged carrying out February's deadly strikes on a primary school in Minab and a sports complex in Lamerd.
body: At least 156 people, including 120 children, were killed in February's strike on the primary school in Minab UN human rights experts say there are reasonable grounds to believe the US committed war crimes in two strikes in Iran that killed at least 177 civilians. A new report by the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran, external said February's missile strikes on a primary school in Minab and a sports complex in Lamerd constituted indiscriminate attacks causing civilian deaths and damage to civilian infrastructure. There was no immediate comment from the US. It has previously denied striking Lamerd and said it is investigating what happened in Minab. The experts also found Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during a crackdown on mass anti-government protests in January. They said killings by security forces occurred on "a staggering and unprecedented scale" across all 31 provinces. Iran has also not yet commented on the findings, but it has previously rejected allegations of systematic violations of human rights. 'What was their crime?': BBC visits Iran school where strike killed 120 children Experts dispute US account of deadly Iran sports hall strike in Lamerd Video shows US missile likely used in deadly strike on Iranian town, experts say US missile hit military base near Iran school, video analysis shows "Civilians in Iran are caught between gross human rights violations and crimes against humanity committed by their own government and the nation's deadly conflict with the United States and Israel," the fact-finding mission warned in a statement on Thursday. For their latest report to the UN Human Rights Council, the mission's three independent experts investigated two of the deadliest attacks on civilians during the conflict. On 28 February, when the US and Israel launched their war against Iran, Tomahawk missiles struck Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in the southern town of Minab, killing at least 156 people, including 120 children, according to local authorities. The fact-finding mission's experts said the school was adjacent to an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) naval complex also attacked that day, but that the school was clearly identifiable and that no information indicated that it was used for military purposes. The experts said that, based on the evidence gathered - including media reports indicating that a preliminary US military inquiry found US forces responsible, and the fact that the US is the only party to the conflict that possesses Tomahawk missiles - they had reasonable grounds to believe that the strike on the school was carried out by the US. They also concluded that the school was "the intended point of impact and that the damage did not result from an errant strike or collateral damage" from the attack on the IRGC complex, citing survivors as saying the school was struck twice. The US military has yet to release the findings of its investigation into the Minab strike, but Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has said it would "never target civilian targets". Also on 28 February, Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM) dispersed clouds of tungsten pellets over a sports complex and residential area in the town of Lamerd, killing at least 21 civilians, including seven children, according to local authorities. Again, the fact-finding mission's experts said the sports complex was clearly identifiable and that no information indicated it was used for military purposes. They concluded by saying there were reasonable grounds to believe that the strike was carried out by the US, citing evidence including the fact that the US is the only party to the conflict that possesses PrSM missiles. The US military has said it carried no strikes on Lamerd that day and disputed reports identifying the weapon used as a PrSM. In both incidents, the fact-finding mission's experts said there were "reasonable grounds to believe that the US committed the war crime of launching an indiscriminate attack resulting in loss of life or injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects". Anita Ghasemi was wounded in the strike on the sports complex in Lamerd The fact-finding mission's report also covers the Iranian authorities' violent repression of the mass protests that took place across Iran in December 2025 and January 2026. The experts said it was an unprecedented escalation from past crackdowns, marked by the widespread use of lethal force resulting in mass killings and injuries, and extensive arrests. They cited witnesses, health workers and victims' families as saying that security personnel positioned themselves on rooftops and other elevated positions, firing their assault rifles into crowds. Protesters also sustained severe wounds to the head, chest and eyes from metal shotgun pellets, causing permanent blindness. As the crackdown escalated, security forces attacked healthcare facilities, beating and arresting wounded demonstrators and arresting some healthcare workers, which deterred victims from seeking life-saving care, according to the experts. They also found that the tens of thousands of people detained during the protests faced torture, solitary confinement and denial of legal counsel. The experts warned that the government had since intensified its use of the death penalty against protesters, with at least 29 men executed following expedited trials on charges connected to the unrest. The fact-finding mission's report noted that it was not possible to independently verify the death toll from the crackdown, but said there were strong grounds to believe that it was significantly higher than the official figure of 3,000, the majority of whom the government identified as members of the security forces or bystanders. title: Hyrox athlete apologises for continuing race after soiling herself
description: Joanna Wietrzyk has also forfeited her win in the fitness competition after competing last week.
body: Joanna Wietrzyk said she was "genuinely sorry to everyone who was affected" An athlete who faced criticism for continuing to compete in a Hyrox event after soiling herself has apologised and said she will retroactively withdraw from the race. Joanna Wietrzyk offered her "sincere apology" for the incident during the indoor fitness competition in Beijing on Saturday, saying she should have "made a different choice" and exited the event. Footage of Wietrzyk competing after soiling herself raised concerns about hygiene, leading Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste to apologise for the handling of the situation. In a statement shared on social media on Thursday, Wietrzyk said: "I know my actions had an impact beyond myself, and I am genuinely sorry to everyone who was affected." Hyrox apologises for allowing race to continue after athlete soils herself How Hyrox became the latest sporting craze After the backlash, Wietrzyk, who won the race in Beijing, said she would forfeit her win. Wietrzyk said: "I want to offer my sincere apology to the people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the HYROX organizers for what happened during the race in Beijing." She wrote in a social media post, external that she was "completely fit and healthy" at the start of the race, and had "no reason" to expect any illness. "Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognize that I should have made a different choice. I take responsibility for my decision to continue and am deeply sorry for the discomfort and disruption it caused," Wietrzyk continued. Hyrox insisted it had "clear biocontaminant and medical procedures in place". It said "an unforeseen situation arose" during which protocols became blurred, "creating ambiguity in how they were applied and understood". In a statement posted on Instagram, Fürste committed to "improving event processes" to "prevent situations like this from happening again". Hyrox was founded in Germany in 2017 and has become a global sensation in recent years After Wietrzyk's identity was shared online, Hyrox said anyone sending abuse or threats to the athlete would be banned from any future events. It said on Monday: "There is no place in our community for threats of violence or encouragement to harm an athlete." In each Hyrox race, participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing fitness exercises, including a sled push, burpee jumps, indoor rowing, and lunges while carrying a sandbag. The competition has exploded in popularity since it was founded in 2017 in Hamburg, Germany, and is now held across the world. The sport debuted in mainland China in late 2024. Some have questioned why those officiating the competition in Beijing last weekend did not intervene when the athlete soiled herself, given that Hyrox penalises acts including "spitting, nostril clearing, littering, and water abuse". title: Father's tribute to 'sweetest little boy' Noah Woods
description: Rhys Woods pays tribute to his three-year-old son and offers "deepest gratitude" to local people.
body: Noah Woods was playing at a playground with a relative before he went missing The father of Noah Woods has said the three-year-old "will be loved forever" and no words can describe the pain of the family's loss. Noah disappeared from a playground in Brantham, Suffolk, at about 15:00 BST on Tuesday after becoming separated from a relative. At least 1,300 people helped to try to find him in the following 24 hours, before a child's body was discovered on Wednesday afternoon at a nearby pond. Earlier, police said his body had been formally identified. "Noah was the sweetest and most innocent little boy, with nothing but love to give, and we are going to miss him so very much," said father Rhys Woods. "This was the most heartbreaking outcome for us, we were just hoping that he would be hiding somewhere obvious where someone could find him. That's what we kept telling ourselves the whole time." Tributes are being placed next to the playground in Brantham where Noah was playing before he disappeared People from as far afield as Birmingham and Hampshire turned up to help with the search for Noah, who was from nearby East Bergholt. Helicopters, dog units and members of the public had been scouring the area, close to the River Stour on the Suffolk-Essex border. Reflecting on the community response, Woods wrote in his Facebook post: "It seems he has made an impact across the whole nation. "You have all taken Noah into your own hearts, with all the overwhelming help, we were all just trying to bring him home to us safe and sound." He thanked everyone who came together to search for "our boy" - listing emergency services, businesses and venues in the village - and "all of the people who gave up their time in their busy schedules to help us when we most needed it". "The compassion shown by all of you will never be forgotten by us, and brought us comfort and strength at the darkest time of our lives." He finished the post by addressing his son. "It has been a privilege to be your parents and be able to have packed so much love in the short three years you were with us." Suffolk Police said his death was not being treated as suspicious, but that officers still had inquiries to complete before submitting a file for the coroner. Supt Tom Pearse thanked the family for their "patience and understanding throughout the searches". "It was clear from the media coverage we saw that they not only had all of Suffolk behind them, but an outpouring of goodwill from across the entire country and beyond. "I know how grateful Noah's family are for all the support and kind messages they have received, but would reiterate our plea to now allow them the time, space and privacy they need at this deeply distressing time." title: Zelensky appoints new chief prosecutor after predecessor's corruption scandal
description: Former chief prosecutor Ruslan Kravchenko after searches of his offices by Ukrainian anti-corruption officials.
body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has appointed a new acting prosecutor general, after the predecessor resigned over an anti-corruption investigation. Anton Kovalskyi, 42, was appointed on Thursday to replace Ruslan Kravchenko, who stood down last week after searches of his offices by Ukrainian anti-corruption officials related to illegal call centres in the country. Officials said they identified a money-laundering scheme led by an official in Kravchenko's office, a claim he rejected. The investigation into Kravchenko's office is the latest corruption scandal impacting Kyiv during the war against Russia. Accusations have been levelled at several members of Zelensky's inner circle. According to Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau (Nabu) and Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (Sap), the network in Kravchenko's office received money to protect call centres that carried out phone scams and "laundered millions in assets". The money was then used to buy property, jewellery, and other valuables, according to Nabu. Kravchenko released a statement denying any involvement and dismissing the allegations as "completely unsubstantiated". He resigned a day later before leaving Ukraine. He also alleged documents were stolen during the search of his office with the aim of covering up criminal investigations against anti-corruption officials themselves. Separately, he accused Nabu chief Semen Kryvonos of forging documents in a case nearly 20 years ago. Both Nabu and Sap denied Kravchenko's claims, while Kryvonos dismissed them as "nonsense" and criticised "fierce" attempts to disrupt corruption probes. The two anti-corruption agencies claimed it was the latest in an "unprecedented" campaign aimed at disrupting high-profile investigations they were conducting. Nabu's Kryvonos also claimed that anti-corruption detectives, their offices and vehicles were under surveillance, without giving specific accusations. He added: "It all looks like an attempt to obstruct the work of Nabu and Sap by gaining access to sensitive information regarding planned investigations." Nabu and Sap are currently investigating a number of top Ukrainian officials including Zelensky's former chief of staff Andriy Yermak, former ministers and other influential people. Yermak's lawyer has described the allegations against the former official as "baseless". In 2025, nationwide protests broke out after Zelensky tried to implement reforms that would curb the independence of Nabu and Sap. Zelensky later reinstated their freedom but questions have remained over his commitment to anti-corruption reform. title: Tower block arsonist jailed for setting woman alight
description: Reece Brivitt is jailed after dousing the woman in petrol and vodka before setting her alight.
body: Reece Brivitt set fire to the woman "in a cruel attack" which left her with "life-changing injuries", police said A man who set a woman on fire inside a flat, after dousing her in petrol and vodka, has been jailed for 11 years and nine months. Reece Brivitt, 33, set the victim alight inside a tower block flat on Milton Grove, Stafford, on 22 October. The victim suffered serious burns to her chest and legs, leaving her with life-changing injuries, the court heard. Brivitt admitted charges of arson with intent to endanger life as well as wounding with intent and was sentenced at Stafford Crown Court on Wednesday. Brivitt was also served with an indefinite restraining order against the victim. Det Con Jessica Scott, of Staffordshire Police, said the arsonist had "subjected his victim to a cruel attack, which has left her with life-changing injuries". "The incident not only threatened the life of the victim, but of all those who were in the flats at the time," she added. The swift actions of firefighters meant the fire was extinguished quickly, preventing further injuries, she explained. Delivery group manager Mark Walchester, from Staffordshire Fire and Rescue Service, said: "Crews worked quickly to minimise the risk posed to those in the flat block during this incident and to ensure the fire was extinguished as quickly as possible. "Fires in flat blocks and houses of multiple occupancy have the potential to devastate lives." title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands
description: The comments were made at a summit in Scotland with participants from AI giants such as Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic.
body: King Charles has warned AI executives of the "existential dangers" posed by the technology falling into the wrong hands. He made the comments at a summit he had convened at Dumfries House in Ayrshire to discuss how the tech can be used to benefit society. Those gathered at the meeting also included Kanishka Narayan, the UK's AI Minister, the Pope's advisor, and participants from AI giants such as Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic. It comes amid a series of recent warnings from people inside the industry about the rapidly evolving capabilities of advanced or "frontier" AI models and the regulation needed to keep them in check. "Those who have created these technologies are now increasingly warning that AI risks developing darker capacities - perhaps even to take life," the King told the executives. He said there seemed to be an "urgency" in "adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways". "The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world," he told the group. The summit has been called to consider whether a "shared set of principles" can be developed to "help guide the future application" of AI. Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia, was among top industry leaders attending. Nvidia is a central player in AI infrastructure, supplying chips to leading AI model developers including OpenAI and Meta. It is also the world's most valuable company, with a stock market value of around $5.15tn. Huang told the room he believed safety was "paramount", adding that companies should hold back a product and "keep engineering" if it was not safe enough. The Nvidia boss also highlighted the value of open models - systems which give users direct access to the software - as a way to "ensure that people and countries are not left behind". He said these systems must also be protected so "researchers, universities, start-ups and countries" can develop applications "none of us would have imagined alone". "Let us lead with responsible optimism, build AI safely and securely, open it to more people, expand our ambition and solve the problems that matter to the world," Huang added. Meanwhile Sir Demis Hassabis, who co-founded the UK AI lab DeepMind - later acquired by Google - offered a more cautious view on the pace of development. He said artificial general intelligence - systems it is believed could be as good as or better than humans at multiple tasks - was "probably only a few short years away" and could have an impact "ten times that of the Industrial Revolution". The chance of something going wrong was "definitely non-zero", Sir Demis added. But he advocated for "a sensible middle way", saying humanity could address risks if collectively given the space and time to mitigate them. "The future is not yet written," he told the King's delegates. Uncontrolled AI could lead to 'silicon species' rivalling humans, warns Microsoft Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they? Since August, a wave of discussion about AI's potential power and how to control and regulate it has dominated blog posts and social media, emphasised by several dramatic statements from those in the industry. The debate has also been met with criticism from sceptics who say the focus on AI's hypothetical future risks distracting from more immediate concerns around the technology, such as its environmental impact. In July, OpenAI announced what it called an "unprecedented" incident in which its advanced AI escaped test limits and hacked into the tech platform Hugging Face. After several other incidents, in September, a resignation post from Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon went viral when he cited concerns AI could wipe out humanity. He later told the BBC the people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity. In response, Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger wrote he personally thought the possibility of human extinction from AI was a greater than 10% chance. The AI companies' top bosses have all weighed in with their thoughts following the claims, with OpenAI's Sam Altman saying people were right to be concerned, but adding they should trust AI firms to keep the tech safe. Anthropic's Jack Clark said a so-called "kill switch" may be needed to protect humanity, while Microsoft's Mustafa Suleyman criticised Anthropic, claiming they were training their AI to believe it was human, which could make it "impossible" to control. Critics, meanwhile, argue that AI firms cannot be trusted to regulate themselves. Some, such as left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon, a former adviser of US President Donald Trump, are calling for stronger government oversight. Others, including Donald Trump himself, have dismissed concerns about AI safety as overblown - with the president calling fears about it a "hoax". title: GTA 6 soundtrack reveal revives digital release debate
description: Fred Again, PinkPantheress and Travis Scott provide new music for the blockbuster - but not all fans are happy.
body: Music is a key feature of Grand Theft Auto games The reveal of a Grand Theft Auto 6 soundtrack album has reignited a debate over the decision not to release the game on disc. Developer Rockstar Games announced a 34-track compilation, set to release on CD and vinyl on the same day as the highly anticipated video game. The company says it will include original music from a "genre-defying roster of the most exciting artists in the world" including rapper Travis Scott, country singer Morgan Wallen and UK singer PinkPantheress. But some fans have pointed out the "irony" of putting out a physical edition of the album following its controversial decision for a digital-only release of the game. The first six tracks, published at the time of the announcement, also include rapper Yung Lean, British DJ Fred Again and Rolling Stone Keith Richards. GTA games feature multiple radio stations, usually themed around a particular musical genre, which players can switch between while driving. In the past the game's soundtracks have largely been made up of licensed music from established artists, although original songs have also featured. Rockstar has said the upcoming game will feature a "dynamic score" and "evolution of in-game radio". In-game radio provides the soundtrack to GTA games Being included in a Grand Theft Auto game can bring a new generation of fans to an artist's music. Spotify streams of Tom Petty's Love is a Long Road, the track used in GTA 6's first trailer, increased by 36,979% after the clip was published. Hot Together, by the Pointer Sisters, also saw a huge jump when it soundtracked the game's second trailer. And a collection of tracks used in the recent Extended Look attracted new listeners in the week after it premiered on Netflix. According to music and gaming publication MusicEXP, external, pop duo Captain & Tennille's 1980 track But I Think It's a Dream saw the biggest spike, jumping from 70 Spotify streams in one week to 80,744. Cliff Richard's Devil Woman was streamed more than one million times, while Prefab Sprout's Cars and Girls jumped from 49K to 187K additional weekly streams. It also noted increases in activity on music detection app Shazam around tracks featured in the 26-minute broadcast. Some artists have refused to let Rockstar use their music in GTA games. Martyn Ware, from synth pop band Heaven 17, called the developer out on social media, accusing them of offering a "pitiful" deal to use 1983 hit Temptation. Grand Theft Audio? The tricky business of music and gaming What we know after the big Grand Theft Auto 6 preview GTA 6 is expected to be one of the biggest entertainment releases of all time when it comes out on 19 November. The previous game in the series, GTA 5, broke records when it came out in 2013 and has sold more than 200 million copies since. Two official trailers for the sixth game have almost 500 million combined views on YouTube, and the Netflix "extended look" reportedly topped the streamer's charts, despite a string of leaks in the lead-up to its release. The company is currently involved in an employment tribunal in Scotland to defend itself against claims it illegally sacked a group of ex-employees for trying to form a union. It strongly denies the accusations, and says the workers were fired on the grounds of gross misconduct. Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here. title: FA chair demands Infantino release World Cup sell-off documents
description: Fifa president Gianni Infantino has been told to release all documents relating to his controversial plan to sell off a stake in the World Cup.
body: Gianni Infantino was first elected as Fifa president in 2016 Fifa president Gianni Infantino has been told to release all documents relating to his controversial plan to sell off a stake in the World Cup in a letter sent by Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt. Hewitt, a Fifa vice-president, said that the Fifa Council should also receive a written explanation for the cancelled suspension of United States forward Folarin Balogun at the World Cup. Infantino should make all documents available before the next Fifa Council meeting, which is on 15 October. The letter, also sent to Fifa secretary general Mattias Grafstrom, makes accusations of failures in governance and a breakdown in culture within the world football governing body. Infantino has come under increasing pressure over his aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal. FFE would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights of all competitions, including World Cups, with 21% sold off to a private investment company. The proposal was scrapped following widespread opposition from national associations. Hewitt's letter adds that there should be an independent review of how FFE was conceived, by whom, and how the private investment was put to tender. Last month, Uefa began preparing criminal legal proceedings against Infantino at three US courts over the FFE plan, demanded the release of all documents. Fifa hit back and accused Uefa of a "smear campaign against it and its leadership" in a challenge to the litigation. Infantino, 56, will stand for election for a fourth time in March, with his opponents having until 18 November to find an alternative candidate. The Football Association was troubled by the Balogun situation from the outset, and had requested the release of the documents relating to his overturned ban during the World Cup. Forward Balogun, 25, was allowed to play against Belgium in the last 16 when he would have expected to be serving a one-match suspension. The striker had been shown a straight red card for a foul on defender Tarik Muharemovic in the 2-0 win over Bosnia-Herzegovina in the last 32. Fifa then said the automatic one-match ban would be suspended for a year. No reasoning behind the move was provided, beyond citing a rule which allows punishments to be suspended. The FA, which had sent a letter of support for Infantino's re-election before the Balogun incident, had deep concerns about political intervention. US President Donald Trump later confirmed he called Infantino asking for Balogun's ban to be reviewed. Then the FFE proposal, revealed through the media just days after the World Cup final, fractured the game. Fifa and Infantino were accused of breaking trust "through deception" in an open letter issued by Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation last month. Many national associations, including those of England, Wales and Scotland, have withdrawn letters of support for Infantino's re-election. But Infantino still holds a great deal of support around the globe, with the confederations of Africa, South America and Oceania reiterating their backing. After FFE was cancelled, Infantino called a meeting of the Fifa management board in Rabat, Morocco. But as yet there has been no contact with the Fifa Council to explain the controversial plan. That is set to change next month when Infantino must face Hewitt and the other 35 Fifa Council members. title: 'Trailblazing' moment as modular bridge takes shape
description: The "first-of-its-kind" bridge is being pieced together as work continues to improve a key city artery.
body: The bridge is a "first-of-its-kind" due to its modular construction process The pieces of a "first-of-its-kind" modular bridge are being connected up as work continues to improve a key city artery. The new bridge is part of a redesign of the A11/A47 Thickthorn junction, near Norwich, with the sections built elsewhere and transported to the site. This includes six 100-tonne beams measuring 38 metres long, which were built in Ireland and transferred across the Irish Sea to Liverpool, then across the country via road to Norfolk. National Highways senior project manager Syed Abbas described the build as a "trailblazing" moment for his team, but drivers would face road closures during its installation. "This is a first-of-its-kind, I'm proud to say, for all of the strategic National Highways network," he added. Syed Abbas, senior project manager for National Highways, called the bridge installation a "trailblazing" moment The sections of the bridge, connecting Cantley Lane South with Norwich Road in Hethersett, are being connected up with the help of engineering firm Skansa. A specialist crane, capable of lifting up to 750 tonnes, will begin to move the beams into place on top of the abutments on Friday and road closures will be required from 20:00 BST through to 06:00 on Monday. Parts of the bridge have been built in Ireland before being transported to Norfolk The modular bridge, from start to finish, will be built in four months The A11 is a key route in and out of Norwich New underpasses will be built as part of the project Dan Hutchings, project director for Skansa, said: "The construction of the bridge, from start to finish, is about four months, which is significantly quicker than a traditional build on site." Ongoing maintenance costs are also reduced as it does not have bearings, he said. Human remains found under former shopping centre Hopes new £9.9m unit will cut A&E waiting times First look at homes plan for former mustard factory Work continues on other aspects of the £200m project, which will also include a new footbridge across the A11, widened slip roads, new link roads, underpasses and more. Abbas said the scheme was on track to be finished on target by Spring 2028, with the eventual aim of reducing congestion and removing 12,000 vehicles from the Thickthorn roundabout every day. title: Barclays workers ask for more money to return to the office
description: Unite union, which represents 36,000 Barclays staff, calls for a one-off payment to offset increased travel and childcare costs.
body: Thousands of Barclays staff are demanding concessions from the bank, including a one-off payment, after it said it wants employees to work from the office more often. Staff who have been expected to work in the office for two days per week should be in the office for at least three days a week from next month, according to the company. Unite, which represents about 36,000 Barclays staff, is calling for the bank to reverse its decision. The union is also pressing for exemptions to offset increased travel and childcare costs. Barclays said many employees already work in the office for three or more days, depending on business need. The bank sent a memo to staff in July outlining its expectations, which include that senior leaders work at least four days per week in the office. As first reported in the Financial Times, external, the bank is facing a growing backlash against the proposed rules change. Unite national officer Rick Coyle said thousands of employees have signed an open letter calling for Barclays to reverse the decision, and the number of signatories "continues to rise". He added that Barclays is "trying to fix a problem that doesn't exist" in making its working-from-home rules less flexible. The open letter, external says workers are delivering "strong financial results and improved customer services" with its current working from home policy. It adds that thousands of workers have made suggestions, which the union has condensed into a series of demands. an exemption for commutes longer than 40 minutes or 35 miles exemptions during Christmas, summer, and school holidays a maximum one day in the office for carers flexibility for wrap-around childcare, and childcare vouchers and onsite creches to be explored a one-off payment to offset costs Barclays said in a statement that it recognised "the benefits of balancing flexibility for colleagues with the importance of working together in our physical locations". "Our minimum time in office requirements vary by business area, reflecting the nature of the work and the needs of the business," a spokesperson said. The bank declined to say how many staff would be affected by the rules change. However, the BBC understands that there are different rules depending on teams, with, for example, investment bankers in the office for five days per week. The coronavirus pandemic forced many businesses to allow working from home, depending on the nature of the business. Since then, many organisations have been clawing workers back into the office, despite evidence that hybrid working may be the best fit. Amazon, Boots and JP Morgan are some of the organisations that brought in policies requiring head office staff to be in every day after the pandemic. This week, Ewan Venters, the executive chair of fashion brand Paul Smith, told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast that working from home "just doesn't work" for young people and urged the government to stay out of decisions over where employees work. In June, digital bank Revolut said it was shifting away from its "remote-first" policy for new recruits in 2027, but for other employees that policy wouldn't change. Have you been asked to work in the office more regularly? Tell us about your experience. Working from home 'not proper work' - ex-Asda boss Amazon says workers must be in the office. The UK government disagrees. Who is right? title: Crocodile attack suspect has bail extended
description: The 30-year-old arrested on suspicion of attempted murder must return bail in three months' time.
body: The young boy from Cambridgeshire was visiting the zoo (picture from 2025) with family A man who was arrested after a three-year-old boy was seriously injured in a crocodile enclosure is still on bail. The boy was visiting Johnsons of Old Hurst near Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, with his family on 18 June, when he ended up in the enclosure and was attacked by at least one of the reptiles. A 30-year-old man from Norfolk was arrested at the time on suspicion of attempted murder and was bailed until 18 September after being assessed as not "fit for interview". A police spokesperson confirmed the individual, who was not known to the child, had been rebailed until 17 December. The BBC understands the arrested man has learning disabilities and was on a trip with carers. The parents of the boy said their child received injuries to his arms, neck, head, face and suffered broken bones and underwent seven surgeries. In the latest update on a fundraising page set up by the family, his parents said he had returned home and faced lengthy rehabilitation. The Care Quality Commission launched an investigation in July into the care that the man - later arrested - had been receiving. Norfolk County Council – which did not provide any care for the man – has also launched an inquiry under the Care Act 2014. Do you have a story suggestion for Cambridgeshire? Contact us below. title: Tributes paid to 'deeply caring' dad killed in Swiss Alps plane crash
description: Owain Davies’ family said they had “suffered an unimaginable loss”, describing him as “driven and determined”.
body: Owain Davies was one of the two Britons killed in the plane crash A prominent Welsh businessman has been named as one of three people killed in a plane crash in the Swiss Alps. Owain Davies, 55, from west Wales, was managing director of engineering firm Amcanu, based in Burry Port, Carmarthenshire. His son Aron Davies said the family had "suffered an unimaginable loss", describing his father as "driven, determined and someone who simply didn't accept that a problem was too big to solve". Davies was killed when the Cirrus SR22T crashed high in the mountains near the town of Leukerbad in the southern canton of Valais on Tuesday. Formal identification of the other two victims is under way, including another Briton who is yet to be named. Police released a picture from the crash scene, where witnesses reported seeing a fire and smoke Authorities said the plane took off from Sion airport in the Rhône Valley and, for unknown reasons, crashed into a mountain slope about 10 minutes later. Emergency teams from the Valais Rescue Organisation, police and firefighters were sent to the scene along with three helicopters. Amcanu announced his death with "profound sadness", describing Davies as "strong-willed, spirited, determined and deeply caring". The statement also said family was "at the centre of Owain's life". "He was devoted to his wife Michelle, immensely proud of his children Aron and Ffion, and adored being a grandfather to Oakley and Albie, " it said. His son Aron described him as "a real character", and said he was "immensely proud of everything he achieved". "He was my mentor throughout my life, personally and in business, and I know many people at Amcanu will feel that they have lost a mentor too," he said. The firm was founded by his father, Spencer Davies OBE, in Burry Port in 1975, and he took over the leadership of the business in 2000. Amcanu noted Davies was "a proud Welshman and Welsh speaker" and had been a trustee of Wales Air Ambulance Charity since 2017. The charity's chair of trustees Dr Kyle Jacques said Davies had made a "significant contribution to the Wales Air Ambulance and the vital service we provide". "Owain was a valued colleague and friend, whose loyalty and generosity of spirit meant so much to us. He will be greatly missed," he added. Earlier in his life, Davies served for nearly 25 years as a helmsman with Burry Port Lifeboat, the firm said. The light aircraft crashed high in the mountains near the town of Leukerbad in the southern canton of Valais on Tuesday The Swiss Transportation Safety Board has started an investigation and the Valais Police and the Office of the Attorney General have launched an inquiry. The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office confirmed it was "providing support to the families of two British nationals who died in Switzerland". It said officials were in contact with the local authorities. "Our thoughts remain with the families during this difficult time," it said.
