title: The Papers: King's 'astonishing outburst' and 'heartbreak' after search for missing Noah
description: Several of today's papers splash on the Palace's response to Earl Spencer's claim in his upcoming book about his sister Diana.
body: Earl Spencer, the brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, has ignited a fresh row with the Palace following claims in his upcoming book, which feature heavily in today's papers. The book claims that King Charles told Spencer in the days after Diana's death in 1997: "Rest assured, we'll forget her soon enough", the Times reports. The paper headlines on a Buckingham Palace official statement that hit back at the book, saying grief can "colour memory". The Daily Mail was the one that published the exclusive extract from Earl Spencer's upcoming book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, which it says "lifts the lid on an incendiary row with the now King over funeral arrangements". Spencer alleged the then-Prince of Wales subjected him to a "stream of anger" after he insisted Diana would not have wanted the young Princes William and Harry to walk in her funeral procession. The Daily Telegraph also reports that Buckingham Palace has "hit back" at accusations made by Earl Spencer, which it describes as a "highly unusual move". In the official statement, the Palace said "pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss," the paper reports. "Recollections may vary...again", the Sun headlines after the "war of words with Prince Diana's brother". The paper points to the Queen's famous "recollections may vary" statement over claims made by Prince Harry and Meghan in 2021, and how they are echoed in the Palace's latest statement. Noah Woods, who disappeared on Tuesday, is pictured on the front page of the Independent after police confirm a body was found near where the toddler vanished. "Heartbreak", the Daily Mirror reports. Three-year-old Noah went missing from a playground in Brantham, Suffolk, after becoming separated from a relative. Police said a child's body had been found in a nearby pond. Meanwhile, Tory leader Kemi Badenoch warns Britain is "paying the price" for Labour's economic failures after inflation rose to 3.1% with warnings it could top 4% next year, the Daily Express reports. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the government "won't take risks with people's living standards" after the 3.1% inflation news, the i Paper reports. According to economists, capital gains tax may be one of the most likely tax rises in the upcoming Budget next month, the paper says. Nine years after the "Putney Pusher" mystery began - when a jogger pushed a woman into the path of a bus during a run on Putney Bridge - the suspect of the incident has been found dead, the Metro reports. Nicholas Brandram was arrested in June this year on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm. Last week he was released under investigation. The "face of Putney Pusher Suspect" is the Daily Star's lead image after the 44-year-old banker was found dead at his home. The paper reports that the man was a direct descendent of Queen Victoria. US interest rates have been raised for the first time in more than three years, the Financial Times reports, despite US President Donald Trump's "calls for lowering borrowing costs". And the Guardian says the prison service in the UK has drawn up plans to "double up" hundreds of prisoners in cells built for one person, according to leaked documents. title: Carrick 'not bothered' by pressure - but should he be after this latest mess?
description: Manager Michael Carrick insists he does not feel under pressure after Manchester United's EFL Cup exit.
body: Manchester United's players were left dejected after squandering a 2-0 lead to lose at home for the first time in 50 years Sir Alex Ferguson was St Mirren manager the last time Manchester United lost at Old Trafford having taken a 2-0 lead. That is the context to the shocking Carabao Cup third-round exit his old club suffered against Brighton on Wednesday. It is a period of time that encompasses the legendary Scot's dynasties at Aberdeen as well as United. The Class of '92 were in nappies when John Pratt scored the winner for Tottenham on 4 September 1976. After holding protests inside and outside the ground before Sunday's loss to 10-man Manchester City, United supporters made their feelings known about their latest embarrassment in three ways. Most fans simply left as the players embarked on their post-match lap of appreciation. Some of those who remained booed, as they had done when their side fell behind 21 minutes from time. By the time they approached the tunnel, close to United's 'singing section', supporters were asking Michael Carrick and his players 'what was that?'. Their wording was somewhat more colourful. It is not certain where 15-year-old JJ Gabriel was while all this was taking place, but nothing happened that would make him think he had got it wrong by turning his back on the club. Indeed, it is quite possible, probable indeed, that the promised senior debut would have been scrapped given the game situation - and the fact skipper Bruno Fernandes was among the experienced players introduced in the frantic final stages. "Of course we can turn it around, we have got some really good players," said Carrick. "It feels bad because we haven't had a great week or two, or three weeks." Man Utd lose to Brighton from 2-0 up to end 50-year record What next for Gabriel and Man Utd? 'Let's go, let's go' - inside catastrophic derby VAR mistake Carrick's side have won twice this season, against newly promoted Ipswich at home after falling behind, and Azerbaijani champions Sabah FK in the Champions League. They have now lost on three occasions, more defeats than he experienced in 17 matches after replacing Ruben Amorim in January. He has been around Manchester United long enough to know the pressure losing runs can build. "I don't feel under pressure," he said. "Either way, that doesn't bother me one bit. "I understand what goes on outside and how the world works, but it doesn't bother me. What bothers me is winning games, having a good feeling around the place and a good feeling around the group to know we're moving in a good direction." The problem is it doesn't feel as though they are moving in a good direction. There were certainly not many positives to take from this mess. The obvious one was Shea Lacey, who marked his first senior start with a well-taken eighth-minute goal. It meant he became the first teenager to score on his first United start since Marcus Rashford in February 2016. Lacey was one of eight changes made by Carrick. Defensively, those changes were not a success. Diogo Dalot was one of the three players to keep their place. His form has deserted him. Noussair Mazraoui is the back-up left-back, which only heightens the debate over the wisdom not to buy one before the transfer window closed. Leny Yoro and Ayden Heaven looked like the inexperienced defenders they are. In midfield Manchester United were overrun. Yet again, Rashford threatened without managing a goal or an assist. He came closest to levelling when he sped beyond the Brighton defence, but his shot was saved by Jason Steele. "The longer the game went, the more we had control," was the concise assessment of Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler. "I thought we deserved to win." Carrick didn't dispute the assessment. His greatest sadness was for Lacey, who should have had his name in lights but instead was part of a team scuttling off the pitch to the sound of boos and harsher criticism. "It's a shame that Shea's moment, such a great moment for him, for his family, his friends and the whole academy; to have an academy player come in and have a moment like that, gets a bit lost, unfortunately," said Carrick. "It won't for him when things settle down but, as we sit here now, it feels that it was a long time ago." Carrick also addressed the JJ Gabriel situation. "He's a young boy, he's 15, and for me, definitely, and from a club point of view, looking after our younger players, their welfare, their wellbeing, their exposure, we've got to be really conscious of that in this situation," he explained. But ultimately, for any manager, the assessment of their work comes through results. "Being here toughens you up over a period of time," he said. "It depends how you deal with it. You've got to deal with it in a way where you can cope with it and you can bring out the best in yourself. However you do that, with your motivation and the confidence deep within yourself to know we can win football matches. "We've gone out of the cup tonight, and the feeling around the place feels bigger than that. I'm honest enough to say that's how it feels. But it doesn't have to be like that. If we win football matches again, it can go in a different direction." Manchester United have one more game before the international break, at Fulham on Sunday. For the general wellbeing of the club, Carrick's team really need to win. Speaking on Sky Sports, former England midfielder Jamie Redknapp said he wasn't sure they will. "Right now, they're miles off it," he said. "It doesn't matter how good the manager is, if you don't have the right players it makes it really difficult. "There's a reason why the other managers have struggled. Sooner or later the pressure's always going to come on. "This weekend becomes a huge game. He doesn't need another poor resul

title: Chelsea chairman and director sell stakes in club to majority owner Clearlake
description: Clearlake Capital acquires full control of Chelsea as chairman Todd Boehly, director Mark Walter and Hansjorg Wyss sell their stakes in the club.
body: Todd Boehly (left) and Mark Walter (right) had been part of Chelsea's ownership group since 2022 Chelsea chairman Todd Boehly and director Mark Walter have sold their stakes in the club to majority owner Clearlake Capital. Swiss billionaire Hansjorg Wyss has also sold his stake, meaning Clearlake - led by co-founders Behdad Eghbali and Jose E. Feliciano - have now acquired full control of the club. Boehly, Walter and Wyss each had a 12.8% stake, with Clearlake previously owning 61.5% of the Blues. American Boehly will leave his role as chairman, a position he has held since 2022, when the consortium bought the club for £2.3bn from Roman Abramovich, who was sanctioned by the UK government in March 2022 over alleged links to Russian president Vladimir Putin - something he has denied. BBC Sport reported in August that Boehly and Walter were exploring selling their stakes. Multiple sources said talks started within Chelsea's ownership group after a rift, first apparent in 2024, led both sides to explore buying each other out. Boehly, who is a co-owner of baseball franchise the Los Angeles Dodgers, said it had been an "honour" to serve as Chelsea chairman. "I would like to thank the many who helped secure a bright future for the club, including the English Premier League, the coaches and players, the talented leadership and staff at Chelsea, and the legions of dedicated fans," he added. "I have valued my partnership with Clearlake and the wider ownership group, and the collective decisions and investment we have made to support the immediate and long-term success of the club. I am confident that Chelsea is well positioned for continued success under Clearlake's leadership." Since the takeover in 2022, Chelsea's highest Premier League finish is fourth in 2024-25, with the club also winning the Uefa Conference League and Fifa Club World Cup that season. The club have also had a remarkably high turnover of players over the past four years, with the initial strategy focusing on signing young players to long-term contracts. Chelsea finished 10th in the Premier League last season and appointed Xabi Alonso as their manager in the summer. Eghbali and Feliciano thanked Boehly for his "time and contribution" as chairman, saying he will "always be a part of the Chelsea story and family". They added their focus is to "continue investing in the club's infrastructure, sporting performance, player development and delivering long-term success for Chelsea and the club's supporters". Chelsea have ongoing plans either to redevelop Stamford Bridge or move to a new stadium, which sources say had created tension at times between Boehly's camp and Clearlake. A club statement said there will be "no changes to the day-to-day operations, leadership or strategy at the club" as a result of Clearlake assuming full control. Walter, the co-owner and chief executive of global finance firm Guggenheim Partners, where Boehly also began his financial career, last month sold the Los Angeles Lakers for a record $12.5bn (£9.23bn) - a year after buying a majority stake in the NBA franchise. Separately, US federal prosecutors and the Securities and Exchange Commission are investigating companies in Walter's business empire. title: Would you buy branded clothing from your favourite tech firm?
description: Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic are all now selling their own limited edition fashion lines
body: Nvidia's clothing lines quickly sell out, bought by fans of the tech giant For Natalie Fratto, putting on her dark green jumper from US microchip giant Nvidia is like wearing the kit from a favourite sports team. On the front of the $178 (£132) woollen garment is a cartoonish image of the tech company's boss Jensen Huang. Fratto doesn't work for Nvidia. Instead, she's a fan of the company. "I have a New Zealand All Blacks rugby jersey, and I think of my Jensen sweater in kind of the same way," says New York-based Fratto, who runs a tech start-up. She explains that it's a representation of a team and ethos "that I am impressed by and root for", and she proudly wears the jumper in videos she posts on social media., external Nvidia certainly plays in the top league of global tech firms. Under Huang's leadership, it has capitalised on the AI boom to become one of the world's most valuable companies. While it sells tens of millions of its chips per year, its clothing is far more exclusive. The lines, which also include t-shirts, hoodies and hats, are typically only available to buy from pop-up stalls at its conferences, and for very limited periods or "drops" via an online store and sell out very quickly. And while it might seem odd that such a tech company is selling clothing, others are getting in on the act too – and also focusing on exclusivity. OpenAI, the operator of ChatGPT, usually only offers its branded fashion to employees, but occasionally it goes on general sale for a few days via its website. Meanwhile, Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, last year opened a temporary, pop-up coffee shop in Manhattan's West Village. For just one week it gave away free baseball hats with the word "thinking" embroidered on the front. Professor Hazel Clark, who teaches fashion at Parsons School of Design in New York, says that by limiting availability, tech firms have taken inspiration from the world of fashion. "It's a very common strategy for brands to use. It elevates the desirability," she says. But why are such companies selling clothing in the first place? It is not as if they need the supplementary income streams. Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic all declined to comment, but it appears to be about brand promotion and reputation management. Take US software firm Palantir Technologies, which has faced criticism due to it work for the military and police, both in the US and overseas. Since launching its own clothing range last year, Palantir now calls itself a "lifestyle brand". Eliano Younes, Palantir's head of strategic engagement, says: "A lifestyle brand isn't defined by what you sell, it's defined by what you stand for and whether people want to affiliate with it. I believe that the store's success and the enthusiasm from our community proves this." Younes adds that "investors, customers, employees, and everyday people" in more than 60 countries have bought Palantir's gear, which includes a cotton jacket. US defence firm Anduril's t-shirts are not subtle One US buyer of Palantir clothing, who didn't want to be named, says it was attracted by the controversy and "amount of people talking about it". He adds: "It's the purest form of anti-fashion…and that is what makes it so interesting and unique." Critics suggest companies like Palantir are using stylish merch "to get their name into a more positive conversations", as Clark puts it. Younes says: "Our clothing, like our software, is not political. It's designed for all people who support Palantir and what it stands for." Some other companies are being more overtly political with their clothing, such as US defence firm Anduril, which makes military drones. It sells a hoodie emblazoned with the words "Rebuild the Arsenal", reflecting its aim of seeing more US defence spending and manufacturing. Jonathan Sargent, a legal assistant in Albuquerque, New Mexico, has bought clothing from both Palantir and Anduril. "A lot of apparel today, whether it's Nike or other large brands, can feel disconnected from anything tangible," he says. "But Palantir and Anduril are companies that people associate with building things that have a visible impact, whether that's defence, AI, infrastructure, or decision-making systems," he adds. Jonathan Sargent says he likes the fact firms such as Palantir and Anduril have a 'visible impact' Back at Nvidia, the popularity of its founder Huang may be driving the sale of its clothing. He has been known to attract crowds of adoring fans, competing for autographs or selfies with the 63-year-old who is known for his trademark leather jacket. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has described Huang as "Taylor Swift, but for tech". Prof Gianpaolo Vignali of the Manchester Fashion Institute says: "People look at them [such big tech bosses] as role models. They want to aspire to them." For Greg Epstein, author of the book Tech Agnostic, who describes the tech industry as a cult or new global religion, wearing tech merch is "a way of symbolising that you're one of the prophetic elite". This can particularly appeal to Silicon Valley insiders who are often "searching for a sense of identity, a sense of purpose, a sense of community". Epstein, who is the humanist chaplain at both Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, adds: "When tech bros put themselves on sweaters, it's more than just a cutesy phenomenon, it's an attempt to sell a cult whose goal is to radically alter the human condition." Whether or not you choose to buy your next shirt or hat from a tech or defence firm, Vignali argues that all clothing choices are loaded with meaning. "The subtle colour of a tie or hair bobble… all of these are signals that allow the wearer to symbolically share their cultural and ideological positions," he says. title: I sent 200 DMs to companies - it was awkward but I got a job
description: From coffee chats to LinkedIn messages, here's how to network your way to your next job.
body: This video can not be played 'I sent 200 DMs': Networking in New York For some, networking comes naturally but for others, the thought of approaching someone they don't know and trying to make a professional connection can fill them with dread. Whether you're looking for your first job, trying to get ahead at work or hoping to change career, building a network can help you find opportunities and make connections. Networking doesn't have to mean working a room at a formal event - it can happen in person over a coffee at work, through a chance conversation or online, through email and social media. Just under half (44%) of Gen Z say not having the right network is the biggest barrier to landing an entry-level role, according to research from LinkedIn, external. Nicole Leverich, chief communications officer at LinkedIn, shares her top tips on how to network and we took the same question to city workers in New York to find out what has worked for them. Everyone can start building their network online and "you'd be surprised how many connections you have once you connect with people you went to school with, former professors, people you met through summer jobs, family and friends," says Leverich. Don't be discouraged if your network is small as "not having a network right now doesn't mean you'll never have a network", she says. And not having obvious industry contacts shouldn't put you off. Leverich grew up in a small town in Oregon and moved to San Francisco after college without knowing anyone who worked in communications. After getting her first job, she says, "I raised my hand for a lot of the grunt work that other people didn't want to do and I built connections as I went along." Leverich has been LinkedIn's chief communications officer for the past two years If you're thinking about reaching out to someone online, the key is to show you've done your homework, Leverich says. In a message you should "reference something they've posted or establish some common ground". Make sure your request is "clear and specific" and something they can do in less than five minutes. And, most importantly, don't forget to say thank you. "You'd be surprised by how many people are willing to help, but I get so few thank yous," she says. "I'm not talking about anything excessive but just a 'thanks' makes you want to help next time." Networking can feel transactional, so to avoid that, try to build relationships before you need something from them, Leverich advises. If you know you want to work in a particular industry, "start finding people in that field a year or two before you're looking for a job". When you reach out to them, think about what you can offer them in return. "If you call me and say you want a job randomly, I'm much less likely to help than if you call and ask for five minutes of advice." You also don't have to start by messaging someone directly, she says. Instead you could react to a post or drop a comment. In-person networking can be more daunting, particularly early in your career, but remember that at a networking event, everyone is there to talk. To begin a conversation, start with something simple like complimenting someone's outfit, introducing yourself and asking why they're there, Leverich advises. "Put in the reps and start by going to an event for just 15 minutes or half an hour and then build from there." When you want to move on, don't overthink it: "I just do the hard cut and say, 'It was great to meet you and I need to make sure I work around the room.' "If you want a softer out, something like 'I need to get a glass of water, it was great meeting you' can work." Taylor and Vicky both say networking helped them get the job they are in now Of course, knowing what you're supposed to do is one thing but actually walking up to a stranger and starting a conversation, or even messaging someone out of the blue online, is another. Taylor Crow who works in sales says she's "fairly good" at networking as it was something she prioritised at university. "I sent over 200 cold DMs on LinkedIn and reached out to people in the companies I wanted to work at while I was studying." She admits it was "so awkward" but it was something she had to do to land the job she wanted. Her colleague Vicky Peterlin, 24, agrees. "It's not about being good at networking but more about not being afraid to reach out to people. "I had thoughts about how I'm not qualified to have these conversations but then you realise there are no rules and sending out emails and messages are free and easy. "The worst that can happen is that they say no and that's ok." Katherine Leopold, a tutor at Greenwich Business School, echoes this. She says the biggest hurdle is making the first move but if you don't take the step you are "ruling yourself out". The number of applications that organisations are dealing with is "absolutely enormous" so try to meet employers in person and show them your total authentic story, she advises. "Ensure you say to them, 'I have this skill, I have this piece of knowledge, so I'm confident that your team is stronger with me in it.'" Madison Brown works in tech partnerships, having previously worked in corporate jobs for 10 years. Madison says it's important to be authentic and intentional when reaching out to people He gets a lot of young people reaching out to him for career advice and opportunities, and says many of them could be much clearer in what they are looking for. "There's nothing wrong with saying what your goal is or what you want to get out of this interaction." He adds that it's important to be yourself and "more doors will open if you are authentic". title: Interest rates hold expected but Bank of England facing tough choices
description: Forecasts of further rises in the inflation rate mean some analysts expect the Bank to act by the end of the year.
body: Policymakers at the Bank of England are expected to keep interest rates unchanged despite price rises accelerating due to the prolonged conflict in the Middle East. The nine-member Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) has been meeting amid a backdrop of increasing global energy prices and interest rate rises around the world. Economists expect the MPC to hold the benchmark Bank rate at 3.75% for a sixth consecutive meeting but analysts are more divided on whether the rate will need to go up before the end of the year. The Bank rate is crucial in setting the benchmark for banks and other lenders in setting interest for individuals and businesses borrowing and saving money. The latest interest rate decision will be announced by the Bank at 12:00 BST on Thursday. Following its previous meeting at the end of July, the MPC indicated it could raise the Bank rate if the Iran war escalated. Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey told the BBC at the time: "If we get a continuation of this conflict going on and oil prices stay above $100 a barrel... the odds are that interest rates will have to go up higher." Oil prices moved above the $100 (£74) level on 9 September, and have remained there since, and there are few signs of a lasting truce in the Iran war. The Bank uses interest rates to control inflation, which charts the rising cost of living. It aims to keep inflation at a target rate of 2%. However, official figures released on Wednesday showed the Consumer Prices Index (CPI) measure of inflation had risen to 3.1% in August from 2.9% in July, pushing it to its highest rate in six months. The acceleration was driven by rises in the cost of petrol, diesel and airfares. Economists expect that higher global energy costs will feed through to food and fuel prices paid by consumers, meaning the inflation rate is yet to peak. The MPC will be aware that, citing the Middle East conflict and warning inflation was "set to remain well above" its 2% target for some time, the European Central Bank recently raised interest rates to 2.5%. In addition, the US Federal Reserve raised its interest rate to 3.5%-3.75% for similar reasons on Wednesday. However, MPC members will also be keen not to put pressure on employers and further lower the prospects for those seeking a job. This video can not be played Households feel the impact of a rising Bank rate through higher borrowing costs, but can benefit from more generous savings rates. Given the global picture, and market expectations of a higher Bank rate, a host of major lenders have already increased the cost of new fixed-rate mortgages in recent days. Andrew Montlake, chief executive of mortgage broker Coreco, said that the latest data showed that "the inflation dragon has not been fully slain". "If inflation proves sticky, lenders' funding costs stay under pressure, which makes cheaper mortgages harder to deliver," he said. "We are already seeing lenders reprice upwards, so this will do little to calm things down. Borrowers should not panic, but anyone approaching the end of a fixed rate should start looking early, secure an option and keep reviewing it." The average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate is at its highest since 11 May, at 5.77%, while the average five-year is at its highest since 8 November 2023, at 5.83%, according to financial information service Moneyfacts. Savers may be offered more generous returns, but the spending power of their savings could be eroded by the rising cost of living. "It's almost impossible to time things just right, so I would urge households to focus on what's best for them now, in the medium term and in the longer term," said Harriet Guevara, chief savings officer at Nottingham Building Society. "For savers, regularly check that your savings are earning a competitive return and that you have the right balance between easy access and money you can afford to put away for longer." title: Electricity discount to be paid to NI households
description: The one-off £63 reduction in electricity bills will be paid from next month.
body: The one-off reduction will be paid from next month All households in Northern Ireland will get a one-off £63 reduction in electricity bills from next month. It is the local outworking of two schemes which apply in Great Britain, which has a separately regulated electricity market. The schemes are being funded by the UK government and will be applied automatically without the need for an application. Bank payment customers will have their bills automatically reduced while pay-as-you-go customers will receive £63 in credit when they top up their meter. The only complication for pay-as-you-go customers is they should not buy more than £112 of credit if they want to get the discount all in one go. That is because meters are set up to take a maximum payment of £175. Top ups over this value means the £63 payment will be split over a subsequent top up. Economy Minister Dr Caoimhe Archibald said the money would help families The Economy Minister Dr Caoimhe Archibald said the money would "provide some help for families as winter kicks in and energy bills rise". Last week applications opened for a separate means-tested scheme to provide a £100 voucher to some heating oil users. It is jointly funded by Stormont and the UK government. The electricity scheme reflects two policies which apply in GB: a temporary cut in VAT and the removal tax of some consumer levies. The UK government decided not to apply the VAT cut in NI as it would have required agreement with the EU which it thought would lead to delay. It comes as energy prices continue to rise, driven by the US conflict with Iran. Data from the NI consumer council suggests 500 litres of home heating oil currently costs around £560, more than twice the price compared to this time last year. title: Two Britons among three killed in Swiss Alps light aircraft crash
description: Authorities say the plane took off from the Rhône Valley and collided with a mountain slope about 10 minutes later.
body: Police released a picture from the crash scene Two Britons are among three people killed in a plane crash in the Swiss Alps. The light aircraft crashed high in the mountains near the town of Leukerbad in the southern canton of Valais on Tuesday. The authorities said the Cirrus SR22T took off from Sion airport in the Rhône Valley and, for unknown reasons, collided with a mountain slope about 10 minutes later. Witnesses reported seeing a fire and smoke. Emergency teams from the Valais Rescue Organisation, police and firefighters were sent to the scene along with three helicopters. The Swiss Transportation Safety Board has started an investigation. And the Valais Police and the Office of the Attorney General have launched a inquiry. Formal identification of the victims is under way. The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) confirmed it was "providing support to the families of two British nationals who died in Switzerland". It said officials were in contact with the local authorities. "Our thoughts remain with the families during this difficult time," it added. title: Photos show charred wreckage from deadly crash of news helicopter in LA
description: A 29-year-old pedestrian who was the third victim of the unexplained crash has been identified.
body: Investigators have released new photos that show the stark aftermath of a news helicopter crash that killed three people in Los Angeles on Tuesday night. A scorched aircraft and charred storage container were being examined at the scene of the incident on Wednesday. The collision claimed the lives of NBC photojournalist Eliana Moreno and pilot George Marciniw. The third victim, a pedestrian, was identified as Edy Gutierrez Mejia, 29, by the coroner's office. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), which is leading the investigation into the incident, said a report on the cause could take up to 18 months. Journalist and pilot among three killed after news helicopter crashes in LA NBC Los Angeles said its NewsChopper4, which also operated for the Spanish-language Telemundo 52, was in the city's suburb on Tuesday night reporting on a deadly bus crash that had killed two people. Several other news helicopters were also overhead in the area. The driver in the bus crash has since been arrested on suspicion of murder. The cause of the aircraft crash has not yet been determined, officials said. Marciniw was reportedly an experienced pilot. Mejia, the pedestrian killed when the helicopter came down, was a Guatemalan national who had only arrived in Los Angeles this week, according to NBC News. This video can not be played Moment NBC anchors confirm their helicopter crash Investigators were collecting data at the crash site on Wednesday. The helicopter will be moved to a secure facility, where the NTSB will continue to examine the wreckage. The NTSB is an independent US government agency that investigates civil transportation accidents. During a news conference on Wednesday, the NTSB's investigator-in-charge Fabian Salazar said a preliminary report on the incident would be issued within 30 days. A final report on the cause of the crash could take up to 18 months to be released, he added. Asked by reporters about video circulating on social media that appears to show the helicopter's viewpoint in the seconds before the crash, Salazar said it is so far "probably the most important evidence" for investigators. Photojournalist Eliana Moreno and pilot George Marciniw In addition to the three people killed, two others were taken to the hospital. During emotional live coverage on NBC4 on Tuesday night, veteran news anchor Colleen Williams confirmed it was the local news station's helicopter that crashed. While news coverage via helicopter is not necessarily unique to Los Angeles, it is more prominent compared to other major metropolitan areas. LA local news stations regularly break into live programming to broadcast high-speed police pursuits from the air, fly over wildfires and show accidents, protests, and holiday traffic jams in often unscripted, real-time aerials. title: No fire alarms or sprinklers at Pakistan neonatal unit where fire killed 14, report finds
description: A firefighter tells the BBC that rescuers had said many doors near the unit were locked, obstructing their route to the babies.
body: A fire tore through the neonatal unit in Islamabad last month, killing 14 newborns An official inquiry into a Pakistan hospital fire that killed 14 babies last month has found the neonatal unit lacked fire alarms and sprinklers, while firefighters reported that escape routes were "locked or obstructed". One firefighter, who asked to remain anonymous, told the BBC he had heard from other rescue workers that entering the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) hospital in Islamabad was "extremely difficult". "The doors were locked so they had to break through the windows to enter. Even after getting inside, the doors leading towards the ward were locked." PIMS has not provided a comment on the report and its findings. The firefighter said he arrived once the blaze had been put out. It was "difficult for me to even describe what we saw," he said. "The medical equipment above [the babies] had melted and collapsed onto them." The report from an investigative committee headed by a retired senior civil servant found "systemic and institutional failure" which meant what began as an electrical spark became a "catastrophe". At least 14 babies die in Pakistan hospital fire Inside hospital after fire kills 14 babies in Pakistan For many inside the hospital on the morning of 26 August, the first warnings were shouts. Abdul Ghafoor was in a nearby ward with his mother, who was a patient, when he heard someone warning that a fire had erupted. He went upstairs to see if he could help. "The entire ward was filled with smoke, we could not see anything," he told the BBC. CCTV from the corridor outside shows how quickly the fire spread. According to the report, the first indication that something was wrong came at 06:38 when a nurse can be seen running from the ward to get help, returning 20 seconds later with a security guard. Another nurse, Razia Noreen, is then seen rushing into the ward, emerging seconds later with one of the babies who turned out to be the only one to survive. Within a minute, the report says, dense smoke had obscured the camera. Hivsa Walid, her newborn niece and sister-in-law were in the ward next door. Hours later she told the BBC that they had heard a loud commotion and then realised it was a fire when they saw smoke emerging from the unit where the babies were sleeping. "In that moment, I couldn't understand what was going on. We just focused on getting downstairs and saving ourselves." Funerals were held last month for some of the babies who died On the day of the fire, authorities suggested the fire had started from a spark in the ward's air conditioner. The report agrees that this was the most probable source of the fire, due to an overheating electrical supply cable - although it remains unclear what exactly the electrical defect was. The fire then spread quickly, igniting plastics, equipment and bins. Several babies in the ward were on oxygen support, but the report says that while oxygen may have intensified the fire, there isn't evidence that it created a pathway for it to spread. The air conditioning units had undergone maintenance, but the report says this is not the same as a safety check. Back in 2018, the hospital's air conditioning units had been approved to be replaced and upgraded, but eight years later this hadn't happened. The report states that there was no functioning smoke detection, fire alarms or sprinkler system. It found no evidence that the staff in the unit had been trained or had ever rehearsed how to evacuate the ward of newborns, many of whom were premature or "medically fragile". It also found staff had not been trained on how to isolate the oxygen supply in the case of an emergency. Several people described chaos and confusion in the hospital. "There should have been fire extinguishers and protocols, but no one was doing anything," Walid said. "Everyone was just running." Ghafoor said that he was part of a group of seven or eight who tried to find a way to relieve the thick smoke; they managed to break glass panels at the end of the corridor before firefighters arrived. The emergency services weren't notified about the fire until 06:54, the report says, nearly 20 minutes after it first began. It says the first rescue workers arrived at 07:01. Like the firefighter who spoke to the BBC, Ghafoor also said rescue staff struggled to get through some of the hospital's doors. At the time, the hospital's executive director had told BBC News that the door to the newborns' ward was not locked, but guarded, because of previous incidents of baby abductions from government hospitals. The report says that while "ordinary access restrictions may be legitimate for security purposes… they cannot render designated emergency routes inaccessible when needed." The report also found that the hospital had received previous warnings about fire risks. A month before, a fire had broken out at its nursing hostel, raising issues with smoke detection, alarms and general fire preparedness. It says that the hospital and its senior management "bear the principal institutional responsibility for failing to convert known risks, prior warnings and assigned duties into an effective safety system". Pakistan's prime minister has directed the inquiry's short-term measures to be implemented within the next three months and ordered fire safety audits of public and private offices and buildings. He has also suspended eight officials and asked for criminal proceedings to be initiated against them. title: Plaid warned not to cut help for poorer children if it wants Labour to back budget
description: Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates makes early years programme Flying Start a red line in negotiations.
body: Ken Skates makes early years programme Flying Start a red line in negotiations with Plaid Cymru's Welsh government Welsh Labour has said it will not support the Welsh government's budget if cuts are made to a flagship early years programme. The party's leader, Ken Skates, said the future of the Flying Start scheme "has to be a red line" in his party's ongoing budget talks with the government. A Plaid Cymru government minister praised aspects of the scheme but did not say whether it would continue in its current form. The Welsh government said support for "disadvantaged children will be enhanced" as it expands its free childcare policy. Plaid Cymru is running the Welsh government without a majority of seats in the Senedd, meaning that it has to strike deals with other political parties in Cardiff Bay in order to pass budgets or new laws. First launched in 2007, the Flying Start scheme was primarily designed to help children in the poorer areas of the country with their language, social and physical development before starting school. It also includes 12.5 hours of free childcare for two-year-olds, and is being expanded Wales-wide as part of the Welsh government's ultimate policy aim of providing free childcare 20 hours a week to all children between nine months and four years. £55m to boost childcare for two-year-olds, Welsh government says Plan to expand free childcare in Wales faces serious challenges, figures show Since May's election, the new government has been under pressure to explain how it was going to fund its flagship childcare policy. The Welsh government's latest estimate, external is that it would require between £250m and £500m of extra funding a year, depending on how many parents make use of the scheme. Speaking at an event held by the Senedd Sources podcast, external on Tuesday, Plaid's Minister for Government Effectiveness, Dafydd Trystan Davies, did not rule out cutting or changing the Flying Start programme. Asked if he could guarantee that the scheme would still be available by the time of the next Senedd election, he replied: "I don't think I can guarantee that any single programme will be in its current form." Davies said: "What is really strong and important with Flying Start is those areas around speech and language therapy, is around the health aspect. "So, can you guarantee that those provisions of Flying Start will be there as part of the [childcare] offer? Clearly, it has to be. "What I've seen with Flying Start is the budget allocated to different councils. Some councils have been far more effective at delivering to a large number of poor and disadvantaged children and therefore, what I'm keen to see there, is that all councils adopt the best practice. "As has been done in various contexts, you can target that provision." The Welsh Labour leader says he would be "deeply disappointed if Plaid didn't commit to the future of Flying Start" Back in July, the government lost a Senedd vote on extra spending plans after failing to strike a deal with Welsh Labour. Plaid and Welsh Labour are currently holding fresh budget negotiations around this year's supplementary budget and next year's full budget. In an interview with BBC Walescast, Welsh Labour Leader Ken Skates said: "It appears they're looking at using Flying Start money to pay for something they never costed during the election or in their manifesto, the childcare offer, which will benefit a lot of middle class and upper class families. "But it's going to be people and children who benefit from Flying Start who will pay the price. "I would be deeply disappointed if Plaid didn't commit to the future of Flying Start." Asked if any change to Flying Start would rule his party out of supporting the budget, Skates replied: "For us as a party, I think it has to be a red line. "If Plaid Cymru think they can take the best of Flying Start and apply it in different areas, I'm afraid they're going to let people down badly. "So, I'm afraid, if they're talking about Flying Start, then they're going to have to do it by themselves, without our consent or support and they won't be getting a budget approval from us." Steffan Evans, head of the Bevan Foundation, said: "The majority of children living in poverty are not in Flying Start areas. "So, if we want to get a childcare system that helps child development in terms of the education and parents back into work and gets to those children in poverty, you do have to strike a compromise, I think, in terms of how that operates. "And that might mean going towards something more universal to get to more children, rather than something that's perfect, but only answers part of the problem." Reform's minister for fairness, families and communities, Cristiana Emsley, said: "Plaid Cymru are raising the prospect of cutting funding for vulnerable children while continuing to spend money on overseas embassies, its Nation of Sanctuary programme and tree planting in Uganda. "At a time when families across Wales are struggling with the cost of living and children are in need of support, it is clear Plaid have the wrong priorities." A Welsh government spokesperson said: "Our offer means that childcare will be more accessible and affordable to all families. "The current phase of delivery which will provide funded childcare for all two-year-olds is being delivered through the Flying Start model. "At the same time, the support available to disadvantaged children will be enhanced as a result of our offer. "We will need to substantially increase the number of providers to ensure that families have childcare options that work for them. "These are all matters under discussion by the Expert Group on Childcare as we work on rolling out the next phase of this ambitious policy." title: Delay to neonatal reform is putting babies at risk, warn doctors
description: The plan to cut the number of neonatal intensive care units from eight to three was announced in 2017.
body: Kelly Dalley's baby Annabel was admitted to Neonatal Intensive Care at Ninewells Hospital The lives of some of the smallest and sickest babies in Scotland are being put at risk because of delays in reorganising neonatal care, doctors have warned. The Scottish government's controversial plan to cut the number of neonatal intensive care units from eight to three was announced in 2017, but has not yet been implemented. Doctors and charities who support the proposals say they would save lives – but have accused ministers of failing to ensure there are enough cots or staff to safely implement the move. Health Secretary Angela Constance admitted that the government could not continue to delay the move and promised: "These changes will be made." Under the plans, neonatal care will be centralised for babies who: Are born at less than 27 weeks Are lighter than 800g (1lb 12oz) Or need specialist complex care The three national neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) will be based at Aberdeen Maternity Unit, Edinburgh Royal Infirmary and Royal Hospital for Children in Glasgow. The five other units - in Dundee, Wishaw, Kirkcaldy, Kilmarnock and at the Princess Royal Maternity Hospital in Glasgow - will become local neonatal units (LNUs), providing a limited amount of intensive care to other babies. A similar move was carried out in England in 2003. The new model in Scotland was due to be implemented by 2026, but there is still no date for when it will be introduced. Health Secretary Angela Constance says the changes will be implemented The British Association of Perinatal Medicine (BAPM) said there had been a lack of progress and that Scotland was "lagging behind England". BAPM president Dr Stephen Wardle said the evidence firmly supported centralisation of services. He said larger centres improved survival chances for the sickest babies, who would have access to highly trained specialist staff, equipment and surgery. Wardle said not implementing the new model was putting some lives at risk and that additional resources should be made available as soon as possible. "Delays in making progress with these proposals will be affecting the outcome for some of these babies", he said. "Ten years is an awfully long time to wait for these changes". Lauren Bruce's baby Grace was admitted to neonatal intensive care at Ninewells hospital in March 2026 He said that the delays were related to a lack of capacity of both cots and staff, alongside the extra space required to adapt these larger centres. BBC Scotland News also spoke to Professor James Boardman, a consultant neonatologist with the NHS and University of Edinburgh. He said the evidence to support centralisation was "unequivocal" and a "matter of life and death" for the most vulnerable, low-weight babies. BBC News has learned that the number of cots in the units earmarked for intensive care has not yet increased as planned. The number of births have been falling in Scotland over the last 20 years, as have the number of babies who need intensive care, according to the available NHS data. The government says only 50-60 of the most premature and fragile babies will be affected by the reorganisation. But there has been significant opposition from some parents. A parliamentary committee is currently considering a petition by campaigners to have the move scrapped entirely. The scrutiny of the petition has descended into a war of words, with the government accusing campaigners and the media of presenting "repeated misinformation". Petitioner Lynne McRitchie says there are "outstanding questions" over the published documents and clinical evidence, including conflicting figures about the number of babies affected. Particular concerns have surfaced around the neonatal unit in Wishaw, with clinicians writing to the committee with their doubts about the new model and its impact on families in Lanarkshire. Lauren Bruce and Kelly Dalley are campaigning for plans to centralise neonatal services to be halted Lauren Bruce from Blairgowrie is one of those who fears any reduction in local intensive care provision will be unsafe because of existing capacity issues across Scotland. Her daughter Grace was born at 37 weeks at Ninewells Hospital in Dundee in March. Moments after the birth Grace became extremely ill and was admitted to one of four NICU cots at the unit. Under the plans, the number of cots will be reduced to one or two. Lauren says three other babies needed intensive care on the night Grace was born, but she was told there was no capacity anywhere in Scotland. "I think that really highlights the pressure that these hospitals are already facing with four intensive care cots there," she said. "What's it going to be like when it's only one?" Kelly Dalley knew her baby had a heart condition and was expecting to travel from Dundee to Glasgow for surgery after she was born. However, Annabel was delivered prematurely at 32 weeks. When she was 12 days old she became seriously unwell. "At that point there was no space in Glasgow, Edinburgh and Aberdeen and staff at Ninewells kept her alive until she was stable," said Kelly. She is also concerned that any reduction in intensive care cot numbers at Ninewells would be unsafe. "I dread to think what the outcome would have been if that capacity at Ninewells wasn't there," she added. Nula Duff needed NICU care in Aberdeen after birth BBC Scotland News has also spoken to parents who are in favour of centralisation. Euan Duff's daughter Nula was born prematurely and stopped breathing shortly after birth. She spent six weeks in the neonatal unit at Aberdeen Maternity Hospital, which is where one of the proposed neonatal intensive care units would be located. He said: "Even though it was a really traumatic experience with Nula, I would want my baby taken care of in the best place. "You can't expect to have all of the most specialised staff in every unit. We would have gone to London if we had to.

title: 'My rent was higher than my student loan' - the booming cost of private halls
description: Private student halls are springing up in Scotland's cities in ever increasing numbers yet rents continue to soar.
body: Lara Reader says her monthly rent was £200 higher than her student maintenance loan You don't have to walk far in any university city before spotting some form of private Purpose-Built Student Accommodation (PBSA). These large blocks of student housing are springing up in cities across the UK, yet rents continue to soar and young people studying at university say they're still finding it difficult to secure a place to live. The increase in PBSA has predominantly been driven by private companies, with many developments targeting more affluent international and postgraduate students, who industry experts say are becoming increasingly important to the sector. Developers say they are meeting a market demand but campaigners argue that they are too expensive for most Scottish students and more affordable housing should be being built instead. Lara, from Kelso in the Scottish Borders, was given accommodation in Brae House Twenty-year-old Lara Reader told the BBC that when she applied for student accommodation at Edinburgh University she did not expect to be allocated the most expensive option on her list. Like many first-year students, Lara selected from a mix of university-owned and privately-operated halls which cater solely to the city's huge student population. She was given a room in Brae House, one of the many private PBSAs in the city. PBSAs typically offer en-suite bedrooms and studio apartments alongside premium facilities such as gyms, study areas and social spaces - but they also come at a higher price point than traditional student halls. The rent for Lara's room was £1,022 per month, more than £200 higher than her monthly student maintenance loan. In case you missed it Why is there so much student accommodation? Despite it being beyond her budget, Lara accepted the offer because of the difficulty of finding student housing in Edinburgh. She said the cost hung over much of her first year at university and she was "constantly stressing" about how much money she was having to put towards rent. To cover the shortfall, she worked 20 hours per week alongside her studies, a decision she says contributed to her failing her first-year exams. "I was exhausted all the time," she said. "I just didn't have enough time to study." "I think when pricing student housing they need to be more realistic. "It makes it so difficult for students like me who don't come from a super wealthy background to find an affordable place to live." The University of Edinburgh said it offered students good value, across a broad range of price points, with entry-level rents being well below the average. A spokesperson said: "We encourage students to select accommodation that aligns with their lifestyle preferences and budget throughout the application process." Across the UK, a total of 206,005 students told the Higher Education Statistics Agency (HESA) they lived in private-sector halls in 2024/25. This is up from 117,995 a decade earlier. The rate of increase is higher in Scotland, up from 5,500 in 2014/15 to 14,640 last year. The growth of PBSA has been particularly visible in Scotland's two largest cities. As of August 2026, Glasgow has 21,655 student beds with a further 18,213 in the development pipeline, meaning the city could host almost 40,000 student beds if all proposed schemes go ahead. Edinburgh has also seen rapid growth, with the supply of PBSA increasing by almost 60% over the past decade. A further 5,917 beds were in the development pipeline as of December 2025. Richard Ward, the head of research at student accommodation marketing website StuRents, said the average cost of privately-operated PBSA in Edinburgh and Glasgow is £268 and £243 per person per week (pppw) respectively. The national average (excluding London) is £191pppw. He said: "The rents you're having to charge are about £250 to £300 per week to make a scheme financially viable "The challenge for the sector is, at that price point, a lot of domestic students cannot afford that." According to industry experts, international students, who are often better able to afford higher rents, are a key part of the PBSA market. It's something Lara, from Kelso in the Borders, noticed in her accommodation too. "A lot of people I was friends with through my accommodation were international students, so funding is very different," she said. "I think for the most part, a lot of people didn't have as much of a struggle paying the rent, but I definitely know a few people who were in the same boat as I was." Saba said PBSAs felt safer than trying to organise a private rental from the other side of the world For many international students, however, PBSA offers reassurance that can be difficult to find in the private rental market. Saba, an international student from Pakistan who had planned to study in Glasgow, said they felt safer than trying to organise a flat from the other side of the world. "I didn't really know where to start," she said. "Every country has different laws when it comes to properties and renting places." After missing out on university accommodation, she considered trying to find a property through a private landlord, however, she says she "encountered a bunch of scammers" during her search, including one man who asked for £500 upfront before sending videos of the property. "As an international student, I feel like you're vulnerable" she said "There are good and bad people everywhere and the bad lot try to take advantage of that." John Boyle said developers were often able to achieve higher returns from PBSAs John Boyle, director of research and strategy at estate agency Rettie, said purpose-built student accommodation had become one of the most "financially viable" forms of city-centre development, with developers often able to achieve higher returns than from conventional residential schemes, making projects easier to fund and deliver. title: Mum's Facebook kidney plea prompts 'mind-blowing' gift from total stranger
description: A woman has undergone a lifesaving transplant after receiving a kidney from a stranger who saw her post on social media.
body: Gary Summerfield told his family "this lady needs one of my kidneys more than I need two of them" A woman who shared a desperate plea for a kidney on Facebook has undergone a lifesaving transplant after a stranger offered to be her donor. Karen Davey, 41, had exhausted every avenue before turning to social media, where she said she did not "want to leave her family without a mother". Gary Summerfield saw the mum-of-four's post and, after learning he was a match, donated one of his kidneys via an operation in July. "I thought this lady needs one of my kidneys more than I need two of them," said Gary. Karen's family said they would never be able to repay Gary for his generosity, adding that it had given her "another chance to be a mum". The average wait for a deceased donor kidney transplant in the UK is two to three years, according to NHS Blood and Transplant, but if you have a living donor it can be about three to six months. Karen says she feels "100 times better" following the transplant in July This was Karen's second lifesaving transplant. She underwent a heart transplant 10 years ago, after having a heart attack aged 31 while watching her son play football. A transplant increases the risk of infection because of the medication patients need to take following the procedure, and complications led to Karen developing kidney failure. "I knew the tablets I was taking following the heart transplant would damage the kidneys so they try and keep the dose as low as possible, but we always knew when I had the heart transplant that I would probably need a kidney transplant at some point, and that is hard to deal with mentally." Karen, from Brynna, Rhondda Cynon Taf, was in stage three kidney failure when she discovered her friends and family were not matches and decided to put a plea on Facebook. She explained in her post that she has a relatively rare blood type and described the kidney failure as putting her life on hold. "My main thing is the kids, I want to be around for them." Karen's eldest is now 22, and she is also grandmother to a one-year-old. "The kids were 10 years younger when I had the heart transplant, and they've been through a lot since then and the kidney was just the next hurdle," she added. Gary seeing Karen for the first time after he donated his kidney to the mother-of-four Gary, a security guard from Tredegar, Blaenau Gwent, stumbled upon Karen's post by chance and felt he had to help. "I saw Karen's appeal and she mentioned the children, and I thought 'Karen's a similar age to my daughter and her youngest child is the same age as my grandson', and I just thought it's terrible for the children. "If It was my daughter, I would be searching everywhere if we had exhausted all avenues through the family and friends, I would want a stranger to come forward. And I thought it would be selfish not to." He added: "I thought this lady needs one of my kidneys more than I need two of them." Although, Gary, 60, had never met Karen, he immediately volunteered to be tested. He underwent extensive assessments, including compatibility testing, psychological evaluations, blood tests, cholesterol checks and other medical examinations. The pair then underwent the six-hour procedure on 15 July at the University Hospital of Wales in Cardiff. Gary said he never had any second thoughts. "It's amazing seeing Karen today, the first time since the transplant and looking so well. "For me, donating a kidney is simply up there with getting married and having my children, it's one of the top three things in my life. "And she's a very deserving lady and a deserving family." Karen, pictured with husband Matthew and son Brandon, who say Gary has given her the "gift of life" Karen said she felt "100 times better" and her husband Matthew said they would always be grateful to Gary. "Everyone knows what's going on in the world at the moment, it's a horrible place at times, but it really does give you hope that there is kindness in the world. "We'll never, ever be able to repay Gary and the family for what they've done, and to give Karen another chance, another chance of being able to be the mother to our children and just live a life that she deserves. "He has given that gift of life." Karen added: "The fact that somebody came forward and has gone through all the testing, because it's a lot of testing. For somebody to put their body through that and having a kidney taken out for somebody that they don't know, it's mind-blowing, I'm just so grateful." The couple's son Brandon, 17, said it was "amazing" to see his mum on the road to recovery after the transplant. "She's looked better now than she has in a long while. "It can be scary, obviously, when she's going into surgeries, but you just have to have hope. It's just amazing there's still good people out there." title: League Two Fleetwood host Arsenal in EFL Cup - full fourth-round draw
description: League Two side Fleetwood Town will host Premier League champions Arsenal in the fourth round of the EFL Cup.
body: Fleetwood reached the fourth round after an own goal by Sheffield United's Rhys Norrington-Davies settled their tie League Two Fleetwood Town will host Premier League champions Arsenal in the fourth round of the Carabao Cup. The Lancashire side reached this stage for the first time in their history with a 1-0 win over Sheffield United on Wednesday night. And their reward was a plum home tie against Mikel Arteta's men, who beat Ipswich Town 4-2 on Tuesday. Holders Manchester City will welcome Brighton to Etihad Stadium if they beat Norwich in Thursday's remaining tie, while Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso will visit his former side Liverpool after the Premier League rivals were drawn together. League One sides Bradford and Peterborough will play for a place in the quarter-finals after they defeated Leyton Orient and Barnsley respectively in the third round. The remaining fixtures are all Premier League affairs with Fulham hosting Crystal Palace, Bournemouth at home to Aston Villa, Brentford travelling to Sunderland and Everton welcoming Newcastle United The fourth round will take place during the week commencing 26 October. title: Watch: Leaked photos reveal extensive damage at US bases in Gulf
description: The photos, provided by active military personnel, show a severed radar jet, flattened trailers and severely damaged buildings as a result of Iranian strikes.
body: This video can not be played The BBC's US partner CBS obtained photos showing widespread damage to multiple US military sites in the Middle East as a result of Iranian strikes. The photos came from an unnamed member of the military, who said: "This is major damage to our bases that hasn't been communicated to the American public". They images show a severed radar jet, flattened trailers and severely damaged buildings. The BBC's State Department correspondent Tom Bateman talks through what the photos show. title: US interest rates raised for first time in three years
description: The Federal Reserve unanimously voted to increase interest rates to 3.75%-4% from 3.5%-3.75% on Wednesday.
body: US interest rates have been raised for the first time in more than three years and could be increased further in a bid to slow rising prices. Rates were hiked to 3.75%-4% from 3.5%-3.75% by the Federal Reserve in a unanimous decision on Wednesday despite fierce opposition from President Donald Trump, who had called for rates to be cut. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said the move was because "inflation is too high and has been for too long", adding that it was a "sober" and "responsible decision". However, Trump said rates "should be 1%, or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World - BY FAR". Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for people wanting to secure loans, mortgages and credit cards, but can lead to better returns on savings. Central banks tend to increase rates when inflation is high to discourage spending and encourage saving in the hope this will reduce the pace of price rises. But it's a balancing act, as higher rates can also encourage businesses to hold off on investing and hurt economic growth. Global oil prices have surged since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran, driving up the price of car fuel as well as the cost of goods and services generally. Yet, despite this, Warsh said the US economy was in a strong position and this was one of the things which encouraged the Fed to cut rates. Ahead of the mid-term elections in November, affordability is one of the top concerns of American voters, who have seen diesel prices hit an all-time high and petrol rise above $4 (£2.99) a gallon on average. The price of oil is also key in to the costs businesses face in transporting goods across the country and around the world to sell. The higher costs can result in companies increasing prices, hitting the pockets of households. Warsh told a press conference following the decision to raise interest rates that the Fed "cannot effect any individual price whether it be oil prices, whether it be food stuffs at the grocery store", but could ensure price rises do not broaden across the economy. He added that those least well off had most to gain from lower inflation. Asked about the message the decision sent to Trump, Warsh chuckled before saying "I have got nothing for you on a discussion with the president," as he batted away similar questions with the same response. The Federal Reserve is independent of the government, but has faced sharp criticism from Trump over its decisions on rates in recent years. Trump was heavily critical of Warsh's predecessor Jerome Powell, who stepped down at the end of his term earlier this year, for not cutting rates. Following Wednesday's announcement, Trump said rates should be cut to "1%, or less". "LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!", he posted on social media. Earlier a White House press secretary Kush Desai told Fox News the president and White House had "reiterated our commitment to the independence of the Federal Reserve on numerous occasions" but added it did not prevent Trump being able to voice his opinions. Warsh said at the press conference that "part of the independence of the Federal Reserve is we stay in our lane". This hike by the Fed is the first move rate move in any direction since they were cut in December 2025. The last time they were raised was in July 2023. A 0.25pp increase will likely add to increasing mortgage rates for homebuyers, as the rates set by banks and other lenders are heavily influenced by the Fed's policy rate. Major US banks JP Morgan, KeyCorp and BNY raised their prime lending rate on Wednesday to 7% from 6.75% in response, which will rates charged on credit cards and personal loans. Mortgage costs have climbed over the past year but remain below peaks seen in 2023. A 30-year fixed deal is 6.76% on average, while a 15-year deal is 6.09%, according to figures from Freddie Mac. Due to many US homeowners having 30-year and 15-year fixed-rate mortgages, changes to interest rates will not impact monthly repayments, though they could affect those looking to secure a loan for a home or refinance. Warsh declined to provide his own view on where he saw interest rates going into the future, but the majority of his fellow policymakers said they believe rates would be hiked again before the end of this year to between 4-4.25%. A small majority said rates could rise further to the 4.25-4.5% next year, before cuts begin in 2028 and 2029. The forecast suggested price rises will ease in the coming years, with inflation, the measure used to assess the cost of living, predicted to fall steadily to the Fed's 2% target by 2029. The US is not alone in tackling the inflation impact from the conflict in the Middle East, with the European Central Bank raising rates last week and the Bank of England set to make its own decision on Thursday.
