title: Painful endgame for Gray as stale Hibs slump
description: A club hero, David Gray ends his time as Hibs head coach not to the sound of euphoria from fans, but to the sound of a support collectively exhaling in relief, writes Tom English.
body: Hibernian have sacked David Gray six league games into his third season as head coach It was the strangest kind of farewell; more sadness than satisfaction, more 'thanks for the memories' than 'never darken our door again'. After a dozen years as a player, a goalscoring and Scottish Cup-winning icon, a coach, an interim manager and, for the last two-and-a-bit seasons, the first team manager, David Gray exited Hibernian on Wednesday evening. He left, not to the sound of euphoria from the fans, but to the sound of a support collectively exhaling in relief. Given what he did on an immortal day at Hampden in 2016, no Hibs supporter wanted to boo the man they called Sir David Gray, nobody wanted to call for his head. It was a painful endgame, for everybody. Hibs have sacked many managers in recent seasons, but this was no Nick Montgomery, no Lee Johnson, no Shaun Maloney. Gray was altogether different. Driven, passionate, honest as the day is long, brutally so when talking about how things were going wrong, which he had been doing too much of lately. Gray's big picture tells us this: he was the first manager at Easter Road to qualify for European football in consecutive seasons since the great Eddie Turnbull in the early 1970s. The kind of slump that Hibs are in right now is entirely in keeping with what's happened at Hibs over the last half century. He's the only Hibs manager to win at Ibrox in three consecutive seasons. He won at Celtic Park last season, too. The flipside is also clear. Six successive home defeats in the league equals a grim club record dating back to 1920. Two shots at European Conference League play-offs - and the finance that would have come had they completed the task - were wasted in the most self-harming way. Six points from six games, ninth in the table, an awful loss to lowly Kilmarnock on Tuesday and a sense of drift did for him. Making the League Cup semi-final, against Hearts, wasn't enough to save him. Gray sacked by Hibs after six league games The style of football wasn't easy on the eye, the lack of energy and entertainment was a problem that was only growing. Hibs just look a bit stale, a bit rudderless. Occasionally they can spark into life and show what they are capable of, but those moments have been too fleeting. Jens Berthel Askou brought zest and enjoyment to Fir Park last season and Alfred Johansson, his successor, is trying to build on that. They both had bad nights on Tuesday but Johansson and Wouter Vrancken at Hearts are attempting to create something compelling and their fans are on board with them all the way. Maybe Hibs fans want something similar, something shinier, something more exotic. There is the feeling that they have a decent enough squad of players but also a belief that these players should be delivering more than they are. If there was a table for under-performance, Hibs would be challenging at the top. Some of those same players must shoulder a chunk of the blame for Gray's demise, but they are a largely protected species, even if a number of them, weak-willed and unreliable, have no right to be protected. You can't sack a dressing room in one day, though. A manager and his assistants? Now that's different. Gray goes but others must look in the mirror; the players, a sporting director in Malky Mackay, a chairman in Ian Gordon, a chief executive in Dan Barnett who could scarcely be more low-key if he lived in a bunker under Easter Road. Gordon, presumably, will lead the search for another manager. It would be interesting to do a poll on the level of trust fans have in him and others to land the right man. David Gray after scoring his famous late goal at Hampden in 2016 Gray took them to third in the league in his first season and fifth last season. There is an argument to be made that on the back of those bottom lines he deserved more time, but he hasn't got it. He had a tumultuous beginning as Hibs manager; one league win in his first 14 games. In November he was bottom of the league. Hearts were second bottom. More than once Gray seemed to be in trouble only to pull out a series of wins that made him safe. That first season was a prime example. From bottom of the table, he got them to third by the end. It was a fine achievement. Fifth last season was reasonable, but it must have felt nightmarish to Hibs fans as Hearts roared on and threatened to win the league. The rise of Hearts adds significant pressure on whoever's managing Hibs. It's just the way it is. Throughout his time, Hibs had a ruinous capacity to concede late goals that checked momentum and made the search for the holy grail of consistency all the harder. In 2024-25 Hibs conceded late goals that cost them points against Kilmarnock, Ross County, Hearts, Dundee twice and Dundee United twice in minutes 88, 90, 90, 90, 86, 90, 87 and 90. Last season that unfortunate habit of caving late on continued too often. They conceded damaging goals against Midtjylland, Legia Warsaw, Livingston, Dunfermline, Dundee and Hearts three times in minutes 119, 90, 98, 90, 90, 90, 88, 90 and 86. This season they lost to Motherwell in the 85th minute and shipped goals in the 84th and 90th minute against Gent to exit the Conference League. They salvaged a point, or three, on other days, but they were on the wrong side of the ledger on so many occasions. Gray will have regrets about that. What-might-have-beens. Plenty of 'if onlys' mark his time in the job. His players have cause for reflection, too. They have no shortage of decent-to-good players at Hibs, but there is something missing, some steel, perhaps, some mentality, some leadership, some coaching nous. Gray did his utmost to improve things. He always struck you as a manager who lived and breathed the job, who was terribly cut up by it when it didn't go to plan. Most sacked managers think they could have improved things if they were given time. The be

title: US House votes to hold billionaire Epstein associate Leon Black in contempt
description: Black - who had business ties to Epstein - declined to appear and provide documents related to the convicted sex offender.
body: The US House of Representatives has agreed to hold billionaire Leon Black in contempt of Congress for defying a legal summons related to its investigation into convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Black, who had business ties to Epstein, did not comply with a subpoena ordering him to appear before the House Oversight Committee earlier this month and share documents related to Epstein. Lawyers for Black, who has sued over the summons, called the contempt move "outrageous". After passage of the measure holding Black in contempt, Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer said: "No-one is above the law. We will continue to seek transparency for the American people and justice for survivors." In a statement shared with US media, lawyers for Black called the House move an "outrageous action that ignores the facts and the truth about Mr Black". "The full House is holding him in contempt without any regard to the active litigation challenging the lawfulness of the Committee's actions and the ethics complaint against Chairman Comer," they said. The measure, which passed by unanimous consent, means the matter will be referred to the US justice department, which will decide whether to criminally prosecute Black. In a written statement, the committee's top Democrat, congressman Robert Garcia, called the contempt vote "an important step towards justice and accountability". "We will continue to center the survivors in our fight to hold those responsible for these horrific crimes," he said. The private equity tycoon walked out of voluntary testimony before the House Oversight Committee in June after he was asked about nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) he may have signed, lawmakers said at the time. Black left Apollo Global Management, which he co-founded, amid scrutiny in 2021 over his Epstein ties. He has denied any wrongdoing with regards to his dealings with Epstein. The subpoenas, which ordered Black to share NDAs and give an on-camera deposition under oath, were issued after he left the committee meeting in June. Black has said he hired Epstein as a wealth management adviser, telling lawmakers in June that he gave Epstein $158m (£118m) for legitimate reasons. The billionaire has said he did not know about Epstein's crimes until he was charged with sex trafficking in July 2019. title: Police boss cancels 'ridiculous' theatre tour
description: Colin Sutton tells a meeting that he has pulled out of a 127-date tour due to residents' reaction.
body: Promoters of Colin Sutton's show claimed it would offer "an unforgettable evening of real-life detective work" An under-fire £79,000-a-year police commissioner said he had cancelled heavily criticised plans to take part in a 127-date national theatre tour. Opposition parties had questioned how Reform UK's Colin Sutton would be able to oversee Norfolk Police while also presenting a live true crime stage show across the UK. Sutton told a council meeting that the number of dates was "ridiculous" and that he had pulled out of the "Makings of a Murderer" tour after being contacted by residents. Conservative Matthew Taylor, who stood against Sutton in the police and crime commissioner election in July, said it had been "a sorry saga". Conservative councillor Matthew Taylor said many people in Norfolk had been left "deeply disappointed by this episode" A high profile former detective who led the investigation to catch Levi Bellfield, the murderer of Milly Dowler, Marsha McDonnell and Amelie Delagrange, Sutton comfortably won the election to become Norfolk's commissioner two months ago. A regular on TV documentaries, he has previously carried out a long national theatre tour talking about his career. Last week, promoters announced his follow-up series of shows would take place next year and Sutton initially said it "wouldn't impinge" on his day job. But on Tuesday, he admitted to the BBC that he was considering cancelling the tour and on Wednesday he told councillors he had now scrapped it. "What surprised me and what made me reflect and think again was the reaction that I got personally from a number of residents," he told North Norfolk District Council's scrutiny committee. "I'm not sure I could do 127 dates because it was ridiculous, but I could have done some. What I don't want to do is to give the impression to anybody that I don't take this role seriously and I'm not going to do a good job on this. "So that's why my decision has been: OK, I'm not legally obliged to do this, I'm not going to do it." Colin Sutton was heavily criticised for his plan to go on tour Taylor, a county councillor who came second to Sutton in the commissioner election, said it had "been a sorry saga, one that erodes public confidence in those who are supposed to represent them". "I know many people across Norfolk have been deeply disappointed by this episode," he added. South Norfolk Labour MP Ben Goldsborough also said it was "good" that Sutton had pulled out. "But the fact it took a huge public backlash to make him realise that being Norfolk's police and crime commissioner should come before his career as a touring personality tells its own story," he said. The promoters of the show, Entertainers, have been contacted for comment. Do you have a story suggestion for Norfolk? Contact us below. title: Trump chief of staff Susie Wiles announces she's cancer-free
description: The 69-year-old White House chief of staff is a powerful figure and particularly close to the US president.
body: Susie Wiles is the first woman to serve as White House Chief of Staff. White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles has announced she is free of cancer, exactly six months after she announced her diagnosis. In a post on X, Wiles said her pathology tests "came back clear" after a visit to the Mayo Clinic earlier this week. Wiles, 69, is considered among the most powerful figures in the Trump administration and someone particularly close to the US president. In her post, Wiles thanked Trump for his "unwavering support" and vowed to continue working to "advance his America First Agenda". Wiles continued working virtually at the White House during the six months of treatment following her diagnosis. In a March statement, Wiles said that one in eight women are diagnosed with breast cancer. "Every day, these women continue to raise their families, go to work and serve their communities with strength and determination," she said. "I now join their ranks." Her post on Wednesday did not reveal any more details about her treatment. Wiles is the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff - widely considered to be the most important role in the White House. In her position, Wiles works to keep the president's agenda on track and serves as a gatekeeper to President Trump, as well as a policy coordinator and political advisor. Before taking the job, Wiles played a significant role in President Trump's 2024 presidential campaign. Her tenure, however, has not been without controversy. In December, Vanity Fair published interviews with Wiles in which she gave a blunt - and occasionally unflattering - assessment of her time working in the Trump White House. For example, she described the famously teetotaling president as having an "alcoholic's personality" but added that there's "nothing he can't do. Nothing, zero, nothing." She also provided candid thoughts about other figures close to the US president, describing Vice-President JD Vance as a "conspiracy theorist" and Elon Musk as an "odd, odd duck." The US president, however, swiftly came to her defence and Wiles described Vanity Fair's reporting as having omitted "significant context" to create a "chaotic and negative narrative" about the administration. President Trump and the White House have yet to comment on Wiles' announcement. title: Verstappen passes 100 amateur karters in 14 laps in exhibition race
description: Four-time F1 world champion Max Verstappen passes 100 amateur drivers in just 14 laps in an exhibition go-kart race at Silverstone.
body: Max Verstappen has won 71 grands prix in Formula 1 Max Verstappen needed just 14 laps and 35 minutes to overtake 100 amateur drivers in an exhibition go-kart race at Silverstone. The four-time Formula 1 world champion had a maximum of 35 laps and 75 minutes to pass everyone on an adapted track at the grand prix circuit in Northamptonshire. Red Bull's Verstappen, 28, was up to 37th by the end of a chaotic first lap in which many drivers crashed or span out, resulting in racing being briefly suspended. The ruthless Dutchman, who warned participants "it's not a charity event" on race radio, moved into 10th by the start of lap six and was in fourth by lap 10, with each driver who he passed having to retire. At that stage, the field - made up of TV, sport and social media personalities, with no professional racing drivers - consisted of just Dutch F1 journalist Jacky Martens, Red Bull engine builder Lewis Osler and YouTuber Zac Alsop. All three were given an extra 'fast lap' where they could cut a corner of the track to try to hold off Verstappen for longer, but he inevitably reeled them in. Martens, who was on pole position after qualifying, was the final driver to be passed as Verstappen completed his challenge with 40 minutes and 21 laps to spare. Verstappen began his racing career as a junior in karting and won four consecutive F1 titles between 2021 and 2024. title: Police officer guilty of series of rapes and sex attacks over 17 years
description: Campbell Petrie, 50, was convicted of nine charges while he was a Police Scotland officer from 2006 until 2023.
body: Campbell Petrie was found guilty of nine charges at the High Court in Glasgow A former Police Scotland officer has been convicted of a catalogue of sex crimes, including two counts of rape, over a 17-year period. Campbell Petrie was found guilty of nine charges at the High Court in Glasgow which took place between 2006 and 2023. Petrie, 50, was a serving officer at the time of the offences, which included indecent assault, assault with intent to rape and assault to injury and danger of life. The force confirmed he was arrested, charged and suspended from duty in December 2023. He retired from the force in December last year. Petrie was remanded in custody and is due to be sentenced next month. More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland Det Supt Adam Brown, of Police Scotland's public protection unit, said: "Our thoughts are very much with the victims in this case and I commend their strength in reporting these crimes and bringing Campbell Petrie to justice." Brown acknowledged how difficult it could be to report such offences "particularly when the perpetrator is a police officer". He added: "I want to reassure the public we will identify and investigate these officers whether they are serving or retired, or whether their crimes are committed on duty or, as in this instance, off duty. "Petrie will now face the consequences of his actions." title: Body found in search for missing Noah Woods, 3
description: About 1,300 volunteers joined police in searching for Noah, who went missing from a playground.
body: Noah Woods was described as looking "happy and healthy" by one of the last people to see him A body has been found in the search for missing three-year-old boy Noah Woods, police have confirmed. Noah disappeared at about 15:00 BST on Tuesday from a playground in Brantham, Suffolk. Supt Tom Pearse of Suffolk Police said dive teams recovered the body of a child from a nearby pond. He said the death was being treated as unexplained but not suspicious. This video can not be played CCTV footage shows the last sighting of Noah at the playground Supt Pearse said formal identification had yet to take place, but Noah's family had been informed. "Our thoughts are with Noah's family and all those who knew him," he said. "We have been overwhelmed by the outpouring of public support and people putting on their boots to help." Police said at least 1,300 members of the public had helped in the search for the missing boy, who was non-verbal and partially deaf. People from as far afield as Birmingham and Hampshire had turned up to help. Supt Tom Pearse of Suffolk Police said: "Our thoughts are with Noah's family and all those who knew him" Searches had widened to include East Bergholt and Manningtree, over the Essex border, on Wednesday. Divers from the Metropolitan Police were called in to search Decoy Pond, a nearby fishing lake. The pond is about 350 yds (320m) away from the playground where Noah was last seen. Police said at least 1,300 members of the public had helped in the search for the missing boy Supt Pearse continued: "Since Noah was reported as missing, a vast number of our officers and staff have been deployed in numerous functions in the search for Noah and support for his family. "We've been supported by Suffolk HART (Hazardous Area Response Team), SULSAR (Suffolk Lowland Search and Rescue), Environment Agency, HM Coastguard, Fire and Rescue Service and the ambulance service. "As a parent myself, I completely understand why people would want to help and such a response is one that typifies the strong sense of community and the heart-warming nature of Suffolk people that make the county such a special place. "I am sure you appreciate the family now need time, space and privacy and I thank you for your understanding in this." title: Ex-BBC presenter questions role of Royal Family in new documentary
description: John Humphrys, who presented Today and the Nine O'Clock News, heads a new Channel 4 documentary on the topic.
body: Humphrys met Queen Elizabeth II alongside other BBC figures at Broadcasting House in 2006 Veteran broadcaster John Humphrys has said the people of the United Kingdom should "be able to choose our leaders" as he releases a documentary exploring the role of the Royal Family. Humphrys, who for decades was one of the most prominent faces on the BBC, is presenting a new Channel 4 documentary called The Royals: Time to Go? Speaking to BBC Radio Wales Breakfast, the Cardiff-born presenter said he "admires" King Charles III in many ways, but said it was a "matter of choice". Buckingham Palace has been approached for comment. In the documentary, Humphrys speaks to both critics and supporters of the monarchy, and makes the case for electing a president as the head of state. He recalled seeing the late Queen Elizabeth III visiting Cardiff when he was growing up, watching her being driven down Newport Road. "My father didn't attend and said he would never bend the knee to anyone. I guess that rubbed off on me," he said. Humphrys asked why it was seen as such a taboo to call for an alternative to the Royal Family, saying that "we can because it's a democracy". "I know the monarch is not a political leader, but he is our leader, and we need to bow our knee to him. "That's what I object to. Shouldn't we get a choice?" He met the Queen throughout his career, including at Buckingham Palace where he said he spoke to her "and the corgis of course". Humphrys, who presented the Nine O'Clock News, the Today programme and Mastermind throughout a decades-long career with the corporation, said he took the opportunity to ask her for an interview. "When I'd finished, she looked up at me and said just one word 'no' and I thought I could build on that," he said. title: Charles said Diana would be forgotten 'soon enough', Earl Spencer claims in book
description: Buckingham Palace has pushed back against the claim, saying grief can "colour memory" of events.
body: Earl Spencer (second from the left) said he disagreed with Charles over whether William and Harry should walk in Diana's funeral procession Earl Spencer, the brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, has claimed King Charles said "we'll forget her soon enough" days after her death, in an extract from his upcoming memoir published by the Daily Mail. He claimed the then-Prince of Wales subjected him to a "stream of anger" after he insisted Diana would not have wanted Princes William and Harry, then aged 15 and 12, to have to walk in her funeral procession. Buckingham Palace has strongly pushed back against the claim. A spokesperson said: "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss." Swan Song: Diana, My Sister is due to be published next week and is expected to be highly critical of the Royal Family. BBC News has not seen the book in full. In the first extract, external from it to be made public, Earl Spencer claims to have been informed by a senior Palace aide that the young princes would walk alongside Princess Diana's coffin, which he objected to. He claims to have received a phone call from Charles shortly after. Earl Spencer wrote in the book: "He [Charles] unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death. 'Rest assured,' he hissed, 'we'll forget her soon enough'." Earl Spencer's book about his sister seems set to open a very difficult time in the recent history of the Royal Family. The death of Diana, a hugely popular figure, in a car crash in 1997, had created a volatile atmosphere, in which the royals were accused of failing to show feeling and empathy, and had seemed out of touch with the public mood. Earl Spencer's emotional and defiant speech at her funeral added to that cloud of grievance hanging over Diana's untimely death. Prince Harry has previously said that walking behind his mother's coffin aged 12 was something no child "should be asked to do". In 2017, he told the BBC he didn't "have an opinion whether that was right or wrong", but "looking back on it", he was glad to have been part of the day. Earlier on Wednesday, it emerged that copies of Earl Spencer's unreleased book had been stolen from a truck in the Netherlands. BBC News understands four copies of the Dutch language edition were taken from a truck while it was en route from the Dutch publisher's printers to their warehouse. title: British soldier who died in Ukraine road accident named by MoD
description: Tributes have been paid to Major Paul Wilks, who was described as a "gifted leader".
body: Major Paul Wilks, 40, died in a road traffic accident in Ukraine last week The member of the UK armed forces who died in a road traffic accident in Ukraine last week has been named as Major Paul Wilks. The Ministry of Defence (MoD) described the 40-year-old as a "gifted leader who earned the admiration and respect of all those fortunate enough to have served alongside him". The incident on Saturday was not the result of hostile action, the BBC understands, with the MoD stating that the accident happened "away from the front lines". Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "Major Wilks served this country with pride and dedication. His loss will be deeply felt by those around him." He said: "The tributes paid by those who worked with Paul illustrate his exceptional talent and ability, underscored by genuine warmth, compassion and a desire to support others. "His loss is a poignant reminder of the enormous sacrifice that our armed forces and their families make in the service of our country." Major Wilks, described by the MoD as a "proud family man", is survived by his wife and two sons. He joined the Intelligence Corps in 2012 and was deployed on multiple operational tours, including to Afghanistan. Major Wilks was the recipient of two operational service medals and a long service and good conduct medal. His commanding officer praised Major Wilks as "a man of great intellect, yet he remained a mate to those he served with". They added: "He spoke often of his love for his wife and two sons, expressing his deep gratitude for the support they provided, which allowed him to serve with such distinction. "It is because of that foundation that he was able to meet the challenges of his role, and it is in the course of his devotion to duty that he made the ultimate sacrifice." title: More than £2m spent by government on influencers since July 2024
description: Departments are using influencers alongside campaigns in traditional media such as TV and newspapers.
body: Government departments have disclosed that they have spent at least £2.4m working with social media influencers since July 2024. Departments have used influencers to promote campaigns on topics including career development, how to access benefits, as well as recruitment of teachers and prison officers. Of those providing figures, the Department for Education (DfE) has spent the most at more than £700,000, followed by HMRC, which has spent nearly £600,000, although this excludes agency fees. Departments said using influencers helped the government to reach people who may be harder to engage through traditional channels, with content creators paid fairly for their time and expertise. They also stressed that all paid marketing campaigns were assessed to ensure they deliver value for money. However, Conservative shadow Cabinet Office minister Mike Wood said: "The government is spending hundreds of thousands of pounds of taxpayers' money on influencers in a feeble attempt to cover for its failures. "It is becoming increasingly clear that if Labour want praise, they must pay for it." The figures - which primarily cover the period when Sir Keir Starmer was prime minister - were revealed in responses to parliamentary questions submitted by the Conservatives and first reported by the Politics At Sam And Anne's podcast, external. Andy Burnham's plan to collaborate with social media creators Previous Conservative governments have also used influencers - who can include celebrities, podcasters, bloggers and social media creators - in campaigns. For example, under Prime Minister Rishi Sunak, the Home Office paid TikTok influencers to encourage people not to cross the English Channel in small boats. In 2025/26, the Department for Education paid 57 social media influencers, who worked on campaigns including supporting career progression for young people, providing parents with childcare advice and recruiting more teachers. The department said this included Strictly Come Dancing's Oti Mabuse and reality TV star Billie Shepherd, who both backed the government's Best Start in Life childcare campaign. The department said spending covered fees paid to individuals and agencies, as well as production costs. HMRC has worked with 44 different influencers, with some taking part in multiple campaigns. In response to parliamentary questions, ministers said the tax agency used influencers to help reach the public with accessible information through "authentic and trusted voices", countering misleading tax guidance on social media. Meanwhile, the Department for Work and Pensions, which has spent more than £200,000 on influencers since July 2024, said content included helping people switch to Universal Credit and sharing advice on how to access career support. The DfE faced a backlash over its collaboration with reality TV star Gemma Collins - although it said she was not paid for the posts While the figures cover Labour's time in office under Sir Keir Starmer, his successor Andy Burnham has continued to use influencers to get the government's message out. On his first day as prime minister, Burnham was already posting videos on TikTok of him running with Sir Mo Farah and appearing on influencer Max Klymenko's "career ladder" podcast. Prof Andrew Chadwick, an expert in political communication at Loughborough University, said working with influencers "chimes with the change of direction since Burnham took over", with the PM using his following on TikTok and Instagram to engage directly with the public. He argued using influencers could be an effective way of telling the public about things like how to file their taxes, or counter health misinformation on social media. Governments have traditionally paid for advertising through newspapers, TV, radio and social media. But Prof Chadwick says paying content creators is increasingly used on top of this. At a time when more people - especially younger age groups - are switching off from traditional media, he said influencers could act as a trusted source of information. "It's taken a while to get to this stage, but I'm surprised in a sense at how little has been spent by these departments," he added. However, Prof Chadwick said there were also risks, as the government had less control over what posts could appear alongside, which could damage credibility. He added that it was difficult to predict what the public response would be to a collaboration. "The comments are there, they're underneath the post, and you'll get these kind of backlash moments," he said. "That undermines the purpose of the original campaign." Earlier this year, the Department for Education faced criticism over its collaboration with reality TV star Gemma Collins to promote post-16 education. The department said Collins was not paid for the content. Defending the campaign, then-education secretary Bridget Phillipson said Collins could reach people politicians could not, suggesting some of the criticism was driven by "snobbery". Government guidelines for influencer marketing have existed since 2023. Under the government's influencer due diligence policy, external, departments must consider the size and demographics of an influencer's following, as well as whether they have previously posted about political issues which could undermine the effectiveness of a campaign. title: 'It's a miracle' - fireball crash victim Millroy praises rescuer Hartog
description: British racing driver Ollie Millroy says it is a "miracle I'm alive" after fellow driver Loek Hartog "did everything right" when saving him from his blazing car.
body: Ollie Millroy is still in hospital in China British racing driver Ollie Millroy says it is a "miracle I'm alive" after fellow driver Loek Hartog saved him from his car when it was engulfed in flames. Millroy, 36, was hit by two other cars during the China GT Championship race at the Shanghai International Circuit 11 days ago, with his Ferrari immediately catching fire before hitting the safety barriers. A barely conscious Millroy was stuck in his car for over a minute before he was pulled from the burning wreckage by Dutchman Hartog after he immediately stopped his car to help him. "He acted instantly and he did everything right," a recovering Millroy told BBC Sport from his hospital bed in China. "Watching the video back, it looks like you're watching a movie and everything's rehearsed. "He ran around to check on me and realised the fire was too bad, and went round to the passenger side and realised he wasn't going to get me out of there; got an extinguisher, kept the fire off me for long enough to get inside the car and get me out of it. "Every single step was perfectly executed. If you look at the photos and videos of the car, the fact I've got out without life-changing burns or even the fact I'm alive - it's a miracle. "It was as though it was meant to be," added Millroy. "I'm not religious in any way, but it was as though someone had pre-programmed him to get me out of that car. "It's created this really strong bond between us. I didn't have any memory of the crash, the first time anyone talked me through it was Loek in the hospital and the two of us were just in floods of tears when he was telling me what happened and what [he] did and how different the result could have been for me." This video can not be played 'I owe him my life' - British racing driver on rivals rescue Millroy, who suffered several fractures and a punctured lung in the impact, says he has no memory of just before and for about an hour after the accident, which is affecting him psychologically as he tries to piece together what happened. "It's a strange feeling - I'm still not coming to terms with it because I don't remember any of it. I was sort of conscious; I was talking to Loek and I took my helmet off because I had run out of oxygen and I was struggling to breathe. "But I wasn't getting myself out of the car. My body had gone into some sort of survival mode because of the amount of the injuries I'd sustained. "Watching the video is like I'm watching something else. I keep waking up at night where my brain is trying to piece together what happened to my body - that frustration seems to be building more and more." Millroy eventually intends to continue racing, but first he is set to be reunited with Hartog, 23, as the Dutchman flies back to China this week so the pair can meet for the first time since the day of the crash. "I remember being scared very briefly," says Hartog, who races a Porsche for various different teams across GT racing. "I tried to run to the car and I was seeing if he was making an effort himself and quickly realised it was a one-sided quest. I saw I needed to free the space around him to get out [of the car]." By the time he saw the scene Millroy's car was already stationary, and Hartog recalled that it was another 59 seconds from when he stopped his car to Millroy exiting his burning vehicle. "I wish it were sooner," Hartog said. "There's a human element to that. I don't know why I went there; why I chose [to help him]. There was no reasoning, and I explain to myself that it was how I have been taught - how I grew up in some way." Millroy's wife Fern has been by her husband's side since hours after the crash, with the couple's three children being looked after by Fern's sister. "It's so emotional. I feel like I need that closure to give [Hartog] a great big hug," she said. "It's incredible how you can instantly love someone you've never met before - we've probably been around the same paddocks over the years, but to love someone who has just taken care of my soulmate and father of our three children, it's incredibly significant." Millroy joked: "I'm just sorry I can't take him out anywhere nicer for dinner [when they meet] but I'm tied to machines in the hospital bed. "We've got to know Loek's parents and you can see how he's come from the most wonderful, amazing family, and that you don't have to be a bad guy to be a great sportsman; you can be a really nice guy and really good sportsman. "He made a decision that day he was going to prioritise something else other than sport, and that's what saved my life." While Hartog wants to "close their chapter" by revisiting Millroy in China, the pair expect to work closely together in the future - in particular on matters of safety. "There'll always be an element of risk," says Millroy. "But we always take that for granted. "I never got in that car on that day and thought: 'I really hope there's a highly trained and expert fire crew down that corner in case something happens.' "I don't want to comment too much until it's been officially investigated. There's a lot of people wanting a lot of answers." Hartog adds: "This specific moment is something we can use to make the sport safer - there was a multitude of things that went wrong: I shouldn't have been the person to help but if it weren't for me, the outcome could have been very different." Millroy added: "As soon as I feel ready I want to get back in the car, but I've not been home yet, not seen the kids - there's a lot of things I want to go through in my head first. "I must have said 'thank you' a thousand times and I'd say it another thousand times that I'm so unbelievably grateful. All the emotions won't make sense until I g

title: Gray sacked by Hibs after six league games
description: Hibernian sack head coach David Gray six games into the Scottish Premiership season, ending the former captain's 12-year stay at Easter Road.
body: David Gray has been removed from his post after Tuesday's home defeat to Kilmarnock Hibernian have sacked head coach David Gray six games into the Scottish Premiership season, ending the former captain's 12-year stay at Easter Road. Tuesday's 1-0 defeat by bottom-of-the-table Kilmarnock leaves the Edinburgh club ninth in the table on six points. It was Hibs' sixth successive home league loss, stretching back to last season. Assistants Liam Craig and Craig Samson are also leaving, with John Potter placed in charge for Saturday's home game with Aberdeen. "Ultimately, this is a decision that we have not taken lightly, but unfortunately, one as a board we had to make due to the recent downturn of results and performances," said executive chairman, Ian Gordon. Gray famously led Hibs to Scottish Cup victory in 2016, heading in a stoppage-time winner against Rangers at Hampden to end a 114-year wait for a third success in the tournament. Having signed two years previously, the right-back retired in 2021 after 177 appearances and joined the coaching staff. Gray 'will continue until told otherwise' - but has Hibs boss lost the fans? Struggling Kilmarnock condemn Hibs to sixth home loss in row Latest Hibs news, analysis and fan views After three shorts spells as interim manager, Gray took on the position of head coach in May 2024, replacing Nick Montgomery. He won just one of his first 15 league games but the team staged a remarkable recovery to finish third, while Hibs were fifth last season. Both campaigns yielded European qualifiers which ended in dramatic, last-gasp Conference League play-off exits. Gray oversaw 107 games, winning 43, losing 35 and drawing 29. He departs with a League Cup semi-final against derby rivals Hearts to come on 1 November. "Dave has been an inspirational figure at the club during his time here, and he has been a true friend and fantastic colleague to so many," added Gordon. "On behalf of my family, I would like to personally thank him for everything he has done for us since we joined the club. "As a person, he constantly set the standard with his attitude, professionalism and general work ethic and he will be sorely missed around the building by all the players and staff. "On the pitch, he has delivered some incredible moments for our fans, and brought a level of stability and consistency that we haven't reached in recent years." We need to be like Motherwell and Hearts and look outside of Scotland and find a manger with an exciting style of play and fresh ideas. No "old school" Scottish manager! Robbie: It was a great run for David. But I think his time was up after the final whistle went last night. Not a great home run. John: I would like to thank David for what he achieved for the club as a player and then coach with two decent seasons culminating in European football. The lack of drive, effort and leadership from the players this season has got him the sack. Good luck and thanks for May 2016. Colin: It's a sad day. It felt inevitable after last night though. I wish David Gray all the best. I hope we take a modern approach to finding a new coach and don't go down the route of Malky's contact book Callum: Unfortunately its all about results and we haven't achieved them with ultimately the highest paid squad in years i think the board need a trusted and experienced manager now. Richard: David Gray is unfortunate - as he is only part of the issue. Malky Mackay [sporting director] should be sacked too - they are members of the same management team and bear equal responsibility. Ben: We got lucky in the end with Gray. After a horrendous start he pulled it back and gave us a third place finish with back to back European qualification. The football and system played however has not been good enough. There is something sad about a club legend coming to thank the fans and instead getting booed, but there was no longer any positives to take, even for the happy clappers. Sam: As a Hearts fan, I'm genuinely sorry to see David Gray sacked. He served Hibs well. I realise that he has to take the rap for the results, but the real truth is that at the moment his players simply aren't very good. These are lean times for Hibs, but they'll come again. Josh: If Hibs could sack Pat Stanton and Frank Sauzee they were always going to sack a Scottish Cup winning David Gray. You see some of the dross in their back line and realise he had no chance of survival. Poor guy. Alex: Sorry it came to that for David and wish him all the best, unfortunately the manager takes the hit. But the players have let him down time after time, clearly not good enough. Send us your views on Hibernian Keith: Truly gutted for Gray as the players need to have a long hard look at themselves. Simo Valakari from St Johnstone is the only manager other than Neil Lennon who we should be looking at. Big Marvin Bartley is for another time. All the best Sir David and thanks for all you've done for us over the years. I'll never forget the Scottish Cup win and the celebrations afterwards as long as I live. Scott: Long overdue. This Hibs team is going back the way. It will take a miracle to get the best out off the dross we have. Need a manager that plays exciting attacking football. Tony Mowbry was the last manager that got me off my seat. It's been a while since I've been excited to watch Hibs. John L: Neil Lennon or could the right offer be made to Alex Neil? Steve Clarke might fancy it. Stay away from Steven Pressley as he'll not go down well. Scandinavia seems to have good young coaches so perhaps there. Ross: Wouldn't be adverse to Kevin Thomson, good motivator. I suspect Lennon will be favourite and that would not upset me one bi

title: Photos show widespread damage at US sites from Iranian attacks
description: A wrecked air force plane and destroyed buildings are among the images obtained by the BBC's partner CBS News.
body: An undated photo shows a car reportedly destroyed in an Iranian strike at Camp Buehring in Kuwait Images showing widespread damage to multiple US sites in the Middle East from Iranian strikes have been obtained by the BBC's US partner CBS. The photos, provided by active military personnel, show a severed radar jet, flattened trailers and severely damaged buildings. The undated photos were taken at US bases and sites in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait. One member of the military, who was not named by CBS, said: "This is major damage to our bases that hasn't been communicated to the American public. "We're standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face." The White House referred the BBC to US Central Command. Centcom did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The photos, which have not been independently verified by the BBC, were published the day after a report from the Pentagon's watchdog confirmed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in the Middle East have been damaged and destroyed by Iran. One of the photos showed a destroyed Boeing E-3 Sentry at Prince Sultan Air Force Base in Saudi Arabia that has been ripped in half, its tail section crumpled into a tangled mess of metal. An undated photo of a destroyed Boeing E-3 Sentry at Prince Sultan air base in Saudi Arabia, about 62 miles (100km) south-east of the capital Riyadh While the photo is undated, BBC Verify previously confirmed a similar photo, apparently of the same radar aircraft in March. The Boeing E-3 Awacs are used to detect and track potential targets at long ranges to provide an early warning of possible threats. At the time, a US official told Reuters that 12 US personnel had been wounded, two of them seriously, in an Iranian attack on the air base. A pair of undated images reportedly from Camp Beuhring, Kuwait, show crumpled trailers, and a large tent-like structure that had been reduced to shreds as smoke billowed from the site. Trailers destroyed by Iranian strike at Camp Buehring, Kuwait Undated photo shows smoke billowing from a structure that sustained damage in an Iranian strike at Camp Buehring, Kuwait Another image shows a four-storey building damaged by an Iranian strike at Camp Arifjan, in Kuwait. Damage to the site was reported in March, including on satellite communications hardware, though it is not clear whether this image is from the same attack. Damage to a building can be seen in this photo from Camp Arifjan, Kuwait The images were published on the heels of a report from the Pentagon's watchdog, which found Iranian strikes had "damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan during the conflict". It also noted that equipment losses have totalled $3.7bn (£2.8bn). Overall, the US spent $33.4bn (£24.7bn) on the war up to 29 June, the report said. In the months after the war began, "dozens of US aircraft were destroyed or damaged", the report continues. The document lists several of the aircraft damaged, including five refuelling aircraft which were "damaged or destroyed on the ground in Saudi Arabia by Iranian munitions". A separate report , externalfrom the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) notes that the E-3 aircraft is no longer in production and would have to be replaced with a more modern equivalent, the E-7. The CBO noted that the E-3 aircraft alone costs $500m (£371m), and the estimated total cost of equipment lost in battle - including planes, drones and a terminal high altitude area defence system - amounts to $1.9b (£1.4b). CBO said that its review was subject to "uncertainty" because the defence department did not respond to its requests for information, requiring the agency to rely on government databases and public reports. Additionally, the extent of repairs and rebuilding that the US military plans to do remains unclear, according to the report. This video can not be played Watch: What does the munitions shortage mean for the US? Public and political pressure has mounted on the White House to find an end to the conflict with Iran, which began on 28 February when the US and Israel launched joint attacks on the country. Since the war began Iran has repeatedly attacked US bases and allied states in the Gulf, as well as Israel. On Tuesday night, the US House of Representatives voted for the third time to end the war in Iran, approving a measure that would force President Donald Trump to end US military action without congressional approval. The vote passed with the help of several Republicans, in what could be the final House vote on the matter ahead of the US midterm elections in November. It faces an uncertain path to passage - the US Senate has not indicated if it will take up the matter. The same day, outgoing Republican Congressman Thomas Massie announced an attempt to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth as new details emerged about the Iran war's price tag for the US. The Trump administration backed Hegseth, with US attorney general Todd Blanche telling reporters he was "doing a phenomenal job". title: Why an escalating Saudi oil crisis could drive up prices everywhere
description: BBC Verify's Ben Chu examines what impact rising energy costs could have on the global economy.
body: Global energy prices have spiked alarmingly again, driven largely in recent days by the escalating conflict between Yemen's Houthis and Saudi Arabia causing chaos for the oil industry. Petrol and diesel costs have risen rapidly in most countries while the wholesale price of natural gas - used for heating homes and generating electricity - has almost doubled in the UK and Europe since July. There are growing concerns of another inflationary shock on the world economy, which could cause interest rates to rise, increase mortgage costs and raise the price of almost everything in the shops including food. So what is behind this latest surge - and what are the implications for the world economy? The global oil price is currently above $108 (£80) per barrel, up from $70 (£52) in June 2026 - a roughly 50% increase. This has contributed to average petrol prices in the UK going above 170p a litre, the highest since 2022 and up from 150p in July. As a result of the near-doubling of UK natural gas costs alongside this the domestic price cap set by energy regulator Ofgem is forecast to rise by 25% in January next year - or about £440 a year for a typical household. In the US, the cost of a gallon (3.8 litres) of petrol has risen from $3.80 (£2.82) in July to $4.32 (£3.20), according to the AAA Gas Prices index. Diesel prices have hit a record level in the US of more than $6 (£4.46) a gallon, higher even than after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Analysts say the main driver has been a reduction in global oil and gas supplies. Before the US-Israeli war with Iran began in late February, about 20% of both global oil products and liquefied natural gas supplies passed through the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway connecting the Gulf and the Arabian Sea. This flow of energy collapsed after February due to Iranian attacks on commercial shipping and the energy facilities of US allies in the Gulf as well as a US blockade of Iran's ports. After the war began, Saudi Arabia stepped up the use of its East-West pipeline - which according to maritime intelligence firm Kpler has a capacity of 3.6 million barrels per day - to export oil via the Red Sea, rather than the Strait of Hormuz. But the pipeline was forced to shut down after it was attacked by drones on Friday, which Saudi Arabia has blamed on Iran-backed militias in Iraq. The Houthis separately attacked several Saudi oil facilities with drones and missiles last week, causing fires which led to operations being temporarily halted. Neil Quilliam of Chatham House said the pipeline could be closed for up to eight weeks for repair - although US Energy Secretary Chris Wright told broadcaster CNBC on Tuesday it will start operating again "very soon". And despite the US government insisting fuel is flowing through the Strait of Hormuz in roughly pre-war volumes, most independent analysts judge that the waterway remains significantly obstructed. Before the war around 21 million barrels per day of oil and oil products were passing through the Strait of Hormuz, according to the US Energy Information Administration. But Kpler estimated this had fallen to about 8.6 million barrels per day by the end of August. Over the past two weeks, the Houthis in Yemen have captured strategic territory from Saudi-backed pro-government forces close to the Bab al-Mandab Strait, another trade chokepoint at the southern tip of the Red Sea which was the transit point for about 5% of global oil supplies before February. About 5% of the global oil supply also normally leaves the Red Sea through the north, via the Suez Canal and a pipeline across Egypt to the Mediterranean. The global market oil price is rising over concerns these shipping arteries could, like Hormuz, be even more severely disrupted by Iran and its proxies. Before the Houthis recent advances on the south-west coast of Yemen the group declared in July it was enforcing a naval blockade of Saudi ships and ports. It said it will not attack vessels from other countries passing through the Red Sea. US President Donald Trump has said "the world's diesel price rise is mostly caused by the Russia/Ukraine War, not Iran". Analysts say the conflict - including Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries - has put pressure on diesel prices as Russia is the world's second largest diesel exporter. But most judge the bigger cause of the recent energy price spike has been the expanding regional conflict in the Middle East. Economists say that higher global energy prices - if sustained - usually lead to even higher prices for households and weaker economic growth, which translates into lower incomes and wages for people. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has estimated that a sustained 10% increase in oil prices increases global inflation by 0.4% and reduces global GDP growth by up to 0.2%. The Bank of England has estimated that a 10% increase in global oil price increases the UK inflation rate by 0.5% in the near-term and reduces UK GDP growth by about 0.4%. The rise in the global oil price since June is about five times larger than in the scenario used by the IMF and the Bank of England in their economic models to assess the impact of rising oil prices. However, it is possible that the global oil price could drop again if there is a peace agreement between the US and Iran. After a preliminary deal was signed between the two warring parties in June, the oil price temporarily fell sharply to pre-war levels, having gone as high as $120 a barrel. title: Part-human part-mouse brain developed in science breakthrough
description: Researchers at Stanford University genetically altered mice to be able to receive and function with human brain cells.
body: The research has raised questions about what it means to alter the way laboratory animals think and feel Neuroscientists in the US have successfully adapted mice to have functioning human cells inside their own brains. The researchers hope that potential treatments for psychiatric and neurodevelopmental diseases that only occur in humans could now be tested on the laboratory rodents. While mice with brains that are partly human might sound like a Kafkaesque experiment, the scientists said these are not "mice that think like humans". The animals are genetically engineered - and surgically altered - so that some of their brain tissue is human. The scientists said their work, published in the journal Nature, external, was carried out with independent ethical scrutiny. In scans of the implanted mice, researchers were able to see connections between the human brain cells and the rest of the mouse brain The aim of this ethically complicated breakthrough was to better understand the biology of brain disorders for which there are currently no effective treatments. Some conditions cannot be studied in a mouse, simply because rodents do not develop some of the brain disorders that we do. As lead researcher Prof Sergiu Pașca from Stanford University explained in a press conference, psychiatry has "one of the lowest success rates for clinical trials". "Even drugs that actually make it to clinical trial - that seem to be working really well in animal models - fail dramatically in clinic," he said in a press conference. "That tells us we're missing a lot of information about human biology and capturing that will be essential." The Stanford researchers said that, for some complex conditions, including epilepsy, autism and cerebral palsy, it has the potential to be "transformative". Pașca said: "Here we have a new model that allows us to actually capture aspects of human brain function in a way that has not been possible before." The hope is that this will provide a new way to investigate the biology of some human brain disorders The human brain is made up of billions of cells, interconnected in millions of circuits, making it difficult to understand its development and what exactly is happening – at the cellular level - when things go wrong. While this research is not the first time human neurons have been implanted in laboratory rodents, external, these scientists took that approach to a new level. First, they genetically-engineered mice to develop almost none of their own cerebral cortex – that is the outer layer of the brain sometimes referred to as "grey matter". It handles higher-level thinking, memory and senses. The researchers then used skin cells taken from humans and "reprogrammed" them, so they grew into pieces of brain-like tissue. These are structures called organoids – they are not whole brains grown in dishes, more collections of connected, living cells. When these organoids were implanted into the mouse brain the cells divided and organised themselves into the animal's existing brain circuitry, connecting with the rest of the mouse's brain and spinal cord. The cortex of the implanted mice is not perfect - normal cortex forms organised, structured layers. And as neuroscientist Dr Ilary Allodi put it, scans of these human-mouse brains look "a bit messy". After a few months though, the human cells started to look and function like the outer layer of the mouse's brain. About six months after the surgery, scientists put the mice through some basic behavioural tests - observing them as they moved around a small table-top arena. Pașca said they performed "largely as [the normal] mice did". "They don't have any enhancement," he added. Dr Sarah Chan, a reader in bioethics at the University of Edinburgh who was not involved in this research, told BBC News there was "no indication that what's being created here are mice that can think like humans, or a human brain in a mouse body." But she said the study "prompts us to think about what it might mean when we start changing animal cognition". "How can we know what it's like to be one of these mice? And how do we take account of that in the ways that we treat laboratory animals," she added. Dr Ilary Allodi, a neuroscientist from St Andrews University, who was not involved in the research, said the work the scientists had done was "very impressive". In particular, Allodi pointed to the fact that cell types that are found only in human and other primate brains - not in the brains of mice – spontaneously formed in the implanted mice. "You're keeping the human program inside the mouse environment – like the mouse is an incubator," she told BBC News. These mice, which the researchers said are engineered and reared under strict ethical and welfare guidelines, will most likely be used in a small number of labs for studies of a few, very specific brain disorders. Prof James Ainge, a neuroscientist who is also at St Andrews University, pointed out that while the development was technically very impressive, these mice could be "of limited use". This, he said, was partly due to the "ethical issues of raising living human brain tissue in a mouse and what that would mean for the experience of the animal". Neuroscientists who study the human brain, Allodi pointed out, all struggle with the same limitations. "We try to understand human disease, and what we have is mice, cells that live on a plate, and neural networks on a computer. "So this is a new avenue." title: Michelin-starred Seoul restaurant fined for using ants as garnish
description: The owner of the acclaimed establishment avoids jail but is made to pay 15 million won (£8,144; $10,965).
body: Most of the ants came from the US, with some coming from Thailand A two Michelin-starred restaurant in Seoul has been fined for using ants as a dessert garnish. The owner of Evett in the South Korean capital was fined 15 million won (£8,144; $10,965), while the company operating the restaurant was fined 10 million won for violating the Food Sanitation Act, local media report. Ants are not among the 10 insect species approved for human consumption in the east Asian nation. The approved list includes grasshoppers, locusts and some silkworms. Prosecutors had sought a one-year prison term for the restaurant's owner, as well as a 20 million won fine - but the judge took the owner admitting the charge and having no prior criminal record into account. However, the judge is reported as saying that, as well as violating food standards, the presence of heavy metals exceeding standards was detected in the ants when they were tested, meaning the "culpability is not light". The owner was said to have been unaware that providing ants in food was prohibited in South Korea, as they are used as food elsewhere. Their use as a topping for sorbets at Evett came to light after the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety found online reviews accompanied by photographs. It said the owner had sprinkled three to five ants on certain dishes to give them a "sour taste", over a period of nearly four years - amounting to approximately 49,000 ants used as a garnish. Most of the ants were imported from the US, while some came from Thailand, the ministry said. The owner had argued that they were used in a "small part" of the restaurant's 15-course menu and that diners were told they could opt for a non-ant alternative topping. Ants are eaten and sometimes even valued as a delicacy in several Asian, African and Latin American cultures. Weaver ants and their eggs are used in Thai and Cambodian cooking, while in Colombia, queen ants are as prized as caviar. The Michelin Guide considers a two-star establishment as one that does "excellent cooking" and is "worth a detour". title: Charlie Kirk's family alleges 'stunning failures' by Utah officials led to his shooting
description: The conservative activist was speaking to a crowd of thousands on the university campus when he was shot and killed by a gunman positioned on a roof.
body: Charlie Kirk speaks at Utah Valley University on 10 September 2025 before he was shot and killed by a gunman Charlie Kirk's family has accused the Utah Valley University and state officials of "stunning failures and reckless decisions" that they say led to the conservative activist's 2025 assassination during a campus event. In a legal notice, lawyers for the family say Kirk's Turning Point USA event at the university campus was not properly secured or monitored, making him an easy target. Kirk, 31, was speaking to a crowd of thousands on the university campus, when he was shot and killed by a gunman positioned on a roof. The university said it was aware of the claim but did not comment further on the allegations, according to a statement shared with the BBC's US partner CBS News. "We are aware of the notice of claim. UVU addresses legal matters consistent with our established processes, " the university said in its statement. "Our focus remains on supporting our campus community." The legal notice was filed on 9 September, a day ahead of the one-year anniversary of Kirk's death, and is typically a precursor to a lawsuit. It names Utah Valley University, local police, the state of Utah, and other university officials as parties who were allegedly aware of the threats against Kirk and did not take steps to protect him. "Through a series of stunning failures and reckless decisions, the UVU Parties created a foreseeable danger to Charlie," the notice alleges. "Placing a politically controversial figure like Charlie Kirk in an outdoor event in the quad surrounded by tall buildings and other elevated observation platforms is accurately described as walking him into a fishbowl," it says. Kirk's family alleges the university failed to conduct a meaningful security assessment ahead of the event, failed to assign enough police officers, and did not have an ambulance available on site. The family also alleges the university ignored warnings about securing the rooftops surrounding the courtyard where Kirk was speaking. "The risk of a rooftop shooter should have been especially top-of-mind given the attempted assassination of President Trump, Charlie Kirk's close friend and political ally, by a rooftop shooter the previous year," the family's attorney D Loren Washburn wrote in the court filing. Tyler Robinson, a 23-year-old man from Utah, who has been accused of shooting Kirk from a roof, is due to appear in court next month to hear the date of his trial. Robinson denies aggravated murder, a capital offence in the state, as well as six other charges. Prosecutors have called for the death penalty. title: Obamas' 'fiery and gorgeous' dog Sunny dies
description: The Portuguese Water Dog spent 13 years with the family, meeting many high-profile visitors in the White House, including Pope Francis.
body: The Obamas' beloved pet dog Sunny has died after 13 years with the family, Barack Obama has announced. "Yesterday, we lost a cherished member of our family," the former US president wrote on X, describing her as a loyal dog who was "pretty much perfect" and always by their side. The family had two Portuguese Water Dogs in the White House. They got Sunny at the beginning of Obama's second presidential term in 2013. Sunny met many high-profile visitors while Obama was president, from foreign dignitaries to Pope Francis. Their other dog, Bo, joined the family in 2009 as a gift for daughters Sasha and Malia to help them settle into the White House. Bo died in 2021. Obama said that when Sunny joined the family they "immediately fell in love". He described her as "full of boundless energy", saying she leapt over the hedges on the South Lawn like they weren't even there. Sunny most enjoyed "having us run around with her, roll on the floor with her, or have her belly rubbed for as long as we were willing", he wrote. "She loved the girls, even if they were pestering her when she was napping. She loved our team, and would often follow them around, helping them on the job." Obama added that Sunny was "a loud and sloppy drinker" who hated getting wet. "For thirteen years, she would be by our side – always loyal, always sweet, always ready for adventure, still fiery and gorgeous till the very end of her days." He said the family would miss her terribly and that she was now with her "big brother" Bo. Sunny and Bo met Pope Francis at the White House in 2015 Sunny was a regular at White House events, meeting children at Christmas parties and international dignitaries on state visits. In 2015, Sunny and Bo met Pope Francis in the Blue Room at the presidential residence. Former chief White House photographer Pete Souza said it was an "honour" to work with Sunny, describing her as a "willing subject" who had "the rare distinction of being petted by both a President and a Pope". There is a long tradition of pets at the White House. Donald Trump is believed to be the only president in the past 100 years to not have a pet. title: 'Putney pusher' suspect found dead at home
description: Nicholas Brandram was a suspect in the incident where a woman was shoved into the path of a bus nine years ago.
body: Nicholas Brandram, pictured in 2013, was found dead on Tuesday The man suspected of pushing a woman into the path of a bus while he was out running on Putney Bridge in south-west London in 2017, has been found dead at his home. Nicholas Brandram, 44, was under investigation in the so-called "Putney pusher" case, after CCTV went viral showing just how close the woman came to be run over by the 430 bus, in a seemingly unprovoked attack. He was arrested in June this year on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm. Last week, the Metropolitan Police confirmed he had been released under investigation. The banker was found dead in his home on Tuesday evening. The Met said his death was being treated as "unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious". This video can not be played The incident happened nine years ago A spokesperson for the force said officers attended the property in Chiswick alongside paramedics "after a man was found unresponsive". "Sadly, a 44-year-old man was pronounced dead at the scene. His next-of-kin have been informed," they said. Brandram, who served as a Captain in the Scots Guards in Afghanistan, was working more recently in private banking for HSBC. He is known to been a distant relative of European royalty - his grandmother was Princess Katherine of Greece, and the late Duke of Edinburgh, Prince Philip, was his father's godfather. While in police custody in June over the Putney Bridge incident, Brandram was also arrested on suspicion of drug possession. title: Pressure for quick VAR decisions obvious in rushed derby review
description: The controversy surrounding the VAR decision to allow Erling Haaland's winner in the Manchester derby has rumbled on for days, so what led to the error?
body: This video can not be played Refereeing decisions were 'baffling' - Rooney "Quick, quick, quick, quick! Go, go, go, go, go!" The words of video assistant referee Matt Donohue as he rushed through the review to award Erling Haaland's winning goal in the Manchester derby. No doubt Donohue was simply trying to be as efficient as possible, but it led to one of the most catastrophic VAR errors the Premier League has seen. Donohue and his assistant VAR, Blake Antrobus, inexplicably failed to notice that Enzo Fernandez was three yards offside before he tried to head the ball. The goal was given, and Manchester City beat Manchester United 1-0. Refereeing has always been a goldfish bowl of scrutiny and pressure, heightened by the introduction of VAR. The Premier League made a "more efficient application of VAR to reduce delays" one of its football principles for the season. Has the game tried to prioritise speed over accuracy? Supporters have grown tired of long delays while the video officials review incidents The urgency in Donohue's voice was all too apparent. "Let's go, let's go, let's go, let's go!" It was a panicked exchange between the VAR and the replay operator. Not calm, collected and methodical. Rushed and chaotic. The opposite of how a video official should operate. Officials hear repeatedly - from fans, pundits, radio phone-ins and newspaper columns - that VAR has to be quicker. That delays are not acceptable. In the Premier League stakeholders' survey - which includes managers, coaches and supporters - the key theme for improvements to VAR was the speed of decisions. This has to create pressure - but it is no excuse for such an error. City boss Enzo Maresca had some sympathy speaking on Wednesday, though he was of course the beneficiary of the gaffe. "To make a decision in 10, 20 seconds is not easy for them," said Maresca. "Sometimes they make mistakes. I make mistakes, players make mistakes. It's part of our job." Referees' chief Howard Webb has taken the desire for quicker reviews on board, but it is still a balancing act. There has been a positive impact, as far as the stats go. VAR delays - including the referee making an announcement to the crowd - have been reduced, from an average of 46 seconds per game to 36 seconds season-on-season. Yet the only other VAR mistake, the failure to award a penalty to Arsenal at Aston Villa, also arguably came about because the incident was cleared too quickly. This video can not be played What would you do to fix VAR? Completing a VAR review in the shortest possible time is not about skipping steps. And it was a critical mistake by Donohue and Antrobus. Speed is a factor, but the most serious error in process came before Donohue tried to rush through the attacking phase. Donohue asked the replay operator to stop the video on the first replay when Josko Gvardiol touched the ball to cross into the area. He then went immediately into the semi-automated offside technology. This should not have happened. The VAR team should have assessed the full picture, from the playing of the cross to the head of Haaland. This would have provided awareness of Fernandez's position and impact. They did not, and the events inside the penalty area were not considered until the attacking phase was looked at. By then, all that mattered to Donohue and Antrobus was whether Fernandez touched the ball. This would have created a new phase and placed Haaland offside. Donohue has received much of the criticism, but arguably Antrobus' involvement, or lack of, was just as influential. The AVAR's contribution to the entire review was to utter "no, yeah" about the potential touch by Fernandez. This was one second before Donohue uttered the words "final decision is goal, check complete". Antrobus' role is to provide the checks and balances, to make sure the VAR has not missed anything. This fell short. There has been only one lengthy VAR delay this season, in the game between Brentford and Sunderland. A Dan Ballard goal was ruled out for a subjective offside against Kevin Danso. Antrobus was the AVAR in this game, too. There was a great deal of criticism in some parts of the media for that delay, which took over four minutes. Could that have played on Antrobus' mind on Sunday? We cannot know for sure. Ironically, Antrobus played a crucial role in steering VAR Tim Wood to the correct offside decision against Danso. There is also the role of the support VAR, who sits in the operations room next to the match hub at Stockley Park and can intervene on points on protocol. Aware of what was unfolding with the review, no action was taken.- It would still have been salvageable in the period between the goal being scored and the kick-off. But when an error of this magnitude happens, no amount of investment can mask the failure. There have been calls to appoint VAR specialists, yet this is exactly what Donohue is - in the Premier League's definition. Three seasons ago, Pro Ref asked for candidates interested in becoming video officials. All those who applied were put through aptitude tests. About 15 made it through to the final stages of training, of which 10 have officiated games in the Premier League. One of those is Donohue, who on Sunday was the video official for the 65th time. title: Fitzpatrick not comfortable with Dubai tour finals
description: Matt Fitzpatrick says he is not "100% comfortable" with the prospect of travelling to Dubai for the season-ending DP World Tour Championship in November when he is due to be defending champion.
body: Matt Fitzpatrick won his third DP World Tour Championship in November 2025 Matt Fitzpatrick says he is not "100% comfortable" with the prospect of travelling to Dubai for the season-ending DP World Tour Championship in November when he is due to be defending champion. Fitzpatrick is concerned that the United Arab Emirates could be a target in the ongoing conflict between Iran, the United States and Israel. "You've only got to look at the hotel that got hit earlier this year," Fitzpatrick told BBC Sport. "I was having dinner the week I won in that hotel. "That's obviously very scary when you think about how it was a few months away but how close you were to that particular spot and for something like that to happen. It's obviously quite scary." Fitzpatrick would like to see the event switched to a different host country, a decision he called a "no brainer, in my opinion" before adding: "But I'm not a sponsor, I'm not paying the bills and all that sort of stuff. "I'm sure there's more to it than just the meets the eye." Led by chief executive Guy Kinnings, DP World Tour officials are assessing safety issues for their final two play-off events in Abu Dhabi and then Dubai. Both tournaments are backed by key sponsors of the European-based tour and provide a lucrative end to the season for the circuit's leading money winners. "I think it's annoying, but at the same time, Guy Kinnings can't control what Iran are doing," Fitzpatrick added. "It is frustrating because as someone who likes to plan and be prepared, it is difficult to kind of figure out what's going on. Obviously, things as they stand are a bit weird over there. "I can't say I'm like a hundred percent comfortable, but I guess you just have to see nearer the time and, you know, I still need to qualify as well." Fitzpatrick's Ryder Cup team-mate Shane Lowry said the tour faces important choices over how to end the current season. "They are huge decisions for everyone," said last week's winner of the Irish Open. "I'm not going to sit here and comment on the whole thing because I think it's up to the powers above to sort that all out. I think if the tournaments are on, the players are going to go. And if they are not, they will find an alternative." A spokesperson for the DP World Tour said: "We are in constant dialogue with our members and their management teams about the tournaments they play in, but ultimately players' individual schedule choices are a matter for them to decide. "As far as our play-offs are concerned, it remains our intention to play as scheduled in the UAE but we continue to monitor the situation and take advice from our international travel advisors."
