title: Very hot drinks may damage the food pipe and increase cancer risk
description: Steaming hot liquid can damage the cell lining on the way down to the stomach, experts say.
body: Regularly drinking beverages like tea and coffee at very hot temperatures increases the risk of cancer of the food pipe or gullet, known as oesophageal cancer, UK research suggests. Researchers say the findings, external, from a study of nearly a million people, make this the largest to date to establish the link. In the study, people who had their drinks "very hot" had around a three times higher risk of the cancer than "warm" tea or coffee drinkers - although experts stress the overall chances of developing this cancer are low. Steaming hot liquid can damage the cell lining of the food pipe on the way down to the stomach. The work by Oxford University, which is published in the International Journal of Cancer, defines any drink at 65 degrees Celsuis or above as "very hot" and posing a potential risk. Consuming six or more hot drinks per day also raises the risk, according to data from 977,282 middle-aged men and women. Although adding milk can cool drinks down slightly, a milky tea or coffee may still be far too hot, researchers say. Tea made immediately after a kettle is fully boiled is touching boiling point, which is 100 degrees C (212 degrees F). Once poured into a cup, that lowers to around 90 or 95 degrees C. The advice is to wait a few minutes before drinking so the beverage cools to a safer temperature. Cancer Research UK says it's difficult to put an exact time on how long a hot drink should be left to cool. "But if you're worried, we'd suggest just waiting until it's comfortable to drink rather than drinking it while it's still very hot," the charity said. Lead researcher Dr Keren Papier said research in South America - where many people drink a very hot herbal beverage called mate - had already shown a similar link between hot drinks and oesophageal cancer. But she said: "More research is now needed to identify the exact drink temperatures linked to this increased risk." A separate study, external of 118 young adults who did multiple tastings of different black coffees found most only deemed the drinks to be too hot if the temperature was 70 degrees C or above. According to one takeaway coffee cup manufacturer, the ideal temperature for hot coffee on the go is between 49 and 60 degrees C. Should a barista want the coffee to stay hotter for longer - if a customer requests extra hot - it can be served at over 82 degrees C, says MTPak Coffee. The researchers suggest that around one or two in every 10 oesophageal cancers could be avoided if people stopped drinking very hot beverages. Squamous cell oesophageal cancer is rare, affecting a few thousand people a year. In the UK, around 1% of the population has a lifetime risk of being diagnosed with this type of cancer. So even if scalding hot drinks might increase someone's risk, the chances of them developing the cancer are still low. And there are other factors, such as smoking, which are a bigger risk for oesophageal cancer. Fiona Osgun from Cancer Research UK, which funded the study, stressed: "The most important ways to reduce the risk of this cancer type are not smoking and cutting down on alcohol." Symptoms of oesophageal cancer can include heartburn, indigestion or a pain in your throat or chest, especially when swallowing, along with weight loss. title: Meta continues to run ads promoting child sexual abuse material in India - report
description: The report follows a BBC Eye investigation that found Instagram running paid ads promoting such material in India.
body: Tech Transparency Project (TTP) says it found 332 adverts with CSAM that ran on Facebook and Instagram Warning: This story contains descriptions of abuse Meta ran hundreds of paid ads with artificial intelligence-generated child sexual abuse imagery, including several in India, over the past 10 months, a new report by US-based campaigners has found. The report comes two months after the Indian government ordered Meta to remove all ads and content promoting child sexual abuse material (CSAM) on Instagram. This was in the aftermath of a BBC Eye investigation which found that Instagram was running paid adverts promoting CSAM in India. Washington-based Tech Transparency Project (TTP), external says it found 332 adverts with CSAM that ran on Facebook and Instagram, the majority of them (274) in August this year. When the BBC wrote to Meta about these findings, they said in a statement, "We don't tolerate nudify apps or any kind of child exploitation, whether real or AI-generated. These criminals constantly shift tactics to evade detection, which is why we keep strengthening our detection and enforcement." The TTP report, published on Tuesday, says that it identified several photos of real children, including a member of a European royal family, that were used in the ads and then manipulated using AI. It says more than a dozen ads appeared on Meta platforms even after TTP made the company aware of its findings. About a quarter (84) of the ads ran in India and 78 of these were published after the Indian government's order on removing CSAM and its meeting with senior Meta officials. After the BBC investigation, several Indian agencies including the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights and the National Human Rights Commission have said they are examining the matter. The distribution of CSAM is a criminal offence in India, while Meta's policy states that ads must not contain content that sexually exploits or endangers children. When the BBC contacted Meta about its investigation, it said that when it becomes aware of apparent child exploitation, it reports it to the US-based National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) in compliance with its legal obligations. The NCMEC is the centralised global reporting system for the online sexual exploitation of children. But Bhuwan Ribhu, the founder of Just Rights for Children, a network of more than 250 organisations working to prevent violence against children in India, says this is not enough. Just Rights for Children has filed a petition in India's Supreme Court, citing the BBC's findings, and asked for directions to social media platforms for mandatory reporting and identification of those promoting child sexual abuse material Bhuwan Ribhu wants India to require social media platforms to identify and report those promoting CSAM "Social media companies are clearly flouting Indian laws by not reporting child sexual abuse content to Indian law enforcement agencies as mandated by our child protection laws," said Ribhu. The TTP, a research initiative of the non-profit Campaign for Accountability that seeks to hold large technology companies accountable, said it found 332 ads featuring CSAM on Instagram and Facebook running in the US, UK, EU, Australia and India. They say they have reported all the ads to NCMEC. According to TTP, almost all the ads they found start with a photo of a child, and, as the video plays, the photo is manipulated by AI to show them engaging in a graphic sexual act. TTP described one ad which ran in India as: A photo of a preteen girl animated so that she performs a graphic sex act, with a voiceover that says, "There are no restrictions. All the characters are real people and there are many options. This is the AI men actually use." The BBC has not seen this ad. According to TTP, the ad was posted by more than 50 different handles in India over a fortnight in August this year. In July, after BBC's investigation, Meta had put out a detailed post on its website, external about how it fights child exploitation on its apps. "Anyone on our platforms can report ads if they believe they violate our policies," it said. TTP said that it tried reporting ads via Meta's own reporting system and that of the 84 ads that ran in India, they were able to report 55. Meta only gives the option of reporting ads when they are live. For 43 of these, TTP got a reply that said, "We've taken a look and found that this ad doesn't go against our Advertising Standards." For 11 ads, they were told that the content had already been removed. They haven't received a response yet for one ad. In July, after BBC's investigation, Meta had put out a detailed post about how it fights child exploitation on its apps When the BBC reached out to Meta for a comment, they said, "we've built strong defenses, including systems that block violating ads as well as ongoing monitoring in case we initially miss something: that's why many of the ads flagged to us had already been removed, most had fewer than 200 impressions, and the total ad spend was under $5,000". TTP said that when it reached out to Meta for a response, all the ads they reported were removed. This was similar to what happened during the BBC's investigation. When the BBC used Meta's reporting system to report one of the ads featuring child sexual abuse to Instagram, the platform did not take it down. Later, when the BBC asked Meta for comment, it said it had already disabled several adverts and suspended the accounts posting them. The company said it had removed additional ads, disabled more accounts and blocked URLs for other content that violated its policies in response to the BBC's findings. TTP said that the vast majority of the 332 ads they found directed users to AI image or video generation apps, mostly from Chinese developers. title: England up in reading, maths and science rankings as Scotland and Wales fall behind
description: The latest Pisa report also warned of a global decline in teenagers' reading skills.
body: English pupils have pulled ahead of the rest of the UK in international reading, maths and science tests, new data suggests, with Scotland and Wales falling further behind. The 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) saw reading and maths scores slump in each UK nation except England, while all four saw an uptick in science, with that rise again most notable in England. The latest Pisa report, which is published every three years, also warned of a worldwide decline in teenagers' reading skills. Teenagers were losing the skills that "matter most in the age of AI", such as being able to critically evaluate information from different sources, it said. The share of "hasty readers", who rush through texts to give quick, incorrect answers, has almost doubled between 2018 and 2025. The report warned the fall was greatest in those from "relatively well off" families. Run by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), the Pisa tests assess teenagers on their ability to solve problems, think critically and communicate, before asking them a wider range of questions about their education in a questionnaire. Although the UK performed well overall, the rankings varied significantly again, with results showing England, where the curriculum is significantly different, pulling consistently ahead of Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales. England's schools minister, Georgia Gould, said the government wanted to "build on" the positive results and "go further so all young people leave school with strong literacy and numeracy". The 2025 Pisa tests were taken by a sample of 760,000 15-year-olds in 91 countries. In the UK, where education differs between the home nations, 15,566 students took the tests in 515 schools. In England, where it was recently announced that technical subjects would soon be available to students from age 14, Gould held up high-performing Estonia as an example of where "academic excellence can go hand in hand with high-quality vocational routes". "Our reforms will build on England's strong academic foundations so future generations not only perform well, but feel connected to school and excited about where their education can take them," she added. But Laura Trott, England's shadow education secretary, said the country's successes were down to previous reforms, and accused the new government of trying to "sabotage" them. Wales falls further behind rest of UK in international school tests Primary teachers hired to teach Glasgow secondary pupils to read While Wales lags behind the rest of the UK overall, on science it is ahead of other European countries such as France, Spain and the Netherlands. As the tests last year were taken by 15-year-olds, the results there largely reflect learning under an old curriculum, which has recently been changed. Anna Brychan, Wales' minister for education and Welsh language, said plans were in place to support schools, adding that the results "highlight our need to improve standards of reading and maths, as a priority". Scotland's education secretary, Mairi McAllan, said the results showed "real strengths in Scottish education, as well as areas we're already working to improve". But Scottish Labour said results had "flatlined since 2022's historically poor results", while the Scottish Liberal Democrats said the education system under the SNP had "tumbled down the rankings, lagging behind England on every measure of performance". Northern Ireland's education minister, Paul Givan, said pupils there had performed well by international standards, but that - like other countries - its education system was facing "significant challenges", adding that "there is much more work to do". Overall, the Pisa tests provide the biggest global snapshot of education systems and an independent view of how teenagers are performing compared with their peers in other countries, so it is a relative measure. Andreas Schleicher, director of education at the OECD, said reading was the "mother of all skills" and that the steep decline was a concern. He said children's ability to read complex texts had declined by the equivalent of "two school years" in the last decade. Longer-term Pisa research suggested students who read longer books performed best, he added, as it helped them to learn to hold complex information in mind. Schools like Meadow Park, in Coventry, are adopting a range of approaches to improve pupils' reading skills, including weekly book club discussions led by tutors. Year 10 pupil Ampaabeng said the sessions have had a "really positive impact" on his reading since they were brought in a year ago. The school has also invested in a wider range of books in the library, where reading for pleasure at lunchtime is encouraged. A mobile phone ban was introduced at the school two years ago to reduce distractions - an approach which is commended by the new report. "In a digital age, it's easier to pick up a phone than it is a book," head teacher Bernadette Pettman said. She said reading together had enabled the school to "break down that fear of reading" and that pupils had "absolutely embraced it". Bernadette Pettman says the school tries to make reading fun with book clubs, creative writing sessions and visits from authors One of the other big changes in education, picked up in the OECD's report, is the use of AI. It warns that excessive use can lead to pupils avoiding looking up information themselves, a process sometimes called "cognitive off-loading". In the UK, the Pisa questionnaire's results suggested a relatively high proportion of teenagers said they had never used AI for their schoolwork. But the OECD's report said countries were allowing the rapid spread of AI without evidence of its impact, likening it to rolling out an untested vaccine on children. Schleicher called on governments to provide clear guidelines, and consider whether AI could be use

title: Track UK's latest migration numbers - net migration, visas, asylum and small boats
description: Use our interactive tracker to explore the latest migration statistics for the UK
body: Track UK's latest migration numbers - net migration, visas, asylum and small boats UK net migration has dropped to the lowest level, outside of the Covid pandemic, since 2012. How does that sit alongside other key migration measures, including asylum applications, small boat arrivals and visas granted? Scroll down to find out more about the latest key figures, and get answers to key questions on a range of topics. Between 1 January and 7 September 2026, a total of 17,281 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 43% on the same period the previous year. These crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020. Nearly all those who arrive by small boat claim asylum. Under international law, this means they are allowed to stay in the country while their asylum application is considered. Small boat arrivals made up 40% of asylum applications between July 2025 to June 2026. Boats that arrived in the UK from 8 September 2025 to 7 September 2026 carried an average of 68 people. This has more than doubled since 2021. Experts say overcrowding in boats makes crossings riskier. At least 84 people died while attempting to cross the Channel in 2024, according to the United Nations (UN). When looking at the scale of small boats crossings, the number of these arrivals is about 5% of the size of total immigration into the UK from January 2025 to December 2025. The government has pledged to “smash the gangs” behind these crossings in order to reduce the numbers. People from Eritrea accounted for 18% of all arrivals from July 2025 to June 2026. In the latest figures covering January 2025 to December 2025, at least 2,335 people who arrived by small boat were found to be potential victims of human trafficking or other forms of modern slavery, according to the Home Office. Another 4,712 people were detected entering the UK without permission via other methods including hiding in vehicles, travelling on ferries or through airports from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 17% on the same period the previous year. There are also individuals who arrive legally, for example via a work or study visa, and then overstay their limit. The total number of people who live in the UK illegally after arriving legally is not known. An asylum seeker is someone who wants to be in the UK because they say they cannot live safely in their own country due to persecution or violence. The government must house an asylum seeker if they cannot financially support themselves while their claim is being considered. There were 89,089 people in asylum accommodation as of June 2026. About 18% of those people, 16,021, were in hotels. These are used when there is not enough shared housing available, such as houses of multiple occupation (HMOs) or former military sites. The government has pledged to stop the use of hotels by 2029. More people are in hotels across the south of England than elsewhere in the UK, while HMOs are more common in the north of England and Scotland. A modern browser with JavaScript and a stable internet connection is required to view this interactive Type in a postcode or the name of a local council below to see how many asylum seekers are housed in the area A total of 85,891 people applied for asylum in the UK from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 21% on the same period in the previous year. Most people who arrive in the UK by small boat claim asylum, but they were only 40% of all asylum seekers from July 2025 to June 2026. The rest include people who arrived by other illegal means or who came to the UK legally and applied for asylum while holding, or just after holding, a valid visa. It can take years for the government to decide whether someone should be granted asylum. In June 2026, 40,168 people - across 32,401 asylum applications - were waiting for an initial decision. The number of people awaiting an initial decision was down by 56% on the previous year. As of March 2026, a further 87,450 refused asylum applications were part of a second backlog, waiting the outcome of an appeal in the courts. This was up by 72% on the previous year. Together, these initial decision and appeal cases form the government’s total asylum applications backlog, which it has pledged to clear. Refugee status was granted in about 38% of asylum decisions made by the Home Office from July 2025 to June 2026. About 39% of asylum appeal cases concluded between April 2025 to March 2026 resulted in a previous refusal decision being overturned. The government requires people who are in the UK, but no longer have permission to live or work in the country, to leave. This is called a return and can happen voluntarily or involuntarily. People can lose the right to be in the UK for different reasons, such as a visa expiring, an asylum claim being refused, or by receiving a criminal conviction that results in deportation. There were 40,605 returns from July 2025 to June 2026. This was up by 8% on the same period the previous year. That number of returns is equivalent to about 6% of total emigration from the UK from January 2025 to December 2025. Of all returns from July 2025 to June 2026: 5,962 had been convicted of a criminal offence12,568 had lodged an asylum claim at some point3,310 had arrived in the UK by small boat People from India made up 27% of all returns from July 2025 to June 2026. The UK is trialing a scheme with France to return people who arrived in the country on a small boat. For every person the UK sends back to France, the UK will accept an equal number of asylum seekers. This is called the "one in, one out" deal. As of 30 June 2026, 1,087 people have been returned through this arrangement. Returns can happen in different ways. "Enforced returns", which includes deportations, means the government arranges transport to return people to a different country. In some cases, people are escorted by officers. title: New mums 'left to get on with it' as C-section numbers hit record high
description: Mothers have described being left to recover from caesarean sections with "no support".
body: Carys Louise Brandon says she was completely unprepared for what came after her first C-section Mothers have described being left to recover from caesarean sections with "no support" as the number of babies being born via caesarean reaches its highest rate on record. A caesarean, or C-section, is a major operation to deliver a baby through a cut in the abdomen, usually just below the bikini line. Carys Louise Brandon, from Swansea, had an emergency C-section to deliver her first child in 2022 and said she was completely unprepared for what came afterwards. The Welsh government said every woman should receive high-quality postnatal care tailored to her needs. Carys Louise says she had many unanswered questions about her recovery Latest figures show 42% of babies in Wales were born by C-section in 2025, with just over half of those operations being emergencies. Carys' first baby was born in 2022. After needing an emergency C-section, Carys, a content creator, said she had many unanswered questions about her recovery. "I think I was thrown in at the deep end and I really didn't know how to deal with it," she said. It was almost three weeks before the 29-year-old said she felt physically able to leave the house. "And even then, I only walked up to the top of the street and back," she added. Carys has since had two more caesareans and said each experience was very different. Both times, she said the care she received in hospital and from her community midwife was good. But after getting home, she was left with questions about how her body should be recovering. "You're thrown so into the deep end and there's no sort of, 'Oh, this is how your scar should look. This is quite normal for this sort of time'." She recalled taking the dressing off her wound and fainting in the shower. "I didn't know - should my scar be recovering in a certain way, should I really be feeling like this? "There's just no support around the fact that after it, you're looking after a baby and recovering from major surgery, and everyone's recovery looks totally different." She has shared her own experiences online in the hopes of helping other women, and said expectant mums often contact her for advice. "I wish I'd had more stories that I could read to be a bit more informed before I gave birth that way." Carys has had three children, all of whom were delivered via C-section The latest figures from the Welsh government showed that 42% of births in Wales were by caesarean section in 2025 - the highest rate on record - while in England around 45% of babies are delivered in this way. According to the NHS, external, a caesarean may be recommended as a planned procedure or carried out in an emergency if a vaginal birth is considered to be too risky. Some women also choose to have a caesarean for non-medical reasons. The health service's website states that most women can go home from hospital one or two days after a C-section, but that recovery is normally slower than from a vaginal birth. A Welsh government report published in February highlighted the rapid increase in caesarean sections and inductions, saying the consequences for women, their families and the NHS had not been evaluated. The report raised concerns about staffing and support across maternity services and said postnatal care was inadequately staffed and supported. The Welsh government has committed to a three-year programme of improvements, but the Royal College of Midwives (RCM) said maternity services had not kept pace with the changing picture. New mums 'left to get on with it' after C-sections Julie Richards, director of the RCM in Wales, said postnatal care for C-sections should include support with pain relief, wound care and surgical recovery, alongside help with feeding and caring for a new baby. She said the rise in caesareans had changed the demands being placed on services. "What we may not have had is the developments in maternity care to respond to the change in landscape for maternity services." Ceri Ann says she waited seven hours to hold her newborn baby Ceri Ann Roberts, 29, from Gwynedd, said the care she received at Ysbyty Gwynedd after giving birth to her second child in 2025 had left her "traumatised". Ceri Ann had an emergency C-section and her daughter, Ania, was taken to neonatal intensive care because she was not breathing. Ceri Ann said she was then left alone on the recovery ward, unable to move. "I just wanted to see my baby but I couldn't, and the staff told me there was no-one available to take me up to see her." She said it was seven hours until she held her baby for the first time, and that was when her husband arrived back at the hospital and took her to the unit himself. "It was awful, I just cried and cried," she said. Ceri Ann Roberts says her post C-section experience was "just awful" Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board said while it could not comment on individual cases, women recovering from C-sections while their babies are in special care are supported by midwives who provide updates on their baby's wellbeing and help to facilitate visits to see their babies as soon as they are medically able to do so. It acknowledged that being separated from a baby following birth could be distressing and said its teams worked to facilitate contact "at the earliest safe opportunity". She said women often tell her they feel left alone to manage their recovery by themselves. title: Support for disability benefits 'remarkably strong' report finds
description: About 7% of those polled wanted disability benefit cuts, according to the latest British Social Attitudes survey.
body: Protesters demonstrating against benefit cuts at a rally in Parliament Square in 2025 Support for disability benefits remains "remarkably strong" and cutting them would be "politically risky" according to a new report. The analysis, from the British Social Attitudes survey, found that fewer than one in 10 people favoured cutting welfare payments for the disabled, with almost half of people saying they would support more being spent on them, even if it led to higher taxes. The report comes amid mounting concerns among several political parties about the growing cost of disability benefits. Spending on the main disability benefit is forecast to more than double in a decade, reaching £41bn by 2030. But the report says that cutting these payments would not be easy. "Despite growing political divisions on welfare, support for disability benefits remains remarkably strong," said Dr Robert de Vries from the University of Kent, who was one of the report's co-authors. "Very few people favour cuts, disabled people are seen as among the most deserving recipients of support, and proposals to reduce disability benefits appear politically risky across the political spectrum." The analysis is based on 4,656 interviews gathered between August and October 2025. The authors noted that the timing of the interviews, just after the Sir Keir Starmer's government had failed to reform PIP, meant it was "possible that people were particularly supportive of disability benefits at the time". They cautioned that public attitudes to disability benefits "crucially depend on which disabled people are in the public's mind", referencing previous research that showed that "some types of disabled people are seen as 'deserving' by the public". The findings come despite the proportion of those who support increasing welfare spending for the poor being at a near record low. Labour, the Conservative party and Reform UK have all said there is a need to reduce the amount of money being spent on health and disability benefits, while the Liberal Democrats, Greens and SNP oppose reductions. Efforts by Sir Keir to introduce cuts last year were opposed by many in his own party, forcing a government climbdown. The proportion of GDP the UK spends on all welfare benefits for those of working age has remained broadly flat over the past 40 years, at just under 5%. It has occasionally increased to over 5%, including in the 1990s, after the financial crisis in 2008, and during the Covid pandemic. Despite that, the survey found that support for increasing welfare payments to help the poor was close to the lowest level the researchers have ever recorded. Asked if "the government should spend more money on welfare benefits for the poor, even if it leads to higher taxes," 27% replied they should while 42% were opposed. While wider welfare spending on people of working age has, proportionately, remained stable, payments for disability benefits have taken up an increasing share of the total. The latest figures show four million people in England and Wales are currently in receipt of Personal Independence Payment (PIP), the main disability benefit. Annual spending has increased sharply from £16.3bn in 2019/20 to £27.3bn in 2024/25, and is forecast to rise to more than £41bn by 2030. But around half of those polled for the survey, 49%, supported higher spending on disability benefits overall even if it led to higher taxes. Just 7% were in favour of cutting such benefits for disabled people who cannot work. A majority also strongly backed extra payments for the costs of having a disability. Around 83% of respondents supported additional payments to help with cooking, 80% for budgeting, and 78% for washing. Just 3% replied that "nobody should get any additional money" for all three tasks. Respondents were not asked if they thought it should be harder to claim those benefits. Proposals to reform PIP are due to be unveiled by the government in the autumn after an interim report published in the summer found the benefit was not fit for purpose. Around 57% of Labour voters polled for the survey favoured more spending on disability benefits. But there was broad political consensus that cuts would be wrong – just 5% of Labour voters, 7% of Conservatives and 11% of Reform UK backers said they supported cuts to those payments. The British Social Attitudes survey, carried out by the National Centre for Social Research, has been gauging public opinion since 1983. title: Mum 'lost trust' in surgeon review hospital
description: One parent says the number of patients involved in a review is "ridiculous".
body: Lynn said she had lost trust in Addenbrooke's Hospital, where her daughter Tammy underwent surgery A mum whose daughter was among more than 200 patients "harmed" after being operated on by a now-suspended NHS surgeon says she has lost trust in the hospital that treated her. Of the 209 patients who "experienced harm" under the care of orthopaedic surgeon Kuldeep Stohr at Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge, 41 were classed as severe and one person died, as first reported by the BBC on Monday. Lynn, whose 13-year-old daughter Tammy was among the first to receive findings from an independent investigation last year, said the number of patients involved was "ridiculous". The hospital trust said it was "deeply sorry". Stohr previously said she was fully co-operating with an investigation. Kuldeep Stohr is being investigated in relation to hundreds of operations An ongoing review by the Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust (CUH) has looked into the care of more than 900 patients so far. Many of the cases investigated in the review involved children operated on by Stohr. The figures were published in a report prepared for the trust's board of directors and was published on its website ahead of a meeting on Wednesday. The trust removed the report after it was contacted by the BBC for comment. It said a "confidential interim update" was "shared by mistake in our public board papers". The city grappling with unreliable phone signal 'Our son's law will save generations of children' 'I want my Bayeux Tapestry next to the original' Tammy's family was among the first to receive findings from an independent investigation last year Lynn questioned who had authored the report, "as us relatives don't trust the hospital and what they say now". "One or two can be classed as a mistake, but this amount – no. It's ridiculous, especially where parents like me have had to see their children go through additional surgery." Her family's lawyers previously said they had received a written admission of substandard surgery after screws on Tammy's hip joints, meant to improve her mobility, were inserted in the wrong place and did not properly connect to the bone. Natasha, pictured with her daughter Neave, is calling for a public inquiry Another parent, Natasha, said she was calling for a public inquiry into how children under Stohr's care – including her 19-year-old daughter Neave – came to be harmed. The trust's final findings are expected to be shared in November. Chief executive Nicola Ayton said it would be shared with patients and their families before it is published. Elizabeth Maliakal from Hudgell Solicitors, which is representing several families, said she expected the final report to be "damning". "Some of our clients, who are children, endured major surgery they didn't need, which had no positive impact on their lives, and left them in pain for years afterwards," she said. "I expect the final report from the trust, once all the findings of the independent review panel are known, to be highly critical, given we already know from those that we represent that fatal harm was caused in at least one case, and many, many more were harmed." Stohr was suspended by the hospital and has not been at work since March 2024, initially for personal reasons. Ayton said the trust was "deeply sorry to the patients and families who came to harm or experienced care below the standards they should expect". "This should never have happened and we are making changes so that something like this could not happen again," she said. Stohr's legal representatives declined to comment about the new report when approached by the BBC. Have you been affected by this story? Contact us below. title: Train station to mark World Suicide Prevention Day
description: As well as offering advice, Wellbeing Week will include poetry, gardening workshops, art and music.
body: L-R: Maria Jones and Kirsten Rose (Rethink), Jade Beddington (The Haven), Cllr Paul Singh and Mrs Ranjit Dhillon (Mayor & Mayoress of Wolverhampton), Sam Passmore and Thomas Harty (WMR) A five-day programme activities has begun at Wolverhampton's railway station to support people's mental health and wellbeing. Wellbeing Week has been timed to coincide with Thursday's World Suicide Prevention Day and is a collaboration between West Midlands Railway and Rethink Mental Illness. The event is being held at The Hub at the station, which opened in May last year to help people in crisis, and activities include poetry performances, gardening workshops, art and music. Visitors would be offered personal support and information, West Midlands Railway said while Kirsten Rose from Rethink Mental Illness said it was about raising awareness and normalising conversations about mental health. title: A&E did not get the basics right - my son's life was ruined at 32
description: Oli's experience is one of a growing number of clinical negligence claims being made in England, BBC analysis shows.
body: Oli Coppock had a career in digital marketing and was feeling positive about his future In May 2024, a few months after having treatment for a brain tumour, Oli Coppock went to Warrington Hospital's emergency department with bad headaches and dizziness. He underwent tests and assessments, but did not have a brain scan, before going home. It was a decision that ultimately ruined his life at the age of 32, his family says. A week later, with fluid building up on the brain, he suffered a cardiac arrest. He did not recover and now lives in almost complete paralysis. Oli's case is just one of a growing number of clinical negligence claims being made in England relating to A&E care. An analysis by the BBC shows there has been a 41% rise in cases over the past five years, with doctors linking it to the long delays and pressures being seen in emergency departments. Oli's father, Stephen, says he knows A&E staff are under pressure, but he cannot understand how a brain scan was not ordered, given his son's medical history. Despite the brain tumour and a recent diagnosis of multiple sclerosis, Oli was otherwise fit and well and positive about his future. He had a career in digital marketing, loved going to the gym and did some DJing in his spare time. Stephen says the whole family – including Oli's six siblings - has been left "angry and broken" by what happened to him. Stephen Coppock says the whole family has been left broken by what happened to Oli "The hospital didn't get the basics right and my son has paid a terrible price – it's ruined his life. It was an awful error. He trusted the health service and believed it was there to help him, not destroy him." He says Oli's body is now twisted and paralysed and he has no ability to move around. His breathing, feeding and toileting are all done through tubes at the neurological rehabilitation centre where he is being cared for. He can only communicate through blinking, but Stephen believes he understands everything going on around him. "There is no worse space for a human to occupy – it's a permanent living nightmare." Oli, who is being cared for in a neurological rehab unit, communicates by blinking North Cheshire and Mersey NHS Foundation Trust, which runs Warrington's A&E, has now accepted a breach of duty in not ordering a CT brain scan, which on the balance of probabilities would have identified the fluid build-up in his brain and led to surgery to address it. In a statement, the trust said: "We are deeply sorry that Mr Coppock did not receive that standard of care that should be expected and we recognise the distress and lasting impact on patients and their families when harm is caused." An interim damages payment has been agreed. However, Oli's solicitor, Tanzeela Aslam, head of medical negligence at Express Solicitors, says the time taken to get to this point – more than two years – has just added to the failings, depriving him of access to funds for therapies and support that could have improved his quality of life. "Oli's case illustrates how preventable errors within the NHS can have devastating and life-changing consequences for individuals and their families." She says she is seeing more and more A&E-related cases – something she too puts down to the growing pressures. "There has been an increased reliance on corridor care for patients, and we are seeing cases across A&E departments of misdiagnoses that have led to serious injury and in some cases death." A BBC analysis of NHS Resolution figures using published data and freedom of information requests showed there were more than 1,623 A&E-related clinical negligence claims in 2025-26 in England – up from 1,151 in 2020-21. It means A&E is now the single biggest area for clinical negligence claims in terms of number. The value of those claims exceeded £550m last year. Not all claims will result in damages being paid – that happens in about half of all cases. The NHS sometimes accepts liability but it is judged compensation is not needed. And there were points during the 2010s when the number of claims were higher per A&E attendance than they were now before falling. But the sustained increase over the past five years is causing concern, say experts. The pattern is not being repeated in other areas, such as maternity or orthopaedics, and the low point in 2020-21 is thought to be unrelated to any behaviour changes by patients during the Covid pandemic as it takes three years on average for a claim to be submitted. The Royal College of Emergency Medicine told the BBC it was worried about the rise, linking it to increasing pressure and long delays being seen in A&E in recent years. Over the last two years one in 10 patients who attended A&E spent more than 12 hours waiting to be treated or discharged. RCEM's Dr Adrian Boyle said the figures were "sobering". "This is a concern. But it is not surprising when you see how busy departments are. People are staying longer and pressure on staffing is increasing." But he said clinical negligence cases were still relatively rare – happening in only around one in every 17,000 attendances. NHS Resolution, which supports NHS trusts with clinical negligence claims, said it was taking action on the "high volume" of claims and has published reports to help the NHS learn from mistakes. Such mistakes include missing the signs of acute deterioration in patients, failing to order the necessary tests and scans and making incorrect diagnoses. NHS England said claim numbers were not a good measure of current safety because of the lag between the incident happening and claims being logged, adding there were signs A&E waiting times had started improving. Matthew Hopkins, of NHS Alliance, which represents hospitals, said health bosses were "making every effort is made to ensure safe, high-quality care, and that lessons are learned when that falls short". For Stephen, "every waking hour" is spent worrying

title: Oasis: Don't Look Back In Anger review - emotional documentary glosses over the hard stuff
description: The film captures the euphoria of Oasis' comeback, but fails to explore the story of their reunion.
body: Noel and Liam Gallagher premiered the documentary at the Venice Film Festival over the weekend "The little things that used to annoy us about each other have all gone away," says Noel Gallagher of reconciling with his brother, Liam. "It's not a power struggle any more." The scene comes towards the end of Don't Look Back In Anger, a sentimental and affectionate portrait of the band's comeback tour in 2025. But it's about as deep as we get into the band's 15-year hiatus. In an opening montage, we hear how Oasis conquered the world in the 1990s with hits like Wonderwall and Roll With It. As their fame grew, so did the brothers' animosity, until the party came to an abrupt halt backstage at a gig in Paris in 2009. Fan shot footage shows the promoter on stage, informing the crowd that the concert is cancelled following "a huge fight together in the dressing room". "The band doesn't exist any more," he announces, sounding more irritated than sad. According to Scottish singer Amy McDonald, who was also on the line-up, the altercation was seismic. "Liam smashed Noel's guitar, huuuge fight!" she tweeted from backstage. The film, however, never tells us what was said. Nobody explains the fall-out. We don't find out who instigated the rapprochement, nor do we hear how it affected their family. Instead, we cut to rehearsals for the comeback tour, with a caption informing us the brothers "didn't speak for 15 years", and an implication that all the wounds have been miraculously healed. Tantalisingly, the first song they practice is Columbia - a fan favourite that never made the tour's setlist - but there's a tension in the room. The band, under Noel's instruction, is piecing together the setlist. Liam won't arrive until later in the process, and no-one's sure which Liam they'll get. When he arrives, he seems fantastically grumpy, complaining about the sound-proofing panels that have been placed in front of Joey Waronker's drums. "They're already giving me the hump," he huffs. The documentary shows that the brothers' reconciliation was as genuine off-stage as it was in front of fans But when he steps up to the mic, the band relax. Guitarist Bonehead - who's strategically placed between Liam and Noel - beams from ear to ear. A couple of hours later, still in the middle of a song, Liam waves goodbye and casually strolls out of the rehearsal space. "I'm not sure whether our kid's enjoying himself," Noel says to his bandmates. In a voice-over, Liam reveals, enjoying himself wasn't the goal. "If you're not on it, chaos can ensue," he says, adding that he's given up cigarettes and alcohol (the intoxicants, not the song) for the duration of the tour. "These songs, they need to be treated with the utmost respect." The Rise and Fall of Oasis Liam's newfound professionalism is probably the biggest revelation in the documentary, scripted by Peaky Blinders' creator Steven Knight, and shot by directors Dylan Southern and Will Lovelace. To their presumable dismay, there are no scenes of the singer quitting the tour to go house-hunting, external; throwing snooker balls at Blur, external; or starting a fight on a cross-channel ferry. Instead, they complete rehearsals without incident and rock up to Cardiff's Principality Stadium for their public reunion. As the big moment looms, everyone limbers up in the corridors like middle-aged dads getting ready for a Park Run. But when they hit the stage, it's electric. The band are rumoured to be staging a second leg of their comeback tour next year Liam grabs Noel's hand and thrusts it into the air, they launch into the opening chords of Hello, and the crowd practically explodes with joy. As the gig continues, they dance and cheer and weep. During Slide Away, a man sinks to his knees and sings the lyrics, his hands clasped together as if in prayer. When the gig ends, cameras capture a young fan in an awe-struck stupor, unable to tear himself away from his spot on the stadium floor. This is where the documentary excels - capturing the sheer surge of affection that greeted Oasis's return. We visit shows in Dublin, Manchester, Sao Paolo, Tokyo and New York - and every one has a fan with a personal story to tell. One woman has named her dog Bonehead. Another is a Haenyeo - a South Korean free-diver - who says Oasis's music helped her out of depression. Noel, in particular, is blindsided by the impact. "The gravity hit me of what it meant to people and it took me by surprise," he reflects. "I have to say it actually knocked me back." During rehearsals, Bonehead jokes that he's been positioned between the Gallagher brothers as a peacemaker Structurally, though, the film has a problem. In a biopic, the triumphant night in Cardiff would have been the final scene - the moment of resolution after 15 years of pain. Here, it comes about 40 minutes into the action. Every subsequent concert just rinses and repeats the same story. The music is still thrilling. The live mix is impeccable. Liam sounds incredible. But Southern and Lovelace are left flailing around for a story. In Manchester, they focus on a priest delivering a sermon about brotherly forgiveness. In London, they follow a survivor of the Manchester Arena Bombing, who reflects on the way Don't Look Back In Anger became an anthem of resilience. But the film sidesteps the fact that Liam spent the mourning period criticising his brother for his failure to appear at charity shows supporting the survivors. It's not the only omission. There's no mention of the dynamic pricing row that overshadowed the launch of the tour (although Liam is heard apologising for the lack of "cheap seats" during one of the concerts). And while Noel praises Bonehead's contribution to the band, calling him "the sound of Oasis," we never hear from the guitarist; and the film nev

title: Faisal Islam: Chancellor's attempts to boost vibes may limit tax rises
description: The new leadership is trying to maintain both confidence and the promotion of economic animal spirits.
body: The chancellor may have thought about shifting the venue of his first major speech this morning. It was an absolute and total coincidence that he chose to make it in the Coventry Manufacturing and Technology Centre (MTC), just a few minutes' drive from the city's totemic HQ of Jaguar Land Rover (JLR). In the event, no one was pulling punches. The 4,000 office-based job losses at JLR were confirmed as John Healey answered questions a few miles away. Healey chose to lean into it as an example of the global turbulence against which the UK needs more resilience. The difference between this chancellor and his predecessor was he also feels that stressing fiscal discipline should instil confidence in consumers, businesses and investors, and not sap it away amid rolling fears of tax hikes. So the prime minister and his chancellor have been engaged in a conscious attempt to boost the economic vibes - "a new story", as he called it. In his speech, and in a BBC interview afterwards, this was clear. There are some positive underlying signs from consumer, business and recruiter confidence measures that indicate this message has been heard, although the hot weather and World Cup have also been factors. The Downing Street duo are trying to maintain this precious commodity of confidence and the promotion of economic animal spirits that have been suppressed by years of political and economic chaos. "Borrowing costs are too high," Healey acknowledged at the start of his speech. The global rise in bond yields is like a boa constrictor squeezing the Budget maths, slowly and relentlessly, occasionally loosening its grip, but never actually slithering away entirely. It raises some reasonable questions therefore about how to balance reining in borrowing with protecting mildly better confidence? The speech did not seem to me to prepare the ground - a "pitch roll" - for significant tax rises, as I heard at the equivalent Budget "scene setters" for the past two years. "Am I right?" I asked the chancellor on this point. A pause as he sought precisely the right word formulation. "I won't comment. I can't comment. No chancellor can ahead of a Budget I will take and announce on October 28th". OK, what about the advice from one of the PM's favourite economists Lord O'Neill that the rise in borrowing rates is a golden opportunity to scrap the triple lock? This lock guarantees the state pension rising each year in line with either inflation, wage increases or 2.5% - whichever is the highest - but some have argued it is unaffordable. "The prime minister has said, like I have, that we must bring down welfare costs, but we are also responding to the extreme pressure that is there in wider markets," Healey said. Neither answer was a denial, but nor were they any type of confirmation. Like a stubborn batsman, the chancellor is going to stay at the crease, giving little away, in his case, about next month's Budget. Chancellor refuses to rule out tax hikes in October Budget UK long-term borrowing costs highest since 1998 ahead of October Budget There was a focus on growth. As he toured the MTC, a centre of excellence for advanced manufacturing, he said the UK's "great talent and latent potential" made it the third most innovative country in the world, and he wanted to translate that into economic growth and success in more areas. Two decades ago, Healey was responsible for the Regional Development Agencies, scrapped by the Coalition Government, that helped fund this very facility. In his speech there was a big clue about how to square the circle of investing in industrial policy at a time of tricky public finances. The "Pufins" - public finance institutions - such as the British Business Bank and National Wealth Fund can invest strategically, less constrained by the government's borrowing rules. Part of the plan is Pufins to breed more unicorns ($1bn tech startups) in the UK. This is the other part of the global backdrop. Amid the tumult of trade and military wars, there is arguably one of the biggest financial events in world history. In the coming weeks, hundreds of billions of dollars will be invested and trillions in value confirmed from flotations of big American AI firms. The UK has some standout technology in this sector. The government wants to promote it. The chancellor was also, however, cautious about the impact of AI on security and on jobs. Some degree of "public control" could be required to make these changes work for everyone. It appeared a little less cheerleading than the stance of the Starmer administration. The chancellor was perhaps mindful of the army of manufacturing robots, laser welders, 3D metal printers, whirring into action around him. Long term, it will be growth that will determine whether his borrowing rules are met, he said. Ultimately he will be judged by his actual policy choices, but where there are trade-offs between balancing the books and economic growth across the country, this sounds like a chancellor who might prioritise the latter. title: Powerlifter wins golds despite endometriosis pain
description: Lhamo Weston says it's important to be open about competing with endometriosis
body: Lhamo Weston trains for her powerlifting competitions at a gym in Redditch A teenage powerlifter managed to win double golds at a world championship despite her endometriosis flaring up to leave her in excruciating pain just before the competition. Lhamo Weston, from Redditch, also landed second on the podium with a silver and a bronze medal, across three events in the World Sub-Junior & Junior Powerlifting Championships, in South Africa last month. The 18-year-old only took up the sport three years ago, after being inspired by her brother to give it a go. Weston now uses social media to speak openly about having endometriosis and being a young woman in the sport of powerlifting, in the hope of empowering others. Lhamo Weston placed second overall at the World Sub-Junior & Junior Powerlifting Championships Lhamo told the BBC she loves competing in the sport because of its inclusivity. "I love how inclusive it is and how we're like a community," she said. "Everyone knows each other and are really supportive of each other, and I just think it's an amazing sport that really brings people together." She stood on the podium in the Under 57kg category at the championship after getting two golds in squat and deadlift, and a bronze in the bench event. "It felt incredible to be completely honest, I went into it with expectations of potentially reaching podium. I didn't initially expect to place second or even have a chance at placing first," she said. This is the first time Llamo has competed at international level But a flare up of her endometriosis, a condition which sees tissue similar to the lining of the womb grow outside of it, meant she was competing in difficult conditions: "That led to excruciating amounts of pain and a lot of issues again with making weight, which really affected me leading into comp," Lhamo continued. "It can affect my training with the pain, I get quite tired and I also get back pain which can feel the same as a back injury. It was difficult but we managed to do it." Lhamo has been celebrating back home with her medals Endometriosis affects one in 10 women in the UK, but she says many people don't know about it. "There's not enough awareness about it and how it actually impacts women and girls," she continued. "I've been dealing with endometriosis since I was 12, and I only got diagnosed last year. It was a very long journey and I just think there needs to be more awareness so we can try and find solutions to help other people. "As for powerlifting, if you want to do it, go for it. At the end of the day, there's nothing holding you back." Sam Pope from Elite Fitness in Redditch says Lhamo is an inspiration to all The teenager trains at Elite Fitness gym in Redditch and, despite recently moving to Worcester, still travels the 45 minutes to get there. Sam Pope, who works there, says Lhamo is an inspiration. "For other young people of her age, it just shows that actually if you put the effort in, the reward is there," he said. "We take pride knowing we house her here as a member because we are very much like a family. "To have her as a role model is very important because it does allow others to think 'I can do this as well' and I think that's very important not just at our gym but every gym as well." title: India's high-stakes exam system faces a crisis of trust
description: As exam scandals persist, critics ask whether fixing the centralised testing agency is enough or if the model needs to change.
body: Millions of students appear for tests conducted by India's National Testing Agency every year In 2017, India introduced the National Testing Agency (NTA) to conduct fair, transparent and standardised examinations. Set up under the federal education ministry, it was meant to make exams more efficient, consistent and trustworthy, after years of paper leaks, administrative errors and cheating allegations. Over the next few years, the agency took charge of some of India's largest and most competitive tests, including medical and engineering entrance examinations, university admissions and eligibility tests for teaching and research. But eight years later, the organisation created to restore trust in India's exams is facing a crisis of confidence of its own. In June, more than two million students had to retake a crucial medical entrance examination after the paper was leaked. The fallout triggered weeks of youth-led protests which eventually led to the resignation of the federal education minister. In response, the government appointed a high-level task force led by tech tycoon Nandan Nilekani to recommend reforms and restore confidence in the examination system. For many Indians, however, the announcement prompted a sense of déjà vu. A similar panel was established in 2024 after irregularities in another medical entrance examination sparked widespread unrest. That committee proposed more than 100 reforms, a little over half of which, external have reportedly been fully implemented. The cycle has repeated: an exam goes wrong, students protest, a committee is appointed and reforms are proposed - only for another crisis to expose the same weaknesses. Experts the BBC spoke to say the problems go beyond paper leaks - from NTA's accountability and capacity to exam centralisation, design and whether India's high-stakes testing system needs a rethink. More than two million students appeared for the NEET-UG retest BJ Rao, who was part of the 2024 panel and is now head of SGT University near Delhi, says India should move more decisively towards computer-based examinations to minimise the chances of paper leaks, increase efficiency and reduce human involvement wherever possible. "Digital connectivity has vastly improved across the country, what we need to do is put in resources and focus on upgrading infrastructure and move to computer-based exams," he told the BBC. "We currently have ad hoc centres for conducting exams. We need to replace them with standardised state-controlled online centres." But technology alone will not solve the problem, he says. Rao points to the NTA's reliance on contract staff: just 24 of its 221 employees are permanent, with many from bureaucratic backgrounds, according to the government. "When you have a large portion of people who work on a temporary basis then there is no sense of belonging, and that has an impact on the functions as well. You need people who are well-versed in academia and experienced in conducting such assessments to ensure better management and oversight," he explains. Some experts argue that repeated crises have exposed flaws not only in how exams are conducted, but also in how they are designed. Keshav Aggarwal, an educationist and president of Educators Federation, says the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (Undergraduate) or NEET-UG - whose paper leak triggered this year's protests - could be restructured along the lines of the country's engineering entrance examination, which is computer-based and conducted in two stages. Rather than relying on a single high-stakes test day, the exams could be held across multiple sessions with different sets of questions, he says. "Different stages and days with varying sets of questions" would reduce the risks associated with any one examination and make the system more resilient to disruptions, Aggarwal explains. The NEET-UG paper leak triggered massive protests in India Experts also question whether an annual exam can work when millions compete for limited university places. India needs a system where students can take important entrance exams more than once a year, as is common in some western countries, said Yamini Aiyar, senior visiting fellow at Brown University. "This would give students another chance if an exam is cancelled or they do not perform well, reducing the risk of losing an entire year," she says. For millions of Indian students, the risk is real. Many spend years preparing and tens of thousands of rupees on private tuition. A leaked, cancelled or delayed exam can suddenly upend months or years of preparation. Pari, 17, experienced that uncertainty first-hand. After taking NEET this year, she had to retake it after the original exam was cancelled following a paper leak. "It was very frustrating. All our preparation had gone to waste, and we had to start all over again," she said. The experience left her angry at repeated exam failures. "The government can form as many panels as it likes. We need a system strong enough to prevent paper leaks from happening again." Mansi Bansal, 23, has a similar story. She spent months preparing for UGC-NET, a qualification for entry-level college teaching jobs. The exam was cancelled after a 2024 paper leak and again this year after the NTA cited errors in three subjects. Bansal took the affected commerce paper and will retest on 9 September. "I put my life on hold all these months, stopping going to the gym, hanging out with friends or even attending family gatherings," she said. "I had planned my entire year but now it has all gone into uncertainty. Can the government promise a leak won't happen again?" Student activists and opposition parties have been demanding to scrap the NTA Such experiences have fuelled calls from student activists and opposition politicians to scrap the NTA altogether. title: What big issues are on the agenda as Stormont returns after summer?
description: What challenges face assembly members and ministers as Stormont returns after the summer recess?
body: Ministers and MLAs are to return to Stormont on Monday It's not even the start of a new Stormont term and already there have been leaks. Albeit it wasn't some big scoop but a rather damp surprise for the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) MLA Colin McGrath, who took to social media saying a water leak over summer had left his assembly office looking worse for wear, external. Even the most casual observers of politics here could guess, however, that Stormont's leaky roof problems are outweighed by the ever-slow drip of political activity inside the building - a place the assembly's freshest face will witness for himself from this week. On Tuesday, Paul Boggs was named Sinn Féin's new West Tyrone MLA after Maoliosa McHugh - who'd already said he wouldn't run in the next election - decided to call it quits. Boggs brings the number of MLAs who have been co-opted since the last assembly election to 14 and that figure could go up still before the upcoming election next May. Co-options aside (that's a whole other piece), the backdrop of said looming election means parties are likely to be in fighting form when Stormont sittings resume on Monday. No time for new minister to fix health service warns top doctor 'Sinn Féin will not walk away from Stormont', says Michelle O'Neill Maolíosa McHugh stepping down as West Tyrone MLA The newly-appointed Health Minister Robbie Butler will be one of those quick to feel pressure, as the 10-year anniversary of the Bengoa report - a major health reform review - approaches next month. Pay pressures in his department and the Department of Education also make for another winter of discontent, with the prospect of strike action yet to be ruled out. We know by now that Butler and other ministers argue that their hands are tied without a budget that can allow them to meet all their outstanding pressures. Executive parties have been taking part in talks with Treasury officials in a bid to break the deadlock but 36 days since the legal deadline to pass a budget expired, there has so far been little sign of light at the end of this tunnel. So much so that it prompted SDLP leader of the opposition Matthew O'Toole to issue a call to public bodies across Northern Ireland this week, asking them how the ongoing lack of financial certainty is affecting their services. Robbie Butler signing the pledge of office at Stormont after being appointed as health minister Whether point scoring or simply making a wider point about the consequences of not having a budget, others are also talking about the problems being stored up at Stormont. Think tank Pivotal published a report, external last week on the issue, noting that several departments are facing massive overspends this year, including deficits of about £800m in health and £250m in education. Money matters are a major sticking point for this executive but whether this can be resolved rests on what comes out of talks with Treasury and the secretary of state - more of those are expected to happen with the parties this week. The budget, as big as it is, is only one item on the executive's to-do list before the assembly dissolves in March ahead of the election. Already ministers have been repeatedly warned by assembly Speaker Edwin Poots that time is running out to pass remaining pieces of legislation through all their hurdles. It's not uncommon for Stormont to sit into the small hours or hold extra days of sittings as the end of a mandate approaches - this one will be no different but there are serious question marks over some key bills. Economy Minister Caoimhe Archibald's so-called "Good Jobs" Bill which aims to massively reform employment laws has yet to get executive agreement, after the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) said it had no support among business groups. Other flagship policies including the redevelopment of Casement Park and the A5 road project also remain mothballed due to financial and legal disputes. The reality is that as the countdown to election day gets closer the harder it will be for the executive to make decisions on major issues, for fear that any misstep could go down badly with their respective bases. The first and deputy first ministers will be feeling the heat in their own ways The largest parties - Sinn Féin and the DUP - will be feeling the heat in their own ways. Sinn Féin, which became the largest party for the first time in the last election, needs to consolidate its support and show that it can deliver - without a legislative win or two in the next few months this may be hard to demonstrate on the doorsteps. The DUP faces its own challenges of going into its first election since the conviction of former party leader Jeffrey Donaldson in June for child sex abuse offences, which he is appealing. In July, the party moved to commission an independent review over Donaldson's actions while he was a member of the DUP, but it is not yet clear when the report will be completed or published. Throw in fresh tensions over Drumcree, continuing rows over Irish language signage and pressure on Alliance's agriculture minister over a controversial cattle cull last month and it all makes for a battle a day. If this current executive has anything going for it, it's that leaks of information and counter briefings against each other are much more rare than in the last executive. Often the mood around the table is described as collegiate, even if ministers disagree on an issue. But as one Stormont source put it recently: "You can't leak anything if there's nothing to leak. This is an executive in a holding pattern." Sooner rather than later this executive will have to circle back to big issues that can't be ducked forever. title: Why Reform UK undercover donations claims are legally complicated
description: A look at the key allegations concerning foreign donations and where they sit with the law.
body: Reform UK has been hit by a row over foreign donations as the party's leaders and supporters gather for their annual conference. The row centres on allegations which surfaced during undercover filming by Verbatim Investigations - founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting - and broadcast by Channel 4 News on Thursday. The party denies any wrongdoing and says it is investigating. Robert Jenrick, Reform's economy spokesperson, said the two senior aides in the film had been suspended, telling the BBC's Today programme: "Nigel [Farage] got rid of the two people who did this…he acted swiftly, they've gone." Both Labour and the Liberal Democrats have reported Reform to the Metropolitan Police, which says it is assessing the claims but has not launched an investigation. The Electoral Commission says it is "in touch" with the police. We have looked at each of the three main allegations and where they sit with the law. In the film, Nigel Farage's senior aide Dan Jukes and Reform's head of policy James Orr suggest a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations for the party, one of which would have totaled £500,000. Jukes meets an undercover reporter posing as a UK-based son of a wealthy American financier, who voices concern that his father could not directly donate to Reform within the law. Jukes tells him: "You do realise that you can do it?" According to Channel 4, Jukes was suggesting that the donation could be in the son's name, even though the money would have come from his American father. A similar arrangement is also mooted in a meeting with Orr. Farage is shown saying "it's all above board" and expressing thanks. On Friday, Farage said he was in fact asking whether it was above board. Channel 4 says the proposed £500,000 donation was never made. Under electoral law, you must be a UK registered voter or a company registered in the UK to be a "permissable" donor to a UK political party. In this instance, the son would be a permissible donor, but his father would not be. Any donation of more than £500 from an impermissible source must be declared to the Electoral Commission and returned within 30 days. If the party keeps it beyond that, it is deemed to have accepted the donation - and that could lead to a fine and potential criminal investigation. Two Reform officials step down after undercover donations report Farage says his aides' donor comments were 'loose pub talk' Channel 4 says Reform commissioned three opinion polls between January and July 2026, costing £32,500 in total. One was on the front page of the Telegraph newspaper under the headline "Labour would face wipeout if elections went ahead"; another on the front page of the Times with the headline "Reform vote in unions at same level as Labour". In the film, Orr suggests to the undercover reporter that perhaps the American financier could pay for opinion polling to help with Reform's campaigns. He is shown saying this would "technically be a donation in kind" but "the reality is we could easily get away with it". The public was not told who had commissioned and paid for the three polls. Polling firm JL Partners, the Telegraph and the Times have all said this was not known to them either. Farage said on Friday the polls in question had been commissioned by an independent third party and that Reform had "not done anything wrong". Any legitimate donations from permissible donors worth more than £11,180 in a calendar year must, by law, be declared to the Electoral Commission. The £32,500 polling payment does not appear to have been declared. The legal definition for a political party donation includes payments for studies and research. This video can not be played Watch: Undercover reporters posing as party donors meet with Nigel Farage The Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000 specifically outlaws knowingly taking steps to disguise or conceal that a donation has come from an impermissible source. As part of this, it can be a crime for someone to conceal money spent on expenses incurred directly or indirectly by the party - and to mislead a party on the source of a donation. The maximum sentence is 12 months in prison. It is in this context that Labour is demanding the police investigate the polling and whether there is evidence of concealing who actually paid for it. But investigating this and the other claims in the film would be hugely complex - and a 30-minute TV report could not be the sole basis for a prosecution. The police would almost certainly ask Channel 4 for all the unused filmed material, research notes and plans for the documentary. Detectives would want to interview everyone involved and understand their intentions. In a statement on Friday, JL Partners said that "sometimes people with a party alignment make suggestions about potential clients who may be interested in commissioning and paying for polling" in the UK and abroad, and that it would not expect to be told the precise relationship between Reform and the US-based company. Nick Vamos, former head of specialist crime at the Crown Prosecution Service, explained: "It is very common for allegations of electoral offences to be reported to the police, especially by political rivals looking to score points," adding the police would assess the evidence neutrally to decide whether a full investigation is required. Such offences very rarely lead to prosecution. Between 2011 and 2021, the Electoral Commission referred eight cases to the Met, none of which resulted in charges. Even if there were an investigation, it would take months to get near specialist detectives or prosecutors. Elsewhere in the film, Jukes appears to list other supporters of Reform UK who have potentially donated to the party through UK residents.
